feat(replay): support map projection replay with marker-based deferral (#3268)

* feat(replay): support map projection replay with marker-based deferral

Projection replay previously only re-ran fold projections, so fixes to
canonicalisation (which happens in the `spanStorage` map projection)
could not be applied to already-ingested spans. Extend replay to
support map projections, with the same live-event deferral guarantees
folds already have.

- `RegisteredMapProjection` type + `ReplayConfig.mapProjections`
- `ReplayService.replayMapProjection`/`replayMapBatch` — same 7-phase
  cycle as folds, with the replay+write phases collapsed into per-event
  `map(event) → store.append(record, ctx)`
- `replayPreset.createReplayRuntime` registers map projections from
  `def.mapProjections`; `MAP_TARGET_TABLE` maps `spanStorage → stored_spans`
  for post-replay `OPTIMIZE TABLE`
- `projectionRouter` now runs `replayMarkerChecker.check` on both map
  dispatch paths (queued + inline), mirroring the fold-side behaviour
- `getProjectionMetadata` returns both fold and map entries with
  `kind: "fold" | "map"`; `BulkReplayWizard` renders a kind badge
- Unit tests cover the three marker outcomes on the map path

* perf(replay): batch map projection writes and unify discovery

Map projection replay was doing one ClickHouse INSERT per event,
causing "Too many parts" errors and ~2 events/sec throughput. Each
map projection also ran its own 7-phase cycle sequentially with
redundant discovery queries.

- Add optional `bulkAppend` to `AppendStore` interface
- Add `insertLogRecords`/`insertMetricRecords` bulk methods to CH
  repositories and append stores
- Create `MapAccumulator` (mirrors `FoldAccumulator`) — buffers map
  records by tenant, flushes via `bulkAppend` in chunks of 5000
- Integrate map projections into `replayBatchOptimized`: single
  discovery pass, single event load, all projections (fold + map)
  applied per-aggregate in one loop, bulk writes for both
- Add `logRecordStorage`/`metricRecordStorage` to `MAP_TARGET_TABLE`
  for post-replay `OPTIMIZE TABLE`

* fix(replay-ui): highlight all active projections and show count badge

When multiple projections replay together (unified path), the UI was
showing the raw "name+name+name" string as a single badge. Now:
- Parse currentProjection into individual names
- Highlight all active projections with orange/solid badges in the list
- Show a compact "N projections" count badge above

* fix(replay-ui): use completedAt for rate calculation after replay ends

Rate was using Date.now() as the denominator, so after replay completed
the rate kept decreasing (3092/500s = 6/s instead of 3092/18s = 172/s).
Now uses completedAt when available.

* fix(replay): correct map projection pause/drain and fold event-type filtering

Address review feedback on map projection replay. Map projections enqueue
as `__jobType=handler` (jobPath `map/{name}`), so pause-set entries and
groupId drain checks that hardcoded `projection`/`fold` never matched
their live jobs — replay could race with in-flight writes. Folds in the
optimized path were also fed events of types they never declared because
the union-discovery + bulk event load skipped per-projection filtering.

- FoldAccumulator now drops events outside its declared eventTypes,
  matching MapAccumulator
- MapAccumulator buffers per-event ProjectionStoreContext so the
  sequential append fallback carries the real aggregateId
- pauseProjection/unpauseProjection take a pauseKey directly; drain
  helpers take projection kind to build the right groupId segment
- pipelineRegistry + replayPreset emit `{pipeline}/handler/{name}` for
  map projections; both registered types now expose `kind`
- replayMapBatch routes through MapAccumulator so the non-optimized
  path also gets bulkAppend instead of per-event INSERTs
- ReplayEvent gains createdAt and idempotencyKey from event_log
- ReplayProgressDrawer freezes the elapsed stat using completedAt

* fix(replay): preserve per-aggregate context on map projection bulkAppend

The optimized map replay path called bulkAppend with a fabricated tenant-scoped
context (aggregateId: ""). Any AppendStore implementation that keys off
context.aggregateId would diverge from the non-optimized append() path. Group
buffered records by aggregateId within each tenant and pass the originating
event's context so the bulk write semantics match the per-event path.

* test(replay): cover map projection orchestration (pause/drain, cutoff, skip)

Adds integration coverage for `replayMapProjection`/`replayMapBatch`:
- happy path: bulkAppend grouped per aggregate with per-event context,
  pause-set held active through WRITE phase, markers cleaned up on success
- resume: aggregates pre-populated in the completed set are skipped

Existing tests only exercised `discover()`; the map orchestration layer
(cutoff marking, pause/drain semantics, skip interactions) was previously
uncovered above the unit-tested `MapAccumulator`.

* test(replay): align map projection test with main type renames

Rebase fallout — main renamed FoldProjection's `lastEventOccurredAtKey`
to `LastEventOccurredAtKey` and tightened the `AppendStore.append`
signature, so the loose `ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>` parameter types no
longer assign cleanly. Type the helper's `append`/`bulkAppend` params
against `MapProjectionDefinition` directly.

* test(replay): cover mixed fold + map replay orchestration

Adds two integration cases against the public `replay()` API to close the
largest untested surface introduced by the map-projection PR:

- happy path: a fold and a map projection in one replay call — verifies
  both projections execute, each is paused only during its own WRITE
  phase (per-batch pause, not whole-session), and per-aggregate
  bulkAppend context is preserved.
- early-exit: when the fold batch errors, the map projection must not
  run — guards the `if (totalBatchErrors === 0)` short-circuit in
  `ReplayService.replay`.

* fix(replay): drain map projections by group-key prefix scan

Map projection jobs are grouped by each projection's custom groupKeyFn
(e.g. span:${event.id}), so reconstructing ${aggregateType}:${aggregateId}
group keys never matched and the drain reported complete while pre-pause
handlers could still be writing. Map-kind drains now SCAN for any active
group under ${tenantId}/map/${projectionName}/ in both waitForActiveJobs
and waitForAllActiveJobs. Adds an integration test with an active
custom-key map job that must block the write phase until it clears.

* fix(replay): apply audit findings across replay engine and ops UI

- MapAccumulator flushes incrementally at writeBatchSize instead of
  buffering an entire aggregate batch in memory
- replayOptimized attaches only projections whose eventTypes intersect
  each discovered aggregate's events; markers are written per matching
  projection instead of the full cross-product
- batchLoadAggregateEvents selects IdempotencyKey, matching the
  optimized loader
- optimized-path progress reports the actual projection kind instead of
  hardcoded "fold"; map replay emits progress per page, not per event
- ops UI: shared parseActiveProjections helper, memoized projection
  metadata lookup, no kind badge when metadata is missing, badge
  highlights gated on running state, single-projection name display
- projectionRouter deferral test throws the real ReplayDeferralError
  and asserts it surfaces in the AggregateError
- add specs/event-sourcing/projection-replay.feature

* test(replay): wait for ClickHouse insert visibility before optimized replay assertion

The per-eventType mapping test inserts a span event mid-test and ran
discovery immediately; on CI the insert was not yet visible, so the map
projection discovered nothing and bulkAppend was never called. Poll for
the event before replaying.

* test(replay): stamp never-expire retention on the mid-test span event

The shared test DB gets the platform retention TTL applied to event_log
by the ttlReconciler (anchored on EventOccurredAt). The freshly inserted
backdated span event was already past retention, so ClickHouse dropped
the part right after insert and map discovery found nothing — passing
locally (no TTL applied) but failing CI. Stamp _retention_days: 0 like
every other backdated fixture in this file.

* fix(replay): address review findings — lean parity, retention, cutoff safety, scoped ids

Resolves the four findings from @sergioestebance's review:

- P1 map replay bypassed leanForProjection: MapAccumulator now leans events
  before projection.map(), matching live dispatch and the fold path, so
  replayed spans/logs carry previews + event refs, not oversized content.
- P1 staged pre-cutoff jobs could re-run after replay: replay no longer HDELs
  the cutoff marker on completion. markCompletedBatch writes a short-TTL
  terminal "done" marker instead; the live checker reads it (in one pipelined
  round-trip alongside the active cutoff) to keep skipping events at/before the
  cutoff while letting newer events process. Short-TTL per-aggregate key so an
  all-tenant/multi-month replay stays bounded to ~throughput × TTL, not one
  marker per aggregate for the whole run.
- P1 replay ignored tenant retention: replay contexts now resolve retention per
  tenant (reusing the live RetentionPolicyCache) and stamp it on fold + map
  write contexts; log/metric bulk stores thread it through insertLogRecords/
  insertMetricRecords (log keeps the claude_code floor), so replay-rebuilt rows
  honour the same policy as live ingestion.
- P2 non-optimized replay ignored aggregateIds: fold and map discovery now
  filter to config.aggregateIds, matching the optimized path.

Regression tests cover the done-marker checker semantics, markCompletedBatch,
map lean parity, and retention stamping on both accumulators.

* fix(replay): make replay-marker pipeline interface chainable

The ReplayMarkerRedis pipeline methods returned `unknown`, so chaining
.hget().get().exec() failed project typecheck (TS2571). Type the pipeline as
a self-referential interface so each command returns the pipeline.

fix(scenarios): take maxRuntime-killed and orphaned QUEUED runs terminal (#3365) (#5008)

* fix(scenarios): take maxRuntime-killed and orphaned QUEUED runs terminal (#3365)

When a scenario worker hit maxRuntimeMs and restarted, it killed in-flight
child processes without emitting any terminal event, so those runs orphaned at
QUEUED forever and the suites page polled them indefinitely. Two layers of
recovery:

- Graceful drain (AC1): the execution pool now tracks in-flight job data
  (running + pending) via `inFlightJobs`; the processor's `close()` emits a
  terminal failure for every in-flight run before draining. worker.ts already
  awaits `close()` before the restart reject, so a killed run goes ERROR
  instead of stuck QUEUED. Covers graceful shutdown too.

- Startup reconciler (AC2): on processor startup a best-effort, non-blocking,
  cross-tenant ClickHouse scan finds runs whose latest status is QUEUED with no
  progress past the orphan threshold and emits a terminal failure. This is the
  belt-and-braces net for hard kills (OOM/SIGKILL) where the graceful drain
  never ran. Gated by age so freshly/healthy QUEUED runs are never falsely
  failed.

Tests (AC3): pool `inFlightJobs`, `drainInFlightRuns` emit-before-drain (incl.
rejection resilience), and the reconciler gate (long-abandoned QUEUED failed;
recent/healthy QUEUED and non-QUEUED untouched), plus a behavior feature spec.

fix(invite): surface acceptInvite failures instead of dead-ending on the loading screen (#5551)

Fixes #5550

Two interacting defects left /invite/accept stuck on the bare loading
screen when acceptInvite failed, with the error only in the console:

1. InnerProviders conditionally wrapped the routed page in PostHogProvider
   only once usePostHog() resolved (after the publicEnv query). The element
   type flip at that tree position remounted the entire page subtree
   shortly after boot. Now the provider always renders with the posthog
   module singleton, so the tree shape never changes.

2. useAcceptInviteOnce's module-scoped one-shot guard (from #3325)
   survives remounts, but the mutation outcome lived only in the unmounted
   instance's useMutation state — a remounted instance stayed idle forever
   and deriveStatus reported 'loading'. Outcomes are now recorded in a
   module-scoped store read via useSyncExternalStore, so any remounted
   instance resolves to the real terminal state.

The error UI also gains a primary 'Go to Dashboard' action (hard
navigation, busting stale pre-invite caches) next to 'Log Out and Try
Again', so the user is never stranded.

recover-leases sweep intentionally crosses tenants (no projectId

* refactor(outbox): collapse onto the main event-sourcing queue (ADR-022 r3)

Drop the langwatch:outbox GroupQueueProcessor. Settle and cadence
payloads now ride the main event-sourcing queue (event-sourcing/jobs),
routed by a stage-discriminator branch on each queue callback.

setup.ts: `setupOutbox` → `buildOutboxRuntime`. The runtime returns
`{ dispatcher, auditAdapter, enqueueSettle, attachQueue }` — no queue
field. `attachQueue` is called by EventSourcing once the main queue is
constructed; `enqueueSettle` and the dispatcher's internal
`enqueueCadence` both forward to whichever queue is attached. `OutboxStack`
is kept as a deprecated alias for the new `OutboxRuntime` so consumers
that still reference the old type compile.

eventSourcing.ts: accept an optional `outbox?: OutboxRuntime` on the
constructor, persist it on the instance, and consult it in
createGlobalQueue. Each of the queue's callbacks (`groupKey`, `process`,
`processBatch`, `coalesceMaxBatch`, `score`, `spanAttributes`,
`deduplication`) peels off `isSettle || isCadence` first and delegates
to the outbox dispatcher; everything else flows through the existing
registry. The audit adapter is wired onto the queue's `auditAdapter`
slot — the adapter already gates internally on outbox-stage payloads
so non-outbox queue events no-op cheaply. After construction,
`outbox.attachQueue(globalQueue)` resolves the producer cycle.

pipelineRegistry.ts: `outbox.queue.send(...)` becomes
`outbox.enqueueSettle(payload, { ttlMs })`. The per-trigger
`traceDebounceMs` override is still the only knob that crosses the
wire — stage-aware dedup (Debounce Mode for settle, per-job for
cadence) is configured once on the main queue's `deduplication` field.

ADR-022 r3 documents the trade-off captured by the collapse: one
Redis prefix / Grafana panel / crash-recovery story, but trigger
dispatches now share the per-tenant fairness budget with span
projections (`TenantRateTracker`). Bounded; not catastrophic; but a
regression in isolation guarantees vs the two-queue split that should
be visible to the next person reasoning about queue scaling.

The reactor-outbox-dispatch spec swaps the "sent to the
langwatch:outbox GroupQueue" assertion for "sent to the main
event-sourcing queue".

* fix(outbox): defer cadence claim post-dispatch so retryable sends retry

Sergio flagged on PR #4498: handleCadenceBatch claimed TriggerSent
before the provider call, so a retryable email/Slack failure on the
first attempt caused the outbox retry to see claim=false on
claimSend, return empty claimedPayloads, and silently log
"fully suppressed" without actually sending anything. The
notification was permanently lost.

The claim now runs *after* a successful provider call. A read-only
isSendClaimed check handles cross-batch dedup (suppressing pairs an
earlier batch or the inline evaluation reactor already dispatched),
the existing seenTraceIds set handles in-batch dedup, and
post-dispatch claimSend failures are swallowed for the same reason
updateLastRunAt is — re-throwing would let the outbox retry the
dispatch and double-send a real notification.

regression test covering the four cadence-stage paths (retryable
re-send, prior claim suppression, post-dispatch claim failure,
in-batch dedup), and a spec scenario under "Dispatch failures route
through the DispatchError contract".

* fix(mailer): trigger emails route To=hashed no-reply, recipients=BCC

Production trigger emails previously rendered every recipient address in
the To: header, leaking the internal recipient list to every receiver,
inviting reply-all storms, and putting user-controlled multi-recipient
content directly into a header (EMAIL_RX blocks CRLF smuggling but
doesn't undo the enumeration leak).

Now:

  - To:  LangWatch Triggers <no-reply+<HMAC>@<domain>>
  - Bcc: configured recipients

The local-part tag is HMAC-SHA256(triggerId, NEXTAUTH_SECRET) truncated
to 12 hex chars — stable per trigger so future bounce processors can
attribute mail back to a row, unguessable without the secret so the
address can't be reverse-engineered or forged.

    BccAddresses, raw-MIME path uses Destinations envelope (no Bcc:
    header rendered to receivers); SendGrid uses bcc / replyTo keys.
    `computeDefaultFrom()` extracted for callers that need to derive
    the no-reply domain from the From: address.
  - sendTriggerEmail: now takes `triggerId`, builds the no-reply To
    via `buildTriggerNoReplyAddress`, recipients ride in bcc.
  - TriggerNotifier.sendEmail: signature changes to
    `{ to: string, bcc: string[], subject, html }`. Test-fire uses a
    "preview" sentinel id so test bounces don't pollute prod bounce
    streams that may key off the hash.
  - Both production dispatchers (outbox + inline pipeline) thread the
    trigger id through.

* feat(outbox): wire .withOutbox to real trigger-dispatch reactors

PR1's `.withOutbox` builder + OutboxReactorDefinition API has been
exported and tested but never invoked by the runtime — `eventSourcing.ts`
read `foldReactors`/`mapReactors` from each StaticPipelineDefinition and
ignored `foldOutboxReactors`/`mapOutboxReactors`, so even if a pipeline
called `.withOutbox`, the reactor would never fire.

Adds the missing wiring:

- `outboxReactorAdapter.ts` wraps an `OutboxReactorDefinition` into a
  regular `ReactorDefinition` whose `handle` invokes `decide(...)` and
  forwards each emitted `OutboxEnqueueRequest` to
  `outbox.enqueueSettle`. The GroupQueue-routed adapter ignores the
  request's `dedupKey`/`groupKey`/`maxAttempts` (those describe the
  spec's row-leased architecture); `enqueueOptions.ttlMs` IS threaded
  because the settle stage's Debounce Mode TTL is the per-trigger
  `traceDebounceMs` knob. When `OutboxRuntime` isn't wired (web
  process, or worker without outbox), the adapter degrades to a
  no-op `handle` so the pipeline registration is harmless.
- `buildServiceOptions` in `eventSourcing.ts` now walks the static
  definition's outbox-reactor maps, adapts each, and merges them into
  the `reactors`/`mapReactors` arrays the runtime already consumes.
- `OutboxEnqueueRequest` grows an optional `enqueueOptions.ttlMs`
  field. The defaults to `DEFAULT_TRACE_DEBOUNCE_MS` (30s) when absent.
- `defineOriginGuardedTraceOutboxReactor` factored out next to the
  existing `defineOriginGuardedTraceReactor` so both `.withReactor`
  and `.withOutbox` trace-pipeline reactors share the same
  origin/age/event-type guard logic (single `passesTraceOriginGuards`
  helper).

Splits the two trigger reactors into NOTIFY-class and PERSIST-class
responsibilities and registers the NOTIFY half via `.withOutbox`:

- `ee/governance/reactors/alertTriggerNotifyOutbox.reactor.ts` — new
  OutboxReactorDefinition; for every active trace-only trigger whose
  action is SEND_EMAIL / SEND_SLACK_MESSAGE, emits an
  `OutboxEnqueueRequest` carrying the settle payload. Registered on
  the trace pipeline via
  `.withOutbox("traceSummary", "alertTriggerNotifyOutbox", ...)`.
- `evaluationAlertTriggerNotifyOutbox.reactor.ts` — same shape on the
  evaluation pipeline; restricts to triggers with evaluation filters
  whose action is NOTIFY.
- `ee/governance/reactors/alertTrigger.reactor.ts` and
  `evaluationAlertTrigger.reactor.ts` keep handling PERSIST-class
  actions (ADD_TO_DATASET, ADD_TO_ANNOTATION_QUEUE) inline; their
  NOTIFY branch is gone. Tests now exercise the persist path with
  `ADD_TO_ANNOTATION_QUEUE` (single-call dispatch path) rather than

fix(trace-processing): stop the hot-trace fold re-fold storm (#5584)

* fix(trace-processing): stop the hot-trace fold re-fold storm

Sharding recordSpan across GroupQueue lanes (#5531) let a hot trace's spans
be handled in parallel, so span_received events reach the trace-summary fold
out of occurredAt order. The fold's out-of-order detector responded by
replaying the whole trace from event_log — and because apply() raises the
checkpoint to the highest occurredAt it has seen, the first replay pinned the
checkpoint at the trace's maximum event time, making every later batch look
out of order too. In two hours of prod one trace re-folded 730 times, re-read
5.66M event rows, and never caught up (36k fold jobs pending, oldest 1h).

The replay bought nothing. The trace summary is an order-insensitive fold:
spanCount and the token/cost totals are sums, timing is min/max, status is an
OR, and every precedence rule decides from data the span carries (output
selection compares span end times, trace naming compares root-span start
times) rather than from arrival order. A span can be folded whenever it lands.

- FoldProjectionOptions.refoldOnOutOfOrder (default true) lets such a fold opt
  out; the executor then applies the batch in occurredAt order on top of the
  loaded state, the same path taken when no eventLoader is wired. traceSummary
  opts out. es_fold_refold_total{projection,outcome} makes the choice visible.

Underneath it, each coalesced batch dispatched every reactor once per event.
Reactors keyed on the trace collapse to one queue job by dedup id, so 99 of
every 100 sends were discarded — each after serializing {event, foldState}
twice, gzipping it, and writing a content-addressed blob into Redis that the
dedup squash immediately reclaimed.

- ProjectionRouter.collapseByJobId dispatches an aggregate-keyed reactor once
  per batch, with the last event that passed its shouldReact — the same queue
  state the dedup would have reached. Per-event job ids (customEvaluationSync)
  and reactors without one are unaffected. alertTrigger / alertTriggerNotify /
  traceUpdateBroadcast take (_event, context) and read only foldState, and
  evaluationTrigger was already squashed to the last event by its per-trace
  job id, so the collapse is behaviour-preserving.
- The origin guard and evaluationTrigger's synthetic-span + span-cap guards
  are pure and read only the payload handle() gets, so they move to
  shouldReact and reject pre-enqueue (ADR-026), as originGate and
  customEvaluationSync already did. They stay in handle as the fail-open path.
- OutboxReactorDefinition gains shouldReact; adaptOutboxReactor forwards it.

specs/event-sourcing/hot-trace-fold-amplification.feature

* Address review findings

- Correct the order-insensitivity claim on TraceSummaryFoldProjection. Three
  fields DO resolve in fold order: `models`, `computedInput` on multi-root
  traces (trace-io-accumulation's `isRoot || computedInput === null` branch has
  no timestamp tiebreak), and a fallback-only `computedOutput`. Note that a span
  event's occurredAt is the ingest wall-clock (Date.now()), so the replay only
  ever restored global ingest order — never span-time order — and these fields

- evaluationTrigger: move the oversized-trace cap guard back into handle(). It

* fix(mailer): trigger emails route To=hashed no-reply, recipients=BCC

Production trigger emails previously rendered every recipient address in
the To: header, leaking the internal recipient list to every receiver,
inviting reply-all storms, and putting user-controlled multi-recipient
content directly into a header (EMAIL_RX blocks CRLF smuggling but
doesn't undo the enumeration leak).

Now:

  - To:  LangWatch Triggers <no-reply+<HMAC>@<domain>>
  - Bcc: configured recipients

The local-part tag is HMAC-SHA256(triggerId, NEXTAUTH_SECRET) truncated
to 12 hex chars — stable per trigger so future bounce processors can
attribute mail back to a row, unguessable without the secret so the
address can't be reverse-engineered or forged.

    header rendered to receivers); SendGrid uses bcc / replyTo keys.
    `computeDefaultFrom()` extracted for callers that need to derive
    the no-reply domain from the From: address.
  - sendTriggerEmail: now takes `triggerId`, builds the no-reply To
    via `buildTriggerNoReplyAddress`, recipients ride in bcc.
  - TriggerNotifier.sendEmail: signature changes to

    "preview" sentinel id so test bounces don't pollute prod bounce
    streams that may key off the hash.

    trigger id through.

* feat(prompts): tab switcher for the prompt playground

Opening several prompts fills the tab strip. The extras scroll off the
right edge behind a fade gradient, with nothing to say they exist and no
way to reach one but to scroll blindly.

Adds a switcher beside each pane's strip: it reports how many prompts are
open and lists them all, jumping to the one you pick and scrolling its tab
back into view. It renders per pane, outside the toolbar's is-this-pane-
active guard, because a pane you are not working in still has tabs worth
reaching.

The strip keeps scrolling and no tab is ever hidden. That is deliberate:
tabs are @dnd-kit sortables, and `display: none` gives an element a
zero-size rect, which corrupts horizontalListSortingStrategy's drop-index
math. Hiding overflowed tabs the way LensTabs and SpanTabBar do would have
broken drag-to-reorder; those strips are not draggable.

Along the way:

- Extract `usePromptTabSummary`, the one place a tab's title, unsaved state
  and version are derived. The tab and its switcher row now render the same
  facts from the same source and cannot drift.
- Extract `shouldShowVersionBadge` into source. It previously existed only
  as a copy inside showVersionBadgeLogic.test.ts, so the test verified a
  reimplementation rather than the shipped code. It now imports the real one.
- Extract `PromptTabStrip`, since each pane needs its own scroller ref and a
  ref cannot be created inside the loop over panes.

Binds all 16 @integration scenarios in specs/prompts/prompt-tab-switcher.feature.
The two strip invariants that jsdom cannot honestly assert — overflow
scrolling and drag-reorder, both needing real layout rects — stay
@e2e @unimplemented rather than becoming green tests that prove nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

The related-specs note claimed this switcher reuses the traces-v2 overflow
menu. It does not, and cannot: hidden elements have a zero-size rect, so
@dnd-kit's sorting strategy miscomputes drop indices for draggable tabs.

Also demotes the two strip invariants to @e2e @unimplemented rather than
leave them as @integration scenarios jsdom cannot honestly assert.

* feat(prompts): shrink tabs to share the strip, switcher only on overflow

The switcher made scrolled-off tabs reachable but not visible: tabs were
`minWidth="fit-content"`, so each claimed ~150px and only about three fit.
Dogfooding made the gap obvious — a dropdown is not what "show me more
tabs" means.

Tabs now share the strip (`flex: 1 1 0`, 88px floor, 180px cap), so they
narrow as more open. Measured live at ~580px of strip: 3 tabs before, 7
after. Only once they hit the floor does the strip scroll.

Shrinking is safe where hiding was not. A hidden element has a zero-size
rect and corrupts @dnd-kit's drop-index maths; a narrow one does not.

The switcher is now the fallback rather than the feature. It renders only
when the strip actually overflows (`scrollWidth > clientWidth`, re-measured
on resize), so while every tab fits there is no dropdown listing what is
already on screen. Verified in the browser: at 1280px, 10 tabs sit at the

same tabs relax to 124px, fit exactly, and the switcher disappears.

QA caught the collision: `data-tab-id` already marks a tab's chat textarea
(SyncedChatInput), which PromptPlaygroundChat queries document-wide.

Getting the shrink to engage needed `minWidth: 0` on every flex ancestor
down to the title Text — flex items default to `min-width: auto`, their
content width, and one ancestor without it pins the whole tab.

ci: add sticky PR impact map comment (#5586)

* ci: add sticky PR impact map comment

Posts one comment per PR summarising which areas of the monorepo the diff
touches, and rewrites that same comment on every push.

`synchronize` is "a new commit was pushed to this PR", so a single
`pull_request` trigger covers both open and push -- there is no separate
`push:` trigger. The changed-file list comes from the pulls/files API, so
the job needs no checkout, no Node setup and no pnpm install, and runs as
a single step.

Categories are ordered and first-match-wins, derived from the path globs
the existing workflows already pass to .github/actions/detect-changes, so
the buckets agree with what CI already believes about this repo. Ordering
is load-bearing: migrations, specs and tests are pulled out above the
general `langwatch/**` rules, and lockfiles above the language buckets so
a dependency bump does not masquerade as a large app change.

Two failure modes are handled explicitly. A `concurrency` group with
cancel-in-progress prevents two rapid pushes from both observing "no
existing comment" and each posting one. Fork PRs receive a read-only
GITHUB_TOKEN and are skipped rather than failing the check.

The comment is descriptive only and gates nothing, so it is not a
candidate for branch protection. It carries no path filter, therefore it
always reports a result and needs no "-unmodified" stub under the
complementary-pair system.

perf(group-queue): run the queue Lua via EVALSHA instead of re-sending 11-23KB scripts per call (#5595)

* perf(group-queue): run the queue Lua via EVALSHA instead of re-sending 11-23KB scripts per call

Every GroupQueue operation shipped its full Lua source on each call — STAGE
is ~11KB and DISPATCH ~22KB once the shared park/water-level helpers are
prepended — at four-digit call rates. Measured on prod Redis (2026-07-09):
eval at 1,042 calls/s was ~33% of engine CPU, the second-largest consumer,
with most of the cost in parsing/hashing the re-sent source.

CachedLuaScript wraps each script: EVALSHA with the precomputed sha1, and a
one-time EVAL fallback on NOSCRIPT (restart, SCRIPT FLUSH, first call on a
cluster node) that loads it into the server cache. The sha derives from the
source, so a deploy that edits a script can never execute a stale body.
Applied to all nine GroupStagingScripts call sites and the blob holder
release/transfer evals; key hash-tagging and call semantics are unchanged.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BUi7eLwDkxpZGUgujjPJ8L

* fix(group-queue): type evalsha mock args so cachedLuaScript test type-checks

The bare `vi.fn(async () => ...)` mock declared no parameters, so vitest
typed `evalsha.mock.calls` as `[][]` and `mock.calls[0]?.[0]` tripped
TS2493 (empty-tuple index) under `pnpm typecheck`. Give the mock a rest
signature mirroring the real `evalsha(sha, numKeys, ...keysAndArgs)` call
so recorded args are indexable. Runtime behaviour is unchanged.

* fix(group-queue): match NOSCRIPT by prefix, not substring

`err.message.includes("NOSCRIPT")` would trigger the EVAL fallback for
any error whose message merely contains that token (e.g. a Lua script
that errors with the word in its own text). Redis' NOSCRIPT reply always
begins with `NOSCRIPT `, so `startsWith` is the precise guard and cannot
misfire on script-level errors.

perf(observability): stop the anomaly baseline reads from dominating Redis CPU (#5596)

* perf(observability): stop the anomaly baseline reads from dominating Redis CPU

Two compounding costs in the per-minute anomaly tick, measured on prod
(2026-07-09) as the single largest Redis engine-CPU consumer — hmget at 29
calls/s costing ~1.8ms each (~37% of engine CPU):

1. perMinuteSeries enumerated every minute of the 7-day window as an
   explicit 10,080-field HMGET, forcing Redis to look up each requested
   field however sparse the hash. It now HGETALLs the hash — one field per
   ACTIVE minute, bounded by the 8-day key TTL — and window-filters
   client-side, so the cost scales with the tenant's actual traffic.

2. A tenant with under an hour of activity never cached a baseline, so
   every 1-minute tick re-paid the full-series read for every quiet tenant
   in the fleet, forever. The not-enough-data verdict is now cached for 10
   minutes (0 reads back as below-floor, the existing skip path); a ramping
   tenant still gets its first baseline within minutes.

Bound spec updated: specs/event-sourcing/anomaly-detection.feature now
states the brief-cache behaviour instead of mandating the re-read.

* test(observability): address review nits on anomaly baseline PR

- complete the truncated baseline-cache scenario step so it names the
  comparison to the 1h baseline TTL
- forward the full arg list in the redis.set test wrapper instead of
  only the first two, keeping the fake consistent with real call shape

* fix(observability): bound the tenant-rate hash so HGETALL stays cheap

perMinuteSeries switched to HGETALL on the premise that the minute-bucket
hash is bounded by the 8-day key TTL. It is not: record() refreshes the
whole-key TTL on every write and never deletes old fields, so a
continuously-active tenant accumulates one field per active minute
forever (~129k after 90 days). HGETALL would then fetch all of them each
cold baseline read, reintroducing the exact engine-CPU spike this change
set out to remove.

Bound the hash on both ends:
- record() HDELs the field aging out of the retention window each write
  (O(1)), so a steadily-active tenant never grows past the window.
- perMinuteSeries() trims any field older than the window it already scans
  from the HGETALL reply (batched, best-effort), which also shrinks hashes
  that grew unbounded before this fix and cleans up sparse-gap orphans.

Regression tests cover both the read-time trim of an over-grown hash and
the write-time drop of the just-expired field.

The retention fix extended setCachedBaseline to a third positional arg,
so `setCachedBaseline(tid, 0, 600)` left two bare numbers at the call
site. Switch to a named-params object per the repo convention and update
the two call sites plus the tests.

fix(event-sourcing): bound out-of-order fold re-fold amplification + remove SDK radar (#5707)

* fix(event-sourcing): bound hot-trace fold re-fold amplification + remove SDK radar

Fold performance / correctness
------------------------------
A hot trace (a Claude Code session streams 100k+ events into one aggregate)
pinned a `traceAnalytics` fold group at ~0 drain with 112k staged jobs. Root
cause: the slim `traceAnalytics` fold shipped (ADR-034 Phase 2) without
`refoldOnOutOfOrder: false`, so every out-of-order batch re-folded the ENTIRE
event history — which raised the checkpoint to the max occurredAt and made every
later batch look out of order too (the 2026-07-09 amplification, O(n²)).

- traceAnalytics + experimentRunState folds: set `refoldOnOutOfOrder: false`.
  Both are order-insensitive (sums / min / max / counters / LWW-by-occurredAt),
  so a late event is applied on top instead of replaying history. Mirrors the
  sibling traceSummary fold; experimentRunState was the other amplification risk
  (dataset-scale aggregate, order-insensitive, no opt-out). suiteRunState was
  considered and left re-folding (bounded aggregate + order-sensitive FinishedAt).
- Streaming store-miss re-fold: `refoldOnStoreMiss` re-folds still ran an
  unbounded read that materialised every EventPayload at once (OOM risk on a
  100k-event trace). Added a cursor-paginated read (`getEventRecordsUpToPaged`
  -> `getEventsUpToPaged` -> `eventLoaderUpToPaged`) and a streaming
  `streamRefoldUpToDelivered` that pages the history and folds page-by-page,
  gated to order-insensitive folds. Cross-page idempotencyKey dedup preserved.
- Fold coalesce batch: DEFAULT_FOLD_COALESCE_MAX_BATCH 100 -> 500, so a
  backed-up group drains ~5x fewer dispatch cycles (pure left-fold; identical
  final state).
- Added specs/event-sourcing/hot-trace-fold-amplification.feature and regression
  tests (fold policy, streaming re-fold, paged repository cursor).

Follow-up (not in this change): a worker-side byte-budget on coalescing so a
batch of large *offloaded* payloads can't OOM the worker. BlobRef carries no
size, so a correct guard needs fetch-with-budget on the hot dispatch path and
deserves its own integration-tested change.

Remove SDK radar / projectDailySdkUsage
---------------------------------------
Fully removes the unused SDK Radar feature and its backing global fold
projection `projectDailySdkUsage`, plus the unwired `customerIoDailyUsageSync`
reactor that piggybacked on it: UI (banner/card/drawer, command-bar entry,
drawer + feature-flag), API (`sdkRadar` router + `sdk-radar` module + version
generator), the projection/store/registration, tests, docs, and the Prisma
model. New Postgres migration drops the `ProjectDailySdkUsage` table (the
create migration is immutable and untouched).

* fix: address review comments on fold re-fold amplification PR

- Fix a real correctness bug: getEventsUpToPaged's store-side dedup could
  drop a page's last row (shared idempotencyKey, different EventId),
  feeding a stale cursor back to the caller and making a full page look
  short — silently truncating a streaming re-fold. Dedup now happens only
  in the executor's cross-page seen-key set.
- Add a page-count safety cap to streamRefoldUpToDelivered so a
  non-advancing cursor bug can't hang the fold worker indefinitely.
- Convert the new paged-read contracts (store + repository + ClickHouse/
  memory impls + callers + tests) to named-object parameters, and split
  EventRepositoryClickHouse.getEventRecordsUpToPaged into private query-
  building/row-mapping helpers.
- Add an IRREVERSIBLE comment + commented-out down migration for the
  ProjectDailySdkUsage drop.
- Restore the 14 reactor/fold-executor spec scenarios orphaned by the
  hot-trace-fold-amplification.feature rewrite (feature-parity was
  failing) into their more fitting homes (fold-coalescing.feature,
  reactors.feature, hot-trace-fold-amplification.feature), and bind the
  previously-unbound "Evaluation folds keep re-folding..." scenario to a
  new regression test.
- Reword an ops-resilience.feature step to describe operator-visible
  behavior instead of the drainTenant/groupIdContains internals.

Plain string literal isn't assignable to the branded TenantId type;

perf: cut redundant JSON work; zstd + size-gated msgpack in the queue (#5712)

* perf(routes): take payload size from wire bytes instead of re-serialising the body

/api/dspy/log_steps and the legacy log_results endpoint each ran
JSON.stringify(body).length purely to feed a Prometheus histogram, then threw
the string away — a full second serialisation of a body capped at 20MB and 10MB
respectively.

Read the size from the raw request text before parsing instead. This also
corrects the metric, which was reporting UTF-16 code units of a re-serialised
string rather than the bytes actually transferred.

* perf(truncate): make the key-dropping fallback linear instead of quadratic

safeTruncate's last-resort branch re-serialised the whole accumulated object on
every key to test it against the budget, so an object with N keys cost N full
JSON.stringify passes. It runs on precisely the inputs already known to be
oversized — raw tRPC mutation args, so workflow DSLs and dataset payloads.

An object's serialised length is the sum of its entries' lengths plus the
separators, so each value can be serialised once and the total accumulated.
Behaviour is unchanged: the existing suites pin exactly which keys survive, and
the no-truncation-regression suite pins the boundary.

* perf(groupQueue): zstd + size-gated msgpack body codecs, behind read-first flags

Three changes to the GQ2 envelope, all measured on Node 24 against payloads
modelled on a real RecordSpanCommand.

1. Drop a redundant full serialisation. encodeJobEnvelope opened with
   JSON.stringify(jobData) whose result the GQ2 path then discarded, having
   re-serialised the payload separately. GQ2 now only ever serialises the
   payload.

2. zstd compression (GROUP_QUEUE_ZSTD_WRITES_ENABLED). Compression, not
   serialisation, dominates this path: gzip was ~75% of encode cost. zstd is
   built into node:zlib on Node 24, so no new dependency, and encodes ~5x faster
   than gzip level 6 on large bodies.

3. msgpack above 100KB (GROUP_QUEUE_MSGPACK_WRITES_ENABLED). Deliberately
   size-gated: below the threshold msgpackr.pack is 1.7-1.9x SLOWER than
   JSON.stringify, because our payloads are dominated by long UTF-8 strings that
   msgpack stores much as JSON does, leaving nothing structural to win back.
   Above it, msgpack's 2-3x faster decode dominates — and GQ2's content-addressed
   dedup means one encode feeds N reactor decodes, so the decode win multiplies.

Rollout is readers-first, matching the GQ1 precedent (ADR-026). Decode sniffs
magic bytes and accepts gzip/zstd and JSON/msgpack from the moment it ships;
writes stay behind flags. Writing first would not be safe: GroupQueue re-stages
only on TransientBlobStoreError, so an old worker meeting a body it cannot
decode throws a plain Error and terminates at the non-retryable fail-safe, which
completes the slot and drops the job.

The codec is folded into the content hash. Blobs are content-addressed, so a
JSON-encoded and a msgpack-encoded copy of the same payload would otherwise
collide on one key with different bytes, and the second writer would silently
dedup onto the first — handing a reader a codec it was not expecting.

* Address review comments

- Drop the "json:" hash prefix: hashing the raw JSON string keeps the
  content hash byte-identical to the pre-rollout implementation instead of

fix(group-queue): move dedup-squash blob-hold transfers into the stage eval (#5598)

* fix(group-queue): move dedup-squash blob-hold transfers into the stage eval

Prod Redis grew 200MB -> 1.9GB in four days: 279k GQ2 blobs + holder sets,
100% orphaned against a 462-job backlog, every holder set pinned by exactly
one never-released hold (2026-07-09 investigation).

Root cause: send() fired the squash's hold transfer AFTER the stage eval
returned, fire-and-forget. Concurrent squashes of one dedup id reorder at
Redis — a late transfer re-adds a token an earlier transfer already
displaced — leaving a phantom hold that pins the blob until its TTL. Two
sibling paths minted the same phantom deterministically: a replace:false
squash and a post-dispatch survive-dispatch squash both report the NEW
value as the orphan, and send() self-transferred it (new == old), acquiring
a hold for a value that was never staged.

The hold transfer now happens INSIDE STAGE_LUA / STAGE_BATCH_LUA, atomic
with the displacement it accounts for (the ADR-030 follow-up the transfer
fallback comment tracked):
- replace squash: the replacement's hold is SADDed and the displaced hold
  SREMed in the eval; a newly-unreferenced redis-tier or GQ1 blob is
  UNLINKed there too. An s3-tier blob is reported via a new reclaimS3
  return element and deleted by the caller (Lua can't reach s3).
- discarded-new squashes (replace off / survive-dispatch): no hold is ever
  recorded; a GQ1 blob (uniquely owned) is UNLINKed, a GQ2 blob is left to
  the holders of jobs sharing its content or the TTL backstop.
- tenant guard mirrors the TS release path (ADR-030 §5): a foreign ref is
  skipped and left to its TTL.

The standalone TRANSFER eval stays for the retry re-stage path, which is
single-flight per group and has no ordering race.

Specs: payload-store-blob-hardening.feature Track 4 rewritten around the
atomic in-eval transfer, with four bound scenarios covering the squash
transfer, the squash chain, and both discarded-new paths.

Tests: 9 new integration tests (GQ2 holds through stage/stageBatch, s3
flag, GQ1 mixed-format, shared-content survival, tenant guard); queue
integration suite 212 passed, event-sourcing unit lane 6737 passed.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BUi7eLwDkxpZGUgujjPJ8L

feat(dev): thuishaven — hostname-based local dev via portless (#5713)

* feat(dev): thuishaven — hostname-based local dev orchestrator (haven)

Give every worktree's dev stack stable hostnames instead of raw ports, so
parallel worktrees never collide over ports. haven (cmd/haven, Go) resolves a
random per-worktree slug and registers app|api|gateway|nlp.<slug>.langwatch.localhost
with the portless proxy; .localhost resolves to loopback natively — no
/etc/hosts, DNS, or sudo.

A single machine-wide daemon hosts the dashboard (langwatch.localhost), an OTLP
telemetry fan-out to every running stack (telemetry.langwatch.localhost), and the
local Grafana LGTM stack (observability.langwatch.localhost); it holds a
cross-worktree registry and reaps stacks whose launcher has exited or gone stale.

Hexagonal (domain/app/adapters/cmd) after services/nlpgo, with pkg/clog logging,
a live TUI (haven watch), and an --agent mode for token-free AI-driven output.
Installable with go install ./cmd/haven.

* feat(dev): route pnpm dev through haven; load .env.portless overlay

pnpm dev now runs haven up, which owns codegen, migrations, alias registration
and process supervision. The resolved hostname URLs + ephemeral ports land in
langwatch/.env.portless, loaded last with override:true by server.mts and
vite.config.ts so they beat anything pinned in .env (which loads with
override:true). start.ts binds the haven-assigned API port; vite proxies /api to
the API hostname. Adds make portless-setup / portless-{list,doctor,down}; the
legacy PORT+offset scheme stays available via pnpm dev:legacy (or PORTLESS=0).

* feat(haven): collapse app + API onto one origin (API at /api)

The app and its API were two hostnames (app.<slug> and api.<slug>), which
routinely confused AI drivers into hitting the wrong URL. Vite already serves the
SPA and proxies /api (plus /mcp, /sse, /oauth, /.well-known/*) to the API, and the
telemetry fan-out already targets app.<slug>/api/otel — so a single origin was
already the real contract; haven was just advertising a redundant second URL.

- Drop `api` from the routed services; the API is now a loopback backend of `app`
  (Stack.APIPort), reached same-origin at app.<slug>.../api.
- Point Vite's /api proxy at 127.0.0.1:<apiPort> in portless mode (no self-proxy
  loop, no TLS/CA), and point server-to-server callers (gateway control-plane,
  LANGWATCH_API_URL) at that loopback port too — robust and one URL.
- Surface the API as an `app/api` sub-row in printStack + the dashboard, so the
  single origin is unmistakable. Groundwork: Stack now also carries the per-slug
  ClickHouse fields used by the next commit.

Other services (gateway, nlp, clickhouse) keep their own hostnames — only the
artificially-split app/api pair is collapsed.

* feat(haven): native ClickHouse managed by haven — one server, a DB per slug

haven now provisions and manages a single native clickhouse-server on the host
and gives every worktree its own database on it (lw_<slug>). This kills the
recurring "the migration count is wrong, use a fresh CH db" pain: each worktree
only ever reads and writes its own database, so counts are always its own.

- adapters/clickhouseserver: locates the clickhouse binary (CLICKHOUSE_BIN → PATH,
  with install guidance when absent), writes a light single-node config (memory
  ceiling, no S3/cold-storage tiering, no zero-copy replication — prod-only
  concerns that only hurt locally), starts it on free loopback ports (never
  competes with a hand-run CH on 8123), and persists the endpoint so restarts
  reuse the same ports + databases. A file lock serialises concurrent `up`s.
- app: ensureClickHouse runs inside provision, so CLICKHOUSE_URL (pointing at the
  per-slug DB on loopback) is in the overlay from the first line and the app's
  existing start:prepare:db step migrates into it. `clickhouse.<slug>` is a
  routed hostname that always resolves to the one shared server.
- `haven clickhouse status|up|url|stop|drop [--all]` for manual control; `haven
  doctor` reports CH health; `haven down` drops this stack's DB (--keep-db to
  keep). The daemon can stop the idle server (LANGWATCH_HAVEN_CH_STOP_IDLE=1);
  by default CH is a persistent singleton like the shared Redis/Postgres.

Verified end-to-end in isolation: started the server on a free port + temp home,
ran all 41 real app migrations into lw_lunar_koala (24 tables), created a second
slug's lw_brave_otter on the same server with independent data (7 vs 2 rows), and
confirmed `haven clickhouse drop` removes only this stack's DB.

* feat(haven): slug is the sanitised worktree name, not a random bird

Hostnames are now predictable: a checkout at .../worktrees/portless is the
"portless" stack (app.portless.langwatch.localhost, db lw_portless), instead of a
random happy-tiger. DeriveSlug takes the worktree's directory basename, lowercases
it and reduces it to [a-z0-9-]; on the rare same-basename collision it appends a
short stable hash of the full path. Drops the adjective/animal/place wordlists.

* feat(haven): always migrate + seed on up, with a stable local API key

Every `haven up` now guarantees a provisioned database is not just migrated but
also seeded, and seeded with the same credential every time — so a fresh stack is
immediately usable and any agent authenticates with a well-known key.

- haven injects a stable LANGWATCH_API_KEY into the overlay (default
  sk-lw-local-development-key, override with LANGWATCH_LOCAL_API_KEY). One key for
  every worktree and every agent, locally.
- `up` always runs prisma:seed (was gated behind LANGWATCH_SEED=1).
- prisma/seed.ts is now idempotent: it no-ops when a project with the API key
  already exists, so running it on every up (and across worktrees that share one
  Postgres) never duplicates the org/team/project nor errors.

* feat(haven): shared-baseline fallback — every URL always resolves

Every stack now defines all service hostnames. A service a worktree opts out of
(LANGWATCH_SKIP_AIGATEWAY / LANGWATCH_SKIP_NLP) no longer dead-ends: its hostname
resolves to a shared baseline stack's copy instead. Mark the baseline with
HAVEN_BASELINE=1 (run it off main); domain.BaselinePort finds a live baseline that
runs the service locally. ClickHouse already embodies this — one shared server,
clickhouse.<slug> always resolves, only the database is per-worktree.

printStack now shows "-> baseline :port" for fell-back services. Adds
Service.Fallback + Stack.Baseline and a unit test for the resolver.

* feat(haven): haven prune — reclaim node_modules + caches from idle worktrees

A ~60-worktree checkout accumulates tens of GB of regenerable node_modules and
build caches. `haven prune` reclaims them from worktrees that are safe to touch —
never one that is up (a live stack) or dirty (uncommitted changes). Dry-run by
default; --yes acts.

- adapters/hygiene: git worktree enumeration, dirty check (conservative: an
  unreadable status counts as dirty), Go-native dir sizing + removal, and safe
  `git worktree prune` of orphaned admin entries.
- domain.ReclaimablePaths lists the regenerable artefacts (node_modules across
  packages, dist, .vite, coverage, server.log).
- The daemon runs `git worktree prune` every ~10 min (the only unattended-safe
  hygiene); node_modules reclamation stays explicit.

Verified on a throwaway repo: reclaims clean worktrees, skips a dirty one, and
the dirty tree's node_modules is left untouched under both dry-run and --yes.

* feat(haven): haven typecheck — machine-wide slot to cap parallel tsgo RAM

Running `pnpm typecheck` in several worktrees at once is what exhausts RAM: each
tsgo run peaks around 3-4 GiB. `haven typecheck` acquires a machine-wide slot,
runs, and releases — a drop-in wrapper any script can call.

- adapters/semaphore: a file-lock counting semaphore under the haven home. flock
  means a slot is held exactly as long as the holder lives — a killed run frees
  its slot instantly, with no daemon bookkeeping to leak, and it works even while
  the daemon restarts.
- domain.TypecheckSlots bounds concurrency by memory (one slot per ~4 GiB) capped
  at the CPU count; HAVEN_TYPECHECK_SLOTS overrides. System.TotalMemory detects
  RAM (darwin sysctl / linux meminfo).
- Unit tests cover the slot maths and the semaphore's mutual exclusion.

* feat(haven): AI-gated HMR — defer Vite reloads while an agent edits

When an AI agent makes many rapid edits, HMR on every save thrashes a human's open
browser through broken intermediate states. haven supervises Vite, so it can gate
this:

- vite/havenHmrGate.ts: a Vite plugin that reads a marker (an expiry timestamp).
  While the gate is live it swallows HMR updates and remembers it owes a reload;
  when the gate lifts (marker cleared or TTL passed) it fires ONE full-reload so
  the browser jumps to the final state. Opt-in (no marker → normal HMR) and always
  time-bounded — a safety timer guarantees the catch-up reload, so HMR can never
  be permanently stuck off.
- `haven hmr on [--ttl 30s] | off | status` writes/clears the marker (stored
  worktree-local, gitignored). An agent runs `haven hmr on` before a batch of
  edits and `haven hmr off` after.

Verified the command lifecycle writes the expiry marker, reports remaining time,
and clears it.

* docs(haven): README reflects shipped CH/prune/typecheck/HMR features

* fix(haven): address review — leak the API key nowhere, escape the dashboard, bound Root

Security:
- /api/registry served domain.Stack verbatim, which carries LocalAPIKey. It now
  encodes a DTO without it.
- The registry JSON and .env.portless both hold the local API key and were

* feat(haven): own the local observability stack — colima, capped, auto-wired

Folds the local LGTM observability stack (PR #5698) into haven and makes it a
first-class managed surface instead of a compose service.

Why haven owns it, not compose:
- Runs on colima, not Docker Desktop, so the VM has an explicit per-profile
  RAM/CPU/disk ceiling — a background telemetry stack can never take the box.
  haven starts colima if down; a profile it creates is capped, one that exists is
  never resized.
- Every `pnpm dev` (haven up) writes the OTLP endpoint into that stack's
  .env.portless overlay and tags telemetry langwatch.worktree=<slug>. One shared
  collector serves every worktree; filter Grafana to your slug. No .env surgery.
- `haven observability up|down|status` (alias obs) is the lifecycle;
  `make observability*` now delegate to it. `haven doctor` reports stack health.
  Opt-in start on `up` via LANGWATCH_HAVEN_OBS=1 — otherwise haven only links to a
  collector already running (won't spend 2 GiB on every pnpm dev).

Resource + retention caps (the stack should be small at local scale):
- Container: memory (== memory-swap, no thrash), CPU, pids-limit, log rotation.
- The bundle ships NO retention for any store — Loki and Tempo keep everything
  forever. haven derives a config for all three from the image's own and mounts
  it back read-only with a short retention (default 2h), a Prometheus size cap,
  and a Loki ingestion-rate cap. Derived via the yaml.Node tree (not a map) so
  untouched scalars survive verbatim — a map round-trip re-emits Loki's schema
  `from: 2020-10-24` as an RFC3339 string it then refuses to parse.

Image pin corrected 0.11.7 -> 0.28.0: on a healthy colima VM, 0.11.7's OTLP
collector segfaults on startup (the collector IS the ingest endpoint, so nothing
lands) while the rest come up. The container healthcheck only probes Grafana, so
a dead-collector stack still reports healthy — `status` reports the running image
and the docs say to verify by round-tripping /v1/*, not by the health endpoint.

Also promotes langwatch.worktree to a Prometheus metric label (its OTLP receiver
only promotes an allow-list; without this, metrics lose the worktree tag that
traces and logs keep for free).

Verified end-to-end on real colima: all three signals ingested (HTTP 200) and
read back, each filterable by worktree; caps confirmed on the container; all
ports loopback-bound; Loki config validates; zero collector segfaults.

Hexagonal, like the rest of haven: pure limits/config/patch logic in domain (unit
tested), colima + otellgtm adapters behind an app.Observability port.

fix(groupQueue): classify redis-tier blob-read errors as transient, await holder bookkeeping (#5736)

The redis tier of TieredBlobStore.fetch() had no error handling, unlike the
s3 tier: any exception from RedisJobBlobStore.get()/.peek() (connection
drop, timeout, an OOM-from-noeviction rejection) propagated raw instead of
being classified. Since a genuine miss is represented by a null return, not
an exception, any thrown error here now maps to TransientBlobStoreError so
the caller retries instead of permanently dropping the job as "missing".

Also: EnvelopeBlobLifecycle.acquire/release/transfer/reclaimOrphanedS3 were
fire-and-forget from every call site in groupQueue.ts. A killed worker
process could silently drop one mid-flight (never even reaching the
existing .catch() warning), and nothing ordered one squash's holder
bookkeeping against the next on the same group. All four are now async and
awaited everywhere they're called; each still degrades to a warn + the TTL
backstop internally rather than throwing, so job completion/retry
semantics are unchanged.

Also logs the actual error message (redacted) on the "Failed to parse
staged job data" / "Failed to parse drained sibling job data" catch-alls,
which previously gave no way to tell a missing blob from a malformed
envelope from a transient store error.

* perf(simulations): stop re-downloading run payloads on timers

The simulations views were heavy for reasons the data model doesn't
require: the run drawer re-pulled the full transcript (incl. tool-call
JSON) every 3s forever, the external-set view re-fetched up to 5000

  stream is down, slow safety-net when connected.

  their timers. A new tiny getSuiteRunFreshness probe (max(UpdatedAt),
  partition-pruned, adaptive 3s/15s cadence, paused while SSE is
  connected) invalidates the heavy query only when something changed.

  from list reads — the drawer keeps reading RUN_COLUMNS.
- Auto-expansion: only the newest execution expands on first load; new
  arrivals still auto-expand; collapsed rows stay collapsed (seen-ids
  tracked separately, localStorage schema migrated).
- Grid cards / list rows prefetch getRunState on hover/focus so the
  drawer opens instantly.

Adds WORKERS_IN_PROCESS=1 (and `pnpm dev:single`) to host the background

  roleRunsWorkers(role): outbox runtime + heartbeat scheduler (presets.ts),
  the GroupQueue consumer (eventSourcing.ts), and the scheduler start()
  guard (heartbeat.scheduler.ts).
- Extract the worker boot from src/workers.ts into a reusable startWorkers()
  (src/server/workers/startWorkers.ts). The standalone worker calls it with
  its own metrics server; start.ts calls it after listen with
  startMetricsServer:false and drains it before closing the shared App.

* fix(dev): address review findings for in-process worker mode

- P0: reactors with a `runIn` filter (runIn:["worker"], ["web","worker"])
  were excluded under the new "all" role — projectionRouter matched the role
  with `runIn.includes(processRole)`, and ["worker"].includes("all") is false,
  so in-process mode booted the worker stack but ran no reactors. Extract a
  pure `roleSatisfiesRunIn(runIn, role)` helper (config.ts) that treats "all"
  as satisfying any filter, and route isReactorExcluded through it.
- P2: start.ts gated in-process mode on `dev` (NODE_ENV !== "production") while
  start.sh gated on NODE_ENV === "development"; an exotic NODE_ENV would spawn
  BOTH the standalone workers lane and the in-process stack. Align start.ts on
  NODE_ENV === "development".
- P3: /workers/metrics proxied to a dead port in single-process mode; serve it
  from this process's shared prom registry (same as /metrics) instead.
- P3: register the SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers before awaiting the in-process worker
  boot, so a signal during boot still drains gracefully.
- P3 (test): unit-test roleSatisfiesRunIn exhaustively, locking the "all"

* fix(haven): autostash local edits before refreshing a reused PR worktree

PR #5743 review (P1): reusing a `haven pr` worktree ran `git reset --hard
FETCH_HEAD` unconditionally, so a developer who made temporary/debugging edits
in pr-<n>, then reran `haven pr <n>` after the author pushed, had those
uncommitted changes silently discarded.

Now a refresh checks for uncommitted tracked changes and, by default,
autostashes them first (the safety net `git rebase`/`git pull` get from
--autostash) instead of losing them — printing the stash's sha so they can
restore exactly those edits with `git stash apply <sha>` (apply, by sha, not a
bare pop, since git's stash stack is shared across the repo's worktrees).
`--discard-local-changes` opts out and overwrites instead.

Scoped to tracked changes (`--untracked-files=no`): `git reset --hard` only
destroys tracked-file modifications; untracked files survive it, and sweeping
them into the stash would drag in the generated artifacts a prior `haven up`
leaves behind. The status probe also fails loudly if the dir isn't a usable git
worktree — a stronger reuse gate than isDir alone.

Tests: porcelainIsDirty cases; a git-backed behavioural test proving the edit is
stashed (working tree back to HEAD) and recoverable via `git stash apply`.

fix(scenarios): reconcile orphaned IN_PROGRESS runs on worker boot, and make a finished run final (#3195) (#5006)

* fix(scenarios): reconcile orphaned runs on worker boot (#3195)

When a scenarios worker dies mid-run (OOM, crash, deploy, container
restart), the in-process failure handler that emits the run's terminal
event dies with it, leaving the run non-terminal in ClickHouse forever:
the UI spins at "Starting"/"Running" and downstream reactors never fire.
Read-time stall detection only paints it STALLED cosmetically; it never
writes a terminal event.

On worker boot, the scenario processor now reconciles non-terminal runs
whose last activity is older than the stall threshold (2x the child
timeout) to a terminal ERROR via the existing idempotent finish path.
The threshold is the multi-pod false-positive guard: a live worker
hard-caps every child at the timeout and emits its own terminal event at
the cap, so a run quiet for longer than that has no live worker.

Also guard the fold's non-terminal status handlers: once FinishedAt is
set, a late started/snapshot event can no longer resurrect Status to
IN_PROGRESS, which would otherwise create an unrecoverable zombie when a
reparented child outlives its dead parent.

Tests: reconciler unit (emit/skip/partial-failure), fold finalized-status
guard regression, and a ClickHouse integration test proving only stale
non-terminal runs are surfaced (healthy/terminal/archived excluded).

* fix(scenarios): scope boot reconciliation to started runs, make finish final

Addresses three review findings on #5006.

Scope the sweep to IN_PROGRESS (P0). The threshold argument this reconciler
rests on -- a worker hard-caps every child and emits its own terminal event at
the cap, so an idle non-terminal run has no live worker -- only closes for a run
that was STARTED. Nothing bounds queue wait: the pool is concurrency-bounded, so
a QUEUED run behind a draining backlog goes stale while a healthy worker is
still working toward it, and failing it is the false positive this reconciler
must never produce. QUEUED orphans are a different failure (nobody ever picked
the run up) and are owned by scenario-orphan-reconciler (#3365), so the two
sweeps are now disjoint by status and cannot double-write a run. Also order the
sweep oldest-first so the cap drops the least urgent orphans, not arbitrary ones.

Make a finished run final (P1). handleSimulationRunFinished sets FinishedAt, so
statusAfter cannot cover it, and it left two ways to build the exact zombie the
guard exists to prevent -- both observed by executing the fold:

  - a second finished() rewrote the first, taking a reconciled ERROR back to
    SUCCESS and splitting the record (ERROR status, SUCCESS verdict). It now
    returns early once FinishedAt is set: a run finishes exactly once.
  - the ingest schema types finished status as z.nativeEnum(ScenarioRunStatus),
    so finished(status=IN_PROGRESS) wrote a non-terminal Status alongside
    FinishedAt -- invisible to the reconciler (FinishedAt IS NULL) and to
    read-time stall detection. A non-terminal explicit status is now refused in
    favour of the verdict-derived one.

Each is covered by a regression test that fails against the un-fixed fold.

* fix(traces): named params for fetchKeyOf + enforce batch-resolver cardinality (#5082)

fetchKeyOf(aggregateId, eventId, field) took three positional strings, so a
caller that transposed two of them compiled cleanly and silently deduped/fetched
the wrong event_log row onto the wrong span. Now takes named params, per the
repo's TypeScript standard (CLAUDE.md).

ResolveTraceSpansBatchFn is INJECTED, so "exactly one resolution per input trace,
in input order" is a convention its type cannot enforce — yet `resolutions[i]!`
relied on it on the hot bulk-read path shared by export, thread, and the
dataset/sample builders. A resolver (or test double) that dropped or reordered
entries would crash with zero context, or silently pair the wrong resolved spans
with the wrong trace summary.

Guard it at the boundary where the untrusted value enters (resolveSpansBatch),
not at the two downstream index sites: that catches the violation while the
offending resolver is still nameable, and covers both `resolutions[i]!` and
`merged[i]!` with one assertion. (`merged` comes from `entries.map(...)`, so its
length already equals `enrichable.length` by construction — a second assert
there would be unreachable.)

The error is a named class, following the ClickHouseClientUnavailableError
precedent, and both read paths' generic try/catch re-throw it unwrapped — a
resolver-contract violation is a code bug, not a fetch failure, and flattening it
into "Failed to fetch traces from ClickHouse" would lose the very context the
guard exists to provide. Covered by a test that drives a genuinely
non-conforming resolver through the real service and observes the throw.

* fix(traces): address review — honour the resolver-order claim, close the third catch, unbreak the spans-less download

Review of the previous commits surfaced four real defects, three of them in code
those commits added.

**The guard overclaimed.** Its message and comments promised "one resolution per
input trace, IN INPUT ORDER" and said a resolver that "drops or reorders" would
fail loudly — but it only compared lengths. A resolver returning the right COUNT
in the wrong ORDER sailed through and scattered each trace's IO onto its
neighbour: precisely the silent-corruption case the guard was added to catch.
Advertising a check that doesn't exist is worse than no check, so the order is
now actually verified (resolved spans carry the trace identity the resolution
itself lacks). Renamed to TraceSpansBatchResolverContractError since it now
polices two distinct violations.

**A doc comment described a mechanism that does not exist.** It claimed this
error escapes "like ClickHouseClientUnavailableError" — but that one escapes by
being thrown OUTSIDE the try, not by an instanceof re-throw. Two opposite
mechanisms; a reader would hunt for an allowlist that wasn't there. Now describes
what the code actually does.

**The unwrapped re-throw missed a third catch.** getTracesWithSpansByThreadIds
sits ABOVE getTracesWithSpans and flattens what that method re-throws, so the
descriptive error was destroyed on a live resolveBlobs path (thread router +
evaluation-execution service). The class doc's "the read paths re-throw this
unwrapped" was simply false there. Allowlisted.

**getAllForDownload had the summary-export bug, untouched.** It still gated
`resolveBlobs` on `includeSpans` — the exact pattern just fixed in ExportService.
A download returns trace-level input/output whether or not spans are included, so
a spans-less download silently truncated any offloaded trace. Same data loss, twin
path, introduced by this PR. Fixed and covered.

Also: the public-share branch is extracted into readPubliclySharedThread (the
handler had grown to ~78 lines with the security-critical sequencing buried in
prose), and it now re-projects onto authorizedTraceIds instead of re-deriving a
chronological sort — those ids already carry the thread's order, so the thread
read stays the single owner of what "thread order" means rather than the
comparator living in a third place. The test fixture that returned an unsorted
thread was contradicting the service's actual contract; corrected.

The audit-log stub now mocks the auditLog function directly, matching
translate/apiKey.myBindings/workflows.generateCommitMessage, instead of reaching
through to the prisma singleton's internals.

test; restoring `resolveBlobs: input.includeSpans` fails the spans-less download
test.

* test(traces): make the public-share exclusion property actually load-bearing

Test review found the security property under-guarded in the one scenario that
matters. The multi-shared case (t1 and t3 shared, t2 an unauthorized sibling

doesn't depend on its args, so a router that regressed to resolving

assertion on the CALL ARGS can catch the unauthorized sibling being de-offloaded,
and there wasn't one.

* fix(traces): close the span-less blind spot in the resolver-order guard

The identity check I added compares spans[0].traceId on each side — but a trace
can legitimately have ZERO spans (fetchTracesWithSpansJoined builds its map from
summary rows and defaults spans to []). A span-less trace has no traceId on
EITHER side, so swapping it with a spans-ful trace was invisible to the identity
check at both indices, and the real trace silently lost its spans: exactly the
corruption the guard exists to stop, in the one case it couldn't see.

Both resolvers derive resolvedSpans by mapping over the input spans, so span
count is a genuine contract invariant. Checking it first catches the swap (the
spans-ful index expects N, gets 0). Two span-less traces transposed remain
invisible and are harmless — their resolutions are empty and interchangeable.

Found by writing the falsifiability check properly. My first attempt at the test
passed with the span-count check removed: it constructed a resolution whose
resolvedSpans were empty but whose SIBLING still carried an identity, so the
identity check caught it and the new check was never exercised. The real hole
needs a trace with no span ROWS at all. Rebuilt the test that way; it now fails
when the span-count check is removed.

* fix(traces): actually resolve blobs on summary reads — the flag was inert

My earlier "fix" for the summary-export data loss did not fix it. Setting
`resolveBlobs: true` in ExportService and getAllForDownload changed nothing at
runtime, because resolution lives inside enrichTracesWithSpans, which only ran:

    if (options.includeSpans && traces.length > 0) { ...resolveBlobs... }

A summary-mode export sets includeSpans=false (`request.mode === "full"`), so
`options.resolveBlobs` was never even READ. Zero event_log reads were issued and
the truncated 64 KB preview shipped exactly as before — while a code comment
asserted the opposite. Same for a spans-less download.

Spans are fetched when the caller wants them OR wants full IO, because those are
not the same thing: the full value is recoverable ONLY by de-offloading the
spans' eventref pointers and recomputing trace IO from them (trace_summaries
holds nothing but the preview). So a content-consuming summary read must fetch
and resolve spans, then discard them — it keeps the recomputed trace-level IO and
returns `spans: []`, so its payload shape is unchanged.

AC5 is preserved by construction: resolveBlobs stays opt-in, so the list grid and
the aggregations resolve nothing and issue zero event_log reads whether or not
they ask for spans. The existing zero-read tests still pass.

Why the old tests couldn't catch this: the router/export tests mock
getAllTracesForProject and assert only that the FLAG IS FORWARDED. Such a test
passes whether or not the flag has any runtime effect — it was green throughout.
The new test drives the REAL service + REAL resolver with
{ includeSpans: false, resolveBlobs: true } and asserts the VALUE comes back full.
Confirmed RED before this fix (getFromEventLog never called).

Cost, stated: summary exports now do a span join + bounded event_log reads where
they previously did neither. That is the tradeoff the reviewer explicitly accepted
on the blocker thread, and there is no cheaper way to recover the value.

* docs+test(traces): make getTracesByThreadId's chronological order a stated contract

The public-share branch re-projects its authorized subset onto the order this
method returns, rather than re-deriving a sort of its own. That is the right call
— one owner for "thread order" — but it silently made an unstated implementation
detail load-bearing on the anonymous, least-exercised path. The router's own tests
mock this service, so deleting the sort here would have mis-ordered public-share
threads with zero test failures anywhere.

Stated in the JSDoc and pinned by a service-level test that feeds the bulk read's
rows back out of order and asserts chronological output. Verified falsifiable:
removing the sort fails it.

* test(export): prove summary-mode blob resolution end-to-end against real ClickHouse

The unit tests could not have caught the bug they were written for. They mocked
getAllTracesForProject and asserted `resolveBlobs` was FORWARDED — an assertion
that passes whether or not the flag does anything. It did nothing (resolution was
gated behind includeSpans), and they stayed green while summary exports shipped

This test asserts the VALUE, through the real stack:

  real ClickHouse (trace_summaries + stored_spans + event_log)
    -> real ClickHouseTraceService  (the includeSpans/resolveBlobs gate)
    -> real resolveOffloadedTracesBatch + real BlobStore (the event_log read)
    -> real ExportService in SUMMARY mode

preview in trace_summaries. UNIQUE_TAIL sits past the preview boundary by
construction, so it exists ONLY in the de-offloaded value — a preview-only export
cannot contain it.

AC5 is guarded in the same file: the list/search read over the SAME offloaded
trace, without resolveBlobs, must still come back as the preview with the tail
absent — so the fix demonstrably did not disarm the heavy-read protection.

feat: harden the pipeline against fat-payload poison (worker outage 2026-07-10) (#5661)

* feat(event-sourcing): claim-side poison guard parks groups that kill workers

A group whose staged jobs seize the event loop dies before any retry
accounting can run: the liveness probe SIGTERMs the process, the next boot
re-claims the same group, and the crash loop survives every restart
(2026-07-10 incident: one recordLog group with ~2,000 jobs stalled all
tenants for 20h).

Claim strikes: processWithRetries records a persistent per-group strike
before decoding and clears it on every surviving code path. A blocked event
loop cannot run the clear, so only genuine loop-killers accumulate strikes;
the claim after the threshold parks the group into the existing blocked set
with a stored explanation. Unblocking resets the count.

Decode cap: staged values over MAX_BLOB_BYTES (legacy bare JSON or
zip-bomb envelopes predating the encode cap) park the group unparsed
instead of dropping to replay, which would re-materialize the same value.

* docs(event-sourcing): document the claim-side poison guard in ARCHITECTURE.md

* feat(traces): bound Claude Code turns with recordLog shard lanes + conversion cap

One agentic turn can stream thousands of log records under its single
per-turn trace. Every record became a recordLog command FIFO'd into one
GroupQueue group, and the span-sync reactor re-read the whole turn on
every debounce; the converter's 'a turn's log set is small and bounded'
assumption was the 2026-07-10 outage's ingest-side flaw.

recordLog now mirrors the span-command sharding: TRACE_LOG_PROCESSING_SHARDS
> 1 spreads a turn's records across traceId:<shard> lanes while the emitted
event keeps aggregateId = traceId, so the fold, the reactor, tool-output
recovery, and the session view are untouched. Trace identity must not be
split further: tool outputs are recovered from the next model call's request
body within the same trace's record set.

The reactor fetches cap+1 marked logs (LANGWATCH_CLAUDE_TURN_LOG_CAP,
default 2000), converts the first cap, and stamps the root span
langwatch.claude_code.truncated_logs + dropped_log_count when the cap
bites.

* style: normalize dashes on branch-added lines

* feat(evaluations): offload oversized evaluator inputs to stored objects (ADR-039)

Evaluator inputs (the full conversation context fed to an evaluator) were
written raw into the evaluation event and evaluation_runs.Inputs. One
tenant's agentic workload produced rows up to GB scale; a background merge
of those partitions has been retrying since 2026-05-23 because a single row
no longer fits the server memory budget, and 10-45 MiB evaluation events
still land weekly.

Inputs over 1 MiB now offload to the content-addressed stored-objects
service (purpose evaluation_inputs, tenant-scoped keys, project-delete
cascade) before the event is built: event_log, the fold state, and the
ClickHouse row all carry a bounded marker with a 16 KiB preview, and the
lazy inputs read the UI already uses resolves the marker back to the full
content. Over 50 MiB stores a preview-only marker. Flag-gated on
release_evaluation_payload_offload and fail-open: an S3 failure keeps the
inputs inline and the evaluation completes.

Unconditional belt-and-braces caps at the repository write
(8 MiB Inputs marker, 256 KiB text columns) keep rows merge-safe for any
writer regardless of the flag.

stored_objects.size_bytes doubles as the per-tenant offloaded-bytes ledger:
getStorageUsageByProject sums it (dedup-aware) so offloaded storage is
chargeable alongside ClickHouse-native bytes, and stored_objects joins
MONITORED_TABLES.

evaluators live side-by-side with fully independent code paths — Pairwise

config even with the filter fixed. This was a latent bug for pairwise
chip evaluators too.

the Phase-1 evaluator filter, the column-style comparison target skip,
and the Phase-2 dependency expansion (which previously only expanded
