* feat(comparison): one door in, a real grid, and structured outputs again (#5101)

Three things, all downstream of the same mistake: Comparison was modelled as
an evaluator you create anywhere, when it is really a question about the
columns of one experiment.

**One door in.** Comparison's `variants` are target ids and its `goldenField`
is a dataset column, both local to a single workbench. Created from the
evaluator catalog there is nothing to bind them to, so that drawer rendered
a name, a model and a prompt, and no way to say WHAT was being compared —
a Comparison you could save and never use. It is removed from the catalog
(the treatment pairwise_compare already had) and left resolvable so saved
ones still load. The Comparison card in TargetTypeSelectorDrawer, which
opens the full form, is now the only way to make one.

**Structured outputs.** PairwiseConfigForm had a per-variant output-field
picker; merging the forms dropped the UI while keeping `variantOutputPaths`
in the schema and the legacy reader. So a variant emitting `{answer, score}`
had no way to say "judge the .answer" and the raw object reached langevals,
where `CandidateInput.output: str` 422s the run — pydantic will not coerce a
dict. The picker is restored per variant, using the app-wide
VariableMappingInput. Belt and braces: the orchestrator now serializes any
non-string candidate rather than failing a run for a user who never opened
the picker, and empties a null one so the judge skips the row instead of
grading the text "null". The old orchestrator test asserted a raw dict was
passed through; it now asserts the string, because the dict was the bug.

**A grid.** The variants were a Wrap, so twelve reflowed to 4/4/3/1 and the
orphan read as a layout bug. `balancedColumns` picks 3 or 4 columns, always
preferring an exact divisor. Its first draft minimised the empty cells in
the last row, which quietly chose 2 columns for 13 variants and orphaned a
card anyway; the tests caught it. It maximises the last row instead.

orchestrator (29, up from 26). 1060 pass across the four suites. Typecheck
clean.

* fix(comparison): surface a picked output field that no longer exists (#5101)

A saved comparison can point at an output field a variant no longer emits —
someone renamed it on the prompt. The target still runs, so the missing-output
check passed the row, but pickOutputPath resolved the field to nothing and the
candidate came out empty. langevals drops empty candidates and skips the row
silently, so a three-way comparison quietly became a two-way, or a two-way
showed a bare "no verdict" with no cause.

Detect an empty candidate after building it and skip the row with its own
reason, the same way a missing output already does — but with a distinct
message. Missing output says "run it first"; empty output says "check the
output field", because re-running won't help when the field is gone or the
output is empty/unserializable.

ComparisonSkipReason gains a `kind` ("missing-output" | "empty-output") and
`missingVariantNames` becomes `variantNames`, since it now names variants for
either reason. The Phase-2 event loop switches message and error_type on kind.

The null / empty / unserializable candidate tests move from asserting an empty
candidate on a built cell to asserting the skip — the honest outcome the old
code only reached by handing langevals a candidate it would throw away.

* fix(topic-clustering): bound the heavy trace fetch to a 49-day hot-tier window

The batch/incremental page fetch reads the heavy ComputedInput payload and
cursor-pages back through a 365-day window. Only the most-recent ~90 days of
trace_summaries live on the ClickHouse hot tier; the rest is S3-tiered, so
paging walked the payload column across cold storage (measured: ~38 GiB / 75%
of the scanned partitions on S3), producing multi-hundred-MB cold reads.

Split the two windows by role:
- MODE decision (fetchCountsFromClickHouse) stays at 365 days. It reads only
  light key columns and must reflect the project's whole history — narrowing
  it flips historically-mature-but-quiet projects out of incremental into the

* fix(scenarios): bound generate LLM dispatch so a failing gateway can't surface as HTML (#5758)

Scenario generation dispatches its LLM call through the nlp-service
/go/proxy gateway — the same path as the scenario User-Simulator (#5760).
When that gateway is broken (e.g. the Azure "endpoint not set" bug fixed
server-side by #5762), the Vercel AI SDK retried the dispatch 3× (its
unbounded default), burning ~6s on an instant config error. The app
itself always answers with JSON (even the 502 is application/json), so

failing/hung dispatch now returns a fast, clean JSON envelope (~6.1s ->
~2.0s, verified live) — never long enough for a proxy to substitute HTML.
Provider-agnostic; #5762 is the fix that makes Azure generation succeed.

The client response.json() guard stays as defense-in-depth for a
front-proxy body that still slips through.

Regression test runs the real handler + real AI SDK retry loop against a
MockLanguageModelV3 and asserts the dispatch is bounded to 2 attempts
(revert the bound -> "Failed after 3 attempts" -> red).

fix(replay): unfreeze live processing and cut weeks off projection rebuilds (#5776)

* fix(replay): unfreeze live processing and cut weeks off projection rebuilds

Production map-projection replays (spanStorage et al.) ran for weeks while
freezing live processing for the entire run. Five compounding fixes, per
ADR-015's original intent (amendment added):

- MapAccumulator now flushes ONE bulkAppend per tenant chunk (default 5000
  records) instead of one awaited ClickHouse INSERT per aggregate — for
  span storage the aggregate is a single trace, so each trace was its own
  ~200ms sequential wait_for_async_insert INSERT. AppendStore.bulkAppend
  takes a tenant-scoped BulkAppendContext (no aggregateId); the live
  append() path is unchanged.
- replayOptimized pauses + drains PER BATCH (only that batch's aggregates)
  and unpauses in a per-batch finally, mirroring the non-optimized path —
  it used to pause all selected projections before the first batch and
  only unpause after the last, and a batch error path depended on a
  run-level finally. The marker protocol keeps correctness across the
  unpaused gaps.
- Cutoff/load queries now carry an EventOccurredAt range computed per
  batch from the aggregates' own event history
  (getAggregateOccurredAtBounds), enabling toYearWeek partition pruning
  instead of scanning every partition (incl. S3 cold storage) per batch.
  Bounding by the replay's `since` would drop pre-since history that fold
  rebuilds need, so the bound is derived from the data instead.
- Per-tenant cutoff and load queries within a batch run in parallel.
- The ops replay lock (1h TTL) is refreshed at least once per batch (and
  time-gated from progress emits), so multi-hour runs no longer silently
  stop updating status when the lock expires; replay-phase progress emits
  are throttled to every 100 aggregates instead of every aggregate.

* fix(replay): address review — pause inside try/finally, bounded fan-out, lost-lock abort

- move the per-batch pause loop inside the try/finally so a mid-loop
  pauseProjection failure can never leave projections frozen (CodeRabbit)
- bound both per-tenant ClickHouse fan-outs in replayBatchOptimized with
  pMapLimited(concurrency) instead of unbounded Promise.all (CodeRabbit)
- abort a stale run when refreshLock reports the lock was lost, and guard
  finalization so a superseded run can't clobber its successor's status
- filter AggregateType in the occurred-at bounds query to restore the
  primary-key binary search; return undefined instead of null
- skip cutoff/load queries entirely when bounds are null (zero-event case)
- make the lock-takeover test deterministic (no 20ms sleep, CodeRabbit),
  type the runtime stub with satisfies, and add coverage: refreshLock Lua
  vs real Redis, multi-tenant replayOptimized batch, narrow-bounds pruning
  proof, time-gated heartbeat, lost-lock abort
- docs: consistent per-batch pause wording in the spec, ADR-015 <-> spec
  cross-links, real Related-ADRs list, comment renumbering, drop dead
  aggregateBatchSize param, fix MapAccumulator JSDoc placement

* fix(replay): type BufferedMapRecord.record as unknown; fix latent ColumnDef variance

- BufferedMapRecord.record: any -> unknown (CodeRabbit); the record is
  produced by a generics-erased MapProjectionDefinition and only handed
  back to the store's append/bulkAppend, so unknown flows cleanly
- buildEvalColumnDef now returns ColumnDef<TraceListItem, unknown> with

- 023 (was 025+030): per-trigger dispatch timing — cadence and
  trace-readiness debounce. Two knobs on the same Trigger row at
  different points in the pipeline; treated as one decision.
- 024 (was 026): Liquid templates for trigger notifications.
  Standalone; moved into one shared module under src/shared/templating
  per the rendering ADR.
- 025 (was 027): typed DispatchError contract. Standalone interface
  decision tied to the outbox worker; small and focused.
- 026 (was 028+029): authoring drawer + dispatch-health view.
  Same data model, opposite ends of the operator lifecycle.

Will ship as part of the three-PR slicing (PR 1 ships 022/023/025;
PR 2 ships 024; PR 3 ships 026). Original ten ADR files (021-030 from
the doc-only PRs #4241 + #4464) are superseded — those PRs will be
closed when the new stack opens.

already shipped to main since the original stack was started.

* feat(outbox): transactional outbox + per-trigger dispatch timing

Ships PR 1 of 3 in the trigger-outbox stack — server-side dispatch
infrastructure with no UI changes.

What lands here:

* fix(outbox): rebase schema onto main + address Copilot review

CI on #4498 was failing on a cascade of typecheck errors plus several
real bugs Copilot caught. Sweep:

Typecheck unblock:
- schema.prisma: re-apply Trigger + ReactorOutbox additions on top of
  current origin/main instead of the stale source-branch snapshot, which
  was removing CostCenter, multi-scope CustomLLMModelCost, and ~40 other
  main-side schema changes unrelated to this PR.
- queues/index.ts: export the QueueAuditAdapter type (groupQueue.ts
  imports it from "../../queues" / "../queues" and the type was missing
  from the barrel).
- outbox/setup.ts: cast `redis` to Redis for RedisCachedFoldStore now
  that the dep type is Cluster|Redis|null.
- alertTrigger + evaluationAlertTrigger reactor unit-test factories:
  add notificationCadence + traceDebounceMs to the TriggerSummary
  default builder so tests compile after the column additions land.

Real bugs from Copilot review:
- triggerActionDispatch.computeScheduledFor: digest cadences now snap
  to the next wall-clock boundary (ceil(nowMs / windowMs) * windowMs)
  instead of returning `now + window`. The old behavior gave every match
  its own scheduled-for, so concurrent matches landed at slightly
  different times and never coalesced through the queue's
  processBatch + coalesceMaxBatch — digest mode silently degraded to
  per-match dispatch. Snapping is what makes ADR-023 digest semantics
  actually work.
- groupQueue.sendBatch audit hook: replace O(n²) `jobsToStage.indexOf(job)`
  with a positional loop index. The indexOf form was both slow and
  potentially mis-associating payloads if two jobs shared an object
  reference.
- groupQueue audit hooks (both send + sendBatch): pass
  JOB_RETRY_CONFIG.maxAttempts on onEnqueue. The PG ReactorOutbox.maxAttempts
  column was defaulting to 8 even though the queue retries up to 25, so

setup.ts: `setupOutbox` → `buildOutboxRuntime`. The runtime returns
`{ dispatcher, auditAdapter, enqueueSettle, attachQueue }` — no queue
field. `attachQueue` is called by EventSourcing once the main queue is
constructed; `enqueueSettle` and the dispatcher's internal
`enqueueCadence` both forward to whichever queue is attached. `OutboxStack`
is kept as a deprecated alias for the new `OutboxRuntime` so consumers
that still reference the old type compile.

eventSourcing.ts: accept an optional `outbox?: OutboxRuntime` on the
constructor, persist it on the instance, and consult it in
createGlobalQueue. Each of the queue's callbacks (`groupKey`, `process`,
`processBatch`, `coalesceMaxBatch`, `score`, `spanAttributes`,
`deduplication`) peels off `isSettle || isCadence` first and delegates
to the outbox dispatcher; everything else flows through the existing
registry. The audit adapter is wired onto the queue's `auditAdapter`
slot — the adapter already gates internally on outbox-stage payloads
so non-outbox queue events no-op cheaply. After construction,
`outbox.attachQueue(globalQueue)` resolves the producer cycle.

pipelineRegistry.ts: `outbox.queue.send(...)` becomes
`outbox.enqueueSettle(payload, { ttlMs })`. The per-trigger
`traceDebounceMs` override is still the only knob that crosses the
wire — stage-aware dedup (Debounce Mode for settle, per-job for
cadence) is configured once on the main queue's `deduplication` field.

ADR-022 r3 documents the trade-off captured by the collapse: one
Redis prefix / Grafana panel / crash-recovery story, but trigger
dispatches now share the per-tenant fairness budget with span
projections (`TenantRateTracker`). Bounded; not catastrophic; but a
regression in isolation guarantees vs the two-queue split that should
be visible to the next person reasoning about queue scaling.

* fix(mailer): trigger emails route To=hashed no-reply, recipients=BCC

Production trigger emails previously rendered every recipient address in
the To: header, leaking the internal recipient list to every receiver,
inviting reply-all storms, and putting user-controlled multi-recipient
content directly into a header (EMAIL_RX blocks CRLF smuggling but
doesn't undo the enumeration leak).

Now:

  - To:  LangWatch Triggers <no-reply+<HMAC>@<domain>>
  - Bcc: configured recipients

The local-part tag is HMAC-SHA256(triggerId, NEXTAUTH_SECRET) truncated
to 12 hex chars — stable per trigger so future bounce processors can
attribute mail back to a row, unguessable without the secret so the
address can't be reverse-engineered or forged.

    BccAddresses, raw-MIME path uses Destinations envelope (no Bcc:
    header rendered to receivers); SendGrid uses bcc / replyTo keys.
    `computeDefaultFrom()` extracted for callers that need to derive
    the no-reply domain from the From: address.
  - sendTriggerEmail: now takes `triggerId`, builds the no-reply To
    via `buildTriggerNoReplyAddress`, recipients ride in bcc.
  - TriggerNotifier.sendEmail: signature changes to
    `{ to: string, bcc: string[], subject, html }`. Test-fire uses a
    "preview" sentinel id so test bounces don't pollute prod bounce
    streams that may key off the hash.
  - Both production dispatchers (outbox + inline pipeline) thread the
    trigger id through.

* feat(outbox): wire .withOutbox to real trigger-dispatch reactors

PR1's `.withOutbox` builder + OutboxReactorDefinition API has been
exported and tested but never invoked by the runtime — `eventSourcing.ts`
read `foldReactors`/`mapReactors` from each StaticPipelineDefinition and
ignored `foldOutboxReactors`/`mapOutboxReactors`, so even if a pipeline
called `.withOutbox`, the reactor would never fire.

Adds the missing wiring:

- `outboxReactorAdapter.ts` wraps an `OutboxReactorDefinition` into a
  regular `ReactorDefinition` whose `handle` invokes `decide(...)` and
  forwards each emitted `OutboxEnqueueRequest` to
  `outbox.enqueueSettle`. The GroupQueue-routed adapter ignores the
  request's `dedupKey`/`groupKey`/`maxAttempts` (those describe the
  spec's row-leased architecture); `enqueueOptions.ttlMs` IS threaded
  because the settle stage's Debounce Mode TTL is the per-trigger
  `traceDebounceMs` knob. When `OutboxRuntime` isn't wired (web
  process, or worker without outbox), the adapter degrades to a
  no-op `handle` so the pipeline registration is harmless.
- `buildServiceOptions` in `eventSourcing.ts` now walks the static
  definition's outbox-reactor maps, adapts each, and merges them into
  the `reactors`/`mapReactors` arrays the runtime already consumes.
- `OutboxEnqueueRequest` grows an optional `enqueueOptions.ttlMs`
  field. The defaults to `DEFAULT_TRACE_DEBOUNCE_MS` (30s) when absent.
- `defineOriginGuardedTraceOutboxReactor` factored out next to the
  existing `defineOriginGuardedTraceReactor` so both `.withReactor`
  and `.withOutbox` trace-pipeline reactors share the same
  origin/age/event-type guard logic (single `passesTraceOriginGuards`
  helper).

Splits the two trigger reactors into NOTIFY-class and PERSIST-class
responsibilities and registers the NOTIFY half via `.withOutbox`:

- `ee/governance/reactors/alertTriggerNotifyOutbox.reactor.ts` — new
  OutboxReactorDefinition; for every active trace-only trigger whose
  action is SEND_EMAIL / SEND_SLACK_MESSAGE, emits an
  `OutboxEnqueueRequest` carrying the settle payload. Registered on
  the trace pipeline via
  `.withOutbox("traceSummary", "alertTriggerNotifyOutbox", ...)`.
- `evaluationAlertTriggerNotifyOutbox.reactor.ts` — same shape on the
  evaluation pipeline; restricts to triggers with evaluation filters
  whose action is NOTIFY.
- `ee/governance/reactors/alertTrigger.reactor.ts` and
  `evaluationAlertTrigger.reactor.ts` keep handling PERSIST-class
  actions (ADD_TO_DATASET, ADD_TO_ANNOTATION_QUEUE) inline; their

  `ADD_TO_ANNOTATION_QUEUE` (single-call dispatch path) rather than

* feat(experiments): reroute legacy pairwise_compare dispatch to select_best_compare

Retires the langevals/pairwise_compare judge from the app's call path
without breaking experiments and monitors saved against it. A dispatch
whose stored evaluator type is the legacy 2-slot judge is transparently
rerouted to the N-way select_best_compare, with its 2-slot request body
translated into the `candidates` shape.

Both the reroute (resolveDispatchEvaluatorType) and the payload
translation (translateLegacyPairwisePayload) happen at ONE site — the
legacy evaluations route — so the dispatched type and the payload shape
can never drift apart. #5528 regressed exactly because those two were
decided in different places (the orchestrator forced the new type while
the payload stayed 2-slot); every upstream caller here keeps emitting
the 2-slot shape it always has, unaware of the reroute.

Also drops a legacy pairwise `prompt` setting that references the old
{candidate_a_output}/{candidate_b_output} placeholders — the N-way judge
only renders {candidates}, so an un-migrated prompt (including pairwise's
own default) would arrive half-literal; falling back to the new judge's
default is correct.

Spec: specs/experiments/comparison.feature — updates "Existing pairwise
monitors keep running" to require rerouting + N-way winner ids, and adds
a structured-output-field-survives-translation scenario.

refactor(errors): rename DomainError → HandledError, match Go herr shape (#5825)

* refactor(errors): rename DomainError to HandledError, match Go herr shape

Rename the app-layer `DomainError` base class to `HandledError` and align its
shape with the Go `herr.E` it mirrors (pkg/herr), so the two languages read the
same at the boundary:

- `DomainError` -> `HandledError` (class + domain-error.ts -> handled-error.ts)
- discriminant `kind` -> `code` (matches herr.E.Code) across the class, the
  serialized shape, wire bodies, frontend readers, guards, and tests. This
  includes the 25 `declare readonly kind` subclass narrowings (typecheck can't
  catch those — they'd read undefined at runtime otherwise).
- flatten `telemetry: { traceId, spanId }` -> top-level `traceId`/`spanId`
  (mirrors herr.E.TraceID/SpanID)
- rename the whole vocabulary: SerializedHandledError, readHandledError,
  handledErrorMiddleware, handledErrorToTRPCCode, isHandledErrorLike, etc.

Wire impact: the tRPC `data.domainError` payload and the packages/api HTTP error
body now carry `code`/`traceId`/`spanId` instead of `kind`/`telemetry`. No
external SDK consumes these; the frontend readers are updated in the same change.

Kept deliberately:
- `httpStatus` and the Grafana `traceUrl` — TS-side conveniences with no herr.E
  equivalent (Go maps code->status via a registry, builds the link elsewhere).
- the `data.domainError` tRPC envelope KEY — it names the payload slot, not the
  error shape; renaming it is out of scope and higher blast radius.
- DDD-sense "domain error" types that are NOT the boundary class (SuiteDomainError
  extends Error; the dataset DOMAIN_ERROR_HTTP name->status map).

Updates ADR-045, the domain-error-contract spec, and packages/api README.

* refactor(errors): address review comments on HandledError rename

- admin.ts: rewrite stale discriminant comment — it said "use `kind`, not
  instanceof" while the code calls HandledError.isHandled (which *is* an
  instanceof check); comment now describes the same-process guard accurately
- automations.ts: fix stale data.domainError shape in doc comment
  (kind/telemetry -> code/traceId/spanId)
- handle-system-prompt-handled-errors: `any` -> `unknown` (the instanceof
  branches already narrow)
- packages/api/errors: drop redundant `isHandledErrorLike as isHandledErrorLike`
  self-alias left by the LSP rename
- evaluations-legacy: HandledError.is -> HandledError.isHandled to match the
  base-class-check idiom used in auth-middleware; both are valid, no runtime bug

Skipped (with rationale on threads): error-handler meta spread (meta/trace is
public-by-contract for a HandledError), automations instanceof->is (no-op:
.is() is instanceof this), handled-error one-line guard docs (pre-existing,
not new), and the feature-file wire references (intentional contract spec).

* feat(errors): keep DomainError→HandledError rename non-breaking (dual code/kind)

Renaming the wire discriminant kind→code is breaking for any client still
reading `kind` during a rolling deploy. Make the transition seamless:

- Emit both: HandledError.serialize() and the packages/api error body now
  carry `code` plus a deprecated `kind` alias with the same value, top-level
  and in nested reasons.
- Read both: the JS data.domainError readers (automations errorExplainer,
  lite-member interceptor, TraceDrawer classifier) resolve `code ?? kind`, so
  new-client↔old-server also works.
- Add `declare readonly code` narrowings to the subscription + triggers
  HandledError subclasses for consistency, and fix a stale `kind` doc comment.

Documented in ADR-045 and the domain-error-contract spec; covered by unit
tests on both the emit and read paths. Typecheck clean; packages/api (85) and
affected app tests green.

The catch sits immediately after parseCustomRolePermissions throws in the same
process, so instanceof on the specific class is the correct idiom (and drops
the now-only HandledError import). The apiKey.ts router mapper keeps its
code-keyed switch — that's a deliberate cross-boundary discriminant dispatch.

fix(scenarios): restore pino as direct dep so child bundle resolves it in prod (#5856)

* fix(scenarios): restore pino as direct dep so child bundle resolves it in prod

The pre-compiled scenario child bundle (dist/scenario-child-process.js) keeps
`pino`/`pino-pretty` EXTERNAL (build-scenario-child-process.mjs), emitting a
runtime `require('pino')`. pino reaches the child only via
`child-logger -> @langwatch/observability`, and #2404 (5fc087619) moved the
pino family out of the app manifest into that workspace package. Because pino
is then neither a direct langwatch dep nor public-hoisted, pnpm never symlinks
it into `langwatch/node_modules/pino`, so the bundle's external require cannot
resolve pino from `dist/` at prod runtime -> MODULE_NOT_FOUND, every scenario
run reported `failure`. `pnpm prune --prod` (Dockerfile) compounds it.

Re-add `pino` and `pino-pretty` (the two bundle externals in the child's import
graph) to the app's direct dependencies. pnpm then top-links them into
`langwatch/node_modules/`, where the external require resolves, surviving
`pnpm prune --prod`. Verified: pino now resolves from the dist/ dir.

Not app-source regression range: 60b9efc1..HEAD changed nothing here; the delta
is #2404, which predates the clean pins (rollback to 60b9efc1 would NOT fix it).

Refs #5855

fix(analytics): monitor cards match the analytics donut pass rate; forward negateFilters/traceIds (#5858)

* fix(analytics): stop fabricating 0% pass rate for days an evaluator never ran

The timeseries row parser defaulted every bucket missing a series value
to 0. Average-type metrics (pass rate, score) are only ever missing when
the evaluator produced no processed runs in that bucket, so the 0
invented a failing day. Combined with the monitor card averaging daily
buckets with equal weight, an evaluator with 6/6 passed runs on one of
four active days showed 25% while the analytics donut said 100%.

The parser now only zero-fills additive aggregations (counts and sums,
where no rows really is zero). The monitor card headline now reads a
single full-period bucket, which is run-weighted by construction and
matches the donut exactly.

* fix(analytics): forward negateFilters and traceIds through the read path

The legacy shim dropped both fields when forwarding to
buildTimeseriesQuery, so the Negate Filters toggle and trace-scoped
graphs were silently ignored on every analytics query. The routed fast
paths (slim and rollup tables) do not implement either parameter, so the
route table now sends any query carrying them to the legacy fallback
table for its source instead of serving non-negated or unscoped results.

* chore(scripts): drop removed Project fields from seed-local-admin

piiRedactionLevel and captured visibility moved off the Project model in
the scoped data-privacy refactor; the seed script still passed them and
failed on a fresh run.

* fix(analytics): full-period summaries stop coalescing empty averages to 0; bind specs

The timeScale full scalar path wrapped every metric in coalesce(x, 0), so
an evaluator with no runs in the period read as a 0% pass rate instead of
no data (the same fabrication the daily path had). The coalesce now
applies only to additive series, driven by a shared
isZeroWhenAbsentSeries predicate used by both the summary builder and the
row parser.

Also binds the new feature-file scenarios to their tests for the
feature-parity check and covers the never-ran evaluator with an
integration test.

* fix(analytics): review round — real-value error fallback, always-fill additive keys, user-visible specs

The monitor card's error fallback now averages the real daily values
instead of the sparkline's filled data (which substitutes 1 for empty
days on pass rates and inflated the average). Additive series that are
null in every bucket now still default to 0, matching the normaliser's
documented contract. Feature scenarios reworded to describe chart
behavior rather than parser and routing internals.

* refactor(analytics): delete the dead legacy timeseries path

ClickHouseAnalyticsService.getTimeseries and its private parse and
normalisation copies had no callers since the app-layer rewrite took over
timeseries reads, but kept the retired zero-fill-everything semantics
alive as a second implementation that could drift or be resurrected.
Timeseries reads now have exactly one parser and one zero-when-absent
predicate; AnalyticsBackend shrinks to the non-timeseries reads it
actually serves.

fix(nlpgo): withhold pod environment from code-block subprocess (#5923)

The code-block executor spawned the Python runner with cmd.Env unset, so
Go inherited the full pod environment into the child. Any os.environ read
in user code could see every variable in the pod — AWS credentials,
service-account token paths, LANGWATCH_* internals, and DB/Redis/ClickHouse
secrets.

Set cmd.Env from a secure-by-default allowlist (interpreter/locale/TLS
plumbing only). cmd.Env is always a non-nil slice, so exec can never fall
back to inheriting os.Environ(). Project secrets already reach user code
via Request.Secrets over stdin, so withholding the environment does not
break the secrets contract.

  - nil allowlist  -> defaultEnvAllowlist (secure default)
  - non-nil empty  -> pass nothing (maximally locked down)
  - populated      -> pass exactly those names, when present

Regression tests assert a parent-set secret is invisible to user code
while allowlisted PATH remains, and that an empty allowlist passes nothing.

Scope: this covers the in-process Go codeblock path. The per-project Lambda
execution path (langwatch-nlp-role) injects creds as env vars into the
function's own process and needs a separate mitigation, tracked separately.

feat(haven): keep the managed ClickHouse's own logs lightweight by default (#5924)

* feat(haven): keep the managed ClickHouse's own logs lightweight by default

Stock ClickHouse never bounds its self-telemetry: the system log tables
have no TTL and the server log runs at trace with a 1000M x 10 rotation.
Measured on one laptop after ~5 days of ordinary dev: 610 MiB of system
log tables (303 MiB of it text_log, 70M rows in asynchronous_metric_log)
plus a 1.3 MiB and growing server log. haven already caps ClickHouse
memory two ways, so unbounded log disk was the odd one out.

By default haven now disables the high-volume system logs (text_log,
trace_log, metric_log, asynchronous_metric_log, processors_profile_log,
query_metric_log), caps the ones worth keeping (query_log, part_log,
error_log, crash_log) at 7 days, and quiets the server log to warnings
with a 50M x 2 rotation. HAVEN_CLICKHOUSE_FULL_LOGS=1 restores stock
behaviour; HAVEN_CLICKHOUSE_LOG_TTL_DAYS tunes the cap.

Two things this needed to actually take effect:

- The config is now written in Ensure, not start(). A container already
  running the correct image was never reconfigured, so any tuning change
  reached new machines only. A changed config now forces a recreate; the
  data dir is a bind mount, so databases survive.
- Config governs table creation, not existing tables, so an already-
  running server kept its unbounded ones. applySystemLogPolicy drops the
  disabled tables and MODIFY TTLs the kept ones. Best-effort by design:
  reclaiming disk must never be what stops a stack coming up.

Verified live: 610 MiB -> 16.7 MiB of system logs, server log 1.3M ->
20K, all 9 stack databases intact, no config errors, doctor green.

Also fixes a misreport in the brew adapters: a cancelled startup context
kills the `brew list` probe too, which was surfaced as "X is not
installed" and sent you off to brew install packages that were already
running. Cancellation now reads as cancellation.

Folding every non-globally-routable address into the nlpgo HTTP block's deny
set was a silent breaking change for self-hosters. A workflow that reaches an
internal service over Tailscale (100.64.0.0/10) — or any other range that was

Split "what an address IS" from "what this deployment does about it". pkg/ssrf
still owns the classification; the HTTP block now decides:

    (168.63.129.16) closes for everyone — no legitimate traffic behind it;
  - private/loopback/link-local/unspecified stay refused, as before;
  - everything else non-public is refused only under strict egress.

Strict egress is off by default and arrives as a dedicated egress knob on
EngineConfig, passed explicitly into SSRFOptions. Nothing under
app/engine/blocks reads the environment for it — what an egress boundary
refuses is deployment policy, so it is declared once and plumbed.

refused is logged with the range, its RFC, and the ALLOWED_PROXY_HOSTS hint.

fix(errors): make HandledError boundary guards survive class duplication (#5932)

* fix(errors): make HandledError boundary guards survive class duplication

`instanceof` compares class identity, so it breaks when a bundler includes the
handled-error module twice — Next.js/turbopack does this across route and server
boundaries. An error raised from the second copy is a genuine HandledError, but
`instanceof HandledError` returns false, which silently downgrades a handled 4xx
into an unhandled 500 and replaces the vetted copy with "An unknown error
occurred".

#5917 already hit this and hand-rolled duck-typed workarounds in sse.ts and
trpc.ts ("a bundler can load a second copy of the package"). This centralises
that instead of spreading it further.

Every instance already carries a `readonly isHandled = true` brand, so match on
that. Hardening the guard fixes every call site at once:

- `isHandled`: `instanceof` OR the brand
- `isUnhandled` / `toUserMessage` / `serializeReason` route through `isHandled`
- 12 call sites across trpc, sse, langy, automations, experiments,
  clickhouse-trace, event-sourcing and error-handler now ask `isHandled`
- the two ad-hoc duck-typed blocks collapse into it

One `instanceof HandledError` now remains repo-wide: the canonical one inside
`isHandled` itself.

`is()` stays instanceof-only on purpose: subclass narrowing cannot be
brand-based (the brand says "handled", not "which subclass"), so cross-boundary
callers compare `code`. The brand also deliberately does not match a
deserialised wire payload — a plain object with no prototype, so the methods
this guard promises would not exist; those go through `handledErrorFromHerr` /
`isHandledErrorLike`. error-handler keeps its `code`+`httpStatus` tail so the
accepted set does not narrow; it only reads fields there.

Verified the 4 new duplication tests fail against the old bare-instanceof guard
and pass after.

fix(api): trust real HandledErrors, and log the ones we swallow (#5934)

* fix(api): trust real HandledErrors, and log the ones we swallow

@langwatch/api duck-typed HandledError to stay standalone. #5917 made that
justification obsolete by extracting @langwatch/handled-error, so this switches
to the real class and drops the parallel Zod encoder.

Three things were wrong:

A ZodError carried neither httpStatus nor fault, so request logging derived a
500 and logged at error while the caller received a 422 — validation noise
landing in the 5xx error budget. Promoting it to a ValidationError fixes both
ends at once, and gives validation errors the fault/tips/docsUrl channel they
were silently missing.

createErrorHandler never logged. Unknown errors flatten to "An unknown error
occurred" and the stack was dropped right there, surviving only incidentally
via loggerMiddleware reading c.error. It now logs handled errors by fault
attribution and unhandled ones at error with their cause. Request bodies are
never logged — automation actionParams carry encrypted webhook headers and
Slack tokens.

The error handler now records the status it sent, so the request logger reports
what the caller received instead of re-deriving it.

Duck-typing also meant any object growing a serialize() could pick its own
status. Only HandledError instances are trusted now; impostors get a 500. The
per-issue schema_failure reasons shape is preserved — serializeReason adds kind
and fault on top, which is additive.

* fix(api): one error record per failed request

The error handler logged the failure and the request logger logged it again
after next() settled, so every failed request produced two error records
carrying the same stack -- doubling error-log volume and any log-derived
alert or error count.

Give the record a single owner. loggerMiddleware writes it; the error handler
publishes the error it sent and the status it sent it as, and logs nothing.
The published error is the promoted one, so a ZodError is reported as the 422
ValidationError the caller received rather than the 500 a re-derivation
guesses. traceId rides along as request-log extra.

createErrorHandler's logger/name options are dropped -- it no longer logs, and
leaving them would be misleading config.

Adds an integration test that counts records per failed request; it fails with
three errors if a second record is reintroduced.

* docs(api): describe the real request-log severity

The README claimed anything unhandled logs at `error`. getLogLevelForRequest
only uses fault when the error is handled and otherwise falls back to
getLogLevelFromStatusCode, so an unhandled HTTPException carrying a 4xx logs at
warn. Describes both halves, and keeps the reason the 500 case still carries
its cause.

The trace pipeline still registers `recordLog` but the canonical cutover

rejectedLogRecords when building a trace contribution threw — the precise thing

partialSuccess is a permanent verdict, so this told the collector to discard a
log we hold. Correlation is best-effort; only preparation may reject, and the
counters are const now to keep it that way.

metricCorrelationFields re-listed the five metric kinds instead of importing
metricKindSchema. A kind added to one and not the other would make a
correlation event the command accepted fail re-validation on replay — the exact

oversight until you notice metric points and log records are immutable and

ADR-055 records the decisions that are not readable off the diff: why both

fix(aigateway): keep non-streaming connections warm during slow dispatch (#5963)

* fix(aigateway): keep non-streaming connections warm during slow dispatch

Large-context requests intermittently hit Cloudflare 524 (edge idle-
connection timeout, ~100s) because the non-streaming path buffers the
entire response and writes zero bytes to the client until dispatch
fully completes. A completion that legitimately takes longer than the
edge's idle window has no way to keep the connection alive.

Once a dispatch runs longer than HeartbeatInterval (default 45s), the
gateway now writes a periodic RFC 8259 insignificant-whitespace byte
and flushes it, resetting the proxy's idle timer without corrupting
the eventual JSON body. Requests that finish inside the interval are
byte-for-byte unaffected. If a heartbeat has already fired and
dispatch later errors, the HTTP status is irrevocably committed to
200 (net/http sends it implicitly on first Write) — the same
trade-off the streaming path already accepts for mid-stream errors —
but the structured error body still reaches the client correctly.
Negative HeartbeatInterval (NON_STREAMING_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL=-1s)
disables the mechanism entirely as an operator kill switch.

Closes #4806.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(aigateway): recover panics in heartbeat dispatch goroutine

Independent review of the heartbeat fix (#5963) found that dispatch
now runs on a background goroutine so the heartbeat loop can keep
writing while it's in flight — but that goroutine sits outside
httpmiddleware.Recover()'s reach (its defer/recover only guards the
goroutine that calls ServeHTTP). An unrecovered panic anywhere in the
dispatch call graph would take down the whole gateway process instead
of producing a 500 for one bad request — strictly worse than the 524
this PR fixes. withHeartbeat now recovers the panic itself, logs it
via clog.LogPanic, and surfaces the same internal_error 500
Recover() would have produced for a synchronous panic.

Also: NonStreamingHeartbeatInterval was a time.Duration env field,
but config.Hydrate parses time.Duration as raw nanosecond integers
(not via time.ParseDuration), so the documented "45s" format would
never have actually worked via NON_STREAMING_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL.
Switched to a plain-seconds field (NonStreamingHeartbeatIntervalSeconds,
env NON_STREAMING_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_SECONDS) to sidestep that
pre-existing parsing gap entirely rather than touching the shared
config parser.

* fix(aigateway): add X-LangWatch-Heartbeat-Active to mitigate the committed-200 trade-off

The one open P2 from the goated-review pass on this PR: once a
heartbeat fires, HTTP status is irrevocably committed to 200 even if
dispatch later errors — inherent to writing body bytes before the
final status is known, unfixable without abandoning the mechanism.
But a client that only checks response.status (not the body) has no
way to know that happened.

heartbeat byte so it survives regardless of the eventual outcome.

key before trusting the status. Caught and fixed a real bug writing

*enabled* (interval > 0, the default for every request) rather than
when a heartbeat actually *fired* — every response would have carried
it, making it useless as a signal. Now tied to the first real tick.

matching the error message, and it matched `/\b403\b/`, `/authentication/i`
and `/billing/i` anywhere in the text — before it checked whether the
failure came from langevals at all. Two things followed from that.

It misattributed our own outages. ClickHouse reading cold parts off S3
raises `403 Forbidden`; a langevals 5xx embeds the upstream body, which
routinely quotes a `401`. Both were classified `model_provider_auth`,
`userActionable: true`, and the customer was told their credentials were
wrong and sent to rotate a key that was fine.

And `userActionable` was the only gate on disclosure: the settings page

internal hostnames, echoed key prefixes. So a mis-scoped regex was a

strength of not recognising an error. All the regexes are gone.

params to langevals — so those failures reach us only as prose inside a 5xx.
Recovering them needs langevals to return a structured provider error. The
codes stay defined for stored rows and that future signal.

* fix(event-sourcing): reconcile process store rename with ADR-052 automations

Rebasing ADR-051 onto main produced a clean merge that did not compile.
This PR renames PipelineRepositories.langyProcessStore to processStore
(the ProcessManager* tables are generic, shared by every domain), while
ADR-052 automations landed on main independently and added three new
call sites using the old name. Git saw disjoint lines and merged both.

The presets.ts site is the dangerous one: EventSourcing.processStore is
optional and falls back to a fresh InMemoryProcessStore, so every
withProcessManager declaration would have silently lost durability had
this been a plain JS rename rather than a typed field.

* feat(event-sourcing): give wake handlers wall-clock and rearm from the present

Prerequisite for moving topic clustering and Langy onto the ADR-052
withProcessManager builder: the declarative wake context could not
express the missed-wake clamp the hand-rolled ADR-051 definition
relies on.

WakeHandler now receives `now` alongside `at` (the slot it was
scheduled for), and a scheduled process manager rearms from
max(at, now) rather than from the slot it missed. Without this, a
fleet that was down for a week replays every skipped interval
back-to-back on recovery, one commit at a time. That affects the
existing automations declarations today, not just the ports to come.

* fix(topic-clustering): schedule from the present, and stop stale runs wedging a project

Three defects in the scheduling arithmetic, all reachable in normal
operation:

1. `settle()` scheduled from event business time. The event branch of
   `evolve` had no clock, so a backed-up subscriber could deliver an
   event whose next daily slot had already passed, writing a nextWakeAt
   in the past. That wake fires immediately, regenerates a messageKey
   the outbox already dispatched, and the duplicate insert is dropped --
   leaving `currentRun` set with no intent in flight. A day of
   clustering disappears with no log. ProcessInput's event variant now
   carries `now` (symmetric with wake) and the branch clamps to it.

2. The stale-run window was measured from the last completed page. A
   backlog walk refreshes `updatedAtMs` per page, so a walk that starts
   at its slot and stalls five hours in still looked fresh at the next
   slot, deferred it, and only recovered a day later -- 48h against a
   documented one-day bound. Staleness now measures from the run's
   start, which is what makes that comment true. `startedAtMs` is
   optional and falls back to `updatedAtMs` so rows written before this
   field cost at most one extra run.

3. Manual "Run now" deferred to any recorded run, including a long-dead
   one, while the route returned success and the UI toasted it. It now
   preempts a stale run -- precisely the state a user presses the
   button in. Run identity still derives from business time so a
   redelivered request cannot mint a second run.

Regression tests drive `evolve` and observe the wrong outcome rather
than asserting on shapes: a lagged event scheduling behind the present,
a stalled walk surviving its next slot, and a manual request swallowed
by a dead run.

* refactor(langy): declare the conversation process on its pipeline (ADR-052) (#5944)

Langy was the last process manager still hand-rolled. It carried a literal
ProcessDefinition with its own evolve switch, a literal intent-handler record,
a bespoke subscriber duplicating the one ProcessRuntime generates, and a
ProcessManagerService / OutboxDispatcherService / ProcessOutboxWorker trio
constructed in pipelineRegistry -- all of it predating the ADR-052 builder.

It is now declared on its own pipeline with .withProcessManager, the same way
triggerSettlement and topicClustering are. The topology -- state, intents, the
content boundary, every event decision, the outbox lease -- lives in one
declaration; the registry only injects effect ports.

No behaviour change: the same events produce the same decisions and the same
two intents. What the substrate adds:

- intent payloads are schema-validated at emit time, not only at dispatch
- message keys are auto-qualified `process:<conversationId>:<key>`, so two
  conversations cannot collide on one turn id
- the inbox keys on `idempotencyKey ?? id`, making a redelivered command a
  logical no-op rather than a second physical event
- ProcessRuntime owns the manager, subscriber and outbox worker, and stops
  them via EventSourcing.close() -- the Langy-specific shutdown handle is gone

Liveness stays out, for the reason ADR-049 gives: durable event activity is
not proof the ephemeral heartbeat is stale. No .schedule(), no wake handler;
agentTurnLiveness remains the sole liveness owner.

The no-decision events keep explicit handlers rather than being dropped: the
runtime derives its subscription from the declared handlers AND throws on an
undeclared event, so omitting them would change delivery and turn any other
path into a hard failure. This mirrors the old `default:` arm.

Intent type strings are unchanged. The name IS the persisted intentType, so
renaming them to the short camelCase form newer processes use would strand
in-flight outbox rows with no handler.

Tests now build the definition through the pipeline's own applier plus the
runtime's buildProcessDefinition/buildIntentHandlers, and the trace-continuity
and Postgres tests drive ProcessRuntime's generated subscriber -- so they cover
the real generated path instead of a re-implementation.

* refactor(event-sourcing): process managers live on their pipelines, not in app-layer

The pipelines/xxx/ directory owns the full event-sourced topology —
projections, process managers, schemas — while app-layer/xxx keeps only
the services and repositories they call. Topic clustering and langy had
their process-manager directories stranded in app-layer; move them next
to their pipelines, matching the automations layout.

* test(topic-clustering): guard the page-fetch memory cap behaviorally, not by source text

The old guard regex-matched clustering.ts as a string — it could only
fail on reformatting, and would keep passing if max_threads were applied
to the wrong query. Drive the real fetchTracesFromClickHouse through a
capturing stub client instead: assert the ComputedInput page fetch
carries a small max_threads and that the page CTE's ORDER BY is the only
one in the query (no outer top-N buffer).

* fix(scheduler): pin the test clock instead of trusting the calendar

The lease-and-retry tests hardcoded NEXT_CRON as the Monday after SLOT
and ran against real wall clock. The policy deliberately schedules from
now when a slot's next instant has passed, so the suite was a time bomb
that detonated the moment the calendar reached that Monday — five
failures on every branch today. Pin Date (and only Date; the loop needs
real timers) to just after SLOT.

* refactor(ee): declare the ingestion-pull process on its pipeline (ADR-052)

The last hand-wired process manager moves onto the builder: the raw
ProcessDefinition (evolve/evolveWake switch), the hand-rolled envelope
bridge subscriber, and the pipelineSet's own ProcessManagerService +
OutboxDispatcherService + ProcessOutboxWorker all collapse into a
.withProcessManager declaration on the ingestion-pull pipeline. The
shared ProcessRuntime now owns its subscriber, outbox and wake workers,
so the registry's enterprise-only ProcessWakeWorker and the
enterpriseWorkers stop composite (plus its presets closeable and test
stub) disappear — EventSourcing.close() is the single shutdown path.

Process-manager code lives under the pipeline
(ee/event-sourcing/pipelines/ingestion-pull-processing/process-manager),
matching the core domains; the puller services and reconciliation stay
in ee/governance. Behaviour is unchanged: same evolve semantics per
event, same wake/stale-run rules, same effect retry contract. The
intent type and message keys adopt the builder conventions (short
'run', process-qualified keys) — safe because this feature has never
shipped; it was born on this branch.

* feat(topic-clustering): run history on the settings page

The settings page showed only the latest run; past outcomes were
overwritten. Add a second, audit-grade read model: a bounded per-project
run history folded from the same run events (spec:
specs/topic-clustering/run-history.feature).

- TopicClusteringRunHistoryFoldProjection: newest-first entries, one per
  logical run (pages accumulate), capped at 50. A new run superseding an
  unfinished one settles it as abandoned; the status service also
  presents a wedged 'running' entry as abandoned past the stale-run
  window, mirroring the scheduler's own clock.
- Raw error text is never part of the model (ADR-051 §8) — errorCode +
  actionability only, same contract as the status card.
- New Prisma read-model table TopicClusteringRunHistoryProjection (one
  row per project, JSON entries, rebuildable by replay); corrupted JSON
  degrades to empty history instead of poisoning the fold.
- topics.getClusteringRunHistory tRPC query (project:view) and a Run
  history table on the settings page: when, started by, outcome badge,
  and the same fixed guidance copy the status card uses.

* chore(queues): delete the last BullMQ scraps

Every queue migrated off BullMQ (topic clustering and pullers were the
final two); what remained was dead code with zero importers — the
queueWithFallback/withJobContext modules, their test, and the bullmq_*
Prometheus helpers nothing calls — plus the bullmq and bullmq-otel
dependencies. makeQueueName stays: it is a Redis Cluster hash-tag
helper used by the custom event-sourcing GroupQueue, not BullMQ.

* feat(topic-clustering): the event stream owns the topic model

Topics become facts on the clustering stream (spec:
specs/topic-clustering/topics-source-of-truth.feature). A new
topics_recorded event (replace|merge) carries the full model — ids
verbatim, so ClickHouse TopicId/SubTopicId references stay valid and
replay recreates identical ids; centroids/p95 ride along so the model is
fully rebuildable. The Topic table is now the topicModel projection's
write-through store (cursor in a new TopicModelProjection row, rows
reconciled transactionally); nothing else writes it.

- storeResults stops writing Prisma and issues recordTopics, keyed
  run:<runId>:page-<n> via run context threaded through the run port.
- Reads go through the topic-clustering TopicService (moved from
  app-layer/topics): topics.getAll, traces.getTopicCounts, and the facet
  name lookup all read the projected model.
- Pre-ownership history: seedProjectTopicModel records existing Topic
  rows as a seed:v1 replace event, preserving each topic's original age
  (the batch cadence gate reads it). Ordering is solved by the aggregate
  log, not coordination: the clustering write path awaits the seed
  append before its own record, so a cutover-time merge can never
  reconcile the table down to its own delta.
- A worker-only boot pass seeds the rest in the background, elected via
  Redis SET NX when available, safe without it — no Helm/compose job.
- New migration 20260720130000_add_topic_model_projection (cursor table
  only).

* fix(ee): drop a stale intentType field from the effects test context

IntentContext never had it; CI typecheck caught the ported stub.

* perf(topic-clustering): make the boot seed free for post-cutover signups

Projects created after the cutover always carry a projection cursor row
(written with their first topics), so they never needed seeding — but
every boot still paid a per-project ownership query. Batch the check to
one query per page, and once a pass finds nothing left to seed (fresh
installs hit this on first boot), set a permanent Redis done-marker so
later boots exit on a single GET. Without Redis the page scan itself is
the cheap fallback, and a failed project blocks the marker so the next
boot retries it.

* fix(topic-clustering): expose the topics read on the app facade, and review cleanup

Full-typecheck round: the app-layer topicClustering facade type never
declared the topics service the routers now read through, and the boot
seed's failure log used a logger that was not in scope. Review sweep:
ADR-049's process-manager path updated to the pipeline location, the
orphaned bullmq-otel packageExtensions block removed, and the Redis
Cluster spec prose updated — BullMQ is gone; the GroupQueue carries the
hash-tag requirement now.

* fix(topic-clustering): release the seed claim, stable dedupe for the manual task

Review round: the boot-seed Redis claim was never released, so a failed
or crashed pass blocked every replica's retry for the full 24h TTL —
'the next boot retries' is the contract, so release it in a finally.
The runTopicClustering task now threads one stable runId through its
walk so re-recorded pages dedupe instead of appending a fresh
topics_recorded chain per re-run. Also documents why the projection's
topic upsert is safe without a compound tenant key.

* fix(deps): regenerate the lockfile for the packageExtensions removal

Dropping the orphaned bullmq-otel packageExtensions block changed the
lockfile's settings hash, so frozen-lockfile installs failed in CI.

* feat(topic-clustering): worker-boot schedule seed replaces the Helm backfill Job

The legacy-project schedule backfill is no longer a deploy-time chart
hook. seedClusteringSchedules runs in the background on worker boot,
elected via a Redis NX claim (released on exit), with a permanent
done-marker so installs that finish the walk never scan again. Without
Redis it still runs safely because the walk is idempotent. The paging
walk itself is ported unchanged from the deleted task, tests included.

The chart Job template, its values block, README rows, and the e2e
override are gone; ADR-051 and the scheduling feature spec now describe
the boot-time mechanism.

* fix(topic-clustering): continuation pages skip the cadence gate; drop dead runsWorkers deps

Batch-mode pagination was structurally dead after page one: page 2
re-entered clusterTopicsForProject, read the topics page 1 had just
written (createdAt = now), and the recently-clustered gate ended the
walk with a skip and no cursor. The gate throttles run starts only now —
a page carrying a searchAfter cursor belongs to an already-approved run
and goes through. Regression tests cover both directions.

Also: the ModelNotConfiguredError comment now describes what actually
happens (propagates, outbox retries, run_failed with a user-actionable
code) instead of a catch that never existed; the langy and
topicClustering runsWorkers fields in PipelineRegistryDeps were read by
nobody and are gone (the enterprise one is real and stays); two
Object.keys(array).length spots use .length like their neighbours; and
the presets boot path now seeds clustering schedules (see previous
commit).

* chore: drop unused imports flagged by review bots

INGESTION_PULL_EVENT_TYPES was imported but unused in the process
module (pipeline.ts imports it where it is used), and the langy
trace-continuity test declared a process definition it never read.

* refactor(topic-clustering): boot seeds own their wiring, presets makes one call

The Prisma page queries and command closures move out of presets into
startTopicClusteringBootSeeds in the topic-clustering module. Project is
a GLOBAL model in the tenancy guard (it IS the tenant), so the fleet-wide
page query carries no projectId predicate by design; the
ProcessManagerInstance lookup is bounded by projectId-in, which the guard
accepts — both documented at the query site now.

* fix(topic-clustering): a stale seed can never replace away the clustering delta

Adversarial audit finding: the seed:v1 idempotency key was assumed but
enforced nowhere on the fold path — recordTopics had no enqueue dedup,
ClickHouse inserts cannot be unique, and the incremental fold never
deduplicates. A boot seed racing the write-path seed during projection
lag could append a second replace-mode seed with a later occurredAt,
fold last, and delete the topics clustering had just recorded (whose ids
ClickHouse already references). It also made live folds diverge from
replay, whose read path does collapse duplicate keys.

Fixed at the fold: a seed is only meaningful as the model's first record,
so one arriving after the state has topics folds as a no-op — closing
the race deterministically and making incremental identical to replay.
Enqueue-side dedup (shared recordTopicsDedupeId, 60s TTL) suppresses the
duplicate append in the common window as belt-and-braces. The repository
also refuses to reconcile an empty state (notIn: [] would delete every
row for the project); no event can legitimately fold to zero topics, so
leaving rows is the recoverable direction. Regression tests cover the
race and the still-applies-when-empty case.

* docs(charts): drop the stale backfill hook-Job prose

values.yaml and the chart README still told operators the schedule seed
was a post-install hook Job and pointed at a task
(backfillTopicClusteringSchedules) that no longer exists; both blocks
are gone, and ADR-051 no longer calls the boot seed a task.

* feat(topic-clustering): per-row event provenance + lifecycle integration tests

The Topic table now says what it is: schema comments (and COMMENT ON in
the migration) declare it a projection of the clustering stream, and a
new nullable lastEventId column records which topics_recorded event
recorded each row — null marks a legacy row that predates event
ownership, so migration state is visible per row. Provenance is folded,
not stamped at write time: a merge keeps untouched topics' original
event id. The table keeps its name; the *Projection suffix stays
reserved for cursor/read-model tables.

Two new integration tests (real commands, real ClickHouse event log,
real folds, real Postgres, read back through the production services)
cover the whole run lifecycle — ask, in-flight, start, topics recorded,
completion, bounded history — and the full migration flow: legacy rows
seeded with ids/hierarchy/ages preserved, re-seed skipped, post-cutover
merge, and a late duplicate seed folding as a no-op.

They immediately caught three bugs mocked tests could not see, all in
the real Prisma layer:
- the projection's topic upsert keyed on bare id violated the tenancy
  guard (every fold would have failed on deploy) — projectId now rides
  along, PrismaProcessStore-style;
- the status repository's ProcessManagerInstance findUnique had the
  same violation — same fix;
- reconciling a batch replace deleted parents and children in one
  deleteMany, which the client-emulated Subtopics relation refuses —
  every re-cluster would have failed. The reconcile now deletes
  children before parents, and the flow test exercises a second
  replace to prove it.

Also verified: every topic read path is index-backed (projectId indexes
on Topic, unique projectId on all three projection cursor tables, the
processName-projectId compound on ProcessManagerInstance); the seed's
one-time Project walk is keyset-paged over the primary key.

* feat(charts): ship no alert rules and no hook Jobs

Self-hosters don't need our alert taxonomy imposed on them, and every
rule change was a chart release: the bundled alerting_rules.yml and the
prometheus.alerting values are gone. The reviewed rules live with the
rest of the Grafana tier in the SaaS infra repo (ADR-054 amended); the
chart's Prometheus keeps scraping the same metrics, so operators can
point their own rules at them.

The chart also ships no hook Jobs anymore:
- the dataset PG→S3 migration Job is removed, implementing ADR-032's
  latest amendment (one-off backfill, runnable as a cloud Job or
  `pnpm run task backfillDatasetContentToS3` — no every-upgrade hook);
- the pre-upgrade Secret-keys preflight Job is removed; missing keys
  surface at pod boot instead. The clickhouse-serverless subchart keeps
  its own preflight for standalone installs (still disabled under the
  umbrella, for its original install-ordering reason).

The e2e dataset-migration suite becomes test_upgrade_strategy_boundary,
keeping the Deployment-strategy upgrade regression (the part that broke
real installs) without the hook. helm lint and a full template render
pass with zero Jobs.

* fix(review): retryable:false on exhausted pulls + 12 bot findings

The one real bug: the ingestion-pull effect recorded retryable: true on
the exhausted-retries failure — nothing retries that run (the next
scheduled wake starts fresh), so the field misinformed operators. Now
false, and the test pins retryable + errorCode instead of a loose
objectContaining that let the regression through.

The rest, per the review bots:
- cron validation consolidated: pullScheduleSchema (schemas/events.ts)
  is the single source; assertValidPullSchedule / isValidPullSchedule
  are its imperative faces there, and the process manager + source
  service import them instead of re-implementing the check;
- per-source reconciliation failures in ingestionPullLifecycle are no
  longer swallowed — sourceId and reason are logged so a nonzero failed
  count is actionable;
- positional→named params: identity (commands), nextWake/settle
  (process), isSuperseded (fold projection), syncPullProcessBestEffort
  (source service), metricValue/evolve (tests), and the topic
  repository/service findNamesByIds/getNamesByIds chain;
- run-history entry: the zod schema now lives in the fold projection
  with the type z.infer'd from it; the repository imports it instead of
  re-declaring the shape;
- status-service history tests get their BDD when-nesting, and the
  newest-first assertion now uses two runs so it actually proves order;
- dropped a redundant as const on a scalar constant.

Declined: renaming langy process-state booleans (autoTitleRequested,
archived, titleTouched) — they are persisted fields inside
ProcessManagerInstance.state JSON for live conversations; the rename is
a state migration, not a naming tweak.

* test(analytics): rollup reads wait for async-insert visibility

The trace_analytics_rollup integration tests read milliseconds after an
acked insert; with async_insert the ack can beat part visibility when a
server profile overrides wait_for_async_insert, and both CI (shard 6)
and a local run landed on 0 rows exactly that way. Each fixture's
beforeAll now deadline-polls until its rows are visible (the
metricsSync.convergence pattern) — a genuinely lost insert still fails,
loudly, after 15s.

Not caused by the canonical-OTLP merge: #5945 is an ancestor of this
branch and the same shard passed three runs today; the failure is a
pre-existing visibility race that finally fired.

* fix(ci): pre-warm the Go toolchain in e2e-ci so the API lane isn't starved at boot

The e2e job auto-starts aigateway + nlpgo via `go run ./cmd/service`
(start.sh dev mode) but never set up Go: both lanes cold-downloaded the
go1.26.2 toolchain and the full module graph in parallel while tsx was
booting the API server, starving it past global-setup's 60s readiness
window on the 2-core runner. Intermittent failures showed as
"API not ready ... backend never served publicEnv" with zero [api]
lane output.

Add setup-go (module + build cache keyed on go.sum) and pre-build
./cmd/service — which imports both services — before the app starts, so
the auto-start lanes hit a warm cache and the API lane keeps the CPU.

fix(mcp-server): move unused runtime deps to devDependencies (npx cold-start 27s -> 2s) (#5965)

* fix(mcp-server): move unused runtime deps to devDependencies

dist/index.js is a fully self-contained esbuild bundle (build.js), but
package.json still listed express, node-pty, vitest, @opentelemetry/sdk-node,
@opentelemetry/context-async-hooks, yargs, zod, chalk, date-fns,
zod-validation-error, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk as production
dependencies. None of them are externally imported by the bundle, so every
fresh `npx -y @langwatch/mcp-server` install (the exact command our own docs

Measured cold, from a neutral directory, real MCP protocol handshake:

MCP clients see the server register but never report its tools before
timing out.

feat(langy): flag-only access, a langy permission family, and no product-managed credentials over the API (#5966)

* refactor(langy): gate access on the rollout flag alone

Langy access was decided by two levers: `release_langy_enabled`, and an
`isLangwatchStaff()` bypass that short-circuited it. In production that
bypass had been narrowed to a hardcoded single-email allowlist, so the
cohort lived in source and every change to it needed a deploy.

Collapse it to one lever. `hasLangyAccess()` and `useShowLangy()` now
evaluate the flag for everyone, with no identity that grants Langy on its
own, which also makes the flag a complete kill switch rather than one with
a hole in it. Rolling out is now an operator-store row (project/org) or a
PostHog rule (single user); local dev uses FEATURE_FLAG_FORCE_ENABLE.

This matters while ADR-033 is unresolved: Langy's opencode workers share
the manager pod's network namespace with an unauthenticated control
server, so a prompt-injected worker can reach a sibling's port and lift
that user's live credentials. The cohort has to stay exactly who was
deliberately opted in, and a flag row is a faster lever than a redeploy.

Also corrects the registry description for the flag, which documented
`RELEASE_LANGY_ENABLED=true` as a blanket on. The env override parses only
`1` or `0` (parseStrictEnvValue) and this flag defines no legacyEnvVar, so
`=true` fell through and silently did nothing. It also claimed the
operator store could target a user; it matches projectId/organizationId
only, and fails closed on any other key.

`LANGY_RELEASE_FLAG` moves to its own module now that the predicate it
shared a file with is gone.

* fix(langy): stop exposing product-managed credentials through the API

Langy provisions three credentials the customer never created: a virtual
key, the project secret holding that key's plaintext, and an ephemeral
per-chat session API key. Only the last was properly hidden.

The schema says the Langy VK's contract is "UI surfaces it as a managed
row and forbids edit/revoke" — but `virtualKeys.ts` never mentioned
`purpose`. The forbidding was a badge and some dialog copy; the tRPC
router and its public REST twin both reach the same service, which let
every by-id mutation through. `rotate` was the sharp edge: it returns a
fresh plaintext secret AND breaks Langy, since the gateway keeps
authenticating against the secret Langy still holds.

Enforce it where the boundary actually is:

- Customer-facing VK listings filter to `purpose: USER`, mirroring how
  HIDDEN_SYSTEM_KEY_NAMES already filters the API-key listings. Internal
  lookups (findById, findByHashedSecret) stay unfiltered — the gateway
  authenticates against these keys and Langy re-reads its own config.
- `requireOwn` rejects product-managed keys, which covers update, rotate
  and revoke in one seam so they cannot drift apart. `getById` returns
  null. Both report not-found rather than forbidden: a distinct error
  would confirm the id exists.
- ApiKeyService.update/revoke refuse HIDDEN_SYSTEM_KEY_NAMES. They were
  absent from every listing already, but absence is not immutability —
  a caller holding an id could revoke the key a live turn was using.
- The secrets router hides `langy_vk_secret` and refuses to mutate it.
  Deleting it did more than break the key: Langy treats its presence as
  "this project already has a VK", so the next chat minted a duplicate
  while the original stayed active.

The composer's model picker read `modelsAllowed` off the customer-facing
VK listing, so filtering the listing would have broken it. It now calls
`langy.modelsAllowed`, which returns just that field and resolves the
organization server-side. The client no longer receives a virtual-key row
at all.

`LANGY_VK_SECRET_NAME` moves to a leaf module so the secrets router can
name a reserved secret without importing the Langy app layer. The
now-unreachable "auto-managed" badge and its Langy-specific revoke copy
are removed, along with `langyVk.ts` — the row they described can no
longer appear.

* feat(langy): give Langy its own permission family

Langy hung off `evaluations:view` — the only permission on the whole
router, with `langyTurnProcedure` adding a rate limit and nothing else.
So a read-only viewer could call `createConversation`, which provisions
credentials, spawns an OpenCode worker and spends the project's model
budget. Starting a turn is not a read.

Add a `langy` resource: `view` reads conversations, `create` starts or
continues a turn (and forks, which creates one), `update` renames,
`delete` archives, `manage` implies the rest via the existing hierarchy
rule. `langy:delete` rather than an `archive` action because delete is
already what the hierarchy helper enumerates, and Langy's delete archives
under the hood anyway.

Granted from MEMBER upward and to org admins; VIEWER and EXTERNAL get
nothing. The permission grain is not what keeps Langy scarce — the
`release_langy_enabled` flag is — so the line is drawn at "can this
person act on the project at all" rather than trying to be finer.

Also closes two gaps the audit turned up:

- `langyGithub` checked no permission at all. `authorizeInResolver`
  authorizes nothing; it just marks the check done, leaving a role-blind
  membership row lookup as the only gate, so an EXTERNAL lite member could
  enumerate the org's private repositories through `listRepos`. Now
  `checkOrganizationPermission("langy:manage")`, still ahead of the
  rollout gate so a non-member's response stays independent of the org's
  flag value.
- `langyEgress` read `project:view`, which DEMO_VIEW_PERMISSIONS grants to
  every authenticated user on the demo project, so the demo project's
  egress allow-list — the hosts Langy's sandbox may reach — was
  world-readable. Now `langy:view` / `langy:manage` plus the explicit demo
  refusal `langy.ts` already had.

`useShowLangy` gains the matching `langy:view` check, so a custom role
without it no longer renders a panel whose every call 401s, and stops
treating the demo project as a place Langy runs — the server refuses it,
so that panel could only 403 on send.

No migration or backfill: built-in role permissions resolve at request
time from TEAM_ROLE_PERMISSIONS, so existing members pick these up on
deploy. Custom roles carry a stored permission array and will not gain
`langy:*` — deliberate, since a role authored as "may view evaluations"
never asked for turn spend.

* fix(langy): wire the credentials service into the app layer

modelsAllowed reads getApp().langy.credentials, but the service was never
registered on the langy app-layer bag — the router did not typecheck.

* test(langy): bind the new authorization scenarios to their suites

api-endpoint-authorization.feature is parity-enforced; its eight new
scenarios needed @scenario bindings. The demo-refusal scenario gets a real
test: the panel stays dark on the demo project even with flag + permission.
Also fixes the one binding that named a scenario that doesn't exist.

* fix(security): apply the reserved-secret-name guard to the REST secrets twin

The tRPC secrets router hid and refused langy_vk_secret, but the public
/api/secrets routes go through SecretsService, which had never heard of
RESERVED_PROJECT_SECRET_NAMES: a secrets:manage API key could list it,
confirm it by id, overwrite its value (silently breaking the key the
gateway authenticates against), or delete it (making the next chat mint a
duplicate VK). Same seam, same not-found posture, on both surfaces now —
plus an explicit reserved-name refusal on both create paths and a test
pinning that reserved names stay outside the creatable (uppercase-only)
namespace.

* fix(security): make reserved API-key names unclaimable by customers

The system-managed guard keys on the name 'Langy session', but nothing
stopped a customer creating a key with that name — or renaming one to it.
Such a key would vanish from every listing while the guard made it
unrevocable by anyone, including org admins: a stealth, permanent
credential. Create and rename now refuse HIDDEN_SYSTEM_KEY_NAMES with a
dedicated api_key_reserved_name error; Langy's own mint opts in through an
explicit systemManaged flag.

* fix(security): gate the REST GitHub install twin on langy:manage

The tRPC langyGithub router demands langy:manage, but the REST install and
setup routes the in-chat popup drives authorized on org membership alone —
a plain member could still connect the App through the second door, and
connecting it grants Langy repository access for every project underneath.
Both routes now run the same permission check between membership and the
rollout gate, preserving the probe-resistant ordering; setup re-checks in
case the role was lowered mid-flow.

* docs(langy): retire stale evaluations:view and virtual-keys-UI references

The chat-entry spec scenario and the langyTurnProcedure docblock still
described the old evaluations:view gate; langyVirtualKey.ts still promised
UI badging and a /virtual-keys listing this branch removed. Also reunites
newCount with its docblock, which modelsAllowed had split.

* test(langy): stub langy.modelsAllowed in the panel test harnesses

* fix(langy): pin projectId with the conversation+turn on the relay

The runToken is cached after frame 1 while apply() re-reads projectId off
each envelope, so a caller holding a valid token could switch projectId on
later frames and sign them with the token they already have — writing this
conversation's frames under another tenant's id. The first verified frame
now pins projectId alongside conversation+turn, and every later frame is
held to it; the end-of-stream summary carries the verified project too.

* fix(langy): tenant-scope the session-key revoke

credentials/revoke looked a key up by id alone and gated only on its name,
so a bearer-secret holder could revoke ANY tenant's live session key. The
revoke now requires the calling turn's projectId (the manager holds it on
the worker's credentials) and the key must carry a PROJECT-scoped binding
for it — the project the session key was minted against. A cross-project id
reads as not-found so it never confirms the key exists. Threaded through
both compensation callers (turn-attempt abort, recovery effect port) and
the Go manager's Revoker.

* fix(langy): bind the internal turn-result ingest to a real turn

The durable result route validated projectId/conversationId only as
non-empty and never cross-checked them against each other or the turn — the

this path had only the shared bearer. It now rejects any (project,
conversation, turn) triple with no matching turn projection row (which
exists only after the turn was really accepted under that conversation in
that project), closing both a leaked-secret forge and a benign projectId
mix-up that would cross-write one tenant's output into another's. 404 so a
probe never confirms a cross-tenant id; the manager treats 4xx as terminal.

today and would write forged feedback onto arbitrary traces once the
trace-event follow-up lands. It now needs langy:create and drops any
conversationId the caller cannot see (and the traceId/messageId with it),
so feedback can never be pinned to another user's conversation or an
arbitrary trace. The demo-refusal middleware, previously copy-pasted three
times, is now one shared refuseDemoProject.

* fix(gateway): refuse customer budgets on product-managed virtual keys

VIRTUAL_KEY was the one budget scope with no cross-org and no purpose
check, so a customer could attach a $0.01 BLOCK budget to the Langy VK and
deny every Langy turn — the same 'customer breaks a product-managed
credential' class the by-id VK mutation guards already close. create() now
requires the target VK to belong to the caller's org and to be purpose=USER;
a product-managed VK reads as not-found.

from the manager-held ActorUserID — server-side truth, overwritten with the

queryable in trace_summaries (cost x user x VK), and tag.tags=langy already

fix(mcp-server): keep zod and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk as real dependencies (#5976)

Follow-up to #5965, which moved 11 packages to devDependencies on the
(correct, for the npx CLI path) theory that dist/index.js is a fully
self-contained esbuild bundle. That's true for index.js, but the package
also exports ./create-mcp-server and ./config (dist/create-mcp-server.js,
dist/config.js) — built by plain tsup, NOT bundled — and those are exactly
what langwatch/src/mcp/handler.ts imports for the live in-app /mcp HTTP
transport.

Verified the regression empirically: ran the actual Dockerfile production
step (`cd langwatch && CI=true pnpm prune --prod`) and imported the real
handler.ts import path afterward. @modelcontextprotocol/sdk turned out
accidentally safe (the app happens to pin the same ^1.29.0 range), but zod
is not — mcp-server wants ^4.3.6, the app has ^3.25.76, and after the prune
ESM resolution silently cross-resolves to the app's v3 copy with no error
(confirmed via require("zod/package.json").version from within the actual
dist/create-mcp-server.js module context).

Moving zod and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk back to dependencies fixes this
(verified: the same dry run now resolves zod@4.3.6 correctly). The other 9
packages stay as devDependencies — confirmed via grep that none of them are
imported anywhere outside index.ts/http-server.ts/__tests__, so they're
genuinely unused by the in-app handler path.

Cold-start impact: still 27s -> ~6.8s (vs the ~1.5-2s the overly-aggressive
first pass measured) — zod and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk are small, pure-JS,
no native compilation, unlike node-pty/vitest/@opentelemetry/sdk-node which
stay excluded.
