- Stop logging requestedBy as an email. The router passes the opaque user

Performance:
- The sweep verdict was one Lua round trip per blob, run sequentially — a

- A resolved delete or a resolving preview can no longer close a newer

- Outcome maps marked as const; ConfirmDialog confirmDisabled doc corrected.

Spec:
- The put-before-stage scenario no longer claims a blob is "never
  destroyed" — it is not reclaimed within that window; an unstaged orphan

* fix(ops): match CleanupVariables to the tRPC input so typecheck passes

runBlobCleanup's `dryRun` carries a Zod default, so the mutation input

which the full-project typecheck rejected (tslsp resolves the tRPC

Ops shows in the main sidebar when your email is in the
SHOW_OPS_IN_MAIN_SIDEBAR env allowlist, or only while you are under
/ops. That means a server config change (or a trip through settings) to

Add a per-browser pin: a new frontend feature flag
`ops_ui_ops_menu_pinned` that ORs into the existing always-show gate.

and is meant to be forced on locally. It never widens access: the

feat(ops): show event subscribers and the per-aggregate manager state machine in DejaView (#6047)

* feat(ops): DejaView lists event subscribers instead of reactors

DejaView's left rail showed reactors — projection-tied side effects. The
event-sourcing model this is meant to reflect is moving to event
subscribers (raw-event consumers with no projection state), so the rail
now lists those.

Adds getEventSubscriberMetadata() alongside the existing projection and
reactor introspection — it walks each pipeline definition's
eventSubscribers map (the .withEventSubscriber / .withSubscriber({events})
seam) and reports each subscriber's name, pipeline, aggregate type, and
the event types it reacts to. The listProjections ops endpoint returns
eventSubscribers in place of reactors, and the LeftPanel renders them
keyed by those event types. Process-manager-generated pm:<name>
subscribers are runtime plumbing, not part of the static definition, so
they are intentionally excluded.

getReactorMetadata stays for now — reactors still run; only the DejaView
surface changes.

* feat(ops): DejaView shows the process-manager state machine per aggregate

When an aggregate is on screen, DejaView now shows the per-aggregate
process managers driving it: each machine's definition joined to this
aggregate's current position and the commands it has emitted.

The state machine is implicit in each manager's evolve() — there is no
declared state set or transition table — so what a machine can advertise
is its definition surface: the event types that trigger it, the intents
it can emit (its cross-aggregate commands), and whether it wakes itself.
getProcessManagerMetadata() introspects that from the live pipeline
definitions, mirroring the projection/subscriber introspection.

The aggregate's position lives in the persisted instance. ManagerExplorer
reads it by ref (processKey == aggregateId) through the existing
ProcessStore port — findByRef for the state, revision and next wake,
findMessagesByRef for the emitted-intent outbox — reusing PrismaProcessStore
rather than duplicating the queries. Scheduled singletons are excluded:
they key by process name, not aggregate id, so "this aggregate's instance"
does not apply to them.

The ManagerPanel is a self-hiding right column — most aggregate types have
no per-aggregate machine, so it collapses rather than take space. Each card
shows triggers, emitted commands, and, when the machine has started, the
current state JSON, revision, next wake, and the outbox with per-message
status and attempts. State payloads are content-stripped at the toPayload
boundary, so they are safe to render directly.

Wired as ops:view behind requireOps().managerExplorer, with an in-memory
store on the null-app path.

* fix(ops): drop the duplicate PrismaProcessStore import in presets

presets already imported PrismaProcessStore from the process-manager
barrel; the manager-explorer wiring added a second direct import of the
same name (TS2300), which failed typecheck and cascaded into the test
shards. Consolidated onto the barrel import (which also exports
InMemoryProcessStore) and removed both direct imports.

* test(ops): loosen the fake ProcessStore override types

typecheck:tests rejected the mocked findByRef: a concrete-returning
vi.fn is not assignable to the store's generic
`<State>(...) => Promise<PersistedProcessInstance<State> | null>`
signature. The fakeStore overrides are typed loosely (the whole store is
cast to ProcessStore anyway), so a plain async mock satisfies them.

* fix(ops): surface manager-panel fetch errors and reuse the process store

- The panel returned null on an errored fetch, which looked identical to
  "this aggregate has no process managers". A debugging tool must not
  hide its own failures, so the error now renders in the panel.
- presets already wraps prisma in a PrismaProcessStore for the pipeline
  repositories; the manager explorer reuses that instance instead of
  constructing a second copy of the same stateless wrapper.

feat(observability): full-stack trace correlation — browser RUM + tRPC context (ADR-058) (#6015)

* docs(observability): ADR-058 + spec for full-stack trace correlation

Plans browser RUM that joins to backend traces, so a click, the navigation
it causes, the calls it fires and the server work behind them read as one
trace.

Decisions worth flagging:

- Telemetry reaches the in-cluster collector through a same-origin proxy
  route on the app, not the public OTLP NLB. Prod deliberately keeps OTLP
  off the internet, and the collector's bearer filter guards only the
  traces pipeline -- the logs pipeline behind the same listener has none.
- Client spans are opened by a tRPC link rather than fetch instrumentation.
  httpBatchLink collapses N procedure calls into one request, and the WS
  and SSE transports carry no per-call headers at all.
- Grafana Faro considered and declined: its non-trace signals need a Faro
  receiver, and we run no Alloy to host one.

Also records two gaps found while planning: the tRPC server tracer never
extracts inbound trace context (so tRPC calls start a fresh root trace),
and PostHog captures carry no trace or tenant identity, leaving nothing to
join on.

* feat(observability): carry trace context across the tRPC boundary and into PostHog

Two independent gaps that each broke correlation on their own.

The tRPC tracer opened a SERVER span without ever consulting inbound
headers, so every tRPC call rooted a fresh trace. Since most of the
product talks tRPC rather than REST, work the browser starts and the
server work it triggers were always two unrelated traces. It now extracts
the caller's context the way the REST middleware already did.

Subscriptions deliberately do not extract: they ride a long-lived
connection, so `ctx.req` is the handshake request, and adopting it would
parent every later message on that socket to whatever trace happened to
open it.

PostHog captures carried no trace identity at all, so an exception and the
request that caused it could only be joined by eyeballing timestamps. Both
capture paths now stamp trace_id/span_id from the active span, placed
after the caller's extras so a colliding key cannot quietly rewrite where
the error was captured. Outside a trace they stay absent rather than
claiming an invalid all-zero one.

Refs ADR-058.

* feat(observability): browser RUM via @langwatch/react-rum

Adds the browser half of a trace, in a package the app consumes rather
than inline: a web tracer, session identity, and a tRPC link that times
individual procedure calls.

@langwatch/react-rum lives beside @langwatch/observability and is
source-only like its siblings. OpenTelemetry is a peer dependency
throughout, because two copies of @opentelemetry/api in one bundle means
two context stores and silently broken propagation.

The browser exports OTLP to /api/rum/v1/traces on the app's own origin
rather than to a collector. Production deliberately keeps OTLP off the
internet, and the collector's bearer filter guards only its traces
pipeline, so exposing it would also expose an unauthenticated log sink.
Same-origin also means no CORS to arrange. The route rate limits per
browser session, caps body size below the collector's own limit, refuses
payloads claiming to be another service, and stamps langwatch.origin
itself rather than trusting the client to send it.

Spans are timed by a tRPC link rather than by fetch instrumentation alone:
httpBatchLink collapses several calls into one request, so a single
POST /api/trpc span says a batch was slow without saying which call was.
The link is fail-open — it sits in the live request path, so any error in
it passes the operation through untouched.

Off unless RUM_ENABLED is set, and inert regardless without a collector
endpoint configured.

Corrects two things the ADR claimed that this does not do: the link does
not inject trace context (fetch instrumentation does, per batch), and
calls on the WebSocket and SSE transports root their own server-side
trace because those transports carry no per-call headers. Both are now
written down as knowingly open rather than described as solved.

Refs ADR-058.

* feat(haven): enable browser RUM whenever the observability stack is up

Ties RUM_ENABLED to the LGTM collector being present in the overlay, so
the app's browser telemetry turns on with the stack and off without it —
the exporter would otherwise post to an ingest route with nowhere to
forward. The frontend half of a trace is exactly what a developer
debugging their own worktree wants.

* fix(observability): harden the RUM ingest route and fix trace parentage

Actions a review of the branch, plus what driving it in a real browser
showed. Two of the findings were reproducible live against a local stack.

Ingest (now a service behind a thin route, per the layering rule, with
typed HandledErrors instead of bare responses):

- Identity attributes are overwritten rather than validated. The previous
  check read the *first* `service.name` while collectors take the last, so
  appending one array element let a payload land in Tempo attributed to
  `langwatch-app`. Confirmed live before the fix and neutralised after it.
- Body size is enforced while reading. `content-length` is a hint a chunked
  request need not send, so the old check ran after the whole body had
  already been buffered into a string — an unauthenticated memory
  exhaustion primitive. Bytes are now counted as they arrive.
- Span count is capped separately. A 500KB body carrying 5,000 spans is
  well under the size limit; it is now refused.
- Limits are enforced globally as well as per caller. Both per-caller keys
  are self-asserted, so rotating either one landed every request in a fresh
  bucket. The global bucket is the actual bound.
- Collector auth headers are forwarded, and the forward has a timeout.
- A collector failure no longer returns 5xx: that is in the OTLP retryable
  set, so an outage would turn every open tab into a retry loop against us.

Tracing:

- tRPC procedure spans are made active for the call, so the transport's
  fetch span descends from them instead of rooting its own trace.
- `callerTraceContext` keeps a local span when one exists. Re-extracting
  parented the procedure to the browser and left the HTTP span a childless
  sibling — visible in Tempo as `trpc.*` beside `POST api` rather than
  under it, now nested correctly.
- Browser tracing no longer clears its started flag on a partial failure,
  which could leave two providers registered.
- `resetBrowserTracingForTesting` is off the package's public entry point.

Tests cover the ingest paths that had none (all of the above), the link's
parenting and teardown contract, and the local-span precedence. Spec marks
the navigation scenario pending — it describes work ADR-058 defers to a
later phase.

* docs(observability): document RUM_ENABLED in .env.example

Deployment surface: the var is off by default and inert without
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, but an operator reading .env.example should
not have to find it in an ADR.

* fix(observability): drop the client tRPC link, tighten the origin match

Actions CodeRabbit's review. Two findings were substantive.

**The client tRPC link never worked, and is removed.** CodeRabbit pointed
out that `StackContextManager` has no async propagation, so the context
made active around `subscribe()` does not survive httpBatchLink's deferred
dispatch. Measured against a running stack: of 700 spans exported from one
browser session, all 32 `trpc.*` client spans were lone roots in their own
traces with no other span in them. So the link added a trace per call and
correlated none of them.

The visibility it was meant to provide already exists on the server: the
`trpc.<path>` spans now nest under the HTTP request span, giving the
per-procedure breakdown of a batch without putting code in the request
path. What is lost is the browser's own view of a call, which needs async
context propagation (zone.js) to do properly — noted in the ADR as
deferred rather than pretended to be solved.

**Trace context could leak to a lookalike host.** The origin match was a
bare prefix, so `https://app.example.com.evil.test` matched
`https://app.example.com`. Now requires a `/` or end-of-string boundary.

Also: the collector forward no longer blocks the browser's response (an
outage tied up a connection for the full 5s timeout per request);
`callerTraceContext` takes the headers it reads instead of `any`; session
tests carry `when` conditions and scenario annotations on the tests
themselves; the realtime spec scenario describes user-visible behaviour
rather than transport internals; and the unused test seam is gone.

PostHog-in-Grafana guidance moves out of ADR-058 into its own operational
reference, since it is a separate decision — now with the rate limits and
costs that actually constrain it.

* docs(adr): state the request-path trade-off accurately

The ADR claimed no code is added to the request path. Not true as
written: context extraction and span activation are server request-path
code. The real distinction is which path — the browser's critical path,
where a bug degrades the interaction the user is waiting on, versus
server-side tracing that already wraps every request.

* feat(observability): SPA navigation spans and session-based RUM sampling

Two gaps ADR-058 left open.

Navigation spans. Only the document load produced a span, so every call a
page made on arrival was an orphan trace with no statement of what the user
was doing. React Router drives a navigation span in the application (the
router is the only thing that knows a navigation happened); the package keeps
the span itself and stays router-agnostic.

Parenting those calls needs context to survive an async gap the
StackContextManager cannot bridge — the page mounts and its queries dispatch
in a later task. Rather than adopt zone.js, an in-flight navigation is
published as an ambient context that spans with no parent at all take
instead. Bounded by the navigation's own duration, and withdrawn a frame
after the route commits.

Sampling. Always-on was the stated starting point and the main cost lever;
it is now configuration (RUM_SAMPLE_RATIO). The ratio is a ratio of sessions
rather than traces: a tenth of the traces from every visit is enough to bill
for and never enough to read, so whole visits are kept or dropped. A browser
decision reaches the server, so lowering it also drops the backend half of
unsampled browser traces — server work with no browser parent is untouched.
Tail sampling biased toward errored or slow sessions remains the better
answer and still needs collector support.

Un-pends the navigation scenario in the spec and adds scenarios for route
naming, superseded navigations, and what sampling must keep whole.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01517Eg1FdMCU8vxqcEkJb2r

* test(observability): cover the router half of navigation spans; document both

The hook is where the router coupling lives, so the test drives a real memory
data router with a lazy child route — a navigation that genuinely passes
through `loading` before it commits — against a real in-memory OTel provider,
and reads the trace that came out rather than the calls that were made.

`useParams` was wrong in the hook: it runs in the root layout, where it
resolves against the root's own match and sees none of the child route's
params, so every route pattern would have been the raw path. `useMatches`
gives the leaf's accumulated params.

ADR-058 gains the reasoning for both halves: why ambient context works for a
navigation when it did not for the tRPC link, and why the sampling ratio is a
ratio of sessions.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01517Eg1FdMCU8vxqcEkJb2r

* fix(observability): treat blank RUM_SAMPLE_RATIO as unset

z.coerce.number() turns "" into 0 and .default() only fires on undefined, so
a bare RUM_SAMPLE_RATIO= in .env silently disabled all browser sampling.
Preprocess blanks to undefined, matching REDIS_DB_INDEX and the PostHog
polling interval.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01517Eg1FdMCU8vxqcEkJb2r

* fix(observability): refuse RUM payloads whose nested shape cannot be walked

The top-level resourceSpans array check let malformed nesting through to code
that reaches inside it: countSpans iterates scopeSpans and stampIdentity calls
.filter on resource.attributes, so a payload making either a string or an
object threw a TypeError and the route answered 500. A body of bare null did
the same, one level up. The endpoint is public, so that is a way to provoke
server errors at will; a shape we cannot read is now refused as the malformed
input it is.

Also drops the removed tRPC link from the package description, and states the
oversized-report scenario as an observable outcome rather than buffering
mechanics.

* fix(observability): stop a nonsense RUM_SAMPLE_RATIO taking the app down

The spec says a meaningless share records rather than silently collecting
nothing, and the sampler clamps for exactly that reason. Nothing out of range
could reach the clamp: the env schema refused the value first and turned it
into a failed boot, so RUM_SAMPLE_RATIO=banana (or 2) took the whole app down
over an optional telemetry dial. The schema now falls back to recording
everything, and is exported so the test drives the real one. An explicit 0
still means zero.

Alongside it, three things the audit turned up:

- the browser is only told tracing is on when a collector exists, so a
  deployment that sets RUM_ENABLED alone no longer has every open tab
  exporting on a batch timer into a permanent 404
- the shared rate-limit bucket is checked before the per-caller one, whose key
  the caller chooses: refusing on the shared bucket first means a flood that is
  already being refused cannot still mint a Redis key per request
- the flood test claimed to rotate identities while using one fixed key, so the
  shared bucket was never exercised; it now pins both limits and there is a
  test for the rotating case, plus one for the ordering above

Also drops a comment describing a function that does not exist.

feat(coding-agent): pipeline with a session aggregate (ADR-056) (#6005)

* docs(coding-agent): ADR-056 — coding-agent pipeline with a session aggregate, plus specs and build plan

The session becomes its own aggregate (keyed by session.id) in a dedicated
coding-agent-processing pipeline fed by span, log and metric contributions —
subscribers, projections and one process manager, no reactors. Two decoupled
surfaces: session views (session tab, personal usage — works for metric-only
sessions) and trace enrichment (terminal transcript, log joins — works for
any trace). Supersedes PR #5708's trace-keyed fold; the plan doc carries the
full port manifest from that branch.

* feat(coding-agent): pipeline scaffold — session aggregate + contribution commands (slice 1)

The coding_agent_processing pipeline mounts with aggregate
coding_agent_session and its write surface: contributeSpanFacts,
contributeLogFacts and contributeMetricFacts, one per OTLP signal
(ADR-056 $2). Payloads carry lifted scalar facts only — content stays
in the canonical rows — and the span status is the OTLP numeric enum,
so PR #5708's silent string-comparison bug is unrepresentable.
Idempotency keys make re-delivered telemetry collapse instead of
inflate; the metric key versions on asOfUnixMs so a newer converged
observation is a new fact ($5: replace, never increment).

Ports the five-agent vocabulary (coding-agent-normalization.ts) and
its tests verbatim from the superseded branch.

* feat(coding-agent): span + log contributors and the session fold (slice 2)

Dispatch subscribers on trace-processing (raw span_received, gated on the
span-name set before any decoding) and log-processing (canonical records,
gated by the vocabulary lift) contribute session-keyed facts into the
coding-agent pipeline. The session fold — ported from the superseded
branch's derivation — is re-keyed to the SESSION: one row per session in
coding_agent_sessions (migration 00051, ORDER BY TenantId, StartedAt,
SessionId), with TraceIds as a bounded array so multi-trace sessions
unify, plus the coding_agent_trace_sessions map so the trace drawer
resolves its session with two keyed seeks.

The store writes every folded session (the dispatchers are the gate now,
so metric-only sessions can exist once slice 3 lands); reads stay on the
IN-tuple dedup pattern, never FINAL. No reactors — fan-in is
withEventSubscriber, per ADR-056 §3.

* feat(coding-agent): metric contributor + converged session_metric_series (slice 3)

A subscriber on metric-processing lifts session-keyed coding-agent
datapoints (session.id rides 100% of them; trace ids ride none) and
contributes CONVERGED units per ADR-056 §5: a cumulative point is its
series' total (a later observation replaces it — the table versions on
AsOf, so arrival order can't clobber observation order), a delta point
is its own unit (sums exactly once; a re-delivery replaces that row).
session_metric_series (migration 00052) is Replacing, never Summing;
the per-session read is SUM ... GROUP BY over IN-tuple-deduplicated
units.

The session fold overlays the metric-fed fields (lines of code,
commits, PRs, edit decisions, active time) by recomputing them from the
bounded unit map on every contribution — replace-not-increment, so
replays converge. Token/cost metrics deliberately do not overlay (the
spans and logs already carry them); their series still land in the
table for the metric-only-session read. Metric-only sessions now
materialize a session row with no spans and no logs at all.

* feat(coding-agent): read layer — session, trace mapping and usage reads (slice 4)

CodingAgentSessionService: getBySessionId (IN-tuple dedup point read,
±7d partition hint), getSessionForTrace (two keyed seeks through
coding_agent_trace_sessions, the mapping's timestamp seeding the
session read's partition hint), and listByUser (UserId + StartedAt
range, newest first — the personal-usage read).

The one read-time overlay left: a metric-only session has no spans or
logs to carry tokens and cost, so those fill in from its converged
series (SUM over IN-tuple-deduplicated units) — and only when the
folded value is zero, so a session that did send spans is never
double-counted. PR #5708's cross-trace merge module and per-open
rollup scan are not ported: the session fold already did both at

fix(langy): harden GitHub App installation binding at /setup (#6067)

* fix(langy): harden GitHub App installation binding at /setup

recordInstallation now rejects rebinding an installation that's already
connected to a different organization, instead of silently overwriting the
existing org mapping. Genuine same-org re-installs still upsert cleanly.
Blocked attempts are audit-logged.

Adds service- and route-level regression tests.

* fix(langy): close the race window in the installation ownership guard

The previous guard checked ownership via a separate read (findByInstallationId)
before writing (upsert), leaving an await-gap where two concurrent /setup
completions for the same not-yet-recorded installation could both observe
"unclaimed" and both write, the second silently overwriting the first's org.

Replace it with an atomic claim: insertOrGetExisting attempts a create and
relies on the DB's unique index (falling back to a lookup on conflict) instead
of a check-then-act pair, so only one concurrent caller can ever win a fresh
installation id. Adds a regression test that races two organizations for the
same installation id and asserts exactly one wins.

LangyGithubInstallationConflictError now takes a single named-params object
instead of three positional (same-typed) strings, removing a swap hazard
between the existing and attempted organization ids.

Also renames the setup-route test to .integration.test.ts — it exercises the
real Hono route end-to-end via app.request with only the app-layer boundary
mocked, matching this repo's unit vs integration test classification. Adds a
popup-mode case for the cross-tenant conflict path alongside the existing
redirect-mode one.

* test(langy): prove the installation race guarantee against real Postgres

The service/route tests mock the repository, so they can only show the
service correctly interprets whatever the repo returns — they can't prove
Postgres actually serializes two concurrent inserts the way the fix assumes.
Per TESTING_PHILOSOPHY.md's mocking guidance (external boundaries only,
prefer real implementations where practical) and this repo's own precedent
for DB-level correctness claims, add a repository-level integration test that
exercises insertOrGetExisting against the real test database: a fresh
install, a race between two orgs for the same installation id (asserting
Postgres's unique constraint — not call ordering — picks exactly one
winner), and a pre-existing id never getting overwritten.

Also narrows the service-level unit test's claim: it was documented as
proving the race is closed, but it only proves the service's branching logic
given an already-atomic fake. Retitled its comment to point at the new
integration test for the actual DB guarantee.

* refactor(langy): rename insertOrGetExisting's inserted flag to wasInserted

Bare boolean fields must carry an is/has/was-style prefix per this repo's
naming guideline (.coderabbit.yaml). Renamed across the repository
interface, the Prisma implementation, the Null stub, the service, and every
test double/assertion that reads it.

fix(security): rate-limit and allowlist POST /api/track_usage (#6071)

* fix(security): allowlist, cap, and rate-limit POST /api/track_usage

The public telemetry endpoint accepted any event name/shape from an
unauthenticated caller with no rate limiting, letting anyone inject
arbitrary events into the analytics pipeline at unlimited volume
(customer security report). It now allowlists the one event
self-hosted deployments actually send, bounds the payload size and
property count, and rate-limits per-IP and per-instance — mirroring
the existing pattern in the RUM ingest and one-click-unsubscribe
routes. Extracted the Hono-context IP resolution shared by both into
getClientIpFromHonoContext to avoid a second copy.

* fix(security): close gaps in track_usage rate limiting and validation

Critical follow-up on the previous commit: per-IP and per-instance
limits alone are bypassable by rotating either attacker-controlled
value (same reasoning as rum-ingest.service.ts), and the catchall
schema still let a spoofed event smuggle arbitrary properties into
PostHog. Adds a global rate-limit bucket as the actual bound, switches
to a `.strict()` schema matching the exact known daily_usage_stats
shape, and sets Retry-After on 429s per the report's ask. Also
reclassifies the test as .integration.test.ts (it exercises the real
route via app.request(), mocking only external boundaries) and tags
it @regression per TESTING_PHILOSOPHY.md.

* fix(security): address CodeRabbit review on track_usage rate limiting

getClientIpFromHonoContext only ever read proxy headers, so any caller
that skipped them (no CDN/LB in front, or one that strips them)
resolved to "unknown" and shared a single rate-limit bucket with every
other such caller across both track_usage and unsubscribe. Falls back
to getConnInfo's raw socket address (populated by @hono/node-server's
getRequestListener, which is how this app is actually served) when no
header resolves, guarded defensively since Hono's app.request() test
helper and other adapters leave c.env without the shape getConnInfo
expects.

Also folds in the track-usage-security test rewrite (strict-schema and
global-rate-limit coverage) that a `git add` scoped to misc.ts alone
left uncommitted in the prior commit despite the file already having
been renamed to .integration.test.ts.

* fix(security): make the track_usage getClientIp fallback actually work, and stop 400ing legacy senders

Self-caught during a ruthless review of this PR before merge, both P1:

1. getClientIpFromHonoContext's getConnInfo fallback (previous commit)
   was dead code in production: honoFetchForNode (src/start.ts), the
   function @hono/node-server's getRequestListener actually calls as
   fetchCallback(req, {incoming, outgoing}), only declared a single
   `request` parameter and silently dropped the second argument. c.env
   was therefore always undefined for every route in this app, so
   getConnInfo(c) threw unconditionally (caught, returns undefined) —
   the exact "unknown" bucket collapse the fallback was meant to fix
   never stopped happening. Fixed by forwarding every argument
   honoFetchForNode receives straight through to honoApp.fetch. No
   existing handler reads c.env today, so this is additive.

2. trackUsageBodySchema's stat fields were all required under
   .strict(). track_usage is a stable receiver self-hosted instances
   at any historical version hit (usageStatsWorker.ts's own docstring:
   "unchanged"), and collectUsageStats.ts's field set has already
   drifted once (totalScenarioEvents, #471) — a required+strict schema
   400s any sender whose shape doesn't exactly match today's, and the
   worker never checks the response status, so the drop is completely
   silent. Made every stat field optional; .strict() still closes the
   actual security gap by rejecting unknown keys.

Both confirmed via a temporary decisive test (executed, then deleted)
before fixing, per the ruthless-review protocol. Added permanent
regression coverage for both.

fix(auth): close open redirect on /auth/signin callbackUrl (#6070)

* fix(auth): close open redirect on /auth/signin callbackUrl

The already-authenticated bounce path validated callbackUrl with a raw
startsWith("/") check, which a protocol-relative value like "//evil.com"
satisfies while the browser still treats it as an off-domain redirect.
Route it through the existing safeRedirectTarget() guard (already used
by every other callbackUrl consumer in this file, and already unit
tested) instead of duplicating ad hoc validation.

Also hardens the analogous referrer check in the auth error page,
which used the same string-prefix anti-pattern (bypassable via a
referrer host like origin.evil.com) instead of a real origin
comparison.

* refactor(auth): consolidate redirect fix into existing test file, extract isSameOrigin

Follow-up to the open-redirect fix: the standalone regression test file
duplicated the mock boilerplate of the existing signin.integration.test.tsx
for the same component and reimplemented safeRedirectTarget's logic inline
instead of exercising the real guard. Merged both new scenarios into the
existing file (spy on the real ~/utils/auth-client module via
importOriginal, only signIn/useSession mocked) and dropped the duplicate
file.

Removed the @scenario JSDoc annotations — those bind to specs/**/*.feature
scenario titles via the parity checker, and there is no feature file for
this bug fix (bug fixes don't get BDD specs). They were failing
`pnpm check:feature-parity` as unknown annotations. Tagged the describe
blocks @regression instead, matching existing convention.

Extracted isSameOrigin() out of safeRedirectTarget() and reused it in the
error.tsx referrer check, which had the same string-prefix anti-pattern
(referrer.startsWith(origin), bypassable via a referrer host like
origin.evil.com) reimplemented inline instead of sharing the one guard.

Verified the new regression test actually fails against the pre-fix
signin.tsx (asserted window.location.replace("//evil.example.com")) before
restoring the fix, per TESTING_PHILOSOPHY.md's regression-test requirement.

* fix(auth): close backslash bypass in safeRedirectTarget, cover error.tsx referrer redirect

CodeRabbit review on #6070 caught a real, confirmed bypass: safeRedirectTarget's
fast path (`callbackUrl.startsWith("/") && !startsWith("//")`) returned values
like `/\evil.com` raw, without ever running them through URL parsing. The
WHATWG URL parser treats a leading `/\`, `\/`, or `\\` as authority-introducing
for special schemes (same as `//`), so `window.location.replace("/\\evil.com")`
navigates off-origin — verified with node's URL implementation before and
after the fix. Removed the fast path entirely; every callbackUrl now resolves
through isSameOrigin()/new URL(), which already handles this correctly (proven
by the existing "bare word" test case). Added regression tests for the
backslash variants, verified red against the pre-fix fast path before
restoring green.

Also added integration coverage for the error.tsx referrer redirect, which
had none: same-origin referrer is followed, a prefix-confusion referrer
(origin used as a string prefix, e.g. `<origin>.evil.com`) falls back to "/",
and a missing referrer falls back to "/". Verified this regression test fails
against the pre-refactor `referrer.startsWith(origin)` check.

Minor test hygiene from ruthless-review: the referrer override was never

* fix(traces): wire the canonical log repository into the app-layer log read

stored_log_records repository; the canonical parameter was optional and
never passed, so every trace-correlated log read through

constructor parameter is required, so a construction site cannot drop it
again. Unit cases pin the canonical delegation and the merge of

fix(metrics): correct oldest-pending-age gauge + reset stale ClickHouse table gauges (#6084)

fix(metrics): correct oldest-pending-age gauge + reset stale CH table gauges

gq_oldest_pending_age_milliseconds could report a group's entire blocked/parked
hold time as "backlog age" (0 -> hours in one tick, e.g. a 4141s spike two
minutes after the alert resolved). Two independent defects:

1. Wrong clock origin: it read the per-group jobs zset, whose dispatchAfterMs
   scores are PRESERVED across a block/park, so a just-unblocked group looked
   like an ancient backlog.
2. Sampling bias: zrange(readyKey, 0, 9) samples the 10 MOST dispatch-eligible
   groups, not the oldest, so a real backlog past index 10 was missed and the
   gauge could also under-report and fail to page.

Fix (metric-layer only, no queue-behaviour change): read the readyKey score
directly over (1, now] — every not-yet-dispatchable state (in-flight
activeUntil, backoff retry, delayed stage) is future-scored and excluded, and
the unblock sentinel (score 1) is dropped by the exclusive lower bound. One
O(log N) ZRANGEBYSCORE ... LIMIT 0 1 replaces the first-10 scan + per-group
fan-out. Known residual (documented): unpark restores a preserved score, so a
long-parked group briefly over-reports on unpark until dispatched — closing
that needs an unpark re-score (queue-fairness) decision.

Also: clickhouse_table_rows/_bytes/_parts are now .reset() before each
repopulation (mirroring the per-disk gauges). Without it a table that
TTL-drops to zero active parts kept its last value forever, feeding phantom
size into the DB-size and trace_summaries alerts.

Adds a unit test for the oldest-pending computation (previously untested).

fix(traces): keep lone UTF-16 surrogate spans via ClickHouse safe-escape insert setting (#6078)

* fix(traces): sanitise lone UTF-16 surrogates before ClickHouse span insert

Span strings serialised into ClickHouse could carry a lone (unpaired) UTF-16
surrogate half (\uD800–\uDFFF) — e.g. a value truncated mid-emoji, or binary
/ garbage text captured by an SDK as a string. `serializeAttributes` passed
strings through untouched, and `format: "JSONEachRow"` emits a lone half as a
`\uD800`-style escape with no second part. ClickHouse's JSON parser rejects it:

  Cannot parse escape sequence: missing second part of surrogate pair.
  ... (while reading the value of key SpanAttributes) ...

The insert throws, the pipeline retries, retries exhaust, and the span is
dead-lettered. In production a single bad character dead-lettered 13 groups for
one project.

Sanitise every string a span contributes to a `stored_spans` row to well-formed
UTF-16 via `String.prototype.toWellFormed()` (replaces each lone surrogate with
U+FFFD) at the write boundary: SpanAttributes / ResourceAttributes / Events.*
/ Links.* map keys and values (in `serializeAttributes`), plus SpanName,
StatusMessage, ScopeName, ScopeVersion, ServiceName and Events.Name in
`toClickHouseRecord`. Lossless for valid input; only touches genuinely malformed
strings. Deliberately does not use ClickHouse's
`input_format_json_throw_on_bad_escape_sequence=0`, which would persist garbage.

Regression tests execute the real serialize / record-build path and observe the
malformed input being sanitised (well-formed UTF-16 + U+FFFD marker); they fail
before the fix. Adds specs/traces/span-attribute-unicode-sanitisation.feature.

* fix(traces): use ClickHouse safe-escape insert setting instead of JS surrogate sweep

Replace the per-string toWellFormed() sanitisation across the whole span
write surface with input_format_json_throw_on_bad_escape_sequence: 0 on the
stored_spans inserts — exactly what ClickHouse's own error recommends.

The previous approach walked and rewrote every string of every span
(attribute keys/values, names, statuses, event names — unbounded per-span
payload) on the hot ingest path to pre-empt the parser, and replaced the
rare malformed byte with U+FFFD. The setting handles it once at the insert
boundary, per batch and O(1): ClickHouse keeps the bad escape as text
instead of throwing, so the span is stored verbatim; valid strings are
never touched.

- span-storage repo: revert serializeAttributes/toClickHouseRecord to
  pass-through; add SPAN_INSERT_SETTINGS applied to both insertSpan and
  insertSpans.
- unit test: drop the in-process sanitisation assertions (behaviour now
  lives in ClickHouse, not JS).
- integration test: real-ClickHouse regression — insert a lone-surrogate
  span through insertSpans and assert it does not throw and reads back
  (without the setting this throws and the span is dead-lettered).
- spec: rewritten to the store-not-reject behaviour.

  track of a batch it already folded (three-attempt chain covered by

  only counts dedup as unavailable when even that set is empty.

* fix(workflows): throw NotFoundError/UnprocessableEntityError from runWorkflow, not plain Error

nonexistent workflow ID returns a raw 500 ("Workflow not found.") while
platform_get_workflow / platform_delete_workflow on the exact same ID

not-found and not-published preconditions. Same bug class as

plain Error has no .status and isn't a HandledError, so it falls through

determineErrorResponse(), same classes get/delete_workflow's route
handlers already rely on for their correct 404s. Message text is
unchanged, only the thrown class changed; checked all 3 other callers
(routes/misc.ts, app-layer/presets.ts, evaluations/runEvaluation.ts) for
message-based error matching -- none exists, so this is safe everywhere
runWorkflow is called, not just the REST route.

feat(event-sourcing): declared fold read windows — width as fold config, miss-coalescing in the executor (#6102)

* feat(event-sourcing): declare fold read windows on the fold, coalesce misses in the executor

The time bound on a fold's read-back was hand-threaded at every layer:
the executor stamped a raw occurredAt hint, each store decided whether to
forward it, and each repository widened it with its own arithmetic — ±7d
here, ±2d there — with its own (sometimes forgotten) miss fallback. The
coding-agent session repository forgot the fallback: a windowed miss on a
live session read back as null, so the executor folded the batch onto
init() and the partial row won the ReplacingMergeTree dedup.

Now the window is config on the fold definition (options.readWindow) and
the miss-coalescing is platform behaviour: the executor computes
occurredAt ± widthMs onto context.readWindow, stores pass it through
verbatim, and a windowed miss is retried once without the window before
the aggregate is treated as new — counted via
es_fold_read_window_fallback_total so a drifting width is visible.

Both ClickHouse-backed folds adopt it: codingAgentSession (±7d, closing
the partial-overwrite bug structurally) and traceSummary (±2d, replacing
the store-side hint plumbing). Width constants live in one place each;
the coding-agent session service derives its API-read window from the
same constant and gets the same unwindowed retry, so a stale hint
degrades to a slower read instead of a 404.

ADR-066 rules updated; behavioural contract in
specs/event-sourcing/fold-read-window.feature.

* fix(event-sourcing): review round 1 — window type on findByTraceId, cache-bypassed retry, single fallback net

Four findings from the PR audit:

- findByTraceId's implementation signature re-declared its options inline
  without `window`, so the store's window never type-checked (TS2339; CI
  red). Use FindByTraceIdOptions.
- The executor's unwindowed retry re-entered RedisCachedFoldStore moments
  after the windowed attempt consulted it — a guaranteed second miss that
  double-counted es_fold_cache_total{miss} for the dominant miss
  population (new aggregates) and skewed the hit-ratio dashboards. The
  retry context now carries bypassReadCache and the wrapper goes straight
  to the durable tier.
- trace_summaries ran two recovery ladders: the repo's internal
  resolve-OccurredAt retry AND the executor's unwindowed retry. An
  explicit window is now applied verbatim with no internal fallback (the
  executor owns the retry, which lands on the repo's resolve path);
  occurredAtMs hint callers keep the internal ladder.
- The recovery warn now fires once per projection per process (debug
  after) so a chronically-narrow window can't flood the logs; the
  recovered counter stays the ongoing signal.

Plus the service-retry test the audit flagged as missing, verbatim-window
repo tests, and a spec line for the cache-bypassed retry.

* fix(ci): bind the stale-hint scenario, drop the test-store cast

- The service-retry test's @scenario annotation referenced a scenario
  that existed nowhere; it now binds to a real scenario in
  specs/coding-agent/session-aggregate.feature.
- getWithApplied is on FoldProjectionStore since #6098, so the readWindow
  executor test assigns it directly instead of casting through
  Record<string, unknown> (TS2352 under typecheck:tests).

* refactor(event-sourcing): review round 2 — named params + given/when test structure

- readWindowAround / withReadHints / loadWithApplied take destructured
  object parameters per the repo convention for multi-arg functions.
- The readWindow executor, cache-bypass, traceSummary store, and service
  retry tests now nest action "when" blocks under state "given" blocks
  instead of describing setup in a top-level "when".

* fix(event-sourcing): audit round 3 — ADR-068 alignment + unwindowed dedup seek

Rebased onto main's queryWindowed (ADR-068, #6107) and applied the
dual-audit findings:

- trace_summaries' explicit-window (fold) path now rides queryWindowed
  with fallback "none", so the read lands on
  clickhouse_windowed_read_total while the executor keeps sole ownership
  of the miss retry. The fold's width is ADR-068's shared
  DEFAULT_PARTITION_WINDOW_MS; the duplicate TRACE_SUMMARY_READ_WINDOW_MS
  constant is gone.
- coding_agent_sessions' inner max(UpdatedAt) dedup seek is now
  UNWINDOWED: windowing it let a session whose latest version's StartedAt
  drifted outside the window dedup to a stale in-window version — a
  non-null result no fallback can catch, re-opening the overwrite door
  this PR closes. Unwindowed, the drifted case reads back empty and the
  executor's retry recovers the true row (integration-tested).
- executeBatch's windowed-miss retry is now covered by a unit test
  (bypassReadCache + fold-onto-recovered-state), and its dead
  ordered[0] ternary is gone.
- The cache-bypass branch documents why it runs no dedup-unavailable
  accounting (the windowed attempt already counted that delivery), and
  the service documents why its own hint retry is intentionally
  unmetered.

fix(aigateway): forward mid-stream provider error events with their payload, cut in-stream retry loops at the relay (#6128)

* fix(aigateway): forward mid-stream provider error events with their payload, cut in-stream retry loops at the relay

A provider can fail a Responses stream AFTER the 200 is established by
emitting an in-stream error event whose detail nests under an error
OBJECT (OpenAI signals insufficient_quota this way). Two layers dropped
it on the floor:

The gateway's stream pipeline only mapped the legacy flat message/code
fields, so the nested payload vanished and the client received
data: {"error":"stream error: "}, an empty message in a shape no
OpenAI SDK recognises. opencode crashed with a Zod parse error instead
of showing the provider's actionable message. The iterator now recovers
the payload from the raw event (rawForwardCtx already carries it) into a
structured UpstreamError, and writeSSE forwards the provider's own error
event verbatim, falling back to the standard
{"type":"error","error":{...}} object for gateway-origin failures.
Pinned by a real-pipeline integration test replaying a captured
api.openai.com quota-failure stream through bifrost via a new
tests-only OpenAIBackendURL override.

With the message flowing, the second layer showed: the worker SDK
treats the in-stream failure as retryable and re-opens a fresh 200
stream forever, the silent-spinner loop #6104 cut for status-code 429s
but which status-based cutting can never see. The relay now sniffs
mediated 200 SSE streams for terminal error events as they pass through
untouched, captures the typed cause for the turn's error frame, and
arms a one-shot terminal 400 with the provider's own payload for the
next retry, on the same strike rules as the 429 cutter.
insufficient_quota and billing_hard_limit_reached join the hard-limit
discriminants for both paths.

Also adds scripts/dogfood/langy-local.sh, a doctor that checks
everything a local Langy turn needs (env block, release flag, opencode
binary, the three services, provider-key validity) and prints the exact
fix for whatever is missing.

Specs: specs/ai-gateway/error-transparency.feature,
specs/langy/langy-turn-recovery.feature,
specs/setup/langy-local-dogfood.feature

The doctor gains overridable provider-check URLs so the bats tests can

fix(coding-agent): monotonic version stamp — two session upserts can no longer tie on UpdatedAt (#6127)

* fix(coding-agent): monotonic RMT version stamp — two upserts can no longer tie on UpdatedAt

The IN-tuple dedup read depends on the repo invariant that no two versions of
one row tie on UpdatedAt (clickhouse-queries.md: "nextUpdatedAt = max(now,
prevUpdatedAt + 1) … no ties possible"). The session repository stamped plain
write time, so two commits inside one millisecond tied — both matched
max(UpdatedAt), and the drifted-window read then returned the stale in-window
version instead of empty (the intermittent "returns empty, not a stale
version" failure in the round-trip suite, and in prod a tied version lets a
read-back resurrect stale fold state).

The stamp is now max(now, superseded version + 1, this writer's last stamp + 1):
the threaded prior covers the read-back path, the per-writer floor covers
writers that did not read back, and per-aggregate group serialization covers
the cross-process window. Pinned by unit tests driving same-millisecond
upserts, a future-threaded prior, and a batch.

* test(coding-agent): move the drifted StartedAt off the retention TTL boundary

The drifted-window fixture backdated StartedAt by exactly retentionDays,
parking v2 on the StartedAt + toIntervalDay(_retention_days) TTL DELETE
boundary: any background merge between insert and read deletes the true
latest version and the reads fall back to v1 (reproduced locally;
OPTIMIZE TABLE FINAL deletes the row at 30d drift and keeps it at 15d).
The scenario only needs the drift to exceed the read window, so 15 days
keeps the TTL far away while still proving the windowed-empty contract.

fix(group-queue): planned shutdowns stop counting as worker deaths in the poison guard (#6122)

* fix(group-queue): a planned shutdown is not a worker death — sweep claim strikes on graceful close

The poison guard counts claims that never reached their clearing finally as
"consecutive worker deaths". A graceful shutdown produced exactly that
signature: SIGTERM → close() drains, but a job the drain budget (or the
platform's SIGKILL) abandoned kept its strike, so every deploy could tick
innocent in-flight groups toward the park threshold — the false-blame parks
observed in prod on rollout days.

Two changes, both preserving the guard's self-discrimination (a worker whose
event loop a poison job seized can never run either path, so real
crash-loops keep their count):

- close() sweeps the in-flight groups' claim strikes FIRST, before the drain,
  while the event loop is provably alive — jobs that complete during the
  drain re-clear harmlessly, jobs the budget abandons leave no strike behind
- a claim made after shutdown was requested records no strike at all; a group
  already at the threshold parks on the next boot's claim instead of during
  the drain

Implements the spec's previously @unimplemented scenario ("graceful shutdown
mid-job does not count as a poison strike") plus the new during-drain claim
scenario; bound by an integration test that asserts the strike is swept while
the handler is still running.

* fix(group-queue): recheck shutdown after the claim registers its strike

recordClaimStrike() awaits before the group is added to inFlightStrikeGroups.
close() can flip shutdownRequested and take its sweep snapshot during that
await — snapshotting a set that does not yet hold the group, so the sweep misses
it. If the drain budget (or SIGKILL) then abandons the job, its clearing finally
never runs and the strike survives: exactly the false "worker death" this guard
must not book during a planned shutdown.

Re-check shutdownRequested on the synchronous heels of the add (no await between
them, so close() cannot interleave there) and clear the group's own strike when
the shutdown began mid-claim. The add and this check are jointly exhaustive:
either close()'s snapshot already saw the group and swept it, or it did not and
we clear it here.

Regression: a new integration test forces the exact interleaving — it parks the
claim after the strike lands but before the add, drives close() past its sweep
snapshot (via the post-snapshot drainAndDisconnect hook), then releases the
claim and asserts the strike is cleared while the handler is still in flight.
Without the recheck the strike survives until a finally the abandon path never
reaches.

* docs(group-queue): make the shutdown park-timing docstring exact

The docstring promised a group at the threshold is "not parked during the drain"
and parks on the next boot. One interleaving escapes that: a claim that begins
pre-shutdown (recordStrikes latched true) whose recorded strike crosses the
threshold while close() flips the flag mid-await still runs the park branch, so
the group parks during the drain. That park is correct — it rides only real
prior-death strikes, and clearing them to defer would discard the very evidence
of poison — but the wording over-promised. State it precisely: parked at most
one claim early, never on a shutdown-born strike.

feat(dev): make local development work with no container runtime (#6135)

* feat(dev): make local development work with no container runtime

A laptop that runs ClickHouse, Postgres and Redis natively still had three
places that reached for docker or colima anyway. Close all of them so a full
`pnpm dev:haven` stack and the integration suite both come up with Docker
Desktop and colima stopped.

- Three integration suites called `new ClickHouseContainer()` directly,
  bypassing globalSetup's native-services path entirely. They now ask
  `startTestClickHouseEndpoints` for the isolated endpoints they need, which
  hands out one database per endpoint on the native server, or one container
  each in CI. The suites assert that a distinct URL resolves to a client that
  cannot see the other's rows, and a database boundary tests exactly that.

- ops-explain hardcoded the `langwatch` database in its queries, so on a
  shared native server it would have created a 4-column stub `stored_spans`
  inside the developer's real dev database. Its qualifiers are now the
  suite's own database.

- haven resolved its own knobs from the process environment only, so putting
  LANGWATCH_HAVEN_CH=0 in langwatch/.env did nothing. It now reads the dotenv
  layers as a fallback, the same precedence Prisma and tsx give the app, so a
  machine-level preference travels with the worktree while an exported
  variable still wins for a single run. Per-invocation switches (slug, agent
  mode, colours) are deliberately excluded.

globalSetup and the new helper share one predicate for "is the native mode
on", so the two can never disagree about which backend a run uses.

Verified with docker and colima both stopped: dev:haven serves /api/health
204 and the UI 200, and the three suites pass 21/21 with DOCKER_HOST pointed
at a nonexistent socket.

* fix(dev): address review on the no-container-runtime change

- The ENVIRONMENT help text claimed everything but three knobs resolved from
  langwatch/.env. Eight are process-only, and two of them (HAVEN_BASELINE,
  LANGWATCH_SEED) would have been read as configurable. Naming them is the
  fix rather than routing them through devEnv: every worktree inherits the
  same .env, so a baseline marker pinned there claims all of them at once and
  a seed flag re-seeds on every up. A test now derives the list from the
  source, so a knob added on plain os.Getenv without being documented fails.

- Extract TEST_CLICKHOUSE_IMAGE so the image is one symbol instead of a
  string in two files kept in step by a comment, and fold the duplicated
  create-root-client/CREATE DATABASE/close pattern into ensureEndpoint.

- Native isolation is by database, not by instance, so say endpoint in the
  suite headers rather than instance.

- With observability off it is the application stack, not a full stack.

- Drop database naming and container provisioning from the feature scenarios,
  leaving the observable outcomes: rows stay invisible across endpoints, dev
  data is untouched, and no container is started.

Verified both backends again on this commit: 21/21 native with DOCKER_HOST
pointed at a nonexistent socket, and 21/21 under CI=1 on real containers.

* test(clickhouse): scope the routing fixture read by project

The fixture read filtered on the row id alone. The id is unique per run so

* fix(ops): stop pointing operators at a file that does not exist

Two runtime messages and a source comment told operators to see

Describe what to provision instead: a langwatch_ops user with a readonly=1
profile and no SOURCES grant.

feat(charts): make Langy self-hostable via the Helm chart (#6138)

* feat(charts): make Langy installable on a self-hosted cluster

Langy shipped to the hosted product first, so every prerequisite it grew
was satisfied by our own infrastructure: a secret created by terraform, an
image in a private registry, a rollout flag flipped from an internal ops
screen, a node pool with a sandboxed runtime. None of that exists for
someone installing the chart, and each missing piece failed somewhere
different. Turning the assistant on is now one value, and everything it
needs is either materialised by the chart or named in one place.

What was broken, in the order an operator would have hit it:

The turn dispatch never left the cluster. Langy turns are driven by the
process outbox in the event-sourcing runtime, which runs in the worker
stack, not the app. The workers deployment had no agent URL and no shared
secret, and the agent's NetworkPolicy admitted only the app pod, so every
turn died in a process that was never wired up while both pods looked
healthy. Workers now get the same pair as the app and the policy admits
them.

The shared secret was never created. Both deployments referenced a Secret
the chart does not materialise, so enabling the agent left the app pod in
CreateContainerConfigError over a key nothing told the operator to add. It
now lands in the app Secret next to the gateway's pair, generated or
operator-supplied like every other key, and an operator who brings their
own Secret is told which key is missing before anything deploys.

The assistant stayed invisible. Its rollout flag is SYSTEM-scoped and
defaults off so the hosted product can open it one cohort at a time. A
self-hosted install has one cohort, so deploying the agent now opens it,
and enableForAllUsers=false keeps the staged path for anyone who wants it.

The image was pinned to a version that predates the agent. The subchart
was absent from the release-please extra-files, so its appVersion stayed
at 3.3.0 while the app moved on, and the tag derived from it would have
pulled an agent two releases behind. It now tracks releases like the
gateway chart does.

A sandboxed runtime was required unconditionally. Most self-managed
clusters have none, which made the assistant hosted-only in practice. The
invariant worth keeping is narrower: nobody runs this unsandboxed by
accident. acceptUnsandboxedRuntime makes it a decision the operator writes
down, and the values file no longer documents an opt-out the template
refused to render.

Trace mirroring needed an endpoint it could work out itself. Supply the
project key and the endpoint now resolves to the install's own control
plane, so watching Langy work takes one secret instead of two values.

Verified on a real EKS cluster: the chart installs with the agent enabled
and nothing pre-created, the agent runs under gVisor, and the app, the
workers, and the agent all agree on the generated secret.

* ci(charts): cover the assistant paths in the chart render matrix

The chart workflow's path filter listed every subchart except langyagent, so
changes to the assistant's own templates never triggered the render matrix that
guards them, and no overlay exercised the assistant at all. Adds the subchart to
both filters and renders it two ways: the default sandboxed posture, and the
unsandboxed one a cluster without gVisor has to accept deliberately.

* fix(charts): give the control plane the in-cluster addresses Langy needs

Two addresses were missing from a chart install, and both failed in the
places hardest to see: every pod healthy, and a turn that either refused
immediately or produced a paid-for answer that was then dropped.

The gateway. Langy mints the worker's key against the gateway, and the app
was never told where it is: the chart deploys the gateway but only ever
handed the app the PUBLIC url, which an install with no gateway ingress
does not have at all. Every turn was refused with a credential-resolution
error naming a variable nothing in the chart sets. The app and the workers
now get the gateway's own Service, with gateway.internalUrl for a gateway
that lives outside the release.

The way back. The agent's workers dial the control plane to push the
answer, finalize the turn, and run every langwatch CLI tool call. That
origin fell back to the app pod's own LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT, which is
deliberately localhost so in-pod runners can self-reference. The agent
resolved localhost to ITSELF, so the model ran, the tools ran, and then
every callback failed against a port nothing was listening on: a turn that
cost tokens, produced an answer, and never delivered it. Both pods now
hand the agent the app's Service address, overridable via
langyagent.controlPlane.callbackUrl for split topologies.

Verified on EKS: with the agent under gVisor, a turn now loads a skill,
runs `langwatch prompt list` against the control plane, answers from the
result, and lands as a langy.turn trace with its model and tool spans in
the project the mirror points at.

* fix(charts): honor the configured Langy secret and guard the half-set mirror

Review follow-ups from CodeRabbit on #6138.

The app Secret materialised a literal LANGY_INTERNAL_SECRET while the app,
the workers, and the agent all read whatever langyagent.secrets.internalSecretKey
names, so a custom key produced three pods pointing at a key nothing created.
It now writes the configured key, and only when those pods actually read this
Secret: an operator who points langyagent.secrets at their own Secret owns it,
and writing a decoy key here would just be noise. NOTES.txt follows the same
values, and prints a separate create command for that Secret rather than
telling them to add the key to one their pods do not read.

The mirror lane is refused at render time when the endpoint is set without the
key. The manager will not boot with one half configured, and the key is the
half we cannot infer — only the operator knows which project to mirror into —
so this fails before deploying instead of crashlooping after. The opposite
pairing stays fine: a key with no endpoint resolves to this install.

The mirror key is now read from stdin rather than passed as an argument. It is
a credential the operator pastes, so an argument puts it in shell history and
in the process list; the generated secrets nearby are unaffected because the
shell records the openssl call, not its output.

Also points the model-provider link at the page that documents it. Kept the
extensionless form: these docs are Mintlify and every link in the tree is
extensionless, so a .md suffix would be the odd one out.

* fix(charts): refuse a Langy secret key that collides with an app secret key

Review follow-up from CodeRabbit on #6138.

langyagent.secrets.internalSecretKey is configurable, and naming it after a
key the app Secret already holds (nextAuthSecret, virtualKeyPepper, either
LW_GATEWAY_* value) emitted that entry twice. The second write wins, so
Langy's generated value would silently become the session secret or the
gateway token — two credentials whose blast radii are meant to stay separate,
conflated by a values typo. The render now refuses and names both the key and
the Secret. Only when the two share a Secret: an operator-owned Secret
elsewhere may name its key whatever it likes.

fix(model-providers): latest alias follows named tier generations (#6147)

* fix(model-providers): latest alias follows named tier generations

The "latest" / "latest-mini" aliases matched OpenAI models by suffix
shape: unsuffixed meant flagship, "-mini" meant the fast tier. GPT-5.6
ships named tiers instead (sol flagship, terra balanced, luna fast) and
no unsuffixed model, so the whole generation was invisible to the picker
and every org seeded with an alias silently stayed on GPT-5.5.

Replaces the shape test with per-variant tier allow-lists, shared by the
server-side alias resolver and the client-side drawer picker so the two
cannot drift. Sorting now falls back to an explicit tier rank, keeping a
same-generation tie deterministic instead of catalog-order dependent.

Against the current catalog openai/latest resolves to gpt-5.6-sol and
openai/latest-mini to gpt-5.6-luna. Sol is the flagship tier and matches
gpt-5.5 token-for-token on price, so the alias tracks the new generation
without changing what a default costs. Terra is deliberately not an
alias target: a balanced middle tier answers neither question the
aliases ask, and stays explicitly selectable.

* refactor(model-providers): remove dead pickFlagshipModel

No production caller ever consumed it: the provider drawer's default
selectors initialise to null and stay unfilled until the user picks,
and its doc comment pointed at a ModelProviderDefaultSection component
that no longer exists in the tree. utils/modelTiers now has one
production consumer, the server-side alias resolver, instead of two.

Moves the same-generation tie-break scenario binding onto the
modelTiers unit test that already covered it, and drops the drawer
pre-fill rule from the feature file along with the behavior it
described.

feat(gateway): full voice support — /v1/audio/speech + /v1/audio/transcriptions for OpenAI and ElevenLabs (#6168)

* feat(gateway): /v1/audio/speech + /v1/audio/transcriptions for OpenAI and ElevenLabs

The contract has declared both audio routes since v0.1; this makes them real.
Bifrost v1.4.22 — already pinned — ships SpeechRequest and TranscriptionRequest
with both an openai and an elevenlabs provider, so no upgrade was needed.

Speech parses the OpenAI wire shape and returns the provider's raw audio bytes
with the right audio/* Content-Type — no JSON envelope, so an OpenAI SDK's
client.audio.speech.create() consumes the response unchanged. Transcriptions
parses the multipart form in the router (the only layer with the *http.Request),
caps uploads at 26 MB (OpenAI's own 25 MB limit plus framing) with a 413 before
any provider is contacted, forwards only the known OpenAI form fields, and
returns the standard JSON transcript.

Both ride the existing sync pipeline untouched, so virtual-key auth, model
resolution and allowlists, budgets, rate limits, and error transparency apply
exactly as they do to chat. ElevenLabs slots in as a Bifrost-native provider:
the ProviderID maps verbatim onto Bifrost's enum and the credential is a plain
API key, so mapProvider and credentialToBifrostKey needed no changes.

Usage lands on the gateway span with the measures audio is actually priced by:
token counts where the provider reports them (gpt-4o-mini-tts, gpt-4o-transcribe),
plus gen_ai.usage.input_chars for TTS and gen_ai.usage.audio_seconds for STT
(ElevenLabs and whisper-1 bill by character/duration and report no tokens).
Catalog pricing entries for audio models are a follow-up — the catalog's mode
union and price fields are chat/embedding-shaped today.

* chore(gateway-audio): stable id tie-breaker for the seeder provider pick

* fix(gateway-audio): request pcm_24000 from ElevenLabs for OpenAI pcm

Deep dogfooding (a Scenario voice run with ElevenLabs models for both
TTS and STT through the gateway) surfaced that Bifrost translates the
OpenAI pcm response format to ElevenLabs pcm_44100, which is gated to
the ElevenLabs Pro tier and carries the wrong sample rate for the
OpenAI contract (24kHz). The gateway now asks ElevenLabs for pcm_24000,
which every tier serves and which matches OpenAI semantics; Bifrost
passes unmapped formats through to output_format verbatim.

- speechResponseFormatFor extracted and unit-tested
- the live EL matrix cell now requests pcm and round-trips at 24kHz,
  so the tier gate and the sample rate are what the cell guards
- spec scenario added for the pcm contract

* test(gateway-audio): bind the audio spec, cover governance parity, fix exhaustive switch

Three real CI findings surfaced once the GitHub Actions outage cleared:

- feature-parity: the audio feature file had zero @scenario bindings.
  All 16 @unit/@integration scenarios now bind to Go tests (annotations
  plus new tests: bare-name resolution incl. allowlist on the bare form,

CodeRabbit flagged that the organization lookup used findFirst, so a

feat(aigateway): implement GET /v1/models behind the virtual key (#5941)

* feat(aigateway): implement GET /v1/models behind the virtual key

The endpoint existed but the provider router's ListModels was a stub, so
every VK got {"object":"list","data":null} and model-picker clients
(OpenWebUI, LibreChat, SDK helpers) showed nothing.

Build the list from the resolved bundle: routing-policy alias names are
always included; when models_allowed is set it is authoritative (listed
with the aliases, no upstream queried — anything outside it is blocked
at dispatch anyway); otherwise models are discovered from credentials
carrying a base URL via their OpenAI-shape GET /v1/models (vLLM,
LiteLLM, and Anthropic-compatible servers all serve it), with a short
timeout and per-endpoint failure isolation so one dead server cannot
blank the response. Models matching policy_rules.models deny patterns
are filtered out; entries are deduped, sorted, and emitted in OpenAI
list shape ({"id", "object": "model", "owned_by"}) with data always an
array — null breaks strict parsers.

Fixes #5939

* fix(aigateway): harden /v1/models discovery — concurrency, allow rules, x-api-key

Three review findings, each reproduced by a failing test first:

- Discovery queried endpoints serially, stacking per-endpoint latency
  (three 400ms servers took 1.2s); now concurrent, latency is the max.
- Allow policy rules targeting models were ignored, so the list promised
  models dispatch rejects with "is not in allowlist"; the filter now
  mirrors dispatch-time semantics (deny drops, allow gates when present).
- Only Authorization: Bearer was sent to endpoints; Anthropic-style
  servers requiring x-api-key rejected the probe and vanished from the
  list. Both headers are sent now.

* fix(aigateway): apply endpoint policy to discovery + bind /v1/models spec scenarios

Review follow-ups:

- Model discovery now runs the same customer-endpoint policy Dispatch
  applies (local-address blocking, HTTPS requirement, host allowlist)
  before contacting a base URL — the probe carries the credential's key,
  so it must not reach endpoints normal traffic would reject.
- Bind the two unbound @unit scenarios: the allowlist test carries the
  "does not query endpoints" scenario annotation, and a new router test
  binds "/v1/models reflects effective VK allowlist" by asserting the
  OpenAI list shape end-to-end through the HTTP handler.

* fix(aigateway): bound model-discovery fan-out and cap response size

ListModels spawned one unbounded goroutine + outbound request per
base-URL credential and decoded the upstream /v1/models response
without any size limit, so a wide bundle (or a client polling the
endpoint) could exhaust goroutines/connections, and a single
misbehaving upstream could OOM the gateway by streaming an
arbitrarily large model list.

Bound fan-out with a semaphore (modelsDiscoveryConcurrency = 8) and
cap the decoded response via http.MaxBytesReader plus a hard limit on
accepted model IDs, matching the MaxBytesReader pattern already used
for inbound request bodies elsewhere in the gateway.

Also fixes gofmt import ordering in models_discovery_test.go.

* fix(aigateway): attribute allowlisted models and log invalid list policy patterns

GET /v1/models had two listing-time gaps flagged in review:

- Allowlisted models (models_allowed) always shipped with owned_by ""
  because domain.Model.ProviderID was never set for them, unlike
  aliases and discovered models. Now attributed to the bundle's
  credential provider when it is unambiguous (single provider in the
  chain); left empty when the chain spans more than one provider
  rather than guessing.

- An invalid policy regex in a model deny/allow rule was silently
  skipped with no log, unlike dispatch-time Matcher.Check which fails
  closed on the same regexp.Compile error. A typo'd deny pattern could
  leave a model listed with no trace of why. filterModelsByPolicy now
  logs a warning when a pattern fails to compile.

* fix(aigateway): harden and complete GET /v1/models

Four defects found reviewing the model-listing implementation.

Wildcard allowlist entries were listed verbatim. models_allowed holds
patterns, not model IDs, so a VK allowlisted to "claude-haiku-*" got a
literal "claude-haiku-*" in its model picker, which dispatch then forwards
upstream as a model no provider has. Wildcards now expand against
discovery, and discovered models are filtered back down by the allowlist
so the list never promises a model dispatch would reject. The glob
matching moves to domain.BundleConfig.AllowsModel, shared with the
resolver instead of duplicated.

Discovery followed redirects. The endpoint policy vets the configured
base URL, not wherever it points next, so a 302 reached an address the
policy never saw with the credential's x-api-key attached (Go strips
Authorization across hosts, not custom headers). Redirects are no longer
followed, and every resolved address is re-checked against the policy
immediately before connect, which also closes the DNS-rebinding window
the pre-flight check leaves open.

Nothing was cached. GET /v1/models sits outside the dispatch interceptor
chain, so the per-VK rate limiter never sees it: one cheap inbound
request fanned out to every configured endpoint, and a polling model
picker became sustained load on the customer's own servers. Catalogs are
now memoised per credential chain for 60s, and concurrent misses collapse
onto a single probe.

The response was missing `created`, and `owned_by` could be empty. Both
are required fields of the OpenAI Model object, so strict clients found a
null where they expect an int / string. Models the gateway cannot
attribute to a provider are owned by "langwatch".

Discovery moves out of bifrost.go into models_discovery.go alongside its
existing test file.

* fix(gateway): ship routing-policy aliases and rules on the config bundle

Dogfooding GET /v1/models surfaced that a VK's model aliases never
appeared in the listing and its models.deny rules never filtered
anything, even though the materialiser produces both correctly.

The internal config route fetched the virtual key with only its scopes.
resolvePolicySideOfBundle reads vk.routingPolicy off whatever the caller
included, so with the relation absent it fell through to an empty alias
map and empty deny/allow lists. The gateway has therefore never resolved
a model alias or enforced a model policy rule in a real deployment.

The materialiser's own integration test does the include itself, which is
why it stayed green. The new test drives the route, so the route's query
is what is pinned.

Also make the model-discovery cache release its waiters if a probe
panics, instead of leaving an entry nobody ever completes for every later
caller of that credential chain to block on.

* fix(aigateway): resolve model aliases to their provider and model name

Aliases arrive from the control plane in "provider/model" form, which is
a routing instruction, not a model ID. The wire mapper kept the whole
string as the model and left the provider empty, so an alias for
"openai/gpt-5-mini" dispatched a model literally named
"openai/gpt-5-mini" to whichever credential came first.

This was unreachable until the config route started shipping aliases, and
GET /v1/models now advertises them to clients: a model picker that offers
"chat" has to be able to call it.

Spec: specs/ai-gateway/provider-routing.feature, "alias resolves to
configured provider".

* style(aigateway): drop em-dashes from the model-listing comments and spec

* fix(aigateway): stop a cancelled caller from poisoning the discovery cache

Review follow-ups on the model-listing cache.

The caller that missed the cache ran the probe on its own request context,
so a client hanging up mid-probe cancelled the fetch every concurrent
waiter was blocked on, and the resulting empty catalog was then cached for
the full minute. The probe now runs detached from the caller with its own
ceiling, and an empty result gets a short TTL so a transient upstream
outage does not blank the model list.

The cache key hashes the credential chain instead of keeping the API key
in plaintext, which is what its comment already claimed. Test flags
written by httptest handler goroutines are atomic, so a regression reports
the intended failure rather than a data race.

* chore: re-trigger CI

The workflow runs for this branch were queued about 78 minutes without a
runner and GitHub evicted them, so nine workflows show red having never
executed a single job. Re-running them through the API does not help: on
a fork pull request the re-run creates an attempt with zero jobs and ends
in startup_failure, while runs triggered naturally complete fine.

An empty commit is the only way left to get a real run. No file changes.
