feat(server): run Langy on npx installs and slim the install to what gets used (#6144)

* feat(server): run Langy on a laptop install, and stop shipping the model nobody asked for

`npx @langwatch/server` had no assistant at all and downloaded 4.7GB before
it would start, a fifth of which was a language model for one evaluator.
Both are addressed here, in the same spirit: install what the person is
going to use, and let them ask for the rest.

THE ASSISTANT NOW RUNS LOCALLY. Langy was built for a cluster — a
sandboxed container runtime under it, a manager running as root so each
conversation's worker gets its own UID. A laptop has neither and cannot be
asked to get them. What it does have is the single trusted user the cluster
went to such lengths to simulate: every worker already runs as that person,
with that person's own credentials, and there is no second tenant to
protect them from. So the workers run unsandboxed as the user who started
the server, and the service says so rather than implying a boundary that is
not there. The manager itself ships inside the mono-binary the gateway
already downloads, so the assistant costs one 41MB runtime and a 4MB CLI —
both fetched once, and only when it is enabled.

THE PII MODEL IS NOW OPT-IN. The evaluator environment installed every
evaluator, and one dominated the rest: presidio's spacy model is 619MB of a
1.6GB environment. Measured on this machine, dropping it takes that
environment to 982MB. Every other evaluator still installs and every one of
their 43 routes still registers. LangWatch's own secret and PII redaction of
traces never used presidio and is untouched.

Absent is not the same as broken, so the product says which it is: the
evaluator pickers mark PII detection "Not installed on this server" with the
one line that installs it, and running it anyway fails with that same
sentence instead of the bare 404 a missing evaluator route produces.

Three things found while doing this, each of which broke the install on its
own:

  - The dev-build fallback wrote a wrapper that hardcoded `aigateway` as the
    mono-binary's first argument, so the NLP engine and the Langy agent both
    booted a second gateway and died fighting over its port. The binary
    answers `--version` itself, which was the wrapper's only other job.
  - Locating the package source counted `../../..` from a bundled entrypoint,
    which is one level short from source — running the CLI from a checkout
    failed after every predep had already downloaded. It walks up now.
  - LW_GATEWAY_BASE_URL was scaffolded as the app's own URL. The gateway
    process reads that name to mean the opposite direction and gets its value
    elsewhere, so this only ever reached the app, which hands it to Langy's
    workers and CLI users as an OpenAI-compatible base URL — pointed at a
    server with no /v1 surface.

Verified end to end on a real `npx` install: the stack comes up on the
lean environment, the assistant answers, and its answer comes from running
`langwatch prompt list --format json` against the local control plane.

* feat(server): opt-in lingua and legacy evaluators, and prune the app tree to production dependencies

Second round of the lean-install work, applying the same judgment to
everything else that taxes a laptop install without earning it.

LANGUAGE DETECTION AND LEGACY EVALUATORS ARE NOW OPT-IN, exactly like the
PII detector: LANGWATCH_ENABLE_LINGUA and LANGWATCH_ENABLE_LEGACY_EVALUATORS
in the scaffolded .env, off by default, one line and a restart to flip.
Language detection stays visible in the pickers as "Not installed on this
server" with the line that installs it. The legacy evaluators instead
vanish from the product entirely: they are deprecated, nobody should adopt
one today, and a card that only says "you cannot pick this" is clutter. A
saved evaluation that still references one fails with the exact switch to
bring them back rather than a bare 404. Measured on this machine the
evaluator environment is now 886MB against 1.6GB for the full set; the
legacy family's marginal weight turned out small because the current ragas
family shares its heavy dependencies, so its case rests on being deprecated,
not on bytes.

THE APP TREE IS PRUNED TO PRODUCTION DEPENDENCIES after its build, in the
exact order the production Dockerfile uses: install everything, build,
prune, regenerate the prisma client. The earlier attempt at --prod failed
because it ran at install time, before the build that needs the dev
tooling; pruning after the build is the sequence every helm and docker
deployment already runs. This drops the build tooling and every workspace
member's dev dependencies from the served tree, including the 204MB
coding-agent binary that reached installs through a test-only dependency.
Verified against a relocated-shaped copy of the tree: 2.3GB of node_modules
became 1.6GB, the pruned tree keeps tsx and prisma (both genuinely run in
production), and what remains beyond them is reachable from production
dependencies. A checkout is never pruned; the guard only fires for the
relocated install under LANGWATCH_HOME.

Two defects found while proving it:

  - The "is the prisma client generated" check looked at the top-level
    node_modules/.prisma path that npm and yarn use, but pnpm generates
    into the virtual store, so the check never passed and every boot
    re-ran the entire prepare step believing the client was missing. The
    check now knows both layouts; a second boot is now a sub-second no-op
    where it used to re-run install, build, and generate.
  - Turning the assistant off left OPENCODE_AGENT_URL and the forced
    rollout flag in the app's env, so the product offered an assistant
    whose agent was never started and every send would hang. The resolved
    feature toggles now ride into the app and workers env explicitly, the
    assistant's variables are stripped when it is off, and installs whose
    .env predates a toggle get the truth instead of the app's
    assume-available default.

Verified end to end on a fresh run: the stack boots on the lean
environment, the evaluator API hides legacy and marks lingua and presidio
not installed with their env vars, every remaining evaluator route still
registers, and the assistant still answers.

* fix(server): survive the previous release's binary, and a keyless boot

The npx smoke caught both, on macOS, in one run.

The smoke tests an unreleased CLI against the PREVIOUS release's mono-binary,
and that binary predates the langyagent service: asked to run it, it exits
with "unknown service" and the whole install failed with it. Three changes
make that window honest instead of fatal:

  - startAll now probes the binary for the langyagent subcommand (an unknown
    command makes the binary print the services it does have) and, when the
    binary predates the assistant, boots without it and prints a notice
    naming the reason, with the app env stripped exactly as if the assistant
    were toggled off. Verified against the real v3.5.0 release binary: full
    stack healthy, notice printed, no assistant.
  - The aigateway predep re-downloads when the installed binary's version
    differs from the release the CLI ships with, instead of accepting any
    binary forever. Without this, an install that upgrades the npm package
    keeps its old binary and the assistant never arrives at all. Dev runs
    (version 0.0.0-dev) are exempt and keep their local builds.
  - The smoke workflow now asserts the assistant outcome explicitly: either
    the CLI reported it healthy (and the port answers), or it printed the
    deliberate-skip notice. A dead langyagent that something else vouched
    for no longer passes, which is what let the ubuntu jobs go green while
    the macOS job told the truth.

The keyless boot: the scaffolded .env ships fill-me-in lines like
OPENAI_API_KEY=, and readEnvFile passed them into the app as empty strings.
An empty string sails past a `?? "bogus"` guard, and the OpenAI client then
throws at module load, taking the server down for every install that had
not configured a provider yet. readEnvFile now treats a blank value as not
configured, and the one guard in the app that could still meet an empty
value uses `||` so it falls back either way. Verified with a keyless boot
end to end: full stack healthy with no provider configured anywhere.

* refactor(server): address review round one

The substantive ones:

  - The assistant is now genuinely optional at boot. It starts before the
    app tier, and a start failure (or a health timeout) flips the install
    to assistant-off with a notice instead of tearing every service down,
    which is what "optional" claimed and the code contradicted. The
    capability probe got the same treatment: a timeout and a failure path
    that read as "not supported" rather than throwing.
  - The opencode predep re-downloads when the pinned version changes, the
    same lockstep rule the ai-gateway predep follows; without it, bumping
    the pin never reached existing installs.
  - The ai-gateway version check now also exempts binaries reporting
    "dev", which the comment promised and the condition did not deliver.
  - The CLI shim single-quotes its paths; inside double quotes a $ or
    backtick in LANGWATCH_HOME would expand.
  - The unsafe-isolation flag is only passed to the manager when the
    resolved ENVIRONMENT is local-like, mirroring the manager's own guard
    instead of leaning on it across a process boundary.

The conventions ones: named parameters for the evaluator-availability
functions, is-prefixed names for the new boolean toggles, the misplaced
service docblock reattached, dead `as never` casts dropped now that the
service name is in the union, test describes that said "when the assistant
is turned off" while testing other conditions split into their own
describes, the venvs test clears all three toggle env keys instead of one,
and the assistant spec scenario describes the observable answer rather
than the CLI mechanism behind it.

* refactor(server): address review round two

One real catch among the conventions: the predep registry resolved the
feature toggles from the shell environment alone, so a persisted
LANGWATCH_ENABLE_LANGY=false in ~/.langwatch/.env still downloaded the
assistant runtime it would never start. All consumers now resolve through
one resolveEffectiveFeatures helper (persisted .env first, shell on top),
which also removes the merge expression duplicated across three files.

The rest: the langy CLI fast path verifies the entrypoint actually exists
before trusting the version marker, so a half-deleted cli/node_modules
repairs itself on the next boot; makeOpencodePredep is split into
detect/tarball/zip helpers under the exported-function size limit, with the
zip cleanup moved into a finally; isHiddenFromUi replaces hideFromUi; and
the reverse-stop-order test now counts all nine handles, with the workers
stub logging its stop instead of being silently uncountable.

feat(scenarios): hand scenario runs to the simulations tab already open (#6137)

* feat(scenarios): hand scenario runs to the simulations tab already open

Running a suite in a loop used to leave a trail of LangWatch tabs, one per
batch, because the SDK had no way to know a tab was already showing the runs.

The simulations page now identifies itself. When the SDK opens a tab it stamps
a per-machine key on the URL; the page lifts that key out of the address bar,
keeps it for that tab only, and registers it for as long as its simulation SSE
subscription is connected. Presence lives in Redis as a TTL'd sorted set of tab
ids, refreshed server-side so a background tab's throttled timers can never
expire the very tab this exists to reuse.

POST /api/scenario-events/browser-tab answers the SDK's question: if a tab on
that machine is listening, the batch is broadcast to it over the existing
tenant channel and the response says so, and the SDK opens nothing. The tab
routes itself to the new batch and offers a toast to stop following. The URL is
built server-side from the project, set and batch ids, so a handoff can only
ever point a browser at this instance.

Scoped by project and by machine key, so CI runs and colleagues never steer a
browser that is not theirs.

* fix(scenarios): keep a followed tab claimable and never lose a handoff

Three defects that only showed up once a real browser and a real suite were
driving this end to end.

A disconnected client left its subscription generator suspended forever. tRPC
v10 callers do not populate `opts.signal`, so the emitter wait had nothing to
abort on: the generator kept its listener, its refresh timer, and its tab
registration until the TTL. The request's own signal now rides in on the tRPC
context, which ends the wait, runs the cleanup, and incidentally stops every
other SSE subscription from leaking a listener per dropped client.

De-registering the instant a subscription ended was too eager. A tab drops its
subscription whenever it routes somewhere — including to the run this feature
just handed it — so the very next run found no tab and opened a new one. A
retiring tab now stays claimable for a few seconds and is restored outright if
it reconnects, while a genuinely closed tab still stops taking runs almost
immediately.

A broadcast is fire-and-forget, so a handoff sent while a tab was mid-reload
was reported as delivered and then seen by nobody. Handoffs are now parked with
a short TTL and claimed by the next subscription for that machine key.

* test(scenarios): bind every tab-handoff scenario to its test

The feature file described de-registration as instant, which the grace window
replaced, and claimed a permission-grain test that does not exist. Both are now
worded as what the suite actually proves, and the parked-handoff behaviour that
came out of dogfooding has scenarios of its own.

* fix(scenarios): harden the tab registry and the parked-handoff path

Review follow-ups, most of them things that only bite in the corners.

A late goodbye could revive a dead tab: `unregister` re-scored an entry that
had already aged out, pushing it back inside the live window for the grace
period. The retire now only ever lowers a score.

Parked handoff pickup is atomic, so two subscriptions reconnecting at once
cannot both claim the same run. The tab also remembers the last run it
followed, so the parked copy of a handoff it already took cannot yank it back
from wherever the user has since navigated.

Path ids are encoded when building the handoff URL — both are caller-supplied
and only length-bounded, so a `#` would have truncated everything after it.

In the Redis-less single-instance mode, empty registry entries and unclaimed
parked handoffs are now evicted instead of accumulating for the life of the
process. The grace-vs-TTL invariant the retire arithmetic depends on is stated
and asserted at load. Tests use the exported key builder rather than
hand-copying the Redis key format, and two of them now do what their names say.

* style(scenarios): drop em dashes from the new comments

* refactor(scenarios): address review on the browser-tab handoff

Fall back to GET+DEL only when the Redis server rejects GETDEL. The client
exposes the method whatever the server supports, so the old capability check
never fired and a Redis below 6.2 dropped parked handoffs outright.

Move the tab-presence lifecycle out of the SSE resolver into
startScenarioTabPresence, so registration, refresh and retirement live
together and the subscription stays focused on relaying events.

Replace the always-false constant comparison with an assertion in the
registry suite, and reword the feature steps as observable outcomes rather
than registry and transport mechanics.

* fix(tracking): stop a gtag poll from crashing once its page is gone

trackEvent polls for gtag for up to ten seconds and nobody cancels it, so a
tick can land after the page it was started from has been torn down. The
getter read a bare window, which is a ReferenceError once that global is
gone, thrown from inside a timer where no caller can catch it.

Read gtag through a typeof guard, and have pollForGlobal end the poll when
its getter throws instead of letting the error escape to the top level.

This is what failed integration shard 2: every test passed and the run still
exited 1 on an uncaught ReferenceError from a stranded poll.

* feat(simulations): swap the follow toast for a connected badge

The toast interrupted the person who started the run to announce the
expected outcome, and offered a Stop following control nobody asked for.
Runs are now followed silently; the only trace of the feature is a quiet
Connected to local run badge in the external set header, with a hover
popover explaining that runs started on this machine land in this tab.

With no control to persist, the opt-out plumbing in useScenarioTabFollow
goes away too. A tab that should not follow is simply one the user opened
themselves, which never registers.

* chore(vite): stop watching .claude working files

A dev-server log teed into .claude/tmp is appended on every request, and
with the directory watched each append reloads the page, the same loop the
server*.log ignore already covers under a different name.

* fix(simulations): drop the old-behaviour line from the badge popover

A first-time viewer has no old behaviour to compare against, so the
sentence was noise explaining a before-state nobody arriving fresh knows
about.

fix(gateway): make guardrails, metrics, budgets and onboarding actually work (#6143)

* fix(gateway): make guardrails actually enforce

The guardrail seam was broken in three places at once, and each one on its
own was enough to let every request through.

The control-plane endpoint was a stub that returned allow and said so in a
log line. It now runs the evaluators bound to the virtual key's guardrails,
scoped by project, filtered by archive state and direction, and aggregates
them into one verdict.

The request schema accepted the storage enum values pre and post, while the
data plane sends the contract's request and response. Every live call failed
validation, and the data plane treated that failure as permission to
proceed. The schema now uses the wire vocabulary from contract 4.6 and the
service exports it so there is one source of truth.

The Go client parsed a field named action while the control plane returns
decision. Every verdict fell through to the allow default, so replacing the
stub alone would not have restored enforcement. The client now reads the
contract shape, and an unrecognised verdict is an error rather than a
silent allow.

Guardrails also failed open unconditionally on any evaluation error, so a
control plane outage quietly disabled every guardrail while the UI still
showed them as active. The pipeline now honours the per-direction fail-open
flags the bundle already carried, defaulting to fail-closed, and reports
guardrail_upstream_unavailable when it stops a request that way.

Contract tests pin the wire shape on both sides, including a check that
reads the TypeScript schema from the Go test, so a rename on either side
fails the build instead of silently disabling enforcement.

* fix(gateway): budgets accrue and enforce on every window, and say so when they cannot

Budget spend is written to the ClickHouse ledger by the trace fold and read
back from the pre-aggregated rollup. The rollup only ever returns a row when
the period the reader asks for is exactly the period the materialised view
bucketed the debit into, and the two had drifted apart on four of the six
windows a budget can be created with:

  minute, hour, total  view bucketed by day, reader asked for the epoch
  week                 view bucketed on Sunday, reader asked for Monday

Spend accrued correctly and was then never read. A budget on any of those
windows sat at $0.00 forever, never warned, and never blocked, no matter how
much traffic ran through it. Only day and month ever worked.

Each window now buckets by its own period, the reader computes the same
thing branch for branch, and an integration test writes a debit per window
through the real repository and reads it back so the two cannot drift again.

Two things that let this stay invisible for so long are fixed as well:

- When spend cannot be totalled at all, the budgets list and detail said
  "$0.00 / $X, 0%" with total confidence. They now say spend is
  unavailable and that nothing is being enforced.
- Traffic is attributed to the project a key is scoped to, so a
  project-scoped budget and a team-scoped key never interact. A budget no
  active key can ever spend against now says so.

Issue #6141

* test(gateway): drive the guardrail check over real signed HTTP

The service-level tests would not have caught the defect that mattered

Closes #6140

* fix(gateway): make the stream-chunk fail-open visible instead of inferred

The stream-chunk direction swallows its own evaluation error on purpose, so a
slow or unreachable policy service never stalls a stream a user is already
reading. That behaviour is unchanged and deliberate. What was wrong is that it
returned a plain allow, so a chunk that passed unchecked and a chunk a
guardrail actually cleared were the same value. An operator watching
enforcement could not tell an evaluator outage from healthy traffic, which is
the same shape of invisible non-enforcement as the stub this changeset
replaced.

GuardrailVerdict now carries FailedOpen and the reason. EvaluateChunk sets
them on its error branch, keeping the action allow and the error nil, and
stamps langwatch.guardrail.stream_chunk_fail_open on the active span per
contract 7b. The reason stays off the metric label, where unbounded text would
explode cardinality.

The metrics decorator counts a verdict that failed open as fail_open, so
gateway_guardrail_verdicts_total{direction="stream_chunk",verdict="fail_open"}
is now a real series. Four docs said that series could never appear; they now
say it is the one to watch, because stream_chunk is the direction that fails
open whether or not the key opted in. The Grafana panel query already grouped
by direction with none pinned, so only the prose changed.

Tests drive the real client against a control plane that refuses the call and
observe the verdict, the span attribute and the counter, rather than asserting
on a message string. A cleared chunk is pinned as not a bypass, so "count
fail_open" cannot be satisfied by counting every chunk as degraded.

* fix(gateway): forward tools and mcps to the guardrail check, and cover the delete

The control plane scores content.tools and content.mcps, but the data plane
extracted only messages and dropped the rest, so a policy written to catch a
dangerous tool or MCP definition scored the prose alone and passed. Both now
travel with the request direction, absent from the wire when the caller sent
none, covered by a payload carrying messages plus both.

That was half a fix landing without the other half: the consumer was taught to
read these fields earlier in this PR while the producer never sent them.

* fix(auth): sign-in works on a non-default dev port, and failures say why

Closes #6148.

Signing in returned 403 INVALID_ORIGIN on any checkout not running on the
default port 5560, which is the normal state once you have a second
checkout. scripts/start.sh aligns BASE_HOST and NEXTAUTH_URL to $PORT for
exactly this reason, but the Node entry points then load .env with
override: true and put the committed 5560 back, so the origin gate in
server/routes/auth.ts and better-auth's own baseURL/trustedOrigins both
ended up checking against a port nothing was listening on. Because .env
wins, no shell variable could work around it.

alignDevAuthUrlsToPort in src/env-create.mjs realigns the app's own
address after every .env file has loaded, at the single point where env is
resolved, so the Hono gate and better-auth cannot disagree. Only a plain
http://localhost:<port> is treated as stale: 127.0.0.1, proxies, tunnels
and haven's hostnames are someone's deliberate setup, the same rule the
shell-side scripts/lib/sanitize-dev-env.sh already applies. Everything
else pinned in .env, including LW_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL, still wins.

The sign-in and sign-up screens replaced every failure with one fixed
sentence and caught with no error binding, so the real reason never
reached the person reading it. Both now map the failure to wording that
says what to do, show it next to the form as well as in a toast, and never
put an internal code on screen. The gate also logs the expected and
received address, which the 403 access-log line alone never carried.

* test(gateway): drop the cast that let the parity test pass through a divergence

The drawer/gateway parity test cast the service result with as unknown as

* fix(aigateway): make the budget warning header actually reach the client

Two independent faults kept X-LangWatch-Budget-Warning off every response.

The precheck never produced a warning for the case customers hit. A budget
with on_breach block had no warning branch at all, so a hard cap on approach
stayed silent until it started returning 402, and a warn budget only spoke at
90% while the control plane, the dashboard banner and the CLI all call 80% a
warning. A QA run sitting at 85.86% of its limit fell straight through that
gap. The precheck now warns from 80% for every applicable scope whatever its
on_breach, matching budget.service.ts.

The transport then dropped whatever survived. Response metadata was written
only after dispatch returned, but the non-streaming keep-alive commits the
header block as soon as it writes its first byte, roughly 45s in. Any
completion slower than that lost the budget warning, the gateway request id,
the fallback count and the cache mode, which is precisely the long call a
customer needs the warning on. The pipeline now accumulates metadata behind a
mutex-guarded accumulator seeded on the request context, so the keep-alive
flushes what is known so far before committing.

The header value carried the literal near_limit, which named neither the
scope nor how close it was. It now carries <scope>:<pct> per contract.md.

Tests drive the real budget checker through the real router over a real
socket and read the header off the client response.

* fix(gateway): carry the guardrail failure mode across the wire (#6157)

failure_mode was emitted by the materialiser, decoded into
guardrailWire.FailureMode, and then dropped when the domain config was built.
GuardrailsConfig.RequestFailOpen and ResponseFailOpen were declared and never
assigned, so they read false forever.

That was invisible while nothing consulted them. It stops being invisible in
this branch, where guardrailOutcome now honours exactly those two flags: a
guardrail an operator explicitly set to FAIL_OPEN would block traffic on any
evaluator error while the UI kept describing it as fail-open. The safe
direction, but the same shape of lie this changeset exists to remove, pointed
the other way.

Both flags are populated from the decoded failure mode now. The flag is per
direction while the mode is per guardrail, because a direction is one call and
an unreachable control plane produces no per-guardrail verdicts to apply a mode
to. A direction therefore fails open only when every guardrail on it opted in:
one FAIL_CLOSED guardrail means the operator asked for the request to stop when
it cannot be evaluated, and an outage is exactly that case. An absent
failure_mode fails closed, matching the Prisma default, so an older control
plane cannot be read as permission to proceed. A direction with no guardrails
is vacuously fail-open, since there is nothing there to bypass.

The regression test drives the real control-plane JSON through the real client
into the real interceptor. Neither half is individually wrong, so a unit test on
either one cannot catch this; only the seam can. Verified red without the fix,
2 of 3 failing. Fixture shape reused from the audit probes on
audit/unenforced-controls rather than rewritten.

feat(gateway): flow VK tags to customer spans as trace labels (#5995)

* feat(gateway): flow VK tags to customer spans as trace labels

VK tags (config.metadata.tags) were stored by the UI but dead everywhere
downstream: the materialiser never lifted them into the bundle, the Go
wire had no field to receive them (BundleConfig.VKTags permanently nil),
spans carried no tag attribute, and cache-rule vk_tags matchers compared
against an always-empty list.

The materialiser now emits a top-level vk_tags, the gateway parses it
into BundleConfig.VKTags, and the customer-span emitter stamps the tags
as langwatch.labels — the exact attribute the trace pipeline ingests
into metadata.labels, so tagged gateway traffic becomes filterable under
the Trace Explorer's "Label" filter with zero explorer changes. Cache
rule vk_tags matchers start working as a side effect.

Fixes #5993

* fix(gateway): bound VK tags before they become per-request span labels

VK tags stop being inert storage once the gateway stamps them on every
customer span: each request writes them into the ClickHouse trace
attribute map, and the Trace Explorer's Label facet aggregates every
distinct value it finds. The tag list was unbounded in both directions,
with no cap on count or length, no de-duplication, and a REST body that
reaches the same field as the drawer, so a single virtual key could put
arbitrary cardinality on every trace it produced.

Tags are now normalised where the config is parsed: trimmed, blanks and
duplicates dropped, each tag capped by code point so truncation can
never split a surrogate pair, and the list capped in length. It is a
normalisation rather than a rejection because the same parse runs on the
gateway's config-fetch path, where a stored key that predates the bounds
still has to resolve to a servable bundle.

Also covers the pipeline hop that carries the tags from the bundle into
the trace params. It has four independent exits (sync success, sync
failure, stream-establish failure, stream close) and had no test, so a
dropped assignment on any of them would have left every other test green
while labels quietly stopped reaching traces.

* feat(gateway): the VK Tags field explains itself behind the label's (i)

The Tags field carried its explanation in a permanent block under the
input, written in vocabulary only someone who has read the gateway code
would recognise ("VKs", "AND-subset semantics", a rule matcher spelled as
a code literal). Every sibling field in the drawer puts its explanation
behind the label's information icon; Tags now does too, and the field
below the input is clear unless it has something urgent to say.

The copy is rewritten for the person typing a tag. It leads with what
tags buy them, then states the consequence this PR introduces: every
trace the key sends carries its tags as labels, visible to anyone with
access to the project. Cache-rule matching is described in plain terms
rather than as set semantics, and the save-time normalisation is spelled
out, since the caps are otherwise applied silently.

Silence on the caps was the real gap. Typing a 33rd tag used to lose it
with nothing said anywhere, so the field now raises a notice while the
typed list is over a cap, and only then. The notice and the copy share
one module with the parsing both drawers do on save, so the two drawers
cannot drift and neither can the numbers: they are interpolated from the
limits normalizeVkTags enforces and pinned by a test.

Also corrects the field's own maxLength. It counted UTF-16 code units
against a per-tag limit measured in code points, so a full list of
astral-plane tags could be clipped by the input before the server ever
saw it. The budget is doubled, which makes clipping impossible for any
list the server would have kept whole.

Covered by an RTL test that renders the real drawer and the real popover
(no shallow rendering, no stubbing of the component under test) plus a
unit test over the copy and the caps. Reverting the change fails 8 of
the 10 RTL cases.

docs(self-hosting): pre-create ClickHouse Secret when autogen.enabled=false (#4452)

#4447 (the ArgoCD-safe gating) added a render-time validator that
hard-fails when clickhouse.chartManaged=true AND autogen.enabled=false
AND clickhouse.auth.existingSecret points at the default
<release>-clickhouse name. The deployment composes CLICKHOUSE_URL at
runtime from a password key only when the operator overrides the
existingSecret name to a non-default value; with the default name the

pre-create, so operators following the docs against >=3.4.1 hit
"clickhouse.chartManaged=true with autogen.enabled=false requires
clickhouse.auth.existingSecret to be set to an operator-owned Secret
name different from the default..." on first install.

  create langwatch-clickhouse-creds with password + clusterSecret,
  add clickhouse.auth.existingSecret: langwatch-clickhouse-creds to
  the Application values stanza, bump targetRevision 3.3.0 -> 3.4.1
- kubernetes-helm.mdx: same kubectl create block in the Production
  Deployment section, add clickhouse.auth.existingSecret to the
  example values file under the existing chart-managed ClickHouse

fix(licensing): personal workspaces no longer consume plan limits (#6189)

* fix(licensing): personal workspaces no longer consume plan limits

Every person on the free plan should be able to track their own
coding-agent usage, which needs a personal workspace. That workspace was
spending the allowance the customer bought for real work: a free
organization gets 2 projects and 1 team, and a provisioned personal
workspace consumed one of each. A user with a personal workspace and one
real project was already at 2/2 and could not create a second.

getProjectCount and getTeamCount now exclude isPersonal rows. Both are
the single source the enforcement path, the usage page, and the license
status panel read, so the number a customer sees always matches the
number that blocks them. Project and team limits themselves are
unchanged: free still stops at 2 real projects.

Personal workspaces are bounded to one per (organization, user) by a
partial unique index, so excluding them cannot be used to evade quota.
Resources created inside a personal project (datasets, workflows,
prompts) still count, since those are not bounded.

Also removes getOrganizationProjectsCount, a zero-caller export that
counted projects without either the archived or the personal filter.

* fix(navigation): a personal workspace is never the ambient organization context

A personal team holds exactly one project, so it satisfied the
unqualified "first team that has a project" lookup that picks the
ambient team, and won it whenever it sorted first. Everything scoped to
the ambient project followed: the Model Providers settings page files
every write against `project.id`, so an organization's model provider
credentials landed inside one member's private workspace, where nobody
else can see or rotate them.

The remembered selection was the stickier half of it. `projectSlug`
falls back to the persisted `selectedProjectSlug`, which the hook writes
on every resolution including personal ones, so one visit to
/[personal-slug]/traces from the personal sidebar carried the personal
project onto every later page that has no project of its own. That path
resolved before the team fallback ever ran, so the reported line was
only half the bug. DashboardLayout already worked around the symptom
with its `isProjectAnchoredRoute` guard, added so the admin banner would
stop firing on sticky-resolved personal teams.

The address bar is the line between intent and stickiness. A personal
project or team named in the URL resolves exactly as before, so the
personal sidebar, the personal chrome, and /me are untouched. Only the
ambient fallback reorders: shared teams with a project, then any shared
team, then whatever is left. An organization whose only team is personal
still resolves to it, so a solo user never ends up without a context.

A shared team with no project now outranks a personal one that has one.
That leaves `project` undefined on such an organization, which is the
existing "Create a project first" state rather than a silent write into
somewhere private.

* feat(onboarding): coding-agent signups get their personal workspace

The coding-agent track ends on /me, which reads the signer's personal
workspace. Provisioning it lazily at the first CLI login meant the page
the track lands on arrived empty and could only point at a command the
user had not run yet.

`initializeOrganization` now calls `PersonalWorkspaceService.ensure()` on
the governance branch. Only the timing changes: the service is
idempotent and bounded to one workspace per organization and user by a
partial unique index, so CLI login still calls it unchanged and the two
paths converge on the same workspace whichever runs first. Provisioning
is non-fatal, matching organization.acceptInvite, so a failure leaves the
organization intact and user.personalContext backfills on the next
session.

This was held twice. Once on plan accounting: a personal workspace spent
a project and a team out of the free plan's allowance of two and one, so
a free customer landed on their first real project already at the
ceiling. Fixed in the commits this builds on, and pinned here by
asserting getProjectCount and getTeamCount stay at 0 and 1 with the
workspace in place. Once on ambient-context selection, where a personal
workspace could win the app's current project and take
organization-scoped writes with it, fixed in the previous commit.

ADR-038 v6 reserved personal-workspace provisioning for CLI login; the
spec and the ADR record that this supersedes it, and why.

fix(traces): deserialize stored span attributes on trace read paths (#4735)

* fix(traces): deserialize stored span attributes on trace read paths

RAG spans came back with contexts: [] from GET /api/trace/{id}: ClickHouse
stores SpanAttributes as Map(String, String), and the trace-details read
path cast the raw map straight into NormalizedSpan, so extractContexts saw
a JSON string and dropped it on its Array.isArray check.

- extractContexts now JSON-parses string values, matching the defensive
  convention of extractInput/extractOutput/getAnnotatedType in the same file
- ClickHouseTraceService.mapSpanRow and the trace-scoped span listing
  repository now run deserializeAttributes/ensureStringRecord (shared from
  the app-layer repository) like every other stored_spans read site, so
  params/timestamps stop leaking JSON-encoded strings
- resolve-offloaded-traces accepts eventref values that arrive already
  parsed (deserialized read paths) as well as raw JSON strings
- the span listing repository's dedup tuple compared the StartTime SELECT
  alias (milliseconds) against max(StartTime) as DateTime64, returning zero
  spans for every trace; the tuple now table-qualifies the raw column like
  the trace-details service does
- removed extractSpanFromRow, dead since the joined-row path was refactored

Covered by specs/traces/rag-contexts-read-deserialization.feature, new
span.mapper unit tests, and a testcontainers ClickHouse round-trip test.

* test(traces): decouple integration tests and drop non-null assertion chains

* fix(traces): keep decoded event references resolvable

fix(traces): stop suppressing audio spans, record audio input and output, show model names as-is (#6191)

* fix(traces): stop eating audio spans, record audio input/output, drop model-name magic

Dogfooding the deployed gateway audio endpoints in the Trace Explorer
surfaced three defects:

- Every successful TTS span was silently suppressed: the zero-cost
  claude-code probe heuristic (no completion tokens, no cost, no
  extracted output) structurally matches every speech span, and also
  swallowed duration-priced STT (scribe) and embeddings spans. The
  suppression is now gated to chat-shaped request types, the only shape
  probes actually have. Proven end to end: gen_ai.speech spans now land
  in ClickHouse.
- Audio traces rendered with empty input and output. Speech spans now
  carry the synthesized text as the input message and transcription
  spans carry the transcript as the output message.
- The trace UI abbreviated model names through a hardcoded table
  (gpt-5-mini rendered as "5-mini"). Model ids are now shown as-is;
  the only remaining transform is dropping Anthropic's [1m]
  context-variant suffix, which is wire metadata rather than identity.

* fix(traces): address CodeRabbit review on #6191

- messages built in the trace bridge now marshal through encoding/json
  (a jsonString helper swept all 13 Sprintf %q sites): Go %q escaping is
  not JSON, so a transcript containing a vertical tab produced an
  unparseable gen_ai message attribute; regression test round-trips a
  control character
- the context-variant suffix strip is scoped to claude ids, bracket
  suffixes on other providers' ids stay untouched, with tests
- the real-generation suppression fixtures are chat-shaped again so
  they keep proving completion tokens and cost prevent the drop

* chore(traces): gofmt the emitter after the jsonString sweep

* refactor(traces): show model ids exactly as reported, delete abbreviateModel

The [1m] context-variant strip goes too: the marker says which context
tier served the request, and Anthropic already bills long-context
differently, so hiding it loses real information. With no abbreviation
table and no suffix strip left, abbreviateModel was the identity
function; all call sites now render the raw model id.

* chore(traces): CodeRabbit quick wins on #6191

- ChatTurnRow comment describes raw model-id labeling, not abbreviation
- long model ids truncate with a title tooltip in the non-wrapping
  summary and group rows (both ConversationSummary variants)
- the control-char test comment is scoped to constructed wrappers, and
  the parsed message is length-checked before indexing

* docs(langy): correct the no-RuntimeClass symptom and ship the EKS installer

Verified against a real EKS cluster while testing this PR.

A missing RuntimeClass does not produce a Pending pod. Kubernetes rejects the
pod at admission, so none is ever created: the documented
`get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=langyagent` lists nothing at all, and the
reason sits on the Deployment's ReplicaFailure condition. That is the state
most EKS installs land in on day one, and both the install notes and the setup
page sent operators to an empty list to look for an event that isn't there.
They now say no pod appears and give the command that prints the reason
(jsonpath on the condition — `describe | grep ReplicaFailure` shows the
condition but not its message).

The EKS recipe also asked operators to build a runsc installer DaemonSet with
pinning and SHA-512 verification without giving them one, which is a lot of
privileged, node-mutating YAML to get right from prose. The manifest is now in
the page, pinned to a reviewed release and verifying the published digests, in
the nodeSelector-scoped and tainted shape the recipe describes. It is the one
used to bring the sandbox up on the test cluster for this review.

* feat(charts): make isolation the default and a sandboxed runtime the hardening step

Flips the agent's default from a pinned gvisor RuntimeClass to the node's
normal runtime, and turns the EKS recipe into a hardening guide.

The controls that bound the attack that actually happens stay on by default
and cost nothing: per-worker UID isolation, the per-worker opencode password,
and a NetworkPolicy that denies egress to the internet. A worker reached by
prompt injection through ingested data is stopped by those, on every cluster,
with no configuration.

A sandboxed runtime guards the rung above: the node kernel, against a worker
that escapes its container, which needs a kernel exploit on top of the
injection. It is the one control in this chart whose behaviour depends on the
operator's node image, containerd version and runsc build, none of which we
test. Mandating it bought the least likely rung at the highest operational
cost, and when the class is absent the pod is rejected at admission rather
than pending, so the assistant silently did not exist.

So the sandbox becomes a documented step taken on purpose. The install states
which posture it got, links the guide, and when the cluster already defines a
sandboxed class that the values are not using, the notes name it. That hint
reads the cluster at install time and stays silent during `helm template`, so
a GitOps render never guesses a posture it cannot see.

The render guard is unchanged in spirit and now protects the case that
matters: blanking the class while acceptUnsandboxedRuntime is false is still
refused, so a cluster that HAS hardened cannot silently lose its sandbox.

The EKS installer DaemonSet is now shipped rather than described, and it
detects the containerd major version instead of assuming: containerd 2.x
renamed the CRI plugin, and writing the wrong stanza leaves containerd healthy
with the runtime unregistered, which fails silently. The version I published
yesterday had that bug, found by running it.

Verified on EKS both ways. Default: the agent runs on the node runtime, Langy
loads a skill, runs `langwatch prompt list` through the CLI, answers, and
mirrors the turn back as a trace. Hardened per the guide, applied verbatim
from the page: digests verified, containerd 2.x branch taken, agent Running
under 4.19.0-gvisor on the dedicated node group, same conversation, same
result.

ci: unblock main and the release PR from three checks that fail on correct code (#6192)

* fix(ci): assert the gateway subchart by its source, not by a label anyone can use

The chart job proved "the gateway subchart rendered" by grepping the rendered
umbrella for `app.kubernetes.io/name: gateway`. That string is not evidence of
the subchart: sibling charts legitimately SELECT that label, and langyagent's
NetworkPolicy has an egress rule to the gateway. Once Langy started shipping
enabled (#6106), that policy renders on a default install, so the opt-out
assertion failed on a chart that had suppressed the gateway correctly, and
main went red.

The positive assertion had the same hole in the other direction: it would have
passed on a genuinely broken dependency, because langyagent's egress rule
supplies the string whether or not the gateway rendered.

Both now grep the `# Source:` marker helm stamps on every rendered file, which
is the actual question being asked. Verified both ways: 6 gateway files with
the subchart on, 0 with `gateway.chartManaged=false`.

* ci: exempt release PRs from the deployment-impact check

release-please writes the release PR description itself from the
changelog, so the check fails on every release PR for a section no
author can add. The impact of what a release carries is already stated
on the PRs it is composed of.

* ci: scope the release-PR exemption to this repository

A fork can name its branch anything, so matching the branch name alone
lets any PR opt out of the deployment-impact gate. release-please only
opens PRs from inside the upstream repo.

* test(sdk): expect the streaming attribute to survive the round trip

The trace read path deserializes stored span attributes, so a boolean
set on a span comes back as a boolean. The assertion still expected the
JSON-encoded string ClickHouse holds it as.

fix(charts): let the gateway find the control plane of its own install (#6194)

charts/gateway pinned the control-plane address to http://langwatch-app:5560
and the ConfigMap used it verbatim, so the gateway only reached the app on an
install that happened to be named langwatch. Under any other release name it
dialled a Service that does not exist: every pod healthy, every probe green,
and every request carrying a virtual key refused, with no usage recorded and
nothing in the install to say why.

The address now derives from the release name like every other cross-service
address in the chart family, and an explicit baseUrl still wins. The port half
is a constant the subchart cannot see past, so an app moved off 5560 with no
baseUrl set is refused at render time and told which value to fill in.

plane blip surfaced to the caller as the terminal no_provider_configured
400 — telling an org with perfectly good keys to go add a provider API

until expiry. This is what intermittently failed the SDK CI lanes and
scenario runs today.

All three call sites now fail right:
- cold miss: retryable 503 auth_upstream_unavailable, nothing cached
- stale-entry refresh: the stale bundle's known-good credentials keep
  serving, transport-failure style
- proactive background refresh: the healthy entry survives instead of
  being replaced by a config-less bundle

A config fetch that succeeds with a genuinely empty credential list still
caches and answers no_provider_configured — that distinction is the
point. auth_upstream_unavailable now maps to 503 (was an unregistered
500) so client SDKs retry.

only /config — cold-cache requests answer 503, and the first request
after the outage clears serves 200 with real credentials.

feat(gateway): route anthropic providers with a base URL to self-hosted endpoints (#5940)

* feat(gateway): route anthropic providers with a base URL to self-hosted endpoints

An anthropic ModelProvider with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL configured now
dispatches /v1/messages (sync and streaming) to that endpoint instead of
api.anthropic.com, so self-hosted Anthropic-compatible servers
(vLLM >= 0.24, Claude-compatible proxies) work behind LangWatch virtual
keys, budgets, and tracing.

Control plane: include anthropic in the materialiser's per-slot base_url
gate; the registry endpointKey resolves the value. Providers without the
key keep emitting no base_url, so stock Anthropic routing is unchanged.

Gateway: Bifrost's Anthropic key has no per-key URL slot and provider
config is resolved by provider key alone, so mapProvider derives a
deterministic per-endpoint custom provider key (base type Anthropic) and
registers the endpoint for GetConfigForProvider to resolve. Bifrost
creates the provider lazily on first dispatch; the sync raw-forward path
and the streaming PassthroughStream path both build URLs from
NetworkConfig.BaseURL. Credentials without an API key produce a keyless
provider config — Bifrost's key selection rejects empty-value keys for
base provider Anthropic — and keyless-ness is part of the key hash so
instances never mix.

Fixes #5938

* fix(model-providers): allow keyless anthropic credentials when a base URL is set

Review follow-ups:

- The anthropic keysSchema required a non-empty ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, so the
  keyless self-hosted flow the gateway supports could never be configured
  through the control plane. Mirror the openai schema: either the key or
  the base URL must be non-empty. api.anthropic.com itself still requires
  the key at dispatch; unauthenticated self-hosted servers no longer force
  a placeholder.
- Add a streaming end-to-end regression: DispatchStream against a keyless
  Anthropic-compatible endpoint reaches /v1/messages, sends no x-api-key,
  and forwards native SSE frames byte-for-byte.
- Replace a single r.Body.Read with io.ReadAll in the sync dispatch test
  (a partial read could truncate the captured body and flake).

* fix(gateway): bound the anthropic-compat endpoint registry and release evicted providers

The registry behind derived anthropic-url-* provider keys was a
process-global sync.Map that only ever grew: every distinct
{base URL, keyless} pair ever dispatched to kept its entry — and the
bifrost worker pool lazily created behind its key (DefaultConcurrency
goroutines + a DefaultBufferSize queue) — for the life of the process,
so endpoint rotation across tenants leaked pools without bound.

Replace it with an LRU registry owned by the router: each dispatch
refreshes its endpoint's recency, inserting past capacity evicts the
least-recently-dispatched endpoint, and eviction fires
bifrost.RemoveProvider on its own goroutine (teardown drains in-flight
work and must not stall the dispatch that triggered it). An evicted
endpoint that comes back into use transparently re-registers and gets
its provider lazily re-created — covered end-to-end against a real
bifrost instance, plus LRU-order unit coverage.

Provider-key derivation is now pure (registration happens at dispatch
time via mapProviderForDispatch), so mapProvider keeps no side effects.

Addresses the P2 resource-management blocker from review on #5940.

* fix(gateway): bound the per-endpoint anthropic-compat worker pools and stop teardown racing a live endpoint

Three review findings on the anthropic base-URL routing.

Per-endpoint worker pools inherited bifrost's provider defaults. Unlike
the OpenAI-compat path, where every customer endpoint shares the single
VLLM provider, each anthropic-compat endpoint gets its own bifrost
provider, and bifrost sizes an unconfigured provider at 1000 workers and
a 5000-slot queue. Measured, the first dispatch to a compat endpoint grew
the process by 1003 goroutines, so a full registry meant ~32k goroutines
that customer configuration alone could add. The gateway now sizes those
pools itself (128 workers, 1024-slot queue): 131 goroutines per endpoint,
with a test that fails if the defaults come back.

Eviction schedules the provider teardown on its own goroutine, so a
dispatch to the same endpoint could land in between and enqueue onto a
queue RemoveProvider was closing, which bifrost answers with "provider is
shutting down". A re-registered endpoint now cancels its own pending
teardown, and the next eviction reschedules it.

prepareEnvKeys read credential names off the provider's keysSchema
through a shape reader that did not unwrap superRefine, so anthropic (and
openai before it) resolved to no credentials at all. Both shape readers
are now one helper that unwraps effects and optional wrappers alike.

Also restates the endpoint-rotation scenario in user-visible terms rather
than LRU internals, per the feature-file convention.

* test(model-providers): cover the wrapper-schema branch of getSchemaShape

* docs(gateway): note that a full compat-endpoint queue backpressures rather than drops

* test(gateway): assert the compat pool size on the config, not just the goroutine count

* ci: retry the goose download so a reset connection stops failing whole shards

An integration shard on this PR failed with `curl: (35) Recv failure:
Connection reset by peer` against the GitHub release CDN, before any test
had run. The download had no retry, so one transient reset took out the
shard and the whole app-CI gate. Same script backs the javascript-sdk and
e2e workflows.

* ci: install goose from a private temp file instead of a predictable path

The download landed on a hardcoded /tmp/goose, so between the checksum
and the install another local process could swap the file (CWE-377).
mktemp gives a 0600 file nothing else can pre-create, a trap removes it
on any exit, and `install -m 0755` places the verified bytes in one step.

fix(model-providers): let an organization with no project add a provider (#6186)

* fix(model-providers): let an organization with no project add a provider

A ModelProvider is anchored to `organizationId` and its reach is the
`ModelProviderScope` rows attached to it. A project is one of the three
scopes it can reach, never where it is stored. The write path took
`projectId` as required anyway and resolved the organization back out of
it, so an organization with no project could not configure a provider at
all, and the gateway therefore had nothing to route with.

`projectId` was never ownership on that path. `repository.update` and
`repository.delete` ignored it outright, `repository.create` only used it
to default the scope set, and the router used it as the permission
anchor. It is now optional context: callers pass an organization or a
project, whichever they have.

Scope authorization is unchanged and still the authoritative gate.
`assertCanManageAllScopes` runs per scope, fail-closed, on both the row's
current scopes and the submitted set. With no project the scope set has
to be explicit, since there is no project to default it from, so the
organization path is fully covered by that same per-scope check rather
than falling through it.

Also removes the "Create a project first" empty state and the comment
claiming a provider "is always stored inside a project", which the schema
contradicts.

* fix(model-providers): authorize the credential probe per scope, not by org membership

The no-project validation path fell through to organization membership,
which MEMBER and EXTERNAL both hold, while the handler sends caller-
supplied keys and a caller-supplied base URL straight out over the
network. Nothing downstream re-authorized it, so a read-only seat could
turn the probe into an arbitrary outbound request from our servers.

It now runs the same per-scope manage check the provider writes use, so
"may I probe for this scope" is answered by the same code as "may I
store a credential at this scope". The project path is unchanged.

Also refuses to act on a provider row carrying no scope grants. The
org-anchored lookup finds rows by (id, organizationId) with no scope
predicate, and assertCanManageAllScopes is satisfied vacuously by an
empty list, so such a row would have been waved through on the strength
of having nothing to check.

Reported by langwatch-agent on #6186. SSRF fencing of the fetch itself
is filed separately as #6205.

* spec(model-providers): state the rule the credential-probe gate enforces

The regression tests cited a scenario the feature file did not have, which
the feature-parity gate caught. The rule belongs in the spec regardless:
checking a credential reaches the network on the customer's behalf, so it
is only for someone who could store one.

fix(server): ship the workspace packages the app imports, and boot smoke from the packed tarball (#6200)

* fix(server): ship the workspace packages the app imports, and boot smoke from the packed tarball

The 3.6.0 npm artifact shipped no langwatch/packages/* and no root
packages/{handled-error,langy}: both .npmignore files still excluded them
from when that dir held only dev tooling, while runtime workspace
packages had since moved in. pnpm exits 0 on a lockfile importer whose
directory is missing, so every install died minutes later at the first
import with a bare MODULE_NOT_FOUND. feature-map.json (read by Langy at
runtime) was missing from files[] too. Ship all of them, assert them in
the publish sanity check (derived from the checkout so new packages are
covered automatically), and fail install-time with a message naming the
packaging gap when any @langwatch/* link dangles.

The smoke never caught this because it booted the checkout, where the
packages exist. It now extracts the packed tarball into a
node_modules/@langwatch/server layout and boots that, exercising the
same relocation and app tree npm users get.

Members living outside langwatch/ (mcp-server, packages/*) cannot reach
langwatch/node_modules by walking up, so their peerDependencies (zod for
@langwatch/langy, @opentelemetry/api for @langwatch/handled-error)
resolve nowhere in the relocated tree. The installer now links each
declared peer to the app's own resolved instance after install. Links,
not dependency entries: both packages must share the consumer's
instance (zod schemas from two majors cannot merge, a second otel api
loses the global registrations), and a dependencies entry resolves
per-workspace — it pulled zod 4 in next to the app's zod 3 and broke
every Langy turn with 'merging._def.shape is not a function'. The repo's
langwatch/.npmrc never ships either (npm pack strips .npmrc
unconditionally), so the installer recreates its hoist patterns before
the first install.

Two boot-lifecycle bugs the rehearsal surfaced: a service failing its
health probe rejected the app-tier Promise.all and discarded the
already-started siblings' handles, leaking live processes that squatted
the port slot; and a rerun that auto-shifted slots kept the old slot's
URLs in .env, so the app dialed data stores this very run had started
elsewhere. App-tier startup now collects handles via allSettled and
stops them on failure, and scaffolding reconciles port-bound .env URLs
to the current allocation, touching only values still in their
scaffolded localhost shape so hand-edited ones survive.

* refactor(server): address review round one

Replace a dangling peer link instead of dying with EEXIST (unlinkSync,
not rmSync — rm stats the target and silently no-ops on a dangling
link), rename the reconcile flag to shouldReconcilePorts, make the
byte-for-byte reconcile test actually diff lines, clear langyCliFn
between tests, drop the unused resolve import, restore the orphaned
--port spec step, and rewrite the publish scenarios around observable
installer behavior.

* fix(ci): probe every port slot in one health-wait loop, budget 30 minutes

The tarball boot adds relocation plus a full on-runner install to the
cold path, which can outlive the old 18-minute window. Probing one slot
per window also meant a boot that outlived the first window was then
sought on ports it never bound, turning a slow build into a guaranteed
three-window failure.

* fix(server): restore shell-script exec bits after relocation, and make the smoke aggregator honest

pnpm pack normalizes file modes, so every *.sh in the published artifact
arrives 0644 — and the app's build chain invokes some directly
(pnpm run build -> ./scripts/build-mcp-server.sh died with exit 126 on
every cold smoke). The relocation step now restores the bit across the
tree. alls-green also stops reporting success over failed or cancelled
smoke jobs: the smoke boots the artifact npm users run, so red is a
shippability signal on every trigger.

* fix(ci): bound each health probe and the whole wait by wall clock

curl without -m can hang on a half-open listener, and an iteration count
does not bound time. Probe with a 5s cap and stop at 1800s of SECONDS.

* fix(server): make the artifact tree buildable — prebuilt mcp-server skip, skills shipped, catalogue kept

The no-prebuilt-dist path (smoke, pack-driven installs) runs the full app
build inside the artifact tree, which surfaced three gaps in order:
build:mcp-server tried to rebuild a package whose build config the
artifact deliberately excludes (it ships prebuilt — skip when the config
is absent and dist is present), generate-langy-skills imports
skills/_lib/frontmatter.js from the repo root (skills/ now ships, 1.1MB),
and the same generator derives from Dockerfile.langyagent which the
artifact rightly omits — it now keeps the committed catalogue when the
tree cannot regenerate, failing loudly only when neither exists.
Verified locally: full production build exits 0 inside the relocated
artifact tree.

* fix(ci): smoke packs the same prebuilt artifact publish ships

Every published artifact carries langwatch/dist and mcp-server/dist (the
publish sanity check asserts both), so the smoke now runs the same app
prebuild before packing instead of booting a tree shape no npm user ever
receives — which also paid a full on-runner vite build inside the health
budget. The buildable-tree fallback stays supported for pack-driven local
installs, and build-mcp-server.sh now names the packaging gap outright
when a tree has neither build config nor prebuilt dist.

fix(server): restart crashed services with bounded backoff (#6203)

* fix(server): restart crashed services with bounded backoff

A laptop install lost its workers process to the OOM killer (exit 137)
while a heavy install phase was running. The CLI printed "workers
crashed (exit 137)" and kept everything else up, but nothing ever
restarted the process, so the BullMQ queues had no consumer and the UI
sat on "Waiting for first trace..." forever.

Supervision now distinguishes boot failures from steady-state crashes.
A service that dies before its first healthy event keeps failing fast
exactly as before. A service that crashes after having been healthy is
restarted in place: up to 3 attempts with 1s/5s/15s backoff, announced
on the bus as "restarting" events and as [supervisor] lines in the
service's log file, with the budget refilled after 5 minutes of uptime.
When the budget runs out the crash falls through to the existing
"crashed" event, and the CLI's crash line now points at the service's
log file.

* fix(server): keep event delivery alive when a tap listener throws

A tap registered via EventBus.tap() ran uncaught inside emit(), ahead
of delivery to the waiter/buffer. One misbehaving tap would abort the
whole emit() call, skipping every other registered tap and dropping
the event for the CLI's own event stream too, since spawn.ts registers
one tap per supervised service and any of them throwing would silently
break log/healthy/crashed/restarting delivery bus-wide.

Each tap now runs in its own try/catch so a throw there can no longer
affect its siblings or the iterator.

* fix(server): address CodeRabbit round two on the restart-policy PR

Four more findings on #6203, two critical:

- npx-server-smoke.yml: the job-level env block set LANGWATCH_HOME
  using the runner expression context, which jobs.<job_id>.env does
  not allow (github, inputs, matrix, needs, secrets, strategy, vars
  only) — actionlint flagged it as an error and the job would have
  failed outright. Moved to an early step that resolves $RUNNER_TEMP
  as a shell variable and exports it via $GITHUB_ENV instead.
  Verified with actionlint directly: the runner-context error is gone.
- cli.ts: the install command's ensureEnvFile call relied on the
  contract's shouldReconcilePorts default (true, the "start" flow's
  need), so a bare `npx @langwatch/server install` would rewrite an
  existing .env to an unresolved PORT_BASE_DEFAULT guess before any
  conflict detection ran. Passes shouldReconcilePorts: false
  explicitly now, restoring the documented install-flow behavior.
- spawn.ts: spawnAttempt only handled the child's "exit" event, so a
  spawn that never started at all (ENOENT/EACCES/EPERM) left the
  process's "error" event unhandled, which throws and crashes the
  whole CLI instead of being caught by the restart policy. Added a
  child.on("error", ...) path that funnels into the same handleExit
  dispatch as "exit", gated by a settle-once guard so a spawn that
  both errors and (platform-dependently) still exits is only
  processed once.
- exitCause was duplicated verbatim between spawn.ts and log-tee.ts.

fix(gateway): chat streams open with the role-carrying delta OpenAI sends (#6214)

* fix(gateway): chat completion streams open with the role-carrying delta OpenAI sends

api.openai.com opens every streamed choice with
delta:{role:assistant,content:""} before any content. The stream engine
forwards a chunk only when its delta carries content, reasoning, audio
or tool calls, so that opening chunk matches nothing and is consumed;
the first chunk the gateway emitted was a bare content delta. Clients
that key their accumulator off the opening role delta then index a
message that was never created: our python-sdk streaming tracer crashed
with KeyError: 0 on every streamed chat completion through the gateway.

Repair in the gateway's own iterator layer: on the first delta-carrying
chunk per choice index, a delta with no role gains role:assistant.
Per choice, so n>1 works; first-chunk-only, so later chunks are
untouched and the steady-state cost is a map lookup; presence-checked,
so a provider that sends its own role passes through unchanged. Chunks
without a delta object are never given one, and usage-only terminal
chunks pass through with no choices invented.

Fixes #6196

* docs(gateway): review fixes on the role-delta spec and tests

Addresses CodeRabbit review on #6214.

Correct a stale doc comment on deltasForChoice, reword the spec's Given
step to describe client-observable behavior rather than the stream
engine's internals, and give the no-delta choice case its own scenario
with the test bound to it.

fix(model-providers): derive credential requiredness from the schema and keep the stored key through base-URL edits (#6210)

* fix(model-providers): derive credential requiredness from the provider schema

The drawer marked a credential required from a static list, while the
provider's schema said something else: openai and anthropic accept an
API key OR a base URL, because a self-hosted endpoint commonly runs
unauthenticated. Customers configuring one were told the key was
mandatory, invented a value to get past the form, and that invented
value then travelled to their own server as a credential.

Requiredness now comes from the schema itself, judged against the values
entered so far, so the marker moves as the customer types: the key stops
being required the moment a base URL is entered and is required again
when it is cleared. `optionalKeys` stays as the floor for fields that are
never required (base URLs, api-version overrides); the schema may only
relax from there, so providers whose fields are `.nullable().optional()`
purely to allow an environment variable keep their markers. Any provider
that adopts the either/or shape inherits the behaviour with nothing to
declare.

The refinement names no single field, so its message had nowhere to land
and Save looked like it did nothing. It now anchors on a required field
the customer left empty, and both providers carry copy that reads as
guidance.

The onboarding provider step read the same schemas through its own copy
of the shape reader and reached the opposite wrong answer (key never
required). It now shares the one rule.

Fixes #6172

* fix(model-providers): warn when a base URL sends the saved key to a new host

Adding a base URL to a provider that already holds an API key changes
where that key goes: from the next request on, it travels to whatever
host was just typed in. The edit looks exactly like adding any other
optional field, and nothing in the drawer said otherwise, so a typo or a
runbook copy could hand a live credential to a host nobody meant to
trust.

The drawer now says so at the moment of the edit, inline under the base
URL field: the saved key follows this change, and requests carry it to
that host from the next save on. Clearing the base URL says the same
thing about the provider's own endpoint. It appears only when there is
something to re-point, so configuring a provider for the first time and
opening a provider without touching its base URL stay quiet.

This composes with the requiredness rule: on a keyed provider, adding a
base URL both drops the required marker and raises this warning, because
the key is no longer demanded yet is still on file and still travels.

Fixes #6173

* fix(model-providers): keep the API key a base-URL edit used to delete

Found while walking the drawer as a customer: edit a provider that has an
API key on file, add a base URL, save, and the key is gone. The next
request goes to the new endpoint with no credential at all, and nothing
in the product says why the provider stopped working.

The drawer shows a stored key masked. On save it stripped every masked
value out of the payload before sending, so the write read as "this
provider has no key" and the stored one was overwritten. The rule that
was supposed to prevent this is real and works, but it only fires when
the placeholder actually arrives. It never did.

The form now sends itself as the customer left it, placeholders included,
and the credential on file is kept. Its unit coverage asserted the merge
against a copy of the merge function, which is how this survived: the
scenario is now bound where the real path runs, once through the drawer
and once through the service against a real database.

Second dead end from the same walk: emptying the base URL did not count
as a change, so Save stayed disabled and an endpoint added by mistake
could never be taken back off. Emptying a field is a change like any
other now.

Two P2s from the langwatch-agent review, both confirmed before fixing —
the second reproduced against real Azurite, which answered 400 Bad Request
exactly as predicted.

portal with its trailing slash sent `//container/blob` while the signature
canonicalised `/container/blob`. Path-style detection was wrong for the
same reason: the empty final path segment meant the account name never
matched. Normalised once where the endpoint is derived, so both readers see
the same value.

destination resolver trims AZURE_BLOB_ACCOUNT_NAME before minting

validation and then addressed `https:// lwacct .blob…` on every
stored-object and tiered-blob operation. Trimmed at the construction
boundary so the two cannot drift.

Both carry the regression test the review asked for: a trailing-slash
endpoint round-tripping through Azurite, and the factory asserting the
credentials the driver is constructed with, including whitespace-only
values treated as absent rather than building a driver with a blank
account.

fix(automations): make the Slack channel picker searchable again (#6233)

* fix(automations): make the Slack channel picker searchable again

Typing in the Channel box cleared it on every keystroke. The box fed
`slice.channelId` — which also holds free-typed text — back as the
combobox's selected value, and the combobox rewrites its own input to the
selected item's label whenever that value changes. Free text is not an item
in the collection, so the label resolved to an empty string and the box was
wiped each time. The filter had already run with the character, which is why
the list appeared to react while the box stayed blank: only the last letter
typed ever reached the search, so any channel that needed more than one
character to narrow down was unreachable.

The same rewrite re-entered the input-change handler with an empty string,
so it also wiped the stored channel — a channel typed by hand (one the bot
cannot list) could never be saved at all.

The selection is now tracked separately from the typed text, so a half-typed
search is no longer mistaken for a pick and nothing rewrites the box while
the author types.

Two more defects surfaced while fixing it:

- Opening a saved automation showed a blank Channel box. The stored value is
  a channel ID, resolved against a list that arrives after mount, and nothing
  re-read it once it landed. The box now shows the ID immediately and upgrades
  to the channel name as soon as the list can resolve it.
- Writing the slice on every keystroke re-rendered the whole config form, and
  the combobox resyncs the input element from a passive effect — so the resync
  landed a render late and ate characters ("#adhoc" arrived as "#ahc"). Free
  entry now commits when the author leaves the field or presses Enter, and the
  list re-filters in a transition; the search itself stays live.

* fix(automations): address review on the Slack channel picker

- Name the typing-guard ref `hasAuthorTyped`, per the repo's boolean naming
  convention.
- Correct the field's doc comment: free entry commits on blur OR Enter, not
  on blur alone.
- Assert with `toHaveBeenLastCalledWith` instead of indexing `.at(-1)!`, so a
  regression in the commit path reports "never called" rather than throwing a
  TypeError on undefined.
- Cover Enter accepting a highlighted suggestion. Both the field's own Enter
  handler and the combobox's fire on that keypress, so the test pins which one
  decides: the highlighted channel's ID wins over the search text typed to
  find it.

* fix(automations): move the selection off a channel that was typed over

Picking a channel and then typing a different one left the old pick as the
combobox's selection, so the list kept a tick beside a channel that was no
longer the field's value.

Clearing the selection is the obvious fix and it reintroduces the bug this
branch exists to fix: the combobox rewrites its input from the selected item,
and "nothing selected" stringifies to an empty string, so the box blanks on
blur. A committed free-typed channel now gets its own collection entry and
becomes the selection instead — an entry whose label is the typed text
survives that rewrite unchanged.

Both halves are pinned: one test asserts the tick moves off the replaced
channel, the other asserts the typed text stays in the box and in the slice.
The second fails against the clear-the-selection version.

fix(langy): resolve the user's own project on /me, not the org ambient team (#6262)

* fix(langy): resolve the user's own project on /me, not the org ambient team or a stale remembered one

useOrganizationTeamProject funnels every route through selectAmbientTeam,
which is right for organization-scoped pages (settings etc: prefer a shared
team over a personal one so org-wide settings never land in one member's
private workspace) but wrong for /me, which is unambiguously the personal
workspace. On a fresh install with no other team activity, or after visiting
any organization-scoped page earlier in the session, /me resolved to the
shared team instead of the user's own personal team and project, leaving
project undefined or pointed at someone else's context.

That silently broke every /me-scoped feature gated on project resolving,
Langy chief among them: the launcher never rendered, and even once it did
on a partial fix, the composer stayed disabled because its projectId was
still empty. The personal-team check has to run before the
localStorage-remembered-team lookup, not just as a fallback after it, since
a team id persisted from an earlier organization-scoped visit legitimately
wins on those pages but must never follow the user onto /me.

Also fixes a DEMO_PROJECT_SLUG === project?.slug equality trap in
useShowLangy and DashboardLayout: with no demo project configured (every
self-host) and project unresolved, both sides read undefined and the
comparison wrongly matched, hiding Langy for users nowhere near the demo
project.

* fix(langy): bind @scenario annotations correctly for feature-parity CI

The feature-parity checker only recognizes a single-line
/** @scenario <exact title> */ block immediately preceding an it()/test()
call; multi-line JSDoc annotations and titles containing a literal
asterisk are invisible to its proximity scan, and one single-line title
did not match any scenario in the feature file. Rewrote each annotation to
the single-line form with an exact match, keeping the explanatory prose as
plain comments, and added the missing scenario to langy-baseline.feature
