fix(deps): support Node 25 and 26 alongside 24 (#6267)

* fix(deps): support Node 25 and 26 alongside 24

The engines field strictly pinned "24.x", so pnpm warned on any other
version even though nothing in the app actually required exactly 24.
Verified empirically rather than assumed: installed Node 25.6.0 and 26.5.0
via nvm and ran typecheck, the full unit test suite, and an integration
spot-check against both, alongside the existing Node 24 baseline.

The one real incompatibility: inside vitest's vm-sandboxed worker pool,
both Node 25 and 26 define a global `localStorage` even without
`--localstorage-file`, instead of leaving it genuinely absent the way a
bare Node process (and every other Node version) does. zustand's persist
middleware defaults to this bare global when no `storage` option is given,
and only falls back gracefully when reading it throws, not when it reads
back something non-functional, so any node-environment test touching such
a store crashed the moment persist tried to call `.setItem`. Fixed once in
the shared test-setup.ts (covers both unit and integration configs): only
replaces a broken or empty global, never jsdom's real, working
`window.localStorage`.

Node 25 is itself already end-of-life (odd releases never reach LTS);
Node 26 is Current until it reaches Active LTS in October. 24.x stays the
default in CI and the volta pin, this only widens what pnpm accepts
without warning.

Also sets confirm-modules-purge=false: node_modules is fully regenerable,
so skipping that confirmation is low-risk, and it's what was turning a
Node-major switch into a hard, non-interactive
ERR_PNPM_ABORTED_REMOVE_MODULES_DIR_NO_TTY failure instead of just a
reinstall.

feat(gateway): a public status-page health endpoint for the AI gateway (#6228)

* feat(gateway): serve a public status-page health endpoint on the AI gateway

status.langwatch.ai had nothing to point at for the AI gateway. The
service already carries the three k8s probes (/healthz, /readyz,
/startupz), but those gate pod lifecycle in-cluster and are deliberately
not exposed: /healthz answers as long as the process is alive, and
/readyz is dependency-free on purpose, so neither is a statement about
whether the service is actually serving.

GET /health (and HEAD, since uptime monitors commonly probe with it) is
the public surface: 200 healthy, 503 unhealthy, JSON body with an
overall status and a component map.

Two properties are structural, not conventions to be careful about:

- A model provider outage can never turn it red. Nothing in the verdict
  path reads dispatch state, so OpenAI or Anthropic melting down leaves
  /health at 200 while completions 5xx. That is their status page's
  news, not ours, and a red gateway on someone else's outage is the
  thing that trains people to ignore a status page.
- A poll never fans out. The endpoint is public and unauthenticated, so
  a per-poll upstream call would be an amplification and cost bug
  wearing a health check's clothes. The statusprobe monitor probes on
  its own clock (15s) and the handler reads a cached verdict under a
  mutex.

The single owned dependency watched is the control plane, reached over
the HMAC-signed internal channel rather than a public liveness path: a
200 proves DNS, TCP/TLS, the app being up, AND the shared internal
secret matching, which is the misconfig where every pod looks green
while every virtual-key resolve is refused. §4.7 adds the
/api/internal/gateway/health route behind the existing gateway policy
for it; the gateway reads only the status code.

Unreachability under 60s stays 200 because the auth cache's
stale-while-error machinery keeps warm traffic serving through a blip
and a status page that flaps on what customers cannot feel is worse
than useless. Past it, cold-cache requests are failing with
auth_upstream errors and the page should say so. A booting pod gets one
full window before it can report red, so a rolling deploy does not
blink the page.

The body is minimal on purpose: status and checks only, no version or
uptime (restart cadence and build identity are nobody's business on a
publicly polled endpoint), and the degraded detail carries a duration
only, never the probe error, which embeds the control plane's host and
port. Tests assert that in both verdicts. /health joins the probes in
the metrics middleware's operational-path skip list so status polling
does not dilute the error-rate ratio.

* docs(specs): correct the readyz scenarios to the dependency-free probe we ship

health-checks.feature described a /readyz that checks the control plane,
the auth cache warmth and redis. None of that exists: the scenarios were
all @unimplemented and the implementation went the other way for two
concrete reasons recorded in services/aigateway/deps.go.

An `auth_cache_warm` check dead-locked cold starts. K8s will not route
traffic until /readyz is 200, and the cache could only warm from routed
traffic, so pods never went ready. A `control_plane_reachable` check
would be worse in production: a control-plane blip would pull every
gateway pod from the load balancer at once, turning a degradation the
auth cache is built to absorb into a total outage, and killing exactly
the warm-cache traffic that was still serving fine.

So dependency health is reported, it just is not allowed to gate
traffic. It lives on the public GET /health status-page endpoint
(gateway-health.feature), where a red verdict informs a status page
instead of removing pods from rotation.

* feat(charts): expose the gateway status endpoint through the ingress

The status page has to reach /health from outside the cluster, and the
gateway ingress only published /v1. Adds an Exact-match path for
/health, on by default, so exactly that one route becomes public: the
k8s probes, /metrics and /internal stay in-cluster because Exact will
not match /healthz or anything under a prefix.

Also documents which side of 200 the states fall on and why, and
replaces the two /readyz troubleshooting entries that described checks
the gateway does not have with the one failure this actually surfaces:
a 503 on /health with control_plane unreachable, whose usual cause is a
mismatched internal secret 401ing the probe rather than a dial failure.

* test(gateway): assert the public health body against a probe that really failed

Both public-safety assertions ran against a monitor with no pinger, so no
probe had ever produced an error and the detail string had nothing to
leak. An implementation that formatted the probe error into the response
would have passed them: verified by mutating the monitor to carry
lastErr into the detail, which left the endpoint-level assertion green.

Both now run the loop against a pinger failing with the shape a dead
control plane produces (dial tcp host:port: connection refused) before
reading the degraded verdict, and the same mutation now fails them.

* docs(aigateway): document the status endpoint and correct the probe page

The health-checks page is what a self-hoster reads before wiring a status
page, and it described a gateway we do not ship. It said /readyz runs
readiness checks and /startupz blocks on an auth-cache bootstrap that
calls the control plane; neither exists. /readyz only reports draining,
and startup is marked complete as soon as dependencies are constructed,
so the CrashLoopBackOff row in the failures table described an
impossible failure.

Adds the /health section: the response shapes, why the body is smaller
than the probes' (no version or uptime on a publicly polled endpoint),
the two structural properties (a provider outage cannot turn it red, a
poll never fans out), the 60s tolerance and what it buys, what the
ingress publishes, and the two failures an operator will actually meet.
Also says out loud that the synthetic completion check belongs on an
internal alert, not on the public page, since that one does go red when
a provider does.

* fix(gateway): fail closed without a pinger, and survive a nulled healthPath

Two half-configured states, both found by walking the change rather than
by a test failing.

A Monitor built without a Pinger can never refresh its verdict. It was
reaching the unhealthy state anyway, since nothing stamps lastSuccess,
but only as a side effect of how the tolerance is computed. That is the
behavior we want on a half-wired deployment (a monitor with no way to
reach the control plane has no grounds to call the gateway healthy), so
it is now stated and pinned by a test instead of being an accident.

The ingress template dereferenced .Values.ingress.healthPath.enabled
directly, so an operator setting `ingress.healthPath: null` to turn the
public path off got a template panic rather than an ingress without it.

* fix(gateway): review round, fail closed on a missing reporter and correct four claims

The substantive one: `/health` answered 200 with only the process
component when no StatusReporter was wired. That is a gateway saying it
is healthy while having no idea whether it can reach its control plane,
which would pin a public status page green on a half-wired deployment.
It now reports `control_plane: not configured` and 503, matching what
statusprobe already does with no Pinger, and every response carries both
components so the body shape does not change with the wiring.

Three claims that were wrong, and one that was imprecise:

- `pathType: Exact` bounds the path, not the method. The chart comments
  said it exposed "only GET/HEAD". It exposes only the path; the method
  guarantee comes from the gateway route, which registers GET and HEAD
  and answers 405 otherwise. Now stated where it is true, and pinned by
  a test so the chart comment cannot drift from the router.
- A mismatched internal secret is a completed round trip that comes back
  401, not a dial error. The troubleshooting entries said "dial error".
- `HEAD` returns the same status and headers but no body, which is not
  "identical to GET".
- The `starting` state is unobservable over HTTP because MarkStarted runs
  during dependency construction, which completes before the listener
  opens. Saying it is "only observed if the process dies" was a guess
  about a different mechanism.

Also: the /health smoke command used `curl -sSf`, and `-f` swallows the
503 body, which is the half worth reading. The degraded-outage
troubleshooting row pointed at the control plane as the only thing to
fix, when a shared secret can be wrong on either side.

Two scenarios were describing mechanism instead of outcome, per
specs/README.md: the no-fan-out one now says polling puts no load
anywhere rather than narrating the monitor's ticker, and the signed-probe
one now says a mismatched secret shows up as a control-plane failure
rather than listing header names.

* test(gateway): make the nil-pinger guard fail on the mutation it exists for

The test asserted the verdict goes unhealthy after the tolerance, but it
read the verdict once, immediately after moving the clock. That is true
the instant the clock moves, before the probe loop has run at all, so a
probe that stamped lastSuccess with no pinger wired would still have
passed it. Confirmed: applying that mutation left the test green.

It now holds the verdict unhealthy across ~200 ticks of a 1ms loop with
Never rather than sampling it once with Eventually, which is what
actually rules out the loop talking itself back to healthy. The same
mutation now fails it.

* fix(gateway): review round two, honest healthy fixtures and an accurate 200 condition

The endpoint summary said /health is 200 when "the control plane is
reachable", which contradicts the tolerance documented three sections
below it: it stays 200 through up to 60s of unreachability, on purpose.
Now says the control plane has answered within the last 60s.

The healthy test fixtures were building a monitor and never starting it,
so they read healthy off the boot grace window rather than off a probe.
They passed, but they would have kept passing if probing broke entirely,
and after the fail-closed change it also read as a contradiction: the
same construction is the unhealthy fixture elsewhere. They now run a
real probe to completion before asserting, via one healthyMonitor
helper. The no-fan-out test deliberately keeps an unstarted monitor,
since a stopped ticker is exactly what makes an observed probe proof of
a poll fanning out.

Also pins HEAD on the wire rather than through a recorder. net/http
discards a HEAD body while still reporting the Content-Length the GET
would have carried, which is what RFC 9110 asks for. Guarding the encode
with an explicit HEAD check reads tidier and measures worse: against a
real server it drops Content-Length and adds Connection: close, so a
monitor polling with HEAD would pay a fresh handshake every time. The
test states the property so the tidier-looking version does not get
introduced later.

* test(gateway): make the healthy fixture prove a probe succeeded

Waiting for calls >= 1 only proved a probe was attempted. The verdict was
still resting on the seed New writes at construction for the boot grace
window, so the helper would have handed back a "healthy" monitor even
with Health failing on every call, and its comment would have been a lie.

It now advances a fake clock past the tolerance first, asserts the
monitor reads unhealthy, and then waits for it to flip. Only a probe
returning nil can do that. Verified by making the test pinger fail
unconditionally: the helper now fails with "a successful probe must move
the verdict to healthy" instead of passing.

fix(automations): expose page-cap and missing-scope gaps in Slack channel listings (#6266)

* fix(automations): expose page-cap and missing-scope gaps in Slack channel listings

The picker could hand back a fraction of a workspace's channels and look
complete doing it. Reproduced against a stand-in Slack that serves pages the
way the real one does: 400 of 601 channels came back, the private channel the
bot belonged to was gone, and `error` was null.

Two things combined. Slack documents that "it's possible to receive fewer
results than your specified limit, even when there are additional results to
retrieve", so the ten-page walk ends long before a large workspace does — the
ceiling is nowhere near what the page size implies, and cannot be predicted
from it. And the listing is sorted after it is truncated, so what is left
reads as an orderly alphabetical list with entries missing throughout rather
than as a list that was cut short.

The contract had no way to say any of it: {channels, error} can express
worked or failed, not "worked, but this is not all of it". Both degradations
collapsed into error: null, and the unit tests pinned that as intended.

Listings now carry the gaps that made them short — the page cap, or private
channels dropped when the app has no groups:read — and the picker names every
gap that applies. Both can hold at once, so they are listed rather than
ranked; showing only the first would have the author fix one cause and still
not find their channel.

Also corrects two pieces of copy that sent people the wrong way: the scope
hint named channels:read for a private-channel problem, and the setup steps
said only "invite the bot", which is unnecessary for public channels
(chat:write.public is in the manifest we hand out) and required for private
ones, without distinguishing them.

The channel picker had no scenarios at all, which is why none of this was
caught; specs/automations/authoring-drawer.feature now covers it, and its
Slack scenario no longer describes the retired webhook flow.

* docs(automations): describe what the page-cap test and scenario actually do

The comment above the page-cap test cited a 40-per-page, 400-of-601
reproduction, but the mock beneath it returns one channel per page — the
figures came from a separate live run and read as if they described this
mock. It now describes the mock: one channel per page and an endless cursor,
so the cap is the only thing that can end the walk.

The private-channel scenario stated an install-time permission as its
precondition. It now states what is observable — the app cannot see the
workspace's private channels — while still asserting the UI names the
permission that would fix it.

fix(export): stop trace CSV losing a row at every batch boundary (#6286)

* fix(export): stop trace CSV losing a row at every batch boundary

`serializeTracesToSummaryCsv` and `serializeTracesToFullCsv` returned
`Parse.unparse(...)` with no trailing newline, and ExportService concatenates
those chunks straight into the response. The last row of each 100-trace batch
was therefore glued onto the first row of the next:

    "id,name\r\n1,alpha\r\n2,beta3,gamma\r\n4,delta"
                              ^^^^^^^^^^^

Four rows in, three out, one of them corrupt (`name: "beta3"`). Silent — the
file parses without error, it just has fewer rows than the project has traces.
A 5,000-trace export lost ~49 rows.

There was a second bug behind it: PapaParse defaults to CRLF while
`stripCsvHeader` searched for "\n", so even a chunk that ended correctly left a
stray carriage return at the head of the next one.

`CSV_NEWLINE` is now stated explicitly and used in three places that had to
agree and did not — the unparse call, the chunk terminator, and the header
strip. JSON export was never affected; it already appended "\n".

Four regression tests cover the batch boundary in both summary and full mode.
They execute the concatenation rather than asserting on the output string, and
all four fail if the fix is reverted (verified).

feat(event-sourcing): read-back stores for the trace/eval analytics folds (ADR-066) (#6126)

* feat(event-sourcing): read-back stores for the trace/eval analytics folds (ADR-066)

Migrate the last two refolding fold projections — traceAnalytics and
evaluationAnalytics — to the ADR-066 read-back pattern so their delivery path
never reconstructs state from event_log. Their stores returned null on a miss
and the executor fell back to refoldOnStoreMiss, a streamed re-fold that
cold-scans event_log (no time filter, walks S3 partitions; 1.3-2.2s/query,
observed continuously in prod worker logs 2026-07-24) — the same pattern behind
the 2026-07-23 TOO_MANY_PARTS outage on codingAgentSession.

Each fold now reads its own last committed row back (get -> findBy*WithApplied
-> fromRow), mirroring the codingAgentSession migration:

- migration 00055 adds typed read-back columns (no JSON blob, no new table) plus
  an AppliedEventIds durable dedup watermark on both RMT fold tables.
- trace_analytics: SpanCount, AnnotationIds, RootSpanStartTimeMs, the three
  name-resolution flags, and LastEventOccurredAt round-trip the working state the
  trimmed row dropped; the hoisted dimensions are re-injected into the attribute
  map on decode, and the langwatch.reserved.* accumulators survive the trim by
  contract, so the trimmed column is a faithful read-back.
- evaluation_analytics: StartedAt/CompletedAt (the operands DurationMs is derived
  from); evaluatorId/scheduledAt/costId default on read-back (feed no persisted
  value), LastEventOccurredAt reconstructs from OccurredAt.
- refoldOnStoreMiss removed from both folds; refoldOnOutOfOrder set false and a
  readWindow declared. refoldOnStoreMiss now has no adopters.

Repositories gain a windowed IN-tuple with-applied read (TenantId first, unwindowed
inner dedup via GROUP BY + max(UpdatedAt), never FINAL) and thread the watermark
through the write path. A pre-migration row decodes with documented defaults —
never a refold; old builds ignore the new columns.

The eval repo keeps its column-specific asNullableMs / asNullableBool local until a second consumer appears.

Also document the pre-00055 latched-boolean read-back limitation: HasAnnotation and a user-overridden TraceName cannot fully round-trip because their backing columns (AnnotationIds / TraceNameUserOverridden) did not exist before 00055, so a pre-00055 row can downgrade the flag on a post-miss rewrite. Corrects the mixed-deploy self-heal note in the migration header and the fold doc.

* chore(clickhouse): renumber the analytics read-back migration to 00056

Rebasing onto main collided with 00055_gateway_budget_scope_totals_period_start
(#6143), which took slot 00055 while this branch was open. goose keys migrations

* fix(analytics): decode DateTime64 as UTC and wait for the read-back write

Two defects found reviewing the read-back migration, both consequences of the
same change: a fold's own last committed row is now load-bearing, where before
a miss simply re-folded the event log.

Decode: the new fromRecord decoders parsed the three DateTime64 columns with
`new Date(str)`. ClickHouse emits DateTime64 without a zone suffix and V8 reads
a bare datetime as LOCAL time, so every timestamp skewed by the host's UTC
offset. This is worse than a display bug — the fold min()s `occurredAt` against
each new span, so a value read back early WINS and is written straight back,
and the drift compounds on every cache miss instead of cancelling. `OccurredAt`
is the table's partition key, ORDER BY column and TTL anchor, so a drifting
value eventually leaves the fold's read window and TTLs early; west of UTC the
same path latches `updatedAt` into the future, which pins RMT dedup on a
runaway version. All six sites now use the repo's canonical
`parseClickHouseDateTimeMs`, which is documented as the single definition of
what ClickHouse means by a DateTime64 string. Prod was masked only because no
TZ is set in the images; any non-UTC host reproduced it.

Write visibility: the executor's live path is `store.store()` -> the single-row
`upsert`, which returned before the async-insert flush. A Redis eviction inside
that window let the next delivery read the previous version, fold onto stale
state and rewrite it with a higher UpdatedAt — silently dropping the
intervening batch's contributions and its applied-id watermark. Both upserts
now wait, matching ADR-066 adopter #1, which waits on both paths.

Regression cover: new unit suites pin the decode against a forced non-UTC zone,
since CI runs UTC where the broken and correct parses agree. They fail by
exactly the offset without the fix.

Also corrects three comments that still described the retired mechanism: both
pipelineRegistry wiring notes claimed `get()` returns null and a miss refolds
from the event log, and BaseAnalyticsFoldStore — left with no consumers by this
PR — still instructed future adopters to enable `refoldOnStoreMiss`.

* fix(analytics): surface an unknown evaluation status on read-back

The read-back decoder coerces a status it does not recognise to "scheduled".
That branch is unreachable for a same-version writer, but this migration is
deliberately mixed-deploy safe, so a newer node can persist a status an older
node has never heard of. Unlike most decode fallbacks this one does not
self-heal — read-back never replays event_log, so the next fold writes the
downgrade over the real terminal state.

Keeps the coercion (a decode on the delivery path must stay total) and logs it,
so the mixed-deploy window is detectable instead of silent.

* fix(analytics): version-gate the read-back and make the deduped read deterministic

Five review findings, all downstream of the same shift: the fold's own last
committed row became load-bearing, so anything it cannot faithfully reconstruct
is now permanent rather than self-correcting.

Version gate (the big one). The read-back columns are only trustworthy on rows
this build wrote, and nothing distinguished those from rows written before the
columns existed. Every pre-existing row decodes with SpanCount 0, no annotation
ids and all three name-resolution booleans false, which meant: a user-renamed
trace could be overwritten by one late non-root span, a fallback-named trace
could never be upgraded by a real root, and the 512-span cap reset and re-added
committed cost and tokens. Both projection versions are bumped to 2026-07-27 —
independently correct, since the projected row shape changed and that is what
the version stamp records — and each store now treats a row stamped with any
other version as a miss, dropping the watermark with it (a watermark without its
state would suppress the very events the rebuild needs). refoldOnStoreMiss comes
back on both folds as the net behind that miss.

The result is self-healing and self-expiring: in steady state every row carries
the current version, so nothing rebuilds and the whole point of the PR stands. A
pre-existing row rebuilds exactly once, then is rewritten at the new version and
never rebuilds again. No backfill migration, no mutation. It also fixes the
persistable-signal gap for free — a state carrying only topic or annotation
signal writes no row, so the miss rebuilds it from the log instead of losing it
to a Redis eviction. The ADR now carries the condition for deleting the flag
(one full retention period after this deploys) rather than claiming it already
has no adopters.

Deterministic dedup read. The IN-tuple narrows to the rows sharing
max(UpdatedAt) but does not order them, and ties are reachable: the monotonic
stamp is computed from the predecessor a writer loaded, so two writers resuming
from the same version land on the same millisecond. A bare LIMIT 1 then picked
arbitrarily and could resume the fold from stale state. Both reads now order the
outer scope by how far each version's fold actually got — a progress watermark,
then monotone completeness signals. The inner dedup stays unwindowed, as
documented; the sort is cheap because the IN-tuple has already reduced the outer
scope to one or two rows. Corrected clickhouse-queries.md, which asserted no
ties were possible and would have propagated the unguarded pattern.

Also: both reads now go through queryWindowed, so the two highest-frequency read
paths this PR adds report clickhouse_windowed_read_total (fallback "none" — the
executor owns the miss retry, so the repository must not widen); and an explicit
coalesceMaxBatch of 128 bounds AppliedEventIds, which rides on every superseded
version until TTL.

Tests: 543 across the affected suites. The tie-break tests apply the ORDER BY the
repository actually sent, so a dropped or misdirected tiebreak fails them —
verified by mutation.

* fix(event-sourcing): version-gate codingAgentSession, keep fold accumulators through the trim

Extends the version gate to ADR-066's adopter #1 and closes a state-continuity
gap that the new fold-equivalence tests found.

codingAgentSession had the identical latent defect the analytics folds just had:
it stamps the projection version on the row but never checked it on read, and it
had dropped refoldOnStoreMiss. Rows written before migrations 00053/00054 decode
with those columns at their defaults, and the damage is worse than the analytics
case. MetricSeries empty means the overlay recomputes totals WHOLE from an empty
map, so every converged series is dropped and ADR-056's replace-not-increment
contract inverts from idempotent to destructive. SubAgentIds empty resets the
count to 1 on the next sub-agent span. StepStartedAt empty decodes every step as
starting at 0, so appendStep's ordering scan never moves and steps land in
arrival order — exactly what the column exists to prevent, since spans arrive
wire-batched and out of start order. PreviousCallContextTokens 0 is the "first
call ever" sentinel, so a cache rebuild can never be detected again. Same fix as
the siblings: version bumped to 2026-07-27, the store reports any other stamp as
a miss, and refoldOnStoreMiss returns as the version-gated net that rebuilds
exactly those rows, once each.

refoldOnStoreMiss already defaulted to false — the executor gates on === true
with no defaults-merge — but nothing said so, and the docblock read as a
recommendation for what is now the expensive path. Documented the default,
reframed the option as opt-in-with-an-exit-condition, and fixed the pinning
test's wording, which called init-on-miss "legacy" when post-ADR-066 that is
the correct default.

The fold-equivalence suite then found a real divergence, which is the whole
reason it was worth writing: langwatch.prompt_ids is a third accumulator the
fold grows by read-modify-write, but unlike the others it carries no
langwatch.reserved. prefix, so past ~8 prompt-bearing spans its JSON crossed the
arbitrary-key cap and was dropped. Before read-back that only shrank the stored
row; now the trimmed map IS the fold's next state, so the union silently
restarted. The trim keeps a named set of accumulator keys under the metadata cap
instead, and the docblock claiming the fold "only ever reads the hoisted
dimension keys and the reserved accumulators" is corrected — it was false, and
the test proved it.

Tests: 828 across the affected suites. The equivalence tests fold real event
sequences through the real handlers and compare every projected column at every
split point, so they catch what write-read-write idempotence cannot: mutating
traceNameFromFallback or rootMetadataFromFallback passes the existing fixed-point
tests and fails these.

* test(analytics): share the ClickHouse repository fakes, correct a stale test doc

Three review comments on the review commits themselves.

The two repository suites had byte-identical copies of the ORDER BY-applying
fake and its sort helper — the same duplication rule the production decoders
were held to, and worse here, because a parser that drifted in one copy would
quietly stop proving the tiebreak in that suite while still proving it in the
other. Extracted to a shared module and re-verified by mutation: deleting the
repository's ORDER BY still fails both tie tests through the shared fake.

The fold-equivalence suite still carried a "KNOWN FAILURE … left red on purpose"
block for the prompt_ids divergence, which this same PR fixes — the comment
described behaviour the code no longer has. Rewritten to say what the fixture

and deliberately does not reach the 4096-char one.

Also switched the event fixture's envelope() to named parameters.

* fix(event-sourcing): close the two ways a read-back row lands degraded

Both blockers from the review are the same shape as the ones the version
gate already closed: a fold's own last committed row is load-bearing now,
so anything that writes or reads it in a degraded shape is permanent
rather than self-correcting.

P0 — a pre-migration write launders itself past the version gate.
`wrapWithDefaultSettings` proxies only `.query`, so an insert carries
exactly what the repository passes; ClickHouse defaults
`input_format_skip_unknown_fields` ON; and the workers Deployment
overrides its entrypoint so it never runs migrations (they run in the app
pod's boot, and the two roll concurrently). In that window an insert
carrying the 00056 columns returns 200 with them dropped AND the row
stamped at the current projection version — so once the migration lands
it PASSES the gate, decodes as all-defaults, and is never rebuilt.
All four inserts across both analytics repositories now set
`input_format_skip_unknown_fields: 0`, so the write fails loudly and the
job retries on normal backoff, matching the read half. Not applied to
coding-agent-session: its read-back columns (00053/00054) are already
deployed, so it has no migration window.

P1 — truncated id-set accumulators nested garbage instead of resetting.
`parseJsonStringArray` returned `[raw]` on any parse failure, so a JSON
array cut by the trim's 4096-char cap became one fake element, was
re-escaped into a fresh array on the next write, and re-nested on every
read-back cycle. The `[raw]` fallback stays — it is legitimately lenient
for a bare `prod` instead of `["prod"]`, which the accumulator and the
origin heuristics both rely on. Only a structurally truncated array
(opens with `[`, does not close with `]`) now returns `[]`, which needs
no coupling to the trim's cap. The FOLD_ACCUMULATOR_KEYS docblock
asserted a reset that did not happen; it now describes what the code does.

P2 — the coding-agent gate rejected rows it can decode. Migrations 00053
and 00054 shipped their read-back columns without bumping the stamp
(verified: the constant is 2026-07-21 at both merge commits and their
parents), so 2026-07-21 spans both sides of the change and strict
equality discarded a live, fully-populated population — a regression
against main on the one adopter that had no `refoldOnStoreMiss` before.
The gate now also accepts 2026-07-21 with `lastEventOccurredAt > 0`,
which separates the two halves by construction: the column arrived in
00053 with DEFAULT 0, `init()`s to 0, and only ever takes a positive
`occurredAt`.

That discriminator was only correct by accident: the repository decoded
its four DateTime64 columns with `new Date(String(...))`, which V8 reads
as LOCAL time, so a pre-00053 row's epoch default reads POSITIVE west of
UTC — the gate would have accepted exactly the rows it exists to reject.
All four now go through `parseClickHouseDateTimeMs` (a no-op under UTC).

P2 — the transitional net is now observable. `es_fold_refold_on_miss_total`
counts the executor's store-miss refold path by projection and outcome, so
ADR-066's "it stopped firing, we can delete the flag" is an observation.
A rising rate is the regression signal.

Nits: analyticsStoreBase said "two" folds, now three; the coding-agent
repository's byte-identical private asNumber/asStringArray are gone in
favour of the shared recordDecode ones.

Documented, deliberately not fixed: the metadata.* deep-merge truncation
case and the over-cap arbitrary-key ownership flip are recorded as
best-effort in the trim service docblock. Both need typed columns with
element caps, not a change to the merge semantics here.

The repository module imports the type for its own signatures but does not

* feat(coding-agent): Claude Cowork sessions + registration-style agent registry

Cowork is the Claude desktop runtime in a VM: same event vocabulary as
Claude Code, same session.id — only the resource-level service.name
(cowork) distinguishes it. Sessions now fold into coding_agent_sessions
labeled claude_cowork, keyed by their own session id, logs-only (Cowork
emits no spans by default).

The per-agent knowledge moves out of one grown-together module into a
registration-style layer mirroring the trace-canonicalisation extractors:
agents/ holds one pure definition per agent (identity predicate, name
prefixes, vendor alias quirks, span-name tool resolution), an ordered
registry resolves precedence (cowork before claude_code — service beats
the anthropic scope), and the normalization engine folds the registry
into the shared tables. Adding an agent is one definition file plus one
registry entry. Alias collisions fail at module load.

Subscribers now thread resource service.name into detection (the log
lane parses resource attributes before the gate), and the contribution
vocabulary lifts Cowork's correlation + attribution scalars (prompt.id,
event.sequence, organization.id, user.account_uuid/account_id, speed,
decision_type, decision_source, mcp_server_scope).

feat(event-sourcing): payload cost is a scheduling input — filter irrelevant events at ingest (ADR-069 phase 1) (#6111)

* feat(event-sourcing): payload cost is a scheduling input — extraction at ingest, ADR-069 phase 1

Every span_received event minted a subscriber job carrying the full raw
span; the coding-agent gate ran after dequeue and the handler rehydrated
multi-MB payloads to lift ~20 fields — the memory-pressure class that
probe-kills workers (and ADR-066's deferred scope-table item).

- the subscriber contract gains enqueue-time filter and project hooks,
  run at the fan-out seam where the committed event is already in
  memory; a throwing hook fails into the routing retry, never silently
- codingAgentSpanFactsDispatch adopts both: non-agent spans never mint a
  job; agent spans stage ~2KB of lifted facts instead of the raw span,
  with routing identity (group key, score, dedup) mirrored exactly
- mixed-deploy safe: pre-upgrade jobs carrying full events process
  through the old path, pinned by test
- es_subscriber_enqueue_total{outcome: filtered|projected|staged_full}
- ADR-069 records the seven payload-cost invariants and sequences
  phases 2-4 (honest stub sizes + byte bounds, memory grants, fairness/
  bulkheads/shedding); specs/event-sourcing/payload-cost.feature carries

* refactor(event-sourcing): ship ADR-069 phase 1 as filter-only, defer the projection

The enqueue-time projection ran span normalization — the full canonicalisation
registry, which can throw on malformed data — on the shared routing-dispatch
path. A throw there fails the whole event's fan-out (fold, state, every
subscriber), widening a poison span's blast radius from one isolated subscriber
lane to all of them. Only cheap, total work belongs on the routing seam.

Keep the filter and leave normalization in the subscriber's own consumer lane.
The observed incident was a non-agent project minting a codingAgentSpanFactsDispatch
job for every span it ingested; the filter alone makes those jobs not exist. The
slice-on-the-wire optimization folds into phase 2, where the event carries a
cost-honest claim-check natively and no per-subscriber projection hook exists.

- drop enqueue.project from the subscriber contract and the router seam
- delete the StagedSubscriberProjection envelope module
- es_subscriber_enqueue_total outcomes collapse to filtered | staged
- ADR + spec record why the seam is the wrong place for the projection

* fix(test): narrow the deduplication union before calling makeId

EventSubscriberOptions types deduplication as the "aggregate" | DeduplicationConfig
union, so makeId needs the config branch narrowed first — the full tsgo tests
project rejects the direct access that per-file diagnostics let through.

* fix(event-sourcing): state the enqueue seam's real failure contract, count staged only after handoff

Review follow-ups on ADR-069 phase 1.

The contract claimed a throwing enqueue hook "propagates into the routing
retry, never a silent drop". It does not. The only production caller of
ProjectionRouter.dispatch is EventSourcingService.storeEvents, which logs a
dispatch failure and continues so a projection fault cannot fail an
already-committed write — nothing re-dispatches subscriber fan-out. A hook
that throws therefore loses that subscriber's job for that event
permanently. Today's hooks are total (a set lookup, typeof checks), so
nothing is broken; the defect was the false safety property the next adopter
would build on.

State the truth instead of implementing the promise: enqueue hooks MUST be
total, blast radius is one (subscriber, event) pair, and the failure is
reported but not recoverable. Making the routing path retryable is a change
to storeEvents error handling with its own blast radius, deliberately not
taken here.

This also sharpens why the projection was cut from the seam: it is not that a
throw widens the fan-out's blast radius, it is that the seam has no retry
while the consumer lane does — so moving fallible normalization there would
convert a retryable per-job failure into a silent permanent drop, for exactly
the malformed spans most likely to need the retry.

Pinned at the production caller, not just the router boundary: a router-level
rejects.toThrow() passes even while storeEvents swallows it.

Also:
- count `staged` only once the handoff succeeds (the queue accepted the job,
  or the handler ran inline), so a queue outage no longer inflates the
  filtered/staged split operators are told to watch;
- tag the phase-1 scenarios @unit so feature-parity enforces their bindings.
  That surfaced two bindings the checker was silently ignoring: its proximity
  scan starts inside the comment, so an annotation only counts when its line
  ends in `*/`. Both are now single-line.

* test(event-sourcing): assert the dispatch failure helper saw a cause

An empty AggregateError.errors would have made the per-cause loop pass
vacuously. Also drops an unused parameter from the metric-count helper.

* feat(event-sourcing): span jobs travel as claim-checks — versioned span_referenced event resolved through the span store (#6117)

* feat(event-sourcing): span_referenced claim-check — versioned reference event + span-store resolution (consumer)

* fix(event-sourcing): claim-check resolution windows on the span's own start

The resolution read centered its partition window on occurredAt, which
is ingest time: a span whose duration plus export lag exceeds the fixed
window (blocked_on_user held over a weekend, offline-buffered
telemetry) sat permanently outside every retry and exhausted into a
blocked group. The reference now carries startTimeUnixMs parsed off the
wire span, and the read centers there: the stored row's StartTime IS
that value, so the read stays a pruned point-read at any span duration,
falling back to occurredAt when the wire carried no parseable start.

Also aligns the two lift paths across the store's lossy attribute
round-trip: purely numeric session keys deserialize as numbers and fell
through to trace_fallback on the claim-check path only, splitting one
session's facts across per-trace aggregates; the key resolution and the
service.version fact now accept finite numbers in canonical string
form. The identical-command test routes its store stub through
serializeAttributes/deserializeAttributes so the round-trip is what the
contract is pinned against.

* docs(event-sourcing): record the early claim-check in ADR-069, and what it does not ship

ADR-069 sequences claim-checks into phase 2 and defines one as always
carrying the payload's true byte size. This subscriber ships the
claim-check half early and `span_referenced` declares no size, so the
merged text reads as current state when it is not.

The amendment states the split: the reference mechanism exists and has
one adopter; invariant 1 is still unmet, so byte-bounded stages and the
grant pool behind them are untouched. The two Sequencing/Consequences
lines that would mislead now point at it.

It also names the two consequences rather than leaving them to be
discovered: span-facts delivery is now dependent on spanStorage and the
ClickHouse read, and a store outage outliving the shared 25-attempt
budget blocks the per-trace group until an operator unblocks it (staged
references preserved — delayed delivery and toil, never loss). A
store-miss-specific backoff was considered and declined: the budget is
one shared platform policy already sized for ClickHouse recovery, and
carving out a per-error-class knob is a queue-contract change with its
own blast radius.

* fix(event-sourcing): bind the claim-check scenarios the parity check was not counting

Two spec-binding defects, both surfaced by rebasing onto the re-based
payload-cost base.

The stage hook's failure test pointed at `a throwing enqueue filter
surfaces into retry, never a silent drop`, a scenario the base renamed
when it split the filter's contract into three. The test was never about
the filter anyway — it pins the *stage* hook throwing — so it gets its
own scenario rather than being re-pointed at one of the filter's.

The four claim-check scenarios carried `@scenario` annotations but no
`@unit` tag, so the parity check counted 9 of 13 and never enforced
them: they read as pinned while being invisible to the check that
exists to prove it. Tagged, now 14/14 bound.

* docs(traces): state which timestamp the claim-check read must centre on

The docblock still said the window hint "comes from the reference
envelope", which is what the start-centred fix replaced. The distinction
is the whole point: this table partitions on `StartTime`, spans export on
end, so a window centred on ingest time excludes any span whose duration
plus export lag exceeded it — and excludes it from every retry, not just
the first. Say so where the next caller will read it.

* fix(event-sourcing): stop id-less coding-agent spans deduping onto one job

An id-less coding-agent span keyed its dedup identity to `spanId: ""`, so two
distinct spans in one trace collapsed onto `…:<tenant>:<trace>:` and the
second one's facts were dropped inside the 60s TTL. The path is reachable —
`makeSpanReferencedEvent` refuses to reference an id-less span and stages it
whole. Dedup now falls back to the event's own correlation id, degrading to
per-event rather than per-trace, and stays stable across the reference upgrade
because a reference copies `event.id` verbatim. The empty string is also no
longer accepted from either shape's span-id field.

fix(coding-agent): take the mutable start time out of the session list read's dedup scope (ADR-071) (#6276)

* docs(adr): ADR-071 — coding_agent_sessions has a mutable storage anchor

StartedAt is a Math.min over every signal the fold has seen, so it moves
backwards after the row is written — and it is simultaneously the RMT dedup
key, the partition key and the TTL anchor.

The ADR prices all four consequences. Three are storage hygiene with long
fuses (orphaned versions bounded by distinct StartedAt values, not by writes;
cross-partition orphans that no merge can ever collapse; a TTL deadline that
moves towards the row, which is the root cause of the flake #6127 fixed). The
fourth is a wrong answer today at any age: findManyRecent range-filters its
inner dedup subquery on the same mutable column, so a session that backdates
out of the window renders from a stale in-window version. A day-bounded view
is enough to reach it.

Decision: the correct end state is ORDER BY (TenantId, SessionId) with an
anchor that does not move, but we are NOT migrating the table to get there.
Every consequence is caused by the column moving rather than by which column
is in the key, and a re-key alone does not even fix the fourth — the list
filters StartedAt because it is the partition key. Freezing StartedAt in the
writer (first-observed, with a new mutable EarliestSignalAt carrying the
business truth) closes all four for a fraction of the cost. The re-key is
recorded as the end state, priced honestly (create-new + chunked dedup
backfill + swap on a live replicated table, where FINAL does not collapse the
orphans because they differ in the old sort key), and deferred behind four
named triggers.

Also settles the MetricSeries question: the embedded column and
session_metric_series do genuinely duplicate — same event, same converged
units, and the persisted attribute dimensions coincide exactly — but they
serve a write-side round-trip and a read-side aggregate respectively, and
ADR-066 step 2 already sequences the removal. Not re-opened, not bundled;
records the one hazard (never let the fold read the sibling table back on the
delivery path) so the shortcut is not taken later.

* fix(coding-agent): make the session point read's latest-version pick deterministic

findLatestRecord ended in LIMIT 1 with no ORDER BY, so two versions sharing
max(UpdatedAt) resolved arbitrarily — handing the fold stale state it resumes
from and rewrites, dropping the other version's contributions and its
applied-id watermark.

This is defence in depth, not a live bug: nextVersionStamp already makes a tie
unreachable while per-aggregate group serialization holds, and the comment says
so rather than overstating the risk. The tiebreak covers the residual — two
processes resuming from the same committed version outside that window.

Ranked by how far each version's fold actually got. The session is fed by three
signal families, so it needs a key for each: the progress watermark, then the
span/log accumulator total (summed, because a metric-only session holds every
one of them at zero), then the converged metric-unit count (that session's only
progress signal), then applied-id count, then StartedAt ASC — smallest wins,
because StartedAt is a minimum and only ever decreases, so it is the
best-informed. Same defence PR #6126 applied to the two sibling analytics
repositories.

Not the ORDER BY <version> DESC LIMIT 1 anti-pattern: the IN-tuple has already
cut the input to the rows sharing max(UpdatedAt), so the sort reads no column
SELECT * was not already materialising. The inner dedup subquery stays
unwindowed, as before.

Tests use a fake client that applies the ORDER BY the repository sent to rows
handed over in adverse order, so a dropped or misaimed tiebreak fails rather
than passing on insertion order. Verified by mutation: deleting the ORDER BY
fails all five new tests and leaves the three stamp tests passing. Local
equivalent of the analytics suites' shared fake, which is on an unmerged branch
and does not parse the summed key.

* fix(coding-agent): take the mutable start time out of the session list read's dedup scope

`findManyRecent` applied the same `StartedAt BETWEEN` filter to both scopes of
its IN-tuple dedup. `StartedAt` moves — the fold takes
`min(state.startedAtMs, occurredAt)`, so a late-arriving earlier signal
backdates it — and range-filtering the INNER `max(UpdatedAt)` subquery on a
moving column drops the true latest version out of its own dedup group as soon
as it drifts past the window edge. The group then resolved to a stale in-window
version, and the outer scope returned it: wrong start time, stale totals,
non-null so nothing caught it.

Reachable on an ordinary day-bounded list, with no TTL or partition boundary
involved: a session whose first telemetry to arrive is a log from 00:10 today
writes `StartedAt = today 00:10`; yesterday's 23:50 span then moves it out of
"today", and today's list kept rendering the first version forever.

The bound is removed from the inner subquery, which now carries only `TenantId`
and the optional `UserId` narrowing — both stable, so neither can move a version
out of its group. The outer scope keeps its full `BETWEEN` and now judges the
true latest: a session whose real start drifted below the window leaves the
window rather than rendering stale.

No bound belongs on the dedup scope, not even an upper one. "The latest version
holds the smallest StartedAt because the fold takes a min" is false — a
read-back store miss re-runs `init()` and re-stamps `startedAtMs` from the next
event's `occurredAt`, which can be larger than what was persisted.

Cost: the inner subquery no longer prunes to the window, so it scans the
tenant's sessions across partitions. It reads only sort-key columns plus
`UpdatedAt` and groups one row per session, so it stays compact, and the outer
scope still prunes — but it is a real increase. ADR-071's next step, freezing
the writer, makes `StartedAt` immutable and lets the pruning bound come back.

ADR-071 is updated: consequence 4 is fixed here rather than deferred behind the
freeze, the sequencing no longer lists it as future work, and the deferral of
the re-key is re-justified on what actually remains (storage hygiene plus
consequence 3's retention-period fuse) instead of on the freeze closing
consequence 4.

Tests: the unit suite's fake client now executes BOTH scopes off the emitted
SQL, and the integration suite lists a drifted session against real ClickHouse.
Re-adding the range filter to the inner subquery fails two unit tests and the
new integration test; removing it again is green.

* docs(adr): ADR-071 targets platform accept time as the storage anchor, and records the defect as systemic

The near-term freeze stays, but it is not the end state, and calling it one
would have left the next person to pick a column by name rather than by
property.

Verified rather than assumed, because it kills the obvious "just rename it to
OccurredAt" reaction — the two sibling analytics tables have the SAME defect
under that name:

  trace_analytics (00039:189-192) anchors partition, sort key and TTL on
  OccurredAt, which is min(state.occurredAt, span.startTimeUnixMs)
  (span-timing.service.ts:36-38, projected at traceAnalytics.foldProjection
  .ts:302) — producer-supplied and min-folded, moving backwards exactly like
  StartedAt. Its own fold docblock already admits the dedup consequence and,
  like ADR-056, priced only that one.

  evaluation_analytics (00041:135-138) anchors the same three jobs on
  OccurredAt, written from LastEventOccurredAt = max(prev, event.occurredAt)
  (abstractFoldProjection.ts:235-238, projected at evaluationAnalytics
  .foldProjection.ts:201). It moves FORWARDS, so consequence 3 inverts — rows
  outlive their retention rather than dying early — while 1, 2 and 4 apply
  unchanged. It also already sets eventOrdering: "acceptedAt", so it refuses to
  trust producer business time for ordering while still anchoring storage on
  it. That inconsistency is the finding in one line.

So the axis is producer business time vs platform accept time, not which
business-time column. A partition key, a sort key and a TTL anchor each need
immutable AND monotonic AND not producer-controlled; only accept time — the
log cursor the codebase already names in eventOrdering: "occurredAt" |
"acceptedAt" (foldProjection.types.ts:130-140) — has all three. This is
strictly stronger than freezing: freezing stops the mutation but leaves the
producer able to pin a row into an old, cold, near-TTL partition permanently
with one backdated first event.

Recorded with the trap for whoever implements it: the anchor must be the event
log's accept time threaded into the row, NOT the projection's own CreatedAt,
which is Date.now() inside init() (abstractFoldProjection.ts:206-213) and
re-stamps on a read-back miss.

Both trade-offs are written up rather than waved through. The TTL semantics
change (from "N days after it happened" to "N days after we accepted it") is
argued for — retention measured from custody is the auditable date, and it
closes a live hazard where a producer backdating past the retention horizon
gets near-immediate deletion — but marked as a compliance decision needing a
human sign-off, which this ADR does not give. Losing direct pruning on business
time resolves in ADR-068's existing shape: bound accept time by
[businessFrom - maxLag, businessTo] to prune, then filter business time exactly
in the outer scope.

The invariant now reads "a storage anchor is platform-assigned accept time,
written once" rather than merely "written once", with freezing named as an
improvement rather than the rule.

Scope unchanged: no table is re-plumbed, no migration ships. The re-key stays
deferred — and the systemic finding argues for doing it once, properly, when a
rebuild happens for another reason, not for three ad-hoc ones.

* docs(clickhouse): add the movable-column dedup-scope trap to the review checklist

CLAUDE.md makes clickhouse-queries.md the mandatory read before writing any
ClickHouse query, and its checklist already says to add a partition predicate
for pruning — but said nothing about where that predicate may NOT go. The
adjacent bug class is exactly the one just fixed in findManyRecent: a range
filter on a column the fold can move, placed inside the dedup subquery, drops
the true latest version out of its own max(<version>) group and resolves to a
stale in-window version.

The rule now lives where an author will actually look, names the three tables
whose anchors move, and records that not even an upper bound is safe, since a
read-back miss can re-stamp the anchor forwards.

* fix(coding-agent): the point read's StartedAt tie-break buys determinism, not progress

The tiebreak's fifth key justified `StartedAt ASC` as picking the
better-informed row because the value 'only ever decreases'. It does not:
on a read-back miss the fold re-runs `init()` (`startedAtMs: 0`) and
re-stamps the anchor from the next event's `occurredAt`, which can exceed
the persisted value — the same forward drift ADR-071 relies on to argue
that no bound is safe inside a dedup scope.

Keep the key, which is still needed to make the ordering total, and state
what it actually is: a deterministic last-resort tie-break chosen for
stability, explicitly not a correctness or progress signal. The unit case
is renamed to match and now asserts the pick is identical under the
opposite insertion order, rather than asserting the earlier start is
'better informed'.

* docs(adr): keep ADR-071 on its own decision and stop the spec promising the freeze

Four review points from the ADR:

- The engine/partition/TTL block was an unlabelled fence (MD040); it is
  `sql` now, and it was the only unlabelled one in the file.
- The MetricSeries section was arguing a decision that belongs to ADR-066.
  Compressed to the investigated verdict (they genuinely duplicate; the
  embedded copy is read only by the fold's read-back on the write path,
  the sibling table only by the totals read) plus the statement that the
  removal is ADR-066's step 2 and why it is not bundled. The one detail
  worth keeping — the hazard of replacing the embedded map with a
  cross-projection read on the delivery path — moves to ADR-066 beside the
  step it constrains, rather than living in both.
- The sequencing entry and the rule both justified `StartedAt ASC` as
  picking the better-informed row, contradicting this ADR's own
  forward-drift finding a few paragraphs above. Both now say what the key
  is: a stable last-resort key that makes the order total.
- `session-aggregate.feature` asserted a retention guarantee that arrives
  with the freeze (step 3), not with this change. Tagged `@unimplemented`
  per dev/docs/TESTING_PHILOSOPHY.md so the target survives as a tracked
  gap instead of as a claim about today's behaviour, with the untag
  condition recorded in the ADR's step 3.

* docs(coding-agent): say that the tiebreak's closing key is not a progress key

The list's preamble still described all five keys as ordering by fold
progress, which key 5 explicitly is not. Separates the two.

* feat(coding-agent): measure the list read's unpruned dedup scan (ADR-071)

ADR-071 sequencing step 2 removed the StartedAt bound from findManyRecent's
inner max(UpdatedAt) subquery, because a bound on a moving column inside a
dedup scope resolves to a stale version. The scope therefore stopped pruning
partitions, and the PR's Deployment Impact stated that cost without measuring
it — leaving "the compact scan is acceptable" and "step 3's freeze can keep
waiting" as claims nothing observes.

coding_agent_session_list_read_duration_milliseconds{table,outcome} times the
read. outcome is hit/empty/error; empty isolates the scan's own floor, since an
empty window still runs the whole unwindowed dedup while materialising nothing
in the outer SELECT *. Labels stop at table and outcome — a tenant label on a
one-row-per-session table would track the customer count.

Duration only: client.query() resolves a ResultSet carrying response_headers
but no parsed summary, the ClickHouse client parses X-ClickHouse-Summary for
insert/command/exec alone, and for a streaming SELECT those counters are
complete only under wait_end_of_query=1. Rows returned is capped by the
caller's limit, so it is not recorded as a stand-in for rows scanned.

Also renames the precondition-only describes in both suites this PR added from
when to given, and gives each the when block naming the action actually under
test.

* fix(coding-agent): read the metric's count off the +Inf bucket, which is typed

prom-client stamps metricName on each value at runtime but leaves it off the
published MetricValue, so filtering on it failed typecheck:tests (TS2339) while
passing typecheck, which excludes test files. The +Inf bucket is cumulative over
every bucket, so it holds the same observation count and is reachable through
the declared label map.

fix(clickhouse): give every ALTER-added Array column an explicit DEFAULT (#6297)

* fix(clickhouse): give every ALTER-added Array column an explicit DEFAULT

An `ADD COLUMN` without a DEFAULT leaves the column unmaterialised in every
part written before the ALTER. For an Array, the absent column's size header
decodes as garbage and ClickHouse allocates whatever it claims — at read time
`Code: 173 CANNOT_ALLOCATE_MEMORY ... max_rows_to_read = 1`, at merge time
Code 241 asking for multi-GiB chunks. The read throws out of the ADR-066 fold
read-back, fails the job, and GroupQueue retries until the group wedges.

This is the second occurrence. 00014 diagnosed and fixed it for
trace_summaries.AnnotationIds, quoting the same error string; 00053, 00054 and
00056 then reintroduced it on three more tables. Every scalar column those
migrations added carries a DEFAULT — only the Array ones do not, which is how
it went unnoticed.

Covers all 11 exposed columns across four tables. trace_summaries.Events.* is
the same defect surfacing as ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF instead, because that
header decodes to a length running off the end of the stream rather than to an
absurd one.

Changing only a DEFAULT is metadata-only: no part is rewritten, no mutation is
scheduled. MODIFY COLUMN is idempotent, so replaying the seven applied by hand
during the incident is a no-op. No ON CLUSTER — with CLICKHOUSE_CLUSTER set the
database uses the Replicated engine (00001), which propagates DDL itself.

Repairing a part whose stream is already partially written needs
MATERIALIZE COLUMN, which is a mutation and belongs in the runbook rather than
in a migration that would block a deploy behind it.

* fix(clickhouse): drop the trace_summaries Events.* modifies from 00057

00025 already DROPped `Events.SpanId` / `.Timestamp` / `.Name` / `.Attributes`
from trace_summaries — the per-span events hoist was retired and the list is
derived from stored_spans at read time. MODIFY COLUMN has no IF EXISTS escape,
so naming a column that no longer exists fails the whole migration:

  Code: 10. DB::Exception: Wrong column. Cannot find column `Events.SpanId`
  to modify. (NOT_FOUND_COLUMN_IN_BLOCK)

That aborted 00057 after its first seven statements, which is why all six
test-integration shards and e2e died together in their shared "Run ClickHouse
migrations" setup step, not on any test.

The ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF on Events.Attributes that motivated the block is
a different column: stored_spans carries Events.Timestamp / .Name / .Attributes
from the original CREATE in 00002, so they are materialised in every part and
are not the ADD-COLUMN-without-DEFAULT defect. Whatever that error is, it needs
its own diagnosis rather than a default this migration cannot apply.

Verified against clickhouse-server 25.10.2.65 (the CI version) on a throwaway
database: 00001..00057 apply clean, all seven columns report DEFAULT [] in
system.columns, system.mutations is unchanged across 00057 (metadata-only), and
replaying the seven ALTERs adds no mutation (idempotent).

Also records why the two remaining candidate groups are out of scope, and marks
the commented-out Down block IRREVERSIBLE: per the repo migration convention.

feat(gateway): reach non-Anthropic models from Claude Code through the router (#6207)

* feat(gateway): translate /v1/messages for non-Anthropic providers

* feat(gateway): translate /v1/messages for non-Anthropic providers

Route /v1/messages by resolved provider family. Anthropic-wire
destinations (api.anthropic.com and the derived per-endpoint keys for
self-hosted Anthropic-compatible servers) keep the byte-for-byte
raw-forward path. Every other destination is translated through
Bifrost's neutral Responses request and reassembled into the Anthropic
event union on the way back.

The gateway owns the streaming framing state machine: exactly one
message_start, every delta inside a matching content_block_start/stop
pair at a dense index, and exactly one message_delta + message_stop at
the end, including when the upstream drops without a terminal event.
That last guarantee is what removes the silent hang.

* fix(gateway): drop a ping that arrives before message_start

* test(gateway): pin that translated messages frames are not re-wrapped

* fix(gateway): a stop for an unopened block must not reserve an index

* fix(gateway): make Anthropic thinking budgets portable across providers

Claude Code always sends thinking.budget_tokens, an absolute count that
only means anything against Anthropic's own limits. Carried across
verbatim it is fatal rather than imprecise: Claude Code asks for 31999
tokens, Gemini 2.5 Flash caps thinking at 24576, and the provider's
converter rejects the whole request, so every Claude Code turn against
Gemini failed. Convert the budget to a portable effort bucket on the
translated lane, which each provider maps onto its own valid range.

Also promote the non-streaming stop reason to tool_use when the reply
carries a tool call, mirroring the streaming framer. Providers that
translate through their own chat shape lose the distinction and answer
end_turn, which tells the client the turn is over and leaves the tool
call unrun.

* refactor(gateway): split the messages translation layer by concern

Addresses CodeRabbit review on #6207.

Split anthropic_translation.go, which had grown past the 300-source-line
limit, into four files along its existing seams: error envelopes, the
framing state machine, the stream iterator, and request building plus
dispatch. Each is now well under the limit.

Also from the review: name 529 as overloaded_error so an Anthropic
overload relayed from upstream stays retryable rather than terminal;
drop a comment that promised a local stream close the cancellation path
never performs; guard the test helpers' index dereferences and the
sequence-length indexing so a framing regression fails as an assertion
instead of panicking; and lock the httptest handlers' captured bodies,
which the test goroutine read without synchronisation.

* fix(gateway): drain the provider stream on Close so abandoned requests do not leak

Addresses CodeRabbit review on #6207.

Next stops reading as soon as the stream terminates, on cancellation, on
a provider error, or once the terminal frames are queued, but the
producer may still be parked mid-send on a 256-slot channel. Close now
drains the remainder in the background, which releases it.

The regression test asserts the contract directly rather than counting
goroutines: a live router retains a varying number of pool and transport
goroutines, so a count cannot distinguish a leak from normal churn.

* fix(gateway): close every content block on the paths that terminate a stream

Addresses the second CodeRabbit round on #6207. Three framing defects,
each reproduced by a failing test before the fix.

A converter-emitted error event set terminated and forwarded without
closing open blocks. finish() short-circuits once terminated is set, so
the upstream-close path emitted nothing and the client kept a half-built
content_block: the same hang class this framer exists to prevent,
arriving by a road the iterator's own BifrostError path already guarded.

A repeated content_block_start for a live index reused that index, so

fix(event-sourcing): follow-ups from reviewing #6111/#6117/#6103/#6126/#6276 together (#6293)

* fix(event-sourcing): close the defects found reviewing #6111/#6117/#6103/#6126/#6276 together

Five PRs landed on main in one batch. Reviewed as a whole, three defects only
exist because of how they interact, and two were one-sided gates that the same
PR's own tests documented without enforcing.

**The claim-check start hint was dead for protobuf traffic.**
`parseStartTimeUnixMs` accepted only decimal strings and numbers, but
`startTimeUnixNano` is a `Fixed64` and an OTLP/protobuf decode yields a
`{low, high}` Long — `parseOtlpBody` decodes without `toObject({longs: String})`.
Every protobuf span therefore staged a reference declaring no start, and the
resolving read fell back to centring its window on ingest time. Mostly that made
the start-centred window inert; for a span that started outside the window it
was fatal, because `fallback: "none"` never widens, so the read missed on every
one of its 25 retries and blocked the per-trace group. It now delegates to the
pipeline's own `normalizeOtlpUnixNano`, which has always handled all three
shapes, with the throw contained so the seam stays total. When no start is
parseable at all the seam now declines to build a reference and stages the full
event, which resolves without a store read rather than windowing on a time the
stored row does not have.

**Cowork counted every turn twice.** The logs-only gate was applied on the log
side only: `applySpanToCodingAgentSession` took no agent and folded
unconditionally. `logsOnly` was documented as "must never also emit the
equivalent spans", but Cowork does exactly that behind its beta trace-export
flag, and the span dispatcher accepts those spans — its own test asserts so. A
Cowork session with traces on doubled modelCalls, toolCalls, every token
counter and cost. The gate is now enforced on both sides, and the contract
comment says what is true rather than what was hoped.

The projection version is bumped to reject rows folded by the one-sided gate, so
affected sessions rebuild. `PRE_STAMP` rows stay accepted deliberately: they
predate the logs-only fold and were never double-counted.

**The session list could return a session twice.** The IN-tuple matches
`(TenantId, SessionId, max(UpdatedAt))`, so versions tied on UpdatedAt both
satisfy it — and tied versions differ in StartedAt, so the RMT never collapses
them either. #6276 closed this tie for the point read and left the list open,
where it is worse: `getUsageTotals` reduces over the rows, so a duplicate counts
that session's cost and tokens twice. The list now applies the point read's
ranking per session.

**The subscriber path had no kill switch.** Every other dispatch path resolves
one; this is the path whose filter drops events irreversibly, since subscriber
fan-out is never replayed. Added on the existing convention, checked before the
enqueue hooks.

**A thrown enqueue hook moved no series.** The seam has no retry, so such a job
is gone — and it was counted as nothing at all, which read exactly like a quiet
day. Added a `failed` outcome, so the outcomes now sum to events routed. The
staged/referenced split also keyed on reference identity, which would miscount a
stage hook that rebuilt the event; it keys on the event type now.

Docs: ADR-069's header claimed only filtering shipped while `stage` shipped in
the same commit, and its amendment omitted that a build predating
`span_referenced` completes the job and drops the facts silently — the reason
#6117 was meant to deploy consumer-first, which the squash lost. ADR-071 gains
the list-read rule and four corrected citations that had drifted when #6126 grew
those files earlier in the same batch; the ADR index gains 071.

* fix(event-sourcing): anchor log-only traces, and make a version rejection say so

**Log-only traces committed their row into 1970.** `OccurredAt` is
`trace_analytics`' partition key AND its TTL anchor, and only spans ever set it.
A trace whose only signal is a log record — Claude Code Path B, Codex Path B,
which `hasPersistableSignal` deliberately persists — folded to `occurredAt: 0`,
landed in partition `197001`, and carried a delete deadline of `1970 + retention`:
expired before it was written. The row was reaped on the next TTL merge, so the
read-back this PR series exists to introduce could never hit for that traffic
class, and every delivery kept refolding from `event_log` — the exact cold scan
ADR-066 was written to remove.

The log fold now supplies the anchor when nothing else has. FIRST-observed, not
`min()`: this is a storage anchor and ADR-071's rule is that an anchor must not
move, so logs will not walk it backwards. A late span still refines it through
the span path, which is unchanged. No version bump is needed — a surviving row
decodes `occurredAt: 0` and the next log contribution sets it, so it self-heals
either way.

**A version rejection was indistinguishable from an absent row.** Both answered
`state: null`, so the executor did what it does for a windowed miss: re-read
UNWINDOWED. That is right when the row might sit outside the window and pure
waste when the row was found and refused — a deliberately unpruned scan per
event, per stale aggregate, for the whole transition. It also spent
`es_fold_read_window_fallback_total{outcome="absent"}`, whose meaning to an
operator is "widen readWindow.widthMs", on a schema condition that has nothing
to do with the window — and left ADR-066's own exit condition ("refold stopped
firing") unfalsifiable.

`getWithApplied` can now report `miss: "absent" | "undecodable"`. Additive and
optional; a store that cannot tell them apart omits it and the executor assumes
`absent`, which is the safe direction. All three read-back adopters report it.

Also: the list-read histogram ran to 5s, so the unpruned scan getting expensive
— the one thing it exists to catch, and ADR-071's stated trigger for promoting
the writer freeze — would have landed in `+Inf` where no p99 resolves. It runs
to 30s now. And `trace-analytics`' tiebreak comment claimed `OccurredAt ASC`
picks the better-informed row because the value only ever decreases; ADR-071
refutes exactly that reasoning (a read-back miss re-stamps it forwards), so the
comment now says what the key actually buys, which is determinism.

ADR-066 gains the deploy-order dependency it never wrote down: `clickhouse:migrate`
runs from the app pod's entrypoint only, the workers Deployment overrides its
command and never migrates, and the two roll concurrently — so an adopter's
migration has to land out of band first. Recorded as a release procedure, with
the reason the loud failure must not be softened, and why making it a pre-upgrade
hook is a deployment-policy call rather than an engineering one.

* test(specs): enforce the session-aggregate and fold-read-back contracts

Both feature files enforced ZERO of their scenarios. `check-feature-parity`
counts only scenarios carrying a pyramid tag, so a file with none reports
`0/0 ✓ all bound` and passes — `session-aggregate.feature` (16 scenarios, the
ADR-071 contract) and `fold-read-back-store.feature` (14, the ADR-066 one) were
both green while enforcing nothing. Deleting either fix would not have failed
CI.

Both are now tagged, and every scenario is bound: 15/15 and 14/14, with one
scenario left `@unimplemented` (the retention guarantee, which records ADR-071
sequencing step 3's target rather than today's behaviour). Most scenarios had a
test already and only lacked the annotation. Eight did not and are written here
— among them: bookkeeping surviving a recovery (a repeat sub-agent is not
recounted, a cache rebuild is still detected), a rename surviving a late naming
span, a total recomputed from recorded parts not being collapsed by the next
one, a sequence keeping the order things happened in rather than the order they
arrived, and a topic-only trace surviving a cold cache through the refold. Each
is paired against the state that lost the field, so it fails if the read-back
stops carrying it.

No scenario was reworded, deleted, or newly marked `@unimplemented` to make the
check pass — that would have recreated the defect in a new form.

Also fixes the same defect in its loud form, which the previous commit
introduced: a `@scenario` annotation naming a scenario that exists in no feature
file. `payload-cost.feature` gains the two behaviours that annotation and the
`failed` counter were reaching for — a subscriber being stoppable for one tenant
without a deploy, and work lost before it was queued being visible as lost.

Worth recording, since it decides when ADR-066's transitional net can go:
`refoldOnStoreMiss` now has three adopters, not zero, and the topic-only
scenario holds only BECAUSE of it — `hasPersistableSignal` writes no row for a
dimension-only trace, so the topic survives a cold cache purely by being
refolded. Removing the net on its stated condition ("the counter stopped
firing") breaks that contract unless a dimension-only state becomes persistable
first.

* fix(event-sourcing): close the defects a six-reviewer audit found in this branch

Revert the log-only storage anchor, and make the subscriber kill switch
actually work.

**The anchor was worse than the bug it fixed.** `occurredAt` is not only
trace_analytics' partition key and TTL anchor — `SpanTimingService` reads
`occurredAt > 0` as its "a span has seeded the timing baseline" sentinel and
computes `currentEnd = occurredAt + totalDurationMs`. Seeding it from a log,
whose time is the platform ACCEPT time rather than producer business time,
measured the first span from the log instead of from itself: TotalDurationMs
inflated by the whole ingest lag, and TokensPerSecond with it, since
SpanCostService divides by that value. It was also order-dependent, so one
trace could report two latencies depending on which signal folded first.

No in-place sentinel works. `spanCount > 0` breaks synthetic-then-real, because
a synthetic span increments the count without seeding timing; adding
`&& occurredAt > 0` then breaks log-then-synthetic-then-real. The real fix is a
storage anchor held separately from the timing baseline — ADR-071 step 3's
target — which needs its own change. Reverting is not a regression: log-only
traces landed in partition 197001 before this branch too. The defect and the
two dead ends are recorded where the next person will look, and the regression
guard folds a log plus a span and asserts the span's own duration.

**The kill switch could not stop one tenant, and could not be reached at all.**
`isComponentDisabled` passed the tenant only as `distinctId`, which is the
rollout bucketing key; rule matching runs against `RuleEvaluationContext`
(`{ projectId, organizationId }`), so every rule naming a project was
unmatchable and the flag fell through to its row-level `enabled` — a switch
meant to stop one tenant stopped all of them. Separately
`getKillSwitchDescriptors` never enumerated subscribers, and `ops.setFeatureFlag`
rejects a key that is neither a registry entry nor a live descriptor, so the key
was not merely unlisted but unsettable. The seam it guards drops events
irreversibly.

The flag is now resolved once per distinct tenant per batch rather than once per
event: the busiest subscribers match every span, so a per-event lookup put a
cache read and a span on the hottest path in the product to answer a question
that cannot change within a batch.

Killed events are counted. A kill is permanent loss and previously moved no
series, so it was indistinguishable from an idle subscriber — exactly when an
operator is looking. `killed` is its own outcome rather than folded into
`filtered`, which would disguise an operator's stop as the subscriber judging
the event irrelevant, and the docblock's summation claim now holds.

Also: declare `miss` on RedisCachedFoldStore, which wraps every ADR-066 adopter
— the executor's skip survived only because `readDurable` happens to return the
inner object unchanged. Assert `miss` against the three REAL stores; the only
test naming `undecodable` fabricated it from a mock, so deleting the
discriminator left the suite green. Correct three store docblocks that still
promised the unwindowed retry, and the router comment claiming a `stage` throw
falls into a routing retry that does not exist.

* fix(specs+hygiene): enforce the read-window contract, and correct a comment I got wrong

`specs/event-sourcing/fold-read-window.feature` carried no pyramid tag, so
`check-feature-parity` reported `0/0 ✓ all bound` and enforced none of its five
scenarios — the same trap this branch closed one directory over, still live on

`producer-append-coalescing.feature` is untagged too but describes nothing this
