Also correct the justification I wrote for reverting the log anchor. It claimed
a synthetic span increments `spanCount` without seeding timing; it does not —
`applySpanToAnalytics` returns before the increment for synthetic names. The
conclusion stands but the reason was wrong: the count is inflated by a span
whose TIMESTAMPS are unusable, where `SpanTimingService` early-returns and the
caller still increments. A comment asserting behaviour the code does not have is

Biome: organize-imports and formatting on the three files this branch left
unformatted. Scoped deliberately — `metrics.ts` is already unformatted on main

* fix(event-sourcing): gate the claim-check producer, and close a second review round

A six-reviewer pass over #6111/#6117/#6103/#6126/#6276 re-read at this
branch's HEAD, so it judges the fixes already applied rather than the merged
PRs. Two reviewers landed on the same top defect independently.

**The claim-check producer shipped ungated, and a rolling deploy loses facts.**
ADR-069 already wrote this down: #6117 was meant to deploy consumer-first, was
merged stacked onto #6111, and the protection was lost. Nothing then acted on
it. A reference staged by a new worker and drained by one still running the
previous build fails that build's type check, RETURNS, and *completes* the job
— no throw, no retry, no drop counter, no log — so every coding-agent span
landing on a not-yet-cycled worker loses its session facts permanently.
`stage` now requires `stageFlag`, resolved per tenant beside the kill switch
and dark by default: off, the whole event is staged, which every build reads.
Resolution failure reads as off, because the seam cannot confirm the fleet has
cycled. It must also stay off where span storage is not ClickHouse-backed —
there a reference never resolves, and the handler's correct "not readable yet"
throw burns 25 attempts and blocks the group.

**A refused row could be quietly replaced by a partial one.** The executor
computed `miss: "absent" | "undecodable"` and both call sites discarded it.
`absent` means fold from `init()`; `undecodable` means a complete state exists
that this build cannot read — folding from `init()` writes a partial state
stamped at the CURRENT version, which the gate that just refused the row then
accepts forever. The corruption launders itself and the original is gone. It
now throws when there is no re-fold path, which is a pairing `refoldOnStoreMiss`
being deleted on schedule would otherwise break silently.

**`UserId` is not the stable column three places claimed.** Spans carry no
identity and a re-fold restarts from `init()`, so a later version can hold an
empty `UserId` AND `max(UpdatedAt)` — filtering the dedup scope on it resolves
to a superseded row and serves stale totals. That is the moving-anchor defect
in a column that never moves in a range sense. Narrowed on the outer scope
only; the rule is corrected in ADR-071 and in the best-practices doc, which had
both copied the false version.

**The list read cut its page before collapsing it.** Two versions tying on
`UpdatedAt` both satisfy the IN-tuple, so `LIMIT` in ClickHouse spent slots on
rows about to merge: a 50-session page returned 49, and through `getUsageTotals`
that is not a short page but a session's cost and tokens silently missing — the
mirror of the double count the tiebreak exists to prevent. It over-fetches and
slices after the collapse.

Also: the Cowork option in the tool catalog could not be selected, because the
drawer gated on a hand-maintained copy of `ASSISTANT_KINDS` that was never
updated (`github_copilot` was missing too, and a stored entry decoded back to
`custom`); the trace→session read had the bare `LIMIT 1` #6276 fixed one file
away, with a batched write making the tie certain and the wrong session opening;
the transcript derivation resolved the agent from spans first, without the
`service.name` that is the only thing telling Cowork from Claude Code; a
duplicate agent id now fails at module load, as a conflicting alias already did;
and both read-back reads log their failures like every sibling.

Tests that could not fail are fixed rather than trusted. The tiebreak suites
moved every key the same way, so the whole ORDER BY could collapse to its last
key and stay green — verified by mutation: collapsing it now fails only the new
conflicting-keys case, and none of the nine that were already there. The
claim-check equivalence test stubbed the read-back instead of running the real
`mapChRowToNormalized`, so the contract the whole design rests on was blind to
every column mapping; it now goes through the mapper. Two scenarios were bound
to tests that did not exercise them.

Four claims are corrected rather than implemented, because each fix is its own
change: the version bump does NOT re-label Cowork sessions (identity comes from
the stored contribution, so a refold reproduces it — only re-ingestion moves
it); `refoldOnStoreMiss` cannot self-expire for two classes of trace, so
ADR-066's deletion condition is unreachable as written; `MAX_METRIC_SERIES`
bounds units, and a delta unit is a point, so a long session's metric fields
freeze silently; `AnnotationIds` has no element cap, so it was no precedent for
one. The log-only storage anchor stays reverted and is now documented where it
bites, including why reusing `occurredAt` is not the fix.

`pnpm test:unit` across the affected tree: 9031 passing. Feature parity: 3177
enforced scenarios bound, up from 3167.

* fix(event-sourcing): drop the claim-check gate, and cut the deploy ceremony

The producer flag is removed. #6111/#6117 are merged and deployed, so the
window it guarded has already passed for the fleet; what remains is a
self-hosted upgrade crossing that boundary in one step, and that is accepted
and recorded in ADR-069 rather than carried as a permanent gate on the fan-out
path.

ADR-066's migration section loses its release procedure with it. A migration is
a migration: it runs when migrations run, and if a rollout lands worker code
ahead of the schema, both halves fail loudly and the queue retries until it is
there — which is what a retrying queue is for. The version-bump section loses

* fix(event-sourcing): close the undecodable-refold hole CodeRabbit found

The guard added last round only proved a re-fold path was CONFIGURED, never
that it produced anything. `refoldUpToDelivered` returns null on an empty
history (`history.length === 0`), and both call sites then fell through to
`loaded ?? init()` and stored — committing a partial state at the current
version over a complete row this build could not read, which is the exact
corruption the guard exists to prevent, reached by a different route.
`assertUndecodableWasRebuilt` closes it after the refold attempt.

The regression test that was supposed to cover this could not: its fold had no
history to rebuild from, so it was already in the null case and passed for the

Also from the review: `events.ts` no longer imports `Fixed64` from a

instead, so the cast cannot drift); the tie-break list-read test binds to its

`loadWithApplied` returns as soon as a state is present, so a store answering

fix(aigateway): preserve upstream provider error identity through the gateway envelope (#6304)

* fix(aigateway): preserve upstream provider error identity through the gateway envelope

While the upstream OpenAI account was out of credits, requests through
the gateway's openai lane surfaced to clients as HTTP 500 internal_error
instead of OpenAI's own 429 insufficient_quota. Root cause chain: raw
forward lanes return provider errors as success-shaped Responses, so
streamed 429s counted as circuit breaker failures while non-streamed
ones counted as successes and none fell back; once the flapping breaker
opened, the retry walk ended with zero attempts and returned a bare
error that writeError could only turn into 500 internal_error.

The fix, layer by layer:

- app/dispatch: non-2xx raw-forward Responses are reshaped into
  UpstreamError inside the walk, so provider quota/rate/5xx answers
  fall back to the next credential on every lane and the terminal one
  is still forwarded verbatim. The credential's provider is stamped on
  the surviving error.
- pkg/retry: only slot-health outcomes (5xx, timeout, network) count
  toward opening the breaker; an answered 4xx proves the slot alive.
  Chain exhaustion surfaces the LAST attempt's error, and a zero
  attempt walk returns a typed ErrNoAttempts sentinel.
- app: ErrNoAttempts translates to a typed circuit_open herr with
  provider fault; httpapi registers it as 503 (previously the code
  existed but was never raised and had no status, defaulting to 500).
- providers/httpapi: the provider's parsed error type/code survive on
  translated lanes with no captured body, and error responses carry
  the documented X-LangWatch-Provider header.
- governance: the account-exhaustion message rewrite also keys on the
  parsed insufficient_quota type/code so bodyless quota errors do not
  leak billing copy to governed users.

* test(aigateway): bind the new error-transparency scenarios for feature parity

Aligns @scenario annotations with the spec scenario titles and adds the

breaker accounting, caller-abandoned requests).

fix(process-manager): key the inbox on a digest, stop tool ids carrying provider payload (#6302)

* fix(process-manager): key the inbox on a digest, stop tool ids carrying provider payload

A Langy conversation stopped dispatching turns for good. The cause was a
Postgres error inside the process manager's commit transaction:

  index row size 3080 exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704 for index
  "ProcessManagerInbox_processName_projectId_sourceEventId_key"

Three independent defects, each fixed here.

1. The inbox indexed a caller-sized value. Its uniqueness spans
   (processName, projectId, sourceEventId), and the source event id is
   `idempotencyKey ?? id` — composed by whichever pipeline emits the command,
   so its length was never the store's to guarantee. Uniqueness now lives on a
   sha256 digest of that value; the raw id stays as an unindexed column for
   diagnostics. The constraint is the same width whatever any pipeline
   concatenates, so this class of failure cannot come back through another
   domain.

2. A tool call id was carrying kilobytes of provider payload. Some providers
   require an opaque blob handed back on the next request, and the agent
   runtime has nowhere to put it, so it staples it onto the id as
   `<id>_ts_<base64>`. Production sent a 2,936-character id, which is what made
   the composed key exceed the index limit. The relay now strips it where the
   frame enters and bounds what is left, so identity is identity — and start
   and end frames, which carried different blobs for the same call, agree again.

3. The failure was deterministic, so the retry ladder ran out and parked the
   conversation's queue group permanently.

Fixing (3) properly meant confronting the staged job id, which appended a
segment per retry and stamped the terminal one from the wall clock:

  event_…/subscriber/pm:langyConversation/r/12/r/16/r/24/r/1785261278310

That id is now immutable for the job's life, and the retry attempt rides on the
message instead — in the envelope header, which is readable without fetching a
blob-offloaded body. See ADR-076. Two consequences had to be designed for
rather than discovered: the unreadable-body ladder now also WRITES the group's
retry chain (removing the id as carrier without it turns a bounded ladder into
an infinite loop), and the worker heartbeat is stopped before the re-stage is
issued (with the id reused, a late beat matches again and would stretch a
sub-second backoff into a multi-minute stall).

Also fixed, found on the way:

- Operator recovery leaked the counters that decide whether a group's next job
  may run. Unblock, drain and dead-letter cleared the poison guard's claim
  strikes but left the retry chain and the failure streak, so a recovered group
  re-blocked on its first failure — and whether it did depended on how long the
  operator took, since the chain expires on its own.
- The ops Lua scripts ran through EVAL, re-transferring and re-hashing the full
  source on every call. They now use the EVALSHA wrapper the queue already has,
  with NOSCRIPT recovery on the pipelined bulk paths — without it a cold script
  cache would make "unblock everything" silently do nothing.
- Row ids and the staged-id fallback now use KSUIDs, not nanoid/randomUUID.
- The queue's machinery fields are checked rather than cast: `??` does not
  catch a non-string, so a numeric or object id would have stringified into a
  malformed Redis key or Prometheus label.

* fix(review): close the heartbeat's cold-cache window, keep the migration rolling-deploy safe

Acting on the review of #6302.

The migration would have caused the outage it fixes. `prisma migrate deploy`
runs at pod boot, so it lands while pods on the PREVIOUS build are still
serving — and those insert inbox rows without `sourceEventKey`. A NOT NULL
column therefore fails every one of their commits with a 23502, inside the
commit transaction, deterministically: the exact "commit fails → ladder
exhausts → group parks" chain this PR exists to end. The column now stays
nullable for the rollout; a follow-up tightens it once the fleet has cycled.
Uniqueness is unaffected meanwhile — btree treats NULLs as distinct, and the
new pods, the only ones that can write an oversized key, are fully constrained.

The heartbeat guarantee had a hole. ADR and comment both claimed that stopping
the interval before issuing the re-stage made a late REFRESH impossible. True
only for the EVALSHA: `CachedLuaScript` retries a NOSCRIPT miss AFTER an await,
so on a cold script cache that one hop is issued behind the re-stage, matches
the now-reused id, and resets the active key to the full 300s — reinstating the
multi-minute stall the ADR says it prevents. The refresh is now cancellable and
the heartbeat withdraws it once stopped, which closes the window completely:
the EVALSHA is ordered ahead of the re-stage, and the only later hop is the one
that can now be withdrawn.

Also from the review:

- The legacy `/r/<n>` reader is anchored to the trailing ladder. Unanchored, a
  producer's own event id containing `/r/25` set another job's retry budget and
  discarded it on its first transient error.
- `DROP INDEX` / `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` are guarded, matching the migration that
  created the old index defensively.
- ADR renumbered 076 → 080: 076 and 077 are already taken on two other branches,
  and this repo already carries duplicate 058s and 059s from exactly that.
- ADR corrections where it overstated what shipped: the `/r/` reader survives as
  a migration artifact (the Consequences said the parser was deleted, which
  would have invited someone to delete a live fail-safe); the heartbeat stops on
  the retry path only, the other re-stage paths being safe because they DEL the
  active key; the wire format was already able to carry the attempt but the
  transient ladder never wrote one; the reader takes the highest in-range
  segment, not the trailing one; and a producer can only predict the id when its
  payload carries one.
- `RESTAGE_AND_BLOCK_LUA` still said it re-stages "with a new ID".
- The `legacyStagedJobAttempt` doc block had drifted above an unrelated function,
  leaving the one function that is dangerous to delete undocumented.

* fix(queue): write the retry chain inside the re-stage script, not before it

Addresses a P1 from review: with the staged id no longer carrying a `/r/<n>`
marker, the group's retry chain became the ONLY attempt carrier a re-staged
SIBLING has — a sibling comes back with its original envelope and no
`__attempt` of its own. `recordGroupAttempt` logged a failed SET and returned,
and the caller then re-staged anyway. A chain write lost to a brief connection
blip, followed by a re-stage that succeeded, therefore handed the next
sibling-led claim a fresh budget: a bounded ladder became unbounded, and a fold
that uses the attempt to recognise a retry discarded its record of what it had
already applied and folded the same events twice.

That gap is one this PR opened. The id's marker used to be the last-resort
carrier for exactly this case.

Both writes now happen inside RETRY_RESTAGE_LUA, after its active-key guard, so
they land together or not at all — and a worker that has lost the slot can no
longer advance a chain it does not own, which the previous ordering allowed
(the caller wrote the attempt before a re-stage that could still return false).
`recordGroupAttempt` is gone; the transient ladder now also checks the return
and stops when another worker owns the slot.

Two scenarios and two tests, both failing against the previous ordering.

* docs(migration): mark the inbox digest migration IRREVERSIBLE

The repo requires a down step or an IRREVERSIBLE block, and this one genuinely
has no safe reverse: recreating the unique index on the raw sourceEventId can
no longer be guaranteed to build, because once this is live the store admits
keys of any length and a single oversized row fails the index creation — the
very row the migration exists to accept. Dropping the digest column alone is
not a rollback either; it removes the inbox's only uniqueness, so idempotency
lapses silently.

Records what a code rollback actually needs instead: deploy the previous build
and leave the schema, which is inert to it.

* fix(test): stop a global SCRIPT FLUSH from flaking unrelated queue suites

The two cold-cache tests reached their state with `redis.script("FLUSH")`,
which is global: it blanks the script cache for every suite sharing the
instance, and a queue still running from an earlier file then fails on a
NOSCRIPT it has no recovery for. It made groupQueue.poisonGuard fail
intermittently in a combined run — a flake this PR introduced.

The behaviour under test lives entirely in `execWithNoScriptRecovery`, so it is
now pinned by a unit test with a fake pipeline: all-NOSCRIPT re-runs every
entry, partial-NOSCRIPT re-runs only those (never re-executing one that already
succeeded), a non-NOSCRIPT failure passes through untouched, a throwing re-run
becomes that entry's error, and a null exec resolves to an empty batch. That is
strictly more coverage than the two integration tests gave, and it harms no one
else's Redis.

Also corrects the ladder-rungs expectation, which encoded the old write
ordering. The chain is now written inside retryRestage, and the test samples on
the way in, so each rung sees what the previous one recorded — the lag IS the
property, since the chain now only advances with a re-stage that landed. Added
a post-condition that the final write did land, so the test is stronger rather
than merely passing.

* docs(migration): stop calling a code rollback free

Review caught that the IRREVERSIBLE block claimed the previous build could be
redeployed with no data step. It runs, but the previous build does not write
sourceEventKey, so its rows carry NULL — and a btree treats NULLs as distinct,
so the new unique index does not constrain them at all.

What actually still protects those writers is the store's read-before-insert
under a transaction advisory lock keyed on (processName, projectId, processKey).
Inbox uniqueness spans (processName, projectId, sourceEventId), ACROSS process
keys, so a same-key redelivery is still deduplicated and the case that loses its
guard is one source event reaching two different process keys concurrently —
exactly what the dropped index caught.

Now says so, in the migration, the schema doc, and the PR's deployment impact,
along with the conclusion that follows: drain before rolling back across this
migration. The nullable column is still right — a NOT NULL fails every old-pod
commit, which is the outage this change ends — but the window it buys has a
cost and that cost should not be discovered during an incident.

fix(gateway): pin budget rollup period truncation to UTC (#6222)

* fix(gateway): pin budget rollup period truncation to UTC

The budget rollup's period truncation ran in the ClickHouse server
timezone: the ledger's OccurredAt is a bare DateTime64, so toStartOfDay,
toStartOfWeek, and toStartOfMonth in the materialised view truncated to
local midnight while currentPeriodStart always computes UTC boundaries.
On any server whose default timezone is not UTC, DAY, WEEK, and MONTH
debits landed in a bucket the reader never asks for: spend accrued,
read back as $0.00 forever, and the budget never warned or blocked.
This is the same never-readable-bucket failure 00055 fixed for window
drift, reachable again through deployment configuration alone. Nothing
in the charts or docs pins the server timezone, and ClickHouse defaults
to the system timezone, so a self-hosted non-UTC server is an entirely
ordinary setup.

The test environment runs ClickHouse in UTC, which is why the 00055
parity test could never see this. The new scenario simulates a non-UTC
server by setting session_timezone on a synchronous insert, which is
the context the view's SELECT evaluates in; it fails against 00055 on
exactly DAY, WEEK, and MONTH and passes with the pinned view.

Two subtleties the migration comments carry: the truncation functions
need the explicit 'UTC', and so does the outer toDateTime64, because
toStartOfWeek and toStartOfMonth return a Date and converting a Date
to DateTime64 without a timezone re-interprets midnight in the server
timezone, which puts the drift right back.

Also makes the periodStart suite deterministic at period boundaries:
debits and the read-back now share one pinned instant, injectable into
getSpendForBudgets, instead of racing the wall clock. A run that
happened to span a minute boundary between the MINUTE debit and the
read failed with spend 0; observed once while building the timezone
scenario.

* fix(gateway): rebuild the budget rollup from the ledger when pinning periods to UTC

Pinning the rollup's period truncation to UTC re-keys every DAY, WEEK,
and MONTH row a non-UTC server ever folded, and the persisted aggregate
states cannot be re-keyed in place. Migration 00056 therefore rebuilds
gateway_budget_scope_totals from gateway_budget_ledger_events, the
durable source of truth, instead of only recreating the view over it.
An org that spent $800 of a $1000 monthly budget before the upgrade
reads $800 after it, and enforcement counts that history.

The rebuild lands in a scratch table while the live rollup keeps
serving reads, is swapped in with an atomic EXCHANGE TABLES, and a
reconciliation pass then adds, per rollup key, exactly the amount
present in the ledger but not yet in the rollup. The view is dropped
before the rebuild snapshot and recreated after the swap, so a debit
arriving mid-migration lands in the ledger, is caught by the
reconciliation delta exactly once, and is never double counted: the
ledger snapshot is taken strictly before the rollup is read, folds are
synchronous with their ledger insert, and deltas clamp at zero. A
re-run after a crash truncates the scratch tables and converges to the
same state from any interruption point.

The upgrade path now has an end-to-end regression: a new migration
replay helper places the schema in the 00055 state, folds non-UTC
history under the old view, applies 00056 for real, and proves the
history reads back in full and blocks when combined post-upgrade spend
crosses the cap. On data already keyed by UTC boundaries the rebuild is
asserted to reproduce identical totals.

periodStart suite 23/23 (twice), budgetEnforcement 9/9, reactor suite
5/5, typecheck and typecheck:tests clean, feature parity 3052 bound.
Full goose up verified on a fresh database, migration runs in 125ms.

* fix(gateway): renumber the rollup rebuild migration to 00058 after main's 00056 and 00057

Main took versions 00056 and 00057 while this branch was in review, so
the UTC rebuild migration moves to 00058. The migration replay tests

* fix(gateway): pin join_use_nulls on the reconciliation insert and harden the replay suites

The reconciliation delta relies on unmatched LEFT JOIN rows carrying
zero-valued Cur* columns; a server profile with join_use_nulls = 1 turns
them NULL and the statement stops repairing missing keys, so the setting
is pinned on the statement itself. Verified live under a hostile session:
unpinned the insert fails, pinned it reconciles correctly.

The migration replay suites now restore the current view in afterAll so
a failure mid-describe can never leave later suites on the 00055 view,
and the enforcement suite replays migrations only in beforeAll, with the
pre-rebuild decision captured during setup. Replay helper takes named
object parameters per the repo rule, the Down section carries the
IRREVERSIBLE marker path instructions require, and the upgrade scenario's
When step describes the operator action instead of the rollup.

* fix(haven,retention): close the play trust bypass, stop clean --yes dropping databases

Four blocking defects found auditing this branch.

Trust gate (tools/thuishaven/app/play.go). The gate read GitHub's
author/committer logins, which GitHub derives by matching the commit's
email header against accounts' verified addresses. That header is chosen
by whoever pushes, and the <id>+<login>@users.noreply.github.com form is
publicly derivable, so anyone could open a fork PR whose commits appear to
be a maintainer's and have `haven play` check out and execute their code
with no prompt at all. Nothing was cryptographically verified.

Trust now rests only on authenticated facts. A same-repo PR keeps the
write-access check, since creating the branch required push access. A fork
PR trusts a commit only when GitHub verified its signature and the verified
signer has write access; every other commit is named untrusted by sha. A
commit listing that hits GitHub's 250-commit cap fails closed rather than
vouching for the head commits it never saw.

Play sandboxes also stopped running the checkout's package scripts:
installs pass --ignore-scripts unconditionally, the guard `haven pr`
already applied to forks. Nothing is lost, since the postinstall is codegen
and the sandbox runs start:prepare:files explicitly straight after.

Retention (langwatch/src/server/data-retention/retentionPolicy.schema.ts).
PLATFORM_DEFAULT_RETENTION_DAYS became a module-load call reading
process.env, but six client modules import this file and the browser bundle
has no `process` — vite substitutes only the specific process.env.<KEY>
reads it enumerates. The data-retention settings page threw
ReferenceError at module load. It now falls back to the production constant
in the browser, where there is no override to honour anyway.

The production guard was also fail-open: it refused only the exact string
"production", so a deployment whose NODE_ENV came through Helm as "prod",
"staging" or unset would silently honour a shrunken default and expire
customer data early. It now honours the override only under an environment
positively recognised as development or test, and bounds the value by
MAX_RETENTION_DAYS so a week-aligned but oversized value cannot wrap the
UInt16 column into a much shorter retention.

Cleanup (tools/thuishaven). `haven clean --yes` called Prune, which drops
every idle worktree's ClickHouse and Postgres databases, while its flag
help, doc comment and spec all promised only "safe categories" — and the
agent report tells non-TTY callers to run exactly that command. Database
reclaim is now opt-in through PruneOptions and reachable only from the
interactive picker, which shows the user what is in scope.

Session viewer. readFresh started a fresh model at offset 0 and allocated
the whole combined stack log, twice, to render a screenful. That file is
append-only and uncapped; existing ones here reach 248MB. First reads now
open at a bounded 256KiB tail window.

Also: exclude .env.portless from the Docker build context so a locally
built image cannot bake in a dev stack's overrides and tokens, and set
HAVEN_SEED_MONTHS on the mass preset so seed:retention actually waits out
the policy cache instead of writing backdated rows pre-expired.

* fix(haven): make up reconcile fully, unbreak --level, stop specs enforcing nothing

Reconcile compared only selection and the langy image tag, so two things
were silent no-ops on a running stack. `haven up --rebuild` reported
"nothing to do" and never rebuilt, contradicting the ADR and the README.
Worse, a changed langy isolation tier was invisible: re-running up after
unsetting LANGY_UNSAFE_CONTAINER said the stack already matched while the
container kept running with the UID sandbox off. Both are now terms in the
comparison, and the message says which one diverged instead of always
blaming the selection.

The reconcile test derived its expected selection with SelectionFromStack,
the same function reconcile compares with, making the assertion f(x) == f(x)
— true for any implementation. It now spells the selection out.

`haven logs --level` matched level words by tokenising the raw line, but
captured output is raw service stdout where the level arrives wrapped in
colour escapes ("\x1b[0m\x1b[33mWARN\x1b[0m"). No token ever matched, so the
filter dropped every line of every real service while the tests passed on
hand-written plain fixtures. Escapes are now stripped before sniffing, the
scan is bounded to a line's leading tokens so prose like "failed to fetch
trace abc" is not read as a severity, and the fixtures are shaped like what
the sink actually stores.

The log sink could recurse forever: open() rotated when the file was over
the cap, rotate() ignored the rename error and called open() again, which
found the same oversized file. A read-only log directory turned capture
into a stack overflow that took the launcher, and the whole stack, down.
Rotation now fails closed by disabling capture, and reopening after a
rotation cannot rotate again.

`haven logs --stack` was joined into a filesystem path with no validation,
unlike every other slug entry point, so `--stack ../../..` walked out of
the haven home. It now rejects anything that is not a valid slug.

Three new spec files carried no tag at all, and the parity gate only
enforces tagged scenarios — so it printed "all bound" while enforcing zero
of their thirty scenarios, thirteen of which have no test anywhere. They
are now @unit at feature level, the scenarios that need a running stack are
marked @integration @unimplemented so the debt is visible rather than
invisible, and the scenarios added for the trust-gate work are bound to
real tests.

Also retires command spellings this PR removed but left behind in places
that now hard-fail: the haven-setup skill an agent loads to bring the stack
up (make haven setup / make haven list), the scenario runner's TLS hint,
the README's HAVEN_LANGY_REBUILD, and the prune/hub/doctor invocations in
three enforced spec files.

* fix(haven): bring haven into CI, content-address the langy image, keep failed teardowns reapable

tools/thuishaven was in none of go-ci's scopes — not the paths filter, not
build, test or vet — so this branch's ~5,000 lines of new Go and its 61
scenario-bound tests were never exercised by CI at all, and the workflow did
not even trigger on a haven-only change. The green checkmark said nothing
about the majority of the diff. It is now built, tested (with -race) and
vetted. Lint stays out for now and says why in the file: haven carries ~230
pre-existing findings, three quarters of them misspell enforcing US spelling
against prose written in British English, plus gosec file modes on a local
dev tool. That is a judgement-heavy sweep and belongs in its own change.

The langy image tag folded file mtimes into its hash, so it was not a
content address at all: `git worktree add`, a branch switch or a fresh clone
moved the tag without a byte changing, forcing the multi-minute rebuild the
hash exists to avoid and guaranteeing a CI-published image could never match
a tag a developer's checkout derives. It now hashes file contents, with
path+length framing so two layouts cannot collide, and a test pins that a
pure touch leaves the tag alone.

Play teardown promised, in its own comment, that the record is removed last
"so a half-finished teardown is still discoverable and re-runnable by haven
clean". It never was: every step ran unconditionally, so the record went
even when containers, volumes or the checkout had failed to go, leaving
them stranded with nothing able to find them. The record step is now skipped
when anything earlier failed. Relatedly, the container and volume removals
ended in `|| true`, which cannot fail — `rm -f` and `volume rm -f` already
succeed on absent names, so that only hid a volume still in use or a dead
docker daemon behind a clean-looking teardown.

In the play viewer, esc quit — and quitting a play sandbox irreversibly
destroys its databases, containers and checkout. Only q was ever advertised
as doing that, and esc is the universal back-out-of-this-screen key. It now
declines and names the key that does quit; on the up viewer, where quitting
merely detaches, esc is unchanged.

Also: `haven typecheck` promised "(args forwarded)" but declared no flags
and had no terminator, so --watch, --noEmit and -p were all rejected as
unknown haven flags and the command could only run bare.

* fix(haven): mark the one-shot seed lanes as development, fill gaps in the seed overlay

The fail-closed retention guard refuses LANGWATCH_DEFAULT_RETENTION_DAYS
outside development and test. haven's long-running Node children get
NODE_ENV=development from the plan, but the one-shot lanes — prepare, seed,
codegen — did not, while still receiving the override through the stack
overlay. Those lanes import the same modules the app does, so a seed would
have died at module load on a stack haven itself provisioned. They now carry
NODE_ENV=development, and a test pins it, since this is exactly the kind of
coupling that regresses silently.

managedStackEnv also validated the freshly-ensured endpoints and then
returned the REGISTERED stack's overlay, which only carries a database URL
if it recorded one. A stack registered while haven was not managing that
server therefore had no URL in its overlay, and the child fell through to
whatever .env names — so the guard vouched for one database while the seed
ran against another. The registered overlay still wins where it has a value,
with any missing keys filled from the endpoints just ensured.

* fix(haven): stop the play sandbox inheriting credentials and running the PR's own haven

`haven play` runs an unreviewed PR's code. Two paths let it do that with more
authority than the trust gate ever granted.

The checkout inherited the developer's .env files. `ensurePRWorktree` used a
bare `git worktree add`, and this repo sets core.hooksPath=.githooks, whose
post-checkout hook copies untracked .env* from the primary checkout into every
new worktree. git fires that hook on `worktree add` with the branch flag set,
so both of the hook's own guards pass — it is written for exactly this path.
The stack overlay supplies connection settings and no credentials, so the
provider keys, Stripe and auth secrets in .env survived into the PR's install,
migrations and dev servers, while the banner said "Nothing is shared with your
worktrees". The play path now disables hooks for its `worktree add`, and sweeps
any untracked .env* from the checkout on create and refresh — the sweep also
covers sandboxes left by an older haven. `haven pr` is a working checkout the
developer drives themselves and keeps the hook it has always had.

The launcher compiled and ran the PR's own copy of haven. selfArgv fell back to
a relative `go run ./cmd/haven`, and startPlayLaunch set cmd.Dir to the play
checkout — the same repository, so it has a cmd/haven of its own. go run
resolves a relative package against the child's working directory, so the
orchestrator that owns the docker socket, the overlay writer and teardown was
the PR's, before --ignore-scripts could matter. `make haven install` is
documented as optional and dev/haven.mk falls back to `go run`, so this was the
default for anyone who had not opted in. selfArgv now resolves the package
absolutely against a trusted root, and children that run inside an untrusted
checkout carry that root forward in the environment — otherwise the daemon they
spawn re-derives the same flaw one level down.

Also: `up` hardcoded ensureDeps(..., true), against the invariant deps.go
states and the comment above the call claimed. `haven pr` re-invokes `up` in
the fork's worktree, and its own sanitised install runs at the worktree root,
which the root workspace deliberately excludes langwatch/ from — so
<fork>/langwatch was always uninstalled, depsStale always true, and `up`
reinstalled it with the fork's postinstall enabled, bypassing --no-install too.
The trust decision now travels through UpParams.

The go-ci comment justifying the golangci-lint exclusion said three quarters of
haven's findings were misspell. Measured at the pinned v2.11.4 it is 75 of 231
(32%), with gosec at 72; the comment now carries the real split. Its
conclusion still holds — every gosec sub-rule outside the existing excludes was
read by hand and none is an exploitable defect in a single-user local CLI — but
the exclusion is package-wide, so it also silences adapters/dashboard's G203
and G704 in files this change never touches. Noted there for that sweep.

Each new test was checked against the pre-fix code and fails on it.

* fix(haven): bound the log read, guard the shared database, stop selection decoding silently

Five defects from the branch audit, plus the tests that hold them.

`haven logs` read every byte of every selected capture to print the last
200 lines. A stack left up overnight makes that hundreds of megabytes for
a view of a few kilobytes, and the follow loop sized its allocation the
same way. Both now read a bounded tail, drop the partial line a mid-file
start picks up, and say on stderr when history was elided rather than
quietly showing less than was asked for. The cap is a parameter so the
test costs what the fixture costs, not what the constant is next set to.

`haven db reset` ran the same ceremony for a worktree's throwaway
database and for lw_main — which is not this stack's data but what every
worktree that never asked for its own falls back to. The shared one now
says so, takes the database name rather than a keystroke, names itself in
the agent-mode refusal, and announces what it is dropping under --yes.
--yes still confirms; scripts have no prompt to answer.

The removed selection env vars were matched against one literal each,
while the consumers outside haven spell truthiness three different ways.
WORKERS_IN_PROCESS=off, =FALSE and LANGWATCH_SKIP_NLP=yes all sailed
through and were silently ignored, which is the exact failure the
refusal exists to prevent: haven running a service the developer
believes they turned off. Both predicates now read intent. A value
blanked to nothing still carries none, so it blocks nothing.

.haven.json decoded straight into a Selection, so every service a file
did not name read as false. A hand-written file naming the one service
you want — the natural thing to write — took gateway and nlp off the
stack. Absent now means "not stated" and keeps its default; stated false
still wins. Writes continue to state all four, and the adapter has tests
where it had none.

The three lifecycle scenarios that were enforcing nothing (piped up,
detached up, switch by name) are bound. That meant extracting the two
decisions they describe — upRunsAttached and detachedUpArgv — from the
closures they were buried in.

Every new test was checked by breaking the fix under it and confirming
it goes red; the switch one only discriminated after it stopped
accepting "nothing matched" for a prefix two worktrees matched.

* test(haven): enforce the lifecycle scenarios that had tests but no tag

Five of haven-lifecycle-usability.feature's scenarios were bound by
passing Go tests and tagged with nothing, so the parity checker held
them to nothing while reporting the file green. Tagging them is the
whole fix: the bindings already existed.

* fix(haven): make accepting an untrusted PR take two steps, not one keystroke

`haven play`'s sandbox isolates the PR's data — dedicated databases, volumes,
hostnames and checkout, and since 4a2b771fe none of the developer's .env files.
It does not isolate the developer. The install, migrations, seed and service
commands are ordinary child processes, so they run under the developer's own
account and inherit the environment haven was launched from: SSH agent socket,
GitHub, cloud and registry tokens, plus a reachable home directory and network.
The gate guarding all of that was a single y/N that disclosed none of it, and a
y/N is cleared by reflex.

The terminal gate now asks twice. The first step is unchanged: it names the
authors without write access and takes a y/N, defaulting to no. The second
spells out what the sandbox does and does not isolate, then accepts only the
PR's own number typed back — 6058 or #6058, with a y, an empty line, or another
PR's number all aborting. A number cannot be muscle memory the way a y can, and
answering it means having read far enough to know which PR is about to run.

The same sentence now rides every route that ends in a stranger's code running:
the second step, the --allow-untrusted warning, and the agent-mode failure.
--allow-untrusted still skips both prompts, because agent mode has no y/N to
answer, but it no longer skips the disclosure. No new flag.

Containerising the sandbox's execution is what would close that exposure rather
than disclose it. ADR-064 now records it as deliberately out of scope, so the
isolation claim is not read wider than it is.

Both steps share one buffered reader: a second reader over the same stdin
discards whatever the first buffered, which is exactly where the second answer
sits. The gate is split behind explicit streams so the two-step shape is
testable without a terminal, and each new test was checked against the one-step
code and fails on it.

feat(gateway): budgets on every dimension and the virtual-key drawer redesign (#6259)

* feat(gateway): provider-filtered budgets, per-member GROUP budgets, explicit routing mode

Adds the data model for budgets on every dimension and collapses the three
hand-mirrored copies of "which budgets apply here" into one resolver.

- GatewayBudget.providerKey (a ModelProvider row id): null counts every
  dispatch, set counts and constrains only that provider's spend. This is
  what makes the targeting matrix n x n without a scope type per provider.
- GatewayBudgetScopeType += GROUP, resolved per member: one row means
  "everyone in this department gets this much, each", bucketed
  <groupId>:<userId> so members never share a pot.
- GatewayBudgetLedger.providerKey so a filtered budget accrues only its own
  spend.
- VirtualKey.routingMode NONE | FALLBACK_ALL | POLICY. New keys default to
  NONE (no silent failover to another vendor); existing keys are migrated to
  FALLBACK_ALL so their behaviour is unchanged. NONE also pins
  fallback.max_attempts to 1 so it is real on gateways that predate the field.
- providers_allowed on the VK config: absence means every provider in scope
  now and in future, an explicit list must name at least one and may only
  name providers the key can actually reach.
- Bundle gains provider_key, providers_allowed, routing_mode and the group
  bucket shape.

* feat(gateway): one resolver for budget applicability, provider-aware debits

check(), the trace fold and the config bundle each carried their own copy
of the same OR list. They now all read budgetResolution.service, so a scope
can no longer be enforced on one path while another quietly ignores it.

The ledger buckets spend by (Scope, ScopeId), so anything that must accrue
separately is separate in that key: a provider-filtered budget appends its
provider, a per-member department allowance appends the member. Debits stamp
the dispatched provider (from langwatch.model_provider_id, now accumulated
into the trace fold) and a dispatch with no reported provider only ever
debits unfiltered budgets — guessing there would mis-bill a governance
control.

* feat(gateway): read virtual-key spend from the cost path, not the budget ledger

The Usage tab read gateway_budget_ledger_events, which the trace fold writes
once per applicable budget and not at all when a key has none. A key nobody
capped therefore reported $0.00 forever, and a key covered by three budgets
reported triple. Both numbers are about to be put on the virtual-keys table
as a clickable column, so they have to be right and they have to match the
page the click lands on.

Spend now comes from trace_summaries via the langwatch.virtual_key_id
attribute the gateway stamps on every span: every key, budget or not, deduped
per trace. The budget ledger keeps the debit list on a budget's own page,
where one row per budget is the point.

Also drops the "keys explicitly scoped to this project" predicate on the
Usage tab: the traces already say which key spent here, and the predicate was
hiding org- and team-scoped keys whose traffic lands in the project all the
same.

Adds virtualKeys.spendThisMonth (the table column) and
virtualKeys.applicableBudgets (the drawer's already-applies list, answerable
for a draft key that has no row yet).

* test(gateway): integration cover budgets on every dimension and key spend

Real Postgres + real ClickHouse, no mocks.

The spend suite pins the two properties the ledger-backed read could not
give us and that the new column depends on: a key nobody capped still
reports what it spent, and a key covered by two budgets is counted once.
It also pins the window as half-open, because the reported symptom was
spend showing up about a day late and the range math had to be ruled in or
out — a request from a minute ago lands inside a rolling 30-day window, and
a request one second before the start does not.

The dimensions suite covers per-member department buckets (including
joining and leaving), provider filters keeping their spend apart from an
unfiltered budget on the same target, the bundle fields the gateway will
enforce from, and the key create / revoke invariants: budget and key in one
transaction, archive rather than delete on revoke, no empty or out-of-scope
provider list, no routing mode that contradicts its policy.

* spec(ai-gateway): budgets on every dimension and the key-creation contract

Extends budgets, gateway-budget-targeting, budgets-principal-cascade,
fallback and provider-routing, and adds virtual-key-creation.

Written after the investigation rather than before it, so they say what is
actually true: where key spend is read from and why it is not the budget
ledger, that the range the pages ask for is a rolling window rather than
whole days, that a key owned above a project must state where its traces
land or admit it is untraced, and that leaving the provider list open means
future providers too.

Scenarios that Wave 2 (gateway enforcement) and Wave 3 (the drawer) will
implement are marked @unimplemented and bind when those waves land.

* docs(contract): provider filter, department buckets, routing mode and where key spend is read from

Documents for the gateway what the control plane now sends: provider_key on
every budget, the <groupId>:<userId> bucket a department budget arrives as,
providers_allowed, and routing_mode with the max_attempts pin that makes
"no fallback" true on gateways that do not read the field yet.

Adds 4.6 for how a provider-filtered budget is enforced: a breach removes
that provider from the candidates rather than refusing the request, and only
an empty chain blocks, naming the budget that emptied it.

Also records the bucket-key table, because two budgets on one target with
different provider filters would otherwise share a pot and each report the
other's spend, and states that per-key spend shown to users comes from the
trace cost path rather than the budget ledger.

* fix(gateway): keep the usage window rolling instead of freezing it at page load

The Usage tab and the key detail page computed their date range once, at
mount. A tab left open overnight kept asking for the window it was opened
with, so spend recorded since then never appeared and the page looked about
a day behind until somebody reloaded it. That is the shape of the reported
freshness complaint, and it needed no ingestion delay to produce.

The window now advances on a one-minute cadence, quantised to the minute so
this costs one refetch a minute rather than one a render.

* feat(gateway): refuse keys whose traces have nowhere to land

Budget spend is accrued from the trace fold, so a key whose traces land

fix(workers): probe an unauthenticated /healthz instead of /metrics (#5524)

* fix(charts): authenticate worker metrics liveness/startup probe

The worker liveness/startup probes were process-only (kill -0 1). Switch
them to an HTTP GET of the /metrics server on :2999 so a wedged event
loop is caught, and send Authorization: Bearer <METRICS_API_KEY> when a
metrics key is configured — the same key Prometheus scrapes with. Without
the header, a metrics endpoint that enforces auth answers 401 and the pod
crash-loops on failed probes. The header is only emitted when the key is
set as a plain value; an unauthenticated endpoint answers 200 either way.

* fix(workers): probe an unauthenticated /healthz, not /metrics

Probing `GET /metrics` crash-loops the workers in two independent
configurations, and the e2e `workers health check` suite caught it:
`helm upgrade --wait` timed out because the pod never went Ready.

1. Stock install. `app.telemetry.metrics.enabled` defaults to false, so
   METRICS_API_KEY is never emitted, and the chart defaults NODE_ENV to
   production. `isMetricsAuthorized` throws on that combination and the
   handler fails closed with 500 — to every caller, header or not. A
   default `helm install` would crash-loop its workers.
2. secretKeyRef install. A kubelet httpGet probe cannot read a Secret,
   so a key delivered via `apiKey.secretKeyRef` can never reach a
   rendered Authorization header. That install gets 401.

Baking the token into the podspec as a plain httpHeader does not fix
either case, and copies a secret out of the Secret into an object
readable by anyone with `get deploy`.

So liveness gets its own path. The worker metrics server now serves an
unauthenticated `/healthz` alongside the bearer-gated `/metrics`, and the
chart probes that. It carries no telemetry, so leaving it open exposes
nothing the gate was protecting, and an answered request still proves the
event loop is turning — the thing `exec: kill -0 1` could never tell us,
which is what this change set out to fix.

The request handler is split out as `createWorkerMetricsHandler` so the
routing and auth branches are testable without binding a port.

Spec: specs/server/worker-liveness-probe.feature

* docs(specs): describe production mode as behaviour, not NODE_ENV

Feature files describe what an operator observes, not the config value
behind it. Both scenarios that set up the fail-closed case now say the
worker is running in production mode.

* test(charts): cover metrics collection with a key, in a live cluster

Every live assertion about /metrics ran in one configuration — the chart
default, where no key is configured — so only the fail-closed branch was
covered. The branch operators actually run (a key is set, Prometheus
scrapes with a bearer) had no live coverage at all, and secretKeyRef
delivery was only ever checked as rendered YAML.

Adds a metrics-collection suite that installs both keyed configurations
and asserts, in-cluster, that the tiers come up and that metrics are
collectable: unauthenticated and wrong-key scrapes are refused without
leaking samples, the correct bearer really serves samples from both the
worker and the app, and the liveness path stays credential-free once a
key exists. The secretKeyRef pass proves the value reaches the process,
which rendering a reference does not.

The probe reports status and sample-presence together — a gate that let a
caller through but returned an empty body would pass a status-only check
while collecting nothing.

* fix(event-sourcing): stop log-only traces committing into partition 197001

`trace_analytics.OccurredAt` is the partition key, the lead sort key and the
TTL anchor, and it was also the fold's span timing baseline — the running
`min(span.startTimeUnixMs)`, which only spans ever set. A trace whose only
signal is a log record (Claude Code / Codex "Path B") therefore folded a zero,
passed the store's persistable-signal gate on its log-record count, and was
written with `OccurredAt = new Date(0)`: partition 197001, TTL deadline
`1970 + retention`, already years past. Before the TTL merge reaped it the
windowed read-back missed it and the executor paid an unwindowed scan per
delivery; after the reap `store.get()` missed forever and every delivery past
the cache TTL refolded the aggregate's whole history from `event_log`.

ADR-071 step 3, applied to this table: the anchor is now its own fold state
(`storageAnchorMs`), frozen on the first contribution of ANY kind that carries
a usable business time — span, log record, metric correlation, annotation,
topic, origin, rename — and never moved after. The span timing baseline stays
exactly as it was, span-seeded, and moves to its own `EarliestSpanStartMs`
column (migration 00058, `DEFAULT 0` per the rule 00057 wrote down) so the
read-back can restore it instead of decoding "no span yet" onto a trace that
has spans.

First-observed rather than `min`, per ADR-071's rule: the anchor is a storage
address, and every consequence that ADR prices comes from the column moving.
For a span-led trace it is the first span's start — the value the column
already held — so no span trace changes partition. Only log-only traces move,
out of 1970 and into real time.

Seeding the baseline from the log instead was tried and reverted: it inflates
`TotalDurationMs` by the whole ingest lag and takes `TokensPerSecond` with it,
and does so order-dependently. That is now pinned by a test rather than by
memory.

The projection stamp goes to 2026-07-29 — both the derivation and the row
shape changed — so pre-split rows are reported as a store miss and refolded
once, self-healing per aggregate with no backfill.

* fix(event-sourcing): heal pre-split rows by decoding them, and bound the anchor a producer supplies

Three defects from the review of this branch, plus the comment drift they left.

1. The version bump re-anchored the whole population. Bumping the projection
   stamp made every existing row undecodable, so each one rebuilt from event_log
   on its next delivery — and a rebuild RE-DERIVES the anchor. For a trace whose
   spans arrived out of order the rebuilt value is later than the min(span start)
   the column held, so the row changes sort key, orphans its previous version
   until TTL, and can cross a toYearWeek boundary. The change whose premise is
   "an anchor is written once" would have opened by moving every anchor it
   touched — ADR-071 consequences 1-3 at population scale.

   The predecessor stamp is now decoded instead of refused. On a pre-split row
   OccurredAt is min(span start), which is at once a valid anchor (it is what the
   row is already partitioned and TTL'd on) and the correct timing baseline (it
   is what EarliestSpanStartMs was split out to carry), so both fields are read
   off that one column and the row heals in place: no refold, no re-anchoring, no
   backfill, and ADR-066's refoldOnStoreMiss retirement clock is not reset. The
   stamp still had to move, because after the split EarliestSpanStartMs = 0 is
   ambiguous between "pre-split row" and "log-only trace" and only the version
   separates them.

2. The anchor had no future bound. isUsableAnchorMs checked only `> 0`, while the
   collector accepts any 13-digit timestamp and bounds only the past edge. One
   span claiming to start in 2286 fixed that row's partition and its
   `OccurredAt + retention` TTL deadline in 2286 — outliving tenant retention
   indefinitely, unreachable by ttlReconciler, and outside every read window so
   every delivery paid an unwindowed scan. Before the freeze this self-corrected;
   freezing is precisely what would have made it permanent, so the bound belongs
   here. A day of skew is allowed, which is well inside the read window.

3. The CreatedAt fallback was unvalidated. ADR-071 names CreatedAt as a trap for
   exactly this use; the deviation is accepted and documented, but every step of
   the chain is now checked, because parseClickHouseDateTimeMs returns 0 on a
   parse failure and an unchecked fallback puts the row straight back in 196952.

"KNOWN DEFECT, deliberately NOT fixed here" block described this fix as still
needed and told the next reader not to write it; the "TWO CLASSES DO NOT
SELF-HEAL" list still named the log-only trace it closed; the refoldOnOutOfOrder
rationale claimed whole-fold order-insensitivity that storageAnchorMs breaks —
load-bearing, because the executor keys on that flag to choose the streaming
refold, so it now states the exception and why it is safe for a storage address.

The migration's "no span trace changes partition" is qualified to the in-order

* docs(event-sourcing): make the anchor's own claims agree with it

An audit of the previous two commits found no correctness defect but a cluster
of documentation that the new code contradicts. One of them is inside migration
00060, which becomes immutable on merge, so it is the reason this commit exists.

- 00060 contradicted itself. One paragraph said pre-split rows are decoded and
  the population is not rewritten; another, four paragraphs later, still said
  they are "reported as a store MISS and refolded once". The code does the
  former. An operator sizing the deploy off the stale sentence would expect a
  population-wide refold, and an engineer reconciling code against it would
  "fix" the store gate and reintroduce exactly what this change removes.

  true: the anchor is validated on every write, not only when first frozen, so a
  row whose committed OccurredAt is more than a day ahead of fold time fails the
  new bound and is rewritten at fold time. That is a partition move on an
  existing row. It is the intent — the row was filed in a future partition with
  a TTL deadline to match, and would have outlived its tenant's retention — but
  denying it in the migration was wrong. Documented there and in the ADR.

- "The stamp move is not a refold trigger" holds forward, not backward. During a
  rolling deploy, pods on the previous build refuse the new stamp (bare
  equality) and refold what new pods wrote. Ordinary for any stamp bump, bounded
  by the deploy window rather than the table, and the reason the decode exists
  on the forward path. Said plainly in the store and the ADR rather than left as
  an unqualified claim.

  decoder still justified trusting AnnotationIds with "only rows at the current
  projection version reach here". Both are now about DECODABLE stamps, with the
  invariant that actually holds it up: every decodable stamp postdates 00056.

  rebuilt anchor lands "strictly later" in one place and "either side" in
  another (the latter is right — a replay's first event may be a log or topic
  assignment predating the first span), and "every derived field commutes" is
  true in value but not of Models' most-recent-first ordering.

- The future-skew docblock listed a log's timeUnixMs and the span envelope's
  occurredAt as producer-controlled anchor sources. Neither is: a log's envelope
  carries acceptedAt and a span's carries ingest Date.now(). The bound is
  justified by the span start alone, which is what a span-led trace anchors on.

  column is never the epoch" is structural rather than a convention every caller
  must keep, and `now` is documented as reaching validation, not just the

* fix(langy): refuse a turn whose runToken cannot be resolved

The runToken is the HMAC key the worker signs every stream frame with. Both
the rejected and the null branch of the allSettled read collapsed it to ,
which is an empty HMAC key: publicly computable, and rejected by the relay
(loadRunToken maps absent to null, handle() rejects as no-run-token).

So a transient Postgres blip on that one read produced a turn that ran to
completion, emitted nothing, and never reached a terminal state - a silent
hang with no error surfaced. Fail fast with the typed LangyAgentUnavailableError
instead, so the sign side and the verify side cannot disagree.

Refs #5881 (finding 1)

* fix(langyagent): close the SNI fragmentation evasion, gate the reaper on PID 1

peekClientHelloSNI read exactly one TLS record. A handshake message may
legally span several, so a hostile worker could split its ClientHello and
leave the SNI in record 2: the peek returned , the caller had no definite
mismatch to act on, and the anti-domain-fronting cross-check - the control
whose own comment names that exact adversary - was skipped. Reassemble across
records (bounded), and refuse an unreadable hello while a policy is enforcing.
Monitor-only and non-TLS tunnels are unaffected.

StartOrphanReaper claimed to be a no-op off PID 1. Wait4(-1) matches ANY
child, and the manager always has worker children, so it raced the pool's own
cmd.Wait() and could turn a clean exit into ECHILD. Gate it on PID 1.

Refs #5881 (findings 2, 10)

* fix(cli): decode daemon frames across chunk boundaries

FrameDecoder did chunk.toString("utf8") per socket read, so a multi-byte
sequence straddling two reads resolved to U+FFFD on both halves. The
surrounding JSON stayed well-formed, so the frame parsed and the corruption
shipped silently: 'langwatch dataset records add --json' with non-ASCII
payloads uploaded mangled records at exit 0, while the same command under
LANGWATCH_NO_DAEMON=1 uploaded correct data.

The module header already warned about exactly this for the base64'd output
path; the framing layer itself had the bug. StringDecoder holds the
incomplete tail until the rest arrives.

Four raw TRPCErrors carried no data.error, which is exactly the signal
ADR-045 uses to distinguish handled from unknown - so the client explainer
could not tell a known condition from an internal crash. The worst was a

HandledError's message on the wire.

* fix(traces-v2): stop keyset cursors outliving the sort that minted them

Two ways the table went blank or lost your place, both in the cursor state

Refs #5881

* fix(cli): close two daemon defects — eligibility bypass and socket deletion

1. The daemon gate read the command as "first arg not starting with -", but
   the root program registers value-taking globals and enablePositionalOptions,
   so their VALUE became the detected command: `langwatch -o json open /traces`
   detected "json", passed DENIED_COMMANDS, and ran `open` inside a detached
   daemon with stdio /dev/null and no DISPLAY — no browser, and for the
   claude/codex/cursor wrappers no output reaching the caller at all. The gate
   now scans every argument. This module is deliberately dependency-free, so it
   cannot consult the real option table; a hand-copied skip-list would silently
   reopen the hole the next time a global is added. Over-rejecting costs one
   cold start, under-rejecting changes behaviour.

2. Both socket deletions unlinked by path with no check the file was still
   this process's own, so two concurrently-spawned daemons could delete each
   other's live socket in a loop — the "daemon keeps disappearing" symptom.
   The inode guard alone was NOT sufficient: libuv unlinks the bound path
   itself on close, unconditionally, before any of our code runs. So the
   daemon now binds a private per-pid path, chmods it 0600 while still private
   (closing a pre-existing 0755 window), and publishes with link() — fail
   closed on EEXIST, where rename() would silently orphan a live
   credential-holding daemon.

* fix(langyagent): close the SNI record-version fail-open

The record-version check added in this PR was itself a bypass. A header of
`16 03 05` — one byte off a real ClientHello — took the `header[2] > 4` exit,
which returned a nil error with `sawHandshake` still false. The adapter's guard
is `sni == "" && sniUnreadable(sawHandshake, err)`, and (false, nil) satisfies
neither term, so the tunnel spliced uninspected while the destination parsed the
very hello we had declined to read (RFC 8446 s5.1 deprecates that field and says
it MUST be ignored). Domain fronting, restored by a one-byte edit.

Content type and version are now separate decisions: a non-22 type is still the
clean not-TLS exit, but anything claiming type 22 that we cannot follow is
UNREADABLE, so the caller fails closed.

The suite passed with the bypass present, so the tests move too:

- the version test asserted the fail-open as intended behaviour, locking it in.
  Inverted, and table-driven across three bad-version shapes.
- BoundsEndlessFragments could not fail: it dribbled a FINITE bytes.Reader, so
  io.ReadFull hit EOF and the loop returned whether or not the bound existed.
  Now an infinite reader, so removing the bound hangs the test.
- the fail-closed branch had no decision-level coverage at all — deleting the
  whole arm left the package green. Three adapter-level tests now drive a real
  CONNECT and assert the destination is never dialled.
- the monitor-only @scenario was bound to a test about IP literals.

CONNECT and ClientHello into one segment lost the hello entirely; an SNI that
differs from the authority but is allowed is now flagged rather than silent; and

fronting inside the encrypted stream is not caught.

* fix(langy): unwedge turn recovery, stop demoting terminal history errors

An armed auto-retry could be cancelled and never re-armed. A history poll
landing mid-retry flips sideEffectsObserved, React runs the previous effect's
cleanup and kills the timer, then the same-failure short-circuit returns without
re-arming and without a cleanup. `pending` then stays set forever: isRecovering
is permanently true, regenerate() never runs, the error card stays suppressed,
and the recovering line shows indefinitely until the user sends a new message.
The retry delays are well inside the poll interval, so this is not a rare race.
sideEffectsObserved is an arming-time input, so it moves to a ref and the timer
now belongs to the failure rather than to the effect instance.

isHistoryStale tested only whether content was on screen, never which error
arrived. Deleting a conversation in another tab made the poll return not-found
forever, and because the engine still held messages the actionable card never
rendered — the user kept reading a transcript that no longer existed, with no
retry and no next step, and it never self-healed. Now gated on the error kind,
as a denylist: an unrecognised infra code stays transient, because the opposite
default would let an unknown code replace a streaming answer with a red card.

Console prose sniffing marked successful shell calls as failed. A `bash` call
running `tail` over a log exits 0, and any line starting "failed to " matched,
so the step was dropped from the receipt and rendered as a red error card. The
fallback now only runs on a console the CLI envelope actually wrote — scoped
rather than deleted, since it still covers a langwatch call that prints a
failure line and exits 0.

unless told not to. On reload, applyFromFragment runs before useLensSync has

* perf(ci): let the integration suite run in parallel, and split shards by weight

Integration was the most expensive thing in this workflow: six shards at
~6 minutes, ~36 runner-minutes, every file strictly serial. Measured per
shard, only ~1.3 min of that was setup and containers -- the rest was
tests running one at a time.

The serialisation was justified, but by something narrower than the
setting. Five suites called redis.flushall() in afterEach against the
shared Redis, and BullMQ keys a queue by name alone so two workers
building the same pipeline share it. Both are Redis. The other two
stores were never the problem: across the 111 integration files that
touch ClickHouse there are five hardcoded tenant ids, one of which
appears in more than one file.

So the five flushall() calls become flushdb(), and each worker gets its
own Redis logical database -- flushdb can then no longer reach past the
worker that issued it. With the contention gone the files run
concurrently, and six shards drop to three.

Both knobs are CI-only. A local run still goes serial on one database,
because a laptop is doing other things at the same time.

Sharding also stopped being blind. Vitest splits by hashing paths into
equal-sized groups, so shards get equal file COUNTS regardless of cost:
402/402/402/401 files ran 2.7, 4.8, 3.3 and 2.9 minutes, and the matrix
waits for 4.8 while a runner sits idle. vitest.sequencer.ts assigns
heaviest-first to whichever shard is currently lightest. It weighs bytes
rather than runtime, because vitest's duration cache is per-machine and
a CI runner is always cold -- so it narrows the spread rather than
removing it.

Coverage moves off every merge to main and onto the weekly schedule. It
costs ~45% of a run and nothing consumes it: no codecov.yml, no status
check, both uploads fail_ci_if_error: false. The provider was already
the fast one (vitest 4 defaults to v8), so frequency was the only lever.

* fix(lint): stop Biome choking on the SDK's bundled API schema

Biome raised an INTERNAL diagnostic -- 'unusually large amount of types
which exceeded the limit of 200,000' -- against
node_modules/langwatch/dist/types-*.d.ts, and repeated it for every file
that imports the SDK.

The published langwatch package inlines the entire REST API schema into
one 525KB declaration file: 'interface operations' is 11,998 lines and
'interface paths' another 2,058. The file is never scanned directly, it
arrives through the type graph, which is why the hard '!!' form of the
ignore is the one that works.

This silences the crash. It does not restore coverage, and the comment
says so: Biome was already aborting on those types, so the type-aware
rules were blind wherever SDK types reach and still are.

The real fix is in typescript-sdk/, which derives its public types as
indexed lookups into the generated schema -- paths["/api/evaluators"]
["get"]["responses"]["200"] and so on. A dts bundler cannot tree-shake
an indexed access; it has to inline the whole paths tree to keep the
lookup resolvable. Emitting resolved named types instead would ship only
what is used, and would help every consumer's typecheck rather than just
this repo's linter. That needs an SDK release and a version bump here,
so it is not this config's job.

* perf(test): tune the vitest pools for CI and for a laptop separately

These knobs were single values serving two environments with opposite
constraints, and the laptop won every time.

pool: vmForks trades ~15% wall-clock for 4.5x less memory (2.56GB ->
573MB on a 68-file sample) because a forked child returns its leaked VM
context on exit while a thread's accumulates in the shared heap. That is
the right trade on a machine running several worktrees. It is the wrong
one on a CI runner with 16GB that does nothing else and is destroyed
afterwards, so CI takes vmThreads and the speed. vmMemoryLimit still
recycles a worker past the limit, which is what keeps threads bounded
rather than merely quicker.

maxWorkers: half the cores locally so a run leaves the machine usable,
all of them in CI. vmMemoryLimit likewise rises in CI, where recycling
costs more than the memory it saves.

The integration config deliberately does NOT switch pools: threads panic
inside @prisma/client's query engine wherever they run. Only its worker
count varies, and locally it is pinned to one because that suite is
serial anyway.

* fix(ci): build the Go images with the toolchain go.mod now requires

Clearing the 13 reachable advisories raised the go.mod floor to 1.26.5,
and three Dockerfiles still pinned golang:1.26.4. The official images set
GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so a tag below the floor does not quietly fetch a

1.26.5 (running go 1.26.4)" and the build stops. That took out

are in the standard library: lowering it would turn CI green while the

* fix(scenarios): give the create path its own function again

The noMisusedPromises fix earlier in this branch wrapped the create
callback in `void (async () => { ... })()` so a promise-returning
function stopped being passed where a void one was expected. That is the
right shape, but it left the whole create flow -- mutate, decide whether
to transition, resolve the outer promise, swallow the handled error --
inside one nested closure, at cognitive complexity 11 against a limit of
10.

So split it where it already wanted to split. createScenario does the
mutation and returns a scenario or null; createNew owns the plan-limit
dance and the promise; handleSave picks between create and update
instead of containing both. handleSave keeps its signature, and the
model-overrides type it shared with the two branches is now named rather
than repeated inline.

This was the one real violation the new Biome gate found on this branch.

* fix(ci): gate Biome on new violations, not on lines the formatter touched

The gate failed on its own PR, and it was right to by its own rule and
wrong about the thing that matters. reviewdog's `filter-mode=added`
attributes a diagnostic to whoever added the line it sits on, and Biome
anchors noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity, noExcessiveLinesPerFunction and
useMaxParams at a function's DECLARATION line. Rewrap a signature -- the
formatter's decision, not an author's -- and that line is "added", so the
PR inherits the whole function's backlog. Measured here: 61 findings, of
which this branch had written none. Complexity 30 in useSpanTreeLoader, 29
in sse.ts, a 221-line function in team.service.ts, all pre-existing, all
reported because a parameter list moved onto four lines.

A gate that reports work you did not do is a gate people switch off,
which lands in the same place as the green-but-meaningless check this
whole branch exists to remove.

So ask the question that matters -- does this PR leave the tree worse
than it found it? -- by counting violations per (file, rule) either side
of the merge base and failing only on an increase. That is
.github/scripts/biome-new-violations.sh.

The base is FORMATTED FIRST, with the head's own config, because the
comparison is otherwise not like-for-like for a rule that counts lines: a
58-line function whose signature gets rewrapped is a 61-line function,
and trips a 60-line limit nobody's edit went near. That step is load
bearing, not tidiness -- normalizing the base took this branch from 77
apparent regressions to 1, and the 1 was real (fixed in the previous
commit). It runs with --linter-enabled=false so it can only move layout;
if it fixed a lint violation the base would look better than it is and
the PR would inherit the difference.

Both sides lint under the head's config and share one node_modules, so a
newly-enabled rule's backlog counts as main's rather than the PR's, and
the type-aware rules cannot disagree for reasons unrelated to the diff.

reviewdog keeps annotating the diff and can no longer fail the job, so
the 200-diagnostic cap that works around GitHub's 65536-character review
body now costs annotations only, never enforcement. Two known gaps, both
deliberate: a renamed file reads as entirely new, and net-zero churn
within one file and rule passes. Both stay visible as annotations.

Verified end-to-end against origin/main: 989 violations removed, 0 added,
exit 0.
