* fix(ci): stop a negation pattern defeating the python SDK path filter

`sdk-python-ci` gates its ~9-minute `test` job on a `relevant` filter scoped
to `python-sdk/**`, but the filter also carried
`'!python-sdk/src/langwatch/__version__.py'`.

dorny/paths-filter evaluates a filter's patterns independently and ORs the
results, so that lone negation matches every path that is not the version
file — which is every path. `relevant` was therefore true on every PR in the
repo, and the suite ran in full on changes that never touched python-sdk/.
This branch is the proof: zero python-sdk files, and the changes job still
logged `Changes output set to ["relevant"]` while `test` burned 8.9 minutes.

The control is in the same run — docs-ci, clickhouse-serverless and
langevals-ci all skipped their heavy jobs and still reported their
aggregators green. The mechanism was fine; this one filter was not, and it
was the only filter in the repo using a negation.

The exclusion cannot be expressed under OR semantics, so it is removed
rather than rewritten. A release-please version bump now runs the suite it
was meant to skip: one run per release, instead of one per PR.

specs/ci/path-filters.feature already forbids negation patterns. Nothing
enforced it — the file carries no binding tag, so check-feature-parity
counts none of its scenarios.

* fix(ci): stop running integration files concurrently inside a shard

The four-shard split assumed a shard could safely run two files at once,
given that the five suites calling redis.flushall() had moved to flushdb()
and each worker took its own Redis logical database. Neither half of that
held up.

The wall-clock did not improve: shards measured 7.4-9.2 min against the ~6
min the six-way serial split took, so the claim that no shard got longer
than before was wrong. Runner-minutes fell 35 -> 26, but this workflow is on
the critical path and the minutes were not what needed buying.

And it broke two suites. groupQueue.decodeDrop and scripts now fail
non-deterministically, both with state vanishing rather than an assertion
disagreeing: a staged job that is never dispatched, and a group set that has
lost `j1`. That is the shape of a flushdb reaching past the worker that
issued it. The isolation meant to prevent that is not obviously airtight —
setupEnv runs once at config load in the main process, where VITEST_POOL_ID
does not exist and the worker id falls back to 1, and again per worker as a
setup file — and nothing in the suite asserts that two concurrent workers
cannot see each other's keys.

So the parallelism moves to where isolation is a property of the topology:
six shards, each its own runner with its own Redis service container, each
running its files one at a time.

VITEST_ISOLATE_WORKER_REDIS and VITEST_MAX_WORKERS stay set. The first is
free when files are serial and keeps the wiring in place for whoever writes
the cross-worker isolation test; the second keeps vitest off all four vCPUs
of a runner that is also hosting ClickHouse, Postgres and Redis.

* ci: supersede outdated PR runs, but never cancel main's

Every CI workflow that runs on both main and PRs carried
`cancel-in-progress: true`. On a PR that is what we want and it was already
working — the group keys on `github.ref`, which is the PR's merge ref, so a
new push cancels the run it supersedes.

On main it is wrong. Two merges landing close together cancel the first
one's run, so the commit in between reaches main with no validation of its
own and nothing says so.

Scoping cancellation to non-main keeps the PR saving and stops main
discarding results it is the only place that will ever produce.

Seventeen workflows, all with the same unconditional `true`. PR-only
workflows (migration-order, no-committed-screenshots, pr-auto-approve,
pr-impact-map) keep theirs — they never run on main. boxd-pr-preview already
had the conditional form.

* fix(ci): keep the shard count next to the shard list

Raising integration to six shards produced `--shard=5/4` and a vitest
startup error: the matrix supplied the numerator from an output, but both
run steps hardcoded the denominator as `/4`.

The count now travels with the array as its own output, so the two cannot
drift apart again.

That also fixes the draft case, which was quietly wrong in the other
direction: a draft got `shards: [1]` and still ran `--shard=1/4`, so it
executed a quarter of its files and reported that as a pass over all of
them. A draft now runs `1/1`.

(This file also picks up the main-cancellation change from the previous
commit; it has the same unconditional `cancel-in-progress` as the rest.)

* fix(test): stop integration suites flushing each other's Redis database

Five integration suites called redis.flushdb() to reset themselves. flushdb
empties the whole logical database, so none of them was resetting itself —
each was deleting every key in the database, including the in-flight state of
whatever else was using it.

That is why the failures never landed on the file that caused them.
groupQueue.decodeDrop and stagedJobIdIdentity scope their own cleanup to a
hash-tagged prefix and were doing nothing wrong; they failed because
poisonGuard, scripts and loopPrevention flushed the database out from under
them. The symptoms match exactly: a staged job that is never dispatched, and
a blocked set that never fills — state that existed and then did not.

Each suite now deletes only what it owns:

- scripts already had a hash-tagged QUEUE_NAME, so it deletes `{test/scripts}*`.
- poisonGuard and groupQueue.integration both minted names under `{test/gq/`,
  which would have had them deleting each other. They move to `{test/gqpoison/`
  and `{test/gqmain/` so a prefix-scoped delete cannot cross the boundary.
- loopPrevention and traceparent-roundtrip flush to clear orphaned reactor
  jobs, not their own keys. They now delete the global queue's prefix, taken
  from makeQueueName rather than hardcoded, so renaming the queue cannot
  silently turn the cleanup into a no-op.

This is the same rule groupQueue/README.md already states for the suites that
were written correctly — no global flush, so suites can share a Redis.

Also corrects maxWorkers in the integration config. Vitest overrides
maxWorkers to 1 whenever fileParallelism is false, so the previous
`isCI ? "100%" : 1` was inert and read as if CI ran four workers when it ran
one.

Parallelism stays off in this commit. The point of it is to make turning it
on possible, and that flip is worth its own run rather than being confounded
with the fix.

perf(clickhouse): add bloom skip-index on evaluation_runs.EvaluationId (#5810)

* perf(clickhouse): add bloom skip-index on evaluation_runs.EvaluationId

evaluation_runs is ORDER BY (TenantId, EvaluationId) and PARTITION BY
toYearWeek(ScheduledAt). Point lookups by (TenantId, EvaluationId) that carry
no ScheduledAt predicate cannot prune partitions, so the primary key lands on
one candidate granule in every part and reads it, even when the evaluation
lives in a single week. EXPLAIN INDEXES on a large tenant shows the lookup
reading 61 granules across 61 parts.

trace_summaries already solves the identical shape with its idx_trace_id bloom
filter, where the same EXPLAIN prunes all 180 candidate granules to 0. This
gives evaluation_runs the same property, mirroring the existing idx_trace_id on
this same table (bloom_filter(0.001) GRANULARITY 1).

* feat(model-providers): make every refusal a coded handled error

Only `provider_unreachable` was handled. The other five ways a credential
check fails were free-text strings on `ValidationResult.error` — invented
server-side, handed to the UI, and read by nobody who could branch on
them. That is the shape #6010 spent a whole PR removing everywhere else.

Now each is a code the customer's client can explain and act on:

  provider_key_invalid       the provider says the credential is wrong
  provider_service_disabled  the key is fine, the API is off for its project
  provider_key_restricted    the key's own restrictions refuse this call
  provider_refused           it answered and said no, in terms we can't map
  provider_key_missing       there was no credential to check
  provider_unreachable       nothing answered (unchanged)

Each is the three edits the convention asks for: the subclass, the code in
`APP_ERROR_CODES`, and the copy in the presentation registry. The registry
is exhaustive, so a code without copy fails typecheck and a code nothing
raises fails `codes.unit.test.ts`.

RETURNED, not thrown, with one exception. Being told no is a successful
question — ADR-045 reserves throwing for the ABSENCE of an answer, which
is why `provider_unreachable` alone still throws. So the refusal rides the
result as `domainError`, following `target_result.domainError`, and the
client reads it with `explainSerializedError`.

The provider's own sentence is no longer shown, and this is the change
with teeth. It is the text that quotes the request back: an OpenAI 401
body reads `Incorrect API key provided: sk-proj-…`, and a Gemini request
carries the key in its query string. An earlier draft of this commit put
it in the handled error's `message` on the reasoning that a message is
server-side — it is not. The REST boundary sends `{ error: code, message }`
verbatim (`error-handler.ts`), which is why the convention says a handled
error's message must be written customer-safe. Relaying via `meta.message`
is not the way round it either: a model provider's rejection was admitted
there once as `llm_upstream_error` and reversed for this exact reason, and
the note on `ALLOWED_PER_CODE` says so.

So the upstream sentence is read, used to RANK the refusal, logged, and
dropped. `serialize()` omits `message`, so nothing the browser receives can
carry it — a stronger guarantee than redacting by pattern, which only ever
masks the shapes someone thought of.

Two scenarios changed meaning rather than wording, so the spec says so:
"A refusal carries the provider's own explanation" is now "A refusal is
explained in our own words, not the provider's", and the redaction
scenario asserts the key appears nowhere in the payload rather than in one
field. The tests assert CODES now, not prose — the code is the contract;
the sentence belongs to the registry and is free to be reworded.

Also fixes the P4 from the review: an empty walk returned "invalid API
key", the one answer that is certainly wrong when nothing was asked. It
raises `provider_unreachable` now. `runProbeChain` crossed the complexity
limit once `probeOnce` was inlined in it, so that shape is its own
function.

so anyone outside the eurozone with an existing EUR subscription hit an

fixed, before getBillingCurrency resolves.

fix(event-sourcing): bound the re-fold event_log reads so they prune partitions (#6336)

* fix(event-sourcing): bound the re-fold event_log reads so they prune partitions

`event_log` is PARTITION BY toYearWeek(EventOccurredAt), but both re-fold
loaders bound only on EventTimestamp — acceptance order, not the partition
key. Neither passed an EventOccurredAt predicate, so every re-fold walked
every weekly partition ever written, including the cold tier on S3.

Measured in production: `event_log` was the ONLY table cold-scanning — 198
scans in 15 minutes across 3 pods, ~30k/day, all from exactly two param
signatures, both of them these loaders. The absence is visible in the
signatures themselves: no occurredAtFromMs. Every other time-partitioned
table (stored_spans, log_records, trace_analytics, trace_summaries, ...) is
already bounded and never trips the cold-scan detector.

The bound and its correctness contract already existed — `getEvents` has
passed `rehydrationLowerBoundMs` since the window was introduced, the
repository already accepted `occurredAtFromMs` and rendered the filter, and
TIME_LOCAL_AGGREGATE_TYPES already whitelists the types whose events all
fall inside the aggregate's own lifetime. These two paths were the only
callers that never supplied it. This wires them up rather than adding
anything new.

Safe by construction in both directions:
  - long-lived types (global, billing_report) and events with no usable
    occurred time get `undefined` back and stay unbounded, exactly as today;
  - rows with an unknown occurred time (EventOccurredAt = 0) are always
    kept, so the bound can never drop an event;
  - the 45-day window is far wider than any time-local aggregate's lifetime
    (a trace spans seconds to hours), and a short read still falls back to
    the unbounded scan.

The paginated path matters more than the unpaged one: unbounded, every PAGE
re-opens every partition, so the cost is paid per page rather than per
re-fold.

The in-memory repository mirrors the filter, so a window that would drop
events in production drops them in tests too — otherwise a too-small window
passes every test and only fails against real data.

Context: this sits upstream of a ClickHouse instance pinned at its 3.50 GiB
ceiling and rejecting inserts (Code 241, OvercommitTracker), which in turn
drives spanStorage retries, worker liveness failures and blocked groups.
Separately, 93.1% of 962 sampled re-folds read back exactly the events the
queue had already delivered — those scans return nothing new; this makes
them cheap. Skipping them entirely is a follow-up.

* fix(clickhouse): cover every partitioned table in the cold-scan detector

`detectColdScan` fails OPEN: it only inspects tables listed in
TIME_PARTITIONED_TABLES, so a partitioned table missing from that map is
silently treated as un-partitioned and never flagged, however expensively
it is queried.

The map covered 11 of 35 partitioned tables. The 24 missing ones included
`trace_analytics` and `trace_summaries` — whose unwindowed reads run at
~350/min against a ClickHouse already at its memory ceiling, and which
were therefore invisible to the very detector built to find them. The gap
went unnoticed precisely because the detector reported nothing.

Adds the 24, and adds a test that parses every PARTITION BY out of the
migrations and fails when one is unlisted. A "keep in sync" comment could
not catch this class of drift, because the symptom of the drift is silence.

The test also asserts the two ways an entry can be wrong but non-empty:
a declared prune column that the PARTITION BY expression does not use
(the detector would demand a predicate that cannot prune), and a listed
table that is not partitioned at all (noise that trains people to ignore
the warning).

feat(model-providers): add Google Agent Platform as a provider (#6352)

* feat(model-providers): add Google Agent Platform as a provider

A customer holding a Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform key could not add
Gemini at all. The key is valid; generativelanguage.googleapis.com refuses
it because its API restrictions exclude that service, so #6252 correctly
reported a restriction — but there was still no provider the key belonged
to.

Agent Platform is one, for the same reasons `vertex_ai` is: its own host,
its own auth header, and a path naming the project and location. Same
Gemini models, different service.

The part that had to be established by probing rather than read from the
docs is that the two endpoints on that host disagree:

    POST .../publishers/google/models/{model}:generateContent   accepts an API key
    GET  .../models                                             401 "API keys are
                                                                not supported by
                                                                this API"

So this provider cannot be validated the way every other one here is. It
is probed by generating one token, not by listing models — validating by
listing would report a working credential as unusable. `ProbeRequest`
grew `method`/`body` for that; every existing provider keeps its GET.

The key rides in `x-goog-api-key`, not `?key=`. Both work; a credential in
a URL reaches access logs, proxy logs and browser history, which is what
#6252 moved the whole flow away from. A test pins the absence.

Omitting the project or location yields no probe candidates rather than a
guessed path, which `runProbeChain` reports as unreachable — nothing was
asked, so there is no verdict on the key.

Verified against the customer's real Agent Platform key: the provider
accepts it, where the Gemini provider correctly refuses it. Two
exhaustiveness gaps the compiler caught on the way in — `iconsMap` and
`ModelProviderKey` — are filled.

NOT done, and deliberately: inference. Routing a provider type to an
upstream is `mapProvider`'s job in the Go gateway, so the credential
materialises but no traffic dispatches yet. This closes "I cannot add my
key", not "I can run models through it".

fix(billing): classify provider failures instead of naming every one (#6353)

* fix(billing): classify provider failures instead of naming every one

Follow-up to #5969, which merged with a blanket catch: every failure of
customers.retrieve became billing_currency_unavailable, whatever the
cause. listInvoices has the mirror-image problem — it never wrapped
anything, so a raw provider error escaped and the client rendered
"An unknown error occurred".

Both are the same mistake in opposite directions, and
dev/docs/best_practices/error-handling.md draws the line: a HandledError
promises the caller we know the cause and they can act on it. "Unknown" is
a correct outcome, and inventing a handled error to avoid it leaks
internals and promises an action that isn't there.

translateStripeError classifies instead, mirroring translate-query-error.ts
for ClickHouse — including its fall-through. Rate limiting and connection
failure become a handled billing_provider_unavailable ("nothing happened,
try again", the documented 'wait' case); everything else is returned
untouched and degrades to unknown with a trace id.

Net effect per call site:

  currency lookup  a rate limit is now retryable rather than opaque, and an
                   unrecognised failure stops being dressed up. Either way
                   it still throws before any write, so the no-orphaned-
                   records guarantee from #5969 is unchanged.
  listInvoices     a rate limit becomes actionable copy instead of
                   "An unknown error occurred"; an unresolvable customer id
                   correctly stays unknown.

fix(licensing): canonicalize PEM before crypto.createSign, and type signing-key failures as HandledErrors (#6274)

* fix(licensing): canonicalize the PEM signing key before crypto.createSign

Signing failed whenever the pasted PEM was indented, prefixed with a space,
or had its newlines collapsed — OpenSSL wants -----BEGIN at the start of a
line and rejects everything else with an opaque ERR_OSSL_UNSUPPORTED, which
the router flattened into "check your private key".

Only the base64 payload carries meaning, so signLicense re-emits the block in
canonical form first (normalizePemKey), making layout irrelevant: indentation,
stray leading/trailing whitespace, a single-line paste, CRLF, a BOM, or
\n-escapes from a .env value all normalize to the same key. It is the one
choke point every caller funnels through — tRPC router, generation service,
Stripe webhook, CLI script.

A PEM file is legally a bundle, so the private-key block is selected rather
than whichever block came first: operators keep a certificate or the public
half in the same file, OpenSSL scans a bundle for the key it needs, and
canonicalizing the first block would have broken a key that worked before.

Signing-key failures are handled errors with three codes the UI keys off —
not a PEM / passphrase-protected / OpenSSL refused — each carrying remediation
tips from the central registry, with copy in the presentation registry.
OpenSSL's own error is kept as a masked reason for the logs, so no key
material reaches a client.

* style(licensing): biome formatting and import order

* test(licensing): split the oversized describes so the lint gate stays green

CI counts NEW biome house-rule violations per file and rule against a
format-normalized base. The added cases pushed both licensing test files past
noExcessiveLinesPerFunction's 60-line limit, which the gate reads as this PR
leaving the tree worse than it found it — correctly, since neither file
tripped the rule before.

Split by what is under test rather than by line count: the pasted-key cases,
the cannot-sign cases, and what the failure carries are three separate
top-level blocks now, and the encrypted-key helper is shared between them.

fix(langy): surface and self-heal GitHub App install failures (#6291)

* fix(langy): surface GitHub App install failures instead of silently dropping them

The /setup callback reports every failure (expired signed state, session
mismatch, permission checks, the cross-tenant installation-conflict guard)
by redirecting back with ?githubError=<message>, but Settings > Integrations
never read that query param — a failed install re-rendered the plain
"Install" button, indistinguishable from nothing having happened even though
the user had just approved the install on GitHub's side.

specs/langy/langy-github-install.feature already documents this: "Then I am
shown that the installation could not be verified". Only the backend redirect
was tested; the UI-facing half of the scenario was unimplemented.

* fix(langy): preserve scroll position on githubError cleanup, prove the toast doesn't repeat

router.replace() resets scroll to top unless {scroll: false} — the setup flow
returns to /settings/integrations#github, so cleaning up ?githubError from
the URL was yanking the user back to the page top right after landing on the
GitHub card.

Also strengthens the cleanup test to actually apply the replacement query and
rerender, proving the toast doesn't fire again once the URL is clean, instead
of only asserting replace() was called.

* fix(langy): self-heal stale GitHub App installation selection

mintTurnToken() always picked the oldest non-suspended installation for
an org, with no check that it was still alive on GitHub. A missed
webhook delivery (or an installation predating the webhook being
configured) left a dead installation row blocking every real one behind
it, minting silently failing and surfacing to the user as "Install the
LangWatch GitHub App" even though it was installed.

On a confirmed 404 from GitHub (not any other error — a transient
failure must not delete a live installation), remove the stale row and
retry the next candidate instead of failing the whole turn.

* fix(langy): address CodeRabbit findings on the self-heal fix

- Self-heal a dead installation whether the 404 surfaces while minting
  or while resolving an explicit repo id (an uncached "all" selection
  falls through to a live listing, which mints a token and can hit the
  same 404 that resolveRepositoryId was silently swallowing).
- Correct a comment that claimed useRouter() returns a fresh object
  each render — it memoizes; the effect is keyed to the error value.

* style(langy): run biome format on the self-heal fix files

* refactor(langy): split mintTurnToken to satisfy cognitive-complexity gate

The self-heal branching pushed mintTurnToken from 0 to a new
noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity violation, which the repo's diff-aware
lint gate treats as a failing new violation, not a pre-existing one.
Split into mintForExplicitRepo/mintForAnyInstallation/
resolveRepositoryIdOrHeal — same behavior, each function under the
complexity limit.

* fix(langy): confirm a cached installation token's installation is still alive

mintInstallationToken() returned a cached token without ever contacting
GitHub, so an installation uninstalled while its ~50min token cache was
still warm kept being served a "valid" token indefinitely if the
deletion webhook was missed — the self-heal path only ever sees
GithubInstallationNotFoundError from a real mint call, which a cache
hit skips entirely. This was the primary missed-webhook scenario the
self-heal fix exists for.

getInstallation() now distinguishes a confirmed 404 the same way
mintAtGithub() does, and a cache hit confirms the installation still
exists before trusting the cached token. Any other liveness-probe
failure (network blip, 5xx) fails open and still serves the cached
token — a flaky check must not block an otherwise-valid one.

* fix(langy): guard the cache-hit liveness probe against a stampede

Every cache hit now confirms installation liveness (previous commit),
but a cache hit is the common path — without a lock, N concurrent turns
for the same installation would each fire their own GitHub liveness
probe, unlike the mint path which already guards its own (far rarer)
GitHub call this way.

Added a single, non-blocking lock attempt (tryLockOnce) rather than
reusing the mint path's retry-for-up-to-3s acquireLock: the mint path
retries because it MUST eventually mint, but a losing liveness-check
caller has a valid immediate fallback (trust the cache) and shouldn't
block waiting for a lock it doesn't need. Whichever caller does hold
the lock still throws on a confirmed 404, so the shared installation
list still self-heals for every subsequent caller.

* fix(langy): stop probing GitHub on every warm-cache turn

The stampede lock only coalesced overlapping callers; it releases right
after the GET, so sequential cache hits (the normal, common case — one
turn after another, not overlapping) each re-acquired it and each paid
for their own GitHub liveness call. For an active installation that
turned the 50-minute token cache into ~one GitHub App API request per
turn, and during a GitHub outage or rate-limit response every turn
would sit on githubFetch's 10s timeout before falling back to the
cached token — reintroducing the exact GitHub-availability dependency
the token cache exists to remove.

A confirmed-alive result is now cached under its own short-TTL marker
(LIVENESS_RECHECK_TTL_SEC, 5min) — a cache hit skips the probe entirely
while the marker holds. A transient probe failure (network blip, 5xx,
rate limit) sets a shorter backoff marker (LIVENESS_FAILURE_BACKOFF_SEC,
60s) instead of leaving every following turn to hit the same 10s
timeout. A confirmed 404 still propagates immediately and unconditionally
— it's the only signal that evicts the installation, and there is
nothing to mark alive once it's about to be deleted.

fix(langy): let the session key reach the experiment surface (#6288)

* fix(langy): let the session key reach the experiment surface

`langwatch experiment list` came back 403
`api_key_permission_denied: experiments:view` for users who can see their
project's experiments perfectly well in the UI. `langwatch status` calls the
same endpoint, so it was quietly degraded too.

Two independent holes, both halves of the contract the candidate list's own
comment describes:

1. `LANGY_CANDIDATE_PERMISSIONS` covered nine resource families and no
   experiments family at all. The minted key is the intersection of that list
   with what the caller holds, so `experiments:view` could never appear in it
   — the one permission `GET /api/experiments` asks for. Every project role
   already holds that read, down to VIEWER and the EXTERNAL lite member, so
   this puts it on the same footing as the `project:view` exception already
   documented there. The family stops at the view: `:manage` is its only other
   action and that is the delete Langy must never hold.

2. `POST /api/experiments/:slug/run` asked for `evaluations:manage`. Starting a
   run creates a run row against an experiment that already exists; it does not
   administer the family. The coarse grain refused every least-privilege key
   holding the create, the Langy session key among them — precisely the failure
   mode the candidate list warns about ("THE OTHER HALF OF THIS CONTRACT IS THE
   ROUTE"). `:manage` still satisfies `:create` via `hasPermissionWithHierarchy`,
   so narrowing it takes access away from nobody.

The session-key integration suite also carried an
`isTestcontainersOnly`/`TEST_CLICKHOUSE_URL` skip guard that permanently
skipped it EVERYWHERE — CI always sets that variable for the
ClickHouse-dependent suites sharing the run. The file only needs Postgres. It
had gone stale unnoticed as a result (a `mintLangySessionApiKey` return-shape
change left an assertion matching a regex against an object). Guard removed,
assertion fixed, with the same warning comment PR #5988 left on the sibling
suite.

Verified live against a haven stack with a real minted session key:
`GET /api/experiments` 403 -> 200, the run route's ceiling cleared
(`evaluations:manage` refused, `evaluations:create` allowed), and both
`langwatch experiment list` and `langwatch status` returning real data through
the actual CLI.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(langy): make the permission gap impossible to reintroduce silently

The first commit added `experiments:view` to `LANGY_CANDIDATE_PERMISSIONS` and
narrowed the run route's grain. Both are right, and both are the THIRD hand-fix
of one bug: `project:view` (`langwatch agent list` refused), `scenarios:create`
against a route asking `scenarios:manage`, and now `experiments:view`. Each was
found by a user, diagnosed by hand, and closed by adding a line plus a comment
apologising for the omission. A fourth was going to follow.

The defect is not any of those three lines. It is that an enumeration cannot
say why something is absent: `experiments:view` was missing because nobody
thought of it, `cost:view` is missing because someone decided against it, and
in the list those look identical — a line that isn't there.

So state the rule the enumeration was always an expression of.
`langyPermissionPolicy.ts` classifies any permission as granted or excluded,
fail-closed on both axes (an unrecognised action and an unrecognised family
shape are both refused), and every exclusion carries its reason.
`langy-permission-coverage` then reconciles three facts that are maintained
independently, so no two can drift into agreement while being wrong together:
the route registry (what the API demands), the policy (what Langy may be
delegated), and the candidate list (what the mint asks for). A route demanding
a permission the policy says Langy should hold, which the list omits, now fails
CI naming both — `experiments:view — demanded by GET /api/experiments` —
instead of reaching a user as a 403.

The rule deliberately does not GENERATE the list. That would grant a brand-new
resource family the moment it appears, which is the wrong default for a
credential. A human still writes the line; the rule makes forgetting impossible.

Coverage alone would not have caught the run route, because a route demanding
`evaluations:manage` classifies as excluded and raises nothing. Two changes
close that:

  - `handlerManagedAuth` now takes the permissions the handler enforces for
    itself. A self-enforcing route was previously invisible to the registry —
    which is precisely how the run route sat on a grain no least-privilege key
    can hold without anything noticing. The experiments-v3 routes declare
    theirs.
  - the session-key suite reads the experiment routes' required grains OFF THE
    REGISTRY instead of hardcoding them, so coarsening one back fails there,
    against a real minted key. Verified: reverting the route to
    `evaluations:manage` fails the suite; reverting `experiments:view` fails
    coverage with the route named.

* fix(langy): make the permission policy fail closed on unknown families

`classifyForLangy` was a blocklist, so anything it had not heard of came back
`granted`. Verified before the change: `billing:create`, `piiExport:create` and
`impersonation:update` — all invented — classified as delegable to Langy.

The file's own comment claimed the opposite ("Fail-closed at every step: an
unrecognised action and an unrecognised family shape both come back excluded"),
which was true only of a string with no colon in it. A false fail-closed claim
in a security policy is worse than no claim, because it is the thing a reviewer
reads instead of the code.

Worse than the default itself was what it did to the coverage sweep. A resource
family invented next quarter would classify as "Langy should hold this", so the
sweep would go RED until someone added it to the candidate list — turning CI
into pressure to grant an assistant a capability nobody had assessed. Exactly
backwards, and it inverted this PR's own stated principle that a new family must
not become delegable just by appearing.

Now an ALLOWLIST: `DELEGABLE_FAMILIES` names the eleven families Langy may be
delegated, and anything else is refused with a reason that names both ways to
resolve it. `OFF_LIMITS_FAMILIES` is now redundant against it and deliberately
kept, so "why can't Langy read secrets?" is answered at the decision rather
than by absence. The default while nobody is looking is "Langy cannot".

`langyPermissionPolicy.unit.test.ts` pins the defaults — unknown family,
unknown action, non-permission string — plus the grants, so the policy cannot
become vacuously strict either.

`setupFiles` entry for the WHOLE integration lane and sets it in both the
testcontainers and native-local modes, and `setupEnv.ts` sets it again from
`CI_CLICKHOUSE_URL` in CI. `isUsingGlobalSetupContainers()` reads it for
exactly that meaning. Skipping WHEN it is present therefore skips
everywhere, permanently — and a skipped suite reports green, so nothing
ever said so. The same trap was caught once before in #5988.

Un-skipping produced 36 failures across 7 files, from four causes. Three
were stale tests; one was a real bug.

REAL BUG — `ModelProviderService.getById` 404s on org/team-scoped rows.
`findById` matches only rows carrying a PROJECT scope for the project, so a
provider granted at ORGANIZATION or TEAM scope — which the settings list
surfaces by inheritance — could not be read from a project context. The
edit path had already been fixed for this exact problem and carries a
comment saying so; the read path never was, because the test that would
have caught it was skipped. Worse, it made `canReadAnyScope` unreachable
for the scopes it exists to judge: a row that never loads is never asked
about. Now org-anchored like the edit path, with the read gate — the actual
security boundary — still deciding.

STALE TESTS.
- Fixtures created `OrganizationUser`/`TeamUser` rows but no `RoleBinding`.
  A bare `OrganizationUser.role = ADMIN` confers only MEMBER's base bag, and
  the legacy TeamUser union deliberately cannot grant `organization:*`
  (ADR-021), so callers were refused before reaching the guard each suite
  was about. Same for the custom-role assignment in the plan-limit suite,
  which set `TeamUser.assignedRoleId` while the guard reads a RoleBinding —
  that one made the suite assert nothing at all.
- `project.regenerateApiKey` expected UNAUTHORIZED; the wire code is
  FORBIDDEN, re-derived by `handledErrorMiddleware` from the handled cause's
  403, and deliberately so. `deleteScope` expected the tRPC `NOT_FOUND`
  where the service now throws `model_provider_not_found`.
- modelProvider read-backs queried the removed `ModelProvider.projectId`.
  The model moved to `organizationId` + N `ModelProviderScope` rows.
- Two plan-limit tests asserted a persisted row through `createTestApp`'s
  NullOrganizationRepository, which by design persists nothing. They now
  assert the call resolves, paired against a sibling proving it rejects
  without the override, which is the behaviour those tests are about.
- `monitors-evaluator` never initialised the app layer, which the evaluators
  router now needs for license enforcement.

PREVENTION. An ast-grep rule bans the inverted guard specifically, not the
env var: `describe.skipIf(!hasTestcontainers)` is correct and stays legal —
several ClickHouse suites rely on it. The rule targets the
`isTestcontainersOnly` idiom that spread by copy-paste, plus the same
inversion written inline. It flags exactly one remaining file,
`langySessionKey.integration.test.ts`, which PR #6288 fixes and this branch
deliberately leaves alone to avoid a conflict.

Not fixed here: `modelIdBoundary.integration.test.ts` fails against the live
Anthropic API with a 404 for a retired model id. Pre-existing, untouched,
unrelated to the guard.

Verified: 14 files / 78 tests pass; typecheck, typecheck:tests and lint
clean; Biome new-violations gate reproduced against the merge base at 0.

Closes #6327

* fix(tests): guard teardown against undefined ids, close two ast-grep gaps

Every afterAll here assigns organizationId/teamId/projectId in sequence
during beforeAll; if an earlier setup call throws, later ones stay
undefined. Prisma treats an undefined filter key as "no filter", so an
unguarded deleteMany/updateMany would touch the whole table instead of
just this run's rows. Guard each cleanup by the id it depends on.

Also closes two gaps in the new no-clickhouse-env-skip-guard rule that
would have let the exact bug this PR fixes reappear unnoticed: the
patterns only covered TEST_CLICKHOUSE_URL (not CI_CLICKHOUSE_URL, which
setupEnv.ts also sets in CI), and the files glob omitted .test.tsx/
.spec.tsx even though integration suites use both extensions.

Addresses CodeRabbit findings on this PR.

* fix(tests): one all-or-nothing teardown guard instead of per-id branches

The per-id guards tripped the Biome delta gate: six branches pushed
workflows.node-llm-materialization's afterAll past the cognitive
complexity limit, which is a new violation on a rule the repo enforces.

Setup is all-or-nothing, so teardown is too. One combined guard keeps
the property that matters — no undefined value ever reaches a Prisma
filter, where it would be dropped and turn a scoped deleteMany into an
unscoped one — at complexity 1, and reads as the invariant it is.

fix(cli): never reroute a run onto the metered gateway path (#6343)

* fix(cli): never reroute a run onto the metered gateway path

Picking "use your own plan, send only telemetry" and getting billed for
model usage anyway is the bug. The wrapper had four ways to end up on the
gateway path without anyone choosing it, and every one of them spends
money through LangWatch-held provider credentials:

- direct-OTLP setup failing (an expired device session, most often) fell
  through to the gateway with a one-line notice
- a non-TTY run with no pinned tool_mode defaulted to the gateway
- cancelling the path prompt with Ctrl-C defaulted to the gateway
- a tool with no ingestion template returned the gateway shape silently

The gateway is now reachable only from the prompt, a pinned tool_mode,
`--tool-mode=gateway`, or `LANGWATCH_TOOL_MODE=gateway`. An expired
session on a TTY explains itself and offers the login inline, then
retries the same path; without a TTY it exits naming
`langwatch login --device`. Ctrl-C exits 130. A tool with no ingestion
template raises instead of routing.

Root cause of the expiry: device sessions issue a 1h access token and a
30d rotating refresh token, and the CLI never called
`/api/auth/cli/refresh`, so every session died an hour after login with
an unused refresh token sitting in ~/.langwatch/config.json. Every
authenticated CLI request now refreshes when the recorded expiry has
passed and refreshes-and-retries once on a 401, and the idle window goes
to 90 days. An actively used session no longer expires; revocation is
unchanged, since it deletes the Redis keys the request path reads.

* fix(cli): pin the gateway in the wrapper e2e suite and address review

The wrapper e2e suite drove the CLI non-interactively with nothing pinning
the path, so it inherited the old implicit gateway default. Now that an
unpinned non-TTY run takes direct OTLP, all 20 gateway-shaped scenarios
resolved a path the fake control plane cannot mint against and exited 2.
The suite pins LANGWATCH_TOOL_MODE=gateway, since the gateway wiring is
what it asserts, and gains two scenarios for the unpinned case: no gateway
credentials reach the child and no request reaches the gateway, plus the
platform-policy exception where the gateway is the only path left.

Review findings:

- REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS reads LANGWATCH_CLI_REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS,
  keeping 90d as the default, so a deployment that wants a shorter idle
  window does not need a fork. Non-positive and unparseable values fall
  back to the default with a warning.
- refreshSession normalizes caught values through messageOf, so a non-Error
  rejection no longer reports "undefined" as the reason a session died.
- authorizedFetch records why replaying a mutating request after a 401 is
  safe, and that the argument does not extend to other status codes.
- aborted becomes isAborted; the recovery prompt field becomes confirmed.
- The shared expired-session sentence lives in one helper.
- New tests for the proactive-refresh path, the sibling-retry network
  failure branch, and the non-Error rejection.
- The precedence docblock described the old gateway default.

* fix(cli): satisfy only-throw-error and keep agent env out of spawned CLIs

The non-Error rejection test throws a bare string on purpose, so the rule
against it is suppressed at the throw rather than worked around, which
would have removed the thing being tested.

`cli-error-propagation-commands.integration.test.ts` asserts on
human-format output but spawned the CLI with the ambient environment, so
running the suite from inside a coding agent inherited the agent-mode
markers, flipped the child into agents format, and failed every message
assertion. It now scrubs AGENT_MODE_ENV_VARS from the child env, matching
what the output harnesses already do.

* test(cli): reject through the mock and name the suite as a precondition

Rejecting via mockRejectedValue keeps the non-Error value the test is
about without a bare throw, so only-throw-error never fires and the
suppression comes out. The new e2e suite is named as a given precondition.

* chore(sdk): drop regenerated openapi client churn unrelated to this PR

* fix(cli): stop a sibling's token rotation from logging the user out

session-api.ts carried its own refresh. Rotation is single-use
server-side, so when two CLI processes overlap the loser is handed an
unauthorized for a token the winner already spent. That path read the
rejection as a revocation and deleted access_token, refresh_token,
expires_at and the cached personal_project, writing that over a config
that by then held the winner's perfectly live pair. The user was logged
out mid-session and lost their personal project cache.

The rotation now goes through session-refresh.ts, which re-reads the
config and retries once with whatever the sibling persisted before
reporting anything, so only a real rejection clears the session. A
network failure now clears nothing, where before any unauthorized did.

Covered by a regression test that fails on the previous implementation:
the sibling's token is never tried and the session is destroyed.

perf(event-sourcing): trust absent fold state — stop rescue-scanning every new aggregate (#6347)

* perf(event-sourcing): make fold-state absence authoritative (HasSignal), stop rescue-scanning new aggregates

Every store miss on the analytics folds paid an unwindowed fallback scan of
the fold's own table plus a full event_log re-fold — measured in prod at
~290/min fallback scans (30 days: 230k+ attempts, 0 recoveries at ±7d) and
~180/min re-folds (93% returning exactly the delivered batch). The root
cause is that absence was AMBIGUOUS: the stores' persistable-signal gates
declined to write dimension-only states, so 'no row' could mean 'new
aggregate' or 'declined to persist' and the executor had to assume the worst.

- Migration 00064: trace_analytics gains HasSignal Bool DEFAULT 1 and
  WriterNonce String DEFAULT ''. The store now ALWAYS writes; the gate's
  verdict rides on HasSignal; analytics readers filter AND HasSignal (one
  chokepoint, dedupedSlim). WriterNonce ends the LWW tiebreak's arbitrary
  LIMIT 1 pick — deterministic winner across reads.
- evaluationAnalytics: gate removed (its identity check was unreachable
  behind the aggregate-id stamp).
- traceSummary readWindow 2d -> 7d: the 2d width's 'clock skew only'
  rationale measured false (138,654 outside-window recoveries in 30 days,
  all in the 2-7d band; zero beyond 7d on any fold).
- Executor: new per-fold option trustAbsentMiss — an absent read folds from
  init() with no unwindowed retry and no event_log re-fold. undecodable
  keeps the full rescue machinery (a complete row exists). Kill-switch:
  ES_FOLD_TRUST_ABSENT_MISS=0. New counter
  es_fold_absent_miss_trusted_total measures exactly what is saved.
- Contract tests: applied-event-id watermark round-trips the write path,
  trusted folds bind only to TIME_LOCAL aggregate types, refoldOnStoreMiss
  keeps a store that can report undecodable.

Verified: pnpm typecheck, pnpm typecheck:tests, 7,494 event-sourcing unit
tests, 1,792 app-layer unit tests.

* refactor(event-sourcing): derive the signal filter from existing columns — no migration

Replaces the 00064 HasSignal/WriterNonce columns with equivalents over data
the rows already carry, so the whole change ships as pure code:

- TRACE_ANALYTICS_HAS_SIGNAL_SQL derives the persistable-signal verdict in
  SQL: SpanCount > 0 OR EarliestSpanStartMs > 0 (that column IS the state's
  occurredAt since 00061) OR the reserved log-record-count attribute (which
  survives trimAttributesForAnalytics by prefix — the ADR-066 read-back
  already depends on that) OR Version < PRE_SPLIT (pre-00056 rows decode
  SpanCount as default 0 but everything written then had passed the gate).
  Defined next to the in-memory predicate it mirrors; fromRecord re-derives
  it on read-back.
- The LWW tiebreak's deterministic last key becomes
  toString(AppliedEventIds) DESC: two writers racing the same committed
  version folded different batches, so their watermark contents differ even
  at equal length; versions equal on all five keys are interchangeable.

Verified: pnpm typecheck, pnpm typecheck:tests, 9,197 unit tests across
event-sourcing + traces/analytics/evaluations app-layer.

* test(event-sourcing): write the trusted-absence scenarios the executor tests bind to

The trustAbsentMiss suite declared seven @scenario bindings with no matching
scenario in any .feature file, so feature-parity failed on the first tag it
could not resolve. Write them into fold-read-window.feature, next to the rescue
scenarios they qualify, with a note on why absence became trustworthy.

The kill-switch scenario is named for the behaviour rather than the env var it
reads, per the specs rule against config literals in scenario text; its binding
tag moves with it.

perf(clickhouse): bound the evaluation_runs JOIN so it prunes partitions (#6383)

buildJoinClause took a spanTimeFilter and applied it only to stored_spans; the
evaluation_runs branch ignored it, so every query carrying an evaluation metric

cold scan of evaluation_runs at 4.8-7.5s.

Bound both scopes on OccurredAt, the partition column, with the same date
envelope plus 2-day cushion the stored_spans pair already uses. All six
buildJoinClause call sites now pass the filter matching their date regime.

* test(event-sourcing): bind the remaining contract scenarios

The first parity pass covered only the executor suite. The fold contract tests

* perf(event-sourcing): coalesce traceSummary deliveries like every sibling fold

traceSummary was the only fold in the pipeline with no coalesceMaxBatch, so it
defaulted to 1: one delivery, one read-back and (while the rescue scan stands)

128 matches its siblings and stays below MAX_APPLIED_EVENT_IDS, which the

* fix(event-sourcing): bind the fold contract scenarios, refuse a trusted windowed absence on a long-lived aggregate

The seven @scenario tags #6347 added never bound: the parity checker's

Each tag moves to the single-line form directly above its `it(...)`, the shape

  trusted folds are on trace/evaluation, so nothing shipping changes.
- The undecodable pairing cannot be settled at registration: by then the store
  is behind RedisCachedFoldStore, which declares getWithApplied whatever the
  durable tier can do. The spec now says what the check is, and the contract

Also binds the reader half of the always-write promise: the has-signal
predicate is what keeps a dimension-only row out of the product's numbers, and
nothing asserted the query still carried it.

Reverts the traceSummary coalesceMaxBatch change. Its premise was that a fold
declaring no ceiling coalesces at 1; initializeFoldQueues resolves an undeclared
ceiling to DEFAULT_FOLD_COALESCE_MAX_BATCH, which is 500, so pinning 128 lowered

feat(charts): consolidated chart hardening — admission control, ingress path blocking, component flags, signed OCI prereleases (#6375)

* fix(chart): block /api/internal at the ingress by default

The Helm chart's ingress routed every path (default `path: /`) straight to
the app, so `/api/internal/*` — the private control-plane surface for the
Langy agent manager (langy-internal.ts / langy-relay.ts) and the AI gateway
(gateway-internal.ts) — was internet-reachable on a default install, with a
single shared bearer secret as the only control. Each route's header says
"Never expose publicly", but nothing enforced it.

Enforce it at the edge, on by default and portable across ingress controllers:

- New `ingress.blockedPaths` value (default `["/api/internal"]`). For each
  prefix the ingress renders a higher-priority `pathType: Prefix` path routing
  to a dedicated no-endpoints blackhole Service (`<release>-blackhole`).
  Spec-conformant controllers return 502/503 for a Service with no endpoints,
  so the block is a hard dead end, not a soft redirect. Longest-prefix wins on
  conformant controllers (`/api/internal` beats the app catch-all `/`), and the
  blocked paths are emitted first for order-sensitive controllers (nginx).
- New `templates/blackhole-service.yaml`: a selector-less ClusterIP Service,
  rendered only when the ingress is enabled and blockedPaths is non-empty.
- Operators can extend the list or set it to `[]` to disable the block.

In-cluster callers (the agent manager, the gateway, the chart's own CronJobs)
reach the app via the internal Service, not the ingress, so nothing legitimate
breaks. `/api/cron/*` and `/metrics` are internal-only in the default topology
but intentionally left out of the default block (external schedulers and
metrics federation are legitimate topologies); operators can add them.

Adds regression assertions to the chart's e2e-overlays test suite.

* test(chart): use --set-json to clear blockedPaths in the overlay e2e

The `blockedPaths=[]` regression assertion used `--set 'x=[]'`, which does
not assign an empty list — Helm's strvals parser assigns the two-character
string "[]". That string is truthy, so the blackhole Service still rendered,
and the ingress template then failed on `range can't iterate over []`.
Under `set -euo pipefail` the non-zero `helm template` inside the command
substitution killed the suite outright, which is why the job died with no
PASS/FAIL line for that assertion.

`--set-json` produces a real empty list — the same value an operator writing
`blockedPaths: []` in a values file gets, which is the behaviour the
assertion is meant to pin. Supported since Helm 3.10; CI pins v3.12.0.

* test(chart): select the ingress app path by value, not by index

The live-install assertion read
`.spec.rules[0].http.paths[0].backend.service.name` and expected `lw-app`.
`ingress.blockedPaths` emits the blocked prefixes FIRST, so `paths[0]` is now
`lw-blackhole` and the assertion failed:

    [FAIL]  Ingress backend → app: expected 'lw-app', got 'lw-blackhole'

The positional read was only ever correct while the app catch-all happened to
be the sole path. Select by path value instead, so the assertion keeps meaning
"the app's catch-all routes to the app" no matter what precedes it.

Also assert the block end-to-end in a live cluster, which the render-only
phase-1 checks cannot prove: `/api/internal` resolves to the blackhole
Service, and that Service has no Endpoints — the property that makes the
block a 502/503 dead end rather than a route to something live.

* test(chart): assert the blocked path is gone, not just the blackhole

The blockedPaths=[] case only checked that the blackhole Service
disappeared. A regression that dropped the Service but left
`path: /api/internal` in the Ingress would route to a nonexistent
backend and still pass, so assert the path is removed too.

Also add `|| true` to the ordering greps: under `set -euo pipefail` a
non-matching grep aborts the suite at the assignment, making the
`fail` diagnostic (and its `${app_line:-?}` fallback) unreachable for
the very regression it guards against.

* docs(gateway): point the internal routes at the ingress block

langy-internal and langy-relay both note that the chart hard-blocks
/api/internal by default; gateway-internal is part of the same
control-plane surface but still said only "Never expose publicly".

* fix(chart): refuse to render app paths nested under a blocked prefix

The blackhole only holds while nothing out-matches it. An operator path
configured under a blocked prefix — `/api/internal/status` against a block
of `/api/internal` — renders alongside the block, wins on length, and routes
the private control plane straight to the app. Nothing looks wrong: the
blocked path and the blackhole Service are both still there.

There is no topology in which a path nested under a blocked prefix is what
you want, so templates/ingress.yaml now fails the render instead of shipping
a block that silently does nothing. Emptying `ingress.blockedPaths` drops the
guard with the block, so opting out knowingly is still a one-line change.

The match is on `/`-separated segments, exactly like `pathType: Prefix`: a
bare `hasPrefix` would also reject `/api/internal-status`, a sibling the
block genuinely does not cover and a legitimate app path.

Also corrects the ordering comment. It claimed longest-prefix precedence
makes the emit-first ordering redundant, but Kubernetes defines that
precedence only for `Exact`/`Prefix`, and the chart's own catch-all `/`
ships as `ImplementationSpecific`, whose matching is controller-defined —
so on default values the ordering is what carries the block.

Regression coverage in tests/e2e-overlays.sh: nested and exact paths refuse
to render (asserting the guard's own diagnostic, not just a non-zero exit),
the `/api/internal-status` sibling still renders, and `blockedPaths=[]`
disables the guard along with the block.

* docs(chart): scope the ingress block and note its 5xx signature

`ingress.blockedPaths` read as an absolute guarantee. It is a property of
this ingress, not of the application: an install that publishes the app by
another route — a NodePort or LoadBalancer `app.service.type`, or an Ingress
the operator writes themselves against the app Service — does not inherit
these prefixes and wants an equivalent restriction where that route
terminates. Say so, so nobody reads the block as covering more than it does.

Also records that blocked requests answer 502/503, so probes against
`/api/internal` land in whatever 5xx alerting runs over the ingress. That is
the block working, and is worth knowing before it reads as an app fault.

* fix(chart): reject the prefixes that turn the block into decoration

Review found three ways to configure a blocked prefix that leaves the block
rendered but inert — the blocked path and the blackhole Service are both still
there, so the install looks protected while the control plane is served to the
internet:

  - a trailing slash ("/api/internal/") made the nested-path guard build
    "/api/internal//", which matches nothing, so a nested application path
    sailed past the guard and out-matched the blackhole;
  - a missing leading slash ("api/internal") rendered an Ingress the API server
    rejects, after the guard had already gone dark;
  - a non-list value — what plain `--set 'x=[]'` assigns, a two-character
    string — is truthy, so the Service rendered while the ingress failed deep
    inside a range with an error naming neither the value nor the fix.

All three are now rejected by name, along with a bare "/", by a single
`langwatch.ingress.blockedPaths` helper that validates and normalises the list.
Both templates resolve prefixes through it, so they can no longer disagree about
whether the block is on. Malformed `ingress.hosts` entries get written errors
too, instead of raw Go-template internals.

Corrects the precedence rationale while here. The previous comments claimed the
emission order was what carried the block, and named nginx as an order-sensitive
controller. Neither is true: the Ingress API defines no precedence for path-list
order, nginx resolves prefix locations by longest match, and what actually
carries the block is that /api/internal is a longer match than /. The ordering
is a hedge for controllers that derive rule priority from list position (the AWS
load balancer controller). The argument now lives in values.yaml only, rather
than in three copies that had already drifted apart.

Also: quote the rendered path, merge ingress.labels as a dict (a colliding key
was emitted twice, which kubectl rejects), use the chart's standard label set,
and drop the inert targetPort.

Tests. The live-cluster "blackhole has no Endpoints" assertion could not fail —
a selector-less Service never gets an Endpoints object, so it compared "" to ""
and passed just as happily when the Service was absent; it now asserts existence
and selector-lessness directly. Adds the pathType assertion (flipping Prefix to
Exact blocks only the literal path and left every other assertion green),
multi-prefix and multi-host coverage (both loops have been narrowed by refactors
before), the default ImplementationSpecific topology, the four malformed-prefix
rejections, and the duplicate-label check. Renders are captured with their exit
code so a failure prints a diagnostic instead of aborting the suite silently.

Verified by mutation: reverting each fix fails the assertion that covers it.

* docs(chart): correct the block's response codes and controller support

The claim that a no-endpoints backend returns 502/503 was stated as a spec
guarantee and used to tell operators their 5xx alerting would show probes
against /api/internal. The Ingress API specifies no behaviour here, and
ingress-nginx in particular swaps a no-endpoints upstream for its default
backend and answers 404 — so the documented signal was one an operator would
never see. Reworded as the per-controller observation it is. Every controller
still fails closed, which is the property that matters.

Adds the caveat that cost the most to find: controllers that route to node ports
rather than pod IPs (AWS load balancer controller with its default
`target-type: instance`, GKE Ingress without NEG) reject a ClusterIP backend and
stop reconciling the Ingress. On a fresh install that fails closed; on an upgrade
it fails OPEN, because the load balancer keeps serving the rules it already had.
Documented with the remedy rather than silently shipping a manifest those
controllers refuse.

Records three other things the review surfaced: /api/ops is a third

* chore(charts): pin ClickHouse container runAsUser: 101

The image already runs as uid 101 via its USER directive, but pinning it on

Jobs, and satisfies runAsUser / MustRunAs policies that read the pod spec.
Addresses CodeRabbit review on #4967.

* fix(charts): right-size minimal/dev overlays so they actually boot

size-minimal/size-dev (and the values-local profile) set the Node app and
workers to 512Mi-1Gi, which OOMs them at boot: they cold-load the TS server via
tsx and below ~2Gi V8 can't size its heap. Bump app/workers to ~2Gi (measured
against ~500Mi steady usage plus boot headroom); the running instance already
validates workers booting at 2Gi.

ClickHouse memory scales with ingest burst size and background merges, so the
sub-1Gi minimal value risked OOM under load: minimal -> 1Gi, dev/local -> 2Gi,
with a caveat in the overlay comments and both READMEs to raise it before real
trace volume.

prod/ha and the hosted/scalable profiles were already sane and are unchanged.

* test(charts): assert size-minimal renders workers (now enabled)

size-minimal enables workers now (so the smoke test exercises them), so the
e2e-overlays template suite must assert the workers Deployment is present, not
absent. The install suite layers values-e2e.yaml (which disables workers to keep
CI light), so its 'workers absent' check is unchanged and still correct.

* test(charts): assert pod-security hardening in overlay e2e

Adds a render-level suite guarding the strict-admission posture so it can't
silently regress: read-only root on every container (>=10) with no writable-root
opt-outs, RuntimeDefault seccomp, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, no privileged
containers, SA token not automounted (incl. the gateway pod specifically),
ClickHouse pinned to uid 101, and the dead Next.js init container gone. Also
checks the strict-admission overlay drops Prometheus, the gateway HPA, and app
metrics scraping.

* fix(charts): set runAsNonRoot at container level so Gatekeeper reads it

A self-hosted install with Gatekeeper's k8sreadonlyrootfilesystem constraint
denied all our containers with 'Only read-only root filesystem container is
allowed', despite readOnlyRootFilesystem being true. Reason: that variant of
the constraint reads c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot (container-level only)
and denies when it's not true. We set runAsNonRoot: true at the pod level,
which Kubernetes inherits, but the rego doesn't traverse pod defaults.

Set runAsNonRoot: true on every container-level securityContext so both
constraint variants pass:
- global.containerSecurityContext (flows to app / workers / nlp / langevals /
  cronjobs via the coalesce)
- postgresql, redis, clickhouse, backup Jobs (hardcoded contexts)
- gateway subchart containerSecurityContext

Extends the e2e-overlays hardening suite to assert container-level
runAsNonRoot: true on >=10 sites so this can't silently regress.

* fix(charts): propagate global.scheduling to postgres + redis

The bundled postgres and redis statefulsets hardcoded their pod spec and
never honoured global.scheduling.nodeSelector/tolerations/affinity, so a
cluster with tainted nodes (Azure AKS 'node=saint:NoSchedule' pattern, etc.)
couldn't get them to schedule from a single values override. Every other
chart-managed workload already coalesced from global.scheduling; align these
two so one global override reaches every pod.

* fix(charts): layer securityContext overrides onto the hardened defaults

A per-component podSecurityContext / containerSecurityContext override now
merges over the global default instead of replacing it: the key the operator
sets wins, and every key they did not mention keeps its hardened value.
Overriding one field is no longer a way to drop the others.

coalesce is all-or-nothing — it takes the component map whole as soon as it is
non-empty — so it cannot express "override this one field". Two shared
helpers (langwatch.podSecurityContext / langwatch.containerSecurityContext) do
the merge in one place, and all ten call sites use them.

PostgreSQL and Redis consumed neither global context, so every cross-cutting
hardening flag had to be retyped into those two files by hand. They now take
global.containerSecurityContext through the same helper, keeping only their
image's own uid at pod level, and gain per-component podSecurityContext,
containerSecurityContext, nodeSelector, tolerations and affinity keys so the
datastores can be pinned without moving every other pod.

* fix(charts): make strict-admission cover the assistant, and size-minimal self-contained

The strict-admission overlay disabled the preflight hook, which no longer
exists, and said nothing about the Langy assistant, which is chart-managed by
default and runs its manager as root with CHOWN/DAC_OVERRIDE/FOWNER/SETUID/
SETGID so it can give each worker a distinct uid. On a cluster enforcing the
restricted standard that pod is rejected, so the overlay now opts it out.

It opts out rather than de-privileging: an unprivileged manager cannot perform
the per-uid handoff, which is what keeps one worker out of another worker's
credentials (ADR-033, specs/langy/langy-deploy-hardening.feature). The comment
says so, because "just set runAsNonRoot" is the obvious wrong fix.

size-minimal pins workers.enabled: true rather than inheriting the chart
default — an overlay stacked after a base values file that disables workers
would otherwise silently drop them — and its header now states the real
footprint (~3.7Gi requests, ~2 CPU) instead of implying it fits anywhere.

* fix(charts): bound ClickHouse scratch volumes and give the backup Jobs the chart SA

The log and /tmp emptyDirs are backed by node ephemeral storage, so a pod in an
error loop consumed the node's disk and pressured its neighbours rather than
being capped itself. Both are now size-bounded via scratch.logsSizeLimit
(2Gi, sized against the shipped 1000M x 10 log rotation) and
scratch.tmpSizeLimit (1Gi), which also applies to the backup/restore Jobs.

The three backup/restore Jobs read serviceAccount.* to decide token mounting
but never set serviceAccountName, so they ran under the namespace default SA
and would miss an IRSA annotation on the chart's own SA — which matters
precisely because backup is the component that talks to S3. They now use the
same ServiceAccount as the StatefulSets.

Dropped the /var/run/clickhouse-{server,keeper} mounts: neither process writes
a pidfile there and the path does not exist in the Keeper image, so the mounts
and the comments describing them were inert. Comments now name what is actually
written and where it lands.

* test(charts): assert the hardening per workload instead of counting strings

test_pod_security grepped the whole render, so "is readOnlyRootFilesystem
present?" passed on one container out of ten, and "at least 10 runAsNonRoot
sites" passed when a workload regressed as long as another gained a field.
Removing the container-level runAsNonRoot the suite exists to guard left it
green. It now fails.

Each workload is rendered with --show-only and asserted individually, so a
regression is attributed to the workload that caused it. Prometheus and the
Langy assistant are listed as explicit exemptions with their reason and the
values key that removes them, and a new check fails on any workload that is
neither hardened nor exempt — so a future subchart cannot ship unhardened

Also: assert the strict-admission overlay by template source rather than by
loose strings; make the app-metrics check differential (render a baseline with
metrics on via -f, since --set outranks every -f, then prove the overlay

live workers assertion at the enable gate it actually exercises; and fix
count_matches and the assert_* helpers, which emitted a second line on zero
matches and mis-parsed any needle starting with '-'.

The Pod Security section claimed every pod passes the restricted standard

* test(charts): fail loudly when a render the overlay checks depends on breaks

tmpl folds stderr into its output, so a failed render is just a string that
contains none of the needles the strict-admission block looks for — every
assert_not_contains would pass and the overlay would look correct precisely
when it had stopped rendering. Both negative-assertion renders now confirm they

* docs(workers): describe how the worker registry is actually scraped

Both comments said the web process scrapes the worker registry at

its own loopback, so it only resolves when the workers share the web
process. The chart's Prometheus scrape config targets the worker pod

* test(specs): tag the strict-admission scenarios so the gap is tracked

An untagged .feature is skipped by the parity checker entirely: it carries no
scenario the checker counts, so the run reports "0/0 all bound" and enforces
nothing. That is how the file shipped, and it is indistinguishable from a
fully-bound one in CI output.

These scenarios are verified by charts/langwatch/tests/e2e-overlays.sh, but the
checker's shell binding roots scan .bats only, so a chart-e2e scenario cannot
bind to a .sh assertion as written. Tagged @e2e @unimplemented, which records
the binding gap as a tracked one instead of hiding it.

* test(server): bind the worker probe specs so the parity gate enforces them

Both feature files shipped untagged. The parity checker only counts scenarios
carrying @unit/@integration/@e2e/@regression, so an untagged file contributes
nothing: the run reported "0/0 ✓ all bound" and every scenario in it was
decorative. That is indistinguishable in CI output from a fully-bound file.

The seven handler scenarios are tagged @unit and bound to the tests that
already covered them via /** @scenario */ annotations; enforced scenarios go

but the checker's shell binding roots scan .bats only, so a .sh assertion
cannot bind as written. Tracked rather than invisible.

Two of those newly-enforced tests could not fail, which matters more now that
they are load-bearing:

- The response fake dropped headers on both paths (a no-op setHeader, and a

Also drops a dead assertion (an exact toBe already implies it) and wraps the

* fix(charts): render the cronjobs template again

The pod securityContext was indented 20 spaces against a nindent 12 body, so
`helm template` failed for any release that defines a cron job:

  YAML parse error on langwatch/templates/cronjobs/cronjobs.yaml:
  did not find expected key

so this broke the only configuration it exists for. It stayed invisible because
the map ships empty and both e2e values files set cronjobs.enabled false — no
