* test(charts): assert the hardening per container, not per document

The pod-security assertions counted matches across the whole rendered
document, which cannot distinguish where a field sits. Moving
readOnlyRootFilesystem and allowPrivilegeEscalation off two of the three backup
containers and up to the pod level — where Kubernetes ignores them — left the
totals identical and the suite green, printing "read-only root on all 3
container(s)" while two containers ran writable-root with privilege escalation
allowed. Seccomp and the SA token were plain presence greps, so a single hit
covered three pod specs. The ServiceAccount check asserted only that the key
existed: setting it to `default`, the exact failure the adjacent comment
describes, passed.

charts/lib/pod-security-report.rb parses the manifest and emits one line per
container, so fields are read off the container object they belong to. All
three regressions above now fail, naming the workload and the container. Ruby's
YAML is stdlib on macOS and ubuntu-latest, so this adds no dependency.

The triage guard read only the default render, so a workload gated off by
default could never be reported as untriaged — which is how the cronjobs
template stayed both untriaged and unrenderable. It now unions the feature-on
renders, and LC_ALL=C pins comm's sorted-input contract, which comm does not
check. Hardening is also asserted under the strict-admission overlay rather
than chart defaults alone, since a per-component override now merges and could
relax a control there. Scratch volumes are checked by count, so one volume
cannot lose its bound while another keeps it.

The temp values file the metrics differential writes is now removed via a
RETURN trap; fail() exits, so the trailing rm never ran on the failure path.

* fix(charts): bound every scratch volume, and stop hand-rolling the datastore context

The Postgres socket dir, both /tmp volumes and the ClickHouse config emptyDirs
were unbounded, which contradicted the rule stated in the ClickHouse values:
an unbounded emptyDir is node-backed, so a looping pod evicts its neighbours
rather than itself. All of them now carry a sizeLimit, via new
postgresql.scratchSizeLimit / redis.scratchSizeLimit knobs and the existing
clickhouse scratch.* pair.

The logsSizeLimit comment claimed the cap tracked the image's rotation ceiling.
It does not, and cannot: the chart renders console logging into config.d but
never disables the base image's file logging, which rotates at 1000M x 10 per
file. The cap is deliberately below that — it exists so a pathological logger
is evicted on its own quota, and the pod logs to stdout regardless. The comment
now says so instead of implying the two numbers agree.

Postgres and Redis hand-rolled the securityContext merge with an identical
inlined dict, duplicating what the helpers exist to centralise. The pod helper
takes an optional "base" for components whose image pins its own uid, so both
call it and a partial override still cannot strip the uid or the seccomp
profile.

* fix(charts): pin the ClickHouse preflight Job off under strict admission

A third component cannot meet the policy set, not two. The ClickHouse
subchart's preflight Job shells out to kubectl to check the Secret's keys, so
it needs an automounted token and a writable root for kubectl's discovery
cache. It renders only when the operator supplies the Secret themselves rather
than using autogen — which is the production path, so leaving it to the
umbrella default was leaving it to chance.

* docs(charts): correct the uid list, the exemption count and the minimal footprint

Three claims were wrong in ways an operator would act on:

- The MustRunAs uid list omitted 65534, which Keeper's init container runs. A
  constraint written from it denies the whole Keeper pod on that container —
  the exact failure class the list was added to prevent. The ClickHouse README
  said "uid 101" for the same reason.
- "Two bundled components cannot comply" is three; the ClickHouse preflight
  Job is the third.
- size-minimal claimed ~3.7Gi / ~2 CPU. Measured over the render it is 4.66Gi
  and 2.42 CPU: the figure omitted the Langy assistant, which ships enabled and
  which that overlay does not disable. Someone sizing a node from it
  under-provisions by ~1Gi, which is what the paragraph existed to prevent.

Also qualifies the SA-token sentence (the bundled Prometheus does mount one),
adds the cron pods to the hardened enumeration, drops a "pid" writable path
that is not mounted, and scopes two spec scenarios that asserted more than the
chart delivers.

* test(server): stop pinning an implementation accident, and clean up unconditionally

expect(captured.status).toBeUndefined() asserted that the success path writes
no explicit status. That is true today and behaviourally irrelevant: rewriting
it as writeHead(200, …) is equally correct HTTP and turned the test red, which
teaches the next person to delete the assertion rather than fix it. It now
pins the outcome a scraper observes — a 200 — and survives either form.

The fixture counter was removed at the end of the test body, so a failing
assertion above it left the metric in the process-wide prom-client registry.
Moved to afterEach. Also renames the liveness test, which drifted when it
gained a content-type assertion.

* fix(charts): stop the temp-file cleanup from failing the suite after it passes

The RETURN trap added to clean up the metrics values file is global, not
scoped to the function that sets it, so it fired on every later function
return — where that local no longer exists. Under `set -u` that is fatal, so
the overlay suite printed "All overlay E2E tests passed" and then exited 1:

  tests/e2e-overlays.sh: line 934: metrics_base: unbound variable
  make: *** [Makefile:70: test-e2e-overlays] Error 1

Temp files are now registered in a list the existing EXIT trap drains, which
covers both the pass and the fail() path without a second trap. Verified
against an empty registry, a successful run and a failing one.

This slipped through because the local driver grepped for PASS lines and never
checked the script's exit status, which is precisely what CI checks.

* style(server): organize the worker metrics test imports

Adding the prom-client and afterEach imports pulled the file's pre-existing
organizeImports diagnostic into the diff, and the lint job's reviewdog step
reports on changed lines — so a diagnostic that had sat unreported on main
became a failure here. Biome's own ordering applied; no behaviour change.

* feat(chart): per-component enable flags, envFrom, Service annotations, priorityClass

Four pass-throughs the umbrella chart was missing. All four default to the
current behaviour, so an existing install renders byte-identical output apart
from comments (verified by diffing `helm template` against origin/main on the
default values and on tests/values-e2e-full.yaml).

langwatch_nlp.enabled / langevals.enabled
  workers and cronjobs already had an `enabled` flag and a guard; these two
  rendered unconditionally, so there was no way to run the app against an NLP
  or evaluations service deployed outside the release — a shared instance
  across releases, or a serverless one. Both default true.

  Disabling only stops the Deployment/Service/PDB rendering. The app still
  expects to reach those services, so an install that turns one off without
  also setting app.upstreams.<svc> fails at runtime rather than at render
  time; documented on the values.

app.extraEnvFrom / workers.extraEnvFrom
  There was no envFrom anywhere in the chart, so an operator whose own tooling
  (External Secrets, SOPS, Vault Agent, Terraform) already materialises a
  Secret holding the app config had to re-declare every key under extraEnvs
  and keep the two in sync by hand.

  Values arriving via envFrom are NOT available for `$(VAR)` interpolation in
  other env entries — Kubernetes only expands names defined in `env` — so
  anything referenced that way still belongs in extraEnvs. Noted on the value.

app.service.annotations
  Cloud load-balancer controllers are driven entirely by Service annotations
  (AWS NLB scheme/subnets, GCP internal LB, ingress-controller hints). Without
  a pass-through, `app.service.type: LoadBalancer` could be switched on but not
  steered, which makes it unusable on any cloud.

global.scheduling.priorityClassName + per-component override
  Follows the existing coalesce pattern used by nodeSelector/tolerations/
  affinity. The chart deliberately does not create a PriorityClass: the object
  is cluster-scoped and its value only means anything relative to the other
  classes an operator has already defined.

Verified: helm lint, the chart Makefile's four template modes, and all 12
configurations in the langwatch-chart CI template matrix.

* ci(chart): publish charts to GHCR as OCI prereleases on merge to main

A cluster that wants to track main currently cannot: charts are only published
when a release is tagged, via chart-releaser into the GitHub Pages Helm repo.

Deliberately a separate workflow rather than an extension of
release-langwatch-chart.yml. That one writes a shared index.yaml, which is the
artifact self-hosters install from; adding a build per merge would grow that
index without bound and push every `helm search` / `helm upgrade` onto --devel
to avoid selecting an untagged main build. OCI has no shared index — each push
is an independent immutable tag — so prereleases and stable releases cannot
interfere with each other, and the Pages flow is untouched.

Versions are `<chartVersion>-main.<run_number>.<shortSha>`, e.g.
3.7.0-main.412.a1b2c3d. Valid semver PRERELEASE, so it sorts below the
eventual 3.7.0 and is never selected by accident; also a valid OCI tag, which
semver build metadata (`+sha`) is not, since `+` is not a legal tag character.

Name and version are read from Chart.yaml rather than `helm show chart`: the
packaged filename uses the chart NAME, which is not the directory name
(charts/gateway packages as langwatch-gateway), and `helm show` needs
dependencies resolved, which is the following step.

Verified by running the package loop locally against all four charts and
asserting each predicted .tgz filename exists; only the `helm push` itself is
unexercised.

* harden(ci): sign chart artifacts, stop persisting the token, drop secret interpolation

Three hardening changes to the OCI prerelease workflow, each matching a
convention this repo already established elsewhere.

Sign the pushed charts with cosign, keyless via the workflow's OIDC identity —
same approach as publish-docker-app and sign-release-images, and pinned to
cosign 2.6.3 for the same stated reason (3.x defaults to the OCI 1.1 referrers
bundle, which not every client resolves). Consumers can then verify a chart
came from this workflow rather than from anyone who happens to hold a token
with packages:write.

Signing binds to the DIGEST, never the tag. A tag can be moved; a digest
cannot, so a tag signature attests to whatever the tag points at when it is
verified rather than to what was reviewed. helm push reports the digest on
stderr, so the push output is captured with 2>&1 and parsed; if the digest
cannot be read the step fails loudly instead of falling back to signing the
tag. Parser and the empty-digest guard both exercised against sample output.

persist-credentials: false on checkout — the job performs no git operations,
so GITHUB_TOKEN has no reason to sit in .git/config where every later step can
read it. Matches coderabbit-config-check, langwatch-app-ci, code-scanners.

Move GITHUB_TOKEN and github.actor out of the run body into env. `${{ }}` is
substituted before the shell parses the line, so an interpolated value
containing shell metacharacters is executed rather than read. No secrets remain
interpolated in any run block.

claims to come from main, carrying a valid Sigstore signature, built from
unreviewed code. The version string is the entire trust signal for these

artifact published and the job red.

transparency-log hiccup, or a bundle format the verifier rejects (the reason
cosign is pinned to 2.x here). Verifying now turns that into a red build rather
than a chart that only fails when someone first tries to trust it. The identity
regexp is pinned to this repository so a signature minted by another repo's
workflow is refused.

* fix(chart): close five ingress-block bypasses and stop `base` shadowing global pod security

Audit found the ingress block did not actually block, and that the pod-security
layering exempted the two workloads holding data. Each bypass below was
reproduced by rendering before the fix and is refused after it, asserting on the
specific error rather than on "helm exited non-zero".

INGRESS — the block rendered but did not block, five ways:

  - `/api/internal//` and `/api/internal ` (trailing space). `trimSuffix "/"`
    strips exactly ONE character, so the first became `/api/internal/` and the
    nested-path guard then compared against a prefix no request path matches:
    the chart emitted a blackhole rule while an app rule for
    `/api/internal/status` out-matched it. Silently repairing operator input is
    what made this reachable, so the helper now REFUSES whitespace, `//`, and a
    trailing slash instead of normalising them. That also makes the Gherkin
    true — it already claimed `/api/internal/` was rejected, and it was not.

  - A regex `pathType: ImplementationSpecific` app path. ingress-nginx ranks
    regex locations above prefix locations, so `/api/(.*)` beats the blackhole
    outright, and segment matching cannot reason about it at all. Refused when
    blockedPaths is non-empty.

  - `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/default-backend`. ingress-nginx defines it as
    the handler for a service with no active endpoints — which is precisely
    what the blackhole IS — so setting it for custom error pages turned the
    block into a working proxy. Refused, matched on the annotation suffix so
    the check is not tied to one controller's prefix.

  - `http: {}` / `http: {paths: []}`. The guard tested `$host.http`, not the
    list, so an empty paths entry rendered an Ingress whose ONLY rules were
    blackholes — a total outage that applies without error. Now tests the list.

POD SECURITY — `base` replaced global rather than layering onto it:

  `.base | default $global` meant a component that pins its own uid discarded
  every other global key. An operator raising the bar globally
  (seccompProfile.type: Localhost, supplementalGroups, fsGroupChangePolicy) got
  it on app/workers/nlp/langevals while the bundled PostgreSQL and Redis stayed
  on whatever `base` named. The two workloads holding data were the two exempt
  from the hardening.

  Now a three-level merge — global, then base, then override — and `base` is
  trimmed at both call sites to the uid keys it actually must pin
  (runAsUser/runAsGroup/fsGroup), so runAsNonRoot and seccompProfile come from
  global and a global raise reaches the datastores. Verified: default render is
  unchanged (RuntimeDefault, uid 999, runAsNonRoot true), and with global set to
  Localhost postgresql now renders Localhost while keeping uid 999.

  Also documents the removal path the layering took away: set a key to `null`
  to drop it rather than change it — needed on OpenShift, where the SCC assigns
  runAsUser from a range.

* fix(ci): stop the OCI publish leaving unsigned, reusable or mislabelled artifacts

Six audit findings on the workflow added earlier in this PR.

cancel-in-progress: false. Cancelling lands between `helm push` and
`cosign sign`, and there is no cleanup path — the chart stays in GHCR unsigned
while the run reports "cancelled" rather than failed, so nothing retries and
nothing reconciles it. A publish run now drains.

run_attempt joins the version. A re-run reuses BOTH run_number and github.sha,
and `helm package` is not byte-reproducible (tgz entry mtimes come from
checkout time), so "Re-run all jobs" silently republished the same version
string with different bytes and orphaned the first run's signature. The header
claimed these tags were immutable; that claim is now qualified rather than
false.

Stop passing --app-version "$short_sha". clickhouse-serverless declares
appVersion "25.10.2.65" — the actual ClickHouse release — and overwriting it
with a git sha destroyed real information AND asserted a correspondence the
chart does not have, since its image tags come from values.yaml, not
appVersion. The sha is already carried in the version string.

Shape-check the digest instead of testing non-emptiness. `awk '/Digest:/...'`
matched anywhere on a line against combined stdout+stderr, so a helm output
change printing ref and digest together would have handed `cosign sign` a ref.
Now anchored on the field and validated against ^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$.

Parse Chart.yaml scalars with the quotes stripped. `awk '{print $2}'` returned
`"0.2.0"` verbatim for any chart that quotes its version — a malformed
--version and a .tgz filename that does not exist. The repo already quotes
appVersion in that same file, so this was one edit away from breaking.

helm lint + helm template before packaging. Nothing between `dependency build`
and `cosign sign` established that the chart renders, so a template error
merged to main would produce a cryptographically valid signature over a chart
that cannot install.

fallback) filters findings by their quoted text instead.

ingest-key traces, was being nuked to [SECRET] by the sensitive-attribute-name

stamped server-side (never client-forgeable), so it is exempt from the name

An exception is the only pattern in this feature that REMOVES redaction, so a

one there only over-redacts. Mirrors the existing over-breadth guard on

* fix(data-privacy): make the api_key.id exemption safe by always overwriting it

`langwatch.api_key.id` carries the id of the ApiKey row that authenticated the
request, not key material, and the sensitive-attribute-NAME deny-list was
nuking it to [SECRET], hiding the one field that says which key produced a
trace. It is exempt from the name rule again, under the name it describes.

A bare name exemption would not be safe: attribute names are caller-supplied,
so a name the deny-list skips is a free slot to park a real secret in. The root
cause was never the name, it was that the receiver only overwrote the attribute
for ingest-key traffic and left every other authenticated request's value
untouched. So the receiver now rewrites it on EVERY authenticated OTLP request:
payload copies are dropped first at resource, span, event and link level, then
the true row id is written when one exists. Legacy project keys have no ApiKey
row, so nothing is written and the attribute stays absent, which is a correct
answer where a caller-supplied value is not.

That makes the exemption safe by construction rather than by trust, and the
doc-comments on both sides say so, including that the rewrite must not be
narrowed back to ingest-key traffic.

The other ingestion paths need nothing: the REST collector maps known fields
through a fixed `ATTR_KEYS` set and custom metadata lands namespaced under
`langwatch.metadata.*`, so no caller can produce this attribute name there.

Tests cover forgery on resource, span, event and link, the no-ApiKey-row
branch, exact-name scoping against near-miss names, and the whole thing end to
end through the real command handler.

fix(aigateway): decode compressed request bodies so codex turns stop failing with missing model field (#6344)

* fix(aigateway): decode compressed request bodies before the model peek

codex 0.145 posts /v1/responses under `Content-Encoding: zstd` once the
user is signed in with an OpenAI account. The gateway read those bytes
as JSON, found no top-level `model`, and answered 400 "missing model
field" before contacting any provider, so every codex turn through
`langwatch codex` failed instantly.

The transport now decodes gzip, deflate, br and zstd request bodies on
every lane that reads a body, drops the Content-Encoding header so the
passthrough lane cannot forward a claim that no longer matches the
payload, and holds the decoded stream to the same size ceiling as the
raw one so a compression bomb answers 413 instead of expanding into pod
memory. A content coding the gateway cannot decode is a bad request with
the coding named.

* fix(gateway): usage page reads the org, not the selected project

The Usage page rendered "No usage in this window" for every key and
every window while the keys table beside it showed real money.

Both surfaces read the same ClickHouse source (`trace_summaries` via
GatewayVirtualKeySpendRepository); they disagreed on tenancy. The keys
table's spend column reads every project of the organization, because a
gateway trace lands in the tenant of its key's trace destination: the
key's explicit trace project, else its single PROJECT scope, else the
org's `internal_governance` project. The Usage page read
`tenantIds: [projectId]`, the project the viewer happens to have
selected, which for org- and team-scoped keys is never where the traces
are. Hence an empty page under a full table.

The usage reads are now org-scoped like the spend column, and the router
is org-scoped with them. Visibility moves to the membership rule the keys
table already applies (`loadMembershipSet` / `isVisibleToMembership`), so
the page totals exactly the keys the table lists, and a non-member reads
an empty summary rather than another org's spend.

`gateway_budget_ledger_events` read that no longer happens; both now
describe the trace-cost path they actually use.

fix(components): clear scheduled timers so nothing runs after unmount (#6394)

* fix(components): clear scheduled timers so nothing runs after unmount

HoverableBigText scheduled its overflow probe with a bare setTimeout in the
render body, so every render armed a measurement that nothing could cancel.
When a shard ran slowly the probe landed after jsdom teardown and threw
"window is not defined" outside any test's stack: the shard exited 1 while
its own summary reported all 950 tests across 122 files as passing, and the
blame fell on whichever file happened to be running, most recently
EvaluationStatusItem.error.integration.test.tsx. A failure that reports
everything green is worse than a flake, because the only sane response to it
is to rerun until it goes away, and a real failure hiding behind the same
exit code reads identically.

The probe now lives in an effect that clears its handle, which also collapses
a burst of renders into one measurement instead of one per render.

An AST sweep over every component and hook found this was the only timer
scheduled directly in a render body. It also found 15 more sites where a
timer or frame armed inside an effect had no cleanup and could outlive the
component; those are fixed here too. Three of them needed more than a
clear-on-rerun and carry a comment saying why:

- OptimizationStudio's expand loop read the panel size through a null ref
  after unmount, so its "below 70" test stayed true and it rescheduled a
  frame forever. It now bails on a missing panel and cancels on unmount.
- BatchEvaluationV2 and VersionToBeUsed re-run while their deadline is
  pending, so an effect-scoped cleanup would push the deadline out forever
  or swallow a one-shot generation. Both track the handle on a ref and clear
  it on unmount.

Left alone, with the mechanism verified in each case rather than assumed: 12
sites whose callback's first reachable statement dereferences a ref React
nulls during the unmount commit, or that only writes a ref field. Observers
were swept the same way and every ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver and
MutationObserver already disconnects.

The new test unmounts before the probe fires and asserts nothing is left
scheduled. It fails against the old component.

fix(analytics): bound the evaluation_runs JOIN so it prunes partitions; env-driven ClickHouse pool size (#6399)

* fix(analytics): bound the evaluation_runs JOIN so it prunes partitions, and make the ClickHouse pool size configurable

The analytics timeseries and filter-values builders join evaluation_runs
through a subquery that filtered on TenantId only — including its IN-tuple
dedup inner scan, which walked the tenant's entire evaluation history
across every weekly partition, S3-tiered cold ones included. The query's
OccurredAt window couldn't help: evaluation_runs partitions on ScheduledAt
per the migrations (UpdatedAt on older deployments), so an OccurredAt
predicate prunes nothing there. Measured in production at ~900 executions
and 6,400s of accumulated query time per 30 minutes on a single worker
pod, starving the projection reads that drain the event-sourcing queue.

Mirror the existing spanTimeFilter pattern: buildJoinClause gains an
evalTimeFilter applied to BOTH the outer subquery and the dedup inner,
and every call site passes lower bounds on both candidate partition
columns with a 7-day margin. Lower bounds only — a re-evaluation updates
rows long after the window and the dedup must still see that latest
version. UpdatedAt is table-qualified because trace_summaries also has
one, and ClickHouse resolves a bare unknown identifier against the outer
scope instead of failing (the hazard the
join-time-bound-partition-column guard test exists for).

Separately, max_open_connections was hardcoded at 25 in both client
construction sites — sized long before GLOBAL_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY=256, and
measured in production as the actual bottleneck: 4 worker pods pinned at
exactly 100 open connections queueing multi-second for queries the
server answered in ~55ms at a third of its concurrency ceiling. Now
env-driven via CLICKHOUSE_MAX_OPEN_CONNECTIONS (default 64, clamped to
[1,1024]) from one shared helper.

* fix(analytics): make the ScheduledAt bound NULL-safe for legacy schemas

Review catch (langwatch-agent): long-lived deployments that predate the
unified DDL carry ScheduledAt Nullable(DateTime64(3)) — there, a bare
ScheduledAt >= x evaluates to NULL for NULL rows and silently drops those
evaluations from every graph. Verified against production: the column is
indeed Nullable there (0 NULL rows in 20.3M today, but the type permits
them and self-hosted installs can't be audited). The bound is now
(ScheduledAt IS NULL OR ScheduledAt >= x); on the unified schema the
column is NOT NULL so the IS NULL branch is statically false and pruning
is unchanged, while NULL rows on legacy schemas remain bounded by the
UpdatedAt predicate — their actual partition column.

Also correct the connectionPool sizing comment (CodeRabbit): the pool is
per client INSTANCE, not per process — a process holding both
construction sites' clients can open 2x the value, and the server budget
must sum every pool.

* fix(langy): stop the explorer link truncating a quoted search phrase

Found by driving the real agent end-to-end, not by reading the code: it
composes its shell command with one quoting level nested inside another

escaped `\"` as a plain closing quote. The phrase ended at the first space

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(traces-v2): re-read the fragment on navigation, not on render identity

Two defects found reviewing this PR's own diff, both in code it added.

1. The navigation guard trusted a value nothing keeps current. It compared
   React Router's `location.hash`, but the write effect moves the fragment with
   a raw `history.replaceState`, which React Router never observes — so its copy
   goes stale the moment a filter is edited. Caching `window.location.hash`
   instead failed the same way: the ref only advances when the effect applies,
   while the writer moves the real fragment without telling it. Both let the
   same sequence through — type a query, follow a link back to the fragment you
   started on, and the deep link is silently dropped, reinstating the dead
   button this PR exists to fix. No cache of "what the fragment was" is
   trustworthy while something else mutates it unobserved, so there is no longer
   one: `applyFromFragment` reads the fragment live and its existing in-sync
   check makes a redundant apply a no-op, exactly as the popstate path has
   always relied on. Pinned by a test that fails against both earlier guards.

2. The effect re-ran on `applyFromFragment`'s identity, so a plain re-render —
   no navigation at all — re-applied the fragment. Against a store whose actions
   are not referentially stable (a test double returning a fresh `vi.fn()` per
   selector call, for one) this clobbered a lens the user had just picked, which
   is how the existing lens-restore suite caught it. The callback now rides a
   ref so the effect depends on `location.key` alone.

Also: stop claiming the 24h default for a half-named window. The CLI defaults
its two ends INDEPENDENTLY (absent start → now-24h, absent end → now), so
`--start-date` with no end is [thatStart, now], not the 24h window. Stamping 24h
on a start three months back would cut the link to a fraction of the search —
and a link that narrows is the one failure this module must not produce, since a
lost filter shows a superset the user can see through while an invented one
hides rows they came to find. With one bound named we cannot reconstruct the
other without knowing when the search ran, so we now assert nothing.

* fix(langy): only the CLI's own search may claim the CLI's default window

Sergio's review catch on #6370, and he is right — the earlier commit made the
24h fallback unconditional, but the invariant behind it is not.

`explorerFragment` stamped `preset=24h` whenever both dates were absent, on the
reasoning that the search "covered the CLI's own default window". That holds for
`langwatch trace search` and nothing else. `buildTraceExplorerHref` is also the
seam for ADR-060 derived-card `explore` hints, which the model authors as

data is from — and this PR had just widened that path to accept origin-only
hints. A card summarising last quarter therefore linked to a one-day window and
showed an empty page: an invented filter, which is the exact failure the
module's own comment forbids ("a lost filter shows the user a superset they can
see through, an invented one hides rows they came to find").

The window's meaning is now the caller's to state, via `unstatedWindow`:

  "cli-last-24h"  the CLI search paths — both trace cards, their row links, and
                  the automation follow-up chip, all reading a settled
                  `langwatch trace search` where an absent window really is the
                  last day.
  "unknown"       everything else, and the DEFAULT — so a caller that forgets
                  lands on the Explorer's own default, a superset the user can
                  see through, rather than on a window we made up.

The derived-hint call site passes nothing and so takes the safe branch.

Tests now assert the hrefs rather than the links' existence, which is what let
this through: the derived-card cases pin `q` with no `preset`, and a new case

* feat(experiments): lead the leaderboard with the decision, not the table

The drawer opened on a sortable table of Bradley-Terry scores. That asks
the reader to do the statistics: compare "1.42 ± 0.18" against
"1.31 ± 0.22", notice the intervals overlap, and conclude the run does not
actually separate them. Almost nobody does that. They read the top row as
the winner — and frequently it isn't one.

So compute the conclusion and say it. computeLeaderboardVerdict compares
confidence intervals and returns one of three answers: a clear winner, a
tie at the top, or not enough signal to rank at all. A missing interval
counts as "cannot separate" rather than "different", so thin data never
manufactures a winner.

indistinguishable on quality and one costs materially less, the ranking
is not the decision — the price is, and the top row is the wrong pick.
findCheaperTiedAlternative surfaces that as "Ship X — same quality, 62%
cheaper", which is the most actionable sentence this drawer can produce
and was previously not derivable from anything on screen.

The drawer is now three numbered steps in the order a reader has the
questions — what should I ship, can I believe it, what is it costing me —
so someone who reads only step 1 still leaves with a defensible answer.
The table and win-matrix move under step 3, where they answer "why" for
people who want it instead of "what" for everyone.

Two supporting changes. Scores are drawn as bars with their intervals as
whiskers, because overlapping whiskers make a tie visible in a way two ±
figures never are. And the three warning banners collapse into a trust
step that states each condition either way — silence is a bad way to say
"this is fine", since the reader cannot tell a clean run from a check
that was never made.

The compact card carries the verdict too, so the answer is on the results
page without opening anything.

* fix(experiments): stop the bootstrap fabricating confidence intervals

Smoothing was decided once, from the full dataset, and then reused for
every bootstrap replicate. That is wrong: a resample routinely contains a
variant that happened to win nothing even when no variant is degenerate
overall. With smoothing off, that variant's strength goes to zero,
400*log10(0) is -Infinity, and the geometric-mean renormalisation throws
its opponent to about 1e300 — which renders as +120000.

Measured on 8-2 over ten comparisons at the shipped defaults: the
interval came out as 120.41 +/- 59982.39.

Three things made this worse than a cosmetic glitch. The bounds are
FINITE, so the isFinite guards added earlier let them straight through.
computeLeaderboardVerdict compares raw interval bounds, so inflated ones
make every pair overlap and the verdict collapses to "too close to call"
— the headline output of the feature, wrong. And the trust step
cheerfully reports "ranking settled", because convergence describes the
point fit and not the replicates.

Worst of all it lands precisely in the regime the feature warns about:
around half of ten-comparison runs were affected, falling to zero by
forty. The panel told you the sample was thin while showing you a number
invented by the thinness.

Decide smoothing per replicate instead, from that replicate's own win
matrix. Identical output on healthy samples, corrective where it was
broken.

The existing tests missed this because all but one disable the bootstrap,
and that one asserts only determinism. The regression test added here
fails at 119999.99 without the fix.

* fix(api-keys): let the ceiling see the access it is supposed to bound

A user whose project access comes from legacy TeamUser membership could
not mint a restricted API key. Every permission was refused with
"exceeds your own access" — including permissions they demonstrably
held, and had just been authorized on.

Two resolvers answer the same question from opposite sides, and only
one of them knew about legacy membership:

  - `batchProjectPermissions` (rbac.ts) decides what a caller HOLDS. It
    falls back to the TeamUser role when the user has no RoleBindings
    anywhere in the org.
  - `checkRoleBindingPermission` reports RoleBindings and nothing else,
    deliberately — its suite pins that ("TeamUser fallback is handled
    by checkPermissionFromBindings, not this resolver"). The tRPC path
    layers the fallback on top; this ceiling never did.

So the mint measured 23 held permissions and the ceiling then rejected
the first one. Not theoretical: Langy mints a per-turn key mirroring
the caller's permissions, so on any workspace still on legacy
membership EVERY Langy turn died with an opaque
`api_key_scope_violation` — an error whose remediation text
("try rephrasing") cannot possibly apply.

Fixed at the ceiling rather than in the resolver, whose narrower
contract is intentional and tested. The legacy role is resolved ONCE
per create, not per permission: langyApiKey.ts records what
per-permission query fan-out already did to this path once — it
starved the connection pool and aborted the 5-second interactive
transaction — and that call site passes ~23 permissions.

Same gate as `loadScopeResolution`, so a migrated user's legacy row can
never stack on top of a real binding, org-scoped keys are excluded (an
org-wide grant is not something a team role should reach), CUSTOM
legacy roles are left to the binding path, and the lookup fails closed
on current org membership.

Verified end to end against a live stack, on a user with zero
RoleBinding rows: langy.createConversation 200, langy.onTurnStream 200,
no scope violation. Was 403 then api_key_scope_violation before.

* fix(langevals): honour allow_tie=False when reconciliation disagrees

`_judge` already respects `allow_tie=False` by leaving "tie" out of the
winner enum, so neither individual call can return it. `_reconcile`'s
disagreement branch then returned it unconditionally — so with

codebase already distinguishes them (a tie is 0.5/0.5 evidence, an
unresolved verdict contributes none and the row is skipped).

rather than falling through to the score branch, where score=1.0 would
have read as a win for label=None and score=0.5 would have been the tie

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(leaderboard): decide separation on the difference, not two intervals

Whether two variants differ is the root of every claim here — the winner,
the tie set, what can be dropped, how much of the order got settled. It
was answered by asking whether their two confidence intervals overlap,
and that is the wrong question.

Every bootstrap replicate resamples the comparisons and re-fits the whole
field at once, so two variants' replicate scores are not independent: a
resample kind to the field lifts both. Each marginal interval therefore
carries all of that shared movement. Subtracting two scores from the SAME
replicate cancels it. Overlap-of-marginals is a strictly stronger
condition than "the difference excludes zero", so the old test could only
under-report.

Measured over 40 synthetic four-variant runs of 60 rows with known
strengths, 240 pairs: interval-overlap separated 26.3%, the paired
difference 39.2% — about half as many again — and neither test separated
a single pair against the true ordering. The old behaviour was reporting
"too close to call" on pairs the run had demonstrably resolved.

The replicate scores needed for this were already being computed and
thrown away; only the pairing was missing.

Also consolidates the separation test. computeSampleAdequacy had its own
copy, and the two had already drifted once — the verdict named a clear
winner while the adequacy panel beside it counted zero separated pairs.
There is now one implementation in scoreSeparation.ts, used by the
verdict, the adequacy count and the Pareto dominance check, so the panels
cannot disagree about a pair again.

Falls back to comparing intervals when the bootstrap is disabled, where
there is nothing better and conservative is the right way to be wrong.

* fix(leaderboard): close the three remaining gaps in what the run claims

1. COST DOMINANCE now uses a paired test, not a guessed threshold.

"Meaningfully cheaper" was a flat 5% relative gap — a stand-in from when
no interval existed, which called a 6% gap on two rows cheaper and missed
a dead-certain 4% gap on two hundred. It is now the 95% interval of the
mean PER-ROW cost difference. Paired within the row for the same reason
the score difference is: both variants answered the same row, and rows
differ from each other far more than variants do, so differencing within
a row removes the variance that otherwise drowns the comparison. The old
floor stays only as the fallback when a run produced no interval.

2. MULTIPLICITY is now stated rather than implied.

Six pairs each tested at 95% leaves roughly a 1-in-4 chance one separated
on luck, and "4 of 6 pairs were separated" read as a joint guarantee.

The textbook fix is simultaneous bands, and it was built, measured and
REJECTED. A max-t construction — largest standardised deviation across
all pairs per replicate, 95th percentile as one critical value — is the
efficient form, since it reads the correlation between pairs off the
replicates instead of assuming the worst as Bonferroni does. Measured on
40 synthetic four-variant runs: 12.9% of pairs separated, against 26.3%
for the interval-overlap test this work replaced and 39.2% for the
per-pair difference. The simultaneous band came out ~1.10x the overlap
test's own effective threshold — the multiplicity multiplier (~2.9 rather
than 1.96) more than cancels the correlation gain.

Shipping it would make every claim weaker than before any of this work,
to fix an overstatement that a sentence fixes for free. So each pair stays
correctly calibrated at 95% on its own, and the trust panel now says what
the count across pairs does and does not mean.

3. REPLICATE NON-CONVERGENCE is no longer swallowed.

`didConverge` describes the point fit, while the margins of error are
built from a thousand other fits whose failures were discarded. A
resample is often harder to fit than the full dataset — it can drop a
variant's only wins — so a run could report a clean convergence beside
intervals drawn from fits that never settled. The share is now tracked
and, above 2%, the panel says the intervals are approximate.

fix(automations): serialize graph-trigger sweeps in one lane per tenant (#6414)

* fix(automations): serialize graph-trigger sweeps in one lane per tenant

The 5s debounce dedup bounds how fast sweep jobs are STAGED, but each
staged job inherited a per-trace queue group, so jobs staged across
successive windows dispatched concurrently. Under sustained tenant
traffic this stacked into a parallel sweep storm: measured 2026-07-31,
~85 concurrent sweeps for one tenant (~8/s where the debounce intends
0.2/s), each a multi-hundred-MiB analytics query, saturating ClickHouse
selects fleet-wide and reversing the queue drain.

A sweep evaluates the tenant's CURRENT trigger state, so concurrent
sweeps are pure waste. One tenant-keyed lane serializes them: queued
deliveries drain sequentially and a backlog degrades to cheap

serialized chunks through an AsyncGenerator so memory stays flat.

  common question needs no parsing.

* fix(app-layer): stop traced() breaking async generator methods

The previous commit registered ScenarioRunExportService on the app-layer, which
routes it through `traced()` — and that broke the export at runtime:

    TypeError: service.exportRuns(...) is not a function
                or its return value is not async iterable

`traced()` wraps every method as `withActiveSpan(name, async () => fn(...))`.
For a normal async method that yields a promise, which is correct. For an
`async function*` it yields a Promise<AsyncGenerator> — and `for await` on a
promise throws, because a promise is not async-iterable. The failure is
invisible at wrap time and only appears when the method is iterated, which is
why typecheck and every unit/integration test stayed green while the endpoint
hung.

Async generator methods are now delegated with `yield*`, so the method stays a
generator. The work is still traced: awaits inside it run under whatever span
is active at iteration time, which for a streamed export is the request span.

This was latent for anything else that gets tracked this way —
`export.service.ts` and `langyTokenBuffer.ts` also expose async generators and
would have hit it the moment they were registered on the facade.

Four tests pin it, including that a throw inside the generator still
propagates. Removing the branch fails three of them.

counts from before the app-layer change.

* fix(scenarios): address Sergio's review — backpressure, injection, dedup

Four of the five findings from the Codex review.

Backpressure. The producer lived in start(), which runs to completion
whatever the consumer does, so a slow client had the whole export swept

scenario set id, run id, batch id and target reference all arrive from
the SDK as arbitrary strings — so `=cmd|...` was a value a caller could
choose, in a cell no one thought to guard.

pages remain: filter to a scenario whose runs sit further back and the
sweep would have found them. It now takes hasMore into account.

Stale versions. StartedAt is mutable across ReplacingMergeTree versions —
the projection opens a run with it null and sets the real value when the
started event lands — so filtering on it inside the dedup subquery picked
the newest version *within* the range. A run whose corrected timestamp
moved out of the window exported its stale earlier snapshot instead of

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(scenarios): propagate a failed sweep instead of crashing the process

Switching the gzip to Node's stream plumbing brought its error semantics
with it, and they differ from pipeThrough's. `.pipe()` does not forward a
source error: it unpipes, leaves the destination open, and the Readable's
own 'error' event goes unhandled — which takes the process down rather
than the one request.

Headers are already sent by the time a sweep can fail, so the only honest
way to report it is to break the body. Destroying the gzip with the error
does that, and the client sees a broken stream rather than a file that
looks complete but stops early.

The regression test reads the response to exhaustion and expects it to
throw; without the handler it fails and vitest reports the unhandled
error, which is the crash.

Also pins the sweep suite's cleanup setting as a string — its number form
does not typecheck against the client's settings type, and `pnpm
typecheck` never looks at test files.

* fix(ops): add a lock-protected full-rebuild replay so an emptied table is not skipped

A replay records every aggregate it finishes in a Redis completed set, and a
run that fails or is cancelled leaves those entries behind on purpose so a
plain re-run resumes rather than repeats. Discovery skips whatever is in that
set (replayOptimizedPath, replayMapPath, replayFoldPath), and the set has no
TTL, so it outlives the rows it vouches for.

That is the wrong default after 00065/00066 swap the analytics rollups in
empty on clustered deployments. Any aggregate an earlier aborted replay had
finished is skipped by the rebuild, which reports a clean run and leaves that
tenant with no pre-deploy history and nothing in the result to say so.

startReplay now takes fullRebuild: it clears the selected projections' markers
under the replay lock, before discovery, and fails the run if that clearing
fails rather than replaying against stale markers. The ops projections page
exposes it as "Rebuild from scratch", and the runbook prescribes it for the
post-migration rebuild, with the flip side spelled out: a rebuild that fails
partway is resumed with the flag OFF, since its markers now describe rows that
are really there and a second full rebuild would double count them.

Covered by an integration test that drives the real ops entry point against
real Redis and ClickHouse across three cells: no marker plus default run
rebuilds the rows, a surviving marker plus default run reports success and
writes nothing, and a surviving marker plus fullRebuild rebuilds the rows.

vi.waitFor retries on a throw, so the wait loop no longer holds assertions

* fix(coding-agent): restore codex terminal, system context, reasoning effort and cache TTL

Four gaps found by dogfooding claude code 2.1.219 and codex 0.146 against a
local instance, plus a context-size signal the trace level never carried.

Codex terminal view was empty. Two causes: the ingest noise filter only knew
the `codex_cli_rs` scope, so `codex exec` sessions (scope `codex_exec`) landed
555 unfiltered infra spans across ~60 fragment traces; and the canonical log
read never surfaced `EventName`, which codex sets on the OTLP LogRecord field
rather than as an attribute, so every reader gating on `event.name` skipped its
records. The transcript now renders codex prompts and tool calls with real
arguments and output, joined span-to-log by `call_id` so a call recorded on
both sides appears once.

The system prompt was missing because the request-body join groups spans and
logs by `query_source`: claude 2.1.x stamps it on the log events but not on the
`llm_request` span, so every body sat in a group no span could reach and each
call fell back to the bare prompt text. Sources only need keeping apart when
the spans declare them, so a trace whose spans carry none now pairs as one
group. A truncated body (claude cuts inline at 60KB, mid-JSON) is salvaged
rather than discarded, and the injected context that rides `<system-reminder>`
blocks is surfaced as one collapsed entry at the top of the transcript.

Reasoning effort and the Anthropic 5m/1h cache-write split were on the wire but
unparsed. Effort now lifts from claude's `api_request` and from codex's turn,
response and log paths; the TTL split lifts from the response body usage and
sums into reserved trace attributes the token popover reads.

Context Size is a new trace attribute and column: the context the trace's first
model call already carried. Deliberately not a sum, which is what makes it
readable next to Tokens, whose cache reads run into the millions for an agent
turn that re-sends its conversation every call. Available in the trace explorer
column picker and default on the personal usage table.

Also: `sdk` query sources count as conversational, so `claude -p` sessions keep
their reply instead of recording no output.

fix(personal-workspace): guard the write paths that hand an organization uncounted resources and brick provisioning (#6227)

* fix(personal-workspace): a ?team= slug matching no team no longer addresses the personal workspace

`isAddressedBySlug` read the raw `?team=` query param, so a slug left over
from a team that was archived, renamed, or belongs to another organization
counted as the user naming a workspace in the address bar. On an
organization-scoped page that was enough to keep a stale personal selection
out of localStorage alive, and the page would then write against one
member's private project without ever naming it.

Key the predicate on the team the slug actually resolved to. A slug that
matches a team the user can see still addresses it, so opening a personal
workspace by its own URL is unchanged.

* fix(personal-workspace): guard the three write paths that could take a personal workspace apart

A personal workspace is one team, one project, one owner, and none of it
spends the organization's plan allowance. Three mutations could break that
shape, and the owner holds the permission each of them checks, so nothing
stopped them:

- `project.update` moved a personal project into a shared team, or a shared
  project into a personal team. `Project.isPersonal` travels with the row and
  plan counting reads it, so the organization ended up with a project no limit
  ever saw. The personal team was also left without its project, which is what
  `PersonalWorkspaceService.ensure()` looks for.
- `team.update` edited members and roles on a personal team, turning a
  single-member workspace into a shared team the allowance never counts.
  Renaming still works.
- `team.archiveById` archived personal teams. The partial unique index
  `Team_organizationId_ownerUserId_personal_key` covers archived rows while
  the service looks up with `archivedAt: null`, so the archived team keeps the
  slot and `ensure()` can neither find the workspace nor create a replacement.

Both `ensure()` failures are permanent for that user and organization: the
next call raises P2002 on `tx.team.create()` and no recovery path exists.
Recovery deliberately stays out of `ensure()`; the write paths are where the
invariant belongs.

The regression suite drives the real tRPC router as the workspace owner, and
proves each rejection twice: the mutation fails, and the state it would have
produced is absent, measured through the real LicenseEnforcementRepository and
a real `ensure()` afterwards.

* fix(licensing): count a project unless both it and its team call it personal

`getProjectCount` exempted a project on `Project.isPersonal` alone. That flag
is a denormalized mirror of `Team.isPersonal`, so one flipped flag was enough
for a project to stop counting against the plan while sitting in a shared team
where the whole organization works.

Require both flags to agree. Counting is the fail-closed side of that
question: a project whose flags disagree is not in anyone's personal
workspace, in either direction, so it counts.

* fix(licensing): stop charging the team allowance for archived teams

`getTeamCount` counted every team row, archived or not, while
`getProjectCount` frees the slot an archived project held. An archived team is
gone from every read path in the product, so a customer who archived one and
still could not create another had nothing on screen explaining what held the
allowance.

Filter `archivedAt: null`, matching how `team.archiveById` archives and how
every team read path already reads.

* fix(teams): surface the server's reason when a team edit is refused

Team settings autosaves on a debounce, and the only error it surfaced was
UNAUTHORIZED. A FORBIDDEN from the server therefore left the form looking
saved while nothing had been written, which is exactly what the new personal
workspace guards return, along with a message saying what to do instead.

Show that message, and use it for the archive dialog too instead of the
generic failure line.

* fix(projects): hold the personal workspace boundary in the app layer too

`PATCH /api/projects/:id` reaches `ProjectService.update` directly and
documents `teamId` as a supported field, so the tRPC guard alone left the same
move open over the REST API: a personal project out of its workspace, or a
shared project into one.

Guard it in the service, where both callers pass, and return 403 rather than
400 since the caller holds the permission and the request is refused on its
own merits. Adds `ForbiddenError` to the shared HTTP errors, which had no 403.

* fix(teams): hold the personal team invariants over the REST API too

Three more doors onto the same invariants, all reachable with an org-scoped
API key that holds every permission they check:

- `DELETE /api/teams/:id` archived personal teams through
  `TeamRestService.archive`, which the tRPC guard never sees. Same permanent
  break: the archived team keeps the uniqueness slot the workspace lookup
  skips.
- `POST /api/teams/:id/members` added members to a personal team.
- `DELETE /api/teams/:id/members/:userId` removed them, and unlike the tRPC
  path it has no last-admin check, so it could strip the owner of access to
  their own workspace.

All three now refuse with 403. The archive guard sits in the service so any
caller passes it; the membership routes write RoleBinding directly, so they
check the team they already loaded. The refusal wording is shared with the
tRPC router rather than restated.

* fix(projects): refuse to archive a personal project

A personal workspace is its project: PersonalWorkspaceService finds the
workspace by the personal team still holding an unarchived personal project.
Archiving it hides the workspace from that lookup while the team keeps the one
slot allowed per (organization, owner), so the next ensure() can neither find
the workspace nor create a replacement. Same permanent break as archiving the
team, reachable from both `project.archiveById` and `DELETE /api/projects/:id`.

Guard both, and share the three project refusal messages between the router
and the service rather than restating them.

* fix(teams): let the global handler own the errors it already handles on archive

The archive dialog's onError showed its own toast for every failure, including
the license and lite-member errors the global handler already surfaces, so
those appeared twice. Matches the update path, which short-circuits them.

* fix(projects): decide the personal guards on a project this organization owns

The app-layer guards read the project by id alone, so a caller could tell a
personal project from a shared one in an organization they have nothing to do
with by the status code the request came back with. Read the project with its
team and only refuse when the organization matches; anything else falls through
to the scoped write, which already answers not-found.

* refactor(projects): define the personal workspace boundary once

The move and archive predicates were written out in both the app layer and the
tRPC router, which do not share a code path, so the invariant was encoded twice
and could drift. Extract them as pure functions the app layer owns and both
callers ask, each wrapping the returned reason in its own error type.

Also from review: the REST membership guard comments described the defect
rather than the branch, the new REST suite's inner describe did not read as a
`when` condition, and the new project scenarios named the service instead of
the behavior a reader can observe.

* fix(projects): refuse to create a second project in a personal workspace

Review finding P2. The new boundary predicate was only asked on move and
archive, so creation was still open: both `project.create` and
`POST /api/projects` accepted any team in the organization, and the owner is
ADMIN of their own personal team, so `project:create` passes there. The result
is a normal project sitting in a workspace that team selection deliberately
hides, which is a project nobody but its owner can find.

Guarded on both paths through a `personalWorkspaceCreateViolation` helper
alongside the move and archive ones, so the shape is stated in a single place.
`PersonalWorkspaceService` provisions the one project that does belong there
without going through either path, so it is unaffected.

The regression test wires a generous plan into the app layer on purpose:
without it the creation fails for want of an app rather than for the reason
under test, and the assertion that no project appeared would pass with the
guard removed.

* fix(role-bindings): hold the personal team invariant where bindings are written

Review finding P1. The team editor's guard only covered `team.update`. Team
membership is really role bindings, and those are written from the role-binding
service, the group router and the groups REST API, the member-role path, the
custom-role assign/remove path and the team service, only some of which share a
code path. None of them read `Team.isPersonal`, so an organization manager
could grant a second user or a group access to a personal team, or take the
owner's own binding away, without the editor ever running. The team stays
flagged personal, so plan limits keep excluding a team the organization is
really using; and a group ADMIN binding defeats the last-admin projection that
is the only thing standing between the owner and removal from their own
workspace.

State the invariant once, in `personal-team-scope.ts`, and ask it wherever a
TEAM-scoped binding is created, changed or removed: creates and deletes alike,
since taking the owner's binding away is as much a membership change as adding
someone else's. Two wrappers because the callers do not share an error
vocabulary: tRPC paths get FORBIDDEN, app-layer and REST paths get
`PersonalTeamProtectedError` and map it themselves.

`PersonalWorkspaceService` writes the one canonical owner ADMIN binding
straight through Prisma, so provisioning never reaches the guard and first
login, invite accept and CLI bootstrap are unaffected.

Wider than the review asked. It named `roleBinding.create` and
`group.addBinding`; re-probing found the delete and mutate sides open too, plus
`organization.updateTeamMemberRole`, the custom-role assign/remove path, which
rewrites any binding to CUSTOM or VIEWER, and `TeamService.removeMember`.

* fix(role-bindings): a personal workspace is reached by its project too

Review follow-ups.

The scope check only resolved TEAM ids, so naming the personal project on a
PROJECT-scoped binding walked straight past it into the same private space.
Both scope kinds now resolve, and the group repository delegates to the one
implementation instead of keeping its own copy.

Also from review, both pre-existing and both on paths this change touches:
`GroupService.create` never validated that its initial binding scopes belong to
the caller's organization, unlike `addBinding`, so a group could be created
holding a binding on another organization's team or project. And project
creation accepted an archived destination team while moving a project into that
same team was refused; it now requires an active team, like moves do.

The licensing scenarios said "role binding" and "the owner's binding", which is
how it is stored rather than what a customer does. They now describe giving and
taking away access to a personal workspace.

* docs(specs): describe the personal workspace rule without naming write paths

Review follow-up. The section comment listed the internal paths access can
arrive through; what a reader needs is that the workspace stays one person's
regardless.

* fix(teams): stop rendering a raw error message, except the sentences we author

Main's handled-errors migration added a guard test that no toast renders an
error's raw message: for a handled error that shows the customer a code slug,
and for an unhandled one it can leak internals. Both toasts on the team
settings page tripped it.

The generic archive failure now goes through `showErrorToast`, which resolves
its copy from the error registry. The two FORBIDDEN branches keep the server's
message and are marked with the escape hatch the rule documents, because a
FORBIDDEN on these mutations is only ever raised by the personal-workspace
guards in this PR, and its message is a sentence written for the customer that
says what to do instead. RBAC failures arrive as UNAUTHORIZED and take the
other branch, so nothing unauthored reaches those lines.

Also clears the two Biome errors the merge left in the new invariants suite and
on this page.

* refactor: keep the Biome complexity ratchet at zero added violations

Main's lint gate compares diagnostic counts against the merge base and fails on
any the PR adds. This one added eight.

Six are gone by extraction, with no behavior change: the destination-team check
in `ProjectService.create`, the create and move guards in the project router,
the update error mapping in the projects REST route, and the team settings save
failure reporter, each now a named function that says what it decides.

The other two are `noExcessiveLinesPerFunction` on integration `describe`
blocks, and that rule is measuring the wrong thing there. A `describe` body is
a suite declaration; the rule counts every nested `describe` and `it` inside
it, so any suite covering more than a couple of cases trips it however it is
written, and the only way to satisfy it is to split coverage by line count
rather than by subject. `e2e/**` is already exempt for exactly this reason, so
the exemption now extends to `**/__tests__/**` for that one rule.
`noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity` stays on there, because it does measure
something real in a test body, and the one violation it flagged in the new
suite is fixed rather than exempted.

fix(ops): stop the pending reconcile and blob sweep scaling with the keyspace (#6457)

* fix(ops): reconcile the pending counter from the queue's group indexes

The total-pending reconcile enumerated a queue's group-jobs zsets with a
keyspace SCAN. SCAN walks every key in the database regardless of MATCH,
so a pass cost as much as the whole Redis instance held rather than as
much as the queue contained, and it got more expensive precisely as the
keyspace grew.

Read the group ids from the queue's own indexes instead — ready, blocked,
and the per-tenant parked zsets reached through parked-tenants — and
build the `group:<id>:jobs` keys from them. Those three are exhaustive
for a group holding jobs: a dispatched group stays in ready (re-scored
into the future, not removed), and every path that removes a group from
ready either moves it to parked or blocked, or does so because its jobs
zset is already empty.

The single-flight marker was also a fixed 55s expiry taken before the
pass, so a pass that ran longer than that was joined by others and they
stacked — worst under exactly the load that makes passes slow. The
marker is now taken on a refreshable lease that is re-armed after every
ZCARD batch, and handed back at the end as the unspent remainder of the
window, so the one-pass-per-window cadence is unchanged while the pass
keeps its hold however long it runs. A compare-and-set script does the
re-arm so a lapsed marker another instance has since taken is never
extended or dropped.

* fix(ops): resume the blob sweep cursor across ticks

The blob sweeper stops after 50,000 matched keys and relies on the next
tick to continue, but `scanNode` started every walk at cursor "0" and
kept the cursor in a local. Nothing carried it between ticks, so each
sweep re-judged the same leading slice of the keyspace and no blob past
it was ever examined, however often the sweep ran.

Two comments already promised the behavior the code did not implement:
`DEFAULT_MAX_KEYS_PER_QUEUE` says "work not reached this tick is reached
the next one", and `BLOB_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS` claims the practical
retention bound for an unreferenced blob is ~1 hour rather than the
4-day backstop. Neither held past the first slice, and reclaim needs the
repair pass to have armed the grace window first, so blobs beyond it
were never even put on the clock.

Park the cursor in Redis per queue, one hash field per node, and resume
from it. It lives in Redis rather than the process so progress survives
a restart and is shared by whichever pod runs the tick; an exhausted
walk stores "0" so the next cycle rewinds and picks up newly written
blobs.

The batch that crosses the ceiling is no longer trimmed. Trimming it
dropped keys the returned cursor had already passed, which was harmless
when every tick restarted and would now skip them for a whole cycle.

Truncation is no longer logged as a warning: with the cursor resuming it
is the steady state for any keyspace larger than one tick's ceiling, not
a fault.

* fix(ops): count pending jobs from a pending-groups index and fence the write

Two concurrency defects from review.

Enumeration read the lifecycle indexes — ready, blocked, and each parked
tenant — one after another. A group moving between them mid-read, from
one not yet visited into one already visited, appeared in none of the
reads even though it never stopped holding jobs, and the shortfall was
written out as ground truth. Transitions go both ways, so no scan order
avoids it and re-scanning only narrows the window.

Count from a `pending-groups` set instead, written in the same atomic
script as every insert into a `group:<id>:jobs` zset. It is keyed on the
property being counted, "has jobs", which no lifecycle transition
changes, so a group holding a job for the whole of a pass is in the index
for the whole of that pass wherever it moves. One index also means one
read, so there is no cross-read gap left to fall through.

Membership is deliberately a superset: an id whose group has drained
contributes ZCARD 0, so removal can be lazy, which is what lets the
`:jobs` safety-net TTL expire a group without corrupting the index. The
reconcile prunes what it observes empty under a script that re-reads the
zset atomically, so a group staged since the observation is never
dropped. The lifecycle indexes are still read but are additive only,
covering groups staged before the index existed; they can go once no
queue predates it.

The lease refresh swallowed both a lost marker and an error, so a pass
that no longer held the marker carried on and could put its stale count
back over a newer pass's. Refresh now reports ownership and losing it
aborts the pass, and the counter write is a compare-and-set against the
holder token so a marker lost in the gap after the final check cannot let
the stale write land anyway.

* fix(ops): adopt legacy groups into the pending index on first sight

A group only enters the pending index when a writer stages a job for it,
so two populations were still being found by reading the lifecycle
indexes in sequence: groups staged before the index existed, and groups
staged by a pod on the previous release while a rollout is in progress.
For those, the read-ordering race the index removes was still live —
blocked to ready, or parked to ready, between two of the reads.

Write any group the lifecycle legs turn up into the index as it is read.
One observation is enough: from the next pass the group is counted from
the index and cannot slip between reads again. That bounds the exposure
at "until first seen" rather than "until the group drains", which is what
matters across a rolling deploy. Adoption is best-effort — failing to add
only leaves the group where it already was — and over-inclusion is
harmless because the prune removes anything that reads as empty.

Also releases the held processor in a finally in the staging test, so a
failed assertion does not leave teardown closing a blocked queue and
charging its shutdown timeout to the next test.

so a large legacy backlog could spend the marker mid-adoption and leave

exists to stop. It now re-arms per batch and abandons the pass on loss.

* fix(licensing): stop a license from lowering the limits a self-hosted deployment already had

Without a license a self-hosted deployment resolves to UNLIMITED_PLAN, where
seats, lite seats and message volume are uncapped. Activating a license then
replaced that plan wholesale with whatever the signed payload encodes, and the
Enterprise template mints 100 members, 50 lite members and 10M messages. So
paying for Enterprise took a deployment from unlimited seats down to 100, on
exactly the axis the uncapped baseline exists to fix, and it contradicts the
self-hosting docs that promise members and lite members are uncapped.

Signed licenses are immutable once issued, so the correction has to happen when
a license is resolved into an active plan rather than at minting time. That also
repairs every license already in the field with no re-issuance, which raising
the template defaults would not do.

and plan identity (type, name, paid status, source) still comes from the
license, because the deployment really is on Enterprise.

* fix(licensing): let a self-hosted license meter seats, and keep older deployments able to read it

Two corrections to the plan-resolution work on this branch.

**Seats bind again.** `floorAtOssBaseline` raised every limit on a
license-resolved plan to the open-source baseline, seats included. A
self-hosted Enterprise license is priced per seat, so that made the seat count
in the signed payload enforce nothing: a ten-seat license accepted the eleventh
member, and every seat clause in every self-hosted contract became
unenforceable by the product.

The floor was built on "a license must never leave you worse off than none",
which is right for capabilities and wrong for the meter. With an uncapped
baseline, any finite seat count is lower than it, so that rule and per-seat
pricing cannot both hold. Seats are now the explicit exception: the license's
numbers apply, and the creation guards stay armed to enforce them.

Everything else still floors, because nothing else is sold by quantity on
self-hosted. Volume is not metered there at all, the data lives in the
customer's own database, and publishing is part of the open-source floor. So
the guarantee narrows to the thing that actually mattered: no capability a
deployment had before it paid disappears when it does.

**Newly minted licenses stay readable by released versions.** `maxProjects` and
`maxWorkflows` only became optional in this branch; every deployment already in
the field requires them and rejects a license that omits them, which lands on
the pre-existing invalid-license path and drops the org to a one-seat free
plan. Since licenses are issued from a continuously deployed control plane to
deployments that upgrade on their own schedule, the first renewal issued after
this shipped would have locked a paying customer out of their own install with
exactly the bug this branch exists to fix.

Both minting paths now go through `buildMintedPlan`, which re-emits those two
fields at the unlimited sentinel, so an older deployment reads them as uncapped
(what they now mean) and a current one ignores them. Key order there is load
bearing: verification re-serializes the Zod-parsed payload, so the order has to
match the schema. The regression test parses a freshly minted license against
the schema as it shipped before the fields were relaxed, so dropping a field
some supported version still requires fails loudly.

* feat(licensing): let an over-seats organization choose who keeps a seat

A self-hosted deployment runs uncapped before it buys a license, so by the time
an organization activates one it can easily hold more members than the seats it
just paid for. Nothing handled that: every member kept working and the seats
were billed but not enforced, which is the leak on one side and, if it had been
enforced bluntly, a lockout on the other.

Activation now always succeeds and the organization lands in an over-seats
state. Everyone keeps working, the license page says how many seats have to come
back, and only new members are refused, since letting the org grow is the one
thing that makes the overage worse. Nobody is signed out by an admin's pending
paperwork.

Disabling is per organization and reversible. `OrganizationUser.disabledAt`
revokes access to that organization only, keeps the role, the department and
everything the person did, and returns the seat to the pool. Re-enabling
restores access, and is refused when it would take the org back over its seats,
so a freed seat cannot be quietly reclaimed. The membership row survives, so
nothing has to be rebuilt when someone comes back.

Two halves have to be true together and both are covered: the seat is really
returned (seat counting excludes disabled memberships) and access is really
gone. The access half is the easy one to get wrong, so every membership read
that grants something filters on it: the two role lookups, the org-with-members
gate, the organization list behind the switcher, and the member roster. Live
sessions are revoked on disable rather than left to expire.

Disabling the last active admin is refused, for the same reason demoting the
last admin is: an organization with no admin who can sign in cannot be
recovered from inside the product.

The license page also stops claiming a license is "required for commercial
use", which the Apache 2.0 floor has made untrue.

* fix(licensing): a lapsed license keeps metering the seats it sold

A self-hosted deployment runs uncapped without a license, so resolving an
expired one back to that baseline handed the customer more than a current
license gives them: the seat cap disappeared and the deployment started
reporting itself as unlicensed. Letting a license run out was worth more than

of what was bought, and reaching its end date does not unmake the purchase, so
the numbers in the signed payload keep binding: seats stay at the count that was
paid for and the capabilities the plan names stay switched on.

organization holding more members than a lapsed license covers lands in the same
over-seats state as one that just activated a license for fewer seats than it
had: everyone keeps working, the license page asks an admin to choose who to
disable, and only new members are refused.

unreadable or tampered key still resolves to the open-source baseline, and the

from the payload's own date, so the status now carries the server's verdict.

fix(event-sourcing): give per-project reactors a per-project queue lane (#6460)

projectMetadata and billingMeterDispatch both build a per-project dedup id
but inherited the default per-trace group key, so the dedup never collapsed
anything.

The queue's dedup key is global to the queue, but the check deciding whether
a duplicate is still squashable looks the existing job up in the group being
staged into. A dedup id that spans groups therefore always misses that
lookup: the key is read as stale and deleted before a fresh job stages,
which also drops the guard protecting the job still pending in the other
group. The result is one live job per concurrent trace for work that is
per-project by construction, each one holding its own serialized lane.

Route both through a per-project group key so the lane and the dedup id
describe the same unit. Squashing is safe for both: projectMetadata is
level-triggered and asserts the project's metadata from whichever trace
carries it, and billingMeterDispatch reads nothing from the triggering
event at all, deriving its dispatch from the project's organization and the
current billing month. Neither loses work when duplicates collapse.

Mirrors the lane fix already applied to graphTriggerActivity.

perf(event-sourcing): collapse map-reactor dispatch across a coalesced batch (#6465)

The map batch path dispatched reactors one event at a time, so the per-reactor
collapse never saw more than one event and could not fire. A drained batch
staged a job per event for reactors keyed on the aggregate, and the queue
squashed all but the last — after every one of those sends had already been
serialized, gzipped and, past the inline ceiling, written to a blob the squash
immediately reclaimed. The fold path has collapsed since it was written; only
the map path missed out.

Dispatch the whole batch in one call so the collapse applies.

A map differs from a fold in the one way that matters here: it produces a
separate record per event rather than one accumulated state for the batch, so
there is no single state to hand the reactor. Rather than pick a representative
record, dispatchToReactors and collapseByJobId now take event/state pairs. A
fold repeats its state across the pairs, a map gives each event the record it
produced, and a survivor keeps its own. No map reactor reads that record today,
but makeJobId, shouldReact and handle are all handed it, so pairing them
correctly costs nothing and removes a trap for the next map reactor.
