perf(event-sourcing): coalesce log and metric record appends (#6462)

* perf(event-sourcing): coalesce log and metric record appends

recordLogRecord and recordDataPoint each processed one queue job per
record: its own Zod validation and its own single-row event_log insert.
Both shard their jobs onto a fixed set of group keys, so a busy exporter
parks many records behind one shard and every one of them pays for its
own tiny insert — exactly the small-parts flood ADR-066 pillar 2 exists
to stop.

Register coalesceMaxBatch on both commands so the dispatcher hands a
worker up to N same-shard jobs in one unit and processCommandBatch folds
them into a single multi-row append. Both handlers derive their event
from their own command alone and never read back a same-batch append, so
they satisfy the batch path's statelessness contract. The bound matches
each pipeline's existing map-projection width; the drain's byte bound
backs it up.

The visibility record meant to catch an un-coalesced high-fan-in producer
keyed only on serializeByAggregate, which is why these two shipped
unbatched in silence. A shard or bucket group key funnels many aggregates
into one consumer just as serializeByAggregate funnels many commands into
one aggregate — same producer shape, same gap — so the detector now
covers both.

Per-group ordering and kill-switch semantics are unchanged: the drain
takes the group head in score order, and the batch path kill-switch-checks
every payload individually.

* docs(event-sourcing): state what the coalescing byte bound actually bounds

The drain's byte budget sums the stored size of each staged job, so an
offloaded envelope body is invisible to it. The comments claimed the byte
bound backed the count up and bound first near the per-record payload
maximum, which is false whenever envelope writes are on. Name the count as
the only reliable bound, and point at the groupQueue change that would fix
the accounting for the command and map stages together.

* fix(licensing): let a self-hosted license meter seats, and keep older deployments able to read it

Two corrections to the plan-resolution work on this branch.

**Seats bind again.** `floorAtOssBaseline` raised every limit on a
license-resolved plan to the open-source baseline, seats included. A
self-hosted Enterprise license is priced per seat, so that made the seat count
in the signed payload enforce nothing: a ten-seat license accepted the eleventh
member, and every seat clause in every self-hosted contract became
unenforceable by the product.

The floor was built on "a license must never leave you worse off than none",
which is right for capabilities and wrong for the meter. With an uncapped
baseline, any finite seat count is lower than it, so that rule and per-seat
pricing cannot both hold. Seats are now the explicit exception: the license's
numbers apply, and the creation guards stay armed to enforce them.

Everything else still floors, because nothing else is sold by quantity on
self-hosted. Volume is not metered there at all, the data lives in the
customer's own database, and publishing is part of the open-source floor. So
the guarantee narrows to the thing that actually mattered: no capability a
deployment had before it paid disappears when it does.

**Newly minted licenses stay readable by released versions.** `maxProjects` and
`maxWorkflows` only became optional in this branch; every deployment already in
the field requires them and rejects a license that omits them, which lands on
the pre-existing invalid-license path and drops the org to a one-seat free
plan. Since licenses are issued from a continuously deployed control plane to
deployments that upgrade on their own schedule, the first renewal issued after
this shipped would have locked a paying customer out of their own install with
exactly the bug this branch exists to fix.

Both minting paths now go through `buildMintedPlan`, which re-emits those two
fields at the unlimited sentinel, so an older deployment reads them as uncapped
(what they now mean) and a current one ignores them. Key order there is load
bearing: verification re-serializes the Zod-parsed payload, so the order has to
match the schema. The regression test parses a freshly minted license against
the schema as it shipped before the fields were relaxed, so dropping a field
some supported version still requires fails loudly.

* feat(licensing): let an over-seats organization choose who keeps a seat

A self-hosted deployment runs uncapped before it buys a license, so by the time
an organization activates one it can easily hold more members than the seats it
just paid for. Nothing handled that: every member kept working and the seats
were billed but not enforced, which is the leak on one side and, if it had been
enforced bluntly, a lockout on the other.

Activation now always succeeds and the organization lands in an over-seats
state. Everyone keeps working, the license page says how many seats have to come
back, and only new members are refused, since letting the org grow is the one
thing that makes the overage worse. Nobody is signed out by an admin's pending
paperwork.

Disabling is per organization and reversible. `OrganizationUser.disabledAt`
revokes access to that organization only, keeps the role, the department and
everything the person did, and returns the seat to the pool. Re-enabling
restores access, and is refused when it would take the org back over its seats,
so a freed seat cannot be quietly reclaimed. The membership row survives, so
nothing has to be rebuilt when someone comes back.

Two halves have to be true together and both are covered: the seat is really
returned (seat counting excludes disabled memberships) and access is really
gone. The access half is the easy one to get wrong, so every membership read
that grants something filters on it: the two role lookups, the org-with-members
gate, the organization list behind the switcher, and the member roster. Live
sessions are revoked on disable rather than left to expire.

Disabling the last active admin is refused, for the same reason demoting the
last admin is: an organization with no admin who can sign in cannot be
recovered from inside the product.

The license page also stops claiming a license is "required for commercial
use", which the Apache 2.0 floor has made untrue.

perf(event-sourcing): coalesce span appends, excluding spooled spans (#6467)

* perf(event-sourcing): coalesce span appends, excluding spooled spans

A trace's recordSpan commands all land in one queue group (or one of its
shards), so a busy trace appended one tiny event_log insert per span.
Register append coalescing so the group's queued spans fold into a single
multi-row append instead.

The bound is a resolver rather than a constant, because a flat count is
unsafe here. An over-threshold span is queued as an ADR-022 spoolRef with
its attributes cleared, so its queued size — the only size the drain's
byte budget can weigh — is a few hundred bytes, while the span the handler
reconstitutes from object storage is over 256 KB and unbounded above.
Folding those by count would let the byte budget wave through a batch whose
true size it never saw. A spooled span therefore caps itself at 1 and is
appended on its own, which is how the oversized-item case is meant to
behave; inline spans are bounded by COMMAND_INLINE_THRESHOLD, so for them
the byte budget is honest and does the real work.

Supporting the resolver meant widening coalesceMaxBatch from a number to
number | ((payload) => number) through the option type and the job registry
entry. The GroupQueue already typed its own knob as a per-payload function;
only the layers in between had flattened it to a constant. Registration can
no longer compare the bound against 1 to decide whether to wire processBatch
— a function is truthy but not greater than 1, which would have silently
left coalescing off — so presence of a resolver is the opt-in.

recordSpan satisfies the batch contract: the handler derives its event from
its own command alone and never reads back a same-batch append, and its
post-store spool cleanup already reads spoolRef from the command argument,
so it runs correctly per command after the single append. Ordering,
deduplication and kill-switch semantics are unchanged.

perf(event-sourcing): coalesce coding-agent session contributions (#6475)

Every contribution command keys its group on the SESSION, so one agent
session is one queue group. With no coalescing wired, that group drained a
single job per dispatch — one tiny event_log insert per contribution — and
a long run's whole transcript queued behind it while the rest of the fleet
sat idle.

Register append coalescing on all three contribution commands so a backed-up
session folds its queued contributions into one multi-row append. All three
handlers are pure payload-to-event: no spool, no read-back of a same-batch
append, so the batch contract is satisfied and a plain count bound is enough
(no resolver needed).

The session key is deliberately NOT sharded, though sharding is what would
give one session parallel lanes. A session's contributions are not
interchangeable: foldModelCall derives previousCallContextTokens (the chain
the next call is compared against for cache-rebuild detection),
finalRequestId (last-call-wins) and stopReason/truncated (last call only)
from the order calls arrive in, and a logs-only agent's API_REQUEST records
fold through exactly that path. A test folds the same calls in two orders and
shows the session changes, so the constraint is executable rather than a
comment. Coalescing needs none of that latitude — it changes how many
contributions share an insert, never their order.

Also adds the `as const` the three command-type constants were missing.
Without it they widened to string and silently dropped out of the CommandType
union that every sibling pipeline's types are members of.

fix(ops): let the keyspace sweep come due again (#6472)

The sweep's deadline was rewritten on every reconcile pass, including the
passes that did not sweep. In the steady state those find nothing to
adopt, so each one pushed the deadline a full backstop into the future
and the deadline outran the clock: after the first sweep, no later one
was ever due. The walk is the only enumeration that cannot miss a group,
so losing it leaves a group the lifecycle reads missed undiscovered for
as long as the queue keeps reconciling — which is exactly what the
backstop exists to prevent.

Only a pass that actually swept may move the deadline.

The reschedule signal is also narrowed to what the sweep itself found
unindexed, rather than everything the pass adopted. The lifecycle legs
turn up groups that hold no jobs — a drained group still listed in ready
or blocked is adopted, pruned for being empty, and found again next pass
— and counting those would answer "sweep again" forever, pinning the
queue to the expensive walk over work that does not exist.

perf(event-sourcing): give level-triggered reactors a real firing window (#6463)

* perf(event-sourcing): give level-triggered reactors a real firing window

Several reactors set makeJobId + ttl expecting a debounce and never got one.
With no delay the job dispatches on its first event; dispatch removes it from
staging, so the next event's dedup lookup misses, the key is deleted and
restaged, and every event ends up with its own job. The TTL never bites.

Add a shared throttledPerWindow helper and adopt it where the consumer can
absorb the wait. It sets the delay the collapsing depends on, and pins the
window with extend: false — a reactor's queue score is the event's own
createdAt, so re-arming on every event would let a continuously-streaming
aggregate push its own job forward indefinitely and never fire. Pinned, the
window fires once per period carrying the newest payload.

The helper also hands the same function to makeJobId and deduplication.makeId.
Two layers read them independently — the router collapses a coalesced batch
before staging, the queue squashes after — and drift between them would stage
duplicates the collapse believed it had removed.

Windows: traceUpdateBroadcast 2s, projectMetadata 3s, governanceKpisSync and
governanceOcsfEventsSync 30s, billingMeterDispatch 30s.

shouldSurviveDispatch is set only on billingMeterDispatch, whose handler reads
nothing from the event it was given and derives everything from the org and
the clock. The rest stay off deliberately: they rebuild their output from the
fold's running state or notify a client that it moved, so discarding an
aggregate's last event would leave a partial write as the final answer.

gatewayBudgetSync and spanStorageBroadcast are excluded. The first is read by
the budget check that blocks requests, and the same handler emits the change
event that keeps the gateway's cached spend fresh. The second drives the open
trace view, which has no polling fallback while the live stream is connected.
Both exclusions are covered by tests so they are not quietly reversed.

perf(metrics): fold a rollup chunk's reads instead of one seek per point (#6481)

* perf(metrics): fold a rollup chunk's reads instead of one seek per point

The time-rollup map projection already arrives as a coalesced chunk and
already writes one INSERT for the whole chunk, but the reads that decide
what to write were still per point: recomputeAffectedRollupsMany looped
over the chunk awaiting one immediateNeighbors query each, then one
affected-bucket query per series. A full chunk therefore cost N+S
sequential ClickHouse round trips to produce a single insert, so the
coalescing bought the write path and left the read path untouched.

Both reads are index seeks, so the round trip is the cost, not the scan.
Fold them: one statement carries up to SEEKS_PER_QUERY successor seeks
across every series in the chunk, and a second carries the affected
buckets the same way, chunked so no single statement grows without
bound. A chunk's reads now track the buckets it touched rather than the
points it carried.

The successor is also the only neighbour that ever mattered.
affectedRollupBuckets takes the smallest point after the inserted one
and ignores everything else, so the predecessor half of the old
neighbour query was fetched and discarded on every point; it is gone.

Correctness rests on the raw points being ensured first, which was
already true. Every chunk point is stored before the seeks run, and each
seek returns the smallest stored point after one chunk point, so the
true successor is always in the union of the chunk and the seek results
and no stored point can sit between the two. Taking the minimum of that

fix(clickhouse): in-band exceptions surfaced as errors; rollup reads slimmed under the memory cap (#6493)

* fix(clickhouse): surface in-band exceptions as errors; slim rollup reads under the memory cap

Root cause of the rollup-lane crashes, reproduced live: the folded
successor seek fetched the full row — including the megabyte-scale
CanonicalPayload column — through FINAL for every folded branch,
pushing a single query past the server's per-query memory cap
(Code 241, MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED while executing ReplacingSorted).
ClickHouse streams over HTTP: rows were already flushed, so the error
could not change the 200 status and was written INTO the output as a
final {"exception": "..."} line. The client parsed it as a data row,
and the decoder crashed on a column the "row" never had — pointing
every investigation away from ClickHouse, through a wrong revert,
until the stack capture landed.

Two fixes, verified against the exact batch that failed:

- The resilient client wraps json() and throws an in-band exception
  row through the same translator as the catch path (typed
  query_memory_exceeded for Code 241). A row only counts when
  "exception" is its sole key AND the value carries the server's
  error signature (Code: <n>. <Class>Exception:), so a legitimate
  one-column result named exception passes through untouched. The
  failure is recorded in the failure log + a dedicated inband_error
  metric outcome at discovery; transport success accounting stays at
  query resolution because a caller may stream() or never consume
  the body.
- The successor seek selects only the sequence fields (SEEK_SELECT)
  and the bucket reads drop CanonicalPayload (AUTHORITATIVE_SELECT) —
  the fold never reads it. The same query that died at the memory cap
  returns its full batch cleanly.

Closes the trigger hunt in #6489.

* perf(billing): the spend fold neither refolds new requests nor replays late confirmations

read that as a lossy store rather than a new aggregate, sending one

state. That option is the transitional net for populations written by an
older row shape, and a greenfield fold at version 1 has none; it returns
with the first version bump, once older stamps report as misses and there
is something to heal.

Out-of-order replay goes for the same reason the option doc names: the
status lattice keys on data, not arrival, with confirmed and failed
outranking settled, so the late confirmation that supersedes a settled
request folds on top of loaded state instead of replaying the aggregate
from the log.

explicitly, since absent-row-means-new only stays true while every
committed row decodes.

lands (the fold's status lattice is built for exactly that ordering).
The outcome handlers dropped the delivery in that case: the ledger row
came out complete and the webhook was never sent.

Outcomes that arrive without attribution now wait in process state and
the admitted handler releases them. Precedence follows the fold's
lattice: confirmed or failed always takes the slot, a settlement only
fills an empty one, so the envelope admission releases is the one the
ledger agrees with. One admission per instance keeps the late deliver
intent single, and the endpoint append's source event id dedups it
against the live path.

* fix(event-sourcing): a job this worker cannot route is retried, never acknowledged

A worker that dequeued a job whose pipeline it has not registered logged a
warning and returned normally. Returning normally tells the queue the job
SUCCEEDED: it is removed, the group advances, and the payload is gone. The
log line naming it lived only in that worker's own output.

The fleet hits this on every rolling deploy. Old and new workers poll one
queue, so a command for a newly added pipeline can land on a worker that has
never heard of it, and roughly that share of the records is destroyed for the
length of the rollout. For a gateway spend command the record is a charge:
the ingest route has already answered 200 and the drainer has already deleted
its spool segment, so nothing upstream can notice or resend, and the request
sits at admitted forever while the ledger, the meters and the webhook feed all
read zero.

Reject the job instead. The queue's bounded retry re-offers it until a worker
that does have the pipeline takes it, which is the behaviour a rolling deploy
needed all along, and a pipeline genuinely retired gets an explicit tombstone
at the send boundary rather than this path quietly deciding a record is
disposable. The rejection logs at error with the tenant, the aggregate and the
gateway request id, and counts on gq_jobs_unroutable_total so a build skew is
visible as a rate rather than as missing money.

Resolution runs several times per job, so the per-lookup miss drops to debug
and the processing path raises it once.

* fix(gateway): name the request when a spend record is rejected at ingest

A per-record reject is reported back by index in a 200 body, and the drainer
does not read that body: it sees 2xx, acks the segment, and the record is
gone. The control-plane log line was therefore the only trace the record ever
existed, and it carried the command name and the batch index but not the
request, so nothing could be reconciled against the gateway's own records.

Log the gateway request id and the tenant, at error rather than warn. A
dropped billing record is not a warning.

* fix(governance): a seat cap sees every request its seat spent

The trace-fold reactor wrote ATTRIBUTED_USER debits to the template's
bare anchor. It has no end user on trace fold state, so the resolver
hands it back the anchor, and the ledger keys rows by (TenantId,
BudgetId, GatewayRequestId) with no bucket in that key. The reactor's
anchor row and the attributed-user process manager's per-user row are
therefore the same row identity, and the insert probe drops whichever
writer arrives second. When the reactor won, the request's spend left
the per-user bucket entirely, and the per-user bucket is the only thing
per-seat enforcement reads. A seat 40% over a blocking cap kept being
admitted.

The reactor now leaves template rows to the process manager that owns
them, which is what the repository's own ownership split always claimed.
Its BUDGET_UPDATED change event still names the templates, so the
gateway's cached bundle is evicted on the same clock as before. The
ingestion-source writer had the same defect for project-anchored
templates and is fixed with it.

Two writers claiming one budget on one request can no longer happen
quietly: the insert probe now compares the bucket it is about to
suppress against the bucket already there, and a mismatch is reported at
error with the request id. A replay, which names the same bucket, stays
silent.

Separately, the process manager dropped an outcome that reached it
before its admission, exactly as the webhook delivery process did before
c5694351de. That guard never fired for this incident, but it is the same
latent bug, so it takes the same remedy: the outcome waits in process
state and the admitted handler releases it under its own intent key. An
admission naming nobody discards the outcome loudly instead of silently.

Also states the ledger's real dedup contract in the migration header: it
is sound only while one writer owns a budget's row for a request, since
GROUP and ATTRIBUTED_USER budgets each own many buckets.

fix(sdk): normalize the configured endpoint so a trailing slash stops 404ing (#6509)

* fix(typescript-sdk): normalize the configured endpoint so a trailing slash stops 404ing

Most services build request URLs by concatenation, and every path already
carries its own leading slash. An endpoint written as
`https://app.langwatch.ai/` therefore produced
`https://app.langwatch.ai//api/experiment/init`, which the router does not
match, so the caller got the server's opaque `{"error":"Not Found"}` with
nothing pointing at the endpoint as the cause.

Five services already stripped the slash inline and the rest did not, so
whether a trailing slash worked depended on which service you called.
`resolveEndpoint()` now owns that decision once: explicit value, then
LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT, then the cloud default, trimmed and stripped. Blank
values count as unset, so an empty `LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT=` in a `.env` falls
through to the default instead of producing relative URLs. The CLI resolver
drops its private copy of the same helper.

The boot-graph pin gains `internal/endpoint.ts`: two pure string functions
over `internal/constants.ts`, which is already on the CLI boot path, so cold
start is unaffected.

* fix(python-sdk): normalize the endpoint there too, and address review

The Python SDK builds the same URLs the same way, so
`LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT=https://app.langwatch.ai/` produced the same
`//api/experiment/init` 404. `normalize_endpoint()` now guards both
`get_endpoint()` branches and the two places `Client.setup` stores the URL,
with a blank value falling through to the cloud default.

Review follow-ups:

- CodeQL flagged `/\/+$/` as a polynomial ReDoS. The pattern backtracks from
  every start index on a run of slashes, so the normalizer scans backwards
  instead. An endpoint is configuration rather than attacker input, but the
  linear form costs nothing.
- `resolveControlPlaneEndpoint` accepted a whitespace-only `--endpoint` flag
  or persisted `control_plane_url` and returned an empty URL. All three
  sources now check for content and fall through when blank.
- `WorkflowsApiService` resolved its endpoint but still built its fallback
  API client from the environment, so a caller supplying only an endpoint
  issued requests to one host and emitted run URLs for another.

`Experiment` and `DatasetService` normalize at construction, which retires
the last two inline strips at the URL-building sites.

* fix(mcp-server): normalize the configured endpoint

The MCP server builds `${endpoint}/api/...` the same way both SDKs do, so
`LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT=https://app.langwatch.ai/` produced the same double slash
and the same opaque 404. A blank value now falls through to the cloud default
instead of becoming an empty base URL.

The Go SDK needs no equivalent change: it joins with `url.JoinPath`, which
collapses the separator itself.

* fix(sdk): fall back to the default when a source normalizes to nothing

Three review findings, all on the same edge: a value that is present but
reduces to the empty string once normalized.

- `Client(endpoint_url="   ")` assigned that empty string, so the REST client
  got a blank base URL and OTLP got a bare `/api/otel/v1/traces`. The explicit
  branch now falls back to the cloud default like the others.
- `resolveControlPlaneEndpoint` guarded on `trim()`, which lets `"/"` and
  `"///"` through to return an empty URL. Each source is now judged on what it
  normalizes to, so a slash-only value falls through to the next one.
- The MCP server's normalizer documents trimming but only had coverage for
  slash removal; a whitespace-around-a-real-endpoint case now pins it.

* fix(python-sdk): normalize the endpoint when reconfiguring an existing client

`Client(endpoint_url=...)` on an already-initialized singleton took a second
path that stored the raw value, so a reconfiguration could still put
whitespace or trailing slashes into the OTLP URL and the REST base URL.

Normalizing before the comparison also means reconfiguring with the same
endpoint written differently, `https://host/` for `https://host`, is
recognized as unchanged and no longer restarts the exporter.

A value that normalizes to nothing is treated as not supplied rather than as
the cloud default. That differs from first initialization, where there is no
endpoint yet and the default is the only sensible choice: here the instance
already has one, and silently moving a self-hosted client to the cloud is
worse than ignoring a blank argument.

* test(python-sdk): pin the exporter-restart behavior on reconfiguration

The claim that an equivalent spelling no longer restarts the exporter had no
test behind it: the existing case changed to a different endpoint and skipped
OpenTelemetry setup entirely, so the restart branch was never reached.

Two tests now spy on the tracer-provider setup and shutdown: an equivalent
spelling of the current endpoint touches neither, and a genuinely different
one still restarts both. The second keeps the first from being vacuous.

refactor(build): single pnpm workspace + restructure into sdks/ platform/ services/ mcp/ infra/ (ADR-076) (#6405)

* refactor(build): merge every JS project into one pnpm workspace (ADR-076)

The repo had six independent pnpm install roots with six lockfiles: the
repo root, langwatch/, typescript-sdk/, mcp-server/, skills/ and
agentic-e2e-tests/. mcp-server was BOTH its own root and a member of the
app's workspace, so CI installed it twice on every app build. skills/ and
agentic-e2e-tests/ sat inside a workspace root without being members of
it, so every install of them needed --ignore-workspace to escape a
workspace they were never in.

Three consequences, all now fixed:

- A fresh clone needed `pnpm install` at the root AND inside langwatch/.
  Skipping the second failed with `Command "prisma" not found`, which
  reads like a broken toolchain rather than a missing install.
- pnpm honours `overrides` only at the workspace root, so each root
  carried its own list and the lists drifted. langsmith was pinned in
  two roots but not the third; esbuild in two but not the app; hono,
  uuid, ip-address, qs, form-data and js-yaml only in skills. A package
  patched in one project stayed vulnerable in the others.
- Shared packages were reachable only from the roots that listed them,
  so the SDK could depend on neither @langwatch/handled-error nor
  @langwatch/langy.

Blocking the merge outright: the app and the SDK had the SAME package
name. langwatch/package.json was `langwatch@3.7.0` and typescript-sdk/
is `langwatch@1.0.0`; pnpm rejects duplicate names in one workspace. The
collision had already produced a latent oddity — the app declared
`"langwatch": "1.0.0"`, a dependency on its own name, resolving to the
published SDK only because the two lived in separate workspaces. The app
is now @langwatch/web (directory unchanged) and keeps resolving the
published SDK; linkWorkspacePackages is pinned false and documented,
because after the merge that default is load-bearing rather than
incidental.

Merging the override lists needed care. pnpm reads overrides from BOTH
pnpm-workspace.yaml and the root package.json `pnpm` field, and
langwatch/ and typescript-sdk/ each carried a second, larger block that
was live only while they were roots — merged naively those go silently
dead, dropping ~50 pins. They are merged here and removed from the
members. Ranged pins (pkg@<x) are safe to share and all are unioned;
unconditional pins are not, so three were deliberately left out, each a
direct dependency whose own declaration governs it: the SDK's
`zod: ^4.0.14` (the app is on zod 3.x and @langwatch/langy compiles
against it via the zod/v4 subpath), and its api-logs/sdk-logs 0.205.0
pins, both older than the app's OTel stack. Where two roots disagreed we
took the stricter value — protobufjs >=8.6.0 over >=8.0.2, glob ^11.1.0
over >=10.5.0.

The published @langwatch/server tarball was the hard constraint: it ships
the app's source plus langwatch/pnpm-lock.yaml and runs
`pnpm -C langwatch install --frozen-lockfile` on the end user's machine
at first boot. It now ships the root workspace, the root lockfile and
every member's package.json, and narrows the install with
`--filter @langwatch/web...` so the SDK, skills compiler and test suites
never install. The prune step becomes a filtered --prod re-install, since
`pnpm prune` takes no --filter and would otherwise reason about every
project. The install-recipe sequence tag is bumped to seq4 so existing
~/.langwatch/app trees redo the cycle.

Verified: single lockfile resolves all 15 projects and satisfies
--frozen-lockfile; no "will not take effect" override warnings remain;
the app resolves zod 3.25.76 while the SDK resolves 4.4.3; a filtered
install of the MCP server subtree completes in 9.8s with workspace links
resolving correctly across two separate directory trees. server-cli
suite is 120 passed / 2 failed, identical to pristine main (both
failures pre-existing and unrelated).

Also updates dependabot: the npm ecosystem now points at the workspace
root instead of three of the six old roots, which additionally closes a
coverage gap — skills/, agentic-e2e-tests/, packages/* and
langwatch/packages/* were never scanned at all.

* fix(npx): publish @langwatch/server from a staging tree (ADR-076)

Packing in place made the tarball's layout a mirror of the repo's, and that
coupling broke the moment the repo became a single pnpm workspace.

npm deletes `pnpm-lock.yaml` from the package ROOT unconditionally — the
same hardcoded rule that eats `.npmrc`. The exclusion is root-only: a
lockfile one directory down ships fine. The old layout satisfied that by
accident, because the lockfile lived at `langwatch/pnpm-lock.yaml`, already
a subdirectory. One workspace puts it at the package root, where npm removes
it, leaving an end user's first boot with nothing for `--frozen-lockfile` to
check.

So the artifact is now assembled into a staging tree with everything nested
under `app/`, and that is packed. The nesting costs nothing on the consuming
side: the CLI already locates the app by walking up for
`langwatch/package.json` (locatePackageSource), so it finds `app/` by itself
and every downstream path resolves unchanged — no CLI code changes needed.

scripts/pack-npm.sh becomes the assembler. It reads `files` from
package.json, still the single source of truth for WHAT ships, and decides
only WHERE it lands. Both .npmignore files are deleted; their trimming rules
move into one explicit exclude list next to the copy that applies them.

Rejected alternatives, all recorded in the ADR: generating a second
standalone lockfile at pack time (two lockfiles that can disagree, only
observable in a published artifact); shipping the lockfile under an
unstripped name and copying it back (a rename dance that leaves the artifact
coupled to the repo layout, so it breaks again on the next move); dropping
--frozen-lockfile (gives up reproducibility on the install we control
least). `pnpm deploy` does not help — --legacy emits no lockfile and does
not rewrite workspace:* specs, so it needs node_modules, which cannot ship
because bcrypt / @prisma/engines / sharp / msgpackr-extract / cpu-features
are native and per-platform.

Also drops a stale `files` entry: packages/server/templates/ named a
directory that has never existed in the tree, and npm was silently skipping
it. The assembler warns on a missing entry rather than failing, matching
npm's behaviour, so the next stale entry is visible instead of invisible.

The publish workflow's tarball gate now asserts app/pnpm-lock.yaml and
app/pnpm-workspace.yaml as required paths and package/pnpm-lock.yaml as
forbidden, so a future layout change cannot quietly return the end-user
install to non-reproducible. packages/server is no longer skipped in the
member sweep — it is a workspace member now, and --frozen-lockfile checks
the lockfile against its manifest.

Verified end to end: pack produces a 17MB tarball; all 22 required paths
present and no forbidden ones; and from inside the EXTRACTED tarball,
`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --filter "@langwatch/web..."` validates and
reports "Scope: 9 of 15 workspace projects" — the app plus its eight
workspace dependencies, with the SDK, skills, e2e suites and server-cli
correctly excluded.

* fix(build): preserve the app's dependency resolutions across the merge

Regenerating the lockfile from scratch quietly bumped the whole app tree
within its declared ranges — shiki 4.3.0 -> 4.3.1, vite 8.1.2 -> 8.1.5 and
a long tail behind them. That combination panics rolldown during `vite
build`:

  Symbol "createJavaScriptRegexEngine" in @shikijs/engine-javascript
  should belong to a chunk

which failed npx-server-smoke on all three platforms.

Pinning the two packages that happened to break would have left the rest of
the silent bump in place. A build refactor should not be a dependency bump,
so the merged lockfile is instead SEEDED from the app's pre-merge lockfile
(importer keys remapped: `.` -> langwatch, `packages/*` ->
langwatch/packages/*, `../mcp-server` -> mcp-server, `../packages/{langy,
handled-error}` -> packages/*), then resolved. pnpm keeps every resolution
that still satisfies its spec, so the app's tree is byte-for-byte what it
was and only the genuinely new members resolve fresh.

shiki is back on 4.3.0 and vite on 8.1.2. Still 15 importers, still clean
under --frozen-lockfile, and the app/SDK zod split (3.25.76 / 4.4.3) holds.

Also fixes the skills compiler, which broke for an unrelated reason. It ran
`npx tsx skills/_compiler/compile.ts` from the repo root, where tsx has
never been a dependency — it only ever worked because npx silently
downloaded tsx on every run. Adding a root .npmrc made npm read pnpm's
settings, fail to recognise them, and leave `tsx: not found`. It now calls
skills/'s own tsx by path: faster, reproducible, and it fails with a
message naming the install command instead of a bare 127.

Review findings from the first CI run, all in changes this branch made.

The serious one: both CD workflows stopped parsing. The bulk edit that
repointed `cache-dependency-path` at the root lockfile deleted the line but
not its leading whitespace, so `registry-url` inherited it and ended up
nested under `cache:` instead of beside it. actionlint and yamllint both
reject it, so mcp-javascript-cd and sdk-javascript-cd could not run at all.
Re-indented; actionlint is now clean across every workflow (its only
remaining finding is a pre-existing unknown runner label in
publish-docker-app.yml, untouched here).

Dropped the "Install TypeScript Native Preview" step from
sdk-javascript-ci. It ran `pnpm install -D -w`, and `-w` means the
workspace root — which used to BE typescript-sdk/ when that was its own
install root. After the merge it would have written into the root manifest

Cause: npm/pnpm pack honours a .gitignore inside an included directory, and

file along with everything else, so packing silently dropped the prebuilt
vite client, the scenario bundle and every generated type — all required at
runtime. Probe-confirmed in isolation: a nested .gitignore listing those
patterns removes exactly those paths from `npm pack --dry-run`.

This is precisely what the deleted langwatch/.npmignore existed to prevent —
an .npmignore overrides the sibling .gitignore, which is why that file had to
restate the broad excludes explicitly, and said so in its header. Removing it
without carrying the intent across is the regression.

Staging is the allowlist now, so no ignore file gets a second say over it:
.gitignore and .npmignore are excluded from the copy.

Also adds a post-pack assertion, because the failure mode is invisible at
pack time and only surfaces ~25 minutes later as a boot timeout. When the
repo has a built langwatch/dist/client, the tarball must ship it or the pack
fails. Proven in both directions: exit 0 with the fix, exit 1 without it.

The assertion had a bug of its own worth noting: resolving the tarball with
`ls` under `set -e` + `pipefail` aborts the script when the glob matches
nothing, so the check silently never ran and the pack step would have exited
non-zero in CI. Both lookups now tolerate an empty glob, and a missing
tarball is reported explicitly.

block, so the shell tries to execute it. The flags it names are already
inlined on the `biome check` invocation four lines above, so the line is

* fix(npx): stop the pack guard failing on its own SIGPIPE

The dist assertion added with the staging fix reported the prebuilt client
missing when it was present — but only on linux, and only in CI.

`tar -tzf "$tarball" | grep -qx <path>`: grep -q exits at the first match,
which SIGPIPEs tar. GNU tar treats that as an error ("tar: stdout: write
error", non-zero), and under `set -o pipefail` the pipeline inherits it, so
the check reported failure even though the match succeeded. bsdtar on macos
exits cleanly in the same situation, which is why the same tarball passed
there and failed on both linux runners — a check whose verdict depends on
how much tar manages to write before grep exits.

Lists once into a file and greps that, so there is no pipe to break. The CI
log is the proof: "tar: stdout: write error" immediately precedes the error
message, on a tarball the macos leg verified as correct.

The staging fix itself is confirmed working — macos logged
"→ verified: tarball ships the prebuilt langwatch/dist/client", and the boot
no longer falls back to a runtime vite build; it now reaches
clickhouse:migrate. Whether that step is a further problem or macos-specific
needs the linux legs, which this unblocks.

* fix(npx): stop an exclude pattern dropping application source

The smoke job failed on all three platforms with the server never reaching
healthy. The real error was in the uploaded cli.log, not the truncated tail
the workflow prints:

  Error: Cannot find module './reports/report-chart.service'
    from langwatch/src/server/app-layer/presets.ts
  inside `pnpm clickhouse:migrate`, ~20 minutes into first boot.

depth, so alongside the GDPR output directory it was written for
(langwatch/reports, a runtime artifact a clean checkout does not even have)
it took two real source directories: src/server/app-layer/reports and
src/components/analytics/reports.

Every other bare name in EXCLUDES was checked against the shipped trees for
the same collision — `test`/`tests` match only genuine test directories, and
`notebooks`/`coverage` match nothing in source. Only `reports` was wrong.

This is the second exclusion bug in this script to ship a tarball that packed
cleanly and died at first boot (the first stripped dist/ via a .gitignore in
the staged tree). Both were invisible for ~20 minutes and cost a full smoke
cycle to find, so the class now has a guard: pack asserts that every file git
tracks under langwatch/src and langwatch/ee is in the tarball. It costs about
a second, and reinstating `--exclude=reports` makes it fail with exactly the
file that broke the boot:

  ✗ the tarball is missing application source the repo tracks:
  langwatch/src/server/app-layer/reports/report-chart.service.ts

Verified both directions, and a full diff of tracked source against tarball
contents now reports zero missing files.

enforces nothing while reading as coverage, and tagging everything
@unimplemented does not fix it either — the checker counts an all-
@unimplemented file as inert too, and tolerates that only for files already
on its legacy ratchet.

So ten of the seventeen scenarios now bind to
packages/server/test/workspace-invariants.test.ts, which asserts the shape
directly against the repo: exactly one lockfile and one workspace definition,
every former install root listed as a member, the app and the SDK on

Every one of those held at some point during this branch and then quietly

Also fixes the SDK lint error the merge surfaced. Unifying six roots onto one

Verified: SDK lint goes from 1 error to 0.

Binding a scenario to a test is not what makes the parity checker treat it as

workspace-invariants.test.ts were left untagged, so the file still reported

* fix(docker): ship the workspace store, or the runtime image dies at boot

The production image was broken by the workspace merge, silently.

Before ADR-076 the install root was /app/langwatch, so pnpm's virtual store
lived at /app/langwatch/node_modules/.pnpm and `COPY /app/langwatch` brought
the whole dependency tree with it. The install root is /app now, so the store
is at /app/node_modules/.pnpm and every entry in langwatch/node_modules is a
symlink into it:

  langwatch/node_modules/react -> ../../node_modules/.pnpm/react@…/node_modules/react

The runtime stage never copied /app/node_modules, so every one of those links
dangled. Docker build succeeds — there is no error to catch it — and the
container dies on its first import.

Verified both directions by replicating each COPY set on disk and resolving
real modules from langwatch/:

  old set: react FAIL, zod FAIL, pino FAIL   (MODULE_NOT_FOUND)
  new set: react OK, zod OK, pino OK, @opentelemetry/api OK,
           @langwatch/langy OK, @langwatch/handled-error OK

(@langwatch/mcp-server resolves its link correctly; it only fails locally
because its dist/ is built during the image build, not in a checkout.)

Also drops the hand-built peer symlinks this stage used to create at
/app/node_modules for zod and @opentelemetry/api. They existed because the
workspace packages sat outside the app's install root; now pnpm links each
member's peers into its own node_modules pointing at the shared store, so the
manual links are both unnecessary and would collide with the real store.
langy and handled-error are copied as whole directories to bring those links.

Checked and unaffected: mcp-server/Dockerfile is single-stage, so its store
stays in the image; Dockerfile.langyagent compiles a self-contained binary in
the stage that holds node_modules; .dockerignore blocks nothing the new COPY
set needs; and the charts keep working because /app/langwatch still exists and
`pnpm run` resolves through the workspace root above it.

* fix(docker): copy the whole packages tree, and build the image on PRs

Two follow-ups to the runtime-store fix.

The runtime stage cherry-picked packages/langy and packages/handled-error by
name. That is the failure mode, not the safeguard: adding a root workspace
package as an app dependency and forgetting a COPY line leaves a dangling
symlink and a boot-time "Cannot find module", which is how handled-error
broke the workers entry point once already. It copies /app/packages whole
now — it cannot be forgotten, and it costs about 1.3MB (packages/server, the

in hundreds. Verified by replicating the COPY set and resolving every one of
the app's eleven workspace dependencies, including the five under
langwatch/packages/* that ride along with langwatch/.

The Dockerfile regression test accepted only the per-package spelling, so it
now accepts the whole-tree copy as satisfying the same invariant more
strongly. It still fails if neither is present. 3 passed.

And the gap that let the broken image through: langwatch-chart is the only
job in CI that builds the app image and runs a stack against it, but it
triggered on charts/** alone — publish-docker-app fires on `release:
published`, so a pull request touching the Dockerfile got no image build at
all. A change to how the image is assembled would have reached a release

haven silently stopped installing dependencies. ensureDeps was handed
langwatch/, and depsStale reads "no lockfile here" as "nothing to install" —
so since the workspace merge, `haven up` in a fresh worktree installed

It takes the workspace root now, which is the only place either the lockfile
or node_modules exists. `haven pr` was already correct — its install has

The existing deps tests could not have caught this: they build a temp dir
with a lockfile in it and are indifferent to which directory that is. Added

last of those can be asserted at all. Full haven suite passes, gofmt and vet

Also proxies the common scripts from the repo root, which is the point of

exist in their target package, and every filter resolves unambiguously —
including `--filter langwatch`, which now means the SDK and nothing else.

Also reverts an accidentally committed regeneration of the SDK's generated
OpenAPI client. The SDK's `prepare` runs on install and rewrites it from the

scope, a provider_key field) into this branch. Worth knowing: a root install

* docs(docker): record what makes the prune step work

Answering "does the Dockerfile actually prune?" with evidence rather than
assumption, since the step is what keeps roughly a gigabyte of vite, vitest,
playwright and biome out of the production image.

It does. Verified on a scratch two-package workspace: after
`CI=true pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile --filter "@app..."`, a
workspace member's devDependency is deleted from its node_modules while its
runtime dependency and the app's link to it survive. `--prod` removes; it does
not merely skip. That is also what makes the whole-packages/ copy in the
runtime stage safe rather than a way to ship test tooling.

The non-obvious part, now written down: CI=true is load-bearing. --prod purges
the modules directory and pnpm refuses to do that without a TTY, failing with
ERR_PNPM_ABORTED_REMOVE_MODULES_DIR_NO_TTY — which is how the scratch run
failed before the flag was added. The root .npmrc carries
confirm-modules-purge=false as well, so either alone suffices; both stay,
because losing this silently would ship a dev-dependency-laden image while
losing it loudly fails the build where the cause is legible.

Also confirmed the ordering still holds: tsx, prisma and @prisma/client are
declared dependencies, so they survive the prune, and `prisma generate` runs
after it because the prune drops the generated client.

* fix(test): make the tarball prefix check actually compare a directory

Two review findings, both real.

* fix(security,docker): stop the tarball shipping secrets, and actually prune

Findings from the read-only audit. Four are mine and two are corrections to
claims I made in this branch's own comments.

SECRET LEAK. `pnpm pack:npm` shipped `langwatch/.env.portless` — mode 0600,
haven's resolved config, with the admin password and access tokens in it —
into a tarball destined for the PUBLIC npm registry. Confirmed by listing a
real packed artifact. Cause: deleting langwatch/.npmignore removed its
`.env*.local` and `*.pem` rules, and because this script also strips
.gitignore/.npmignore from the staged tree, the EXCLUDES array became the ONLY
filter — and it named `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.*.local` individually while
the working tree carries `.env.portless` and `.env.dev-up`. Now excludes every
dotenv variant (re-including `.env.example`, which must be ordered first
because rsync takes the first matching rule), plus `*.pem`/`*.key`/`*.p12`,
`.npmrc` and debug logs. `.npmrc` matters because npm's own strip is root-only
and this script deliberately stages one level down, which disables it for
every nested one.

A blocklist is one filename away from being wrong, so the pack now also
refuses to publish anything secret-shaped, checked against the packed tarball
rather than against intentions. Proven both ways: with the exclude removed it
exits 1 naming `package/app/langwatch/.env.portless`; with it restored the
file never reaches the tarball.

THE PRUNE DID NOT PRUNE. This branch claimed, in a Dockerfile comment, that
`pnpm install --prod` "really does remove, not merely skip". Measured again
properly: it removes the member's SYMLINK but leaves the package in
node_modules/.pnpm — and the runtime stage copies /app/node_modules wholesale,
so vite, vitest, playwright and biome were all still shipping, merely
unreferenced. `pnpm prune --prod` does remove them from the store. Both now
run: the filtered --prod install fixes the member trees, prune reclaims the
store, and prisma generate still runs last because prune drops the generated
client. The earlier verification tested the wrong thing.

EVERY NPX BOOT REBUILT. `prismaClientGenerated()` was handed
langwatch/node_modules, but ADR-076 moved the store to the root — so both its
branches were permanently false and every `npx @langwatch/server start`
re-ran the install and prisma generate before booting. Verified: langwatch/
node_modules has no .pnpm and no .prisma; the root does. It takes several
roots now and checks the root first, keeping the langwatch/ path for trees
installed before the merge. This is the same regression its own docstring
records having fixed once.

LOCAL PACK PRODUCED NOTHING. With no --pack-destination the tarball landed
inside the staging dir and the EXIT trap deleted it, so `pnpm pack:npm` exited
0 having written no file and `pnpm release:dry-run` then failed on an
unmatched glob. Defaults to the repo root now, and both flag spellings are
parsed. All three invocation forms verified to produce a tarball with all
three guards passing.

SECURITY PINS WERE CEILINGS. Exact-valued override targets pin a version
rather than setting a floor, and merging the six lists made ten previously
INERT entries live — langwatch/pnpm-workspace.yaml's overrides never applied
on main, which is why nobody saw them resolve. Effect: express-rate-limit
8.3.2 -> 8.2.2, protobufjs 8.6.5 -> 8.6.0 with 7.5.6 reintroduced, minimatch
gaining an older 5.1.8. Eighteen selectors rewritten as `>=` floors and
protobufjs restored to the unconditional form three roots carried. After a
targeted re-resolve: express-rate-limit 8.6.0, protobufjs 8.7.1 alone,
minimatch 5.1.8 gone — all at or above what main shipped. The app's own
resolutions are untouched (shiki 4.3.0, vite 8.1.2, zod 3.25.76/4.4.3,
react 19.2.7) and --frozen-lockfile is clean across all 15 projects.

server-cli suite: 130 passed, 2 failed — the same two cli-doctor failures
present on pristine main.

* fix(test): make the DateTime64 TZ suites survive a reused vm context

test-unit (3) has been failing intermittently — on this branch AND on main —
in the ClickHouse DateTime64 decode family, always with the same collapse:
"expected +0 not to be +0" from the guard that requires a non-UTC zone.

Deterministic repro first: TZ=UTC, one vmForks worker with isolate:false, a
Date-using suite loaded before the TZ suite → 3 failures, every time. The
same files alone in a fresh worker → green, every time. Mechanism: the
`process` global vitest hands a vm context wraps the real one, and assigning
TZ on the wrapper misses Node's NATIVE env setter — the thing that flushes
V8's cached timezone. First Date use in the worker warms the cache; after
that the module-top assignment silently does nothing. Whether a TZ suite
landed in a warmed or fresh context depended on the sequencer's file
grouping, which is why #6305's weight-balanced sequencer turned a latent
coin-flip into a steady red on main — the suites were order-dependent from
the day they were written, and every earlier green was placement luck.

The fix is three lines per suite: assign through node:process instead —
`import { env } from "node:process"` reaches the real object, whose setter
flushes the cache even mid-context. Hypothesis tested against the repro
before rollout: 118/118 with the experiment applied, 149/149 with all three
suites fixed under the worst case (UTC host, one shared worker, warmed
cache), 41/41 under the normal config. The vm-pool comment in
vitest.config.ts gets a breadcrumb so nobody "simplifies" the import back to
the global and reopens the coin flip.

* fix(pricing): name every billable family in the short answer, not just spans

The meter bills seven event types across four families: spans, evaluations,

Both now name all four in the customer's words, with the arithmetic that bites
(a sweep is many events, a simulation counts each turn) stated rather than left
for the full list to reveal. The full list keeps the counting rules, the
never-billed list and deduplication.

A test pins this to the meter instead of to prose. It imports
orgBillableEventsMeterProjection.eventTypes, so a newly billable event type
fails until someone documents it, and a documented type the meter does not
subscribe to fails as overclaiming. Confirmed both ways: the three copy
assertions failed against the old wording, and adding an undocumented type to
the projection fails the drift check by name.

The short answers are checked by family, not by event type, and against the
definition itself rather than the surrounding section — the section already
linked to the full list with the word "experiment" in it, which would have
satisfied a looser check while the definition still left experiments out.

"Testing is not free" is a double negative that leaves the reader

fix(helm): size the evaluations worker pool to the container, not the node (#6479)

* fix(helm): size the evaluations worker pool to the container, not the node

The evaluations service sizes its gunicorn pool from its own get_cpu_count(),
whose "Kubernetes" branch reads /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.shares. That is a cgroup
v1 path, and current nodes run cgroup v2, so the lookup raises and it falls
through to sched_getaffinity() and counts the node's cores. A container limited
to 500m forks one worker per node core.

Each worker lazily loads its own copy of every local model it serves, so memory
climbs ~2.1Gi per worker as requests round-robin the pool. Measured on the
published images, one CPU limit, an 8-vCPU node: 11Gi and still climbing, having
OOM-killed at the chart's own 8Gi default. Pinned to one worker the same load
holds flat at 2.5Gi.

The chart now derives CPU_COUNT from langevals.resources, so asking for less CPU
gives a smaller pool and a smaller footprint. An operator's own CPU_COUNT in
extraEnvs still wins. The profiles set WEB_CONCURRENCY to contain this, which
does nothing: the service passes an explicit worker count to gunicorn, which
overrides the environment default. Dropped it rather than leave it claiming a
bound it never had.

The four small profiles also could not hold what they started. values-local and
values-test capped memory at 512Mi against a 543Mi resting footprint, so they
were killed while importing, before serving anything. The documented Kind
quickstart points at values-local. size-dev and size-minimal capped at 1Gi,
which boots and then dies the first time someone runs an evaluator that loads a
model. All four now request 768Mi and cap at 4Gi, covering one worker with every
local model resident. A limit is a ceiling, not a reservation, so the larger one
costs nothing until a model loads.

None of this reached CI: the chart e2e either disables the evaluations service
or grants it 4Gi, and helm template only proves the YAML renders.

Verified end to end on a cluster. A chart-rendered install with the size-dev
sizing gets CPU_COUNT=1, runs one worker, and holds flat at 2528Mi against its
4Gi limit with zero restarts across 40 evaluator calls.

* test(helm): verify the worker count by rendering, not by reading the template

The worker-count assertions read _helpers.tpl as text and matched on `dig`,
`ceil` and `max`. That proves the template mentions those words, not that the
pipeline computes anything. `ceil` could become `floor` and every assertion
would stay green, which is exactly the class of bug the helper exists to avoid.

charts/langwatch/tests/langevals-sizing.sh renders the chart instead and
asserts what reaches the pod: the CPU_COUNT for each shipped profile, the

fix(datasets): stop the dataset list counting every tenant's entries (#6559)

* fix(datasets): stop the dataset list counting every tenant's entries

Opening the datasets page or the "Add to Dataset" drawer took several
seconds on production projects, and the picker gave no sign it was
working: an in-flight dropdown renders exactly like a project with no
datasets.

Both surfaces call `dataset.getAll`, which counted entries through
Prisma's relation-count include. Prisma compiles that into a subquery
with no tenancy predicate at all:

    LEFT JOIN (SELECT "datasetId", COUNT(*) FROM "DatasetRecord"
               WHERE 1=1 GROUP BY "datasetId") ...

so every list aggregated the whole `DatasetRecord` table across every
tenant. Measured against production, that is a 4.36s parallel sequential
scan of 2.58M rows / 3.2GB, paid on every open, by every project,
including projects with no datasets at all. Datasets kept in object
storage made it worse rather than better: their rows are not in that
table, their count already sits on the dataset row, and the number the
scan produced for them was discarded.

Counting now stays inside the project and inside the datasets that
actually store rows there, and a composite index serves it as an
index-only scan. On a faithful reproduction of the production
distribution: 251ms -> 3.5ms for a typical project. A project entirely on
object storage issues no count query at all.

The picker now shows a loading placeholder while the list is in flight,
and says "No datasets yet" when the project really is empty.

Also brings the dataset lists' three storage layouts under test against a
real database, which nothing covered before.

* fix(datasets): say 'Loading datasets' outright in the picker

A skeleton in place of the dropdown is easy to miss, which leaves the
reported complaint half-answered: the drawer still gave no sign it was
working. The trigger now shows a spinner and says so.

* fix(datasets): stop a failed dataset request reading as an empty project

Review caught that when `dataset.getAll` fails, the picker showed
"No datasets yet" and disabled itself: `isLoading` is already false and
the data is undefined, so the empty branch won. Telling someone they have
no datasets when we simply could not ask is worse than saying nothing
worked. Only a list that actually arrived empty counts as empty now, and
a failure says so.

Also from review: the loading state carries `role="status"` so it is
announced rather than only named, the migration carries its manual
rollback, and the picker tests cover the create action, the loading to
loaded transition, and the failure.

* refactor(datasets): split the picker's state out of its render

CI's Biome gate flagged the third branch as new cognitive-complexity and
lines-per-function violations, which is fair: the render was carrying a
nested ternary over four states. The state is now a small pure function
returning one of loading / unavailable / empty / ready, with the copy in
a lookup and the loading row as its own component.

feat(mailer): smtp and resend gateways, outbound proxy support, EMAIL_PROVIDER registry (#6445)

* feat(mailer): SMTP and Resend gateways, outbound proxy support, EMAIL_PROVIDER registry

Self-hosted deployments could only send email through SendGrid or AWS SES,
chosen implicitly by whichever credentials were present. Corporate networks
that reach the internet only through an HTTP proxy, or that are only allowed
to relay through an internal SMTP server, had no working option at all: the
AWS SDK ignores HTTPS_PROXY, so SES failed with a TLS read timeout.

The chart and docs already advertised an EMAIL_PROVIDER variable that no app
code read, and exposed only SendGrid.

- Provider registry keyed by EMAIL_PROVIDER: ses, sendgrid, smtp, resend.
  Deployments that predate it are still inferred from their credentials, so
  upgrading changes nothing for them. A named-but-unconfigured provider fails
  loud instead of silently sending from an unexpected gateway.
- SMTP gateway via nodemailer, covering internal relays, Azure Communication
  Services, Office 365, Postmark, Mailgun and anything else speaking SMTP.
- Resend gateway over fetch, no extra SDK.
- SES honours HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY with NO_PROXY exclusions, and
  AWS_SES_ENDPOINT for VPC endpoints. Resend routes through undici's proxy
  dispatcher. SMTP deliberately ignores the proxy, since a relay is normally
  an internal host that must be reached directly.
- Blind recipients ride the SMTP envelope rather than a Bcc header, matching
  the privacy guarantee SES and SendGrid already gave.
- Chart gains ses/smtp/resend provider blocks; docs document every variable
  and the proxy behaviour.

The mailer's public interface is unchanged, so none of the twelve sendEmail
call sites move.

* chore(mailer): keep only the reusable live QA harnesses

* docs: regenerate llms-full.txt for the email provider section

* chore: apply biome formatting to the email gateway QA script

* refactor(mailer): extract resend payload building to keep complexity in bounds

* fix(mailer): address review — real spec bindings, scheme-less host parsing, port validation, gateway timeouts

- add connect/greeting/socket timeouts to SMTP and a request timeout to Resend
- share one header-sanitizing helper, and strip control characters from header
  names as well as values
- drop the backwards-compatibility re-exports and point the consumer at the

- chart: stop emitting empty AWS_REGION/SMTP_HOST, which shadowed extraEnvs
- correct the SendGrid proxy claim: its client cannot be given a proxy agent

* fix(mailer): reuse proxy agents across sends, redact smtp credentials in QA output

A proxy agent owns a socket pool, so building one per send accumulated pools
and file descriptors under a burst of alerts. SES caches its request handler
per proxy URL and Resend memoizes its dispatcher, with a test pinning the reuse.

* docs: regenerate llms-full.txt after the email provider corrections

* fix(mailer): keep the resend response body out of logged errors

Resend echoes the request on failure, so the body can carry recipient
addresses. The status identifies the failure class without it.

Also tightens the QA harnesses: the unicode scenario now rejects duplicate
deliveries, and the proxy probe derives its expected route from the mailer's
own NO_PROXY matcher rather than assuming any NO_PROXY value is a bypass.

* fix(qa): print only scheme and host of SMTP_URL

Pattern-replacing the userinfo leaked a fragment when a password contained a
raw @. Parsing and rebuilding drops credentials entirely.

* refactor(mailer): named parameters for the provider send contract, cancel failed resend bodies

The send port took positional (content, defaultFrom) against the repo's named
object parameter convention; updated the contract, all four providers, the
caller and the tests together.

Not reading the failed Resend body to keep recipient addresses out of logs left
it unconsumed, which keeps the connection out of undici's pool. Cancel it.

* fix(mailer): resend proxy never applied, global fetch rejects an undici dispatcher

Node's global fetch is bound to the undici bundled with Node, which rejects a
dispatcher built by the installed undici package with "invalid onRequestStart
method". The request failed outright with a proxy configured, so proxied
deployments could not send through Resend at all.

Calling undici's own fetch makes both come from the same package. Proven live
against a real Resend key and a logging CONNECT proxy: CONNECT api.resend.com:443
now appears, and NO_PROXY still goes direct.

The unit tests stubbed globalThis.fetch, which is why they passed against the
broken code. They now mock undici's fetch, with a test asserting the global is
never called.

* fix(mailer): correct the bcc rationale, self-diagnose a chart upgrade break, keep secure=false

The claim that nodemailer renders a Bcc header from a bcc message field was
wrong: captured against an SMTP sink that records DATA, 9.0.3 strips it either
way (keepBcc defaults false) and delivers via the auto-computed envelope. The
earlier observation came from streamTransport, which is not the wire format.
The explicit envelope stays, but as a stated guarantee rather than a bug fix,
and the comment, test name and PR body now say so.

Reading EMAIL_PROVIDER breaks one real pre-existing helm shape: provider left
at its sendgrid default while SES came through extraEnvs was inferred as SES
before and is now taken at its word. The error names a configured alternative
so that shape self-diagnoses.

an operator forces STARTTLS on 465.

SES raw headers now go through the shared sanitizer, so all four gateways strip
header-name tokens identically. Docs note reframed to current behavior.

The email env block lived only in the app Deployment, but scheduled reports and

Selecting a provider the chart cannot configure now fails the render instead of
the first send. Skipped when extraEnvs/extraEnvFrom are set, since those can
carry the settings and the chart cannot see inside them.

The claim that SendGrid is not proxy-aware was wrong. Its client is axios-based
and reads HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY itself: a logging CONNECT proxy saw
api.sendgrid.com tunnelled through it, and stopped once NO_PROXY covered the
domain. Corrected in the code comment, the chart note and the docs, and the
proxy harness is now provider-aware instead of assuming SES.

Attachment filenames outside ASCII were emitted raw into a quoted parameter,

The lint-template matrix never enables email, so nothing in CI would have

instead of aborting the run on a bare helm error.

fix(event-sourcing): budget coalesced batches by payload bytes, not stored bytes (#6473)

* fix(event-sourcing): budget coalesced batches by payload bytes, not stored bytes

The drain's byte bound was measured against the stored Redis value. A body
over the inline ceiling lives in the blob store and leaves a ~250-byte
reference behind, and a body over the compression threshold is stored
compressed, so the budget was reading a number one to three orders of
magnitude under what the coalesced batch would actually hold. A 256-wide
drain of megabyte payloads passed a 4 MiB budget untouched — the byte bound
stopped existing in exactly the backlog it was built for.

The encoder now records the pre-compression, pre-offload payload size in the
envelope header (`s`), and both the TS starting point and the Lua drain spend
the budget against that. Values with no `s` — legacy bare JSON, envelopes
written before this field — keep the old stored-length reading and remain
bounded by count, as they were.

Covers every coalescing consumer at once: the command producers and the
existing map/fold projections all drain through this one path.

* docs(event-sourcing): pin the payload-size helpers to each other

`readJobPayloadBytes` and the Lua `gqPayloadSize` are one byte budget read
from two ends — TS sets the starting point, Lua spends it inside Redis. Nothing
in the type system ties them, so an envelope-format change that lands in one
and not the other makes the two disagree silently. Each now names its twin and
says so.

* fix(event-sourcing): cost a pre-`s` compressed or offloaded body at the cap

Falling back to the stored length for every envelope with no recorded size
reinstated the defect for the one window that matters. During a rolling deploy
old workers keep staging pre-`s` envelopes while new workers drain them, and a
deep backlog — the condition the byte bound exists for — does not age out
promptly. A pre-`s` blob reference read as its ~200 stored bytes let the same
256-wide batch of megabyte payloads through.

The stored length is only honest for a plain inline body (`e:"j"`) and legacy
bare JSON. For `gz`/`ref`/`redis`/`s3`, and for a header that names no encoding
at all, nothing in the value says how far under it reads, so it costs
MAX_BLOB_BYTES: an unreadable payload is worth the largest payload we accept.
Any sane coalesceMaxBytes is far below 50 MiB, so such a job drains alone. The
rollout loses coalescing on those jobs instead of losing the bound — coalescing
is an optimization, the bound is what keeps a worker from assembling a batch it
cannot hold.

Both ends move together: the Lua drain interpolates the same constant.

* style(event-sourcing): satisfy biome formatting in the rollout tests

The parameterised rollout case tripped `biome ci`'s format check — the only
blocking-severity diagnostic in the tree. Lifting the encoding list and the
two-job staging into named bindings makes the canonical formatting readable
rather than an exploded inline array.

* fix(event-sourcing): only trust a recorded size that is a byte count

`typeof s === "number" && s >= 0` let a corrupt or forged header talk the
budget down. `1e999` is valid JSON and parses to Infinity, which passed that
test and would have reached the Lua drain as an unparseable ARGV; a fractional
or string `s` under-reported quietly. Both ends now require a finite
non-negative integer — Lua needs the explicit math.huge bound because
math.floor(inf) == inf — and anything else falls through to the encoding rule,
so an offloaded body still costs the cap rather than its reference.

Also tightens the end-to-end regression, which asserted only an upper bound and
so would have passed if coalescing stopped happening altogether.

* fix(event-sourcing): give the Lua size check the same ceiling as its TS twin

The TS side used Number.isSafeInteger while Lua accepted anything finite and
integral, so 2^53 was admitted by one helper and refused by the other — the
exact drift the two-ends-of-one-budget comment says must not happen. Lua now
bounds by MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, interpolated from TS rather than hand-typed, and
that single bound also rejects the infinity cjson decodes 1e999 to. Both
regression lists now carry 9007199254740992.

* test(event-sourcing): bind the shipped ADR-069 invariant and pin the byte boundary

The contract this PR implements was already written down and marked unbuilt.
specs/event-sourcing/payload-cost.feature carried "an offloaded payload's
reference advertises its true cost" tagged @planned, with a note saying it was
not yet implemented — while its two Then clauses describe exactly what
EnvelopeHeader.s and gqPayloadSize do. @planned is not a tag the parity checker
recognises, so the scenario was among the 5651 it cannot see: the code shipped
and the spec kept reporting a gap. Retagged @integration and bound to the gq2
regression, which moves the enforced count from 4333 to 4334.

Also pins the boundary. The drain admits a job when (accumulated + size) is not
greater than maxBytes, so a job landing exactly on the budget is included. The
existing test only proved that 300 > 250 stops, which a >= implementation would
satisfy just as well. The new case fails when > is flipped to >=, so the
boundary is now held by a test rather than by the absence of one.

perf(build): bundle server entrypoints so prod runs on node, not tsx (#6557)

* perf(build): bundle server entrypoints so prod runs on node, not tsx

esbuild bundles the four server entrypoints (server.mts, workers.ts, task.ts,
and the scenario child process) into dist/server/*.cjs, so production runs on
plain `node` and the prod image ships no tsx, typescript, or esbuild — all
three move to devDependencies and `pnpm install --prod` drops them.

esbuild is a transpiler here, not a packer: only first-party code is bundled
(app source, tsconfig aliases, workspace: packages — raw TypeScript only tsx
could load). Every other bare specifier stays a real require resolved from
node_modules, so OTel's require-in-the-middle patching, native addons,
Prisma's generated client and asset-reading packages load exactly as they did
under tsx. Two guards make the policy self-enforcing: the build fails on any
external not declared in dependencies (the class that used to surface as
MODULE_NOT_FOUND at image boot), and on any bare side-effect import missing
from the explicit sideEffectImports set — the sideEffects:false waiver that
keeps frontend packages tree-shaken out of the server graph would otherwise
drop it silently. Dependency moves in the lockfile are pure section moves at
identical versions.

CJS is deliberate: __dirname is native (goose resolves migrations from
dist/server/migrations, copied by the build), and import.meta.url is defined
to the bundle's directory URL. Bundles emit linked source maps with
sourcesContent:false and run under --enable-source-maps, so prod stack traces
name real files and lines.

Around the bundles:
- src/env-load.ts: .env + the .env.portless overlay load as the FIRST import
  of every entrypoint, so no imported module reads process.env before the
  overlay applies (workers.ts used to resolve Redis before the overlay and
  dispatch on the wrong db).
- scripts/generate-task-registry.mjs: task.ts discovers tasks via a generated

feat: gateway billing follow-ups: anchored cycles, idempotency keys, one webhook pipeline, CodeQL, docs sweep (#6511)

* feat(gateway): anchor a budget's cycle to an instant instead of the calendar

Cyclic budget windows have always been calendar aligned: a month budget
starts on the 1st, a week budget on Monday. A customer whose own billing
runs from the 17th had no way to say so and had to reconcile a gateway
period that did not line up with the invoice it was meant to cover.

A budget may now carry a cycleAnchorAt. NULL, which is every existing row
and every budget created without one, means exactly what happened before.
Set, the window cycles from that instant, Stripe billing_cycle_anchor
style, so an anchor on Jan 17 09:00Z with window month rolls every 17th at
09:00Z.

The clamp for months reads the day off the original anchor every period
and never rewrites it, so a 31st anchor gives Feb 28 and then springs back
to Mar 31. Rewriting the day on the short month would walk the cycle
backwards a few days a year until it settled on the 28th, quietly moving
the customer's billing day.

Anchored budgets need no new read path. Every spend read already flows
through budgetPeriodFloorMs, and an anchored budget simply takes the
raw-ledger branch the MANUAL windows already take, since the rollup
buckets by calendar period and holds no row matching an anchored one. The
same floor is stamped into the breach idempotency chain, so a crossing
fires once per anchored period. No ClickHouse migration, no rollup change.

cycleAnchorAt is a required parameter of budgetPeriodFloorMs and
bucketPeriodFloorMs rather than an optional one, so a caller that forgets
it is a compile error rather than a silent calendar floor counting another
period's spend.

Also adds effectiveBudgetPeriod, which computes the period a budget is
actually in at read time. The stored currentPeriodStartedAt and resetsAt
columns are written at create and at each explicit reset and nothing
sweeps them forward, so a calendar budget past its first boundary reports
its creation date and a reset instant in the past while enforcement has
long since moved on. The read surfaces switch to this in a later commit.

Nothing can set the column until the wire lands, so this commit is
behavior neutral for every existing budget.

* test(gateway): prove anchored cycles against real ClickHouse and Postgres

The decisive case for an anchored budget is a debit that sits in the
previous CALENDAR month but inside the budget's own period. Anchored to
17 June, a debit on 20 June counts when read on 15 July and stops counting
on 20 July, because the anchored period rolled on the 17th while the
calendar month did not. Both halves are asserted against real ClickHouse,
with the debit written by the real spend pipeline.

An anchored month and a calendar month on the same virtual key are read
side by side: the backdated debit counts on the anchored one only, a fresh
debit counts once on each, and neither is doubled.

Resetting an anchored budget zeroes its read, reports the next ANCHORED
boundary rather than one month from the reset, and hands the floor back to
the anchor's schedule exactly at that boundary. An anchored per-seat
template floors its bucket read at the anchored period start, so a seat's
allowance covers the customer's period rather than the calendar's.

Crossings are stamped with the anchored period start rather than the
calendar one, which makes the idempotency key and the webhook envelope id
stable within an anchored period and new after it rolls. A customer billed
from the 17th is therefore warned once per period they are actually
invoiced on.

One production fix came out of writing these. getSpendForBudgets and
getSpendForBudgetsAcrossTenants take an injectable `now` and pass it to
the rollup read, but the period floors were computed from the wall clock
regardless, so the two halves of a read could disagree about which period
they were totalling. It never showed with a calendar or MANUAL window,
whose floors barely move; an anchored floor moves with the clock and makes
it visible. `now` is now threaded into spendTargetsForBudgets. No
production caller passes an explicit `now` today, so nothing changes
outside tests.

* feat(gateway): cycle_anchor_at on the wire, and a truthful reported period

Budget creation accepts an optional `cycle_anchor_at` over REST, tRPC, the
TypeScript SDK, the CLI and the budgets drawer, and the budget DTO returns
it. Omit it and nothing changes: the window stays calendar aligned, which
is what every budget does today.

The reported period is now computed at read time everywhere it is served.
`current_period_started_at` and `resets_at` were rendered straight from the
stored columns, and those columns only move at create and at an explicit
reset. A calendar budget created in March and never reset therefore
reported a period starting in March and a reset instant already in the
past, printed next to July's spend. The pair now brackets the figure it
sits beside, on the REST DTO, the tRPC DTO, the gateway config bundle's
