* Trim trailing slashes without a backtracking regex

Every SDK service and CLI command that normalises an endpoint did it with
`.replace(/\/+$/, "")`. CodeQL flagged four of those as polynomial regular
expressions used on uncontrolled data, and it is right to: the endpoint
arrives from user config, an environment variable or a CLI flag, and a long
run of trailing slashes makes the engine backtrack across the whole run once
per start offset.

One loop-based helper replaces all of them. It scans back from the end of the
string and slices once, which is linear whatever the input. Its unit test
asserts equivalence with the regex it replaces across every input shape, not
only the ones the fix was written for, so the swap is provably behaviour
preserving.

Swept the whole SDK rather than only the four flagged constructors. The same
expression sat at 32 call sites; the alerts landed on the four CodeQL could
trace to uncontrolled data, not on the four that were somehow different.
resolveEndpoint's local wrapper is gone with it, since it now only forwarded.
The CLI boot module graph test gains one entry: the helper has no imports and
is thirty lines, so putting it on the boot path costs nothing measurable.

Left alone deliberately: the single-slash form, which is linear already and
trims exactly one slash, and the skills installer's both-ends trim, which is
a different operation.

* Fold the CLI onto the endpoint normalizer main landed

#6509 landed the same fix for the same reason while this branch was in
flight: one linear scan replacing `/\/+$/`, exported from
internal/endpoint.ts, wired through every client SDK service. Two helpers
that trim trailing slashes is one more than the SDK needs, so the one added
here is gone and the CLI now calls main's.

What that leaves is the half main did not cover. #6509 stopped at the
client SDK; the CLI carried the same expression at 24 further call sites,
across the login and device-code flows, the governance wrapper, the
telemetry endpoint builders and the command surface. Those are the sites
that read an endpoint straight from a flag, a config file or the
environment, so they are the ones where the input is least controlled.

normalizeEndpoint also trims surrounding whitespace, which the expression
it replaces did not. Every one of these call sites is building a base URL
out of user configuration, which is exactly the case main wrote it for, so
the wider normalization is the point rather than a side effect.

The merge also restores cycle_anchor_at to the budgets service. Both sides
had rewritten that constructor, and resolving in favour of main's took its
copy of the whole file with it.

* Make the control-plane creates safe to retry

A create is the one request a caller cannot retry safely on its own. When the
connection drops after the write but before the response, a lost request and a
lost reply look identical from the outside, and the obvious move mints a second
virtual key, budget, cache rule or webhook endpoint. `Idempotency-Key` is how a
caller says the two attempts are one request; a receipt table is what lets the
second one answer with the first one's response.

The header is optional and the unkeyed path is byte-for-byte what it was:
no receipt is written, no query is made. A key is unique within the tenancy its
family authenticates at, so it is the project on the gateway platform and the
organization on the webhook platform.

Only successful outcomes are stored. Stripe stores failures too, but Stripe
cannot re-run your handler and we can: a create that failed left nothing behind
and is safe to run again, while a deterministic 4xx recurs on the retry anyway.
Storing failures would instead pin a rate limit or a moment of database
unavailability to the key for a day, so a caller's retry would get the stale
failure rather than the success it would now get.

Two details worth naming. The receipt row is inserted BEFORE the handler runs,
because a read-then-write lets two concurrent retries both find the key free,
which is the exact race the key was sent to prevent; the unique index is what
actually decides, so it is what the outcome is read from. And a pending row
older than sixty seconds is treated as a crashed original and superseded,
because without that a process dying between the insert and the update would
hold the key locked for its full 24 hours and the caller could never complete
the create it was trying to make.

`responseBody` is `json` rather than the `jsonb` used everywhere else in the
schema. jsonb normalises key order, which would make a replay answer the same
document with different bytes than the original caller received.

The virtual-key and webhook-endpoint creates return a secret that is otherwise
stored only as a hash, so their receipts hold that secret in clear for 24 hours.
That is deliberate and it is the point of the feature on those two routes: a
replay that withheld the secret would hand back a resource nobody can ever use,
which is a worse outcome than the duplicate the key was sent to prevent.

* Register the gateway debits process under its own name

The process writes one budget ledger row per applicable budget for every
gateway request. It was still registered as `attributedUserDebits`, the name of
the narrower thing it started as, which meant the one string a reader could use
to find it in the queue logs, the process tables and the wake scan named
something it stopped being.

The rename cannot be code-only, so it comes with a migration. The process
manager keys its instance, inbox and outbox rows on the process name and every
lookup filters by it: the wake scan only considers registered names and the
outbox lease reads `WHERE processName IN (...)`. Rows left behind under the old
name would not fail, they would go unread in silence, and the outbox ones are
pending money intents. Collision-free by construction, since nothing has ever
registered under the new name and each table's unique index leads with it.

One gap is accepted rather than solved. Between the migration running and the
last old-code pod draining, those pods keep writing rows under the old name,
and any still pending when they stop are orphaned. That window is seconds of
drain lag, and the ClickHouse ledger's ReplacingMergeTree key collapses
anything written twice across the straddle.

Verified against the running stack rather than only in tests: a completion
through the gateway still lands its debit in ClickHouse, the three process
tables hold zero rows under the old name and are growing under the new one, and
the worker log shows `pm:gatewayDebits` waking and completing its jobs.

* Encrypt the stored idempotency response at rest

Two of the four creates that take an `Idempotency-Key` answer with a secret
that exists in readable form nowhere else. A virtual key's secret and a webhook
endpoint's signing secret are both shown once and otherwise kept only as a
hash, which is exactly why replaying those responses is worth doing: a caller
whose connection dropped has no second way to read the secret it was sent. That
also means the secret transits the receipt, and the receipt should not be the
one place in the system where it sits in the clear.

So the stored body is AES-256-GCM ciphertext under CREDENTIALS_SECRET, through
the shared encrypt/decrypt the automations webhook already uses for its custom
headers. Expiry keeps bounding how long it exists at all.

The receipt now stores the response's exact serialised bytes rather than a JSON
document, which makes the guarantee simpler than it was. Byte-identical replay
used to rest on the column being `json` instead of `jsonb` so that Postgres
would not reorder keys; it now rests on a string round trip, with nothing in
storage in a position to reorder or renormalise anything. The column is text
holding ciphertext, and the replay path writes those bytes through instead of
parsing and re-serialising them.

A receipt that no longer decrypts is treated exactly like an expired one:
dropped, and the request runs as a first use. The realistic cause is
CREDENTIALS_SECRET being rotated inside the receipt's 24 hours, which leaves
rows that are authentic and unreadable, and the model provider repository
already drops customKeys it can no longer read for the same reason. Refusing
instead would leave the caller with a create it can never make and a key it
cannot reuse.

Migration 20260804120002 is edited in place rather than followed by an ALTER.
It has not merged, so one clean CREATE reads better than a create-then-alter
pair that only ever existed inside this PR.

No wire behavior changes: same status codes, same error codes, same replay
semantics, and the integration tests that pin byte-identical replay pass

last thing anyone should be writing by hand. The header carries MORE THAN

that keeps a single one refuses every delivery for the length of the
rotation. Our own demo hand-rolled three verifiers and all three had that

* Total a budget in the unit it was priced in

A request is priced exactly once, as an integer number of nano-USD, and the
spend events publish that integer. A budget is the same money seen from the
other side, and the REST surface says so in as many words: "_nano_usd is the
canonical integer in the same nano-USD unit the spend events carry, so a

in float64 and formatted six decimals, and the ledger column it wrote into
could not have held more, so every debit was rounded to the nearest micro-USD

number as adding and then rounding, and the difference compounds with request
count rather than cancelling. On live data one budget read 219000 nano against
a true 212250, and one serving small requests read 100000 against a true 55050,
overstating by 81%. Reads then rounded a second time, and the wire published
the result as the canonical integer.

The money is now the integer the whole way: the ledger carries AmountNanoUSD,
the rollup aggregates it, both spend reads sum it, and the display string is
rendered from it. The decimal column stays for the audit read that shows one
debit beside the request that caused it, and is summed nowhere.

Backfilled history is the micro figure scaled up rather than recovered
precision; those digits were destroyed at write and survive only in
gateway_spend.CostNanoUSD. Requests priced from here carry the true integer.

exact figure instead of an already-corrupted one.

* Hold an idempotency claim by liveness, not by age

A pending receipt was superseded once it was older than 60 seconds, on the
assumption that whoever claimed the key had crashed. Age does not carry that
information. A request merely slow past the window, waiting on a row lock or a
saturated connection pool, is still going to write its resource, so taking the
key off it minted the second resource the key was sent to prevent, and did it
exactly when the platform was least able to absorb it.

The claim holder now reports itself alive every 5 seconds while its handler
runs, and a claim is only takeable after 20 seconds of silence. A slow request
keeps beating and keeps its key; a dead one stops and its key frees up in
seconds rather than in minutes, so the crash case recovers faster too.

Behind that, a fence. A takeover rewrites the row's claimId instead of deleting
the row, and every write a claim holder makes names the claim it holds, so a
process that resumes after being declared dead cannot overwrite the receipt of
the request that replaced it. That write affecting no rows is logged as the
signal that one key may have produced two resources, replacing a failure that
was previously silent.

The migration is edited in place rather than followed by an ALTER, as this
branch has done for its other unmerged migrations.

stayed green. Each of the 14 paths that were unowned is now registered with a

* ci: stop the vite cache key changing on every commit

The build job's vite cache key hashed platform/app/src/**, so the primary
key moved with every commit. That guarantees a miss on the primary key
and still writes a fresh multi-MB entry each run, so the cache was pure
quota churn against the repository's 10GB budget — and hashing that tree
costs time before the build even starts.

The entry is Vite's dependency pre-bundle, which is a function of the
dependency set rather than app source, and Vite re-optimizes on its own
when its internal hash moves. Key it on the lockfile and vite.config.ts,
and let restore-keys cover the rest.

feat(clickhouse): a shared client package for pooling, logging and retries (#6604)

* feat(clickhouse): a shared client package for pooling, logging and retries

Three ClickHouse client rules were decided independently at each construction
site, and each of them was wrong in production on its own terms.

Pool sizing was a fixed 64, reasoned about as "4 pods x 1 client". The fleet
is 10 worker pods and 3 app pods, and a process holding both the raw client and
the app-layer factory opens two pools, so the real ceiling was several times
the server's 300. On 2026-07-31 that surfaced as ~37k
TOO_MANY_SIMULTANEOUS_QUERIES rejections, each retried straight back into the
same wall. Sizing now derives from the server's own budget divided by the
fleet, once a deployment sets CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT_REPLICAS. Until it does, the
old fixed default stands, so adopting this changes nothing by itself.

The vendor client logged an error for every failed HTTP attempt and cannot
know whether the caller then retried and succeeded, so those records carried
no verdict - and were roughly half of one service's error volume. They are
dropped. A call under the retry wrapper is reported by the wrapper, which knows
the outcome, and an unwrapped call throws.

No cause is attached under a field named `error` any more, in either the vendor
adapter or the retry notice. Loki derives detected_level from that field, so
successful retries were being counted as failures. The retry notice also warns
only on the first attempt, rather than 25 times per failure.

The package is pure and reads no environment of its own: callers pass the
numbers in and get a decision back, which is what makes the rules testable
without mocking a process and identical wherever they are applied.

* fix(clickhouse-client): ship the new package in the npm tarball's files[]

The root package.json's files array didn't list packages/clickhouse-client/,
so the ADR-076 workspace-invariants test (every workspace member needs a
files[] entry) failed CI across all three smoke jobs and the lint job.

* fix(clickhouse-client): address CodeRabbit review findings

Two real correctness gaps in pool.ts:
- deriveFleetPoolCeiling accepted fractional replicas/clientsPerProcess,
  which could inflate the derived ceiling instead of shrinking it
  (e.g. clientsPerProcess: 0.5 derived a *larger* pool than 1 would).
  positiveOr now requires positive integers.
- resolvePoolSize's derived-size path hardcoded exceedsBudget: false. A
  fleet so large the raw ceiling floors below 1 (e.g. 151 replicas) still
  resolved a pool of 1, but exceedsBudget stayed false because the
  MIN_POOL_SIZE clamp that keeps the ceiling usable also erased the signal
  that the true budget was already gone. resolvePoolSize now tracks the
  unclamped ceiling to detect this and reports it.

House-rule fixes:
- decideVendorLog, emitVendorLog and isTransientClickHouseError now take a
  single named-parameter object instead of positional args, matching the
  project's named-parameter convention. Call sites (clickhouseLogger.ts,
  the package's own tests) updated.
- tsconfig.json's tsBuildInfoFile moved under node_modules/.cache/tsbuildinfo/,
  matching every other workspace package.
- Fixed a misleading tsconfig comment (Vitest types are consumed by tsc, not
  "at runtime").
- Test suites now nest describe("when ...") under describe("given ..."),
  and a backoff test's description was corrected (attempt 40 doesn't
  overflow - the delay is clamped because it exceeds maxDelayMs).

* feat(clickhouse-client): tenant safety, limiting and tracing as composable middleware

Everything the client does to a statement is now a middleware over one
function type. There is no base class and nothing to extend: behaviour is
added by wrapping, and the order of the wrapping is the order of the
behaviour, visible at the call site.

  compose([tenantGuard(), trace(), rateLimit(), retry()])(driver)

Tenant routing fails closed. The previous resolver cached tenant to
organisation in an unbounded Map that was never invalidated, so a project
moved between organisations kept reading its old organisation's ClickHouse
until the process restarted - a data-leak class of bug, not a stale-read one.
The router here bounds the cache, expires it, and exposes invalidation. An
unknown tenant raises rather than falling back to the shared instance, because
the shared instance is where a routing mistake is least visible: the query
succeeds and returns plausible rows belonging to someone else.

The tenant guard refuses a statement with no `TenantId = {param:String}`
predicate. No other id in this schema is unique across tenants, so an omitted
predicate returns another customer's rows and looks healthy doing it. It also
refuses an inlined literal, which cannot be checked against the caller's
tenant and is the shape that eventually becomes an injection. Statements that
genuinely span tenants declare `unscoped: { reason }` - a written sentence, not
a boolean, so it survives review and lands on the span for audit.

Bounded concurrency, with shedding. Pool sizing bounds sockets; it does not
bound how many statements a process will attempt, which is what actually broke
on 2026-07-31. The limiter holds one slot for a whole statement, retries
included, so a retrying query keeps its place instead of rejoining the queue
behind fresh work. Its wait queue is bounded and sheds when full, because an
unbounded queue does not prevent overload, it hides it.

Spans carry the tenant, table, operation and result shape - never the
statement text or its parameters. Neither has been through redaction, and a
span backend is not a place customer content is allowed to reach.

Still no dependencies, still no `process.env` read inside the package, and
still builds without `@types/node`: `AbortSignal` is declared structurally as
the narrow port this actually uses.

130 tests.

* fix(clickhouse-client): drop the cache expiry, the mapping it guarded is immutable

The previous commit justified a TTL on the tenant-to-organisation cache with a
project moving between organisations. That cannot happen: a project belongs to
a team and a team to an organisation, and nothing reassigns either - `teamId`
appears only in the create path, and no update writes it.

So the expiry protected against nothing and cost a periodic lookup per tenant.
Gone, along with the clock port and the per-tenant invalidation that existed to
serve it. What stays is the bound, which is real: a long-lived worker sees a
great many tenants and the map would otherwise grow for the life of the
process.

Also states, and now tests, that a failed lookup is deliberately not cached -
a tenant that does not exist yet is a different thing from one that never will,
and caching the negative would leave a newly created project unroutable until
eviction.

* refactor(clickhouse): move the retry loop out of the resilient client

The app kept its own copy of the retry policy: a transient classifier, a
jittered backoff and the loop that drives them, all duplicating what the
package now owns. Two copies of "is this worth retrying" is the shape that
drifts, and it had already drifted once - the app's classifier and the outer
group-queue classifier agreed only because a comment asked them to.

`runWithRetry` in the package is now the single implementation. The retry
middleware is a thin wrapper over it for pipeline callers, and the resilient
client calls it directly, since it wraps the vendor client's own query/insert
rather than a pipeline request.

What is left in resilient-client.ts is the part that is genuinely an adapter:
attaching queryWindowed, translating errors, guarding ClickHouse's in-band
exceptions, and the query logging and metrics. 461 lines to 402, and none of
the remainder is policy.

Deleting the file outright needs every repository moved off
ResilientClickHouseClient and onto the pipeline. That is a wide mechanical
migration and is not this commit.

* fix(clickhouse-client): close the review's fail-open and data-disclosure findings

An independent code and security review found three things worth fixing and a
handful of smaller ones.

The routing table's `<label>__<organizationId>` split is ambiguous when either
half contains the separator, and taking the last one is a guess. Guessing wrong
is not a parse error, it is a silent fail-open: the intended organisation ends
up with no route, so every one of its tenants falls through to the shared
instance and reads and writes there. LangWatch ids are prefix plus nanoid and
nanoid's alphabet includes `_`, so this is reachable. Nothing in the parser can
tell which split was meant, so it now reports the guess in `ambiguous` for the
caller to surface loudly, rather than making it silently.

`trace` promised the statement never reaches a span and then handed the raw
error to `recordError` on the failure path. ClickHouse embeds the failing
statement in its own error message, so that re-opened the hole on the path
nobody inspects until an incident. Spans now carry a classified descriptor -
name, code, status - and never a message. The existing test only covered the
success path, which is why it passed.

The tenant guard now strips SQL comments before matching. Commenting out a
WHERE clause while debugging is the exact scenario the guard exists for, and it
was passing. The bypasses a regex genuinely cannot see - a disjunction, a UNION
with an unscoped arm, a JOIN scoped on one side, a scoped subquery under an
unscoped outer query - are now named in the docblock and pinned by tests, so
they stay documented limits rather than becoming folklore.

Also: `runWithRetry` rejects a non-positive `maxAttempts` instead of throwing
an uninitialised `undefined` that every instanceof handler upstream would miss,
and the vendor log adapter strips an `error` key out of the vendor's own args,
which could otherwise defeat the Loki detected_level rule the module exists to
enforce.

142 tests.

* fix(clickhouse): stop retrying inserts at the client, the queue already does

Production says the retry policy was aimed at the wrong half. Over two days the
worker logged 14,442 insert retries against 1,789 read retries - 89% writes -
while the code justified the whole mechanism on the grounds that reads are
idempotent.

Inserts are the half that should not have been retrying.

They are only ever issued from a job on the group queue, which retries the whole
job on its own backoff, so a client retry adds no resilience. It multiplies:
four attempts here inside up to twenty-five there, so one insert could be tried
around a hundred times against a server that was rejecting precisely because it
was overloaded. That is the amplifier from the 2026-07-31 incident, living in
the write path.

It was also unsafe. These are async inserts (`async_insert` +
`wait_for_async_insert`) and `async_insert_deduplicate` is set nowhere, so it
takes ClickHouse's default of off. The commonest insert failures in production
are `Query was cancelled` and the memory limit hit while executing
`WaitForAsyncInsert` - both raised after the server has taken the batch into its
buffer, where it can still flush. Retrying then writes the rows twice.
ReplacingMergeTree collapses that for the tables keyed to collapse it; the
rollup and analytics tables just double-count.

Reads keep retrying. They are idempotent, nothing above them retries, and they
were never the volume.

The spec said inserts retry, so it says the opposite now, and the tests that
pinned the old behaviour now pin the new one - including that no retry warning
is emitted for an insert, since there is no retry. The transient-classification
cases moved onto the read path, which still exercises the same classifier.

Wanting insert retries back means making them idempotent first: set
`async_insert_deduplicate`, or pass a deterministic `insert_deduplication_token`
per batch.

* fix(clickhouse): close a tenant-scope bypass and stop telemetry failing queries

Review round on the client package. The two that matter:

The tenant guard accepted `WHERE TenantId = {t:String} OR Status = 'x'`,
which contains the predicate and returns every tenant's rows. That is not
an exotic statement, it is what operator precedence produces from `AND A OR
B`, so it is refused now: an `OR` at or above the predicate's bracket depth
weakens it, one nested deeper cannot. Bracketing the disjunction satisfies
the guard and fixes the query.

Comment stripping was `/\/\*[\s\S]*?\*\//`, which rescans to the end of the
input from every unterminated `/*` - quadratic, and reachable from any
caller that builds SQL from input it did not write (CodeQL flagged it).
Replaced with a single-pass scanner that also masks string bodies, so a
literal containing `OR` or `--` cannot steer any of the checks.

The rest:

- Host observability could fail a query it only observes. A throwing
  `onRetry` replaced the ClickHouse error with a logging one and cancelled
  the remaining attempts; a throwing tracer or completion hook failed the
  query outright. Both are isolated now.
- Retry checked the abort signal before the backoff but not after, so a
  caller that gave up during a 30s wait still paid for another attempt.
- `maxQueued` and `maxCacheEntries` went unvalidated, and `NaN` made both
  bounds false forever - an unbounded wait queue and an unbounded cache,
  each silently removing the only thing its module exists to provide.
- Named parameters for the multi-argument functions, `stats?: T | undefined`
  for `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, and the nested `when` blocks the test
  convention asks for.

167 package tests, 143 app tests.

fix: seven production defects found in a five-day error review (#6602)

* fix(data-privacy): default the cached policy's collections on read-back

Old and new pods share the Redis policy cache for the whole of a rolling
deploy, so a cached blob can predate any field added since the writer last
shipped. #6324 added `pii.exceptPatterns` and read `.length` on it unguarded,
so upgraded pods deserialised an old blob and threw on a field the type says
is always there.

Span processing fails closed on a redaction error, so those spans stopped
rather than leaking. The queue's 25-attempt budget rides out a deploy
comfortably, so they landed on retry - this cost ingest latency and a retry
storm on 2026-07-31, not data.

Defaulting at the cache boundary rather than at the ~20 sites that walk the
shape, since every one of them is exposed to the same skew. A blob missing
`categories`, `pii` or `secrets` is past defaulting, so it reads as a miss
and the cascade recomputes.

* fix(otel): stop shipping rejected OTLP bodies to the logs and PostHog

The three ingest routes dumped the whole request body as base64 twice on a
parse failure, once into the log record and once into captureException, with
no size cap on either and no cap on the routes themselves.

That body has not been parsed, so it has not been through PII redaction. The
bytes carry prompt and completion attributes, hostnames and OS usernames, and
one misconfigured client sent roughly 219MB of them into Loki over three days
with a matching copy into PostHog, which is a third-party processor.

Only the length survives. The routes also pick up the 10MB cap the collector
route has always had.

* fix(usage): answer a spent plan limit with 402, not 429

429 sits in the OTel SDKs' retryable set, so an exporter that hits a plan
limit re-posts the same batch until its elapsed-time budget runs out. A plan
limit is terminal for that payload, so the retryable status turned one
rejection into an unbounded loop - one free-tier project spent five days
retrying a quota rejection every ~30s and could never have succeeded.

402 is outside every SDK's retryable set, so this holds for any OTLP client
rather than only ours. The `ERR_PLAN_LIMIT` discriminant is unchanged, which
is what the SDKs and the AI gateway actually match on.

The middleware now throws a typed PlanLimitExceededError instead of hand-
rolling the response, so the boundary classifies it as customer fault and
logs it at warn. Its serialised body is a superset of the old one: same
`error` and `message` fields, plus the counts and a tip.

* fix(experiments): bound the Run via API poll loop and give up on a 404

The shell snippet behind the Run via API button polled `while true` and
matched on `.status` parsed from the body. A 404 has no `.status`, so jq
returned null, no case matched, and the loop ran forever.

Runs stay readable for 24h and SDK-logged runs never write run-state at all,
so 404 is permanent for whole populations of run ids. 57 distinct runs were
polled ~361 times each over five days, from a snippet we hand customers, in
their CI.

Now branches on the HTTP status, caps at 1800 polls (an hour at 2s), and
breaks on `interrupted` alongside the other terminal states. Also drops the
trailing note advertising an events stream: there is no
/api/experiments/runs/:runId/events route.

* fix(usage): make UsageLimitResult a discriminated union

blockTraceUsageExceededMiddleware now constructs PlanLimitExceededError
directly from result.message, which needs message: string. The old
interface left every field optional regardless of `exceeded`, so tsgo
correctly rejected string | undefined. exceeded: true now carries
message/count/maxMessagesPerMonth/planName as required fields, which is
what checkLimit always returns on that branch anyway.

* fix: address CodeRabbit review comments on PR #6602

- runSnippets.ts: give up on any non-200 poll response, not only a 404.
  A 401/403/5xx carried no .status either, so the loop burned attempts
  parsing an error body instead of failing fast.
- otel.ts / collector.ts: throw PlanLimitExceededError instead of
  hand-rolling the 402 body, matching the HandledError convention the
  trace-limit.ts middleware already uses in this same PR. The lookup
  failure try/catch is split from the thrown limit error so the error
  is never mistaken for a lookup failure and swallowed.

* fix(otel): use a named-parameter object for enforcePlanLimit

CodeRabbit flagged the three positional args against the project's own
convention (named parameters via object destructuring for multi-arg
functions). Object-destructure project/customerTraceIds/logger and
update the three call sites.

* fix(usage): narrow UsageLimitResult in tests instead of asserting past it

checkLimit() became a discriminated union in d68e65d2b5, but its own test
file still read result.message/.count/.maxMessagesPerMonth/.planName right
after expect(result.exceeded).toBe(true) — a real assertion, but one that
doesn't narrow the type for TS, so tsgo saw those reads against the
{ exceeded: false } branch and typecheck failed.

assertExceeded() gives the seven affected cases a real type guard. It
throws rather than calling expect() so biome's noMisplacedAssertion rule
(assertions must live inside it()) stays clean.

* fix: contain two error-volume and blast-radius problems (#6603)

* fix(logs): stop a malformed collector body reading as a platform error

The three body-validation sites answer a 400 and return rather than throw, so
they never reach the boundary that classifies a customer fault as warn. At
error level they were about a fifth of the app's real error stream, all of it
callers sending the wrong content-type or invalid JSON.

The HTTP response is unchanged.

* fix(traces): cap the joined span read's memory instead of the server's

The joined span read selects every heavy column, and its window falls back to
"none" when a page's summaries carry no usable OccurredAt, so it scans every
partition including the cold S3 tiers. Uncapped, the pathological tail was
stopped by ClickHouse's OvercommitTracker, which picks its victim across the
whole server - so one bad trace read degraded unrelated queries.

A per-query cap fails the offending read on its own request instead. Mirrors
what the single-trace read path already does.

Containment, not a cure. The window goes null because trace_summaries rows
land on an OccurredAt sentinel; #6306 anchored trace_analytics against exactly
this and left trace_summaries alone.

* fix(usage): narrow UsageLimitResult in tests instead of asserting past it

checkLimit() became a discriminated union in d68e65d2b5, but its own test
file still read result.message/.count/.maxMessagesPerMonth/.planName right
after expect(result.exceeded).toBe(true) — a real assertion, but one that
doesn't narrow the type for TS, so tsgo saw those reads against the
{ exceeded: false } branch and typecheck failed.

assertExceeded() gives the seven affected cases a real type guard. It
throws rather than calling expect() so biome's noMisplacedAssertion rule
(assertions must live inside it()) stays clean.

* fix(otel): bound the decompressed body, not just the compressed one

`bodyLimit` weighs the bytes on the wire, and the sender picks the ratio
between those and the bytes we end up holding. So the advertised 10 MiB cap
was one any holder of an ingest key could walk straight past: a compressed
body comfortably inside it expands to hundreds of megabytes, or to gigabytes
at Node zlib's own default, and the process is exhausted before anything
downstream gets a chance to reject it. Cheap to send, expensive to receive.

The cap goes in `readOtlpBody` rather than at each route, for two reasons.
The compressed limit cannot express it, and the governance ingest routes have
no compressed limit at all - they were the more exposed of the two receivers.

zlib enforces it via `maxOutputLength`, so an oversized body stops being
written the moment it crosses the line. Buffering it whole and measuring
afterwards would concede exactly the memory being defended.

`OtlpBodyTooLargeError` is a 413 rather than a 400: the request is
well-formed, and the sender's remedy is a smaller batch, which is something
OTLP exporters are already configured to do. The `/api/otel/v1` routes
surface it through the service app's error handling. The governance ingest
routes still acknowledge and record a hint, which is their existing contract
for every receive failure and not something this change should alter - they
get the memory bound regardless.

Pinned across all three encodings, plus the just-under-the-cap case, and a
test that states the asymmetry as a number: the bomb costs under 1% of the
wire budget to send.

* test(traces): pin the memory cap to the span read, not merely to the flow

The include-spans test asserted the returned spans and nothing about the
query, so it stayed green if `clickhouse_settings` were dropped altogether or
drifted onto the summary query. A cap on the wrong query reads as protection
while protecting nothing, which is the failure the cap exists to prevent.

Asserts the setting is present on the span call specifically, rather than
restating the byte count the source already states.

* fix(otel): bound the wire body too, not just the decompressed one

The decompressed cap only ever sees a body that went through zlib. An
identity-encoded request skips it, and `readOtlpBody` then read the whole
thing with `req.arrayBuffer()` before anything could object.

That leaves the receiver the two receivers do not agree on: the OTLP handler
routes carry `bodyLimit`, so their wire bytes were capped at 10 MiB all along,
but the three governance ingest routes carry no middleware at all. Their only
limit on an uncompressed body was the memory of the process, available to any
holder of an ingest key. The last commit called those routes the more exposed
of the two and then fixed only the half of the problem that needs compression.

The wire bound goes in `readOtlpBody` for the same reason the decompressed one
did: it is the one function both receivers share, so neither can be left out,
and each still answers in its own contract — the OTLP routes with a 413, the
ingest routes with their existing ack-and-hint. The read consumes the stream by
hand rather than calling `arrayBuffer()`, because measuring after the fact
would concede exactly the memory being defended.

`OTLP_MAX_BODY_BYTES` now lives beside the reader and `otel.ts` imports it, so
the cap the middleware advertises and the cap the reader enforces cannot drift
apart. An unsupported Content-Encoding is also settled before the read now,
rather than after paying for a body that was always going to be refused.

Narrows DECOMPRESSORS to its three real keys with `as const` while there, per
CodeRabbit. The lookup widens back to a shared signature at the call site: the
entries differ in their options type (ZlibOptions vs BrotliOptions), so the
indexed union is not callable as it stands.

* fix(collector): answer a json null body with the 400 it already means

`typeof null` is "object", so a request body of literal `null` walked past the
guard meant to catch exactly this and reached `"metadata" in body` further
down, which throws on it. An array walked past too — it does not throw there,
but nothing below treats one as a payload either.

Both are the caller sending the wrong thing, which is the same class the warn
level change above this line was for. Left as it was, the null case turned that
mistake into a TypeError and a 500 in the platform's error stream, which is
precisely the noise this branch is trying to remove.

The response for a body that is not a json object is unchanged: 400, same
message, now logged at warn like its two neighbours.

perf: cut the server's resident memory (browser UI out of the backend, env-gated DLP & OTel) (#6023)

* perf(server): keep the browser UI stack out of backend processes

Every backend process held the entire browser UI stack, and one import edge
caused it: `server/routes/evaluations-legacy.ts` pulled the display-name
constant `evaluatorTempNameMap` out of a React component, and that single edge
dragged in Chakra UI, Ark UI, Emotion, react-dom and react-router. Measured on
a single-process boot: 8,525 -> 6,505 modules, 676 -> 464 MB RSS.

The constants move to framework-free modules both sides already import:
`server/evaluations/evaluatorDisplayNames.ts` beside the evaluator catalogue,
and `iconsMap.tsx` (pure JSX, imported only by the UI) into `components/`.
`@langwatch/react-rum` gains a `./constants` subpath so the three backend
files that wanted two numbers stop resolving the barrel, which re-exports
`startBrowserTracing` and with it browser OpenTelemetry.

`server/__tests__/frontend-boundary.unit.test.ts` keeps it out. It walks the
real import graph transitively — a direct-import check would not have caught
this, since evaluations-legacy never imported Chakra itself — and follows
value imports only, so `import type` of a component's types stays legal.
`server/mailer/**` is an allowed terminal because react-email renders
templates server-side. The walk is a backwards flood from each browser-only
package rather than a recursive descent, so import cycles cannot make a
"cannot reach" answer unsound, and it settles in well under a second.

* feat(observability): env-gate Google DLP and load only the OTel instrumentation we use

Two heavy dependencies were resident in every server process regardless of
whether anything ever called them.

`@google-cloud/dlp` (generated protos over google-gax/grpc, 118 modules) is
now a type-only import, loaded on first use inside `getDlpClient` and only
when a google_dlp check actually runs with credentials configured. The load
is `await import()` rather than `require` so vitest's `vi.mock` still
intercepts it. `LANGWATCH_DISABLE_GOOGLE_DLP` refuses the check outright and
guarantees the SDK never enters the process. `getDlpClient` caches the
in-flight promise, so concurrent checks share one gRPC channel instead of
building one each.

OpenTelemetry loaded `auto-instrumentations-node`, which pulls all 41
instrumentation packages even though 28 were configured off and most target
frameworks this server does not run. It now names the five it uses: aws-sdk,
ioredis, openai, pino and runtime-node. The SDK and instrumentations load
through a gated `require` — instrumentation.node.ts compiles to CommonJS, so
top-level await is illegal there — and only when observability is configured.
With OTel unset, nothing loads at all.

Measured A/B on the boot graph with OTel on: 9,018 -> 8,524 modules, DLP 7 ->
0, gax 118 -> 0, OTel instrumentation 252 -> 44, heap 480 -> 446 MB.

* feat(haven): disable Google DLP by default for local stacks

No local workflow should ship trace text to Google, and the opt-out also keeps
the DLP SDK out of the process. haven now sets
`LANGWATCH_DISABLE_GOOGLE_DLP=true` in the stacks it starts, including
sandboxes started by `haven play` — which run unreviewed branches and so want
the default most.

It stays a default, not a lock: when the operator sets the variable to any
non-true value haven emits nothing and leaves `.env` to govern.

Reading that opt-in correctly needs care, because haven both reads and writes
this knob. The overlay it writes (`.env.portless`) is loaded last with
`override: true`, so reading the merged layers means that from the second
`haven up` onward haven reads back its own output: it sees the "true" it wrote
last time, concludes the operator asked for it, and rewrites it, and a `.env`
opt-in can never win. `operatorEnvLookup` therefore reads the process
environment and `platform/app/.env` only. The general rule, worth stating
because it will come up again: any knob haven both reads and writes must
exclude the overlay, because an overlay is output, not input.

* fix(server): keep NODE_ENV a runtime mode, not .env configuration

`env-load.ts` loads `.env` with `override: true` so pinned values beat what
start.sh exported. NODE_ENV is a runtime mode rather than configuration, and
the comment there already promised it stays shell-only — but nothing enforced
it, so a stray `NODE_ENV=development` line in a dev machine's `.env` silently
de-productionized `pnpm start`: the API port moves to PORT+1000, no CSP, no
static serving, while the process composition stays production.

`keepProcessNodeEnv` restores the process-level value after dotenv runs and
warns once. It lives in env-load.ts, so every entrypoint that shares the load
(server.mts, workers.ts, task.ts) is covered by the same guard.

It deliberately does nothing when the process declared no mode of its own.
There is no production boot to protect in that case, and deleting the variable
would leave NODE_ENV unset, which env-create.mjs rejects outright since it
validates NODE_ENV as a required enum — turning a boot that used to succeed
into an invalid-enum crash. An exported-but-empty NODE_ENV names no mode, so
it counts as unset, matching what every shell reader here already does.

* fix(dev): don't gate the free-port suggestion on a port in-process workers never open

When ports are busy, check-ports.sh suggests the next free PORT slot. It
required the worker-metrics port to be free at every candidate slot, but the
single-process topology serves worker metrics through the app's own /metrics
and never binds that listener. So the search skipped otherwise-usable slots,
and if every candidate's metrics port happened to be held it printed no
suggestion at all — the one thing the script exists to do.

It now applies that condition only when the topology actually binds the port,
reusing the `IN_PROCESS_WORKERS` decision computed above rather than
recomputing it.

* docs(adr): ADR-070 modular package architecture, and the footprint spec

ADR-070 records the architecture this PR's point fixes kept running into: a
single boundary-less module graph with no enforced dependency direction, which
is why both the RAM a process holds and the files the compiler re-checks keep
growing. It is Proposed, not Accepted — the phases are sequenced so the
landable footprint wins can ship without waiting for the whole thing. It
builds on ADR-076, which has since made the repo a single pnpm workspace, so
the package moves it proposes inherit a layout rather than inventing one.

`specs/setup/memory-footprint.feature` specifies what a server process loads:
the DLP SDK, the OTel instrumentations, the browser UI boundary, and the
NODE_ENV guard. Process topology is a separate concern and stays in
`specs/setup/in-process-workers-dev.feature`.

ADR-004 loses a limitation that is no longer true: it said the web entrypoint
does not load `instrumentation.node`, so in-process workers produce no-op
spans. server.mts does load it, before the app graph evaluates, precisely
because the standalone workers lane no longer runs under the single-process
default. Worker spans are real.

ci: publish container images to artifacts ECR via OIDC (#6610)

* ci: publish container images to artifacts ECR via OIDC

The OSS build already produces every image the SaaS deployment runs, but
SaaS could not consume them: they only landed on Docker Hub, so the private
pipeline rebuilt the same source from a git submodule. This publishes the
same four images to the LangWatch shared artifacts account ECR as well, so
SaaS can pin an OSS-built `git-<sha>` instead.

Auth is GitHub OIDC into `langwatch-oss-ecr-push` (langwatch/langwatch-saas#486),
which trusts `refs/heads/main` and `refs/tags/langwatch@v*` only — no
long-lived AWS keys in a public repository. There is deliberately no
`pull_request` trigger: a PR-ref assume-role is denied by that trust policy,
so such a run could only ever fail.

Tag policy: always `git-<short-sha>`, plus `<version>` on a `langwatch@v*`
release. Never `:latest` — the SaaS pipeline still owns that tag on these
repositories and racing it would silently repoint production.

publish-docker-app.yml is untouched; Docker Hub keeps its own triggers,
credentials and `:latest`.

Supersedes #3709, which was opened while the IAM role did not yet exist and
against a tree that has since been restructured (ADR-076).

* fix(ci): tag every image on every publish, and validate tags in meta

Two problems with the path filter as written, both from review.

The filter gated the TAG, not just the build. A commit touching only
platform/app/** published langwatch-app:git-<sha> and nothing else, so the
one thing this workflow exists to provide — a single git-<sha> SaaS can pin
across the whole deployment — did not hold. create-manifest now runs for all
four images every time: a rebuilt image assembles its index from the per-arch
tags just pushed, and a skipped one has this commit's tag pointed at the index
it already has. `imagetools create` from a single index writes a manifest and
moves no layers, so the cost of a skipped image is one PUT and the build saving
is unchanged. Nothing to re-tag yet is a warning, not a failure; a dispatch run
builds all four and seeds them.

`meta` also turned two pieces of external input into Docker tags without
looking at them. A `langwatch@1.2.3` tag (no `v`) left VERSION as the whole
ref, and `@` is not a legal tag character; a dispatched image_tag went through
verbatim. Both now fail in meta, where the run has cost nothing, rather than
after eight images are pushed.

The validation uses `case`, not `grep -E '^…$'`. grep matches line by line, so
a value whose first line is well formed passes even when the rest is not —
which is the input that matters here, since the `key=value` writes are
line-oriented and a second line defines further step outputs. Verified: the
grep form accepted $'ok\nis_release=true' and set is_release twice.

* fix(ci): reject a 'latest' tag, and stop swallowing ECR lookup failures

Two more holes in the same two steps, both from review.

`assert_docker_tag` accepted `latest`. Nothing this workflow computes can
produce it, but a dispatcher can type it into the input box and a
`langwatch@vlatest` release tag reaches the same place — and publishing it is
the one thing the file's own header says must never happen, because the SaaS
pipeline owns that tag. Now rejected in meta for both paths.

The previous-manifest lookup ran `describe-images | tr | grep | head` as one
pipeline with `|| true` on the end. The `|| true` was there so a no-match would
not trip `set -e`, but it swallowed a failed `describe-images` just as happily:
an AccessDenied or a throttle would leave PREVIOUS empty, take the bootstrap
branch, log a warning and exit 0 — reporting success while writing no tag at
all. The AWS call is now its own statement so a failure stops the job, and the
match is awk, which exits 0 on no match without needing `|| true`.

Verified with `aws` and `docker` stubbed: a stubbed AccessDenied now exits 254,
where it previously exited 0 with a bootstrap warning.

ci: build ECR images for arm64 only (#6617)

Every consumer of these ECR images runs on Graviton. The EKS node groups
are AL2023_ARM_64_STANDARD on m8g — including the module defaults, so the
backbase and DR clusters too — and every Lambda is
`architectures = ["arm64"]`.

The amd64 half of the matrix was building four images per run to produce
manifest entries nothing has ever pulled. Dropping it halves the build
table, and takes the four `ubuntu-latest` runners with it.

Docker Hub is untouched and still publishes both arches for the community;
that is where multi-arch actually matters. This registry serves one
private, all-arm64 deployment.

create-manifest still wraps the per-arch tag in an index rather than
pushing the bare manifest, so the consumer-facing tag keeps the same media
type whether an image was rebuilt this run or re-tagged from a previous
one.

feat(app): serve content-hashed assets from a runtime-configurable CDN base (#5535)

* feat(app): serve content-hashed assets from a runtime-configurable CDN base

During a rolling deploy the app replicas serve two builds at once behind one
Service, so a browser that fetched the HTML shell from build A can have a lazy
import() load-balanced to a build-B pod lacking that content hash — a hard 404.

Host content-hashed assets on a commit-prefixed, immutable CDN and choose the
base at container start rather than build time, so the single published image
still serves self-host same-origin, unchanged.

- vite.config.ts emits every JS-referenced asset URL as window.__lwAssetUrl(path)
- src/server/asset-base.ts normalizes LANGWATCH_ASSET_BASE, defines the resolver
  bootstrap and rewrites /assets/ entry refs; static-handler.ts injects it
- charts/langwatch gains app.assetBase, empty by default
- scripts/upload-assets-to-cdn.sh syncs dist/client/assets to the origin bucket

Rebased onto the restructured tree (langwatch/ -> platform/app/). Two changes
were needed beyond the path move:

- The CSP builder this originally added as src/server/csp.ts now duplicates
  src/server/securityHeaders.ts, which landed on main in the meantime and is
  richer. Dropped the duplicate and extended buildSecurityHeaders with an
  optional assetOrigin instead, admitting the CDN into the six fetch directives
  the browser needs. Its test cases moved to securityHeaders.unit.test.ts.
- Renumbered the ADR 038 -> 086. ADR-038 is now intent-forked onboarding
  governance on main; 086 is what the langwatch-saas infra already references.

Tagged the nine scenarios in specs/server/cdn-asset-base.feature @unit and bound
each to a test — the feature-parity gate now fails closed, so the untagged file
would have failed CI.

* docs(adr): correct ADR-086 paths for the restructured tree

* fix(app): address the outstanding CDN asset-base review findings

- normalizeAssetBase rejects a query or fragment. The resolver concatenates
  the asset path onto the base, so "…/build?rev=1" + "assets/x.js" resolved to
  "…/build?rev=1/assets/x.js", putting the path inside the query string — the
  same silent 404 the scheme check already guards against.
- injectAssetBaseIntoHtml and insertBootstrap take object parameters, per the
  repo standard for functions with more than one argument.
- Label the ADR's fenced code block (markdownlint MD040).

* test(app): execute the bootstrap body directly instead of regexing it out

The test pulled the script body back out of the rendered tag with
/<script>([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/, which meant it reverse-engineered the output of
the function it was testing, and tripped CodeQL's bad-HTML-filtering rule (the
pattern does not match <SCRIPT>). Nothing here filters HTML — it was extracting
a body we had just generated — but the indirection was not worth keeping.

Export assetBaseBootstrapBody and have assetBaseBootstrapScript wrap it, so the
test runs exactly the JS the browser runs. Output is byte-identical: verified
against the previous implementation for the same-origin sentinel, a CDN base,
a percent-encoded base and a base containing $1.

* docs(adr): correct how the SaaS pipeline uploads CDN assets

ADR-086 claimed the SaaS deploy pipeline invokes
platform/app/scripts/upload-assets-to-cdn.sh. It does not — langwatch-saas
inlines the same aws s3 sync in build-and-push-artifacts.yaml, which the
script's own header already documents. The two descriptions contradicted
each other.

State the script as this repo's reference implementation and the prefix
contract it fixes, and say the pipeline inlines the same sync, so the ADR
matches the script.

* docs: name the CDN prefix git-<short-sha> everywhere

ADR-086 already said the prefix is the deployed image tag, git-<short-sha>,
in the sentence fixing the contract — but described it as <commit-sha> two
paragraphs earlier, and the same loose placeholder had spread to the spec,
the upload script's header, the asset-base docstring and the chart values.

The two are not interchangeable: the running app requests git-<short-sha>
via LANGWATCH_ASSET_BASE, so anyone implementing the S3 sync from the
<commit-sha> spelling writes to a prefix the app never asks for.

Comments and docs only.

fix(ci): render the prerelease smoke check with autogen enabled (#6615)

fix(event-sourcing): floor the group queue's ready score so the age gauge cannot report 56 years (#6618)

* fix(event-sourcing): floor the group queue's ready score at a plausible epoch

gq_oldest_pending_age_milliseconds occasionally reported ~1.786e12 ms, about
56 years of age. Observed in production on 2026-07-31 14:00-15:00 and
2026-08-03 12:00-13:00 UTC. The Events Backed Up alert reads max(...)/1000, so
every one of those samples was a guaranteed spurious fire.

The mechanism was `??`, not the empty-queue case (the collector already returns
0 there, and the unblock sentinel was already excluded). queueManager's
standalone-job score function returned `payload.occurredAt ?? 0`, and
GroupQueue.send coalesced with `this.score?.(payload) ?? Date.now()`. `??` does
not catch 0 or NaN, so a payload with no usable occurrence time staged at the
epoch and stayed the oldest thing in the queue.

Three layers:

- the producers pick a meaningful fallback. A missing occurredAt means "we
  never recorded when this happened", so it scores now, which is what every
  un-scored producer already did.
- GroupQueue validates whatever a score function returns, at all four score
  sites (send, sendBatch, the exhausted-retry re-stage, the poison park),
  against MIN_PLAUSIBLE_EPOCH_MS (2020-09-13).
- both age gauges refuse to read a score below that floor, and raise
  gq_ready_score_implausible_total for each row they refused, so the corruption
  is a signal rather than a silent skip.

This removes one specific false signal. It does not by itself quieten Events
Backed Up - that gauge is legitimately enormous much of the time.

specs/event-sourcing/ready-score-integrity.feature

* fix(event-sourcing): bound the ready score two-sided against the staging clock

Review found the fixed 2020-09-13 floor was the wrong shape. The score for the
highest-volume producers is a customer-supplied OTLP timestamp (recordDataPoint,
contributeMetricFacts, contributeLogFacts), whose domain is unbounded on both
sides of any constant:

- a tenant shipping logs stamped 2021-01-01 cleared the floor and still read as
  ~5 years of backlog, i.e. the identical spurious fire one day above it
- there was no upper bound at all, and dispatch scans ZRANGEBYSCORE "-inf" now,
  so a clock set to 2030 hid a group from dispatch for four years while its jobs
  counted against totalPending. The previous test suite blessed this.

So the bound is now relative to the staging clock and two-sided:
MAX_SCORE_PAST_SKEW_MS (24h) and MAX_SCORE_FUTURE_SKEW_MS (5min), with
MIN_PLAUSIBLE_EPOCH_MS kept as the absolute backstop the relative bounds cannot
provide - a worker booting before NTP reads Date.now() in 1970 and every score
is then plausible relative to that, so the fallback is checked too. Same shape
and vocabulary as isUsableAnchorMs in traceAnalytics.foldProjection.ts.

Nothing legitimate needs the future side wider: every registered score function
returns a past time, deferral is expressed as `delay` added after the score, and
the retry paths compute Date.now() + backoffMs without passing through here.

Also from the review:

- the counter is raised at the staging fallback, not by scanning the ready set.
  The scan could never fire: the guard replaces the bad score before it is
  written, so it would report zero for ever while the producer carried on.
- a fifth score-writing site, restageDrainedSiblings, staged originalScore
  unvalidated. A legacy row at 0 was rewritten at 0 on every batch failure and
  never healed, and because the exhausted-retry path did re-score, one failure
  left siblings ordered ahead of the job they were drained behind.
- the score functions no longer repair a supplied value, so it reaches the queue
  where the producer can be named. An absent occurredAt is still scored now and
  is not reported, because that is the design rather than a defect.

The integration test the review asked for earned its place immediately: it
caught a missing gqReadyScoreImplausibleTotal import that every unit test
passed over, because none of them constructs a GroupQueueProcessor.

specs/event-sourcing/ready-score-integrity.feature

* fix(event-sourcing): keep the implausible-score counter to producers only

Three review threads on #6618.

restageScore no longer raises gq_ready_score_implausible_total. Two files
document that counter as staging-only ("Jobs staged with a producer score the
queue rejected"; "Only a value the producer actually supplied counts"), and a
re-stage is not a producer supplying anything.

It cannot be, structurally: originalScore is always read back out of Redis
(scripts.ts:2042/:2151) after this queue wrote it, and staging already required
it to clear MIN_PLAUSIBLE_EPOCH_MS - an absolute floor, so a score that cleared
it once clears it for ever. restageScore can therefore only fire for a row
staged before the guard existed, or one corrupted in Redis. Neither is a broken
score function, so counting them diluted the single signal that is with our own
bookkeeping. The docs were right and the code was wrong.

The counter had no test at all, which is how this got through. The integration
test that already stages a rejected score now asserts the count is exactly 1,
pinning the producer semantics.

Also: `rejected` -> `isRejected` for the boolean-prefix rule, and a grammar fix
in a test title.

fix(scenarios): scope reasoning compatibility to affected judges (#6620)

* fix(scenarios): stop the gpt-5.6 judge 400 with an endpoint-scoped reasoning capability

Scenario runs on a gpt-5.6 judge fail outright: the provider rejects
function tools combined with reasoning on /v1/chat/completions, and the
judge always sends tools with a forced tool choice, so it can never
return a verdict.

We never send reasoning_effort for the judge, so the model applies its
own server-side default and rejects on that - there is nothing in the
request to strip. All six gpt-5.6 entries also mis-declared themselves,
listing reasoning_effort and tools together with no reasoningConfig at
all, so the registry actively asserted the combination works.

Declare the constraint on the model rather than pattern-matching it, and
scope it to the endpoint the provider scopes it to:
reasoningConfig.toolsIncompatibleOn. Enforcement is three-way - the
model reasons, the conflict is declared on this endpoint, and reasoning
can be disabled - so the reasoning models that handle tools perfectly
well are left alone.

nlpgo enforces it at the dispatch chokepoint every chat-completions
caller passes through (the proxy and the in-process executor), silently
and automatically: refusing the request would leave the judge with no
verdict, which is the bug. The capability table is generated from
llmModels.json by cmd/modelcapsgen, so a future model is adopted by
registry data alone.

A model that declares the conflict and cannot disable reasoning is left
exactly as the caller wrote it and logged; the provider's own rejection
stands. Routing those to /v1/responses is the follow-up.

* fix(scenarios): narrow the capability to the endpoint the runtime can honour

Review follow-ups on the endpoint-scoped reasoning capability.

The rule used the endpoint as a predicate, but the rewrite was written to
the chat-completions wire shape: a top-level reasoning_effort string plus
the alias collapse. The generator nonetheless accepted `responses` and
`messages`, so declaring either produced a table entry that would destroy
a legitimate Responses-API `reasoning: {effort, summary}` object, or
Anthropic's `thinking`, and replace it with a key the endpoint rejects.
/v1/responses is the follow-up this work names, so it is the declaration
the next person is most likely to reach for. Refuse it at generation
instead, with the type staying wider than the runtime on purpose.

allowedValues were copied from gpt-5.2, and adding a reasoningConfig also
gives these six models a playground Reasoning dropdown they did not have
before. xhigh is absent from plain gpt-5.1 and its codex siblings, so it
is per-model rather than family-wide and there is no evidence for it on
gpt-5.6. Offering it would be a provider 400 we introduced, so it is
trimmed; none/low/medium/high hold across every non-pro gpt-5.x entry.

The TypeScript resolver had one importer, its own test, and had already
drifted from the Go rule it mirrored (it honoured parameterName, which
the Go side hardcodes and the generator drops). Two implementations that
disagree are worse than one, and the disagreement is what made the
endpoint gap look safe. Delete it; findUndeclaredReasoningModels stays,
being what the baseline test runs on.

Also: both call sites logged the same decision under different event
names and levels, so alerting on the irreconcilable path saw half of it -
unify on one event with an outcome field. And the generator hand-aligned
struct padding, which silently breaks gofmt on the generated file the
first time a longer field appears; run it through go/format instead.

* fix(scenarios): follow the registry's -pro precedent for gpt-5.6 pro tiers

The three gpt-5.6 -pro entries were declared by copying their non-pro
sibling, which contradicts the only -pro evidence the registry holds:
gpt-5-pro and gpt-5.2-pro both carry allowedValues ["high"], defaultValue
"high" and canDisable false.

That was defensible while allowedValues was inert. It stopped being inert
when the reasoningConfig was added, because the playground's Reasoning
dropdown is driven off it - so a user on gpt-5.6-sol-pro was being offered
none, low and medium, and if the -pro precedent holds those are values the
model rejects. Same user-facing 400 as the xhigh case, moved to the other
end of the range, except here we would be introducing it on three models
rather than inheriting it.

Mirror the precedent instead. canDisable false also gives the honest
enforcement outcome: the rule reports the conflict as irreconcilable,
leaves the body byte-for-byte and lets the provider's own 400 stand,
rather than pretending we can fix a tier we cannot reach. Widening later
if gpt-5.6 -pro turns out to accept lower efforts is a data change with no
behaviour risk; declaring canDisable true on a guess is the direction that
cannot be safely undone, because it makes us rewrite a request body.

Side benefit: the irreconcilable path is now reachable from real registry
data instead of only from a fixture, so it is exercised rather than merely
covered.
