feat(charts): alert when a ClickHouse backup stops succeeding (#6436)

* feat(charts): alert when a ClickHouse backup stops succeeding

The clickhouse-serverless chart schedules backups and nothing watched
whether they worked. Adds Prometheus alerting rules, off by default,
built entirely on kube-state-metrics so the chart ships no exporter.

The primary rule is freshness rather than failure: a CronJob that is
suspended, deleted, or silently rescheduled produces no failure event at
all, so a failure-only alert stays quiet while backups stop happening. It
carries a second branch for a backup that has never succeeded even once,
which has no kube_cronjob_status_last_successful_time series and so is
invisible to the obvious form of the query.

Each target also gets a faster failure alert scoped to recently created
Jobs, a suspension alert, and an absent-metrics alert so that losing the
CronJob or kube-state-metrics is noisy rather than silently resolving
every other rule.

* fix(charts): let backup alerts target a CronJob this chart does not create

Adds cronjobName for an exact CronJob name, alongside cronjob for a
suffix the release fullname is prepended to. The README already promised
targets could name CronJobs the chart does not create; only the prefixed
form existed, so such a target selected a name that does not exist and
ClickHouseBackupCronJobMissing would have fired forever. Setting both or
neither now fails the render.

Extends the tests to cover the PrometheusRule output mode and to assert
the disabled cases by the manifests that come out rather than by how helm
reports an empty --show-only selection.

fix(ui): give the onboarding accent surfaces a dark mode, and stop the assistant tabs disagreeing with the docs (#6653)

* fix(ui): give the onboarding accent surfaces a dark mode, and stop the assistant tabs disagreeing with the docs

A customer evaluating the product hit two things on the first screens they
saw. The onboarding intent card's title became unreadable the moment they
picked it: the selected background was `orange.50`, a raw palette step that
renders the same near-white in both modes, under a title on `color="fg"`,
which flips to near-white in dark mode. Same untreated value sat on the icon
chips of three onboarding screens.

The fix is one accent-surface module naming both sides of every accent, so
there is a single place to change it. SelectableIconCard already had the
right pair hardcoded and now reads it from there too.

Separately, the Token Created dialog offered two coding assistants while
the docs publish the MCP server for more than that, and the same file
listed five *different* editors for its config-path chips. Both surfaces
now come from one CODE_ASSISTANTS list. Assistants with a published
installer (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) get their terminal command; the
rest name the config file they read instead of being handed a command
that does not exist.

Regression coverage reads the injected stylesheet rather than computed
style, because jsdom cannot resolve Chakra v3's emitted rules and returns
a transparent background in both modes — the obvious assertion proves
nothing.

The wider defect class — no written rule, no lint check — is #6652.

* fix(api-keys): drop the Gemini tab rather than ship an mcp add command that does not run

Review caught that the Gemini builder emitted

  gemini mcp add langwatch --env LANGWATCH_API_KEY=… -- npx -y @langwatch/mcp-server

which Gemini's CLI does not parse: its options must precede the server
name, and `--` separates Gemini's own flags from arguments passed to the
MCP server process rather than introducing the command. It was modelled
on the Codex builder, where `--` genuinely is the separator.

That string sits behind the "you won't be able to see it again" warning,
so a user who copies it spends their one look at the token on a line that
fails. Removing the tab is the honest state until the command is checked
against a real CLI; the whole fix is #6654.

Codex loses its config-path chip for a related reason: the chip row is
rendered from every entry carrying a configPath, and Codex reads TOML
while the block above it renders JSON. The base branch deliberately
omitted it. Also tracked in #6654.

Claude Code and Codex commands are unchanged and were proven byte-identical
to main across every flag combination.

* test(api-keys): stop the Gemini-exclusion guard claiming to cover a spec scenario

The guard added alongside the removal carried
`@scenario "An assistant without an install command points at its config
file"`, which it does not exercise — it asserts an entry's absence by key.
The scenario was already correctly bound by the test above it, so parity
stayed green while an annotation pointed at the wrong test: exactly the
vacuous-binding shape the repo warns about, in miniature.

Dropped the annotation and renamed the test to say what it actually does,
including the issue that retires it.

* fix(api-keys): bind the spec annotations that bound nothing, and test the rendered tabs

check:feature-parity was FAILING and the earlier runs missed it — the summary
was never read, only one feature's line was grepped.

Four annotations referenced scenarios that do not exist:

  - Three in the onboarding colour-mode test invented titles for scenarios
    never written to a .feature file. This is a bug fix, and the repo does not
    open feature files for bug fixes, so the annotations go rather than the
    scenarios arriving.
  - The fourth was self-inflicted: a comment saying the test carries no
    "@scenario" annotation contains the literal token, so the parser bound the
    prose that followed it. Reworded.

Also from review:

  - The unselected-card assertion only checked that Chakra emitted a class,
    which a raw background does too. It now asserts the background reaches for
    a semantic `bg` variable and names no palette step. That surface is
    mode-aware by a different route than the selected one — a semantic token's
    value flips at :root, so it has no element-scoped `.dark` rule to find.
  - The assistant tests poked the registry from a file named `.integration.`.
    They now render the dialog, click a tab and read what the user is shown;
    the registry's own shape moved to the unit test where it costs no render.
  - accent-surface's pairs use `as const satisfies`, keeping their literal
    types per the repo's constant guidance.

* test(api-keys): pin each installer's exact command, and make the tab tests selection-sensitive

CodeRabbit reached the same conclusion the review did: asserting a command
merely contains the token and the package name lets a builder swap its
executable or move a flag to the wrong side of the `--` and stay green. That
is exactly how the Gemini command shipped wrong (#6654).

Each installer now has its full expected string pinned, across cloud and
self-hosted and with and without a project id, plus a test that fails if an
installer is added without pinning one.

The tab tests were also passing vacuously: Claude Code is the default tab and
also has a command, so "select Codex, expect a terminal heading" held whether
or not the click did anything. They now start from a config-only assistant so
the selection is what is actually measured, and the config-only case checks
two different assistants so the message is shown to follow the selection.

The command string itself cannot be asserted in the rendered dialog —
ShikiCommandBox is `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` and renders nothing in
jsdom — so the exact strings live in the unit test and the integration tests
prove which treatment the tab selects. Both files say so.

* test(api-keys): cover the project-id and self-hosted flags independently

The four pinned command cases paired a project id only with cloud mode and
self-hosting only with no project id, so the combination where BOTH flags are
present was never built. That is the densest line either builder emits, and
Claude Code's is the awkward one: the project id goes before the `--` while
the endpoint goes after the api key at the very end. Nothing checked it.

Now a full 2x2 per assistant, driven by a combo table so the matrix is
visible rather than implied, with every expected string still written out in
full. Eight cases, up from four.

The table is `as const` — it is a static fixture and nothing should mutate it.

feat(auth): support AWS Cognito and OneLogin as self-hosted SSO providers (#6606)

* feat(auth): support AWS Cognito and OneLogin as self-hosted SSO providers

Both speak OpenID Connect, so both are wired the way Okta already is: the
operator supplies a client id, a client secret and the issuer, and every
endpoint is read from the issuer's discovery document.

For Cognito that discovery document is what carries the hosted-UI domain, so
the operator never has to find and copy that domain separately, and the three
COGNITO_* variables the app already validated are enough on their own.

Cognito was previously advertised without working. The chart README documented
six cognito values, _helpers.tpl validated them, and env-create.mjs accepted
COGNITO_CLIENT_ID/SECRET/ISSUER, but values.yaml had no cognito key and the
Deployment never emitted the variables, so setting NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER=cognito
logged "cannot mount" and silently fell back to email mode. The chart now
renders both providers, and a render test asserts what the container receives
rather than what the template says.

Verified against a real Cognito user pool on lw-dev.

* docs(auth): correct the stale next.config.mjs reference on the pinned callback path

The Next rewrite it named has not existed since the Vite migration. The path
works because the genericOAuth plugin registers each config in
ctx.socialProviders, which is what the core callback route resolves against.

* style(auth): drop em dashes from the comments added here

* feat(auth): route legacy callbacks for every generic-OAuth provider, and add a generic OIDC one

Two review findings, both real.

The legacy-callback rewrite table in api-router.ts only listed auth0 and okta,
while cognito and onelogin pinned the same legacy path. That did not 404: the
request fell through to the /api/auth/* catch-all and better-auth's core social
callback picked the provider out of ctx.socialProviders, so sign-in worked while
quietly taking a different code path from the two that are rewritten. The table
is now derived from the provider list itself, so the two halves cannot drift,
and legacyCallbackParity fails if they do.

A reviewer pointed out they had already run LangWatch against their own OIDC
identity provider by claiming it was auth0. Naming a provider should buy
documented setup steps, not capability, so `oidc` joins the list: any issuer
publishing a discovery document now works without pretending to be something
else. The named entries stay because operators look for their provider by name
and Cognito's issuer-vs-hosted-domain distinction is worth spelling out.

Also from review: the chart test renders once per flag set instead of eight
times and surfaces helm's error text, its provider count was wrong and its
third case had no scenario binding, the duplicated auth0 @param annotations are
gone, and the .env.example provider comments are complete sentences.

Verified against the real Cognito pool through the rewritten path, and again
with NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER=oidc pointed at that same pool.

* test(auth): assert the PKCE challenge reaches the identity provider

The config carries pkce: true and the unit test checks the flag, but only the
emitted authorization URL shows whether it arrived, and the integration suite
is the only place that looks at that URL.

* fix(auth): a trailing slash on NEXTAUTH_URL no longer breaks the redirect URL

Identity providers compare redirect URLs by exact string, so a deployment
URL written as `https://host/` produced
`https://host//api/auth/callback/cognito`, which does not match the
`https://host/api/auth/callback/cognito` the operator registered, and the
provider refuses the sign-in. NEXTAUTH_URL is written by hand in a values
file or an env var, which is exactly where a trailing slash comes from.

Verified the new unit test fails without the fix rather than passing
vacuously.

Along with it, from the same review pass:

- The parity test read the router source through an inline `import()`,
  which the repo bans outside the SDK CLI boot path.
- The env schema comment said the generic provider is "configured by
  issuer alone" directly above the three variables it needs.
- The docs said a discovery document returning `authorization_endpoint`
  meant the issuer was correct, which reads as a compatibility check when
  it only proves the issuer resolves. They now name the three endpoints
  LangWatch reads and the flow the client has to allow.
- Two comments in the chart test counted providers, so adding one made
  them wrong. They no longer count.
- The comments in `auth-client.tsx` listed the generic-OAuth providers by
  name, which is the same drift that put the legacy-callback rewrite out
  of sync. Generic OAuth is the fall-through there on purpose, so a new
  OIDC provider links correctly without being listed, and the comments
  now say that instead of enumerating.

* test(auth): prove the callback URL an identity provider actually receives

The unit test pins what the provider config carries, but an identity
provider only ever sees the emitted authorization URL, and the redirect it
compares against its registration is a query parameter on that URL. This
asserts it there, through real BetterAuth, which is the only place the
value can be observed the way the provider sees it.

Verified it fails without the normalization: `redirect_uri` comes through
as `http://localhost:5624//api/auth/callback/cognito`.

* test(auth): gate every OIDC provider from the table, not a copy of it

The license-gate tests listed cognito and onelogin by hand, so the generic
oidc provider added later was never gated by them. The gate is
provider-agnostic, so nothing was broken, but these tests are what would
notice if that ever stopped being true for one provider, and one of them
was outside their reach.

They now take the list from PLAIN_OIDC_PROVIDERS, the same source the
legacy-callback rewrites take it from, so a provider added there is
covered without anyone remembering to come back.

* refactor(auth): stop restating the provider list where it can go stale

Two more copies of it, found by sweeping the diff for the drift shape that
produced the legacy-callback bug: a doc comment on
`buildGenericOAuthConfigs` enumerating provider ids, written before the
generic one existed and so missing it, and a hardcoded triple in the
callback-URL test.

Both now come from `PLAIN_OIDC_PROVIDERS`. Places that legitimately
enumerate providers, the chart templates, the env example and the docs,
are left alone: there the list is the content, not a copy of it.

* fix(auth): say on screen when an identity provider could not be started

A licensed deployment that mistyped its provider name or left a client
secret unset lands in email mode, which is the no-lockout guarantee working
as designed, but nothing on screen said so. The gate logs it once at
startup and the sign-in page looks identical to a deployment that never
configured single sign-on, so an operator could believe federation was
being enforced when it was not.

The authentication settings page already explains the other cause of the
same symptom, a deployment that is configured but unlicensed, with the
reasoning that nobody reads server logs to explain a login screen. That
reasoning covers this case too, so it now reports both. They are kept apart
because they are fixed in different places: one by activating a license,
the other by correcting the provider name or its credentials.

Verified both new assertions fail when the notice is restricted back to
the license case.

This deliberately does not change what happens at sign-in. Falling back to
email on a mount failure is a bound guarantee, and failing startup instead
would lock every user out of a licensed install over one typo.

fix(ci): scope the secrets gate to the pull request's own commits (#6683)

* fix(ci): scope the secrets gate to the pull request's own commits (#6681)

TruffleHog's git source walks `git log --all` — every ref in the clone —
unless it is given a `--branch`. `--since-commit` is not a substitute: it
only stops the walk on reaching that exact commit, and `--all` interleaves
other refs' newer commits ahead of it, so they are scanned first. One
branch's finding therefore failed every open pull request in the repository.
gitleaks beside it was already scoped.

Both scanners now go through .github/scripts/secrets-scan.sh, which pins the
range to one local ref (actions/checkout leaves HEAD detached on a pull
request, so there is no branch name to hand TruffleHog otherwise) and fails
loudly if the scan reaches no commits at all — a mis-aimed scope reports the
same green check as a clean one.

The scoping is tested against throwaway repositories built to match the ref
layout actions/checkout produces, running the real scanners, in the same job
that installs them.

* fix(ci): harden the secrets gate per review

- Tolerate a failed base-ref fetch when the ref is already local, so a
  transient network error cannot paint a red check that has nothing to do
  with secrets.
- Extend the empty-scan safeguard to gitleaks — the spec rule is "both
  scanners are scoped the same way", and a scope can be mis-aimed on either.
  The guard now takes the scanner's parsed work counter (chunks for
  trufflehog, commits for gitleaks) and an unparseable report fails too.
- Verify both scanner tarballs against their release checksum files before
  extraction, under pipefail.
- Reference #6684 from the allowlist comment instead of "deferred half" —
  the non-narrowing AND entry now has a tracker.

fix: make missing-model and relayed LLM failures handled errors (#6619)

* fix(aigateway): make the missing-model rejection diagnosable

/v1/messages returned 154,597 HTTP 400s over five days against roughly
20,000 successes, all of them one virtual key posting bodies with no
top-level "model" in a round-the-clock retry loop. Neither the response
nor the metrics could have told anyone that.

The response said "missing model field", which names no field, no body
and no endpoint, so the operator on the other end had nothing to
correct. It now names the field, its type, where it belongs, the
endpoints that require it and a worked example, and it states
"fault": "customer" the way errProviderNotAllowed already does - model
resolution runs before SetRequestLabels, so a rejected request is
recorded with model="unknown" and the message is the only place the
detail can live.

The metrics could not see it either. gateway_http_requests_total carries
no caller identity, and customer faults log at info, correctly, which is
also why nothing an operator watches moved while six figures of
rejections accumulated. gateway_client_rejects_total{code, vk_id} counts
them at the one point that has already decided whose fault a failure is
(faultForCode in the writeError choke point), so the counter cannot
drift from the log line.

The label set is deliberately small. Project is redundant with the
virtual key and model is caller-controlled on a key permitting arbitrary
names, which is the unbounded-label trap modelLabel exists to cap; code
is a closed enum and vk_id is control-plane-minted, the same pairing
gateway_rate_limit_denied_total already uses. The choke point reaches
the recorder through the request context, seeded by the metrics
middleware alongside the dispatch labels, because writeError is called
from two dozen sites that never received the router's dependencies.

* fix(langyagent): stop the relay discarding the LLM error body it needs

The relay logs "otelrelay llm error body not a typed envelope; captured
best-effort", and five turns in the same five-day window failed with
"agent error carried no captured LLM cause". The causes were recoverable
in principle - the relay does log the provider's own sentence, which is
the one place that sentence is allowed to go - but two gaps threw the
body away before it got there.

The probe read three known dialects (error.message, detail, message) and
then fell back to the raw text only if the body did not open with a
brace or a bracket. Every other JSON shape yielded "": a JSON:API
errors array, an error nested one level deeper than the probe looks, a
bare code with no prose. The line was left holding a byte count and
nothing else. Anything the probe does not recognise now travels as the
bounded raw body under raw_body_snippet - a distinct field, because a
snippet nobody has parsed must not be read as the provider's own
sentence. boundMessage already caps at 2048 bytes on a rune boundary, so
the field is bounded by construction.

The bound is not enough for the second case. One production failure was
a 41 KB Cloudflare Access login page returned to the agent's proxied
model calls, and bounding an interstitial records two thousand
characters of stylesheet. An HTML body now contributes its title and
nothing else; with the status already on the line, "Sign in ·
example.cloudflareaccess.com" plus a 403 is the whole diagnosis. HTML is
detected from the declared content type and from the leading markup,
because an edge that returns a login page in place of an API response is
not reliably careful about its headers.

None of this changes what a customer reads. The provider's prose stays
out of the error frame and off the card, exactly as before; this is
about what reaches our logs.

* test(aigateway): prove the reject counter cannot be minted before auth

gateway_client_rejects_total carries a per-virtual-key label, which is
only bounded if every value is control-plane-minted. That claim was
resting on reading the middleware order, so assert it by driving the
real stack instead: a caller with no API key, and a caller whose 64-char
bearer token the control plane rejects, both leave the counter with no
series at all, and the caller's token never appears in a scrape.
AuthMiddleware answers both with herr.WriteHTTP directly rather than
through writeError, so neither reaches the choke point that records.
The counterpart is asserted too - an authenticated caller posting a body
with no model is counted against vk-test, the key the control plane
minted.

Two corrections fall out of establishing that. The docs entry listed
invalid_api_key as an example code, which the test shows can never land
on this counter, so it now names reachable codes and points operators at
gateway_http_requests_total{status="401"} for auth failures instead. The
recorder's keyless case was described as an unauthenticated rejection;
it is unreachable through the pipeline and is really a check that the
placeholder is a fixed constant rather than caller input, so it says so.

* fix: address review - per-surface model message, counter scope, relay guards

Five findings from the independent review.

The missing-model message named the wrong endpoints for four surfaces.
ModelResolve is an unconditional interceptor, so it also fires for
/v1/embeddings, /v1/audio/speech, /v1/audio/transcriptions and the Gemini
/v1beta passthrough - and those disagree about where a model comes from.
Transcription reads a multipart form part and Gemini reads the URL path,
so a caller was told to add a top-level JSON field to a request carrying
no JSON, and that none of the three named endpoints was theirs. The old
message was vague; that one was misleading. Resolve now takes the
request rather than the bare model string (three arguments still, so the
argument-limit rule is untouched) and names the caller's own surface. A
request type with no entry stays surface-agnostic rather than inheriting

fix(event-sourcing): bisect a failing coalesced batch instead of retrying it whole (#6555)

* fix(event-sourcing): bisect a failing coalesced batch instead of retrying it whole

A coalesced batch is all-or-nothing: the fold state is written once at the
end, so any throw discards the work for every payload in the batch, and the
retry re-drains the same siblings into the same batch. One unprocessable
payload therefore took up to `coalesceMaxBatch - 1` healthy payloads down
with it on every attempt until the group blocked. Recovery from a
size-driven failure was equally undirected — a batch too heavy for a
downstream query's budget only succeeded if the retry happened to
re-assemble a lighter set.

On a retryable batch failure the dispatch now splits the batch in half and
runs each half in sequence, recursing until it either fits or the failure is
attributable to a single payload. One mechanism covers both cases, because
both are "this set fails but a smaller set might not".

Ordering is preserved: halves are contiguous and awaited sequentially, never
concurrently, because a fold derives fields from arrival order. That same
invariant bounds what this can do — a throw propagates immediately, so
payloads after the offender are not attempted; stepping over one would apply
later payloads across a gap the fold cannot see. So bisection recovers
everything before the offender and names it, rather than losing the whole
batch. Rescuing what queued behind it needs an explicit decision about that
gap (#6482).

Re-running a payload that already applied is safe: fold redelivery is
idempotent via the store's applied-event-id set (#6016), which is what makes
a partially applied batch recoverable rather than a double-count.

Non-retryable failures are not split — they fail identically at every size.

Adds `gq_batch_bisections_total`, which counts splits rather than batches:
isolating one payload costs log2(batchSize), so read it as a rate.

Closes #6510

* docs(event-sourcing): state the bisection counter's real cost, and count commits rather than distinct ids

Two review findings on the bisection change.

The counter's doc claimed isolating one payload costs `log2(batchSize)`
increments. That is wrong twice: for a single unprocessable payload the
count moves with the payload's POSITION (a batch of 5 costs 2 or 3, not
2.32), and a batch failing purely on size keeps splitting until every part
fits, approaching `batchSize - 1` — far above `log2(batchSize)`. Say what
the counter does (one increment per split) and give both cost shapes.

The poison test recorded committed payloads in a Set, which cannot tell
"committed once" from "committed twice" — exactly the failure worth watching
when a dispatch applies part of a batch before failing. Record an array and
assert the healthy prefix's per-payload counts are all equal: the prefix
commits as a unit, so equality holds under any number of redeliveries while
one payload applied an extra time breaks it.

Scope is deliberate: this pins that bisection does not re-run a payload it
already committed. Cross-dispatch redelivery is at-least-once by design and
made safe by the fold store's applied-event-id set, which has its own suite;
this handler is a mock with no such guard, so asserting it here would test
the mock rather than the queue.

* fix(event-sourcing): name the payload a bisection isolates, and pin the split schedule

Five review findings on the bisection change.

The isolate was anonymous. When bisection narrowed to a single failing
payload it rethrew the error unchanged, so nothing recorded WHICH payload
was at fault — and the terminal record anchors to the dispatched job, which
for a failing drained sibling is the wrong job entirely. That identity is
the whole reason bisection beats a plain retry, so it is now carried:
batch members travel as {payload, stagedJobId} pairs, and narrowing to one
logs the offending staged-job id and stamps it on the span. Only a batch
that a split actually produced is reported as an isolate — an un-split
single is just a job that failed, and claiming otherwise would send an
investigator hunting for a bisection that never happened.

The ordering test proved each sub-batch was internally sorted and
contiguous, which two concurrently-running halves would also satisfy. It now
pins the exact left-first descent ([8, 4, 2, 2, 4, 2, 2] for a batch of 8
capped at 2) and asserts no batch ever overlaps another, with the handler
yielding so an overlap would actually be observable.

The non-retryable fast-fail branch was documented but untested; it now has a
test asserting a CRITICAL-category error is never split.

A comment claimed a split singleton reaches the single-payload handler. It
does not — a one-payload batch still goes through processBatch. Corrected.

HEALTHY_PREFIX gets `as const`, per the repo's convention for internal
constants.

The failure path moves into splitFailedBatch so the added branch does not
push processBatchBisecting past the cognitive-complexity gate.

* test(event-sourcing): wait on the applied set itself, not on a handler-call count

CI caught a real interaction with bisection. This test sends a three-event
chain into a coalescing group whose handler fails twice, waits for two
handler applications, then asserts all three ids are in the applied set.

Counting applications was a sound barrier while a failing batch retried
whole: the chain could only ever land together, so a count of two implied
the third had landed with it. A failing batch is now bisected, so the chain
can land in separate sub-batches within a single attempt, and a count of two
no longer implies anything about the third. CI observed exactly that —
["chain-0", "chain-1"] with chain-2 still in flight.

The accumulation being tested is unaffected; only the barrier was too weak.
Poll the applied set directly, which is immune to however the queue divides
the work and still fails within the timeout if accumulation is genuinely
broken.

* fix(event-sourcing): carry the applied-id watermark across bisected sub-batches, forward the delivery, and bound the descent (#6578)

Two review findings (langwatch-agent) plus the pre-existing gap they exposed.

The applied-id watermark was lost across bisection leaves. A fold commit
REPLACES the applied-event-id set on a fresh delivery — deliberate garbage
collection that keeps the set bounded at one delivery's ids, resting on the
assumption of one save per delivery. Bisection makes several: each later
leaf's commit erased the ids the earlier leaves recorded, so the redelivery
after a failed later leaf re-applied the committed prefix. Counters, sums
and appends double-count silently, with no cache loss required.

Worse, the merge-on-retry branch that should at least protect retries never
ran in the deployed system at all: the shared queue's wrappers dropped the
delivery argument on both the single and batch paths, pinning
deliveryAttempt at 1 everywhere. The idempotency suite could not see it —
its harness wires its own queue definition and forwards the delivery
itself.

The chain now holds end to end:
- both wrappers forward the delivery (eventSourcing.ts);
- JobDelivery carries a continuation flag, set by the bisector for every
  sub-batch call after the first successful commit of a dispatch;
- the flag travels queue manager → read context → router → store context;
- the commit rule becomes: replace only on the first save of a fresh
  delivery; merge on continuation saves and on retries. The bounded-set
  property is preserved and its lifecycle test still passes.

Each link is pinned by a test that its removal fails (mutation-checked):
the wrapper by eventSourcing.deliveryForwarding, the queue-manager and
router links by projectionRouter.continuationForwarding — the router link
because the batch callback rebuilds the context field-by-field and
silently dropped the flag in the first version of this change — and the
end-to-end behaviour by a foldRedeliveryIdempotency scenario that drives
real bisection through a real store: root fails, a two-event prefix leaf
commits, a later singleton fails, and the retry folds each event exactly
once (count 6-vs-4 without the fix).

Bisection work within one locked attempt is now bounded. A batch degrading
toward singletons walked the entire tree — ~2N sequential handler calls —
while the heartbeat kept renewing the group's active key, holding the lock
and a worker slot instead of yielding. After
MAX_BISECTION_SPLITS_PER_DISPATCH (32) splits the failure propagates
un-split: committed prefixes stay committed, the remainder re-stages, and
exponential backoff takes over. Sized to cover every useful descent
(isolating one poison payload in a 256 batch costs 8 splits; converging to
sub-batches of 8 costs 31) while cutting off only the pathological walk.
Pinned by driving the bisector directly with a 64-entry singleton-only
handler — dispatch-level shapes vary with staging timing, the contract
must not.

The existing retry-chain lifecycle test also swapped its barrier: it waited
on a handler-call count, which was a sound proxy only while a failing batch
retried whole. It now polls the applied set itself, immune to how the queue
divides the work.

* fix(event-sourcing): prefix the new booleans, de-race the descent tests

Three review findings.

The new booleans lacked the repo's required is/has prefix: JobDelivery's
continuation is now isContinuation, the store contexts carry
isDeliveryContinuation, and the bisector's dispatch state reads
hasCommitted / isNarrowed. Names only — no behaviour change; the
mutation-checked forwarding tests pass unchanged after the rename.

The exact-descent and poison ordering tests staged their payloads already
due, so the dispatcher could claim the first job before the rest finished
staging and assemble a partial root — failing the exact-sequence assertion
with no self-heal. They now future-date the batch, the same treatment the
fold-suite scenario already carried. The ordering test's contiguity check
moves from payload values (which the retiming repurposed as timestamps) to
payload ids, which is what arrival order is actually made of.

* fix(event-sourcing): record delivered ids at commit, and treat a throwing call as a write

Self-review found the bisection change amplified an existing double-apply
rather than closing it: 4 applies is correct, main does 5, this branch did 7.

Two causes, each now pinned by a test that fails without its fix.

A commit recorded only the ids it folded FRESH. An id dropped as
already-applied is still an id the committed state absorbs, so a
first-attempt commit — which replaces the set as bounded garbage collection
— EVICTED any redelivered id riding along with new ones. Whoever saw that id
next treated it as new and folded it twice. The batch commit now records the
delivered ids; the other three commit sites already did, so the parameter is
renamed `deliveredIds` to stop the name lying at one of four call sites.
Bounded exactly as before: one delivery's ids, against MAX_APPLIED_EVENT_IDS.

`dispatch.hasCommitted` was set only when the handler RETURNED, so a handler
that stored and then threw — a reactor failing after the fold committed —
left the flag false and the first sub-batch ran as a fresh delivery, its
commit replacing what the failed call had just recorded. The flag is now set
on both outcomes and before the split recurses: it means "an earlier call in
this descent may have written", which is what a later commit needs to know.
It only ever turns a replace into a merge, so over-setting is the safe
direction.

Also from the review, both non-blocking:

The split budget moves behind LANGWATCH_GQ_BISECTION_SPLIT_BUDGET, mirroring
the quarantine and claim-strike knobs, with 0 disabling bisection outright —
so restoring pre-bisection behaviour is an env change rather than a deploy.
Covered by a test asserting a zero budget produces exactly one call.

An over-broad `\bnarrowed\b` rename had reached operator prose, including the
log line whose whole job is naming the offending payload during an incident.
Reverted to English in the message and the two comments.

feat(model-providers): fold Google Agent Platform into Gemini — one provider, two doors (#6633)

* feat(model-providers): fold Google Agent Platform into Gemini — one provider, two doors

Gemini is sold through two Google services and a key opens exactly one:
an AI Studio key answers on generativelanguage.googleapis.com, an Agent
Platform key on aiplatform.googleapis.com at a path naming the project
and location. Same models, same wire shape, same auth header — verified
live with one key of each kind. So Agent Platform is not a provider with
its own (empty) model list, which is why #6352 left it unlocking zero
models: it is a second door into the gemini provider.

The gemini credential now optionally carries GEMINI_PROJECT and
GEMINI_LOCATION. Pair present: validation probes and the gateway
dispatches through the Agent Platform door (a derived Bifrost provider,
base type Gemini, whose base URL names the path — the anthropic-compat
mechanism generalised with a baseType). Pair absent: everything works as
before. An Agent Platform key pasted without the pair gets Google's
API_KEY_SERVICE_BLOCKED answer surfaced as a named restriction telling
the customer to fill the two fields — not "invalid key".

Model names stay gemini/* everywhere: no catalog rows, no new stored id
format, nothing downstream learns a new prefix. Stored
google_agent_platform rows fold in via pnpm task
migrateAgentPlatformToGemini (field rename inside the encrypted blob +
provider flip; scopes and enabled state untouched).

* fix(model-providers): the fold migration could never read a row

ModelProvider is a tenancy-scoped model: the multitenancy middleware
rejects a where-clause carrying neither a row id, an organizationId nor
a scope predicate, so the task's bare { provider } scan threw on its
first query — the migration was dead on arrival in a real environment.
Found by running it against a seeded legacy row, not by a test: the unit
tests mocked Prisma wholesale, so the guard never ran.

Walks organizations and scans per organizationId, which satisfies the
guard via the ADR-021 anchor every row carries and — unlike the
per-project walk the sibling task uses — also reaches rows granted at
ORG and TEAM scope. The test mock now enforces the same contract, and
fails with the production error message against the old scan.

* chore: revert generated-file churn from start:prepare:files

* fix(model-providers): embedding availability follows the row that runs, and the fold walk is bounded

Two review findings, both real.

The embedding filter asked "can any accessible Gemini credential serve
embeddings", but a catalog model is listed in no credential's own model
list, so execution keeps the scope-collapse winner — enabled first, then
narrowest scope. An Agent Platform credential shared with one project and
an AI Studio one shared with the organization therefore ran against the
project's, which answers 404 on the embeddings endpoint, while the picker
happily offered the models. The rule now asks the question execution asks:
the winning scope tier decides, and a tie inside that tier hides, because
either row could win.

The answer also moved server-side. It depends on the API key's presence
and, for an env-fed credential, on the server's own environment — neither
of which the browser can see, and one of which it must never receive. One
helper (geminiDoor.ts) now decides the door for both the request path and
the read path, so the picker and the request cannot disagree.

The fold migration loaded every organization and fired one query per
organization at once, then held every matching row. ModelProvider's
tenancy guard takes organizationId as a string and not an `in` list, so
the per-organization query stays; the walk is now paged, each page folds
before the next loads, and at most five scans are ever in flight.

* refactor(model-providers): drop the fold migration from this change

Converting stored google_agent_platform rows into gemini rows is a
one-off data migration run per deployment, and it ships separately. This
change stops at making both doors work.

Nothing here depended on the migration having run: the retired provider
stays a known, deprecated provider, so existing rows keep validating
through the Agent Platform door and keep dispatching under their old
name. The registry entry (and its validation and materialiser branches)
can only be deleted in a release after those rows have been converted —
the comment now says so without naming a task that no longer exists here.

* fix(model-providers): a retired provider refuses new credentials on the server, not just in the menu

Hiding the tile is not enforcement. updateModelProvider only checked that
the provider key exists in the registry, so a direct API call, an SDK, or
a page open since before the change could still create a brand-new
google_agent_platform row — and a population that keeps growing never
reaches zero, which is the one condition for ever deleting the
compatibility entry and its validation and materialiser branches.

The refusal is keyed on there being no existing row, so editing,
disabling, re-scoping and deleting a stored row all stay open: that is
what keeps a deployment mid-fold from being stranded, and it is the half
that has to keep working.

The flag now names what replaced the provider, which is what turns the
refusal into something a caller can act on — the customer is told to add
Gemini rather than that a thing they asked for is unavailable. One
narrowing helper replaces the cast the settings page was already doing,
so the flag has a single reader.

* chore: stop reverting the generated API client's docs to an older wording

The earlier churn revert restored this generated file to its pre-change
state, but main had meanwhile regenerated it with clearer prose for
cycle_anchor_at. The branch was therefore undoing a docs improvement it
never meant to touch — six comment lines, no behaviour.

It also had a cost nobody would guess from the diff: this file is the
only thing on the branch matching the TypeScript SDK path filter, so it
pulled the expensive real-HTTP e2e suite into every run of a PR that
changes no SDK code.

* test(model-providers): the allowed-edit binding now proves the write lands

Both "still allowed" assertions were `rejects.not.toMatchObject({ code })`,
which passes when the call fails for ANY other reason. Executed, the
stored-row edit was rejecting with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of
undefined (reading 'update')` from the test's own stub — the transaction
handed the repository an empty object. So the scenario "an already-stored
credential under the retired provider can still be changed" was bound to a
test that could only ever prove the guard did not fire, never that the edit
lands. That is the half of the fold contract that has to keep working.

The fake now passes the transaction the same client the outer prisma
carries, plus the tenancy tables a create reads to resolve its
single-organization anchor. Both tests assert the write itself: the edit
records `enabled: false` against the row, the replacement-provider create
records a `gemini` insert.

Both fail on the mutation they are meant to catch: making the guard
unconditional reddens the edit test, removing it reddens the refusal test.

* test(errors): pin the retired-provider copy to the registry slug

Which provider to add instead comes from two places nothing joins:
`deprecated.replacedBy` in the provider registry, and the slug -> brand
name table in presentation.ts. Executed against the real presentation
module, an unmapped slug renders "It has been merged into another
provider" — safe, no raw identifier at the customer, but the one fact the
error exists to give them is gone, and nothing notices.

Drives every deprecated registry entry through explainHandledError and
asserts the copy is not the unnamed fallback. Reddens when the registry
slug and the copy table disagree.

* fix(errors): build the wire payload the copy test reads, instead of casting

`pnpm typecheck:tests` rejected the cast: HandledErrorShape has no
`message` and does require httpStatus, tips, docsUrl, traceId and reasons,
so the object overlapped it too little for TS2352. The cast was hiding
that — the test was asserting against a payload the client can never
actually receive.

Constructs a real HandledErrorShape instead. It also fails honestly if the
shape grows a member, which a cast never would.

feat(model-providers): test a credential you have already saved (#6657)

* feat(model-providers): test a saved credential from the settings list

A customer asked to be able to check a provider they had already set up —
"just a quick hello world or a ping, to make sure I filled in the credentials
in the right way". Until now a credential was only ever checked while it was
being typed, and the form deliberately never shows a stored key back, so
re-checking one meant re-entering a value you cannot see.

Adds a Test Connection action to the provider row. It reuses the existing
probe and sends nothing new: the row id goes out, the stored credential is
resolved server-side, and a verdict comes back.

Three things are load-bearing.

The check has three answers, not two. Five paths through the probe used to
return the same value as a successful check without having sent a packet, and
that was safe only while the answer stayed inside the save path, where a skip
correctly means "do not block the save". Read by a customer it becomes a claim
we cannot support — six of the sixteen registered providers reach one of those
paths, so a two-state result would have reported more than a third of the list
as working. `valid` still says what the save path needs; `outcome` says what a
reader needs.

azure_safety joins the providers we will not probe. It is a content-safety
service that authenticates with a subscription-key header and has no models
route, but nothing in the validation module excluded it and it carries an
endpoint field — enough for a stored endpoint to send it down the bearer
branch and have a perfectly good credential reported as refused. The only
thing standing in the way was a gate in the settings form, which is one
caller. The rule now lives where every caller passes.

The new procedure takes a row id and no endpoint. The save-time path accepts
a base URL from the caller, which is reasonable there because the caller
supplies the key too. Here the credential comes out of storage and may be one
the caller is never allowed to read, so accepting a destination would let
anyone who can edit a provider have this server post the key wherever they
liked. It is also anchored by id against the organization rather than looked
up by provider name inside a project, so the org- and team-scoped rows the
list displays resolve instead of reporting no credential, and it applies both
of the guards the delete path applies — the scope-carrying check is not
redundant in front of the per-scope check, which an empty scope list satisfies
vacuously.

Rate limited per organization and then globally, after authorization, so an
unauthorized caller is refused rather than throttled.

Out of scope, deliberately: a persisted health badge, background
re-validation, and coverage for azure, bedrock and vertex_ai, which need a
real inference call rather than a listing. Those answer "did this credential
expire", which is a different question from "did I fill this in right".

* fix(model-providers): drop connection verdicts when a row may have changed

Review of the preceding commit found the failure it was written to prevent,
displaced in time. A verdict is about the credential that was in the row when
it was asked, and nothing about a row's identity changes when its key does. So
a customer could test a provider, be told the connection works, then edit the
row, paste a bad key, save — and the row would still read "Connection works".
A success claim about a credential nothing ever checked is the one thing this
feature must not produce.

The drawer closing is the moment a row may have changed underneath us, so the
verdicts are dropped there. All of them rather than the edited one: re-asking
is a click, and reasoning about which row was touched buys nothing.

`useCredentialProbeGate` makes the same argument for the save-time probe — a
refusal must not outlive the credential it was about. This is that rule, one
surface over.

Also from the same review:

An unreadable credential no longer presents as an absent one. A row written
before the encryption secret was rotated decrypts to null, which is
indistinguishable from nothing being stored by the time it reaches the copy,
so "no credential is stored" sent that customer off to re-enter a key they
had already entered. It now says the credential could not be read, which is
true either way.

The rate-limit comment no longer promises a ceiling every deployment has. The
shared limiter counts in Redis when one is configured and in a process-local
map otherwise, so several replicas without Redis get the budget per replica
rather than per fleet.

* fix(model-providers): close the in-flight verdict window, and stop the service reaching into the router

Review found that clearing the verdicts is not enough on its own. A probe
already in flight when the map is cleared still resolves afterwards and writes
its answer back, so a customer who edits a row mid-check sees a verdict about
the credential that was there before — the failure clearing was added to
prevent, arriving a second later. `test` now stamps the generation it was asked
in and a write from an older one is discarded. Verified by removing the guard
and watching the new test go red.

Also moves credential validation out of the delivery layer. The service
imported `validateProviderApiKey` from `server/api/routers`, which points the
dependency the wrong way round: a service that needs the router to do its job
cannot be called from anywhere the router is not. It now lives in
`server/modelProviders/` beside its only consumers, with its tests.

That move pays for itself immediately — the hook can now `import type` the
verdict shape from the module that owns it instead of redeclaring it. Types are
erased, so nothing reaches the browser bundle, and a renamed field or a new
outcome becomes a type error rather than a sentence that quietly stops being
true.

The rest, smaller:

- The router's anonymous input schema is now exported from the service and the
  service's input type inferred from it, so runtime validation and the
  compile-time contract cannot drift.
- `testConnection` takes one destructured object rather than two positional
  arguments.
- The retry delay is rounded up before it is rendered. The server sends whole
  seconds today, but this is a client contract read by whatever raises the
  code, and a fraction would print "about 30.427 seconds" and slip past the
  singular check.
- The verdict renders in a polite live region. It arrives well after the click
  that asked for it, and without this a screen reader announces neither the
  transition nor the answer — a button that appears to do nothing.
- `ConnectionTestVerdict` had been inserted directly beneath the doc comment
  for `AddModelProviderMenu`, orphaning it. Moved above it.
- The skip tests assert which reason came back, not merely that the check did
  not run. A wrong reason shows the customer the wrong guidance and passed
  before.
- Four steps in the feature file began with `Or`, which is not a Gherkin
  keyword. `And` reads identically and parses.
- Import order in the service, which is what the lint job was failing on.

* fix(model-providers): send the credential probe through the SSRF validator

The review round on the last push found the hole the "no caller-supplied
endpoint" rule does not close, and it was right.

Refusing an endpoint on the test request stops one route, not the capability.
Several providers expose a configurable endpoint, and the update path preserves
a stored key when the submitted one is the mask — so someone who can manage a
provider but cannot read its secret can save an endpoint they control, run the
test, and have the server deliver the credential there. The address on the row
is a customer-supplied value; it is only the moment of supply that differs.

So the probe now goes out through `ssrfSafeFetch` rather than a bare `fetch`.
That brings the cloud-metadata denylist that applies regardless of
configuration, private-address blocking, and IP pinning so a name cannot
resolve to something else between the check and the connection — the same
protection the webhook destination has had all along, on the path that carries
a credential rather than a payload.

Redirects are refused outright, for the reason `httpDestination.ts` gives:
hop re-validation falls back to the weaker env-gated validator, and measured on
this repo's Node a cross-origin redirect strips `Authorization` but carries
`x-api-key`, `x-goog-api-key` and `xi-api-key` straight through to the new host.
A models listing has no need of a redirect.

This also closes the same hole on the save-time path, which shared the fetch.

The probe tests now stand in for `ssrfSafeFetch` instead of `global.fetch`,
which is the seam the code actually uses; mocking the global would have left
the real validator in the path and made every assertion here about DNS.

Also from the same round:

- The hook no longer casts the mutation result. The cast defeated the point of
  importing the server's type, and an unhandled outcome fell through to
  "can't be tested automatically" — a confident sentence about a verdict nobody
  classified. A `never` check makes a fourth outcome a compile error.
- The hook test is `.ts`; it contains no JSX, and the `.tsx` path matched a
  glob meant for hook implementations.
- `NOT_PROBEABLE` is a `ReadonlySet`.

* fix(model-providers): tell a redirecting endpoint apart from an unreachable one

Refusing to follow a redirect was right — a hop carries the credential to a
host the SSRF validator never saw — but every refusal came back through the
same catch and was reported as "could not reach the provider". An endpoint that
redirects is reachable. Something answered; it just wants us somewhere else.
Saying "unreachable" sends the customer to check their network when what they
need to change is a URL, which is the misdiagnosis this module exists to remove
and the subject of three previous fixes.

A redirect now has its own code and its own sentence, naming the usual cause
(an http:// base URL redirecting to https://). Detected by matching the
helper's message, since it raises a plain Error — the coupling is pinned by a
test, so rewording the helper fails loudly rather than folding the case back
into "unreachable".

Also converts `validateKeyWithCustomUrl` to a named parameter object. It has
four positional parameters, which the repo caps at three; the count only
surfaced now because moving the file made the pre-existing warning read as new
against the merge base.

* refactor(model-providers): pull the branchy parts out of the probe and the hook

The lint gate counts violations per file and rule against the merge base and
fails on an increase, so three complexity warnings the plain lint run does not
fail on were still red in CI. Both are worth fixing on their merits rather than
suppressing.

`validateProviderApiKey` had grown five early returns before it asked anything.
The reasons we decline to probe now live together in `whyNotCheckable`, which
returns the reason or null. Having them in one list is what stops a future
branch quietly returning a pass instead — the failure the third verdict exists
to prevent.

The hook's `test` callback carried the whole verdict-to-copy mapping inline.
That mapping is the part worth reading on its own, so it moved to a pure
`toState`, which also makes the exhaustiveness check the single place a new
outcome has to be handled.

No behaviour change; the same 1345 tests pass. The gate now reports no new
violations and two fewer than the merge base.

* fix(model-providers): pin the redirect marker to its source, and stop the throw carrying a payload

Four from the latest review round, all of them real.

The redirect marker was a copy of a message `utils/ssrfProtection` owns, and
the test reproduced the same copy — so the two agreed with each other and
pinned nothing. Reword the helper and every redirect would have gone back to
"could not be reached" with both sides still green. The message is now exported
from the helper and imported at both ends, and the test mock keeps the rest of
the module real so the constant it asserts against is the true one.

The unhandled-outcome throw serialized the whole verdict into its message. That
message reaches `describeError` in the caller's catch, which can render a plain
Error's text to a customer, and nothing promises a future outcome's fields are
free of credential material. It carries the discriminator now.

`whyNotCheckable`'s comment claimed to gather every reason a check declines to
run. Two of them — an unrecognised provider, and one whose auth we cannot
exercise — are decided by the callers, because both need the registry entry
that function is deliberately not given. The comment says so.

And the provider name is read through the same narrow cast the rest of the file
uses rather than `any`.

* fix(ssrf): let a refused redirect out as itself, not as a connection failure

The redirect handling shipped two commits ago did not work, and its test
passed anyway.

`fetchWithResolvedIp` raises the refusal inside its try, and the catch below
funnels every `Error` through `formatConnectionError`, which rewrites it as
"Connection failed to host:port: …". So the message a caller receives is not
the message this module writes, and the consumer — matching on exact equality
after the last review round tightened it from a substring — never matched.
Every refused redirect was still being reported as "could not reach the
provider", which is the misdiagnosis the whole change was meant to remove.

The test did not catch it because it mocked the fetch helper wholesale and
rejected with the bare message, so the wrapping it was supposed to survive
never ran.

Now a `RedirectRefusedError` type, thrown by the helper and re-thrown
unchanged by that catch, matched by `instanceof` at the far end. No string
crosses the boundary, so there is nothing left to drift.

`fetchWithResolvedIp` had no coverage of `followRedirects: false` at all,
which is why this was invisible. There is a test now, at the real seam, and it
fails when the passthrough is removed.

* test(model-providers): give the settings page tests the mutation the page now calls

Both page tests stub `~/utils/api` with only the procedures the page used
before this branch, and the connection-test hook asks for `testConnection` at
render time. So every test in both files died on a TypeError before reaching
anything it was about — 18 in one, 3 in the other.

Nothing local caught it: `pnpm test:unit` silently drops
`*.integration.test.tsx` from a multi-path run, so the sweep that reported
1345 passing never loaded either file. CI found it. Verified the fix by running
both against native services rather than assuming.

* test(model-providers): watch the seam the probe actually uses

The authorization tests here record outbound requests to prove a refused
caller's credential never leaves. They recorded `globalThis.fetch`, and the
probe now dispatches through undici inside `ssrfSafeFetch`, so the recorder
stopped seeing anything.

One test noticed — the one asserting the admin DOES reach the network, which
went red. The three asserting nobody else does went quiet instead, passing on
an empty list that would have been empty either way. Their own comment had
already named the hazard: "a test that passed because the fetch merely failed
would be worthless". Passing because no fetch is observed at all is worse.

Both seams are recorded now and every assertion reads the union, so a request
cannot leave by a route no assertion is watching. Verified against real
Postgres rather than assumed: 24 in the file, 73 across the directory.

* test(model-providers): bind the row action and the verdict to the page

The connection test was covered at the hook and nowhere else, which left the
wiring itself unbound: the menu item could stop calling the hook, or the verdict
stop rendering, and the suite would have stayed green. That gap has been called
out in this PR's description since the first commit; the page test now has the
mutation mocked, so closing it is three tests.

They drive the real page: pick the action, assert the row id goes out and no
endpoint travels with it, assert the verdict lands on the row, and assert a
provider that could not be checked is never rendered as working.

Verified by neutering the click handler and watching all three go red.

* test(model-providers): pin what the probe actually puts on the wire

Every other test of this module stands in for `ssrfSafeFetch`. That is the
right seam for what the probe decides and the wrong one for what it sends: the
SSRF path tears a URL down to its parts and rebuilds it, so anything riding
outside a header could be dropped in between without a mocked test noticing.

Gemini is why this needs its own file — its key travels in the query string,
and nothing else in the suite would have caught it going missing when the
transport changed under it.

Mocks undici instead, one layer further out, so the real validator and the real
rebuild both run. Written while reviewing this branch, where reading the code
said the query string survived and running it was the only way to know: it
does, along with the bearer header, the POST body, and a non-standard port.

* fix(model-providers): keep both halves of the never-probed fix through the rebase

Main's Gemini fold (#6633) and this branch attacked the same defect from
opposite ends, and the rebase put them in the same three lines.

Main narrowed WHEN validation declines to ask: a credential naming the Agent
Platform door needs no base URL, and without the exemption a legacy row was
declined without a request. This branch changed WHAT a decline says: `unchecked`
rather than a value indistinguishable from a pass. Either alone leaves half the
bug — a row that is never probed, or one that is probed but reported wrong.
Both are kept: the exemption now guards the condition inside `whyNotCheckable`,
which returns the reason.

The fold's two-door branching pushed `validateProviderApiKey` back over the
complexity gate at 19. Two extractions rather than a suppression: which pair of
field names carries the door (two eras of credential reach the same place), and
which door a refusal should name (telling a customer to fill the project and
location when they should clear them sends them the wrong way).

One assertion main added while this branch was open read `toEqual({ valid: true })`.
It now asserts `outcome === "verified"`, which is what that test is actually
about — its own comment says a green check without a request would pass a
revoked key, and `unchecked` also carries `valid: true`, so the old form could
not tell the two apart.

* test(model-providers): pin which of Google's two doors a refusal names

Found by reviewing the rebase: nothing anywhere asserted `meta.googleDoor`.

That matters beyond the refactor. The copy in `presentation.ts` branches on it
to tell a customer whose key was refused either to FILL IN the project and
location or to CLEAR them — opposite instructions, and the wrong one sends them
away confidently doing the wrong thing. The value reaching that branch was
unpinned, so the two-door work and my extraction of it were both riding on
nothing.

Five cases: the pair present and absent, half a pair (which cannot reach Agent
Platform, so must not be offered the clear-it advice), a legacy row reading the
retired field names, and a single-door provider naming no door at all.

Two of them redden when the door is forced to a constant.

fix(mcp-server): authorize every request to the standalone HTTP server (#6641)

* fix(mcp-server): authorize every request to the standalone HTTP server

The standalone MCP HTTP server treated a session id as a credential and
never checked that an API key was real. A coordinated disclosure from an
external security researcher covered four issues, all reproduced against
main and all fixed here.

Origin and bind address. The server validates Origin against an allowlist
on every request, as the MCP transport specification requires. Loopback
origins are always accepted, because DNS rebinding reaches the server
under an attacker-controlled hostname and the browser sends that hostname.
Any other origin has to be listed with --allowedOrigin or
LANGWATCH_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS. The listener now binds 127.0.0.1 by
default, with --host or LANGWATCH_MCP_HTTP_HOST to opt into a wider bind,
and the CLI warns when it is not on loopback. Responses reflect an
allowed origin with Vary: Origin instead of returning a wildcard. The
container image opts into 0.0.0.0 explicitly, since it is unreachable
otherwise.

Credentials in the query string. The ?apiKey= fallback on /sse is gone,
along with its scanner suppression. The SSE session id still travels in
the query string because the transport hands the client its POST endpoint
as a URI, but it is now only an identifier: the Bearer token is what
authorizes the request.

Session ids no longer authorize. Every request that names a session
re-reads the Bearer token, resolves it, and requires a constant-time
match against the key the session was created with. A missing or
mismatched token is a 401 regardless of session validity. Sessions carry
a 30 minute idle TTL and a reaper closes them, matching the in-app
handler.

Verification before allocation. Keys are checked against the LangWatch
API before a transport or MCP server is allocated, so an unverified
bearer can no longer allocate anything. Verification results are cached
briefly and concurrent checks of one key collapse into a single upstream
request, so re-verifying per request costs no round trip and a flood
cannot be amplified upstream. Failed authentication is rate limited per
IP, each key is capped at 20 concurrent sessions, and the OAuth token
endpoint verifies client_secret before minting a token.

Sessions moved from plain objects to Maps so a session id of __proto__
cannot reach the prototype chain.

Adds SECURITY.md with a reporting address, scope, response targets, and
a safe-harbour statement for good-faith research.

BREAKING CHANGE: three behaviors change for callers of the HTTP server.
A client that authenticated once at initialize and then sent only the
session id must now send Authorization: Bearer <key> on every request.
GET /sse?apiKey=<key> no longer authenticates; use the Authorization
header. A deployment relying on the implicit 0.0.0.0 bind must pass
--host 0.0.0.0, which the published container image already does.

* fix(mcp-server): re-verify the key on session requests and scope OAuth tokens per server

Session requests matched the bearer against the session's key but did not
re-check that the key was still live, so a revoked key kept working until
the session TTL. They now run the same verification as initialize, which
the short-lived cache makes free on the common path.

OAuth tokens moved from a module-level map into the server instance, so
two servers in one process no longer share a token namespace, and the
reaper that sweeps them belongs to the server that minted them.

Trust in proxy headers is now explicit via LANGWATCH_MCP_TRUST_PROXY,
since the per-IP rate limiter keys on the client address it produces.

SECURITY.md points at GitHub private vulnerability reporting alongside
the reporting address.

* fix(mcp-server): expose the session id header to allowed browser origins

A cross-origin client cannot read a response header that is not on the
expose list, and the Streamable HTTP transport reads the session id off
the initialize response. Without this an allowlisted browser origin can
reach the server but cannot complete a handshake.

* docs(mcp-server): surface the proxy trust tradeoff where operators hit it

The per-IP rate limit on failed authentication keys on the client address
that forwarded headers produce, so a port reachable without a trusted
proxy in front of it can be fed any address. The off-loopback startup
warning now says so and names the setting, and the README documents it as
defense in depth behind key verification rather than as a boundary.

Adds coverage for untrusted-proxy rate limiting and for an SSE session
losing access when its key stops verifying.

* fix(mcp-server): enforce the auth failure rate limit on session requests too

The session paths recorded failed attempts against the per-IP limiter but
never checked it, so an attacker guessing tokens against a known session
id was counted and never stopped. Both paths now check before doing any
work.

* test(mcp-server): align the container test with verified bearers

The container test asserted a wildcard CORS origin and drove the
authenticated paths with a placeholder key, both of which the hardened
server now rejects. Authenticated cases use a key the LangWatch API
accepts and skip without one; the wildcard assertion is inverted; and the
shipped image now also has to prove that it turns away an unrecognised
bearer and a session id presented with no token.

* refactor(mcp-server): address review on the hardened HTTP server

Rate limiting no longer keys on a caller-supplied address. Forwarded
headers still resolve the external scheme for the OAuth metadata, but the
limiter reads the socket peer unless LANGWATCH_MCP_TRUST_PROXY=true, so a
caller reaching the port directly cannot rotate X-Forwarded-For to reset
its own counter. Where that default is wrong it is wrong in the strict
direction, counting a proxy as one client rather than not counting.

The Bearer scheme is matched case-insensitively per RFC 7235 and the
token is trimmed. Key verification carries a request timeout, so an
upstream that accepts a connection and never answers cannot park every
request for that key behind one unsettled promise.

DELETE /mcp and the SSE message endpoint authenticate before resolving
the session and answer the same way for a session that does not exist and
one the caller does not own, which removes an existence oracle. Opening
an SSE session cleans up if connect throws rather than holding a per-key
slot until the reaper.

startHttpServer is assembly only, at 54 lines against the 60 line cap,
with origin handling, authentication, OAuth, and each transport in their
own factories taking the per-server state explicitly. authenticate and
authenticateForSession were near-duplicates and are now one function with
an optional expected key. Multi-argument exported helpers take named
object parameters.

Adds nosniff and DENY framing headers, and corrects the rate limiter
comment: the window is fixed, not sliding.

* test(mcp-server): split the HTTP server suites and fix two weak assertions

The bounded-cache test asserted against a second verifier with its own
empty cache, so it re-tested negative caching and never exercised the
eviction it was named for. It now fills one verifier past maxEntries and
asserts that the oldest key has to be fetched again while the newest does
not. The cache-expiry test raced a 15ms sleep against a 5ms TTL and now
uses fake timers.

The concurrent-session test asserted only a 429, which any future limiter
would satisfy; it now asserts the session-cap body. Reading the SSE
session id waits for the endpoint frame rather than assuming it arrives in
the first chunk.

Both new test files were over the 300 line cap, so they are split by
concern into origin, session auth, and allocation suites over a shared
harness, which also removes the duplicated verifier stub and the repeated
loop-until-429 blocks.

The container no longer runs the network-reachable server as root, and an
IPv6 bind address is bracketed before being printed as a URL.

Documents that HTTP mode authenticates before routing, so the
documentation tools are not reachable without a key the way they are over
stdio.

* fix(mcp-server): correct the proxy trust warning and the docs it matches

Splitting proxy trust so that only the rate limit key is gated left the
startup warning describing the old behavior, and inverted: it fired when
forwarded headers were not used as the rate limit key and stayed silent
when they were. It now fires on LANGWATCH_MCP_TRUST_PROXY=true, which is
the case that carries the risk.

The README said the same thing the wrong way round and told operators to
set the variable to false to get a behavior that is already the default.

* test(mcp-server): authenticate the documentation SSRF suite

The suite drives the real HTTP server to prove the documentation tools
cannot reach a loopback target. It now stubs the key check so the cases
stay on SSRF rather than on authentication.

* fix(mcp-server): make session admission atomic and bound OAuth token state

Reserve the per-key slot before initialize is awaited, so admission no
longer depends on the transport reporting the session as initialized
before another request is served. Cap the OAuth token map per key with
oldest-first eviction, which the per-address rate limit does not bound
because one key can be presented from many addresses.

Scope the README's authentication wording to MCP requests and document
the three routes that do not take the bearer.

* fix(mcp-server): parse the Authorization header without backtracking

The header is attacker controlled and can be kilobytes long, and a
scheme-then-token regex backtracks over runs of whitespace. Splitting on
the first space is linear and still accepts the case-insensitive scheme
RFC 7235 allows.

* refactor(mcp-server): key the digests derived from API keys

The identifiers used for per-key counters and for constant-time
comparison are now HMACs under a per-process secret rather than bare
digests. They only index in-memory maps within one process, so they
never need to be reproducible, and keying them means exposure of those
maps does not let candidate keys be confirmed offline.

* feat(evaluators)!: remove the legacy Ragas evaluators

The seven legacy/ragas_* evaluators and the langevals-legacy Python
package are gone, along with the LANGWATCH_ENABLE_LEGACY_EVALUATORS
toggle that gated them.

The evaluators were served by a Lambda with a 100% failure rate: 30,258
invocations and 30,258 errors over seven days, broken for roughly two
months, at $212/mo to fail. An evaluation still referencing one now
fails at validation with the accepted types listed, instead of timing
out against a Lambda that could never answer.

catalog (scripts/generate_evaluators_ts.py), the uv workspace lock, the
Mintlify llms.txt aggregations, and the API reference navigation.

legacy/ragas_* evaluator type stop working. Their current equivalents
in the ragas/* family remain available.

* perf(studio): right-size the per-project studio Lambdas to 1024 MB

Across 806,383 production invocations over 30 days these functions peak
at 507 MB of Max Memory Used, with 194 MB at p50, 235 MB at p99 and
333 MB at p99.9. At 2048 MB they were provisioned four times above their
own ceiling.

1024 MB clears the observed peak twice over. 512 MB would sit at 1.01x
that peak, which is not headroom, and memory also sets the CPU share, so
cutting further trades duration back against the GB-seconds saved.

Newly created project Lambdas pick this up on their own. The existing
ones keep 2048 MB until an operator updates them.

create-path assertion pinning the studio Lambda memory size.

no longer attempt a real AWS call per run.

The page documenting ragas/faithfulness sat at ragas-faithfulness-1
because the deprecated evaluator held ragas-faithfulness. The suffix
leaked into user-facing text, with llms.txt titling the entry "Ragas
Faithfulness 1", so the slug now matches the evaluator's name.

* fix(evaluators): keep monitors saved on a retired evaluator recoverable

Migration 20250105132258_migrate_legacy_ragas rewrote customer Check rows
onto the seven legacy Ragas slugs. Removing those slugs from the catalog
left every one of those rows naming an evaluator that no longer resolves,
and the monitor edit page dereferenced the missing definition, so the page
threw on render and stayed unreachable: the ErrorBoundary catches it, but
Try again re-renders and re-throws. Update was closed too, because
validateCheckSettings rejects a checkType that is not in the catalog, so
delete was the only exit.

The form now resolves the definition once and treats "not in the registry"
the same as "no checkType", falling through to the picker with the saved
slug named. The form resolver looks the settings schema up by presence for
the same reason.

metric rather than by name. Four move: faithfulness and answer_relevancy
to their renamed selves, and both context-precision variants to
ragas/response_context_precision, which picks the with-reference or the
without-reference scorer depending on whether an expected output is
present. Three stay put: context_relevancy has no successor upstream,
response_context_recall newly requires the model output these rows were
never configured to supply, and factual_correctness drops the embedding
half of answer_correctness, so its score is not the number the monitor has
been reporting. Those keep their saved type and go through the picker
rather than being rewritten into a quietly wrong evaluator.

runEvaluation reached AVAILABLE_EVALUATORS unguarded, so an unknown slug
threw a bare TypeError that degraded to a generic unknown error. It now
raises EvaluatorNotFoundError, matching the sibling path in
EvaluationExecutionService. This covers a class wider than the legacy
slugs: a code/<id> type already reached the same line.

getEvaluatorMissingMappings reported a built-in evaluator with no catalog
entry as fully mapped. Its mappings are beside the point when the
evaluator cannot run, so the evaluator is now the finding.

* revert: keep the studio Lambdas at 2048 MB

The 1024 MB resize reversed a reproduced incident using data that cannot
observe the failure it reverses. The 806k-invocation distribution peaking
at 507 MB of Max Memory Used was collected with these functions at 2048 MB.
The failure mode is Python multiprocessing.fork() needing RSS headroom that
only exists at the larger size, so Max Memory Used measured at 2048 MB does
not predict it at 1024, and an invocation that dies on the wall never
becomes a clean data point. The surviving sample is selected on not having
hit the ceiling.

The comment being replaced recorded the counter-evidence directly: 805 of
1024 MB mid-request on lw-dev, fork() failing to clone parent pages, the
uvicorn worker pool dying and /studio/* returning 502s. The 300 MB gap
between the two observations was never reconciled.

The resize was also unrelated to removing evaluators, which put a change
most likely to need reverting inside one that should not be. If the saving
is worth chasing it belongs in its own change, behind a canary on one new
project rather than on every future one.

Six call sites passed the id, the evaluator type, the input definitions and
the mappings positionally, so a swapped pair of adjacent strings read as a
valid fixture.

The Proxy get trap branched four ways to decide between an override, a
query hook, a mutation hook and a deeper stub. One keyed table answers all
four, which drops it under the cognitive-complexity ceiling the repo
enforces on new code.
