is an object to `typeof`, so a document carrying either would have had
`security` stamped onto it and stopped validating. Filtered by method name
now, in one predicate the generator and its test both import, since the test
had the same hole and would have failed on a correct document.

The end-user spend description named a nullable `cap` and the schema has
always had a non-nullable `caps` array. Its pinning test asserted the string
contained "cap", which "caps" satisfies, so the drift was never visible; it
pins the field name and the empty-array case now.

`resolveApplicableBudgets` and `memberGroupIds` take named parameters, like
everything else in that module after the earlier rounds. The debit path was
the one caller outside `src/`, and missing it would have been a typecheck
failure rather than a silent one.

`CLASS_BY_APP_SCOPE` keeps its literal types, matching the security map next
to it.

The refusal copy for an unreachable budget said it "would never spend and
never block", which reads as permanent when a later key can reach it.

Not taken, with reasons on the threads: deriving an API-key class for a
service or session app must not throw, which is the correction already made
in c5687fbe3b for nineteen live routes; and the no-active-keys exemption is
not organization-scoped only, it covers team, project and group budgets too,
so narrowing the docs would describe behaviour the code does not have.

* feat(spend): one filter vocabulary on both reads, and a grouping that refuses to lie

A reconciliation checksums the rollups and then diffs the events when a
checksum disagrees. It can only do that if it can ask both surfaces the same
question, and it could not: /spend-events offered four filters, /spend-summaries
offered one, and neither offered provider, principal, request type, label,
metadata, team or the customer's own external id.

One module now owns the vocabulary, the domain type and the SQL, and both
routes spread it, so the two cannot drift. A test asserts the parity against
the published document rather than the source, since the document is what a
caller reads.

Three things worth naming:

A filter that is present but resolves to nothing emits its predicate anyway.
Collapsing an empty list into an absent predicate would hand back the whole
organization's spend under a narrowing the caller asked for, which is the
worst possible answer to "show me this one team".

Metadata is filtered through a MATERIALIZED expression column rather than a
stored one the fold writes. Verified against the pinned server that the
expression is evaluated for parts written before the ALTER, so history is
correct from the moment this lands with no backfill window during which a
filtered reconciliation silently agrees on a subset. The rejected alternative
is recorded in the migration: a real Map backfilled by re-insert would carry a
higher EventTimestamp, which is this table's replacement version, and would
erase the fold's next legitimate write.

Grouping gained model, provider, project, principal, request type and an
hour/day bucket, and with them a guard. The fold replaces the requested model
and provider with the ones that actually served the request, and its admitted
handler sets the occurred-at unconditionally while every outcome handler
preserves it, so over an unsettled window a row can change group mid-walk and
be served twice or skipped. Those groupings are refused until the window is
older than the settlement grace, which is read from the settlement process
manager so an operator who widens it widens this too. allow_unstable serves it
anyway for a caller who only needs the shape.

Nine skip indices back the new filters. They apply to parts written after the
migration and MATERIALIZE INDEX is left as an ops task, so an unmaterialized
index costs a granule read and never drops a row.

* docs(spend): describe the filters and say when a grouping is refused

The route descriptions still described a rollup that could group one way and
a walk that took four filters. Both now name the shared vocabulary, how
repeating a parameter widens it, and the `key:value` metadata form.

The refusal gets the most words because it is the one thing a reconciliation
script cannot discover by trying: it only fires on recent windows, so a script
written and tested against last month's data meets it first in production.
`meta.settles_at` is there so a scheduler can wait rather than guess.

Also fixes the docs-to-metrics contract test, which had four documented
`gateway_*` REST error codes that no collector registers. Three predate this
change and one is new here. The test reads them as undocumented metrics, and
because it iterates a map it names a different one on each run, so it has to
be swept rather than patched. It stayed invisible because the Go job is
path-filtered and neither this work nor the budget-reach work before it
touches Go: the failure would have surfaced on whichever unrelated Go PR
landed next.

* feat(sdk): carry the spend filters and the new grouping through the SDK and CLI

The API grew a shared filter vocabulary and a wider grouping; a customer
scripting a reconciliation reaches them through the SDK, so they land here in
the same shape rather than as a set of query strings to hand-assemble.

`SpendFilterOptions` is one interface both reads take, mirroring the server's
one module. Every field accepts one value or many, and many means any of
these, which is what repeating a query parameter does on the wire. Metadata is
a record rather than `key:value` strings, because an SDK caller already has
the pair as two values and joining them only to have the server split them
again is a step that can go wrong.

`SpendSummariesOptions` carries the grouping, and its docstring is where the
refusal is explained: a caller meets `gateway_spend_group_by_unstable` only on
recent windows, so a script written and tested against last month's data
meets it first in production.

`SpendSummaryRow` gains `group` and `bucket_start`. `key` keeps its meaning as
the first dimension's value, so code reading it today is untouched.

On the CLI, `--group-by` takes one or two dimensions and still refuses a typo
rather than silently reporting on virtual keys, which on a reconciliation
surface is the failure worth being loud about. `--metadata` is written
`key=value` rather than the wire's `key:value`, because a metadata value may
itself contain a colon and `key=value` is what a shell user expects.

Formatting note: this package is on eslint, not the repo-root biome, so it is
deliberately left in its own style.

* feat(sdk): carry the spend filters through the python SDK, and name group_by in its own refusal

The python SDK offered five singular filters while the TS SDK and the REST
surface took the whole vocabulary, so a python reconciler could not narrow a
walk to what a checksum had covered. It now takes the same twelve filters,
each as one value or many, plus the multi-dimension grouping, the time bucket
and its timezone.

A comma-split group_by piped into an array schema reported an invalid value
against `group_by.0`. The caller sent one string, so an index they never wrote
maps onto nothing a client can point at, which is the whole purpose of
meta.fields. It is validated inside the transform now and names `group_by`.

The Billing events screen test asserted the pre-vocabulary tRPC input shape.

* test(sdk): pin the python spend filters to the published contract

The SDK lagged the REST surface by seven filters and nothing failed. A
reconciler just could not narrow a walk to what its checksum had covered,
which is the one divergence a reconciliation cannot detect on its own.

Asserted against the published OpenAPI document rather than the server
source, because the document is what a caller reads, and it fails loudly
when the document is missing rather than skipping.

* fix(spend): the ways a filter could quietly answer the wrong question

Review round on the filter vocabulary. Four of these returned wrong spend
rather than failing, which on a reconciliation surface is the expensive kind.

`allow_unstable=false` turned the guard OFF. `z.coerce.boolean()` is
JavaScript `Boolean()`, so every non-empty string is true and the most obvious
way to spell "off" meant "on". A caller opting out of an inexact walk got one.
Query booleans now name the spellings they accept and refuse the rest.

`metadata=tier:` matched every row with no `tier` at all. ClickHouse answers a
missing Map key with the value type's default, so an empty value read as
`'' IN ('')`. Both halves of a pair must now be non-empty, in the query
spelling, the structured one and the SDK.

The summaries cursor decided its format by looking for a leading bracket.
Group keys are caller data, so an end-user id or model opening with `[`
refused that caller's own cursor and restarted their walk from page one. The
format is decided by parsing now, never by sniffing.

No filter bounded how many values it could name, so one request could build an
unbounded query. Capped at 100 per filter, which the published contract now
states as `maxItems`.

Also: an unknown `timezone` is a 400 naming the parameter rather than a
ClickHouse error the caller cannot act on; the summaries window gets the
`.safe()` guard the events window always had; `group_by` publishes what it
accepts; the CLI validates `--bucket` and prints the whole row identity now
that a row can be two dimensions and a bucket; and a metadata key carrying a
colon is refused rather than sent to address a different key.

Tests: a second organization with real spend of its own, because "a key from
another organization" and "a key nobody minted" were the same test and only
one of them exercises the tenant fence. Provider, end-user and label filters
were seeded but never asserted. The fixture window is anchored to the run, so
it cannot age out of the 13-month ledger. The parity check refuses to pass by
finding nothing, and compares schemas rather than only names.

The migration says IRREVERSIBLE and why, which is the form the rule accepts
for a down step we deliberately do not run unattended.

* fix(spend): close the last gaps between the two metadata spellings

The structured input still accepted a metadata key with a colon, so the
Billing events screen could set a filter no reconciliation script could
reproduce over REST. That gap is the thing this module exists to prevent, so
the domain schema now enforces the same limit the query spelling documents.

The CLI refused an empty metadata key but not an empty value, and passed
`--metadata key=` straight to a server that has refused it since the last
commit. Refused locally now, with the reason.

Docs: the grouping example says out loud that its window is the closed month
declared above it, since the same call on a recent window is refused. And the
event-level diff compares per-id counts rather than set membership, because
one request dropped and another booked twice leaves the id sets looking close
and the money wrong.

* docs(spend): say the whole filter list, and name the option each client spells

The events read still advertised five filters after gaining twelve, and the
paragraph next to it said both grains take the same ones, so the page
contradicted itself. The live-view escape hatch was written only in its
TypeScript spelling, which a REST caller can copy and get nothing.

Reconciliation: matching per-id counts rule out drops and duplicates, not a
repricing, so "the ids whose counts disagree are your fix list" hands an empty
fix list to the one divergence counts cannot see.

The two structured-metadata refusals asserted only that something threw, which
would keep passing if the rule under test were deleted and an unrelated one
tripped instead. They now name the field the refusal has to land on.

* ci(gateway-matrix): stop release PRs from evicting real ones from the VK lock

The matrix serializes on one concurrency group because every run dials the
same matrix-* virtual keys. With cancel-in-progress false GitHub keeps a
single pending run per group and cancels the older one, so anything queued in
that group evicts whatever was already waiting.

Release PRs land in it by accident: release-please bumps the chart version,
charts/gateway/** is in the path filter, and the branch re-pushes on every
merge to main. Twenty of the last sixty runs came from one, each spending live
provider calls to prove a version string still answers, and five runs were
evicted, including two consecutive pushes of one feature branch.

They now skip the job and sit in a group of their own. The two go together: a
run outside the shared group must be one that never touches a shared key.

* fix(test): the pre-migration probe built a table name it could not parse

The name is an identifier, so it is spelled into the DDL rather than bound,
and it carried the suite's nanoid suffix straight through. nanoid's alphabet
includes a hyphen, which ends an unquoted identifier mid-token, so about a
fifth of runs died with a syntax error instead of exercising the property.

It reproduces on the pinned server: CREATE TABLE probe_a-S04f_ is rejected
with code 62, and probe_a_S04f_ is accepted. The local runs that passed had
simply drawn hyphen-free suffixes, which is what made this read as a CI-only
failure of the ClickHouse behaviour under test rather than a flake in the
harness around it.

* ci(gateway-matrix): make the lock exemptions match the guard's, all four

The previous commit said the concurrency group had to stay in step with the
job guard and then moved one of the guard's three classes out of it. Drafts
and forks kept queueing in the shared group, and a run parked there evicts a
real PR's queued run whether or not its own job ever executes, because the
eviction happens when the run queues, not when it starts. Finishing in
seconds is no mitigation. Eleven of the last sixty runs were cancelled, and
they were not all release PRs: a draft PR and two feature branches are in
that list.

Dependabot was in neither the guard nor the group, and its runs are not
skipped at all. One took five minutes and forty-five seconds inside the
shared lock to bump the action SHAs pinned in this file, reading the
Dependabot secret store rather than the Actions one, so it either bills real
provider calls for a SHA bump or reports green on empty credentials.

Both expressions now list the same four exemptions, and the release prefix
carries the double dash release-please actually emits so a hand-written
release-please-config branch is not swept up with it. YAML cannot share an
expression between `concurrency` and a job `if`, so the comment saying they
move together is the only thing holding them together; it now names all four
rather than describing a rule the code did not implement.

* fix(openapi): stamp the operations whose route pins its parameter to a pattern

Hono may pin a route parameter to a matcher pattern, `/:id{.+}`, and the
translation into the document's `{id}` spelling did not take the pattern
off. Eight operations under /api/prompts and /api/evaluators therefore
matched no registered route and kept the document-wide security default
instead of the class their route enforces. They happen to sit on project
apps, so the default was the right answer and nothing looked wrong; the
first such route on an organization app would have published a
credential class that cannot reach it, which is the defect the stamping
exists to prevent.

The translation moves to the security module, where it can be tested
without the generator's import graph, and a documented operation under an
app prefix that matches no route now fails the generator rather than
inheriting quietly. The two surfaces are added to the credential-class
property test, which is what makes the failure visible: it reports all
eight against the pre-fix document.

The same merge brought a second copy of the request body cap, added
independently on main as routes/_lib/body-limit.ts while this branch
added server/api/bodyLimit.ts. Both were imported in all six consumers,
which typechecks as a duplicate identifier. Main's copy stays: it is
stricter about a Content-Length it cannot trust and carries the abort
signal. Its tests gain the one guard this branch had and it lacked,
that hono's own middleware still answers 500 to the chunked request the
module exists to serve, and the spec scenarios rebind to it at the layer
that actually runs them.

Also excludes TruffleHog's Lob detector from the secrets gate. It matches
`test_` plus exactly 35 characters and its verifier accepts the match, so
two ordinary shell functions in charts/langwatch/tests arrived as
verified secrets that --only-verified could not filter and blocked pull
requests that had not touched them. Nothing here integrates Lob, so the
detector can only produce false positives; excluded by name rather than
by path, so a real credential in those files is still caught.

* fix(gateway-spend): read allow_unstable off the wire, and test that it is read

The critical defect this branch already fixed was that
`z.coerce.boolean()` made `allow_unstable=false` mean true, so the
clearest way to decline an inexact read turned the guard off. It was
fixed without a test that could observe it: the four grouping scenarios
were bound to a unit test calling the grouping check directly with a
boolean argument, which cannot see how a query string becomes that
boolean. They now run through the route, and one of them sends the
`false` that used to be served.

The parameter also refused `True`. `requests` renders a Python bool with
a capital letter where `httpx` renders it lower case, and this parameter
is documented for Python callers, so the surface was rejecting the exact
request the documentation asks for. Case is folded now, while a spelling
it does not know is still refused by name rather than guessed at, and
the published parameter says so.

The scenarios move to the layer that runs them rather than being counted
at one and executed at another. check-feature-parity treats @unit and
@integration as one set and never checks that the binding test matches
the tag, so nothing else would have caught the mismatch.

* fix(gateway): a project the customer deleted is not a trace destination

Project deletion is soft, so the three lookups behind resolveTraceProjects
constrained the id, the organization and the kind, and nothing else. An
archived project therefore still answered, which meant a key could name one
as its explicit destination and pass the write-path guard: the create was
accepted, the gateway went on exporting the key's traces into a project the
customer had deleted, and its spend went on being attributed there. That is
the gateway_trace_project_unknown case this change's own guard exists to
refuse.

archivedAt: null now applies to all three stages, so an archived project is
passed over as an explicit destination, as a single project scope, and as
the governance inbox. The write path refuses a key that names one, and the
read path degrades the way it always has for a destination that stopped
answering: it falls through to the next rule, because the deletion happened
on another screen and failing here would take the key's live traffic down
with it. The key's own stated destination stays visible next to the rule
that actually answered, so the disagreement is readable rather than hidden.

The ambiguity guard counts live projects for the same reason. Counting a
deleted one made the two refusals contradict each other: the key was told
to name a project while every project it could name was refused as unknown.

* fix(gateway): the offer to keep an unreachable budget stops at the scope it was refused for

"Create it anyway" resubmits the form as it stands with allowUnreachable
set. Picking a different scope kind cleared it, picking a different target
within the same kind did not, so the button stayed on screen and sent the
override for a scope the server was never asked about. The one budget the
admin had already been warned about was the one the guardrail then skipped.

Both selectors now clear the refusal, and the negative control is in the
test: with the target selector left as it was, the button survives the
change and the second submit carries allowUnreachable to the new scope.

* refactor(gateway): the budgets route asks the service for reach, not Prisma

The create route read reachability by calling resolveScopeReach with the
Prisma client directly, which is a route reaching past its service into
persistence. GatewayBudgetService.scopeReach now owns it, and the reason it
is a separate read rather than a value carried out of the create guard
moved onto the method with it: the guard only runs for the three scopes it
can refuse, and a create response missing the field would not equal the row
the very next read returns.

* fix(gateway-spend): the rollups refuse a status they could only answer with zero

The summaries query drops in-flight rows with a fixed predicate, and the
shared filter contract let a caller narrow to exactly that status. The
conjunction is provably empty, so /spend-summaries?status=admitted returned
a confident zero while /spend-events?status=admitted returned the envelopes.
A reconciliation that checksums against that zero decides the books agree.

The two reads now publish two status enums derived from one tuple: the
events read takes the whole vocabulary, the rollups take it minus the
in-flight status, by exclusion so a status added to one reaches both. The
boundary refuses with the ordinary validation_error naming the status field,
the published parameter says why and where the answer lives, and the
repository throws rather than serving the empty intersection to any other
caller. The TypeScript SDK narrows the same way through Exclude, and the
docs, the route descriptions and the Python facade name the one exception
instead of promising a symmetry that no longer holds.

Bound by a cross-route regression test through both routes: the same query
serves admitted envelopes on the events read and is refused on the rollups,
while a completed status still rolls up.

* perf(gateway-spend): give the rollup walk a deadline

LIMIT bounds the rows a page returns, not the rows it aggregates: under
FINAL the whole group set is rebuilt on every page before all but one page
of it is discarded, so a 30-day window bucketed by hour and grouped on two
dimensions is paid for once per page of the walk.

max_execution_time caps that. Memory is left to the server profile and the
shared query defaults, which already enforce a per-query ceiling and spill
GROUP BY state to disk; a client-side max_memory_usage could only raise the
ceiling, which is why queryDefaults.ts omits it deliberately.

* docs(sdk): move the organization-key note out of the breaking PR

release-please applies a whole commit message to every component the change
touched, so a PR carrying a breaking marker and touching two components
proposes two majors. This one breaks the gateway API, at the root component,
and its only other files were two SDK doc comments, which would have taken
the published TypeScript SDK to 2.0.0 for a paragraph of prose.

The note lands on its own, in a PR with nothing breaking in it. See
dev/docs/RELEASES.md, "A breaking change belongs to one component".

* docs(gateway-spend): fold the two group_by doc blocks into one

* chore(release): pin typescript-sdk at 1.5.0 under the inherited breaking marker

This stacked branch still carries the base PR breaking-marked commit, and the squash body would major every component this PR touches. The TypeScript SDK changes here are additive filters, a minor.

Release-As: 1.5.0

* chore(release): pin python-sdk at 1.2.1 under the inherited breaking marker

Nothing is pending for the Python SDK since 1.2.0, and this PR adds tests and docstring constraints only, a patch.

Release-As: 1.2.1

* chore(release): pin langwatch at 3.11.0 under the inherited breaking marker

The open release PR already proposes 3.11.0 and this PR app surface is a feature, so the pin holds the version the release was already going to be.

Release-As: 3.11.0

* fix(spend): close the review round, from the cursor arity to the zone the store cannot load

A cursor whose arity does not match the grouping was ignored, so the
walk served page one again under a fresh cursor with nothing saying it
had reset, and a reconciliation folded those groups into its checksum
twice. Refused at the route now, naming what to do instead, with the
repository throwing behind it.

A fixed offset like +05:00 passed the timezone check because the runtime
builds a formatter for it; ClickHouse loads zones by name only and
answers "Cannot load time zone", so a value the caller chose came back
as an unknown error from somewhere they cannot see. Refused at the door.

`normalizeStatusFilter` restated the four lifecycle statuses instead of
deriving them, so a status added to the published vocabulary would pass
the boundary and then throw inside. `parseMetadataFilters` cut on an
absent colon, turning "tier" into key "tie": both now derive or refuse.

`from` and `to` published Zod's safe-integer bounds, documenting a
negative epoch as acceptable while the server refused it, and never said
whether the unit was seconds or milliseconds. They now publish
exclusiveMinimum 0 with the unit and an example.

The Python facade accepted a metadata key carrying a colon that the
other two clients refuse, and the CLI called N model-by-hour rows
"N models". Both corrected, both pinned.

Workflow: the two automation exemptions take the opening account as well
as the branch prefix, so a human branch named dependabot/... keeps its
gateway coverage, and `ready_for_review` joins the triggers so a draft
marked ready runs the matrix without waiting for another push.

Regenerated the OpenAPI document, the docs copy, llms-full and the
TypeScript client; a further run produces no diff.
Release docs (auto-release on merge to main) [skip ci]

fix(aigateway): propagate routing-policy and cache-rule edits through the change feed (#6737)

* feat(aigateway): propagate routing-policy and cache-rule edits through the change feed

A RoutingPolicy edit only reached a running gateway when the cached bundle
crossed Options.ConfigTTL, a 60s safety net rather than a propagation path.
Every sibling mutation (budgets, cache rules, VK config) appends a change
event and lands in seconds. Cache rules were worse than that: the control
plane has emitted CACHE_RULE_CREATED/UPDATED/DELETED since they shipped, but
no Go code named those kinds, so the switch in applyChange dropped them
silently and the documented behaviour never existed.

Control plane:

- New GatewayChangeEventKind values ROUTING_POLICY_UPDATED and
  ROUTING_POLICY_DELETED, matching the vk-disable precedent.
- RoutingPolicyService.update now runs in a transaction: update the policy,
  bump the revision of every VK that references it, append the event. The
  event is unconditional rather than gated on which field moved, because
  every stored field except isDefault reaches a bundle and a gate that must
  track that list will one day drop an edit silently. The revision bump has
  no consumer today (the gateway never sends If-None-Match) but the 304 path
  exists server-side, so a policy edit that left the revision alone would
  strand every referencing key the day the gateway starts sending one.
- RoutingPolicyService.delete now runs in a transaction and releases the keys
  that pointed at the policy. relationMode is "prisma", so there is no SQL
  foreign key behind onDelete: SetNull, and it would only reach
  routingPolicyId anyway. Deletion used to leave keys on routingMode POLICY
  with a dangling id, a state the schema says cannot exist. They now move to
  FALLBACK_ALL, whose behaviour is closest to the multi-provider chain the
  policy was giving them.
- create and setDefault deliberately emit nothing: isDefault is read by list
  ordering and at VK issuance, never by the materialiser, so it cannot change
  an already-issued key's bundle.

Gateway:

- applyChange handles the two routing-policy kinds and the three cache-rule
  kinds, evicting the polled organization. A bundle carries the resolved
  routing mode and a pre-sorted cache-rule array with no id to join either
  back on, so the organization is the finest key available, the same position
  a budget event without a project_id is in.
- evictWhere reads with Peek instead of Get. Get takes the exclusive lock and
  promotes what it reads, so a full-cache scan queued every in-flight request
  behind it once per entry and dragged keys it merely looked at ahead of keys
  real traffic touched after the Keys() snapshot.
- Deleted the unreferenced ChangeKind block in controlplane/client.go. It had
  no callers anywhere in the repo, including its own package tests, and had
  drifted to missing VK_DISABLED, VK_ENABLED and every CACHE_RULE kind. Kinds
  cross that boundary as opaque strings; the enumeration lives in
  authresolver, where the switch over it is.

Docs and specs said 30 seconds for a mechanism that never existed anywhere.
Both now state the real path, the change feed and the next long-poll, without
inventing another number.

Tests: three Go cases in authresolver over the new kinds, and a new
integration suite against real Postgres pinning what each mutation writes,
which keys it bumps, and that a rejected edit writes nothing at all.

* fix(aigateway): report a change kind this build has no case for

The switch in applyChange had no default, so a kind it did not name was
dropped without a trace. That is how CACHE_RULE_CREATED, UPDATED and
DELETED stayed unhandled from the day the control plane started emitting
them: the events arrived, nothing acted on them, and the only symptom was
staleness nobody could attribute. Adding the three cases fixes today's
instance; the missing default is what let it happen, and what would let
the next one happen just as quietly.

Not acting on an unrecognised kind is still the behavior. The control
plane is free to emit kinds a running gateway predates, and evicting on
one it cannot interpret would be worse. It is reported at warn now, by
name, so the next drift costs a log search rather than a bug report.

* fix(aigateway): make a change-feed eviction reach the shared cache tier

An invalidation event removed the entry from L1 only. On a gateway with L2
configured that is undone by the very next request: it misses L1, finds the
invalidated bundle in the shared store and rehydrates it, so the mutation the
event announced does not take effect until the config TTL expires.

The rehydrate made it worse than no eviction at all. storeL1 stamped
configFetchedAt as now, so an entry 50 seconds into a 60 second ConfigTTL came
back with a fresh 60 and config staleness could approach twice the TTL.

This is the shared eviction seam, so it holds for every change kind, not only
the routing-policy and cache-rule kinds this branch adds.

- L2Store gains Delete, and evictWhere drops the hashes it removed from L1
  from the shared store too, after the L1 walk. Best effort: a store that
  cannot be reached is reported at warn and leaves those copies to the config
  TTL, which is the bound the gateway had before the change feed existed.
- An L2 value is now an envelope carrying the moment its config was fetched,
  and a rehydrate inherits that instead of stamping now, so the TTL clock
  keeps running across nodes. An entry that arrives already past its TTL
  refreshes on the spot. An undatable value degrades to stale-now, never to
  fresh.
- The key prefix moves to gw:auth:v2:, retiring values written in the old
  shape rather than guessing an age for them. They expire on their own TTL.

A cold entry living only in L2, with no node holding it in L1, still cannot be
enumerated for deletion: the key is a hash of the raw credential. Carrying the
fetch time is what bounds it, at one config TTL from the original fetch rather
than two.

* fix(aigateway): batch the shared-tier deletes, and never serve a bundle past its cap

Review follow-ups on the cache-tier invalidation.

- serveFromL2 had no expiry guard. The L2Store interface promises no
  filtering, so a store handing back a long-dead bundle would have that
  bundle served, while the L1 path refuses the same thing. Past the hard cap
  is now a miss, checked before the hit is counted so one lookup cannot
  report both, and the request resolves fresh instead. A bundle merely past
  its JWT exp still rehydrates, and the next hit takes L1's existing
  refresh-or-serve-stale path.
- deleteL2 spent one 5 second budget on the whole batch, one round trip per
  key. An org-wide eviction is thousands of keys, so the budget ran out part
  way through and every key after that point was abandoned, which is the
  opposite of what the comment claimed. L2Store now takes DeleteMany, Redis
  issues one DEL per chunk of 256, and each chunk gets its own budget, so a
  chunk that fails costs its own keys and nothing else.
- The evict reason is the lowercased change kind rather than one hardcoded
  word per branch. Deletes used to log as updates, and revoke, disable and
  rotate all logged as one label, which is unreadable for the operator the
  line exists for.
- Documented the cache-rule evaluation timing consistently: resolved once per
  bundle refresh, then matched per request against the baked array. One
  paragraph said each, and only one of them was true.
- Marked the enum migration IRREVERSIBLE, since Postgres cannot drop an enum
  value. Forward-only by design, no down step.
- A rejected-edit describe block now reads as a given, per the BDD rule.
- Added the three REST error codes that main documents but never registers as
  metrics to the docs-contract allowlist. They are error.code values, not
  series, and the contract test has been failing on main because of it.

* fix(db): move the enum migration off a timestamp main already took

Merging main brought 20260808120000_add_trace_edit_overlay, which claims the
same ordering key. Two migrations on one key is ambiguous ordering, and
cmd/migrationorder fails the build on it. The migration has never run
anywhere, so renaming it costs nothing.

* fix(aigateway): a cold cache is not a weaker door than a warm one

Three review follow-ups on the shared cache tier.

- A bundle past its JWT exp but inside the grace window was served straight
  out of the shared store with no control-plane contact, while an L1 entry in
  exactly that state goes through refreshOrServeStale first. So a key revoked
  during the grace window kept working on every node whose L1 was cold, one
  request per node, until something else happened to refresh it. The
  rehydrated entry now takes that same path synchronously: revocation is
  enforced before anything is served, and a control plane that is merely
  unreachable still gets the stale bundle served, which treating it as a
  plain miss would have thrown away. L1 and L2 no longer have different
  answers for the same state.
- DeleteMany sent a chunk as one variadic DEL. The store takes a
  redis.UniversalClient, which is a cluster client whenever it is built from
  more than one address, and these keys carry no hash tag, so that command is
  refused with CROSSSLOT the moment the chunk spans slots and the whole chunk
  counts as failed. It is a pipeline of single-key DELs now, routed per key
  and still one round trip per node.
- VK_CREATED had no case, so every key creation logged auth_cache_change_
  unhandled at warn. It is named as a deliberate no-op with its reason,
  nothing cached to evict, and the warn is left for kinds this build genuinely
  does not recognize. The new test reads GatewayChangeEventKind out of the
  Prisma schema, so a kind added upstream fails a test here instead of
  arriving as a warning in production.

* fix(aigateway): check a bundle's own expiry before the cap, on both tiers

The L2 guard tested the hard cap first. A negative HardGrace puts the cap
BEFORE the JWT exp on purpose, which is the documented stale-while-error
opt-out and reachable from LW_GATEWAY_AUTH_CACHE_HARD_GRACE_SECONDS, so under
that setting a bundle with ten minutes left had a cap in the past and the
shared tier discarded it. L1 never did: it tests soft expiry first and serves.
A node with a cold cache could therefore reject a still-valid credential that
a warm node was happily serving, and worst when it matters most, with the
control plane unavailable and nothing to re-resolve against.

The ordering is now stated once, in classifyEntry, and both tiers ask it
rather than each testing the fields themselves. Fresh, stale and dead are
named, so the three-way decision reads the same in Resolve and serveFromL2 and
there is nowhere left for the two to drift apart. Splitting newEntry from
storeL1Entry also means a bundle classified dead is never published to L1 at
all, rather than added and immediately removed.

Table-driven test over positive, zero and negative grace against both tiers,
asserting they return the same credential and consult the control plane the
same number of times. With the old cap-first guard, exactly one case fails:
negative grace, unexpired bundle, shared tier.

fix(model-providers): an extra header no longer deletes the stored Azure credentials (#6730)

* fix(model-providers): an extra header no longer deletes the stored Azure credentials

An Azure provider that already holds an API key loses it, and its endpoint,
the moment an extra header is saved. The row comes back holding only the
header. Nothing warns, and the credential is gone rather than hidden.

Headers were folded into `customKeys` for Azure on the way out. When no
credential had changed the credential branch had correctly settled on
`undefined`, meaning "leave the stored keys alone", and the fold spread that
`undefined` into an object holding only the headers. The empty-object safety
net below it did not catch that, because the object was not empty. On the
server, `mergeCustomKeys` restores a stored value only where the payload sends
the masked placeholder for that key, so keys the payload never mentions were
simply dropped.

The fold is removed. Headers are not credentials: they have their own column,
their own masked-placeholder merge, and both readers already take them from
there. `prepareLitellmParams` builds `extra_headers` from
`modelProvider.extraHeaders` and the gateway materialiser reads
`mp.extraHeaders`. Nothing reads a header out of `customKeys`, so the fold
wrote a value no one consumed and destroyed the credential bag doing it.

It also fired without anyone adding a header. Stored header values come back
to the drawer masked, and dirty detection compared the header objects whole
while the form's copies carry a `concealed` flag the stored ones lack. Every
Azure provider holding a header therefore read as dirty the moment its drawer
opened, so Save was live over an untouched form and a rename or a scope change
was enough to wipe the key. Headers are now compared on key and value only.

Widening that comparison exposed a second gap: emptying a credential field was
invisible to dirty detection, so Save stayed disabled and a credential could
not be removed at all. That was already true on main for any provider without
a header; the header bug had been accidentally papering over it. Dirty
detection now uses the same helper the submit path uses to decide whether to
send credentials, so the button and the payload cannot disagree.

Finally, the server refuses a payload that would drop every stored credential.
Azure's schema is `.passthrough()` with every field optional, so a header-only
payload validated cleanly and the loss was silent; the same silent loss has now
arrived twice by different routes. Omission is the signal, not emptiness:
clearing a credential sends the field empty and still goes through, and a row
with nothing stored yet is unaffected. This also closes an empty-object payload
on the REST upsert that emptied the bag the same way.

* test(model-providers): spec the header, dirty and refusal behaviour

The four new tests annotate scenarios that had nowhere to land, so
check-feature-parity failed on unknown annotations. Adds them next to the
masked-placeholder scenario they extend.

* test(model-providers): review follow-ups on the credential guard

- Customer copy for the refusal says what to do rather than describing the
  request shape.
- New suites use the given/when hierarchy the ast-grep rule asks for, instead
  of topic labels.
- Cover the guard on `custom` and `azure_safety` too, since it reads the
  provider's own schema rather than a list of names. Which layer says no
  differs by how strict that schema is: `custom` strips the unknown key and
  the guard catches it, `azure_safety` demands a URL and a non-empty key so
  validation rejects it first. Both keep the stored credentials, and the
  difference is the reason the guard exists, because a loose schema never
  objects.

* test(model-providers): state the header scenarios as outcomes, not mechanics

Feature prose is the behaviour contract, so it describes what a customer can
observe rather than columns, payload shapes and schema strictness. The
header scenario also now asserts the header is saved, so a regression that
drops it cannot pass on credential preservation alone.

* fix(model-providers): a partial save no longer deletes the credentials it leaves out

The guard added earlier only refused a payload that named no credential at
all. A payload naming one of several passed it, and the merge then dropped
every field the payload had not mentioned: a caller rotating an Azure
endpoint deleted the API key it never sent, and the provider stopped working
with nothing on screen to explain it. The REST upsert is where that shape
arrives, since a script sends the one field it means to change.

A secret is masked on read, so no caller can resend one it did not type, and
leaving it out cannot be a request to delete it. Leaving out anything else
still drops it, because the visible configuration is stated in full on every
save, and that is how the Azure API-Gateway toggle switches over. The merge
now says so in one place, `mergeStoredCustomKeys`, which the unit test calls
instead of restating: the copy that used to live in the test stayed green
through both rounds of this bug.

The guard stays for the payload that names nothing, which still cannot be a
credential edit and would still wipe the endpoint.

Also makes the credential-loss copy provider-neutral rather than naming an
API key and endpoint, since the error is raised for every provider.

feat(gateway): store the trace destination at creation instead of deriving it per read (#6769)

* feat(gateway): store every virtual key's trace destination, and backfill the ones that exist

Where a key's traces and costs land was derived on every read: the key's own
traceProjectId, then its single project access scope, then the organization's
oldest live governance project. Three lookups, each of which had to remember
that a deleted project is not a destination, and one of which forgot.

The column becomes the answer instead. This is the specs, the schema comment,
the migration that fills the column for keys that already exist, and the
read-only report that says what it will do before it does it.

The backfill answers the old chain once, with its own rules, so no key's
traffic moves: a pointer at a live project of the key's organization is kept,
one that is deleted or foreign is passed over, a single live project scope is
taken, and everything else gets the governance inbox. An organization with no
governance project has nothing to write, so those keys stay null and keep
taking the path they take today, where the gateway skips span export rather
than failing. It is idempotent: every value it writes satisfies the predicate
that would have cleared it.

The column stays nullable and the invariant is enforced in the app. A NOT NULL
would fail the migration on exactly the self-hosted data that cannot satisfy
it, mid-deploy.

* refactor(gateway): delete the trace-destination chain and read the column

Creation now decides the destination once, using exactly the rules the chain
used, and stores it. Reading it back is a column read and one project lookup.

What goes: the three-stage resolver, its batch precedence machinery, the
source discriminant, and the org-scoped key pairing the batch needed. What
stays is one org-pinned archived-aware lookup that write-time validation uses,
and one plain lookup that follows the stored pointer wherever it goes.

Two behaviors change on purpose.

Editing a key's scopes no longer moves where its traces land. That used to
happen silently, because the destination was re-derived from the scopes on
every read: two decisions, made on two screens, one of which never mentioned
the other. The pointer moves only when trace_project_id is set, validated the
way create validates it.

Deleting the project a key traces into no longer reroutes its traffic. The
materialiser follows the pointer as it stands, so the spans keep landing
there, whole, and reappear if the customer restores the project. Rerouting
would scatter one key's history across two projects for an act performed on a
different screen, and failing would take its traffic down for the same. The
write-time refusal for naming a deleted project stays.

Tests that wrote key rows straight to Postgres now carry the destination:
nothing derives it for them any more.

* feat(gateway): say on the key when the project it traces into was deleted

A key goes on sending its traces to a project the customer deleted, which is
the right thing to do and the one thing a reader cannot work out for
themselves: the destination still resolves, the traces still arrive, and
nothing on the row says the project behind it is gone.

So reads publish trace_project_archived, computed once per page rather than
per row, and the key's drawer badges it with a line saying the traces are
still going there and how to change that.

trace_project_source leaves the DTO with the chain it described. It named
which of three rules answered, and there is one rule now: the column.

* docs(api): publish the stored trace destination and drop the rule that named itself

Regenerates the API description and the generated client, and says the two
things a caller now has to know: trace_project_id is decided when the key is
written and a scope edit does not move it, and trace_project_archived means
the key is still tracing into a project that was deleted.

The CLI marks a deleted destination where it prints the key, since that read
is the only place it surfaces for anyone working from a terminal.

* docs(aigateway): describe the trace destination as stored, not resolved per read

* fix(gateway): follow an existing key's stored destination when previewing its budgets

The "already applies" list serves a draft in the create drawer and a real key
in the edit drawer through one shape. Deciding the destination again is right
for the draft and wrong for the key: a key whose destination the customer
deleted previewed no project or team budgets while the gateway went on
enforcing them, because the decision refuses a deleted destination and the
materialiser follows the pointer as it stands. A key that exists now follows
its pointer, the way the bundle does.

Also from review:

- The migration says IRREVERSIBLE and why, as the repo requires, and spells
  out the one step worth reading twice: clearing an archived pointer is what
  keeps those keys' traffic where the chain is already sending it, since
  keeping the pointer would move it into a project the customer deleted.
- No semicolon anywhere in the migration but at the end of a statement. One
  inside a comment splits the file for anything that replays it, this repo's
  own backfill test included.
- The published update description says what an explicit null does, which is
  re-resolve under the create rules rather than clear the destination.
- The report script walks the keys a page at a time, so "safe against
  production" means bounded and not only read-only, and counts organizations
  missing a governance project from Organization rather than from the
  projects, which left out the ones with no projects at all.
- Named object parameters on the DTO helpers.
- The archived-destination note no longer offers a move the drawer does not
  provide, and the idempotency test seeds the shape most at risk of a second
  write.

* refactor(gateway): split the backfill report's key walk from its page fold

* docs(gateway): say precisely what an explicit null destination re-resolves to

Second review pass, all of it about saying what the code does rather than
roughly what it does.

- The update contract said explicit null refuses a shared key whenever the
  organization has projects. It is narrower: null re-runs the create rules, so
  a key with exactly one live project scope takes that project, and only a key
  with none to take is refused. Fixed on the published description and in the
  docs, and the PATCH example carries the field now.
- The report script's header claimed it holds one page whatever the size of
  the instance. It also holds the projects and the organization ids, so it
  says so, and it no longer claims a walk with no snapshot around it cannot
  miss a row written while it runs.
- Named object parameters on the draft-destination helper, and the comment
  over the page fold explains why it is split out rather than restating it.

* fix(gateway): true up the null-destination copy, the spec's claim shape, and the CLI labels

The edit drawer's fallback copy said a destination-less key's traces land in the governance inbox, which is exactly backwards under stored destinations: null means the organization had no governance project to give, so nothing files those traces. The copy now says so and names the remedy. The ownership tooltip stops claiming attribution stability comes from frozen ownership; it comes from the destination being stored, and both scopes and the destination move through the management API. The config-bundle spec now states the claim is present and null rather than omitted, matching what the materialiser sends and the integration coverage asserts. CLI labels spell out Trace project and Routing policy, and the deleted suffix variable says what it holds.

* chore: retrigger ci after a dropped push event

* docs(gateway): state every branch of explicit-null destination re-resolution

The published re-resolution rules stopped one branch early: they named the single-project-scope case and the ambiguous refusal, but not that only a live project qualifies, nor the fall-back to the organization's oldest live governance project when there is nothing else to choose from, nor the trace_project_required refusal when there is no governance project to fall back on. A client reading them could expect gateway_trace_project_ambiguous in exactly the case the resolver quietly succeeds. The wire description, the management docs, and their llms-full mirror now walk all four branches of decideTraceDestination. The ownership tooltip stops calling visibility set-at-creation, since the update contract replaces scopes, and the null-destination note drops the implementation history for what the customer needs: no destination means nothing files this key's traces.

* docs(gateway): say which legacy keys can carry a null destination

Only a key written before the destination was stored, in an organization that had no governance project to give it, carries null. Saying every legacy key can invited clients to treat null as a normal legacy state.

refactor(aigateway): one auth cache tier, and a conditional config refresh (#6768)

* refactor(aigateway): drop the shared auth cache tier

The auth resolver had an optional L2 store in front of the control plane,
implemented once against Redis. Nothing in production wired it: deps.go
never set Options.L2, no env var reached it, and the Helm chart's
redis.url only ever gated a NetworkPolicy egress rule. So the tier was
dead code that the change feed still had to reach, which is where its one
real cost landed, an invalidation path that has to delete from a second
place or the next request rehydrates the bundle the event just
invalidated.

What it was meant to buy is a warm start for a new pod. That cost is
already paid on every rolling deploy, one control-plane round trip per
key per pod, and if a scale-out burst ever does hurt, singleflight plus a
warmup pull answers it without a second store to keep coherent.

Deleted: L2Store, CachedBundle, RedisStore and its gw:auth:v2 keyspace,
serveFromL2, setL2, the chunked deleteL2 path, the l2_redis metric tier,
and Options.L2. classifyEntry stays: it is L1's rule, and its
grace-window test keeps binding a scenario. go-redis leaves go.mod with
nothing else importing it.

The chart's inert redis.url and networkPolicy.egressToRedis go with it,
along with the docs that promised the tier and the CI helm render that
set redis.url to exercise a branch that no longer exists.

* feat(aigateway): revalidate the config safety net instead of re-downloading it

The control plane has served an ETag on /api/internal/gateway/config since
the endpoint shipped, and answers 304 to a matching If-None-Match. It keys
that ETag off VirtualKey.revision, which every mutation bumps. Nothing
consumed it: the Go client fetched the config unconditionally and the
control plane materialized, serialized and sent the whole bundle every
time.

That fetch runs on a timer. The change feed is what propagates a config
edit; the ConfigTTL refresh underneath it is the safety net for the
mutations that emit no event, and it fires per cached key, per TTL, per
pod, almost always to learn nothing changed. Conditional, that becomes a
revision lookup instead of a materialization, which is the difference
between a control plane that shrugs at a high-volume rollout and one that
spends its query budget re-answering the same question.

The cache entry now carries the ETag its config came back under, and the
staleness refresh offers it. A 304 keeps the bundle and lets
endConfigRefresh restart the staleness clock, which is what a
confirmation is worth. A 200 swaps in the config and the new ETag. A
response with no ETag stores none, so the next refresh goes out
unconditional rather than revalidating against a token nobody issued, and
any error leaves the cached config in place.

The cold path stays unconditional on purpose: it is materializing config
for a bundle that has none, so "still current" would be an answer about
nothing, and both the client and populateConfig refuse a 304 that answers
a request which offered no ETag.

FetchConfig now returns domain.ConfigFetchResult rather than a bare
BundleConfig, so "not modified" is a state the caller has to handle
instead of an empty config it might cache over a working one.

* fix(charts): stop the SSO provider test failing on its own SIGPIPE

The test's render() ended in `cat "$out"`, and every reader pipes that
into an awk that stops at the first thing it was looking for. Once the
rendered manifest is larger than the pipe buffer, cat is still writing
when awk exits, takes SIGPIPE, and `set -o pipefail` reports the run as
failed against whichever assertion happened to be reading. `cat big |
awk 'NR>1{exit}'` under those options exits 141 every time.

Whether it fires depends on how far into the manifest the awk finds its
match, so the script has been one env-var reshuffle away from a red run
since it landed, and it went red on a change that only shrank a subchart's
values.

render() now prints the path to the cached manifest and each reader opens
the file itself. No pipe, so nothing to signal, and the readers keep
stopping as early as they like.

* docs(aigateway): reconcile the auth-cache and admin-listener claims

Review follow-up on the pages this PR already touched.

The admin/pprof surface is documented three different ways. The gateway
binary opens no admin listener at all, which is what the helm page's own
"Admin listener" section and the chart's deployment comment say, and
grepping the Go tree for pprof or an admin address finds nothing. Two
other places described a loopback-bound listener with a bearer token and a
startup refusal as if it were live. That is the dangerous direction to be
wrong in, so the NetworkPolicy note, the timeout note and the security
page now say what ships and mark the protected listener as planned.

The helm upgrade steps claimed the cache survives restarts, which an
in-process LRU cannot. The runbook's pod-failure row claimed no impact and
a PDB holding two replicas: the chart default is minAvailable 1 against 2
replicas, and a PDB bounds voluntary disruptions, so it says nothing about
a crash, which does cut the streams pinned to that pod.

The config TTL note oversold the conditional refresh: a cached config with
no ETag is refreshed unconditionally and does cost a full bundle.

contract.md §9 said the L1 TTL is the JWT exp, which skips the whole
stale-while-error window that follows it, and gave a 64k entry bound
against a 10k default. It now describes the grace window and the real
default, and the bootstrap flag is named the way §6 names it, with the
feature file's aspirational scenario moved onto that same name so the two
documents stop reserving two names for one unbuilt feature.

The conditional-refresh rule promised that a failed or unreadable refresh
leaves the cached config in place and bound nothing to it. Two @unit
scenarios now cover it: the existing keeps-serving test picks up the
annotation plus an assertion that the failure is reported, and a new
client test proves an unparseable 200 yields an error rather than an empty
config or a stored token.

configServer's captured headers move behind a mutex and a snapshot
accessor, matching etagConfigFetcher, so the assertions do not depend on
net/http internals under -race.

llms-full.txt is regenerated from the sources rather than hand-edited.

* fix(aigateway): refuse a config body that did not arrive whole

FetchConfig dropped the error from io.ReadAll and unmarshalled whatever
had arrived. A stream cut after the closing brace of the top-level object
leaves bytes that parse perfectly well into a bundle missing everything
that came after them, so a truncated response could be cached as config,
with a fresh ETag stamped on it, and a key would quietly lose whatever
was in the tail. The read error is now checked before the body is
trusted. Its regression test writes a Content-Length longer than the
valid JSON it sends, and fails without the check.

The other two readers of this response (the resolve-key and budget calls)
have the same dropped error. They are untouched here: that is the auth
hot path, and it belongs in a change that can carry the behavioral risk
on its own.

Also: the config TTL note now says a changed key still answers 200 with
the whole bundle, so the saving is on the keys nobody edited rather than
on every refresh, and contract.md writes the reserved bootstrap flag as
an assignment rather than an expansion.

* docs(aigateway): say what the config read-error guard actually protects

The comment claimed a truncated body unmarshals into a bundle "missing
whatever came after" the closing brace, which cannot happen: a JSON
object's fields are all before its closing brace, and trailing bytes make
Unmarshal fail rather than silently drop anything.

What the guard is really for is that a read ending in an error leaves the
response's integrity unknown, and the arrived bytes parsing says nothing
about that, since a prefix can be a complete object cut out of a message
that never arrived whole. Accepting it stamps the server's ETag on config
this node never fully read, and every later refresh revalidates against
that token. Comment only, no behavior change.

fix(members): desired-state access edits, group-aware guards, Lite Member rows store the truth (#6698)

* fix(members): apply member access edits as desired state, and list group access on every plan

A customer admin swapping seats hit three different errors in one
afternoon, all from the same dialog. Re-adding an access row the member
already held failed as an unknown error: the duplicate insert tripped the
partial unique index and the P2002 degraded to the generic toast. Removing
a row while picking a Lite Member seat failed with "one or more bindings
not found": the seat change rewrites the member's team rows before the
binding batch lands, so the staged ids were stale. And every save fired a
refused group.listForMember request, because the read was gated to
Enterprise while the member dialog issues it for every organization.

applyMemberBindings now treats the batch as the state the admin wants:
deletes skip ids that are already gone, and creates skip rows the member
already holds. Writing the repro also proved the delete filter accepted
any binding id in the organization, so a member's save could remove
another member's or a group's rows; deletes are now scoped to the member's
own direct bindings. applyGroupEdits gets the same treatment, since two
admins editing the same group hit the identical stale-id class.

group.listForMember loses the Enterprise gate: permission resolution
honours group bindings on every plan, so the read either misreports
effective access or refuses every dialog open. The management surfaces
keep theirs.

The dialog now re-reads the member's access after a failed save, since the
role change lands before the binding batch and the failure toast used to
sit on top of rows the server had already rewritten. It also refuses to
stage an access row identical to one already listed.

* fix(members): stop churning binding ids on role sync, and save a filled access row without Add

Every role sync deleted and recreated the binding row, four separate
times in the organization repository, which is the root the stale-id
class grew from: the member dialog stages removals by id, the seat
change applied first and replaced every id, and the binding batch then
named rows that no longer existed. setUserScopeBinding updates the row
in place, so an id stays valid across the whole save, rows keep their
creation order in the access list, and a removal the admin staged
before the seat change lands instead of being silently superseded. The
integration test asserts the id survives the correction and the
removal actually removes.

The input row now reports draft completeness, so filling in an access
row without pressing Add enables Save, which flushes it. The two spec
scenarios that described dialog internals are reworded to observable
behavior.

* fix(teams): the team form keeps the last-admin guard, and refusals reach the person saving

Dogfooding the seat flows end to end found the one write path with no
last-admin awareness: team.update saves the whole member list as a diff,
so demoting the team's only admin, or leaving them out of the list,
reported "Team updated successfully" and left the team with nobody who
can administer it. The save now recounts admins inside its transaction
and refuses with team_last_admin_required when it would take the last
one away. A team that already has no team-scoped admin, which a seat
correction can legitimately produce, stays editable here, because this
form is also where somebody gets promoted back.

The refusal used to vanish even where it was raised: the team page's
autosave error handler only had words for FORBIDDEN and UNAUTHORIZED,
so anything else silently reverted the form. It now falls through to
the registry copy, which names the team and the remedy.

Also from the same session: the organization-scoped row that mirrors
the member's seat appeared in the dialog as a removable access row
after a seat round trip, inviting a delete that would desync the seat
from its binding. The mirror row no longer offers removal; custom-role
and off-seat organization rows still do. And the duplicate-collapse in
setUserScopeBinding now breaks createdAt ties by id, so repeated runs
keep the same row.

* fix(event-sourcing): name the rejected cache write as its own consistency hole

ADR-066 claimed that running Redis with noeviction leaves a miss meaning TTL
expiry and nothing else. It does not. Under memory pressure noeviction rejects
the SET, the entry is never created, and the next read finds nothing and counts
an ordinary miss, which no expiry preceded. That is the same non-settlement a
pre-TTL eviction would have been, moved from the read side to the write side.

The trade is still worth making, because the write side is counted where the
read side would have been silent, so the ADR now names the third hole and says
the write counter is what to watch under pressure. A scenario and its test pin
it: the rejected write increments the write-error counter, and the read that
follows reports a plain miss rather than a fallback.

Also from the same review: a comment claimed the sorted column draws a heavier
label, which the code deliberately does not do (it reads lighter when forced),
and three fixtures carried a Haiku identifier that no product data uses.

* spec(automations): retention sweep, overflow coalescing, condition requirement and runaway containment

Specs first, before any implementation.

New:

Both amended files leave LEGACY_INERT in check-feature-parity: they now carry

* feat(event-sourcing): reap process-manager inbox and outbox on a schedule

The substrate's two traffic-bound tables had no working deletion path.
ProcessManagerInbox had none at all. ProcessManagerOutbox had a per-process
prune that six of twelve process names never registered, and the highest
volume one got its retention by piggybacking on an unrelated pipeline's
daily prune behind an unguarded await. Production reached 2.8M inbox rows
and 473k outbox rows in twenty days on a database with autoscaling off.

- New process_manager_maintenance pipeline with an hourly processRetentionSweep
  singleton that reaps by predicate across every processName, so no process
  manager has to opt in and none added later can be forgotten.
- Three batched store methods, bounded by an id subquery so one statement's
  lock footprint stays small, drained 5,000 rows at a time up to 200 batches
  per family per wake, each family isolated from the others' failures.
- Windows: dispatched outbox 24h, dead outbox 30d, consumed inbox 7d.
- Migration adds a partial index on dispatched rows and one on consumedAt,
  the two shapes the existing indexes cannot answer.
- The overflow log entry is keyed per trigger per minute of event time
  instead of on a cumulative counter, so a storm coalesces to one row per
  trigger per minute rather than one row per overflowed match.
- Drops the webhook-prune piggyback the global sweep now covers.

* feat(automations): require a condition on every automation write path

The drawer has always refused a condition-less automation, but only in the
browser. Every server write path accepted one, and the REST create went
further: filters carried a .default({}), so the smallest possible create
call produced an automation matching every trace forever. That is the one
genuinely customer-facing hole behind the volume incident.

- hasActionableTriggerFilters mirrors the drawer's filtersAreSet on the
  server; a present-but-empty field selects nothing and is not a condition.
- TriggerFiltersRequiredError (trigger_filters_required, 422) with its
  sorted code entry and its customer-facing copy.
- Enforced on tRPC create, tRPC upsert, tRPC updateTriggerFilters, REST
  create and REST patch. Alerts and reports are exempt: their condition is
  a threshold or a schedule.
- REST create no longer defaults filters. Omitting the key is now the same
  as sending an empty one, and both answer a typed 422. Breaking change.
- Rows saved before the rule keep firing unchanged. The trigger cache logs
  them once per fill so the remaining population stays visible.

BREAKING: POST /api/triggers now requires a non-empty filters object.

* feat(automations): plan-tiered daily ceiling and runaway containment

An automation that matches a large share of a project's traffic produces
real work, and nothing bounded it: the existing caps only ever covered
email and webhooks. One customer's two triggers produced roughly 300k
process-manager rows in a day for about two annotation items of output.

The blame split is the design. Only CONFIRMED persist dispatches count
toward the ceiling: matches whose filters genuinely passed and that were
about to create a dataset row or an annotation item. Match records,
unconfirmed matches, debounce fan-out, overflow flushes and retries are
our pipeline's amplification, so they are measured on team metrics and
never charged to a customer.

- Per-trigger daily ceiling, plan-tiered and env-overridable: 100 for free
  and entry tiers, 1,000 for paid, 10,000 for enterprise, with
  PlanInfo.maxTriggerPersistDispatchesPerDay as a per-contract raise.
- The ceiling sits after confirmSettledMatch and before dispatchTriggerAction.
  Retry-safe via a SET-NX claim on the (trigger, trace) pair, and the counter
  keeps climbing past the cap so the overshoot stays measurable.
- Over the ceiling is a throttle, not a punishment: terminal drop, trigger
  stays active, one email that day, works again next UTC day.
- Pausing is reserved for misconfiguration: a grandfathered condition-less
  automation, or one whose confirmed matches cover 90% of at least 100
  traces of project traffic in 24h. Resuming clears the pause record.
- Migration adds Trigger.pausedReason and pausedAt.
- Containment can never break the dispatch it watches: it is guarded at the
  call site as well as internally.
- The automations list shows a paused badge or a skipped-today count.
- New metrics: automation_match_records_total, automation_overflow_flush_total,
  automation_ceiling_breach_total, automation_auto_paused_total{reason}.

* refactor(automations): keep the new code under the repo's complexity budget

CI compares Biome violation counts between base and head and fails when a
PR adds any. This adds none.

- persistCap: the plan-tier ternary becomes capForPlan, the two memory
  sweeps share one generic helper, and the Redis and in-memory counting

- runaway-containment: pauseAndNotify takes an object rather than four

- The ceiling gate moves out of dispatchPersistMatch into
