* fix(automations): close the review gaps in retention and containment

Addresses the review on the retention and ceiling work. The substantive
ones:

CONTAINMENT COULD LOSE A PAUSE FOR A WHOLE DAY. The once-only claim was
taken before the pause write, keyed on the UTC day, so a single failed
write left the runaway automation active until the day rolled over with
one warn line as the only trace. The claim now gates the ATTEMPT on a
short window, which still absorbs the storm of in-flight dispatches, and
the day-long claim moved onto the mail, after the write has landed.

THE CEILING COULD DRIFT PERMANENTLY HIGH. The Redis claim and the INCR
were separate commands. A failure between them held the claim with the
count unmoved, so the dispatch was allowed from the fallback and the
retry re-read a count that never saw it. Both now run in one Lua script.

A VACUOUS FILTER COULD STILL SAVE. The write validation counted a key
selector as a condition while the matcher discarded its empty leaf, so
`{"metadata.labels": {region: []}}` saved cleanly and then fired on every
trace. Validator and matcher now share one recursive vacuity check.

THE INDEX BUILD COULD BLOCK INGESTION. `prisma migrate deploy` runs on
pod start, and a plain CREATE INDEX on these two tables blocks INSERT for
as long as the build takes. Each build now carries its own lock_timeout
and statement_timeout and degrades to a warning, so a deploy against a
backlog leaves the index for the operator instead of stalling writes.
Verified against Postgres in the single-query-message form Prisma uses,
with and without a competing lock.

THE FALLBACK MAPS GREW WITHOUT BOUND. Both in-memory claim maps are keyed
per dispatch and lived 25h, so a long Redis outage grew them for the
whole outage while a size-gated sweep put an O(n) scan on every dispatch
that deleted nothing. Sweeps are time-gated now and the claim map has a
hard ceiling with oldest-first eviction.

THE SWEEP COULD OUTLIVE ITS LEASE. 600 delete statements can outlast the
15-minute outbox lease, after which a second worker starts a concurrent
sweep. It now stops at a deadline well inside the lease and leaves the
rest for the next tick.

Also: a runnable ops script replaces the runbook's placeholder command; a
single typed definition for the pause reason instead of three loose
copies; focusable badges so the list tooltips reach keyboard users; the
in-memory store reaps dead rows by updatedAt like the durable one does;
and the test suites gain given/when contexts, guarded fixtures, and
coverage for the paths above, including the Lua script against real
Redis.

* fix(prisma): move the retention sweep indexes out of the deploy migration

A deploy-time CREATE INDEX holds a SHARE lock that blocks INSERT on the two
highest-volume write tables for the whole build. The lock_timeout guard only
bounded the wait for that lock, not the hold, so an acquired lock could still
stall ingestion for the full statement_timeout during an automatic deploy.

The indexes are ops-managed now: built with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY as an
explicit runbook step after the backlog purge, over a near-empty heap. The
schema no longer declares them, so prisma migrate dev cannot regenerate a
blocking build, and the sweep never depended on them for correctness.

* fix(automations): validate purge env numbers and drop the Redis 7 EXPIRE dependency

The purge script read its env overrides through Number(), so RETENTION_DAYS=0
widened the window to now() and would have emptied both tables under APPLY=1,
RETENTION_DAYS=7d reached Postgres as NaN and aborted mid-run, and BATCH_SIZE=0
deleted nothing while reporting success. Every override now goes through one
validator that takes the fallback when the variable is unset or empty and
otherwise demands a whole number at or above its minimum, printing why and
exiting 1 before any connection is opened.

The daily cap Lua script gave the day counter its TTL with EXPIRE ... NX, an
option that needs Redis 7. On Redis 6 the whole eval throws, and the catch
quietly degrades the fleet-wide ceiling to per-worker counters for self-hosted
installs. The script now reads TTL first and sets the expiry only when the key
carries none, which keeps claim, INCR and expiry in one atomic script and keeps
the TTL from sliding on retries.

The daily cap status test used fixed project and trigger ids against real Redis,
where the counter carries a 25h TTL, so a rerun on the same UTC day inherited
the previous run's counters and claims and its skipped assertion went stale. It
now builds run-unique ids and deletes the keys it wrote, following the
tracked-keys pattern the persist cap suite already uses.

The whitespace-only query case asserted that nothing narrows the automation
while sitting under "given something narrows the automation". It moves next to
the other no-condition cases, with the assertion unchanged.

* fix(automations): drop the Redis 7 EXPIRE dependency from the email caps too

Same defect the persist cap carried: EXPIRE with the NX option needs Redis 7,
and on Redis 6 the throw lands after the INCR already ran, leaving an immortal
counter key and degrading the cap to per-worker in-memory counting for
self-hosted installs. The TTL guard keeps the no-slide property (a window that
is ticking is never reset) and the re-attempt property (a lost first EXPIRE is
retried by every later hit).

* feat(automations): warn in the drawer when a condition would outrun the daily ceiling

The ceiling was discovered after the fact: the first a customer heard of it
was the skipped-matches email. The drawer already counts what the drafted
condition matched over the last 7 days, so it now derives a matches-per-day
estimate from the same preview and, for persist-class actions only, warns
when that estimate exceeds the plan's resolved daily limit.

Advice, never a gate: a failed preview, a failed cap read, or a notify-class
action all render nothing, and saving is untouched in every case.

* fix(automations): make the limit emails actionable and suppression-aware

The limit email asks the customer to narrow the condition, but its deep link
opened the legacy structured-filter drawer, which cannot edit a query-based
condition at all. The link now opens the automation authoring drawer, and the
same broken link is fixed in the four platformUrl fields of the REST triggers
API. The legacy drawer stays registered so previously mailed links resolve.

Limit email recipients are now filtered through the ADR-031 suppression list,
failing open so an unreadable list never swallows the one mail that explains
why an automation stopped producing records.

The legacy filter drawer's save error handler also surfaced a hardcoded
string instead of the server's registered copy; it now goes through
showErrorToast, so a rejected condition explains itself.

The automation limit email template gains the unit coverage the sibling
templates already had.

* fix(docs): concurrent invalid-index drop and honest post-purge index timing

The invalid-index recovery step told operators to run a plain DROP INDEX,
which takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that blocks reads and writes on the same
hot tables this runbook exists to protect; it is DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF
EXISTS now, outside an explicit transaction. The step-5 rationale also
overclaimed the post-purge heap as near-empty: a plain VACUUM only marks
pages reusable, so the honest benefit is fewer live tuples to sort and write.

The cap-status test teardown deletes its Redis keys one per DEL, since a
multi-key DEL fails with CROSSSLOT on a cluster connection and a failed
teardown would strand 25h keys.

* test(scripts): deflake the check-queue overlap assertion with a real hold window

* fix(automations): keep both cap keys in one Redis Cluster slot and make the email-cap TTL guard atomic

* feat(automations): offer an Upgrade Plan way out on the cap advice, align names and runbook checks with review

* fix(process-manager): hand each retention family its share of the wake

* fix(automations): absorb breach storms before the traffic query, read cap counts per key, fail closed on unreadable conditions

* fix(automations): align pausedAt with timestamptz, name the toggle for screen readers, pin resume through the real mutation

* fix(process-manager): ramp the retention sweep's first wakes instead of opening at the ceiling

The batch size bounds one statement's lock footprint and the batch ceiling
bounds how many statements a wake issues, but neither bounds the write-ahead
log, the dead tuples or the index churn the deletes leave behind. Opening at
the full ceiling meant the very first wake, the one that meets the whole
historical backlog on the least free space, could ask a database with 2.8 GiB
left to absorb over a million deletes per family in ten minutes.

The per-wake budget now opens at 5 batches per family and doubles every wake up
to the existing 200, and each statement is followed by the same 200 ms pause the
supervised purge script already uses. A multi-million row backlog still drains
within a day, steady state never notices because an hour of traffic is a few
batches, and the one-time purge runbook becomes an accelerator rather than the
thing that makes the deploy safe.

* fix(process-manager): clamp the sweep's batch budget at the ceiling on use

The wake handler already caps what it writes, so an over-large budget could
only arrive on a payload this code did not write. Bounding it in the schema
would answer that by failing the intent, exhausting its retries and
dead-lettering the sweep, which stops retention and regrows the tables it
exists to bound. Clamping holds the delete loop to the same ceiling and keeps
the sweep running.

* fix(automations): bind the purge script's SQL and keep old automation links useful

Two review findings from the same pass.

The purge script spliced RETENTION_DAYS and BATCH_SIZE straight into its SQL.
intEnv rejects anything that is not a whole number, so nothing could be
injected today, but the safety lived two screens away from the splice and the
next override added there would not necessarily be an integer. The counts and
the ctid batch deletes now bind their values; the VACUUM keeps a literal
identifier because Postgres takes no parameter in that position.

The deep link the REST API returns moved from the filter-only drawer to the
authoring drawer, and every producer moved together, but URLs handed out
earlier live in inboxes and in whatever callers stored. The old drawer name now
resolves to the authoring drawer, so those links open the editor that can
change a query condition instead of the one that never could, and the drawer
they used to open is gone rather than left unreachable.

* fix(automations): stop three error paths from failing in the wrong direction

Review asked for a pass over the handled errors. Three were pointing the wrong
way, and they are the ones a customer or an operator would feel.

A plan read that failed cached its fallback for the whole cache window. The
fallback is the paid ceiling, which is open against the free tier and a tenth
of the allowance against the enterprise one, and matches over a ceiling are
dropped terminally. One transient read turned into ten minutes of an enterprise
account quietly losing most of its automation output. The fallback is now
returned without being cached, so it costs one dispatch instead.

The day-long claim that makes the limit email once-only was held across the
send. An SMTP refusal therefore bought a whole day of silence about an
automation that had stopped producing records. The claim is released when the
send throws, and the containment rate limit in front of it keeps a broken
mailer to one attempt a minute. The mailer itself also stopped treating one
unroutable admin address as a failed batch.

Containment failure logged at warn while a mere breach logged at error, so the
loudest signal was "an automation is busy" and the quietest was "the thing
that answers that did not run". It now logs at error and increments
automation_containment_failed_total, and the retention sweep gained
process_manager_retention_failures_total so a family that fails every hour no
longer looks like a family with nothing to sweep.

Also, while in these files: the project-not-found throw in the automations
router is a HandledError rather than a bare Error, the daily-cap status query
and its caller share one constant instead of two numbers that had drifted, and
the purge script reports how far it got before a failure.

* test(automations): drive the legacy automation link through the real drawer path

Asserting that two registry keys point at the same component proved the mapping
and nothing else: it never resolved a URL, so it could not tell whether a link
still reaches a drawer at all. The test now renders CurrentDrawer with the
legacy query string and lets the real registry and its lazy import answer,
stubbing only the drawer's body.

* fix(automations): specify the REST edit contract and soften the purge's stop warning

The REST patch that empties a condition was tested for its 422, its
machine-readable code and the stored condition surviving, but no scenario
claimed that test, so the contract most likely to leave a half-applied
automation behind was the one the specs did not state.

The purge's batch-ceiling warning asserted that rows remain. Reaching the
ceiling only proves the last batch was full, and a full batch can take the last
eligible rows, so it now says they may remain.

* docs(process-manager): record the executed purge and correct what VACUUM returns

The purge ran against production on 2026-08-09 ahead of this PR. The runbook
now carries its numbers as the record of that run, and the sweep's ramp is
described as defence in depth for a future backlog rather than as the thing
that makes this deploy safe, because there is no longer a backlog for it to
meet.

The verify step also told operators to expect the file sizes not to move. That
is only half true: a plain VACUUM does hand back empty pages at the end of the
heap, which is why this run finished with more free space than it started. The
step now says the sizes move only to the extent that the deleted rows sat at
the end, warns against planning on it, and keeps the point that either outcome
is a successful purge.

* fix(automations): cover every automation's cap badge, and stop two failures from crossing a boundary

Three findings from the review round on the current head.

The daily cap status took its automations from the caller, capped at 500. The
list renders every automation in the project, so any automation past that cap
lost its "skipped today" badge with nothing to say why, and it landed on
exactly the projects with enough automations to want it. The status now reads
the ids itself: the work is bounded by what the project owns rather than by
what a caller asks for, and the count reads chunk so a project with thousands
of automations does not open one Redis command per automation at once. The
authoring drawer only ever wanted the ceiling, so it takes a cap-only query
instead of asking for counts it discards.

A containment claim released by key alone crossed workers. A worker that
claimed while Redis was unreachable, whose send then failed after Redis came
back and another worker had claimed and mailed, would delete that worker's
claim, and the next breach would mail the customer a second time. A claim now
hands back a lease carrying its own token, and both stores drop the key only
while that lease still holds it.

A mail provider quotes the envelope back in its rejection, so logging the
failure text wrote the admin's address into the log and into the error the
containment path re-logs. The failure is reported by its code or SMTP status
instead, which is the part that says what went wrong and names nobody.

fix(observability): let a gateway log join its trace, and a JS log name its build (#6702)

* fix(observability): let a gateway log join its trace, and a JS log name its build

Two gaps found while auditing what each producer actually sends to Loki. They
are mirror images: the Go gateway has a version and no trace correlation, the
JS app has trace correlation and no version.

**The gateway's access log carried no trace_id — 0 of 10,762 records.** Not
missing instrumentation: it exports spans to Tempo, the tracer middleware is
wired, and it calls clog.WithSpanContext. The two middlewares were registered
in the wrong order. Telemetry captures its context up front
(`ctx := clog.With(r.Context(), ...)`) and logs `request_completed` with that
same value AFTER the inner chain returns, so anything a LATER middleware puts
on a derived context is invisible to it. Registered after Telemetry, the tracer
stamped the ids onto a context the access log never reads.

langyagent wires the same two middlewares the other way round, says why in a
comment, and carries a trace_id on 98.7% of its records. That is the control
case: same code, opposite order, opposite outcome. nlpgo registers Telemetry
with no tracing middleware at all, which is a separate gap and not fixed here.

Three tests: the correct order correlates, the real NewRouter correlates (so
the registration order is what is guarded, not a chain reassembled in the
test), and the broken order does not — the last so the first two cannot pass
for the wrong reason. All three use a real SDK provider set as the global,
since the middleware resolves its tracer from there and a no-op would make them
vacuous. Verified the NewRouter test fails when the order is put back.

**No JS log line named its build.** The deployment already states it —
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES carries service.version=<tag> and envDetector merges
it into the OTel resource — but that resource only reaches telemetry we EXPORT.
These logs go to stdout and are read back off the pod's log file, a path the
resource never touches. Measured against prod: service_version appeared on no
record in the entire fleet.

The pino bindings now read the same env var rather than introducing a second
way to state the version, which is how the two would drift. SERVICE_VERSION is
accepted as an explicit override, and an unset environment adds no field at all
rather than an empty one.

* fix(observability): decode the version, and test the wiring not just the parser

Both from review, and the first one is the same mistake this branch's other
commit exists to fix — testing the layer above the thing that can break.

**The tests only called serviceVersionField().** A parser test passes perfectly
well while the emitted record carries nothing, because the field only reaches a
log line if the parser is wired into pino's `bindings` formatter, and a direct
call proves nothing about that. There is now a test that goes through
createLogger and reads what lands on the stream. Verified it discriminates:
removing the one `...serviceVersionField()` line fails the two emitted-record
tests while every parser test still passes, which is precisely the gap.

**OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES values are percent-encoded** — the spec's W3C
Baggage octet string, which is how a value containing `,` or `=` survives a
format that separates on both. The OTel SDK's envDetector decodes them and this
did not, so a log could have said `git%2Dabc` where the trace said `git-abc`.
That is exactly the drift reading this variable was meant to prevent. A
malformed escape falls back to the raw text: decodeURIComponent throws on a
stray `%`, and a version printed imperfectly beats no version.

fix(observability): make the prod error signal mean something (#6687)

* fix(observability): make the prod error signal mean something

A 24h review of prod logs found 143k records at ERROR, of which about 190
were a real defect. The rest were expected 4xx rejections and one retried
infrastructure condition, all of which either were emitted at error level or
were promoted to it. Six changes, in the order they matter.

**The measurement was wrong in both directions.** Loki derives
`detected_level` from the presence of a field named `error`, and that guess
beats the `severity_text` we emit. `logHttpRequest` attached the cause under
`error` even at warn, so 128k handled 402s a day arrived as errors — while
28,129 of 32,242 genuine worker errors were stamped `unknown` and were
invisible to anything filtering on it. The cause now moves to
`requestError` on any record below error level, with `errorType` restated
flat so the grouping survives. At error level nothing changes, so existing
5xx dashboards are untouched. Same rule, same reason, as
`VENDOR_CAUSE_FIELD` in @langwatch/clickhouse-client.

**500s on POST /api/otel/v1/traces (~190/day).** Every way `readWireBody`
can fail is the sender's — an exporter that gave up mid-upload, an already
consumed body, an unsupported encoding, a body that will not decompress —
and none was classified, so all reached the boundary unhandled as 500s.
They now raise `OtlpBodyUnreadableError` / `OtlpUnsupportedEncodingError`
(400, customer fault) with the cause on `reasons`. Releasing the reader also
moves out of the bare `finally`: a throw from `finally` REPLACES the error on
its way out, which is why the logs named a stream-internals TypeError rather
than the disconnect behind it.

**Validation failures now say what was wrong, not what was sent.** The
collector logged the whole body and the whole span — customer prompts and
completions into the log sink and Sentry — while the useful part stayed
buried in a serialised error. `validationMeta()` replaces the payload with
the failing path, the rule that rejected it, and the keys we refused. Those
are our schema's vocabulary, so they are safe to log and safe to aggregate:
a key refused across many projects is how we learn the schema, not the
sender, is what needs to change. Fields are copied by an allow-list per
issue code because zod's `message` and `received` both embed the value.

**ClickHouse attempts stop claiming a verdict they do not have.**
`logFailure` reported every failed attempt at error with the cause on
`error` — 17k records a day against zero jobs actually dropped, since reads
surface their translated error at the boundary and inserts are issued from
jobs the queue retries. Now warn, cause on `queryError`, still counted.

**Two ClickHouse timeouts are now numbers someone chose.** `request_timeout`
was the driver's own default and the queue in front of the pool was bounded
by depth but not by time, so an observed 46-second failure was assembled out
of two limits, neither of which was 46 seconds. Both are stated, and the
wait bound sits inside the request bound. The wait timer is armed only when
the limiter is already saturated, and cleared on admission.

**The transient classifier stops reading query text.**
`/timeout/i.test(error.message)` matched anywhere in the message, and
ClickHouse echoes the failing statement back in its errors — so a syntax
error on a query mentioning "timeout" burned the full retry budget. The
driver's own timeout is matched on the whole message; every other timeout
already arrives as a code, a status, or a caller fragment.

Specs: specs/observability/ingest-validation-diagnostics.feature,
specs/otlp/otlp-body-read-failures.feature, plus scenarios added to
specs/analytics/clickhouse-structured-logging-alerting.feature and
specs/clickhouse/single-client-access.feature.

* fix(observability): correct the detected_level mechanism these comments claimed

Measured against prod on 07-08 and the stated cause was wrong. Loki 3.3 reads a
record's level by parsing the LOG LINE as JSON and looking for level / severity
/ lvl. Our lines are not JSON - fluent-bit promotes the pino fields to
structured metadata and ships the bare message as the line - so Loki never sees
a field called `error` at all. It falls back to scanning the message text, and
"error handling request" contains the word. That, not the field, is what
promoted 129,127 handled 402s a day.

The same window shows 1.15M WARN records stamped `unknown` and not one stamped
`warn`, because no level word appears in their messages. So detected_level is
noise on this pipeline in both directions.

Moving the cause off the `error` field stays, on its own merit: a record logged
at warn should not carry a key asserting it failed, and it puts requestLogging
on the same convention as VENDOR_CAUSE_FIELD and RETRY_CAUSE_FIELD. It is not,
and never was, what fixes detected_level. The real fix is
`discover_log_levels: false` in the Loki limits_config, which lands separately
in langwatch-saas, plus severity_text as the only level anything queries - the
alert rules already do.

No behaviour change. Comments, one spec line, and one test docblock.

* fix(observability): serialize the re-keyed cause, and bound the issue walk

Three findings from review, all of them real.

**The re-keyed cause was being emitted unserialised.** pino matches serializers
by exact property name, and `logger.ts` registered one for `error` only. Moving
the cause to `requestError` therefore took it off the serialiser: an Error has
no enumerable own properties, so it went out as `{}` and the message and stack -
the only reasons it is logged at all - were gone. Every existing assertion still
passed, because they check the object handed to the logger rather than the line
that comes out.

REQUEST_CAUSE_FIELD moves to constants.ts, which is what lets logger.ts register
the same serialiser for both keys without importing from request/requestLogging
and forming a cycle. The serialiser map is exported as NODE_LOG_SERIALIZERS so
the new test drives the real one instead of a copy of it. Removing the second
key from that map fails the two assertions that matter.

**maxIssues bounded the output but not the work.** collectIssues materialised
every issue, including every nested union branch, before slicing to 20. The
input is an untrusted body of up to 10 MiB against union schemas, so the array
thrown away could be far larger than the one kept. Counts all, builds only what
is kept.

**timedOut / fired now read as booleans.** hasTimedOut / hasFired, per the
prefix rule in CODING_STANDARDS.

* fix(event-sourcing): make a shed statement retryable, and tighten the specs

The substantive one came out of review and is a defect I introduced a claim
about. `classifyClickHouseError` unwraps a HandledError and classifies its
`reasons`, but the shed signals - `QueueFullError`, and the expired wait added
in this branch - carry neither a ClickHouse code nor a transient message
fragment. So every shed statement classified CRITICAL: a job refused precisely
BECAUSE the platform was busy was dropped rather than re-staged, which is the
one outcome shedding exists to avoid. `clickhouse_overloaded` is now read off
the handled shell, where that verdict actually lives. The pre-existing
queue-full path was wrong the same way and is fixed with it.

Everything else is review follow-up:

- the spec now names `queryError` rather than "any field except error" - log
  queries read it by name, so a rename to another wrong key breaks them just as
  thoroughly
- the wait-expiry scenario asserts the recoverable classification, not just the
  overload label, which is what the fix above makes true
- a bound scenario for a body that does not decompress; it had a test and no
  contract
- `parseOtlpBody.readFailures.test.ts` -> `.unit.test.ts`
- the spec said Sentry; this repo captures through posthogErrorCapture
- `rejectionLog()` throws with what it did see, instead of letting a missing
  record surface as "cannot read .issues of undefined" from whichever assertion
  ran first

Left alone deliberately: `...validation` stays spread at the three collector
rejection sites rather than nested under one key. `issueCount` is the field
worth aggregating on and flattening keeps it directly queryable; the three keys
it adds collide with nothing at those call sites.

* docs(observability): specify the request-log level and cause contract

Review was right that this shipped as unit tests with no specification behind
them. The behaviour is a contract - which level a handled failure is logged at,
which field carries the cause, and that the cause survives being moved - and it
had none, so the seven scenarios now exist and the existing tests bind to them.

The last two read the emitted line rather than the object handed to the logger,
because that is the only level at which the serialisation regression this
branch introduced was visible at all.

Also completes a step sentence in the ClickHouse logging spec that ended
without a predicate.

fix(clickhouse): three audit defects — dropped EventVersion, decimal money sums, unbounded events read (#6627)

* fix(event-sourcing): project EventVersion on every event_log read

getEventRecords left EventVersion out of its SELECT list while the row
type declared it and the mapper read it, so every event rehydrated
through that read carried version undefined. getEventRecordsUpTo and
getEventRecordsUpToPaged projected it; nothing failed, because the three
reads answer the same EventRecord through the same mapping and a column
one of them forgets to ask for simply decodes as undefined.

The version is what a version-gated fold reads to decide how to decode a
payload, and one projection writes it back to the log, so the gap
propagates rather than staying local to the read.

One EVENT_LOG_SELECT_COLUMNS constant now feeds all three queries and one
mapEventLogRows maps their rows, which removes the seam the drift lived
in. The repository test's fake client projects the stored row through the
query's own SELECT list the way ClickHouse does; the previous fake handed
back every column whatever was asked for, so it could not have failed on
this.

* fix(governance): sum the ledger's integer money on personal usage

The /me ingestion-ledger union read spend from AmountUSD, the
Decimal(18, 6) column budget.clickhouse.repository.ts documents as
never-summable: `any(AmountUSD)` per request, then sum() across the
window in three places. Rounding each debit to a micro-USD and then
adding them is not the amount anybody spent, and the gap grows with
request count rather than cancelling. A month of sub-micro requests
reads as zero.

Money now rides AmountNanoUSD, the integer column migration 00070 made
the money column, summed there and stringified so a total past 2^53
arrives with its low digits intact. parseSummedNanoUsd refuses a figure
past the safe integer range rather than publishing one that has silently
lost digits, and nanoUsdToDecimalString reads the USD figure out of the
digits instead of dividing by 1e9. The per-model read orders by the sum
itself, since its alias is now a string and would otherwise sort
lexicographically.

The subquery also gains `Status = 'success'`. It was the only read of
this ledger without it: the materialized view behind the budget rollup
filters it, and so do both enforcement reads. A provider error and a
guardrail block each write a debit row, and neither is spend the user
made — so both the amount and the request count now exclude them, which
is the semantics every other reader of this table already has.

The /me integration seed writes the nano integer the way the debits
process manager writes it, with an amount carrying digits below a
micro-USD so the assertion fails for any read that goes back to summing
the decimal, plus a provider_error row that must not count.

* fix(webhooks): require a created range on the emitted-events log

GET /api/webhooks/v1/events declared `from` and `to` optional. Omit both
and the listing reads gateway_spend FINAL with no predicate on
OccurredAt, so ClickHouse sorts every month the organization has ever
written — thirteen of them, cold tier included — to answer one page of
fifty, and again for every page after it.

The sibling route over the same table, GET /api/gateway/v1/spend-events,
has required them since it shipped and says why in a comment. This
mirrors it exactly: same `.int().positive().safe()` bounds, the same
`from <= to` refinement and message, and so the same 422 with the
offending fields named, which is what the shared validator answers for
any schema failure.

That is a breaking change in the request shape for a caller who omits
the window today, so every in-repo caller moves with it:

  - The TypeScript SDK's eventsPage/iterEvents take `from` and `to` as
    required options, matching SpendEventsApiService.listPage/iterate.
  - The Python facade's events_page/iter_events take from_ms/to_ms as
    required keyword arguments, matching SpendEventsFacade.list_page.
  - `langwatch webhooks events` defaults to the last 24 hours when the
    flags are absent, exactly as `langwatch spend-events list` does, and
    parses the flags through the shared instant parser so a bad value is
    a clean error rather than a NaN on the wire.
  - Both generated clients are regenerated from the spec rather than
    hand-edited; the OpenAPI document and its docs copy carry the
    required flags and the reason.

Two scenarios cover the refusal — no range and half a range, then an
inverted one — bound to the route's integration suite.

* fix(event-sourcing): restore EventType on the shared event_log row type

Extracting the three reads' duplicated row shapes into one `EventLogRow`
dropped `EventType` from the interface while the mapper still read it, so
`pnpm typecheck` failed on that one property. Runtime was never wrong —
the column was in the SELECT list and in the record — but the type said
otherwise, and it was the only error the job reported.

Alongside it, the review points worth taking:

  - `mapEventLogRows` and the test's `queryOf` take named object
    parameters, per the repo's rule for functions with more than one.
  - The webhooks integration suite's `eventsWindow` reads the clock once.
    Two reads let a backward step invert the range, turning an assertion
    about the page into a 422 about the window.
  - `langwatch webhooks events` anchors its default `from` to the
    resolved `to`, so `--to` alone reads the day before the instant the
    caller named instead of a range that ends before it starts.
  - The events-log docs state the ordering constraint, not just that both
    bounds are required.
  - The Python facade tests assert the forwarded `from` and `to`, on the
    first page and on every page of a walk. They passed before without
    them, which is to say they would have passed had the facade dropped a
    bound.
  - `WINDOW` in the TypeScript SDK test is `as const`.

* fix(webhooks): refuse an unbounded events read with this surface's own 400

The two new scenarios asserted 422, which is the status the shared
validator raises but not the one this family publishes. Every REST family
on the canonical envelope routes a `validation_error` through
`canonicalErrorFor`, which pins it to 400 (`canonical-error.ts:59`) — the
sibling spend-events suite asserts 400 for its inverted window, and the
webhooks suite's own body-validation scenario asserts 400 two hundred
lines above these. So "the same error shape as the sibling" is 400, and
the tests now say so.

They also assert the shape rather than only the status: the canonical
envelope, `code: validation_error`, `meta.target: "query"`, and the
missing bound named in `meta.fields`. A status on its own would pass for
any 400 the route happened to raise.

The docs and the spec drop the number and name the refusal instead.

* fix(webhooks): tighten the events-log refusal tests and their copy

Review follow-ups, all in the new material:

  - The reversed-range case asserts `meta.target: "query"` as the
    missing-bound cases do. `expectCanonicalError` does not check the
    target, so without it the case passed for a validation error about
    anything at all, including a body this route does not take.
  - The case table is `as const`, so `missing` keeps its literal type and
    a field name the route never names stops compiling.
  - The two scenarios name the 400 and the code rather than saying
    "canonical validation error", matching how the rest of this feature
    file states a status.
  - The docs sentence drops its em dashes.

* test(governance): type the ledger-money double as the resolver it stands in for

The money reads moved into PersonalUsageClickHouseRepository when the
repository seam landed, so this test follows them there rather than
driving the service and mocking the module. Its stand-in client is typed
as a ClickHouseClientResolver, which is what the repository takes.

* test(governance): answer the trace-summary side with a row, not null

findSummary returns a row whether or not there is usage, so a double
handing back null tested a state the repository cannot produce — and the
service's own dereference is what failed. The point of the case is the
LEDGER read refusing while the rest of the dashboard stands.

* docs(webhooks): say that the required range has to be the right way round

The route refines `from <= to` and answers a 400, and nothing said so:
an OpenAPI parameter schema cannot express an ordering between two query
parameters, so a client reading the spec learns the bounds are required
and not that one has to precede the other. Said in the description, which
is the only place the constraint can live, in the route and in both
copies of the document.

Also: `parseInstant` takes named parameters, and the read-projection
tests get the `given` block their `when` blocks were missing.

fix: ship the ADR-069 R2 producer flip and bound the graph-trigger query that was killing workers (#6814)

* fix(coding-agent): stage the lifted span facts instead of the racing claim-check (ADR-069 R2)

The `span_referenced` claim-check reads the canonical span back from the
span store, and that read races the sibling spanStorage write. #6621 only
re-centred the read window on the span's own start time; it left the race
itself in place, because the producer flip was deliberately held back a
release (ADR-069 deploy order: consumers must be able to read the new
shape before anything stages it).

The consumer half has been live since #6621, so flip the producer: the
enqueue seam now lifts the span's facts and stages them ON the job, and
the handler contributes them with no read-back at all.

Why this is the fix rather than tuning. The claim-check's retry budget is
finite (25 attempts, ~2h27m). spanStorage is sharded into 128 lanes per
tenant and coalesces 256 spans per dispatch, while this subscriber keys
one group PER TRACE — so a tenant pushing coding-agent traffic mints
thousands of per-trace groups contending with those 128 lanes for the
same per-tenant in-flight cap. The harder the tenant pushes, the later
its spans land, the more claim-checks burn attempts, and each failure
re-queues and adds contention. Removing the read-back breaks the loop at
its source. On 2026-08-10 that loop had 88 groups blocked and the error
rate up ~10x over its 24h baseline.

The stage hook is total, as the routing seam has no retry: normalization
is wrapped, and the lifted payload is validated against the very schema
the consumer parses with. Anything that does not validate stages the
WHOLE event instead — never a claim-check, so a malformed span costs
scheduling-plane bytes rather than re-introducing the race.

Flips the spec's producer scenario from @unimplemented to @unit and binds
it; untagged/@unimplemented scenarios enforce nothing.

* fix(automations): stop an unbounded graph-trigger query killing the worker

A graph-trigger evaluation collapses its whole timeseries to ONE number,
but the query it issues carries the graph's `groupBy`, so ClickHouse
returns `buckets x distinct group values` and the group axis is summed
away in Node — after every row has been materialised as a JS object. The
time axis is already capped at 1,000 buckets; cardinality is not, and
cannot be, because it comes from the data.

The result was not an error. The process died mid-read, so the job
neither completed nor failed. Three of those in a row trip the poison
guard, which parks the tenant's whole graph-trigger lane — which is how
one project's misconfigured graph silently stopped ALL of its alerts for
19 hours, with 4,184 jobs stranded behind it.

Bound the read at the ClickHouse boundary (`max_result_rows` +
`result_overflow_mode: "throw"`) for this caller only. `throw` is the
load-bearing half: ClickHouse defaults to `break`, which silently returns
a TRUNCATED result, and a threshold quietly computed on partial data is
worse than a failed evaluation because nothing reports it.

An oversized result is a configuration fault, not an outage, so it skips
that one trigger rather than throwing. Throwing would be redelivered and
re-fail forever until it quarantined the lane, taking every other trigger
in the project with it. Any OTHER read failure still propagates, so a
transient ClickHouse blip cannot silently skip evaluations.

Sets `log_comment` on the analytics timeseries reads. Result sizes per
call site are then answerable from `system.query_log.result_rows` grouped
by `log_comment`, with no new metric and no new mechanism:
`@langwatch/clickhouse-client` already records rows on the span
(`db.response.returned_rows`) and already exposes `onComplete({ rowCount
})` for counters. Nothing is added under `src/server/clickhouse`.

Drops the `release_event_sourced_analytics_read` gate. It is permanently
on, so it spent a feature-flag round trip per query to be told "yes".
Routing to the legacy tables is unaffected — that is a property of the
query's SHAPE, never of the flag.

* fix(analytics): keep the reports chart reader on its single-argument getTimeseries

The row-ceiling threading widened this call site by accident. It wires
`loadReportCharts`, whose `getTimeseries` dep is declared single-argument
(report-chart.service.ts) — reports render the data they fetch, so they
are not a caller that wants a scalar-reader's ceiling.

The graph-trigger deps are built in automationDispatch.wiring.ts, which is
the one construction site of GraphTriggerEvaluationDeps and does pass the
options through, so both the real-time and heartbeat paths keep the bound.

* fix(tests): read the dedup strategy from options, not options.enqueue

`deduplication` is a sibling of `enqueue` on the subscriber's options, so the
new dedup-identity assertion did not typecheck. Only `typecheck:tests` covers
test files (`tsconfig.tsgo.json` excludes them), which is why the plain
typecheck step passed over it.

* fix: address CodeRabbit review — bound the tripwire read, stop retrying an unnormalizable span

Three real defects from the review, plus two cleanups.

**The tripwire's legacy read ran unbounded.** `runRouted` got the caller's
row ceiling; the legacy comparison query beside it did not. The bound would
therefore have held everywhere EXCEPT the projects we had turned an extra
read on for — precisely the ones doing double the work.

**An unnormalizable span would have blocked its trace's group.** The seam
stages the whole event when it cannot lift a span, and the handler's
full-event path then re-ran the SAME normalizer. Normalization is a pure
function of the span's bytes, so it fails identically on every redelivery:
25 attempts spent re-deriving one failure, then the TRACE's group parks and
every other span's facts in it are lost to save one span that was never
recoverable. That is the blocked-group class this PR exists to remove, so
the path now completes quietly and logs for an operator instead.

The regression test drives `handle` rather than asserting on the staged
shape, because the staged shape is exactly what could not observe this.

**A tautological assertion.** The dedup-identity test compared two
`makeId?.()` results, so it passed with both `undefined` if the subscriber
ever stopped declaring a dedup strategy. It now asserts the strategy exists
and that the key carries the span id.

Also: `resolveAnalyticsTable` had two stacked docblocks, the older one still
describing the removed flag-off fallback; and the stage helper takes named
parameters per the repo convention.

* fix: narrow the dedup union in the test, and reformat the presets revert

`DeduplicationStrategy` is `"aggregate" | DeduplicationConfig`, so `.makeId`
needs narrowing — the surrounding tests already do this and the new one now
matches them, which also removes the optional-chain that let the comparison
degrade into undefined === undefined.

The reports-path revert was written as one line that exceeds the formatter's
width. Biome skips a path passed to it directly here, so it only surfaced in
the repo-wide `lint` job; verified locally this time with
`biome check ./src ./ee ./scripts ./e2e ./prisma ./vite --diagnostic-level=error`
(0 errors) and `typecheck:tests` (exit 0).

* refactor(coding-agent): make handle a dispatcher over the three staged shapes

The lifted-facts path and the normalization guard pushed `handle` past both
`noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity` and `noExcessiveLinesPerFunction`, which the
lint job's delta gate counts as new violations.

Extracting `handleFullEvent` (and `normalizeOrReport` inside it) is the fix
that also reads better: `handle` now dispatches over the three staged shapes —
lifted derivation, claim-check, whole event — instead of dispatching over
three while inlining one of their implementations.

No behaviour change; the 188 coding-agent tests cover both paths.

feat(sdk-go): native instrumentations, REST client, and gen_ai-first telemetry (#4998)

* feat(sdk-go): native instrumentations, REST client, and gen_ai-first telemetry

Replays the Go SDK parity work onto main's post-ADR-076 layout: the tree
moves sdk-go/ -> sdks/go/ and the module path becomes
github.com/langwatch/langwatch/sdks/go throughout.

- Dependency-free core tracing SDK: exporter, Tracer/Span helpers, typed
  input/output, span filtering, data capture, evaluations and events.
- Shared streaming HTTP base (otelhttp) that passes bodies through to the
  caller while capturing a bounded copy off the critical path.
- Native instrumentations, each its own Go module so importing one never
  pulls another's SDK: OpenAI (+ compatible), Anthropic, Gemini/Vertex,
  Bedrock, Ollama, Azure, go-openai, Genkit. The OpenAI-family extraction
  is centralised in a dependency-free openaiformat package.
- Typed REST client (own module) with streaming JSON decode and
  iter.Seq2 auto-paginating iterators.
- gen_ai-first telemetry: one canonical key per datum, token usage
  single-sourced on gen_ai.usage.*, SpanMetrics slimmed to cost.

* feat(langwatch): canonicalise gen_ai v1.41 signals and sync tracked events from span events

Backend half of the Go SDK parity work, replayed onto main's post-ADR-076
layout (langwatch/src -> platform/app/src).

- Canonicalisation reads the OTel GenAI v1.41 signals (reasoning tokens,
  time-to-first-chunk, stream flag) and closes a cache-read cost gap. The
  additions are aliases only; gen_ai/langwatch.metrics precedence is
  unchanged and is now pinned by the sdkMetrics and otelSemconv suites.
- New trackedEventSync reactor turns langwatch.event span events into
  tracked events, mirroring the existing customEvaluationSync reactor.
- Predefined event schemas move out of track-event.service into their own
  module so the REST route and the reactor share one definition.

The stale biome-format commit that churned misc.ts by ~590 lines is
dropped: main has since been formatted the same way, so the file's real
delta is a three-line import repoint.

* build(sdk-go): unify OpenTelemetry on v1.44.0 and cover every module in CI

The modules had drifted apart, mixing otel v1.43.0 and v1.44.0 — e2e even
mixed otel v1.44.0 with otlptracehttp v1.43.0 in one require block. Pin all
twelve on v1.44.0, matching the root module, and re-tidy.

sdk-go-ci only ran 'go test ./...' in the core module. Because each
instrumentation is a separate module by design, that covered none of them:
the typed REST client and all eight provider instrumentations had no CI at
all. Run test-all.sh instead, which vets, tests and gofmt-checks every
module, and widen the build cache to sdks/go/**/go.sum.

* fix(event-sourcing): stop the tracked-event reactor feeding itself

recordTrackedEventSpan emits a span whose span event is named after the
recorded event_type and always stamps an event.type attribute. A tracked
event typed 'langwatch.event' therefore produced a span matching this
reactor's own predicate, and dedup could not break the cycle: each hop
derives its event id from the newly minted span id, so every iteration
minted a fresh span and re-fired. The staleness guard never tripped
either, because each hop is freshly timestamped. That is unbounded
amplification reachable from user-controlled span content.

Skip spans this path emitted itself, by name, before any event scan, and
reject the envelope's own wire name as an event type.

Also repoint the logger import: '../../../../../utils/logger/server' does
not exist post-restructure, so the module could not load at all.

* fix(sdk-go): stop double-billing cached input tokens on OpenAI and Gemini

LangWatch costs the token buckets additively — input at the input rate
plus cache-read at the cache-read rate — so cost.ts requires the caller
to pass an exclusive split, the convention Anthropic and Bedrock report
natively. OpenAI's prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens and Gemini's
cachedContentTokenCount are subsets of the prompt count, and both were
being forwarded alongside the inclusive total. A 1000-token prompt with
800 cached was costed at 1080r instead of 280r.

Subtract the cached portion at the three subset-style extraction sites,
leaving the field unset when the remainder is not positive so a provider
reporting cached > prompt cannot go negative. CachedInputTokens and
TotalTokens are unchanged.

Six existing assertions encoded the inflated arithmetic across openai,
gopenai, azureopenai and googlegenai; they are corrected and now show the
split explicitly. azureopenai, openai and gopenai all route through
openaiformat, so one fix covers them; ollama has its own usage mapping
but reports no cached tokens.

* fix(analytics): keep gen_ai attributes the extractor cannot interpret

The four v1.41 blocks took their source key out of the attribute bag
before coercing it, then wrote to the output only when coercion
succeeded. Because the span is merged as the bag's remainder overlaid by
the output, a value that failed to coerce was deleted from the bag and
never written back — so gen_ai.request.stream: "yes" vanished from the
span entirely, where on main it passed straight through. The same applied
to a time_to_first_chunk that parsed but was then rejected by a guard.

Peek with get() and consume the key only once the value is actually
used, which is the pattern coerceStringNumberAttrs already follows in
this directory. Restoring through the bag rather than the output also
keeps the attribute visible to the fourteen extractors that run after
this one.

* refactor(sdk-go): target OTel semconv v1.41 with typed constants

The branch advertised gen_ai v1.41 telemetry while importing semconv
v1.40.0 and hand-rolling the v1.41 keys as raw strings, which the
compiler cannot check. otel v1.44.0 ships semconv v1.41.0, so move all
44 import sites over and replace the four hand-rolled keys with their
generated constructors.

The emitted keys are byte-identical; the existing assertions in
genai_test.go pin them as raw strings and still pass. The scope
schema_url does move to 1.41.0, which is the point of the bump.

Eleven raw gen_ai.* literals remain, each verified absent from v1.41.0
and now annotated. Also correct a doc comment pointing at
GenAIProviderNameGroqCloud, which exists in neither version.

* build(sdk-go): refresh provider SDKs and normalise the core pin

The branch had been open long enough for every provider pin to go stale.
No call site needed adapting.

  openai-go/v3          v3.41.0 -> v3.50.0  (openai, azureopenai, e2e)
  anthropic-sdk-go      v1.51.0 -> v1.61.0
  google.golang.org/genai v1.61.0 -> v1.67.0
  firebase/genkit/go     v1.9.0 -> v1.11.0
  sashabaranov/go-openai v1.41.2 -> v1.42.0
  aws-sdk-go-v2         v1.42.0 -> v1.43.4, bedrockruntime v1.54.0 -> v1.57.1
  smithy-go             v1.27.2 -> v1.27.6
  oapi-codegen/runtime   v1.4.1 -> v1.6.0

ollama stays at v0.23.0. Every release from v0.23.1 onward declares
go 1.26.0, so taking one would drag this module's go directive past the
1.25 floor that sdk-go-ci and .golangci.yml both target. The bump itself
compiles and tests clean, so it is available as soon as the SDK's Go
floor moves.

Three modules pinned the in-repo core SDK as v0.2.0 or v0.0.0 while the
rest used the standard replaced-module placeholder; they are uniform now.
otel stays at v1.44.0 everywhere and the go directive is untouched.

* fix(sdk-go): address review findings across the SDK, client and instrumentations

Resolves 95 CodeRabbit review threads on the rebased branch. Six were
correctness bugs rather than polish:

- Bedrock's stream accumulator released its lock before reading the
  accumulator, racing the pump goroutine. Reproduces under -race before
  the fix.
- The REST client shared one math/rand source across concurrent requests.
- otelhttp marked a span Ok on 200 response headers, and OTel refuses to
  downgrade Ok, so a mid-stream provider error exported as a successful
  generation. Anthropic and OpenAI were both affected.
- Gemini's reasoning tokens were never priced: candidatesTokenCount
  excludes thoughtsTokenCount, so they were recorded as informational.
- DataCaptureNone leaked content twice over: langwatch.rag.contexts
  carries retrieved document text and was not stripped, and the filter
  covered attributes only, so free-text feedback in span events passed
  through untouched.
- go:generate pointed at an OpenAPI path the restructure had moved.

Eight findings were rejected with reasoning on the threads, most of them
resting on a house style the repository does not hold or on a semconv
package layout that does not exist.

The Go SDK's spec scenarios now bind for the first time: sdks/go joins
the feature-parity checker's Go roots, taking
specs/go-sdk/span-attribute-parity.feature from 6 of 19 enforced to
20 of 20.

BREAKING CHANGE: the provider middlewares now capture input and output
content by default (langwatch.DataCaptureAll), and the opt-in
WithCaptureInput() / WithCaptureOutput() options are removed. An
existing user who upgrades without passing WithDataCapture will begin
exporting full prompts and completions, which routinely contain end-user
PII. Opt out with WithDataCapture(langwatch.DataCaptureNone).

BREAKING CHANGE: the REST client no longer retries non-idempotent
requests. Retries now apply to RFC 9110 idempotent methods, plus POST
and PATCH carrying an Idempotency-Key. Evaluations.Create and
Events.Track are POSTs and are no longer retried on 429/5xx, because a
retry there duplicates an evaluation or a tracked event.

* fix(sdk-go): distinguish repeated span events, list Go in the feature map

Two same-type feedback events on one span hashed to the same tracked-event
id, so idempotent recording collapsed them and one was silently dropped. The
doc comment claiming a span carries at most one event per type was false --
nothing rejects the second. The reconstructed event now carries its index
within the span's own event list, and that index joins the id hash, so the
ids stay distinct and remain stable across a replay.

Alongside it:

- ollama: /api and /api/ reported the operation as "api"; they now fall
  through to unknown, since no operation segment follows the prefix.
- anthropic: correct the stream extractor's note about the shared tracer --
  it defers codes.Ok for streamed responses precisely so this SetStatus lands.
- bedrock: drop a write-only test field.
- feature map: the Go SDK was absent entirely, so every generated surface
  still described LangWatch as a two-SDK product. Ten features gain a Go
  value; Projects is Go-only. FEATURE_MAP.md gains the matching column and
  records the gaps.
- .gitattributes: mark the generated Go OpenAPI client, the docs llms.txt
  aggregates, the generated evaluator and skill manifests, the redaction
  mirror, and the pnpm and Helm lockfiles. The Go client alone is 56k lines
  and was dominating this PR's reported diff.

* fix(sdk-go): strip request content when data capture is off

Disabling data capture left three content-bearing attributes on the span.
gen_ai.request.tools is the worst of them: six extractors write the tool
schemas before the capture gate runs, so a customer who chose
DataCaptureNone for compliance still exported every function name,
description and parameter JSON schema. langwatch.prompt.variables carried
the compiled prompt variables verbatim and langwatch.params an arbitrary
caller-supplied map. All three now sit in the input strip list.

gen_ai.request.tool_choice deliberately stays. It names at most a tool
whose schema is now redacted, and it keeps a redacted span debuggable; the
doc comment records that as a decision rather than an omission.

Two more, both found by auditing what the tests could not catch:

- mergeUsage could not clear a field, so a streamed response whose later
  usage chunk supplied a cache split kept the earlier non-cached input
  count alongside it. That is the additive double-bill dadd05f0a3 removed,
  reappearing on the streaming path. The prompt side now merges as a unit.
  The old tests folded a single chunk into an empty destination, which is
  why this survived them.

- sdk-go-ci ran the suite without -race, so the SDK had never been race
  tested, though test-all.sh has always forwarded the flag. It passes now,
  and the whole SDK is green under the detector.

And three tests that could not fail:

- the only backend test guarding cached-token cost compared against the
  full-input baseline. Cost is monotonic in prompt tokens, so it held with
  the canonicalisation removed. It now also compares against the
  no-cache-attribute baseline, which is the comparison that discriminates.
- nothing asserted the trackedEventSync reactor was registered, so
  deleting the wiring shipped green.
- the tenant assertion could not tell context.tenantId from
  event.tenantId, because both fixtures said tenant-1.

Finally, the feature-parity gate: this branch added sdks/go to the parity
scanner's roots without adding it to the workflow's path filter, which the
comment above that filter forbids by name. plugins was missing the same
way and has real bindable suites. Both are listed now.

* fix(sdk-go): stop retrying bodies that cannot be replayed

A request whose body is not rewindable was still retried. The loop guarded
the replay but not the attempt, so a 503 on a streaming PUT sent the same
request three times with the second and third bodies EMPTY — a silent
overwrite of the resource with nothing. It is attempted once now, which is
what the doc already claimed. The doc also said the body was buffered up
front via GetBody; it is not, GetBody comes from http.NewRequest.

Three more that were mislabelled as documentation nits:

- googlegenai replaced the caller's whole http.Client to install its
  transport, dropping Timeout, CheckRedirect and Jar, which live on the
  client rather than the RoundTripper. It shallow-copies now and repoints
  only the Transport.
- openaiformat accepted the Responses-API input_tokens/output_tokens when
  reading a whole response but not when consuming a stream, so streamed
  Responses usage was silently lost. Both paths share one probe now.
- span.go wrote prompt.ID unconditionally while guarding the version
  fields beside it, so an empty SelectedPrompt emitted a blank prompt
  identity — enough to render an "Open in Prompts" affordance that
  resolves to nothing.

A 2xx whose body fails to decode reported "200 200 OK", an error that
reads as a success and names nothing. It carries the decoder's cause and
unwraps to it.

The rest are comments that restated their own code, a doc comment naming a
statusErr sentinel that does not exist, an options doc claiming every
default has an Option when two do not, a README link that resolved to a
CONTRIBUTING.md one directory too high, a ThumbsDown example that
swallowed the error its ThumbsUp neighbour handles, and a duplicated
metrics merge in ollama.

Tests: the opts aliasing guard in Start had none, so nothing stopped
append from writing into the caller's backing array. The HTTP-exclusion
filter test only counted filters rather than applying one. A Finish
counter replaces a boolean that could not tell one call from two. Two mock
transports classified any JSON containing "data:" as an SSE stream.

* test(event-sourcing): name the subscriber wiring test for the shard it runs in

It mocks no boundary — it hands the pipeline inert dependency objects and
asserts registration metadata — so it belongs in the unit shard, and the
bare .test.ts suffix left that implicit. The .unit.test.ts name says it.

Not .integration.test.ts: that suffix is a routing decision here, not a
label. vitest.config excludes it and vitest.integration.config includes it,
so the rename would move the file into a suite configured for real
infrastructure.

* fix(release): tag the Go SDK the way Go can actually resolve it

No version of the Go SDK has ever been installable. proxy.golang.org

* fix(sdk-go): make the sibling modules resolvable, and tag them with the core

The SDK is twelve Go modules, and every one except the core required the
core at v0.0.0-00010101000000-000000000000 — a placeholder that cannot
resolve. So `go get github.com/langwatch/langwatch/sdks/go/instrumentation/openai`,
which the README tells people to run, could never have worked, even once
the core was tagged.

The replace directives stay. Go ignores a replace in a dependency's
go.mod — it applies only from the main module — so they are what makes
in-repo builds work under GOWORK=off and are invisible to consumers. Only

consumer requiring only the openai module, built with GOPROXY=off, asks
