fix(trace-processing): fold the trace-side correlation appends (#6827)

* fix(trace-processing): fold the trace-side correlation appends

A trace's log records and metric exemplars each reach the trace pipeline
as their own command, and neither `recordLogContribution` nor
`recordMetricCorrelation` declares a group key. Both therefore fall back
to the aggregate — the trace — so one chatty agent trace funnels every
correlated item into a single queue group and appends one tiny event_log
insert at a time, while every other trace's correlations wait behind it.
Observed live at 2,275 pending on one group, oldest 59 minutes.

Give both the append coalescing (ADR-066 pillar 2) their log_processing
and metric_processing counterparts have had all along, so a backed-up
group drains as one multi-row insert per batch instead of one insert per
item. Safe to fold: each handler derives its event from its own command
alone, never reads back a same-batch append, and stamps a per-item
idempotency key. The events still carry aggregateId = traceId, so the
trace-summary and trace-analytics folds are untouched.

The group key is deliberately left alone. Sharding would spread one
trace's correlations across groups, but it is a second lever; taking the
group off the per-item write path is what the backlog needed.

Why it shipped un-coalesced: the registration-time warning for a grouped
producer without coalescing reads a producer's *declared* grouping, so it
sees an explicit group key or an explicit serialized aggregate and misses
a funnel arriving by the default key. Recorded as an @unimplemented
scenario rather than widened here — fan-in per aggregate is a domain fact
the registration site cannot infer, so closing it needs a signal a
producer states.

Take producer-append-coalescing.feature off the parity checker's
LEGACY_INERT list. Every scenario in it was already bound by a real test
but none was tagged, so the file reported "0/0 bound / all bound" and
enforced nothing — which is why the rule it states did not hold for these
two commands. It now enforces 7 scenarios.

* fix(trace-processing): address review on the correlation coalescing

Review round on #6827. The coalescing change itself stands; what follows
fixes what the audit found around it.

Tests — the registration assertions were blind to the bound's VALUE.
Coalescing only engages above 1 (`(coalesceMaxBatch ?? 1) > 1`), so a bound
edited down to 1 would have disabled the fold and left every test in the PR
green: the fix could regress to a no-op undetected. Add a test that runs the
real registrations through the real QueueManager and asserts `processBatch`
is installed (verified: it fails at a bound of 1, and it is the only one
that does). The same test pins the negative case on a low-fan-in command.
Also read the group key the way queueManager resolves it (option OR class
static) and resolve the registration first, so the assertion cannot pass for
a command that is no longer registered; and assert the metric idempotency
key under batching, which only the log side had.

Correctness of the explanation — the claim that a hot trace made "every
other trace wait its turn behind it" is wrong. The group key is
`<tenantId>/command/<cmd>/trace:<traceId>`, so each trace has its OWN group
and other traces are not queued behind it. What actually happens: that one
trace's items drain a claim at a time, adding a part per item and holding a
fleet slot per claim, and the contention with other traces is for slots and
merge headroom. Corrected in the constant's doc and the spec.

Spec — the visibility scenario claimed the guard names any un-coalesced
high-fan-in producer, which is what the new @unimplemented scenario says is
missing; the file asserted and denied the same behaviour. Narrow it to the
grouping the guard actually reads. Drop the new scenario that duplicated
"many items for one aggregate become one insert" and bind the behavioural
tests to that scenario instead. Revert the "low-fan-in producer" annotation
that pointed at a fixture already bound to the opposite scenario; it is now
bound by a test that observes the behaviour.

Dispatcher — `persistBatch` ran `cleanupAfterStore` for commands that
produced no events, where the single path gates on `events.length > 0`.
No live bug (no batched handler had both a cleanup and a drop path), but
recordMetricCorrelation is the first can-return-empty handler to be
coalesced, so restore parity before it matters. Regression test added.

Docs — ADR-066 said un-coalesced producers "are logged at registration, so
the gaps are enumerable". They are not, and that is why this gap survived
three pillar-2 sweeps; correct it, record both adopters, and mark recordSpan
shipped. The log and metric bounds claimed the byte budget cannot see an
offloaded body — true before the envelope's `s` header, false since — so
all three docs now describe the same budget.

* test(trace-processing): make the durability clauses executable

CodeRabbit review on #6827.

The 'coalescing preserves every item' scenario promises two things nothing
executed: that the batch completes only after the insert is durably
acknowledged, and that a retry neither duplicates nor drops. Cover both —
one test holds the append open and asserts the batch has not completed
while it is in flight, the other runs the same batch twice and asserts the
event identities are unchanged and distinct, which is what the event log's
dedup collapses on. (The log's own collapsing is already covered by
recordSpanCommand.dedup.integration.test.ts.)

Also drop two fixture doc comments that restated their function names, and
replace them with the non-obvious constraint each fixture actually encodes.

Not taken: the nested `describe("given ...")` blocks flagged as needing to
be `when` conditions. given -> when IS the repo's BDD structure (CLAUDE.md)
and matches spanCommandCoalescing.unit.test.ts exactly.

* docs(adr-066): British spelling in the pillar-2 correction

* test(trace-processing): make the registry-count check a precondition, not an assertion

The biome delta gate counts noMisplacedAssertion, and an expect() inside the
registryFor helper added one. It was never an expectation — it guards against
a renamed command silently wiring fewer registrations than the test names —
so express it as a throw.

fix(workers): drain the queue before closing ClickHouse on shutdown (#6825)

* fix(workers): drain the queue before closing ClickHouse on shutdown

App.close ran the event-sourcing drain and the graceful closeables
concurrently, so the ClickHouse HTTP client was destroyed while the
GroupQueue consumer was still issuing statements over it. The drain has a
20s budget in production; the close finished in milliseconds.

Every worker pod termination therefore severed its in-flight ClickHouse
work. ClickHouse logged it as `Broken pipe, while writing to socket ...
ParallelFormattingOutputFormat (NETWORK_ERROR)` and the worker logged the
same event back as `socket hang up` on inserts, event-store writes and
canonical log/metric persistence. In prod on 2026-08-10 this fired the
new-error-signature alert three times over (one incident, three renderings)
and recurred on each of that day's three termination events: rollouts at
~11:30 and ~16:50, and a node-eviction wave at 14:20-14:30. Immediately
before the 16:50 rollout ClickHouse held ~200 statements in flight with
~1000 queued behind the concurrency cap.

Three changes:

- App.close now awaits the drain, then closes ClickHouse/Redis/Prisma. The
  drain gets a 25s backstop so a hang cannot strand the connections.
- classifyClickHouseError treats Node socket errnos as RECOVERABLE. It only
  checked ClickHouse's numeric codes, so `socket hang up` (ECONNRESET)
  classified CRITICAL, which isRetryableJobError treats as non-retryable —
  dead-lettering suite/simulation/experiment run-state jobs and blocking
  their groups instead of re-staging them. The code set is imported from
  @langwatch/clickhouse-client rather than restated, so the queue classifier
  cannot drift from the retry policy the shared client applies to reads.
- The workers Deployment gets terminationGracePeriodSeconds (60s, override-
  able). It had none, so it ran on the k8s default of 30s against a drain
  that can legitimately take 20s plus teardown, and a missed grace period is
  a SIGKILL. workers.ts gains a 45s watchdog so an overrun exits on our own
  terms with a log line rather than dying silently.

* refactor(shutdown): derive every shutdown clock from one budget

Four clocks run during a pod's termination and they are nested, not
parallel: the kubelet's terminationGracePeriodSeconds, the entrypoint's
force-exit watchdog, App.close's drain backstop, and the GroupQueue drain.
They were four independent literals in four files, agreeing only by comment
— and they did not agree.

start.ts force-exited after 5s, which is inside the GroupQueue's own 20s
drain budget. Under the `all` process role (the app hosting the worker
stack) a drain could therefore never finish however long the queue was told
it had. The previous commit made that worse: with the drain now awaited
first, the 5s timer could fire before ClickHouse/Redis/Prisma were closed at
all.

server/shutdown/budget.ts is now the single source of truth. One
configurable number — the drain budget, SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS — and the
rest derive from it with fixed slack for work whose cost does not scale with
queue depth:

  queueDrainMs      = 20s (2s in dev), overridable
  appCloseMs        = drain + 5s
  processDeadlineMs = appClose + 15s
  required grace    = processDeadline + 10s kubelet slack  (= drain + 30)

Raising the drain moves every clock above it, so they cannot drift apart.

server/shutdown/runGracefulShutdown.ts is now the single implementation.
start.ts and workers.ts each had a hand-rolled sequence; they agreed on the
order but not the deadline, and anything living in only one copy (the
re-entrancy guard, the watchdog, phase logging) was missing from the other
by accident. Both now declare ordered, named phases and share one runner
that logs a failing phase and steps over it rather than skipping the rest.

On the chart side, `langwatch.terminationGracePeriod` validates rather than
derives, mirroring the gateway subchart: an operator draining behind a slow
load balancer wants their own margin, so the chart only refuses to install a
release the kubelet would kill mid-drain. The app Deployment gets a grace
period too — it had none either, and it shares the same entrypoint.

Both guard directions are covered: too short a grace period fails the
render, and raising shutdownDrainSeconds alone fails it as well.

* fix(shutdown): stop the langwatch SDK exiting the process mid-drain

The `langwatch` SDK's setupObservability() registers its own SIGTERM/SIGINT
handlers by default and calls process.exit(0) as soon as its OTel flush
resolves. Node runs every listener registered for a signal, so this is not a
race that could be won by ordering — whoever calls exit() first ends the
process. A second or two into a shutdown, with a queue drain entitled to the
full budget still running, the SDK killed it.

The platform was not opted out: instrumentation.node.ts passed `advanced: {}`.
So every worker rollout severed its in-flight ClickHouse work even with the
ordering fixed, and observability tooling was terminating its own host.

The metrics MeterProvider did a milder version of the same thing — its own
SIGTERM/SIGINT handler for a best-effort flush, the comment conceding it was
racing the exit and dropping the last periodic export whenever the exit won.

Both are now shutdown phases. server/shutdown/telemetry.ts is a registry that
instrumentation.node.ts writes to on the boot path (dependency-free by design,
it loads before the app graph), and the runner appends those flushes after
every other phase — so the spans and logs describing the shutdown are
themselves exported, and nothing but the runner decides when to exit.

Budget is now 25s in production and 5s in dev, and the chart sets
SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS on both Deployments from the same
shutdownDrainSeconds that sizes terminationGracePeriodSeconds. A process
running a budget its pod was not sized for is the drift the pair exists to
prevent; the suite asserts both halves come from one value.

Checked the Go services: no change needed. aigateway, nlpgo and langyagent all
run the shared pkg/lifecycle Group with SERVER_GRACEFUL_SECONDS, and their
budgets already nest inside their grace periods (gateway 60+3 in 75, the other
two 10 in 30). The gateway chart's validateShutdownBudget is the pattern this
change copied for Node.

The SDK's own default is fixed separately — it is a footgun for every customer
with a graceful shutdown of its own, not just for us.

* fix(shutdown): bound each phase, and refuse a budget that would crashloop

Review findings on #6825. Four were real defects in the fix itself.

**A hung phase swallowed the drain.** runGracefulShutdown awaited each phase
with no bound, and the first phase closes the websocket server — which
resolves only once `wss.clients` is empty, and `ws` never terminates clients
for you. One suspended laptop tab held it open indefinitely, so the queue
drain never started and the watchdog exited with nothing flushed: the incident
this PR exists to fix, reached through the new code path. Every phase now has
a timeout; the app phase carries the drain and gets the whole budget.

**The timeout path re-caused the incident.** App.close closed ClickHouse,
Redis and Prisma after the drain timed out — but a timed-out drain is still
running, so that severed exactly the in-flight statements the method protects.
A drain that *threw* is different: it has finished, and its connections are
safe to close. settleWithTimeout now reports which happened, and only the
timeout case leaves the transports to process teardown.

**Junk Helm values shipped a crashloop that rendered clean.** `--set-string
workers.shutdownDrainSeconds=abc` (or a fraction, or 0) made Helm's `int`
yield 0: SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS="0", which the app rejected at boot, while
the required grace period collapsed to the bare margin so the guard passed and
the release installed looking correct. langwatch.positiveSeconds now refuses
anything that is not a positive whole number, and distinguishes an absent
value from an explicit 0 rather than letting `default` rewrite it.

**A bad env var could crashloop the fleet.** budget.ts threw at module load,
on the boot path of every process, over a value that only matters at death.
It now reports the bad value and keeps a working budget.

Also: the watchdog is ref'd and cleared in a finally, so a stalled phase that
empties the loop can no longer exit 0 silently; extraEnvs may not set
SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS behind the pod's back; the http-server phase closes
idle connections and lets in-flight requests finish instead of destroying them
outright; and the chart workflow now runs on changes to the shutdown module,
which it previously ignored.

Tests. The ordering assertion lived inside a closeable, where App.close's
try/catch swallowed it — it passed only by the accident of a skipped push.
It now records the observation and asserts outside. The chart-margin
assertion restated the implementation; it now reads the margin out of
_helpers.tpl and the chart suite, so retuning one alone fails. Added coverage
for the phase timeout, the re-entrancy guard, and the junk-value and
extraEnvs refusals. Shell assertions guard against a non-numeric render and
name the component so an app-side failure cannot satisfy a workers-side
scenario.

Spec: the budget scenarios described arithmetic and internal module names
rather than behaviour, and three Then-steps asserted things no test checked.
Rewritten as behaviour with the consequence spelled out. 28 scenarios, all
bound.

Known and deliberately not fixed here: EventSourcing.close() does unbounded
work (processRuntime.stop awaits in-flight outbox dispatches) before the queue
drain starts, so a slow outbox can still eat into the drain's budget; and the
app has no preStop hook, so endpoint removal still races SIGTERM. Both deserve
their own change.

* fix(shutdown): named params for settleWithTimeout, cover both socket messages

Two review comments worth taking:

- settleWithTimeout took positional parameters, against the repo guideline for
  multi-argument functions. Now a named-parameter object.
- The transient-message test only covered "socket hang up". "other side
  closed" is the same failure from undici rather than Node's http module, and
  the classifier lists both, so both are now covered by a table.

The rest of that round is answered on the threads rather than applied. The
flush-order concern is not a defect — the metrics MeterProvider is a separate
global provider with its own exporter, so the SDK shutdown does not tear down
anything it needs. The inline `import()` in workers.ts is load-bearing and
predates this PR: the app graph must not be imported before setEnvironment()
and initializeWorkerApp() run, which is why the presets import above it is a
gated require for the same reason.

* fix(shutdown): gate the timeout skip on terminating, pin the drain across layers

Second review round on #6825. Three real findings.

**The timeout skip leaked handles outside shutdown.** App.close returned early
on a drain timeout without closing the transports, on the reasoning that a
dying process reclaims them anyway. That reasoning holds for the shutdown path
and not for the other caller: resetApp() does not terminate, and its own
comment says orphaned closeable handles keep vitest's fork worker from exiting
between files. close() now takes `terminating`, defaulting to false so the
safe answer is the one you get without thinking about it; only the entrypoints
pass true.

**The app phase's timeout was decoration.** It was set to processDeadlineMs,
which is exactly the runner's own watchdog deadline, so it could never fire
first. Now appCloseMs + 5s: enough for App.close's internal bound plus the
transports, and genuinely below the watchdog.

**The drain default was not pinned across layers.** The margin was, but
DRAIN_SECONDS=25 in the chart suite, shutdownDrainSeconds in values.yaml and
the helper fallbacks could all drift from DEFAULT_DRAIN_MS with every
assertion still passing. A test now reads all three and compares them; I
mutation-checked it by moving the suite to 30 and confirming it fails.

Also replaced a fixed 10ms sleep in the re-entrancy test with vi.waitFor —
the sequence is async and the sleep could expire before exit(0) landed.

* fix(shutdown): type the telemetry phases, bind the drain-drift scenario

Both caught by CI on the previous commit.

**typecheck.** The telemetry flushes were mapped into anonymous objects with
no `timeoutMs`, so `all` widened to a union and `phase.timeoutMs` did not
exist on it. Annotated the map and the array as ShutdownPhase. I cannot run
the whole-project typecheck locally by standing rule, so CI is the gate for
this class — worth noting rather than pretending otherwise.

**feature-parity.** The drain-drift test carried a `@scenario` annotation for
a scenario I never added to the feature file, which the checker reports as an
unknown annotation. The scenario now exists. Note for next time: a per-file
"29/29 bound / all bound" says nothing about the global unknown-annotation
check, which is what actually failed.

* test(shutdown): count the helper fallbacks before comparing them

A loop over zero regex matches passes happily, so if someone reformats the
helper's arguments the drain-drift guard would quietly become decoration —
the same vacuous-pass class this test exists to catch elsewhere. Now asserts
both fallbacks were found before comparing their values.

feat(gateway): view traces from a virtual key, and teams/projects management in both SDKs (#6807)

* feat(sdk): manage teams and projects from both SDKs

Provisioning a team and a project was reachable only from the CLI and raw
HTTP. Both SDKs now expose the same surface, so an integration that opens a
project per end customer can do it in the language it already uses.

TypeScript: TeamsApiService and ProjectsApiService are exported from the
package entry point, and the LangWatch client carries `teams` and
`projects`. They are built on first use, since the management families
resolve their credential when constructed and refuse an empty one.

Python: new langwatch.teams and langwatch.projects facades, lazily loaded
like every other facade. Create, list (following pagination to exhaustion)
and, for projects, archive. A project create returns the service API key
minted with it, served exactly once.

* feat(gateway): view traces from a virtual key

A key's traces were only reachable by knowing the destination project and
writing the attribute filter by hand, which is the one thing an integration
that runs a project per end customer does constantly.

The row actions on the virtual keys list and the key's own page now offer
"View traces", opening the destination project's Trace Explorer filtered to
that key over the last 30 days. The gateway already stamps
langwatch.virtual_key_id on every span it proxies and the fold hoists it onto
the trace summary, so this is a link, not a new read path.

The action only appears when it leads somewhere: the key has a destination,
that project is not deleted, and it sits on a team the viewer belongs to.
A deleted destination keeps its badge and offers no link.

The key's page now states its trace destination too, by rendering the same
read-only ownership section the edit drawer already used instead of a second
copy of the scope chips.

* fix(gateway): drop an em dash from the default cascade copy

* fix(sdk): name a malformed page at the walk, and specify the unreachable trace destination

The numbered-page walk treated a missing or null data field as an empty
page, so the facades reading rows off it failed as a bare KeyError or
TypeError with nothing naming the malformed answer. It now rejects
anything that is not a list of rows where it is detected.

A virtual key whose trace destination sits on a team the reader cannot
open already offers no View traces, but no scenario said so. Adds the
requirement to the feature file and binds the two tests that cover it.

* test(sdk): hold the python entry point's teams and projects wiring

The package resolves a facade the first time its name is read, so a wrong
module path or class name in the lazy registry surfaces only when a
caller reaches for it. Reading both names through the package covers the
python half of the reachability scenario the TypeScript suite already
binds.

* fix(tests): give the impatient queue run a hold wide enough to observe

The run that gives up waiting held the slot for zero milliseconds, so
its start and its end landed in the same millisecond of the event log.
The overlap scan settles ends before starts, which is what keeps a run
ending exactly as another starts from counting as an overlap, and that
same rule read the impatient run as having been serialized behind the
holder: maxOverlap came back 1 where the test wants 2.

Holding for a quarter second gives the overlap a width. The scan is
left alone, since ends settling first is correct for every other run
in the file.

* test(sdk): reach the facade modules through one import style

The entry-point test aliased langwatch.teams and langwatch.projects as
modules while the file already imported the facade classes from them.
Monkeypatching by dotted path drops the aliases and leaves one import
style per module.

fix(analytics): keep Attributes-backed metrics in scope in the dedup CTE (#6819)

* fix(analytics): keep Attributes-backed metrics in scope in the dedup CTE

A metric whose field mapping resolves to the trace-level `Attributes` map —
metadata.thread_id, user_id, customer_id, labels, prompt_ids — is aggregated
in the OUTER query of the arrayJoin CTE path. That query reads
`FROM deduped_traces` and has no `ts` alias in scope, so the read has to be
hoisted into the CTE under a name, exactly as the typed passthroughs
(`ts.TotalCost AS trace_total_cost`) already are.

Only three hardcoded `langwatch.reserved.*` token keys were hoisted, so every
other Attributes-backed metric emitted a raw `ts.Attributes[…]` into the outer
SELECT and ClickHouse rejected the entire query with "Unknown expression or
function identifier `ts.Attributes` in scope". Seen in production 2026-08-10
on a thread-id count grouped by label; the analytics panel simply failed.

`transformMetricForDedup` already had a guard for precisely this — it throws
when a rewritten expression still references `ts` — but it only ran inside
`if (rewritten !== selectExpression)`, i.e. only once some substitution had
matched. The expression that reaches production unrewritten is exactly the one
that matches nothing, so the guard's own precondition excluded the failing
case and it fell through to "return as-is". The guard now wraps every path.

The hoist is conditional on a requested metric actually reading the attribute:
pushing all five would widen the dedup subquery with the wide Attributes map
for every grouped query, which is the cost the existing conditional
cache-token hoist exists to avoid.

The regression test drives the real builder and asserts on the generated SQL's
outer scope. Verified against the pre-fix builder: 3 of its 5 cases fail there,
on the `ts.` leak and the missing hoist.

* test(analytics): pin the hoist table to the Attributes field mappings

The defect was never a wrong expression — it was a mapping nobody added to the
hoist table. A hand-written list of metrics in the test reproduces that same
"someone must remember" gap one layer up.

This enumerates `fieldMappings` instead and asserts the hoist table covers
every Attributes-backed `trace_summaries` mapping, so adding a mapping without
a hoist fails here rather than in production.

Documents why the metric loop stays at three: `metadata.labels` and
`metadata.prompt_ids` map to `Attributes` but are group-by / filter fields, not
metrics (the registry exposes only thread_id, user_id, customer_id), so they
cannot reach the outer aggregation. The hoist table still covers them, and the
new invariant is what keeps that honest.

* test(analytics): pin the guard relocation, and stop the leak detector failing open

Findings from the /review-pr audit on this PR.

**The guard relocation was pinned by nothing.** Moving the `ts.` check back
inside `if (rewritten !== selectExpression)` — reverting the half of this fix
the docblock names as root cause — left all 346 tests green. Every expression
the SQL-shape cases exercise now DOES rewrite, so the guard fires from either
position; the case that distinguishes them is the one that matches NO
substitution, which is exactly what reached production. Added a direct case for
it (verified: it fails when the guard is moved back), plus the partial-rewrite
case so a refactor cannot trade one for the other.

**`outerQuery()` failed open.** An unmatched regex returned `""`, and
`expect("").not.toContain("ts.")` passes — a leak detector reporting success
when it cannot see. Now anchored on `FROM deduped_traces` like the sibling
event-metric suite, and throws rather than returning empty.

**`metadata.customer_id` asserted nothing.** It has no `translateMetadataMetric`
case, so it falls through to `count()` and never emits an attribute read. Only
`thread_id` and `user_id` do. Dropped from the metric loop, with the reason
written down; all five keys remain covered by the field-mapping invariant.

**The conditional-hoist assertion named only unhoistable columns.** Swapped in
`trace_attr_user_id` — an attribute that CAN be hoisted, so it actually catches
an over-broad hoist.

**The invariant filter was form-sensitive.** `startsWith("Attributes[")` would
silently skip a future mapping written as `toFloat64(Attributes['x'])` and
still read green — the same "someone must remember" gap it exists to close.

Also documents the scope of the guard: the identical `ss.` (stored_spans) leak
is a known pre-existing limitation, left alone deliberately because rewriting a
value aggregation to `uniqExact(trace_id)` would turn "average score" into
"count of traces".

perf(ci): stop fetching 175 MB of media into every checkout, and pin one Go version (#6820)

* perf(ci): stop fetching 175 MB of media into every checkout

docs/ and assets/ are the two largest directories in the tree and hold none
of CI's inputs: 138 MB and 37 MB of .gif and .mp4 marketing media against
81 MB for platform/, the thing we build. Every job cloned all of it, and
langwatch-app-ci alone runs a dozen checkouts per PR.

Naming a sparse-checkout makes actions/checkout fetch with --filter=blob:none
(git-source-provider.ts:184), so those blobs never cross the wire. Measured on
a depth-1 clone of this repo, back to back on one machine:

  full      180 MB .git   490 MB tree   78s
  lean       39 MB .git   175 MB tree   15s

It compresses the tail as well as the median, which is what sets wall clock.
In run 31396568900 the six integration shards spent 9s, 9s, 10s, 19s, 151s
and 185s in checkout for identical work, and the job totals tracked it: 599s
against 891s.

Non-cone mode is deliberate. Cone mode takes an include list, so a new
top-level directory would silently stop reaching CI; the negation form says
what we drop and lets everything else through.

specs/ci/lean-checkout.feature states it as an invariant over every checkout
rather than a list of today's jobs, because the failure mode is a new job
added without one — nothing breaks, CI just gets slower again. The bound test
fails on 11 of the 13 checkouts as they stood before this change.

Deliberately not touched: code-scanners. Narrowing what gitleaks, trufflehog
or semgrep read is a security decision, not a performance one.

Also here, found while measuring:

- langwatch-chart and clickhouse-serverless-chart had no concurrency group.
  Their e2e jobs are the most expensive in the repo (697s and 348s), so every
  push to a chart PR left its predecessors running alongside it.
- langevals-publish-pypi was the one setup-uv call site of four with no
  cache, so every publish re-resolved the whole dependency tree.
- Four setup-python pins were commented "# v5" on a SHA that is v7. The
  comment is the only human-readable record of what a pinned SHA is.

Not done, because measuring refuted it: caching the pinned pip installs.
`Install pinned semgrep` is 11s against a 21s checkout in the same job.

* fix(ci): exclude the media under docs/, not docs/ itself

Dropping docs/ wholesale failed three test-unit shards.
error-remediation.unit.test.ts resolves ../../../../../../docs and asserts
that every remediation link maps to a real .mdx, so with docs/ absent every
one of those assertions failed.

The media was always the point. docs/media and docs/images are 128 MB of
docs/'s 138; the .mdx tree is the other ~10 MB and CI does read it. Excluding
the two media directories plus assets/ keeps 165 MB off the wire and keeps
the test green: 180 MB -> 42 MB of .git on a depth-1 clone, against 39 MB for
the version that broke it.

Verified against a real sparse clone rather than the local tree: docs/media,
docs/images and assets/ absent, and docs/platform/data-retention.mdx,
docs/platform/rbac.mdx, docs/evaluations/overview.mdx and docs/pricing.mdx —
four of the paths that failed — all present.

Two scenarios added and bound, because the spec as written did not forbid the
thing that broke:

- prose under docs/ is kept, so a future edit cannot go back to `!/docs/`
- exclusions are root-anchored, so `!/assets/` never reaches
  services/langyagent/internal/assets, which
  shipped-evaluator-types.unit.test.ts reads

* refactor(ci): move the lean-checkout guard to .github/scripts

A workflow invariant is not an app-script test. It was under
platform/app/scripts/__tests__ only because ci-ingest-path-filter lives there
and I copied the nearest precedent; the right neighbours are
guard-pull-request-target.ts and guard-breaking-change-scope.ts.

That move costs the js-yaml dependency — these guards run on a bare runner
under `node --test --experimental-strip-types` with no install — so the
checkout steps are line-scanned the same way guard-pull-request-target
already scans job blocks. Verified equivalent: both implementations find the
same 13 checkout steps across the two workflows and classify the same 2 as
gates.

The guard is now a script with a CLI, not only a test, so CI fails with the
offending job named rather than with an assertion diff. Both run in
ci-scripts-test, next to the shell-script tests.

Fixture-driven, so the negative cases are real: a bare checkout, a docs/
wholesale exclusion, a missing cone-mode flag and an unanchored pattern each
have a test that fails without the guard logic. The last test runs it against
the live workflows.

.github/scripts joins DEFAULT_TEST_ROOTS. Without it the parity scanner never
reads these files, and specs/ci/lean-checkout.feature would have reported
"all bound" while binding nothing — the same vacuum specs/ci/migration-order
is in today. It now reports 6/6 bound.

* refactor(ci): rewrite the lean-checkout guard as a Go CLI

Dev and CI tooling in this repo is a Go CLI, not a script. The guard was
TypeScript twice over — first under platform/app/scripts/__tests__, then under
.github/scripts — and both were the wrong call.

It lands as tools/ciguard with the shared reading in pkg/ciscan and a
cmd/ciguard entry point, alongside thuishaven, herrgen and migrationorder.

Going to Go pays for itself immediately: gopkg.in/yaml.v3 is already a direct
dependency, so the workflows are parsed rather than line-scanned. The
TypeScript version hand-rolled a block scanner because .github/scripts runs on
a bare runner with no install and had no YAML library to reach for. Parsing
also made the guard stricter — StringWith renders a mistyped scalar instead of
dropping it, so `sparse-checkout-cone-mode: "false"` is still understood while
a genuinely absent one is still caught.

Verified equivalent to the implementation it replaces: same 13 checkout steps
across the two workflows, same 2 classified as gates, same 6 scenarios bound.

The guard runs in go-ci rather than app-ci, where the Go toolchain already
is. It gets its own `ciguards` filter key because its inputs are workflow
files rather than Go source — a checkout added to langwatch-app-ci touches no
.go file and must still be caught.

Parity roots follow it: .github/scripts comes back out of DEFAULT_TEST_ROOTS
and tools/ciguard goes into DEFAULT_GO_TEST_ROOTS. specs/ci/lean-checkout
still reports 6/6 bound, now from the Go tests.

golangci-lint is clean on all three packages. Four of its twelve findings were
British spellings in my own comments — behaviour, modelled, honour twice —
which misspell rejects.

* perf(ci): one Go version, and stop two buildx caches evicting each other (#6823)

Two findings from measuring CI, plus the guard that keeps the first fixed.

It lived in eight places and had already drifted:

    go.work                              1.26.5
    go.mod                               1.26.5
    infra/clickhouse-serverless/go.mod   1.26.1
    infra/clickhouse-serverless/Docker*  golang:1.26-alpine   <- floating
    sdks/go/go.mod                       1.25.0 (deliberate)
    sdk-go-ci.yml, sdk-go-cd.yml         "1.25"
    clickhouse-serverless.yml            "1.26"

Nothing failed. Different jobs compiled the same code with different
toolchains, and the clickhouse-serverless image was built with a third — its
floating tag resolved to whatever 1.26.x was newest that day.

Every workflow now reads `go-version-file` from the module it builds, so
there is no literal left to drift. That is also more correct than the
hardcodes were: sdk-go tested at "1.25" while its module declared 1.25.0, and
now tests at exactly its declared floor.

The SDK keeps that floor. Its go directive is what consumers must meet and
raising it drops support for anyone below, which is why sdk-go-ci and -cd
build it standalone with GOWORK=off. That is recorded as an exemption
carrying its reason rather than left as a silent difference.

clickhouse-serverless moves to 1.26.5 in both its module and its Dockerfile.
It is internal, not published, so its floor is ours to set. Verified it still
builds: `GOWORK=off go build ./...` is clean (the missing-go.sum failure you
get in a fresh worktree is pre-existing and identical before the bump).

Dockerfiles cannot read a go.mod, so `ciguard go-version` is what keeps them
honest — it rejects a mismatched patch, a floating tag, a go.work that
disagrees, and any workflow that pins a literal.

langevals-ci and langwatch-nlp-ci were the only unscoped `type=gha` caches
left, which means they were not merely unscoped — they shared buildkit's
default scope and evicted each other's layers on every run, both at mode=max
against a 10 GB per-repo budget. Now scoped, like every other buildx cache
here.

I had this down as a finding: go-services builds linux/arm64 under QEMU on
main pushes while publish-docker-app uses native arm64 runners. It is not a
finding. Dockerfile.go_service pins its build stage to $BUILDPLATFORM and
cross-compiles with GOARCH=${TARGETARCH}, and its runtime stage is
distroless/static — there is nothing to emulate. setup-qemu-action registers
binfmt handlers the build never uses, which costs a second or two, and
converting it to a native matrix would have been a large rewrite of a
publishing path for nothing.

* fix(ci): close four holes in the guards themselves

Review found the guards passing on exactly the mistakes they exist to catch.

**BoolWith accepted typos.** `sparse-checkout-cone-mode: flase` returned
"present, and false", satisfying the cone-mode check. It now distinguishes
valid-false from unparseable, and the guard names a typo separately from a
missing setting, because the fix is different.

**Child modules were never scanned.** GoVersion read the root go.mod and
nothing else, so infra/clickhouse-serverless could drift straight back to
1.26.1 unnoticed — and ExemptModules, the whole mechanism for letting sdks/go
keep its floor, was never consulted at runtime.

Its test asserted the reason string contained the word "floor", which passed
whether or not the map was ever read. That is a constant asserted back at
itself. It now asserts the exemption changes the outcome: an exempt module at
a different version produces no problem, a non-exempt one does.

Turning it on immediately found two modules I had not known about —
sdks/go/examples and sdks/go/e2e, both at 1.25.0. go.work documents them as
deliberately outside the workspace, pinned to the SDK's floor, so they are
exemptions with that reason recorded rather than a version bump.

**setup-go with neither key passed.** A step with no go-version and no
go-version-file installs the action's own default: a third source of truth,
and a silent one. Now reported.

**The Dockerfile FROM pattern was uppercase-only and column-anchored.**
Dockerfile instructions are case-insensitive, so `from golang:1.26.1` was
valid and unchecked. Now `(?mi)` with optional indent.

Also: tools/ciguard joins the pinned golangci-lint package list in go-ci. That
list enumerates packages, so a new one is not picked up on its own — the same
trap as the go test list.

Two review points not taken:

- "the first scenario has no binding" — it does; all 16 titles across both
  feature files match a @scenario annotation, and check-feature-parity reports
  9/9 and 7/7 bound.
- "add an explicit gofmt step" — goimports is enabled in the pinned
  golangci-lint config and already fails on unformatted files; it caught one
  in this very change. A separate gofmt step would duplicate it.

Scenario titles renamed where they overstated: "Every Go toolchain reference
in the repo agrees" now says "non-exempt", and "A workflow states the version
by reading the module" now says what its test actually asserts.

* fix(ci): the media was timing migration-order out mid-clone

CI failed this PR on migration-order, and the cause turned out to be the
thing the PR is about rather than anything in it.

migration-order runs under timeout-minutes: 5 with a fetch-depth: 0 checkout.
Across its last 34 runs, 9 ended cancelled — and the cancelled ones sat at
297-298s in the checkout step, which is that 5-minute budget expiring during
the clone. Runs that finished averaged 22.8s in the same step. It was failing
roughly a quarter of the time because a full clone of this repository
occasionally takes longer than its entire job.

It reads Go source and migration files and never touches the media, so it
takes the same exclusion as the rest: 180 MB down to 42 MB, and the timeout
stops being reachable.

Added to the guarded set so it stays that way.

* style(ci): prefix the guards' boolean locals

House rule: a boolean gets an is/has/should/can prefix. `cone` and `valid`
both read as nouns at the call site, where the question is whether cone mode
is on and whether the value parsed.

Renamed the BoolWith return too, since that is where the name is documented.

* fix(ci): let the SDK tree keep its floor without going unchecked

#4998 landed nine new modules under sdks/go — a REST client and eight
provider instrumentations — all at the SDK's 1.25.0 floor rather than the
repo's 1.26.5. The go-version guard flagged every one of them on rebase,
which is the guard working, but the fix it asked for was the wrong shape:
listing each module in ExemptModules means the next provider package
breaks the check the day it lands.

Exempting the whole subtree instead would have been worse. It reads as
tidier and leaves nothing inside sdks/go checked at all — including the
failure that actually reaches a customer, where one instrumentation module
drifts above the floor the SDK publishes and someone who meets the
declared directive cannot build it.

So the exemption is now from the ROOT version, not from agreement.
sdks/go is a family whose own go.mod declares the floor, and every module
beneath it must match that floor. Reports name whichever file is the
authority, so a disagreement inside the family points at sdks/go/go.mod
rather than at the repo root.

perf(ci): give the last 20 workflows a concurrency group (#6831)

Every workflow now declares one except issue-link, which fires on
`types: [opened]` and so cannot have a second run to collide with.

Two shapes, chosen by what the workflow does rather than by what it costs.

Gates cancel. Their verdict describes the PR as it is *now*, so an
in-flight run is answering a question that no longer exists:

  release-scope-guard              29 of last 100 runs superseded
  pr-conventional-commits-title    18
  deployment-impact-check          18
  workflow-security-guard           3
  coderabbit-config-check           2

The first three take `edited` in their trigger list, so re-titling a PR
or editing its description starts a run — and all three read the title,
body or labels as they stand at read time. They cancel on PR refs and
never on main, the idiom the other 20 workflows here already use, so a
commit that lands keeps its own validation.

Writers queue instead. A cancelled publish has no cleanup path: it
reports "cancelled" rather than failed, so nothing retries and nothing
reconciles it. This is the reasoning prerelease-charts-oci already
carries, applied to the rest of them.

Two of those are not theoretical:

release-please-sdks had 12 of its last 60 runs still in flight when the
next merge to main started another. Overlapping runs compute a release
plan from the same history and then race on the same release PRs, which
shows up as a duplicate release PR or one run reverting the other's
version bump.

release-langwatch-chart and release-clickhouse-serverless-chart both run
`cr index --push`, and `cr index` rebuilds index.yaml from the release
list and force-pushes it to the same gh-pages branch of the same repo.
Run together, the loser pushes an index built before the winner's
`cr upload` registered, and a chart version that published fine vanishes
from the index — the release still exists, `helm repo update` just stops
seeing it. They share one `helm-chart-index` group, because the race is
between the two workflows and a per-workflow group would not have
touched it.

langwatch-chart and clickhouse-serverless-chart are the only other
workflows without a group; they get theirs in #6820.

fix(typescript-sdk): stop the observability SDK exiting its host on a signal (#6826)

* fix(typescript-sdk): stop the observability SDK exiting its host on a signal

The auto-shutdown handlers called `process.exit(0)` as soon as the OTel flush
resolved. Node runs every listener registered for a signal, so any host with its
own graceful shutdown — draining a queue, finishing in-flight database writes,
closing connections — lost the rest of it a second or two into SIGTERM. This cost
the LangWatch platform severed in-flight ClickHouse statements on worker
rollouts. Observability tooling must never terminate its host.

The handlers now flush and hand the process back to whoever else is listening.
The one case that still needs an exit is a one-shot script whose only listener is
ours, because a signal with any listener no longer performs Node's default
action: after flushing, the SDK removes its own listeners and re-raises the
signal only when that leaves the signal with none. The process then dies exactly
as it would have without the SDK loaded, reporting the signal instead of the
success status `process.exit(0)` faked.

`disableAutoShutdown` still turns the whole thing off.
`advanced.UNSAFE_exitProcessAfterAutoShutdown` restores the old exit for the one
shape that regresses: a host whose own signal handler never terminates the
process and relied on the SDK to do it.

Spec: specs/typescript-sdk/observability-auto-shutdown.feature

* refactor(typescript-sdk): clearer count name, scenario under the right rule

Both from review, both cosmetic:

- otherListeners held a listener COUNT, and read as an array at the check and
  in the interpolation. Renamed to otherListenerCount.
- The repeated-signal scenario sat under "Draining the event loop still

fix(traces): reject pageOffset, and pin the updated-axis scroll to a snapshot (#6812)

* fix(traces): pin the updated-axis scroll to a snapshot so mid-scroll writes are not lost

UpdatedAt is a mutable sort key — that is the point of the updated axis — but
the keyset cursor is a snapshot of a position computed from the versions
visible when the scroll began. Version resolution was re-run per page against
current data, so a trace bumped above the cursor mid-scroll matched no
remaining page (later thresholds only move further away) and left the scroll
entirely. The next incremental window starts where this one ended, and the
trace's new UpdatedAt now sits behind that, so it was never recovered.

Pin a scrollStart in the cursor on the first page and bound version resolution
by it, in both stages of the read: the id/count query and the row fetch. Both
resolve versions independently, so capping only the first left the second
returning a newer version than the page was selected on — wrong sort position
and a cursor minted from a timestamp that never appeared in the ordering.

The bound goes inside the dedup subquery rather than on the outer rows: it is
version RESOLUTION that has to be stable, not just which rows survive. Capping
the outer filter leaves the cursor predicate excluding the row anyway.

Occurred axis is untouched — OccurredAt is immutable, so its cursor is already
stable and its SQL is byte-identical. Cursors minted before this field existed
carry no scrollStart and keep the old uncapped behaviour, so scrolls in flight
across a deploy do not break.

Known residual, covered by a test asserting current behaviour: a backdated
write landing above the cursor but before the scroll started is still dropped.
The bound is expressed in UpdatedAt, and nothing in the row records when it was
written, so separating the two needs a write-time column.

Fixes #6810

* test(traces): pin what the backdated scroll delivers, not only what it drops

The known-limitation assertion was a bare not.toContain, which passes just as
happily on a scroll that returned nothing at all — a total breakage would have
read as the documented residual.

* fix(traces): reject a malformed scrollStart instead of binding it to ClickHouse

scrollId is client-supplied base64 JSON parsed with no shape check, and
scrollStart binds as {scrollStart:UInt64}. A tampered cursor carrying a string,
a null or a negative reached the query and failed it outright rather than
degrading. It now drops the cursor like every other mismatch in that block.

Legacy cursors also now stay genuinely uncapped, which is what the field's own
documentation already claimed: the previous fallback pinned a bound taken after
that scroll's earlier pages had been served, describing a moment it never read
from.

Also moves an assertion out of a test helper — outside a test body it reads as
a check that passed when it never ran.

* test(traces): cover the tampered-scrollStart guard

The guard silently restarts a scroll, which is the failure class this PR family
exists to close, and nothing exercised it. Three cases — a string, a null and a
negative — each asserting the request degrades to a fresh first page rather than
failing the query. Verified they go red with the guard disabled.

Own tenant, seeded and never mutated, so page 1 is stable regardless of when the
assertions run relative to the live-bump scenario.

* docs(traces): the backdated case is unreachable, not a shipping gap

UpdatedAt is stamped Math.max(Date.now(), prev + 1) by abstractFoldProjection
and written by exactly one repository, so nothing in the ingest path can emit a
backdated version. Event occurrence time is a separate column.

The test stays as a characterisation of that assumption — if a bulk import or
backfill ever writes a chosen UpdatedAt it starts failing — but calling it a
known limitation invited a write-time column to be built against an input that
cannot occur.

* fix(api): reject pageOffset instead of accepting it and returning page one

Offset paging was dropped when trace search moved to ClickHouse, but the
parameter stayed on the schema and in the published spec and nothing read it.
A request carrying one was answered with the first page and HTTP 200, so an
export that paged by offset repeated that page for as long as it ran, and no
part of the response said so.

It is now rejected at the boundary with a message naming scrollId. Rejected
rather than deleted: the v1 route validates non-strictly, so removing the field
would let an unknown key be stripped and the request succeed — the same silence,
with the explanation removed too. The published spec now carries that
explanation, since a zod refine has no JSON Schema form and the field would
otherwise still read as an ordinary accepted number.

0 and absent stay valid. Every caller that does not paginate sends one or the
other, and rejecting those would break working clients to no purpose.

pageSize gains non-negative-integer validation (#2163), which was only ever
worth adding once the parameter beside it stopped being a no-op.

The UI half: the footer inferred its pagination mode from whether a scrollId
happened to be in the URL, so the first page of a cursor list looked like an
offset list and "next" wrote a pageOffset the API does not read. Mode is now
declared by the caller. Trace search declares cursor; the experiments list and
the audit log page by real offset against Prisma skip and keep working.

Fixes #6808. Closes #2163.

* fix(traces): declare cursor mode in the footer regression test, and mark the filter-reset scenario as a gap

The #4077 regression test called the hook with no mode, so it took the offset
default while asserting cursor behaviour — it had been relying on the mode being
inferred from the URL, which is exactly what this PR removed. It now declares
cursor the way the Traces tab does, and asserts the same thing it always did.

pnpm test:unit never ran it: the file is .integration.test.ts, which that script
excludes, so the earlier component runs reported green without executing it.

Also: nothing clears scrollId when a filter changes, so 'applying a filter
starts the scroll over' described behaviour that does not exist. Kept as the
requirement, moved under an explicit known-gap heading so it cannot be read as
a description of what ships.

* fix(traces): clamp the updated-axis window to the snapshot and return the boundary

The scroll reads every trace as of the moment it started, so a trace created
after that instant is in no page of it. A request can still ask for an endDate
beyond that point, and reporting the requested window while delivering a
shorter one is how a client loses rows: it resumes from the end it asked for
and steps straight over the difference.

The window is now clamped to the snapshot, and the bound comes back as
`updatedThrough` on the result and in the v1 response's pagination object, so
the next incremental pull can start exactly where this one stopped. Covered by
a round trip: a trace inserted after page one is absent from that scroll and
present in a pull resuming from the reported boundary.

Also tightens the cursor guard from isFinite to isSafeInteger. 1.5 and 2**53
are finite positives that UInt64 will not take, so both reached the query and
failed it — the two new tamper cases go red against the old check.

Test helpers take named parameters, per the house rule.

* docs: sync the API reference spec with the trace-search schema changes

The published spec is mirrored into the docs site, and check_generated_files
compares the two. Regenerating platform/app's copy alone left the mirror stale.

* test(api): cover the updatedThrough wiring on the search route

The service-level test asserts the boundary is computed; nothing asserted it
reaches the response. Two cases now: present when the service reports one,
absent when it does not — a null a client might resume from is worse than no
field. Confirmed both catch the wiring by removing it and watching the first
go red.

* fix(traces): drop the scroll cursor when filters change

A keyset cursor describes a position in the result set it was minted against.
Applying a filter mid-scroll carried it into the new one, so the list resumed
partway down: the first rows matching the filter just applied were the ones the
user never saw, while the footer still read "page 3" and nothing signalled it.

shallowPush is the choke point every filter write goes through — setFilter,
setFilters, clearFilters and setNegateFilters — and all four change which rows
match, so the cursor is dropped there rather than at each call site. It leaves
the display URL and the router query together; stripping only one would leave
the two disagreeing about which page is shown.

Found by an adversarial read of the scenarios rather than of the code: the
feature file claimed this behaviour, nothing implemented it, and I had first
written it off as an aspirational scenario rather than the bug it describes.

Also retags "changing the search query starts the scroll over" as @integration:
observing it means rendering the hook against a mocked router, and the existing
test for that hook is already an integration test.

* chore(sdk): regenerate the TypeScript client from the updated spec

Carries the trace-search changes to the published client: pageOffset's
deprecation notice and the new updatedThrough on the search response.

Two unrelated deltas ride along because the committed client had drifted from
the spec on main — a webhooks-events description and a dropped `@default {}`
on an action-params field. Both are already-merged work catching up; a generated
file should equal what its generator produces, and cherry-picking hunks would
leave a state no regen reproduces.

* fix(traces): drop a spec-binding annotation that named no scenario

The occurred-axis pagination test carried an annotation pointing at a scenario
title that exists in no feature file, so feature-parity reported it as a stale
binding and failed. Bug fixes do not get BDD scenarios here, so the annotation
should never have been written — the test stands on its own.

Worth knowing: the checker matches the annotation token anywhere in a comment,
including a comment explaining why there isn't one. The first attempt at this
fix failed for exactly that reason.

* fix(sdk-go): page trace search by cursor, not by the rejected offset

Traces.All walked by pageOffset. Trace search has not read that parameter
since trace storage moved to ClickHouse, so every request was answered with
page one — and a repeated full page never looks short, so the walk never
terminated. Now that a non-zero offset is rejected, the same walk fails with
422 on its second request instead.

It follows the scroll cursor each response carries, which is the only
pagination the endpoint has ever honoured, and stops when a response carries
none. An empty page also stops it, so a server that kept returning a cursor
cannot spin the loop.

TraceSearchResponse was aliased to the shared openapi.SearchResponse, whose
page/limit/total envelope this endpoint does not send; decoding into it
dropped the cursor silently, so ScrollID could be sent but never received and
a manual scroll was impossible to drive. It is written out here with the shape
the API actually returns.

Also drops the dead pageOffset parameter from the MCP server's searchTraces,
which advertised something the API now rejects and had no caller.

* fix(traces): reset the offset on resize, and unblock a cold-opened cursor link

Two footer defects, one of them mine.

Introduced here: making the offset conditional dropped the `pageOffset: 0`
reset from changePageSize and from the search-query reset. Cursor lists were
unaffected — the offset is stripped from their URLs regardless — but the
experiments list and the audit log page by real Prisma `skip`, so both kept an
offset counted in the old page size and landed on the wrong rows, or on no
rows. The existing test mounted at offset 0, where the reset is invisible; the
new one starts deep in the list, which is the only place it shows.

Pre-existing, and fixed here because this change owns the cursor-mode footer:
"previous" was disabled from an in-memory page counter, so a shared or
refreshed cursor link opened with a dead back button on a page plainly past
the first, under a label claiming to be page one. It is keyed on the cursor in
the URL instead, and the handler behind it already did the right thing — with
nothing walked it drops the cursor and returns to the first page. Where the
position is genuinely unknown the footer now says so rather than printing a
number nobody computed.

* docs(traces): say that the updated-axis window boundary is inclusive

A reviewer asked what a consumer should do at the boundary. The field told
them where to resume but not that both ends are inclusive, so a trace last
written at exactly that millisecond arrives in this pull and again in the
next. That is the axis's at-least-once guarantee working — a duplicate is
recoverable by an idempotent apply, a gap is not — and it is why resuming at
the value is the advice rather than one millisecond past it.

Regenerated spec, docs copy and TypeScript client.

* fix(sdk-go): stop a scroll whose cursor is not moving

Found reviewing my own diff. Following the response cursor unconditionally
means a server that returns the same cursor with full pages walks forever —
which is #6808's failure exactly: the client is served one page repeatedly and
has no way to notice. The offset walk had the same hole, so this is not a
regression, but repeating it in the replacement would be.

An unchanged cursor is now reported as an error rather than followed, so the
caller learns the walk stalled instead of watching it consume API quota.

Also corrects two claims that were not true of the code:

- the PaginationMode doc said the audit log pages through this hook. It
  renders the footer component but drives it from its own offset state and
  handlers, so the mode never reaches it; the experiments list is the only
  caller in offset mode.
- a scenario asserting the offset reset was added to a feature file whose
  Background puts the reader on the Traces tab, which has no offset mode — it
  contradicted the Background it inherits, and being @unimplemented, nothing
  would ever have caught that. Replaced with a note pointing at the test that
  actually binds the behaviour.

fix(tests): repair mock specifiers that silently resolved to nothing (#6586)

* fix(tests): repair mock specifiers that silently resolved to nothing

`vi.mock("<specifier>")` does not fail when the specifier names no file.
Vitest registers a mock under a module id nothing ever requests, the real
module loads instead, and the suite goes green while asserting against the
thing it set out to replace.

Twelve specifiers were in that state. Nine were off by one directory level,
a path copied out of the module under test into its `__tests__/`
subdirectory. Three were vestigial, their mock target deleted while the
mock stayed behind. Two vitest configs also aliased
`@injected-dependencies.*` at a `src/injection/` tree that no longer
exists and that nothing references.

Two of the repaired mocks changed what their suite exercises.
SuiteFormDrawer rendered the real Chakra portal rather than the
`data-testid="drawer"` stub it declares, and its only drawer assertion was
a negative one that passed vacuously; a positive assertion now pins the
stub. useTraceNewCount read the real store defaults rather than the search
text, time range and SSE state the test feeds it, and asserted nothing
about the query it builds from them; it now captures the query input and
pins the filter passthrough, the live-range flag, SSE suppressing polling,
and paused live updates disabling the query.

A new scan guards the class: it parses every tracked test file with the
TypeScript compiler API, collects each vi.mock / doMock / unmock /
doUnmock specifier including the typed `import(...)` form, resolves it
against the alias tables read from the vitest configs themselves, and
fails listing anything that names no module. Run against the tree before
this change it reports exactly these twelve.

Spec: specs/setup/test-mock-specifier-resolution.feature

* fix(tests): read array-shaped alias tables, and name TargetPicker for what it is

Review follow-ups on the mock-specifier guard.

The alias reader only understood `alias: { ... }`, but vite also accepts
`alias: [{ find, replacement }]`. An array table was walked straight past,
so every specifier relying on it stopped looking like a path, was taken for
a package name, and was skipped: the exact silent skip the guard exists to
stop. It now reads both shapes, and rejects loudly what it cannot resolve
by prefix substitution, a regular-expression find, an entry carrying a
customResolver, a table that is neither literal, an entry spread in from
elsewhere, and a config composed with mergeConfig whose table is therefore
only partly in the file being read. Each shape has a snippet case.

The repository walk moves into beforeAll. In the describe body it ran
during collection, so a missing .git or an unreadable alias entry aborted
collection and surfaced as a file-level error with no test name on it.

The walk's file-count tripwire drops from 2000 to 100. It exists to prove
the walk still sees a tree, and a count that tracks the repo census goes
stale on merges and fails outright on a partial checkout.

TargetPicker's test renders the component and mocks the Checkbox boundary,
which makes it an integration test by the repo's own rule, and the three
scenarios it binds were already tagged @integration while the file was
named .unit. Renamed to match its siblings, which are already
.integration.test.tsx. It runs under the integration config unchanged.

* fix(tests): apply aliases in declared order, and split the scanner by concern

Review follow-ups on the mock-specifier guard.

Alias precedence was wrong. The resolver sorted the table by find length so
the most specific entry won, but vite applies the FIRST entry that matches,
in declaration order. With `[{ find: "@/" }, { find: "@/generated/" }]` vite
resolves `@/generated/x` through `@/`, and the guard would have gone looking
somewhere the runner never would: a false pass or a false failure depending
on which path happened to exist. Matching the runner is the whole premise of
the check, so the sort is gone and the table is applied as declared. Two
cases pin it, one on the reader keeping declaration order and one on the
resolver taking the first match with both candidate files present.

Alias-table reading moves to its own module. It is a separate concern from
the mock rule, and both files were over the 300-line limit for a new file
(scanner 334 source lines, its test 375). The split puts the vitest-config
reader and its tests beside each other and leaves the mock rule, its
resolver and the repository walk together: 161 / 225 / 265 / 189 lines.

Helpers take one named parameter object rather than positional arguments.

Merged latest main, which moved under the branch, and regenerated the
Prisma client and task registry that the gateway billing change invalidated.

* fix(tests): stop the guard skipping doMock files, and expand alias paths per callee

Review follow-ups on the mock-specifier guard, both of them the guard being
wrong about the thing it exists to check.

The walk decided whether to parse a file by looking for the substring
"mock". `vi.doMock` does not contain it: the capital M means a file whose
only mock call is written that way was dropped before the rule ever ran, and
reported clean. Proven with a fixture using only `vi.doMock` and a specifier
naming nothing, which the walk reported zero offenders for while the scanner
found one the moment it was allowed to look.

The root cause is that "what counts as a mock call" lived in two places, so
the pre-filter is now derived from MOCK_METHODS and exported beside it. The
method names share no common case-sensitive substring, so any filter written
out by hand drifts from the set it mirrors, and the drift is invisible
because the file it wrongly skips comes back clean.

Alias paths were expanded with `resolve` whichever function the config
called. The two part company on an absolute segment: `join(dir, "/src")`
keeps the directory, `resolve(dir, "/src")` discards it. Each is now
expanded by the function that was actually called, and the trailing
separator is normalised to one rather than assumed absent, since `join`
keeps it and `resolve` drops it. No config in the repo uses an absolute
segment today.

Both are pinned by tests, and the two new spec scenarios bring the feature
file to 10.

feat(otlp): serve the paths a misconfigured exporter posts to (#6822)

* feat(otlp): serve the paths a misconfigured exporter posts to

An OpenTelemetry exporter builds its own URL: given a base endpoint it
appends /v1/traces, /v1/logs or /v1/metrics itself. A customer who pastes
our signal-specific URL into the base setting therefore posts to
/api/otel/v1/traces/v1/logs, and one who pastes the collector URL posts to
/api/collector/api/otel/v1/traces. Both are live in production and neither
is visible to the customer, because an exporter surfaces a 404 nowhere a
human looks - the telemetry simply never arrives.

A base endpoint of the site root was worse than a 404: /v1/traces fell
through to the SPA fallback, which answered the HTML shell with a 200. An
exporter reads that as success and drops the batch.

These paths are now served from the canonical handlers. Not by redirect:
OkHttp, under the Java exporter, refuses to replay a POST across 307/308,
and the Node exporter issues its request with no redirect handling at all,
so a redirect would repair part of the fleet and go on silently dropping
the rest. The request is replayed internally instead, the same shape as the
experiments-v3 legacy alias.

The signal comes from the suffix the exporter appended, never from the base
it was given. Only paths a known misconfiguration produces are accepted -
canonicalOtlpPath is an allow-list, and anything else is passed straight on
to keep its own routing and its own 404.

Nothing else about the request changes. The replay enters the canonical
route, so auth, the body limit and the plan check all apply exactly as they
do on the canonical path; a corrected path with no key is refused like any
other. The original path travels to the receiver behind a per-process
secret, so a caller cannot claim a correction that did not happen, and it
is logged with the project id - which is what makes it actionable.

* style(dev): keep the vite config's own formatting

The proxy entry went in via `biome check --write`, which also reflowed
imports and line widths across the whole file - 450 lines of noise around
a 9-line change. The file's formatting is left as it was; only the OTLP
root-path entry is added.

* fix(otlp): address review comments on the path canonicalisation

- The ordering comment on the alias mount claimed it was last of the
  ingestion apps; ingestionRoutesApp mounts after it. State the real
  constraint: after otelApp and collectorApp, whose namespaces it overlaps.
- Report a corrected path at most once per (project, path) per ten minutes.
  A misconfigured fleet posts continuously and every batch carries the same
  pair, so a line per request cost money on an ingestion hot path and said
  nothing the first one did not. The map is bounded, not grown.
- The metrics bypass matched a bare `v1`, so `/v1/profiles` slipped through
  and the comment's claim of three bounded labels was wrong. Spell the three
  signals out in the alternation.
- The dev proxy required the path to end at the signal name, so `/v1/traces/`
  reached the API in production and fell through to the SPA in dev. Accept
  the trailing slash on both sides.
- Pin that a streamed payload survives the replay. The correction rebuilds
  the request around a new path, and a body dropped there would be answered
  with a 200 - the failure this feature exists to remove.

* fix(otlp): escape the NUL separator instead of embedding the byte

The throttle key joins project and path on a NUL, which cannot appear in
a URL pathname and so cannot collide. It went in as a literal NUL byte
rather than the \u0000 escape, which noBinarySourceFiles caught: a NUL in
a tracked file makes git and GitHub treat it as binary and stop rendering
the diff. Same separator at runtime, plain text on disk.

* fix(otlp): named parameters, and anchor the metrics matcher

- `correctedPathIsDueToLog` and the test's `post` helper took positional
  arguments, against the repo's named-object-parameter rule.
- The metrics bypass matched `/v1/traces` as a prefix, so `/v1/traces-anything`
  and `/v1/traces/foo` slipped in and the claim of three bounded labels was
  still not true. The OTLP branch is now anchored at the end, with the
  trailing slash and query string it actually receives; the other branches
  stay prefixes, as they were.

fix(scenarios): never show a runner crash dump as the run's verdict (#6817)

* fix(scenarios): never show a runner crash dump as the run's verdict

A customer report showed a simulation whose verdict reasoning was Node's
raw module-loader dump: the interpreter's own source path, the stack
frames, and the absolute path of our bundle inside the container.

The classifier added in the infra-error work already kept most raw dumps
out of the drawer, but a runner that fails to boot matched none of its
rules, and the generic fallback took the dump's first non-brace line —
which for a loader crash is `node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1520`.
Internal, and useless to the reader.

Two changes:

- A named `scenario_runner_unavailable` code for a runner that can't
  start. The cause is always our build or deployment, so the copy says
  that plainly instead of guessing at something for the user to fix. It
  needs an actual Node crash dump alongside the module-resolution
  wording: a customer's own agent can fail with `Cannot find module`,
  and blaming our deployment for that would send them looking in the
  wrong place.

- The generic bucket now skips runtime noise — stack frames, interpreter
  locations, `Require stack:` lists, the property block Node prints under
  the trace — and drops any candidate that still carries a frame or an
  absolute path in favour of a plain sentence. The line filter works by
  enumeration and enumeration lags the next crash shape, so the guard is
  what makes "no internals" hold rather than the list.

The underlying missing-module bug is separately prevented: since #6557
the bundler fails the build when an external require isn't declared in
dependencies, and the reported path predates that layout.

* fix(scenarios): only blame our runner when our runner is what died

Follow-up to the review of the previous commit. Three real defects in it.

The runner-unavailable gate asked "is this a Node crash dump", which is
not the same question as "is this OUR Node crash dump". Every marker it
looked for is printed by the customer's process too, and
http-agent.adapter.ts embeds the agent's HTTP response body verbatim in
the error it throws — so an agent that boots with its own missing
dependency arrived looking identical, and got told the fault was on our
side. It now also requires the child-exit wrapper, which
scenario.processor.ts adds only when our own child died without
reporting anything.

The internals guard matched any two-segment slash path, which also
swallowed the adapter's `HTTP 502: … from <url> (request-id: …): <body>`
— the status, the URL, the request id and the agent's own error body,
all of it the customer's own data, suppressed to hide nothing. It now
names our artefacts: node: locations, stack frames, /app/, dist/,
node_modules/, .cjs. That also closes two leaks the old pattern missed,
both needing no leading slash: bundle-relative frames, and `at async X (`.

The suppression fallback reused "failed before it could run", which
asserts the run never started. That is false for anything suppressed
mid-run, and it lands in the verdict a customer reads.

Also: a block now opens only on a line starting with `{`, so a stray
bracket in prose can't swallow the dump, and an unclosed block (the
adapter truncates bodies mid-string) falls back to a bracket-blind
rescan rather than losing a real sentence.

* refactor(scenarios): address review on the error classifier

- `as const` on the marker tables (NOISE_LINE_PATTERNS,
  INTERNALS_PATTERNS, NODE_CRASH_MARKERS, and the test's
  INTERNAL_MARKERS), per the internal-constants guideline.
- Rename the `hit` local to `hasMatchingNeedle`, per the boolean
  naming rule.
- Cover our bundle path with a backslash separator and behind a UNC
  prefix. The guard keys on our artefacts rather than on path shape, so
  both were already caught; the tests pin that. A bare `C:\app\runner.js`
  stays unsuppressed on purpose — it names nothing of ours, and blanket
  path suppression is the bug the previous commit removed.
- Widen the test's own stack-frame marker to the `at async X (` form so
  the test contract matches the code's.

fix(evaluations): stop display and export surfaces from inventing verdicts (no-verdict family) (#6839)

* fix(traces-v2): verdict-less processed evaluations render neutral, not green PASS at 0.00

A processed evaluation with passed == null mapped to 'pass' and a
fabricated score of 0, so the eval card showed a green PASS with

fix(typescript-sdk): disable the live LangWatch exporter in logger integration tests (#3296) (#5811)

* fix(typescript-sdk): disable the live LangWatch exporter in logger integration tests (#3296)

The 7 setupObservability calls in logger.integration.test.ts ran without
langwatch: "disabled", so setup attached a BatchLogRecordProcessor pointed at
the live endpoint alongside the test's in-memory processor. That is the same
anti-pattern #3097 identified and #3294 fixed for the proxy tests.

Adding the flag on its own turns the file red, because its green depended on
that exporter. The LangWatch span processor was the only thing registering a
concrete tracer provider, which made every setup after the first hit the
"already set up" early exit and return a no-op handle. The shutdown calls were
therefore no-ops, and the module-shared log record processor survived. With the
exporter gone the setups become real, the first shutdown tears the shared
processor down, and every later test records nothing.

Give each start its own exporter and processor so a shutdown cannot poison a
later test, and shut the handle down in afterEach. The six data-capture tests
now genuinely re-configure observability instead of having their setup silently
discarded.

Build the custom logger provider test its own LoggerProvider as well. It read
the global api-logs provider, which is registered once and cannot be replaced,
so it only passed by sharing the module-level exporter and never exercised a
caller-owned provider. This also drops an inline import().

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(typescript-sdk): stop the logger test fixture leaking process listeners

Review catch. Disabling LangWatch leaves the tracer provider non-concrete, so
every start now reaches a real NodeSDK instead of the already-set-up early exit.
With disableAutoShutdown omitted that registers beforeExit, SIGINT and SIGTERM
handlers per start, and shutdown() never removes them, so the suite leaked three
listeners per test and emitted MaxListenersExceededWarning three times where
main emitted none.

Set disableAutoShutdown in the test helper, since afterEach already owns
teardown, and guard it: the new test fails if the option is dropped.
