fix(licensing): an enterprise plan carries its entitlements however it was resolved (#6847)

* test(licensing): specify how a plan's entitlements are resolved

Three files, one question: what does a plan grant, and who decides. The new
file states the rule (the tier decides what the payload leaves unanswered,
and an explicit answer always wins), the generation file extends its
entitlement rule to what the mint form produces, and the subscription page
file gains an enforced rule for a licensed enterprise plan being the current
plan rather than an upgrade candidate.

That last file was on the parity ratchet's inert list because every scenario
in it was parked. It now enforces three, so it comes off the list in the same
commit that puts them there.

* fix(licensing): decide tier entitlements where every plan is resolved

An entitlement sold with a tier was written into each contract at mint time,
so it only reached contracts minted after the flag was written. Every
enterprise license signed before that carried nothing, and absent was read as
no.

The tier now answers it, at the one point both legs and both deployment modes
pass through. Only fields the plan leaves unanswered are filled, so an
explicit false still means false, and a plan with nothing to fill comes back
as the same object it went in as.

For that to work the license leg has to stop turning absent into false, which
it did while resolving defaults. Saying nothing and saying no are different
answers, and only one of them is a decision the customer made.

* fix(billing): state the webhook entitlement on the enterprise preset

An enterprise organization with no license resolves from this map, and the
map did not mention the entitlement, so those customers were refused too.

Stated on the enterprise plan only, not in the features every paid plan
shares, and stated as well as inherited from the tier map: the preset is what
this plan sells, the tier map is the net under contracts resolved some other
way.

* fix(subscription): show a licensed enterprise plan as the plan it is

A plan resolved from a license could never be "the enterprise plan" on this
page, because the check excluded license-sourced plans by construction. Every
licensed enterprise customer was shown an upgrade badge, a smaller plan's
feature list, and a card inviting them to buy what they already exceed.

Enterprise is now enterprise on either leg. A licensed plan below enterprise
reads its features from its own numbers rather than borrowing another tier's
marketing copy, and the plan name falls back to its type instead of naming a
plan it is not.

The capabilities builder is renamed for what it does now: it describes any
plan from its numbers, not only the legacy tiered ones.

* fix(licensing): mint the license the operator asked for

Two mint paths quietly dropped what they were given. The generator form had
no field for the webhook entitlement at all, so every license issued through
the product left it unanswered, and re-issuing a license was not a fix. It is
now a checkbox in Plan Limits, defaulted from the plan template, cleared when
the operator switches to a plan that does not include it, and sent as a
definite answer so what is ticked is what the license carries.

The CLI script took seats from its flags and everything else from the plan
template, so a contract with negotiated numbers was minted with the
template's: it now takes the lite-seat count, the message volume and the
expiry as flags. An expiry in the past is refused where the license is built,
the same refusal the license router already made, because an expired license
reads as no license and silently drops the organization onto whatever sits
underneath it.

The script's comment about forcing a validation cache is dropped. There is no
cache and no TTL: the license is read and verified on every request.

* fix(billing): pick the same subscription every time

An organization is not supposed to hold two active subscriptions, and some
do. The query that picks one had no ordering, so which contract answered was
whatever the database returned first, and it could differ between calls.
Newest created wins now, with the id as a total order behind it.

A read-only report goes with it: which organizations hold more than one
active subscription, which row this ordering picks for them, and a census of
the pending rows abandoned checkouts leave behind. It proposes nothing.
Deciding which of a customer's duplicate rows is the real contract is a
billing question, not a query result.

* fix(licensing): resolve the subscription ordering from one rule, and refuse what the mint cannot mean

The ordering that picks among duplicate active subscriptions existed as a
query literal, a hand-written comparator and a test literal, with a
comment asking a human to keep them in step. It is now exported once from
planTypes and read by all three, so the report cannot describe a winner
the product would not pick. The report also orders ids relationally
rather than through localeCompare, which is what Postgres does.

The SaaS provider's non-SaaS branch answered Enterprise. It stays
unreachable through the wiring, but this change gives the top tier
webhook entitlement, so a deployment that reached that line by mistake
would have been handed signed webhook delivery it never bought. It
answers the free baseline instead.

The mint accepted values it could not mean: parseInt read "50GB" as 50
seats and "1.9" as 1, and an impossible calendar date rolled forward
into a license expiring on a day nobody chose. Both are refused at the
flag now, and an unparseable date can no longer slip past the expiry
check to fail later as a RangeError naming nothing.

The subscription-selection test asserted a copy of the query's own
orderBy, which passes even where the database ignores it. Its mock now
honors the ordering it is handed, so the test says which row is
selected.

* docs(specs): state the license precondition as the customer's own

The subscription-page scenarios opened on the plan resolving from a
license, which is the pipeline's vocabulary rather than anything the
reader has. Holding a license is the fact; how it becomes a plan is what
the scenarios exercise, not what they assume.

feat(stored-objects): sign in to Azure Blob without a shared account key (#6181)

* spec(stored-objects): Azure Blob sign-in without a shared account key

Issue #6087, stacked on #6092 (issue #4133).

The Azure backend shipped in #6092 speaks SharedKey only. Enterprises
routinely set allowSharedKeyAccess=false — often via Azure Policy — which
makes the backend unusable rather than degraded: every request is refused.

Amazon S3 already has the equivalent capability and has had it all along.
createS3Client falls through to the AWS SDK default provider chain (IRSA,
EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, ~/.aws/credentials), so keyless
sign-in works there for free. Azure was hand-rolled REST to avoid the
Azure SDK, and that decision is precisely what costs us this. So this is
a provider-parity gap, not a new capability.

Locked decisions in the spec:
- AZURE_BLOB_AUTH_MODE is an explicit toggle, never inferred from which
  variables happen to be set (same reasoning as STORED_OBJECTS_BACKEND).
  Values: sharedKey (default, unchanged), workloadIdentity, managedIdentity,
  azureCli.
- No credential fallback. A misconfigured identity fails loud; it never
  silently reverts to the account key, which would undo the security
  posture the operator chose at the moment they are least likely to notice.
- AKS is the only federated-Kubernetes target. Webhook-free clusters are an
  explicit non-goal; those operators use managedIdentity or sharedKey.
- One resolver decides Azure credentials for every consumer. Three sites
  decide independently today and two would crash without a key.

The spec was adversarially reviewed before landing; findings folded in
include the write-path outage hiding behind the driver-registration gate,
the unkeyed token cache versus per-project BYOC (#6088), federated-token
rotation on disk, 401-versus-403 retry semantics, sovereign-cloud authority
hosts, and retagging the chart scenarios as integration because grep
assertions cannot prove render behaviour.

Scenarios are tagged @unimplemented so the design can be reviewed before
code exists; #6087 tracks binding each one to a test.

* feat(stored-objects): Azure Blob sign-in without a shared account key

Implements the core of #6087. AZURE_BLOB_AUTH_MODE selects how the app
authenticates to Azure Blob: sharedKey (default, unchanged), or one of
workloadIdentity / managedIdentity / azureCli, which present an Entra
bearer token and need no stored secret at all. Enterprises that set
allowSharedKeyAccess=false could not use the backend before this — every
request was refused.

Amazon S3 has had the equivalent since #4058 via the AWS SDK provider
chain, so this closes a provider-parity gap rather than adding a new one.

- azure-credentials.ts: ONE resolveAzureCredentials() owning the decision
  for every consumer, returning a discriminated union so the compiler
  forces each construction site to handle both arms. Fixes two latent
  keyless-install breakages: the factory gate that registered no driver
  without a key (a write outage, since the registry throws on an
  unregistered scheme) and the Buffer.from(undefined) crash in dataset
  storage.
- azure-token-provider.ts: token cache keyed on
  (authorityHost, tenantId, clientId, audience) — module-scoped because
  drivers are per-request, keyed because an unkeyed cache would hand one
  project's token to another once per-project BYOC (#6088) lands. Stores
  the in-flight promise so a cold start under load performs one exchange,
  refreshes before expiry, and re-reads the federated assertion every
  exchange since the platform rotates it.
- azure-blob-driver.ts: signedRequest() became a strategy — SharedKey HMAC
  unchanged, or Bearer with no canonicalisation. 401 refreshes and retries
  once; 403 never retries and names the role assignment to grant, because
  a fresh token cannot fix a missing permission.
- Chart: global.serviceAccount (opt-in) wired into app, workers and
  cronjobs — the chart previously set serviceAccountName nowhere, which
  blocked AWS IRSA just as much as Azure identity, so this also closes
  #6182. azureBlob.authMode emits AZURE_BLOB_AUTH_MODE and requires the
  account key only under sharedKey, refusing a stray key that would be
  silently ignored and refusing workloadIdentity with no ServiceAccount
  to bind to.
- Docs: every mode, the Storage Blob Data Contributor role (and the trap
  of granting control-plane Contributor instead), no-fallback rule, and
  the AKS-only limit for federated Kubernetes identity.

Chart behaviour is asserted by running helm template and reading the
rendered YAML, not by grepping template source — the spec review noted a
string check cannot prove "renders successfully" or "fails with this
error". 10 such cases pass, including one that caught an assertion being
satisfied by a comment in my own template.

Verified: both typechecks, 561 unit tests, 10 helm render tests, and
check:feature-parity (2963 bound). 10 scenarios remain @unimplemented —
byte-path integration, secret hygiene, throttle backoff, Azurite OAuth
mode, and the @manual real-account run.

* feat(stored-objects): redact authorization material and prove keyless byte paths

Three additions on top of the Azure identity core:

Secret hygiene. Storage errors quote response bodies verbatim, and Azure
answers a failed request with a body that can echo signed-request detail
back. In bearer mode the Authorization header is a live credential for the
token's whole lifetime, so one leaked error string is a usable credential
until it expires. redactAuthorizationMaterial strips Bearer/SharedKey
values and echoed assertion elements; redactStorageErrorText composes it
with the existing URI redactor so a caller cannot apply only half. Both
body-quoting driver paths now route through it.

Keyless byte paths. The regression these guard against is a wiring bug
invisible to the driver's own tests: a resolvable Azure destination with no
registered driver means every write throws "unregistered scheme" while a
healthy driver sits next to it. Asserts the destination resolves, the
driver registers, dataset storage is selected rather than crashing on an
absent key, and every consumer receives credentials from the one resolver.

Throttle backoff. Removed as a thing we build. @azure/identity ships
@azure/core-rest-pipeline, whose retry policy already honours the
provider's Retry-After; a retry loop of ours would nest inside that one and
multiply attempts against an endpoint asking us to slow down. The scenario
now records that delegation, and the test pins exactly one attempt so
nobody reintroduces a compounding retry.

Also fixes a test-setup gap the stricter validation exposed: the dataset
integration suite stubbed only the account key, and now needs the full
shared-key set because credentials resolve through one validating path.

Verified: both typechecks, 574 unit tests, 19 Azure integration tests
(Azurite + real Postgres + helm renders), check:feature-parity 2968 bound.
Four scenarios remain @unimplemented — three needing an Azurite OAuth+TLS
harness, and the @manual real-account run.

* fix(stored-objects): address review findings on Azure identity auth

BLOCKER — the chart never emitted the pod label that makes workload
identity work. Azure's admission webhook only mutates pods carrying
azure.workload.identity/use: "true"; without it the federated token is
never injected, so a chart that rendered green produced pods that failed
every storage write at runtime with an error blaming the operator's
cluster. Worse, values.yaml and the docs both claimed the label was a
chart value, and my own helm test asserted only the ServiceAccount and
annotation — so nothing caught it. Now rendered on app, workers and
cronjobs from the same value that selects the auth mode, and asserted.

Read outage for deployments migrating OFF Azure. maybeAzureDriver() gated
registration on STORED_OBJECTS_BACKEND === "azure", so flipping the toggle
back to s3 while keeping the account vars — the mirror of the
legacyS3ReadBucket path we document for the other direction — stranded
every historical azure-blob:// object behind "unregistered scheme". The
resolver now takes a purpose: a read driver being available is not
symmetric with Azure being chosen for writes.

Secret hygiene, two real gaps:
- The new 403 message echoed the account and container in the clear, the
  exact two segments redactStorageUri strips everywhere else. It names the
  role to grant instead; the existing test had pinned the leak, so it now
  asserts non-disclosure.
- The redactor only matched XML, but the identity endpoint speaks JSON and
  form-encoding — a quoted access_token or client_assertion passed
  straight through. Added a key/value arm (including quoted JSON field
  names), allowed attributes on the XML tags, and put a 20-char floor on
  the scheme match so "SharedKey authentication is disabled" stays prose.

Also: corrected the token-cache docstring, which claimed the key was
"already shaped" for per-project identities (#6088). It is not — tenantId
and clientId come from process-global env, which per-project identities
cannot vary. Recorded as a caveat with what must change, rather than left
as a claim someone would trust. Plus .env.example coverage for the new
vars, a docs contradiction where the warning still said the account key is
always required, and two unused imports.

Verified: both typechecks, 578 unit tests, 19 integration tests, parity
2968 bound, and helm renders for workloadIdentity / sharedKey / non-Azure.

* fix(charts): survive a values tree without global.serviceAccount, assert helm stderr

Two CI failures, both mine, both real.

The chart's ServiceAccount template dereferenced
.Values.global.serviceAccount.create directly, so any values tree that
overrides `global:` without carrying the new key died with "nil pointer
evaluating interface {}.create" rather than rendering nothing. Found by
rendering the chart against the base branch's values — exactly the shape
an operator upgrading with their own values file presents. Now uses safe
navigation, verified by rendering with global.serviceAccount explicitly
null.

The helm integration test asserted on the thrown Error's `message`, but
Node only folds a subprocess's stderr into that message on some versions:
it passed locally and failed in CI against the useless "Command failed:
helm template …". Failure assertions now read helm's own stderr, so the
four negative render cases test what they claim to.

* test(charts): build chart dependencies before rendering, or skip honestly

The helm suite failed in CI for a reason that had nothing to do with the
chart: `helm template` refuses to render until every Chart.yaml dependency
is present under charts/, and the built .tgz files are gitignored. A
developer checkout has them, a fresh runner does not, so all ten tests
died on "missing in charts/ directory" before reaching an assertion.

Only visible after the previous commit made failures report helm's stderr
instead of Node's "Command failed" — the first fix is what exposed this.

The suite now builds the dependencies itself when absent (three are local
file:// subcharts, one is remote), and skips if it cannot — same honesty
as the existing helm-not-installed guard, rather than reporting a chart
bug that isn't one. Verified both paths: with deps present, and with the
built charts/ directory moved away, where it rebuilt them and ran all ten.

* test(stored-objects): verify Entra identity auth against real Azure

Runs the driver against a real storage account with
allowSharedKeyAccess=false — the enterprise posture this whole feature
exists for, and the one thing no mocked test or emulator could confirm.

Evidence, in order:
- Shared key against that account: 403 KeyBasedAuthenticationNotPermitted
  on every operation. The blocker reproduced for real, not described.
- The same operations on a bearer token: write, read, size via signed
  HEAD, delete, and a zero-byte blob — all pass.

Also closes the earlier gap where host-style SharedKey signing had never
been exercised: Azurite is path-style only, so every signature the emulator
suite verified took the other branch of canonicalisedResource. Five
shared-key tests now pass against real host-style Azure.

azureCli is the mode a developer can actually run; workloadIdentity is the
same code path with a different credential class, so this proves the bearer
request shape Azure accepts. Both blocks self-skip without credentials, so
CI is unaffected.

The @manual scenario keeps its tag — it needs a subscription and cannot run
in CI — but is no longer @unimplemented, and carries the verification date.

* feat(stored-objects): surface the AADSTS code on a failed token exchange

Research into what the azureCli verification does and does not prove
turned up a gap worth closing.

The token exchange previously discarded the SDK error entirely, on the
grounds that it can quote the request and the assertion. That is true of
the message, but it also threw away the AADSTS code — which is an error
identifier, not credential material, and is the single most useful line an
operator can get. AADSTS70021 means the federated identity credential does
not match the token the cluster presented, and per Microsoft's own
troubleshooting guide it is the most common workload-identity
misconfiguration by a wide margin.

The code is now extracted and surfaced, and for the two federated-identity
codes the error names the three things to check: issuer (including the
trailing slash — a documented footgun, and the issuer changes if the
cluster is recreated), subject in the exact
system:serviceaccount:NAMESPACE:NAME form, and the
api://AzureADTokenExchange audience. Everything else from the SDK error is
still discarded; a test pins that an assertion quoted in the message does
not ride along.

Docs gain the same three requirements, since the federated credential is
configured on the Azure side and is the one piece the chart cannot do.

* test(groupQueue): prove the durable blob tier works on an Azure-only install

The durable tier is labelled tier: "s3", which raises a fair question for a
deployment with no S3 anywhere: does offloading a large job body fail?

It does not, and this executes the proof rather than arguing it. A real
TieredBlobStore against a real Azurite emulator, azure destination, no S3
configured: a body over the threshold lands in Azure Blob, reads back
byte-identical, and deletes through the same branch. Redis is asserted
untouched, so the durable path is the one under test.

The reason it holds is worth stating, because the name suggests otherwise:
tier never selects a provider. Both branch points test tier === "redis" and
fall through otherwise, and the fall-through calls mintUri(), which
re-derives the destination from resolveProjectStorageDestination and yields
an azure-blob:// URI that the registry dispatches on scheme. Deriving the
provider fresh instead of reading it off the ref is also the ADR-030
tenancy rule — a tampered envelope must not be able to redirect a read.

Closes one of the remaining @unimplemented scenarios.

* docs(groupQueue): say what the "s3" blob tier actually means

The durable tier is named "s3" but selects nothing — it answers "redis or
the durable store", and the provider is re-derived per operation by
mintUri, so an Azure-only deployment produces tier: "s3" refs whose bytes
are in Azure Blob.

That name reaches a human in exactly one place: "tier" is a label on
gq_blob_release_grace_total, so a dashboard split by tier shows "s3" for
Azure. The metric's help text now says so, and the BlobRef type carries the
same note plus a pointer to #6096.

Fixing the words rather than the value is deliberate. "s3" is also the job
envelope wire format (header.e), so renaming it needs read-both, drain,
write-new across two releases on the queue that carries trace payloads —
a migration to correct a label nothing branches on.

* chore(docs): regenerate llms-full.txt after the stacked rebase

* fix(stored-objects): follow ensureAzuriteContainer to its named-parameter form

The helper moved to named parameters on the base branch (CodeRabbit, repo
rule for multi-argument functions). Its three call sites there were updated
in the same commit; this suite lives only on this branch, so it needed the
same change to compile.

* fix(stored-objects): carry the endpoint and credential normalization forward

Rebase adaptation for the two langwatch-agent fixes from the base branch.

The endpoint normalization landed in this branch's refactored shape rather
than the base's: signedRequest became an auth strategy here, so the value is
derived once in resolvedEndpoint() — a better home for it than the inline
version, and isPathStyleEndpoint reads the same normalized value.

The credential trimming needed nothing: maybeAzureDriver now routes through
resolveAzureCredentials(), which already trims all three vars, so the fix
is preserved by construction instead of being restated.

Test adaptations: the trailing-slash regression test needed this branch's
`mode` discriminant, and the padded-credentials test needed
AZURE_BLOB_CONTAINER, which is part of "is Azure usable" here — padded too,
so the same normalization is proven to cover it.

* fix(charts): give sovereign clouds the identity authority they require

P1 from the langwatch-agent review, reproduced: `helm template` for a
sovereign endpoint emitted AZURE_BLOB_ENDPOINT and neither the authority
host nor the token audience. Since resolveAzureCredentials refuses a
non-public endpoint in a token mode without a matching authority — asking
the public-cloud issuer for a sovereign token fails confusingly — the chart
rendered green and the deployment died on its first storage call.

Adds authorityHost and tokenAudience to the azureBlob provider (value or
secretKeyRef, like its siblings) and emits them when set.

More usefully, the chart now mirrors the app's rule: a non-public endpoint
in a token mode without an authority fails the RENDER. The operator learns
at deploy time, from the values file they are already editing, rather than
from the first dataset write. The public cloud is untouched.

The secrets gate fires on `azure-secret-hygiene.unit.test.ts`, which exists

like a real leak for that test to mean anything, so gitleaks flags it on

Decoded, it is a header of {"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT"}, a payload of
{"aud":"https://storage"}, and a signature that is the ASCII word
`signature`. No key signed it; it names no tenant, account or subject.
There is nothing to revoke.

key or SAS token landing in the same file is still caught. Entry names the
value and says why it is not a secret, as the top of that file requires.

* docs(charts): scope legacyAzureRead to stored objects, not datasets

Review finding: the Azure->S3 migration flag reads as though it carries
everything written to Azure. It does not, and an operator following it on an
install with datasets loses access to them.

Stored objects survive the switch because each carries an `azure-blob://` URI
whose scheme selects the driver, so a read re-derives its own provider
independently of the write toggle. Dataset chunks are addressed by
{projectId, datasetId, index} with no provider recorded on the row, so dataset
reads follow the CURRENT toggle and cannot reach chunks written to Azure. The
bytes are intact — they are unreachable until the toggle is reverted.

Says so plainly in values.yaml and the self-hosting env table, and tells
operators with datasets not to use the flag until per-dataset storage
provenance lands (#6323). No behaviour change; this closes the gap between
what the flag promises and what it does.

Both let a misconfiguration render green and fail on the first Blob call,
which is the failure mode this chart validation exists to prevent.

annotation passed the guard, which only checked that a name resolved. The
labelled pods came up healthy while the admission webhook had no identity to
bind them to, so resolveAzureCredentials() failed at runtime on the missing

account — one the operator names lives outside the chart and its annotations
cannot be read, so that stays a documented prerequisite.

The sovereign-authority check read only endpoint.value, so supplying the
endpoint through a Secret bypassed it entirely: a sovereign endpoint in a
token mode with no authorityHost deployed fine, then had every token request
refused for asking the public-cloud issuer. Helm cannot read the Secret, so a
secret-backed endpoint is now treated as unknowable and requires an authority
host. That costs a public-cloud install nothing, since it need not set the
endpoint at all.

Six render tests cover both, including the paths that must still succeed: a
supplied account name, an authority configured alongside a secret endpoint,
and an install that sets no endpoint.

resolveAzureCredentials required it for both purposes, so maybeAzureDriver()
returned undefined without it.

feat(billing): collect annual event overage during the year via billing thresholds (#6609)

* feat(billing): collect annual event overage during the year via Stripe billing thresholds

Annual Growth subscriptions accrue metered event usage for twelve months
and collect all of it in a single renewal invoice — a payment far more
likely to be declined than the same amount collected as it accrues.

Set billing_thresholds (750.00 in the subscription currency,
reset_billing_cycle_anchor: false) on every subscription carrying an
annual Growth events price:

- new signups: applied from the checkout-completed webhook, since Stripe
  Checkout rejects the parameter at subscription creation
- existing customers: one-time idempotent backfill script

Stripe then invoices and charges the accrued overage automatically each
time it crosses the threshold; the annual included-events quota keeps its
cumulative semantics and the billing anniversary never moves.

- add the IRREVERSIBLE: disposition block to the backfill script: it

  un-issued, so there is no meaningful down step
- extract the threshold application into a private helper so
  handleCheckoutCompleted stays under the cognitive-complexity gate

- the one exception: reset_billing_cycle_anchor=true would move the
  billing anniversary on every threshold invoice, contradicting what
  the customer was sold — it is corrected to false while keeping the
  existing amount (new anchor_pinned result).
- the backfill walk now lives in a tested module
  (annualEventsThresholdBackfill.ts): candidate query shape, annual-only
  updates, one failure not stopping the walk, and dry-run making no
  update calls are all covered; the script is a thin CLI entrypoint.
- spec grows three scenarios for the above; the backfill scenario now

Review follow-ups: state blocks now read 'given ...' per the BDD

The one-time backfill walks live Stripe billing data for existing paying
subscriptions. That is SaaS-only operational work: it belongs with the other

repo, where it ships to self-hosted users who can never run it.

What stays here is the part every deployment needs: the shared
applyAnnualEventsBillingThreshold helper and the checkout-completed webhook
that sets the threshold on new annual subscriptions.

* fix(billing): alert when an annual subscription misses its billing threshold

Checkout completion answers Stripe with a 200 whether or not the threshold
was applied — a non-2xx would make Stripe redeliver the whole checkout
webhook, which must not happen. That means Stripe's own retry never covers
this failure, and until now the only trace was a single log line. A transient
Stripe error would silently drop that subscription back into the
single-large-renewal-invoice risk this feature exists to remove, discoverable
only by grepping logs.

The failure now also raises a Slack alert on the existing subscriptions
channel, carrying the subscription id and the reason so it can be re-applied
manually. Extends the billing NotificationService rather than adding a
parallel alerting path.

The alert is separately guarded: a broken Slack webhook must never be what
fails an otherwise-successful checkout. The test for that case failed first —
the initial version propagated the alert error straight out of the handler.

backfill script for pre-existing subscriptions". That script left this repo
in 9e44abe, so the comment described a caller that no longer exists here —
and left `isDryRun` looking like dead code with no caller and no reason.

States the real contract: the checkout-completed webhook is the only caller
here and covers new subscriptions only; the backfill lives in the
langwatch-saas task runner, imports this function, and its safety story is
the dry-run preview, so the flag is a seam for that caller rather than
something to delete.

Also records that Stripe returns `items` as a paginated list (default 10)
while a Growth subscription carries two, so a plan that ever grows past ten
line items would silently read as not_annual_events and skip the threshold.

* docs(billing): stop claiming the langwatch-saas backfill already exists

The comment added in 37e5956 said the backfill "lives in the langwatch-saas
task runner, which imports this function" — present tense, about something
that has not been written. That repeats the defect it was fixing: a comment
describing a caller that is not there.

States the real position instead: the backfill is not written yet and is

fix(traces): stop a deleted span reaching the dataset, and show removals where the reader can see them (#6855)

* fix(datasets): stop the AI-readable column quoting deleted spans, and let the Expansions switches be switched

The "Full Trace (AI-Readable)" column is filled from a read of its own,
and that read never asked for the reviewer's corrections. Every other
column in the same mapping did, so a span the reviewer deleted was gone
from spans.* and from the traces list, and still spelled out in full in
the one column that quotes the whole trace. It now reads the trace the
same way the rest of the mapping does.

The Expansions switches all sat inside one field. A field describes a
single control, so it handed the same input id to every switch in it, and
each switch's label pointed at the first switch's input: clicking one
moved another. They now sit outside the field, where each owns its id and
its own name.

Turning the last expansion off also did not stick. An empty selection read
as "nothing chosen yet", so the host's re-read of the stored mapping put
the old expansions straight back, including one the reader never touched.
After the first pass the selection is the whole truth, empty included.

Mapping a column to the spans source no longer turns "one row per span" on
by itself. A dataset built from traces is a row per trace until someone
asks otherwise; annotations and events, where expanding is the point of
mapping them, are unchanged.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01CiNRWuXMuubAUKW1ujoJk2

* fix(traces): stop re-serialised JSON reading as an edited attribute

A correction rewrites a whole attribute record, so an attribute holding
JSON comes back re-serialised whether or not the reviewer touched it:
different spacing, different key order, sometimes text where the capture
held the structure. The comparison behind the "Edited" marker was on the
rendered string, so all of that counted, and rows nobody had edited came
back marked. A marker that fires on rows nobody edited is one readers
learn to ignore.

Values are now compared by what they say. Key order is formatting and does
not count; array order is content and does. Text is only read as JSON when
it parses to an object or an array, so a correction that turned the string
"123" into the number 123 still reads as the edit it is.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01CiNRWuXMuubAUKW1ujoJk2

* fix(traces): show what a correction removed on the corrected trace, not the captured one

A span a correction deletes used to vanish from the corrected trace and
carry a "Deleted" badge on the captured one. That is backwards on both
counts. The corrected trace is where a reader goes to see what the
correction did, and a row that simply disappeared reads as a row that was
never captured, so the removal was the one edit the reader could not see.
The captured trace is the trace as it arrived, and nothing the correction
did belongs on it.

A removed span now stays on the row it had in the corrected trace, marked
and struck through along with the model or tool pill under its name, and
reads plainly in the captured one. Attributes a correction removes get the
same treatment: still listed, struck through, marked Removed rather than
Edited, since a removal is not an edit to the value.

The tombstones are a rendering of what the correction did, not spans the
corrected trace has. The tree the drawer draws keeps them; everything that
asks what the trace now contains -- the header's span count, whether a
comment still points at something, what a dataset row is built from --
reads the tree that leaves them out.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01CiNRWuXMuubAUKW1ujoJk2

* fix(traces): let every expansion switch answer to its own click, and stop a removal reading as a change

Two things dogfooding found after the first pass.

The Add to Dataset drawer wrapped its mapping and its preview in one
field. A field describes one control and hands that control its id, so
every expansion switch and every preview checkbox came out carrying the
same id and announcing the field's label. A click on a switch went
wherever that id resolved first, which was usually nowhere the reader
aimed: the switches simply did not respond. Each heading now holds a
field of its own, with no control inside it.

On the captured trace, a span the correction only deleted still carried
the changed colour. That colour promises a captured value the reader can
go and compare, and a removal replaces nothing, so the changed set is now
the rows whose values the correction replaces. A span it renamed before
removing still reads as changed.

* fix(traces): keep a removed attribute out of what gets copied, and bind each test to what it proves

Copying a corrected span's attributes, and reading them as JSON, quoted the
struck-through rows too, so an attribute a correction took away travelled back
out as one the span still carries. The table now lists one map and hands on
another.

Mapping a column also rebuilt the expansions from the render's filtered set
rather than the latest state, so an expansion the reader had turned on was lost
once its column was remapped away and back.

Also renames keepDeleted to shouldKeepDeleted, gives sameExpansions a named
parameter object, and puts two doc comments back on the functions they describe.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01CiNRWuXMuubAUKW1ujoJk2

* docs(specs): say which corrections leave a span reading plainly on the captured trace

A span the correction renames before deleting does keep the changed colour

right below it, and the comment claiming nothing the correction did belongs on

* fix(traces): keep the AI-readable digest on previews while it reads the correction

Teaching getFormattedSpansDigest about corrections also gave it the

Tag teardown must not raise, so every failure was swallowed and a cleanup that
gave up looked exactly like one that worked. Two tests also created tags
outside the factory entirely. Between them, 167 orphan tags accumulated in a

returns whether the tag is confirmed gone, which is what makes that count mean
something; a 404 counts as clean, because nothing is left behind either way.

fix(ops): publish the pending-drift metric so every collector reports the same figure (#4703) (#6669)

* fix(ops): publish the pending-drift metric so every collector reports the same figure (#4703)

The reconcile is single-flighted through a shared Redis marker, so on any cycle
only the instance that wins a queue recomputes it. The drift it measured was
then kept in process memory and surfaced through that instance's own dashboard,
which made the signal disagree with itself once more than one collector ran: an
instance that won no marker reported 0 drift for a queue that had plenty, and an
instance that won some of the queues reported a partial total. The counter
itself was never affected, only the number an operator reads.

Publish the drift to a shared key under the same fence as the counter it
describes, and have every instance read the published figures rather than its
own measurement. Writing it outside the fence would let a pass write the
counter, lose the marker, and still announce a drift for a heal it did not land.

The figure expires after three reconcile cycles. It has to outlive the gap
between passes or every instance reads nothing for most of the minute, and it
has to expire or a queue whose reconcile has stopped pins its last drift on the
dashboard forever.

The other half of the ticket, SCAN double-counting keys, is already fixed on
main: collectPendingGroupIds collects into a Set and no longer walks the
keyspace as its primary enumeration. Evidence on the issue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ops): reject a partly numeric published drift instead of half reading it

A lenient parse stops at the first character it cannot use, so a stored
"7oops" read as 7 and landed in the dashboard total looking exactly like a
figure some instance had measured. The read already skipped values it could
not parse at all, so the half parsed case was the one gap where junk was
believed rather than dropped.

* refactor(billing): route webhook notifications through a bestEffort wrapper (#5591)

Stripe retries any webhook answered with a 5xx, so a notification that
throws does not merely lose a message: it replays a handler that has
already written. The rule was kept by remembering to wrap each call in
try/catch, and it was kept at one call site out of four.

handleSubscriptionUpdated's active branch, syncInvoicePaymentSuccess and
the checkout analytics emit were all unguarded. They were safe only
because sendSlackMessage swallows send errors internally and posthog
happens not to throw, which is a property of the callee rather than a
decision at the call site.

bestEffort logs and never throws, so the posture is a named rule instead
of per-call discipline. The one guard that already existed is rewritten
to use it rather than left as a second way of doing the same thing.

Scoped to the webhook handlers, which is where the rule comes from.
subscription.service.ts has the same shape but is not a webhook, so
swallowing there would be a behaviour change rather than an application
of this rule.

fix(mcp): make /sse transport work across replicas and harden the OAuth path (#6860)

* spec(mcp): describe cross-replica SSE, OAuth discovery and consent error scenarios

The in-app MCP surface had no scenarios for the SSE transport, the OAuth
discovery documents, or where an authorization failure is reported. Adds
them so the behaviour the fixes below implement is written down first.

* fix(mcp): make the SSE transport work across replicas and harden the OAuth path

Production runs several app replicas with no session affinity. GET /sse
opens a stream that lives only on the replica that answered it, but the
session was recorded nowhere else, so each POST /messages landed on the
right replica about one time in four and was rejected with
400 "Invalid or missing session ID" otherwise. Claude and ChatGPT
connectors pointed at /sse therefore listed no tools.

An SSE stream cannot be recreated elsewhere, so the message travels to
the stream instead: the session is recorded in Redis, the replica holding
the stream subscribes to a per-session channel, and a replica that
receives a message for a session it does not hold publishes it there and
answers 202. A publish nobody receives means the owning replica is gone,
so the record is dropped and the client is told to reconnect.

Alongside that:

- POST /sse/messages is routed too. The stream advertises /messages, and
  some clients resolve that by appending it to the path they connected
  on. The standalone server already mounted both.
- The OAuth discovery subtree is claimed, so the path-suffixed documents
  clients try first are served instead of reaching the single-page-app
  fallback, which answered 200 text/html and left the client parsing
  markup as JSON. Documents that do not exist answer a JSON 404.
- The token endpoint accepts client credentials as HTTP Basic, and tells
  a client whose registration is gone to register again rather than
  reporting its code as invalid.
- Rate limiting keys on the caller address the proxy reports, not the
  socket address, which behind Cloudflare is the proxy for everyone.
  Registration and token exchange get a budget each, and a throttled
  request answers an OAuth error with a retry hint.
- SSE sessions now count towards the per-project session limit, and
  reopening a streaming session through another replica recovers it the
  way the POST path already did.
- Every MCP request writes one access log line. These routes return
  before the app's Hono stack, so nothing recorded them at all.

* fix(mcp): report authorization failures back to the waiting OAuth client

The advertised authorize endpoint is a page in this app, so every
validation failure rendered as a toast here and the client's popup was
left waiting with nothing to report.

RFC 6749 section 4.1.2.1: once the client_id is registered and the
presented redirect_uri is one it registered, the failure belongs back at
that redirect_uri as an OAuth error. Those failures now return a redirect
carrying error, error_description and the request state, and the page
follows it. Failures that cannot be attributed to a verified client, an
unknown client_id or an unregistered redirect_uri, have no safe
destination and keep showing on the page.

* docs(mcp): point the client config at the endpoints that exist

The sample config advertised https://app.langwatch.ai/api/mcp, which is
not a route. The transports are served at /mcp and /sse.

* fix(mcp): proxy the OpenID configuration probe to the API in dev

Every other MCP discovery path is proxied; without this one dev answers
the single-page app's HTML where production answers a JSON 404.

* test(mcp): clear recorded SSE sessions around the cross-replica suite

An interrupted run leaves session records in Redis, which would make the
next run's first connection hit the per-project session limit.

* fix(mcp): authenticate a streamable reconnect before rebuilding the session

Recovering a session from Redis decrypts the stored key, connects a server
bound to it and puts the session in this replica's map. That ran before the
bearer token was checked, so naming a session id was enough to make any
replica do all of it for a caller who was then answered 401.

The caller's key is now resolved first and the record only rebuilt when it
matches, on both the POST and the GET path.

Also from review:
- await the session releases on shutdown, so a process that exits does not
  leave slots allocated against the per-project session limit
- clear both transports' session records in the relay suite, which was
  leaking a 30-day streamable record per run into the same limit
- fail openSseStream loudly when the server answers no stream, instead of
  hanging until the suite times out
- move the SSE harness into __tests__/support, build form bodies with
  URLSearchParams, and split the discovery loops into per-resource cases
- guard the consent page's redirect with the scheme check the deny path
  already had

* refactor(mcp): read every request body through one size-limited reader

The three handlers that read a body each carried their own copy of the
413 branch. The JSON reader and both form readers now share it, and each
form reader keeps the parse failure its own OAuth error needs.

* fix(mcp): refuse redirect URIs the browser executes, from one shared list

The authorize route and the consent page each carried their own copy of a
three-scheme deny-list. They now share one, which also closes the same-origin
schemes the copies missed: blob: and filesystem: resolve against the origin
that created them, so they belong with javascript:, vbscript: and data:.

The list stays a deny-list rather than an http/https allow-list because
native MCP clients complete the flow through a custom-scheme callback they
register with the OS (RFC 8252 section 7.1), and an allow-list would refuse
every one of them.

Also from review: split the cross-replica suite per transport so each file
stays under the size ceiling, move the two-replica fixture into the shared
harness, name sessionSetKey's parameters, and unref the harness timeout so a
won race does not hold the event loop open until teardown.

* fix(mcp): refuse a PKCE method the token endpoint cannot verify

The authorize endpoint accepted any code_challenge_method while advertising
only S256, and the token endpoint verifies every code as S256 regardless. A
client asking for plain was handed a code it could never redeem, and only
found out at the exchange. It is now told at the request.

Also from review:
- freeze the shared redirect-scheme deny-list, so an importer cannot mutate a
  security policy both the route and the page read
- drop the local alias for that check, leaving one greppable name
- drain the one-shot Prisma mock queues between tests, and assert the scheme
  gate really does run before the client registry is read
- survive a failed beforeAll in the replica suites instead of masking its
  message with a TypeError, and fail loudly when a replica reports no address

* chore(mcp): drop a suppression marker that suppresses nothing

The lgtm comment is legacy syntax that current code scanning ignores, so
it read as a control that was not there. The reasoning stays in the
docstring, and the alert is dismissed the way the identical production
one is.
Release docs (auto-release on merge to main) [skip ci]

fix(automations): decode middle-dot in metadata filter keys for in-memory matching (#6870)

* fix(automations): decode middle-dot in metadata filter keys for in-memory matching

The UI encodes dots as middle-dots (·) in filter keys (e.g. metadata·environment).
The ClickHouse query path decoded these back to dots, but the in-memory
precondition matcher used the raw encoded key to look up customMetadata —
which always returned null, silently discarding every dispatch.

This caused all automations filtering on custom metadata to stop firing
platform-wide once the filter was saved through the current UI.

Decode the middle-dot and strip the metadata prefix before lookup, matching
the ClickHouse path's behavior.

standalone npm lockfiles, so the workspace-wide pnpm overrides never reach
them and their transitive deps drifted behind. Extend each example's existing

(#2092, #2093, latest published is the vulnerable 2.0.2) and

* fix(security): tighten the axios override floor in the langgraph example

`^1.15.0` resolves anywhere in the 1.15.x line, which the repo's own policy
marks vulnerable: the root pnpm-workspace.yaml carries
`"axios@>=1.0.0 <1.16.0": ">=1.16.0"`. The example's standalone npm lockfile

fix(clickhouse): stop metering tables that have no _size_bytes column (#6453)

* fix(clickhouse): stop metering tables that have no _size_bytes column

Metering enrolls a table by listing it in the retention map, but summing
_size_bytes only works if that table's migration declared the column.
Nothing connected the two, and the four ADR-034 analytics projections were
enrolled without it: migration 00032 added _size_bytes to the tables that
existed then, later tables declare it themselves, and 00038 to 00041 do
neither.

Metering them raises UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER instead of returning a number, and
that is not contained to those four. They are summed in one UNION ALL with
every other metered table, so the single-query total fails outright and
every metering call falls back to the per-table breakdown, which is the
path whose byteSize(...) recompute on un-materialized parts is the known
memory and timeout hazard. The four then fail again individually and
degrade to zero.

Exclude them from the metered set. Reported totals are unchanged, since
the failing queries already contributed zero, and the single aggregate
works again for the tables that can answer. Metering them for real needs
the column added and a decision on whether their bytes are billed.

perf(analytics): add column pruning to the documents and feedbacks stored_spans JOINs (#2643) (#5780)

* perf(analytics): prune the stored_spans JOINs in documents/feedbacks queries

The three hand-written `JOIN stored_spans` in buildTopDocumentsQuery (top-10
+ total-count) and buildFeedbacksQuery joined the full stored_spans column
set and bounded StartTime on the outer alias. They were missed by the #2605
sweep that routed the other analytics JOINs through buildJoinClause with
column pruning (the same class that caused the #2551 OOM).

Route all three through buildJoinClause so the join reads a pruned subquery:
identity columns plus SpanAttributes (documents) or the Events.* arrays
(feedbacks), with the 2-day-padded StartTime window pushed into the subquery
for partition pruning before the join. Behavior is unchanged: the required
columns cover every reference in each query, and the pushed StartTime bound
is byte-identical to the outer filter it replaces (SPAN_TIME_FILTER_START_END).

Closes #2643.

fix(ci): keep integration test files serial so the budget rollup replay cannot collide (#6581)

* fix(ci): keep integration test files serial so the budget rollup replay cannot collide

The gateway budget periodStart suite fails intermittently on the
test-integration (4) shard with every window reading zero spend,
including the TOTAL window that does no period arithmetic at all, and a
rerun with no changes passes.

Vitest resolves `fileParallelism: false` by forcing maxWorkers to 1, and
then reads VITEST_MAX_WORKERS and assigns it over the value it just
resolved. The workflow sets that variable to keep vitest off all four of
a runner's vCPUs, so a cap meant to lower a ceiling raised a floor and
the integration shards have been running two files at a time.

The two files that share the shard are the only two that replay the
rollup rebuild migration. That migration is database-wide, so a per-run
tenant id isolates nothing from it: it drops the rollup's materialised
view, re-derives the table from the ledger, swaps it in, recreates the
view, then reconciles by reading the rollup and writing a delta back. A
debit written by the neighbouring suite while the view is missing lands
in the ledger and never reaches the rollup, which is the zero every
window reports; the reconciliation repairs it a moment later, which is
why the rerun is green. Two replays running at once produce the other
two shapes seen in CI, a scratch table that already exists or has just
vanished, and totals counted twice.

Strip the worker cap while files are serial, and give the schema itself
a lock so a replay and a neighbour's fixtures cannot overlap under any
scheduling. Both suites hold that lock for their whole run; it is
re-entrant, so they still replay migrations inside their own tests.

Closes #6580

* fix(ci): hold the ClickHouse schema lock in every suite that reads or writes the budget rollup

A third file on the same shard failed the same way on an unrelated PR:
budgetBucketBreakdown, with a row count one short rather than the
all-zeros shape. That is the reader half of the same race. The rollup
rebuild re-derives every row from the ledger and swaps the table in, so
a suite reading the rollup while that runs sees it partway through, and
a suite writing the ledger while the materialised view is dropped loses
rows it never folded. Neither suite has to replay a migration to be hurt
by one.

Every suite that writes gateway_budget_ledger_events or reads spend back
through gateway_budget_scope_totals now holds the lock for its whole
run, which is seven files beyond the two that replay the rebuild. The
helper moves to file scope so it also covers a file with several
top-level describes or its own root hooks.

Stale locks are now broken on holder liveness rather than on elapsed
time. The pid is already in the lock file, so a worker killed hard
enough to skip its exit handler frees the lock on the next waiter's
poll, while a suite that legitimately runs for minutes keeps it.

* fix(ci): never recover a schema lock whose holder is still alive

Review found the age fallback could evict a live holder. The lock file's
mtime is written once at acquisition and never refreshed, so it measures
how long the holder has had the lock rather than how long it has been
idle, and recovering on it would take the lock away from a suite in the
middle of the critical section this exists to protect. A living owner
now keeps its lock however long it needs, and the age fallback is left
to the one case it was written for, an owner line that cannot be read.

The process exit handler verifies the token before unlinking, so a
process exiting after its lock was taken away cannot free the new
holder's, and it is registered only while the lock is held so a process
that builds many locks does not accumulate listeners.

The test for a lock changing hands mid-recovery did not exercise that
path: recovery completed synchronously before the timer that was meant
to open the window. The window is a few synchronous calls wide, so the
lock now exposes an onBeforeClaim seam and the test opens it exactly
once. Removing the token verification makes that test fail, which is
what it should have been proving all along.

* fix(ci): keep the schema lock under the cognitive complexity limit

The new-violations gate counts warn-tier rules too, and the lock added
three: recoverIfAbandoned at 19, acquire at 14, and the journal reader
in the contention test at 11, against a limit of 10.

Split rather than suppressed. Recovery now reads as its two questions,
whether there is an owner this process may remove and how one specific
owner is removed, and the acquire loop hands its timeout message to a
named builder instead of assembling it inline.

- new subscription_not_linked handled error (409) for an ACTIVE row that
  was never linked to its Stripe counterpart, with copy that does not
  suggest retrying; subscription_sync_failed keeps meaning transient drift
- 409 added to the client do-not-retry statuses (extracted to
  queryRetryPolicy.ts): the seat dialog shows the real error immediately
  instead of retrying a conflict 4 times behind a spinner
- updateSeatEventItems throws its named failures instead of returning

- tsconfig.tsgo.json excludes dist/ so pnpm typecheck stays green after

* revert: drop unrelated tsconfig exclude from this PR

platform/app/dist/ is gitignored and only exists on a machine that has run
pnpm build:server, so CI and clean checkouts never see those errors. Narrowing
what the whole team's typecheck covers does not belong in a billing fix; if the
build-then-typecheck friction is worth solving it gets its own change.

* fix(billing): quote the seat change that is actually charged

A refutation panel killed most of the first pass. What it found:

- The preview and the update described different operations. The update
  reverses a scheduled cancellation before applying the new quantity; the
  preview modelled the subscription as still cancelling. On an annual plan
  billed next to a monthly meter, cancellation truncates the seat line to the
  monthly boundary, so one 6->8 seat change quoted EUR 54.25 and charged
  EUR 639.91. Both now build the same change object, so they cannot drift.
- The preview netted out prorations the subscription already carried, but
  always_invoice bills those too, so the quote was under the debit. Counting
  them removes the second Stripe call as well: one preview, not two.
- subscription_not_linked could not fire for the customers it was written for.
  cancel() keeps stripeSubscriptionId, so a churned subscription is a
  permanent tombstone that a 'most recent row with an id' lookup returns
  forever - masking an ACTIVE unlinked row behind subscription_sync_failed,
  whose copy promises it catches up on its own. Candidates are now ranked:
  active+linked, then active-unlinked, then cancelled+linked. The throw site
  logs the organization and subscription so support can act on it.
- Not retrying every 409 was wrong in both directions: previewProration is the
  only 409-producing query in the app, and its 409s are mostly transient. The
  rule now reads the handled error's code, so subscription_not_linked stops
  and subscription_sync_failed keeps retrying, as its own copy says it should.
- specs/licensing/proration-preview.feature required the customer see the
  amount charged immediately; it was computed, never rendered, and its
  scenario parked as unimplemented. The dialog now shows 'Due today' and
  labels the recurring total with its period. 19/19 scenarios bound.
- The success toast fired without reading result.success, so the non-seat
  path could still report 'Seats updated successfully' over nothing.

Closes #6638

* fix(billing): quote the taxed invoice total, not a page of pre-tax lines

Found by an adversarial review pass on the branch's own diff.

Summing proration line amounts was wrong twice over, and this PR was about to
put that number in front of a customer as "Due today":

- Line amounts are pre-tax. Where tax is added on top rather than included
  (verified against a real checkout-created USD subscription with automatic
  tax and an EU address), the sum came to 24.58 on an invoice charging 29.74 —
  a fifth short. Currencies where tax is inclusive were unaffected, which is
  why the local EUR fixture never showed it.
- `lines` is a paginated sublist with a ten-line page. A subscription carrying
  enough pending prorations silently dropped everything past the first page;
  reproduced at 14 lines, sum 1000 against a subtotal of 1400.

`preview.total` is the invoice total, post-tax and page-independent, and for an
always_invoice preview the invoice carries only the proration lines (verified:
zero non-proration lines on increase and decrease). Signed, so a seat reduction
still previews as a credit — `amount_due` clamps a negative invoice to zero.

The miscalculation predates this branch; displaying it did not, which is what
made it worth blocking on.

Fixtures now carry tax-exclusive and paginated invoices so a return to summing
lines fails.

* fix(billing): name every billing period, and say when a seat sync fails

Three review findings, all real:

- `SeatsContent` printed "per month" for any interval that was not `year`.
  The value comes from the payment provider, which can also say `day` or
  `week`, so a weekly seat price labelled a charge with the wrong period.
  Each period now has its own words and an unrecognised one says nothing
  rather than something false.
- `seatSyncService` folded every handled error into a bare `false`. Several
  of them are `fault: "platform"` and need an operator — an unlinked
  subscription above all — so the fold now logs the code and the
  organization first.
- `HTTP_STATUS_TO_NOT_RETRY` is an internal constant and takes `as const`,
  per the repo's TypeScript guideline.

* test(billing): nest the retry-policy cases under a given block

The repo's BDD structure wants describe("given ...") above the when-level
contexts; these sat at the top level.

* fix(billing): refuse to quote a seat price the provider does not carry

`unit_amount` is null for tiered and metered prices, and the `?? 0`
fallback turned that into "$0 per year" printed beside a button that
charges the card — the same class of lie the rest of this change removes.
The seat line is always one of four flat licensed prices today, so this is
unreachable; it becomes reachable the moment a tiered seat price enters the
catalog, and then a named failure beats a wrong number.

Also corrects the proration-preview spec header, which still claimed the
modal had no component-test fixture and pointed the backend scenarios at
the wrong test file.

* fix(billing): quote what the card is charged, at the instant it is charged

Three ways the seat dialog could still print a number the customer is not
about to pay.

**Credit on the account.** The quote read the invoice `total`; the charge is
raised for `amount_due`, which is the total after any credit the account is
already holding is spent against it. Measured on one purchase against two
accounts: clean, total 293.70 and charged 293.70; holding 200.00 of credit,
total 293.70 and charged 93.70. So the dialog told a customer with a balance
they were about to pay 293.70 while their card took 93.70.

`amount_due` is not simply the better field — it clamps a negative invoice to
zero, so a seat reduction previewing -587.39 reports 0 and the dialog would
say nothing happens over a 587.39 credit. Hence a branch, not a swap: a credit
is described by the signed total, a charge by the amount actually due. The
credit spent is now shown on its own line, so a "Due today" smaller than the
change itself is explained rather than merely surprising.

**Two live plans on one account.** Seat changes preferred whichever ACTIVE row
still carried a provider link. Nothing in checkout produces this state — both
paths only turn ACTIVE a row resolved by its provider id — but the backoffice
subscription form writes any status against any organization, and there is no
unique index on `organizationId` behind it. The linked row is not reliably the
one an operator meant to keep, so preferring it is a coin flip against a card.
Refuse instead, under `subscription_ambiguous`: it costs a support message and
charges nothing.

**A quote priced at a different moment than the charge.** Mid-term changes are
priced by the instant they are applied, so previewing at one time and
confirming at another are two different amounts. The quote now issues its
instant and the confirmation sends it back, pinning both calls to it. Past
fifteen minutes the pin is refused (`billing_quote_expired`) rather than
honoured — the further it drifts the more it bills for time already paid for,
and across a period boundary it is a different invoice entirely. Callers with
no quote on screen, such as the background seat sync, are priced at the moment
they run, as before.

Both new codes are permanent failures: neither is fixed by trying again.

* refactor(billing): lift the quote's two money figures out of the preview

`previewProration` had grown to 95 lines, most of it the reasoning for which
field on a previewed invoice is the one a customer is actually charged. That
reasoning is about the invoice, not about previewing a seat change, so it now
lives in `quotedAmounts` next to the type it reads.

No behaviour change: same branch, same two figures, same tests.

Also splits a comment that had run two unrelated thoughts together — why the
failures throw, and why the quote's freshness is checked before the provider
is called.

* refactor(billing): move the seat-change pure helpers out of the closure

`seatChangeParams`, `resolveProrationDate` and the quote-validity window take
everything they need as arguments — none of them reads the injected Stripe
client or database handle, so none of them needed to live inside the factory.
Sitting there made the factory 21 lines longer than it had to be and implied a
dependency they do not have.

Module scope instead. Behaviour and tests unchanged.

* refactor(billing): name the invoice shape quotedAmounts is allowed to read

The helper accepted any Stripe.Invoice while its arithmetic is only true of
an always_invoice preview, where the invoice carries nothing but the
proration lines. AlwaysInvoicePreview narrows the parameter to the two
fields the quote reads and puts the premise in a name a future caller has
to look at, instead of a comment they can miss.
