feat(haven): seed a play sandbox from the shared preset registry (#6903)

* feat(haven): seed a play sandbox from the shared preset registry

`haven play` gave its sandbox an identity-only seed, so a PR opened on the
onboarding "waiting for your first message" screen with an empty project —
the wrong place to stand when the change under review is about anything
afterwards. Filling it meant knowing that the play checkout's directory name
(pr-<n>) is not its stack slug (play-<n>), and passing LANGWATCH_SLUG by hand.

`haven play <pr> --seed <preset>` now takes the same presets `haven db seed`
takes, from the same registry — no second list, no play-only variants. The
preset's switches go to the sandbox's own seed; data that has to travel
through the collector is ingested in a lane beside the supervised services,
which waits on the sandbox's own /api/health rather than guessing at a delay.
The preset is validated before the PR is even resolved, so a typo costs a line
of output instead of a checkout and a container set, and it travels to the
backgrounded launcher as a positional (a preset the parent parsed and dropped
would have left the sandbox silently empty).

A failed ingest is a warning, never a stop: it names the step and the command
that retries it, because a PR that broke the collector is precisely one worth
watching run. Teardown does wait for the seeder to stop, though, rather than
racing a `docker volume rm` against a process still writing.

PlayLaunch is split into named steps along the way (runtime, databases, stack
registration, checkout preparation) — it was over the cognitive-complexity and
argument limits the moment it was touched, and the seams were already there.

Spec: specs/setup/haven-play.feature, ADR-064.

* Address review comments

- guard `haven play-launch` against an empty argument list: the parser caps
  positionals but never requires them, and the command is dispatchable by
  hand, so a bare invocation indexed an empty slice and panicked
- log the error on the codegen and seed warn-and-continue paths, matching the
  ingest lane; a sandbox that came up unseeded gave no reason why
- exercise the give-up path: an ingest whose app never answers runs nothing
- name `mass` in the seed-preset spec's shared list, and say in the README
  which presets actually load data

* Give the two negative paths scenarios of their own

Both tests were annotated with a scenario title that already had its own
test, so the parity checker counted them as bound while the spec described
neither behaviour: a sandbox whose app never answers, and a launcher invoked
with no PR number. Two scenarios, two bindings, 28/28.

* Say what bare actually seeds in the play --seed line

It was grouped with onboarding and post-onboarding as a preset that "only
moves the flags", but bare drops the env-derived model providers and keeps
stock feature flags: it is the identity alone.

* Say what the never-serving sandbox actually loses

"never seeded" was wrong: the base seed and the preset's switches run before
the services, so a sandbox whose app never answers still has its identity —
what it loses is the data that has to travel through the running stack. The
scenario says that now, and the test asserts the base seed ran anyway.

The launcher's empty-argument guard loses its scenario: play-launch is
internal, hidden from help and spawned by `haven play`, so its argument
handling is not behavior the feature file should describe. The test stays.

fix(traces): route the edge spool through the shared storage layer (#6253)

* fix(traces): route the edge spool through the shared storage layer

The ADR-022 edge spool wrote over-threshold span payloads straight to AWS S3
through `createS3Client`, bypassing `stored-objects` entirely. It was the one
byte-writing surface left behind when everything else moved onto the shared
storage layer, so it silently ignored a deployment's configured destination.

On an Azure-only install the spool PUT threw, `maybeSpool` swallowed it
fail-open, and every oversized span logged "oversize protection skipped" while
the container stayed empty. Worse, mid-migration (Azure configured, legacy
S3 bucket still set for reads) the spool resolved the legacy bucket and kept
writing trace payloads to S3 while the operator believed storage had moved —
a data-residency problem, not just a missing feature.

Neither state was reachable in a shipped deployment: `release_trace_blob_offload`
defaults off and appears in no chart or `.env.example`. This closes the gap
before the flag is ever recommended.

- `BlobStore` now resolves the destination and writes through the
  `stored-objects` registry, injected rather than constructed, so the spool
  lands in Azure Blob, S3, or the local filesystem as configured.
- `mintUriForDestination` becomes the single destination-to-URI mapping,
  replacing three copies of the same switch (content-addressed objects, the
  GroupQueue durable tier, and the spool's absence from that list).
- The object path is unchanged, keeping `trace-blobs/spool/` above the tenant
  segment so existing lifecycle rules still match.

Also closes a tamper channel the spool carried since ADR-022: the reference
travelling in the queue message was the object key, and the read path parsed
the tenant id out of it to pick a bucket. Commands now carry an opaque marker
and the worker re-derives the location from its own authenticated tenantId and
span ids, matching ADR-030 §5. v1 keys still resolve for one release, but only
when their tenant segment matches the command's.

Fixes langwatch/langwatch-saas#800

* refactor(traces): named constructor params + surface refused cross-tenant deletes

Review follow-ups on the spool change.

- `BlobStore` takes a named options object. The third positional dependency had
  ~30 call sites threading a positional `undefined`, against the repo's
  named-parameter rule; a fourth would have been unreadable.
- A refused cross-tenant v1 delete now logs instead of vanishing into
  `deleteSpool`'s best-effort catch. That swallow is for storage blips; a
  reference naming another tenant is a tamper signal and should be visible.
- Cover the `MAX_SPOOL_BYTES` read cap, which nothing exercised — a regression
  dropping the argument would have passed green.
- Settle the orphan-cleanup window: code said 3 days in five places, ADR-022
  said 24h in three. 3 days is the intended value (it covers a weekend
  incident); the ADR amendment now supersedes both 24h statements.
- Drop redundant `as string` casts on span ids. The span schema already types
  them as strings, and the casts made a safe derivation read as unchecked.

* chore(adr): drop the stale ci-trigger marker from ADR-022

A debug artifact from an older branch. Removing it while the file is open.

* style(traces): satisfy biome after the rebase onto main

Import ordering that main's biome pass now enforces, plus a dead
PutObjectCommand import the spool change left behind.

* style(traces): drop two dead imports and revert an unrelated generated file

The spool no longer writes through the S3 client, so PutObjectCommand is
unused in the service and in the event-log test that lost its putSpool
case. Also restores langySkills.generated.json to main — a regenerate
swept in by git add -A, unrelated to this change and unformatted.

* test(traces): flatten the spool suites to satisfy the new-violation gate

Each 'given' block is now its own top-level suite, operation-prefixed, so
none exceeds the per-function line cap the repo gates new code on. Same
16 assertions, same BDD nesting below the top level — this matches how
blob-store.event-log.unit.test.ts already organises its suites.

* fix(traces): confine spool path segments and drop the local destination

Two review findings on the spool change, both real.

**Path traversal.** Percent-encoding the id segments was not enough.
`LocalFilesystemDriver.parseFileUri` round-trips the URI through
`decodeURIComponent`, which turns `..%2F..%2F` straight back into
`../../` before `mkdir`/`writeFile` see it. `idSchema` accepts arbitrary
strings, so a span id of `../../…` resolved outside the object root —
reproduced at `/var/etc/evil/span-1`.

Ids outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` are now replaced by a hash of the id. A hash
cannot carry a separator whatever decodes it downstream, and it stays
deterministic, so the read and delete paths re-derive the same location.
Ordinary hex ids are untouched and stay legible in a bucket listing.

`LocalFilesystemDriver` additionally refuses any `file:` URI whose decoded
path is not already canonical. That is the backstop: a caller that
percent-encodes its segments is not protected by having done so, and this
makes the next such mistake fail loudly instead of writing outside the
root.

**No orphan bound on the local filesystem.** The spool deletes eagerly
after the event_log INSERT and leans on a lifecycle rule to reap what a
crash between those steps leaves behind. A filesystem cannot express one,
so an orphan there is permanent and the volume is what fills. The spool
now refuses a `file` destination and ingestion continues inline.

Not a regression: before this consumer moved onto the shared storage
layer it built an S3 client, which on a local install resolved to the
hardcoded `langwatch` bucket, so the write already failed and the same
fail-open path already ran. This makes it explicit.

Also names the concrete v1-removal marker (langwatch/langwatch-saas#837)
in place of "for one release", and states in ADR-022 that provisioning
the lifecycle rule is the operator's prerequisite for enabling the flag,
not something enabling it creates.

* test(traces): cover the spool against a real Azure account

Azurite is path-style only; production Azure is host-style, and the two
canonicalise differently in the SharedKey string-to-sign. A signature bug
on the host-style path produces a well-formed header that only real Azure
rejects, with a 403 the emulator can never produce — #6181 was bitten by
exactly that. The spool mints a deeper object path than any other caller,
which is the shape where such a bug hides.

Self-skips without LANGWATCH_TEST_AZURE_*, matching the sibling driver
suite, so CI is unaffected and anyone with an account gets the coverage.

Run against a real (now deleted) storage account: 4/4 pass. Independently
confirmed with `az storage blob list` that the object appears at
trace-blobs/spool/{project}/{trace}/{span} with the exact byte count and
is gone after the eager delete, and that a `../../` trace id lands as a
hash — five path segments, no `..`.

* fix(traces): fail the spool closed on Azure until retention is provisioned

Review follow-up. The local-filesystem refusal removed the unbounded-orphan
case there, but left the same case open on Azure: a crash between the spool
write and its delete is bounded only by a lifecycle rule, and nothing
required that rule to exist. An operator enabling the flag without creating
it accumulates trace payloads that outlive the documented 3 days — a
retention problem, not just storage growth.

`mintSpoolUri` now refuses an azure destination unless the deployment sets
AZURE_BLOB_SPOOL_RETENTION_CONFIRMED (chart:
app.dataplane.providers.azureBlob.spoolRetentionConfirmed). Default false, so
an Azure install that has not thought about retention degrades to inline
payloads rather than leaving objects nothing reaps. The error names the
policy to create and the setting to flip.

It asserts rather than verifies, deliberately. The policy is a
management-plane resource (Microsoft.Storage/.../managementPolicies) and this
deployment holds a data-plane key; checking it would mean requiring ARM
credentials, a subscription id and a resource group the feature otherwise has
no use for. The affirmation sits in the same config that turns the spool on,
and the default is the safe one.

S3 is deliberately not gated: its lifecycle requirement is the long-standing
ADR-022 rule that predates this change, so gating it would silently disable
the spool for every existing install. Covered by a test.

The flag is injected through SpoolStorage rather than read from env in
BlobStore, keeping that class env-free and testable; the composition root
owns the env read.

* fix(traces): bound the v1 spool read by the same cap as v2

The v2 read goes through `streamToBuffer(..., MAX_SPOOL_BYTES)`; the v1
compatibility read called `transformToByteArray()`, which buffers the whole
object before anything can check its size. So the cap documented as stopping
a tampered or corrupt object from OOM-ing the worker did not apply to the
one input it exists to distrust — an object written before this deploy.

Splitting the original read into a v1 and a v2 path is what introduced the
asymmetry; the cap went on the new path only. The legacy read now consumes
the SDK stream through the same helper, and the explicit no-body error is
preserved ahead of it.

Regression test covers an oversized legacy object. Confirmed it fails
without the fix.

* test(traces): match the coalescing stubs to the named getSpool signature

main added spanCommandCoalescing.unit.test.ts while this branch was open,
and its BlobStore stubs take the old positional `getSpool(ref: string)`.
This branch moved that call to a named object so the spool derives its
location from the command's own tenant and span ids, so the stub received
an object and `ref.slice(-16)` threw.

The behaviour under test is unchanged and still worth pinning — a spool is
deleted once per span after the single append, and a handler that throws
partway drops none of them. Only the stub shape moves, and the first one
now reads `spanId` directly instead of slicing it back out of the
reference, which is what the real call passes anyway.

Surfaced by CI's --changed run: the edit to env-create.mjs pulls a wide
module graph into scope, which is what reached this file.

* fix(traces): apply the spool destination guard on write only

Turning AZURE_BLOB_SPOOL_RETENTION_CONFIRMED back off — the documented
remediation, and what a chart rollback does — made every already-spooled
span unreadable and un-deletable: getSpool threw
SpoolDestinationUnsupportedError (and does not fail open, so the payload
was lost outright, the edge having already cleared the attributes), and
deleteSpool skipped the eager cleanup, manufacturing the exact orphan the
guard exists to prevent.

The guard is a rule about creating new objects, so it now runs only on
the write path. Reads and deletes of objects already out there are always
allowed.

* fix(storage): scope the file-URI containment check to '..' segments

The check asked whether the decoded path was already canonical, which is
a stricter question than whether it escapes. A storage root configured
with a trailing slash — accepted by both LANGWATCH_LOCAL_STORAGE_PATH and
the chart's app.storedObjects.localFilesystem.path — mints
file:///root//project/object, whose decoded form is non-canonical and
entirely harmless. That refusal broke every local-filesystem write on
those installs, dataset uploads and scenario media included, neither of
which this guard is about.

Only '..' escapes, so only '..' is refused; the path is still resolved
before use.

* docs(adr): record that the spool retention gate is write-path only

* test(traces): cover the retention-flip read and delete against real Azure

The write-only guard fix needs proof on the destination it is about, not
just against a fake object store: an object written with retention
confirmed must still read back and still be deleted once the assertion is
flipped off, and a NEW write must still be refused.

* test(traces): tag the spool suites' Azure credentials with the shared-key mode

main turned AzureBlobDriver's credentials into a discriminated union over the
auth mode, so a bare account name plus key no longer typechecks. Both spool
suites drive the emulator and a real account with a shared key, which is the
`sharedKey` arm.

feat(sdk): judge n-way target comparisons from the experiment SDKs (#6863)

* feat(sdk): judge n-way target comparisons from the experiment SDKs

Code-first experiments could run several targets over a row and score each
one on its own, but not ask the question that actually decides between them:
which of these is better? That verdict only existed inside the evaluations
workbench, behind the browser.

evaluation.compare() hands every target that recorded an output for the row
to the same judge the workbench uses, in one call, and returns a verdict
naming the winner. Two candidates or twenty is the same call.

The verdict's five statuses stay distinct, because collapsing them is how a
comparison starts lying: a tie is a measurement, an inconclusive row is the
absence of one, and an error is not a finding about the candidates at all.
Neither a thin row nor an unreachable judge raises, so one bad row never ends
a loop over a thousand.

The SDK never restates a server default. An option left unset is absent from
the request, which is what lets the judge pick the right one of its four
adaptive prompts per row, and the SDKs ship no copy of any judge prompt. A
test parses the judge's own source and byte-compares all four against the
config form's copies so they cannot drift.

No server or storage change was needed: the batch protocol already carries a
row-level evaluation, and the results page already renders one. CSV export
now carries the verdict too.

Also fixes three pre-existing bugs that dogfooding surfaced, all of which
affect the workbench as well:

- The judge explained its verdict in slot letters the reader had no key for.
  The reasoning is now translated with the same mapping the winner is, per
  judge pass, since swap-and-reconcile reverses the slot order between them.
- langevals judges send a forced function tool with no reasoning_effort,
  which gpt-5.6-sol and -luna reject. The project default openai/latest
  expands to gpt-5.6-sol, so the Comparison judge failed on every row for
  those orgs.
- An inconclusive row lost the cost of the two judge calls it paid for.

And one unrelated red test: three published recipes were missing from the
docs skills manifest.

* fix(sdk): keep a comparison row numeric, and bound the judge call

Review follow-ups on the n-way comparison work. Every finding was valid.

The comparison row key is a number again. `ComparisonOptions.index` accepted
`number | string`, but the server validates `evaluations[].index` as
`z.number()` and parses the body before dispatch, so a string row label failed
validation and took the whole batch down with it, the row's dataset entries
included. Narrowing matches Python, which already coerced and raised.

The evaluator fetch now carries a timeout. A judge that accepted the socket
and never answered held its slot in the concurrency window for the life of the
process, so one dead connection stalled a run rather than costing it one row.
The ceiling matches the one the Python SDK already applies to that endpoint.

`_current_trace_id()` pads to 32 hex characters like every other trace id in
that file. Roughly one trace in 256 starts with a zero byte, and an unpadded
id for one of those stopped joining its evaluation to its dataset entry.

The async litellm wrapper is covered. Awaiting is what makes translating a
provider rejection possible, and every test drove the blocking wrapper.

Documentation corrections, all verified against the code rather than assumed:

- A comparison weighs every candidate together, and the judge is called twice
  per row by default, not once. The workbench page claimed one call and half
  the cost of swap-and-confirm; `swap_and_reconcile` defaults to true and the
  config form never writes it, so that was wrong there too.
- Candidate shuffling is the default, not the only behaviour.
- The CSV winner column reads `unresolved` only when the judge's answer
  matches none of the candidates it was shown. A winner naming a target the
  run no longer lists is written under its own name.
- `npx langwatch report` scrubs the title, summary and transcript by pattern.
  It does not redact everything: an address passed with `--email` is spliced
  in after the redactor runs, and only IPv4 is scanned.

Also: the comparison test suite is split along behaviour lines and under the
file-size rule, the compatibility spec describes what a person observes
instead of request internals, and the eviction test stopped opening four
thousand real spans to prove one bound.

* docs(sdk): say what the comparison judge and the login flow actually do

Second round of review on the n-way comparison SDK. Every finding was a
sentence that claimed more, or less, than the code does.

What a candidate is. "Recorded an output" was missing the condition all
three layers agree on: Python gates on a truthy output, TypeScript returns
early on an empty string, and the judge itself filters candidates without
one. The page now says non-empty everywhere it describes a candidate.

What the CSV winner column can hold. It listed three values and there are
four: a processed verdict whose winner resolves to no candidate position
exports `unresolved`.

That shuffling is a default. `randomize_order` can be turned off, and then
the judge sees candidates in the order their targets were registered.

That an unsettled row is a third outcome. The workbench page described only
wins and ties. A row whose two passes disagree is neither: the reconcile
step returns no winner, the row never becomes a processed verdict, and it
lands on no bar of the win-rate chart. Saying it is a tie would claim the
candidates are equally good, which is the one thing that run did not
establish. The module docstring made exactly that claim and now agrees with
its own code.

That a custom judge prompt exists. "No judge prompt to choose" read as
though there was nothing to choose from.

How to log in without leaking the key. The setup guide warned against
putting a secret in argv and then recommended `login --api-key <key>`.
Plain `langwatch login` never touches the terminal with a credential: you
pick the project on the browser approval page and its key comes back over
the same channel. That is now the local path, `--api-key` is described as
what it is, the way automation writes a key it already holds, and the
`--endpoint` note says it pins the CLI while the instrumented app still
reads the environment. One clause of the original warning went too: a key
typed at an application prompt does not reach the shell history file.

Also here: the IPv6 comment in the session-report redaction claimed
coverage that does not exist (there is no IPv6 pattern; a mapped address
merely loses its dotted-quad tail to the IPv4 one), the comparison test
suites now share one lifecycle helper instead of six copies, the logged
`index` fixture is numeric like the wire contract it stands in for, and a
login comment claimed the endpoint environment variable skips a prompt that
only the flag skips.

* fix(cli): stop telling people a login mints them a new project key

`langwatch login` in project mode never creates a key. It returns the
existing `Project.apiKey` of whichever project you pick, verbatim, and the
server comment and an integration test both already said so. Every surface
a user sees said the opposite.

The approval page offered a "Generate API key" button under the heading
"Generate an SDK key", and on success announced "A fresh project API key
has been minted for X". The CLI agreed, printing "API key generated for
project X". The CLI guide said the mode "mints a fresh project API key",
`login --project` advertised itself the same way, and the requirement the
whole flow was built from was written that way too, which is where the copy
came from.

That is worth more than a wording nit. A reader who believes a fresh key
was minted has no reason to think the key now in their `.env` is the same
one their teammates and CI are already using, and every reason to think the
old one was rotated out from under them.

Now the page reads "Connect a project to the CLI", the button says "Send
API key", and the confirmation says the key is in your terminal. The CLI
says "Connected to project X", one line above where it already reports
saving to `.env`.

Checked for a path where a key really is created and there is none:
`Project.apiKey` is non-nullable, so there is no lazy-create case, and
`generateApiKey()` is reachable only from project creation and the
regenerate mutation in settings. The device-session mode does mint a
personal virtual key, so its wording is untouched.

* fix(sdk): keep a concurrent row's comparison on its own row

`Experiment` kept the current trace id and row index on mutable instance
fields while `run()` dispatched iterations concurrently against them. That
is a race, and `compare()` read both.

The window is narrow but certain. `evaluationUsesTargets` is a run-wide
latch flipped by the first `withTarget()` call, so row 0 is the only
iteration that takes the branch writing `currentTraceId`, and it holds that
value until its callback returns. Every row that compares inside that window
sent row 0's trace to the judge and persisted it on the verdict. The row
index was worse: a `compare()` with no iteration context fell back to
whichever row the experiment last touched, so a background caller got a
confident verdict about a row it never asked about instead of the error it
should have got.

Neither field is needed. `IterationContext` is already an AsyncLocalStorage
object that exists, by its own comment, to prevent exactly this, so the
trace id rides there and both instance fields are gone rather than guarded.

In targets mode the row's trace id is null on purpose. Each `withTarget()`
opens its own root trace, so a row genuinely has no single trace, and naming
one would file the verdict against a trace that judged something else. A
verdict on the wrong trace is worse than a verdict on none: opened from the
results page it shows another row's run, so it reads as evidence about
candidates the judge never saw.

Three tests, and the last two are what make the first worth anything. The
first drives four rows at concurrency 4 and holds row 0 open on a deferred
until the others have compared, so the window is deterministic rather than
hoped for; it installs a real tracer, since under the no-op tracer every row
reports the same all-zero trace and a misattributed verdict is
indistinguishable from a correct one. The second pins that the row which
does own a trace keeps it, because dropping every trace id would satisfy the
first while destroying what it protects. The third covers the index, and
asserts the background caller gets `ComparisonError`.

Reverting the implementation and keeping the tests fails the first and
third, which is the evidence that they test the bug rather than the fix.

* docs(cli): correct five claims the login and comparison docs still overstated

Review round three. Each of these said something the code does not do.

The approval page announced delivery before it had happened. Approving only
records the approval; the key reaches the terminal on the CLI's next poll,
and the CLI writes `.env` after that. The card could render before any of it,
so "is now in your terminal" and "your .env is updated" were both claims
about the future. It now says the key is on its way and the CLI will save it.

`--project` advertised only half of itself. With a slug it authenticates
through an existing device login and opens no browser at all; only the bare
flag shows the picker. The help text describes both.

`_reconcile` still promised a tie. The module docstring and the caller had
already been corrected to say a swap disagreement leaves the row with no
winner, but the function's own docstring, sitting directly above the code
that argues at length why a tie would be wrong, still said the opposite.

The setup guide told you to keep the key off the command line and then put
it there. Its own automation example expanded a secret into `--api-key`. The
environment variable is the answer for a runner, and it is the whole of the
setup: every command resolves the key from the environment, so there is no
`login` call to make. `--api-key` stays, described honestly for the case
where something downstream needs the key on disk, next to the way to write
that file with nothing in argv at all.

Two scenario titles were written in internals. A reader of a feature file
should not need to know what a device-code poll or a first-trace watcher is,
and the second scenario's own Then steps already said the observable thing.
Both `@scenario` annotations moved with their titles.

* test(cli): prove the daemon serves commands at once without timing it

The concurrency test dispatched five commands scripted at 20ms each and
asserted the batch finished in under 100ms. Serialised, those five would
take at least 100ms, so the bound sat exactly on the floor it was trying to
clear with nothing left over for socket, dispatch and event-loop overhead.
It was therefore asserting an idle machine as much as a concurrent daemon,
and it failed twice in four full-suite runs under load, once at 144ms.

Widening the number would only move the load level at which it lies. The
commands now meet at a rendezvous instead: none emits its output or its exit
code until all five are inside the daemon at the same moment. A daemon
serving them one at a time never gets past the first, which waits on four
peers that cannot arrive until it returns, so concurrency is what lets the
test finish at all and the clock decides nothing.

Verified by falsification, since a test that can only pass is worth nothing:
dispatching the five sequentially instead of together makes it fail on the
15s timeout. The diagnosis is the first line of the test body, because a
bare "test timed out" is otherwise the only thing vitest prints.

The per-command assertions are unchanged, and `cancel` is load-bearing now:
whatever is still waiting at the rendezvous has to settle its caller when
the daemon gives up on it, or a failing run hangs in teardown.

Ten consecutive runs pass, as do four copies of the file running at once,
which is the condition that broke the old bound.

* test(sdk): count the comparisons a concurrency check actually compared

The attribution check dropped every entry whose trace id was empty before
comparing anything, and in that run three of the four rows have no row-level
trace, so it compared one entry per side and reported a clean result. A
regression that blanked every trace id would have passed it.

Instrumenting the real run showed exactly that: three entries per side
carrying `""` and one carrying row 0's trace. The count is now part of the
assertion, so "no mismatches" means something. It is one per side rather
than four because the switch to target-rooted traces is a run-wide latch:
only the row that runs before any `withTarget()` call gets an iteration
span. Giving every row its own trace raises the number, which is a change to
make here deliberately rather than discover as a still-passing test.

Falsified three ways by blanking every trace id in the implementation: the
new check fails, the old one passes, and the sibling test that pins the
traced row fails under both. That last one is why the suite was never
entirely vacuous, only weaker than it looked.

Also here, three claims that were wider than the code: `--project` without a
slug needs an interactive terminal and exits 1 in a non-TTY; appending
`LANGWATCH_API_KEY` to `.env` from a shell can leave two lines and an
ambiguous credential, where `login --api-key` rewrites the existing one; and
no flag answers prompts globally. `-o json` picks an output format, so the
troubleshooting row now names the flag each command actually takes, from
`--force` on `prompt tag delete` to `--force-local` on `prompt push`.

* fix(ui): close expanded cells and the image lightbox on Escape

Every expandable cell in the batch results table opens its full content in
a Portal over a fixed, full-viewport backdrop, and every one of them was
wired to close on a backdrop click and nothing else. Escape did nothing.

That is more than a missing keyboard shortcut. The backdrop stays in the
DOM and keeps intercepting pointer events, so pressing Escape leaves the
reader with a page that looks dismissed and is not: the toolbar above the
table, the run selector, the column controls all stop responding until
they happen to click somewhere the backdrop is, which is the one gesture
they just decided against. The comparison verdict cell even prints "click
outside to close", so the overlay is self-describing, but Escape is what a
reader tries first and its failure is silent.

Adds useEscapeKey, which attaches a document keydown listener only while
the overlay is open and removes it on unmount, and wires it into every
overlay built this way: all three cells of the results table (the
comparison verdict, the target output and the dataset value), the
workbench target cell the read-only one is copied from, and the expandable
image lightbox, which is the surface where the expectation is strongest
and the trap most complete, since it fills the screen. One overlay
answering Escape while the one beside it ignores it would be worse than
the original behaviour.

The verdict cell's hint now names both ways out.

* fix(comparison): keep the winner's tally and the judge's letters readable

Two defects found by dogfooding the results page for a screenshot. Both take
the thing the reader came for and drop it.

The win-rate chart hid the number it exists to show. Its axis tops out at the
highest tally, so the leading bar reaches the top of the plot area exactly and
the count drawn above it lands outside the chart and is clipped. On a run of
4, 0 and 3 wins the "3" appeared over the short bar and the winner's "4"
appeared nowhere, and since the leader is always the bar that touches the top,
it is always the leader's number that goes. The room is reserved as a fixed
strip rather than by padding the axis, because headroom measured in wins is
worth fewer pixels the higher the tally climbs, which would lose the label
again on a long run.

The judge kept explaining itself in slot letters after a preposition.
Candidates are shown to it as anonymized slots and the reasoning is translated
back, but the words after which a bare capital cannot be an article were only
verbs and "than", so "compared with A (too brief)" came through untouched.
That was 3 of the 7 decided rows on a ten-row run, in prose a customer reads.
The comparison prepositions join the list. Title case is still left alone,
which is what makes them safe to add: a capitalized article turns up there and
nowhere else.

A bare letter opening a sentence can still survive, because "A incorrectly
introduces an unrelated vendor" and "A concise answer wins" are told apart
only by grammar this translation deliberately does not attempt. Leaving a
letter standing stays the better failure: it is unhelpful, where a wrong
substitution is a sentence that says something the judge did not.

* fix(evaluations): carry the judge cost of a row that reached no verdict

The claim that an inconclusive row no longer reports as free was only half
true. langevals was fixed to carry the spend, and the platform threw it away
again on the way out: `handleEvaluatorCall` rebuilds the response field by
field, and the skipped branch named only status and details. So every row
whose two judge passes disagreed, the most expensive kind of row there is
because both calls were made and billed before they were found to disagree,
still landed in the experiment with a null cost.

Found by reading the column rather than the code. A ten-row dogfood run
stored a cost on each of its three decided rows and null on all seven
inconclusive ones, which is what sent me looking for the hop that drops it.
The path was otherwise already correct end to end: the batch schema, the
projection and the SDK all carry cost independently of status.

The same gate existed on the workbench path, where the orchestrator only
recorded a cost when the status was "processed". Both now record it for
anything that is not an error, so a comparison costs the same whether it was
judged from the SDK or from the browser. A row that declined before calling
the judge still reports no cost, which is different from reporting zero.

Billing was never affected: the Cost row is written for every status, so the
money was always charged and only the experiment's own view of it was wrong.

Verified against three running processes rather than by reading: langevals
returns the cost on a skipped result, the platform route dropped it before
the fix and carries it after, and a real log_results POST lands it in
EvaluationCost. Both fixes were falsified by reverting them and watching the
new tests fail.

* fix(evaluators): ask the judge to name candidates instead of writing bare letters

Translating slot letters back into candidate names after the fact can only go
so far. A bare "A" is also the English article, so the translation rewrites it
only where the surrounding words rule the article out, and the word after it
comes from an open vocabulary: "A strikes the best balance" reads exactly like
"A concise answer wins" to any list of followers. On a real ten-row run four of
the seven decided rows shipped reasoning with a letter still standing.

So stop producing the ambiguous form. The judge is now told to write "Candidate
A" rather than "A", which the translation already resolves unconditionally, and
the guard stays as the fallback for whatever still gets through.

The instruction goes in the system message, not in the four prompt templates.
`settings.prompt` is a documented escape hatch, and a hand-tuned prompt still
gets anonymized slots, so the rule that makes them readable cannot be something
a user can delete. The system message is also where the existing rule of the
same species lives, the one telling the judge to ignore presentation order, and
it has no mirrors, where each template is copied into the config form and two
generated catalogs.

The sentence ends by exempting the winner field, which takes the bare label
through a tool-call enum whose out-of-enum fallback silently awards the row to
slot A. A blanket "never write a bare letter" could have corrupted every
verdict, so a test pins that exemption.

Measured on live gpt-5-mini output rather than assumed: over 24 rows the rule
took responses containing a bare letter from 24 to 9 and bare letter tokens
from 53 to 11, at the cost of about 11% longer reasoning. Saying it a second
time on the reasoning field was tried and dropped: compliance moved within
noise while reasoning grew by a third, because a judge told twice starts
enumerating every candidate. Both the measurement and the decision not to
repeat it are pinned by tests.

Some bare letters still reach the reader, and the spec now says so instead of
implying the translation is complete. Leaving a letter standing beats
corrupting a sentence.

* docs(evaluations): list the setting that doubles the judge cost per row

The workbench settings table omitted swap_and_reconcile, so a reader who
checks the table rather than the prose above it never learns that the judge
runs twice per row by default.

fix(charts): stop the install notes reading cluster-scoped resources (#6842)

* fix(charts): stop the install notes reading cluster-scoped resources

A customer upgrade failed outright because the Langy install notes list
the cluster's RuntimeClasses to offer an optional hardening tip:

  Error: UPGRADE FAILED: template: langwatch/templates/NOTES.txt:102:11:
  ... error calling lookup: runtimeclasses.node.k8s.io is forbidden: User
  "..." cannot list resource "runtimeclasses" in API group "node.k8s.io"
  at the cluster scope

Helm swallows only NotFound from `lookup`; a 403 comes back as a template
error, and a Go template cannot recover from it. So advice printed after
the install has already succeeded was able to take the whole upgrade down
for any operator whose RBAC stops at their own namespace.

Nothing about their cluster was unsupported. Langy has not required a
sandboxed runtime since the defaults became an empty runtimeClassName with
acceptUnsandboxedRuntime=true; only the hint needed the permission.

- NOTES.txt prints `kubectl get runtimeclass` for the operator to run
  instead of listing the classes itself. Same guidance, no permission.
- The Langy secret guard probed cluster visibility by reading kube-system,
  a cluster-scoped read with the same failure mode. It now reads the
  release namespace's own default ServiceAccount, which asks for nothing
  the Secret lookup beside it does not already need. Trade-off recorded in
  the template: with --create-namespace on a first install the probe finds
  nothing and the guard stays silent, degrading to the pre-guard
  CreateContainerConfigError rather than blocking a correct install.
- tests/restricted-rbac.sh fails the build on any cluster-scoped lookup,
  and on any lookup at all in NOTES.txt. This has to be a static check:
  every `helm template` in the matrix renders with no cluster behind it, so
  a forbidden lookup returns empty there and the branch is simply skipped.
  The bug was invisible to a fully green CI.

Also corrects a stale scenario claiming a default install leaves the pod
Pending on a cluster with no RuntimeClass. It does not — that only happens
once an operator has chosen to pin one.

* fix(charts): match the lookup CALL, not the word

The NOTES rule grepped for 'lookup ', which the template comment
explaining why the rule exists matched on 'every lookup returns empty'.
Every real call names its apiVersion as a string literal, so 'lookup "'
separates the call from prose about it. Caught by the gate on its own
first run.

* fix(charts): make the rbac guard fail when it scans nothing

Two review findings on the guard itself.

The corpus was never asserted. GNU xargs, which is what CI runs, executes
grep even on empty input; with no file operands grep reads the drained
stdin, finds nothing and succeeds. So any breakage that emptied the file
list — the script moving, a templates/ rename, the wrong cwd — turned the
gate into a green tick that checked nothing. It now anchors on the file
the rule exists for and fails loudly instead. Dropping 2>/dev/null on the
greps stops a genuine grep error being swallowed the same way.

The helper comment also overstated its case: ServiceAccount and Secret are
different resources, so a role could grant one and refuse the other. The
claim that matters is narrower and still holds — the read is namespaced,
and no RBAC reachable by a namespace-scoped installer makes a
cluster-scoped read succeed.

* docs(specs): claim only what the notes test actually proves

The scenario asserted two things and the test enforced one. Enforcing the
second means grepping the notes for the command's own text, which passes
by finding a string we wrote rather than by testing behaviour. Dropping
the Then is better than leaving one unenforced inside a scenario the
parity checker reports as bound; the intent stays as rationale.

* fix(charts): address review — drop the secret probe, harden the scan

_helpers.tpl: the ServiceAccount probe traded a cluster-scoped read for a

mechanism kept as rationale.

* test(charts): prove langyagent.chartManaged=false removes Langy completely

The opt-out is documented as a single values key, and it is the escape
hatch we point locked-down clusters at, so it has to be genuinely single.
Nothing asserted that before: lint-template only proved the disabled
overlay renders, not that anything was actually removed.

Asserts all four surfaces, because nothing links them. The subchart goes
via a Chart.yaml condition; the app's and workers' references are separate
if-guards in the umbrella chart, each its own edit and each forgettable on
its own while the Deployment correctly vanishes and the render stays green.
So: no langyagent objects, no OPENCODE_AGENT_URL, no forced rollout flag,
no LANGY_INTERNAL_SECRET key — with enabled-side negative controls, since a
failed render arrives as a string that would satisfy every absence check.

Verified it fails: dropping one umbrella guard to 'if true' is caught.

* fix(charts): propagate template-discovery failure in the rbac guard

Feeding the loop with `done <<< "$(templates)"` discarded find's exit
status, so a discovery that failed part-way still fed the loop whatever it
had reached and the scan succeeded over a partial corpus. The anchor check
does not cover this: it catches a corpus that is empty, not one that
quietly lost a subtree — and a skipped subtree is exactly where an
unreviewed lookup would sit.

Capture the status first and exit 2 on failure. Verified with an

* docs: correct the missing-RuntimeClass failure mode and the sandbox default

A pinned RuntimeClass the cluster does not define does not leave the pod
Pending. Kubernetes' RuntimeClass admission plugin refuses to create the pod
at all (`pod rejected: RuntimeClass "..." not found`), so no pod object
exists and `kubectl get pods` lists nothing — which reads like the install
skipped Langy rather than like a failure. NOTES.txt has said this correctly
since #6106; the spec scenario and the langyagent README both contradicted it.

The README also claimed the default pins the pod to gvisor. It has not: both
charts ship runtimeClassName empty with acceptUnsandboxedRuntime true, so
Langy installs and runs on any cluster. Stating the opposite is what makes
operators on locked-down clusters believe the assistant is closed to them.

The notes replaced a cluster-scoped `lookup` with `kubectl get runtimeclass`
for the operator to run. That command needs the same cluster-scoped read the
lookup did, so the operators this fix is for may well be denied it as well.
The difference that matters is that a denial in their own terminal costs them
nothing, and the notes never said so — leaving them at a Forbidden error with
no idea whether the install is fine. It is. Say that.

fix(aigateway): repoint controlPlaneRoot after ADR-076, and make the skip-guard unfakeable (#6898)

* fix(aigateway): repoint controlPlaneRoot after ADR-076, and make the skip-guard unfakeable

Fixes https://github.com/langwatch/langwatch/issues/6895 — main is red at tip
with five controlplane contract failures.

Chain, not a single cause:

1. #6405 (2bbeb7dd2, ADR-076) renamed langwatch/ -> platform/app/.
   controlPlaneRoot was not moved with it.
2. readControlPlaneSource skipped rather than failed when the directory was
   absent, so every run for eight days skipped silently and the stale constant
   stayed invisible.
3. #5748 (a5784bedb) added one misplaced test file under the old path,
   re-creating langwatch/src/server. The os.Stat sentinel flipped to "found",
   the tests stopped skipping, and the dormant breakage went live as five hard
   failures.

The constant is repointed to platform/app. That alone would restore green and
leave the same trap armed for the next rename, so the guard is rebuilt too.

The class fix is that both witnesses are IDENTITIES, not directories. A
directory is re-created by any stray file, which is exactly what happened. Skip
now requires BOTH to be absent: the pnpm workspace manifest at the repo root,
and a package.json at controlPlaneRoot whose parsed name is @langwatch/web.
Either one alone runs the tests.

The ambiguous case fails, it does not skip. A workspace present without the
control plane under it -- the precise shape of the ADR-076 rename -- is now a
hard failure that names the stale constant. A false red costs one path edit; a
false green costs an unenforced cross-language contract nobody is watching.

Not in this commit, deliberately: the misplaced test file from step 3 is left
where it is. It is dead code (langwatch/ is not in pnpm-workspace.yaml, so it
runs nowhere), and moving it would activate a ClickHouse integration test that
has never executed anywhere, which is a separate risk that does not belong in a
main-is-red fix. The new guard is unaffected by the stray tree -- verified
below. Tracked in https://github.com/langwatch/langwatch/issues/6895.

Verification, run with the stray tree present, i.e. the state this lands in:

  go test -count=1 -v ./services/aigateway/adapters/controlplane/...
    all five named tests RUN and PASS, no --- SKIP

  Mutation, constant reverted to langwatch/ and nothing else changed:
    --- FAIL: TestControlPlaneSchemaAgreesOnTheWireShape
        this checkout carries the monorepo (pnpm-workspace.yaml is at the repo
        root) but ../../../../langwatch holds no @langwatch/web package
        manifest: the control plane moved and controlPlaneRoot did not move
        with it. Repoint controlPlaneRoot.
    Restored -> green again.

  Old guard, langwatch/src/server present as an EMPTY dir -> passes the old
  os.Stat sentinel, proving a bare directory was never a witness.

* test(aigateway): cover the control-plane guard's own branch logic

The guard added in the previous commit decides whether the five
cross-language contract tests run, skip, or fail. Nothing tested that
decision. It is the same trap class the guard exists to close: a branch
that skips where it should fail is invisible in a green CI run.

Split the decision out as a pure controlPlaneVerdict(root) returning
ok/skip/fatal plus a reason, with requireControlPlane reduced to a thin
wrapper over dispatchControlPlaneVerdict. Observable behaviour of the
five existing tests is unchanged; they still run, not skip.

Adds an 11-row t.TempDir() table over the verdict and a 3-row dispatch
table over the verdict-to-action mapping, including the ADR-076 shape
(workspace present, control plane gone) and the bare-empty-directory
case that defeated the original sentinel.

One deliberate behaviour change: a package.json that is present but
malformed, unreadable, or naming another package is now fatal
regardless of whether the workspace manifest is around. It previously
skipped in the no-workspace case. A present-but-broken witness is drift,
not the signature of a checkout with no TypeScript side; a Go-only
vendored tree carries no platform/app/package.json at all and still
skips.

Evidence, re-run independently before landing rather than taken from the
implementing agent's report: restoring the old bare-directory sentinel
inside the verdict leaves all five existing contract tests green (ok,
exit 0) while the new table fails on 7 rows. That is the whole argument
for this commit, demonstrated. gofmt and go vet clean; full package
green.

Closes the review thread on #6898.

* fix(aigateway): fail when the workspace witness will not stat

controlPlaneVerdict consults two witnesses and treated them
asymmetrically. The package.json witness already distinguished absent
from unreadable:

    case !errors.Is(readErr, fs.ErrNotExist): -> fatal

The pnpm-workspace.yaml witness did not. It tested only `err == nil`
and fell through to controlPlaneSkip, so EACCES, EIO or ELOOP on that
path read as "no TypeScript side in this checkout" and silently skipped
the five contract tests.

That is the same trap class this file exists to close, and it
contradicted the file's own stated contract: skipping requires BOTH
witnesses to be absent. An unreadable witness is present, not absent, so
the premise for skipping was never established.

The workspace witness is now exactly as strict as the manifest witness.
Present -> fatal and genuinely-absent -> skip are unchanged.

Covered by a twelfth row in the verdict table, using a self-referential
symlink so os.Stat fails with ELOOP rather than ENOENT. That fixture is
deterministic and, like the directory-as-manifest fixture beside it,
holds when the suite runs as root, which a permission bit does not.

Reproduced here rather than taken on report: with the new branch
disabled (case !errors.Is(statErr, fs.ErrNotExist) -> case false), the
new row is the ONLY failure in the package while all five pre-existing
contract tests still pass. The existing suite is blind to this defect.

Also clears the six golangci-lint findings the previous commit
introduced: gosec G301 on two MkdirAll calls (0o755 -> 0o750), G306 on
WriteFile (0o644 -> 0o600), and three misspell hits. Both CI lint steps
were run locally with CI's pinned v2.11.4 and its verbatim args:
0 issues each.

fix(release): a pin no longer exempts a break from the scope guard (#6919)

* fix(release): a pin no longer exempts a break from the scope guard

release-scope-guard used to accept a multi-component breaking pull request
as long as the extra components were pinned. #4998 showed that exemption
was unsound in two independent ways.

A pin overrides the version and nothing else. Even when it applies, the
other component's note still lands in the pinned component's changelog, so
the Go SDK's two breaks were filed under the platform's release while the
platform sat at its pinned version.

And squash is this repository's only merge method. The per-component pin
commits the old procedure asked for collapse into one commit carrying every
footer and touching every path, so at most one pin survives. Only the
sdks/go pin applied; the platform went to 4.0.0, release pull request #6787
stalled on a major nobody wanted, and the #6842 Helm chart fix waited behind
it because the chart ships from the app release train.

So the guard now fails a breaking marker that spans components, pins or no
pins. Pins are still read and still reported — they remain the right tool
for a version release-please got wrong — but they no longer exempt. The
multi-component-major label stays as the deliberate override.

This is stricter, and worth naming: a stacked branch that inherits a marker
from its base, which is what motivated pin detection in #6656, now has to
split the incidental part into its own non-breaking pull request or take the
label. Splitting is the only thing that keeps one component's break out of
another's release entirely, so that is what the guard now asks for.

specs/ci/breaking-change-scope.feature covers the rule, with the #4998 replay
bound to it. Binding needed .github/scripts as a feature-parity test root:
CI guards run under `node --test` from the workflow that uses them, and
their tests live beside them, so scenarios about what a guard refuses could
otherwise only ever be @unimplemented.

* docs(release): state only what the squash collapse is proven to have done

Both breaking-change footers sit mid-message too and release-please did read
those, so a trailing-block-only rule cannot be the explanation. What is
established: the squash left two competing pins in one 402-line body, and
the platform's did not apply — it released 4.0.0 rather than the 3.13.0 it
asked for. One message cannot carry one pin per component however the parser
resolves that, which is what one-pin-per-pull-request follows from.

* fix(release): address review on the scope-guard change

Name the noun in "the platform pin did not apply", across the guard
comment, the replay test comment and both places in RELEASES.md. The
elided form read as a sentence fragment.

Restate the incidental-file scenario as behaviour rather than layout. It
named the specs directory, which is where the root package's exclude-paths
happen not to reach today; what it actually pins is that one incidental
file in another component widens the scope and fails the check. The
directory detail stays in the test comment, which is where it belongs, and
the @scenario binding follows the new title.

fix(event-sourcing): confirm worker deaths before parking a group (#6922)

* fix(event-sourcing): confirm worker deaths before parking a group

The poison guard inferred a worker death from the absence of a Redis
delete: processWithRetries INCR'd a per-group strike before decode and
deleted it on every path where the process survived, so a surviving
strike WAS the death signal.

That inference is only sound if the delete is guaranteed, and it is not.
It is issued fire-and-forget, and process.exit(0) discards whatever Redis
has not yet read. Production parked roughly ten healthy groups a day that
way, accelerating (4 -> 6 -> 10 over three days), 81% of them on one
high-fan-out subscriber. None of them were poisoned: the parks sat hours
from the nearest deploy, on pods with zero restarts and peak memory well
inside the limit, for jobs whose p99 is 25ms and which had never retried.
Every operator unblock worked first time, because nothing was wrong with
the group — the guard was the only thing wrong.

Evidence is positive now. A claim marker names the process holding it;
each consumer publishes an `alive` beacon on a heartbeat and overwrites
it with a `retired` tombstone on graceful shutdown. A leftover marker is
booked as a death only when its owner is in neither state. A live owner,
a retired owner, and a worker re-claiming its own lapsed lease are all
ordinary and count for nothing, so a dropped release, a torn-down
connection and an abandoned drain can no longer park a healthy group. A
pod the job actually killed still has no beacon, so a genuine poison
group parks in the same number of laps as before.

This also removes what the old signal needed to stay honest: the
in-flight strike set, the shutdown sweep over it, and the post-claim
recheck guarding the race between the two. One tombstone answers for
every claim a worker holds, however the drain ends.

Also fixes the park path leaving its own marker at the threshold, which
made an unblock inside the marker's hour re-park the group on its very
next claim — so whether the operator's click worked depended on how long
they took to press it.

* fix(event-sourcing): close the beacon-arming race, bind the new scenarios

Three follow-ups found by re-auditing the diff and by CI's feature-parity gate.

close() may run while the constructor is still awaiting its FIRST beacon
publish. It then finds no timer to stop and writes the tombstone, and the
constructor arms the refresh interval afterwards — putting an `alive`
write after the retirement, which expires into exactly the false death
the tombstone exists to prevent. The beacon setup now returns without
arming if a shutdown began while it was publishing. Its test fails
against the unguarded version.

The new scenarios were tagged @integration/@unit but three of them bound
nothing: a `@scenario` annotation only binds from a SINGLE-LINE JSDoc
directly above the `it(` — the proximity scan stops at the `*/` of a
multi-line block. Rewrote the one that had prose above the tag, and wrote
the two scenarios that had no test at all: a vanished owner booking one
death and accumulating to the threshold, and the tombstone outliving the
marker it answers for.

Removed the spec from LEGACY_INERT now that it enforces its scenarios;
the checker fails a file that is on the list but no longer inert.

* fix(event-sourcing): address review on the poison-guard rewrite

Two findings were real defects, both in the new code.

A worker whose beacon write failed still stamped claim markers with its own
id. `publish()` swallows the error, so `livenessReady` resolved either way,
and every peer inheriting one of those markers would find an owner with no
beacon and book a death — the same false-park class this PR removes, entered
through the beacon write instead of the release. The guard now stands down
while the beacon is unconfirmed and resumes when a refresh lands: a real
death goes uncounted, which is the cheap direction to be wrong in, rather
than a healthy group being parked, which is the expensive one.

`recordClaim` passed numKeys=0, so ioredis had no key to route a cluster
EVAL by and would send it to an arbitrary node, where the derived claim and
beacon accesses can fall outside the slot that node owns. Every sibling
script passes its keys (3 to 8 of them); this one is now consistent, with
the claim marker as KEYS[1] and the beacon still derived from the
same-hash-tag prefix.

Also from review: hoisted the threshold to a read-once construction field
beside the other two guards' thresholds, so it is no longer re-parsed from
the environment on every job in the fastq hot path; renamed
DEFAULT_CLAIM_STRIKE_THRESHOLD to DEFAULT_CONFIRMED_DEATH_THRESHOLD to match
what it now counts, leaving the env var and the Prometheus label alone as
deploy and dashboard contracts; renamed the one scenario still saying
"poison strike" while its steps said "death"; and moved the duplicated
claim-marker fixture into a shared module that seeds the production TTL, so
the two suites cannot drift from CLAIM_GUARD_LUA or from each other.

Fixing the beaconless case surfaced a mock leak: this suite spies on
GroupStagingScripts.prototype but never restored, so a broken collaborator
escaped into whichever test ran next. afterEach restores now.

* docs(specs): describe the beacon-failure scenario by its outcome

The scenario named the liveness beacon, Redis and the claim marker, which
is how the guard is built rather than what an operator observes. Restated
as a worker temporarily unable to report itself as running, with the
matching annotation updated in the same commit.

* fix(event-sourcing): release a claim marker only when still its owner

Adversarial review found a real bug in the release path.

The release was an unconditional DEL keyed by group alone. Heartbeat
failures are warn-and-continue, so a worker paused or partitioned past the
active-key TTL keeps executing while its group is redispatched to someone
else. When its job finally returned, the release deleted the NEW owner's
marker — erasing the owner AND the accrued death count. A genuinely
poisoned group therefore lost its progress toward the threshold and parked
later than it should: with no marker left, the next claim finds no previous
owner to check and books no death at all.

Same shape as releasing a Redlock you no longer hold, and the same fix:
compare-and-delete, with the worker id threaded through. The release is now
`releaseClaim({groupId, workerId})`; the unconditional delete survives as
`discardClaim`, used only by the park, where the group leaves the dispatch
path and a surviving marker would re-park it on the operator's next
unblock. Its test fails against the blind delete.

Two claims in the doc block were too strong, and are now stated with their
limits. "Nothing healthy parks" holds against every failure of our own
writes, but not against Redis being gone: an outage longer than the beacon
TTL expires healthy beacons, and a handoff claimed after recovery but
before the previous owner's next refresh reads as a death. "The same number
of laps" is about crash-loops — a hang overlapped by a routine SIGTERM is
deliberately not counted, because the tombstone lands before the platform's
SIGKILL and hangs belong to the exhausted-retries path.

Detection also rests on an inequality between constants in two modules: a
dead worker's beacon must expire before its group can be redispatched. That
is now pinned by a test, along with the refresh-to-TTL ratio and the
tombstone outliving the claim marker, so a future retune of either side
cannot silently invert it.

Operability: the claim guard returns what it observed the previous owner to
be, and the park line carries it. A crash-loop and a Redis outage that
expired healthy beacons previously parked with an identical message.

minutes at a time, and the obvious diagnosis is wrong. Measured mid-session
on an 11-core / 18 GiB machine: 17 node processes, 24 threads each, 550-712
MB each, PIDs inside a 250-PID range. One simultaneous burst, about 10.5 GB,
next to an 8 GB colima VM. Those are vitest vmThreads workers. maxWorkers is
"50%", which is 5 workers PER RUN on 11 cores, so three or four agents
testing at once is 15-20 workers. The guardrail is per-run and does exactly
what it says.

#6598 already built the right mechanism for typecheck, lint and format: one
counter shared by every worktree, terminal and agent. ADR-087 extends it
rather than replacing it, and closes three gaps. Tests were not on the
counter, and they are the larger problem. The limit derived from
os.totalmem(), which counts the 8 GiB inside a VM the process cannot use.
And a wait could cost more than it saved.

That last one shapes everything else. A blocked tool call issues no API
requests, and the prompt cache expires on idle with a five-minute floor, so
an agent parked past it re-reads its whole conversation at cache-write rates
(1.15x base input) instead of cache-read (0.1x). Across ten agents that
costs more than the RAM the wait protects. So: narrow before queueing (a
2-worker run that starts now beats a 5-worker run that starts in six
minutes), bound every agent-facing wait under the floor, and treat a fast
deny as the gentle option rather than the harsh one.

ADR-088 covers the seam that lets an agent's tool call reach any of this
without haven driving the agent: a PreToolUse hook. The agent calls haven,
haven answers. It rewraps commands rather than holding locks, because the
hook exits before the command runs and leases would need a TTL and a reaper
that flock already gives for free. The same hook sees cache-invalidating
actions before they happen, which is the second spec — pricing a model
switch or a tool-list change against the bust constant, warning rather than
deciding, and denying only the two things that are unambiguous waste.

Certainty is ranked and stated throughout. The cache multipliers, the
invalidation hierarchy and the 20-block lookback are documented behaviour.
Whether editing an instructions file invalidates depends on where the
harness places it in the prefix, which is not verified, so the spec says so
rather than asserting it. The 20-block window is the highest-variance
unknown: if it trips the cost is continuous rather than per-event, and if it
does not that check is worth nothing. It is a measurement, not an
assumption.

Spec only. Nothing is implemented, every scenario is @unimplemented with its
pyramid tag, and tracking issues for the missing tests are not yet filed.
Stacked on #6598: specs/setup/check-slots.feature and check-queue.mjs arrive
with it, so those references dangle until it lands.

* docs(setup): apply review findings to ADR-087/088 and the four specs

Two Fable reviews, one per half. 3 P0 and ~24 P1 between them. Both
reviewers independently found the same P0, which is the one worth leading
with: the two ADRs deadlocked against each other. ADR-087 put pnpm
test:unit on the shared counter and ADR-088 rewrapped the same command
under `haven run --class heavy`, so the outer run took a slot and then
waited for the inner one to get another. At a limit of 1 it waited for
itself. #6598 had already solved this for `haven typecheck` by passing
CHECK_SLOTS=0; I specced the mechanism and missed its own lesson. Both
ADRs now spec the handoff and both features pin "admitted once, not twice".

THE DESIGN CHANGE. The sharpest finding was that a running tool call
issues no API requests either. The whole argument for narrowing was that a
parked agent goes cache-cold past the five-minute floor — but so does a
narrowed run that takes ten minutes. So "a 2-worker run that starts now
beats a 5-worker run that starts in six minutes" compared the wrong pair
whenever base runtime exceeded a couple of minutes, and the success metric
counted only parks, so narrowing could burn the same money while the
dashboard read zero.

That resolves rather than defeats the design. The cache only discriminates
between admission options for runs that finish INSIDE the floor; above it
the cache is forfeit either way and queueing is strictly better for the
machine. So narrowing is now conditioned on projected duration, an
unobserved command is treated as long and queues, and the doctor gained a
second counter for narrowed runs whose actual duration crossed the floor.
This also settles the tension with CLAUDE.md, which calls --maxWorkers=1 an
anti-pattern because it extends residency: bounded narrowing inside the
floor caps that extension by construction, and above the floor the ADR
agrees with CLAUDE.md and queues.

Factual errors, all confirmed against the source rather than taken on
trust. The workers are vmForks, not vmThreads — platform/app/vitest.config.ts
picks it deliberately and measures 573 MB per fork, which is exactly the
observed 550-712 MB, so the correction makes the measurement more coherent.
The cache write rate is 1.25x; 1.15x is the premium over the 0.1x read, and
ADR-087 had been quoting the premium as the rate while ADR-088 had it right.
`taskpolicy -b` does not retroactively demote already-running children, so
demotion walks the process group. haven already sweeps orphans via
procsupervisor.reapOrphans. monitorLoop reads neither GroupRSS nor
TotalMemory; those live in report.go and typecheck.go.

Structural fixes. One precedence table in ADR-087 replaces three
conflicting readings of amber, and every scenario is now a row of it.
Fail-open is scoped to pressure-derived behaviour only — an absent daemon
must not disable the slot counting #6598 already gives, which the previous
draft would have done. The refusal leg finally has scenarios. Agent and
interactive callers are distinguished, unknown provenance gets the agent
cap, and only agent parks count against the metric.

Gate fixes. tool_input.command is a shell string, not argv, so the rewrap
passes it as one escaped argument instead of splicing after a separator,
where `&&` would have left half the line outside the slot. The gate returns
defer rather than allow, because allow bypasses the permission system and a
resource governor must not approve what the user's rules would ask about.
Exit code 2 is the code that blocks and an unrecovered Go panic exits with
exactly that, so the crash discipline is specced rather than assumed. The
repeat detector is scoped to consecutive calls with no intervening edit,
because the previous version denied the red-green loop. The spawn cap gained
decrement events and expiry so it cannot fail closed. Every warn scenario
now names its channel, since there is no primitive that shows the model a
price and still lets the action proceed.

Hedges added where I had asserted. The telemetry claim was a guess: the
settings set OTEL exporters but no enable flag and no auth, so whether any
of it reaches LangWatch is unconfirmed and confirming it is now the first
deliverable. Three hook contract details need one smoke test — matcher
syntax, whether updatedInput survives defer, and whether /model raises a
hook at all — and the scenarios that depend on them say so.

Still spec only. Every scenario @unimplemented with its pyramid tag,
tracking issues not yet filed, stacked on #6598.

* docs(setup): replace the unverified assumptions with measurements

Everything the last revision listed as unverified has now been probed, and
two results came back the opposite way to what the specs assumed. Both
change decisions rather than wording.

CLAUDE CODE TAKES THE ONE-HOUR CACHE TTL. A headless probe reports its
writes as ephemeral_1h_input_tokens with ephemeral_5m at zero. The whole
first draft was built on a five-minute idle floor, and at an hour the
picture inverts: #6598's existing 30-minute failsafe already sits inside
the floor, so a queued agent keeps its cache through any wait the failsafe
permits, and waiting costs nothing in tokens. Queueing also dominates
narrowing for the machine, because a queued run holds no RAM and a narrowed
one holds some.

So narrowing goes from primary lever to a fallback for one regime. Sessions
in usage overage fall back to the five-minute TTL, where the original
argument holds, and that regime is detectable rather than assumed — a
session's transcript reports which lifetime its cache writes went to. Where
it cannot be read, assume the long one and queue. The first draft's central
mechanism is now the third draft's edge case, and the reason is that nobody
had measured the TTL.

The bust is worse than either earlier draft said, though: on the one-hour
TTL a write costs 2x against a read's 0.1x, so the premium is 1.9x and a
300k-token prefix costs about $2.85 rather than $1.73.

updatedInput IS HONOURED WITH allow AND SILENTLY IGNORED WITH defer. Same
hook, same replacement input: under allow the substituted command ran, under
defer the original was handed back untouched. ADR-088 had chosen defer
specifically to avoid widening the permission boundary, and that choice does
not work. Since rewriting requires allow, and allow bypasses the permission
system, the gate may only rewrite where permission_mode already
auto-approves; under default or plan it observes and may refuse but does not
rewrite. That is a real reduction in reach and it lands in the right place —
unattended fleets run auto-approving and are the case this exists for, while
an interactive session keeps its prompts.

Also measured. The matcher shape in the specs fires exactly as written, and
the payload carries no agent_id in a main session, as documented. A compiled
Go panic exits 2, so the exit-code discipline is justified — the earlier
check said 1 because `go run` masks the child's status. taskpolicy -B
un-demotes and -p works on a running process, so the restore scenario is
implementable. And a model whose command was silently substituted ran it,
noticed the output did not match, and reported its environment as
untrustworthy — so a rewrite has to explain itself, which is now a scenario.

One premise corrected while being precise about premises: macOS does offer
a per-process memory bound, via taskpolicy -m at spawn. It stays rejected,
but on its merits — jetsam kills the process that breaches its limit, which
is the lost-work outcome the design exists to avoid — rather than on a false
claim of impossibility.

Still unverified, and still marked as such: whether /model raises a hook,
where CLAUDE.md sits in the cached prefix, whether the 20-block lookback is
ever tripped in practice, and whether the OTel export reaches LangWatch.

* docs(setup): the cache floor depends on the caller, and sub-agents get five minutes

Alex pushed back on the previous revision's claim that Claude Code takes the
one-hour cache TTL. He was right, and the reason the probe missed it is that
`claude -p` is a main session.

A scan of 40 real transcripts — 14,121 cache-writing requests, about 53M
cache-write tokens — is perfectly bimodal:

  sub-agent transcripts    100% ephemeral_5m   (5,960 requests, 28.3M tokens)
  main-session transcripts 100% ephemeral_1h   (8,161 requests, 25.4M tokens)

Not one request wrote both, so this is not a breakpoint split within a
request. Claude Code gives a main session the one-hour cache and a sub-agent
the five-minute one.

That matters more than either earlier reading, because the population these
specs exist to govern IS the sub-agents. Ten parallel agents on a worktree
are ten five-minute caches, so a queue deep enough to hold one past five
minutes really does cost a cold re-read — which is what the first draft
claimed on instinct, what the second draft kept, and what the third draft
wrongly relaxed on the strength of a single main-session probe.

So narrowing comes back, for sub-agent runs that fit inside five minutes,
with the fit condition the reviews correctly insisted on. A sub-agent run
too long to fit is queued anyway, because its cache is lost by running.
Main sessions and terminals queue on the existing thirty-minute failsafe,
which sits comfortably inside their hour.

The bust differs by population too, in the opposite direction to the floor.
A five-minute write costs 1.25x against a read's 0.1x — a 1.15x premium,
about $1.73 on a 300k-token prefix. A one-hour write costs 2x, a 1.9x
premium, about $2.85. Sub-agents park cheaply per token but expire fast;
main sessions park expensively but almost never expire. A warning that
quotes one figure at the other kind of caller is off by nearly two times.

The detection also gets simpler rather than harder. The previous revision
specced parsing a transcript to work out which lifetime was in force. That
is deleted: the hook payload already carries agent_id inside a sub-agent and
omits it in a main session, which is the same field the specs had already
documented for a different reason. A caller that cannot be identified is
treated as a sub-agent, because that keeps the tighter ceiling.

Recording the sequence, because it is the useful part: the premise went from
asserted, to attacked by two reviews, to measured wrong by a probe, to
measured right by a transcript scan, and the design is different at each
step. Nobody had looked at a transcript until now, and the answer was
sitting in forty of them.
