* feat(haven): pressure levels and the admission precedence table

The pure half of ADR-087's governor. ClassifyPressure reads a level from
compressor occupancy and swap rather than summed RSS, because GroupRSS sums
ps output and double-counts shared pages. Either signal alone can raise the
level, so a machine with swap disabled still registers a thrashing
compressor.

DecideAdmission implements the precedence table. Red is the only level that
refuses and only with no slot free; amber stops admitting at full width
rather than refusing work. Narrowing is reached only by a sub-agent whose
observed duration fits inside its five-minute cache floor — an integration
suite is never narrowed (specs/setup/integration-file-serialism.feature owns
its concurrency and treats an environment worker count as a failure), a
single-process run has nothing to divide, and an unobserved command is
treated as long.

CallerKind carries the measured finding that a sub-agent holds the
five-minute cache and a main session the one-hour one, read off the hook
payload's agent id. An unidentifiable caller gets the tighter ceiling.

Binds 14 scenarios across memory-pressure-governor and heavy-run-admission.

* feat(haven): a wait too long to serve becomes a background task

Alex asked whether the thing holding off the machine could queue work and
send periodic IPC back to the agent. A true push channel does not exist —
hooks are request/response, and a blocked agent issues no API calls, so
there is nothing to push to. But a probe found something better one field
away from what was already verified: updatedInput can set run_in_background
on a Bash call.

Measured, not assumed. The nested agent got control back immediately, read
haven's explanation out of the replacement description ("haven queued this
behind other heavy runs; it is running in the background"), and received a
completion notification with the exit code when the run finished. Periodic
updates during the wait fall out of the same mechanism: haven writes queue
position to stdout, so an agent polling the background task sees live depth
rather than silence.

That dominates both alternatives for a wait the caller cannot afford.
Blocking parks it past its cache floor. Refusing costs a turn and sends it
back into the same queue. Backgrounding does the work, keeps the agent free
so its cache never goes cold at all, and reports the outcome later.

Scoped deliberately. Backgrounding breaks causality — an agent that runs
tests then edits based on the result gets an immediate return and could
proceed as though they passed — so it only applies where the alternative was
a refusal, and the agent was not getting its result this turn regardless. A
wait that fits inside the ceiling still queues inline and blocks. Red still
refuses outright, because deferring work the machine cannot take only moves
the burst a few seconds.

Also in this commit, the rest of ADR-087's pure core: ParseVMStat and
ParseSwapUsage, tested against real output from the machine that motivated
the ADR rather than invented fixtures — which is the point, because the two
traps only show up in genuine output. The page size comes from the vm_stat
header (16384 on Apple silicon; assuming 4096 understates the compressor
four times and the governor never fires) and the occupied line is read
rather than the stored line (128k pages against 679k on that machine — five
times the difference). An unknown swap suffix is a parse failure rather than
a guess, since a figure off by 1024x would pin the governor at red forever.

Extracting the two vm_stat line readers also removed a latent panic: the
first draft indexed Fields(...)[0] on the header without checking length.

Domain package: tests pass, golangci-lint clean, gofmt clean.

* feat(haven): quote the wait, do not hold the place

Alex proposed a loket: a refused caller takes a number, keeps its place
across its absence, and is told when to come back. Asked whether it was a
good idea, and on reflection two thirds of it are and one third is not yet.

BUILT. A refusal now carries the caller's position and a time to try again,
and that time is capped by the caller's own cache window. The cap is the
part worth having: the wait ceiling already sits under the prompt-cache
floor, so a time quoted inside the ceiling is always one the caller can
afford to honour. It turns "never send an agent away past its own window"
from a guideline into an invariant, and WithinWindow is written as a
function so a test holds the design to it rather than a reader checking by
inspection. A queue too deep to quote inside that window yields no hint at
all and the run is backgrounded instead, rather than the caller being sent
away with a comfortable lie. A command haven has never timed gets no
estimate, because there is no honest one to give.

NOT BUILT, and this is the interesting half. Actually HOLDING the place is
what fixes starvation, and it is the only part that costs anything: a store,
an expiry, a reclaim, and a reconciliation between who holds a place and who
holds a slot. That is exactly the bookkeeping ADR-088 is pleased to have
avoided by rewrapping, and a reservation cannot lean on a flock, because a
flock's defining property is dying with its holder while a reservation exists
to outlive one. It also has a failure mode nothing else here shares: it needs
the model to cooperate. A flock does not care what anyone believes; a held
place is prose handed to a client that may come back early, come back late,
lose the reference, or rephrase the command and retry.

So starvation is measured before it is solved. Starving() counts consecutive
refusals of the same command, the doctor reports it, and if that number is
ever meaningfully non-zero the reservation earns its cost. If it stays zero,
a subsystem was saved. Same discipline that corrected the cache TTL twice:
build the cheap half, instrument the expensive half's justification, let the
measurement decide.

Removing the ticket as a DECISION also simplified the ladder. Without a
reservation it is not a fifth branch, it is information attached to branches
that already existed — and a wait that fits inside the ceiling should simply
block, because forty seconds of blocking beats a round trip and keeps the
tool call meaning what it says.

Domain: build green, tests pass, golangci-lint clean, gofmt clean.

* feat(haven): the daemon samples pressure, demotes, and sweeps orphans

Wires ADR-087's governor onto the tick the daemon already runs. It samples
the machine, publishes the level for every other process to read, sweeps
orphaned test workers, and slows down what it can.

It never kills. macOS can bound a process's memory — taskpolicy -m sets a
jetsam limit at spawn — and that is rejected on its merits rather than on a
false claim of impossibility: jetsam kills what breaches the limit, which
turns a slow machine into lost work. Demotion is reversible.

Demotion walks the process group rather than signaling the launcher, because
the background band is inherited only by processes forked after it is set and
a live stack is a tree already running. The focused worktree is exempt: it is
the one being watched, and Stacks() is ordered most-recently-updated first,
so the head is it. Red names the largest stack and the command to stop it
without stopping it, because the daemon did not start that work.

The orphan sweep is deliberately narrow — matching the vitest worker path AND
owned by PID 1, which together mean an interrupted run left it behind and
nobody is coming back for it. It is the same rule procsupervisor.reapOrphans
already applies at every up, widened to the workers CLAUDE.md currently asks
people to pkill by hand.

Publishing happens before any of that, so a failure to demote still leaves
readers a current level. A failed publish is logged and not retried: readers
treat a missing record as green, which disables narrowing and refusal and
leaves slot counting exactly as it was.

Binds 6 scenarios in memory-pressure-governor. Build, tests, gofmt clean.

* feat(haven): haven run and haven gate, wired end to end

Completes the A+B+C scope. The governor now has a way in.

`haven run --sh '<command>'` takes a machine-wide heavy slot, runs the
command, and releases. The command arrives as ONE argument rather than
trailing argv, because the gate hands over a shell string and splicing it
bare would let everything after an && run outside the slot. The wait is
bounded by the CALLER's ceiling rather than a constant: a sub-agent holds the
five-minute prompt cache and a main session an hour, so one limit for both
would either park the first past its floor or needlessly hurry the second.
Reaching the ceiling starts the run anyway — a wedged queue must never be
able to block work outright.

`haven gate` answers a PreToolUse hook. Every path defers: exit code 2 blocks
the tool call and an unrecovered Go panic exits with exactly 2, so the gate
recovers in its own defer and the cmd wrapper never returns an error. It only
rewrites in a session whose permission mode already auto-approves, because
rewriting needs "allow" and allow bypasses the permission system — a resource
governor must not hand out an approval the user did not give.

Occupancy is a directory of pid-named entries whose liveness IS the count, so
a killed run frees its place with no bookkeeping. Durations are an
exponential moving average in one file: no growth, and a suite that gets
bigger is tracked within a few runs rather than anchored to whatever the
first one cost.

Naming, per ADR-064's one-meaning-per-flag rule: caller identity is
--agent-id, NOT --agent, which already means plain token-free output across
this CLI. Both new commands and the two new environment variables are in
--help, and the summaries say what the command is for rather than what it
does mechanically.

Two bugs the smoke test found that the unit tests could not. WrapCommand
emitted the flags without the `run` subcommand, so a wrapped command would
never have executed — the marker and the wrapper had been written separately
and drifted; they now share one constant. And the wait was reported even when
it was zero, which would have trained the reader to ignore the line that
matters.

Verified end to end: the gate defers an ordinary command, defers a heavy one
on an unloaded machine (correct — a free slot admits unchanged), and --help
renders both commands with their flags.

Build, tests, gofmt and golangci-lint all clean.

* refactor(haven): layer --help, and install the gate hook explicitly

`haven --help` had grown to about 200 lines: a prose preamble on hostnames,
every flag of every command, thirty-odd environment variables, and
twenty-five examples. That is a manual, and top-level help is not read like a
manual — it is read when you have forgotten a command's NAME, and a wall that
size buries exactly the line you came for.

Now 42 lines, and nothing is deleted, only re-homed:

  haven --help          names and one-line summaries, eight examples
  haven help <command>  what it does, how it is called, every flag
  haven help env        the environment variables, grouped by what they touch
  haven help hosts      the hostname scheme and the machine-wide URLs

Unknown topics list what is available rather than failing blankly. The env
block gained headings (identity and routing, machine load, services and data,
ClickHouse, Postgres and Redis, containers) because thirty flat entries are
unsearchable by eye even when you are looking at the right page.

On installing the gate. `setup` was removed from this CLI deliberately —
`haven up` bootstraps the machine itself — so the obvious home for the hook
was `up`. It is not there, on purpose. Installing portless and trusting a CA
are things haven does to make ITSELF work; registering a PreToolUse hook
reconfigures a different tool, globally, for every project on the machine.
That is a decision to ask for rather than assume.

So `haven gate --install` writes it, and it merges rather than replaces: an
existing hooks block survives, an entry that is already there is left alone
instead of duplicated, and the previous settings are backed up next to the
file so a bad merge is one mv from undone. It also says that hooks are read
at session start, since otherwise the first question is why nothing happened.

Build, tests, gofmt and golangci-lint clean.

* refactor(haven): register the gate hook per worktree, from up

Two objections, both right.

`haven gate --install` was a command whose job is answering hooks also being
the thing that installs them — two jobs, one name, which is what ADR-064
exists to prevent. It is gone.

And the target was wrong. It wrote ~/.claude/settings.json: global, shared by
every project on the machine, and checked-in-adjacent. The right home is the
checkout's own .claude/settings.local.json, and that changes the calculus
completely. .gitignore carries `**/.claude/settings.local.json*` while
.claude/settings.json is tracked, so writing there configures this developer's
checkout without committing a hook into everyone else's. And repoRoot comes
from `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, which in a worktree resolves to that
worktree — so each one gets its own file, which is exactly right when each
already gets its own stack, slug and .env.portless.

Because it is scoped that way, it belongs in `haven up` after all. Reaching
into ~/.claude to change how a different tool behaves everywhere is a decision
to ask for; writing a dev-environment setting into the checkout haven is
already provisioning is the same thing it does with the overlay two lines
earlier.

The write merges and reports whether it changed anything, so a second `up` is
a no-op rather than a duplicate hook or a pointless rewrite. A settings file
that will not parse is left alone with an error rather than replaced by our
idea of its contents. A failure never fails `up`: a stack that would not start
because a hook could not be written is a worse trade than a machine with no
governor. And with no resolvable absolute path for haven the hook is skipped
entirely, since one that cannot exec would fire on every tool call.

Build, tests, gofmt clean; golangci-lint clean on every line this branch adds.

* fix(ci): renumber the governance ADRs to 090/091, unpark the bound scenarios, split the two over-complex functions

* feat(haven): haven setup — optional integrations, chosen rather than assumed

`up` no longer installs the gate hook. It should not have: everything up
bootstraps (portless, the CA, the proxy) is something haven needs to work at
all, and this changes how a DIFFERENT tool behaves. Offering it and assuming
it are not the same thing.

`haven setup` is where those live now. `setup` had been retired from this CLI
with the note that up bootstraps the machine itself — true then, and the
reason the name was free. What it means now is different: optional features,
per checkout, none installed unless asked for.

    haven setup              interactive: each feature, described, y/N
    haven setup gate-hook    name what you want
    haven setup --list       what there is and what each one does

A human with a terminal is asked one feature at a time with the detail in
front of them, and the default is NO — hitting return through the prompts
installs nothing, which is the safe direction for something that edits your
editor's configuration. An agent, or any non-terminal caller, is never
prompted: it names what it wants or it gets the list and an error. A picker
that blocks forever on a pipe would be the worst of both, and installing
"everything" because nothing was named is the surprise this command was split
out of `up` to avoid.

Re-running is a no-op: features report whether they actually changed
anything, so a second setup says "was already installed" instead of writing a
duplicate hook. Input that ends mid-prompt declines the rest rather than
erroring, so a closed pipe leaves the machine untouched.

The gate-hook feature itself is unchanged and still writes this worktree's
own .claude/settings.local.json — gitignored, per checkout, resolved through
git's toplevel so a worktree gets its own. It now refuses rather than
half-working when haven has no absolute path, since a hook that cannot exec
would fire on every tool call.

Build, tests, gofmt clean; golangci-lint clean on every line this branch adds.

* feat(haven): cost safety — price a cache bust, deny unambiguous waste

I deferred this citing ADR-088's measure-first rule. That was over-applied:
the measurement gates WHICH cache-invalidation warnings are worth surfacing,
not the whole duty. The repeat detector and the spawn cap need no measurement
at all, and the pricing mechanism is needed either way.

Pricing. BustPremium is the DIFFERENCE between the write and the read, not
the write rate — an earlier draft quoted 1.15 as the rate and was wrong by
the read it forgot to subtract. It follows the caller: a sub-agent on the
five-minute cache pays 1.15x, a main session on the one-hour cache 1.9x, so
the same bust costs a main session nearly twice what it costs a sub-agent
($2.85 against $1.73 on a 300k prefix). Prefix size is a stat of the
transcript divided by four — crude on purpose, because the alternative is an
API call and pricing a warning must not cost tokens.

Credibility is the design constraint. Below 100k tokens nothing is said at
all: a warning on a cheap action trains the reader to dismiss the expensive
one. Above it, a documented invalidation (tool-set change, model switch) is
worth one interruption; an instructions edit only notifies, because whether
it invalidates depends on where the harness places instructions in the
prefix and that is not verified. The copy hedges accordingly, and a test
holds it to that — the documented case must NOT hedge, the unverified one
must.

Wired: the instructions-edit warning fires on Edit/Write from the payload
alone, via a system message, which the developer sees and the model does not.
There is no primitive that shows the model a price and still lets the action
proceed, so warnings are for the human and nothing here ever blocks.

Denied, because both are waste with no legitimate reading. The repeat
detector stops a command that has run past three times with NOTHING changing
in between — any intervening file edit or different tool call resets it,
which is what keeps the red-green loop working, and a test drives that loop
explicitly to prove it is never denied. The spawn cap holds machine-wide
fan-out at 12, and is allowed to lose count: PreToolUse fires before the
permission check, so a rejected spawn is counted and never runs and drift is
one-directional, so entries expire and an unverifiable count admits rather
than refusing every spawn on the machine forever.

Also priced: N sub-agents launched together on a shared prefix all pay the
write, because an entry is readable only once the first response using it
begins streaming. That is a better argument for the cap than RAM is.

Domain logic and tests are complete for all four checks. Two of them — repeat
detection and the spawn cap — need a per-session state port to reach the
gate, which is the remaining wiring, not a design gap.

Build, tests, gofmt clean; golangci-lint clean on every line added.

* fix(haven): the gate's decision now reaches the run it decided about

Review round on #6623. The largest finding is one seam: `rewrap` encoded none
of what `decideHeavy` had just worked out. The rewritten command carried
neither the caller's agent id nor the narrowed width, so `haven run` re-derived
both from an empty command line — every sub-agent resolved as a main session
and took the one-hour ceiling, and `Narrow` was indistinguishable from `Queue`
at the point where it was supposed to mean something. WrapOptions carries both
across; `haven run --workers` applies the width through the environment rather
than rewriting the caller's command line.

Amber had the same shape of problem from the other end: pressure.go and ADR-090
both say it stops admitting at full width, and DecideAdmission admitted at full
width regardless, so the middle level changed nothing anybody could observe. It
now narrows a run that has width to give up — whoever is asking, since this is
about the machine — and leaves a human at a terminal alone.

The two settings-file defects were the dangerous ones. An unreadable
.claude/settings.local.json (EACCES, EISDIR, a symlink loop) fell through the
guard, which only fired on unparseable JSON, and the developer's settings were
replaced by a file built from an empty map. And the "is the gate already
installed" test was `strings.Contains(entry, " gate")`, which any hook running
`gateway-lint` satisfies — setup would report success having written nothing.
It now matches the ` gate` suffix, replaces a haven entry whose path has moved
rather than appending a second, and refuses a hooks block whose shape it does
not recognise.

The rest, briefly:

- processAlive returned false on EPERM while its own comment said EPERM counts
  as occupied, so a run under another uid freed its slot while still running.
- Heavy-run markers now expire on their own timestamp; a recycled pid otherwise
  holds a slot indefinitely.
- Two waiters could pass the same poll before either wrote its marker, so the
  claim is verified and given back if it over-subscribed.
- A failed run no longer files its duration: a suite that died after two
  seconds narrowed the next caller on the strength of a crash.
- DurationKey keys on the classified kind, not on which substring matched
  first — `npx vitest run --config vitest.integration.config.ts` was filing a
  ten-minute suite in the unit bucket.
- The orphan sweep matches the command column, not the whole ps line including
  the pid columns. Its result is group-killed.
- LauncherPID == 0 is guarded before every group operation: pid 0 addresses the
  daemon's own process group.
- Every external command the governor shells out to runs under a 2s deadline;
  one that blocks would stop the tick and blind every reader on the machine.
- haven's queue notices go to stderr, so a caller piping the wrapped command
  gets its output and nothing else.
- The recovered panic in the gate is logged rather than swallowed.
- `haven help <unknown-topic>` exits non-zero.
- EnsureClaudeHook moves off Store onto its own ClaudeSettings port; Store
  persists haven's state and this writes another tool's config. New()
  takes a Deps struct rather than fourteen positional arguments.
- Out-of-range float sizes, future-dated spawn entries, and unquoted paths
  containing spaces are all rejected rather than silently mishandled.
- Comments corrected where the code disagreed with them: HeavySlots sizes from
  total-minus-compressor and now says so, an unidentified caller keeps the
  main-session ceiling (decided rather than left ambiguous across three
  places), and the gate hook is documented as opt-in and worktree-local in
  ADR-091 and in the CLI's own help.

Test fakes that could not observe a defect now can: the duration fake is keyed,
and the orphan sweep's marker is recorded and asserted.

* fix(haven): identify the gate hook by its executable, not by the word "gate"

Second review round on #6623, all of it against the code the first round added.

The hook-identity fix was still too loose. `strings.HasSuffix(cmd, " gate")`
matches `run quality gate`, which belongs to whoever wrote it — and the update
path replaced the entire PreToolUse entry, so a real haven gate sharing an entry
with a sibling hook took the sibling with it. Identity is now the executable:
last word is the subcommand, first word names a file called haven. The update
writes the nested hook's own `command` in place, so siblings survive. Both cases
are tested, including that the stranger's command comes back byte-identical.

The rest:

- Future-dated heavy-run claims are expired, not counted. Same defect the spawn
  counter had — a negative age is under the TTL by arithmetic — and it holds
  machine-wide capacity for as long as the timestamp says.
- `TotalMemory` and `GroupRSS` shell out on the report and pressure paths and
  were still unbounded, so the comment claiming every governor command carries a
  deadline was not true. They go through `probe` now.
- Two comments corrected where they misdescribed the code: the main-session
  ceiling is the thirty-minute failsafe (one hour is the cache FLOOR), and
  defaulting an unidentified caller to a sub-agent would hand every main session
  the tighter floor and ceiling rather than unconditionally narrowing it.
- Naming: `changed` → `isChanged`, `installed` → `isInstalled`, and the
  type-assertion results say what they tested.

Build, tests, gofmt and the house-rules lint clean; feature parity 4563 bound.

* fix(haven): read back a quoted haven path as one word, not four

`haven setup gate-hook` installs its own absolute path, shell-quoted
because a checkout can live under a directory with a space. The
already-installed check then split that command on whitespace, so
`'/src/my worktree/haven' gate` read as four words beginning `'/src`,
failed to name a file called haven, and was taken for a stranger's hook.

The effect was one more gate appended on every setup in any checkout with
a space in its path, each one gating every tool call again.

Quoting is only safe if it survives the round trip, so the inverse now
exists next to it: `domain.ShellWords` reads back what `ShellQuote`
wrote. It is a reader for our own output rather than a shell — no
expansion, no substitution, no operators, only where one word ends and
the next begins.

* fix(haven): close three ways governance could quietly switch itself off

`ParseVMStat` reported success on a header with no occupancy line, so a
renamed or missing line answered "compressor empty" rather than "cannot
read this" — and the governor sat at green while the machine thrashed.
Both values are now required. `ParseSwapUsage` had the same shape at the
other end: `ParseFloat` accepts "NaN", which is neither negative nor over
the bound, so it walked through both guards into the conversion they
exist to protect.

`ObserveDuration` read the whole timings map, updated one key and
published all of it. Two runs finishing together each wrote a map built
before the other's update, so the later writer dropped the earlier one's
key and that command read back as never timed — in a tool built for
several agents at once. The read-modify-write is now held under a lock
file, since the writer renames over the durations file and a lock on the
old inode would guard a name nothing lives at.

The daemon's pressure tick published first and then did every slow thing
in the same breath: a sweep, a process list, a taskpolicy call per stack
and, at red, two more probes per stack. Each is deadline-bound alone,
but together on a degraded machine they can outlast the 90-second
staleness window — at which point every reader falls back to green and
governance switches off exactly when it is needed. Sampling and
publishing stay on the tick; the rest runs behind a single-flight guard.

Also: `haven run --class` accepted any value and always took the heavy
pool, `haven setup` prompted when stdout was a terminal but stdin was a
pipe that never answers, and the governor's pid-0 guard — the one
standing between a demotion and haven demoting itself — had no test.

* fix(haven): route the gate to the tools it actually answers for

The installed hook matched Bash and Agent. The cache-cost warning ran only
for Edit and Write. So the whole cost half of the gate could not fire: the
arithmetic was right, the tests passed, and no payload it was written for
ever reached it. Caught in review, not by a test, which is the second half
of the problem.

The tool set was one decision written in two places, so it is now one. The
matcher haven installs is derived from domain.GatedTools, and a test drives
every tool named there through Gate() and fails if one reaches an
unconditional defer. Reintroducing the exact drift fails it by name.

Agent leaves the set. The spawn cap that would read it is complete in domain
but not wired, and waking the gate for a tool nothing handles spends a
process launch per sub-agent to decide nothing — the same defect pointing
the other way. Whoever wires it adds Agent back, and the test makes that
mandatory rather than something to remember.

Widening the set reached nobody who had already run setup: haven's path
usually has not moved, so the merge found the command equal, reported no
change, and left the old matcher. It now reconciles the matcher too, and
declines when haven's gate is not alone in the entry — the matcher belongs
to the entry, and widening a shared one re-routes the developer's own hook
onto tools they never pointed it at.

The three cost scenarios this makes real lose @unimplemented, which took
llm-cost-safety.feature out of LEGACY_INERT; the parity checker caught that
too. The instruction-edit scenario is now bound end to end rather than at
the pricing function alone, since that binding proved exactly nothing about
whether a developer ever sees the line.

Also fixes two ADR references left dangling by the 088 -> 091 renumber.
They pointed at the Terraform provider ADR.

* fix(prompts): derive selected snippet instead of effect-syncing it

GenerateApiSnippetDialog synced selectedSnippet via a useEffect keyed on
[snippets, selectedTarget]. Callers that build snippets in their render
body (GeneratePromptApiSnippetDialog) hand it a fresh array identity every
render, so the effect re-armed and setState'd on every pass — during route
transitions this cascaded past React's nested-update limit (minified
error #185) and starved the router commit.

memoizes its snippets/targets so the identity is stable.

useOrganizationTeamProject wrote lastVisitedHomeKind on every effect
re-run — org/project/team object identities change on each refetch — and
each write dispatches a synchronous usehooks-ts storage event that
setStates every mounted subscriber of the hook. During a route transition
this fan-out cascaded past React's 50-nested-update clamp, throwing #185
in a ~1s loop and wedging navigation (URL updates, page never commits).

value isn't already "project". Introduced in #6190.

removed in this PR; describe it as the previous implementation.

The dialog test counts commits under snippet-identity churn (the old
effect-sync doubled them, 10 vs 5 under mutation); the hook test logs
lastVisitedHomeKind setter calls and asserts idempotence plus the
validated-slug gate on reserved routes and slug-less pages. Both fail

CodeRabbit flagged that the stubbed usehooks-ts setter never dispatched

* fix(readme): repair nine dead links and check them in CI

Seven docs pages had been renamed under docs/integration/ (openai ->
open-ai, crewai -> crew-ai, vercel-ai -> vercel-ai-sdk, azure ->
open-ai-azure, google-cloud -> vertex-ai, aws -> aws-bedrock), Groq and

readme-links workflow runs it on pull requests and weekly, so the scheduled
run catches the rot that needs no commit here to happen.

Only 404 and 410 fail. A bot block, a rate limit or a timeout is reported

Review follow-ups, keeping the ones that decide whether CI is correct:

- cmd/linkcheck had no tests, so the verdict-to-exit-code step — the only

- The run is bounded end to end, not just per request. Sequential fetches
  at the per-attempt timeout could outlast the job's timeout-minutes and
  turn a slow third-party host into a red build, which is the opposite of
  reporting an unanswered link as unverified.
- Links inside fenced code blocks are skipped; a link in a bash sample is
  illustration, and checking it makes a documentation example a failure.
- The spec said the check runs on pull requests that touch the README.
  It has no path filter and runs on all of them.

The toggle ended a block on any delimiter, so a ``` line inside a ````
block closed it early and the rest of the sample was checked as prose.

* fix(linkcheck): a line with an info string does not close a fence

Only the marker and its length were compared, so "```bash" inside an open

refactor(redis): make Redis an owned client, not a module singleton (#6829)

* refactor(redis): make Redis an owned client, not a module singleton

`src/server/redis.ts` opened a live IORedis/Cluster connection as an import
side effect and exported it as `export let connection`. Importing that module
— from a route, a service, a test, or any file the browser bundle happened to
reach — opened a socket.

Three costs followed from that one property:

- It needed `shouldSkipRedis()` reading raw process.env (NEXT_PHASE,
  BUILD_TIME, SKIP_REDIS) and sniffing `typeof window`, purely so it could
  survive a build, a test, or jsdom. None of those branches describe a product
  requirement; they exist to stop an import from connecting.
- The app-layer could not use it and built its own through
  `clients/redis.factory.ts`, so every process held TWO connections to the same
  server, with the `db` index kept in sync by a comment.
- ~20 test files carried `vi.mock("~/server/redis")` to stop the unit under
  test from constructing a Redis client.

ClickHouse already had the answer: a pure package for the contract, and the
composition root owning the instance. This applies the same rule to Redis.

- Adds `@langwatch/redis-client`: configuration resolved from a supplied
  environment, standalone/cluster construction with TLS and database-index
  handling, and a readiness probe. Reads no ambient env; importing it creates
  nothing. Absorbs `redis.factory.ts` and `redis-db-index.ts`.
- The App owns the one connection, exposed as `getApp().redis` and closed with

* fix(ops): carry the peaks and chart history across a writer handover

Alex caught this: the stat strip's accumulated values did not survive
failover, and the single-writer topology is what broke them.

`restoreState()` ran once, at `start()`. Non-writers return from
`collect()` before doing any work, so a pod that spends hours losing the
election holds peaks and the rolling 30-minute buffer frozen at its own
boot. When the lease moved, the new writer published those stale values —
blanking the chart and resetting every peak tile for the whole fleet —
and then `persistState()` wrote them over `ops:metrics:state`, destroying
the only durable copy. Not lost for a cycle: lost for good, on every
rolling deploy.

This could not happen before ADR-090, because every pod scanned and so no
pod ever held stale accumulators. Peaks and history are ACCUMULATED
rather than derived from Redis, so they are the one thing the handover
had to carry and the one thing it did not.

A pod now reloads the fleet's accumulators when it ACQUIRES the lease,
before it scans, and therefore before it publishes or persists. The
restore merges instead of assigning: field-wise max on every peak, union
by timestamp on the two histories. Assigning either direction loses a
real observation — the incoming writer would either publish its stale
numbers over the fleet's, or discard a peak it genuinely saw before the
handover. At boot the local state is empty, so a merge is a plain load
and that path is unchanged.

The spec scenario for this existed and I had tagged it @unimplemented,
which is why nothing caught it. It is @unit now, joined by one for the
clobber, and both fail against the previous code with exactly the
reported symptom (peak 999 -> 0).

* fix(ops): fence writes on a per-acquisition token, and reset the typed confirm

Third review round. Two were defects in code written this session.

**The typed run-now confirmation was bypassable on the second use.** A
CONFIRMED run closes through the parent's success handler, not through
`onClose`, so the reset in `close()` never ran. Reopening the same row
found the project name still in the box and Confirm already enabled — one
click, second real report, guard entirely defeated. Resetting on the
`open` prop covers both exits.

**Fencing on `writerId` did not actually fence.** The id is stable for
the life of the pod, so a detail scan that started under lease A, lost
the lease, and finished after the same pod reacquired as lease B passed
the check. Its completion-time `computedAt` is also later, so the
monotonic guard could not catch it either — the stale scan overwrites
newer state, which is the exact hole the fence was added to close. The
lease key now holds a token minted per acquisition; scans capture it at
START and writes are fenced on that.

- `getBadgeCounts` stamped `new Date()` on the degraded path — my own fix

* fix(ops): refuse run-now on a claimed slot, and show the operator how stale the page is

Two findings from @drewdrewthis's NOT-READY review, both confirmed against
the code before fixing.

**run-now could deliver a customer artifact twice.** `requestImmediateRunForOps`
guarded on `active` and `nextRunAt` but never `currentSlot`. Once `claim()`
leases a slot, `nextRunAt` holds the lease instant — an ordinary-looking
future timestamp — so an operator reading that row and pressing run-now
passes the fencing guard cleanly. The row becomes due again while its
worker is mid-run, and `claim()` guards only on `nextRunAt` too: its
`COALESCE("currentSlot", …)` PRESERVES the pinned slot rather than
refusing, so a second worker takes the same slot and the target fires
twice. That COALESCE is correct for a retry wake or a crash-refire, where
the first worker is gone; it is not a defence against this.

This is the exact outcome ADR-091 declines to offer even behind a second
confirmation — reachable here by accident. Guarded in three places:
`currentSlot IS NULL` in the UPDATE predicate, an early refusal in the
service, and `canRunNow` no longer offering the control while a schedule
reads as running or retrying. New `schedule_run_in_progress` code with
its own copy, because "the scheduler got there first" describes a race
that did not happen here.

**The page could not tell an operator its numbers were stale.**
`DashboardData.snapshot.computedAt` reached the client and nothing
rendered it; `ConnectionStatusIndicator` showed SSE state only. That
connection is between the browser and its OWN pod, and every pod keeps
serving the last snapshot it read — so a dead writer with the lease not
yet handed over shows a green "Live" light over numbers nobody has
refreshed. ADR-090 asserts this was already surfaced; it was not. The
indicator now takes `computedAtMs` and reports the age once it passes
30s, and staleness outranks a healthy socket, since the socket being fine
is what makes the numbers misleading.

Also corrects the `leaseEpoch` comment in `types.ts`, which still carried
the "changes exactly when the writer changes" claim fixed elsewhere.

Both fixes verified non-vacuous by reverting them: the run-now guard test
reports `did-not-throw`. 502 tests pass, both typechecks clean, parity
16/16 and 18/18 bound.

* feat(haven): reap leaked testcontainers and tighten shared-resource defaults

An interrupted integration-test run leaves its testcontainers running in the
shared colima VM forever — the library's own reaper (Ryuk) dies with the run.
A two-day-old stray ClickHouse was found holding 1.65 GiB and ~1.7 cores next
to the managed one it starves. The daemon now sweeps testcontainers-labelled
containers older than HAVEN_TESTCONTAINER_TTL (default 1h, 0 disables) on the
same hygiene tick as idle-database pruning; fresh ones are left alone and the
sweep never boots the VM.

Alongside the reaper, the shared-resource defaults tighten:

- HAVEN_DB_TTL 14d -> 4d: a dozen dead worktrees' databases were sitting on
  the managed ClickHouse's 1.5 GiB cap before the first prune ever fired.
- LANGWATCH_HAVEN_CH_STOP_IDLE now defaults ON: with no stack registered
  nothing queries the server, and the next up restarts it over the same data
  in seconds. =0 keeps it always-on.
- The managed ClickHouse config bounds background work for the small VM it
  shares (merge/schedule pools, max_concurrent_queries), with the merge_tree
  free-entries thresholds shrunk to match so large merges and mutations still
  schedule under the smaller pools.
- The observability bundle gets a seventh of the machine (was an eighth) and
  up to 2.5 CPUs — it sat pinned at its 2-CPU cap with two stacks feeding it.
- New colima VMs may take up to 6 CPUs (was 4); existing profiles keep their
  shape.

specs/setup/haven-testcontainer-reaper.feature covers the sweep; the
background-work bound is pinned in specs/setup/haven-resource-caps.feature.

(LANGWATCH_TEST_CLICKHOUSE_URL) and CI machines run no haven daemon.

Test-spawned ClickHouse containers now get the same low-footprint config.d
treatment as haven's managed server: a 768 MiB ceiling, optional caches
zeroed, background pools sized for one test run, and the noisy self-telemetry
tables off (a stock container idles at whole cores writing metric logs).

Review findings addressed (internal audit):

- A running container's age says nothing about current use: withReuse keeps
  the original CreatedAt across runs, so a birthday-based 10m rule would
  delete a server out from under a live suite. Stopped containers keep the
  10m TTL; running ones now get HAVEN_TESTCONTAINER_RUNNING_TTL (default 2h,
  clamped to never undercut the stopped TTL).
- Ryuk carries the testcontainers label too; force-removing a live Ryuk
  severs the running client's cleanup socket. Ryuk is never a candidate.
- Removal is per container and tolerates the benign vanished-container race;
  successes are reported alongside the joined errors instead of one failure

- docker stderr now reaches the daemon log (Output() discards it from the
  error text), and a listing where every labeled row fails to date surfaces
  as an error instead of a silent permanent no-op.
- ShouldStopClickHouseIdle reverted to opt-in: native-mode tests
  (LANGWATCH_TEST_CLICKHOUSE_URL) and haven db url clickhouse reach the
  server with no stack registered, so a default-on stop would break the
  documented workflow.
- Test-container tuning: memory ceiling raised to 1 GiB (backstop, not the
  win) and a tuning-version label added at both start sites so the withReuse
  hash — which excludes post-create file copies — cannot alias tuned and
  untuned containers.

  failing-sweep branch are now all exercised by tests; the headline spec

ClickHouse validates at BOOT that
number_of_free_entries_in_pool_to_execute_optimize_entire_partition (stock

start when it does not — a sanity check, not a warning. The shrunk pools

how big each gets, its ledger is separate from haven gate's, and tsgo LSP

whack-a-mole, so the guarantee moves to where every process is visible.

node, bun, claude — and enforces limits on tsgo only: runs past

(4 GiB) or idle past HAVEN_TSGO_LSP_IDLE_TTL (45m, CPU-clock based), and
over HAVEN_TSGO_TOTAL_BUDGET_MB (two thirds of RAM) the youngest run until
the rest fits. node and claude are the user's own work and are observe-only
by principle; killing regenerable tooling follows the existing
vitest-orphan-sweep precedent, not ADR-090's no-kill rule for stacks.

Every watched class's footprint ships to the local Grafana over OTLP

so a down stack never produces a spam stream. That history is what decides

it. The engine's config declared the variable and never read it, so the
one path that actually runs agents was the one path the setting missed.

The test button now dispatches the same node an evaluation builds. One
client, one policy, one renderer, one JSONPath. The engine reads
BLOCK_LOCAL_HTTP_CALLS as the rest of the product does, spelled as a
permission so an unfilled options struct keeps refusing, and the chart
passes it and the allow-list through so a self-hosted operator can
reach them at all.

* fix(agents): name a refused address, and carry the endpoint's answer back

Three things the browser found once the test button ran through the
engine for real.

The engine reported a refused destination as http_error, which presents
as "couldn't reach the agent, check the URL and that the service is
running" — advice about an endpoint that is running fine and was never
dialed. It has its own code, and copy written for it.

stateEvent hand-projects NodeState field by field, so the status,
response headers and rendered body the HTTP node records reached nobody.
A test pins that projection now.

The panel sent messages as text containing a list, which the engine
escapes for embedding in a string, so the endpoint received a body with
every quote backslashed. It travels as the list it is.

* chore(errors): regenerate the Go error codes and format the seed script

ssrf_blocked is now produced as a workflow NodeError as well as an herr
code, so its generated entry lists the node site too.

* fix(agents): keep credentials and transport detail out of what the test reports

A test result travels further than the screen it renders on: it is written
to the agent's test trace, and for a real run the same node diagnostics land
in the workflow's execution state.

- A dispatch that never reached the engine is our failure, and its message
  names our hosts and ports. It is logged and presented as the generic
  failure, per ADR-045. The engine's own messages, which are the ones worth
  reading, come back on the node's state and are unaffected.
- The trace sanitiser only knew about the Auth tab. An author who types
  X-API-Key on the Headers tab had configured a credential it stored
  verbatim. Credential-shaped names now lose their values while keeping
  their names, and X-Api-Version keeps both.
- The engine's new response-header diagnostics carried Set-Cookie through
  in full. The name survives, the session does not.
- A node timed at one end only reported the epoch as a duration.
- The failure alert follows the result rather than the presence of a
  message, so a failure we could not name still says so.

* fix(nlpgo): redact every credential-bearing response header, not just cookies

Convention says Authorization and X-Amz-Security-Token are request headers.
An upstream can send them in a response anyway, and Go hands us whatever
arrived, so the deny-list now covers them by name and matches credential
words in custom names. X-Api-Version and X-Idempotency-Key keep their values:
half the value of reporting headers at all is the ones an author came to read.

* fix(agents): redact auth and cookie header variants, and drop an unused knob

One rule, spelled the same way in the engine and the app: a header whose
name reads like a credential loses its value, whole words only.

X-Authorization and X-Auth were reaching trace storage intact. So was
Set-Cookie, which convention calls a response header and nothing stops an
author typing into a request. WWW-Authenticate keeps its value: a 401 is
undebuggable without the challenge that caused it.

sanitizeHeadersForTrace takes a named-parameter object. The test fixture's
componentId option had no caller, so the fixture is single-argument and the
behaviour it existed to reach, a state change belonging to another node
being ignored, is covered by a test instead.

feat(langy): key-authed Langy turn surface, behind its own rollback switch (#6821) (#6844)

* feat(langy): bridge a project API key to the Langy access gate (#6821)

Langy is reachable only from a browser session today, so scripts and CI
cannot drive it. Opening a key-authed surface needs an answer to a
question the browser path never had to ask: a key authenticates the
caller, but the access gate judges a *user*.

This lands the identity half. `resolveLangyKeyIdentity` derives the
actor from the credential — the key's `apiKeyUserId` — and runs it
through the same `hasLangyAccess` gate the browser surface uses, so
there is one cohort and no second definition of who may use Langy. The
actor is never read from a request payload, which is the trap the
internal relay plane fell into: `services/langyagent/transport/rpc/http.go`
authenticates with a shared secret and then takes `actorUserId` from the
body on assertion.

An ownerless key is refused rather than evaluated on its project alone.
Per-project Langy keys are deliberately owned by no individual, and
falling back to a project-only flag check would hand Langy to every
project whose flag is on regardless of who was opted in — the exact
identity hole `langyAccessGate` documents as forbidden.

Also adds the feature file for #6821. All 11 acceptance criteria are
mapped; the five scenarios this slice implements are bound, the rest are
tagged `@unimplemented` as tracked gaps for later slices. The route
itself, streaming, and the GitHub capability question follow.

No behaviour changes: nothing calls the bridge yet.

* feat(langy): key-authed public turn surface, behind its own rollback switch

Slice 2 of #6821. Adds the REST route a project API key uses to start and
continue a Langy turn, on top of slice 1's identity bridge.

POST /api/langy/conversations                        — start
POST /api/langy/conversations/:id/messages           — continue

Mounted under /api/langy, deliberately NOT /api/internal/langy where the
worker-plane routes live: the Helm chart blocks /api/internal at the ingress
by default, so a customer-facing route there would be unreachable or would
force that block open for everything behind it (AC 10).

Create and continue are the same service call, exactly as the tRPC router
does it — conversationId present or absent is the only difference. The route
owns transport only; ownership, idempotency, capacity and model policy stay
in the app layer and arrive as HandledErrors mapped from their httpStatus.

Two decisions worth review:

- The acting Session is LOADED from the owner's user row, never synthesised.
  The turn service reads more than the id off it: mintSessionKey scopes the
  per-turn sk-lw-* key to session.user.id (ADR-047), and
  resolveActingGithubLogin derives the Co-authored-by trailer from name and
  email. A hand-built session with a placeholder name would mint a correctly
  scoped key but sign real commits with an identity belonging to nobody. If
  the owning row is gone we refuse rather than fall back to a stand-in.

- release_langy_api_key_turns_enabled is a new SYSTEM flag, default off,
  ANDed with release_langy_enabled and strictly narrower than it (AC 11).
  Off means the surface 404s rather than 403s, so rollback looks like the

The flag is checked AFTER authentication so an unauthenticated caller learns
only that its token is bad, never whether the surface exists.

files; check:feature-parity exit 0 with 8/8 scenarios bound on

  did not.

* fix(langy): make the dark /api/langy surface actually indistinguishable

Two ways the flag-off 404 announced the route it was meant to hide.

The refusal was thrown, so it came back through createServiceApp's
canonical envelope as JSON carrying trace_id and span_id. A path that was

matched; Content-Type and body did not. The refusal now returns

The ceiling ran before the flag, so a valid key without `langy:create`
got a 403 while the surface was supposed to be dark, and no unmounted
route can answer 403. The flag check moves ahead of it. It stays after

argued for: an unauthenticated caller still learns only that its token

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(langy): narrow the dark-surface claim, and pin the refusal chain

The docblock said an unauthenticated caller "learns only that the token is
bad, never whether the surface exists". That is not true. Credential
resolution runs before the flag check, so a caller with no credential gets a
401 whether the flag is on or off, while a genuinely unmounted path answers
the same request with a plain-text 404. An anonymous prober could tell the
difference.

The ordering itself is not the bug and is not changed here: the flag is
evaluated per project, so there is no project to evaluate it against until a
credential resolves. Returning 404 for a missing credential would also mean
the live surface never answers 401, which is a worse API for the sake of a
property this route was never able to offer. So the claim is narrowed to what
is actually guaranteed — a caller holding a real project key cannot tell
whether Langy is here — and the limit is stated plainly so no one later reads
this as a defence against anonymous route enumeration.

The chain had no tests at all; only the two extracted pure helpers did. Both
load-bearing properties are now pinned, and both were confirmed to fail for
the right reason before being kept: reordering the ceiling above the flag
turns two tests red, and swapping c.notFound() for a JSON 404 of the same
status turns the parity test red.

* fix(langy): correct the 404 wire shape, cover continue, bind the rollback properties

Four blocking review findings on the previous round.

The docblock said an unmounted path returns plain-text "404 Not Found". It
does not. honoFetchForNode (src/start.ts) intercepts every 404 leaving the app
and rewrites Hono's "404 Not Found" sentinel to {"error":"Not Found"} JSON, so
production serves JSON here. Parity still holds — the rewrite keys off that
exact body, so it applies identically to the dark refusal and to an unmounted
path — but the rationale described behaviour that does not happen, and it
silently depends on a bridge in another file with a carve-out: a 404 carrying

now stated rather than left implicit. Same correction applied to the test
docblock, which also notes the assertion compares at the Hono layer.

Coverage: nothing pinned that the credential's project and session actually
reach startConversationTurn, so a route handing the service the wrong tenant
would still have passed on status alone. The continue route
(POST /conversations/:id/messages) was never requested at all — neither its
conversationId forwarding nor that it stays dark on the same terms.

The identity fixture used reason "no_langy_access"; the type is

reached 202 — passing for the wrong reason.

counted none of this. Both added as @unit scenarios in the existing

reddens only the continue test, restoring the bad reason value fails

fix(model-providers): one default-models config per scope, wide-to-narrow inherit, no 500 on save (#7002)

* fix(model-providers): one default-models config per scope, wide-to-narrow inherit, no 500 on save

Saving a config now claims each attached scope: the scope moves to the
saved config, the previous holder loses that attachment, and a config
with no scopes left is deleted. A migration collapses duplicates that
were written before this rule, keeping the config the resolver already
picked (newest per scope).

The drawer builds its inherit entry only from the server's cascade
answer for the picked scopes, so an organization config can no longer
offer "Inherit (from project)". With no wider value the entry reads
"Not configured". Save is disabled while a new config has no model
and while an edit target is still loading, an all-inherit edit toasts
that the config was removed, and a note warns when a picked scope
already has a config.

Permission and validation failures on the write path are handled
errors now (model_default_scope_forbidden, validation_error) instead
of unknown 500s. Table cells resolve inherited values through the
row's own scope chain instead of matching any team in the
organization.

* fix(model-providers): order default-model writes per organization and re-hydrate the retargeted drawer

Review follow-ups on the one-config-per-scope work.

Concurrency. A per-scope lock only covered the scopes a write attaches,
while claiming a scope also detaches and sometimes deletes whichever
config held it, and that config can hold scopes the write never named.
Two writes could therefore reach the same rows through disjoint lock
sets. Every config a claim can reach is anchored to the same
organization as the claimed scope, so every write path now takes an
organization lock first and its scope locks after, in one order. The
deletes in updateConfig and deleteConfig moved inside that transaction
instead of running unlocked, and config removal is idempotent, so a
save that lost the race is a no-op rather than an unknown 500. Lock
ordering compares bytes, not locale.

Drawer. CurrentDrawer renders the drawer without a key and the drawer
is not modal, so the pencil behind it retargets the same mount. The
hydration latch is keyed by target id, so pointing it at another row
reloads that row instead of saving the first row's models onto it.
Create mode resets for the same reason.

Migration. The exact-createdAt tiebreak compares COLLATE "C": nanoid
ids contain - and _, which a linguistic collation orders differently
from byte order, so two databases could otherwise keep different
configs from the same rows. Carries the IRREVERSIBLE block, and a new
integration test replays the shipped statements against real Postgres,
which closes the last unimplemented scenario in the cascade spec.

Also: the replace warning is announced to screen readers, the prisma
schema comment states the invariant it used to contradict, and the
tests cover the states they bind, a project with no team, the
unsettled-to-settled transition on one mount, the saved payload, and
no row written when the scope guard refuses.

* fix(model-providers): budget the default-model write transactions and assert the resolver after a claim

Two review follow-ups.

A write queues on the advisory lock and the wait counts against the
interactive-transaction timeout, whose Prisma default is 5 seconds. A
save queued behind another one in the same organization could exceed
it and fail with P2028, an unknown error for a save that only needed
to wait its turn. Both write paths now carry an explicit timeout that
covers the queue, and a maxWait for connection acquisition.

The claim test asserted the attachment rows but never resolved, so a
claim that detached the old attachment while the resolver still read
the losing config would have kept it green. It now resolves a
DEFAULT-role feature for a project in that organization.

* fix(model-providers): say what actually serialises the deletes, and budget the migration replay

The id sort in the two delete helpers was documented as a lock-order
guarantee. It is not one: a single deleteMany locks rows in whatever
scan order the planner picks, and an IN list is not an ordering
directive. What keeps concurrent writes apart is the organization
lock every write path takes first, so the comments say that instead,
before someone drops the lock trusting the sort.

The migration replay seeds, collapses and asserts inside one
transaction, so it carries the same explicit budget as the write paths
rather than Prisma's 5 second default.

* fix(model-providers): route the per-test config cleanup through cleanupTestRows

The raw deleteMany filtered by a let-declared organizationId, which is
undefined exactly when setup threw, and Prisma drops an undefined
filter instead of matching nothing: the teardown would then delete
every ModelDefaultConfig row in the shared database (#6219). The
teardown scan guard caught it.

* docs(model-providers): describe what the guarded teardown actually does

The comment claimed the id is undefined "exactly when setup failed",
which is one direction only: beforeAll can assign it and throw later.
It also described Prisma dropping an undefined filter as though that
were what happens here, when cleanupTestRows refuses an entry that
identifies nothing and never reaches Prisma with it.

feat(coding-agent): a Sessions screen, full-session terminal replay, and conversations back to their name (#6815)

* feat(coding-agent): a Sessions screen, full-session terminal replay, and conversations back to their name

The coding-agent work so far built the capture and a pull-request-shaped read
of it. The session itself had no home, so the context-window numbers that
motivated the whole effort (peak context, compactions, cache rebuilds, time
spent working versus waiting) were recorded and never shown.

/me/sessions lists them. Each row names the session by the title the agent
generated for it, and carries what it cost in context rather than only in
tokens. Clicking one replays it: the drawer opens on the session's last turn
as a terminal, and scrolling up loads the turn before it, and the one before
that, so the whole session reads end to end in one screen.

A session drives more than one pull request. It finishes one, it is merged, it
moves to the next, sometimes three at once. The fold only ever remembered the
branch a session ended on, so every earlier branch, and every pull request
reached from it, was silently dropped. Sessions now keep the set of branches
they drove, and the pull request rollup counts a session toward the work it did
on a branch it has since left.

Two smaller corrections. The traces explorer groups traces into conversations,
so its labels say Conversations again; Sessions now means the sessions table
and only that. And an injected notification in a transcript is not something a
person typed, so it reads as a drawn-back note rather than as raw XML in the
reader's own voice.

Also: the pull requests table drops its sessions count, which was always one
or two and never worth its width, and devices move into a tab on the personal
settings page instead of holding a page of their own.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XRYUK1mbAWQ18rUFdjminD

* fix(traces-v2): read the drawer from the trace's own project

The trace drawer resolved its project from the app chrome, which is
whichever project was last visited. The personal pages read the caller's
own workspace instead, so a session opened from /me/sessions queried the
wrong project and the drawer said the trace did not exist.

The opener now names the project. It travels in the drawer store and in
the URL, so deep links and reloads keep it, and an opener that names
nothing keeps the project already open rather than resetting: every
in-drawer move stays inside the trace's own project.

* fix(coding-agent): write the drive-key separator as an escape, not a raw NUL

driveKeyOf built its (session, branch) composite key around a literal NUL
byte typed into the template literal. NUL is the right separator, it
cannot occur in a session id or a git branch name, but a raw one in the
source makes git and GitHub treat the file as binary, which is what
src/__tests__/noBinarySourceFiles.unit.test.ts guards against.

Same runtime string, written as \u0000.

* fix(coding-agent): lead the context column with the total, and ellipse a long branch

Total is what the column sorts by and what keeps growing, so it leads and
the bar compares it against the heaviest session on the page. Peak sits
under it in the secondary line: it says whether a session was about to
compact, but it saturates against the context window rather than ranking.

A long branch name ran under the next column instead of ellipsing. The
column is capped, but a column flex box sizes its children to their
content, so both lines now have to be told they may not grow past it. The
full value is on hover.

* fix(coding-agent): gate the devices panel on readiness, and split the sort header

`usePersonalContext` falls back to a placeholder organization id while the
session and organization load, so `organizationId` is never falsy and the
two guards built on it were dead: the list query fired against the
placeholder and its empty result rendered "No devices signed in", telling
the reader nothing is signed in when the truth was that nothing was known
yet. A revoke could be dispatched against the placeholder for the same
reason. Both now gate on the `ready` flag the hook already exposes, and
the loading text covers the not-ready window, which a disabled query does
not report as loading.

The confirmation strips used raw palette values, which do not follow the
color mode; they use the semantic red tokens now, like the rest of the app.

SortableColumnHeader was 68 source lines against the 60-line limit for a
new exported function. The chevron and the aria-sort mapping are their own
small pieces now, leaving 48.

* refactor(coding-agent): split the sessions table into named units, and replay a session from its pull request

The Sessions table had grown into one 816-source-line file holding the
query, the narrowing, the page, every cell, the overflow menu and the
replay. It comes apart into units a reader can name: the row shape and
its mapping, the search and period filters, the toolbar, the header, the
row, one file per cell, the row actions, and the replay hook beside the
open and prefetch helpers it drives. The file that keeps the name is now
the query, the narrowing and the page, and nothing else.

Nothing about the behaviour moves with it. The table's own tests are the
contract and they were not touched: the same 21 pass before and after.

The replay hook only ever read a session id off the row it was handed,
so it now asks for exactly that. Which means the pull request drawer can
use it as it stands: the sessions that drove a pull request open their
terminal replay from there too, over the drawer rather than instead of
it, so closing the replay comes back to the pull request. The project
travels with the trace, as it does from the table, because these rows
are read from the caller's own workspace while the chrome is still
sitting in whichever project they last visited.

Also from review:

- the scrollback hook's parameter type is named rather than inline
- the turn cap is one constant, interpolated into the copy that states it
- the peeled context blocks are read from the parser that already split
  them instead of being cut apart a second time on the same rule
- the relative-time ladder is one formatter rather than two copies
- the devices tab is addressable, so /me/devices lands on it, and the
  tabs mount lazily so the inventory is not read until it is looked at
- the sessions page waits for its workspace before saying it has none
- a swallowed pull-request lookup failure is logged
- comments and copy corrected where they described something the code
  does not do

Tests: the epoch guard, the load-earlier distance threshold and the
turn-cap status are now observed by tests that fail when the code they
describe is removed, rather than by assertions that could not fail. Two
fixtures no longer depend on declaration order.

* docs(coding-agent): say what the pull request sort actually orders by

The comment claimed the lowest-numbered pull request is the one a session
started on. Nothing establishes that: the numbers come from the
repository's own counter, so a session can open a higher-numbered pull
request first and later land work on an older branch, and the list is not
in chronological order either. It now describes the ordering that is
implemented.

* fix(coding-agent): reach the replay from a keyboard, and open it once

A click handler on a table row cannot be reached without a pointer: a row
takes no focus and has no activation behaviour, so the replay was the
one thing on these two surfaces a keyboard could not do. The session name
now carries the action as a real button with its own accessible name, on
the sessions table and on the pull request detail alike, which is what
makes it focusable and what gives Enter and Space their meaning. The row
stays clickable for a pointer, and the button stops the click from
reaching it so the replay is asked for once rather than twice. A row with
nothing to open renders the name and no control at all.

Two clicks on the same session were two lookups and two drawers. A ref
holds the sessions being looked up, because both clicks land before React
has re-rendered either of them, and the second is dropped. Clearing the
spinner is now conditional on it still being this session's: a reader who
chose a second session while the first was resolving was having its
spinner taken away by the first one finishing.

The sessions page waited on `ready`, which covers the session and the
organization. The project is read only once those land, so `ready` alone
still left a window with no project id, and the page spent it saying "No
sessions yet" to someone who has sessions. `usePersonalContext` now says
whether that read has answered, and the page waits for both.

* fix(coding-agent): carry the branch set into attribution, not only into the fetch

The branch read matched a session on any branch it drove, then attribution

fix(aigateway): make graceful shutdown actually happen, and give a stream the budget it is promised (#7003)

* fix(lifecycle): charge the drain delay on top of the graceful budget

The shutdown context was built before the drain delay was waited out, so
the wait came out of the graceful budget instead of being added to it. A
handler configured for 60s of drain actually got 57.

Build the context after the drain wait, so a service's Stop always sees
the full configured budget and total wall time from SIGTERM is
drainDelay + graceful. That is the arithmetic the gateway chart's own
guard already assumed when it required terminationGracePeriodSeconds to
cover preDrainWaitSeconds + timeoutSeconds.

ServiceNames exposes the registration order so which service drains
before which can be asserted.

* fix(aigateway): stop the spend drainer wedging the lifecycle group at startup

lifecycle.Worker calls its start function synchronously and documents it
as fire-and-forget. The spend drainer's Start ran its loop inline, so it
never returned, and the group's start loop blocked there forever.

The group therefore never reached signal.Notify. With the spend emitter
on, which is the default, SIGTERM fell through to the default signal
disposition and killed the process outright: measured at 0.08s from
SIGTERM to exit, with no drain, no readiness flip and no stop of any
service.

Launch the loop in a goroutine. The cancel func is still installed before
the launch, so a Stop landing straight after Start cannot miss it.

* fix(aigateway): drain the listener before the spend pipeline, and warn on the real stream ceiling

Services stop in reverse registration order, and the spend spool and
drainer were registered after the listener, so they were torn down first.
Spool.Append counts and discards every record handed to it after Close,
so the spend of every request that completed during the drain was thrown
away. Measured on a running gateway: one 'spend spool closed, dropping
record' for a stream that had already been admitted, leaving an admitted
spend that was never confirmed.

Register the spend services before the listener, so stop order is now
http, statusprobe, auth, spend-drainer, spend-spool, customer-trace-bridge,
otel. Telemetry stays first in and last out, so the shutdown itself is
still traced.

The startup check also only compared the graceful budget against the 45s
heartbeat interval, which is why 60s against a 14 minute stream ceiling
was silent. Nothing gateway-side bounds a streaming response: the server
sets ReadHeaderTimeout only. Compare against the upstream provider
timeout as well, keeping the heartbeat check.

* fix(aigateway): default the graceful budget to the longest legitimate stream

The default was 60s while a stream can legitimately run for the 14 minute
upstream provider timeout, so a deployment that set nothing severed long
streams on every rolling deploy. Default to 900s: the 840s ceiling plus a
minute for the response to finish flushing and the spool to seal behind
it.

It is a ceiling and not a sleep, so an idle gateway still exits at once,
and it cannot outlive the platform's clock because the kubelet still
SIGKILLs at terminationGracePeriodSeconds. The chart sets the value
explicitly and is unaffected.

The README also still documented the default as 10, which was two
defaults out of date. Note on listenSvc.Stop that Shutdown never covers
hijacked connections, which matters for any future websocket work.

* fix(aigateway): bind the new shutdown scenarios and give the test server a header timeout

The five new tests carried @scenario annotations with no matching entry in
any feature file, so feature-parity failed on unknown annotations. Add the
scenarios to specs/ai-gateway/gateway-service.feature: three for the new
upstream stream ceiling bound, two for the stop ordering that keeps the
spend spool open until the listener has drained.

The rule covering the startup warning now names both bounds it checks, and
records that the chart's timeoutSeconds of 60 trips the stream bound on
purpose, since that is the correct signal for a 75s pod grace period.

The two ordering tests built a bare http.Server literal, which gosec reads
as a Slowloris risk because it has no ReadHeaderTimeout. That server is
only ever registered and never started, so the value has no effect, but a
shared helper sets one rather than silencing the linter.

* fix(aigateway): wait for an in-flight spend drain before closing the spool

Stopping the drainer only canceled its context and returned, so a drainOnce
part way through reading or acking a segment kept running while the next
shutdown step closed the spool underneath it. Registering the listener ahead
of the spend pipeline put the two in the right order but did not make the
stop itself a guarantee.

Stop now waits for the drain loop to exit. lifecycle.Worker already bounds a
Stop by the shutdown budget, so a shipper that ignores its context costs that
budget instead of hanging shutdown forever.

The new test parks a shipper mid-drain and asserts Stop stays blocked until
it returns. It fails against the old Stop, which returned immediately.

Also in this change:

- addManagedServices took four arguments, one past the revive limit. The two
  services Serve builds for itself now travel together in ownServices.
- The graceful-shutdown docs said in-flight requests finish "before the
  listener closes", which is backwards: the listener stops accepting first
  and the budget covers what is still running after that. Reworded to name
  the drain delay it follows and the work it covers, and llms-full.txt
  regenerated from it.
- The spend ordering scenarios described service registration rather than
  behavior. They now describe the operator-visible outcome, that a request
  finishing during shutdown still has its spend recorded.
