fix(experiments): let a row the judge could not settle explain itself (#6928)

* fix(experiments): let a row the judge could not settle explain itself

A comparison row that reaches no verdict is the most expensive kind in a
run: swap-and-reconcile pays for two judge passes and keeps neither answer,
and the judge writes 1,300 to 1,500 characters saying why. That text was
stored and then dropped: the results table rendered a bare dash and the CSV
wrote three empty cells, which read as missing data rather than as a
finding.

An unsettled row now carries its own verdict, marked `isUnsettled`. The cell
reads "No verdict" with the judge's account beside it, and the export writes
`no_verdict` plus the candidates and the reasoning. The three empty cells now
mean only what they always should have: the judge never ran on this row.

`winnerId === null` already meant tie in four places, so each one opts in
deliberately rather than inheriting a result nobody produced: the win-rate
chart skips these rows instead of counting a tie, Bradley-Terry takes no
0.5/0.5 evidence from them, the CSV keeps `tie`, `no_verdict` and
`unresolved` apart, and the cell checks unsettled before tie.

The export says `no_verdict` rather than the SDK's `inconclusive` because a
recorded row cannot tell an unreproducible verdict from a row too thin to
judge: both reach the platform under the same status, so naming either one
would be a guess. The reasoning cell says which it was.

Also stops a malformed judge answer from erroring the row. A forced tool
call is not a guarantee, and two of roughly 200 live calls came back with no
tool call or no winner in its arguments, turning a row red with nothing to
read. Those now report no verdict with an explanation, and still report the
cost of the call that was paid for.

Fixes #6910
Fixes #6905

* fix(experiments): treat a judge answer naming nobody as no verdict

Review caught a hole in the previous commit's guard. It checked that the
`winner` key was present, so `{"winner": null}` passed, and the slot lookup
below it deliberately degrades an unrecognised slot LETTER to the first
candidate. A judge that named nobody was therefore recorded as candidate A
winning: a row nobody judged, reported as decided. The check now requires a
non-empty string, and a tool call carrying no arguments at all is caught
rather than raising an AttributeError one level out.

Two tests cover the pair, and removing the guard fails the null-winner one
with a processed result naming candidate A.

Also from review: the internal bucket field is `isUnsettled` like the verdict
property it feeds, the CSV test helper takes a named-parameter object, the
docs no longer promise the reasoning cell is always in the judge's own words
(the evaluator writes it when the judge never answered) and say plainly that
`no_verdict` is the shared export token while `verdict.status` keeps the two
apart at the point of comparison, and the scenario preconditions describe an
answer that names no winner rather than the tool call carrying it.

* fix(experiments): give a no-verdict row a colour of its own

Dogfooding this change for screenshots showed the last place the two
null-winner states were still indistinguishable: the page. "No verdict" and
"Tie" both resolved to the gray subtle badge, which computes to
rgb(248,250,252) on a white row, so both read as plain text and as each
other. Separating the states everywhere except where a customer looks is
most of the way to not having separated them.

No verdict is now orange, tie stays gray, a winner stays green. Orange and
not red: the row is unresolved, not broken.

`resolveWinner` is exported so the colour is assertable. Chakra compiles
colorPalette into an emotion class with no attribute to read back, and jsdom
cannot resolve its stylesheet, so the decision has to be pinned before it
reaches the Badge rather than after.

* fix(experiments): break an unsettled row's account into readable blocks

The reasoning for a row that reached no verdict arrived as one unbroken
paragraph. Each judge pass writes prose already carrying its own commas,
semicolons and parentheses, and joining two of them with more of the same
nested to a depth nobody could follow: the reader could not see where one
pass's account ended and the other's began, which is the first thing they
need. A dogfooded row came out 900 characters wide with no seam in it.

The finding is now the opening line, each pass gets its own block under its
own heading, and the caveat about what may be blamed for the disagreement
lands last. The agreement branch gets the same treatment. The cell already
rendered with pre-wrap, so this was never a display problem.

Also from review: gray is documented as the tie AND the fallback for a winner
this snapshot cannot place, which is what the code has always done;
`resolveWinner` takes a named-parameter object; and the skipped-comparison
comments no longer claim the judge always ran, since a row can also be
skipped before any judge call for having too few outputs. The docs row for
`inconclusive` now says it also covers an unusable judge answer and that
those calls are still billed. That went on `inconclusive` rather than
`skipped`, which the review suggested: `toComparisonVerdict` maps a no-label
response to `inconclusive`, so the SDK's `skipped` really is only its own
pre-flight check, with no judge call and no cost.

* fix(experiments): keep a judge reason that is not text from raising

`reasoning` is free text in the tool-call schema, so a provider that does
not strictly enforce the schema can put an object, a list, a number or a
boolean there. The value was read straight into the slot translation, where
a regex substitution over a non-string raises. The judge had named a
winner, so this took down a row that was decided, on the explanation
rather than on the verdict. It is the same class as the null `winner`
already guarded above it: shaped like an answer, unusable as one.

Anything that is not text now falls back to the default explanation, and
the row keeps the verdict it earned. Six parametrized cases pin it, and
five of them fail on the previous read.

Also from review: the comments on the results cell and the CSV token no
longer say every no-verdict row was judged. A row with fewer than two
candidate outputs reaches the same state with no judge call behind it. The
docs row for `inconclusive` says the judge ran and no winner came out of
it, which covers a disagreement and an unusable answer without reading as
a deliberate finding of no winner.

* feat(scenarios): scenario run parameters and http secret references

Scenarios declare typed parameters with defaults; runs override them from
the run dialog, POST /api/suites/:id/run, both SDKs, and a repeatable
--param flag on the suite, scenario, experiment and workflow run commands.
Values render into the situation and criteria through {{ params.NAME }}
and reach every target type: http url and body templates, prompt
templates, code agents as native params.NAME, workflow entry inputs.
Resolved values are recorded on the run, shown in the run detail drawer,
and exported in the CSV. Http targets also resolve {{ secrets.NAME }} in
url, headers and auth fields, mirroring the workflow engine semantics:
missing references stay verbatim and resolved values are scrubbed from
error messages.

* fix(scenarios): address review findings on run parameters and secrets

Security and correctness:
- A resolved secret is no longer fenced with {% raw %} before the Liquid
  render. Liquid ends a raw block at the first literal {% endraw %}, so a value
  carrying that text closed its own fence and handed the rest of the template
  back to the engine as source. References are lifted out behind a nonce
  placeholder and restored after the render, so a value never reaches the
  engine at all.
- redactSecrets replaces the longest value first. With `abc` and `abcdef` in
  one project, replacing `abc` first left `[redacted]def`.
- Parameter names cannot be __proto__, constructor or prototype, and the

  prototype setter, so whether a value survived depended on which side of the
  merge it arrived from.

  TypeError instead of the ordinary validation error, and `--param __proto__=x`
  was dropped without a word.
- --param is a repeatable single-value option rather than a variadic one. A
  variadic option keeps eating argv, so `--param env=prod my-suite` swallowed
  the id.

  other way, a parameter called `input` replaced the conversation turn.

  value undefined, which flipped a form field to uncontrolled.

* fix(scenarios): the editor says it is loading, and slow work warns

A customer reported that opening a scenario left the Edit Scenario fields
empty for a few seconds with nothing to say they were still coming, so it
read as an agent having written nothing.

The query is not the problem. Measured locally, scenarios.getById takes 8ms
and its batch completes in 11 to 43ms. On a force reload with the drawer
open, 1815ms of the 1853ms elapses before the request is issued at all:
943ms to load and parse the bundle, 241ms for the session and organization,
279ms for two shell batches, and 285ms to fetch and mount the drawer's lazy
chunk. The query is gated on the project, so it can only fire at the end of
that chain. The drawer rendered a complete blank form for the whole of it.

What changes here:

- The editor shows a placeholder while it reads an existing scenario, so an
  unread scenario no longer looks like an empty one.
- The editor titles itself "Edit Scenario" during that read. It keyed the
  title off the loaded record, so it said "Create Scenario" over a scenario
  the person had just clicked.
- The save actions stay busy until the read lands. Saving before it arrived
  took the scenario as absent and created a second one.
- Postgres operations warn when they pass a budget (500ms, POSTGRES_SLOW_QUERY_MS).
- API calls warn when they pass a budget (3000ms, TRPC_SLOW_CALL_MS). A call
  that succeeded slowly used to log exactly like one that succeeded fast.

Both warnings are throttled to one line per identity per minute, and each
states how many calls it stands for. That is the part the ClickHouse
slow-query warning lacked: it warned per query on a global 3MB response-size
default, flooded the logs, and was removed entirely in #6114. Neither warning
reports a failure, which the caller already logs with its cause, and neither
logs argument values or raw SQL.

Known and not addressed here: httpBatchLink delivers a batch only when its
slowest member resolves. Proven locally, scenarios.getById goes from 8ms to
36ms when batched with one slow sibling. Its real sibling
prompts.getAllPromptsForProject returns every prompt in the project with its
full latest version and no pagination, which is the member that scales with
customer data. That is the likely amplifier in production and wants its own
change.

* perf(prompts): the prompt list stops aggregating the whole platform per call

The scenario editor sat blank for two seconds because its request batch
waited on prompts.getAllPromptsForProject. Measured in production, that
procedure spent one to three seconds inside Postgres. Two causes:

1. The _count include for copies. Prisma builds it as an uncorrelated
   join that aggregates all 192k prompt configs, and the planner re-ran
   that aggregate once per listed row: 96 sequential scans of the table
   per call, 2364ms in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, 336k calls on record. The count
   is now one grouped query over the listed prompt ids (0.14ms on the
   same table). It counts live copies only, the set a push to copies
   can reach.

2. No index covers (organizationId, scope), and one large organization
   owns 99.6 percent of the table, so the org side of the list filter
   scanned everything. The composite index replaces the single-column
   one, which stays covered as its prefix.

Around the root cause:

- The prompt catalog query travels unbatched. It is regularly the
  slowest query on a screen, and batched it delayed every sibling call
  in the same request, which is what blanked the scenario editor.
- The slow tRPC call budget drops to one second. This regression ran at
  1.5 to 2.3 seconds per call and a three second budget never saw it.
  The Postgres slow-query warning already fires at 500ms and names
  exactly this query, so the spec prose that claimed the slow work was
  in ClickHouse is corrected.

* fix(ai-gateway): fail fast on unbound explicit providers; exclude safety providers from dispatch

Two fixes for the opaque provider errors seen in production traces.

1. Gateway (Go): when a request names an explicit provider prefix
   (e.g. gemini/...) and no credential in the VK chain matches it,
   candidateChain previously fell through to the full chain. Bifrost
   honours the prefix over the credential's own provider, so it then
   read a mismatched credential through the wrong provider's key-config
   shape and surfaced errors that named neither the real cause nor a
   fix: "no keys found that support model", "deployments not set",
   raw provider HTML. It now returns 400 model_provider_not_bound
   naming the provider and how to bind it. Implicit model names keep
   the fallback safety net, where each attempt dispatches under the
   credential's own provider and surfaces that provider's real error.
   Implements the previously @unimplemented scenario in
   specs/ai-gateway/model-disambiguation.feature.

2. Control plane (TS): scopeResolver admitted azure_safety — registry
   type "safety", an evaluator credential with no Bifrost adapter —
   into materialised dispatch chains, which is the only way a chain
   can fail with "unsupported provider: azure_safety". Candidates are
   now filtered to llm-type providers; providers absent from the
   registry pass through, since they may postdate this build.

fix(data-privacy): keep identifier-shaped attribute values out of phone redaction (#7017)

* fix(data-privacy): keep identifier-shaped attribute values out of phone redaction

The native phone detector has no checksum and no context word, so any digit run that parses as a dialable number matched. A datestamped identifier such as hosted-eu-20260812-09 holds 2026081209, a valid US number, and was stored as hosted-eu-[PHONE_NUMBER].

An attribute value that is exclusively one identifier-shaped token now runs only the recognizers that prove their own finding (checksum, or a marker no identifier holds by accident). A phone number inside a longer identifier token that carries letters is dropped everywhere, free text included.

Values of digits and separators alone keep no exemption, and structure that holds data (minified JSON, URLs) is not an identifier, so bare phone numbers, cards, emails and secrets are redacted as before.

* refactor(data-privacy): prefix the new redaction booleans with is

The repo lint rule require-boolean-name-prefix-ts asks every boolean property and parameter for an is/has/should/can prefix.

fix(coding-agent): link a pull request the moment GitHub announces it (#6849)

* fix(coding-agent): link a pull request the moment GitHub announces it

Branches were linked to their pull requests only by polling, and the
polling backoff grew on the reading that a branch which has answered
empty four times will never have a pull request. That reading is
inverted for how the work actually happens: branches are cut first,
worked for hours, and turned into a pull request last, so a branch was
sitting on its 24 hour cap exactly when its pull request appeared.

Subscribe to the pull_request webhook and write the mapping from the
delivery, which already carries the repository, the head ref and the
pull request itself. The route keeps its existing HMAC verification and
stays idempotent; the event normalises through the REST path's own
toPullRequestSummary and lands in the same recordAnswer write, which
clears the branch's negative cache.

A session folding on a branch now also brings its next question forward
to the first rung, bounded rather than reset, so an actively worked
branch never inherits a day-long wait on an instance that misses or
never receives deliveries. The periodic recheck stays as the backstop.

* chore(coding-agent): drop an em-dash from the repository doc comment

* fix(coding-agent): align the connection status with install readiness, and validate the webhook action

`getConnectionStatus` reported token readiness while `installUrl` required
the App slug, so an instance missing the slug told the settings page
GitHub was available and then disabled both install actions. That is the
same contradiction this branch set out to remove from the install link,
left in place one caller over. Both now take the same reading.

The installation action was cast rather than parsed, and the dispatcher
has no default case, so an action GitHub adds later would have reached the
service and been silently ignored. It is a Zod enum now, and an
unrecognised action falls through the acknowledgment guard that already
exists for unrelated events.

A dropped pull_request delivery logged nothing at all, on any of the four
paths the parser declines, so a linkage outage looked from the outside
like an unbroken run of successful deliveries. It logs the GitHub delivery
id, which is enough to find the delivery in GitHub's own redelivery view.
The payload is deliberately not logged: a raw body here would put customer
repository content in the logs.

Also renamed `exhaustive` to `isExhaustive` for the boolean naming rule,
and dropped a cast that was hiding drift between the webhook schema and
the pull request interface. Removing it typechecks clean, which is the
evidence the schema really does satisfy the interface.

* fix(coding-agent): parse the installation webhook envelope before reading it

The type assertion on the installation payload is erased at runtime, so a
delivery whose body is a valid JSON null threw on property access and
answered 500, instead of falling through to the acknowledgment that exists
for exactly this case. It is a Zod envelope now, parsed before any field
is read, with the action schema and the installation id normalisation
unchanged for valid payloads.

* refactor(coding-agent): give applyPullRequestEvent a named parameter object

Two positional parameters, one of them an opaque `unknown`, is exactly the
call site the named-parameter rule exists for: `applyPullRequestEvent(payload,
header)` reads no differently if the two are swapped.

* fix(coding-agent): order pull request snapshot writes by GitHub's own update time

GitHub permits out-of-order webhook delivery, and both writers into the
stored pull-request snapshot were last-write-wins. A delayed `opened` or
`edited` landing after `closed` reopened a merged pull request and cleared
prClosedAt and prMergedAt, which are the two columns session-to-pull-request
attribution reads, so post-close sessions were priced under the wrong pull
request. A slow REST listing racing a webhook did the same.

Both sources now carry GitHub's `updated_at`, stored as `prUpdatedAt`, and
every write to the row is guarded by it: a strictly older snapshot is
skipped, an equal one still writes so a redelivery stays idempotent, and a
row with no stored timestamp accepts the next write.

The GitHub App registration docs now subscribe to the `pull request` event,
which the webhook handler needs to fire at all.

feat(gateway): model tiers, routing policy editor, and the allowlist that aliases skipped (#6923)

* fix(gateway): close the two model-policy holes an alias could walk through

Aliases returned before any allowlist check ran, so naming a forbidden
model in an alias was enough to reach it while the docs promised the
opposite. The allowlist now judges what the alias resolved to.

policy_rules.models was evaluated on the body as sent, which is the name
the caller typed, so the same alias walked around a deny rule. Model
rules move to the resolver, on the resolved id. The interceptor order is
unchanged: Policy also covers tools, MCP and URLs, and reordering it
would change which rejection a request carrying several violations gets.
The deliberate consequence is symmetric: a denied name that resolves to
a permitted model is now served, because nothing denied ever runs.

Both checks judge either spelling of the same model, so an operator who
wrote "openai/gpt-5-mini" and one who wrote "gpt-5-mini" reach the same
model rather than one of them quietly matching nothing.

fallback.on[] and timeout_ms leave the wire. Neither was ever read; the
token vocabularies did not even match between the two sides, honoring
the control-plane default would have removed 404 and network fallback
from every existing key, and timeout_ms would have capped long
generations at 30s. Which failures walk the chain stays where it is
decided from the real upstream outcome. Old bundles carrying the keys
still decode, in both directions, which a rolling deploy needs.

specs/ai-gateway/advanced-routing.feature goes with them: 223 lines
describing cost and latency routing, a decision now reversed.

* feat(gateway): model tiers, and a routing policy editor that says what it does

## Model tiers

Three reserved names a client can send instead of naming a model:
complex, reasoning and fast. A policy decides what each one means, so a
client written once keeps working when the organization moves to a newer
model.

The wire does not change. A tier reaches the gateway as an ordinary
entry in model_aliases, which the resolver already looks up by exact
name, so the data plane needed no changes at all. The whole feature is
one column, RoutingPolicy.defaultModel, and one function that fills in
the tiers a policy named no target for.

The fallthrough covers the tier names and nothing else. A catch-all
would serve a caller a model they never named, bill every typo, and make
models_allowed unenforceable, because a request would always resolve to
something instead of reaching the rejection.

Three tiers rather than four. A "simple" tier alongside "fast" reads as
a synonym and resolves to the same small model in every real catalog,
while permanently taking one more name out of the caller's namespace. A
fourth is additive later; removing one after customers script against it
is not.

The editor offers "newest flagship" semantics through the same
latest-alias resolver the model provider drawer uses, but persists the
concrete id: writing openai/latest into a policy would make the gateway
dispatch a model literally called "latest".

## The editor

pages/settings/routing-policies.tsx was 1,523 lines holding five inline
components, a hand-rolled composer and no test. It is now 120 lines: a
list, and a drawer registered in drawerRegistry and reached by its own
address, so a link to a policy reopens that policy.

Sections in the order the decisions are made: what the policy is, where
it applies, which providers it routes through, what the tiers mean, then
name mapping, then restrictions in an accordion that carries a rule
count and opens itself whenever anything is set. Hiding configured deny
rules would be a footgun, so collapsing is the empty state only.

Row actions move into the single overflow menu the rest of settings
uses, and the duplicate Cancel goes: the drawer's close already cancels.
validateModelAliasesAgainstBoundProviders was orphaned since it was
written and is now wired, so a mapping naming a provider the policy does
not route through is refused while it is being typed.

A copy pass throughout. The page used to show operators
fallbackPriorityGlobal, "409 at issue time", "RE2 regexes", "503
fail-closed", tools[].function.name and a raw credential id under every
provider row.

## Two dead fields

RoutingPolicy.modelAllowlist and RoutingPolicy.strategy are dropped, in
their own migration after the additive one so a revert is clean. Neither
ever reached the gateway: the allowlist the data plane enforces is
models_allowed on the virtual key, and the four documented strategies do
not exist. Deleting modelAllowlist also deletes ChipListEditor, its only
consumer.

Deliberately not backfilled. Because the column denies nothing today,
folding it into policyRules.models.allow would start refusing live
traffic on deploy day.
platform/app/scripts/report-routing-policy-dead-fields.ts reports what
is being dropped, and prints the per-policy patch with --emit-sql for
support to apply where a customer actually wants it enforced.

* fix(gateway): close the review findings on model policy and the policy editor

Three that could let something through:

A model allow list compiled lazily and stopped at the first match, so
["^gpt-.*", "["] admitted gpt-5-mini and only noticed the broken rule for
models the good one missed. Enforcement depended on rule order. Every
pattern in the set is compiled before any of them is matched now, so an
unreadable rule refuses the request wherever it sits in the list.

A build with no model resolver dropped every model rule and logged a
warning. A bundle carrying a deny rule reached dispatch unenforced, which
from the outside looks exactly like a working one. Such a bundle is now
refused.

A routing policy accepted a moving name. openai/latest resolves in the
product and never in the gateway, which looks a model name up literally,
so storing one would make every tier falling through to it dispatch a
model called "latest". The editor already wrote the concrete id; the
service now refuses the paths that do not go through the editor.

And three in the editor itself:

Restrictions used defaultValue, which only applies on first render. The
rules arrive with the form reset that follows the policy query, so an
existing policy's rules rendered under a closed section, which is the
footgun collapsing exists to avoid. The accordion is controlled now, and
still closable by hand.

A policy whose first scope row was missing or named a scope kind this
build predates matched no section and vanished from the page, leaving an
operator unable to see, edit or delete a policy still routing traffic.
Unbucketed policies get their own section instead.

The form schema was only inferring types, so its required-field messages
and the name length limit never ran. zodResolver is wired.

Plus: one ROUTING_POLICY_SELECT constant replacing fourteen copies, since
a missed copy silently drops tier fallthrough rather than failing; the
report script refuses --json and --emit-sql together instead of letting
argument order pick the format; a proper UseFormRegister on the name
mapping section; and comment, naming and migration-marker corrections.

* docs(gateway): say what a cross-provider chain does with a model only one side serves

The Codex known-good setup pairs an OpenAI primary with an Anthropic
fallback while permitting both gpt-* and claude-* models. The chain
carries the resolved model name to the next provider, so a failover for
gpt-5-mini asks Anthropic for a model it does not serve.

That answers 404, which is itself fallback-eligible and moves the request
along rather than failing it, so the setup works. It just costs an
attempt, and the page never said so. Points at the routing policy's name
mapping and at model tiers as the ways to make one name reachable on
both providers.

* docs(gateway): describe fallback the way the classifier actually decides it

Three claims this branch wrote that the code does not make.

An upstream 429 was documented as always triggering fallback. It is
fallback-eligible: a key with no chain, or one whose attempt budget is a
single attempt, answers the caller instead.

A provider-reported 504 was documented as classifying as timeout. A
forwarded upstream response classifies on its status, so a 504 is a 5xx.
The timeout reason comes from the adapter reporting that the upstream
never answered at all. Both retry, so only the reason on the attempt
differs, which is exactly the kind of detail a contract is read for.

And 400, 401 and 403 were grouped as client-fault. They are terminal,
which is not the same thing: a 401 or 403 is usually the operator's
provider credential, and the reason not to mask it is that switching
credentials would hide what they have to fix.

* fix(gateway): make the accordion regression test actually fail without the fix

The test asserted the rule text was in the document. Chakra keeps a
closed accordion's content mounted, so it passed just as happily with
the section shut: reverting the controlled accordion to defaultValue
left all six tests green. It proved nothing.

It asserts aria-expanded on the trigger now, and the same revert fails
it. A second case pins the other direction, so a policy with no rules
still arrives collapsed.

Two documentation claims corrected against the code they describe.

The Codex page said a cross-provider chain answers 404 on the fallback
slot and moves along. eligibleCredentials trims the chain to credentials
whose provider can serve the resolved model, and infers the provider
from a bare model name, so a request for gpt-5-mini never reaches the
Anthropic slot at all: it has one attempt, and an OpenAI outage reaches
the caller. Says that, and points at the two ways to give a model real
failover.

And NamedScope described ScopeTriadEntry as having an optional name.
ScopeTriadEntry is the id pair alone.

* docs(gateway): state the rolling-deploy case as what the customer sees

The scenario described a decode: a payload carrying two keys, the
gateway reading it, max_attempts taken from it. That is the shape the
guideline names outright, a config value asserted instead of a
behavior, and it read as a unit test transcribed into Gherkin.

The behavior underneath is worth a spec line, so it is reworded rather
than deleted: while a deploy is half done and the two sides disagree
about what the fallback block contains, a request is still served and
the key still gets the attempt budget its operator configured, whichever
side is the newer one. The Go test that binds it is unchanged; it now
says which of those it is proving.

* docs(gateway): rewrite the routing policy page for the fields that exist

The page documented two fields this branch deletes and four routing
strategies the gateway never had. It named the wrong permissions, gave
a tRPC snippet with an argument the router does not take, and had no
tiers section.

What it says now: the real shape, model tiers with the request a client
sends, model name mapping, restrictions, provider order, defaults, the
app, and tRPC.

Two claims were dropped rather than reworded, because nothing in the
code makes them. The four strategies never existed; only the order of
the provider list does. And the project-over-team-over-organization
cascade is not resolved anywhere: isDefault is read by the policy
service and the editor, and by nothing on the request path. A key
routes through the policy it names.

Also fixes the tooltip in VirtualKeyRoutingSection, which pointed at
/ai-gateway/routing-policies. That page is under /governance, so the
link has never resolved. Every other docHref in the app was checked
against the file tree; the rest resolve.

* fix(gateway): hold the destructive drop, and make the model list agree with dispatch

Two review findings, both correct.

The migration that drops modelAllowlist and strategy runs on deploy and
cannot be undone, and the production census it was supposed to record
has not run. Merging it would delete the values before anyone counted
them, and the migration comment claimed those counts were already in the
pull request, which was not true. The drop leaves this branch. The
columns stay in the database, unread: the schema no longer declares
them, nothing selects them, and the census script reads them with raw
SQL for exactly this reason. The drop ships once the counts exist.

GET /v1/models and POST disagreed about three things, so a caller could
be offered a name the next request refuses. Aliases were listed whatever
they resolved to, while dispatch now checks that target against
models_allowed. Discovered models were matched on the bare id, so a
provider-qualified allowance hid every model it meant to allow. And the
policy filter judged the listed id, which for an alias is the alias
name, so a deny rule that stops the request never hid the entry.

All three now use the resolved target and both of its spellings, the
same rule the dispatcher applies. The predicate is built once per
listing so an unreadable pattern is still reported once.

The parity test walks both directions and fails on either: it caught two
of the three disagreements above after the first fix, and a probe
confirms it fails when each rule is reverted.

* fix(gateway): only suggest models a tier can actually use, and attribute every model refusal

Live dogfood surfaced four things the tests did not.

Tier suggestions offered models the request would fail on: music and
speech models the catalog marks "chat", models it cannot price (which
sorted to the top of "most capable"), and, when a policy had no
provider picked yet, the whole catalog rather than the organization's
own providers.

Two of the resolver's three model refusals carried no fault, so the
same model_not_allowed code reached one caller annotated and another
not, and the provider-qualified branch named the bare model, describing
a rule the caller did not hit.

* fix(gateway): refuse a provider the request named and the key cannot reach

Sending "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6" through a key with no Anthropic
credential dispatched it to Gemini, which answered with its own
model-not-found for a model nobody asked it about. A key exists to bound
which providers it reaches, so serving the request from another vendor
is a governance hole, not a convenience.

The trim now refuses when the request named the provider, through a
prefix or through a policy alias, and keeps the whole chain when the
provider was only inferred from a bare model name, where the guess must
not refuse a request the key could have served.

The listing follows: an alias or an allowlist entry pointing at a
provider the key cannot reach is no longer offered, so what GET
/v1/models advertises stays what POST accepts. Both sides now read a
name's provider through one domain function.

* feat(gateway): record the model name the client sent when a policy rewrote it

A trace carries the model that was dispatched. With model tiers the two
are routinely different, so a trace of a tier request said nothing about
the tier, and repointing a tier changed what every past trace appeared
to have asked for.

The name the client sent now rides the customer span as
langwatch.requested_model, present only when it differs from what was
dispatched, and the trace fold carries it into the trace attributes. It
is what answers which tier a caller uses and who still sends an old
model name.

* test(gateway): bind the refusal-attribution and requested-model scenarios

span-shape.feature now enforces scenarios, so it leaves LEGACY_INERT.

* docs(gateway): say which tiers the model list shows

* docs(gateway): write the routing pages in Simplified Technical English

One sentence carries one instruction. The voice is active. One term
names one thing: the app is the app, the gateway is the gateway, and
a rejection is a refusal. The content does not change.

* chore(migrations): renumber the routing-policy default-model migration above main

The newest migration on main is 20260814120000. A migration numbered below it
sorts first, so a database that already ran the newer one skips this one and
the column never appears. The number now sits above it.

* fix(gateway): judge a listed model on what it resolves to, and rank only priced models

ListModels judged an alias on its target and every other name on the string it
displays, so the same rule read differently per source. One helper now takes
the name a client sends and the model it resolves to, and applies the
allowlist, the policy rules and provider reach to the resolved model. That is
what dispatch judges. providers_allowed narrows the chain at dispatch, so a
credential it excludes now makes no name reachable in the listing either.

A model the catalog prices on one side only is no longer ranked. A missing
input rate read as zero priced a model at a quarter of its output rate, which
sorted it to the front of the cheapest tier.

The requested-model span attribute no longer reads an accepted provider
spelling as a rewrite of itself. The sent name is split the same way the
resolver split it, and the two halves are compared by what they mean.

The census script builds its own client through the Postgres adapter, so it
runs. It reported 1 non-empty allowlist over 18 policies on a local database.

* chore(migrations): renumber the routing-policy migration above main

Main took 20260814120001 while this branch was holding it, so the migration

feat(webhooks): deliver to SQS as a per-endpoint destination (#6925)

* refactor(aws): one place an AWS SDK client is configured

Every AWS client wants the same things right, and each has been wrong at least once: credentials omitted rather than emptied (a half-filled pair built from unset environment variables is what shut IRSA out on EKS), the SDK's own retries off when a ladder above is already counting attempts, HTTPS_PROXY actually wired in, and one cached socket pool per proxy so SES and SQS can share it.

SES moves onto the builder with no behavior change: same region, same endpoint, same proxy handler, same default credential chain, and its own retries stay on because an alert send has no ladder above it to take them over. The proxy resolver moves out of mailer/providers, since it is generic outbound-proxy resolution that AWS clients now share.

* refactor(webhooks): a transport answers with a verdict, not a status

The recorder used to re-derive retry-vs-terminal from an HTTP status code. A queue has no status code, so a transport now classifies its own failures and the recorder trusts the verdict. The HTTP transport is a wrapper over the untouched sender that reads the same classification function the throwing assertion does, so it cannot drift from what the platform has always done.

The hourly dispatch cap moves out of the HTTP sender into a function every dispatch boundary calls, because a transport that never passes through that sender would otherwise be uncapped.

The schema gains the destination kind and makes url nullable, which is catalog-only in Postgres: instant, no rewrite, every row keeps its value and takes the http default. A hand-written CHECK pins the per-kind shape, including that a static credential pair is all-or-nothing, since a half-filled pair is exactly what the AWS SDK reads as an answer and stops looking with.

* feat(webhooks): deliver to an Amazon SQS queue as a per-endpoint destination

The body is byte-identical to the HTTP body and the signature, delivery id and attempt ride as message attributes under the same names they use as headers, so a consumer verifies with the same call over the same bytes and a customer can move an integration across without touching its verification code.

Credentials come in three modes: a role we assume with a generated ExternalId (the one to market), a static pair encrypted at rest, and the deployment's own identity, which is gated behind WEBHOOKS_UNSAFE_ALLOW_AMBIENT_CREDENTIALS because without that gate anyone who can create an endpoint could name any queue this deployment's role can write to.

The queue URL never meets the SSRF fence, since the AWS SDK dials it rather than us, so its shape is pinned to a canonical Amazon SQS queue URL and the region and owning account are read off it. FIFO queues are refused with a sentence about FIFO; a batch over the message limit is terminal and names the batch-size control, because the same bytes will never fit.

ADR-053 is amended: it still recommended SQS as an internal durable transport, which is now rejected, since durability comes from the transactional outbox and requiring an AWS account to deliver a webhook would break self-hosted.

* feat(webhooks): surface the destination kind across REST, tRPC, the drawer, the SDK and the CLI

Create takes destination_kind with a superRefine, so a body missing its kind's address is a 400 naming that field rather than the whole body. Update accepts the kind only when it repeats what the endpoint already has, and refuses a change, because batches planned against the old transport are already in the outbox.

The drawer asks which destination before it asks for an address, and locks the choice once the endpoint exists. The list carries a badge and the address that goes with it, which for a queue endpoint is the queue, since it has no URL at all. The secret box is never prefilled and an empty one keeps the stored secret.

The CLI selects the destination by which address you pass, so there is no kind flag to keep in agreement with the address. Creating a queue endpoint prints the external id for the role's trust policy and the ReceiveMessage footgun, which is the one thing every queue consumer gets wrong on its first run.

Also repoints the sync-all-openapi target at platform/app, where the task script has lived since the workspace move; it had been failing with a missing-script error.

* docs(webhooks): document the Amazon SQS destination, footgun first

The ReceiveMessage note leads, because a consumer that forgets MessageAttributeNames: ["All"] sees no signature and rejects everything while the body in front of it looks fine.

Then the three credential modes with assume-role first, the trust policy with a placeholder principal (the deployment's own identity is not a property of the endpoint and is not derivable from this repository), the queue rules, and how to say retry on a queue. The self-hosting page carries the ambient-credentials gate with the reason to leave it unset anywhere more than one organization is served.

* fix(webhooks): address review on the SQS destination

The findings worth naming:

A credential-mode switch left the other mode's credentials in the row. Adding a role to an endpoint that had static keys kept the encrypted key pair at rest, unused and unreachable through every read surface, while the view reported assume_role because the role wins. The modes are now exclusive at storage, and an integration test proves the key pair is gone from the row.

A new SQSClient per delivery discarded the assumed-role session cached inside the provider, so every attempt re-assumed the role, and destroying the client per send paid a TLS handshake per delivery. Clients are cached per queue and per credential, keyed on a hash of the secret rather than the secret, so a rotation still produces a new client.

The CLI no longer takes --secret-access-key: an argument lands in shell history, in ps output and in CI logs. It reads LANGWATCH_SQS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY instead and says so when the key id arrives without it.

The tRPC surface could neither clear a credential nor refuse a destination-kind change: the credential fields are nullable now, matching the service's absent-versus-null contract, and the kind is accepted so the router refuses a change instead of silently dropping it and answering success where REST refuses.

The integration tests restored the ambient-credentials flag on the last line of each body, so an assertion that threw first left it set for every test after it, in a serial worker. It moves to a hook.

Also: the queue URL pattern accepts the FIPS and legacy spellings a regulated or older customer is actually handed; the CHECK constraint is added NOT VALID and validated separately so it never holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE over a table scan; the destination cast that could have laundered an empty queue URL is a narrowed type; the IRSA invariant that broke production once now has a test; and the docs stop overstating the FIFO limit and say plainly that consumers deduplicate on the envelope id.

* fix(cli): keep the SDK lint clean and drop the removed flag from the help text

* chore(migrations): renumber the webhook SQS migration above main

The newest migration on main is 20260814120000. A migration numbered below it
sorts first, so a database that already ran the newer one skips this one and
the columns never appear. 20260814120001 is taken by the routing-policy
default-model migration on another branch, so this one takes the next slot.

* fix(webhooks): show the external id, and say which queue a row delivers to

Hand testing the drawer found the recommended credential mode impossible to
finish. The role field says that saving generates an external id to paste into
the role's trust policy. The server does generate one. Nothing ever showed it:
not the create dialog, which shows only the signing secret, and not the edit
drawer. Without it the trust policy cannot be written, so every delivery to a
role-based queue fails with AccessDenied. The edit drawer now shows the id with
a copy control, and the tooltip says where it goes and why AWS needs it.

The list truncated the queue URL from the right, which cut the account and the
queue name. Every Amazon SQS URL opens with the same host, so two different
queues read identically. A queue row now shows the account and the queue name,
and keeps the full URL in the title.

Both are proven by reverting the change: the tests fail on the old rendering.
The queue assertion compares the text exactly, because toHaveTextContent matches
a substring and the full URL contains the pair it asserts.

* fix(webhooks): a repaired queue credential takes effect without a restart

A refused identity is repaired in the customer's account, and we are never
told. The cached client holds a credential provider that has already resolved,
so the repair did not take effect until the process restarted.

Hand testing found it: a trust policy corrected while the app ran kept
answering AccessDenied for as long as the process lived, while the AWS CLI
assumed the same role with the same key and the same external id at that
moment. A restart, with nothing else changed, delivered.

A failure that names the identity now drops the cached client for that queue,
so the next delivery resolves credentials again. Throttling and network
failures still reuse it, because rebuilding on those would re-assume the role
on every delivery, which is the cost the cache exists to avoid.

The key separator is now one constant used by the builder and the eviction, so
the two cannot disagree about where a key's queue ends.

* chore(migrations): renumber above main, and validate the shape check separately

Main took 20260814120002 while this branch held it, so the migration is
renumbered to 20260815120000. Two other corrections to the same file:

The header now begins with IRREVERSIBLE and carries the rollback statements
as commented SQL, which is the repo's convention for a migration with no
executable down step.

VALIDATE CONSTRAINT moves to its own migration. prisma migrate deploy runs one
migration file in one transaction, so validating beside the ADD CONSTRAINT that
recorded the constraint held the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock through the table scan
and blocked every read and write on the endpoint table. In a transaction of its
own the scan takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, which readers and writers pass
through. The comment claiming the benefit is now true.

* fix(webhooks): refuse a mixed destination body, and let a credential switch take

Three defects on the endpoint write surface.

A create body naming one destination kind and the other kind's address answered
201 and dropped half of it. `destination_kind: "http"` beside an `sqs` object
saved the URL and discarded the queue; the reverse discarded the URL. Both are
now a 400 that names the field which does not belong, the same way a missing
address already named itself. The update path already answered correctly, in
the service, because it knows the endpoint's stored kind.

A credential switch from a role to a static key pair changed nothing. The
update merged the sent fields over the stored ones and only then resolved the
mode, and a role outranks a key pair, so the stored role won, the new key was
dropped, and the API answered 200. The mode is now read from what the request
named: sending an access key clears the role and its external id, sending a
role clears the key pair, and naming both is refused. The CLI sends the same
intent explicitly and refuses --role-arn with --access-key-id before the round
trip.

A failure verdict with no message wrote an empty string into the delivery log,
so a failed attempt showed no reason. One fallback now serves the log row and
the throw.

The endpoint response is a discriminated union on `destination_kind` in the
published OpenAPI, so a generated client narrows to one address instead of
null-checking two fields that the document said could both be set.

* fix(aws): bound every AWS request, and prove the assume-role parameters

@smithy/node-http-handler reads 0 as "no timeout" and 0 is its default, so a
client left to build its own handler had none. The SQS destination also turns
the SDK's retries off, because it sits behind a retry ladder that counts
attempts, and its send carries no AbortSignal: a silent proxy or a half-open
socket held a delivery attempt open with nothing to end it. Every client now
gets a handler with a 5s connection budget and a 20s request budget, direct or
proxied, and the AssumeRole leg gets the same treatment. That leg is a second
request to a second host, it runs before every delivery on a cold client, and
it was the one still unbounded.

The assume-role test asserted that a function came back, which stayed true with
the ExternalId spread deleted. ExternalId is the control that proves an
AssumeRole request came from us rather than from anyone who learned the role's
name, so the provider call is now mocked and its parameters asserted, along
with the master credentials and the STS timeouts.

Two tests under "given an incomplete credential pair" supplied complete pairs.
They move to a describe whose precondition holds.

* docs(webhooks): the 256 KiB cap is ours, and the region-less queue URL is refused

Amazon SQS raised its message limit to 1 MiB in August 2025. The docs, the
module comment and the refusal message all called 256 KiB the SQS limit; it is
a LangWatch delivery cap, and saying so is the difference between a customer
lowering their batch size and a customer filing a bug against AWS.

The queue URL module listed the region-less legacy spelling,
https://queue.amazonaws.com/<account>/<queue>, as supported and then rejected
it as an unrecognizable shape. It stays rejected, deliberately: the region is
read off the URL precisely so it cannot disagree with the queue, and that
spelling carries no region to read. A test pins the refusal, and the module
says to re-copy the URL from the console.

Also a comma before an essential because clause, in the self-hosting page.

* test(webhooks): state the cached-client precondition as a given block

Both cache-eviction tests needed a cached client before they act, and said so
by calling resetSqsClientCache at the top and the bottom of each body. The
precondition moves into `given a cached queue client`, with the reset in hooks,
and the two cases split into their own `when` blocks: the identity is refused,
and the failure says nothing about the identity.

* test(mailer): direct SES egress is a handler with no proxy agent, not no handler

Two assertions read `requestHandler` being absent as proof that no proxy was
used. Every AWS client now carries a handler, proxied or not, because one left
to the SDK has no timeouts. The no-proxy case asserts that no proxy agent was
built, and the excluded-host case asserts it gets the same shared direct
handler a deployment with no proxy gets, which a proxied handler would fail.

* fix(aws): the China partition serves STS under its own hostname

`sqsQueueUrl` admits China-partition queue URLs, so the region reaching
`resolveCredentials` can be `cn-north-1`, and the STS host was spelled
`sts.cn-north-1.amazonaws.com`. That name does not exist. It is only ever
handed to the proxy resolver, so the effect is a bypass decision taken against
a host nobody can write a rule for: a rule for `.amazonaws.com.cn` never
matches, and the STS leg takes the opposite proxy path from the queue leg.

Three test corrections beside it. The handler assertions no longer reflect on
`NodeHttpHandler`'s private `configProvider`; the class is mocked as a recorder
of its own arguments, which is app-owned and survives a smithy upgrade.
`paramsOfLastCall` reads `mock.lastCall` rather than the first call, so it
stays correct once a test builds two configs. The credential-mode refusal is
asserted by reading the row back unchanged instead of matching error copy: a
refused switch that landed half of it would leave the endpoint holding
credentials nobody asked it to keep, and the code alone cannot see that.

The CLI checks the mode conflict before the missing secret. With both flags and
no secret set, the old order sent the caller to set a secret and then refused
the command a second time, for the real reason.

perf(navigation): the scenario library fetches the editor before the click (#7032)

* perf(navigation): the scenario library fetches the editor before the click

Opening a drawer downloads its code first, and until it arrives the page
shows only a spinner at the right edge. The scenario library knows its rows
open the editor, so it fetches that code while the person reads the list.

The warm-up covers both halves of the wait: the module download, and the
lazy wrapper's own record of whether it is ready, which otherwise still
costs one suspended render and a spinner flash. That record is primed only
after the download succeeds, because a wrapper that records a failure keeps
it for the life of the page.

* feat(analytics): default-deny AST validator for governed SQL (#6480)

The gateway-side query gate for the governed analytics SQL API. The
database-layer isolation is already shipped and proven in
`governed-sql/provisioning.ts`; this is the defense-in-depth half that
refuses a query before it can exercise a bug in the layer meant to
contain it.

The walk is an allowlist over node kinds AND over each kind's fields. A
node type the rule table does not name is refused, and so is a field the
rule for that node does not name. The second half is what a kind-only
allowlist would miss: `INTO OUTFILE` is a plain string literal hanging
off a field of an ordinary SELECT, so a walk that only checked kinds
would step straight over it. Every field is walked, accepted as an inert
scalar, restricted to enumerated values, or refused — there is no fourth
state. New ClickHouse syntax therefore arrives refused and stays refused
until someone adds a rule, which is why `@clickhouse/parser` is pinned
exactly rather than caret-ranged.

Table functions are refused positionally, with no name list of our own:
the rule is stronger than `TABLE_FUNCTION_RE` in `ops/explain-core.ts`
and would always be a superset of it. ADR-081 records why, and is careful
to state the measured database behaviour accurately — grants already
refuse url/s3/remote/file/postgresql (497), `merge()` respects row
policies, and numbers/values/view/generateRandom reach no data at all.
The AST rule keeps the surface uniform; it is not standing between a
caller and a leak.

Rejections never throw: `validateGovernedSql` returns a discriminated
result, and `governedSqlValidationError` turns one into the handled
error the REST boundary serialises. Two new codes, both customer-safe and
both with presentation and remediation copy.

Binds two @unimplemented scenarios: the dependency-manifest guard and the
table-function/SSRF ADR. The gated-field and AST-policy scenarios stay
@unimplemented — both are @integration and describe gateway behaviour a
unit test cannot honestly claim.

* feat(analytics): governed analytics.* schema catalog and views (#6480)

The curated namespace the governed SQL API queries: a typed catalog of four
views over the real fact tables, generated into invoker-rights views with
column-scoped grants and row policies, proven against the shipped ClickHouse
migrations as the restricted database identity.

The catalog is data with three consumers — the schema endpoint, the AST
validator's allowedTables/gatedColumns, and the view generator — so the exposed
surface is one artifact rather than three lists that drift. Content gating is
derived from the data-privacy policy's own key catalog rather than hand-listed,
and the unit guard takes its expectation from that module so it can disagree
with the catalog.

Three findings, each measured rather than assumed:

- The IN-tuple dedup pattern is pathological inside a view. Only its outer
  scope prunes; the max() subquery cannot receive the caller's predicate, so a
  one-week question reads 4,518 rows against 4,010 for reading the whole table
  undeduplicated. FINAL costs exactly what no dedup costs, prunes the full 8x,
  and stays correct when a version moves partitions. Re-measured every run.

- A source column named bare inside a view body resolves to the projection
  alias of the same name: the span view exposes a content-filtered
  SpanAttributes and reads captured input out of the unfiltered one, and
  CapturedInput came back empty for every span while every other assertion
  passed. Column expressions now take a qualifier rather than trusting an
  author to remember one.

- Row-policy coverage was audited within the governed database only, which
  would have read clean while the grants that matter — on the physical tables
  under the views — went unexamined. Widened to every database, with an
  explicit invoker-view carve-out.

Column grants cannot gate keys inside a Map and an invoker view needs a grant
on every column it reads, so map-key content gating rests on the gateway's
table allowlist. Stated in ADR-082 rather than left implied.

The governed objects stay provisioning statements; deployment wiring is a
later slice.

Also corrects two factual errors in the ClickHouse query guide that this work
depended on: evaluation_runs partitions by ScheduledAt, and simulation_runs
deduplicates on (TenantId, ScenarioRunId).

* feat(analytics): make the governed SQL API callable over REST

Composes the three landed layers — the catalog, the default-deny AST
validator, and the database-side isolation model — into the two endpoints
issue #6480 names:

  POST /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/analytics/query/clickhouse
  GET  /api/v1/projects/{projectId}/analytics/schema

The execute path resolves the caller's project from the authenticated
credential and its content permissions from the same policy stack every
other API-key read path uses, derives the validator's allowedTables and
gatedColumns from the catalog *for those permissions*, validates, and then
executes as the restricted database identity carrying the caller's tenant
capability. Isolation stays where it was proven: the row policies. A bug
anywhere in the gateway costs a wrong refusal, never another tenant's rows.

Two ceilings, two behaviours, and the distinction is deliberate. The
settings profile pins readonly, max_execution_time and max_memory_usage
CONST, so a query that outgrows the database's budget is killed by the
server and surfaces as a coded error. The ceilings added here bound the
*response* — rows and bytes — and truncate rather than throw, always marked
with `truncated` and a RESULT_TRUNCATED diagnostic. Neither is reachable by
a caller: the first because readonly=1 refuses the setting change, the
second because it is not in the request shape.

The path's projectId is a cross-check, never the scope. It selects nothing;
a path naming any other project is reported as not found, so tenant scope
still derives exclusively from the credential.

Schema discovery publishes per-column gate kinds (input|output|costs) rather
than a collapsed boolean — the open question the catalog slice left. A
withheld column stays listed with `available: false` and names the
permission that would unlock it, because that is what makes the refusal
actionable for an agent with no UI. `available` is derived from
governedGatedColumns, the same function the validator's policy is built
from, so the endpoint cannot advertise a column the gate would then refuse.

Two new error codes: governed_sql_unavailable (fail-closed when no
restricted identity is provisioned — refusing is the only correct answer,
since the alternative is running customer SQL as the application's own
identity) and governed_sql_parameter_missing (caught at the gateway, where
ClickHouse's UNKNOWN_QUERY_PARAMETER would have reached the caller as an
unknown 500). The two resource ceilings a caller can act on reuse the
platform's existing query_timeout / query_memory_exceeded via
translateClickHouseQueryError rather than minting a second vocabulary.

Binds nine previously-@unimplemented scenarios, including the gateway-framed
table-function one the validator slice deliberately left open, plus two new
scenarios for behaviour that had no spec line. Schema discovery stays
@unimplemented on purpose: the scenario also demands per-column units and
dataset-level permission scoping, and the catalog has neither.

* feat(analytics): reach PostgreSQL-resident data from governed SQL (#6480)

Maps six PostgreSQL-resident datasets into the governed catalog — annotations,
experiments, experiment runs, projects, prompts and prompt versions — so the
three question classes the ClickHouse slices could not answer become
answerable: agreement between human annotations and evaluator verdicts, cost
attributed to dimension names rather than identifiers, and comparisons across
experiment runs. Each catalog entry generates its whole chain: an approved
PostgreSQL view, a reader grant on that view alone, a policed PostgreSQL-engine
table, and the governed view over it.

The tenant predicate lives in the governed view's body, not in the gateway.
Injecting it into the caller's statement was the plan and is impossible: the
bound scenario that submitted SQL is never rewritten asserts the logged query
differs from the caller's by nothing but FORMAT JSON. Two alternatives were
measured and rejected — additional_table_filters does not push down and breaks
any query not already naming the tenant column, and a row policy in any form,
including a constant one, never pushes down at all. What works is a scalar
subquery over the self-policed key map: ClickHouse folds it to a constant
before planning the PostgreSQL read, so the predicate ships while the caller's
SQL stays untouched.

It is a performance control and never a security boundary. The row policy on
the engine table still decides the answer, proven directly rather than argued:
with the predicate hard-coded to a foreign tenant, PostgreSQL really does read
and ship that tenant's rows and the caller receives zero. Removing the key
map's self-policy makes the subquery multi-row and the view unreadable — a
broken query rather than a leak, with every isolation assertion still green.
Reading through the view, PostgreSQL reads 2 rows where the engine table alone
reads 10,016. ADR-084 records the decision and what it costs.

Also fixes a defect no test could see: making the version column optional for
PostgreSQL datasets, which keep one row per key and have nothing to collapse,
left the in-tuple dedup path calling it unguarded. The suites stayed green
because vitest strips types without checking them. It now refuses at
provisioning time, matching the field's own contract that a forgotten version
column is an error rather than a view that silently double-counts.

* fix(analytics): bound the key-map lookup and stop re-implementing the key digest

The tenant predicate a PostgreSQL-resident view carries read the key map with a
bare scalar subquery. The key map is a MergeTree ordered by KeyHash and enforces
no uniqueness, so a retried provisioning step or a re-issued key leaves two rows
the self row-policy both admits, and the subquery fails the whole query with
INCORRECT_RESULT_OF_SCALAR_SUBQUERY -- taking out every PostgreSQL-resident
dataset for that key at once, with nothing in the query text to explain it.
Reproduced against a live preview box on experiment_runs, annotations, prompts
and projects. Bounded with LIMIT 1, which keeps the shape scalar: the scalar
form is what folds to a constant and pushes down, and an IN (subquery) would
hand the primary the full scan this predicate exists to prevent.

Three test sites re-derived the key digest with their own createHash, which the
module's own doc comment argues against. The harness fixture now derives it
through governedTenantCapability, so it cannot seed a digest production never
computes; the two assertions state the expected digest as a literal, which is a
stronger check than re-running the algorithm under test against itself. That
also leaves one site hashing an API key, and capability.ts now documents why a
slow KDF is the wrong tool there -- the value is a deterministic join key over
a 48-character random keyspace, not a password verifier.

* fix(analytics): refuse identifier-typed bound parameters, which walked past the content gate

A red-team pass against the preview box found that a column withheld by a
caller's data-privacy policy could be read by binding its name as a parameter.
Spelled literally the query is refused with GATED_COLUMN; spelled as
SELECT {c:Identifier} it returned the withheld value.

The mechanism is that there is no column reference in the parse to gate. The
name arrives as a bind-time substitution the database performs after this
validator has finished, so gateColumnReference never sees a reference and the
walk completes clean.

The file already contained the argument it failed to apply. readTableReference
refuses a table whose name is not literal, because 'a table chosen at bind
time is a table the allowlist cannot see -- which would mean the allowlist was
not one.' A column chosen at bind time is a column the gate cannot see, for
the same reason. Identifier-typed parameters are now refused outright, in
every position: a check on the bound value would be reasoning about a string
the parse does not commit to.

A test claiming to cover this already existed and did not. It binds the

* feat(governed-sql): persist saved workbench charts behind one governed write path

The record is { sql, parameters, vegaLiteSpec }, versioned and Zod-parsed, in
the CustomGraph.graph column under kind 'workbench_sql'. It is versioned
because it lives in a Json column, which promises nothing: a row is only ever
read through the schema, so a definition a different build wrote is refused by
name instead of half-understood.

The service is the only writer, and both governors run on the way in — the
governed SQL validator for the statement and its declared parameters, the
Vega-Lite policy for the specification. Refusing at write is what stops the
database becoming the way around them: SQL nobody could execute and a
specification nobody could render must not sit in a row waiting to be handed
to something that trusts it. Create and update share one private gate, so
there is no edit path that skips either check.

What the save deliberately does not decide is whether a viewer may see the
rows, and whether the specification's fields match a result's columns. Both
are facts about an execution, re-evaluated per viewer at render time — which
is also what keeps a chart saved by a member with wider protections from
disclosing anything to one with narrower protections.

Three new codes, with presentation copy and remediation tips. A statement the
governed validator refuses keeps its own code: the cause is identical whether
the member pressed Run or Save, and a parallel code would fork copy and client
rendering that already exist for the same mistake.

- saved_workbench_chart_not_found (404) — also the answer for another
  project's id, so ids cannot be probed for other tenants' charts
- saved_workbench_chart_specification_refused (400) — carries the policy's
  own rule and JSON path so the editor can point at it
- saved_workbench_chart_definition_invalid (500, platform fault) — a stored
  row that cannot be read back is our defect, not the customer's

fix(ai-gateway): a provider-native route decides its own vendor (#7049)

The Gemini surface at /v1beta sends the caller's body and URL path to
Google as they arrived. The model id comes from that path, so it carries
no provider prefix, and the credential chain picked the vendor instead. A
key with an OpenAI credential and no Google one sent the body to OpenAI,
which answered 404 for a model it never had.

The 404 is the small part. The prompt had already left for a vendor the
caller never named, which on a mixed-provider key is a data-handling
problem, not a routing one.

The route now states its own vendors. domain.GeminiSurface() names
/v1beta and the two providers that serve that wire, Gemini and Vertex,
and surfaceCredentials trims the chain to them before model resolution
runs. A key with neither is refused with 400 model_provider_not_bound
naming both slots, and no provider is dialed.

Vertex is on the list with Gemini because Bifrost's Vertex passthrough
rewrites an inbound Google path into the project-and-location form, so a
caller who sends the Vertex path shape to /v1beta is served by a Vertex
credential. Pinning to Gemini alone would refuse a key that can serve
the request.

Translated routes are untouched. Under /v1 the body is rewritten per
provider before it leaves, so any provider can serve it and the resolved
model makes the choice. A bare model name still falls back across the
key's own providers: it names no vendor, and a key whose only credential
is Azure has to keep serving "gpt-4o". That case now has its own test.

Four tests asserted the old lenient path. All four POST to /v1beta with a
bundle holding only an OpenAI credential, and their 200 came from a mock
provider ignoring the credential it was handed. Their subjects are body
decoding, heartbeats and stream selection, so each now binds the Google
slot its own scenario implies.

* feat(gateway): add the billable quantity columns to gateway_spend

gateway_spend stores five token classes and nothing else, so a character
or second priced call has nowhere to put its quantity. Adds CharsInput,
AudioMS, TokensCacheWrite1h, TokensInputAudio and TokensOutputAudio, all
UInt64 DEFAULT 0. No projection version bump: zero is the true value for
every row written before the columns existed.

* feat(gateway): widen the spend quantity vocabulary on the wire and the stores

spendUsageSchema gains input_chars, audio_ms, cache_creation_1h_tokens,
input_audio_tokens and output_audio_tokens, every one defaulting to zero
so a payload an older gateway wrote still parses. The fold store writes
and reads them back, and readForFold decides a row has usage from any
quantity rather than from the token counts alone, so a late admission
folding over a confirmed request restates them instead of zeroing them.

The two outbox schemas take the same fields with the same defaults: a
frozen intent without a key would otherwise fail to parse for eight
attempts and lose the debit. movedNothing() now tests every quantity, so
an unpriced audio call is a visible record instead of a silent drop.

rateSpendNanoUsd passed only four token counts to estimateCost, so
characters, seconds, hour-long cache writes and audio tokens rated at
zero. It now passes all of them, converting audio_ms to seconds at this
one seam.

estimateCost gains input and output audio token terms. The input rate
comes from the catalog's audioCostPerToken, populated on 23 models and
read by nothing until now; the output rate from a new
audioOutputCostPerToken, derived as twice the input rate for OpenAI's
audio families when the catalog carries no figure. Both fall back to the
matching text rate, so a model with no audio price bills a split payload
exactly what it billed the flat total.

Catalog: openai/gpt-realtime, openai/gpt-realtime-mini and
elevenlabs/convai, every rate checked against the vendor's pricing page
and cited in the entry. The two realtime entries land together because
the prefix-anchored match would otherwise price mini at the full rate.

* feat(gateway): read the audio token split off every provider response shape

ReasoningTokens, and SplitAudioTokens takes the audio counts out of the
prompt and completion totals the provider reports them inside. Pricing
both would charge the audio portion twice at rates that differ by eight

that does not add up leaves the totals alone.

Populated at four sites: chat, responses, speech and the passthrough
stream accumulator, which merges the audio counts on the same last-seen
rule as the cache counts so a streamed audio turn keeps its split.

The customer span folds the audio tokens back into its token totals. It
has no audio-token attribute to price them from, so a trace costs what

fix(costs): let the hand-written overlay override a wrong generated price (#7046)

* fix(costs): let the hand-written overlay override a wrong generated price

The model catalog merged the overlay under the generated base file, so the
base won on key collision. That made the overlay unable to do the one job it
exists for. Its own comment said it covered "models where the upstream rate
lags a provider price change", and that was never true: any model the base
file carried ignored the hand-written entry entirely.

It stayed hidden because every overlay entry happened to name a model the
base file did not carry, so the collision case never came up. gpt-audio-mini
is the first one. One upstream source reports its audio input rate as its
text rate, $0.60 per million against the published $10.00, and audio was
billed at a sixteenth of what the provider charges. Writing the correct rate
into the overlay did nothing.

The merge order is now base first, overlay second. Measured against the
current catalog, exactly one id collides, so the change affects gpt-audio-mini
and nothing else: every other overlay entry is byte-identical under both
orders and the model count is unchanged at 373.

The cost of this direction is that a stale overlay entry now overrides a
corrected upstream price instead of quietly losing to it. The weekly sync
audits every overlay entry against upstream and fails on a disagreement it
has not already accepted, so an override keeps having to earn its place.

Also adds a price coverage guard. A model the gateway can route must not be
able to bill a confident zero, and three different faults do that:

- no rate at all
- a rate in a unit the model never reports, which is how gpt-4o-transcribe
  billed zero while looking complete: it carried a per-second rate and the
  transcription response returns tokens and no duration
- a rate on an entry the cost matcher never selects because a shorter model
  id prefix-matches first

The guard covers all three, and run against the catalog as it stands it
fails on the two transcribe entries, which is the defect that reached
production. Both are corrected on another pull request, so they sit in a
named baseline that a second test forces to shrink once they are fixed.

* test(costs): drop an unused binding and hoist the overlay import

The coverage loop destructured an entry it never read, and the precedence test
called require inside a loop, re-resolving the overlay on every iteration.
Both flagged by the code quality bot. Behaviour is unchanged, 9 tests still
pass.

* test(costs): nest the coverage suite in given/when blocks

Follows the repo testing convention in CLAUDE.md: nested describe("given X")
and describe("when Y") blocks carry the BDD structure, not comments. Same 9
cases, same assertions.

Also stops the gpt-audio-mini description from restating the audio output
rate. The entry has no field for it, so a number written only in prose reads
like pricing data that nothing enforces. The output side is twice the audio
input rate and the cost layer derives it, so the description now says that
instead of repeating the figure.

* docs(costs): say the audio output rate is not derived yet, because it is not

The previous commit replaced a hardcoded figure with a claim that the cost
layer derives the audio output rate. On main it does not: getStaticModelCosts

* perf(automations): persist-match reader accepts pages and sheds per-trace fixed costs (#7016)

One outbox message per matched trace paid the full fixed cost every
time: the active-trigger list, a claim check, the plan cap, the project
row, and for annotation actions a whole-trace ClickHouse read it never
looked at. The handler now normalizes both payload shapes, resolves the
fixed reads once per page, filters prior claims in one batched query,
runs the per-trace confirm and action through a bounded pool, and
reports a ceiling breach once per page. The emitter still writes one
intent per trace until every pod can parse pages.

* fix(automations): a page whose claim write failed gives up its retry

Paging turned a safe swallow into a double-dispatch. With one trace per
intent, a failed `TriggerSent` claim after a successful dispatch could be
swallowed: the intent still completed, so the outbox never retried it.
With a page, an unrelated page-mate's retryable failure retries the whole
page, `filterSendClaimed` cannot suppress the trace that never claimed,
and its side effect runs a second time. One database blip produces both
conditions at once.

A trace that dispatched without a claim is now recorded, and the page
drops its retry when any such trace exists. The retryable traces lose
this settlement's attempt and re-settle on their next match, which is
the cheaper loss: a duplicate dataset row or annotation-queue item is
customer-visible and cannot be taken back. Every dropped error is logged
and reported.

Other review fixes:
- Split dispatchPersistMatchPage. Per-trace dispatch and failure triage
  are module-level functions taking an explicit page context, so the
  at-most-once rules are readable and testable outside the closure. This
  also clears two new biome complexity violations.
- Assert on the DispatchError classification instead of the message
  string, and cover retryable: true, which is the shape real dispatch
  failures carry. The bare-Error default keeps its own case.
- Cover the page dedup: a repeated trace in one page dispatches once.
- Wrap the new dispatchTriggerAction suites in a given context.
- Revert evaluators.generated.ts and langySkills.generated.json, which
  were swept into the branch by a local regeneration and are unrelated
  to this change.

* fix(automations): a persist page keeps its retry when a claim write fails

A page can hold a trace that dispatched but whose claimSend failed, and a
different trace that failed retryably. Dropping the page retry in that case
lost the second trace's dataset row or annotation-queue item for good,
because a settled trace has no guaranteed next match.

The page now always retries for its retryable failures. Persist dispatch is
at-least-once: a duplicate dataset row or annotation-queue item is visible to
the customer and can be removed, a lost one is not visible at all. The
unclaimed traces are logged at warn and reported before the page retries.

The claim write itself now retries inline (200ms, then 500ms) before the
trace is recorded as unclaimed, which keeps the duplicate window small

* test(automations): pin that two automations keep separate persist pages

Two automations on one project can persist the same trace in the same
settle window, which gives their pages a byte-identical body. The runtime
prefixes every builder-authored key with `process:<processKey>:`, so the
outbox keeps the two pages apart. Nothing pinned that, and the comment on
