after the lease query returned while the store anchors the lease before

exactly under the degraded conditions it exists for. The persist page

depend on the process locale or ICU version.

was the last place the cause could be named and it carried only a count,
so a page that retried to its attempt ceiling told an operator "one trace
failed" and nothing more.

fix(observability): keep request bytes out of the logs, and name an uncaused 5xx (#6992)

* fix(otel): keep the request body out of a decode failure's diagnostics

Nothing in parseOtlpBody logs the request body. The body reached the log
sink anyway: V8's JSON.parse SyntaxError quotes about ten characters of
its input inside the message, and we interpolated that message straight
into our own. So a slice of the customer's payload was published by code
that never touches the payload.

Those characters are arbitrary bytes, and arbitrary bytes are routinely
not valid UTF-8. The collector folds this message into `error.message`,
Loki stores it as the `error_message` structured-metadata label, and
Grafana's Loki datasource then cannot parse the label set at all:

  {deployment_environment="prod"} | severity_text=~"(?i)(error|fatal)"
    -> 500  failed to parse series labels to categorize labels:
            1:210: parse error: invalid UTF-8 rune

Confirmed on /api/ds/query, the endpoint Explore itself calls, and
deterministic across limits and repeats. Appending `| drop error_message`
returns 200. Three dashboards read that query and have been broken by it:
errors-new-and-anomalies, operations-home and errors-debugging — every
panel that shows all errors rather than filtering by logger.

A JSON failure is now rebuilt rather than filtered: a fixed phrase plus,
where the parser offers one, a numeric position. Nothing from the input
can survive a construction that never reads it. A protobuf failure keeps
its own words, because "index out of range: 57 + 1307648 > 2070" is the
sentence that says whether the sender truncated the body or we mis-read
it, and protobufjs describes structure rather than content. It is still
stripped of quoted spans and unprintable characters, so a future decoder
that starts echoing bytes cannot reopen this.

Fixed in parseWithFallback, so traces, logs and metrics are all covered,
and the sanitised message is what reaches Sentry too.

specs/observability/ingest-validation-diagnostics.feature already
required that the body not be logged. This closes the stage it did not
reach: decoding, before the schema ever sees the payload.

* fix(observability): say so when a 5xx arrives with no cause attached

A route can answer 5xx by returning the response rather than throwing,
so nothing reaches the middleware to attach. The status still forces
error level, and the record then read `request handled` with no cause on
it — indistinguishable from a successful request unless you happened to
read the statusCode field.

In one hour on 2026-08-13 production logged 12,367 of these, every one a
500, and between them they said nothing at all about what had failed.
That is the hour it mattered most, and the logs were unusable for it. A
record that cannot be told apart from a healthy one is worse than no
record: it is found only by whoever already suspected it was there.

The record now says `request failed without a cause attached` and
carries `errorType: UncausedServerError`, so these group and count like
any other failure shape. It still cannot say WHY — that has to be fixed
at the routes returning those responses — but it can now be found,
counted and traced back to one.

Successful requests are untouched: they are still reported as handled,
and carry no errorType.

Also runs the @langwatch/observability suite in CI. The app's vitest root
is platform/app, so a suite under packages/ is unreachable from it, and
without this step the package that decides the level and shape of every
request record the fleet emits had no test running anywhere.

* test(otel): narrow the decode result instead of asserting inside a helper

The biome delta gate fails on any NEW noMisplacedAssertion, and the
helper introduced one. Nothing is lost by removing it: what each test
asserts is what the message may and may not contain, which belongs in
the test. A fixture that decodes is a broken fixture rather than a
failed expectation, so it throws.

* fix(otel): report the body size a decode failure was already specced to carry

The scenario "A body that cannot be decoded reports the stage that rejected
it" has always had two Thens, and only the first was true: the failure named
the stage but never the size. It was bound to a test that asserted the stage
alone, so parity read green over a guarantee nothing delivered.

The size is the one thing about the body that is ours to state — it says
whether the sender truncated it or sent something else entirely, and a byte
count cannot carry a byte of it. The new test fails against the previous
commit, so it pins the behaviour rather than describing it.

Bounding the whole message is now stated once rather than re-derived from the
widths of its parts, since a variable-width byte count is exactly what makes
that arithmetic stop holding.

Also drops fieldprobe.sh, an ad-hoc production log probe that rode into the
previous commit unmentioned, and moves the test helper to a named-parameter
object.

* refactor(observability): take the new request-log helpers by name

The named-parameter rule was applied to a test helper in review and missed
the two functions this branch had just added beside it. Both are new and
private to the file, so they cost nothing to bring into line.

* docs(otel): say what the byte count is actually good for

It was written as though the size alone told you the sender had truncated the
body. It does not. It is context for the decoder's own numbers — an "index out
of range: 57 + 1307648 > 2070" is unreadable without knowing how much arrived,
and a JSON position says little without the end it stopped short of.

* test(observability): give the success case its own when-block

It was nested under "when the response is a server error but no cause reached
the logger" while asserting a 200, so the reported test name contradicted its
own context and it bound a different scenario from the three around it.

feat(observability): continuous profiling with Pyroscope (#7000)

* feat(observability): continuous profiling with Pyroscope

Traces say which call was slow and metrics say the process was busy.
Neither says which function burned the CPU, so the last step of every
performance investigation was a guess or a laptop reproduction that never
quite matched production. This adds the fourth signal next to the other
three, tagged with the same identity so an investigation moves between
them without leaving Grafana.

Dev needed almost nothing: the pinned grafana/otel-lgtm bundle has run
Pyroscope for several releases and already provisions a datasource over
it, but haven published only Grafana and the two OTLP ports — so the
profiler was running, reachable from Grafana inside the container, and
unreachable from any process on the host that wanted to push it a
profile. haven now publishes :4040 (loopback, like every other port) and
names it in the worktree overlay as PYROSCOPE_SERVER_ADDRESS.

Absence of that variable is the off switch, and a real one: no profiler
starts, and in the TS app the native @datadog/pprof binding never enters
the boot graph. Same bargain the OTLP exporters strike, for the same
reason — a profiler with nowhere to push to still samples on a timer and
still fails every upload.

Identity is read from the OTel variables rather than a second set, so a
flame graph lines up with the trace beside it. One wrinkle that is easy
to get silently wrong: Pyroscope label names follow the Prometheus
grammar and reject the dot in langwatch.worktree. A verbatim copy does
not error — the push succeeds and the label is simply gone — so both
wrappers rewrite it to the underscore spelling Loki already uses.

Also surfaces a failure mode none of the existing checks caught.
Pyroscope's embedded raft metastore can stop while the process keeps
serving: /ingest still answers 200, so pushes look fine and nothing logs
an error, while every read times out and the flame graph is empty. Found
it on the shared stack, up four days. haven status now probes readiness
directly and prints the reason Pyroscope gives, which is what separates
"it just started" from "recreate the container".

The Node profiler samples wall time where the Go one samples CPU. Kept
rather than papered over: this server spends most of its life waiting on
Postgres, ClickHouse and model providers, and a pure CPU profile of a
request that took four seconds and burned forty milliseconds answers the
wrong question. collectCpuTime adds the CPU dimension to the same
samples. Documented, because a Grafana panel defaulting to process_cpu
looks empty for the TS app.

Verified end to end against a real Pyroscope: both SDKs push, the flame
graphs render with real frames, and the worktree and environment tags
land under the normalised names.

  cadence, which is what made it look absent.

* fix(observability): give a chart install the environment its profiles claim

The spec has said "the profile is labelled with the deployment environment"
since this feature was written, and instrumentation.node.ts reads ENVIRONMENT
to supply it — but the chart only ever injected NODE_ENV, so a chart install
pushed profiles with no environment label and nothing failed. NODE_ENV is a
different question anyway: it selects a runtime mode and is "production" in
most staging installs. ENVIRONMENT names which install this is, which is what
aigateway, nlpgo, langyagent and cmd/service already read.

Also spells the Go tag-key normalizer the way every other Go identifier in the
repo spells it. The prose in this repo is British and stays that way; the Go
identifiers are uniformly US (normalizeHost, NormalizeMirrorTier,
normalizeMediaType), and pkg/profiling was the one that disagreed.

* fix(observability): label a chart install's profiles without repricing its IDs

The spec has said "the profile is labelled with the deployment environment"
since this feature was written, and instrumentation.node.ts read ENVIRONMENT to
supply it — but the Helm chart only ever emitted NODE_ENV, so a chart install
pushed profiles with no environment label and nothing failed. The unit test
binding that scenario passes an environment in directly, so it never saw it.

The obvious fix is to teach the chart to emit ENVIRONMENT, and it is wrong.
That variable also feeds @langwatch/ksuid, which prefixes every generated ID
with it unless it reads exactly "prod" — so injecting it chart-wide would move
every self-hosted install's new IDs from `local_…` to `production_…` on
upgrade. Relabelling a flame graph is not worth changing the shape of
customers' identifiers, so the fallback lives at the profiling call site, where
its blast radius is the profile tag and nothing else.

NODE_ENV stays the fallback rather than the source: it answers a coarser
question (which runtime mode, hence "production" in most staging installs).
Deployments that set ENVIRONMENT — ours does — are unchanged.

* fix(haven): stop publishing an ephemeral port for a disabled profiler

LW_OBS_PYROSCOPE_PORT=0 reads as "off" in both places that consume it:
profilingUnready skips its probe, and the worktree overlay names no
PYROSCOPE_SERVER_ADDRESS. Docker does not read it that way. `127.0.0.1:0:4040`
does not mean "no mapping", it means "pick a host port for me", so the profiler
came up reachable on a port nothing had been told about while haven reported
profiling as disabled.

The port mapping is now conditional, and a test pins it — it fails against the
previous code with the literal `127.0.0.1:0:4040` rather than only asserting the
argument list looks different.

feat(simulations): run simulation execution on the process-manager substrate (ADR-094) (#6946)

* feat(simulations): run simulation execution on the process-manager substrate

Simulation side effects ran through fire-and-forget reactors: a queued run
could be dropped silently if the execution pool was not yet bound, a lost
cancellation pub/sub message left a child process running, and a stall was
painted at read time rather than recorded, so nothing downstream ever fired.

Move the pipeline onto the ADR-052 process-manager substrate:

- `simulation_run_execution` process manager, one instance per run, with
  execute/cancel/finish intents on the leased outbox and deterministic message
  keys, plus stall and cancel-grace deadline wakes that force a terminal event.
- The four surviving reactors become event-carried subscribers driven by the
  event payload alone; `lw.simulation_run.finished` carries the ids they used
  to read from the fold, backfilled by the finish command from the event log.
- Per-trace cost and latency move to a `simulation_run_metrics` ClickHouse
  table written by a map projection, aggregated at read time.

Deletes the simulation-processing reactors, read-time stall derivation, and
both boot-time orphan sweeps.

* fix(simulations): broadcast the cancel for a queued run, and bind the specs

Self-review of the process-manager migration turned up one real defect and a
set of specs that were enforcing nothing.

The defect: cancelling a QUEUED run finished it CANCELLED without emitting the
cancel intent, on the reasoning that a queued run has no child to kill. But
`queued` is not `undispatched` — the execute intent goes out the moment the run
is queued, so the pool may already hold the job, buffered behind a busy slot or
in prefetch. `pool.wasCancelled`, the only thing that stops it spawning, is set
by the cancellation subscriber and nothing else, so the run read CANCELLED
while the scenario ran to completion and billed for it. The queued path now
broadcasts too, unless the process never initialized (the cancel overtook the
queued event), in which case no execute intent was ever emitted.

The specs: several scenarios were renamed reactor -> subscriber / process
manager without moving their `@scenario` annotations, so four scenarios bound
nothing and two annotations pointed at titles that no longer existed. All are
bound now, with real tests rather than vacuous ones:

- the queued-cancel broadcast, the stall backstop for a run that never left
  queued, execute-intent durability, cancel-grace force-finish, execute
  dispatch on queued, and skipping already-cancelled runs;
- a real-Redis integration test that drives the process manager's own cancel
  executor, so the intent-to-channel mapping is covered end to end;
- Customer.io first-simulation immediacy, asserted with fake timers that are
  never advanced so a deferred call would fail.

`queued-run-orphan-recovery.feature` moves into the enforced `specs/` root —
`platform/app/specs/` is not a parity root, so nothing under it can bind — and
`event-driven-execution-prep.feature` leaves LEGACY_INERT now that it enforces.

Also registers both new tables in TIME_PARTITIONED_TABLES (the rollup prunes on
PartitionMonth, since its OccurredAt is an AggregateFunction state), and
corrects the ADR: the metrics table is additive, the fold keeps its aggregate.

* perf(scenarios): inline the scenario SDK into the child bundle

The scenario child is a fresh Node process per simulation run, so every
module it resolves at boot is paid again on every run. The pre-compiled
bundle kept the scenario SDK external, so each spawn still walked that
package's whole dependency graph across the pnpm symlink tree before the
child could read a byte of job data.

Inlining it, and the rest of that graph with it, turns those file reads
into one. Measured on a quiet machine, interleaved A/B over six runs
each: median 1127ms -> 567ms per spawn.

OpenTelemetry stays external deliberately, and that is a correctness
requirement rather than an optimisation: the child flushes spans at exit
through the globally registered provider, so a second inlined copy of
the API would take registration and flush to different registries and
drop every span while still exiting 0. A test pins it.

Also sets NODE_COMPILE_CACHE for the child, so it stops recompiling the
same bundle on every spawn.

The bundle's dependency check gains an allowlist for optional peers that
are required behind a runtime guard (ws's utf-8-validate, the SDK's lazy
@google/genai), shared with the resolution guard in the tests so the two
cannot drift.

The feature file moves to specs/ and every scenario is bound: under
platform/app/specs it was outside the parity roots, so it enforced
nothing.

* fix(scenarios): keep the logger external so the child keeps its transport

Inlining the child's whole graph took pino and thread-stream with it, and
they locate their transport's worker thread with
`join(__dirname, "worker.js")`. Inlined, __dirname is dist/server, the
lookup misses, and thread-stream reports it by rethrowing on nextTick —
an uncaught error, so the transport's own try/catch never sees it and the
child dies rather than degrading to stdout.

Every ordinary configuration reached it: pretty console logs (the dev
default) and the telemetry log transport both create a transport.
Verified against the pre-change bundle, which does not crash in any of
them.

The regression test spawns the real bundle under both configurations
rather than asserting on bundle text, because the failure is a runtime
crash on a worker thread and no string check would have caught it.

NEVER_INLINED now carries the rule that explains all of its entries: a
package that resolves a FILE relative to its own location cannot be
inlined, because inlining is what moves that location.

Startup is unchanged by this: median 1090ms -> 565ms.

* docs(specs): name child-process scenarios by outcome, not mechanism

The scenarios this PR added were titled after the build mechanism — SDK
inlining, require paths, package names, NODE_COMPILE_CACHE. The repo's
convention is that a feature file states what is observable, with the
mechanism in the body, so they now lead with the outcome that would be
lost: a simulation still reports its spans, configuring log output does
not stop one starting, repeat runs do not repeat the same startup work.

Assertions are unchanged; only titles and their bound annotations move.

* fix(app-layer): drop the App's scenarios accessor, and load env for the seed

Two loose ends the rebase onto main surfaced.

The App still declared and assigned `scenarios`, whose only member was
the orphan reconciliation this branch deletes. `AppDependencies` no
longer carries it and no preset sets it, so the accessor was a reference
to a property that does not exist — caught by CI typecheck, which reads
what `pnpm typecheck` alone does not.

`prisma:seed` runs `tsx prisma/seed.ts` directly, and unlike the Prisma
CLI that loads no env file, so the seed died on env validation and every
`haven up` logged "seed failed (continuing)" and left the stack with no
organization, project or admin login. It now loads .env then
.env.portless. Node applies those without overriding variables already
in the environment, and applies the later file over the earlier, so
haven's injected DATABASE_URL still wins and .env.portless still beats
.env — verified both directions rather than assumed, since getting it
backwards would seed the wrong database.

* fix(seeds): load env in the remaining seed scripts too

prisma:seed was not the only one running bare tsx: seed:sample-traces,
seed:realistic-platform, seed:mass, seed:retention and
seed:langy-prompts all died the same way on env validation, so
`haven db seed demo` got as far as the identity seed and then failed
before writing any scenarios, suites or traces.

Same flags and the same reasoning as prisma:seed — .env then
.env.portless, neither overriding a variable already in the
environment, so haven's injected DATABASE_URL still wins.

* perf(scenarios): issue the prefetch lookups together

The scenario, the project, the target adapter and the suite config are
independent lookups keyed off ids the caller already holds, but they ran
as four sequential awaits. This is on the path between a run being
queued and its child starting, and it runs once per simulation.

The checks keep their original order, so the error reported for a given
failure is unchanged; a doomed run may now have issued the other queries
before finding out, which is the trade for removing three round trips
from every healthy one.

* feat(scenarios): announce the child's environment as soon as it is known

Groundwork for starting the child while the prefetch is still running,
rather than after it. The child's environment needs exactly two
prefetched values — the scenario's labels and the project's API key —
and both land well before the adapter data, suite config and model
params that make up the slow half.

prefetchScenarioData now takes an optional onChildEnvReady, called once
those two resolve. Nothing calls it yet, so behaviour is unchanged; the
next step is the processor spawning against it.

It stays silent for a run that is already doomed — no scenario, a failed
project lookup, or a project with no API key — so a child is never
started for a run that is about to fail. Failures are still reported by
the ordered checks that follow; this signal never decides a run.

Note this keeps one fresh process per run. The child is started earlier,
never reused.

* refactor(scenarios): give the child's environment one definition

The child may soon be started at either of two moments — as soon as its
inputs are known, alongside the rest of the prefetch, or on the ordinary
path once the prefetch has finished. Two callers building that
environment separately is how they drift, and the symptom would be a
child behaving differently depending on when it happened to start.

So it moves to one module with one entry point, buildChildEnvironment,
which composes the OTEL resource attributes, the log context, the TLS
resolution and the variable whitelist. The processor now calls it rather
than assembling the pieces itself.

Everything it needs is derivable from the job data, the parent's own
process env, and the two prefetched values in ChildEnvInputs — which is
precisely what makes starting a child early possible.

No behaviour change: same variables, same values, same single fresh
process per run.

* fix(simulations): address review findings on the execution path

Five real defects, from CodeRabbit's pass:

The queued handler stamped lastActivityAtMs from business time while
every other writer and the wake used scheduling time. That is the bug
schedulingRef was added to prevent, fixed for nextWakeAt but not for the
stored stamp: a backed-up subscriber delivers a queued event older than
the stall threshold, and the first wake calls a run that just started
stalled.

finishRun detected an identity gap with a falsy check but filled it with
??=, so an empty-string id was detected, paid for the loadPriorEvents
lookup, and then kept its empty value anyway.

The metrics repository picked the target ClickHouse from rows[0] and
asserted the single-tenant invariant in a comment. It now checks, so a
mixed batch cannot write one tenant's rows into another's database.

The bundle's transport regression test asserted only the absence of
errors in stderr, which is also what an unlaunched child produces. It
now pins the exit first.

Plus comments that contradicted their code: the ADR called outbox
dispatch unbounded when it is five attempts, the execute payload claimed
to need no mapping when the handler renames two fields, and cancellation
still said queued runs are never picked up.

Also: two test describes renamed to conditions, and the stalled spec's
dead section headers, wrong pending count, and watchdog-naming Given.

* fix(simulations): validate the queued target instead of casting it

buildSimulationRunEventView accepted any non-null object as a target.
The view is persisted and parsed back on the way in, so a malformed one
did not degrade — it threw there, and a throwing handler redelivers,
turning bad data into a loop rather than a run that fails once.

It now parses against the schema's own target shape and normalises a
failure to null, which is the case handleRunQueued already answers by
finishing the run unexecutable with a named error.

Also pins the lastActivityAtMs clock fix from the previous commit: the
late-delivery test asserted only nextWakeAt, so the stored stamp could
have regressed to business time unnoticed.

* docs(events): state the real reason the finished-event ECST fields are optional

The comment said they were optional so events written before 2026-08-06
still parse. They do not: the schema pins `version` to a literal, so an
event written under an older version fails that check long before these
fields are read.

The optionality is still right — the caller need not supply them and
FinishRunCommand backfills from prior events — so the comment now says
that instead of claiming a compatibility guarantee the schema does not
offer.

* docs(subscribers): correct the broadcast recovery claim for terminal events

The comment said a premature refetch is corrected by the next event's
broadcast. Mid-run that is true. On `finished` it is not — nothing
follows the last event, so there is no later broadcast to correct
anything.

The real mitigation for the terminal case is already in the design and
was buried in the same sentence: `finished` carries `status` in the
payload, so a client that refetches early learns the terminal state from
the message rather than from what it read back. Says that now.

* fix(seeds,tests): seed the default prompt tag, and mirror the real cancel payload

The seed creates no prompt tags, but `production` is the one
resolveLangyPrompt reads by default — so seed:langy-prompts fails on
every fresh stack with "Invalid tag" until someone creates it by hand.
It is now upserted alongside the organization, with the same fixed id as
the rest of the local identity.

The cancellation integration test's publish mock sent
`batchRunId: null`. The real handler passes only projectId and
scenarioRunId, and the field is `batchRunId?: string` — optional, not
nullable, with a doc comment saying the cancel intent does not carry it.
The mock was proving a message shape production never sends.

* fix(ci): restore the generated files and satisfy typecheck:tests

Two self-inflicted CI failures.

The generated files were swept into a commit by `git add -A` after a
local regeneration wrote them with spaces where the committed copies use
tabs — 178 lines of pure whitespace churn, and biome's formatter check
rejects it. Restored to main's copies; neither had a content change.

The typecheck failure was four latent errors in test files. They were
invisible until now because the job runs `typecheck` before
`typecheck:tests`, so the earlier app.ts failure stopped the job before
the test project was ever checked. Fixing the first exposed the second.

Of those: the process test imported SimulationRunProcessEventView from
the module that imports it rather than the one that exports it, and the
finishRun test's partial event literals and vi.fn() deps needed casts
the widened mock types no longer inferred.

* fix(simulations): record a duration for runs that actually ran

DurationMs was null for every run a customer executed and populated only
for seeded ones, so the UI showed no duration for real work.

The cause is that the field is optional on the finished event and the
live path never supplies it: the SDK ingest dispatches finishRun with
results and status only. Nothing was broken — it was simply never set.

The fold already holds both ends of the run, so it derives the duration
when the event omits it, and no new field has to cross the wire. A
supplied value still wins, since the runner knows its own elapsed time
better than two projected timestamps do, and a run with no StartedAt
stays null rather than inventing one.

Predates the process-manager migration; the ingest path is unchanged on
main.

* fix(haven): stop two stacks sharing a Redis database

RedisDBForSlug hashed the slug into 16 databases with no collision
check, and with a handful of live worktrees a collision is ordinary
rather than unlucky — three concurrent stacks were observed all holding
db 15.

That is not a mild clash. Redis carries the GroupQueue, so colliding
stacks share one job queue while writing to SEPARATE ClickHouse
databases: whichever worker claims a job projects it into its own
database. And because every stack seeds the same fixed local identity,
the tenant ids match perfectly, so nothing about the misplaced work
looks wrong.

AllocateRedisDB now probes from the slug's preferred index for a free
database, and the result is persisted on the stack. The read sites read
that persisted value rather than recomputing the hash — recomputing
would report a different database than the stack actually runs on, for
exactly the stacks a collision affected.

With all 16 held it warns and carries on rather than refusing to start,
naming the consequence so the collision is visible instead of silent.

* fix(simulations): stop runs sitting on "running" until a manual refresh

Two independent causes, both ending the same way: a finished run kept
rendering as running until the page was reloaded by hand.

The broadcast carries the terminal status as event-carried state, and
the client never read it — it only invalidated and refetched. The
broadcast can beat the fold commit, so that refetch can read back the
pre-terminal row, and `finished` is the last event, so no later
broadcast arrives to correct it. The status is now applied from the
event after the refetch settles, and only over a non-terminal cached
value, so a settled read is never downgraded.

Separately, an update arriving while the tab was hidden was dropped
rather than deferred, and nothing re-fired on return — so a run that
finished while you were on another tab stayed running regardless of the
race above. It is now deferred and flushed when the tab comes back.

isTerminalStatus joins isCancellableStatus in the enums. The two are not
complements: RUNNING is neither, so they do not partition the enum.

* fix(process-manager): budget the commit transaction for its lock wait

Observed in local dev: "transaction timeout was 5000 ms, however 7737 ms
passed" on the process-store commit.

Prisma's 5s interactive default measures the whole transaction, and the
first thing this one does is take a BLOCKING advisory lock on the
process reference. So the budget has to cover however long a concurrent
commit for the same process holds that lock — and a suite finishing
several runs at once produces exactly that contention. The transaction
was being killed for waiting, not for working.

The work inside is untouched and still small: a lock, a dedup read, a
compare-and-swap, and the inbox/outbox inserts. Only the allowance for
waiting moves, and maxWait moves with it — a commit that cannot get a
connection within maxWait fails before its timeout is ever relevant.

* fix(simulations): stop losing run metrics silently

When computeRunMetrics exhausts its retries it returns no events, so the
run's cost and latency never exist. Nothing repairs that afterwards —
the retry WAS the repair path — and it was logged at warn, so a run
permanently carrying no metrics looked like routine noise.

Now an error, with the trace and run ids and the window actually waited.
The window matters: "the trace was slower than 30s" and "the trace never
arrived" want different responses, and the log could not previously tell
them apart.

The trigger itself is untouched. Inverting it — trace-processing
emitting completion instead of the command polling for it — needs a
trace-settled event that does not exist, and deciding when an open-ended
trace is complete is the question the pull-and-retry design exists to
avoid answering. That wants an ADR, not a refactor.

* perf(scenarios): use the child bundle in dev while it is current

The bundle was gated behind NODE_ENV===production, so every other
environment shelled out to `pnpm exec tsx` and transpiled the child's
whole import graph at runtime — measured at 4-6s alone, and ~10s each
with the pool's three running at once. A simulation pays that per run,
so a suite spends minutes before any scenario starts.

Dev now uses the bundle too, but only while it is demonstrably current:
currency is mtime against everything under scenarios/execution, so
editing any child source sends the next spawn back to tsx by itself. The
fast path can never run code you did not build, and every failure
direction — missing bundle, unreadable directory — lands on tsx rather
than on stale code.

Measured: ~10s -> ~0.7s per spawn.

* refactor(scenarios): give the child's execution contract no outside importers

`execution/types.ts` is the wire contract between the scenario worker and the
child process it spawns. It is meant to move to the child's own package, so the
app can stop depending on the scenario runner and the production image can stop
shipping it.

One thing stopped that. `FieldMappingSchema` — how one agent input is filled,
from a scenario source or a literal — lived in the same file, and two callers
outside the child needed it: the suite target schema and the optimization-studio
DSL. The DSL is frontend-reachable, so the browser bundle reached into the
child's execution contract to read one small schema.

It now lives in `scenarios/field-mapping.ts`: zod and nothing else, so either
side can import it without dragging a dependency across the boundary. Nothing
outside `scenarios/execution/` imports the contract any more.

A guard test walks the real source tree and fails on a new outside importer,
because a boundary nobody checks is a boundary that lasts one PR. A second
scenario pins both schemas to the same mappings — a split that let the two
definitions drift would be worse than the coupling it removed, since a suite
would save a mapping the child then refused to parse.

* refactor(scenarios): take prefetchScenarioData's arguments by name

The Biome delta gate fails on violations a PR *adds*, and this branch added
one: `onChildEnvReady` made `prefetchScenarioData` a four-positional-argument
function, tripping `lint/complexity/useMaxParams` (1 -> 2).

Named parameters are this repo's house style for exactly this reason, so the
fix is the standard one rather than a suppression: one options object, and the
call now says which argument is which at every site.

The orphaned docblock is folded back onto the function it documents — the
`ChildEnvInputs` interface had been inserted between the two — and
`onChildEnvReady`'s contract moves into it as a `@param`.

No behaviour changes. The remaining `useMaxParams` violation in this file
(`fetchCodeAgentData`) predates the branch and is left alone, which puts the
count back at the base's 1.

* fix(simulations): address the review findings from the folded-in PRs

Seven follow-up branches are now merged here, so their review feedback belongs
here too.

The one that mattered: the test named "stamps the terminal status after the
refetch settles" could not observe that ordering. Its invalidate mock resolved
immediately, so stamping *before* the refetch passed it just as well. Replaced
by one that holds the promise open, asserts nothing is stamped while it is in
flight, then settles it. Verified by mutation — dropping the `await` fails the
new test and leaves the other 22 green, which is exactly the gap it was
reported to have.

Also:
- `applyRunUpdate` takes a named-parameter object, per house style.
- `missedWhileHiddenRef` says *why* one boolean covers every missed update:
  the flush refetches current state rather than replaying events, so N missed
  updates cost the same single refresh.
- `DurationMs` gains the finish-before-start case. The guard existed and was
  untested, so nothing pinned it against a negative duration.
- `COMMIT_TRANSACTION_OPTIONS` no longer conflates its two knobs. `timeout`
  covers the callback body, which is where the blocking advisory lock is
  waited on; `maxWait` covers connection acquisition before the body runs.
  The old comment implied maxWait covered the lock wait. Same values.
- `resolveChildProcessSpawn`'s docblock admitted the production fallback it
  actually has, instead of claiming production always uses the bundle.
- The child-source scan explains why it stops at the first match.
- The Redis allocation tests assert the documented cyclic probe order and the
  preferred-index fallback, not just uniqueness and range — either would have
  passed for an allocator that picked arbitrarily.

Declined, with reasons, in the PR discussion: globalising haven's `up` lock to
close the cross-slug allocation window, and "flush a debounced hidden update on
visibility" — the second is not a defect, the timer still fires and the update
is delayed only by the debounce it would have paid anyway.

* fix(simulations): record the stall reason on the terminal event

The stall watchdog put error: "stalled" on its finish intent, but the
finishRun command schema had no error field and the handler never read
one, so the reason was silently dropped and a stalled run recorded ERROR
with no explanation. The command now accepts the bare error and
synthesizes the same failure-results envelope the in-process failure
path writes, via buildFailureResults extracted to a shared module.

* feat(simulations): add a one-shot backfill closing historical stalled runs

Runs abandoned before the process manager existed have no process
instance, so no watchdog can ever finish them, and with read-time stall
derivation deleted they would render as in-progress forever. The
backfillStalledSimulationRuns task closes that population for good:
run once per environment after the deploy, it finds every non-terminal
run quiet for over a day across all ClickHouse instances and finishes
it ERROR "stalled" through the same idempotent path in-process
failures use. Its --dry-run mode measures the population first.

* refactor(simulations): drop the non-null assertion in the metrics batch guard

Destructuring the first row and guarding on it proves the same
invariant the rows.length check did, without rows[0]!.

* fix(simulations): put the stalled-run finder behind the repository door

The backfill task resolved ClickHouse clients directly, which the
client-access boundary test rightly rejects. The finder and the
per-instance enumeration now live in a repository module; the task only
consumes finders and never holds a client.

* test(simulations): pin that pre-parameters inbox rows still parse

* fix(simulations): move the metrics migrations past main's 00078

Main took key 78 for gateway spend billable quantities while this branch
was open. Both files move together - the rollup's materialized view reads
the base table, so the base must keep the lower key.

* test(scenarios): assert the prefetch mock against the object call shape

refactor(clickhouse): a client class, and a cluster name on every failure (#6947)

* fix(clickhouse): name the cluster on every ClickHouse failure

A ClickHouse error said what failed and never which server refused it. An
organization can be routed to its own private instance, so a rejection from a
customer's dedicated cluster and one from the shared cluster were the same log
line. On 2026-08-13 that ambiguity cost an afternoon: ~5.6k rejections in three
hours had to be attributed by reading the concurrency limit out of the vendor's
error text ("Maximum: 25") and matching it against terraform, because 25 is the
private-instance default and the shared cluster runs 300.

The name already existed and was thrown away. `CLICKHOUSE_URL__<label>__<orgId>`
carries a human label, documented as "ignored by code". Keep it, and stamp it on
every failure line as `cluster`.

Kept separate from the existing `instance` field rather than replacing it:
`instance` is a metrics label, and repointing it would move every existing
series and break the dashboards built on them. `cluster` only has to be readable
by a person looking at one error.

Parsing moved to its own module. It is a string split, and it lived in a file
that imports Prisma — so testing it meant generating a Prisma client first,
which is why the edge cases had no tests. Now pinned: a label containing the
separator still routes on the trailing org id (splitting on the FIRST "__" would
send "acme__eu" to org "eu"), and an unlabelled variable falls back to the org
id so the field is never empty.

Also stops logging a private ClickHouse URL verbatim. Those URLs embed
`user:password@host`, and the duplicate-URL branch put one straight into the log
sink; it now logs the cluster name.

* wip(clickhouse-client): replace the middleware pipeline with a client class

INCOMPLETE — 14 tests in tracing.test.ts and retry.test.ts still call the old
middleware forms. Committed so the work is not lost, not for review.

Drops compose()/QueryMiddleware/QueryExecutor and replaces them with
ClickHouseQueryClient, which holds its collaborators and runs them in a stated
order rather than one implied by a list's index. The order is unchanged and
still load-bearing, so it is written out as nesting in query():

  tenant guard   outermost — refuse before spending a span, a slot or a socket

feat(api): add v.rpc(), and fix an endpoint's success status at registration (#7077)

* feat(api): add v.rpc() for RPC-named endpoints

Mounts a dotted `<resource>.<verb>` name as a real POST, following the
existing `v.sse()` precedent: a pseudo-method over the same pipeline,
no new concepts. Endpoint identity is already `${method}:${path}`, so
versioning, forward-copying, `withdraw()`, the policy registry and the
OpenAPI generator all work unmodified.

Two grammars are asserted at registration rather than in review:
`assertRpcPath` pins the dotted lower-camelCase name, and
`assertRpcConfig` refuses `params` / `query`, so "every argument travels
in the JSON body" is enforceable instead of aspirational — a dotted path
has no `:param` to bind, and a query schema would smuggle arguments back
into the URL that the operation name is supposed to own.

See dev/docs/adr/094-rpc-endpoint-naming.md.

* fix(api): fix an endpoint's success status at registration

`serializeEndpointResult` chose between 200 and 204 by inspecting what
the handler returned, so an `output` schema accepting `undefined` gave
one operation two shapes: a body on the request that found something, an
empty 204 on the one that did not. Callers, the published document and
both SDKs each have to pick one.

`assertStatusInvariant` decides it once, when the endpoint is
registered. No `output`, or `z.void()` / `z.undefined()`, means the
endpoint never sends a body and always answers `status ?? 204`; any
other schema means the body is always present and it always answers
`status ?? 200`; a schema accepting undefined AND a value is refused.

That also retires a latent bug. The undefined branch used
`config.status ?? 204` while the value branch used `?? 200`, so an
endpoint declaring `status: 201` with an optional output answered 201
with an empty body — a created response whose own schema promised a
representation.

No endpoint declares such a schema today, so no wire behaviour changes;
what changes is that the next one cannot.

* fix(api): scope the status rule to value-returning handlers

Review was right that the comment overstated it. A handler that builds
its own `Response` owns status and body outright — that early return
predates this change and already bypassed output validation, because a
redirect, a file stream and a hand-built error all need it. `Handler`
in fact requires a `Response` when no `output` is declared, which makes
the no-output branch unreachable from typed code rather than the
guarantee the comment claimed.

Also takes the named-parameter convention on the two private helpers,
and gives the README's grammar block a fence language.

* feat(api): reject a bad RPC registration in the editor, not just at startup

The two RPC rules were runtime asserts only, so the first an author knew of
a malformed name or a `params` schema was a thrown error at service build.
Both are now stated at the type level as well, one line from the assert that
states the same thing:

- `RpcPath<T>` walks the dotted lower-camelCase grammar character by
  character. An illegal name reports as not assignable to
  `'"/endpoints" & RpcPathMustBeDottedLowerCamelCase'` — the alias carries
  the rule into the message, where the `never` that two intersecting string
  literals collapse to would have said only that something was wrong.
- `RpcConfig` closes `params` and `query` off as `never`, so the error lands
  on the key the author wrote rather than on the call.

The asserts stay, and are not redundant: types are erased, so they remain the
only guard for a JavaScript caller, for a config widened to `EndpointConfig`
through a helper, and for anything that arrived behind an `any`. The existing
grammar test feeds names in as a `string` and so cannot be judged by the type
— it now casts past the signature deliberately, which is exactly the caller
the asserts exist for, and says so.

`rpc-types.unit.test.ts` drives both statements from one table of names. Both
conditionals distribute over the union, so a single name the two disagree on
widens the result to `boolean` and stops the file compiling.

@langwatch/api: 154 unit tests pass (137 before), typecheck clean.

* feat(api): make the API description findable, and project the RPC surface from it

An agent pointed at a LangWatch instance had no way to reach the API
description. It was already public — `/api/gateway/v1/openapi.json` has
served it since the gateway contract pinned that URL — but the document is
titled "LangWatch API" and covers all 42 families, while the URL reads like
it belongs to the AI Gateway, and nothing pointed at it.

So this adds no second description of the API. It adds the locations a
client tries first:

  GET  /.well-known/openapi   the same document, by convention
  GET  /api/openapi.json      the same document, inside the namespace
  GET  /llms.txt              ~1 KB: what this is, how to authenticate
  POST /api/rpc.discover      the RPC operations and their schemas

All four read one `apiDocument` module — `gateway-openapi.ts` now reads it
too rather than importing the JSON a second time — so they cannot disagree.

`rpc.discover` is a projection, not a registry. Nothing registers with it
and it holds no state; it filters the published document to dotted
operations and reshapes them, so it cannot report an operation that does
not exist, omit one that does, or disagree about a schema. It recognises a
dotted name by calling `isRpcPath`, newly exported from `@langwatch/api` —
the same grammar `v.rpc` refuses a registration with, rather than a second
regex that agrees until one of them changes. It is itself a dotted POST,
because an endpoint describing a convention should obey it. It returns an
empty catalogue today, which is the derived design working: nothing needs
backfilling when the first family adopts RPC naming.

`/llms.txt` exists because of size. The document is 632 KB minified across
257 operations, and an agent that fetches it to answer "what is this
service" has spent most of a context window on one sentence. It leads with
`Authorization: Bearer`, because `auth-middleware.ts` accepts three
credentials and calls `X-Auth-Token` legacy in its own comments; leading a
new reader with it would teach the header we intend to retire.

Two traps, both of which fail silently:

Root-level paths. `start.ts` routes only `/api/*` and the OTLP aliases into
Hono, so `/.well-known/openapi` and `/llms.txt` would have met the SPA
fallback and been answered with the HTML shell and a 200. A discovery URL
that returns HTML and calls it success is worse than one that 404s. They
are dispatched on `isRootDiscoveryPath`, and proxied in dev by vite.

Two route files, not one. `check-openapi-route-coverage` reads a file's
declared `/api` basePaths and applies each to every registration in it. A
single app based at `/` declared none, so the gate saw none of the four
routes and went on reporting OK while covering nothing — the blind spot
`openapi-route-coverage.feature` names as the one it cannot catch about
itself. Splitting by basePath puts the two `/api` routes under the gate and
keeps its reported paths truthful; both carry a written reason in
UNPUBLISHED, with `rpc.discover` recorded as a `gap` to publish once the
catalogue stops being empty rather than pretended away.

No information is newly exposed: the same document has been public at the
gateway URL all along, nothing is read from the database, and no tenant
data is involved.

Route coverage 351 routes, up from 349 — the two is the evidence the gate
now sees them. 16 integration tests, 10 unit tests.

* fix(api): bind the discovery scenarios, and sort the import the merge moved

Two CI failures, both mine, both silent in the way their gates exist to
prevent.

`feature-parity` reported three unbound scenarios. I had merged their
`@scenario` annotations into the prose JSDoc above each test, which reads
better and does not bind: `collectAllBindings` scans forward from the end of
the annotation and requires the next token to be `it(`, skipping only
whitespace and complete comments. With the annotation inside a block, the
`*/` on the following line is what it meets instead, so the binding is
dropped — and a dropped binding is not an error anywhere, it just quietly
stops enforcing the scenario. The standalone `/** @scenario "..." */`
immediately above the test is the form that binds; the prose keeps its own
block above it.

`lint` reported `assist/source/organizeImports` on start.ts. Moving
`isRootDiscoveryPath` to `./server/openapi/discovery-locations` in the
two-file split put it out of order, and merging main reshuffled the
neighbours again.

@langwatch/api 154 unit tests, catalogue 10, discovery + gateway 16,
typecheck clean, lint exit 0, feature-parity exit 0 with 16/16 scenarios
bound in the new file.

* refactor(api): name the per-operation projection in the RPC catalogue

The Biome delta gate flagged one new violation: `buildRpcCatalogue` scored 13
against a limit of 10. That was worth taking rather than overriding — the
function was doing three things at once, and the loop body was the part with
a name it had never been given.

`rpcOperationFor` is that name: one path in, one operation or null out, which
is also the clearest statement of the rule that a dotted path documented
under anything but POST is not an RPC. `describedFields` replaces three
conditional spreads with one loop, and keeps the same contract — an absent
field is omitted rather than set to undefined, so the JSON carries no
null-valued keys a client has to reason about. `buildRpcCatalogue` is left as
what it always was: map, filter, sort.

Behaviour is unchanged; the 10 unit tests pass untouched, which is the point
of them being written against the projection rather than the loop.

Worth noting for anyone reading the earlier commits: `pnpm lint` exits 0 on
this rule, because complexity is a warning. The delta gate is what fails, on
the difference against the base — so a clean `lint` run is not evidence there
is nothing to fix here.

* fix(api): close the review findings, including two the tests were not catching

Ten CodeRabbit findings on the discovery and type-guard work. Two were real
defects; the rest were correctness of documentation and convention.

**The status invariant refused schemas whose status cannot move.**
`assertStatusInvariant` tested whether the output schema ACCEPTS `undefined`.
`z.string().default("x")` and `.catch("x")` accept it and then replace it with
a value, so they were refused at registration — but `serializeEndpointResult`
branches on what the schema PRODUCED, and these never produce `undefined`.
The endpoint always sends a body and always answers `status ?? 200`. Testing
the parsed value instead of acceptance is the property the status actually
depends on.

**The compile-time table was half vacuous.** `RpcPath<T>` does not distribute
— its checked type is `IsRpcPath<T>`, not a naked `T` — so
`CompilerAccepts<(typeof ILLEGAL)[number]>` collapsed twelve names into one
verdict. `IsRpcPath` of a mixed union is `boolean`, `boolean extends true` is
false, and the assertion reported "all rejected" whether one name leaked or
none did. It passed for the wrong reason and would have gone on passing.
`CompilerAcceptsEach` maps over the tuple so each name keeps its own verdict.
Verified by injection this time, in both directions: a legal name moved into
ILLEGAL, and an illegal one into LEGAL, each fails the typecheck.

The claim in ae4c29f's message that "both conditionals distribute over the
union" was wrong, and this is the correction.

**ADR-094 is the simulation process-manager ADR.** The RPC work cited that
number for an ADR that was never written, and the README linked a file that
does not exist — a live link to a real ADR about something else. Removed from
all four sites; the README section and the spec are the record until one is
written, with a note not to take the next number from main alone.

Also: `isRootDiscoveryPath` accepts a trailing slash and `root-discovery`
registers both spellings, so `/llms.txt/` cannot fall to the SPA and be
answered with the HTML shell and a 200; `vite.config.ts` derives its proxy
matcher from the same path list rather than repeating it, so a new location
cannot work in production and return HTML in development; named parameters on
the two test helpers; and the README no longer says "Both rules" above a list
of three.

refactor(typescript): move the workspace to TypeScript 7, and stop a typecheck filling a 9 GiB ceiling (#7081)

* refactor(typescript): move the workspace to TypeScript 7

TypeScript 7.0.2 is released. The repo had been typechecking with a
pinned preview of the same compiler (@typescript/native-preview, a dev
build from July) whose channel has since stopped moving, while the
workspace carried three compiler versions across its packages.

tsc IS the native compiler now, so the typecheck scripts invoke it
directly and the typecheck:legacy lane is deleted: under 7 there is no
second implementation for it to be a second opinion from, and CI never
ran it.

Two packages stay on TypeScript 6. sdks/typescript and mcp/typescript
publish bundled .d.ts through tsup's dts, which drives the old
programmatic compiler API; 7 does not expose it. Six is not free either
- tsup's dts worker sets baseUrl itself, which 6 makes a hard error, so
both need "ignoreDeprecations": "6.0" to build. That flag does not exist
in 7, so this is a runway of one major, not a resting state.

The compiler API moved behind typescript/unstable/*, and nothing parses
a string in-process any more. src/test-utils/tsAst.ts owns one API
session for the process and serves text through a virtual filesystem.
Two constraints in it were found by its tests rather than reasoned out:
a synthetic path inside the repo gets claimed by the app's tsconfig and
loads the whole 52 MB project, so parsing happens under a temporary
directory instead; and parsing is now a round trip, so the tree-wide
scans batch (4.5s) where per-file did not finish at all. The scan
functions therefore take a parsed SourceFile and the caller does the
parsing.

See ADR-099.

* perf(dev): stop a typecheck expanding into a nine gibibyte ceiling

A typecheck was seen using 9 GB on an 18 GiB laptop. The number is
exact, and that is the tell: CheckGoMemLimit resolved GOMEMLIMIT to half
the machine clamped to [4,10] GiB, so 18 gives exactly 9, and Go treats
that as a ceiling it expands toward rather than a reservation.

Sampled cold at four ceilings, the working set never left 2.3-3.5 GB
while the footprint tracked whatever it was allowed (9 GiB gives
9.08 GB, 6 gives 6.57, 3 gives 6.13). So the clamp drops to [3,6]: 6
cannot be what constrains a run that never needed it, and the floor
stays at 3 because a ceiling below the live heap is missed anyway, at
the price of collecting continuously to miss it.

The specific 6 is a judgement between measured points, not a measured
optimum - the laptop was at a load average of 80 and the wall clocks
were noise. ADR-099 records what the samples do and do not establish.

Separately, the app's tsconfig swept in a 7.7 MB generated Ajv
validator on 19 lines: a seventh of everything the compiler parsed,
carrying @ts-nocheck, with a sibling .d.ts the import resolves to
anyway. Excluded.

* refactor(typescript): carry the authz packages onto 7, and time the walk honestly

packages/authz and packages/authz-server landed from ADR-092 while this
branch was open, both on 5.9. The version guard added here caught them
on the rebase, which is the guard doing its job on its first day.

The tracked-file walk in mockSpecifierScan also grew past vitest's 10s
default hook timeout, because that tree gained a lot of test files in
the same window. The walk is one exchange with the compiler carrying
every candidate's text and now takes around 15s, so it says 120s and
says why: batched it is 20x cheaper per file than asking file by file,
which does not finish at all, and what is left is the price of a
compiler with no in-process parser.

* ci(mcp): typecheck the MCP server with tsc, not the removed tsgo binary

The MCP workflow invoked ./node_modules/.bin/tsgo directly. That binary
came from @typescript/native-preview, which this branch drops, so the
job exited 127 - command not found - and took mcp-javascript-complete
down with it while build_and_test passed.

mcp/typescript is one of the two packages held on TypeScript 6, so its
own tsc is the compiler to use. Verified by running the job's exact
command in the package.

Also drops "tsgo" from the app workflow's cache comment, which now
describes a binary the repo does not install.

* Address review comments

- Split the ADR in two. dev/docs/adr/README.md asks for one decision per
  ADR, and this recorded two: ADR-099 is now the compiler move, ADR-100
  the memory ceiling. Every reference repointed to whichever half it
  meant.
- Drop the stale two-row table from the ADR context. It carried a wall
  column that the paragraph below it said was deliberately absent, which
  was true of the table that replaced it and not of the one left behind.
- Correct the CLAUDE.md queue guidance. It claimed a bare tsc run does
  not take a slot; the bin shim means a whole-tree one does, as the

- Clear the overlay, the scratch directory and the counter when the AST
  session closes. Only the compiler child was being released, so a
  process that cycled sessions kept a copy of every file it had parsed.

  The scenario promises an operator's limit survives and the test only

perf(api): serve the OpenAPI document from bytes, and name the endpoint in logs (#7084)

* perf(api): serve the OpenAPI document from bytes, and name the endpoint in logs

Three routes published the OpenAPI document with `c.json(apiDocument)`, which
re-serialised a 5.8 MB object graph on every request. Measured on the real
artifact: 2.8 ms and 1.3 MB of garbage per hit, on the one surface an agent
polls speculatively to find out whether anything changed.

The document is a build artifact. It cannot change while the process is
running, so the result was identical every time.

    c.json(obj)             2.23 ms/req
    precomputed string      1.33 ms/req   (still re-encodes UTF-8 per write)
    precomputed Buffer      ~0 ms/req

Bytes rather than a string is most of the saving: a JS string is UTF-16 in
V8, so writing one to a socket encodes it again on every response, and the
Buffer lives in external memory where it adds no GC pressure. `Content-Length`
comes off `byteLength` rather than a second pass over the text.

Serving goes through one module, so the three locations cannot drift in how
they answer, and it now sets a content-derived ETag: a polling agent gets a
304 costing ~200 bytes instead of 688 KB, and two replicas of one artifact
agree on the tag without a build stamp. `If-None-Match` is parsed as the list
it is, weak prefix included — missing a hit there is not a wrong status so
much as 688 KB sent to a client that did not need it.

`rpc.discover` is projected once at module load for the same reason. An
earlier comment of mine claimed it was not worth caching because caching would
introduce staleness; both halves were wrong, and it re-walked 166 paths per
call for an answer fixed until the next deploy. It is still a projection, not
a registry — derived from the document exactly as before, just once.

Separately, the request log recorded the path that ARRIVED. With ids in it
that is a distinct value per request, so "which endpoint is failing" could not
be asked of it. `route` is the endpoint that matched, as registered —
`GET /things/:id` — set by the version-context middleware, which is first in
every endpoint stack, so it covers dated mounts and withdrawn 410s too. `url`
stays, because losing it would take the id with it.

That also fixes the error this started from:

    Response failed output validation for GET /things/:id

It stays a plain `Error`. We know the cause, but the caller cannot act on it —
the handler returned something its own declared schema rejects, which is our
bug — so it correctly degrades to "unknown" plus a trace id at the boundary
(ADR-045), and logs at 500/error precisely because it carries no `httpStatus`
or `fault`. What it lacked was saying which endpoint broke its own contract.

* fix(api): recognise a no-body output schema from either zod major

`isNoBodySchema` reads zod's internal type tag directly, because no probe can
separate `z.void()` from `z.object({...}).optional()` — both reject every
sample value a caller would think to try, `{}` included. It read only v3's
spelling.

The two majors name it differently. v3 carries `_def.typeName: "ZodVoid"`;
v4 carries `_def.type: "void"` and no `typeName` at all. So a v4 `z.void()`
output was not recognised as no-body, fell through to the ambiguity check,
accepted `undefined` and parsed it to `undefined` — and was refused at
registration. The service would fail to build, and the error would say the
schema "accepts undefined as well as a value", which is not what happened and
sends the reader looking at their schema rather than at the version boundary.

Nothing in this repo authors v4 schemas yet, so this is not a live bug. It is
a landmine on a path someone is currently walking: a repo-wide zod v4
migration is being planned in a parallel session, `zod@3.25.76` already ships
the v4 engine at `zod/v4`, and the first family to move would have hit this at
startup. The framework should not be the thing that breaks.

The docstring already anticipated exactly this — it said the test pins the tag
"so an upgrade that renames it fails there rather than silently reclassifying
every no-body endpoint as ambiguous". It now pins both spellings against the
real v4 engine rather than a hand-made shape, and the other half of the rule
is pinned across the boundary too: a v4 schema that genuinely admits both is
still refused.

Verified by reverting the fix: the two v4 recognition tests fail, and the
v4-ambiguity test keeps passing.

* fix(api): stop copying the document on every response

Review caught that the shared buffer was buying nothing on the 200 path, and
it was right. `new Response(bytes, ...)` COPIES the `Uint8Array`. Measured
over 200 responses against one shared 688 KB buffer:

    new Response(sharedBuffer)          arrayBuffers +134.4 MB
    new Response(stream(shared))        arrayBuffers +  0.0 MB
    new Response(shared.slice())        arrayBuffers +134.4 MB   (control)

134.4 MB is exactly 688 KB x 200 — a full copy per response, identical to
passing an explicit `.slice()`. So precomputing the bytes kept the CPU saving
and threw the allocation saving away, and the comment claiming "one allocation
for the life of the process" was simply false.

The body is now a `ReadableStream` that enqueues the shared bytes, which
measures at zero. Safe to enqueue the same array into concurrent streams: a
non-transferable stream does not detach or mutate what it is given, and
nothing writes to it. One caveat left in the comment rather than claimed away
— the Hono Node adapter may still copy on its way to the socket, but that is a
transient write buffer rather than a retained allocation, and below what this
module controls.

Also from review: `jsonBytesResponse` takes named parameters, and three
scenario titles that described implementation ("served from bytes prepared
once", "the tag is derived from the bytes") now describe what a caller
observes instead, with their `@scenario` annotations renamed to match.

perf(ci): run integration tests in the lane their dependencies call for (#7080)

* perf(ci): run integration tests in the lane their dependencies call for

The integration matrix took 12-13 minutes a shard, and measuring where that
time went contradicted the obvious explanation. It is not slow tests: per-file
durations on shard 4 are two outliers (90s, 40s) and then a cliff, with
everything else between 3 and 13 seconds. It is per-file fixed cost multiplied
by 1024 files, plus a lane that provisions three datastores for tests that never
open a socket.

Measured across the six shards of run 31977691802:

  import       1,664s   43%
  tests        1,408s   37%
  environment    381s   10%
  setup files    261s    7%
  transform      134s    3%

Loading modules cost more than running the tests.

SPLIT THE LANE. 546 of the 1024 `.integration.test.*` files declare jsdom and
name no database, queue or cache. They now run on `test-component`: no service
containers, no Prisma migration, no goose, no ClickHouse replay, no Helm, files
concurrent, module registry shared — the unit lane's configuration, which is
what those files always wanted. The datastore lane keeps the other 478 and drops
from six shards to four. Both configs derive their file list from
partitionIntegrationFiles, so the lanes are a total and disjoint cover by
construction rather than by a list someone has to maintain. Default is the
datastore lane, so a new test is never silently run without what it needs.

REUSE THE MODULE REGISTRY. `isolate: false` on the datastore lane. This is not
the concurrency knob that was tried and reverted: `fileParallelism` stays off,
files still run strictly one at a time, and only the per-file rebuild of the
module graph goes away. The unit lane has run this way across 1,688 files.

STOP REBUILDING THE NLPGO BINARY. The cache was restoring correctly and the
build ran anyway, every time, because staleness was decided by mtime — and git
records none, so checkout stamps every source with the current run's time while
the restored binary carries the time it was built in an earlier one. Every
source looked newer than every cached binary. Now a stamp beside the binary
records the digest of the sources it was compiled from.

BALANCE BY MEASURED COST. The sequencer weighed file size and the spread showed
it: 547-766s across near-identical file counts, with the matrix paying 766.
Weights now come from a committed manifest, falling back to size for files it
does not know. Committed rather than cached because every shard computes the
split independently and must reach the identical answer. Refresh by dispatching
the workflow and committing the artifact.

CACHE THE GENERATED FILES. `start:prepare:files` is 30-35s of pure function of
committed inputs, paid by every job. Now cached on a hash of those inputs, with
a verifier so a key that stops covering a generator fails at the step that owns
it instead of as a missing module minutes later.

CUT THE JOBS PER PUSH. One push fans out to 27 runs and 98 jobs against a
Team-plan allowance of the same order, which is why shards were measured waiting
286-590s for a runner while their only dependency finished in 8 seconds. Draft
gating goes from 8 workflows to 18 via a `heavy` output on the shared
detect-changes action, and CodeQL's matrix now follows the languages that
actually changed instead of running every analyser whenever any of six trees is
touched.

Verified: 546+478=1024 with zero overlap on the real tree; 162 component-lane
files (1336 tests) pass with no datastore; 50 new unit tests; all three specs
fully bound; actionlint and biome clean; scoped typecheck of the changed configs
clean.

Note: `src/pages/[project]/` made this nearly a silent disaster — handed to a
glob engine unescaped, `[project]` is a character class, and those twelve files
would have been selected by neither lane while both reported a clean pass.
Include patterns are escaped, with a test.

* fix(navigation): wait on a drawer warm-up promise from any realm

The component lane's first CI run failed one test: a warmed drawer rendered its
spinner instead of opening at once. It reproduced locally under `pool: vmForks`
and passed under `pool: forks`, which named the cause.

`primeLazyComponent` settles a drawer's ready-state by reading its `lazy()`
wrapper outside render. A wrapper that is not ready reports that by THROWING the
promise it is waiting on, so the warm-up has to recognise a promise to know it
must wait — and it asked `pending instanceof Promise`.

`instanceof` asks which realm made the value, not whether it behaves like a
promise. A browser has one realm, so this held everywhere it had ever run. Give
each test file its own VM context and the thrown promise comes from the other
realm, fails the check, and the warm-up returns WITHOUT waiting: the drawer is
reported warm while still pending, and paints the spinner after all.

Duck-type the thenable instead. `then` is what React itself looks for and what
the promise contract specifies; realm identity was never the question being
asked. Same class of bug as the `dedupe: ["zod"]` note in CLAUDE.md.

Not a production bug — one realm in a browser — but the check was wrong on its
own terms, and it was only ever going to be found by something that runs the
code in more than one place.

Pinned by a unit test that builds a genuinely foreign promise with
`runInNewContext` and asserts both halves: that `instanceof` rejects it, and
that it is awaited anyway.

* fix(ci): keep the component lane on vmForks, and quarantine the location mockers

Three corrections from the first CI run and a full local pass of the lane.

TYPE ERROR. `isThenable` narrows to PromiseLike, and `PromiseLike.then` returns
PromiseLike — not the `Promise<void>` primeLazyComponent declares. Adopt the
foreign thenable with `Promise.resolve()`, which is both what the signature
wants and the right semantics: a bare PromiseLike carries no catch/finally.

POOL. `pool: "forks"` looked right on the reasoning that these files ran on
forks under the integration config for their whole history, so a move should not
change the environment. Measured, that is backwards: forks + isolate:false
failed 87 of 236 files in src/components, against 4 under vmForks. They ran on
forks with isolate:TRUE — a fresh registry per file. Reusing one registry inside
a plain process is what leaks module state between files; a VM context is what
makes reuse survivable, and it is why the unit lane runs 1,688 files that way.
The two settings are a pair, not independent knobs. Reverted, with the
measurement written down so the next person does not retry it.

WINDOW.LOCATION. Five files replace `window.location` wholesale via
defineProperty. Measured directly in a VM realm, jsdom defines it as a
NON-CONFIGURABLE ACCESSOR: it cannot be deleted ("Cannot delete property
'location'") and cannot be redefined ("Cannot redefine property: location"). The
setter means assignment still works; replacing the object never will. That is
incompatible with a VM context wherever it runs — these files would fail the
same way on the unit lane — so it is not something the split caused. They are
held in the datastore lane by a named list that says exactly why and how to
convert them, so 541 files move while the incompatibility stays attributed.

Also fixed, both real bugs on their own terms:
  - test-setup.ts's matchMedia polyfill omitted `configurable`, so a test could
    assign it but never redefine it — which is how you swap matchMedia to
    simulate prefers-reduced-motion. A stand-in for a missing browser API has no
    business being less replaceable than the API it imitates.

Local state: 453 of 455 component-lane files pass (3,201 tests). The two that
fail pass in isolation, so they are order-dependent under the shared registry —
the documented isolate:false risk, and the reason CI's own sharding is the
place to judge it rather than a local run with different file ordering.
`pnpm typecheck` is clean; `typecheck:tests` was OOM-killed locally twice with
no diagnostics, so CI is the authority on that one.

* refactor(navigation): put full-page navigation behind a seam, and delete the quarantine

Replaces the "hold these five files back" list with the fix it was standing in
for. The list is gone; all five run in the component lane.

The five replaced `window.location` wholesale to observe a navigation. Measured
in a jsdom VM realm, every way of doing that fails:

  Object.defineProperty(window, "location", ...)  -> Cannot redefine property
  vi.spyOn(window, "location", "get")             -> Cannot redefine property
  vi.spyOn(window.location, "reload")             -> Cannot redefine property
  vi.stubGlobal("location", ...)                  -> Cannot redefine property

`location` is a non-configurable ACCESSOR and its methods are non-configurable
and non-writable. Assigning `href` is the one thing that works, and jsdom then
logs "Not implemented: navigation" and records nothing — so a test cannot
observe a navigation a component performs directly, by any means. The tests that
appeared to were relying on a pool where jsdom left `location` replaceable.

So the fix is a seam, not a workaround: src/utils/browserNavigation.ts exports
hardNavigate / replaceLocation / reloadPage, the three call sites use it
(auth/error, auth/signin, LegacyTracesDeprecationBanner), and the tests
`vi.mock` the module and assert the call. A module import is substitutable in
any environment, which a global accessor is not. It is better production code on
its own terms too — a component writing `window.location.href` directly is
untestable by construction.

LangyEvalRunCard needed none of that: it only READS `location.origin`, so it now
declares the document's URL with `@vitest-environment-options` and reads the real
origin. A true URL is a better fixture than a stand-in object.

useLicenseActions keeps its regression guard. The hook must NOT reload — a
reload used to tear the restart toast off the screen — and the guard now asserts
`reloadPage` was not called rather than spying on an unspyable global.

Also from review: the draft gate in detect-changes checked only `pull_request`,
so a draft `pull_request_target` still ran everything heavy. Both event names
carry the same payload; both are checked now.

Verified: all ten files across the five previously-quarantined suites pass in
the component lane (45 tests); partition back to 546/478 of 1024 with no
overlap; biome clean.

* fix(ci): isolate the component lane, so a passing run means the same thing twice

Measured over the full 546-file lane, twice each way:

  isolate: false -> 545/546. A DIFFERENT file fails each run —
                    GlobalUpgradeModal and LangyComposerRecordedTurn one run,
                    SavedChartsToolbar the next. All pass in isolation.
  isolate: true  -> 546/546, 3,987 tests, no failures.

The files this lane took are React component suites, and a shared module
registry turns "has this lazy chunk resolved yet" and "what is in this zustand
store" into global state that the FILE ORDER decides. The result is a rotating
one-file flake: the most expensive kind of red, because it accuses an innocent
file and does not reproduce when you run it.

Registry reuse came in by inheritance from the unit lane, not by choice, and
nothing about this lane's purpose needs it. The win is not booting a Postgres, a
ClickHouse and a Redis, not running two migrations and a Helm setup, and running
the files concurrently rather than one at a time. All of that stands. A
deterministic suite is worth more than the import time reuse saves.

The pool stays inherited (vmForks), and the note explaining why is kept: forks
with a shared registry was measured worse still, 87 of 236 files failing.

* fix(ci): address review — CodeQL gate, cache key, empty manifest, draft e2e

Seven findings from review, six of them real bugs.

CODEQL COULD SKIP ITSELF. `relevant` is the outer gate, and it had drifted from

* fix(ci): keep isolation on in the datastore lane too

The full CI matrix returned the verdict: with `isolate: false`, three of four
integration shards went red, and shard 2 alone failed 30 of its 120 files.

The errors name the cause rather than hinting at it — "Cannot resolve ClickHouse
client", "App not initialized", ECONNREFUSED. These suites build and tear down
an application container per file, and that container lives in module scope.
Share one registry across files and the first file's teardown takes the next
file's client with it.

That is not the `fileParallelism` hazard — nothing here runs at once — but it
has the same root: this suite keeps real per-file lifecycle state in module
scope. The unit and component lanes can share a registry precisely because they
build no containers.

So R2 comes out. It was the second-largest projected win (1,664s of import
against 1,408s of test execution, 43% of integration runner time), and it is
simply not available while a fresh module graph is what gives each file its
container. Reclaiming it means giving the app container an explicit reset
between files — a real change to the harness, and its own PR, where the
failures it causes are the subject rather than collateral.

What the measurement leaves standing, and what CI has now confirmed:
