fix(langevals): stop self-hosted evaluators crashing on dspy thread-affinity and retry-storming 400s (#7129)

* fix(langevals): stop llm_answer_match crashing on a long-lived server

dspy 3 pins global-settings ownership to the thread that first calls
dspy.settings.configure. The answer-match evaluator called it on every
evaluation, so on a long-lived server with a request threadpool the first
request configured dspy and every later request on another pool thread raised
"dspy.settings can only be changed by the thread that initially configured
it." On the SaaS lambda tier each request is a fresh process, so the crash
only showed on self-hosted deployments.

The configure call sets experimental=True, which dspy 3 no longer needs for
dspy.Predict, so removing it fixes the crash with no behaviour change. A
regression test runs the evaluator from two worker threads and fails on the
old code with the exact error.

* fix(langevals): fail fast on provider 400s instead of retrying them

A content-policy block or a bad parameter is a deterministic 400: retrying it
three times only burns time. Worse, on a real Azure content filter the retry
loop took about 138s, past the control plane's 120s request timeout, so the
customer saw an opaque timeout instead of "content policy violation". The
retryer now skips litellm.BadRequestError (the parent of
ContentPolicyViolationError) and returns the real error on the first attempt,
which brought the same case down to about 44s. Transient errors still retry.

* test(langevals): guard the dspy thread crash with a test CI actually runs

The thread regression test lived in `evaluators/langevals/tests/`, which
langevals-ci ignores wholesale because the LLM-judged tests in it are
non-deterministic. The guard therefore never ran outside a developer's machine.

It was also unreliable where it did run. dspy compares `threading.get_ident()`
values, and CPython gives a new thread the identifier of one that just exited,
so starting a worker and joining it before starting the next handed the second
worker the first one's identifier and dspy's owner check passed by accident.
Measured on this repo: 10 runs against the pre-fix evaluator, sequential
start-then-join reproduced the crash only some of the time.

Replaced with a version that holds 4 workers on a barrier, so they overlap and
every one gets an identifier of its own. That is also the real shape of the
server, which serves requests from a threadpool. It reproduces the crash 10 out
of 10 times against the pre-fix evaluator and passes 10 out of 10 with the fix.

The call out to the provider is stubbed with litellm's `mock_response`, so the
test needs no API key, makes no provider request and answers the same way every
time. Everything else stays the real path: the real `model_to_dspy_lm`, the real
`dspy.Predict`, the real adapter parsing. langevals-ci names the file in a step
of its own, which also means it runs on fork pull requests, where no secret is
available.

* test(langevals): stop the retry tests waiting out the real backoff

The transient case walks all 3 attempts, so it sat through the evaluator's real
`wait_random_exponential` backoff: about 4 seconds per run, and a different
number of seconds every run because the wait is randomised. These tests assert
how many attempts happen, never how long the evaluator waits in between, so the
wait bought nothing.

An autouse fixture swaps the wait for `wait_none`. The file now runs in 0.2s
instead of 4.5s and takes the same time on every run.

* fix(langevals): keep the server responsive and size workers by the real CPU limit

Three load-behavior fixes for self-hosted langevals, found by running the
published image in a 1 CPU / 2Gi container and blasting it with evaluations:

1. The evaluate endpoint was an async handler running the fully blocking
   evaluate_batch on the event loop, so one evaluation froze every other
   endpoint including /healthcheck (13.8s observed against a 5s readiness
   probe timeout). The endpoint is now sync, so it runs in a worker thread,
   with a process-wide lock that keeps the existing one-evaluation-at-a-time
   environment-variable semantics and returns 503 when the queue is full
   instead of letting requests pile up forever.

2. get_cpu_count read only the cgroup v1 cpu.shares file, which no current
   Kubernetes or Docker runtime has, so a limited pod booted one heavy worker
   per HOST core: the 1-CPU test container booted 5 workers idling at 1.7Gi
   of its 2Gi, and 5 concurrent PII evaluations got 3 workers SIGKILLed by
   the kernel while the pod stayed Running with 0 restarts. The function now
   reads the cgroup v2 cpu.max quota first and also honours WEB_CONCURRENCY.
   The same blast on 1 worker: all requests pass, no kill.

3. The per-request evaluation parallelism (50) is now configurable via
   MAX_EVALUATIONS_IN_PARALLEL for CPU-bound evaluators on small pods.

The responsiveness regression test drives the real ASGI app in-process with
no API keys; it fails on the old handler and passes on the new one. The
worker-count tests fake the two cgroup files.

* chore(langevals): sync uv.lock with the 3.0.0 workspace versions

The lockfile still recorded the workspace members at 2.2.0 while every
pyproject says 3.0.0, so uv treated the lock as invalid: each uv run or
uv sync re-locked, rewrote the file, and re-anchored the rolling
exclude-newer stamp. Locally that dirtied the tree on every command and
in CI it meant dependencies resolved at install time instead of coming
from the pin.

The refresh changes only the nine workspace member versions and the
recorded exclude-newer anchor. No external package version moves, and
uv lock --check now passes, so the file stays put.

* fix(langevals): never let worker-count detection stop the server booting

Review findings on get_cpu_count, all three confirmed against the code by
running the new tests on the previous version:

- An empty override raised `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10`
  and killed the boot. `CPU_COUNT: ""` is what a manifest produces for a value
  an operator left blank, and this PR had just added a second variable with the
  same problem, `WEB_CONCURRENCY`. An override that is empty, not a number, or
  not positive is now treated the same as unset.
- A cpu.max period of 0 raised `ZeroDivisionError`, which the surrounding
  `except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError)` did not catch.
- A cgroup file that exists but cannot be read raised `PermissionError` out of
  the function, because only `FileNotFoundError` was caught. Both cgroup reads
  now catch `OSError`, so an unreadable file falls through to local detection
  the same way a missing one does.

get_cpu_count runs while the server boots, so any of these took the pod down
instead of falling back to the next source.

Also strengthened one existing test and fixed leaking test state:

- `test_cgroup_v2_without_limit_falls_through` asserted `>= 1`, which
  get_cpu_count satisfies by construction, so it passed no matter what the
  function did. It now sets cpu.shares and asserts the exact fall-through
  result.
- test_server_responsiveness set sys.argv and DISABLE_EVALUATORS_PRELOAD at
  import time and never put them back. pytest imports every test module during
  collection, so the whole session inherited fake command-line arguments and a
  disabled preload. Both are restored right after the import, which is the only
  point they are needed, and the app is still built with the same routes.

16 keyless tests pass, up from 9.

* fix(langevals): let bad queue-knob values fall back instead of stopping boot

LANGEVALS_QUEUE_TIMEOUT and MAX_EVALUATIONS_IN_PARALLEL were parsed with
bare float()/int() at import time, so a blank value in a manifest crashed
the server at boot, the same failure class the worker-count overrides had.
Both now go through shared positive-value parsers that read blank,
non-numeric and non-positive values as unset. The float parser also
rejects nan and inf, which make a lock timeout meaningless.

The responsiveness test now waits for the evaluation to hold the lock
instead of sleeping a fixed 0.2s, so the healthcheck is provably sent
while an evaluation runs, and it times the healthcheck call itself.

* feat(governance): the pulled_usage aggregate, one priced record per usage item

ADR-088 rung 1. The shipped ingestion-pull aggregate is per-source and its
RUN_COMPLETED carries only an event count, so a pulled usage item has nowhere
to be priced. This adds its sibling: `pulled_usage`, one ordered stream per
usage ITEM, carrying `PulledUsageObserved` and the `RecordPulledUsage` command
that mints it.

Two keys, and the difference between them is the correction mechanic. The
aggregate id is the restatement key — dimension-only, cost and quantities
excluded — so every version of one bucket lands on one stream and a
correction can match the figure it corrects. The idempotency key is the same
coordinates WITH the money and quantities, so an unchanged re-pull produces an
identical key and never appends at all, while a corrected bucket differs and
does. The no-op is structural rather than a downstream comparison.

Time carries two fields on purpose. `observedAtMs` is the monotonic pull
instant and is the only field a restatement can be ordered by; `occurredAtMs`
is the provider's business bucket, which a restatement of that period leaves
unchanged and so cannot order anything. Neither is named `occurredAt`: that is
a command-envelope field the envelope strip would delete from the event data.

No writer yet — the ledger write, the puller seam and the adapters are the
rungs above this one.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019NundTW7Sdt3UeSgUf9GN1

* feat(governance): price a pulled usage item once, and say whether it is exact

ADR-088 rung 3. Two paths into one integer. A provider that reports its own
cost has that figure carried verbatim, scaled from the decimal STRING rather
than the float, because `Number * 1e9` on a six-decimal amount lands cents off
at the sums an invoice reaches. A provider that reports only quantities is
priced through the same `rateSpendNanoUsd` the gateway spend spine uses, so
pulled and gateway cost can never be rated by two different tables and then
compared to each other.

`costStatus` is not derivable from `costBasis` and the code says so in its
types. A provider-reported figure can be the invoice (an Anthropic cost report)
or an approximation of one (a metered-unit charge), so the adapter declares it.
A computed figure has exactly one honest answer, so that path does not take a
status as input at all and cannot be argued into `exact` — there is a test that
smuggles one past the type to prove the runtime agrees.

Binds the two @unit scenarios in specs/governance/pulled-usage-cost-reporting.feature,

* fix(governance): stop betting on Databricks' timestamp unit, and on a message being finished

Two ways the Genie sweep could report nothing wrong while losing the records
it exists to capture. Both were found by an independent review of the diff.

**The timestamp unit was a guess.** `created_timestamp` is an integer and
Databricks does not document what it counts. Its REST reference and its Genie
guide both example the field as `1719769718` — ten digits, seconds — while
most other Databricks APIs stamp milliseconds. The adapter assumed
milliseconds and compared the value straight against the watermark.

If the wire format is seconds, every message lands in January 1970, sits
behind a first run's `now - 30 days` watermark, and the source pulls zero
messages forever with no error anywhere. We cannot settle the question
without a live workspace, so the adapter no longer bets: values below 1e11 are
seconds and are scaled. That boundary is 1973 read as milliseconds and the
year 5138 read as seconds, so no real timestamp is ambiguous.

**A message is not immutable while it is being answered.** Databricks fills
`attachments` progressively; a message read at `IN_PROGRESS` or
`EXECUTING_QUERY` carries the question but not the generated SQL. Both sinks
replace on the message id, so a later read corrects the earlier one — but a
completed sweep moved the watermark past it, so no later read ever happened.
A question whose warehouse query outlived the sweep kept its record and lost
its SQL, permanently and silently.

Such a message now holds the watermark through the existing `hadGap`
machinery: the record still lands immediately, and the sweep comes back for
it. `pending` is kept distinct from `failed` because they mean opposite
things — one is something we could not read, the other something we read too
early — even though both have the same consequence. A message that never
settles is let go after an hour, so a stuck one cannot pin the window forever.

The file header claimed the opposite ("a message is immutable, so restatement
never happens here"). That claim was the reasoning that would have stopped the
next reader from finding this, so it is corrected rather than merely
outvoted. Its neighbouring claim that all three API facts were verified
against a live workspace is also corrected: the live evidence tier is skipped
without a credential, and these two rest on the docs.

Reviewing my own previous commit. Holding the watermark for an in-flight
message was right; making that hold a boolean was not.

`pending` fed the sweep-wide `hadGap`, which is all-or-nothing: one message

being answered is neither — a workspace with real traffic has something

* fix(governance): pin where a pull source may send its stored credential

A source's config named any host `z.string().url()` would accept, and the
worker attached the decrypted upstream token to every request it sent there.
Reaching an attacker's host needed no knowledge of the secret: the config was
readable, the credential travelled in it as an opaque envelope, and
re-encryption is deliberately idempotent — so anyone who could edit a source
could hand the envelope back unchanged beside a new `workspaceUrl` and have
the next scheduled run decrypt a token they had never seen and post it there.
`ssrfSafeFetch` is no defence: it rejects private destinations, which is a
different threat.

- Genie configs must name an https Databricks workspace host, checked on
  create AND update, where the rejection can still be shown to whoever made
  the change. Adapters with no fixed destination are left alone rather than
  given a rule that would be disabled immediately.
- The stored envelope is no longer sent to clients, and one arriving FROM a
  client is refused. Rotating means sending a new secret.
- An update that carries no secret keeps the stored one, so a rename cannot
  silently clear it now that the client no longer echoes it back.

the host changed, and the ciphertext was preserved verbatim.

  list from its new text filter — the confirmation and the act cover
  the same groups by construction.
- Per-attempt error history: ProcessManagerOutboxAttempt records each
  FAILED delivery (successes write nothing), with the DispatchError
  diagnostic preserved for the ops surface and untyped errors still
  redacted. Attempt rows cascade with their message under the existing
  retention sweep. The Dead Letters row expansion shows the attempts
  oldest first, so why a message died is on the page, not only on a
  span.
- One vocabulary: redrive/discard on both substrates; the DLQ card's
  'Replay' verbs renamed so replay stays reserved for projection
  rebuilds.
- The /ops stat strip's dead-letter tile is now the union of both
  substrates ('N queue · M outbox'), red when nonzero, linking to the
  dead-letters page — it read 0 while 94 outbox messages sat dead.

* fix(ops): reap discarded rows, and order attempt history by time

Audit findings on the dead-letter work, plus the CI gates it tripped.

Retention: the sweep has three families - dispatched, dead, inbox - and
none of their predicates match `discarded`. Left as it was, the one
terminal state an operator writes would have been the only one that
never ages out, on the highest-volume table in the system. Discarded
rows now ride the dead family, on the same window and the same index:
both are a record of work that will never run, kept for as long as
someone might ask about it.

Attempt history: a redrive resets `attempts` to 0, so a message that
failed, was redriven, and failed again holds two entries numbered 1.
The number was the React key and the sort key, which made it a
duplicate key and an interleaved history. Rows now carry their id and
order by `occurredAt`.

Also: the in-memory store now drops attempt rows with their message, so
the fake stops modelling a leak the durable store does not have.

Typecheck: two stub stores in the test tree were missing the new
interface methods, and a mock's `useQuery` took no argument. Only
`typecheck:tests` sees these - `tsconfig.tsgo.json` excludes test files.

Biome delta gate: this PR added 7 complexity violations. Fixed by
extraction rather than override - the Dead Letters page and the DLQ
card each grew a mutations hook, the DLQ card's header, table and row
became their own components, the two explicit-id Redis paths now share
one batch runner, and the toast handlers the three hooks were each
spelling out moved to one place. Net: one fewer violation than main.

* fix(ops): confirm before an irreversible discard, and stop leaking on failure

Review findings from CodeRabbit on #7127. Verified each against the code
before acting; the ones that held up:

Pending state leaked on failure. The shared toast handlers called
`onSettled` from the success path only, so a failed redrive or discard
left the row spinning and the confirm dialog open, forever. It now runs
on both paths, which is what the name promised.

Discard asked nothing. Nothing un-discards a message - no redrive path
selects a discarded row - yet a single click on a row discarded it, and
the fleet-wide API form was reachable by simply omitting `processName`.
Per-message discard now confirms on both surfaces, and the fleet-wide
form takes an explicit typed confirmation, the same shape the blob-store
delete uses. Redrive and release-lease stay one click: both are
recoverable.

The union tile lied while loading. `?? []` made the outbox count zero
during the first fetch, so the headline rendered the queue figure as the
union and then jumped and turned red - the exact failure the comment
above it rejects. It reads as unknown until both figures exist.

Bulk writes were unbounded, and every redriven message came due at the
same instant. Both are now capped per act, and the redrive spreads its
due times over a minute so a recovery does not become the next incident.

Raw job errors reached a durable audit row. A thrown error's text is
arbitrary and can carry customer payload, so the discard audit records
the SHAPE of the failure instead.

Tests: two assertions could not fail, and one test claimed two scenarios
it never exercised - the second of which was that scenario's only
binding, so parity was reporting covered what nothing asserted. It now
has a test that actually renders a row from each substrate and holds
them to the same verbs.

Also: a status lookup map instead of a four-deep ternary, attempt rows
dropped on every in-memory deletion path rather than one, nested BDD
contexts in the Redis suite, and the biome complexity budget kept by
splitting both mutation hooks by what they act on.

* fix(ops): record a fleet act honestly, and gate the attempt log on provenance

Two more review findings.

Fleet-scoped audit rows were inventing identity. The two fleet-wide acts
passed `projectId: "__fleet__"` and `processKey: "__all__"` because the
sink typed them non-nullable - while `QueueAuditRepository`, added in
this same PR for the identical cross-cutting scope, writes null with a
comment saying inventing one would mislead. The sink now takes nulls,
the fleet acts pass them, and the scope lives in metadata where it can
be read without being mistaken for a real project.

(The reviewer's stated failure mode does not apply: `AuditLog.projectId`
is a plain nullable column with an index and no relation to `Project`,
so a placeholder would not have thrown. The reason to fix it is that the
value is untrue and inconsistent with its sibling, not that it breaks.)

The attempt log trusted the wrong signal. It preserved `error.message`
for anything carrying a boolean `retryable`, which any thrown object can
have. It now requires the stable `DispatchError` name as well - by name
rather than `instanceof`, since the error may have crossed a boundary
that stripped the prototype. Everything else stays redacted, with a
regression test for an impostor that claims to be retryable while
carrying a secret in its message.

* fix(ops): record only recognized error classes in the discard audit

The redaction added a commit ago kept the first three words when an error
carried no recognizable class, which is not a safe fallback: an error's
opening words are no safer than its closing ones. "alice@example.com
payment failed" leads with the address, so the reduction stored it.

Only a leading error class survives now; everything else records a fixed
`untyped_error`. The test that was supposed to catch this passed because
its fixture happened to bury the address past the third word, so it now
carries a message that leads with one.

Also nests the recovery-vocabulary suite under when-blocks, per the
repo's BDD structure convention.

* fix(ops): stop building an instance target for an act that has no instance

Two more review findings.

`targetId` was assembled from a name plus two nulls for a process-scoped
bulk act, giving `webhookDelivery/null/null` - a string that reads as an
instance which does not exist. The triple is now built only when all
three parts are real; anything else records the fleet marker, with the
scope in metadata where it already was. The integration suite caught
this properly: its audit lookups keyed on the old shape, so they now
assert the fleet target, a null project, and the scope.

The view-only case in the vocabulary suite claimed to cover "each
surface" while rendering only the queue row - the same overclaiming this
suite was written to fix. It now renders the outbox table too, and both
fixtures moved into shared builders.

* fix(ops): guard the bulk updates, and make the fleet discard ask a human

The full re-review turned up a real race and a real usability bug.

Both bulk UPDATEs kept their status guard only in the id subquery. The
subquery picks ids under one snapshot and the UPDATE locks them under
another, so a single-row redrive landing in between was clobbered - which
is exactly what the single-row paths repeat the guard to prevent. Both
now repeat it on the UPDATE itself.

A DLQ filter matching nothing removed every control, canary included,
because the toolbar derived its queue list from the filtered rows. The
canary samples a QUEUE rather than the shown rows, so it now reads the
unfiltered list; the bulk buttons still follow the filter.

The fleet-wide discard token was supplied by the UI, which made the
"typed confirmation" theatre - the reviewer's word, and a fair one. The
operator now types the phrase, using the typed-confirmation support
ConfirmDialog already had. The API still requires the same phrase, which
is what stops a script reaching that breadth by omitting a field; the two
layers guard different things.

Also: the port promised "every dead message" while every implementation
moves at most one batch, so it now says bounded and says why; the redrive
stagger had no test and now has one; the instance drawer's discard
confirmation names the intent it is about to bury; the migration states
that the enum change is forward-only, because Postgres has no ALTER TYPE
DROP VALUE; `outboxKnown` reads as `isOutboxCountKnown`; and the sweep
scenario says what its test actually drives.

* refactor(ops): object params for the new queue APIs, and an is-prefixed boolean

Follows the repo's own conventions, which the new code was the outlier
on: QueueService now takes { repo, audit } like SchedulerOpsService and
ManagerExplorerService already do, bulkActionFor takes an object rather
than three positionals, and `filtering` reads as `isFiltering`.

* fix(ops): stop a prose comment binding a spec, and bound the attempt read

The sharpest of this round: a comment explaining why a test is
deliberately unbound spelled the binding token out, and the parity
scanner matches that token anywhere in a comment - so the sentence saying
"this is not a binding" was registering one, for a scenario that does not
exist. Reworded, with a note not to write it again.

`findAttempts` had no ceiling while sitting behind a tRPC query an
operator can open on any message, and a repeatedly-redriven message
accumulates a row per failure. Capped.

Every canary button read "Go", so a screen reader heard the same control
once per queue; each now names its queue.

The unknown branch on the dead-letters tile had no test, which is what
let the original half-union bug through in the first place. It has one.

And the spec promised "the refusal says the message is not dead" while
the act returns a boolean and the UI supplies those words, so the
scenario now claims only what is asserted.

* fix(ops): prefix the remaining new booleans, and bind the jitter window to the redrive

The naming rule was applied to the four other booleans this branch adds, not
just the two flagged: an unprefixed name reads as a value rather than a
question at the call site.

The bulk-redrive test measured its 60-second jitter window from module load,
so a serial suite that reached the test a minute late would fail a spread
that was in fact correct. It now brackets the recovery call itself, which is
the instant the window is actually measured from.

fix(observability): bound the reads and level the logs that hid a six-day fleet crash (#7125)

* fix(observability): a layer that rethrows logs warn, not error

`error` claims something bad and final happened. A failure about to be
retried is neither, and four repository call sites were claiming it on
every attempt of work the queue then retried successfully. Three
overnight New Error Signature pages on 2026-08-17 turned out to describe
143 ClickHouse writes that all eventually landed and zero jobs lost.

GroupQueue already had this right — warn on "Job attempt failed,
re-staged with backoff", error once on "Group blocked after exhausted
retries" — so this makes the layers underneath it agree, and writes the
rule down where it was missing. ADR-003 and logging-and-tracing.md
covered log shape but never said when a level applies.

The inverse mattered more. ProjectionRegistry.dispatch discards events
when it has no router, throws nothing, and logged it at warn — so no
layer above ever reported the loss and nothing alerted. 55 dropped
batches in the 48h to 2026-08-17, every one on a rolling deploy. Its
message also blamed "before initialize()" when prod is overwhelmingly
the opposite end, dispatches in flight when SIGTERM lands and close()
has already cleared the router.

- metric-data-point + evaluation-analytics repositories: error -> warn
  on the three log-and-rethrow catches, identifiers kept
- evaluation-analytics: pass the Error instance, not error.message — a
  bare string loses the stack and the log collector drops the field
- projectionRegistry: warn -> error, state the event count, and name
  both ways the router can be absent
- specs/observability/retryable-failure-log-level.feature, 7/7 bound

* fix(event-sourcing): close the projection registry after the queue, not before

All 55 dropped event batches in the 48h to 2026-08-17 landed AFTER their own
pod's SIGTERM — 55 of 55, zero before initialize — the latest 26 seconds into
the drain. The log line said "called before initialize()", which is why it
read as a startup race for five days. It never was one.

`EventSourcing.close()` closed the projection registry before the global
queue. Closing the registry only releases its router, and every dispatch
arriving afterwards discards its events: the guard logs and returns, nothing
is thrown, and the one caller (eventSourcingService) catches the dispatch
failure and carries on. Two swallowing layers, nothing above either to retry.
Because the queue closed last, that window was the entire drain — during which
the workers are still processing jobs and still storing events.

Ordering is the whole fix and it is free: QueueManager.close() is a no-op for
the globally-owned queue, so the registry's close releases nothing the queue
still needs.

Considered and rejected: draining in-flight dispatches inside the registry.
`this.router` is read before the await, so an in-flight dispatch cannot lose
its router — that path logs "Failed to dispatch events to global projection
registry", which is at zero in prod over the same window. It would have been
machinery for a failure that does not occur.

- eventSourcing.ts: global queue closes first, registry after
- projectionRegistry.ts: document that close() order is load-bearing
- eventSourcing.closeOrdering.unit.test.ts pins the sequence; it fails on the
  previous ordering
- worker-graceful-shutdown.feature: 32/32 bound

* fix(clickhouse): bound the reads that took the worker fleet down

Two unbounded-read bugs that compound: an unbounded read is what makes a
result set big enough to exhaust memory, and the recovery from exhausting
memory is what killed the process.

**The ceiling.** When a joined trace read exceeds ClickHouse's per-query
memory cap, the fallback re-runs it in batches of 25 and merges every batch
into one map. That bounds ClickHouse's peak memory and not ours — the same
full result set is rebuilt on this side of the socket, and the comment
claiming it bounded memory "without dropping data" is why the trap survived.
A 980-trace read did exactly that on every worker at once: 50 V8 heap deaths
over 08-12..16, 16:48 UTC daily, 6-12 pods a day, nothing alerting. The read
had already failed in ClickHouse before the fallback ran, so refusing it
costs the caller nothing it had — what it buys is that the failure stays
inside one job instead of taking the process.

**The floor.** The evaluation_runs ScheduledAt resolver probes a recent
window and, on a miss, re-ran with no lower bound at all. evaluation_runs is
partitioned on ScheduledAt, so that prunes nothing and walks every partition
including cold S3 — the single largest source of coldScan queries in prod,
208 of 300 in one sampled window. Now floored at the tenant's OWN retention,
resolved through the existing RETENTION_TABLE_CATEGORY_MAP, so a project on a
long custom policy keeps its long lookback and one on a short policy stops
paying for someone else's. Safe because anything past retention is TTL'd
away. A resolver failure falls back to the platform default, never to an
unbounded read — that is the failure being fixed.

The floor helper is generic and table-aware rather than a constant in one
repository, so the other cold-scan sites can adopt it without reinventing it.

Also here:
- 90 log-and-rethrow sites across app-layer / event-sourcing / traces /
  gateway demoted error -> warn, continuing 1c7e0f4b04. Detection is
  innermost-catch: a nested rollback catch that swallows sits inside an outer
  catch that throws, and attributing by "any throw in an enclosing block"
  converts genuine swallows. 13 such sites were caught and left alone.
- getTracesWithSpans now preserves the cause when it wraps a failure. It
  discarded it, so the only record of why a read failed was one warn line.

specs/clickhouse/bounded-reads.feature, 7/7 bound.

* fix(clickhouse): make the span read's retention floor follow the tenant

`SPAN_READ_FLOOR_LOOKBACK_MS` was a hardcoded 90 days, and its own comment
admitted the reasoning: "90 days rather than the 49-day platform retention
default: it covers the default with room for a longer tenant policy". That is
a guess in both directions. A project on a 400-day retention policy got a
90-day floor and simply could not see its own older spans on the hint-less
path — a correctness gap, not just a cost one — while a project on a 7-day
policy paid to scan 90 days it has no rows in.

The floor now resolves through the tenant's own policy, via the same
table-aware helper the evaluation_runs fix uses, with the previous 90 days
kept as `minLookbackMs`. So adoption can only widen a read, never narrow one:
a longer policy reaches further back than before, a shorter one still reaches
at least as far as before. That guarantee is what makes this safe to apply to
the remaining cold-scan sites.

specs/clickhouse/bounded-reads.feature, 8/8 bound.

* refactor(clickhouse): move the retention floor into the client package

Two corrections to the previous commit, both raised in review.

**Wrong home.** The floor lived in `platform/app/.../clients/clickhouse/`
because it needed the retention cascade, which is app-side. That avoided the
dependency question rather than answering it. The mechanism — floor
arithmetic, the never-narrower guarantee, the cache — is now
`packages/clickhouse-client`, dependency-free, with the policy inverted out
behind a `RetentionDaysProvider` the caller supplies. The app side is what is
left over: map table to retention category, ask the project cascade, hand it
to an instance. Any other caller that can answer the question gets the
mechanism for free.

**Loose functions.** It was a module of exported functions; it is a class with
its dependencies injected, per dev/docs/best_practices/repository-service.md.

**And the lookup is cached.** The provider walks PROJECT -> TEAM ->
ORGANIZATION, so uncached this put a database round trip in front of every
read it was meant to make cheaper. Five-minute TTL — retention changes on
human timescales — keyed per tenant AND table, bounded at 10k entries with
oldest-first eviction so a long-lived worker serving many projects cannot grow
it without bound. A failed lookup is cached too: a cascade that is down is
exactly when it can least afford to be re-asked on every read.

Also here, continuing the level work: 13 swallow sites whose own message
contradicted their level. Eleven logged at error while saying they recover
("non-fatal", "the next poll will retry", "the next sweep retries it") and are
now warn; two logged at warn while saying work is lost ("orphan bytes may need
manual cleanup", "bytes may be orphaned") and are now error.
`groupQueue.ts:1664` was deliberately left at error — "skipping retries" is
terminal, and the phrase only matched because it contains "skipping".

packages/clickhouse-client: 205 tests pass. specs/clickhouse/bounded-reads.feature, 9/9 bound.

* Address review comments

- Refuse an over-budget joined-span batch at the query, not after decoding

* Address review comments: object params and CI gates

* style: reformat the retargeted ConstructorParameters casts

The cast rewrite ran after the format pass, so the eight widened lines went

* fix(observability): wire the retention resolver into the production paths

The tenant-aware floor was inert. `retentionResolver` was an optional
constructor parameter on both `ClickHouseTraceService` and
`EvaluationRunClickHouseRepository`, and no production path passed one — so
`createRetentionFloorService(undefined)` ran in both and every project got the

resolvers, and the behaviour the PR describes never reached a customer.

* fix(cli): make scenario run --wait count only its own batch

The simulation-runs list route applied the batchRunId filter only when
scenarioSetId came with it, and fell through to the unfiltered project
listing otherwise. The CLI's --wait polls with the batch id alone, so
the tally counted stale in-progress runs from old batches and the wait
timed out even when the batch finished in seconds.

Server: GET /api/simulation-runs?batchRunId= now filters by the batch
id on its own; the scenario set id stays as an optional narrowing.
CLI: fetchBatchRuns keeps only runs carrying the polled batch id, so
the wait also works against already deployed servers.

* fix(simulations): keep an empty scenario set id as a default set filter

The batch query dropped the scenario set predicate for any falsy set id,
which made an explicit empty string behave as if no set was asked for.
An empty string is a value that selects the default set, and it covers
rows written before the set id got its "default" name. Only an absent
set id now drops the predicate.

The predicate is built once for both the outer query and the dedup
subquery, and the review's lowercase "when" naming is applied to the
route test blocks.

* test(simulations): cover both default set storage values in the batch query

The default set filter expands to "" and "default", because rows written
before the set id got its name carry the empty string. The test proved
only the empty string half, so it now inserts one row of each value in
the same batch and asserts both come back while a named set row does not.

docs(agent-simulations): use the skill card on the connect-your-agent page (#7155)

* docs(agent-simulations): use the skill card on the connect-your-agent page

The page carried the connect-agent setup prompt as a raw text block,
written before the skill card pipeline could render outside docs/skills.
Manifest keys are now docs-root-relative paths, so any docs page can
carry a generated section, and the page shows the same accordion card as
the skills directory: install via CLI, slash command, copy full prompt,
download SKILL.md. The prompt content now comes from the compiled skill,
so the page can no longer drift from the released skill text.

* docs(agent-simulations): adopt the traceparent in middleware, not in the handler

The adoption snippet opened a span with the extracted context inside the
handler body. That pattern cannot cover a handler decorated with
langwatch.trace(): the decorator opens its root span before the body
runs, so the agent's spans land in a separate trace and the judge sees
nothing. Verified against the python SDK across tracing styles, with
regression tests in sdks/python (test_traceparent_adoption.py). The
skill and the page now put attach(propagate.extract(headers)) in a
middleware that runs before any tracing starts, which covers decorators,
context-manager traces, autotrack and plain OpenTelemetry spans.

* docs(agent-simulations): commit the regenerated skill card artifacts

* docs(agent-simulations): state the OpenTelemetry runtime prerequisite for the TypeScript middleware

The context.with and propagation.extract calls are no-ops without a
registered context manager and propagator. The skill and the page now
say so and name what registers them: the LangWatch SDK's
setupObservability() or the OpenTelemetry NodeSDK.

feat(cli): create the HTTP agent on the spot when agent dev finds none (#7156)

* feat(cli): create the HTTP agent on the spot when agent dev finds none

Without --agent, the dev session already reuses the agent remembered for
the directory, auto-picks a lone HTTP agent, and offers a picker over
several. The remaining edge failed with instructions even in a terminal:
a project with no HTTP agents yet. An interactive session now offers a
name and registers the agent pointing at the local server, so the first
agent dev run needs no separate create step. Sessions without a terminal
keep the exact fail messages that name the command to run instead.

* fix(cli): refuse credentialed local URLs and harden the create prompt

Review fixes: resolveLocalUrl now rejects a --url carrying userinfo,
since the session stores that URL in the agent's platform config and
prints it; the offered agent name falls back to my-agent when the
current directory has no basename; the --agent help text states that
on-the-spot creation needs an interactive terminal; the resolve tests
restore the original isTTY descriptors instead of forcing false into
the shared worker process; and the directory-name default is now pinned
by the spec and asserted against the prompt call.

* test(cli): bind the my-agent fallback for a rootless directory name

The prompt assertion now mirrors the code's fallback expression, and a
new case stubs the working directory to / and expects the offered name
to be my-agent, so the fallback cannot regress unnoticed.

test(python-sdk): pin traceparent adoption across tracing styles (#7158)

* test(python-sdk): pin traceparent adoption across tracing styles

LangWatch simulations send a W3C traceparent on every scenario call and
the judge fetches the agent's spans by that trace id. These tests pin
which extraction pattern makes each SDK tracing style join the caller's
trace: attach() before any tracing starts covers plain OpenTelemetry
spans, the langwatch.trace() context manager with nested spans, and
handlers decorated with @langwatch.trace(), whose root span opens before
the handler body runs. A with-block carrying the extracted context only
covers traces started inside it, and a decorated handler without early
extraction starts its own trace, which is why the docs put the
extraction in middleware.

* test(python-sdk): make traceparent adoption tests independent of suite order

The "no early extraction" test read the first exported span and asserted it
had no parent. That holds only when nothing is current when the test starts,
and the suite leaves an evaluation.loop_iteration span active, so the handler
opened its root under that span and the test failed in the full run while it
passed on its own. The handler now runs under an empty context, which is the
condition the scenario describes.

The with-block test also proves its boundary: a span opened before the block
keeps a different trace id, while the block's own span and the trace started
inside it carry the remote one.

fix(scim): a group PATCH that names no members no longer empties the group (#7136)

* fix(scim): stop a group PATCH that names no members from emptying the group

A SCIM `replace` operation that was not a `displayName` rename fell through
into the full-member-replace block, which read the absence of a member list as
`[]` and computed every current member as the set to remove. Replacing an
unrelated attribute — or renaming a group with the no-path form Entra ID
writes — revoked access for everyone in the group, with a 200 and a valid
ScimGroup body to show for it.

`extractMemberList` now returns `null` when the operation carries no member
list at all, and the replace block returns early on it. An explicit
`members: []` still clears the group; that is a legitimate request.

The suggested `return` after the no-path rename is deliberately not taken: a
no-path value object carrying both `displayName` and `members` is a single
operation that must do both, and returning early would drop the membership
half of it.

Fixes #7131

* test(scim): pin the bare-array PATCH value, where an array is an object but names no members

* fix(scim): a malformed member list no longer reads as an instruction to clear the group

Review findings on the previous commit. All of them land in the same few lines
of extractRequestedMemberIds and its call site, so they share a commit rather
than splitting one function rewrite across five.

Naming "members" was not enough on its own: `{"op":"replace","path":"members"}`
with no value, or a string where an array belongs, still reached
extractMemberIds, which returns [] for anything non-array. That [] read as a
written-out empty list and removed every member — the exact defect this branch
set out to close, one shape further in. Only an explicit null is now honoured as
a written-out empty list.

Also here:
- `if (!members)` is now `if (members === null)`. [] is falsy, and truthiness is
  the idiom that erases the absent-vs-empty distinction this whole change rests on.
- extractMemberList -> extractRequestedMemberIds. Both it and extractMemberIds
  return user ids; the difference is nullability, not list-vs-ids.
- A warn line when a replace matches no known attribute. Doing nothing is the
  safe answer but a silent one, and the old behaviour at least failed loudly. An
  IdP sending a shape we do not parse should be findable without an access-loss
  incident pointing at it.
- Tests for the three malformed shapes, for an explicit null, and for a
  no-member operation preceding a real member replace in one request — proving
  the early return ends the operation and not the loop over Operations.

Verified: the three malformed-shape tests fail against the previous commit and
pass here; ee/scim is 61/61 green.

* docs(scim): say what a malformed member list does, and mark the externalId gap as a gap

The supported-operations note now covers the malformed case, and the test that
uses externalId as its 'unrelated attribute' example says so is a gap (#7141)
rather than a decision it is pinning in.

* fix(scim): stop warning about a rename that was understood perfectly well

The warn added for unparseable group PATCH payloads fired on ordinary
renames too. A no-path `{"value":{"displayName":"..."}}` — the form Entra
ID writes — was applied, then fell through to a check that found no
member list and logged "matched no known attribute; leaving the group
unchanged". Both halves were false: the attribute was recognized and the
group was renamed. A warning on the common case is a warning nobody
reads, which costs the log the one job it was added for.

Membership answers are now three-way instead of two: a list, a malformed
member value, or nothing said about members at all. The last of those
only warns when the operation went entirely unrecognized, and a
malformed member list gets its own message, because "you named members
but did not give a list" is a payload worth fixing while "this was about
something else" is not.

Also corrects the docs on two points CodeRabbit was right about: an
explicit null clears a group, so "you have to say so with a list" was
wrong; and only the member replacement is left unapplied, so a combined
operation still renames.

* fix(scim): treat a member array with malformed entries as malformed, not empty

A non-empty array whose entries lack a string `value` key (e.g. `[{}]`)
was silently filtered to `[]` and treated as 'clear the group'. Now any
array where extracted ids don't match the input length returns malformed,
preserving the group's membership. Only `[]` and explicit `null` clear.

Also fixes the docs contradiction where `null` was included in the set of
non-list values that preserve membership, even though it clears membership.

* fix(scim): a member list nobody can read is not an empty member list

The same bug this PR exists to fix, surviving in a narrower shape.
`{"path":"members","value":[{"display":"Alice"}]}` is plainly an
attempt to name somebody, but no entry carries a `value`, so the id
filter reduced it to `[]` — which then read as a written-out empty list
and emptied the group. A list is only a list we can act on when every
entry in it can be read; the entries that fall out are precisely the
members that would be removed.

Only `[]` and an explicit `null` clear a group now. A partly-readable
list is malformed and leaves membership alone, warning like any other
malformed member value.

Docs updated to match, and to stop describing `null` as a non-list value
that preserves membership when it is the one non-list value that clears.

* fix(scim): a blank member id names nobody, so it cannot mean "these are the members"

`[{"value":""}]` is a well-formed member list by every check we had: the
entry is an object, it carries a string `value`, and the list is not
empty. It also names nobody, so every current member falls outside the
requested set and gets removed — a group emptied by a mapping expression
that returned blank.

Blank and whitespace-only ids are now malformed, alongside entries with
no `value` at all. An id that refers to somebody outside the
organization stays allowed: that is a membership question and it is
resolved later. This one is a shape problem, and only `[]` and an
explicit `null` may clear a group.

fix(governance): anthropic_admin cost_report 400 — default too recent + log error body (#7178)

* fix(governance): anthropic_admin cost_report 400 — default too recent + log error body

The cost_report puller always 400s because:

1. defaultStartingAt() returns 24h ago, but Anthropic's daily cost buckets
   have a ~1-day processing lag — no completed bucket exists, so the API
   returns 'Invalid date range: ending date must be after starting date'.
   Fix: cost reports now default to 3 days back at midnight UTC.

2. The HTTP error handler discards the response body. HTTP/2 has no
   statusText, so the log shows 'HTTP 400 ' with no explanation.
   Fix: read response.text() and include it in the thrown error.

3. Form hint said 'Empty = 24 hours back' — updated to reflect the
   report-specific defaults.

Closes #7177

* fix(governance): limit ingestion source detail events to 20

The event list on the per-source detail page fetched 50 rows, producing
an excessively long list.  Cap at 20 — the backend already respects the
limit parameter.

* fix(governance): extract error helpers to fix cognitive complexity + bound error body + clarify hint

* fix(governance): fix typecheck (duck-type Response) and formatting

feat(authz): the grants ledger - same position, event-sourced (ADR-092 PR 1) (#7143)

* docs(authz): stage C sign-offs close, and permissions are never called scopes

D2 and D3 were the only two open blockers on stage C, and both closed on
2026-08-17 in a way that removes the customer-visible change the ADR had
been carrying.

D2: no legacy-key sunset. Old keys keep working indefinitely, so C3 stops
being a deprecation and becomes a compatibility backfill — bindings mirror
what each key can do today, and a key the backfill missed mints its own on
first use. The permissions JSON becomes a dormant source rather than a
decision path, which retires the bypass branch without a deadline anyone
has to meet. AUTHZ_LEGACY_KEY_ENFORCE is retired unshipped.

D3: an empty custom role means deny. Measured against production first:
of 464 custom roles, zero are empty and zero carry only strings outside
the 126-permission registry, so the semantics change lands with nobody
behind it and needs no remediation path.

Also records the vocabulary ruling. traces:view reads like an OAuth scope
and on a key it even behaves like one, but scope is already the customer's
word for where — ScopeChipPicker offers organization, team and project on
every scoped-resource surface. Calling a permission a scope would put two
senses of the word in one settings page, so it is permission for the what
and scope for the where, in code, API docs and UI copy alike.

Two things found while checking rather than assuming: the plan pointed C2
at scim.service.ts, which no longer exists, and the shadow soak cannot
currently produce evidence — it logs nothing on agreement and logs its own
failures at debug while cloud runs at info, so a shadow throwing on every
call looks exactly like the silence we have. Both are written down where
the next person will meet them.

* docs(authz): the rollout becomes build-dark, cut over per org, contract at the end

Alex's restructure. The stages A-F still describe the work but stop being
the unit of rollout, because the thing we actually want is to run one of
our own organizations on the engine in production, end to end, before any
customer moves.

Three rules replace the staged fleet-wide soak. Everything ships dark
behind a per-organization gate. An organization then cuts over all at
once - one composite migration rewrites its data, proves parity, and flips
it - so a tenant is on the old flow or the new one and never half. Every
deletion waits for 100 percent, which is why the roleKey tighten, the four
quirk branches and rbac.ts itself all collect into a final contract phase
rather than riding the next stage's PR.

The fork replaces the codemod. Stage D was going to move ~380 call sites
onto .permission() before enforcement could flip, and it does not need to:
the shadow already found every decision point. Ten call sites across
rbac.ts and role-binding-resolver.ts carry every legacy permission
decision and each already calls authzShadowFor, so making them ask the
per-org gate which engine answers is a change inside two files. The
codemod becomes cosmetic cleanup once the direction is proven.

Only the doctrine and the shape are rewritten here. The per-stage sections
still read as the old sequence, and finishing them waits on the open
question of whether the migration itself is event-sourced - that decision
changes what the migration section says.

* docs(authz): the final plan - a grants ledger, born clean, one writer, two views

The delivery plan is rewritten end to end around the decisions of
2026-08-17 and is now the consolidated reference: fifteen dated decisions,
the final data structure, the event vocabulary with occurredAt carrying
business time so 'member since 2024' survives the migration, the two
dispatch disciplines, a four-plus-one PR map, the pre-flight fact table
with the two production measurements already banked, and the testing
doctrine - real containers, one scenario per failure mode, revocation
proven with Redis stopped.

The mandate that shaped the last pass: this is the final rewrite of this
flow, so correct beats expedient wherever they diverge. Two compromises
died for it. Grant and Role are born as new clean tables in PR 1 rather
than evolving RoleBinding in place and renaming it live at the end. And
nothing ever dual-writes - the ledger is the single writer with two
projections, the future-shaped tables and a legacy-shaped compat view,
until the contract PR deletes the latter. That opens the door to the
genesis import: every existing binding, role and floor fact becomes
events backdated to their real creation time, so the whole grants state
is replayable from the beginning of history.

* docs(authz): review resolutions land in the plan - subscriber audit log, SCIM reconciler, the epoch stays until contract

* docs(adr): ADR-092 storage and rollout become the grants ledger, in place; ADR-007 gains the immediate-discipline amendment

* spec(rbac): ledger scenarios land - immediate revocation, collectives, cutover facts, SCIM reconciler; stale stage pointers swept

* feat(authz): the grants ledger core - pure reducer, deterministic ksuid grant identity

* docs(authz): dispatch is the queue, best-effort FIFO - revocation is instant as enforcement, and the two-discipline idea leaves the record

* feat(ops): the operator rollback lands on the migrations page - finalized to rolled_back, with handled refusals

* docs(authz): the Redis-loss breaker becomes ADR-007's shared amendment, and the identity programme's doors are named

* feat(authz): the ledger pipeline takes shape - event schemas registered, Grant/Role/cursor/cutover tables born, decisions 22-23 recorded

* feat(authz): the ledger pipeline goes live dark - commands, reducer-backed projection, the two-headed store, and the org tenancy guard

* feat(authz): shadow mode proves itself in the logs

Enabling shadow (or moving the sample rate) is announced once; every
comparison logs its outcome - info on agreement, warn on disagreement -
and a failed comparison is a warning, never a debug line invisible at
production log level. The info line is the denominator: silence now
means "not comparing", never "no news". Three bound scenarios in
in-place-authz-migration.feature; plan updated - reads stay on the
legacy tables through PR 1, the collector repoint is PR 3's.

* feat(authz): the backfill speaks ledger - attachGrants batches, a waited projection, and the parity proof as a fact

TeamUserBackfillMigration no longer writes role bindings: it emits
batched attachGrants commands (source backfill-b, business time = the
legacy row's own createdAt, deterministic commandIds), waits for the
projection's compat head to land every expected row, and records a
clean sweep as migration_parity_proved before finalizing. The epoch
bump stays exactly as before (decision 19). Held organizations record
no proof fact. The app binds the emitter to the authz_grants pipeline
lazily, and a disabled event-sourcing stack parks the organization
with an honest report instead of letting DisabledPipeline swallow the
send. in-place-authz-migration.feature scenarios pass unchanged.

* feat(authz): runner lifecycle transitions become ledger facts, and the breaker becomes doctrine

Every SystemMigrationTenantState transition is witnessed as a
migration_tenant_state_changed event through a decorating repository -
the synchronous write stays the finalized latch (it never waits on a
queue), the witness is best-effort, and the projection re-applies
transitions under a monotonic updatedAt guard so a lagging fold can
never regress a newer direct write. Replay onto an empty table rebuilds
it; onto a live one it converges to no-ops. The runner package stays
generic - witnessing is this migration's behaviour.

The Redis-loss breaker is simplified to doctrine (ADR-007 amendment
rewritten): when Redis is down, appends still land, revocation-class
operations enforce synchronously - the enforceGrantRevocation seam
ships here, its caller arrives with PR 2 - and everything else waits.
No inline processing, and no replays run during an outage.

* test(authz): the replay proof - one stream, byte-identical rows, every run

PR 1's definition of done: the pure chain from legacy rows to projected
rows (emission mapping, attachGrants handler, wire schemas, fold, row
mappings) runs twice and produces byte-identical Grant and compat rows,
equivalent to the imperative M1 writer's output - equivalent, not
byte-identical, because ids are deterministic now and a custom binding's
role column normalizes to CUSTOM, neither of which can change a
decision. Applying a stream twice folds to the same state as once.

* fix(authz): command classes must carry the aggregate-id static the queue binds

* fix(authz): give the projection test helper the union the wire schema already knows

* fix(authz): the package root is browser-reached, so grant identity moves behind a server-only subpath

* refactor(authz): the grants projection rides the typed fold helper like every other pipeline

* fix(authz): the registry's grants store dep speaks the fold state type

* fix(authz): close the review's real holes - a permanent park, an ungated rollback, and two lying contracts

Three of these change behaviour:

- A legacy TeamUser row of CUSTOM with no custom role parked its
  organization forever. `roleKeyForTeamRole` is lossy (CUSTOM and VIEWER
  both map to `viewer`), so the row projected back as VIEWER and
  `bindingKey` - comparing legacy rows against projected ones on the raw
  enum - never recognised it. Both sides now normalise through the same
  mapping. Regression test included, and it fails without the fix.
- `rollBackSystemMigrationTenant` pinned a whole organization onto the
  legacy authorization path with neither of the guards `deleteBlob`
  requires. `requireBlobStoreWriteAuth` generalises to
  `requireDestructiveOpsAuth` and now covers all three sites.
- The cutover fields are last-write-wins over one row, unlike the grant
  heads, so the reducer takes a monotonic guard (`changedAtMs`,
  persisted) and stale cutover facts no longer take an organization back
  off the engine.

And two contracts that promised what the code did not do: `wireToFact`
said "an event type outside this aggregate throws" with no default arm on
any of its three switches, and the command/event schemas accepted
`tenantId != organizationId`, a null-id `user` principal, and resource
terms at a non-RESOURCE scope.

The grant-identity finding was a false positive worth keeping: the hash
pre-image already joins on a real 0x1f byte, but written as a literal it
renders invisibly and reads as `join("")`. Now an escape, with a test
that pins the boundary case.

Also: rollback guidance and a both-or-neither CHECK on the new migration,
the principal-scan index made partial while the table is empty, ADR-092's
Redis paragraph reconciled with ADR-007's amendment (folds pause; there is
no in-memory processor), a bounded wait on the ledger witness, memoized
and typed command senders, the glossary table un-split, and coverage for
`writeMigrationStates`.

* fix(authz): the projection store test builds the fold state, stamps and all

`store()` is typed against `AuthzGrantsFoldState` - the reducer's state
plus the base class's three bookkeeping stamps - not the bare
`GrantsLedgerState` the new helper was returning. Caught by
`typecheck:tests`, which runs a different project to the one the language
server answers from.

* fix(authz): the resource tier is a scope AND a principal set, enforced at both ends

Follow-up review pass. Two invariants were half-stated:

- `Grant_resource_terms_check` only enforced that token and permission
  travel together, so a tokenized TEAM row still passed - a share
  credential for a scope no share link may reach. Tied to `scopeType`
  now, so neither that nor a termless RESOURCE row is representable.
- The `anyone` and `project` principals are resource-tier only (the
  delivery plan's `Grant` shape says so outright). `anyone` names no
  subject, so an `anyone` grant at ORGANIZATION scope is a standing
  public grant over the whole tenant, held by nobody and revocable by no
  principal. Refused at the wire boundary on both the event schema and
  `attachGrantEntrySchema`.

`wireInvariants.unit.test.ts` covers all of it - 12 cases over the
identity, principal and resource-shape rules, which had no direct tests
before.

* chore(authz): the scoped typecheck project was scratch, not a deliverable

tsconfig.tmpcheck.json rode in on f3a46345fd. It is a local scoped
project for typechecking the three touched test trees, referenced by
nothing and ignored by nothing - a working file, not a change.

* fix(authz): a grant id is content, never the ambient environment

deriveGrantId passed getEnvironment() into the KSUID, so the id it
returned carried whatever ENVIRONMENT the deriving process happened to
read. Two processes that disagree - a worker and a web pod, a backfill
and the fold that replays it - derived two different ids for one legacy
row, and every "idempotent by deterministic id" upsert in the projection
stopped converging.

The environment is now a pinned constant ("prod", the library's own
default, i.e. no prefix), so every byte of the id comes from the
arguments. The determinism test drives setEnvironment() across two
values and proves the id does not move.

* fix(authz): the shadow match line drops to debug

Agreement is the expected outcome of a comparison that runs on the
permission-check hot path, and it was logging at info - one line per
sampled check, which is production traffic multiplied by the sample
rate. Mismatches stay at warn and the rate announcement stays at info,
so the proof that shadow mode is running still costs one line per
change rather than one per check.

* fix(authz): the ledger's tables carry business time and a legacy role, and keep the scan index partial

Three schema corrections, all inside PR 1's own undeployed migration.

SystemMigrationTenantState gains occurredAt. The projection guarded
folded transitions on updatedAt, which is wall clock: a replay onto an
empty table created its first row with updatedAt = now, every LATER fact
in the same stream then failed the lte guard, skipDuplicates dropped it,
and the table converged to the OLDEST status in the stream. Business
time, stamped by whichever writer moved the row, orders a folded
transition against a directly written one honestly.

Grant gains legacyRole - the role column an IMPORTED custom binding
carried, which roleKey cannot express and the legacy resolver still
reads. Persisting it is what lets load() reconstruct the fact rather
than a lossy copy of it.

And the principal-scan @@index comes OFF the Grant model. The index is
partial in the database (WHERE scopeType <> 'RESOURCE'); declaring it in
schema.prisma means the next prisma migrate dev drops the partiality and
rebuilds it over every share-link row - the one thing the WHERE clause
exists to avoid. RoleBinding's six partial uniques are handled the same
way: a comment pointing at the migration, no declaration.

* fix(authz): an imported custom binding keeps the role the resolver falls back to

The compat mapping turned any custom:<id> roleKey into role = CUSTOM,
discarding the legacy row's real role. That is not cosmetic: when the
custom role's permission list is EMPTY, matchers.ts falls through to
builtinRoleGrants(roleKeyForTeamRole(role)), and CUSTOM resolves to
viewer where the legacy row would have answered admin. The retired M1
writer copied row.role verbatim; the ledger silently downgraded it.

The legacy role now rides the FACT - legacyRole on GrantFact, on the
attachGrants entry, on the grant_attached event, and through wireToFact
- so it comes from event content and never from a read at fold time.
The backfill sets it from the legacy row it is importing; ledger-born
custom grants have no legacy row and stay CUSTOM.

replayDeterminism's third block now expects the legacy role on every
row, and its description says what it actually does: it pins the compat
row's shape against a hand-written expectation, it does not execute the
retired writer to compare against.

* fix(authz): store() writes a delta, guards every legacy-owned write, and never prunes on an unreconstructed fold

store() re-upserted EVERY grant's compat RoleBinding on EVERY event for
the organization, and re-wrote migration-state rows it had merely read.
Each of those cost something real:

- a compat row the legacy write paths had deleted or edited (they still
  own those rows until PR 2) was resurrected or reverted by the next
  unrelated event;
- a member removed and re-added at the same role gets a fresh grant id,
  and re-upserting the OLD id's row violates
  RoleBinding_user_builtin_role_scope_key - a P2002 thrown before
  writeCursor, which parks that organization's projection lane forever;
- every event bumped updatedAt on all of the tenant's
  SystemMigrationTenantState rows, which both lies to the ops page's
  "last transitioned" and made the witness ordering unsound.

store() now reads what storage holds once, under the queue's per-org
lock, and writes only what the fold changed - fingerprinted per grant,
per role, per (status, occurredAt). Identical state stored twice issues
no head or compat write at all.

Four more holes closed in the same pass:

- P2002/P2003 on a compat binding or a compat custom role are warned and
  stepped over, never thrown. Neither is retryable, and a throw parks
  the whole lane over one conflicting row.
- Roles are upserted BEFORE the grant compat rows that reference them
  and deleted AFTER the grants, so a batch carrying role_deleted with
  grants still on custom:<id> cannot raise a foreign-key violation. Per
  fact, the compat row is written before its head and deleted after it,
  which makes the head the fact's commit marker.
- A departed CustomRole is only deleted when NO RoleBinding and no
  TeamUser still references it. Those are SetNull relations and imported
  roles keep their legacy CustomRole id, so deleting one nulled
  customRoleId on legacy rows whose role column stays CUSTOM - and
  CUSTOM with no custom role is viewer. A projection may not author a
  permission downgrade.
- When there is no cursor row, load() returned null and the executor
  folded from EMPTY - so the state in hand describes this batch alone.
  Pruning against it would have deleted every other grant and compat row
  the organization owns. Departed-fact pruning is now skipped entirely
  in that case.

The migration-state guard moves onto the occurredAt column both writers
stamp, so a replay converges to the newest status instead of the oldest,
and the direct write in PrismaSystemMigrationStateRepository stamps it
too - otherwise a replayed fact from last year could overwrite the latch
a live transition had just set.

The store's write paths had only the migration guard under test. They
now cover idempotent convergence, the delta write order, departed-fact
deletion, both conflict guards, the unreconstructed-fold guard and the
CustomRole reference guard.

fix(coding-agent): terminal session viewer opens at the end, anchors totals, zero scroll jumps (#7055)

* fix(coding-agent): terminal opens at the session end, anchors footer totals, preloads scrollback without jumps

The Terminal tab now opens pinned to the session's latest line and fills
the screen with the turns before it, instead of showing one turn
top-aligned over an empty screen. Earlier turns preload two viewports
ahead of the reader, so a short turn no longer loads in front of their
eyes, and content shorter than the screen sits against the bottom bar
the way a terminal keeps its prompt.

The bottom bar's cost, tokens, and elapsed time are now anchored at the
session's first turn: the turn list carries each turn's totals, so the
bar counts the turns above the loaded window without reading their
transcripts, and loading one moves nothing. Before, the totals only
covered loaded turns, so they grew as the reader scrolled up and
disagreed with themselves at the same position.

Context-size notes are no longer drawn from a guess: while earlier turns
are unloaded, the crossing at the first loaded call is unknowable, and
the note it produced vanished when the truth arrived, shifting the
transcript under the reader. A note now waits for the call before it. A
resize observer keeps the prepend correction exact when a row changes
height outside a commit (an expanded tool output, syntax highlighting).

The sessions table's Agent and Last update columns hug their content, so
their values stay inside their own column and the freed width goes to
the Session column, which truncates.

Verified in the browser: the shrink-to-fit Agent and Last update columns

they read as one run of text. A minimum width keeps clear air after the
label. The bottom bar's clock, now anchored at the session's first turn,
runs into hours, so it reads "5h 36m" the way the sessions table says

* fix(coding-agent): gate per-turn spend behind cost:view

The conversation read now carries each turn's totalCost so the terminal
footer can count the turns above its loaded window. That value followed
traces:view only, while the sessions rows and the trace header gate spend
on the reader's own cost:view (ADR-057), so a reader without cost:view
could add the session total up one turn at a time.

The turn mapper nulls the cost for a reader without the permission, which

conventions ask.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XRYUK1mbAWQ18rUFdjminD

* refactor(coding-agent): split the scrollback hook and the marker walk

The Biome gate counts violations per file and rule and fails on an
increase. Two of them crossed the line in this branch: the context
marker walk went past the cognitive complexity limit when it started to
track whether the band it reads is the truth or a guess, and the
scrollback hook went past 60 lines when it gained the session baseline.

The marker walk now hands one model call to markersForModelCall, which
returns that call's notes and the band after it. The hook now reads its
position, its opened turn and its baseline from three named helpers.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XRYUK1mbAWQ18rUFdjminD

* fix(coding-agent): the terminal footer states no total it cannot count in full

A turn of the session carries its own token and cost totals in the turn
list, and the bottom bar adds the turns above the loaded window to what
the loaded window has counted so far. A turn that carries no total was
counted as zero, so the bar reported a session total short by that turn
and the reader had no way to see that it was short.

Each field is now null when one of those turns does not carry it, and
the bar leaves that stat out. The two fields are independent: cost is
null for a reader without cost:view, since the turn list carries no
spend for them, while the token total still counts in full.

* fix(coding-agent): the terminal follows the reader's row, and counts a transcript that renders nothing

The screen corrected a prepend by its own height delta, which cannot tell
what arrived above the reader from what appeared below them. When the
session's oldest turn carries no model call, completing the history lets
the walk draw a context note at a call further down, below the reader.
The delta counted that note as history and pushed the reader past it. The
screen now follows the row the reader is on, by the row's own key so a
prepend shifting every index does not lose it: what arrives above moves
the screen by exactly that, and what appears below moves nothing.

The bottom bar stood on the row the reader is on. An agent that reports
economics and no content renders no rows at all, so the bar stood on
nothing and counted zero, under a message that calls those totals real.
It now counts the whole loaded window in that case.

Also from review: the multi-argument helpers take named parameters, and
the turn-list loading flag carries the boolean prefix the repository
asks for.
