feat(langevals): run same-credential evaluations concurrently (#7190)

* feat(langevals): run same-credential evaluations concurrently

The server ran strictly one evaluation at a time per process, because each
request's env (the caller's model credentials) is written into os.environ
for litellm to read implicitly, and two evaluations with different
credentials must never overlap. That made a burst of N judge evaluations
take N times the single-call latency: a customer's 23-question experiment
against two targets ran 46 sequential judge calls and took half an hour.

Requests that carry the same credentials write identical values, so they
can safely overlap, and on a self-hosted install that is nearly every
request. The endpoint now admits evaluations through a generation gate:
evaluations whose model-credential env matches run together, up to
MAX_CONCURRENT_EVALUATIONS (default 8), and a request with a different env
closes the running generation, waits for it to drain, and starts the next
one, so a steady stream with one env cannot starve another tenant. The
process environment is restored when the last evaluation leaves, and
saturation past LANGEVALS_QUEUE_TIMEOUT still returns the 503.

Measured on a 1-worker pod (the size-minimal chart shape) with the real
image and a live azure judge: 8 concurrent distinct evaluations completed
in a strict one-per-0.85s staircase before, and together in about one
call's latency after. The same 46-call experiment through the platform
went from 45.8s to 24.4s at the SDK default of 4 threads, with per-call
p50 dropping from 3.4s to 1.1s (the queue wait), and to 8.6s at 16
threads.

* fix(langevals): make generation switching first-come fair and the test baseline clean

The starvation guard closed the running generation but did not decide who
runs next: at drain time, waiters for the old env and the new env raced,
and a continuous stream with one env could win every race until the other
tenant timed out. Waiting env keys now queue in first-arrival order and
only the front key may start or join a generation, so generations run
strictly in the order their first waiter arrived. Timed-out waiters leave
the queue and wake the rest, so an abandoned key can never block it.

The concurrency tests also rebase the server's original_env snapshot after
the guarded import: it was captured while the temporary
DISABLE_EVALUATORS_PRELOAD flag was set, so every drain restore leaked the
flag back into the test process. The restore assertion now compares the
whole environment, not one credential.

* fix(langevals): reject a queued evaluation whose deadline passed even when capacity frees

Condition.wait can return because capacity freed a moment after the
deadline, and the loop admitted that request instead of returning the 503.
Its caller already gave up by then, so running it only delayed the live
requests behind it. The admission loop now checks the deadline before every
admission attempt after queueing, and a boundary test holds the gate past
three waiters' deadlines, frees it, and verifies none of them ran, the
queue is empty, and a fresh request admits immediately.

* test(langevals): drive the post-deadline capacity release with a manual clock

test_capacity_freed_after_the_deadline_does_not_admit named a case it never
reached. Its three admissions ran one after the other and all expired 0.15s in,
while the holder released capacity at 0.3s, so the queue was already empty when
capacity freed. The admission-order defect it was written for passed it.

Real time cannot reach that state: a waiter wakes on its own timeout the moment
its deadline passes, so capacity can never free while the waiter is both queued
and expired. The gate now reads the clock through an injectable attribute, and
the test blocks a waiter, moves the clock past its deadline, and only then
frees the capacity it waits for. Reversing the check order in admit makes the
waiter come back admitted instead of timed out, so the test guards the fix.

* test(langevals): pin the queue order when one environment repeats

A request that arrives while its own env is still queued joins that queued
generation. That is the batching the gate exists for, and it costs the env
behind it one generation, never more: once the generation starts, its waiters
leave the queue and the front belongs to the next env, so later requests of the
running env queue behind it. The new test walks that whole sequence and asserts
the order, with spare capacity left in the gate so the front-of-queue rule is
what holds the late request back. Removing that rule makes the test fail at 'The
late B never queued behind C'.

Also renames the admission loop's queued flag to is_queued, and adds a
waiting_evaluations count next to the existing gate counters.

* perf(langevals): let the knob decide the evaluation width, not the thread pool

MAX_CONCURRENT_EVALUATIONS defaulted to 8, which made the server the limit
for any client that fans out wider. It is now 64, so a caller can raise its
own concurrency whenever it wants without the server capping it.

The knob alone would not have delivered that. Sync endpoints run on AnyIO's
shared worker-thread pool, which holds 40 threads, so the gate could never
admit more than 40 evaluations however high the knob was set, and the
requests above 40 would wait for a thread BEFORE reaching the gate, where
nothing knows their credentials and the queue cannot order them. The server
now sizes that pool from the knob at startup.

Both new tests fail without the sizing: the burst test measures a peak of
exactly 40 concurrent evaluations, which is the cap it exists to remove.

* fix(langevals): key the evaluation gate on the whole request env

The gate keyed on the model provider allowlist in set_model_envs, but that
function is not the only writer of the process environment. The custom LLM
evaluators (llm_score, llm_boolean, llm_category, pairwise_compare,
select_best_compare) and every Ragas evaluator, through prepare_llm, copy the
whole request env into os.environ while they run.

Any credential outside the allowlist therefore did not reach the key. Bedrock
is the clear case: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY belong to no
provider list here, so two tenants using Bedrock both keyed to the empty tuple,
the gate admitted them together, and whichever evaluator wrote last supplied
its credentials to both model calls. Serial execution hid this before; running
same-key evaluations together exposes it.

The key is now the whole env. Requests that share it write identical values,
which keeps the batching this feature delivers, since a project's burst carries
one set of credentials. Requests that differ in any variable stay in separate
generations.

Restoring the old projection makes the new tests fail: the AWS pair keys to ()
against (), and the two tenants overlap with the second starting before the
first finished.

* fix(langevals): carry request credentials per call, never through os.environ

Evaluators bridged the request env to litellm by writing it into os.environ,
several of them the whole dict (the custom LLM judges, the ragas helper, and
the azure branch of four older evaluators). The process environment is shared,
so two in-flight evaluations with different credentials could read each
other's: that is the cross-request boundary a reviewer flagged, and the reason
the server had to serialize different-credential evaluations at all.

Now nothing about a request touches os.environ:

- langevals_core.request_env binds each evaluation's env to its own context.
  BaseEvaluator binds at construction for library callers, and _evaluate_entry
  scopes it around every batch entry on whatever worker thread runs it.
- The litellm patch layer resolves that context into explicit call arguments:
  provider credentials by model prefix (api_key, api_base, api_version,
  vertex_credentials), the X_LITELLM_* passthrough, and the azure deployment
  rewrite, all request-first with the server's own environment as litellm's
  fallback. Every model call in the fleet funnels through this layer: the
  custom judges call litellm directly, dspy passes kwargs through, and the
  ragas langchain shim wraps litellm.completion.
- The evaluators that pinned AZURE_API_VERSION globally now pin it on their

* fix(automations): create the dataset inside the automation drawer, not a second one

The add-to-dataset section created its dataset by mounting
AddOrEditDatasetDrawer from the section itself. Drawers are URL-routed
singletons, so that stacks a second drawer over the automation drawer,
and the routed path would unmount the automation drawer and discard the
draft the user is in the middle of writing.

The section now creates the dataset inline: a name field and a create
button, the default trace columns, and the same under-the-field message
for a name already in use. The created dataset becomes the automation's
target with its mapping derived, as picking an existing one does.

The drawer rule is now written down in the drawers doc and in CLAUDE.md,
because the rule is what makes this a bug and it was not stated
anywhere.

* fix(automations): navigate to the dataset drawer and back, instead of stacking one

The add-to-dataset section mounted AddOrEditDatasetDrawer from inside the
automation drawer, which puts a second Drawer.Root over the open one and
sits outside the drawer stack the hook keeps.

The section now navigates the way the rest of the app does:
openDrawer("addOrEditDataset") with onSuccess and onClose, and goBack
returns to the automation drawer with its params restored. onClose is
passed because the target drawer closing itself clears the whole stack,
which would drop the caller.

The push unmounts the automation drawer exactly like a close, and the
unmount resets the draft. The drawer now announces a sub-flow first, so
the reset is skipped for the round trip and the draft is waiting on the
way back. The flag lives in its own module because the provider clients
are imported by the store's reducer, so importing the store back from
them closes an import cycle.

The picker clears its selection when it hands over, so an ending with no
created dataset puts the earlier target back rather than leaving the
section silently incomplete.

The drawer navigation rule is now in the drawers doc and CLAUDE.md.

* fix(automations): discard the draft a sub-flow was abandoned in

The departure into the dataset drawer skips the unmount reset so the
draft is waiting on the way back. Nothing collected that draft when the
user never came back: leaving the page while the dataset drawer is open
left it in the singleton store, and the next new automation opened
holding the abandoned one, name, conditions and all.

The drawer now opens on a blank draft unless the mount is the return leg
of a sub-flow, and the return is the one place that knows, because it
calls goBack itself. An abandoned sub-flow announces nothing, so the
stale draft is discarded the next time the drawer opens.

Found while dogfooding the round trip in a browser.

* fix(automations): assert the opened drawer in the test, not in its helper

The helper that reads the openDrawer call asserted the drawer name with
expect, which biome's noMisplacedAssertion flags because an assertion
outside a test case does not report as a test failure. The helper now
guards with a throw and the test asserts the drawer it navigates to.

* fix(automations): read the drawer stack instead of a one-shot sub-flow flag

React replays every effect once on mount in development. The unmount reset
consumed a "leaving for a sub-flow" flag, so the replay found it spent, read
the departure as a close, and wiped the draft the author was coming back to.

The drawer stack answers the same way however often it is asked: a sub-flow
leaves the authoring drawer in the stack, closeDrawer empties it. The return
leg has no such state to read, so it stays a one-shot and the mount latches
its answer in a ref.

The StrictMode test needs StrictMode outside the Chakra provider. Nested
inside it React skips the replay, which makes the test pass against the very
bug it covers. Both traps are now in the drawers guide.

* refactor(automations): take the dataset drawer's own success payload type

The callback annotated its parameter with a copy of the payload the drawer
already declares, which can drift from it. `openDrawer` types the props from
the drawer component, so the callback reads the real contract instead.

Names the created flag for what it asks.

fix(coding-agent): a row exists once the session says something, and its orchestrator can name it (#7197)

* fix(coding-agent): a row exists once the session says something, and its orchestrator can name it

A fleet of scheduled agents resuming at boot with expired credentials
produced twelve trace rows and twelve session rows in one morning, every
one empty: no spans, no input, no cost, a dash in every column, untitled,
and the trace list rendered them as "20684d ago". A process that starts
and dies before its first prompt still emits lifecycle and error records,
and both folds counted any record as a row.

Three changes on the platform, one on the CLI:

The trace-summary persist gate now asks for content, not a count. A span
always persists; a log-only state persists once it carries an input, an
output, cost, tokens or a model. The records stay stored either way. The
list and the drawer header also fall back to the ADR-087 storage anchor
when the span baseline is 0, so a legitimate log-only trace shows the
time its first signal was accepted instead of the epoch.

The session store gains the same gate: a row exists once the session has
a prompt, a call, tokens, cost, work counters, a name or a repository.
Metrics-only sessions keep their contract
(specs/coding-agent/session-aggregate.feature).

Sessions can now be named by whoever launched them. The capture seams
(the claude hook and the codex harvest) read LANGWATCH_SESSION_TITLE and
carry it on the session-context record as
`langwatch.session.title_explicit`; the fold stores it in its own column
(migration 00083) and the read ranks it above the generated title and
the prompt-derived name. A fleet whose sessions all open with the same
scripted greeting reads as its agents' names instead.

And the context record now posts without a git identity when it has a
title to carry. A codex session appears in the sessions screen only
through this record, so a codex agent running from a plain directory was
invisible while its claude neighbours were listed.

Replace the orchestrator-declared title design (LANGWATCH_SESSION_TITLE,
TitleExplicit) before it ships. The harnesses already name their sessions
and can rename them, so the capture mirrors that instead of inventing a
parallel channel:

- The claude hook posts the session's own name: the SessionStart payload
  carries session_title, and claude's live session registry
  (~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json) answers on every later hook, which is

- The codex harvest posts codex's own thread name from
  session_index.jsonl, the same name codex resume and codex archive
  resolve. The prompt-derived title stays the fallback.
- Both ride one wire attribute, langwatch.session.name. The fold writes
  the newest name onto the single Title column in place, ranked
  name > generated > prompt through a TitleSource column (00083, replacing

  the row and the title alone cannot say whether a regenerated topic
  title may replace it.
- The read is just Title again: no coalesce, no second title column.

Also lands the shared deriveTraceTimestamp helper so the trace list and
the drawer header cannot drift on the storage-anchor fallback.

fix(charts): serialize stored-objects PVC consumers across upgrades (#7196)

* fix(charts): serialize stored-objects PVC consumers across upgrades

In local-filesystem stored-objects mode the app Deployment and the workers
Deployment mount the same ReadWriteOnce PVC. Each Deployment already uses a
kill-then-start rollout and the workers carry a required podAffinity to the app
pod, but a helm upgrade rolls both Deployments at the same time and nothing
orders them. On a cluster with more than one node the new pod of one Deployment
can be scheduled on a fresh node while the old pod of the other still holds the
volume attachment on the old node, and both wedge in ContainerCreating with a
multi-attach error.

A pre-upgrade hook Job now scales the workers to 0 and waits for their pods to
go away before helm applies the new manifests. The app then rolls as the only
holder of the volume, which maxSurge=0 handles correctly, and the workers come
back at workers.replicaCount when helm applies the release.

The hook renders only when local-filesystem is the active backend, the workers
are enabled, and app.storedObjects.localFilesystem.serializeUpgrades is on. Its
Role is namespaced and holds get on the workers Deployment, patch on its scale
subresource, and read on the namespace's pods. The wait is derived from the
workers' own terminationGracePeriodSeconds, so it outlasts the time a
terminating pod can keep the volume attached.

Closes #7191

* fix(charts): hold the workers at zero until the app rollout finishes

The pre-upgrade hook alone does not close the race. Helm's apply restores the
worker replica count from the manifest, so a new workers pod is created at the
same instant as the new app pod. Its required podAffinity matches the OLD app
pod, which is still terminating on the old node, so the scheduler puts the
workers back on the node the app is leaving, where they take over the volume
attachment and wedge the new app pod for good.

Measured on a four node EKS cluster: with the pre-upgrade hook alone, an upgrade
that moved the app to another node left it in ContainerCreating with
"Multi-Attach error ... Volume is already used by pod(s) <release>-app-<old>",
which did not clear.

A post-upgrade hook Job now scales the workers to 0 again, waits for the app
rollout to finish, and then scales them back to workers.replicaCount. The
workers therefore follow the NEW app pod. It never fails the release over a slow
or broken app: if the rollout does not finish in time it says so and brings the
workers back anyway, because leaving the workers at 0 would be a silent capacity
loss on top of whatever is wrong.

The Role gains get on the app Deployment by name. The rollout wait polls that
Deployment rather than calling kubectl rollout status, which LISTs Deployments
and so cannot run under a Role restricted by resourceNames.

* test(charts): record the stored-objects upgrade hooks as a known pod-security exception

The hook Jobs call the Kubernetes API to scale the workers Deployment, so they
carry an automounted ServiceAccount token and a writable root for kubectl's
discovery cache. The chart's hardening gate requires
automountServiceAccountToken: false on every workload, which these Jobs cannot
have, so they join the ClickHouse preflight Job in EXEMPT_WORKLOADS.

An exemption is only legitimate when the strict-admission overlay removes the
workload, so that overlay now sets
app.storedObjects.localFilesystem.serializeUpgrades to false. A locked-down
cluster should not be on local-filesystem stored objects in the first place:
that mode shares one ReadWriteOnce volume between the app and the workers and is
the documented hobby tier. With app.dataplane the hooks never render at all.

* docs(charts): drop em-dashes from the stored-objects upgrade prose

* fix(charts): decide the app rollout from the new pod, not from readyReplicas

Review round on #7196. Seven findings, all addressed:

1. The post-upgrade wait read status.readyReplicas, which counts ready pods
   across every ReplicaSet. During a kill-then-start rollout there is a window
   where the controller has recorded the new generation while the still-Ready
   OLD pod satisfies the count, so the hook could give the workers back against
   the node the app is leaving, which is the wedge it exists to prevent. The
   check now applies the same condition kubectl rollout status does:
   observedGeneration >= generation, updatedReplicas == replicas,
   status.replicas == updatedReplicas, availableReplicas >= updatedReplicas.
   The jsonpath is pipe-separated so an absent field, which is how the API
   reports zero, keeps its position instead of shifting every later field left.
   A new test extracts the function out of the rendered Job and runs it against
   a fake kubectl over nine states, so the fix is executed rather than matched
   as a string.
2. NOTES.txt claimed the hooks exist even with workers.enabled=false or the
   knob off. The block is now gated on the same condition the template uses,
   and the knob-off case prints the manual ordering warning instead.
3. The hook pod ignored global.scheduling.affinity, which can leave the
   fail-closed pre-upgrade Job Pending. It now honors it.
   topologySpreadConstraints stay out on purpose: a spread rule for replicas can
   only make a single-run Job unschedulable, and the helper comment says so.
4. The hook Jobs run under their own ServiceAccount, so pull secrets attached to
   the namespace default ServiceAccount do not reach them. Added
   app.storedObjects.localFilesystem.serializeUpgradesPullSecrets.
5. Bumped the hook image to alpine/k8s:1.34.9. kubectl 1.30 was outside the
   supported skew for current clusters. Documented that the value accepts a
   digest and why the tag can be changed.
6. The test used app.dataplane.s3.bucket and .region, which the chart does not
   have. Uses app.dataplane.provider and app.dataplane.bucket now.
7. Two numeric guards concatenated a pair of values before testing them, so an
   empty one hid behind a numeric one and the arithmetic that followed errored
   out, which reads as false and printed ok. Each value is checked on its own.

Also removed a Gherkin continuation line with no keyword.

Verified on lw-dev EKS (Kubernetes 1.34): both Jobs run to completion on the new
image, and the API server confirms the Role's scope. kubectl auth can-i for the
hook ServiceAccount: patch the workers' scale yes, patch the app's scale no,
patch either Deployment itself no, get both Deployments yes, get an unrelated
Deployment no, list pods yes, delete pods no, get secrets no, anything in
another namespace no.

* fix(charts): treat an app parked at zero replicas as a finished rollout

Second review round on #7196.

The API omits a zero-valued updatedReplicas, replicas or availableReplicas, so
an app at replicaCount 0 reported them as absent, the rollout check read that as
unfinished, and the post-upgrade Job spent its whole 655s timeout before it
brought the workers back. The three status counters now default to 0. The
desired count stays mandatory, because with it missing there is nothing to
compare against, and defaulting the counters does not weaken the check: a
rollout that has not produced its pods yet reports 0 against a desired count
above 0 and still reads as unfinished.

The suite gains two states. '5|5|0|||' covers the parked app. '5|5|2|1|1|1|'
isolates the updatedReplicas == spec.replicas comparison, which the existing
two-replica state did not: it also had an old pod left over, so dropping that
one comparison still failed on the next one. Removing it now makes exactly the
new state fail.

* fix(charts): run the stored-objects hooks on rollback as well as upgrade

The hooks were registered for pre-upgrade and post-upgrade only, but helm
rollback fires pre-rollback and post-rollback. Neither the worker drain nor the
app-rollout gate ran there, so a rollback of both shared-PVC Deployments could
recreate the multi-attach wedge this change exists to prevent. A rollback is the
worst place to lose the protection, because it is most often run while
recovering from a rollout that already went wrong.

The drain Job now runs on pre-upgrade,pre-rollback and the restore Job on
post-upgrade,post-rollback. The ServiceAccount, Role and RoleBinding carry all
four, or a Job would run during a rollback with no identity and no permissions.
Weights and delete policies are unchanged.

One case the chart cannot cover, now documented in the template header, the
values comment, NOTES.txt and the README: on a rollback helm runs the hooks
stored in the TARGET revision, so a rollback to a chart version from before
these Jobs runs no Jobs at all. That path needs a manual worker scale-down, and
the README gives the four commands. The same rule makes the restored replica
count correct: it renders from the target revision's workers.replicaCount, which
is the count that revision asks for.

The suite now reads the helm.sh/hook value whole rather than as a substring,
because a substring test for pre-upgrade passes just as happily against
pre-upgrade alone as against pre-upgrade,pre-rollback. A new rollback test
asserts the events on each of the five documents and counts them, so a document
added later cannot quietly skip the rollback events. Verified by mutation:
dropping pre-rollback fails two tests.

The pin resolved 1.1.29 and the app server died at boot with
ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED, taking the sdk e2e suite and two unit shards
with it. Verified: back at 0.3.59 the ./llms/ollama export is present again.

Those two medium alerts stay open, on the same grounds as the four langchain
ones in langevals: no patched release exists on the major line we are on, and
moving majors is a migration with its own PR. Every other floor is unchanged
and still met.

docs(agent-simulations): group the connect pages, add the PM testing guide, and screenshot the flows (#7175)

* docs(skills): add a static always-open variant of the skill card

A manifest entry with "static": true renders the card with data-open baked
in, no chevron and no toggle affordance, and posthog.js skips it in the
header click handler. The connect-agent card on the connect-your-agent page
uses it, so the prompt actions are visible without a click.

* docs(agent-simulations): nest the connect pages and add the testing guide for product managers

Connect your agent becomes a sidebar group holding remote traces, local
development, run parameters and authenticated agents, with the page itself
as its Overview. The new Testing Your Agent page walks product managers
through creating scenarios in the interface, with AI, with Langy from
pasted material, and over the MCP integration, then running run plans and
reading verdicts. Screenshots come from a real run of the platform against
a live agent, and the connect guide's register and verify steps carry them
too.

* fix(ci): chunk the Slack release changelog and fail on a rejected notification

Slack caps a section's text at 3000 characters and rejects the whole
payload as invalid_blocks past it, which the 3.14.0 release hit with a
10476 character changelog while the script still printed success. The
changelog now splits into up to four section blocks at line boundaries
with a truncation notice pointing at the releases page, an empty
extraction sends no empty block, and the script reads the webhook's
response body and exits non-zero on anything but ok.

* fix(ci): cut oversized changelog lines and time out the Slack webhook

The chunker split the changelog only at line boundaries, so a single line
longer than Slack's 3000 character section limit still went out whole and
the webhook rejected the payload as invalid_blocks. The chunker now runs in
jq, which measures and slices strings in characters like Slack does, and it
cuts a line that is longer than the limit into pieces of its own.

The webhook call now has a connect timeout and a total transfer timeout, so
a stalled webhook cannot hold the release job open until the runner limit.

A new test drives the script with a curl stub. It covers an oversized
changelog, a single oversized line, a small changelog, a missing version, a
rejected webhook body and a missing webhook URL, and asserts that no section
block goes past 3000 characters and that no block is empty.

docs/llms.txt and docs/llms-full.txt are regenerated, so the machine readable
docs carry the static skill card and the new testing guide.

* docs(agent-simulations): tell readers to remove personal data before they paste

The testing guide tells readers to paste support tickets, complaint emails
and conversation transcripts. That text is saved as a scenario the whole
project can read, and the AI draft step sends it to a model. A note now says
to remove personal data first, or to replace it with invented equivalents.

The notify-slack-release test now also asserts that the blocks joined back
together still hold the whole oversized line. The cap assertion alone passed
an implementation that dropped the remainder.
Release docs (auto-release on merge to main) [skip ci]

feat(navigation): product switcher becomes the default, and the sidebar matches the design (#7198)

* feat(navigation): product switcher becomes the default, and the sidebar matches the design

With release_ui_navigation_v2_enabled on, a device that never picked a
navigation mode now runs the product switcher. Picking "Old navigation"
stays an opt-out. The sidebar column takes the design's width and type
size, and its marks read as quiet grey rather than violet.

* fix(navigation): make the content panel hairline visible in light mode

The panel already asked for a 1px top and left border, but it used
border.muted, which resolves to the same grey as bg.page in light mode.
The border painted in the colour of the background behind it, so the
panel edge never showed. It now uses the default border token, which is
the value the design uses. Dark mode keeps the muted token, which
already contrasts against the page there.

* feat(navigation): foldable settings groups, and the sidebar shows where you are

The settings menu groups collapse and expand like the LLM Ops sidebar
sections, through the same SidebarSection control, and all start open.
The sidebar scroll region now spans the full column, so the scrollbar
sits against the content panel instead of a padding away from it, and
the slim custom scrollbar renders again on Chromium, which treats the
standard scrollbar-width property as an opt out of the webkit styling.
A page opened by its address scrolls the sidebar to its own entry.

* fix(navigation): the cross-organization teleport follows the flag answer

The redirect that sends a member from an organization with no project to
another organization's project read the navigation mode once, from the
device-wide cache. A reader who came from an organization with the new
navigation on kept the v2 behavior in an organization the flag is off
for, and the effect never ran again when the flag answered. It now reads
a subscribed store value, so the answer brings the legacy teleport back.

Also from the review:

* `lastKnownFlag` becomes `isLastKnownFlagEnabled`, so the boolean says
  what true means.
* `persist` takes named parameters.
* The pending-flag scenario title now says what the scenario proves.

* test(navigation): the settings groups test covers the whole scenario

Every group starts open, and the fold survives the next visit to Settings. The test only proved one group and the current render before.

* fix(navigation): a pointer-closed Support menu leaves no focus ring

feat(authz): the ledger becomes the writer, one organization at a time (ADR-092 PR 2) (#7147)

* feat(authz): the runtime command family, the app-side ledger writer, and the 409 the contract always promised

The pipeline gains the six runtime commands (changeGrantRole, revokeGrants,
defineRoles, deleteRole, offboardMember alongside attachGrants), the app
gains GrantsLedgerWriter - append waited, bounded read-your-writes
convergence, instant revocation enforcement (decision 7), epoch bump
(decision 19) - and AuthzGrantsRepository's storage engine becomes command
emission via LedgerAuthzGrantsRepository. The package's duplicate error now
speaks role_binding_already_exists at 409 (decision 21's frozen REST
contract), reconciled before any write path moves. GrantsService stops
writing AuditLog directly (decision 17 - the ledger's subscriber owns that
trail) and stamps a write actor onto every fact.

* feat(authz): the genesis inventory port - legacy rows, member facts, and the ledger heads

The genesis import needs to read three things before it can emit a single
fact: the legacy RoleBinding and CustomRole rows it is importing, the
OrganizationUser rows that say who is a member at all, and - afterwards -
the Grant and Role heads the ledger projected, so the import can prove it
converged rather than assume it did. Those reads are storage, so they
belong behind a port; what a row MEANS stays in the migration.

AuthzGenesisRepository is that port, and the existing Prisma migration
repository implements it, since it already owns the same tables and the
same organization scoping.

* refactor(authz): the app authz composition moves inside the app layer, where it always belonged

The authz folder is a composition root: it wires Prisma repositories, Redis,
the audit writer and the ledger senders into the services the rest of the app
asks. That is app-layer work by definition, and it sat one directory above the
app layer only because it was written before the app layer existed. Standing
rule: authz lives inside app-layer.

Pure move plus import rewrites - no behaviour, no signatures, no composition
changed. Every '~/server/authz/...' becomes '~/server/app-layer/authz/...',
the folder's own relative reaches out gain a level ('../db' -> '../../db')
while its reaches into the app layer lose one ('../app-layer/app' -> '../app'),
and system-migrations' runtime now finds its neighbour next door rather than
a floor up. The prose in both packages' READMEs and the ADR point at the new
address too, since a stale composition-root path is a wrong answer to the one
question those docs exist to answer.

* feat(authz): the genesis import - all existing grants become ledger facts, adopted in place

Every RoleBinding, CustomRole and inferred membership fact becomes an event,
so the grants state is event-derived from the beginning of history and
replayable from genesis rather than from the day the ledger shipped.

Adoption, not re-creation: a binding's row id becomes the grant id and a
custom role's row id becomes the role id, because those ids are the upstream
identity the REST surface already hands customers, and the compat head then
converges onto the very same rows. The two facts the legacy schema only ever
inferred - the org-member floor row (decision 11) and an org-scoped admin
grant per zero-binding ADMIN, which is what the legacy admin fallback serves
today (decision 20) - have no row to adopt, so they live in the Grant head
alone. That is why the compat write for this source is update-only: minting a
new legacy-visible RoleBinding is the one thing that would stop PR 2 being
dark. The compat upsert also stops throwing on a unique violation - two
identical attaches map onto one compat slot, and a fold that is not total
parks an organization's lane forever.

The proof is that the compat projection byte-equals the rows it imported
from, with one carve-out: a custom row's role column is not compared, since
the fold normalizes it to CUSTOM and the partial unique indexes never keyed
on it. Drift holds the organization with bounded diffs; a clean sweep
finalizes it. No epoch bump and no parity fact - this import changes no
decision.

* feat(authz): the audit trail becomes an insert-only ledger subscriber

ADR-092 decision 17. The grant write paths each wrote their own AuditLog
row, which is how a trail drifts: a path that forgets leaves no trace, and
one that writes twice leaves two. The ledger already records every access
fact, so the trail becomes a subscriber over the runtime event family
rather than a second thing to remember.

Insert-only, never an update, keyed by an id derived from the event id —
so the one path that can re-deliver, a retried job, collides with the row
it already wrote and is dropped. Subscribers are excluded from replay
(ADR-098), so a projection rebuild cannot reach these rows at all.

The cutover sources (genesis-import, backfill-b, read-through-mint) are
skipped before the job is even staged: they replay history that already
happened, and auditing them would bury a customer's audit page under
thousands of changes nobody made. Role events carry no source, so the
genesis import's role facts are recognised by the only actor that writes
them. The guard runs again in the handler, because `when` fails open by
contract and failing open here is exactly the flood.

The pipeline stays storage-free — the dep is an interface with one insert
method, and Prisma lives in the app layer's authz repositories.

* feat(authz): the role-binding service and rest surface speak ledger

Every binding mutation on RoleBindingService is now a grants-ledger command:
create attaches (rejecting a duplicate), update changes the role, delete
revokes with instant enforcement, and the two batch surfaces revoke first and
attach with skip-duplicates second. The tables the service used to write are
projections now, so it must not touch them.

The duplicate signal moves with the writer. There is no P2002 to sniff any
more - the writer checks binding identity before it emits and answers
DuplicateBindingError - so the service catches that instead and keeps the same
role_binding_already_exists surface the REST contract froze.

Batches lose their transaction and gain an order. applyMemberBindings is pure
grants, so it becomes revoke-then-attach: a crash between the two leaves the
member with less access than asked for, never more, and the retry converges.
applyGroupEdits keeps a transaction for the rename and the membership rows -
those are not grant facts - and emits its binding commands after it commits.

Every write carries its actor, threaded from the tRPC session or, on the
management API, from the credential's principal. The REST handlers stop
emitting management.roleBinding.* audit rows: the ledger's insert-only
subscriber owns that trail now (decision 17), and writing both would record
one mutation twice.

* feat(authz): org, team, project and group grant writes become commands

Organizations, teams, projects and groups stop writing RoleBinding and start
emitting grants.* commands. The rule is the same everywhere: membership rows -
OrganizationUser, TeamUser, GroupMembership, the group and team rows themselves
- keep their imperative writes and their transactions, and the grants those
scopes carry are emitted once that transaction commits, revocations first.

The seat correction was the hard one. It read and rewrote a member's grants at
three scopes inside the transaction that moved the seat, so the writes are now
planned inside it - which rows collapse away, which one keeps its id and
changes role, which is new - and the plan is emitted after. The ids survive
exactly as they did, which is what keeps the member dialog's staged removals
addressable across a save.

Two last-admin guards used to read their own post-state back out of the
half-written table. They now hold the decision against the plan: the team form
projects the direct admins its edit leaves and unions the group-derived ones it
cannot edit, and team creation asks the request whether anybody is an admin,
because a team born this second has no group bindings to count. Nothing is
emitted when a guard refuses.

Organization deletion stays imperative on purpose, with the reason written
down: it is a tenant purge, not a grant write, and there is no access left to
describe once the aggregate is gone.

* feat(authz): the role editor and api-key bindings speak ledger

Custom roles stop being table rows the application writes. `role_defined`
carries the whole role, so a create and an edit are the same verb and the
repository re-states the fields the caller left out; the id is minted where
the row's default used to mint it, so ids keep their shape. Deleting a role
checks that nothing still references it and then emits `role_deleted`.

The raw guarded DELETE goes with it, and so does the P2002 backstop behind
the rename. Those were the database refusing the write; the ledger writes the
row through the fold, where a collision would stall an organization rather
than refuse a caller, so the natural-key check now sits immediately before
the append and answers custom_role_name_taken itself. The residual race is
the one the pre-check always had - two renames onto one name in the same
instant - and it is written down where it lives.

API keys follow: a key's grants and its private system role are commands, so
create, update and revoke lose their transactions and gain an order. Every
refusal a request can earn is decided before the key row is written, because
there is no longer a transaction to roll a late one back with, and replacing
a key's grants revokes before it attaches. Retiring a role a key owned checks
whether any other credential still holds it instead of leaning on a partial
delete filter.

The tests move onto the writer seam and keep their assertions. Two get
sharper for it: a role shared with another key is now asserted to survive by
name rather than by trusting a delete filter, and reusing a role in place
versus minting a fresh one is told apart by the role id the event carries.

* feat(authz): invites, signup bootstrap and the scim reconciler emit the difference

Applying an invite stops being a transaction and becomes an order. The
membership row and the invite's own status stay imperative, the grants it
carries are commands, and the status flips to ACCEPTED only once everything
before it has landed - so the stuck state the transaction guarded against is
now just a retry: an invite still PENDING is an invite still to apply. Both
callers drop the transaction they used to wrap it in, because a grant command
cannot be rolled back by one.

The SSO signup bootstrap follows the same shape, and so does the personal
workspace: the team, the project and the legacy TeamUser row keep their
transaction, and the owner's admin grant is emitted once the scope it points
at exists. Neither is anybody's decision, so both are attributed to the
system principal that made them rather than to the person signing up.

SCIM becomes a reconciler (decision 18). A directory does not push edits - it
re-pushes the same declarative truth on every sync and again after every
failure - so the handler reads what the projection holds, diffs the asserted
state against it, and emits only the difference. A replayed push emits
nothing, which is what keeps a nightly full sync out of the ledger and off
the customer's audit page. Removals go first and carry instant enforcement,
because an IdP deprovision is the fired-employee case.

The reconciler is one function with its own tests, and the slice it is
authoritative over is an explicit filter - so a membership push can never
revoke a grant an administrator made by hand at another scope.

* test(authz): the remaining suites move onto the writer seam, and the port's actor lands in its own tests

The last callers of the changed signatures: the role API suite, the group
service's scope guards, and the bound-role delete. Their assertions are the
same rules against the same behaviour - a role redefined in place versus a
fresh one, a team role replaced revoke-first, a role kept because something
still holds it - read off the commands instead of off table writes.

The write port's `actor` was threaded in PR 1 but its own adapter tests were
never given one, so the tests project would not compile on this branch. They
get it here rather than leaving the stack red.

Also drops a NUL byte that had crept into the SCIM reconciler's key separator,
which the no-binary-source guard catches.

* feat(authz): legacy api keys mint their grant on first read - no sunset, ever

Decision 1 says old keys keep working with no deadline and no customer
action; what moves is where their access LIVES. A credential minted before
grants were rows carries no binding of its own, so on the day the engine
decides, an implicit grant that only ever existed as a branch would be an
outage. It states itself instead, the first time it authenticates.

The seam is ApiKeyService.verify, beside the SHA-256 hash upgrade that
already rides it: the same shape of legacy credential quietly brought up to
date on first use, fire-and-forget, unable to fail the answer to "is this
credential real". What is minted is not a guess - `create` states the
implicit grant in code, so a service key with no bindings mints exactly the
org-wide ADMIN that mint path would have given it, and a key owned by a user
mints nothing, because `create` refuses to make one with zero bindings at
all.

Identity is derived, not random: the grant id is a function of the fact and
the key's own createdAt (its business time), and the command id is derived
from the key, so two requests racing before the projection lands carry the
same idempotency key and dedupe at the event store instead of racing two
org-admin rows into a partial unique index - and the same derivation is what
makes this converge with the cutover import rather than duplicate it.

attachBindings grows the three options that shape a write nobody is waiting
on: a derived commandId, the fact's own occurredAt, and awaitProjection off.

* docs(authz): pr 2 scenarios bound, the plan records the ledger as the only writer

Everything PR 2 built was behaviour nothing in specs/ described, and an
untagged or unbound scenario enforces nothing at all - so the genesis
import, the single-writer rule, the audit subscriber's import-source guard
and the instant revocation are written down as scenarios and each one is
tied to the test that actually proves it, in the file that already owns
that half of the story.

The Redis-stopped revocation drops @unimplemented and gains the doctrine's
second integration test: the queue leg severed, the Redis handle
disconnected, and both heads - the Grant row and its compat RoleBinding -
gone from Postgres before revokeBindings returns. It runs on the datastore
lane in CI; this machine has no LANGWATCH_TEST_* URLs.

The role-binding service's prisma double gains create/update/deleteMany
spies so "writes no binding row of its own" is asserted rather than
implied by a mock that would have thrown.

* feat(authz): grant writes fork per organization - legacy until genesis lands, ledger after

PR 2 as written flipped every organization onto ledger-emitting grant writes the
moment it deployed. That is the all-at-once behaviour change the in-place doctrine
exists to avoid; the whole point is that all the code can live on production and
organizations move one at a time.

So the fork is per organization now, and it lives in exactly one place. Every verb
on GrantsLedgerWriter asks the new write gate first: an organization is on ledger
writes iff its SystemMigrationTenantState row for authz-grants-genesis-import reads
migrated or finalized. Absent, pending, parked and rolled_back all mean the
imperative write it always took - create, createMany skipDuplicates, update,
deleteMany, and the role upsert that collapses the editor's create and edit the same
way role_defined does. No converted call site changes at all, and none of them
learns which side answered.

The deploy is therefore inert. Nothing about anybody's writes moves until their
genesis import lands, and putting one organization back is the operator writing
rolled_back on its row - fleet-wide inside the gate's cache TTL, no release. Rows
written imperatively meanwhile are adopted by the next genesis pass under their own
ids, so flip, rollback and re-flip converge rather than divide.

Decision 17 holds either side of the fork. A migrated organization gets its audit
rows from the insert-only subscriber; an unmigrated one has no event to subscribe
to, so the writer inserts the same-shaped row itself - same action vocabulary, same
metadata-is-the-fact-minus-actor rule, id from the column default because there is
no event id to derive one from. Best-effort, as the call sites' separate audit
writes always were: a trail that did not land must not fail a write that did.

Read-through minting is gated the same way. A legacy key in an unmigrated
organization states nothing and keeps the branch that decides for it today; the
guard is released rather than latched, so the first request after the organization
migrates mints as it should.

The gate is modelled on the read fork's legacy-fallback-gate next door - same
short-TTL cache in both directions, same fail-safe reading of an unreadable state
table as "not migrated", same test seam.

* fix(authz): a key is born inert, minted legacy only when it predates the ledger

* fix(authz): revocation heals at the fold, and the ledger's failures speak typed

* fix(authz): every crash window leaves less access, and routes speak to services

* refactor(authz): one identity key, one actor seam, and comments that state the invariant

* test(authz): the fold proven end to end, and every new verb bound to its scenario

* Address review comments, lint gate, and the role-delete 500

- role delete: the cross-organization RoleBinding reference check moves to
  raw SQL with a tenancy opt-out (the guard rightly refuses the model client
  for that question), fixing the 500 every role delete hit in CI
- lint: all 13 new Biome violations are gone — updateWithMembers,
  deleteMember, the personal-workspace ensure path and the better-auth
  signup hook extracted into cohesive helpers; the three useMaxParams sites
  collapsed to object params with every caller updated; dead test variables
  deleted rather than underscored
- group attach: a duplicate binding now rejects and maps to
  role_binding_already_exists instead of returning a caller-minted id for a
  row that was never created; regression test added
- better-auth: the P2002 race-loser re-asserts the organization grant, and
  the personal workspace re-asserts the owner grant on every created:false
  path; both pinned by unit tests
- ledger: partitionByIdentity batches into one findMany; the enforcement
  dependency narrows to the one method it uses; isOnLedger rename;
  LedgerActor aliases the package's GrantWriteActor
- tests: ledger-write-fork split along the fork seam with a shared harness;
  hooks tests assert emitted bindings rather than call counts; acceptInvite
  pins membership-before-grant ordering; SCIM mock keeps the forbidden write
  methods as throwing stubs
- docs/comments that promised pre-ledger atomicity or the "ships dark" state
  rewritten to describe the per-organization gate reality

* Genesis import carries legacyRole, and the audit's concrete fixes

- genesis import: a custom binding's role column now travels as legacyRole
  (exactly as the stage-B backfill does), so the fold's compat upsert
  reproduces the adopted row instead of rewriting its role to CUSTOM while
  the legacy resolver is still authoritative; the parity proof now compares
  the role column unconditionally, and the test that excused the rewrite
  became a drift case
- spec: the "declares no error codes" claim was stale — once an org's grant
  writes ride the ledger, an unavailable event-sourcing stack refuses with
  authz_ledger_unavailable; scenario added and bound to a unit test that
  also pins the refusal not poisoning the memoized handle
- api keys: deleteExclusiveToApiKey's exclusivity count now carries
  organizationId — the tenancy guard refuses an api-key predicate of
  `{ not: ... }` alone, which 500'd every retirement of a key with custom
  roles; tests added
- test fixes: DuplicateBindingError takes no constructor argument; two new
  test files formatted

* Keep grant identity off the browser-evaluable package root

The root of @langwatch/authz-server is evaluated by the client bundle (it
reaches the shadow fork through permissionsConfig), and the re-export of
bindingIdentityKey/deriveGrantId pulled node:crypto into that graph — Vite
externalizes it and every page rendered blank, which is what failed the e2e
auth setup. The identity helpers move to the server-only
@langwatch/authz-server/migration entry (whose header already states this
doctrine); ledger.ts and the SCIM reconciler import them from there, and
only the erased types stay on the root.

Also dismissed the CodeQL js/insufficient-password-hash alert on
deriveGrantId as a false positive: the sha256 input is the grant identity
tuple, and "api_key" is a principal type string, not a credential.

* Address the re-review: two real bugs, bounded caches, and convention sweeps

Functional fixes:
- createWithFoundingAdmin sliced the prefixed team id for its slug suffix,
  leaving almost no entropy; it now slices the nanoid like its sibling
- decidePlanAndRename carried the last-admin row-touch without the
  Serializable isolation that makes the touch conflict; a losing racer now
  gets 40001 instead of committing on a stale admin snapshot
- the SSO-join P2002 catch covered applyInvite too, so an unrelated unique
  violation read as "already a member"; it now guards only the membership
  insert
- the remaining OrganizationUserRole-to-TeamUserRole double cast uses
  ORGANIZATION_TO_TEAM_ROLE_MAP, which moved to the framework-free
  utils/memberRoleConstraints so the repository does not pull the invite
  service's graph
- the ledger-write-gate's per-organization cache and the projection test
  fixture's read-ordinal switch are both bounded/explicit now
- duplicate-binding detection matches by error CODE, not instanceof, per the
  package's own contract (survives a second bundled copy)

Convention sweeps, all callers updated: the remaining positional contracts
(RoleService verbs, both createBinding ports, SCIM/personal-workspace deps),
inner describes renamed to `when` conditions, `system:personal-workspace`
registered in SYSTEM_ACTORS, boolean renames, a roleBindingService factory
for the router, and the oversized legacy-grant-mint test split along its
describe seam. Decision 23 in the delivery plan now documents the delivered
chunk-keyed commandId shape and records the per-row re-keying question as
explicitly open.

* docs(authz): say why the role map exists instead of restating its name

* fix(authz): genesis import reconciles the deny direction and keys commands by content

The re-import now diffs genesis-owned Grant-head facts and custom Role heads
against the current legacy rows and emits compensating revocations, so a
binding revoked imperatively while an organization was rolled back no longer
survives as a zombie fact at read cutover. The parity proof gains
binding_extra/role_extra diff kinds so a fact the sweep could not clear parks
the tenant instead of finalizing over it.

Genesis command ids are now derived from the chunk's content (sha256 of the
sorted fact identities), not the chunk index, so a legacy row set that shifts
between passes can no longer land a new fact on an already-consumed
idempotency key and park the organization forever.

grant_role_changed drops legacyRole from the fact, so reassigning an adopted
binding to a custom role projects role=CUSTOM instead of resurrecting the
pre-migration built-in role. The witnessed migration-state head gains an
occurredAtMs monotonic guard mirroring the cutover fact's.

* fix(authz): ledger writer failure paths - replace ordering, stranded-row adoption, gate visibility

replaceBinding establishes existence with a scoped pre-read before appending
anything, so a lagging fold can no longer make it revoke the broad grant,
attach nothing, and report the binding missing. changeBindingRole adopts a
grant absent from the head with an attach fact carrying the new role instead
of emitting a role change the reducer silently drops while the caller is told
success.

The write gate's fallback-to-legacy path now increments
authz_ledger_write_gate_read_failures_total alongside the warn, the legacy
fork of revokeBindingsWhere is a single deleteMany again so a row created
mid-window cannot survive the sweep, and the legacy defineRole upsert maps
P2002 back to custom_role_name_taken instead of leaking a generic 500 to the
losing racer. revokeBindings/revokeBindingsWhere gain an opt-in
skipAppendWhenNoMatches so call sites that do not rely on the sweep stop
writing no-op revoke rows into the customer's audit trail.

changeBindingRoleImperatively scopes its update by organizationId in the
filter, and the attach epoch-bump test clears its mock so it can fail.

* fix(teams,orgs): knowable refusals throw handled errors, and a refused removal keeps the survivor's grants

team.service and organization.prisma.repository threw TRPCError for failures
we can name - team/member not found, last-admin refusals, custom-role
validation - which ships transport errors from the service and repository
layers and leaked raw user and role ids into customer-visible prose. Every
site now throws the existing handled error for its code, so the registry copy
is what a customer reads.

deleteMember snapshots the member's bindings before revoking and re-attaches
them when the locked last-admin re-check refuses the removal, so losing the
race no longer strips the surviving admin's grants while keeping their seat.
removeMember re-checks the team's effective admins after its post-commit
ledger write and reports loudly when a concurrent demote left zero. The
last-admin concurrency test now asserts the loser's error code and that
exactly one admin remains.

* fix(authz): repairable invite crash window, resilient sign-in, sweeping SCIM offboard, honest mint boundary

applyInvite re-asserts the invite's grants when the same user retries after a
crash between the acceptance transaction and the grant tail, instead of
refusing on the ACCEPTED guard and leaving a member with zero bindings
permanently. Invite acceptance passes skipAppendWhenNoMatches on its two
narrowing revokes so migrated organizations stop logging a no-op revoke on
every acceptance.

Personal-workspace ensure() no longer fails sign-in during a ledger outage:
the owner-admin grant attach skips the projection wait and treats
authz_ledger_unavailable as a logged retry-next-session, while every other
error still propagates. SCIM deprovision uses offboardMember's
principal-scope sweep so a grant the fold has not surfaced yet cannot survive
the fired-employee case. The read-through mint's era boundary reads the
cutover transition itself rather than the state row's first appearance, so
weeks spent parked no longer classify that period's keys as ledger-era.

* feat(authz): the guarded ops rollback accepts migrated organizations

The write fork engages at migrated, but rollBackSystemMigrationTenant refused
anything but finalized - so an organization held at migrated by parity drift,
the population most likely to need the documented no-deploy rollback, could
only be flipped back by direct database surgery outside the ops:manage guard
and its audit attribution. The service now accepts both statuses, the error
is renamed migration_rollback_requires_migrated_or_finalized to stay honest,
and the spec gains the migrated-rollback scenario with a bound test. The
runner already treats a rolled_back tenant identically regardless of origin;
a test now pins that.

* refactor(authz): one name for the actor - LedgerActor

The PR coined both GrantWriteActor (the package's port type) and LedgerActor
(a documented app-side alias of it) for the same concept. LedgerActor wins:
the package now declares it under that name and every consumer imports it
from @langwatch/authz-server directly, with the alias indirection removed.
GrantsLedgerActor is a distinct wire-schema type from PR 1 and keeps its
name. Comments saying "imperative path" now say "legacy path", the name the
delivery plan already uses.

* fix(authz): address review comments - fail-safe orderings, bounded caches, registry actors

Behavioral: group-membership edits revoke before the membership transaction
commits, so a failed revoke can no longer leave removed access active; the
API-key update flow always mints a fresh exclusive role and lets the orphan
sweep delete the superseded one, instead of mutating the live role's
permissions before the bindings swap; the SCIM duplicate-membership race
reconciles the organization grant before reporting success; the invite
acceptance transaction builds both operations from the root client it runs
on; awaitProjection deadlines run on the wall clock rather than injectable
business time; the legacy-fallback gate's cache gains expiry sweeps and a
hard size bound; the offboard proof transaction carries explicit
timeout/maxWait; port-signal errors are lifted by code rather than
instanceof.

Consistency: the SCIM actor joins SYSTEM_ACTORS; the role router uses
ledgerActorFor; role repository create/update/removeFromUser take a single
destructured parameter; updateTeamMemberRole emits its binding plan once;
team-removal revokes carry a reason; audit verbs are a typed union; the
genesis compat update warns when it matched nothing; the personal-workspace
transaction returns its grant target instead of capturing it mutably; the
delivery plan scopes the commands-only contract to migrated and finalized
organizations; test suites gain ordering assertions, teardown coverage, and
when-styled describe blocks.

* fix(ci): repoint the stray LedgerActor import, extract the grown functions, spec the new scenarios

The scim-grants reconciler still imported LedgerActor from the app ledger
module after the rename removed that alias - it now imports from
@langwatch/authz-server like every other consumer. changeBindingRole and
defineRole shed their on-ledger and pre-ledger branches into named helpers,
and the fallback gate's eviction loop moved into evictUntilUnderCap, clearing
the three complexity findings the lint delta gate caught. The eight scenario
titles the new tests bind are now real @unit scenarios in
in-place-authz-migration.feature, beside their thematic siblings.

* fix(tests): type the mint mock and reach stubs through vi.mocked

The genesisImportMoment tests pass a two-method mock where the function's
parameter demands Pick<PrismaClient, ...> - the mock now carries that type
via an unknown cast at its one declaration site. The restricted-permissions
suite reached mock methods through the helper's honestly-typed PrismaClient
return, which the tests-lane typecheck rejects; the five stub sites now go
through vi.mocked. Caught only by tsconfig.tsgo.tests.json - the editor
config does not include test files.

* fix(tests): assert the call-order indices non-null for the ordering proof

noUncheckedIndexedAccess types invocationCallOrder[0] as possibly undefined;
toBeLessThan takes only numbers. Same pattern as the acceptInvite ordering
assertion.

* fix(tests): stub the prisma fixtures through a loose Mock cast

vi.mocked restores the real Prisma signatures, so mockResolvedValue demanded
full model payloads the fixtures deliberately do not carry. A single
as-unknown-as-Mock cast per stub site keeps the helper's honest PrismaClient
return without fabricating twelve-field fixtures. Verified against the exact
CI command scoped to this file, with a control run proving the scoped project
reproduces the CI error.

* style(tests): let biome rewrap the recast stub lines

fix: unify money type — string for USD amounts, BigInt for nanoUsd (#7145)

* fix: unify money type — string for USD amounts, BigInt for nanoUsd

costUsd and spendUsd were inconsistently typed as number, string, or
number|string across 5 governance files. Number() on decimal strings is
lossy past ~15 significant digits, and float accumulation drifts.

Changes across 19 sites in 5 core files + consumer updates:

- activityMonitor.service.ts: all spendUsd/costUsd interfaces → string,
  accumulation through usdToNanoUsd()/nanoUsdToDecimalString() instead of
  float addition, Zod schema validates as string with finite-number guard
- canonicalCostExtractor.service.ts: costUsd → string, new
  costUsdStringOrNull() helper preserves decimal strings from OTLP attrs
- anthropicAdmin.puller.ts: amount schema → .transform(String), removed
  Number(amount) coercion
- pulled-usage-pricing.service.ts: ProviderReportedPrice.costUsd → string
- budget.clickhouse.repository.ts: AmountNanoUSD comparison via BigInt()
  instead of lossy Number()
- pullerAdapter.ts: NormalizedPullEvent.cost_usd accepts string|number,
  transforms to string
- All puller adapters + frontend consumers updated for string types

Closes langwatch/langwatch-saas#1090

* fix: guard empty-string cost_usd from passing through as valid

Number('') === 0, which is finite, so the Zod transform and
costUsdStringOrNull both let '' through. Downstream usdToNanoUsd('')
throws because whole === '' && fraction === ''.

The old z.coerce.number() handled this (coerced '' to 0). Add an
explicit s !== '' guard so empty strings fall back to '0'/'null'.

* fix: update remaining test files for string money types

* fix: remove unused numberOrNull (replaced by costUsdStringOrNull)

* fix: guard Number(nano) with safe-integer check in budget debit path

* fix(test): update costUsd assertion from number to string in integration test

* fix: restore cost_usd validation and remove float round-trip in pullers

B1: normalizedPullEventSchema.cost_usd now validates against DECIMAL_PATTERN
and rejects negative values at the parse boundary, matching the constraint
usdToNanoUsd enforces downstream. Malformed strings like "banana" are
caught at the schema seam instead of throwing deep in the pricing service.

B2: httpPollingPullerAdapter and s3PollingPullerAdapter now use asDecimalString()
which preserves string inputs directly, avoiding the lossy Number() round-trip
that String(asNumber(...)) performed on sub-cent amounts.

Addresses review findings from drewdrewthis on PR #7145.

Data pulled from the Aug-19 dependency-alert-backlog burst: mcp/typescript's
uv.lock only typechecks Python fixture files under tests/fixtures/ for the
MCP server's instrumentation-codegen — nothing in CI installs or executes it.
Its first scheduled sweep dumped 24 individual PRs for zero coverage gain,
adding real load against the org's ~76-slot concurrent-job ceiling. Dropping
the entry entirely is strictly better than grouping it.

(#6804/#7207), each moving part of a coupled-release family out of lockstep
and each breaking imports on its own. A root-npm langchain group (matching
sdks/typescript's real @langchain/* + langchain dependencies) and the
existing per-uv-project langchain groups now open one PR per family instead,
which only opens once every member resolves together.

Also groups arize-phoenix pre-emptively in services/langevals — a single
package today, but upstream ships sibling packages that release in step
with it.

fix(ci): exempt manifest-only diffs from deployment-impact-check (#7294)

* fix(ci): exempt manifest-only diffs from deployment-impact-check

The check's `services/**` trigger path matches every dependency-lockfile
bump in services/langevals, services/aigateway, and services/nlpgo, but a
pure uv.lock/pyproject.toml/package.json diff can't add an env var, a helm
value, or change `helm install` behavior — it has no deployment surface by
construction. Dependabot never writes a "## Deployment Impact" section, so
this was a hard block on every services/* dependency PR (#7293, #7289,
#7288 all failed on it).

* Address review comments

- Scope the manifest-only skip to dependabot[bot]: pyproject.toml/package.json/
  go.mod/Cargo.toml are hand-edited manifests, not pure lockfiles, so a human
  PR touching only one could slip in a real deployment-relevant change
  alongside a version bump.
- Tag the new spec's scenarios @unimplemented (matches
  specs/ci/no-docker-integration-tests.feature convention) — untagged
  scenarios report as vacuously bound in check-feature-parity.ts, which was
  already failing CI on this PR.

* Address review comments

- Add Chart.lock to the always-safe (any actor) lockfile tier: it's an
  auto-generated helm dependency-resolution snapshot, same guarantee as
  uv.lock/pnpm-lock.yaml/go.sum/Cargo.lock. Split the manifest check into two
  tiers so the trigger paths under charts/** aren't left with a Chart.lock-only
  gap.
- Rewrite the spec in user-facing terms (dependency-bump author's
  perspective) instead of naming workflow internals, trigger-path globs, and
  specific project directories.

* Address review comments

- Judge the exemption by the PR author, not github.actor: the workflow
  triggers on `edited`, so a maintainer tidying a dependabot PR's
  description withdrew the exemption it qualified for when it opened.
- Move the manifest classification out of inline YAML into
  .github/scripts/guard-deployment-impact.ts, so the rule has a test
  rather than a `case` statement nothing can run.
- Bind the spec's four scenarios to that test and retag them @unit;
  every scenario was @unimplemented, so the file enforced nothing and
  feature-parity failed it as newly inert.

refactor(api): migrate hono-openapi 0.4.8 -> 1.3.1 (#7286)

* refactor(api): migrate hono-openapi 0.4.8 -> 1.3.1

v1 drops the per-library validator peers and converts schemas through
Standard Schema, so `hono-openapi/zod` no longer exists — 33 files import
`resolver` and `validator` from the package root instead. zod 3.25 already
implements `~standard`, so no schema changed.

The upgrade is only half the work. v1 differs from v0.4 in four ways that
reach published clients, and none of them fail a build:

`packages/api` has its own hono-openapi. Left on 0.4.8 it kept its own
`uniqueSymbol`, and v1's `generateSpecs` cannot see a route registered
against a different instance — so the organization, roles, role-bindings
and scim-tokens families vanished from the document entirely. 23
operations, no error, exit 0. Both packages move together.

Validation hooks changed container. v0.4 handed the hook zod's `ZodError`;
v1 hands over the Standard Schema failure, which is the issue array bare.
`result.error?.issues` on an array is `undefined`, and `undefined ?? []` is
an empty violation list, so the 422 kept its status and lost every field
name. `packages/api` had the matching bug one level up — it threw the array
itself, which reached `onError` as an unrecognisable value and answered 500
"Unknown Error" where a 400 belonged. The issues themselves are unchanged:
zod's Standard Schema issues ARE `ZodIssue`s.

operationIds are derived differently. v0.4 capitalised the first character
of a path segment; v1 pascal-cases the whole thing, so
`getApiCoding-agentPull-request-usage` became
`getApiCodingAgentPullRequestUsage` — 49 of 264 operations, and
`openapi-python-client` turns these into the Python SDK's function names.
Restored by rewriting only ids that match what v1 derives, so a hand-written
id is untouched. Passing the scheme through `defaultOptions` looks right and
is not: the validator's fragment merges after `describeRoute`'s, so the
default clobbered 24 explicit ids instead.

Response schemas are read as input. v0.4 read requests as input and
responses as output; zod 3 exposes no such split through Standard Schema, so
v1 reads everything as input and a `.default()` field stops being required.
30 entries across the 8 prompts response schemas — `messages`, `inputs`,
`tags`, `parameters`, all always returned — would have become `Unset` in the
generated Python client. Corrected on the finished document, where request
and response are still distinguishable; `loadVendor` cannot express it,
since its hook sees neither the caller's options nor the direction.

Verified by regenerating the document before and after: 264 operations
either side, zero operationId changes, zero `required` content changes. What
does change is v1 marking request bodies `required: true` (75), dropping
empty `parameters: []` (73) and redundant `required: false` (36), and moving
parameter descriptions to the parameter level (11).

Two things found and deliberately left alone, each wanting its own change:
v1's operationIds are the better ones, and `nullable: true` appears 80 times
in a document that declares OpenAPI 3.1, which removed it.

Unblocks the zod 4 path: hono-openapi no longer pins zod at all. What
remains is `@hono/zod-validator` (0.4.3, zod 3 only, 145 call sites) and
`zod-openapi` v4, both now ordinary bumps rather than transitive
constraints.

* fix(api): declare hono-openapi's peers on packages/api

The version bump landed without them. `packages/api` declared
`hono-openapi` and `hono` and nothing else, so four of v1's six peers were
resolved from `platform/app`'s declarations instead of its own:
`@standard-community/standard-json`, `@standard-community/standard-openapi`,
`@types/json-schema` and `openapi-types`.

Three of those are load-bearing at runtime, not just for types —
hono-openapi's entry point statically imports `@hono/standard-validator`,
`@standard-community/standard-json` and `@standard-community/standard-openapi`
at module load. `@hono/standard-validator` is marked optional in
`peerDependenciesMeta`, which is misleading: a static top-level import is not
optional, so it is declared here too.

It worked by accident and would have kept working until it didn't. pnpm keys
a package's store entry by its resolved peer set, so two workspace packages
that disagree about peers get two physically distinct copies of
hono-openapi — and a route registered against one copy's `uniqueSymbol` is
invisible to the other's `generateSpecs`. That is exactly how 23 operations
vanished from the document earlier in this branch. Undeclared peers are the
mechanism that brings it back.

Verified both packages still resolve one instance: identical version strings
in the lockfile and the same realpath from each package. Document regenerates
byte-identical — 264 operations, no operationId changes, the 26
organization/roles/role-bindings/scim-tokens operations still present.

* refactor(api): split the two spec-correction walkers

CI's Biome gate compares violation counts against the merge base, and both
new modules added one `noExcessiveCognitiveComplexity` each — a nested walk
over paths, methods, responses and media types in a single function.

Split along the nesting: one function per level, each named for the level it
walks. `subSchemasOf` and `defaultedPropertyNames` also pull the composite
recursion and the property scan out of `requireDefaultedProperties`, so the
recursion happens in one place rather than twice down two branches.

No behaviour change: the document regenerates to the same 264 operations,
with no operationId and no `required` content differences.

* refactor(api): take hono-openapi v1's operation ids

Reverts the rewrite pass added earlier in this branch. It preserved v0.4's
derived ids on the premise that renaming them would break generated clients.
That premise was wrong, and checking it costs less than the machinery did.

`openapi-python-client` snake-cases the operationId, and both a hyphen and a
camel boundary collapse to `_`. So `postApiDatasetDirect-upload` and
`postApiDatasetDirectUpload` are the same function to it:

    both -> post_api_dataset_direct_upload

That holds for all 49 ids the two schemes disagree on — zero produce a
different Python identifier — and 44 of the 49 predicted names match modules
already checked in under sdks/python, so the rule is measured rather than
assumed. The committed Python client contains none of the hyphenated ids at
all; it never referenced them.

The TypeScript client is keyed on `paths`, not `operations`. The one place
that reaches for an operation type asks for `putApiPromptsByIdTagsByTag`,
which both schemes spell identically.

So the ids move to v1's spelling, which is the better one:
`getApiCoding-agentPull-request-usage` becomes
`getApiCodingAgentPullRequestUsage`. An id that genuinely must not move is
declared on its route — 53 operations already do exactly that, and the
`packages/api` builder takes `docs.operationId` for the same purpose. That is
the mechanism for pinning an id, not a post-hoc pass over the document.

Regenerated with the shim gone: 264 operations, 49 ids updated, no `required`
content changes. The docs copy and its api-reference pages re-sync with no new
or orphaned pages, and the TypeScript client regenerates and still typechecks.

* docs(api): drop comments that restate the code they sit on

Four one-liners said what the function name and signature already said.
Removed. The ones that survive explain something the code cannot: why the
recursion sits in the property scan, why `SpecLike.paths` is
`Record<string, unknown>`, and why request bodies are deliberately untouched.

Splitting the walkers in the previous commit also stranded the exported
function's doc block above `requireInOperation`, two comments deep, leaving
`requireDefaultedResponseFields` undocumented. Moved back onto it.
