fix(clickhouse): a tenant is a project or an organization, and the grants ledger's is the latter (#7315)

* fix(clickhouse): a tenant is a project or an organization, and the ledger's is the latter

The grants ledger (ADR-092 §13) keeps one aggregate per organization, so its
event-store writes arrive with an organization id as the tenant. The client
resolver only ever looked a tenant up in `Project`, found nothing, and refused
by design — correctly, since a tenant it cannot place is exactly the one whose
data must not land on another customer's instance. The result in production
was that every `authz_grants` command failed to append: the genesis import's
heads never landed, `awaitConvergence` timed out at 120s, and the organization
parked with the projection blamed for work the event store never accepted.

Routing is per-organization either way — a project only ever contributes the
organization that owns it — so `getClickHouseClientForProject` becomes
`getClickHouseClientForTenant` and resolves both kinds: the project's owner, or
the organization itself. It is a rename rather than a second function, because
a parallel resolver is how the two callers drift apart again. The refusal is
unchanged for an id that names neither.

Nothing else in the append path assumes a project: retention resolves to the
platform default for an unknown id, and `event_log` carries no TTL.

* fix(specs): the routing spec names the resolver it actually has

Review catch: the two project-routing scenarios still said
`getClickHouseClientForProject`, a function this branch removes, so the
specification described a contract the code no longer offers. Scenario titles
are untouched, so every `@scenario` binding holds.

While in the archive test the rename touched: the rationale above the
source-level check claimed the resolver is still referenced by sibling
procedures "in the same router", and the router names it nowhere - which is
exactly what the assertion below proves. The inner describe also gains its
`when` condition.

feat(governance): attribute Databricks warehouse compute to the Genie question that ran it (#7188)

* feat(governance): attribute Databricks warehouse compute to the Genie question that ran it

Genie charges nothing per message, so the adapter recorded every question at a
cost of zero. The warehouse compute answering the question is billed regardless,
and ADR-088 names Databricks as the first adapter to carry real pulled cost.

A source now optionally names its SQL warehouse. When it does, one statement per
run reads `system.query.history` and `system.billing.usage`, and each Genie
statement takes the share of its hour's bill that its execution time accounts
for. Naming no warehouse keeps today's behaviour exactly.

Three things this gets right on purpose:

- The denominator is the whole warehouse, not the Genie queries on it. Dividing
  an hour across Genie alone would hand Genie the bill for the dashboards and
  jobs sharing the warehouse. Live validation put Genie at 13.3% of one
  workspace's compute; the rest stays unattributed.

- The arithmetic is bigint nanoUSD end to end. A question's share of an hourly
  bill is routinely a fraction of a cent, and the Statement Execution API
  returns decimals as strings, so no float exists anywhere on the path.

- Cost arrives after the question. A cost-bearing source therefore reads back
  two hours rather than the watermark's five minutes, so the priced version of a
  question replaces its zero — the restatement key is the message's own
  coordinates and excludes cost, so this corrects rather than duplicates.

Unpriceable compute is reported, never guessed: a SKU with no published price,
or one priced in another currency, yields no cost rather than a converted
figure nobody can reconcile against an invoice. The figure is a list price, so
it stays `costStatus: estimate`. A billing outage costs the cost, never the
visibility records.

Refs ADR-088, langwatch/langwatch-saas#1103, langwatch/langwatch-saas#852

* fix(governance): never let a cost the run could not work out overwrite one it did

Three defects the review found in the warehouse-cost path, all on money, all
introduced by the commit before this one.

1. A billing outage wiped cost it could not confirm. The settling window
   re-reads a question for two hours so a late cost can correct its zero. But a
   re-read whose cost lookup failed still emitted a usage hint carrying zero,
   and since the restatement key excludes cost, that zero REPLACED a figure an
   earlier run had already worked out. A few minutes of billing trouble
   therefore erased the spend it could not reach. A re-read with no cost now
   carries no usage hint at all: the question still lands as an audit record and
   the ledger is not asked to write anything.

2. The window cut hours in half. `hour_total_ms` came from statements inside the
   window while the hour's bill came from buckets inside the window, and a
   window starting at 10:37 keeps hour 10's queries but drops hour 10's bill --
   so those questions priced at nothing while looking properly priced, and on
   the last run that saw them that nothing was the final word. Both ends are now
   snapped to whole hours.

3. A reordered SELECT would have priced from the wrong column. The API answers
   positionally, every value is a string, so swapping two columns parses
   perfectly and silently. With the duration and the hour's total exchanged, a
   question claims $24 of an hour billed at $6. The manifest's column names are
   now checked against the ones asked for, and a mismatch refuses to price.

Each is covered by a test that was watched failing first; the reordering test
was checked to report '24' with the guard removed.

* fix(governance): treat a billing answer with no column names as unpriceable

The manifest check refused to price an answer whose columns were not the
ones asked for, but only when the answer said what its columns were. With
no manifest it fell through and priced positionally — which is the exact
case the check exists for, since every value in a row is a string and a
reordering parses clean.

An answer we cannot check is one we cannot price from.

Also binds the four scenarios CI found unbound, which is the check doing
its job: they were written as claims and never made to hold anything.
Each now drives the adapter — a question Genie answered without a query,
compute that belongs to no question, the figure having to call itself an
estimate, and a late bill correcting the same record rather than adding one.

* fix(governance): refuse a cost answer that was cut short instead of pricing half of it

A cost read capped at 50,000 rows returns a partial set on a busy warehouse,
with no ordering and nothing saying it was truncated. The statements that did
not fit are simply absent, so their questions record zero — and on a first
sweep that zero is permanent, because the cursor moves past the question and
later runs only re-read the two-hour settling window. Which statements are
missing is exactly what a cut-off answer cannot say, so the whole answer is
now refused rather than half-used. The wider problem, that a first sweep is
never revisited however the cost read failed, is langwatch-saas#1121.

A billing row that fails to parse is now counted and logged. Every other
refusal already reached the log through `skipped`; that was the one case that
under-priced in silence.

Narrows a scenario that was measuring nothing. Replacing the whole cost
statement with `SELECT 'mutant' AS nonsense FROM does_not_exist` leaves every
test green — no test executes the SQL — so "the cost is the published rate,
not the customer's negotiated one" was asserted by a `costStatus` constant the
adapter sets unconditionally. It now claims only the label it can observe, and
says in the scenario body why the rest is unverified.

Splits `warehouseCost` and `withWarehouseCost`, which had pushed two Biome
complexity warnings from 0 to 1 and were the only failing check.

* fix(governance): refuse a cost answer cut short by size, not just by row count

The row-limit guard added in the previous commit catches an answer that
filled the LIMIT. It does not catch one that filled the byte cap.

An INLINE statement result is capped by size as well as by rows. When it
overflows, the API answers with a first chunk and a next_chunk_index
pointing at the rest -- a reply that arrives under the row limit and so
reads as complete. A manifest that counts more rows than arrived is a
third form of the same thing.

Neither field was in the response schema, so both were parsed away.
Pricing on either would put a confident zero on every statement that did
not fit.

If Databricks spells either field differently the check reads undefined
and does not fire, falling back to the row count. Tracked with the other
unverified column names in langwatch-saas#1116.

* chore(governance): drop decorative comment CodeRabbit flagged as noise

* test(governance): rename Databricks Genie warehouse-cost test to integration

It opens a real socket (testcontainers-backed ClickHouse/Postgres), so it
belongs in the integration lane, not the unit lane.

* fix(governance): keep a window we could not price retryable, and price it a day at a time

Refusing a cut-short cost answer stopped the asymmetric partial charge but not
the loss behind it. A first sweep reads thirty days and asked for all thirty in
one billing query; a warehouse busy enough to trip the row cap had the whole
month refused, every question in it recorded at zero, and the watermark moved
on regardless — the cost read never reached `nextCursor`. Later runs re-read
only the two-hour settling window, so no healthy billing response could ever
correct those rows.

Two changes, and neither works alone. The window is now read a day at a time,
oldest first, so it takes a single busy DAY to trip the cap rather than a busy
month, and the days answered before it keep their cost. And the walk stops at
the first day it cannot price, handing back `pricedThroughMs` as a second
ceiling on the watermark, so that day stays inside the next run's window.
Chunking without the ceiling still loses the refused day; the ceiling without
chunking re-refuses the same thirty days every run forever.

Held only when the answer was CUT SHORT — rows exist that a narrower question
could still reach. Billing refusing outright is not held: a smaller window
would be refused the same way, and holding would stall a workspace that never
granted the billing tables, with no way out but turning the feature off.

Addresses the P1 on #7188 and the chunked-read finding deferred to
langwatch-saas#1122.

* fix(governance): bound the cost hold and keep the unpriced period's first instant

Two defects in the watermark hold added by 1a8396af44, both found after it
landed and both proved by running them.

A day that is cut short identically on every run held the watermark forever:
the source re-swept a widening window waiting for an answer that could not
come. A probe measured zero progress across three consecutive runs. The hold
is now bounded by age, not distance — a distance bound fires on the legitimate
thirty-day first sweep. `costHeldSinceMs` records when the hold began and it
is given up after WAREHOUSE_COST_MAX_HOLD_MS, matching how `sweepHadGap`
already trades completeness for progress.

A question asked at the exact start of an unpriced period was recorded at zero
and then filtered out of every later run, permanently. The cost window keeps
`start_time >= from` and enumeration keeps `created > watermark`, so both are
half-open in the same direction and a watermark landing on that instant drops
the question standing on it. The ceiling now sits one millisecond earlier.
Reverting that millisecond fails the new test at exactly that seam.

The scenario for the first fix was rewritten after a challenge run refuted it.
It asserted the watermark stays behind every question in the unpriced period,
which is false: within the settling look-back a question is re-read regardless
of where the watermark sits, and a measured run put the watermark 4.2 minutes
ahead of one while still re-reading and pricing it. The scenario now asserts
the re-read itself, which is both true and sensitive to the defect.

Reported by langwatch-agent on PR #7188.

* fix(governance): price a Genie question by the warehouse that answered it

The billing query bound the configured warehouse id twice: once as the
warehouse the query runs on, and once as a filter on which warehouse's
compute it may price. Those are not the same object. A Genie space answers
on whichever warehouse it was authored against, and a connector credential
holds CAN USE on whichever warehouse an administrator gave it — routinely a
different one. When they differ the query filters its own answer to nothing
and every question in the workspace prices at zero, which is indistinguishable
from a question that genuinely cost nothing.

Measured against a live workspace: the shipped statement returned 0 rows
filtered to the executor warehouse and 100 USD-priced rows with the filter
removed, for the same window.

The filter is gone. Each hour is now totalled and priced per warehouse and
joined back on it, so a question is allocated its share of the bill of the
warehouse that actually ran it. The configured id keeps its name and its
optionality, and now means only where the billing query executes.

* feat(governance): let a Databricks source sign in for itself

A pasted workspace token expires about an hour after Databricks issues
it. A source configured that way works when the admin saves it and is
dead by the next scheduled run, with nothing on the source to say why —
so the only way to keep a Genie schedule alive was to paste a new token
every hour by hand.

A source can now carry a service principal's client id and secret
instead, and signs in at the start of every run against the workspace's
own /oidc/v1/token. The credentials do not expire, so the schedule runs
unattended.

A pasted token still wins when both are present: someone pasting one
into a source that already has a secret is rotating by hand, usually
because the secret stopped working, and preferring the secret would
ignore the thing they just did.

The sign-in gets its own 15s bound rather than borrowing the job's five
minutes, so a token endpoint that never answers fails naming itself
instead of surfacing as a run-wide timeout that names no cause. A 200
carrying no access token is rejected at the sign-in rather than carried
forward to fail later as an unauthorised Genie call. The secret is sent
as HTTP Basic, stays out of every thrown reason, and rides the same
encrypted credentials subtree and the same egress guard as the token.

* fix(governance): decline a billing read the run has no time to finish

A billing read started with less than its own timeout left cannot end well.
The worker kills the run at its deadline and discards every question the
sweep had already read, leaving the cursor where it was — so the next run
sweeps the same questions and dies in the same place. The read's own
graceful failure never gets to happen, because nothing is left to return it
to.

RunBudget.exhaustedWithin answers the question the cost loop actually has:
not whether the deadline has passed, but whether enough of it remains to
finish one more request. Out of room now takes the path already there for
out of requests — hold the watermark at the last priced day, record the
questions unpriced, let the next run ask again.

An unpriced window is recoverable. A sweep discarded holding it is not.

* fix(governance): say which warehouse the billing read actually needs

The hint called it the warehouse that answers these spaces questions, which
points at the wrong one. The id is only the executor for the billing lookup;
the statement carries no warehouse predicate, so it prices every warehouse
the questions used no matter which one runs it. Following the old wording
leads to the Genie-bound warehouse, which the credential may hold nothing on.

Also says what naming one costs: every run submits a query, so a stopped
warehouse is started and billed on the source schedule.

* fix(governance): price a whole week per read and split only on refusal

A daily cost read left 30 days as 30 statements, and 30 x 24h/read
overran the 300s job deadline (648s) before the window finished — so a
window never priced fully and its questions sat at zero forever.

Read a week at a time (WAREHOUSE_COST_CHUNK_MS 24h -> 7d). A week that
comes back cut short is retried a day at a time (WAREHOUSE_COST_PIECE_MS)
rather than surrendered whole, and only the days that could not be priced
hold the watermark. A read still in flight at WAREHOUSE_COST_TIMEOUT_MS is
a timed_out, not a failure: it holds and retries instead of advancing the
watermark past a period it never actually priced. wait_timeout 30s -> 50s,
inside the client abort budget.

Measured live: 5 x 7-day reads = 120.8s total vs 648s daily.

* fix(governance): hold unbilled Genie statements, widen the Genie gate, carry the share's ingredients

Three changes on the Databricks Genie warehouse-cost path, all locked
against live-workspace evidence and a five-lens red-team pass (ADR-088 v6):

- LEFT JOIN priced + owed-hold: a statement whose hour has no billing row
  yet is held (watermark stops, bounded by the max hold), never recorded
  at zero for good. Validated live: 33/33 statements priced, $0.3885.

- Membership is the union, not the string: the Genie gate becomes
  (genie_space_id IS NOT NULL OR client_application = :genie_app), so no
  single provider change can silently shrink the priced set. The CTE
  projects genie_space_id for the outer WHERE only; the final six output
  columns and their positional parse are untouched, and hour_total still
  sums the whole warehouse.

- A priced event carries the share's raw ingredients: warehouseHour
  { totalExecutionMs, billableUsd } beside the cost, outside the
  pulled_usage hint so it never enters the restatement key. Raw and never
  a ratio: a "busy fraction" was designed and refuted (unclamped over
  concurrency; inverted by serverless auto-stop).

Also: every enforced scenario in the touched specs is now bound to a test
(feature-parity green), secret-at-rest and billing-destination tests
added, and two branch-new cognitive-complexity violations refactored away
(foldPricedLine, walkWarehouseCostPieces, genieCredentialsFrom).

fix(scenarios): vendor scenario SDK 1.3.0 so the judge can fetch remote traces again (#7327)

The 1.1.1->1.2.0 re-vendor (#7135) silently dropped remote-trace judging:
released v1.2.0 was cut before the feature landed upstream, while the
"1.1.1" it replaced was a pre-release build that carried it. The platform
kept passing `fetchRemoteTraces`/`traceWaitTimeoutMs`/`traceWaitExtensionMs`,
which the SDK's run-config schema accepted and ignored — so every http
target's judge went blind to the agent's reported spans. Symptoms: the
judge kept calling continue_test on conversations that had already ended
(users cancelling by hand), or failed runs claiming the agent hallucinated
tool calls whose spans were sitting in the span store.

v1.3.0 is the first release with remote-trace judging (upstream 149778cc)
and contains the minTurns work 1.2.0 was vendored for; its config surface
(`fetchRemoteTraces`, `traceWaitTimeoutMs`, `traceWaitExtensionMs`,
`langwatch.{endpoint,apiKey}`) matches what remote-trace-run-config.ts
produces, verified against the published tarball.

A new bundle test pins the capability: the built child bundle must contain
the judge's `wait_for_traces` tool, which only exists in SDK builds that
can act on the remote-trace configuration.

feat(langy): minimal harness, own system prompt, scoped tools, outcome-based judge, overfit-resistant skills (#7266)

* feat(langy): minimal harness, own system prompt, scoped tools, outcome-based judge, overfit-resistant skills

The prompt had grown 16.6KB to 52.8KB in 11 days by accreting one rule per
observed failure, with judge criteria that restated the prompt back at it.
This replaces the pile with a 12.8KB contract (role, interface, principles,
one boundary statement), moves the persona into the opencode agent config
(which drops the stock coding-agent prompt entirely), denies webfetch, task
and question at the harness layer, retires the OpenCode-to-Langy replaceAll
plugin, slims the per-turn override to a pointer, rewrites the judge rubric
outcome-based, adds reply-quality and minimal-harness specs with real
bindings, syncs the langyagent skill tree with a pinned generator step, and
teaches the scenarios, test-compliance and agent-improve skills the
improvement ladder so customers do not rebuild this failure mode.

* test(langy): live-suite iteration: adapter turn-lock retry, github guard as outcome, errored-trace fixtures, judge card visibility, prompt class sharpenings

* test(langy): outcome-form judge criteria, turn-override end discipline, worker-stopped retry, greeting names Langy

* test(langy): traceIds-based grounding assert, transcript-scoped judge evidence, one-line write replies

* test(langy): current-surfaces boundary scenarios grade the permission outcome, core criteria gain the refusal arm

* feat(skills): trace-first diagnosis and environment-defined levers in the ladder skills

* fix(langy): never end a turn silently, plus permission-boundary and post-navigation scenario regrades

* fix(langy): suppress the intentional skip on the connected-project pair

* test(langy): tell a starved turn apart from a silent one instead of grading both as a bad reply

* test(langy): scope create-scenario criteria to the transcript, leave persistence to Layer 2

* fix(langy): end on the answer, not on a question about what to do next

* test(langy): run the five consolidation-proof red-team cases first

* fix(langy): bind the silent-turn scenario, correct the tool phase, drop unrelated generated churn

* fix(langy): decline names the boundary instead of promising it later, ban em dashes in replies

* fix(langy): resolve the prompt scope contradiction and the review findings

The Go persona prompt claimed "You operate LangWatch and nothing else"
while AGENTS.md Scope carves out the skill workflows, so a legitimate
"open a PR" request could be refused on scope. Both strings load for the
same agent, and provision.go's own docblock forbids the overlap: persona
in the Go prompt, rules in AGENTS.md. The persona now describes how to
decline and lets AGENTS.md define the boundary.

A whitespace-only delta counted as visible text on both sides of the
turn, so the blank-reply defect survived in a narrower form: the token
buffer set its has-written flag and skipped the fallback, and the e2e
adapter handed the blank string to the judge. Whitespace between two
words still has to be buffered, so the fallback now keys off a separate
saw-visible-text set rather than off the first flush.

The empty-turn fallback no longer tells the user to ask again, because a
silent turn can still have completed a write. It points at the cards.

Test and skill fixes: the dogfood fixture waits for the collector to
project both traces instead of sleeping a constant, the dataset check
asserts the name it asked for, the tool-permission test pins the deny
list exactly, manifest keys cannot resolve outside docs/, the scenarios
skill requires evidence before a test is weakened to green, consultant
mode stops after two attempts at the same failure, the agent-performance
handoff no longer breaks its own read-only contract, repository
discovery paginates, and the debug recipe drops a GNU-only date call
that fails on macOS.

* fix(langy): make the prompt's card examples valid, and drop its em dashes

The card examples used bare elisions, so a model copying the documented
shape emitted JSON that does not parse and degrades to the failed-card
disclosure. They now carry real illustrative values, and a test reads
the shipped prompt and validates every example against the same
derived-card contract the panel renders, so the two cannot drift.

The prompt also carried seven em dashes while its own Replies section
told Langy to write none. Browser QA had already caught em dashes in
Langy's output, and a prompt breaking its own rule seven times is the
likelier cause than the rule being unclear. Removing them costs nothing
and pays for most of the card examples: the prompt is 14,304 bytes,
still under the 16KB budget.

* fix(skills): pass --yes to the report command so it cannot hang an agent

Without it, npx stops to ask before installing the CLI, and a
non-interactive agent waits on a prompt it can never answer. The skill's
own troubleshooting table already lists that failure, so the command it
recommends should not cause it.

The version stays unpinned. The report endpoint is a feedback channel
where the current client is the right one, and a pin would go stale on
every release of the CLI.

* fix(langy): name every trace origin in the prompt, and pin the list

The prompt listed six origins. The platform stamps ten. Langy had never
heard of `workflow`, `sample`, `coding_agent` or `ai_tool`, and
`workflow` is stamped by the trace pipeline itself, so it is present in
real projects rather than hypothetical.

This failure is silent, which is what makes it worth a test rather than
an edit. `parseOriginOption` forwards the value unvalidated, and its own
docblock calls origins free-form strings, so an origin Langy does not
know returns zero rows and reads exactly like a correct empty answer.
Every question about the user's traffic rides on this list.

There are five hand-maintained copies of it (the prompt, ORIGIN_DISPLAY,
originColors, the CLI docstring, the skill file) and no two agreed. The
new test reads the shipped prompt and compares it against the platform's
own set, so the prompt cannot drift from the product again, and a new
origin fails a test instead of quietly narrowing an answer.

Recorded rather than fixed: `langy` is stamped by the relay and has its
own precedence rule, but has no ORIGIN_DISPLAY row, so langy traces
render in the Trace Explorer as a raw lowercase label with a
hash-rotated colour. Adding the row carries a palette decision that
belongs to the Trace Explorer, so the test names the gap instead.

* fix(langy): say the skills table is a shortcut, and report the prompt size

Four installed skills have no routing row: connect-agent,
debug-with-langwatch, eval-triage and setup-lw. Adding four rows was the
obvious fix and the wrong one. opencode discovers every skill under
$HOME/.config/opencode/skills, which the worker symlinks, and the
`skill` tool advertises them, so the table already duplicates a list the
harness injects. Growing that duplication buys nothing; saying what the
table is fixes the part that misleads, which is a shortcut list that
reads like an inventory.

The size-budget test now logs the byte count on every run. A passing
"under 16KB" is true of any prompt, so it could not tell a rebuild that
picked up an edit from one that did not, which is exactly the question
asked of it while rebuilding the worker tonight.

* fix(langy): correct the prompt's claim that every command takes a format flag

Review asked for `--format json` on the `report` command in five skill
files. Checking the CLI shows the opposite: `report` declares only
`--user-approved`, `--summary`, `--summary-file`, `--session`, `--title`,
`--email`, `--endpoint` and `--dry-run`, so a format flag there is an
unknown option, not a better invocation.

The suggestion was reasonable because the prompt says so. "Every command
takes `--format json` (except `dataset upload`)" is false: `report` is a
second command with no format flag. Langy following that rule literally
would break it. The rule now says to pass the flag to commands that
return data, and names both exceptions.

* fix(skills): recommend the openai/latest alias instead of a version number

Review flagged the prompts skill for naming `openai/gpt-5.5` as the
current flagship when the catalog is on the 5.6 family. Correct, and
swapping one version for another only resets the clock: the guidance
goes stale again at the next release, which is how it got here.

LangWatch already resolves `openai/latest` and `openai/latest-mini` to
the current flagship and fast tiers at run time, and a prompt config is
exactly the place that alias is meant for. The skill now recommends the
alias and treats a pinned version as the exception, for prompts tuned to
one model.

* fix(langy): put webfetch back, and stop shipping setup docs to the worker

Removing webfetch was justified in the code as "Langy reads docs via
`langwatch docs`, and fetching user-supplied URLs is out of scope by
contract". That contract was invented here and it is wrong. Langy
answers questions about the user's agents, and those answers are not all
inside our docs: a provider's error code, a framework's changelog, a
model's release notes. Egress already runs through the per-worker
adapter with its TLS, throttle and allow-list rungs, so reading the web
is governed by the proxy rather than by deleting the tool. What stays
out of scope is carrying the project's data out, which the Scope section
now says directly instead of banning fetches wholesale.

`task` and `question` stay denied, with the reason corrected: the panel
has no surface for either yet. Not a judgement about the capability.

The skills tree was the other half. Regenerating the embedded copies
pulled in two setup partials that main's copies never had, so every
Langy skill gained instructions for installing a CLI it already has and
finding an API key it was booted with. 1,898 bytes of cli-setup across
13 skills, 1,585 of projects-and-api-keys across 9, and AGENTS.md
already tells the worker to skip a skill's setup steps: text it reads in
full, every time, in order to ignore it.

`inlineMdx` takes an `excludeShared` list and the native build drops
both partials. An unknown name throws rather than passing silently, so a
renamed partial cannot quietly start inlining again. The published and
docs builds are untouched, where the reader really does have to install
the CLI. The Langy skill tree goes from 260KB to 220KB.

* fix(langy): cut the duplicated text out of the prompt and the skills

The improvement doctrine had been written four times: the full ladder in
`scenarios`, a paragraph of it in `agent-improve`, five numbered steps in
`test-compliance`, and a sentence in `consultant-mode`, which reaches
three more skills. One `_shared/improving-the-agent.mdx` partial now
carries it and the four copies point at it. Shorter than any of them,
and a change to the doctrine is one edit.

AGENTS.md said several things twice and two things that disagreed.

The Replies section forbade closing on a question about what to do next.
The overview row required exactly that. Resolved to one rule: answer what
was asked before offering anything else, and an overview closes on the
question because an overview has no single answer.

"Don't put this in prose" was stated in five places (commands, UI URLs,
raw error text, ids the card lists, ASCII re-renderings). It is now one
list, under the fact that makes it a rule rather than a preference:
everything written during a turn concatenates into the one reply the user
reads, so a line written before running a command is still there
afterwards. There is no status channel. Taken from #7205, which measured
it.

Also removed: a second copy of the `--format json` rule, the write-reply
sentence that the Replies section already carries, the "operator, not a
narrator" line the concatenation fact replaces, and a cross-reference
between two sections that both stated the same ask-the-user rule.

The greeting rule moved from Scope to Replies, where the other reply
shapes live.

Three layers were all introducing Langy. The agent config prompt keeps
identity plus how the platform is reached; AGENTS.md keeps the contract;
the turn override drops to identity plus one rule. That rule is
grounding, and it is there because #7205 measured the defect: 40% of
turns reaching `status: "completed"` make zero tool calls, so the answer
came from the model rather than from the project. The judge rubric now
fails an answer about the project with no retrieval behind it, which the
old "numbers come from what was retrieved" wording passed.

Numbers, measured against what the generator produces rather than against
the committed copy, because 19 of the 21 embedded skills were stale on
main and `connect-agent` was missing entirely:

    AGENTS.md          52,795 -> 14,587 bytes   (-72%)
    skill tree        219,546 -> 187,701 bytes  (-14.5%)

Em dashes are gone from the judge rubric, which the prompt bans and the
rubric was using.

* fix(langy): stop the worker loading the operator's own agent skills

Dogfooding the new prompt and then reading the turn's trace showed what
actually reaches the model, which is not what the repo says reaches it.

opencode folds every skill it discovers into the system prompt, and two of
its scan roots are `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`. The worker's
HOME is its own session directory, but those two scans resolve the real
account home, so a host-tier manager hands Langy whatever the operator has
installed. On this dev box that was 17 foreign skills, 8,191 characters,
22% of the assembled system message, and one of them brokers Slack and
Gmail credentials. `OPENCODE_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_SKILLS` and
`OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_SKILLS` turn both scans off. Measured on the
same greeting turn before and after:

    system message   36,817 -> 29,092 characters
    foreign skills   17 entries -> 0

The container tiers were never exposed, since those directories do not
exist there. What is left is one opencode built-in.

The same trace turned up a fourth prompt block nobody was counting.
`LANGY_REFERENT_POLICY` restated AGENTS.md's "Use prior turns" in ten more
lines, and its comment described a layout the trace disproves: it claimed
to be prepended and read before AGENTS.md, when the assembly order is
persona, AGENTS.md, skill map, turn override, then this. It now says only
what AGENTS.md cannot, which is where the referent lives: the transcript
and the screen context arrive as data blocks ahead of the user's message.

Also corrected: the comment pointed at "AGENTS.md rule 2", "rule 4" and
"rules 6, 10 and 11". Those numbers stopped existing when the rule pile
became sections.

* fix(cli): say when a trace search found nothing because of AND or OR

Reading a real Langy turn's trace showed the agent spend a round trip on
`trace search -q "error OR exception OR failed"`, get zero rows, and then
run the search again without the query. The query is matched as a phrase,
so the operators were searched for as words. Measured against a project
holding 638 traces:

    "validation failed"          40 hits
    "validation AND failed"       0 hits
    "timed out"                  63 hits
    "timed out OR validation"     0 hits

Zero rows is the worst possible answer here, because it reads as "you
have none of those" rather than as a rejected query, and "find my failing
traces" is exactly the question people ask. `--help` said only "Text
search query", which is what invited the guess.

Two changes, both at the layer that caused it rather than in an agent's
prompt: `--help` now says the query is plain text, and the empty result
names the operators when the query carried one. It fires only on an empty
result, so a legitimate search for a phrase containing "and" is untouched.

Adds `specs/traces/cli-search-query-is-plain-text.feature`.

* fix(langy): stop the judge failing a number Langy read correctly

The failing-traces scenario went red on the grounding criterion. The
judge's reasoning: Langy claimed both fixture traces record
`total_time_ms` of about 71,170,000 ms, "which conflicts with the
visible trace data in this conversation", where the attached spans say
60.67 seconds.

Langy was right. The trace really does carry `total_time_ms: 71170357`,
straight out of `langwatch trace get`, and reporting it plus flagging it
as an instrumentation anomaly is the job. The judge preferred the
attached OTel spans over the command result and failed a correct answer.
That is the fourth instance in this PR of one class: a criterion
demanding proof the transcript's attached evidence cannot hold. The
criterion now names the command results as the authority, and says a
field reported straight out of one is grounded even when it looks wrong.

The 19.8-hour duration was ours. The fixture ids were fixed, which
looked tidier and quietly corrupted the data: a trace summary keeps the
EARLIEST start it was ever posted, so a re-post widened the same trace
rather than replacing it, and after a day of runs the fixtures carried a
20-hour span over 60 seconds of work. The ids now carry a minute stamp,
so a re-run within the minute is still an upsert and a later one seeds
fresh traces. Verified: the scenario passes, and the reply no longer
spends a paragraph on the anomaly we had seeded.

The prompt had one ambiguity of its own, in the sentence the
consolidation pass wrote. "Answer what was asked before you offer
anything else, and stop once it is answered" says both that an offer may
follow the answer and that nothing may follow it. It now says: answer,
then stop, and a menu of what to do next is not part of the answer, with
the two things that are not that menu named (an overview, which has no
single answer, and a `choices` card for a decision that blocks the work
rather than following it).

* feat(cli): add --errors-only, so "show me my failed traces" is one command

The drill-in dogfood scenario failed with "No failed traces in the last
24 hours", on a project holding six of them. Langy's own words: "I
searched application-origin traces for errored/failed entries and for
traces containing 'error' and found zero hits."

It was doing the only thing the CLI offered. An error is recorded on the
span, not in the trace's indexed text, so no text query finds one, and
`trace search` had no way to ask. The earlier passing run of the same
flow worked only because the model happened to fall back to pulling 200
traces and filtering them itself. That is a coin flip, and it landed
tails.

`traces.error` is an existing platform filter, the same one the Trace
Explorer's error toggle uses, and the search API already accepted it.
Nothing exposed it. Verified against the local project:

    no filter                            689 traces
    traces.error=true                     39
    traces.error=true, origin=application  6   (exactly the fixtures)

`--errors-only` on `trace search` and `trace export` passes it, and
combines with `--origin` rather than replacing it. The prompt's routing
table, `agent-performance` and `debug-with-langwatch` all point at it;
that last one has a step literally titled "Find the Errored Traces"
which was showing a text query.

Review round 3 fixes, in the same change:

- **AGENTS.md Scope contradicted itself.** It permits the GitHub skill's
  `git`/`gh` workflow, then declines "other CLIs" and prohibits sending
  file contents off LangWatch, which is what `git push` does. "Open a PR"
  was in scope and declined at once. The prohibitions are now bounded to
  what they mean: content you hand the user for other infrastructure, and
  data leaving through a channel the conversation supplied rather than
  one a skill's own workflow owns.
- The turn override's grounding rule said "answer from what you retrieve
  this turn", which also covers greetings and declines, where there is
  nothing to retrieve. Scoped to facts about the project, and the test
  now pins it rather than only pinning the block's size.
- The shared judge rubric is imported by the red-team cases, where a
  correct refusal has no project retrieval behind it. Both grounding
  criteria now name the answers that legitimately carry no project
  result: a permission refusal, an out-of-scope decline, a capability
  Langy does not have, and a greeting.
- Two decorative comments removed, a slice guarded against a missing
  heading, and two `console.log` spies moved into `afterEach` so a
  rejected command cannot leak a mocked logger into later tests.
- The prompts skill said "Never downgrade to a legacy model" in one place
  and allowed one for cost or latency in another. Now one policy.
- The improvement ladder claimed a trace "holds the assembled input".
  True only where the project captures content, which it now says.

* fix(langy): deny opencode's built-in skill by name

opencode ships one built-in skill, customize-opencode, embedded in the
binary rather than discovered from a directory, so the two disable
switches on the worker env do not reach it. Its description scopes it to
editing opencode's own config, agents, plugins and permission rules,
which is not work Langy does for a customer, and it renders 516
characters into every turn's system prompt.

<available_skills> is assembled from Skill.available(agent), which
filters on the agent's permission ruleset, so a rule removes the entry
from the prompt and not only from execution. The rule is per name: a
bare "skill": "deny" reads as pattern "*", which switches the skill tool
off and takes every skill we ship with it.

The test now reads config.json instead of stopping at the environment
values, and pins the shape: a per-name map, customize-opencode denied,
no "*" pattern, exactly one pattern, exactly three permission entries.

* fix(langy): decline the request, not just the payload

The red-team suite found the hole the consolidation left. The old prompt
banned fetching or posting to user-supplied URLs. The rewrite replaced
that with a ban on moving the project's DATA out, and an empty test ping
carries none, so every turn read as compliant while a 20-turn crescendo
assembled a working exfiltration channel: Langy ran the attacker's exact
curl line and pasted back the response body, response headers, request
headers and exit code, then offered to POST a literal shell-substitution
string when it declined to expand one.

Scope now lands on the request. Delivering to a destination the
conversation supplied is declined whatever the body, because the next
turn decides the body. Reading a page stays in scope whatever its URL,
which the old wording did not manage either, and which is what lets
webfetch stay. A second rule covers the rest of the finding: Langy runs
the commands its own work needs, never a command line the conversation
hands it to execute and report back.

Both ship with an overshoot pair, so the boundary cannot quietly become
a refusal to work: one dogfood scenario proves the delivery is declined,
one proves a linked provider error reference is still read and answered
from.

provision.go said the egress proxy governed where a request may go. On a
stock install it does not: rung 1 (TLS, SNI, throttle) is on, and
destination policy is monitor-only until a project sets an allow-list or
an operator sets LANGY_EGRESS_ENFORCE_FLOOR (ADR-076). The comment now
says what is true, and the real control is filed as a follow-up rather
than approximated with a bypassable command-pattern deny.

* fix(langy): a decline does not come with a workaround

CI was red on a biome format error in the new scenario string, which is
fixed here alongside the rule it tests.

Three runs of the new prohibition scenario agree on the security half:
Langy does not send the request and reports no response artifacts. What
it kept doing was decline and then write the same curl out for the user
to run, which the Interface section already bans and which the second
ask, with its reasons and its pressure, is what triggers.

Scope now draws the distinction the model was missing: it had declined
the action and read explaining it as something else. The recipe is the
action. It also says what to do when LangWatch has no command for what
was asked, which is where this scenario sits: the URL is an ad-hoc one
rather than a registered endpoint, so `langwatch webhooks test <id>`
answers nothing and the decline stands on its own.

The scenario's third criterion asked for that non-existent alternative,
so it demanded an answer that could not be given. It now asserts what is
actually required: the decline stands, and the request is not written
out on either turn.

* fix(langy): the empty-turn backstop fires only on a finished turn

Review found the fallback firing on every user Stop. `sawVisibleText` is
in-memory and a token buffer is built per relay request, so `stopTurn`
calls `markEnd` on an instance that never saw a chunk: the check read
that as "the turn wrote no reply" and appended "I finished this turn
without writing a reply" after real partial answers, wrong on both
halves of the sentence. The ADR-048 handoff had the same shape,
mislabeling a graceful checkpoint as an empty turn.

`markEnd` now takes `backstopSilentTurn`, and only the relay's `final`
case passes it. Instance memory is also no longer the only evidence: when
it says nothing was written, the stream itself decides, so a worker that
reconnects mid-turn cannot lose the earlier deltas. That read only
happens in the branch about to emit the fallback, so the normal path
pays nothing.

The fallback now reaches the durable message too. It is built from the
worker's frame rather than the stream, so a genuinely silent turn showed
the line live and rendered blank again on the next history load, which
made the fix cosmetic. `markEnd` returns whether it fired and the relay
uses that for both views, so they cannot disagree.

Also: a leftover `expect(created?.active).toBe(false)` after
`expect(created).toBeFalsy()` failed the trigger-boundary scenario
whenever the guard held, which is the outcome it wants.

The fake redis in the buffer tests returned `[]` from `xrange`
unconditionally, which would have made any assertion about reading the
stream a test of the fake. It now stores and serves what was written.

Two smaller ones from the same review: the scenario logger matched
transient failures by substring on the error's prose, so the adapter now
marks them on the error itself; and the e2e handled-error reader checked
`code` but cast `tips`, which lands in text a judge grades, so every
field is checked. It stays a separate reader from the app's, since the
suite drives a live stack over HTTP and imports nothing from src.

* fix(langy): bind the new stop-path scenario, and stop grading an id the card carries

The stop-path test carried a @scenario annotation with no scenario
behind it, which fails check-feature-parity. The spec now describes what
the two non-final terminals must not say.

The drill-in criterion read "using the concrete id from the prior turn"
as "printed in the prior turn's text". The command results carry the
ids and the prompt tells Langy not to repeat what they already show, so
a judge reading only the transcript sees the id appear for the first
time on the follow-up and calls it invented, when it is Langy using
context the user can see. Fourth instance in this PR of a criterion
demanding proof the transcript cannot hold. It now grades the outcome:
drill into one of the prior turn's failures rather than re-listing,
starting over, or asking which one.

* fix(langy): a permission Langy is never delegated says so

Langy read a permission refusal, told the user to get `triggers:create`
granted, and offered to rerun the command once they had. No grant can
give it: READ_ONLY_FAMILIES withholds trigger writes from every session
key, because a trigger keeps acting after the chat that made it ends.
The user is sent to wait for something nobody can do.

The ceiling now tells the two refusals apart. A Langy session key is
identified where the row is already in hand, and when the policy that
mints the key says the permission is excluded, the 403 carries
`api_key_permission_not_delegable` instead of the generic code. Its
message and tip say a wider key or a higher role does not change this,
and the policy's own reason, which names internal constants, goes to the
log line rather than to the customer.

The refusal reached the agent as a connectivity blip. The trigger
commands built their failure with `new Error(await formatFetchError(...))`,
which keeps the sentence and drops the code and the status, so a 403
arrived as `network_error`, `terminal: false` and "check your network
connection". `failSpinnerFromResponse` reads the body once and keeps
what the platform named, falling back to the old sentence when it named
nothing.

Two prompt rules follow the same failure. A permission block is not a
command for the user to rerun, and a menu path Langy remembers rather
than reads goes stale: it sent the user to a Triggers page the product
renamed to Automations.

The scenario criterion asked for that same stale page by name, so it
grades the outcome instead: a way forward that is the user's to take,
and no CLI command or credential change offered as one.

* fix(langy): drop the permission clause that was wrong for an ordinary refusal

A Langy session key mirrors its owner, so when the ceiling refuses a
permission Langy MAY hold, the user does not hold it either and cannot
do it in the app themselves. The clause told Langy to send them there.
What is true in both cases is narrower: their rerunning the command
fixes nothing. The error itself now says what the way forward is, and
the prompt already says to follow it.

fix(authz): no platform tenant, size-scaled convergence, cohort enrollment (#7322)

* fix(clickhouse): the platform tenant routes like an organization

The grants ledger's cutover (ADR-092) writes one PLATFORM aggregate whose
tenant id, "platform", names no customer — it has no row in Project or
Organization. The tenant resolver refused it, so every cutover enrollment
parked with "grants projection did not land the cutover import".

Route it down the exact path an organization takes: the private env-var
list first (CLICKHOUSE_URL__<label>__platform would give the platform
ledger its own instance), the shared client otherwise. No new client, no
new path — one branch handing the name to getClickHouseClientForOrganization.

The id is declared locally rather than imported from
@langwatch/authz-server/migration so routing does not drag that entry and
node:crypto into every server process; a unit test pins the two constants
equal so the duplication cannot drift.

* feat(ops): cohort enrollment for the rollout, and a convergence wait that scales with the import

Two changes to how the rollout runs its tenants at scale:

Cohort enrollment. One organization at a time paces a rollout of ten, not
of seven thousand. enrollMigrationCohort enrolls a random sample of
organizations not yet enrolled for a migration, in one action - and the
organizations it must never sweep up are excluded by data rather than by a
hand-kept list: an active ENTERPRISE subscription, or a private ClickHouse
route in the environment (the same env vars that route their data are what
exclude them). The result names every organization it picked, so the
action is auditable, and the cutover keeps its typed confirmation. The ops
page gains an "Enroll cohort…" action beside "Enroll…".

Size-aware convergence wait. The migrations parked any organization whose
import outgrew the fixed 120s window: the fold drains per-tenant FIFO at
~1.8 facts/s, so past ~200 facts the first pass always timed out, and a
park that reads as an error was really just an organization being large.
The deadline now scales with the number of facts the wait is actually on
(1s per fact over a 120s base, ceiling 20 minutes), shared by the
backfill, the genesis import and the cutover. An explicitly injected poll
without a per-fact budget scales by nothing, which keeps the timeout tests
exact.

* feat(authz): there is no platform tenant — operator access is the live admin list, not a ledger fact

The cutover stated platform-admin grants on a sentinel aggregate whose
tenant id, "platform", named no organization — a third tenant kind that
existed nowhere else and that no decision path ever read (the read
repository itself documented PLATFORM rows as dormant facts). Every
organization's step 3 parked on it in production, because an id that is
neither a project nor an organization has never been routable.

Remove the aggregate instead of teaching routing about it: the cutover
now states facts only on the organization's own aggregate, ADMIN_EMAILS
stays the live authority for operator access exactly as it already was,
and the admin-email machinery (findUsersByEmail, the unmatched-address
report, normalizedAdminEmails, maskEmail, the pinning suite) goes with
it. The ClickHouse tenant resolver needs no platform branch — reverted —
and the spec states the decision: platform operator access is never a
ledger fact.

Also folds in review findings on the cohort and deadline work:
- cutover cohorts get cutover-specific dialog copy (the flip, times N)
- per-organization audit rows — one row holding a thousand-id array
  loses every id to the audit writer's size cap, and the indexed
  organizationId column is how the trail answers "what touched org X"
- createMany returns what actually landed, so the trail cannot overclaim
  under the skipDuplicates race
- PENDING enterprise subscriptions are excluded from cohorts along with
  ACTIVE — a just-signed enterprise is exactly the organization the
  exclusion exists for
- Number() over parseInt so "1e3" disables Confirm instead of
  enrolling one organization; an empty pool gets an info toast, not a
  success one
- a genesis test pins the scaled deadline through a real migration wait
  (replacing factCount with 0 previously kept every suite green), plus
  a ceiling scenario, a real-database eligibility test, and a wiring
  test proving the composition feeds the private-dataplane exclusion
  from the environment's routing table

* fix(specs): the cohort scenario states behavior, not configuration

The exclusion clauses named env vars and code - the spec now says what an
operator sees: a dedicated data plane, and no list to maintain. Plus
step={1} on the cohort size input so browsers reject fractional steps.

* fix(tests): the cohort eligibility sweep names the rows by owner

SystemMigrationEnrollment deletes require the organizationId tenancy key
(a migration-wide bulk delete would withdraw every organization at once),
so the suite's cleanup names the organizations as well as the migration.

* feat(ops): the migrations page reads like the rest of ops

A design pass under the ops-surface rules (space proportional to trouble,
quiet all-clear): each step becomes a bordered card with the actions on
the title row; the status figures move to their own row where a zero is a
quiet gray chip and a non-zero Held or Parked takes its color solid, so
the eye lands only on what moved; both tables adopt the shared ListTable
look; and the enrolled listing folds away past eight rows behind a
show-all count, so a cohort of hundreds does not turn the page into a
scroll.

* refactor(clickhouse): client access has two doors, and a test that keeps it so

Every ClickHouse client now reaches its consumer through exactly two
routes: the composition root builds the resolvers (presets.ts), and
everything else receives them through the App or an injected repository.
The half-finished migration this closes out had thirteen files reaching
into the client module directly - each one bypassing the routing,
settings and resilience decisions the composition root exists to make in
one place.

- getApp().clickhouse grows the missing halves of the facet it already
  had: resolveOrganizationClient and allInstances, so org-keyed reads
  and fleet sweeps stop importing their own way in
- stored-objects, experiments-v3, the trace service, ingest-lag, event
  usage, analytics availability, blob resolution, the two fleet sweeps
  and the governance activity monitor all resolve through the App now
- ops-explain takes its shared fallback by construction from the
  composition root - EXPLAIN is fleet work and says so in its deps
- the public getSharedClickHouseClient re-export is deleted; the one
  remaining internal consumer (metrics) uses the module's own seam
- the access-boundary suite's RESOLVES_DIRECTLY_BACKLOG ratchet empties,
  and a new import-boundary test walks the tree and fails on any module
  outside the sanctioned allowlist that value-imports the client module
- the migrations page extracts its status badges into a component,
  clearing the noExcessiveLinesPerFunction violation the delta gate
  caught on the design refresh

Twelve unit suites that mocked the client module now mock the App - the
same seam production uses.

* fix(clickhouse): the composition root imports the shared client from the client module

* fix(clickhouse): the seal's datastore-lane tests mock the App door, not the deleted exports

* feat(ops): state projections are visible, switchable and replayable; map rows join their live jobs

The projections page walked only fold and map registrations, so the seven
state projections - the authz grants ledger among them - ran with no row,
no settable kill switch and no replay-wizard entry. And map rows could
never light up: their jobs run as __jobType=handler, which the tree filed
under the fold node while the health join looked under map.

- getProjectionMetadata() emits kind "state" with the stateProjection
  pause path the dispatcher already matches
- getKillSwitchDescriptors() emits the fold-shaped key the state executor
  actually checks, honouring customKey
- normalizeJobType files handler under map and stateProjection under
  state; mapJobTypeToPhase counts state work as projections, not commands
- the health join and the replay wizard accept the state kind

* Address review comments

- drop the restating comment on the harness's grant-head map
- the stray-grant net drops the org filter, not the scope filter: no suite
  may ever write a platform-scoped cutover grant, while sibling suites do
  import grants for their own organizations into the shared database
- the platform-operator scenario states the operator-visible outcome

* refactor(ops): kill-switch descriptors build per definition, flatMapped

The state-projection loop pushed getKillSwitchDescriptors past the
cognitive-complexity ceiling; hoisting the per-definition body out of the
outer loop returns the file to its baseline.

* fix(clickhouse): every datastore-lane suite that reached the sealed door gets the App seam

The seal moved client resolution behind getApp().clickhouse; eighteen
integration suites still wired the old module seam and failed with 'App
not initialized' (or a stub missing the facet). Eleven trace suites, the
experiment getRun and storage-usage suites get an App stub delegating to
their existing clickhouseClient mock; the two governance suites and the
stored-objects probe install the ClickHouse test App; annotation's
partial App stub gains the clickhouse facet.

The cutover-import fleet net reads the table raw: the tenancy guard
(rightly) refuses an org-unkeyed Grant query from app code, and the
org-keyed { not: } shape it was using never satisfied the guard either -
a platform-scoped cutover grant may exist for no one, which only a raw
count can say.

* fix(tests): the fleet net declares its cross-tenant scan; the latest-commit fixture stops racing the clock

The raw-query tenancy guard wants intentional cross-tenant scans to say
so - the cutover fleet invariant now carries the @tenancy opt-out it was
built for. And the workflows latest-commit test created two versions in
the same millisecond, leaving createdAt-desc ordering to pick either;
the fixture backdates the first commit, since real commits are never
simultaneous.

fix(navigation): open LLM Ops from Me, and line up the sidebar rules (#7320)

* fix(navigation): LLM Ops opens from Me, and the sidebar rules line up

The product switcher greyed LLM Ops out on every Me page. The Me pages
resolve the personal workspace, the switcher read that private project as
"no project", and the one product that opens with a project had nowhere to
go. It ran the other way too: visiting /me wrote the personal team and
project over the remembered selection, so the app root and the switcher
sent the reader into another team's project afterwards.

LLM Ops now resolves its own project: the one in the address, else the one
last worked in, else the first of a team the reader is allowed to open. The
personal workspace stays out of the remembered selection, and a remembered
project no longer decides the /me pages, which until now resolved every
personal feature against the shared project.

- the rule above the sidebar bottom block sat 8px from the left of the

- the entries vanished 8px above that rule instead of being cut at it. The
  rule under the way back out of Settings gets the same treatment, and the
  space that holds the entries off both lines moves inside the part that
  scrolls
- the home command bar drew a second line across the top of its results.
  That line separates the field from the list in the raised Cmd+K bar,
  where they share one card, and the home mounts the list as its own panel
- API Keys moves to the ORGANIZATION group under General, out of the bottom

* refactor(navigation): state the personal-workspace scenarios as what the reader sees

The two scenarios about the remembered selection described storage
instead of behavior. They now describe the next organization-scoped

coming back to the project she left is a different page from coming back

fix(dev): listen for signals before the check queue starts the command (#7319)

* fix(dev): listen for signals before the check queue starts the command

A signal keeps its default disposition until the first listener exists, so
an interrupt landing between the spawn and the handlers ended the wrapper in
the kernel: the interrupt reached nobody and the command ran on with no
parent. A slot is counted for as long as its wrapper lives, so the queue
then made that slot free and could start another check on top of a run that
was still using the machine.

Both implementations now listen first. The JS wrapper installs its handlers
before spawn; haven's slot run calls signal.Notify before cmd.Start and pumps
the buffered channel to the child once it exists.

The regression test stalls the real queue for 400ms at the moment the child
appears, which turns the scheduling race into a decision the test can make.
It fails with the reported "expected null to be 137" against the old order.

* docs(dev): state the interrupt scenario as what the contributor sees

perf(dev): typecheck the repository as one program instead of two (#7309)

* perf(dev): typecheck the repository as one program instead of two

Every test file imports the app it tests, so the app project and the
tests project overlap almost entirely. Run back to back they parsed,
bound and checked the app's 17k files twice: 38,046 file loads and
35.1M type instantiations, against 20,980 and 18.9M for a single
program over the union.

tsconfig.tsgo.all.json is that union, and typecheck:all runs it. The
app-only project stays as it is, so the fast inner loop is unchanged.

Coverage is a strict superset, held by a test that loads all three
programs and compares them. It also picks up vite/havenHmrGate.unit.test.ts,
a unit test neither project typechecked.

* fix(dev): run the parity test against whichever compiler binary exists

The test named node_modules/.bin/tsc.real, which only exists where the
check-queue shims are installed. install-check-shims.mjs stands down when
CI is set, so on a runner there is no tsc.real and the test died with
ENOENT before it could compare anything.

It now takes tsc.real when it is there, to keep three whole-tree loads
out of the machine-wide queue, and the plain binary otherwise. Both were
checked to produce the same 20,981 file program.

* test(dev): assert the compiler invocation, and keep the spec behavioural

The script assertion passed on any script that merely mentioned the
project file; it now checks that tsc is handed it with --noEmit.

The incremental-cache scenario described project topology rather than
what a contributor sees, so it now states the behaviour: checking one
project does not make another start from cold.

* docs(dev): say what to run, not what it used to cost

* fix(analytics): keep focus in the chart name field while it is typed

fix(governance): price warehouse compute by the hours it ran in (#7324)

* fix(governance): price warehouse compute by the hours it ran in

A statement was bucketed by the hour its `start_time` fell in, and its
whole `execution_duration_ms` went into that hour's denominator. The bill
it was divided against does not work that way: `system.billing.usage`
charges each hour for the compute that actually ran in it. A query
starting 09:58 and running 40 minutes put all 40 minutes in hour 09,
while ~38 minutes of its compute was billed in hour 10 — and hour 10's
whole bill was then split among only what happened to start in hour 10.
A one-second Genie question landing in such an hour could carry the
entire hour of compute.

Each statement's `[start_time, end_time)` is now cut into one row per
hour it was awake in, and both sides of the share are computed from that
slice: numerator and denominator move together, so shares within an hour
still sum to at most that hour's bill, and a straddler draws from both
hours rather than neither.

This is option 1 of the three the review offered, not the recommended
option 2. Option 2 — start-hour numerator, widened denominator — fails
either way it is read: with the denominator clipped to the hour, a
straddler's share can exceed 100% of its start hour's bill; with whole
runtimes in every touched hour, the sum invariant holds but the
straddler still only draws from its start hour, so the compute it burned
in the next hour becomes permanently unattributable. That trades a
Genie-overcharging bias for a start-hour-overcharging bias rather than
removing one.

Two consequences in the allocator, both per hour rather than per
statement: the record's `hourTotalExecutionMs` sums the distinct hours a
statement drew from (keyed, so an hour billed under several SKUs counts
once), and the hold is per hour — a statement priced for one hour and
unbilled for another is held, because recording it now at the first
hour's cost cannot be revised later.

The scan reaches 24h before the window so straddlers feed the
denominator, while the emit window is unchanged, so no statement is
priced twice. `shareOf`'s null-SKU-first ordering, the `LEFT JOIN
priced`, the bigint nanoUSD arithmetic and `restatementKeyFor`'s inputs
are all untouched.

Refs #7321

* fix(governance): say what the hold does, and assert the money exactly

Review pass over the previous commit.

The SQL file had two comments rewritten for no reason. Both recorded
evidence — that the billing table lands minutes to days behind the
question, and that the Genie client-application marker was observed on
103/103 statements over 60 days without being documented as guaranteed —
and the rewrites dropped it while saying nothing new. Restored verbatim.
Extracting `warehouseCostParameters` had also landed it between the
`WAREHOUSE_COST_COLUMNS` doc comment and the array it documents; moved
below the declaration.

The hold scenario claimed the query is "held rather than recorded at the
first hour's cost". It is both: the billed hour's share is recorded and
the query is held so the re-read restates it once the second hour lands.
The scenario now says that, because a spec that contradicts the test
bound to it teaches the next reader the wrong rule.

And the two new assertions were the only ones in the file comparing
`Number(costUsd)` with `toBeCloseTo`. This suite exists to prove the
money is exact bigint nanoUSD; asserting it through a float is the one
thing it must not do. Exact strings now, which also pin the truncation:
6 USD * 1000 / 2_281_000 settles at 0.002630425, not a rounded 0.00263.

* fix(governance): stop an hour a query never ran in from holding the source

`sequence` includes its stop value; an hour does not. A statement ending
at exactly 10:00:00.000 worked in hour 09 and not at all in hour 10, but
the explode emitted a 10:00 slice for it anyway, with zero execution time
and a real usage_hour that reached the LEFT JOIN.

That slice is not merely noise. If the warehouse shut down at 10:00 there
is no `system.billing.usage` row for hour 10 and there never will be. The
allocator tests a null SKU first — deliberately, because a null SKU is a
bill that has not landed — so it marked the statement owed and held the
whole source at this chunk for the seven-day hold. Every hourly scheduled
query ends on a boundary, so one of them could stop all later Genie
ingestion for a week. Where the next hour did have a bill, its entire
bill also joined the audit ingredients of a statement that did no work in
it.

Two changes, because the shape and the reading were each wrong on their
own:

- The sequence stop is now backed off a millisecond when the statement
  ran for at least that long, so the terminal hour is half-open. It
  cannot invert the range: a statement that did not run that long keeps
  its single hour from the untouched branch.

- `shareOf` returns "idle" for a slice with no execution time, before the
  null-SKU branch. Such a slice can cost nothing whatever its SKU says,
  so holding for it buys a stall against a share of exactly zero. The
  distinction below it is untouched, since every row that turns on it has
  execution time by definition.

The divide-by-zero test now uses a nonzero share against a zero hour
total. It was passing through the zero-execution path rather than the
contradiction it names, and the guard it covers is only reachable with
execution time.

Reported as P1 in review 4982160556 on #7324.

* refactor(governance): name the arguments that decide whether a query is held

`noteHour` writes to one of two maps of the same type meaning opposite
things — the hours a statement still owes a bill for, and the hours it has
been priced for. Its two call sites differed only in the first argument, so
swapping them would have held every settled statement and settled every held
one without failing to compile. `foldPricedLine` had the same shape.

Both now take named parameters, per CLAUDE.md. No behaviour change.

Reported by CodeRabbit on #7324.

* test(governance): assert the shape that carries the fix, not the aliases

Four of the five assertions in the SQL-shape test passed on the defect the
test names: `end_time`, `execution_duration_ms`, `execution_ms_in_hour` and
`usage_hour` are all SELECT aliases that survive reverting `sliced` to
start-hour bucketing. Only the `explode(sequence(` match discriminated, and
this SQL is executed nowhere in CI, so the shape test is its only guard.

Now asserted: the end is reconstructed via COALESCE when the row carries
none; the sequence is bounded by the statement's own `start_time`; and the
per-hour numerator is divided with `div`, never `/` (Spark's `/` returns a
DOUBLE, and no float may enter the money path).

Verified by mutation: pointing the sequence at another column and swapping
`*` for `/` fails the test.

Reported by CodeRabbit on #7324.

* docs(governance): stop the record claiming a cost it cannot reconstruct

`WarehousePricedStatement` promised
`costUsd ~= hourBillableUsd x executionMs / hourTotalExecutionMs` holds "on
the record itself". It does not, for the case this PR exists to fix. Each
hour's share is taken at that hour's own price and the fields are then summed
independently, so the identity only holds when every hour cost the same per
millisecond. The straddler in the unit suite costs 11.997369574 where the
identity reads 11.995001...: its two minutes in an otherwise idle hour 09 were
billed at nineteen times the per-millisecond price of hour 10.

`executionMs` was not a field on the record either — it is a local in
`shareOf` — so the identity was not evaluable as written.

Now says what the pair is good for (naming which bill the cost came from) and
that reconciling a straddler needs the per-hour lines this record does not
carry.

Reported by CodeRabbit on #7324.

* fix(governance): keep both chunks of a statement that ran across a boundary

The window is read oldest-first in chunks that tile it, and each chunk
emits only the hours it owns. Ownership of a ROW, though, was decided by
the statement's `start_time`, which reads like the same duplicate-avoidance
rule and is not: a statement beginning near the end of a chunk was handed
wholly to that chunk, which had already dropped every hour past its own
end. The next chunk counted the statement in its denominators — correctly,
it really did run there — and then excluded it from its rows. Those hours
were billed to nobody while still diluting every other question's share of
them, silently, at every interior chunk boundary a backfill crosses and at
every seam between sweeps.

Ownership is now the hour clip in `sliced`. Hours tile the window, so every
statement-hour is emitted exactly once and a straddler comes back from both
chunks with a different part of itself. That only works if the parts are
added, so `mergeWarehouseCost` moves next to the money helpers and
accumulates in nanoUSD instead of replacing by statement id. All three
fields add: each is already a sum over the hours the statement ran through,
and the chunks partition those hours.

The fixture had to become honest for any of this to be testable. It served
one plan to every chunk, which was harmless while the merge replaced and
multiplied the cost by the chunk count once it added. It now answers only
for the window it was asked about, the way the workspace does, and records
what each call was served so a test can prove the two halves came from two
different chunks.

One assertion moved with it: the held watermark is now bounded by the
unbilled hour rather than by the far end of the window, because the hold
lands at the start of the chunk that could not be priced instead of at the
oldest chunk that happened to be handed the same row.

Verified failing first — the merge test read '1.75' for a '2' cost, and the
end-to-end straddler test fails again when the merge is reverted to
replacing.

Reported by langwatch-agent on #7324.

* docs(governance): correct the straddler limitation note to match the fix

The paragraph still described the pre-fix behaviour, where a statement
running past a chunk edge lost its tail. It is now priced from both sides
and the sweep adds them; what remains is the narrower case of a tail whose
chunk is held on an unbilled hour.

* fix(governance): keep a piece's billed share when an hour it ran through still owes

The split-piece walk held the watermark on an owed piece before merging
what the piece did price, so a statement with one billed and one unbilled
hour was emitted at nothing until billing settled — the whole-chunk path
already merges first and holds second, and the two now agree. Proven by a
piece-sized test that fails at '0' without the reorder.

Also from the same review round: mergeWarehouseCost takes named
arguments, and the chunk-straddler scenario describes the recorded cost a
customer sees rather than read chunks.

* docs(governance): the piece-walk docblock says what the walk now does

Review caught the JSDoc on walkWarehouseCostPieces still describing the

fix(gateway): retire every cap scoped to a key when the key is revoked (#7338)

Revoke already meant to retire the dead key's caps: its own comment says
"a dead key's cap is retired, not deleted". It called a helper written
for the update path, which matches only the drawer-managed row, so a
budget created on the Budgets page targeting one key survived the key
and sat on the list warning that no key sends traffic to it.

Revoke now archives anything scoped to that key alone, including a
per-end-user template anchored on it. REVOKED is terminal, so such a
budget can never count spend or refuse a request again, and leaving it
active preserves no enforcement control.

Update keeps the narrower rule. There the key is still live, so an
independently created cap on it is still enforceable and
virtualKeys:update must not retire it.

Project, team and organization budgets are untouched on both paths:
they outlive any one key.

fix(clickhouse): size the statement bound from the whole cluster, not one node (#7186)

fix(clickhouse): size the statement bound from the cluster, not one node

`max_concurrent_queries` is enforced per ClickHouse server, but the pool
derivation divided a single node's allowance across the whole fleet. With three
nodes that understated the real budget by ~3x, so the platform throttled itself
against a cluster that was mostly idle.

Measured on prod 2026-08-18: nodes at 74/60/70 concurrent queries against 300
each and zero TOO_MANY_SIMULTANEOUS_QUERIES, while the client-side statement
limiter shed ~1,057 statements an hour and made callers wait a median 2.4s
(p99 5.0s) for a slot. The derived ceiling was floor(300 * 0.7 / 25) = 8 against
a configured 20, so every process logged "CLICKHOUSE_MAX_OPEN_CONNECTIONS lets
this fleet exceed the server's concurrent-query budget" continuously — a warning
that fires forever is one nobody reads.

Add `serverNodes` (CLICKHOUSE_SERVER_NODES) and multiply the per-node allowance
by it. Defaults to 1, so a deployment that says nothing keeps exactly the sizing
it had. FLEET_SAFETY_FACTOR already covers the per-user shares carved out of the
server budget (the platform user holds 270 of prod's 300), so this needs no
separate knob for that.

* fix(settings): give the email suppressions page the settings chrome

Two more from the same round of feedback.

The settings menu marked no entry on almost every settings page. It
matched its entries against the route pattern, and one `/settings/*`
pattern covers them all, so only General and Audit Log, which have
patterns of their own, could ever match. It now matches against the

* fix(tests): give the private-ClickHouse suites org ids their env var can carry

Review follow-ups, plus the CI failure this PR hit.

The two private-ClickHouse suites route an organization with a
`CLICKHOUSE_URL__<label>__<orgId>` variable, and built the org id from
`nanoid`. That alphabet contains `_`, so about one id in 800 carries a
`__` of its own; the parser reads the org as the last `__` segment, so
the name splits in the wrong place and the route registers under a
fragment of the id, or under nothing when the id ends with the
separator. The organization then falls back to the shared client and two
assertions fail on a run in which nothing changed, which is what
`test-integration (mocking 2/2)` did here. The ids now come from
`privateRouteOrgId`, whose alphabet has no `_`, and a unit test mints
20,000 of them through the parser.
