describe blocks with "when", and the two feature files drop comments
that described route matching and width arithmetic.

* fix(tests): refuse a private-route namespace that carries the separator

privateRouteOrgId drew its random suffix from an alphabet without `_`,
but copied the caller's namespace through unchanged, so
`privateRouteOrgId("foo__bar")` still minted an id the parser reads back
as `bar-xxxxxx`. It now refuses such a name rather than repairing it: the
suite that asked has a line to fix, and a quietly rewritten namespace
would hide it.

fix(governance): the codex harvest caps a long conversation in one pass (#7336)

* fix(governance): the codex harvest caps a long conversation in one pass

Codex runs `langwatch ingest codex --notify` after every completed turn, so
the whole transcript is parsed again on every turn. Each turn's request body
is capped before it is sent, and the cap measured the whole conversation
again after every message it dropped. The cost grew with the number of
messages times their total size.

On a background agent that had run since the start of the month, the parse
of its 47MB transcript took 242 seconds. Codex started the next harvest
before that one finished, so the session never posted its conversation, its
repository, or its title, and it read as "Untitled session" in the product.

Each message is now capped and measured once, and the running total is
tracked as messages are dropped. The same transcript parses in 138ms, and
the turns it yields are byte for byte the ones it yielded before.

* fix(lwql): fail the deploy on a failed key-map backfill, converge reader grants, drop the wrong-grain batch_evaluations dataset

Three review findings on #7194.

1. The key-map backfill was non-fatal while the views above it were fatal,
   and the comment justifying the asymmetry was wrong: the inline sync on
   project creation only covers projects created *after* a failure, so a
   first-deploy failure leaves every existing project without a key-map row
   until some later deploy happens to re-run the task. Nothing in the request
   path detects that — the row policies resolve an absent hash to an empty
   tenant set, so queries return zero rows with HTTP 200 rather than
   lwql_unavailable. It now fails the deploy like everything around it, which
   costs nothing in availability terms: it shares the admin ClickHouse client
   with the already-fatal steps.

2. The reader role's grants were issued only out of band, against whatever
   approved views existed when that job last ran, so a view added by a later
   deploy had no grant and every query touching it failed ACCESS_DENIED until
   someone re-ran the job by hand. The app now re-grants its own views right
   after creating them, guarded on the role existing so it is a no-op where
   the reader is not provisioned. Grants only — no CREATE ROLE, no password.

3. batch_evaluations declared `one row per ExperimentRunId` and published
   ExperimentRunId as a join key. BatchEvaluation has no run-id column; `id`
   is one row per evaluated datapoint. Its only remaining writer is the legacy
   POST /api/dataset/evaluate route — the SDK batch path writes experiment
   runs to ClickHouse — so it answered experiment questions from a subset with
   a grain that does not exist. Removed rather than shipped as a public schema
   contract; the scenario it bound is @unimplemented against #7334, which
   tracks a truthful ClickHouse-resident replacement.

The amount schema's z.number().transform(String) branch can mint "1e-7",
which the digit-shift regex rejected — and a throw there holds the cursor
and replays forever. Shift the exponent instead of the digits; the money
parser downstream reads exponents exactly. Found in self-review of #7287.

* test(governance): cover legacy flat cache-creation fallback; use named params in multi-arg cursor helpers

* fix(governance): reject unsafe-integer exponents in centsToUsd instead of emitting eInfinity

* fix(governance): rewind the watermark on query-identity change so the 100x cost rows self-repair

* fix(governance): query-identity rewind must never move the watermark forward

* fix(governance): only rewind cost cursors on query change; usage keeps its watermark

Usage identity is not stable across a query change (this PR itself adds
serviceTier and contextWindow to it, and it embeds the config bucket
width), so the rewind that repairs the 100x cost rows would make a usage
source re-read its history under NEW keys beside the old rows —
duplicated spend, not restatement. Usage now drops only the dead page
token and keeps the watermark; cost keeps the full rewind.

* fix(governance): fall back to the configured start when a kept usage watermark is not a date

A corrupt watermark passed through as starting_at would 400 on every
retry forever (the cursor holds still on failure). It certifies no
history, so the fallback duplicates nothing. Found by convention scan:
the cost rewind path had this guard, the usage keep-watermark path
did not.

* fix(governance): bind configured startingAt into the cost cursor identity

A legacy source with no configured startingAt first repairs only the
default window, then mints the new query identity — after which the
cursor matches forever and widening startingAt could never reach the
older 100x rows short of deleting the cursor by hand.

The configured start is now part of the cost identity, so widening it
mints a mismatch and the existing rewind (with its never-forward guard)
fires once more, reaching the deeper window. Usage identity deliberately
still excludes it: usage never rewinds, so binding it there would only
drop a live page token over an edit that changes nothing.

* fix(governance): resume stale usage cursors from the in-window watermark

A run cut off at the deadline or MAX_PAGES_PER_RUN persisted only the
window start beside the page token. When the identity check later voids
that token, the usage branch restarted the window at its start, re-reading
every page already emitted — under the new dimension keys, so the re-read
rows land beside the old ones instead of superseding them: duplicated
spend, up to 20 pages per source.

The cursor now records the newest bucket actually emitted (watermark)
whenever a page token is in hand, and a usage identity mismatch resumes
from it — re-reading at most the one bucket the token sat inside. Cursors
minted before the field existed carry no record, so their in-flight window
is still re-read once; that bounded one-shot is now stated in the
cursorSchema doc instead of denied.

fix(governance): a walk id keeps the events pager's latest walk from losing to a stale failure (#7347)

fix(governance): a walk id keeps the events pager's latest walk from losing to a stale failure (#7346)

Two initial walks overlap whenever the mount effect runs twice, as it
does in development. They shared one generation and one in-flight flag,
so the first walk to settle claimed the outcome: a failure set `error`
and cleared `isFetching`, and the second walk's successful landing was
then dropped by the same guard that was meant to swallow a duplicate.
The table showed "Couldn't load this source's events" with a page of
events in hand.

Each walk now carries an id issued from a ref when it starts, and the
latest start records it in the reducer. A landing counts only when both
the generation and that id match, so the newest walk wins whichever
order the two settle in — which is what the old `isFetching` half of
the guard was reaching for, and could not express with one flag shared
by every walk in flight.

Also renames the test-local `failNext` to `shouldFailNext`.

fix(traces): a trace's media is wherever its spans put it (#7339)

* fix(traces): a trace's media is wherever its spans put it

The trace list and the drawer summary read media from the refs the fold
derives, and the fold derived them from the span that won the trace's
headline input and output. Those are two different questions. A wrapper
span sets the headline text and the model call underneath it holds the
picture, which is the shape every framework integration produces, so the
refs came out empty for the most common trace there is and only the Trace
tab, which reads span payloads directly, showed anything.

Refs now accumulate across every span, with the winning span's own media
first so it stays the trace's thumbnail. The url is the identity, so one
recording reached through two paths is recorded once instead of drawing
the same player twice.

Two capture gaps alongside it. The Go NLP engine replaced every attachment
with a "[media-type, N bytes]" summary at any size; the guard was written
for a 20 MB fetch and cost a 2 KB thumbnail the same way. It is now sized
against the collector's 10 MB body limit, with one budget shared across

The URL a customer pastes into their own ElevenLabs dashboard moves to

customer-facing voice URL is then on one host: both mints, the usage report
and the webhook.

Two reasons. A webhook has to be reachable from the vendor's network, so
whatever serves it must be public. The gateway is public by design, while the
app is the admin UI that self-hosted customers keep behind a VPN, and hosting
the webhook there would force a public hole in the admin surface. On the
gateway it works in every topology where voice already works, with no ingress
change, because the chart already publishes /v1 as a prefix. Second, no
customer has registered the URL yet, so this is the last moment the change
costs nobody a dashboard edit.

because the vendor's HMAC covers them, the signature header is passed
verbatim, and the app's status is returned unchanged so 404-when-unconfigured
still keeps provider ids unprobeable. Verification stays on the app, which
holds the per-tenant secret. The app's own route is unchanged and still
mounted: it is the relay's target and is simply not the documented URL.

A delivery is read before it is sent rather than streamed. Streaming an
unknown-length body goes out chunked, which is not the shape the vendor sent,
and io.LimitReader truncates in silence, so an oversized report would arrive

not retry. An ack the gateway invented would report a landing that never
happened and hide a broken relay, and the reconciler bills the call anyway.

virtual key, so chi resolves the leaf before auth rejects. A 401 on

fix(data-privacy): catch vendor API keys the allow-list missed, and stop custom patterns erasing trace text (#6816)

* fix(data-privacy): catch vendor keys the allow-list missed and stop custom patterns shredding text

Secrets redaction failed in both directions from one root cause: the built-in
rules were a fixed allow-list of nine shapes, so a live third-party key pasted
into a coding-agent prompt was stored in the clear, and teams working around
that narrowness hand-wrote patterns that were compiled exactly as typed.

Matching now works in three layers: known vendor prefixes, shape alone (a
vendor-style prefix plus a high-entropy body, which needs no vendor knowledge),
and context (a credential named in prose and then given a value). Layers two and
three are gated on Shannon entropy and character-class mix.

Custom patterns get a leading word boundary unless they already state where they
start, and their match clamp is widened to whitespace and brackets. A pattern
like sk-.* no longer fires inside "task-notification" and no longer takes the
rest of the line with it.

Over-redaction is treated as the equal of a leak: the negative corpus asserts
that commit hashes, identifiers, timestamps, paths, model names, placeholders
and real coding-agent transcript text survive verbatim, under the built-ins and
under a customer-supplied pattern alike. Rules stay linear-time, about 2 ms per
200 KB, with ReDoS guards pinned as tests.

Neither fix is retroactive: already-stored traces keep the leaked key and keep
the mangled text.

* fix(data-privacy): reject custom secret patterns that would erase ordinary text

An over-broad custom pattern was waved through at save time on the reasoning
that it "only over-redacts". Redaction runs at ingestion and rewrites the text
for good, so an over-broad pattern is data loss, and one saved as sk-.* is what
destroyed a customer's own transcript tags.

The compile-time guard now has an authorship-time counterpart: a pattern is
probed against strings carrying no credential at all, and one that matches
ordinary prose, a transcript tag, a source path, a timestamp or a model name is
refused with the text it would have erased. The probe compiles the pattern
through the exact guard the ingestion path applies, so the settings page, the
server and the pipeline cannot disagree about what a pattern does.

The settings page runs the same probe, so an over-broad pattern is blocked
before save rather than only rejected afterwards. PII exception patterns keep
their own anchored breadth rule, which tests the opposite failure.

A pattern naming a real credential shape is unaffected, including sk-.*, which
the word-boundary guard already makes safe.

* ci(secrets): scope the generic-api-key rule off the redaction test corpus

The secrets-redaction suite exists to feed credential-shaped strings to
redact() and assert they come back as [SECRET], so its fixtures trip
gitleaks' generic-api-key rule by construction: five of them did, failing
the blocking secrets gate.

Allowlisted the way the four existing fixture entries are, by path and
scoped to generic-api-key alone, so every provider-specific rule still
applies to the file. Verified by planting a GitHub PAT and a Stripe live
key in it and watching github-pat and stripe-access-token still fire with
the allowlist active.

* fix(data-privacy): close three detection gaps and make the name rules reach log and metric attributes

Detection, three shapes that passed and should not have:

- Our own key prefixes were not known vendors. `ik-lw-` was covered by
  nothing at all and `sk-lw-` only once the body reached the generic
  `sk-` rule's 20-character floor, so a short or truncated one survived.
  Both, plus the legacy `pat-lw-`, are matched on the prefix now the way
  every other vendor is. The literals are duplicated rather than imported,
  because the package ships inside the SDK and stays dependency-free, so a
  test mints tokens with the real generator and fails if the two drift.
- An all-hex body after a vendor prefix was refused by the character-mix
  gate. That is right for a bare hex run, where a commit, a trace id and a
  digest are the same shape, and wrong when the token names itself a
  credential. A hex body is accepted only behind a credential segment
  (`_live_`, `_test_`, `_secret_` and friends) and never behind an
  identifier prefix such as `commit` or `trace`.
- The shape rule read lowercase prefixes only, missing every vendor
  minting `LW_`-style keys. It takes upper and mixed case now; the length
  floor and the character-mix gate are what keep a bare environment
  variable name like AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY readable, which is pinned.

Reviewer findings, all three reproduced first:

- `SELF_ANCHORED_PATTERN` read a named capture group as a lookbehind, so
  `(?<key>sk-.*)` skipped the word-boundary guard and shredded
  `task-notification` exactly like the unguarded pattern this PR exists
  to tame. The lookbehind arm is `(?<=` or `(?<!` now.
- A blank pattern compiled to something matching every probe, so an empty
  row in the settings UI reported itself over-broad on sight.
- The breadth probe accepted `[0-9a-f]{6,}`, which then redacted commit
  hashes and shredded UUIDs. Commit, UUID and trace-id probes added.

The name rules on the log and metric pipelines (#6818):

Those pipelines flatten a decoded OTLP tree into one record keyed by a
JSON path, because two attributes may share a name and each value still
needs its own address. A path can never satisfy a rule written against an
attribute NAME, so `isSensitiveAttributeKey("log.0.value.stringValue")`
was false for every attribute and the sensitive-name deny-list never ran
there at all: an `authorization` or `x-api-key` attribute was left to the
value-shape rules, and a plain-text one survived them.

The attribute's real name now travels beside the path and the name rules
match on it, which closes that gap and makes the `langwatch.api_key.id`
exemption apply on purpose rather than by accident. The receiver-side
invariant the exemption rests on is untouched, and the exemption stays
exact-match, so a client cannot smuggle an exempt-looking name.

Redaction cost is unchanged: 5.05ms median per 200 KB against a 4.5 to
6.6ms baseline, and 14.7ms on a pathological unbroken high-entropy run.

Fixes #6818

* fix(data-privacy): stop the shape rule eating record ids, and close the scan-cap bypass

A sweep of real traces found the shape layer firing about three times more
often on things that are not credentials than on things that are, and
redaction is irreversible at ingestion, so that is worse than the gap it
was widened to close.

Record ids. `prefix_<random body>` is how this product and the APIs it
talks to mint an id, which is the shape a key is minted in and carries the
same entropy, so nothing in the string separates them and the prefix has
to be named. `project_`, `card_`, `scenario_`, `langyconv_`, `provider_`,
OpenAI's `chatcmpl-` and Anthropic's `toolu_` were all being redacted;
`langwatch.thread.id` and `langwatch.model_provider_id` are attributes the
product groups and attributes traces by, so this broke thread grouping and
provider attribution. The exclusion the digest prefixes already used now
covers record-id prefixes too, and applies to the shape rule rather than
only the hex one. On the swept corpus this costs no recall: no credential
in it used any of those prefixes. `toolu_` had been surviving only by
sitting two characters under the length floor, which is not a margin.

The prose cue. `key is <value>` was accepted as a cue alongside `:` and
`=`, and across the corpus it caught zero credentials while being the only
source of English-prose redactions: "a bare digest of an API key is
offline-checkable against a list" lost everything after "key is", and so
did a sentence about an Authorization header. Removed, with both sentences
pinned in the negative corpus.

The scan cap. Text over the limit was returned untouched, which was a
bypass rather than a budget: an 885 KB agent input carrying a live provider
key went through ingestion completely unscanned, and being oversized was a
reliable way to smuggle one past. It is sliced on newline boundaries now,
so cost per pass stays bounded and no region goes unscanned. A test pins a
credential past the first slice boundary.

Standard base64 bodies. A `+` or `/` early in the body cut the match short
of the length floor, measured at a 57% miss rate for standard-base64
bodies against 0.5% for base64url, and 100% for an AWS secret access key.
The body class takes both alphabets now, which needs no vendor named.

Redaction cost is unchanged: 5.46ms median per 200 KB against a 4.5 to
6.6ms baseline, 15.8ms on a pathological unbroken high-entropy run.

* fix(data-privacy): read camelCase credential names, gate the loose separator, and stop slicing through a credential

The cue layer was blind twice over.

It read attribute names on separators only, so every camelCase and
PascalCase name was one opaque word and none of them fired: signingSecret,
bearerToken, webhookSecret, masterKey, encryptionKey, SecretAccessKey,
AccessKeyId, AuthorizationToken, PasswordHash, verificationToken,
rootPassword, credentialsJson, and AWS Secrets Manager's own SecretString
and SecretBinary, which is the field holding the secret itself. Names are
tokenised on separators AND camelCase boundaries now. Bare `key` and
`token` still need a qualifying word in front, so idempotency_key,
partition_key, cacheKey and a count of input_tokens stay readable.

And it accepted only `:` and `=`, so `Authorization <token>` was missed.
Whitespace is accepted now on a higher bar rather than not at all:
ungated it matched 5,816 further spans over 309 shapes, mostly prose, so
the value must look like key material in its own right, which brings it to
338 over 19 at roughly 87% precision. Four ordinary sentences that used to
lose their tail are pinned as negatives.

The remaining false positives came from JSON encoding. Span content
carries literal two-character escapes, and the value class allowed
backslash, so a value ran through one, crossed logical lines, and slipped
past the guards that recognise `$VAR` and a code expression. That is why
`api_key = $OPENAI_API_KEY` was kept with a real newline and redacted with
an escaped one, and why a Terraform `local.` reference was being eaten.
Backslash is out of the value class.

Slicing could also cut inside a credential, which is the same leak the
slicing was added to close: neither half matches, so it passes through in
two readable pieces. Cuts land on whitespace, which no single-line
credential contains, and an unbroken run moves the cut forward rather than
into it. A PEM block spans newlines by design, so an unterminated BEGIN
pulls its END into the same slice. Both are pinned by walking a key across
the boundary region.

Redaction cost is unchanged: 5.49ms median per 200 KB against a 4.5 to
6.6ms baseline, 15.0ms on a pathological unbroken high-entropy run.

* fix(data-privacy): a second pass over the vendor list, and stop catching PostHog's public project key

From a sweep of what real payloads carry. `vk-lw-` is ours and was
reaching only the generic shape rule, so it survived on a short body;
`GOCSPX-` and `mb_` had no rule at all; `PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK` broke the
PEM anchor on its own suffix, and `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` was not in the
armour list; PuTTY's own key format carries no PEM armour; and a
kubeconfig embeds its client key and certificate as bare base64.

The non-Bearer Authorization schemes needed care rather than a wider
alternation. `Token`, `OAuth` and `Splunk` are ordinary English words, and
adding them beside `Bearer` immediately redacted the sentence "token
acme_live_abcd1234 end" in this suite's own fixtures. They count only
inside an actual `Authorization:` header now, which is where they appear,
and three prose sentences are pinned to keep it that way.

PostHog's `phc_` goes the other way and closes a disagreement between the
code and its own comment. The vendor list has always said `phc_` is
deliberately omitted, being a client-side project key that ships inside
published web bundles by design, so blanking it hides telemetry
configuration and protects nothing. The shape rule was catching it anyway,
against the stated intent. It is excluded for real now, the same
over-redaction argument as a record id, and `phx_`, the personal key that
IS a credential, still redacts.

Also pinned the qualifier rule's negatives, `idempotency_key`,
`partition_key`, `cacheKey`, `sortKey`, `primaryKey`, `tokenCount`,
`keyboardLayout` and `monkeyPatch`, since the rule separating them from
`encryptionKey` is subtle and easy to break by widening the noun list.

Redaction cost is unchanged: 6.0ms median per 200 KB against a 4.5 to
6.6ms baseline, 17.4ms on a pathological unbroken high-entropy run.

* fix(data-privacy): bound every scan slice, and assert match counts on the boundary tests

The forward hunt for a cut point had no ceiling. A payload carrying no
whitespace came back as one slice however long it was, which rebuilds the
unbounded scan the budget exists to prevent: the cut can no longer look
further than a fixed lookahead, and past that the run is an order of
magnitude longer than any credential this file matches, so cutting inside
it cannot split one. A megabyte with no whitespace now round-trips in
about 100ms instead of forming a single slice.

The boundary tests inferred success from the absence of a substring, which
passes just as well if nothing ran at all. They assert the match count
too: exactly one replacement at every offset, since a split would give
zero and a double-counted overlap would give two.

Redaction cost is unchanged: 5.0ms median per 200 KB, 14.6ms pathological.

* test(data-privacy): make the JSON-escape test exercise the bug, and move the log test to the integration lane

The JSON-escape test was built on a real newline where it meant the two
characters a backslash and an n. A real newline already terminated the
value before this change, so the test passed without exercising anything,
the same failure mode as the boundary tests inferring success from an
absent substring. It carries a literal escape now, asserts the fixture
holds no real newline so it cannot silently regress, and covers the real
newline separately. Verified by reverting the value-class fix and watching
this test, and only this test, fail.

canonicalLog.unit.test.ts imports two production units and stubs the
redaction boundary three times, which is an integration test by the
repository's own definition, so it moves to the integration lane and
passes there.

The path-keyed log attribute suite gets its `when` blocks, and the scan
boundary is derived from one named constant rather than written inline at
five call sites, where a change to the budget would have left them passing
while testing nothing near the boundary.

* fix(data-privacy): declare attributeNames on the public redactLog signature

applyNativeLogPass reads log.attributeNames, but redactLog's own parameter
type omitted it, so the public contract promised less than the method
honours and a caller building the argument inline could not pass it at
all. The log pipeline only compiled because it types against the
LogRedactionService interface, which does declare it.

* fix(data-privacy): keep the PEM fixtures past the secrets gate, and drop a dead assignment

The suite has to hand the redactor a real armour block to prove it redacts
one, and `MIIabc` between BEGIN and END markers is a private key to any
scanner, so the gate failed on two of them.

Two changes, because either alone is not enough. The armour is assembled
at run time now, so no complete literal exists at the tip and nothing new
is added by later work, which is the technique the vendor tokens in the
same file already use. That does not clear the failure on its own:
gitleaks scans the whole commit range rather than the tip, so the earlier
commits that carried the literal still report. The allowlist entry for
this path therefore names `private-key` alongside `generic-api-key`.

Scope verified rather than assumed, the same way the first entry was:
with the allowlist active, a planted GitHub PAT, AWS key and Stripe live
key all still fire on this exact file, under `github-pat`,
`aws-access-token` and `stripe-access-token`. Only the two named rules are
suppressed here, so a real credential landing in the fixtures is still
caught.

Also dropped the useless initial value on `end` in `sliceEndAfter`, which
every branch overwrites.

* fix(data-privacy): a bare key field is a map entry, not a credential

The free-text cue read any unqualified `key` as proof that what followed
was a credential, so a map entry like {"key":"<content hash>"} was
blanked at ingestion. It was blanked only there: the same id, the same
UUID and the same record id on their own are all kept by the negative
corpus, so the cue was the one thing destroying them.

`key` now needs a credential word in front of it, the way the name rule
already required. Both rules read one qualifier list rather than each
carrying its own, which is what let them disagree.

* refactor(data-privacy): the PEM cut proves its own terminator, the doc sits on its function

sliceEndAfter kept a branch for close === -1 that the close >= end guard
already rules out, and the redactSecretsInText doc block had drifted onto
sliceForScan.

* chore(gateway): dogfood seed for budget-overview spend

fix(traces): read the Vercel AI SDK's own metadata channel, and stop telling ADK users to break their trace (#7368)

* fix(traces): read the Vercel AI SDK's own metadata channel

experimental_telemetry.metadata is the only metadata channel the AI SDK
gives a caller. It flattens the object onto every span it emits as
ai.telemetry.metadata.<key>, and the trace summary read langwatch.*,
gen_ai.* and tag.tags only, so a call tagged that way arrived with no
labels, no user, no conversation and no custom keys.

The legacy collector mapper has understood the shape since the Vercel
integration shipped, which is why the gap was hard to see: the same
payload behaved differently on the two read paths, and the one the trace
list reads was the one that ignored it.

An explicit langwatch.* value still wins.

* docs(adk): a decorator parents Google ADK spans only over run_async

Runner.run starts a plain threading.Thread and calls asyncio.run inside
it. The OpenTelemetry context lives in a context variable, which a new
thread does not inherit, so the agent spans open a second trace and the
metadata set on the wrapper never reaches them. Measured on a real ADK
run: two trace ids under the sync entry point, one under run_async.

The page showed the wrapper around the sync run twice, as the way to
attach metadata. It now shows run_async, says why, and names the symptom
in Troubleshooting. An <Info> component sitting inside a Python code
fence is removed with it.

The Vercel page said a span attribute overrides the value you pass to

fix(build): anchor the npm pack filters, and run them where they can fail (#7367)

* fix(build): anchor the npm pack filters, and run them where they can fail

The pack script filters the shipped trees with rsync patterns, and rsync
matches a pattern without a slash against every path component. Six working
tree artifacts were named there by their bare name, so `--exclude=licenses.json`
also removed a source data file of that name in any shipped tree and
`--exclude=quickwit` removed a source directory called that at any depth. The
same class already reached npm as `--exclude=reports` and killed the published
server at first boot. Those six move to a list written from the repository
root and anchored there. `Dockerfile*` becomes `Dockerfile` and `Dockerfile.*`,
which stops it matching a source file whose name only starts with the word, and
`server.log` becomes `*.log`, so no log ships from anywhere.

The script's own guard was reporting the wrong cause. It compared what git
tracks against the tarball and blamed a too-broad exclude for every gap, but
the filters also strip ignore files on purpose, and its exemption list did not
say so. A `.gitignore` added under dev/scripts therefore read as lost source.
It is now two guards with one cause each: staging against git, which needs an
exemption list and names it, and the tarball against staging, which needs none
because whatever survived staging is the package. The guard also reads every
tree the root `files` list names instead of a chosen subset.

The check could not run where it fails. npx-server-smoke has never run on push
to main, so main carried the defect green while every branch that merged main
went red, and the nightly is the only cover. Main is back on the push trigger,
and the fast half of the guard runs on every pull request and every merge as
`pack-npm.sh --check-filters`, which needs no build and takes ten seconds.

* fix(build): name every deliberate strip in the guard, and read the staged tree

Review round.

The guard's exemption list named the test, notebook, container, ignore, dotenv
and key classes but not the build output, tool caches and editor state the
filters also drop, so a tracked file under coverage/, .github/ or .vscode/, or
any tracked .log, .map or .tsbuildinfo, would have failed the pack as lost
source. Nothing in the tree hits that today; the list now says what it means.

npm-packlist drops *.orig, .*.swp and ._* at every depth whatever the manifest
says, so a working tree holding one staged a file the tarball then refused and
the staged-versus-tarball guard failed the pack. They are excluded at staging
now, which puts the two back in agreement.

`--stage-to DIR` stages into a directory and leaves it there. The filters
decide what every npm user receives and their verdict was only visible in a
temporary directory the script deletes, so a person debugging a missing file
had nothing to look at, and the tests could read the answer only through the
guard's error text. Both probes now assert on the tree itself, and the
.env.example case asserts the re-include ordering positively and the dotenv
exclusion negatively, which its name claimed and its body did not.

The test fixture copies the script with node:fs rather than spawning cat, and
`write` takes named parameters.

* fix(build): refuse a --stage-to that is empty or already holds something

Review round two.

`--stage-to=` and `--stage-to ""` set the value to an empty string and the
script fell back to a temporary directory, so it staged somewhere the caller
never asked for and said nothing. The flag is now tracked apart from its value
and an empty one is refused.

A directory that already holds something is refused too. rsync adds and
overwrites but never deletes, so a stale file would read as staged and, on a
full pack, ship: the published manifest lists `app`, so the whole preserved
tree goes out. Refusing is the safe half of that choice, because the
alternative is this script deleting a directory a caller named.

The test helpers take named parameters.

fix(model-providers): tell an unreadable credential apart from no credential (#7369)

* fix(model-providers): tell an unreadable credential apart from no credential

`decryptCustomKeys` answered `{}` for a column that holds nothing and for one
that will not decrypt, so no caller could tell a provider an operator left
keyless from a provider whose secret the server can no longer read. It now
answers one of three states and is named `readCustomKeys`, which puts every
call site through review once.

The repository kept its own private copy of the same rule, with a different
sentinel and one defect the shared helper was written to remove: its `catch`
covered `JSON.parse` as well as `decrypt`, and it logged `err.message`. A
SyntaxError quotes the text it choked on, and that text is the decrypted
provider key, so a row that decrypts to something malformed writes the
credential into the log line meant to warn that the credential could not be
read. The copy is gone and the repository reads through the shared helper,
which logs the error name and the input length only.

One caller was acting on the collapsed answer. An unreadable row reads back
with `customKeys: null`, so a save that names no credential field passed the
guard that refuses to drop stored credentials, and the merge then replaced the
ciphertext with what the payload carried. The same save is refused on a
readable row. It is now refused here too, with its own error and its own
message, because the two need different advice: there the stored value is fine
and the save has to stop leaving it out, here the stored value cannot be read
and only a new credential moves it forward. Sending a credential still goes
through, which is the way back.

The gateway config materialiser and the ElevenLabs credential service read the
keys and fail closed on an empty bag, which is correct for both states, so they
keep today's behaviour.

* fix(model-providers): make the guard hold for the save the drawer actually sends

Review round. The guard was refusing the wrong shape.

It asked whether the payload named a credential field, which is the right
question for a readable row, where an empty value is a customer clearing
something they could see. It is the wrong one here. The drawer renders the
masked placeholder for every secret field of an enabled row it found no
credentials on, and empty for the rest, so the ordinary save from an unusable
row names the full set of fields and carries no credential at all. It passed.
The guard now asks for a value that could serve a request.

`mergeStoredCustomKeys` stored that placeholder as though it were a credential
whenever there was nothing behind it, so the provider came away holding
`HAS_KEY...` as its API key and failed every request with a credential that was
never real. A placeholder with no stored value behind it is dropped now, the
same rule the extra-header merge already followed.

`readCustomKeys` accepted whatever `JSON.parse` returned. `null`, an array and
every scalar are valid JSON, and a caller indexing one of those throws where it
expected a missing key, so a stored `"null"` crashed the gateway config
materialiser instead of reading as no credentials. Only a plain object reads
as credentials.

The integration case is now a table over the three payloads that carry no
replacement, empty, masked and absent, and asserts the error code rather than
the message. The scenario describes what the customer sees.

fix(ai-gateway): a rotated provider credential reaches a running gateway, and dogfood seeding stops replacing working keys (#7068)

* fix(ai-gateway): a rotated provider credential reaches a running gateway

The gateway holds a materialised bundle per virtual key, in memory, carrying
the decrypted provider credential it dispatches with. Two things were meant
to carry a rotation into that cache and neither did.

The change feed was never written. ModelProviderService updated and deleted a
row without appending MODEL_PROVIDER_UPDATED, so the gateway's change poller
had nothing to evict on. The event kind already existed and the gateway
already handled it; only the Codex token-refresh path emitted it.

The config version token could not see the change. It came from
VirtualKey.revision alone, and a credential rotation writes ModelProvider and
leaves every key untouched, so the 60 second revalidation kept getting 304 for
a bundle carrying the replaced key.

The service now appends the event inside the write transaction, on update and
on delete, following the mechanism budget.service and cacheRule.service
already use. The token is now the key's revision plus a digest of the
organization's provider rows, which also covers a write the change feed never
sees, such as a seeding script. A digest rather than a newest-updatedAt
summary because updatedAt is TIMESTAMP(3): two writes inside one millisecond
would leave a summary where it was.

The provider-and-project delete resolves the set, deletes the part of it still
inside the scope, then emits an event for each row that actually went. Each
statement gets its own READ COMMITTED snapshot, so the resolved set can name a
row that left the scope before the delete, and the count says how many went
without saying which.

Dogfood seeding no longer replaces a working credential. The seeders wrote
whatever provider key the shell held straight onto an existing org-wide row,
so a run with a stale key in the environment replaced a credential other
people were using, unrecoverably. Seeding now fills a gap: an empty row gets a
key, a row that already has one keeps it, and replacing takes --force-keys.
Forcing swaps one key for another and never empties the column, so a run with
an unset environment variable leaves the row alone. A row whose credential
cannot be decrypted is left alone and kept out of the seeded routing chain,
because enabling it makes every request through it fail at credential
materialisation. Every row a seeder looks at produces a line naming the
organization, the provider, the row and both credentials masked.

seed-governance-refactor-dogfood.ts had a second failure in the same place:
with the env var unset it wrote DbNull and cleared the stored key outright.
Both seeders now point at platform/app/.env for provider keys.

* fix: address third review round on credential rotation

The config version token now digests eligibleModelProvidersForVk, the
resolver the materialiser itself calls, instead of a provider query written
in configETag.ts. A hand-written approximation of the provider set has to be
kept in step with the resolver by hand, and it fell behind three times:
a newest-updatedAt summary that could not separate two writes inside one
millisecond, then a scalar column list that could not see the
ModelProviderScope rows deciding reachability at all, then the ordering that
fallbackPriorityGlobal and createdAt settle. Digesting the resolver's output
cannot fall behind the resolver.

Measured before changing anything: revoking a scope row left the token
byte-identical at 1.995a5c2ea74e1b12, so the control plane answered 304 to a
bundle whose provider set had changed. That is worse than a stale credential,
because scope membership decides whether a key reaches a provider at all.

A seeded row that cannot serve a request is now skipped rather than kept.
Nothing stored and nothing to write used to report keep, and both seeders then
enabled the row, so a row with no credential became routable. A skipped
provider is also removed from the default routing policy, which a merge that
only added ids left in place from an earlier run.

maskSecret no longer prints a one or two character value in full.

The seeding rule and its tests moved under src/server/modelProviders, because
integration discovery only searches src and ee, so the test would never have
run from scripts.

The version token is exposed as GatewayConfigMaterialiser.versionToken, so the
route holds one materialiser for both the token and the payload, and the token
sits beside the output it versions.

* refactor(dogfood): split the credential decision into its two questions

The new-violations gate flagged one added Biome violation in this file:
cognitive complexity over the limit, from stacking the no-replacement case
inside the has-replacement one.

They are two different questions and now read as two functions. With a key in
hand the question is whether it may replace what is stored; with no key it is
only whether the row can serve a request at all. Forcing belongs to the first
and has no meaning in the second, which is what keeps a run with an unset
environment variable from emptying the column.

readStoredCredential is flattened the same way, with the encrypted-blob and
the record cases as their own functions.

No behaviour change: the same 27 unit cases pass unchanged.

* fix(dogfood): a blank replacement is not a credential

The replacement check asked only whether the record had a key, while the
stored check asked whether any value was non-blank. That asymmetry meant a
record like {OPENAI_API_KEY: " "} counted as something to write, so a forced
run replaced a working credential with whitespace, which empties the column
by another name and contradicts the guarantee that forcing never clears a key.

Both sides now use hasAnyValue, so eligibility means the same thing wherever
it is asked.

* fix(dogfood): an unset key is not a reason to drop a provider the org has

The audio seeder only looked at a provider when its environment variable was
set. An organization with a working stored credential and no variable exported
had that provider ignored, so it never entered the seeded routing policy, and
a run with neither variable set failed outright against an organization that
was already configured. That contradicts the rule this change added: seeding
fills a gap and preserves what is there.

The row is now always consulted, with the replacement passed as null when the
variable is unset, so the same decision covers it: a readable stored
credential keeps the provider in the chain, and only a row that cannot serve a
request drops out. A provider with no row and no key creates nothing rather
than an empty row the gateway cannot build a credential for.

rowIsUsable is that question in one place, shared by the seeder and its tests
instead of being re-derived at the call site.

Also converts the parameterised cases to object form and rewrites the feature
scenarios to state what a caller observes rather than how the change reaches
the gateway.

perf(data-privacy): redaction rules search for their own literal first (#7366)

* perf(data-privacy): the connection-URL rule searches for its own literal first

The rule led with the scheme, a run of lowercase letters, so every letter in
a payload started a scan for a "://" that was usually not there. It cost 6.2 ms
of a 200 KB scan, more than every other rule together, and 2.4 ms on prose with
no URL in it at all.

The scheme moves into a lookbehind, so the first thing the engine searches for
is the literal ":". The scheme was already kept out of the replacement, so the
redacted text is the same: proven over a corpus and 300,000 random strings.

200 KB, mean, same benchmark on both sides:

  prose, no URL             4.13 ms -> 1.68 ms
  coding-agent transcript   7.13 ms -> 3.68 ms
  connection strings        5.97 ms -> 3.69 ms

Adds the benchmark that produced those numbers, since no unit test can hold a
2x change without flaking on a loaded runner.

* perf(data-privacy): the phone detector skips text too short to hold a number

libphonenumber treats every digit as the start of a number and then tries to
parse it, so the detector was the most expensive thing in the essential-PII
pass by two orders of magnitude. It had no gate of its own, while the regex
recognizers have carried one since #7092.

200 KB, median, whole essential-PII pass:

  prose with a version number   165.3 ms -> 1.2 ms
  json with numeric fields      247.6 ms -> 4.3 ms
  hex hashes                     33.0 ms -> 2.7 ms
  timestamps                    189.4 ms -> 178.8 ms   gate passes, as it should
  real phone numbers             89.6 ms ->  90.4 ms   gate passes, as it should

The floor is six digits in one window, one below the shortest example number
the phone metadata holds for any country, and the window allows the four
separators the library allows between digit blocks over a character class that
is a superset of the punctuation it accepts. The gate can therefore only err
towards running the detector.

Proven against the detector itself rather than against the annotation: 1715
example-number shapes across every country, and 300,000 random strings of which
235,713 are skipped by the gate, with no case where the gate skips text the
detector would have found a number in. Raising the floor fails the new test.

* test(data-privacy): the gate cases nest by condition and name their parameters

Adds the when layer the file's other block already has, switches shapesOf to
an options object, and takes the detector internals and the benchmark numbers
out of the feature file. The numbers stay in the implementation comment, which
is where the code that spends the time is.

* fix(data-privacy): a reported connection URL still spans its scheme

The anchor change moved the scheme out of the regex match, so
detectSecretsInText reported url_credentials starting at the colon. Redaction
was unaffected, the scheme was never part of the replacement, but the span is
part of what the scan reports and the evaluator collapses overlaps with.

A rule can now name the text it requires in front of the match, and the
detection path widens the reported span by it. Spans are identical to the
engine before the anchor change over a 17-string corpus and 200,000 random
strings. Removing the declaration fails the two new span tests.

Also takes the regex reasoning out of the secrets feature file, the same way
the phone one moved, and nests the gate cases by condition.

fix(governance): one projection hold per ingestion-key rotation, and a spinner while the wrapper sets up (#7395)

* fix(governance): one projection hold per ingestion-key rotation, and a spinner while the wrapper sets up

Minting an ingestion key rides the grants ledger: revoke the prior key's
bindings, delete its private role, define the new key's role, attach the
new key's binding. Every write held the request until the grants
projection landed it, and the organization's queue delivers writes in
order, so one rotation stacked up to four full fold pickup cycles. A
fresh mint measured 14.9 seconds in production, and the first
`langwatch claude` after a logout sat well over twenty, in silence,
right after the "langwatch saved" line.

Only the last write of the chain holds now. The queue is FIFO per
organization, so the final grant attach's projection landing proves the
earlier writes landed too. `defineRole` and `deleteRole` gained the same
`awaitProjection` option `attachBindings` already had; the API-key create
and the hard-cut rotation pass it; every other caller keeps the default
hold. The key row itself is revoked imperatively either way.

The wrapper also shows a spinner ("Setting up telemetry for claude...")
while mode resolution reaches the control plane, stopped before any
feedback or error prints, with stdin left cooked so Ctrl+C still works.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BUKKUiZbSBHmrLK9JJj4Ba

* fix(governance): default awaitProjection instead of a conditional spread

The biome gate reported one new cognitive-complexity point in
ApiKeyService.revoke: the conditional spread that only forwarded
awaitProjection when it was set added a branch. The ledger writer already
defaults the flag to true, so a plain default parameter is the same
behaviour with no branch. The two matching spreads in RoleRepository move
to the same form.

Also lowers the entropy of the fake token in the rotation test, which the
gitleaks scan read as a generic API key.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BUKKUiZbSBHmrLK9JJj4Ba

* fix(governance): keep the role definition hold, drop only the holds nothing reads

The command queue groups jobs per command name, not per organization
(`QueueManager.buildGroupKey`, jobPath `command/${cmdName}`), so
`defineRoles` and `attachGrants` sit in different groups and the attach can
be picked up first. The private role of a restricted key is a foreign key
target for the binding attached right after it, so skipping the definition's
projection hold could let the binding write hit a role row that is not there
yet. `defineRole` holds again, and its `awaitProjection` parameter is gone
rather than left as an option no caller can use safely.

The rotation path keeps its skip, on its own merits: the prior key is dead
the moment its row is revoked, and its private role is named after that key
id, so no later mint waits for the name. `deleteRole` documents that reason
instead of the queue ordering one.

Also drops the intermediate positional helper in the CLI wrapper (the two
calls now wrap `resolveWrapperMode` directly), renames the wrapper spec
scenarios to describe telemetry setup rather than mode resolution, and
replaces the `mode resolution failed` stderr line with copy that names the
tool.

refactor(authz): a grant is its own aggregate, and finishing the migration is the switch (#7358)

* docs(authz): ADR-101 — a grant aggregate is a grant, not an organization

The grants ledger made organizationId both the tenant and the aggregate,
citing the billing_report precedent. That precedent never appends an event,
so its fold state is permanently empty and the shape's one weakness could
not show. Copied into a pipeline that does append, it makes a single
aggregate's fold state every grant the organization has ever held, and the
state store reloads all of it on every event batch.

Measured on the organization that has been parked all day: 69,826 grant rows,
326 genesis facts landed over six hours (~0.015 facts/sec against the ~1.8
the convergence budget assumes), and a cutover needing ~10.7 hours of folding
against a 20-minute ceiling. The import decelerates as it progresses and the

* docs(authz): the aggregate id rule is stability across retries, not determinism

key only dedupes within one aggregate. An id minted freshly per attempt
defeats idempotency outright: the retry lands on a different aggregate,
nothing collapses, and every pass adds another copy of the same fact.

Restates the rule accordingly. Derivation is how a writer with no memory
satisfies it - a migration retries across processes and days with nowhere to
record what it minted, so the id must be recomputable from the fact. A live
write already mints commandId once and reuses it on retry, so a KSUID minted
alongside it is equally stable and derivation buys nothing there.

over them, one of which — TiersPresentIn — was never used. The tiers now

internal helpers become four; PermissionDeclarationError becomes

The declaration sweep now checks agreement, not just presence. For every
procedure it reads the input schema's required scope fields and the
declaration, and refuses an id that no declared check resolves a scope
from, a declaration whose input carries no usable id, and an input schema
it cannot read at all — the last so an unreadable schema can never pass by

declaration that names no permission, so nothing verifiable covers the id

* refactor(authz): the projection never reads, so the fold is gone

Every authz event carries everything needed to apply it to exactly one row,
so there is no prior state to compute from. That makes the fold — and the
580-line reducer behind it, and the cursor table, and readStoredHeads' org-
wide findMany — unnecessary rather than merely misconfigured. What replaces
them is a projection that maps an event to one guarded statement.

Two properties make it safe without a cursor. Every write is state-setting,
never incremental, so re-applying an event is a no-op under at-least-once
delivery. And a revoke now MARKS its row instead of deleting it, so a late
redelivery of an older event loses to the occurredAt guard rather than
resurrecting a grant no row was left to contradict. The two upserts are raw
SQL because ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE is the only way to put that
guard inside the same statement.

The reducer's 580 lines become 132 of facts. The revocation selector goes
with it: sweeping every grant matching a principal was a fold's privilege,
and a grant is its own aggregate now, so a revoke names an id.

role = legacyRole ?? CUSTOM, so an adopted ADMIN binding reassigned to a new

the row said viewer. The store clears it; the regression test moved to the
app beside the projection that owns the behaviour now.

* fix(authz): restore the compat writes, and make the guard say what it means

Four reviewers converged on one defect from different angles, and it is the
same shape as the purge: this branch deleted one half of a dual-write and left
every consumer of the other half standing.

The fold wrote FIVE tables — Grant/Role and the legacy RoleBinding, ShareLink
and CustomRole. Its replacement writes two. Nothing else writes the other
three, so on an organization served by the engine: revoke-by-filter resolved
its target ids from RoleBinding and therefore revoked nothing; duplicate
detection read RoleBinding and so every re-attach minted a second live grant;
three read-your-writes waits polled tables that would never be written and
burned the full convergence timeout; share-link creation read its own row back
and threw; and ledger-born custom roles were invisible to every role screen.

ADR-110 lists this as Open — "whether the projection's compat writes survive at
all". They survive. Rollback to legacy has to stay possible after an
organization switches, and an organization whose grants exist only in Grant
cannot be rolled back to a head that never saw them.

The writes go back where the fold had them, through the mappers that were left
in place when the writes were removed, and stay best-effort: Grant is the
authority and these are a view of it, so a unique or foreign-key conflict is
warned and stepped over rather than parking the aggregate's queue lane.

The guard now differs by what a write states, which is how equal timestamps are
made safe. A full-row write must be strictly newer, because on equality it
restates every column and a redelivered `attached` would revert a
same-millisecond `role_changed` and restore legacyRole — an escalation, not a
lost update. A field-setting write may tie, since it cannot revert anything.
attachBindings stamps one occurredAtMs per batch, so equal timestamps are
ordinary rather than exotic.

Not fixed, and deliberately: a partial update still writes nothing when its row
is absent. Per-aggregate FIFO makes that unreachable except for a back-dated
append after a live revoke — a migration hazard. A tombstone would need
principalType, scopeType and scopeId, which a revocation event does not carry,
and inventing them would put a fabricated scope in the table that DECIDES
access. So the miss is logged instead, and the constraint is written down where
the migration author will find it.

Also: offboarding counted a user's remaining grants without excluding revoked
rows, so now that a revoke marks, a departing member who held any grant failed
their own offboarding and rolled the membership deletes back.

The store had no tests at all, which is how the compat writes came to be
deleted without anything noticing. It has eight now.

The client legitimately imports `server/api/rbac.ts` — `useOrganizationTeamProject`
and the settings permission picker need its permission-matching functions to
decide what to render. So whatever rbac.ts imports, the browser gets. main's
cutover gate had no dependencies at all, which is why this worked; the
consolidated engine gate added a logger and `./metrics`, and `./metrics` imports
prom-client, which runs `register.removeSingleMetric` as a side effect of BEING
IMPORTED. That reaches `process`, and the bundle dies before the app mounts.

The gate is dependency-free again. Its failure reporting is now installed by
the server composition instead of imported, because the counter cannot live in
a module the browser loads. A no-op nobody replaces would be the other failure
— a reopened legacy-fallback window with nothing said about it — so a test
pins that `initializeDefaultApp` installs the real one.

`Actions`/`Resources` also move to `src/utils/rbacVocabulary.ts`, a leaf module
with no imports. They are plain data that both halves of the app read, and
having them live in rbac.ts is what dragged server code into a React component
in the first place.

Note what did NOT catch this: typecheck, lint, and 31,000 unit tests all passed
with a broken client bundle, because none of them load a browser. The new test
therefore checks the import list rather than the behaviour — the cheapest thing
that would have failed. `@langwatch/observability` is deliberately not on its
list: the cached-flag helper in the same graph constructs a logger at module
scope and has done for as long as the file has existed, with the client build
green, because pino defers touching process.stdout until something logs. The
rule is "runs at import", not "is a Node package".

- The compat writes minted legacy rows for every grant fact. For
  migration-sourced facts they are update-only now: an adopted row

Review findings from three parallel audits plus CodeRabbit, one iteration:

Deny direction — a share link deleted while an organization was held kept a
live bearer-token Grant row forever: the sweep read only the non-resource
heads. It now revokes stale migration-owned resource rows too, and

never touch a live-write row whose compat write was stepped over.

- A CUSTOM TeamUser row imported as a viewer grant where the legacy

- The membership suppression keyed on role, stating an extra grant beside

  any binding covering the user at the scopes in play, group-held
  bindings included (new findGroupMemberships read).

Convergence wedges:
- Repair command ids fold in the pass's occurredAtMs, so a value
  oscillating back to one it held before is not swallowed by the event
  store's idempotency key.
- A drifted role is restated WHOLE via defineRole at today's business

feat(aigateway): serve ElevenLabs' own speech and text routes (#7405)

* feat(aigateway): serve ElevenLabs' own speech and text routes

The gateway already reaches ElevenLabs through the OpenAI-shaped /v1/audio
routes. That only helps a caller willing to write OpenAI-shaped requests. A
caller using the ElevenLabs SDK posts to that vendor's own paths with that
vendor's own body, so its traffic went straight to the vendor and none of it
was metered.

Add POST /v1/text-to-speech/{voice_id} and POST /v1/speech-to-text, mirroring
the vendor's paths so an ElevenLabs SDK reaches the gateway by base URL alone.
Both take the vendor's xi-api-key header, run the same interceptor chain as
every other route, and forward the caller's body, form parts and query string
as written.

Bifrost cannot forward this wire (its ElevenLabs provider answers Passthrough
with unsupported-operation), so the gateway calls the vendor itself over the
SSRF-checked client the session mint already uses. Both routes pin the
ElevenLabs provider: the body is that vendor's own shape, so falling back
would spend a credential the caller never named on an API that cannot read
the request.

Metering reuses the existing audio measures. Synthesis reports the runes of
the request text in input_chars, the same count the OpenAI-wire route
reports, so one call costs the same on either wire. Transcription reports the
audio_duration_secs the vendor states in audio_ms, falling back to the last
word timing when a response carries no duration.

* fix(aigateway): address review on the ElevenLabs audio routes

Refuse the vendor's asynchronous transcription mode. With a truthy webhook
form part ElevenLabs answers before it has transcribed anything, so the
response carries no duration and the spend record would confirm at zero
seconds for audio the customer was charged for. The gateway has no settlement
path for the delivery that follows either: the existing /v1/convai/webhook
relay carries Conversational AI post-call reports, a different payload keyed
on a different id. Verified against the live API, which names the parameter
"webhook" in its own validation errors.

Marshal the synthesized model body instead of concatenating strconv.Quote.
The model is a caller-supplied form part and Quote emits Go escapes such as
\x01 for a control byte, which is not JSON, so one control byte would break
every downstream stage that parses the body. The OpenAI-wire transcription
route had the same defect and now shares the fix.

Cap the native transcription upload at 26 MB, the same limit the OpenAI-wire
route uses, rather than the gateway-wide 32 MB request ceiling. The upload is
held in memory twice, as the parsed file and again in the multipart body
rebuilt for the vendor, for as long as the vendor call runs. A caller with a
larger file sends a cloud_storage_url part, which the vendor fetches itself.

Assert the billed cost in the live matrix cell. The two scenarios it binds are
about billing, and the cell only proved that audio crossed both routes, so
incorrect metering passed it. It now stamps its own traceparent, reads the
call back from the trace API, and requires the rated cost to match the
vendor's published price.

Add the tests review found missing: the redirect refusal that keeps the
customer's provider key from reaching a redirect target, and the HTTP-boundary
branch that accepts a cloud_storage_url with no file part.

State in the spec and the docs that model_id is the one body field the gateway
replaces, since a body carrying a resolved model is not byte for byte what the
caller sent.

* docs(aigateway): correct the ElevenLabs upload limit and metering wording

The native transcription section said 26 MB and called it the same limit as
/v1/audio/transcriptions, which documents 25 MB. Those are two different
numbers: 25 MB is the audio a caller may send, and the 26 MB constant is the
request body that carries it plus multipart framing. State the audio limit,
which is what a caller can act on, and which does match the sibling route.

Say that the gateway itself returns the 400 for an asynchronous transcription,
before ElevenLabs is contacted. The previous wording opened with the vendor's
behaviour and could be read as the vendor refusing the request.

Say characters are Unicode characters rather than bytes, since that is what a
customer billing per character needs to know.

* docs(aigateway): separate the refusal from what it prevents

The asynchronous-transcription line ended on "the call would be billed as
free", which sits next to a sentence saying the request is refused and can be
read as describing the refused request. Say plainly that nothing is called and
nothing is billed, then give the free-metering outcome as what forwarding the
request would have caused.

* docs(aigateway): name both settings an ElevenLabs SDK has to change

The opening line said changing the base URL was the whole change. The key
value changes too: the header carries a LangWatch virtual key, not the
customer's ElevenLabs key, which stays on the provider row. A reader who
stopped at that line would point their SDK at the gateway with the vendor key
still in it and get a rejection. Both settings are now named where the claim
is made, rather than one paragraph later.

* docs(aigateway): say where the ElevenLabs key actually lives

The line read "an ElevenLabs key on the virtual key", which points a reader at
the wrong object. The vendor key sits on the organization's ElevenLabs provider
row; what the virtual key needs is provider access that still includes
ElevenLabs. The same line now also says what the refusal is, since a key that
cannot reach the provider is refused rather than served by another one.

fix(langy): composer typing performance, session resume, and cards that tell the truth (#7403)

* fix(langyagent): resume the session a worker home still holds

A reaped worker's home directory survives, but a respawn always created a
fresh opencode session, so the relay re-injected the whole transcript as a
seed on every respawn. The seed changes every turn, so provider prompt
caching missed on every message, and with the transcript in its prompt the
model re-typed its working directory from memory, truncating the session id
and running commands in a directory that does not exist.

OpenSession now lists the sessions persisted in the home and resumes the
newest one; a resumed session skips the transcript seed (its own history is
the single copy), and a failed listing degrades to a fresh session. The
agent instructions now also forbid passing a workdir or retyping
/workspace/sessions paths.

* fix(sdk): passive capture reads never crash an uninitialized SDK

getObservabilitySdkConfig threw whenever NODE_ENV=development and
setupObservability had not run, and the prompt tracing decorators ask
shouldCaptureInput() on every call, so langwatch prompt push failed with
'Please call setupObservability()' in any development-mode environment,
including the Langy worker. An explicit throwOnUninitialized option now
wins over the development-mode check, and getDataCaptureMode reads the
config with throwOnUninitialized: false: code that only asks 'may I record
this value?' degrades to the defaults instead of crashing the operation it
decorates.

* fix(langy): a local prompt scaffold is not a created platform resource

langwatch prompt create writes a file on disk and exits 0 with
{ name, path, dependency: 'file:...' }. Its name key passed
namesCreatedResource, so the panel drew 'Created and ready to use.' with a
deep link to a prompt the platform does not hold, while the push that would
have created it had failed. A payload that declares a file: dependency now
passes only on a server-minted id, never on a name alone; the local
scaffold draws no card and the push or sync result speaks for the
platform.

* feat(langy): a conversation keeps the model it was last used with

Coming back to a conversation in another tab or after a reload snapped the
composer's picker to the resolved default even when the conversation ran on
a different model. The agent_turn_accepted event now carries the turn's
model, the conversation fold keeps the latest as LastModel (new projection
column), the history read returns it, and opening a conversation seeds the
picker from it. A model the user picked since opening the conversation is
never replaced, a model the allowlist refuses is not restored, and a new
chat starts on the resolved default again — a pick lives with its
conversation, which is also what the make-default dialog's 'Just this
conversation' promises.

* fix(langy): panel fixes from a dogfooding session

- Typing lag: the draft subscription lives in a memoized ComposerInputRow
  leaf, the model pill is memoized, useModelSelectionOptions derives its
  options in one useMemo, and the focus ring is a CSS :has rule — a
  keystroke re-renders the input row, not the panel tree.
- The 'Type # to add anything' teaching banner is gone, with its store
  state.
- The last finished tool stays visible as its own settled card while the
  model thinks, folding into the receipt when the next call starts, text
  streams, or the turn ends.
- A prompts result offers no Experiments/Scenarios chips.
- Stopping a turn renders 'Interrupted' instead of 'No content'.
- Saving or removing a default model in settings reaches an open panel
  without a reload (syncLangyAfterDefaultModelWrite), and picking a model
  in the composer offers to make it the default at the scope that holds
  the current one, when the user can manage that scope.
- The plan card marks every step as a checkbox and counts done out of
  total, never 'left'.
- A receipt row with a recorded result opens to show what the tool
  returned.
- The polled history snapshot drives the same durable catch-up as the
  freshness signal (catchUpConversationFold), so a tab whose live stream
  dropped keeps converging on the turn instead of freezing mid-turn.

* fix(langy): green the CI checks and act on the first review round

Four red checks, four causes.

typecheck: two errors `pnpm typecheck` cannot see, because
tsconfig.tsgo.json excludes tests. A forked conversation's
ConversationDetail was missing `lastModel`, and the projection
repository's `row()` helper was missing `LastModel`.

test-component: the Default Models drawer now awaits the langy
cache sync after a successful save. The sync threw on a query
client that does not answer `modelProvider.invalidate`, so a
landed save toasted "Couldn't save the default model". The
sync's own contract says a cache-refresh failure may never read
as a failed write, and now the code says it too.

lint: six new Biome complexity findings, fixed by extraction
rather than an override. `mergeProviderRowsByKey`,
`composerKeyHandler`, `ComposerSendControl` with its two
buttons, `ResultDisclosureButton` / `RawDataToggle`, and a scope
lookup table in `makeDefaultOffer`.

deployment-impact-check: the description had no
`## Deployment Impact` section.

Review findings that changed code:

- The held "just finished" card opens to show what the call
  returned, the same disclosure the receipt row has.
- The catch-up page ceiling refetches the history instead of
  leaving the fold behind the durable record. Multi-page paging,

- `DefaultModelEffective` carries the resolver's own source and

- Five duplicated `modelProvider` mock blocks are one

- `LangyPlanCard.unit.test.tsx` renamed to `.integration`, and

- The migration carries its commented rollback, new booleans

* fix(langy): drop a tail that lands after a conversation switch

The local turn fold is one document for whichever conversation is
open, and selecting another one resets it. A durable tail fetched
for the conversation the user just left arrived afterwards and was
folded into the new conversation's fresh projection, so the panel
showed a turn that conversation never ran. Every page now re-checks

The freshness suite drove the hook with a conversation id the store

Also from the review:

* fix(langy): make the default-model ask one line

The dialog stacked a title, the model in bold, and a four-line explanation for a yes or no question. It now asks the question itself and nothing else, so the sentence is also the dialog's accessible name.
