feat(scenarios): secret run parameters and a truthful batch completion signal (#7397)

* docs: the first body heading names its own section, never the page title

Mintlify renders the frontmatter title as the page H1 and the description
as the lede, so a body heading with the same text showed the title twice,
stacked. Sixteen pages swept. The Remote Traces page is now Linking Your
Traces: remote described our perspective, not the reader's. The rule is in
the CLAUDE.md pitfalls table so it does not come back.

* fix(scenarios): the batch summary tells the truth about completion

Fixes #7363
Fixes #7364

The batch aggregate counted only IN_PROGRESS and PENDING as running, so a
batch of queued runs reported runningCount 0 and a non-null allCompletedAt
while the queue still held all the work. The running set now carries QUEUED
and RUNNING, allCompletedAt stays null until the last run settles, and the
mapper stops subtracting stored STALLED runs from runningCount, a leftover
from read-time stall derivation that no longer exists.

The summary also gains settledCount and a derived isComplete, and a batch
becomes addressable on its own: GET /api/simulation-runs/batches/{batchRunId}
returns the counts for one batch, so a CI job polls one request and one
flag. allCompletedAt is deprecated in the OpenAPI description. The new
docs page covers the recipe, including the totalCount >= jobCount guard
for the async run creation window.

failCount keeps excluding STALLED on this endpoint on purpose: stalledCount
is a separate field here, and folding it in would double-count.

* feat(scenarios): secret run parameters

Fixes #7365

A scenario parameter can be declared secret. The run-time value arrives on
the same parameters field, splits from the plain values before any merge,
and is encrypted before it enters the event store. The ciphertext rides the
queued event beside the metadata, never inside it, so an old worker's fold
cannot stamp it into simulation_runs during a deploy window. The fold and
the run mapper strip any secretParameters key anyway, as defense against
metadata written by external SDKs.

Delivery reuses the secrets namespace: the prefetcher decrypts once and the
run values overlay the project secrets, so an http target reads
{{ secrets.NAME }} and a code target reads secrets.NAME with zero adapter
changes, and the existing error scrubbing covers the values. Scenario text
cannot read a secret: the params record that renders situation and criteria
carries plain values only, and a reference to a secret name is a 422 at
request time. Clear names ride metadata.secretParameterNames for display.

Audit log entries stop recording run parameter values: redactAuditArgs
keeps the names and drops the values for suites.run and scenarios.run, the
same for httpProxy.execute template variables, and the error-path audit
middleware now runs its args through the redactor too.

All new error codes carry parameter names only, in meta and in message.

* feat(scenarios): secret parameters in the editor, the run dialog, the drawer and the docs

The parameter editor gains a Secret switch: a secret declaration drops and
disables its default value, and the footer chip shows a lock. The suite
run dialog renders a required password input for every secret parameter
and holds the run until each one has a value, so the server 422 never
reaches the user. The run detail drawer lists secret parameter names with
a masked value, after the plain parameters.

The docs gain a Secret parameters section on the run parameters page, the
three secret error codes in the rejection table, and a cross-link from the
authenticated agents page, whose warning about credentials in parameters
now points at secret parameters.

* chore(api): regenerate the OpenAPI spec, the docs reference and the SDK clients

The regen carries the new batch summary endpoint and the settledCount,
isComplete and deprecated allCompletedAt fields into the spec, the docs
copy, the generated reference page, the TypeScript client types and the
Python client. The Python regen also produced repo-wide drift from a
stale committed client; only the simulation-runs files are kept, the
rest needs its own regen pass.

* fix(scenarios): fail closed on a secret the run cannot deliver, and address review

The queued event carries the secret parameter names in clear on its metadata
and the values beside it, encrypted. The process manager read only the values,
so an event that declared a name and carried no readable value for it started
the run anyway: the target then ran with no credential, or with the project
secret of the same name. It now compares the two and finishes the run ERROR
before it is submitted, for a name with no entry and for an empty one.

The run request also refused only a missing secret value, not an empty one. The
run dialog cannot send an empty field, but a caller that goes straight to the
API can, so the check now rejects it with the same error.

Review follow-ups in the same change:

- The CI guide says a first 404 means the runs are not stored yet, and carries
  a poll script that keeps polling through it and exits nonzero on failCount or
  stalledCount. A stalled run settles without failing, so failCount alone
  reported success for a batch that never finished its work.
- The secret parameter docs and the feature file say the value is encrypted
  before storage and kept out of the runs store, the APIs, the exports and the
  audit log, instead of claiming it is never stored. The CLI example reads the
  token from a CI variable.
- The OpenAPI document marks allCompletedAt deprecated as a keyword, not only
  in its sentence, and describes the secret and defaultValue fields.
- The error-path audit test runs at a path the redaction rules cover. The
  middleware sits before the input parser, so it holds no input to store; the
  test now says so instead of passing on an empty record.
- Three tutorial pages give the first section its own heading.
- Feature file trimmed to observable behavior, HTTP template syntax corrected,
  and the drawer scenario named for what it masks.
- redactAuditArgs, readBatch and the request helper take named parameters.
  ParameterChip takes isSecret.

Lint: ParameterDefinitionsInput splits the default value and secret cells out
of the row, redactAuditArgs moves its field rules into helpers, and
executeScenarioRun builds the prefetch context in one.

* fix(scenarios): the CI recipe stops on a bad read, and headers redact fail closed

The polling example in the CI guide retried every status that was not 200, so
a wrong token or a server error became a batch timeout thirty minutes later.
It now retries 404 and a request that did not complete, and stops on anything
else with the status and the body. The request carries a connect timeout and a
max time, so a hung read cannot hold the job past its own deadline.

The audit redaction of `extraHeaders` returned an entry it did not recognise
unchanged, so a header sent as a bare string, or with the value under another
field name, reached the audit row in clear. Every entry that is not the
declared `{ key, value }` shape is now replaced whole.

The secret parameter documentation said the value never appears in clear,
which is wider than what the platform does: the target under test reads the
value while the run executes. The text now states the bounded guarantee, that
the value is encrypted before storage and kept out of the stored run, the
APIs, the exports, the audit log and the interface.

Also from review: the row update callback of the parameters editor takes a
named object, the batch completion scenario asserts the completion flag and
not only the counts, and the batch summary tests are grouped by condition.

* docs(scenarios): the CI poll states how close to its deadline it stops

The loop reads the deadline between requests, so a request that starts just
before it, and the sleep that follows, carry the job past it. The page states
the bound rather than adding remaining-time arithmetic to an example whose
subject is the batch endpoint.

more than eight projects: it opens with a focused search field, filters
by project and team name, and answers the arrow keys and Enter. The list
stays grouped by team with the per-team create entries; eight or fewer

* fix(tests): set the combobox query with one change event

Per-character typing races Ark's machine-controlled input and drops
characters on a slow CI runner, even with a typing delay. One change
event with the whole query removes the race.

* fix(navigation): make the mobile menu a modal and split the project combobox

The mobile menu overlay now carries dialog semantics: it takes focus on
open, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the menu button. Its bar
button prop is named for what it does instead of promising a toggle.

The project combobox moves its item building and its popup into their
own modules, so each file stays inside the size limits, and its search
input carries an accessible name of its own.

Also renames the sidebar fullWidth prop to isFullWidth, and adds
coverage for the single-select scope picker search.

* fix(navigation): keep the keyboard inside the open mobile menu

The overlay declares aria-modal, so the page behind it must not hold a
tab stop. It is marked inert while the menu is open, and Tab wraps from
the last entry of the menu back to the first. A menu that portals its
list outside the overlay keeps its own keyboard handling.

* fix(navigation): let the mobile menu keys reach the layer that owns them

Two faults browser QA found, both invisible to jsdom.

A menu the overlay opens restores focus to its own trigger while it
answers Escape, so by the bubble phase the focus no longer says who
owned the key and the overlay closed with it. The overlay now reads the
key in the capture phase and stands aside while another layer holds the
focus, so Escape closes that menu first and the overlay second.

An inert element takes no focus, so restoring focus to the menu button
in the same step that closed the menu sent it to the body instead. The
button now gets the focus back in the render that lifts the inert.

fix(langy): show what a tool returned, and stop reading a rejected command as an empty result (#7408)

* fix(langy): a rejected CLI command is no longer read as an empty result

The CLI documents its --jq flag with the example .traces[].traceId. The [] in that sentence parses as JSON, so every usage text and every --help was recorded as the document []. langwatch trace search --start now-1d names a flag the command does not have, so the agent read the rejection as no traces in the last day and reported that as a count. A document now has to open its own line.

* fix(langy): show the tool result itself, under the command that produced it

An opened receipt row printed the transport envelope on one line, so the reader saw {"kind":"json","payload":[]} instead of the data. It now shows the payload indented, and names the command above it: a row groups calls by what they did, so two trace searches that differ only in their flags shared one label and neither said which result was whose.

* fix(langy): keep scanning past a log line that opens a bracket, and name the command on the held card

Three review findings.

A log line can open its own line with a bracket and never close it
("[retrying request"). The scan read that as a truncated outer result and
stopped, so a valid JSON document under it was lost. It now reads the first
token after the bracket: a document opens with a key, a value, or its own
close, and anything else is prose the scan walks past. A truncated result
still stops the scan, because its first token is valid.

The card the turn holds open showed each grouped result with no command over
it, so the same question the receipt row answers was unanswerable there. It
now renders through OpenedToolCall, and its truncated command gives way to
the full one while open.

The receipt scenarios named the CLI transport. They now state what the reader
sees.

* fix(langy): read a whole JSON token, not its first letter, before the scan stops

A log line can open a line with a bracket and spell a JSON value right after
it: "[notice] using the cache", "[null pointer while reading", "[2026-08-22
fetching traces". Taking the first character for the value made all of those
read as a truncated result, which stopped the scan and hid the document under
them.

A scalar now counts only when what follows it is what a document puts there, a
comma or the closing bracket. "[true, false" is still a result cut short and
still stops the scan; "[true retrying the request" is a sentence.

The four helpers in the file take named parameters, per the coding standard.

* docs(langy): cite log lines that actually reach the value check

* fix(langy): tie the scalar end anchor to the output, not to a lookahead window

The check read a fixed 40 character window, so `$` matched the end of the
WINDOW rather than the end of stdout. A scalar padded that far from the prose
after it, `[true` and then 36 spaces and then `retrying`, read as a result cut
short. The scan stopped and the document under the log line was lost.

The pattern is sticky now. It reads the token at the position without copying
the rest of stdout to get there, and `$` means the end of the output again.
`^` goes with it, since with `y` it would pin the match to index 0.

The anchor still does its job: a result that ends at its first scalar has
nothing after it, and stops the scan.

* fix(langy): read the scalar with a forward pass instead of a backtracking regex

CodeQL flagged the pattern as a polynomial regular expression on uncontrolled
data, and the data is uncontrolled: this reads whatever a tool wrote to its
stdout. `[1-9]\d*` in front of an optional fraction, an optional exponent and
an optional whitespace run is the construct it names.

The scalar and the separator after it are read by one forward pass now, which
never reconsiders a character. It matches the file, which already walks stdout
by hand in findBalancedEnd, and it holds the same rule: a scalar counts only
when a comma, the closing bracket, or the end of the output follows it.

Measured on the shape the alert names, a line of `1` characters that never
closes its bracket: 100k in 1.0ms, 1.6M in 12.95ms, each doubling costing 1.96
times the last.

* fix(langy): reject a leading zero, so a numbered log line is read as prose

`numberEnd` consumed every digit after the sign, so it read `01` as a number.
JSON does not: a number is `0` on its own, or a non-zero digit and the digits
after it. `[01,` therefore looked like an array cut short, the scan stopped,
and the document printed under the log line was lost.

Calling that conservative was wrong. Stopping the scan costs a document, which
is the failure this whole change exists to remove.

The classifier is now pinned to the authority instead of to a restatement of
the grammar: a test asks JSON.parse whether each of 33 scalars is real, and
requires the scan to agree. It covers 01, -01, 007, 00, 1., .5, 1e, 0x1f,
Infinity, NaN and the truncated spellings of the literals.

feat(cli-auth): langwatch login mints a user-scoped key that inherits the user's permissions (#7410)

* feat(cli-auth): langwatch login mints a user-scoped key that inherits the user's permissions

`langwatch login` now mints a user-owned restricted ApiKey instead of
handing the CLI the personal project's own key. The key carries the
scopes and permissions the user picked on the authorize screen, and every
request re-intersects those bindings with what the owner holds right now,
so a demotion narrows the key without touching it.

What the user sees:
- /cli/auth shows the scopes and permissions the key will carry,
  preselected to the widest access the user holds, and lets them narrow
  both before approving
- `langwatch whoami` states the login key's reach
- `langwatch projects list` lists exactly the projects the key can view
- trace and session commands take --project <id|slug> to run against
  another project the key reaches

Deliberate calls:
- the key is minted at exchange, not at approve, so an approval that is
  never exchanged mints nothing
- the default permission list keeps project:manage, because model
  providers and project settings ride on it
- the default data target stays the personal project, so every command
  that worked before still points where it did
- organization-exclusive permissions are filtered out, not refused, when
  the user holds no ORGANIZATION binding

Specs: specs/ai-governance/cli-onboarding/login-user-scoped-key.feature
and specs/typescript-sdk/cli-cross-project-access.feature.

* fix(cli-auth): keep the biome gate at zero new violations

resolveDefaultSelection splits its team lookup and its cross-team
intersection into named helpers, and the device-flow test helper throws
with the server's answer instead of asserting inside a non-test function.

* fix(cli-auth): close the project-administration gap and the exchange poll loop

The RBAC hierarchy promoted a project:create or project:delete check to
project:manage, so the separate Project administration permission
category withheld nothing: every key holding project:manage could create
and destroy projects, the CLI login key included. project:create and
project:delete are no longer implied by manage. No built-in role loses
anything, since team ADMIN lists both outright and team MEMBER lists
create; only a custom role holding manage alone is narrowed, which is the
separation the category exists for.

A mint refused at exchange left the device code approved for its whole
600-second TTL, and the CLI reads a non-200 as keep polling, so one
permanent refusal became roughly 150 ceiling walks with no terminal error
on screen. A scope refusal now burns the device code and answers
access_denied, which the CLI already treats as fatal.

Also from the review:
- the authorize screen intersects the default permission list with the
  user's ceiling, so a member is never sent a selection the mint refuses,
  and approve stays unavailable while the bindings are loading
- an account with no access in the organization is told so, instead of
  reading a permanently disabled Approve button
- the projects listing reads the typed resolved token rather than casting
  the loose context key, and the binding lookup refuses a falsy key id
- the visibility resolution is bounded, and refuses over the cap rather
  than truncating to a wrong answer
- the edit drawer shows the same ceiling the create drawer does
- the scope summary is resolved before the mint, so a read failure can no
  longer strand a live key
- assertSelectionWithinCeiling takes CUSTOM bindings by type
- booleans carry the required prefixes, and the inline import() type
  annotations are gone

* fix(cli-auth): keep the role model whole, and mint before revoking

The previous commit stopped `project:manage` from implying `project:create`
and `project:delete`, so the separate Project administration category would
withhold something. That change is wrong twice over. It breaks the platform
invariant that a resource's `:manage` reaches every route of that resource
(`api-endpoint-authorization` fails on POST /api/projects, DELETE
/api/projects/:id and DELETE /api/agents/:id), and it silently narrows every
key and custom role already holding `project:manage` in production, with no
migration.

The role model stays as it was, and the category stops describing a
separation the request path does not make: Project settings and Project
administration are one Project category again, the CLI default names
`project:create` and `project:delete` instead of excluding what a manage
grant still answers, and the docs say plainly that a key which configures
model providers can also create and delete projects in its scopes.

Also from the review:
- the login key is minted before the key it replaces is revoked, so a failed
  re-login leaves the key in the user's CLI config working; a failure in the
  revoke step takes the replacement with it
- the API key edit drawer intersects the ceiling across every selected scope,
  through one shared `getUserPermissionsAcrossScopes` the authorize screen
  uses too, so a multi-scope key cannot be offered a permission the save
  would refuse
- the authorize screen reads "there is nothing here for you" from the scopes
  the user can actually bind, not from the teams the organization happens to
  list

* fix(cli-auth): say what the login key can do, not what it cannot

The permission summary on the authorize screen said the key cannot create
projects. It can: the default carries project:manage, and the role model
answers a project:create check with it. The line now names project settings
among what the key gets, and keeps the two exclusions that do hold, members
and roles, and the organization itself.

* fix(cli-auth): keep the permission rows inside the ceiling they are read against

Three findings from the review round on e9e13e9a6e.

The customized permission rows kept the level chosen under the previous
scope selection. Adding a scope that grants less shrank the ceiling, the
rows stayed checked, and the approval was refused with
`api_key_scope_violation` for a level the screen still showed as granted.
`clampSelectionsToAvailability` now re-reads each row against the ceiling
of whatever is selected now: write falls back to read where read survives
and to none where neither does. The API key edit drawer had the same gap
against a key's stored level, so both surfaces call the one helper.

Two logins racing on one device could revoke each other. Each mint
excluded only its own key, so the second exchange handed the CLI a token
the first exchange revoked a moment later. A mint now clears only the
keys created before its own, which both racers agree on without a lock,
and the newest key always survives.

The permission partition test counted with a Set, so a permission owned
by two categories read as healthy. It now tracks which categories claim
each permission and fails on a second owner, on a missing one, and on a
platform-tier permission named by any category.

feat(ai-gateway): catalog model routing and per-instance provider handles (#7396)

* feat(ai-gateway): route a model name by what the bound providers declare

The resolver read every slash in a model name as a provider prefix, so a
custom provider declaring "stealth/ox-alpha" resolved to a provider called
"stealth" that no key can hold. GET /v1/models on the same key listed the
model, so the gateway advertised a name it refused to route.

The first segment is now a prefix only when it names a provider family the
gateway knows (a new closed KnownProviderFamily predicate) or a routing
handle the key carries. Everything else is a whole model id, matched against
the models each provider slot declares, then the model-name guess table, then
the providers that declared nothing, then a lone credential. Past that the
request is refused with the new model_not_recognized code, which names the
prefixes the key can reach.

NormalizeProviderID keeps its passthrough: credential decode, exclusions and
deployment maps rely on it. Only the request-side vocabulary is closed.

* feat(model-providers): a routing handle names one provider instance

Two instances of the same provider type answer to the same family prefix, and
which one serves a request was decided by the key's chain order with nothing
in the product saying so. A routing handle is the missing name: an
organization-unique slug on the ModelProvider row that pins that exact row in
a gateway model string.

The provider slot now also carries the models it declares, so the gateway can
route a bare model name to the provider that owns it: the customer's declared
custom models, plus the shipped catalog for the hosted families.

Reserved names are every provider family spelling the gateway knows, so a
handle can never shadow a family. Uniqueness is a partial unique index, which
is what makes two racing saves safe; the service translates the violation into
the refusal a person reads.

* feat(ai-gateway): surface how a request reaches a provider, and document it

The provider drawer now shows the spellings that reach the provider and takes
its routing handle. The virtual key rows show, per provider, the names that
reach it and which one answers a bare provider type, which is only honest at
key level because the order is the key's.

A declared custom model whose first segment spells a provider type is flagged
in the models editor: the gateway reads that segment as the provider, so the
model is only reachable with a "custom/" prefix.

Both refusals carry the reachable prefixes as data rather than as a finished
sentence, so the words a customer reads stay in the client presentation
registry and no relayed message is rendered back to them.

docs/ai-gateway/model-naming.mdx described a save-time ambiguity refusal that
was never built, an error code that does not exist, and prefixes (grok,
ollama, openrouter) the gateway never accepted. Rewritten to what the gateway
does.

* chore: re-trigger checks with the deployment-impact section in the description

* fix(model-providers): a handle set at create time reaches the gateway, and its spelling stays readable

Dogfooding the routing handles found two problems.

A handle set while CREATING a provider did not work. Only the update path
appended MODEL_PROVIDER_UPDATED, so a running gateway kept serving a bundle
that predates the new row and never learned the handle. The failure was
silent rather than loud: an unknown first segment is read as part of the
model name, so "oxbeta/stealth/ox-alpha" became a model nobody declares and
landed on whichever bound provider declared no catalog. In a live org that
was Bedrock, which answered 200 with null content. Creating a provider now
evicts on the same terms as updating one.

The addressable spellings were unreadable in dark mode. The code chips
hard-coded background gray.100, so the muted helper text sat on a light grey
at about 1.3:1. They now use the bg.muted semantic token, which measures
16.6:1. The same sentence also built its trailing clause as a separate flex
child, so the comma took its own line and read as a dangling fragment; the
sentence is now one inline run.

Verified against a live gateway: a provider created with the handle
"oxgamma" routes "oxgamma/stealth/ox-alpha" to its own upstream on the first
request, with no second edit and no restart.

* fix(ai-gateway): a handle addresses its instance in the listing, and a refusal names what the caller wrote

Review findings from the first round on this branch.

The model listing and the dispatcher have to agree about which name reaches
which provider. Two instances of one family serve the same model ids, and
discovery deduped on the id alone, so the second instance's catalog was
dropped entirely: exactly the instance a routing handle exists to address.
Discovery now dedupes per instance and GET /v1/models lists a handled
instance under the handle-qualified id ("europe/claude-sonnet-5"), which is
the name that reaches it. owned_by goes back to the provider family, because
that is the vendor a model picker groups by; a handle there filed an
Anthropic model under "europe".

A handle whose row the request cannot reach was refused by naming the family.
The family is often still reachable through another row, so the message denied
a prefix it went on to offer in the same sentence. It now names the handle.

SplitModelSpelling passed the raw qualifier to NormalizeProviderID, which
matches its aliases literally, so "OpenAI/gpt-5-mini" became the provider id
"OpenAI" and matched no credential.

The discovery cache key did not cover the routing handle, which rides on every
model the credential contributes, so a rename kept serving the old spelling
for a full TTL.

The unique index over (organizationId, routingHandle) is now declared in
schema.prisma. An index Prisma cannot see is drift to it, and the next
migrate dev writes a DROP INDEX for it. The partial WHERE was unnecessary:
Postgres treats NULLs as distinct in a unique index, so every row without a
handle already fits. The migration carries its rollback block.

Also: the tRPC schema took 64 characters where the store takes 32, both now
read the same constants; the reachable list renders through listLabels like
every other list in the registry; the new helpers take object parameters and
the new boolean reads as one; and the docs state that a handle routes only
for a key that can reach the provider.

Specs: the refusal about one instance does not deny its family, and the
fallback steps after the guess table are written down.

* fix(model-providers): the routing handle field says one thing and accepts only what it stores

Review of the drawer in the browser.

The handle field explained itself in two paragraphs and listed two spellings
at once, before the operator had typed anything. It now shows one line that
updates as they type, so the spelling they are creating is on screen while
they create it, and the provider type is the placeholder because that is what
the field falls back to.

The input sanitizes on the way in rather than flagging afterwards. A handle is
stored lowercased and refuses spaces, so a field that let "OpenRouter EU"
stand showed a spelling that never reaches the gateway.

The reserved-prefix warning under a custom model is gone. It fired on a name
the customer had already chosen, told them about a prefix rule they were not
asking about, and the model still reaches the provider either way.

The virtual key provider rows go back to name, scope and model count. Listing
every spelling that reaches a provider, and badging which one answers a bare
provider type, put routing internals on a screen about access.

* docs(ai-gateway): the one-provider fallback is its own step in the resolution order

It was the last sentence of the step about providers that declared nothing, which reads as though it only applies to those. It applies to any lone provider, whatever it declared, and that is what the resolver does.

* test(model-providers): the handle lifecycle scenarios assert what reaches the gateway

The rename and create scenarios asserted the change event and the audit row.
That proves the cache was told to refresh, not that the refreshed config
carries the new name, so a handle that never reached the wire would have
passed both.

They now materialise the bundle a running gateway fetches and assert the slot
for that provider carries the handle. Keyed by provider id, because a renamed
handle is released and the row that takes it puts the old name back in the
bundle legitimately.

Verified by breaking handle propagation in the materialiser: both assertions
fail, and both pass again with it restored.

* fix(model-providers): the routing handle sits under the connection fields

The handle is a routing detail, not identity, so it does not belong
directly under the name. It now follows the credentials and the extra
headers, next to the custom models it addresses.

* fix(migrations): the routing handle migration sorts after the one on main

The migration was numbered below 20260821180001, which merged first.
Migrations run in name order, so a database that already ran the newer
one skips this one and never adds the column.

* fix(tests): the routing handle test wires the App singleton

The service now authorizes writes through getApp().permissions, which main
introduced with probeProjectPermission. Without a composed App the singleton
is empty and every write dies with "App not initialized".

* fix(aigateway): the model list reads a handled alias the way dispatch does

An alias target keeps its routing handle on the wire, because only the key's
config tells a handle from a model id that contains a slash. The listing
judged the target whole, so models_allowed, the policy rules and reachability
answered for a model no provider serves: the endpoint dropped aliases dispatch
serves and offered ones it refuses. The spelling reader moves to BundleConfig
so both sides read one rule, and an alias pinned to a row the key cannot reach
is left out.

Also from review:
- the refusal cap drops provider families and keeps routing handles, which
  name one instance and cannot be guessed
- buildModelAlias calls domain.SplitModelSpelling instead of repeating it
- drop the unused KnownProviderFamilies
- the routing handle refusal reuses ROUTING_HANDLE_RULE, so the copy cannot
  drift from the limit it states
- the reserved-handle test reads the gateway's own family list, so a family
  added on one side and not the other fails
- correct the unique index and RoutingHandles comments, and the discovery
  routing claim in the model naming docs
- named parameters on the new model provider write helpers

fix(cli): the codex harvest reads the checkout, so a session reports the branch it is on (#7415)

* fix(cli): the codex harvest reads the checkout, so a session reports the branch it is on

A codex session could not attribute to a pull request. The harvest built its
session-context record from the rollout's session_meta alone, and codex writes
git identity there only when the session STARTED inside a repository, then never
revises it.

Both halves of that hurt. Every agent on our box starts codex a directory above
its checkouts, so session_meta carries `git: null` and the session reported no
repository for its whole life, however many pull requests it reviewed. A session
that does start inside a checkout is no better off over time: it reports the
branch it opened with, so a reviewer moving from one pull request to the next
keeps naming the first.

The harvest runs on the machine that ran the turn, moments after it, so it now
reads the working directory itself through the same helper the claude hook uses,
and keeps the transcript's values as the fallback for a rollout harvested away
from its checkout.

Verified on the agents box: a codex turn in a checkout on a pull request's branch
reported github.com/langwatch/langwatch@feat/home-pill-setup-menu, and the
pull-request usage API attributed 38,473 tokens to that pull request. Before this
the same session reported nothing at all.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BUKKUiZbSBHmrLK9JJj4Ba

* test(cli): one contextAttr helper, taking named parameters

The new module-scope helper took positional parameters, against the repo
convention for functions with several arguments, and it collided with a
describe-scoped helper of the same name that already took named ones. The
inner one shadowed it, so the file carried two helpers with one name and
two different signatures.

There is now one helper, at module scope, taking named parameters. It keeps
the inner one's guard on the logs POST being present, which reports a
missing session-context record instead of throwing a TypeError that hides
which expectation failed.

feat(langy): pi harness on by default, and panel-open pre-warm (#7407)

* feat(langy): harness joins the credential signature, and stop reaches the worker

The credential envelope gains a harness field (opencode | pi) that folds
into the worker signature through NormalizeHarness, so a harness change
replaces the worker and a deploy that introduces the field keeps every
running worker (empty normalises with opencode). The probe carries the
same field so a flip is a probe miss.

The manager also gains the token-burn half of Stop (ADR-078): a new
POST /worker/cancel route delegates through App.CancelTurn and
Pool.CancelTurn to Worker.AbortTurn, turnId-guarded, on agents that
implement the TurnAborter capability. Opencode does not, so the route
stays a fail-open no-op there; the pi adapter will implement it.

Specs: new langy-pi-harness.feature (6 bound scenarios) and a bound
stop-abort scenario in langy-stop-and-resume.feature.

* feat(langy): langy-worker, the pi-harness worker process

New workspace package @langwatch/langyworker (services/langyworker): a
thin wrapper that embeds the pi coding-agent SDK and speaks a JSONL
stdio protocol to the langyagent manager (PROTOCOL.md, version 1).

The wrapper owns per-turn system-prompt recomposition (persona +
AGENTS.md + turn system, served through a before_agent_start extension
because a direct state assignment does not survive prompt()), abort and
preemption with a terminal-last guarantee per turn, a shutdown handoff
digest capped at 64KB, 1MB field bounding, and a single ordered stdout
writer that flushes terminals on the write callback so they cannot be
lost on exit.

Tools: todowrite keeps the opencode schema on pi's official extension
pattern so the plan panel and AGENTS.md stay unchanged; a thin skill
tool lists and loads SKILL.md files, which AGENTS.md requires by name.
Model config passes through to a generated pi models.json with the API
key written as an env reference, never the secret.

Builds to a standalone binary with Bun (darwin-arm64, linux-x64,
linux-arm64 verified) with node dist as fallback; --version and a
dead-endpoint smoke script cover the image smoke test. 77 unit tests.

pnpm-workspace.yaml registers the package and pins the pi SDK release
in minimumReleaseAgeExclude.

* feat(langy): panel-open pre-warm and the pi-harness flag on the control plane

Opening the Langy panel now warms the conversation's worker before the
first message. A new langy.warmWorker mutation resolves the same
credential surface a turn would (model allowlist, egress, mirror tier,
GitHub PR-cap parity in check-only mode, harness), probes for a live
worker, and only on a miss mints a conversation id plus session key and
calls the manager's warm endpoint. Warm failures never surface: the
first real message cold-starts and reports errors as before.

The frontend fires the warm once per panel open through a new
useLangyWarmWorker hook after model queries settle; the returned id is
kept as pendingConversationId and adopted by createConversation on the
first message (adoptUnknownId, the REST path's existing mechanism).

New flag release_langy_pi_harness (SYSTEM scope, default off) resolves
per project into LangyCredentials.harness, rides probe, dispatch and
the handoff stash, and stays off the frontend flag surface.

Specs: langy-worker-prewarm.feature (12 bound scenarios) and a warm
exception scenario in langy-session-key-lifecycle.feature.

* feat(langy): the pi adapter drives langy-worker over stdio, selected by harness

New adapters/pi: a stateful per-worker agent implementing the
CodingAgent port plus the TurnAborter capability over the langy-worker
JSONL protocol. One persistent reader goroutine (ReadSlice with
skip-recovery, mailbox routing by turnId, dead channel on EOF),
mailbox-before-write posting under a stdin mutex, 5 second heartbeats,
and the full terminal table: ok and aborted settle clean, handoff
emits the resume seed then the handoff sentinel, an error terminal
maps to agent_error, and process death mid-turn stays a plain error so
it routes to worker_stopped. Spawn wires os.Pipe pairs directly,
closes child ends after start, and never calls Wait; provisioning
mirrors the opencode ordering (permissions before secrets) and writes
the .langy-worker.json contract with per-model lanes: anthropic
models ride the gateway's native messages route, codex pins
supportsStore off, chat-completions pins supportsDeveloperRole off.
Worker env always carries NO_PROXY for the loopback LLM host.

The pool's spawn now switches on the normalized credential harness;
the opencode block is unchanged in the default branch. The turn id
rides app.Turn so an abort names the exact wire turn.

The otel relay learns the worker's harness: pi workers export no OTLP,
so the LLM proxy synthesizes one gen_ai span per mediated call (usage
parsed from all three response dialects, token accumulation skipped so
the gateway span stays the meter) and forwards the anthropic-messages
lane with x-api-key virtual-key injection and /v1 path dedupe.

Shared tool mapping moved to internal/toolmap; both adapters delegate
and opencode behavior is unchanged. Config gains
LANGY_PI_WORKER_BINARY_PATH (default langy-worker).

* fix(langy): agent-driven navigation resolves every resource the platform can

A chained lookup-and-open compound (langwatch prompt list && langwatch
navigate open prompt_x) never seeds the conversation link store (sole
invocation stdout provenance, unchanged), and the fallback resolver
knew only the scenariorun_ prefix, so every other navigate silently
dropped. The customer saw Langy claim it opened the page while the
browser did nothing.

The fallback is now a prefix-keyed resolver table: prompt_, dataset_,
workflow_, experiment_, monitor_, evaluator_, agent_ and scenariorun_.
Every resolver looks the id up with the project's own access and
builds the same address the app's UI or REST API hands out; unknown
prefixes and ids outside the project still resolve to null and drop.

Tests reproduce the reported compound against an empty link store at
the relay level, cover each prefix in and out of project (unit +
integration on real Postgres), and a new dogfood scenario asserts a
navigate href lands on the turn stream. The relay is
harness-independent; pi's bash tool emits name bash with a command
arg, which the CLI envelope already recognizes.

* ci(langy): the langyagent service joins go-ci, and the image ships langy-worker

services/langyagent was never in go-ci's test, vet, or lint runs, nor
in the Makefile lint target. Adding it surfaced 177 findings; the
mechanical and real ones are fixed (misspell, tagalign,
usestdlibvars, errorlint, staticcheck, testifylint, noctx via
net.ListenConfig, exhaustive, nilerr, funlen, predeclared renames),
and the structural rest is scoped in .golangci.yml with justifications
(0700 worker homes, test fixtures, protocol-inherent complexity,
interface-mandated signatures). golangci-lint now exits clean.

Dockerfile.langyagent compiles services/langyworker in the cli-builder
stage (per-arch Bun target, same pattern as the CLI) and ships it as
/usr/local/bin/langy-worker with a --version smoke check. The
langwatch-app-ci unit shard 1 gains typecheck and test steps for
@langwatch/langyworker, and both app-ci and go-services path filters
learn services/langyworker.

Haven's langy image plan referenced the Dockerfile at its pre-move
root path; corrected to infra/docker/Dockerfile.langyagent.

Also hardens the harness pool tests: tolerant temp roots so the
pool's async worker-home teardown cannot race t.TempDir cleanup.

* feat(langy): page destinations for agent-driven navigation

"Take me to my prompts" names a page, not a resource, and the id-only
fallback dropped it: the model then reached for browser-only commands and
reported failure. The fallback now resolves a closed set of page names
(prompts, datasets, evaluations, online-evaluations, evaluators, traces,
simulations, experiments, workflows, agents, analytics, annotations,
automations) to the project's own addresses, AGENTS.md documents the page
form and bans `langwatch open`, and the dogfood suite seeds a prompt so
the navigation scenario always has a resource to surface.

* fix(dev): pin a worktree's Redis DB with LANGWATCH_HAVEN_REDIS_DB

haven's allocator avoids only the databases haven-managed stacks hold; a
plain pnpm-dev process from another worktree sits on its .env database
invisibly and then shares the event-sourcing group queue, which lands
folds in the wrong stack's database. The pin makes the assignment
deterministic for a worktree that must route around such a neighbor.
Also settles the changed-line lint findings go-ci raises on the branch
(test dir permissions, a justified nolint on the tolerant temp dir).

* fix(langy): a gate trip keeps the tool card, and scenario judges see command results

The GitHub gate cancels the stream from inside the sink's observer, and
observing before the push dropped the very command card the gate judged:
the user saw the install prompt with no trace of the command behind it.
The sink now accumulates, pushes, then observes, with a regression test.

The scenario suite had the matching blind spot: the adapter folded tool
frames down to a boolean, so no judge ever saw a command result even
though the rubric names them as the grounding authority. Settled cards
now join the judged reply as langy-tool-card blocks in the panel's
order, the transcript helpers strip exactly those blocks so structural
assertions keep grading only Langy's own prose, and the PR scenario
asserts the tripping gh/git card really reached the stream. Rubric
clarifications ride along: text inside a tool card is the tool talking,
and a run where no create is rejected satisfies the retry criterion.
The navigable-prompt seed retries over the loaded-machine first-fetch
stall.

* fix(langy): recovered tool output and a strict document boundary keep evidence whole

pi's bash tool keeps the tail of an output past 50KB and saves the full
text to a file named in the result's details.fullOutputPath. The wrapper
now reads that file back (capped at 1MB, tail fallback on any read
error) so the reduction pipeline sees the document head again.

parseCliJson only accepts a bracket at column 0 as a document start. A
tail fragment's first balanced nested value ("stacktrace": []) was
promoted to the whole command's result, which rendered an empty-array
card for a trace search that found 44.

* fix(langy): AGENTS.md routes activity questions to traces, not the agent registry

"What has my agent been up to" matched the agent-registry row, so the
model listed configured agents instead of reading trace activity. The
activity row now owns "been up to" and "what failed", the registry row
is scoped to "configured agents", and the observability row notes that
errors live on spans, not text. 16382 of the 16384-byte budget.

* test(langy): judges grade native tool traffic, and criteria scope to Langy's prose

The e2e adapter folded tool frames away, so no judge ever saw a command
result while the rubric named them the grounding authority. The adapter
now returns each turn as ModelMessage[]: an assistant message with the
tool calls, a tool message with each result (bounded at the server's own
8KB reduction size), then the assistant prose. Judges grade real tool
traffic, the user simulator sees the framework's compact summary of it,
and the prose helpers keep structural assertions on Langy's own text.

Criteria follow the same attribution rule: a tool result's text is the
tool talking, a worker-side address in a tool result is correct behavior
on a local stack, and the PR flow reads the platform's install prompt as
retrieved evidence for the blocker claim.

lwGet/lwPost retry timeouts three times, and the createConversation
budget is 180s: the server was measured completing it in 135s under fold
backlog, and a blind retry races the accepted first attempt into
langy_turn_in_progress.

* test(langy): the transient-infrastructure retry reads the flag through the cause chain

The scenario library rethrows adapter errors as new Error(..., { cause }),
so the transientInfrastructure marker arrives one level down and the one
retry in runScenarioAndLog never fired. isTransientInfrastructureError
now walks the cause chain. Seen live: an SSE turn stream closed at ~120s
with no terminal marker while the turn completed server-side 11s later;
the scenario failed instead of retrying.

* fix(langy): delete and admin boundaries route to a decline before any attempt

On the pi harness the model drew toward attempting the action and
relaying the API's refusal; the designed behavior is the decline first.
AGENTS.md now routes delete intent from the skills table (no delete
command; deletion is the user's own action, name the page), names
re-authentication as the workaround it is, and turns the billing decline
into decline-then-offer of the spend analytics. Paid for byte by byte
with meaning-preserving compressions; 16376 of 16384.

The boundary delete scenario seeds the evaluator its premise names
(ensureEvaluator), so it exercises the decline instead of a name miss.
Boundary suite: 4 of 4 pass on pi.

* fix(langy): pre-warm never starves a real turn, and a new chat warms again

Browser QA on a two-slot local pool found the wedge: a panel-open warm
took the last slot, the first message did not adopt the warmed
conversation, and every dispatch then failed max_workers_reached into an
outbox retry loop while warm workers sat idle.

Four fixes, each tested:
- Pool.Acquire (the turn path) evicts the least-recently-active idle
  worker at capacity, in the reaper's own pick order, and only refuses
  when every worker is busy. Warms go through AcquireWarm, which refuses
  at capacity instead of evicting.
- useLangyWarmWorker re-arms the fresh-chat warm once a conversation
  takes the panel over, so the new-chat button warms (and re-mints the
  pending id) instead of cold-starting.
- The transport's create sends only the user's own messages: starting a
  new chat mid-stream left the previous reply in useChat state and
  seeded the new conversation with it.
- The conversation title comes from the first USER message, never
  messages[0] verbatim.

specs/langy/langy-worker-prewarm.feature carries the new rule with four
bound scenarios.

* fix(langy): claude-5 thinking rides pi's own model catalog, and in-band LLM errors are captured

The wrapper generated pi's model registry from the manager's config alone,
which lost what pi's catalog knows about the model. Claude 5 models need the
adaptive thinking request shape, selected by the catalog's
compat.forceAdaptiveThinking flag, so every turn on them failed on the first
call. The registry entry now starts from pi's own catalog entry when the
model is known for the same API dialect; the manager's explicit fields win,
the id keeps its provider prefix for gateway routing, and the catalog's own
endpoint never rides along.

The failure also went uncaptured: the gateway forwarded the upstream 400 as
a 200 whose Content-Type says event-stream but whose body is one bare JSON
error object with no framing. The stream sniffer only read framed data
lines, and the clean-end rule then CLEARED the capture, so the turn failed
with no cause on record. A body that opens with a brace is buffered whole
and inspected at EOF as the same error payload.

* fix(langy): replies end on the answer again, with AGENTS.md last in the pi system prompt

On the pi harness the model closed replies with a next-actions menu
("which would you like next?"), which the reply rubric bans. The rule was
already in AGENTS.md, but the wrapper composed the system prompt as
persona + AGENTS.md + turn system, leaving the Replies rules mid-prompt
where the model's own habit wins. opencode appends instructions AFTER the
per-message system block, so AGENTS.md's ending held the recency position
in every run the rubric was tuned green against. The wrapper now composes
persona + turn system + AGENTS.md last; both blocks stay byte-stable per
conversation, so provider prompt caching is unchanged.

The prompt text also sharpened while diagnosing this, and both edits stand
on their own: AGENTS.md opens its Replies section with the stop rule and
scopes the overview exception ("show me recent traces" names traces, a
list question), and the per-turn override block gains the ending rule as
its last-position pointer beside the grounding rule, pinned by a unit
test.

* fix(langy): the failed-traces route filters to application origin, and judges read elision as elision

Two defects from one scenario draw. The skills-table row for "what
failed" named the search command without --origin application, so the
model's own langy-origin runs poisoned the failure analysis; the row now
carries the filter the origin rule already requires. And the scenario
judge grades from the panel frames, where toolmap reduces oversized tool
outputs structurally: real seeded trace ids cited from the elided array
tail were judged hallucinated. The adapter now appends a display note
when the elision marker is present, so the judge reads items beyond the
shown head as elided evidence, not fabrication.

* fix(langy): monitor creation is operating the project now, and dataset creates declare their columns

Two chunk-C findings. The monitor-boundary scenario expected POST
/api/monitors to refuse Langy's key, but main lowered that route to
evaluations:create (the grain the product's own create button uses) one
day after the scenario was written, and this suite only runs against a
live stack, so nobody saw it go stale. The scenario is now a positive
create with a Layer 2 presence check; deletion keeps evaluations:manage
and the boundary suite still covers that decline.

The dataset flow hit a dead end instead: a bare create makes a
zero-column dataset, records add validates rows against the schema, and
schema update needs datasets:manage, which Langy never holds. The skills
table's exemplar now creates with --columns so the rows have a schema to
land in.

* fix(langy): creative writing is named out of scope, and judge criteria match the tool traffic they now see

The out-of-scope reply bullet now states the class (whatever neither
operates this project nor reads for it), which is what stops a haiku
request from being answered as a favor; the scope example list alone
never classified it. Paid for inside the byte budget by compressing
four sentences that taught nothing extra.

Two main-46 criteria are rescoped to the designed behavior. The
evaluations scenario banned every clarifying question, but the skills
table itself says a bare "set up evaluations" asks batch versus live
first, the one decision the design leaves with the user; the criterion
now accepts that single choices card. The GitHub connect scenario
failed on error text that lives in a tool-result card: judges now see
native tool traffic (this branch made that true), and a failed clone's
stderr on a command card is product surface, not Langy relaying an
error, so the criterion is scoped to the reply prose.

The scenario runner also rides out the auth limiter now: every vitest
run signs in once, chunked suite runs burst past the sign-in window,
and a 429 there is the runner being throttled, not a scenario failing.

* test(langy): scenario runs survive slow turns, reduced outputs and shared-project leftovers

Three measurement defects the final ladder runs exposed, all in the
validation harness, none in the product:

- The e2e turn request aborted at 180s while an opencode failure-analysis
  turn was still working, so the judge graded a one-token reply. The turn
  budget is now 300s and the vitest testTimeout 600s so a two-turn
  scenario has headroom past two turn budgets.
- A tool result cut between the agent and the judge (the manager's
  structural array-tail elision, or this adapter's own 8KB byte cap) made
  grounded claims look fabricated: a result count past the byte cap, ids
  and evaluation errors from the elided tail. The adapter now states
  every cut it makes, and the shared grounding criterion tells the judge

  item or a stated total fails.
- Monitors and evaluators leaked by earlier runs changed model behavior
  in the shared project: finding a monitor matching the request, it
  correctly asked reuse-versus-create, a branch the criteria do not
  describe (and a leaked live monitor evaluates every ingested trace).
  langwatch-api gains deleteEvaluator and resetEvaluationResources; the
  two clarifying scenarios restore the designed empty state on both
  edges, and the monitor-create scenario sweeps what it created by
  before-diff, evaluator included.

* chore: regenerate the lockfile after rebasing onto main

The rebase carried main's lockfile through the conflicted commits; one
root install re-adds the langyworker workspace and its pi dependency on
top of main's entries.

* fix(langy): AGENTS.md absorbs main's workdir rule inside the byte budget

The rebase brought main's session-path rule (never pass a workdir, never
retype a /workspace/sessions/... path) into a file already at its 16384
byte ceiling. The rule stays, restated tighter, and the difference is
funded by compressing existing sentences; the ceiling is not raised.

* feat(langy): a respawned pi worker resumes the session its home still holds

Mirrors the opencode session-resume fix from main: the worker home
outlives the process on an idle reap or a crash, and a respawn that
started a fresh session was re-seeded the whole transcript, which
changed every turn, broke the provider prompt cache, and taught the
model to retype paths from memory. The wrapper now continues the newest
persisted pi session (SessionManager.continueRecent), announces the
resume on its ready handshake, and skips a turn's handoff digest when
the session already carries the history. The Go adapter relays the
announcement through OpenSession, so the pool skips the transcript seed
exactly as it does for a resumed opencode session. A corrupt or missing
session file degrades to a fresh session and the seed path, never a
failed spawn.

haven: an explicit LANGWATCH_HAVEN_REDIS_DB is refused when another managed

Config never pins database 0, and the host tier warns when the pi worker

budget, but each call can mint a conversation, mint a session key and ask for a
worker. It now takes its own looser per-minute budget on its own Redis key
namespace; over it the answer is the same silent one every other warm failure
gives, no error to the panel and a cold first message.

reads that id whenever no conversation is active, so an id left behind sent the

adoptConversation cleared it, and the panel never calls it.

promise, so the outer try cannot see a rejection and Node's default would end

start. resolveAndWarm takes one named-parameter object. The monitor_ resolver
goes through MonitorService, and the resolver lookup is a named function rather
than an await-ed IIFE inside a ternary.

prompt seeder throws an HTTP error status instead of retrying it; the langy-card

* fix(langy): the review round lands across the worker, the agent and CI

The turn handoff inside the pi agent could cross turns. app.go starts the
Stream goroutine BEFORE PostMessage, so a turn abandoned between the two
left its handle in the channel and the NEXT turn's Stream could take it:
that Stream attached to a dead mailbox while the live turn's mailbox
filled its 256-event buffer and blocked the reader. Draining in Post
raced the very Stream it had to beat. The drain moves to a turn
boundary instead, a new optional app.TurnBoundary the worker calls from
Release, which is the one point where both Post and Stream have
returned.

A command write held the stdin mutex for as long as the write took. A
worker that stops reading fills the pipe, and every path that needs that
lock (Post, AbortTurn, the shutdown notice, the reader lookup) waited
behind it forever, so a wedged worker wedged its own cancel. Writes are
deadline-bounded now, and a write that fails part-way latches the pipe
broken rather than letting the next command concatenate onto a partial
line.

Also in the manager: a wide flat object could not be reduced under the
tool-output cap, because only arrays and strings were capped, so the
byte cut severed the document the reducer exists to keep parseable; map
width is capped too, on sorted keys so the same document always reduces
the same way. The SSE error prefilter matched the byte-exact
`"type":"error"` and would have dropped a provider that writes a space
after the colon. The prompt taught a progress example with a colon that
the parser does not accept, so measured progress was never drawn from
it; a test now binds every documented example to the pattern.

In the worker: a content block that is null threw and the resumed
session was seeded with an empty digest, losing the conversation. A
digest budget under the truncation header returned more bytes than
asked. The unserializable-value fallback ignored the cap. A model config
could carry baseUrl, provider or apiKey through the passthrough and
point pi past the mediated gateway. A skill with an empty frontmatter

fix(authz): a pass states only the facts the heads do not carry (#7429)

A held organization restaged its whole fact set on every pass, and a pass
runs on every worker boot. The restated facts dedupe — command ids are
content-derived, so the event store swallows them — but that happens
downstream of the queue, which has already paid to enqueue, dispatch and
fold-check every duplicate. Since ADR-101 a grant is its own aggregate, so
the cost is one group per grant, per pass.

Measured on the organization it was found on: 428,720 share links, one fact
each, of which 4,254 had ever folded. Every pass restaged all 428,720 and
the queue carried ~1M pending and ~800k parked groups while real progress
was starved by duplicates of itself.

`state()` already had what it needed. The pass reads the heads once at the
top, before it states anything, and now filters the staged set against that
read using the check's own predicates. "Safe to skip" and "neither
outstanding nor a diff" are therefore the same condition, so the report a
pass produces is unchanged by what it skipped. Anything the heads lack, hold
revoked, or disagree with is still stated; a first pass over an organization
still stages everything; and a projection that is behind under-reports the
heads, which restates a fact needlessly — the pre-existing cost, still
idempotent. Convergence now shrinks each pass instead of repeating.

Also fixes the ops dashboard number that hid it. `Staged/s` is derived, not
counted: the change in in-flight work plus completions. Parked groups were
missing from that sum, so every group that parked read as work LEAVING the
system and the rate under-reported real staging by exactly the parking rate
— the books balanced only while nothing was parking. The in-flight total
moves to its own module with the reasoning and a test that pins it.

perf(authz): grant commands share a sharded organization lane (ADR-114) (#7435)

* perf(authz): grant commands share a sharded organization lane (ADR-114)

ADR-110 made a grant its own aggregate, which fixed the whole-organization
fold and stands. Because a command's group key defaults to the aggregate id,
it also gave every grant its own QUEUE LANE — a lane of one, which nothing
else can join and so nothing can batch with.

That is the right shape for interactive access changes and the wrong one for
a bulk producer. On 2026-08-23 a migration restated 428,720 share-link facts
for one organization and each fact appended its own single-row insert into
event_log. Measured in production:

  ClickHouse statements in flight   200  <- the limiter's entire budget
  ClickHouse statements queued    ~1,090
  mean wait for a slot              5.7 s
  mean job duration               6,300 ms  (5.7 s of it waiting)
  jobs completed                    200/s
  worker CPU                    0.2 cores/pod, flat
  active groups                   ~1,270, flat

Concurrency was never the constraint — the fleet was full of jobs all asleep
on the same semaphore. Nor was the blast radius the migration: recordSpan,
the customer trace ingestion path, averaged 13.5 s a job for ninety minutes
because a background import held every statement slot.

So the lane becomes the organization, sharded 32 ways, and the three grant
commands a bulk producer emits in volume coalesce their appends. The fold is
untouched: state is still one grant keyed by its own id. Aggregate identity
and lane identity were the same string only by default, and `getGroupKey` on
CommandHandlerOptions exists precisely to separate them.

Sharding is safe here in a way it is not everywhere — coding-agent coalesces
WITHOUT sharding because its derivation depends on per-session order. Two
commands about the same grant share an aggregate id, hash to the same shard
and stay ordered; two commands about different grants are different
aggregates whose order was never meaningful; and different command types
already sat in different lanes, since the job path carries the command name.

The role commands keep the default per-aggregate lane. A role is a rare,
human-sized entity and an organization has a handful, so there is nothing to
batch.

`commandShardKey` moves from trace-processing into pipeline/, since two
pipelines now share it, rather than being copied.

Tests assert the REGISTRATION, not just the helper: an option that never
reaches the registry looks identical to one that does and would leave the
queue silently in its old shape.

fix(authz): every command about one grant rides one ordered lane (#7440)

#7435 sharded an organization's grant commands across 32 lanes so their
appends would coalesce. It justified itself with this claim:

  "Different command TYPES already sat in different lanes (the job path
   carries the command name), so nothing that was ordered stops being
   ordered."

The first half is true. The second half does not follow, and this reverts
the mechanism because of it.

`buildGroupKey` composes `${tenantId}/${jobPath}/${aggregateType}:${key}`,
and for a command `jobPath` is `command/${commandName}`. So one grant's
attach and its revoke have ALWAYS lived in two lanes. Before sharding both
held ~one command and drained immediately, so the skew was microseconds and
the reordering theoretical. Sharding exists to make lanes DEEP — that is the
whole point — so it makes the skew proportional to the backlog, next to a
revoke lane holding almost none.

The projection cannot recover that order. `revoked` is a conditional UPDATE:

  revoke first  -> UPDATE ... WHERE id = g -> matches 0 rows, writes NOTHING
  attach second -> INSERT ... ON CONFLICT  -> inserts a LIVE row

The `occurredAt` guard adjudicates two writes to a row that exists; it cannot
defend one that does not. authz-grants-write.prisma.repository.ts says so and
assigns the fix to the migration — sound only while ordinary traffic does not
reorder, which is the premise deep lanes break.

Exposure was bounded: enforceGrantRevocation writes revokedAt synchronously
before queueing, so the enforcing path never waited on the queue, and the
migration's check reports a grant_revoked diff and holds the organization. A
detectable divergence, not silent access. Still a hazard #7435 claimed not to
introduce.

`serializeByAggregate: true` is strictly stronger than either shape: it keys
the lane on the grant id AND drops the command name from jobPath, so all
three commands about one grant share one FIFO lane — closing a gap that
predates ADR-114 entirely. It also scores by arrival rather than business
time, so a retry cannot sort ahead of a newer command.

  BEFORE   attach -> <org>/command/attachGrant/authz_grant:g
           revoke -> <org>/command/revokeGrant/authz_grant:g    two lanes
  #7435    attach -> <org>/command/attachGrant/authz_grant:14
           revoke -> <org>/command/revokeGrant/authz_grant:14   two DEEP lanes
  NOW      attach -> <org>/command/authz_grant:g
           revoke -> <org>/command/authz_grant:g                ONE lane, FIFO

What this gives up is the 428,720 -> ~8,500 statement reduction, and it is
affordable for one reason: #7429 removed the volume at source. A pass now
states only facts the heads do not already carry, and the migration has since
finished. Buying throughput we no longer need with an ordering guarantee we
do need is the wrong trade. If another bulk grant producer appears, the answer
is ADR-114 decision 2 (a per-producer share of the statement budget), not a
wider lane that reorders a grant's own history.

coalesceMaxBatch stays and now means something narrower: it folds ONE grant's
queued same-command jobs into a single insert — the shape queueManager names
("many commands, one aggregate"), safe because they share an aggregate and
drain in order. It also keeps the registration out of the "grouped producer
without append coalescing" gap the queue manager logs.

commandShardKey.ts moves back to pipelines/trace-processing/commands/, its
only home again. Trace-processing's own sharding is untouched throughout:
spans are ReplacingMergeTree-deduplicated by business timestamp and carry no
cross-command ordering requirement, which is why sharding is right there and
wrong here.

ADR-114 is amended in place rather than superseded — its measurement of the
incident and its deferred decision 2 both stand.

  5/5 scenarios bound, scoped typecheck and biome clean.

Cohort enrollment leaves out two classes by data rather than by a list in
code: an active or pending ENTERPRISE subscription, and any organization in
the environment's private ClickHouse routing table. That is the right default
for an experimental cohort and the wrong one for finishing a proven rollout.

The authz-engine migration is now finalized for 7,193 organizations, and the
ones still not enrolled are exactly the two held-back classes. The only way
to take them over was the single-organization enroll — which never applied
either exclusion — one id at a time.

So each exclusion can now be lifted for one draw:

  enrollCohort({ ..., includeEnterprise?, includePrivateDataplane? })

Both default to false in the service, in the repository and in the tRPC
input, so a caller that names neither gets the pool it always got.

SEPARATELY, not one switch. The risks differ in kind — an enterprise
organization is a commercial relationship, a private-dataplane organization
keeps its events in a ClickHouse instance of its own — and a single "include
everything" control would hide that from whoever ticks it. The dialog is two
checkboxes, and its description names which classes the draw will include
rather than always claiming both are left out.

Lifting the private-dataplane exclusion is implemented as NOT naming the ids,
so the environment's routing table stays the only place those organizations
are listed — the same reason the exclusion reads them from the environment
instead of a constant. Lifting the enterprise one omits the `subscriptions`
key entirely rather than setting it to undefined: identical to Prisma, and to
a reader "this filter does not apply" is what lifting an exclusion means.

Both flags are recorded in the log line AND on each per-organization audit
row. "Was this organization drawn because someone lifted an exclusion?" is a
question asked of one organization, and the trail is where it is answered.

makes the draft state starting fresh on every open structural rather than a

feat(authz): release the migration for self-hosted installations (#7442)

* feat(authz): every organization ends up on the engine

Two halves of finishing the ADR-110 rollout, neither of which changes an
organization that has already migrated.

NEW ORGANIZATIONS ARE CREATED ON THE ENGINE.

The migration exists to carry an organization's EXISTING access across: it
states the legacy rows as events and proves the projection agrees. An
organization created after the migration has none to carry, so there is no
proof to run and a pass over it would be empty work whose only product is the
status row.

Nothing wrote that row for a new organization, so every organization created
after the rollout was born on the LEGACY path and stayed there: never
enrolled, never processed, permanently behind. `createAndAssign` and
`createForProvisioning` now write the finalized authz-engine status row inside
the same transaction that creates the organization.

Order is the point. The gate is what every authorization write forks on, and
the founder's two ADMIN grants are attached moments after the transaction
through `attachBindings`. The row is written before the membership row and
before those grants, so they take the engine path. An organization whose first
grants went down the legacy path would be a legacy organization that merely
claims to be on the engine. A unit test asserts the ORDER of the recorded
writes, not just that they happened.

There is no window where the founder lacks access: on the engine path
`attachBindings` appends the events and then AWAITS the projection before
returning, so the bindings are readable by the time creation completes.

The status string comes from `ON_ENGINE_STATUS`, newly exported from
engine-gate.ts and used to build its own `ON_ENGINE_STATUSES`, so the write
and the read are one decision.

No enrollment row accompanies it: enrollment means an operator paced an
organization into a rollout, nobody paced this one, and naming its founder as
the enroller would put a fiction in a table the ops page attributes by name.
The report carries its own kind rather than the migration's, because an
operator reading it must not be told a parity proof ran over facts that never
existed.

THE MIGRATION IS RELEASED FOR SELF-HOSTED.

`runsAutomaticallyOnSelfHosted` flips to true. There is no enrollment off
cloud, so from this release every self-hosted installation migrates every
organization it has, automatically, at worker boot.

This is the prerequisite for removing the legacy authorization path
altogether. That removal cannot be safe until every installation that might
upgrade into it has already had a release that runs this migration, and this
is that release. The declaration is pinned by a test rather than left to a
comment, because reverting it would silently reopen the hole.

The first pass after an upgrade states an organization's whole fact set, since
its projection heads start empty. That is unavoidable and happens once; every
later pass states only what the heads do not already carry (#7429).

This repository is public. ADR-110 and ADR-114 carried a production

None of it is needed for the reasoning. An incident is explained by its shape:

`putNewOrganizationOnAuthzEngine` takes a named parameter object. CLAUDE.md
requires it for two or more arguments and I wrote it positionally.

The ordering test now records `attachBindings` in the SAME sequence as the
transaction's writes, so it checks the half of the contract that actually
matters: the status row must precede the founder's grants, not merely the
membership row. Provisioning gets its own ordering case too — it attaches no
grants of its own, so there the row only has to precede the rest of the

Declined in part: the suggestion to add an amendment mapping the removed

* fix(authz): drop born-on-engine — it makes creating an organization need the queue

CI caught what no unit test could. `organizations-provisioning-rest-api`
returned 503 instead of 201, and the code in the log is
`authz_ledger_unavailable`, 30 times over.

The chain: writing the finalized status row at creation put the organization
on the engine immediately, so `attachBindings` — the founder's ADMIN grants,
and the admin key `legacy-grant-mint` hands back — took the LEDGER branch
instead of the legacy one. The ledger branch needs the event-sourcing stack.
When that stack is not up, the send refuses with AuthzLedgerUnavailableError,
whose httpStatus is 503, and organization creation fails.

That is not a test artifact. It means creating an organization would have
gained a hard dependency on the grants queue: signup and provisioning break
whenever the pipeline is down, still coming up, or backed up. Self-hosted
first-run provisioning — the failing test — is precisely when the stack is
least likely to be there, and a queue incident would have taken signup with
it. Before this change a new organization was on the legacy path, so its
first grants were written synchronously and creation worked regardless.

So the born-on-engine half is removed: the repository, the exported
ON_ENGINE_STATUS, its unit test and its scenarios. What made it attractive
was avoiding an empty migration pass; what it cost is worse than the pass.

What stays is the prerequisite we actually wanted, and it is unaffected by
