fix(authz): a pass finishes, and stops holding organizations it cannot clear (#7460)

* fix(authz): a buried role head is a deletion applied, not work outstanding

The migration's role head read took every `Role` row for the organization,
tombstones included, without the `deletedAt IS NULL` fence that `liveRoles`
exists to make unforgettable. A head the fold had already buried therefore
read back as a live head with no legacy row behind it, which the check counted
`outstanding` and the sweep answered with another `deleteRole` - every pass,
for as long as the migration ran.

Neither ever converged, because a role's name stays taken after a delete: the
row never leaves that read. One organization sat held on a single API key
someone had deleted between two passes, and its report named the tombstone
each time.

The read now says whether a head is buried rather than hiding it, so the proof
can tell a role the fold has never seen from one it has already deleted:

- an extra head already deleted is that deletion applied - neither
  outstanding nor a diff, and never swept again;
- an expected head that is buried is a named `role_deleted` diff, the
  `grant_revoked` treatment one tier over. It is not restated, because
  `role.upsert` leaves `deletedAt` alone and the delete moved the row's
  business time past anything a restatement could carry.

Refs ADR-110.

* fix(authz): the view budget handover costs statements, not round trips

The budget seed is the one step of a pass no head filter covers, and it is
right that it rides every pass: while an organization is held, views keep
landing on `ShareLink.viewCount`, and the proof compares the two counts
exactly, so re-seeding is what lets the count heal.

Its shape was the problem. A `createMany` landed the missing rows, and then a
guarded `update` per seed raised the ones legacy had outgrown - 25 at a time,
awaited in sequence. On a converged organization every one of those updates
matches nothing, raises P2025, and is swallowed as the no-op it means. An
organization with 428,720 share links therefore spent 17,149 sequential round
trips per pass, and the exceptions they raised, to change nothing at all.

It never finished a pass. The state row is only written when `migrateTenant`
returns, so that organization recorded no status of any kind - not finalized,
not held, not parked - and was invisible in every counter while its 429,187
heads sat complete in the projection, waiting for a check that never ran.

Create-or-raise is now stated once per chunk: an insert whose conflict clause
updates only where the seeded count is strictly higher. Every property the two
writes had is kept, and kept in the statement rather than around it - the
refund guard, and the organization and project match the per-row WHERE carried
- so a consume landing mid-flight still cannot be walked back by a filter
resolved in an earlier SELECT.

Refs ADR-110.

* fix(authz): a pass converges however large the organization, and however busy

The budget handover now runs BEFORE the pass takes its projection read rather
than after it. Seeding afterwards meant the check compared a count the seed
had already superseded, so a share link viewed at any point between one pass's
seed and the next pass's read counted outstanding all over again — and an
organization whose links are viewed at all could never finalize, however many
passes it was given. The budget is a direct write, not a fact the pass states
and waits on, so the read that follows it simply sees it.

The budgets are now read FOR THE ORGANIZATION rather than by naming every
grant. Postgres binds at most 65535 parameters in a statement, so the named
spelling failed outright at exactly the size where this migration is hardest —
and only once an organization had heads to compare, never on the empty first
pass that would have shown it. GrantUsage is organization-indexed, so both
spellings select the same budgets.

Also from review: the buried-role scenario is split into the two cases it
described at once (Gherkin reads `But` as `And`, so one scenario could not
hold both states), stated without internal vocabulary; and the chunking test
asserts both chunk sizes rather than only the second, which a statement that
dropped rows would otherwise have passed.

Refs ADR-110.

* test(authz): the budget read is pinned to one call, and its limit is stated

The organization-scoped budget read asserted its shape but not its count, so
an implementation that kept a second per-link read beside it would still have
passed.

The comparison's doc overstated what the project-mismatch case covers. A usage
row on the wrong project is only visible to the proof while its COUNT also
disagrees; one already at the right count reads as agreement and the
organization finalizes over it. That is deliberate — the row is not the seed's
to move, the mismatch fails toward fewer views because the consume fences on
the same three columns and simply misses, and holding on it would be a hold no
later pass could clear. Say so where the claim is made rather than implying a
coverage the code does not have.

Refs ADR-110.

* docs(authz): name which project the proof checks, and which it does not

Two `projectId` columns are in play around the resource comparison and only
one of them is checked. Review read the doc as describing the checked one and
concluded the code and its documentation disagreed; they do not, but the
wording did not make the distinction findable.

`head.projectId` is the GRANT row's and the comparison table covers it, so a
share whose grant sits on the wrong project is a `resource_changed` diff
whatever its view count says. `GrantUsage.projectId` is the BUDGET row's, and
`findResourceGrantRows` selects only `grantId` and `viewCount` from that
table, so it never reaches the comparison at all. Only the second can finalize
unnoticed, and only when the counts agree.

Comment only — no behaviour, comparison or assertion changed. The test the
review pointed at puts its grant on the RIGHT project and differs by count
alone, which is why it is lag and why asserting `resource_changed` there would
have made a green test red.

Refs ADR-110.

refactor(authz): the migration's proof says less and proves the same (#7466)

* refactor(authz): the migration's proof says less and proves the same

Follow-up to #7460, which fixed four faults and then explained them at
length. The behaviour is unchanged; this is what the explaining cost.

Two scenarios described internals rather than behaviour, against the repo's
own rule that feature files are written from the user's side. "The view budget
handover costs statements, not round trips" asserted the shape of a SQL
statement, and "A pass is not limited by how many share links an organization
has" asserted that a query does not name every row. Both are real properties
and both keep their unit tests; neither is a requirement, so neither belongs
in a .feature file. A third leaked the same way in one step, naming the order
two internal calls run in - removed, leaving the behaviour it existed to
state.

The migration harness had grown an `unseededGrantIds` escape hatch so a test
could model the seed guard refusing a row. A fake that reimplements production
semantics can go green while production is wrong, and that branch is already
covered where it belongs - the repository test asserts the guard as SQL. Gone,
along with the white-box test that asserted the seed and the read happen in
that order: the behavioural test one line below proves the same thing by
observing the outcome instead of the call sequence.

The rest is prose. The comments retold what the tests already demonstrate;
they now keep the why and drop the retelling.

278 tests pass, 20/20 scenarios bound.

* test(authz): the budget harness only shows its raise to a pass that awaits

The stub pushed the seeds synchronously, so the raise was visible the instant
the migration CALLED it. In a test whose whole subject is that the handover
lands before the read, that meant a pass which dropped the await - leaving the
write in flight while it read a stale count - would still have gone green.

Landing the push on a later microtask closes it. Verified by removing the
await in `migrateTenant`: the behavioural test fails, and passes again once it
is back.

Raised in review on #7466.

fix(haven): make PORTLESS=0 actually bypass the proxy (#7182)

* fix(haven): make PORTLESS=0 actually bypass the proxy (#7117)

haven help env documented PORTLESS=0 as bypassing portless entirely, but
nothing in the code ever read a bare PORTLESS var — `up` always installed,
trusted, and routed through the proxy regardless. On a machine where the
proxy's TLS handshake won't complete (curl/Chrome see ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED /
SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL), there was no way to reach the app short of hand-patching
.env.portless and killing the API process.

Config.ShouldUsePortless (resolved from PORTLESS=0, same precedence as the
other LANGWATCH_HAVEN_* knobs) now actually gates the proxy: `up` skips
install/trust/start, `provision`/`ensureClickHouse` skip proxy registration
and serve each service plain HTTP on its own loopback port instead of the
shared proxy port, and `down`/cleanup skip proxy teardown too — so bypass mode
never has to touch the (possibly broken) portless binary at all. Hostnames are
unchanged (app.<slug>.langwatch.localhost still resolves to loopback with no
proxy needed); only the scheme and port differ.

* fix(haven): detect a flipped PORTLESS setting on an already-running stack

An upfront self-review of the PORTLESS=0 change (#7182) surfaced two real
gaps before any external comment did:

- reconcileRunningStack compared Selection/LangyTier/image but not the
  portless mode. The primary journey for this whole fix is "stack already up
  under the broken proxy → set PORTLESS=0 → `haven up`" — and that reported
  "nothing to do", silently leaving the stack on its old proxy URLs. Add
  Stack.PortlessDisabled (zero value false, matching every stack persisted
  before this field existed) and compare it explicitly in reconcile, same
  treatment as LangyTier's isolation-posture check.
- ensureClickHouse's new scheme/port branch had zero test coverage (ch is nil
  in the existing provision fixtures, so it never ran). Added direct tests for
  both modes.

Also folds the scheme/port decision (duplicated between provision's loop and
ensureClickHouse, each written slightly differently) into one
Orchestrator.serviceEndpoint method both call. proxy.Endpoint() only reads
portless's own local state files, never invokes the binary, so it's safe to
call unconditionally now instead of gating it — one less thing for the two
call sites to agree on.

Config.ShouldUsePortless is renamed to PortlessDisabled (inverted) so its Go
zero value matches every existing test fixture and the historical default,
instead of silently reading as "bypassed" wherever a Config literal omits it.

* fix(haven): address CodeRabbit review comments on #7182

- Down used this run's PORTLESS setting to decide whether to remove proxy
  aliases, not the mode the stack actually registered them under. A stack
  that came up with portless enabled and is torn down with PORTLESS=0 was
  leaving its aliases dangling — routes that can later point at a reused
  loopback port. Use the stack record's own PortlessDisabled when one exists.
- Fixed the now-stale Up doc comment ("runs in portless mode" — it runs in
  either mode since this PR).
- Removed the @scenario annotations from portless_bypass_test.go: they don't
  bind to any .feature file (none exists for this knob, matching the existing
  precedent for LANGWATCH_HAVEN_CH etc.), so per the repo's own binding rule
  they were vacuous.

* refactor(haven): split Up's prep and langy lanes into named helpers

The PORTLESS=0 work touched Up, which put the whole function under the
delta gocognit gate at complexity 26. The pre-boot lanes (deps, codegen,
migrations, seed) move to prepareWorktree/runSeed and the colima prep to
langyContainerHost; Up keeps the guard-and-registration choreography.

fix(docs): keep internal notes out of the published site, and gate what Mintlify cannot (#6824)

* fix(docs): keep internal notes out of the published site, and gate what Mintlify cannot

The docs site publishes every page file it finds, whether or not the navigation
references one. Twenty-six pages had fallen out of the navigation and were still
being served, four of them engineering notes that belong in the repository rather
than on the site. Internal notes now live under dev/docs/, which is not
published, and a check keeps them there.

Nothing in CI could have caught this. `mint validate` builds the site and
`mint broken-links` follows links, but an unreferenced page builds and serves
fine, so no upstream tool reports one. The link step also swallowed the CLI's
exit code and decided pass/fail by grepping console prose for "no broken links
found" — any new failure mode, or a change to that wording, read as green.

Structure
  - move four internal engineering notes to dev/docs/{research,adr}/
  - delete twelve dead pages: eight api-reference leftovers shadowed by
    redirects or naming operations the API does not have, and four pages of

  - give the nine remaining orphans a home in the navigation; two sit in the

  - collapse three two-hop redirect chains and repoint one that dead-ended

Content

    Mintlify has no opinion on: orphaned pages, redirect chains, and a release

Also adopts the docs.json keys we were leaving on the table — description, seo
with JSON-LD organization, metadata.timestamp, search.prompt, a real 404 instead

note reaches every page served as markdown, and the contextual options for

--check-anchors stays off: it reports 47 pre-existing broken heading anchors, and

Specs: specs/ci/docs-structure-check.feature, 10/10 scenarios bound.

* fix(docs): repair the two largest broken-anchor clusters

Sixteen of 67 broken heading anchors came from two causes, neither of
them a typo:

- concepts.mdx headings were retitled at some point ("Traces" became
  "Traces: One Task, End-to-End"), which moved their slugs. Eleven links
  already used the new slugs and ten still used the old ones.
- Six links pointed at /ai-governance/overview#open-core-licensing, a
  heading that page does not have. Open-core licensing has had its own
  page for a while, so they now point at it.

Mintlify's [#custom-id] heading syntax does not work on this version —
it is taken as heading text, so it moves the auto-slug instead of
pinning it, and the count went from 67 to 73. Fixing the links is the
change that actually holds.

51 broken anchors remain (42 unique), untouched here: they need each
target page's real headings checked one at a time. `mint broken-links
--check-anchors` lists them, which is why that flag stays off the gate.

* fix(docscheck): refuse an unreadable navigation instead of blaming every page

A docs.json with no `navigation` key made collectNavPages return no
pages, and the orphan rule then reported every page on the site: 639
findings whose real cause was one absent key. It now exits 2 with that
sentence, because a gate that buries its own diagnosis is worse than no
gate.

Adds the loader's first tests. collectNavPages, the servable-page walk
and the appVersion match are pure enough to test directly, and they are
where the subtle cases live — a group nested inside another group's
pages, an anchor name that must not be mistaken for a page, an external
href, and `version` vs `appVersion`. Sibling order is compared as a
multiset on purpose: Go randomizes map iteration, so the collected order
genuinely varies between runs. Verified the reported findings do not:
eight runs over a fixture that trips all seven rules produce
byte-identical output, because Check sorts them.

* fix(docs): address review — temperature on gpt-5, and two holes in the new gate

Review found a regression this PR introduced and two gaps in the checker
it added.

The regression: the model sweep moved examples to `gpt-5-mini` and
`claude-sonnet-5` but left `temperature` set alongside them. Neither
model accepts it — `supportedParameters` in llmModels.json omits
temperature for both, `defaultParameters.temperature` is null, and the
repo's own generated skills docs say "the gpt-5 family rejects a custom
`temperature` — do not add". Two examples would have failed on the first
call. Dropped from the ci-cd experiment target and the langgraph
`init_chat_model`, and the CSV column example now illustrates `seed`,
which those models do accept.

Two holes in docscheck, both of which it was reporting "sound" over:

- The version rules only recognised an image tag, a `tag:` line and
  `VERSION=`, so `--version 3.0.0` in the two upgrade guides and
  `targetRevision: 3.5.0` in the ArgoCD manifests were invisible. The
  ArgoCD one matters most: readers copy those manifests verbatim, so the
  docs were deploying a release seven minors old. Both forms are now
  matched and all four references corrected. The image pattern also names
  the three release-tracking images explicitly instead of using a
  character class, so `clickhouse-serverless:0.2.0` — versioned
  independently — stays excluded on purpose rather than by accident.
- A wildcard redirect that carries `:path*` through to its destination is
  Mintlify's documented way to move a section, and the checker called it
  a dead end. The first person to move a section would have hit a red
  gate whose suggested remedy did not apply. External destinations are
  now classified by URL scheme too, so a protocol-relative `//host/path`
  is not treated as internal and an internal slug beginning with "http"
  is not skipped.

Also from review, on the workflow:

- pin Node 24 for the CLI steps. The CLI refuses Node >= 25, and the job
  was using whatever the runner image shipped, so the next image bump
  would have reddened every docs PR with nothing having changed.
- `--ignore-scripts` on the install: the tree reaches puppeteer, whose
  postinstall downloads Chrome, and none of the three checks needs a
  browser.
- the a11y step now separates "issues found" (exit 1, the untriaged
  baseline we are not gating on) from "did not run" (127, 137, a crash),
  which previously printed the same warning.
- add pnpm-lock.yaml, both composite actions and go.mod/go.sum to the
  path filter. detect-changes is the gate itself, so a change to it has
  to re-run the gate.
- declare `permissions: contents: read`. Nothing here writes, and the
  repo default being flipped later should not hand a write token to a job
  that runs an npm dependency tree.

Honest correction in the same pass: the pin comment claimed an unpinned
CLI was the risk being closed, but `mint validate` downloads the current
Mintlify build client at run time, unpinned and unchecksummed. Pinning
that is only possible through an undocumented hidden flag, so the comment
now states the exposure instead of implying it is covered.

Specs: 13/13 scenarios bound (was 10/10); the loader's tests now cover
the redirect and version cases above.

* fix(docs): temperature is optional, and the GPT-5 family rejects it

Following the same thread as the last commit. Reviewing the remaining

data-model.mdx marked `model`, `temperature` and `maxTokens` as

* fix(docs): repair the repo-style links in the two newly navigated pages

Adding the governance architecture pages to the navigation exposed links
written for a repository, not a site. One was broken by this PR's own
rename: activity-monitor-event-sourcing.mdx pointed at
`./architecture.md`, which stopped resolving when that file became

* fix(docs): scope the version rules to LangWatch charts, and correct the SDK examples

Second review round, three threads, all valid.

The version rules were context-free. `--version`, `tag:` and
`targetRevision:` say nothing about whose release they pin, so a
cert-manager or Prometheus example would have been reported as drift with
a remedy telling the author to change it to the LangWatch version —
corrupting the page. They now count only when a LangWatch chart or image
is named within eight lines, which reaches both ways because the real
shapes differ: a `helm upgrade langwatch langwatch/langwatch` line
precedes its `--version` continuation, while `VERSION=` precedes the loop
that names the images. Verified both directions: forcing the chart to
9.9.9 still reports all eight real references, and cert-manager,
Prometheus and an unrelated values block report nothing.

The prompt SDK examples were wrong in a way the `Required` labels hid.
Against the schema and both SDKs: only `handle` is required on create,
`scope` defaults to PROJECT, and `prompt` and `model` are optional. Worse,
the Python examples passed `model=`, `temperature=` and `max_tokens=`,
none of which are parameters of `prompts.create` or `prompts.update` —
there is no `**kwargs`, so both calls would have raised TypeError — and
the update example omitted `scope`, which is required there. The Python
examples now call only real parameters, and a note says which fields are
TypeScript and REST only rather than leaving the tabs silently different.

The `./architecture.md` link raised in the first round is already fixed;
the remaining comment was on generated output from before that commit.

* fix(docscheck): pair a tag with its own repository, not with any nearby langwatch

Third review round, one finding, and it was a false positive I had just
introduced. The context matcher accepted `repository:.*langwatch/`, which
matches `repository: langwatch/clickhouse-serverless` — so a `tag: "0.2.0"`
under it became a release reference and was reported as drift against
3.12.0, on a correct block. Reproduced it on a fixture before changing
anything.

Inspecting the rest of that matcher, `langwatch/langwatch` on its own was
worse: it matches every `github.com/langwatch/langwatch` source link in
the docs, so almost any page counted as chart context.

Two narrower rules now, each with the window its shape needs:

- a `tag:` is paired with a `repository:` naming one of the three
  release-tracking images, over three lines — they are adjacent in a
  values block, and the pairing is the whole point.
- `--version`, `targetRevision:` and `VERSION=` need chart context over
  eight lines: a tagged release image (including the mirroring loop's
  `langwatch/$image:`), a `helm ... langwatch/langwatch` chart reference,
  an ArgoCD `chart: langwatch`, or a `repoURL:` on langwatch.github.io.

Verified both directions rather than trusting the regexes: the
clickhouse-serverless block now reports nothing, and forcing appVersion to
9.9.9 still reports all eight real references — the four in
docker-images.mdx, both in argocd.mdx, and both upgrade guides. Negative
fixtures cover the clickhouse tag, a GitHub source link, and an unrelated
repoURL containing "langwatch".

* fix(docscheck): anchor the langwatch namespace instead of matching by suffix

Every one of these patterns matched `langwatch/` as a bare substring, so
somebody else's namespace counted as ours: `notlangwatch/langwatch:1.14.5`,
`registry.example.com/notlangwatch/langwatch` with a tag under it, and
`https://notlangwatch.github.io` as an ArgoCD source. Each would have
produced a VersionDrift finding on a correct reference.

The review named the repository and repoURL patterns. The
self-identifying image pattern had it too, and that is the one that
produces findings directly rather than qualifying them, so it mattered
most.

`langwatch` now has to be a whole path component — start of line or a
character that cannot be part of a path component — and the ArgoCD host
is exact rather than a suffix. The helm-chart alternative already had its
boundary in the preceding `\s+`, which is why adding another would have
broken it: there is only one space between the release name and the chart
reference.

Verified both directions again. The three hostile forms report nothing,
the mirrored-but-legitimate `registry.example.com/langwatch/langwatch_nlp`
still counts, and forcing appVersion to 9.9.9 still reports all eight
real references.

fastq_pending, 28,467 groups pending — but that took a live measurement to
establish rather than a metric.

DISPATCH_BATCH_LUA now returns [results, overrideDispatched] and the dispatcher
increments gq_jobs_dispatched_override_total. The count rides back with the
results instead of living in a Redis key so it stays per-process: one shared key
reported by every pod would multiply under sum(), as the blocked-groups gauge
already does. Old and new pods parse only their own script's return, so a
rolling deploy is unaffected.

Also drops work-conserving-fair-dispatch.feature from LEGACY_INERT, since it now
enforces the two scenarios these tests bind.

* fix(event-sourcing): validate the dispatch reply before counting overrides

A reply with partial tuples dispatches nothing, and the override count is
only believed when it does not exceed the tuples that rode back with it —
the count is a subset of the batch, so anything larger is corrupt. Spec
wording drops the least-served-tenant dispatch internals for the

fix: quick fixes for the top recurring prod errors (#7465)

* fix(topic-clustering): customer-actionable failures skip the retry budget

A run that fails because the project has no model configured cannot be
fixed by retrying — only the customer changing their configuration can.
Record the durable run_failed (whose code the settings page renders as
guidance) on the first attempt, log it at warn as a customer fault, and
count it as failed_customer so failed_final stays an internal-fault
signal. ~276 projects were burning 3 attempts each on this daily, at
error level.

* fix(scenarios): prefetch blocked by project configuration logs at warn

A disabled provider or bad model format already fails the run with its
remediation message; logging it at error made ~16/day of customer
misconfiguration read as platform failures.

* fix(shutdown): destroy straggler connections inside the http phase

The force-close lived in a finally behind 'await closed', so when a
long-lived response (an SSE stream, a stuck keep-alive) never ended the
runner's phase timeout fired first and the destroy never ran: the
http-server phase failed on every rolling deploy (~28/day) while the
sockets it was meant to reap survived to the process deadline. The
drain grace now lives inside the phase, so in-flight requests get 8s
and only the leftovers are destroyed.

* fix(health): canary failures are handled errors with platform fault

The /api/health/collector self-POSTs could throw uncaught (surfacing as
a causeless 500) and the non-ok branches hand-rolled c.json 500s outside
the handled-error contract. Both now throw health_check_failed with
fault: platform, the failing transport and upstream status in meta, and
the network error attached as a reason — so the monitor's alert names
the broken half without anyone re-running the probe by hand.

* fix(langevals): pin gpt-5-family temperature to its only accepted value

Evaluators default to temperature 0 for deterministic verdicts, and
gpt-5-family models reject every value but the default (1). drop_params
cannot help — it strips unsupported params, not restricted values — so
every gpt-5 judge call failed before it started unless its evaluator
carried its own guard (only llm_answer_match and select_best_compare
did). Normalized centrally in patch_litellm_params, covering topic
naming, ragas, and user-configured judge models at once.

* fix(logs): demote non-fatal metadata sync and dataset 4xx to warn

The project-metadata subscriber called its own failure non-fatal in the
message while logging it at error, and the dataset API error handler
logged every status at error — a caller polling a missing dataset put
'Dataset API Error [404]' in the error stream. Level now follows fault:
4xx and self-healing sync failures are warn, 5xx stays error.

* fix(scenarios): lift the prefetch-failure log into its own helper

* fix(shutdown): derive the http drain clocks from the shutdown budget

The first cut declared HTTP_DRAIN_GRACE_MS in start.ts and left the phase
ceiling to the runner's 10s default, which is the shape budget.ts exists to
prevent: independent literals agreeing only by comment. They did not agree —
8s of grace plus teardown overran the 15s of PROCESS_SLACK that also has to
pay for the worker stack and the telemetry flush.

Both clocks now come from ShutdownBudget, so the grace cannot drift outside
the ceiling that makes the destroy reachable at all. Three defects in the
phase go with it:

- the grace timer started after the MCP session teardown, so a slow teardown
  silently spent the budget in-flight requests were given
- a teardown that threw skipped the drain race and the destroy entirely,
  leaving the sockets to the process deadline — the failure the phase was
  written to end
- the hand-rolled timer promise is now node:timers/promises

Tests cover what the earlier ones could not fail on: that the grace is
actually waited out, the close/teardown ordering, a rejecting teardown, and
the ceiling sitting outside the grace. Scenarios added to the spec and bound.

* fix(health): every probe answers a failed canary the same way

/collector threw the new handled error while /processor still hand-rolled
`c.json({ message }, 500)` around an unguarded fetch, so the probe the PR
did not touch kept the anonymous 500 the change set out to remove. Both now
go through sendCanary.

Three things the first cut got wrong:

- the cause reached nobody. `serializeReason` masks a non-handled reason to
  `unknown` on the wire and pino renders a bare Error inside `reasons` as
  `{}`, so the connection-refused / DNS detail was still gone. It is logged
  where it survives.
- `meta` is a client contract, and `check` carried the transport rather than
  the probe. It now names both, and nothing diagnostic.
- the fetch had no deadline, so a wedged collector held the probe open and
  the monitor saw a hang instead of the coded 500 this exists to produce.

The route had no test file at all; it has one now, with a spec behind it.

* fix(scenarios): recognise every prefetch failure the customer can fix

Two defects in the first cut. The classification was a negative list, so a
reason added later would be called the customer's fault by default — the
opposite of what the sibling clustering classifier argues for, and in the
same PR as it. It is an explicit set now, and an unrecognised reason stays
ours.

And the failure it most needed to catch was not caught: a project with no
model configured for scenarios returns no reason at all, so the dominant
customer-actionable case kept logging at error. It names itself now.

Covered by tests, which the classification had none of, and a spec.

* fix(langevals): match the pinned-temperature models more carefully

`"gpt-5" in model` was wrong at both ends. It claimed openai/gpt-5-image and
gpt-5-image-mini, which do accept a temperature — 46 of the 48 gpt-5 models
in llmModels.json refuse one, those two do not — so an evaluator that chose
0 on an image model was silently overridden.

And it missed the Azure path entirely: patch_litellm_params rewrites the
model to azure/<deployment> before the check ran, and a deployment name is
arbitrary, so an Azure-hosted gpt-5 judge kept sending temperature 0 and kept
failing with the BadRequestError this exists to prevent. The check now also
reads the model the request originally named.

The override is deliberate where the sibling reasoning treatment is not, and
the docstring and spec now say so, along with what it costs: a judge on such
a model does not get the determinism temperature 0 was asked for.

Tests cover the image models, the Azure deployment, and the request-setting
route the platform actually sends temperature through.

ADR-054 section 4 enumerates the outcome labels and is the contract behind
the substrate alert, so adding a fifth value that never reaches failed_final
changes what that alert observes. Written down rather than implied.

The spec said a failing effect always retries three times, which stopped
being true for the dominant failure, and the file was in LEGACY_INERT so
nothing caught the drift. Scenario added, both bound, file removed from the
list — it enforces now.

Also classify the error once instead of twice on the way to recording it.

* fix(logs): level the dataset boundary by fault, and keep discarded work loud

Two log-level changes from the first cut, both corrected.

The dataset handler levelled on a status that is always 500 for a handled
error — HandledError names it httpStatus, not status — so a handled 404 or

resolves the status the response will actually carry, and levels with
getLogLevelForRequest, the shared fault-aware rule tRPC and the request
middleware already use, so the boundaries agree and a 404 is not warn.

The projectMetadata demotion is reverted. specs/observability/retryable-

only one: the onboarding milestone is lost with nothing above warn to say so.

Review feedback: the route module had grown the failure classification and

the request and serializes the response. HealthCheckFailedError, sendCanary
and the canary deadline move to server/health-probes, tests with them.

Also from review: name the prefetch boolean isCustomerActionable, and put
the shutdown phase's when-blocks under the given-block the suite convention
asks for.

* fix(shutdown): wrap the phase run in the HTTP/2 test, which is void | Promise

* ci(langevals): run the core tests on fork PRs too

langevals_core/tests/ only ran on the secret-bearing step, which fork and
dependabot PRs skip, so a contributor could change what actually leaves for

* fix(test): point the traces docs assertion at the page that survived

#6824 removed twenty-six orphan docs pages — served by the site but absent
from the navigation — and update-metadata.mdx was one of them, the twin of

fix(authz): a disabled membership is not a membership (#7476)

* fix(authz): a disabled membership is not a membership

`OrganizationUser.disabledAt` was read by visibility code and by nothing on
the authorization path. The organization switcher filtered it, so the
organization vanished from a disabled person's UI — while
`findOrganizationRole`, every binding fence, the API-key ceiling and the
virtual-key membership set read the row as if it were live. A member an admin
disabled to reclaim their seat kept every permission they had, reachable by
direct URL, tRPC call or REST call. Both heads had it, so this is inherited
rather than introduced by the engine.

Membership now means ACTIVE membership everywhere authorization asks:

- The read port returns the row as a fact (`{ role, disabled }`) and the
  collector applies the policy. Filtering in SQL would make a disabled
  membership indistinguishable from an absent one, and the denial could then
  only claim the person was never here.
- Binding reads keep filtering in SQL, since they return grants and have no
  fact to hand back.
- Denials say `membership-disabled`, not `no-membership`: we know the cause
  and an admin can act on it, which is the ADR-045 test for a named error.
  The reason comes from one indexed read on the refusal path rather than a
  second walk, so it is the same answer on the legacy head and the engine one.
- Disabling and re-enabling bump the organization's authz epoch. Disabling is
  a plain column write, so nothing else retired the snapshots §12 caches.

Covered at every live path, not just the engine: the prisma, grants and
cutover read repositories, `virtualKey.authz.ts` (where `isOrgAdmin`
short-circuits visibility to every virtual key in the organization),
`role-binding-resolver.ts`, and the legacy `rbac.ts` reader.

The scenario that was supposed to cover this asserted through
`repo.getUserOrgRole` — the one reader that already filtered `disabledAt` and
is not on the permission path — so it passed throughout. It now asserts
through the engine. The reader tests that pinned the query shape WITHOUT
`disabledAt`, which is where the gap was frozen, now pin it with.

Separately, a lite invite naming no team produced somebody who could sign in,
see nothing, and hold a seat: a lite seat grants only what its teams grant.
The form now warns before the invite is sent. A warning rather than a refusal,
because assigning the team afterwards is a legitimate way to work.

Deployment Impact: the ADR-092 §9 owner ceiling means a disabled member's
personal API keys stop working, since effective(key) = grants(key) ∩
grants(owner). That is the intent — a person cut off from an organization must
not keep a live credential to it — but it reaches past their own session, so
an automation running on a disabled person's key stops with them. Service
keys, which have no owner, are unaffected. No migration; no config change.

Refs ADR-092 (amended), ADR-045

* fix(authz): name the disabled seat on every tier, and fence the CLI key endpoints

Review follow-ups on #7476.

- rbac.ts: the membership gate both heads share carries the row as a fact,
  so project and team checks refuse a disabled seat by name instead of
  falling back to "no permission"; both engine branches forward the
  engine's denialReason; organizationDenialReason takes named parameters;
  the TeamUser legacy fallback is fenced on disabledAt like the RoleBinding
  query beside it.
- auth-cli.ts: ensureActiveOrgMemberOr403 and /approve read disabledAt. A
  project key has no owner and the gateway honours a personal virtual key
  on its own status, so these were the credentials the owner ceiling never
  reached.
- MembershipDisabledError carries no meta: nothing rendered it, and the
  scope id it held was a project or team as often as an organization.
- Spec wording describes the observable result; the form test walks the
  path the feature describes (remove the assigned team, then send).

* test(authz): membership fixtures carry disabledAt on every rbac path

The legacy resolver now reads the row as a fact, so a mock returning only
{ role } reads as a disabled seat. Six suites shaped their fixture that way.

* fix(authz): re-derive membership at /exchange, and name the seat on the legacy middlewares

Second review round on #7476.

- /exchange re-checks active membership before either credential branch
  and consumes the device code on refusal: approval is not the last word,
  and both branches hand out keys the owner ceiling never reaches.
- checkProjectPermission / checkTeamPermission (still live as building
  blocks for the tenant-anchored compositions) raise MembershipDisabledError
  ahead of the role-shaped denials.
- Re-enable is pinned to bump the epoch too; the CLI guard test asserts
  every resource the scenario names and cleans up unconditionally.

* fix(auth-cli): a disabled seat at /exchange answers the fatal 410 the CLI already knows

The mint below already burns the code with access_denied/410 for a removed
member, and two tests pin that; the earlier recheck now answers the same
way. The guard test asserts consumption on the store, since an immediate
second poll meets the exchange throttle first.

* fix(auth-cli): a disabled seat cannot renew its CLI session

Third review round on #7476.

- /refresh re-derives active membership before rotating, like every other
  endpoint that mints a credential; refused, the presented refresh token is
  revoked. Bearer-only routes keep honouring the access token in hand until
  it expires (one hour), the same window a removed member already has;
  this stops that window rolling forward for ninety days.
- The /exchange denial also drops the poll-rate key, so the CLI's next
  poll learns the code is gone (408) rather than that it polled too soon.

* docs(authz): mark the legacy rbac surface deprecated (#7477)

`server/api/rbac.ts` answered every permission question before ADR-092, so it
is still what autocomplete offers and what a nearby file imports out of habit
— while the engine it was replaced by sits one import away. Nothing said so in
a way an editor could show.

Tags, not deletions. Three kinds of thing live in there and they are not the
same kind of legacy:

- **Role bags and permission maths** (`teamRoleHasPermission`,
  `getTeamRolePermissions`, `hasPermissionWithHierarchy`,
  `EXTERNAL_MEMBER_PERMISSIONS`, `canView` and friends) are second copies of
  what `@langwatch/authz` owns. They agree today only because
  `roles-parity.unit.test.ts` holds them cell-for-cell against the engine's —
  a guard, not a reason to read them. Each names its exact replacement.
- **The hand-`.use()`d tRPC middlewares** are replaced by declaring
  `.permission("…")` on the procedure (ADR-092 decision 25). The prose already
  said "do not `.use()` it on a new procedure"; now the tag says it too, so an
  editor strikes it through.
- **The fork resolvers** (`resolveProjectPermission`,
  `hasOrganizationPermission`, the `batch*` helpers, and the api-key ceiling in
  `rbac/role-binding-resolver.ts`) still RUN: each asks the engine for a
  migrated organization and walks the legacy tables for one that is not. Their
  tags say "not for new callers" rather than implying dead code, because they
  are what the contract PR deletes, not something already gone.

Both modules gained a header saying which of the three a reader is looking at.

Deliberately NOT deprecated, and the header says so: `authorizeInResolver`,
the ops-scope surface (`checkOpsPermission`, `resolveOpsScope`), the
demo-project predicates, and `organizationDenialReason`. Those are current.

JSDoc only — no behaviour change, and nothing in the repo treats a deprecated
usage as an error, so existing call sites keep building.

Refs ADR-092, ADR-110

fix(ui): a markdown link is an inline box again, so long URLs wrap instead of escaping the message (#7434)

Chakra's preflight already puts `word-wrap: break-word` on `*`, so ordinary
paragraph text has always wrapped. Two shapes escaped it:

- Chakra's link recipe is `display: inline-flex`. That makes an anchor an
  atomic inline box — it cannot be split across line boxes at all, so no
  inherited wrap rule reaches it. An autolinked signed URL grew the box to
  its full text width and painted outside the bubble: 1990px of overhang in
  a 320px container.
- A markdown table is `table-layout: auto`, which sizes columns from
  min-content. `overflow-wrap: break-word` deliberately does not shrink
  min-content, so one unbreakable cell widened the whole table by 3445px.
  `anywhere` is the one value that lets a break count towards intrinsic size.

Both markdown roots are fixed the same way. `& pre` keeps `overflow-x: auto`
— breaking a code block mid-token is worse than scrolling it — and a test
guards that.

The test fixture is a run of one repeated character rather than a mixed
alphanumeric literal. Line breaking does not care which characters these are,
only that none of them offers a break, but a secret scanner does: the first
version tripped gitleaks' generic-api-key rule.

Refs #7433

* fix(langevals): a stalled model call can no longer wedge the service

"Evaluation queue is full" was not overload. The gate bounds how many
evaluations run at once, and a request holds its slot until its batch
returns. An evaluation waits on a model call, litellm ships a 6000 second
request timeout, and nothing else bounded the batch, so one stalled
provider parked a slot for 100 minutes. Sixty-four of those and the gate
never admitted anyone again: every caller waited out the 300 second queue
and got the 503, including callers whose work took a second. Only a
restart cleared it.

Two bounds now. One model call may not run longer than
LANGEVALS_MODEL_TIMEOUT, default 120 seconds, so the socket dies and its
worker thread with it. One request may not hold its slot longer than
LANGEVALS_EVALUATION_TIMEOUT, default 300 seconds: the batch keeps the
results it has, answers the rest as EvaluationTimeout, and gives the slot
back. The overrunning work is abandoned rather than waited on, because a
thread parked in a socket read cannot be interrupted and waiting for it
is the hang itself.

The moderation evaluator replaced evaluate_batch with a narrower
signature, so the server could not call it at all. It takes the base
signature now, and a test binds the server's own call against every
loaded evaluator so the next narrow override fails in CI instead of as a
500 for one customer.

Proven against a provider that accepts the connection and never answers:
both slots stalled, both abandoned on the deadline, real work served
while they were still in flight, server healthy afterwards.

fix(haven): `up` builds the api bundle it runs, and names the CA-serial trap (#7508)

* fix(haven): `up` builds the api bundle it runs, and names the CA-serial trap

Two independent reasons `make haven up` could report a live stack that
serves nothing. Both are hit on a clean machine.

The api lane runs the PRODUCTION bundle (`start:app` -> node
dist/server/server.cjs), but no step of the up ever built it: codegen
writes generated source, the migration step only touches the database,
and dist/ is gitignored — so a freshly-created worktree has no bundle at
all. The lane crash-looped on MODULE_NOT_FOUND while the vite lane sat
behind its /api/health ready-probe and never served the hostname: a
stack that reports itself up and then answers nothing. `up` now builds
the bundle when it is missing, and stops if that build fails. An
existing bundle is left alone, so only the first `up` in a worktree pays
for it.

Separately, a ca.srl left root-owned by an earlier sudo run makes
openssl fail to sign every per-host certificate — silently, leaving a
ZERO-BYTE .pem behind rather than erroring. The proxy then serves that
hostname with no certificate and the handshake dies with "no peer
certificate available", which is indistinguishable from the SAN gap of
 #7117 — a bug whose fix already shipped. `up` now checks the serial is
writable before starting the proxy and, when it is not, says what is
actually wrong and gives the commands to clear it. Reporting only:
the file is root-owned because something outside haven ran as root, and
deleting another user's files is not a dev tool's call.

* fix(haven): a play sandbox builds the api bundle too

Self-review caught the first commit fixing one of two callers. A play
sandbox supervises the SAME child plan as `up` (play.go passes
planChildren), so its api lane also runs dist/server/server.cjs — and
the PR checkout it was cut from has no dist/ either. The sandbox came up
serving nothing, for exactly the reason `up` did.

Fatal here as well: stale codegen is survivable in a sandbox ("still
worth looking at"), but a sandbox that never serves its hostname is not.

Two things the first pass left half-done, both about a promise that was not

fix(gateway): a codex request carries only what its backend accepts (#7507)

* fix(gateway): a codex request carries only what its backend accepts

The ChatGPT codex backend keeps an allowlist of its own and answers 400
"Unsupported parameter" on anything outside it, before a token is generated.
A removal list therefore costs one production outage per refused field, and
it took two to learn that: #7484 removed prompt_cache_retention and only
uncovered pi's own default max output tokens, with the same dead card for
the user.

So codexRequestBody keeps the caller's Responses body to the fields that
backend accepts, then pins the invariants it already owned: the bare model
name, stream on, store off. Probed live, one field at a time, the backend
refuses max_output_tokens, max_tool_calls, prompt_cache_options,
prompt_cache_retention, temperature, top_p, top_logprobs, truncation,
metadata, service_tier, background, user, safety_identifier and
previous_response_id, and accepts model, input, instructions, stream,
stream_options, store, include, tools, tool_choice, parallel_tool_calls,
reasoning, text and prompt_cache_key.

sjson reads a path, not a name, so a field name could break the very call
this filtering exists to save. ".", "*", "?" and ":" select something else:
deleting ":input" deleted "input", the one field a turn cannot go out
without, and kept itself. "|", "#" and "@" make the path complex, which
DeleteBytes refuses outright, failing the whole request. sjsonKey escapes
every byte rather than a chosen set, because sjson decides what an operator
is and its list can grow, an escape before an ordinary byte means that byte,
and a multi-byte character survives byte by byte.

The failure log carries the provider's own reason too, read from the four
fields providers write to explain themselves, so a codex 400 names the
parameter it refused instead of saying only "codex backend HTTP 400". A body
in none of those shapes is described by its size and never quoted: an HTML
edge page or a plain-text rejection can reflect the request that caused it,
and a prompt, a key or personal data must not reach a log line.

* fix(langy): a model pick that matches the default is still the user's pick

The composer's model pill reverted to the previous model after a failed

* fix(gateway): the codex body is built from what we accept, not stripped of what we do not

A caller's field name was turned into an sjson path, and that one decision
produced three separate ways for a name to break the call it rode on:
".", "*", "?" and ":" select something else, so ":input" dropped "input", the
one field a turn cannot go out without; "|", "#" and "@" make the path
complex, which DeleteBytes refuses; and an empty name has no path at all, so
a legal body carrying one failed outright.

Escaping covered the first two and would not have covered the third. So the
outgoing body is now BUILT by copying the accepted fields under our own fixed
names, and a name we do not know is simply never copied. A field name is data
again, and no name can address anything but the field we mean. sjsonKey is
gone with the class of bug it was patching, and the test reads the result's
own top-level names rather than looking each one up by a path, since the
names under test are exactly the ones a path cannot express.

* fix(gateway): a codex body that is not an object is refused here, not upstream

Only an object has fields to filter. Anything else read as no fields at all
and was rebuilt into the pins alone, so "null", "[]", a truncated body or
plain text went upstream as a well-formed request with no turn in it. The
caller then paid a provider round trip to be told what the gateway could see
before it dialed. The body is checked for valid JSON with an object root
first, and the caller already turns the error into a bad request.

An empty body still means an empty object, which is the one case where the
pins alone are the intended request.

* feat(lwql): period_granularity_seconds reserved parameter — the granularity contract

Slice 3 of #6582 (#6713), S1 of the plan v2 stack: the server-side contract
the dashboard widget will ride on.

A saved chart declares `{period_granularity_seconds:UInt32}` beside the two
period bounds and uses it as the multiplier of a fixed-unit interval --
`INTERVAL {period_granularity_seconds:UInt32} SECOND`. ClickHouse compiles an
interval unit to a function name, so only the multiplier can be a bound value;
fixing the unit at seconds is what leaves the surface one value to inject.
The validator accepts that shape -- proven first, it is the mechanism's
load-bearing premise (A5).

Rules, all enforced in one resolver so workbench, REST and the later dashboard
cannot drift:

- Declared type must be exactly UInt32; refused at save as well as run.
- Declaring it requires both period bounds; refused at save -- without them
  the bucket budget is uncomputable exactly when it matters.
- A caller-supplied value is refused, same as the window bounds.
- The bucket budget: ceil(window / step) against LWQL_GRANULARITY_MAX_BUCKETS
  (10,000). Caller-owned surfaces refuse with lwql_granularity_too_fine; the
  dashboard auto-coarsens to the finest fitting offered step and names what
  happened via coarsenedFromSeconds.
- Offered steps are sub-day only -- 1s, 1m, 1h. O1 resolved by probe before
  any implementation: over the Amsterdam fallback night the timezone-argument
  seconds form shifts its bucket boundary mid-day (02:00 local -> 01:00 local)
  while toStartOfDay holds 00:00 throughout, so fixed seconds cannot express a
  25-hour local day. Day-scale waits on period_timezone.

Also: the surface-reserved sweep now covers the granularity name, so a caller
supplying it hits lwql_reserved_parameter_supplied like the window bounds.

Tests: resolution rules incl. boundary-exact and one-past-ceiling; the A5
validator probe; save-time declaration rules. Feature scenarios appended to
lwql-workbench.feature (two @unimplemented pending the run-path wiring PR).

feat(authz): a grant states which surface authored it (#7519)

* feat(authz): a grant states which surface authored it

`GrantsService.attach` took who, what and where, and nothing that said
where the grant came from — so `source` was pinned to "grants-service" in
the app's writer, and the vocabulary's own "scim" and "invite" values were
unreachable through the one write surface. The actor cannot stand in for
it: a directory sync and an approved request to join both act as the
platform, and only the source separates them.

`attach` now takes an optional `source`, defaulting to "grants-service",
threaded through the write port and the ledger-backed repository onto the
emitted `grant_attached` fact. Every existing call site keeps its meaning
untouched. `join-request` joins the vocabulary, and `system:join-requests`
the actor registry, for the policy-driven auto-approval path.

Two restatements of the vocabulary went with it: the app writer kept its
own four-value `LedgerWriteSource` union, which a new source could not
travel through, and its legacy-path audit guard restated the skip list the
subscriber owns. Both now read the shared lists, so a source added in one
place is accepted everywhere and audited unless it says otherwise —
`join-request` is a change a customer made and stays on their audit page.

* feat(authz): a grant write can be attributed to a surface, not only a person

The source half of the seam shipped without the actor half. `GrantsService`
took `actor: { userId: string }` and `writeActor` built `{ type: "user" }`
from it, so `SYSTEM_ACTORS.scim` and the `joinRequests` entry added
alongside it were unreachable through the one write surface — an entry
nobody can pass is inert.

`GrantActor` is now `{ userId: string } | Actor`, the second half being the
shared vocabulary from `@langwatch/actor`. Taking that union outright would
have invalidated every existing `{ userId }` call site, so it is admitted
alongside rather than in place of it; `writeActor` routes BOTH halves
through `toLedgerActor`, which keeps one serialization seam and keeps a
`"system:..."` string unbuildable at a call site.

This settles offboard and revoke rather than deferring them. `grant_revoked`
carries no `source` field and now needs none: the actor names the surface
and the existing `reason` carries the rest, so D08's de-enroll is
attributable with no change to the durable event or to the audit page's
metadata allow-list. Tests drive the real chain and assert on the commands
the writer emits — a system actor on `attachGrant` and on `revokeGrant` —
and pin that a system-actor revocation is audited rather than filtered as
backdated history.

Also fixes the `Grant.source` schema comment, which still listed the
pre-ADR-110 vocabulary and omitted the current values.

feat(governance): the edit drawer can edit what pull mode actually runs on (#7430)

* feat(governance): the DTO answers whether a source has already pulled

The edit drawer needs to know whether a backfill start is still in play,
and `status` cannot tell it. A source that pulled successfully but
recorded zero events stays `awaiting_first_event` while holding a cursor,
and one disabled before its first run never held one — so the proxy fails
open and closed at the same time.

`hasPollerCursor` reports it directly, without shipping the cursor, which
is adapter-internal and of no use to a client. It is not a `!= null`
check: the column is a Prisma Json field that stores JSON `null` for a
source that has not pulled, and Prisma surfaces that as either JS `null`
or a sentinel object depending on version. Betting on one of those is how
this silently answers "yes" for every source and hides a setting that was
still editable. The cursor has been seen both as an object and as
serialised JSON, so neither encoding is assumed either.

`pollerCursor` is required rather than optional in the row type, so a
future `select` clause that stops fetching it becomes a compile error
instead of a flag that is quietly false everywhere.

* feat(governance): the edit drawer can edit what pull mode actually runs on

A pull-mode source was created with an admin key, a schedule and adapter
config, and from then on none of it could be changed. The drawer offered
name, description and team, and told the admin the rest was immutable —
which was never true of the database, only of this form. A mistyped key
meant archiving the source and building a new one, losing its history.

The server side already supported this and already defended it: an
incoming encrypted envelope is refused outright, stored hidden keys carry
across when the incoming value is undefined, and the destination is
checked before anything is written. Nothing there needed to move.

So the work is on the form:

- `seedComposerParserConfig` is the inverse of `buildParserConfig`. It
  fills the composer from a stored row and forces every secret field to
  blank, because a secret must never be seeded — the DTO strips
  `credentials` and a blank field is what tells the server to keep it.
- `buildAnthropicAdminPullConfig` and `resolvePullConfig` take
  `requireCredentials`, defaulting to strict so the create path is
  unchanged. On edit, a blank token omits `credentials` entirely rather
  than sending an empty one.
- `ParserConfigFields` takes a mode. On edit a secret says it may be left
  blank to keep the current key, and stops being required.
- `buildEditedParserConfig` merges the result. Every adapter-owned key is
  deleted before the rebuilt config is applied, because the builders omit
  blank optional keys and a plain `Object.assign` therefore leaves a
  cleared field at its old stored value — cleared in the form, unchanged
  in the database, with nothing on screen to say so.

Editing is limited to `anthropic_admin` for now. Databricks Genie accepts
either a workspace token or a service-principal pair, so a blank edit form
there is ambiguous rather than meaning "keep what you have".

* feat(governance): the source detail page offers an edit affordance

The detail page could rotate a secret and archive a source, which meant
the only way to reach the edit drawer was to go back to the list. An
admin who navigated straight to a source had no way to change it from
where they were standing.

The Edit button sits inside the existing `canManage` block, so it is
gated by the same `ingestionSources:manage` permission as the other two
actions rather than introducing a second answer to who may edit.

`SourceEditDrawer` is imported from the list page, which is a page
importing a page. Extracting it properly means first moving the shared
composer helpers into a third module, or the two files import each other;
that is worth doing and is not this change.

* docs(governance): the cursor predicate stops justifying itself with a fiction

The comment claimed Prisma surfaces JSON null as a sentinel object on some
versions, and a test asserted the predicate handles that sentinel. Neither
holds: the generated read type is `JsonValue | null`
(src/generated/prisma/models/IngestionSource.ts:265) and the sentinels appear
only in the write shapes, so no sentinel reaches a read.

What is actually true is narrower and still worth the predicate. The writer at
ingestion-pull-run-projection.prisma.repository.ts:87 stores `Prisma.JsonNull`
or a string, both of which `!= null` would have handled. Object-shaped rows are
the case it would not, and `cursorOf` in ingestionPullLifecycle.ts:27 still
stringifies them, so they are not hypothetical.

Drops the sentinel test rather than repairing it — it asserted an input that
cannot arrive, and the replacement attempt was itself wrong (a computed class
key evaluated before its static initializer, keying on the string "undefined").

* refactor(governance): the edit drawer's decisions move out of its render

The lint gate caught what the PR description had already admitted: three new
Biome complexity violations, all of them the same mistake in three places —
decisions that belong to the edit path were written inline in a React render
function, where nothing can reach them.

`buildEditSubmission` is the important one. Whether the pull config gets
rebuilt at all, whether `pullSchedule` rides along, and what a cleared field
means were a 40-line closure inside `SourceEditDrawer`, so the whole edit path
was reachable only through a surface no test renders. It is now a module-level
function returning the submission or null, and the eleven cases that matter are
asserted directly — including the one that distinguishes an omitted cadence key
from a null one, which is the difference between leaving a push source's column
alone and writing over it.

`parserFieldPresentation` gathers the four things that change about a secret
field between create and edit. Spelled out as separate ternaries in the JSX,
they were one edit away from contradicting each other — a field reading "leave
blank to keep the current key" while still rendering a required marker.

`isEditablePullSource` replaces the three-part inline check, and narrows, so
the callers stop re-casting the DTO's bare `sourceType` string.

The drawer keeps the chrome: `useSourceEditForm` owns the seeding rules,
`SourceIdentityFields` and `PullConfigEditFields` own the markup. That also
settles the reviewdog annotation on the function, which this PR had grown from
64 lines to 108.

Two stacked JSDoc blocks on `SourceEditDrawer` are merged into one, and the
stale half corrected — it still claimed the drawer edited only name,
description and OTTL.

No behaviour change. The gate now reports the branch net-removing one
violation; ee/governance is 50 files / 443 tests green.

* fix(governance): a cleared cadence means the default, not a stopped source

Two behaviour gaps in the edit path, both found in review.

Clearing the cadence field saved `pullSchedule: null`. The field's own
contract is that blank means "the recommended schedule" — create resolves
it to an explicit cron for exactly this reason, because the pull lifecycle
reads a null schedule as `disable`. On edit nothing resolved it, so an
admin who cleared the field stopped the source, while the drawer went on
showing the recommended cadence: the rebuilt parser config had substituted
the default that the column had just lost. The blank now resolves against
the same table the field reads, so the column and the config cannot
disagree.

The backfill start was also locked for every source holding a cursor. Only
the usage cursor is one-way. The cost cursor binds `startingAt` into its
query identity, so moving the start mints a new identity, discards the
cursor and re-reads the widened window — the documented repair lever for a
source whose early figures are wrong. Locking it told a cost admin the
setting could never take effect and sent them to archive-and-recreate over
a control built to work. The lock is now usage-only, and a cost source says
what moving the start will do instead.

The cadence regression runs the edit path's output through the lifecycle
that consumes it: neither half was wrong alone, so only a test spanning
both fails.

* fix(governance): an empty cursor reads the same in both of its shapes

`cursorOf` turns an object-shaped cursor into a string, so the same absent
cursor could arrive at `hasPollerCursor` as `{}` or as `"{}"`. The first
answered "no cursor" and the second "cursor", which is enough to lock the
backfill start on a source that never pulled.

The predicate now reads content out of the serialized form rather than out of
its length, so both shapes agree. An opaque page token is not JSON and keeps
its answer by falling through the parse.

It also moves next to `cursorOf`, the function whose output it has to agree
with, because a second caller is about to need it and a second copy is how the
two would come to disagree about what "has pulled" means.

* fix(governance): the report kind is fixed once a source has pulled

The Anthropic adapter offers two reports for the same consumption — usage
priced by our rate card, cost as the provider's own figure — and its header
states the rule as "Never both", because the same spend arriving down both
paths is counted twice.

The edit drawer made "both" reachable. Only `startingAt` was locked, so a
source with history could be switched from usage to cost; the adapter derives
its query identity from the report, so the stored cursor stops matching, the
new report replays from the backfill start, and its events land under `cost:*`
beside the `usage:*` ids already recorded. Nothing collides and nothing is
overwritten, which is exactly why nothing catches it.

The guard lives in the service, because the invariant is a property of the
stored events rather than of the drawer: a caller that skips the form would
otherwise walk straight past it. The form declining to offer the edit is the
courtesy half, and it explains why rather than simply greying the field out.

Both halves read "has pulled" through the shared cursor predicate, so neither
can drift into a different answer than the DTO gives.

* fix(governance): the edit drawer stops offering what it cannot deliver

Three things the drawer said that were not quite true.

The report is now shown locked once a source has pulled, with the reason
written next to it rather than left for the admin to infer from a greyed-out
field. The service refuses the change either way; this is the form agreeing
with it.

A locked field is no longer `disabled`. It is shown precisely so its value can
be read, and `disabled` drops it out of the tab order where a keyboard or
screen-reader user cannot reach it — which makes it closer to hidden than to
shown. `readOnly` alone prevents the edit and keeps the field reachable, which
is what the Textarea branch beside it already did.

Save is gated on the same cadence check the create drawer uses. The server
already refuses an invalid cron, so this is not what keeps a bad schedule out
of the column — it is what stops one drawer submitting a value the other would
have refused, after the field has already marked it invalid on screen.

The spec drops its claim that the rotate control is hidden for pull sources.
It is not, in either the detail header or the list row, and hiding a
credential control is an access decision rather than a form-editing one. What
ships is the narrower thing the drawer actually does: it stops describing an
ingest secret that a pull source does not have.

* test(governance): the edit-path suite splits along the units it tests

The file had grown to 474 source lines, over the 300 the repo asks of a new
one, and it had three separable subjects sitting in it: what the builders
submit, what the form shows before anything is rendered, and what happens when
a saved edit reaches the pull lifecycle.

They are now three files, each named for its subject, and the composer state
they all start from moves into a fixture so the split does not leave three
copies of it to drift apart.

The presentation suite also picks up the report lock, including the transition
that motivated it: a source with usage history switched to cost, in both
directions, and the cases where nothing should be locked at all.

* fix(governance): the edit drawer follows its page through the Inventory rename

Main renamed `ingestion-sources.tsx` to `inventory.tsx` when the nav unified
Tool Tiles and Sources (15d54d1005). Rebasing onto that moved this branch's
edits into the renamed file correctly — git follows content — but the import

So the detail page and all four edit-path test files still asked for

The kind of break a rebase cannot flag, because at no point were two versions
of a line in conflict.

* fix(governance): an omitted report is refused for what it is

The immutability guard treated a missing `report` as a request to change it,
and said so: an update carrying no report at all was told it could not switch
reports, naming an edit the caller never made.

Refusing is still right — `data.parserConfig` replaces the stored JSON
wholesale, so letting an omitted report through would delete it rather than
preserve it, and the source would come back configured for neither. But that
is a serialization mistake, not a deliberate switch, and sending someone to
look for an edit they never made is how the wrong thing gets debugged.

Also tidies two comments the split and the new mutation left stale: the
lifecycle rationale follows its suite into the file that holds it, and the
detail page counts three mutations rather than two.

* refactor(governance): the credentials flag says what kind of thing it is

`requireCredentials` became part of a public signature when the edit path
needed it, and the repo asks a new boolean to lead with `is`/`has`/`should`.
Renamed to `shouldRequireCredentials` at all seven sites in one pass so the
parameter and its callers cannot disagree.

The single-letter `c` and `p` in the same builders are left alone: they are
the convention every sibling builder in the file already follows, and
renaming only the one function that happens to be exported would make the
file argue with itself.

* refactor(governance): the save gate becomes a decision the drawer can be asked

Adding the cadence check inline pushed `SourceEditDrawer` to 62 lines, two
over what the linter allows, which is the linter noticing the real thing: the
gate is a rule about when a form is submittable, and it was sitting in a JSX
attribute where nothing could ask it a question.

`isEditSaveBlocked` now holds it, with five tests covering the cases the
inline version had none for — a blank cadence meaning the recommended
schedule rather than an error, and a push-mode source having no schedule to
judge in the first place.

* feat(governance): the anthropic composer's closed domains become pickers (#7509)

Report, bucket width and backfill start all have domains the adapter
already declares, and all three were free-text inputs. The domain lived
in a hint, and a mistyped value came back as a toast after the save.

Report and bucket width become selects; backfill start becomes a date
control. Both selects lead with an entry carrying no value — a controlled
<select> holding "" with no "" option displays its first real option, so
a required field would show a report the admin never chose.

The bucket width list collapses to that entry on a cost source, and a
width already chosen is cleared when the report switches to cost. That is
not politeness: validBucketWidth refuses any width on cost, so leaving it
would reject the whole save for a field the form no longer offers.

The date control is display-only truncation. Every startingAt that reaches
storage has been through normalizeStartingAt, which returns an ISO instant,
so the edit form always seeds an instant and a plain date input handed one
renders blank — which on an edit form reads as "no backfill start" and
would drop a setting nobody touched. The held value is left alone until
the admin picks a different day.

Option lists are asserted against anthropicAdminPullConfigSchema rather
than a second hand-written copy, so the form and the adapter cannot drift.

The spec lands under specs/, not platform/app/specs/ — the latter is a
stray tree check-feature-parity never scans, which is why the sibling
governance feature file enforces nothing.

Closes langwatch/langwatch-saas#1157

* fix(governance): the report guard holds the row still until it has written

`assertReportUnchangedOncePulled` clears a report change by reading that the
source has no poller cursor. That read and the update it clears were separate
statements with nothing between them, so a pull run finishing in the gap gave
the source a cursor and the update landed on a source that had pulled — the
exact state the guard refuses whenever it can see it, reached by arriving a few
milliseconds late. Nothing looks wrong afterwards: no row collides, no
constraint fires, and the same spend is counted once under each report.

The guard now says which kind of yes it gave. Every other permission it grants
stays true however the row moves — a config naming no report has none to
protect, an unchanged report is not the edit that breaks the invariant — but
this one is true only of the row as it was read, and the verdict carries that
obligation to the caller rather than making the caller re-derive it and be
wrong about it independently.

The pinned write is a transaction whose first statement is an `updateMany`
carrying that cursor in its `where`. It does two jobs: a cursor written in the
gap makes it match nothing, so the transaction is abandoned with the row
untouched; and because it is a write rather than a read, Postgres holds the row
lock until commit, so a pull arriving after the check waits instead of
interleaving. A plain `SELECT` inside the transaction would give neither — under
READ COMMITTED it takes no lock at all.

Only that path pays for it. Pinning every edit would fail a routine rename for
the sole reason that a scheduled pull happened to land in the same second.

The pin is `Prisma.AnyNull` for an absent cursor, because the column's two
writers disagree about which null they leave: a JSON null from the projection
repository, SQL NULL from a source that never ran. Both read back as JS `null`,
so a pin matching only one of them would refuse the ordinary case it exists to
allow.

Closes the blocking finding on #7430 and the CodeRabbit thread raising the same
gap from the other side.

* test(governance): the report pin is proven against a real Postgres

The unit suite drives a prisma double, so two things in the pinned write
were assertions about a mock and nothing more:

  - `Prisma.AnyNull` inside an `updateMany` where-clause on a `Json?`
    column. Had the query builder rejected it, every report change on a
    never-pulled source would throw — on exactly the path the pin exists
    to keep working.
  - That `AnyNull` matches both nulls the column can hold. A source made
    without a cursor leaves SQL NULL; the pull-run projection clears one
    by writing `Prisma.JsonNull`, the jsonb value 'null'. Both read back
    as JS `null`, so nothing reading through the client can tell them
    apart, and a pin matching only one would refuse a legitimate edit on
    half the table.

Six cases against real Postgres, through the app's own guarded client:
both null flavours and an empty serialised cursor accept the report
change, an already-pulled source refuses it, a rename on a pulling
source still lands (the pin is not a lock on everything else), and a
cursor arriving between the guard's read and the write refuses with the
report left as it was.

The interleaving is staged at the outermost boundary rather than by
racing two connections: a real race is timing-dependent and would trade
a flaky test for evidence this already gives. So this proves the pin
refuses a moved cursor; it does not prove Postgres orders two
simultaneous writers.

* test(governance): the report pin's refusals are asserted by code, not by copy

The sibling integration test in this directory says it plainly: every
assertion is on `code`, never on message prose, because since #5984 the wire
message for a handled error is the code slug. The atomicity test arrived
matching `/already pulled/i` and `/started pulling while the change was being
saved/i`, so a reworded complaint would have failed it for no behavioural
reason.

Both refusals are `validation_error`, though, so the code alone cannot say
which one fired — a race test that only checked the code would pass even if
the pin had never run and the guard had refused for the ordinary
already-pulled reason. So the race case takes its error once, asserts the
structure, and then pins the single phrase that separates the two, with a
comment saying why the prose is there and nowhere else. It takes the error
once because that client is stateful: a second call would read the cursor the
first one landed.

fix(governance): the edit drawer reads the cadence the scheduler runs on (#7522)

* fix(governance): the edit drawer reads the cadence the scheduler runs on

The `pullSchedule` column never reached the client, so the drawer seeded its
cadence field from `parserConfig.schedule` — the adapter's own copy, which the
composer writes on create and nothing keeps in sync afterwards. The update
mutation takes the column on its own, and seeds and migrations touch neither,
so the two drift.

Two costs, and the second is the expensive one. The field showed a cadence the
source was not running on; and because the save path writes that same field
back to the column, opening a drifted row and saving an unrelated edit — a
rename — silently rewrote the live schedule to the stale value.

`toDto` now carries the column, and seeding prefers it, keeping the parser copy
as a fallback for rows that only have one. A cron expression is not a secret:
it says how often we poll, nothing about the credentials we poll with.

Closes #7521

* test(governance): the drifted row is followed all the way to the scheduler

Review of the fix found its own coverage split down the middle. One suite
proved the drawer now seeds from the column; another proved the DTO carries
it. Nothing ran the path where the harm actually happened: open a drifted
source, change only the name, save, and watch what the process manager is
re-addressed to.

Three cases in the suite that already crosses that boundary on purpose:

- a rename leaves the source running on the cron it was already running on,
- the save converges the parser config's stale copy onto the column, so
