fix(event-sourcing): let a queue drain accept the work it produces (#7520)

Every worker rollout shed a burst of "Failed to dispatch event to
subscriber queue", all carrying the same cause — "Cannot send to queue
after shutdown has been requested". 1,185 across two deploys on the
morning of 24 August, ~200 more on the next, and none outside a
rollout window.

There is one global group queue; the projection, subscriber, map and
fold queues are facades over it. close() set shutdownRequested at the
top and send() refused from that instant, so for the whole length of
the drain the queue rejected the work its own drain was producing: a
job still in flight stores its events, dispatches them onward, and is
turned away by the queue that is draining it.

Nothing above retries. projectionRouter collects the failure into an
AggregateError, eventSourcingService catches it and carries on, so the
job SUCCEEDS while its projections never see those events. The events
themselves are durable in the event store; the projections built from
them quietly skip a rollout's worth, and nothing reports the gap.

Refusing was never protecting anything. send() stages into Redis over
redisConnection, which the drain leaves open — only the blocking
connection is closed there, and the shared connections go afterwards,
in App.close, once the drain has finished. Staged work is durable and
shared, so anything staged during a drain is picked up by another pod.
Throwing turned work that would have survived into work that was lost.

So the gate moves to the end of the drain. A new stagingClosed flag is
set in close()'s finally, which the timeout path reaches too: a drain
that overran was abandoned, not finished, and either way nothing
further should be staged. shutdownRequested keeps its other job, which
is stopping the liveness beacon from re-arming after the tombstone.

Accepting the fan-out cannot prolong the drain: the dispatcher has
already been told to stop claiming, and staging writes to Redis rather
than adding to the processing queue the drain waits on.

Covered by specs/background/queue-drain-send-gate.feature, 5/5
scenarios bound. The tests hold the drain open by controlling the
dispatcher's waitUntilStopped, which is the only window the defect
lives in — and reverting the flag alone makes two of them fail.

* docs(adr): ADR-101, ADR-115 and ADR-116 — identity truth, packaging, and the storage adapter

* feat(identity): the behaviour specs for identifiers, the storage adapter, and the packages

* feat(identity): @langwatch/identity — the isomorphic identity core (ADR-115)

The vocabulary, the identifier normalizer, the fact and command schemas, the
one reducer and the refusal family, in a package the frontend and the backend
both import. `types: []` is the boundary — a `node:*` import or a Buffer
reference does not compile here — so nothing that reads or writes a store can
drift in. The reducer the app's projection folds is the one the replay proof
runs, so the two agree by construction rather than by review.

* feat(identity): @langwatch/identity-server — services over ports, guards, and the better-auth storage adapter (ADR-115, ADR-116)

Service classes over repository interfaces, in the app-layer shape: no storage
engine, no event-sourcing framework and no environment read inside the
package. The write gate, the clock and the command-id minter arrive as
closures.

Guards veto before a write, and the same instance runs on the calling path and
on the queue's staged re-run. `./better-auth` is the only contact with the
library: the ceremonies say what a row write means, and the storage adapter is
better-auth's whole `database:` entry, with a per-user branch inside it.

* feat(event-sourcing): the identity pipeline, and the framework owns the commandId:index key

Five commands, the event schemas and the fold that builds the projection, with
the guards running inside the handlers so the queue's staged re-run vetoes on
the same rules as the calling path. `<commandId>:<index>` moves up to the
framework now that two pipelines stamp it.

* feat(identity): the Identifier projection, AccountCredential, and the reservation lock

`Identifier` is the event-truth projection the fold builds, `userHashKey` the
per-user key its hashes derive from, and `AccountCredential` the secret half —
secrets can never be events, and OAuth refresh rewrites them on a cadence no
log should carry.

The reservation table is the address lock: the claim is taken atomically
before the proof is consumed, so a racing verification of the same address is
refused synchronously and nothing about it is recorded. Every table here is
additive and dark.

* feat(identity): the app layer — runtime, ceremonies, the write gate, backfill and sweeps

The composition root: the one place Prisma, the migration-state table and the
pipeline handle meet the packages' services, and the only place an identity
service, a guard or a ceremony is constructed.

The write gate ships closed and stays closed for a user until that user's
identifier backfill finalizes, so deploying the adapter changes nothing on its
own; a held user performs the protocol write alone, and rollback is an ops
action rather than a deploy. The backfill pass adopts the legacy rows and
proves them, and the sweeps reap the entrances and claims a fact never landed
behind.

* feat(identity): better-auth composes the identity adapter, and the identity surface is tRPC

One `database:` entry, forever. The adapter is the implementation
`createAdapterFactory` is built around, which puts better-auth's own join
emulation and its transactions on it rather than below it, and the per-user
gate routes between the stock Prisma behaviour and event-sourced storage
inside it.

The app's own identity operations go on tRPC: each acts on the caller's own
identity, so the credential is the session and the caller is always this
app's frontend. The versioned, API-key surface stays for callers outside it.

* feat(auth): the verification page, and identity refusals render from the presentation registry

* chore(identity): ship both packages in CI and the server manifest

* feat(authz): the engine migration enrols every organization automatically

A migration now declares whether cloud enrollment gates it. The
authorization-engine migration declares that it does not: its
per-organization rollout is finished, and what enrollment would still
decide is only whether an organization created SINCE ever migrates —
which must not depend on an operator remembering it.

`organizationMigrates` reads the declaration, so a declared migration
admits every cloud organization with no enrollment row. The enrollment
read stays for the migrations still paced by it — both identity
migrations declare `false` and keep today's behaviour exactly.

The automatic path leaves out an organization running a private data
plane, as every cohort draw always has; an operator naming one
deliberately still enrols it.

Enrollment actions refuse for a declared migration rather than writing
rows nothing reads, the ops page says every organization runs the step
instead of offering an enrollment count, and a targeted run no longer
asks for an enrollment that cannot exist.

* fix(authz): a private data plane does not hold an organization back

The automatic cohort carried a private-dataplane exclusion over from the
bulk-enrollment suggestion pool. On this axis it was wrong: these
migrations are rooted in the ORGANIZATION, and
`getClickHouseClientForTenant` resolves an organization-id tenant to that
organization and routes to its own ClickHouse instance when one is
configured, refusing to fall back to the shared client rather than
leaking. Their appends already land on the customer's own instance, so
the exclusion bought nothing and would have stranded exactly those
customers on the legacy authorization path permanently.

`organizationMigrates` no longer takes `hasPrivateDataplane` at all,
rather than taking an argument nothing reads.

The user-rooted exclusions stay: a user tenant resolves to neither a
project nor an organization, so `userMigrationPassCohort` and the
targeted-run refusal are genuine correctness there and are untouched.
The bulk-enrollment suggestion pool keeps its own exclusion too.

* feat(migration): drive passes at boot until the fleet stops moving

One pass was never enough on its own. A pass cannot observe its own
events, so an organization it adopts reads as held and only a LATER pass
finalizes it — which made convergence a function of the deploy cadence,
or of a self-hosted operator clicking "run a pass" until the counts
settled. The boot loop now runs passes until one advances nothing.

The stop condition is no progress, not "everything is terminal": a held
tenant is re-proved on every pass and may never reach a terminal state,
so a terminal-based condition would spin forever. No existing summary
field could carry that meaning — `held` counts a `migrated` write, and a
held tenant is re-written `migrated` every pass — so the summary gains
`advanced`, the count of state TRANSITIONS a pass made, including a
tenant's first record. A tenant parked the same way twice does not count
either.

Bounded anyway: a five-second gap between passes, which has to clear a
fold round trip so the next pass can finalize what this one stated
rather than re-holding it, and a 25-pass cap that logs loudly if it is
ever reached, since that means a status that keeps changing without
settling. A failed pass ends the run rather than retrying on a
five-second cadence against whatever is already down.

The ops page's manual single pass is unchanged.

* test(identity): drive an enterprise SSO sign-in through the adapter

Enterprise SSO is the population D02 moves across, and its latched
sign-in was the one path the end-to-end suites never drove: they cover
credential and social only. Adds a latched user holding an identifier
that arrived from a generic-OAuth IdP, signing in through the callback
with every legacy Account row cleared, so whatever answers came out of

Asserts the folded vocabulary never leaks back: `providerId` returns

echoing back.

The fourth case, two IdPs minting the same subject, is committed SKIPPED

reads `Identifier.providerId`, so the two collapse onto one identifier
and production's `ORDER BY attachedAt ASC LIMIT 1` signs the second

* fix(identity): key the provider-subject lookup on the verbatim provider id

An OIDC subject is unique only WITHIN an issuer, but every lookup on the
identity branch matched on `Identifier.provider` — the folded vocabulary
that collapses auth0, okta and every custom OIDC connection into `oidc`.
Two enterprise IdPs minting the same subject string therefore resolved to
one identifier, and production's `ORDER BY attachedAt ASC LIMIT 1` handed
the second customer the first one's account. Legacy never had this:
`Account` is unique on the verbatim pair.

Both ports, the adapter and both Prisma repositories now key on
`(providerId, providerAccountId)` — the same pair `Account` is unique by —
and a partial unique index over the live states enforces it, so the
identity branch namespaces IdPs exactly as legacy does. The folded
`provider` keeps its semantics everywhere it carries them; it simply
stops being a match key.

The index is unique where `value` cannot be: one user legitimately holds
several proven identifiers for one address, but a provider subject names
exactly one account at exactly one IdP. Partial on the live states so
re-linking a previously unlinked provider account still works.

Forward constraint, written into the migration, the schema and ADR-116: a
subject is unique PER CONNECTION, and `providerId` only stands in for the
connection while there is one connection per configured provider. The
Auth0 exit ends that, so when connections become data every connection
must get its own provider id or the index must gain `connectionId`. A
test pins that no two configured providers collapse onto one id today.

The fold stays total if the constraint is ever violated anyway: the
incumbent keeps the subject and the newcomer is parked with a WARN naming
both identifiers and both users, so that user stays held rather than the
projection stopping for everybody.

* docs(identity): the live-states constant names the index that copies it

Migration 20260824120004's partial unique index enumerates ATTACHED,
VERIFIED and PRIMARY as SQL literals, because a migration is immutable
history and cannot import LIVE_IDENTIFIER_STATES. Everything else that
needs the list reads the constant, so adding a fourth live state would be
followed silently by isLiveIdentifierState and every repository IN clause
while the index stayed on three — and a row in the new state could then
duplicate a provider subject with nothing stopping it, which is the
cross-tenant sign-in that index exists to close.

The note lives on the constant, where that change would actually be made,
and names the migration so it is greppable. The migration carries the
reciprocal pointer.

* fix(identity): the address lock answers with a row that exists

`claim()` inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and then read the holder
back in a second statement. A `release()` or `reapOrphans()` deleting the
incumbent between the two made that read return nothing, and the caller
was handed its own claim — told it held a lock with no row behind it. The
next caller, inserting into the now-free key, was told the same. Two
users then stage facts for one address, which is the cross-user
double-verification this table exists to prevent, and nothing downstream
catches it because `Identifier.value` deliberately carries no unique
constraint. `reapOrphans` cannot help: the defect is a MISSING row, not a
stale one.

One statement now. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING returns the row
that ends up holding the key — this caller's on an insert, the
incumbent's on a conflict — where DO NOTHING ... RETURNING returns
nothing. Concurrent claimants on one key serialize on that row lock,
which is what we want. Structural rather than a retry, so the race cannot
be reasoned about wrongly again, and the comment now states what holds
instead of rationalizing the hole.

The pipeline test takes USER_IDENTITY_AGGREGATE_TYPE from the constant
rather than casting the string.

* fix(migration): the rollback pin works for every organization

Automatic enrollment removed `withdraw` as a lever and pointed operators
at `rollBack`, which then refused the two cases that need it most: an
organization that parks every pass, and one the migration has not
reached. Both were unstoppable at runtime, and the boot loop now
re-drives a parked one up to MAX_PASSES per boot.

The pin is now placeable from any status and from no record at all,
because stopping the pass is the point. The rollback EFFECT still runs
only for statuses that could have reached the ledger — a parked
organization and one with no record never cut over, so there is nothing
to undo and an effect written for a cutover has no defined meaning
against one that never was. `ROLLBACK_ELIGIBLE_STATUSES` and its two
handled errors are gone rather than left vacuous; per-migration refusals
still live in `rollbackGuards`, whose record is now nullable. Ops page
and dialog copy say what is actually true.

The convergence loop no longer reads its own shut-out as convergence.
`lease.acquire` fails safe to false on contention AND on any Redis
error, so a pass where every tenant was claimed reports exactly what a
converged fleet reports; several pods booting together was enough to
stop them all. Nothing advanced now means convergence only when the pass
got to look at something, with an empty fleet still converging.

The detach fallback keys on the verbatim `providerId`. It matched on the
folded vocabulary, so with one live `oidc` identifier a user unlinking a
different enterprise account detached the sign-in they still use —
reachable via the collision park, which leaves an `Account` row with no

The collision-park containment claim was overstated and is corrected in
place: it holds for a user the backfill still visits, and not for one
already finalized, whom the runner never revisits.

fix(langy): the transcript reads in the order the turn happened (#7510)

* fix(langy): keep a turn's real order in the record, and stop the workbench blaming the reader

Two things the reader sees, both wrong for the same reason: the record did not
keep what happened, and the page said a change came from somewhere else when it
came from Langy in that very tab.

## The record keeps the turn's real order

A turn was recorded as every tool call first and the reply after them, built
from the text the agent wrote after its LAST call. Everything written between
calls lived only on the live edge, so a reader who refreshed got a pile of cards
and one closing paragraph, and the account of the work was gone. A real
optimization turn recorded 31 calls and one paragraph.

The live stream already carries the true order, so the relay reads it once at
finalize and folds it into the turn's own account: consecutive deltas become the
paragraph between two calls, and a call takes its place where it STARTED, which
is where its card belongs and where the panel already draws it live.
`buildFinalAssistantParts` records that order. The agent's own final text stays
authoritative for the reply, so nothing is written twice.

Without an account the record keeps the shape it always had, so a turn that
outlived its buffer, or one finalized by the agent's HTTP post, still records
honestly. Only one path ever stores a turn, so the two shapes never mix.

The skill was telling the agent to hoard its text until the end, and it named
this bug as the reason. It now says to narrate as it works.

## The workbench stops blaming the reader for Langy's work

A tab with unsaved edits already has a save on the way, and that save's answer
is the authority: a new version, or a refusal that banners with the server's own
account. Bannering on the version signal instead told the reader their work
clashed with "somewhere else" while Langy was driving THAT TAB, seconds before
their own save landed and settled it. A tab now waits for its own answer, and
banners only once autosave has stood down and nothing else is coming.

The version probe also passed no actor and the endpoint returned none, so even a
change Langy made read as a stranger. `getWorkbenchVersion` returns who wrote
the version and the probe carries it into the banner.

Specs: specs/langy/langy-capability-cards.feature (four scenarios under "The
transcript reads in the order the turn happened"),
specs/langy/langy-ui-actions-fallback.feature (the tab waits for its own answer,
and a change Langy made is named as Langy's).

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01G8hWrvamDKFMpH6DJQUWSW

* fix(langy): read a turn's order where the turn is recorded, and name who wrote a refused save

Two paths finish a Langy turn and race each other: the live relay's terminal
frame, and the agent's own result post over HTTP. The ingest keeps whichever
lands first. The order was read in the relay, and the relay loses that race
almost every time, so a real optimization turn was still recorded as 25 tool
cards followed by one closing paragraph.

The account is now read by `ingestAgentTurnResult` itself, through a reader
injected next to the other Langy stores. Both paths assemble the same parts,
and the shape no longer depends on who won. `LangyRelayBuffer` drops the
`readTail` it only needed for this.

A turn that goes quiet after its last call hands over its WHOLE narration as
the reply, because there is no closing paragraph to hand over instead.
Recording that reply after the account printed every paragraph a second time,
below the cards it was written between, so `orderedParts` tells the two endings
apart: a turn that ended on a paragraph replaces the account's copy of it with
the authoritative one, a turn that ended on a call is recorded as it stands.

Proven on the running stack. A full optimization loop now records 27 cards and
18 paragraphs interleaved, where the same task recorded 25 cards then one
paragraph, and the reloaded page reads in the same order the live panel drew.

## A refused save says who holds the newer version

A tab with unsaved edits reaches the banner through its own refused save, not
through the version signal, so the refusal is the path that most needs the
name. It carried only the version number, so the banner said the change came
from "somewhere else" while Langy was driving that very tab.
`StaleWorkbenchStateError` now carries the author of the current version, read
on the save's own transaction, and autosave passes it into the banner.

Specs: specs/langy/langy-capability-cards.feature (a turn that ends on a call
does not repeat what it already wrote, the order does not depend on which path
finished the turn, and a turn whose order cannot be read is still recorded),
specs/langy/langy-ui-actions-fallback.feature (a refused save names who holds
the newer version).

The Langy rollout levers are SYSTEM with `envOverridable: false` on purpose, so

* fix(experiments): a refusal names the version the server holds, and a failed save stops silencing the tab

Four findings from review, each with the test that fails without the fix.

## A refused save reports the version the server holds now

`refuseAsStale` reported the version read at the top of the transaction. At
READ COMMITTED the compare-and-set can lose to a write that committed after
that read, so the loser of a race was told to reload to the version it already
had, under the winner's author. It now reads the row again on the same
connection and reports what it finds, and an archived row reads as not found.

## An actor label names the version it belongs to

`latestAuthorLabel` took the newest version row whatever version it described.
A workflow evaluation moves the counter without writing a version row, so the
newest row can be older than the current version, and the read named a person
for a write the platform made. `authorOfVersion` now names an author only when
the row's version matches the one being reported.

## A tab whose save failed still hears the next version

`thisTabWillAnswerFirst` treated every dirty workbench as one with an answer on
the way. A save that failed for any reason other than a newer version leaves
the workbench dirty and schedules no retry, so there was no answer coming and
the tab stayed silent about every later version until the reader happened to
type again. An errored autosave now reads as stood down, which is what a
refusal already did.

## hasProse

`wroteProse` carries no `is`/`has`/`should`/`can`/`will` prefix, which is the
repo rule and what ast-grep flags.

Specs: specs/experiments-v3/workbench-versioning.feature (a refusal names the
version the server holds now, a version with no row of its own names nobody),
specs/langy/langy-ui-actions-fallback.feature (a tab whose autosave failed
still hears the next version).

TypeScript 7 shipped and the native binary was renamed. getExePath
picks "tsc" when the package is `typescript` and "tsgo" only when it is
not, so an installed typescript@7 resolves to a binary called tsc - and
tsc.js hands the process to it with execve, leaving no node wrapper
behind. haven selected the governor's candidates with
binaryBase(command) == "tsgo", so on a TS7 machine the ADR-095 governor
was selecting nothing: no per-run ceiling, no combined budget, no
runaway reclamation, over the single largest transient memory consumer
in the repo. ClassifyWatchedProcess did not know the name either, so a
typecheck was not even observed.

The selection rule is now name-neutral - one predicate over both
binaries, still matched on the binary base name rather than on args, so
`grep tsgo server.log` is still not a compiler. Both names resolve to
ONE class, so a mixed sample is one budget rather than two half-budgets.
The class string stays spelled "tsgo", now behind a constant: it is an
OTel attribute on four metrics and a persisted ReapEvent kind, and
renaming it would cut the recorded history in two at exactly the moment
the point of the change is to join the two binaries. The governor's
types and its four documented HAVEN_TSGO_* knobs keep their spelling
for the same reason.

The gate could not take the same shortcut. heavyCommands is matched
with strings.Contains, and "tsc" is a substring of tsconfig.json - so
`cat tsconfig.json`, `git diff tsconfig.json` and every
`-p tsconfig.tsgo.json` argument would have classed heavy, which is the
over-match that list's own comment warns about. Binaries are matched as
words by last path segment instead. DurationKey needed the same fix:
a binary-matched run fell through to no bucket, and an unbucketed
command is treated as long, which silently disables narrowing.

Nothing regresses for tsgo: the preview package is still live on this
machine and both paths stay governed. Narrowing the predicate back to
tsgo alone fails six tests across two packages.

ADR-095 gains a dated amendment rather than a rewrite.

test(process-manager): the fencing test waits for the lease instead of sleeping (#7527)

* test(process-manager): the fencing test waits for the lease instead of sleeping

The case pins what happens when a delivery is still running as its lease
lapses and a rival finishes the message: the superseded acknowledgement is
reported as fenced rather than silently dropped. It set that race up by
starting the slow dispatcher, sleeping 150ms, and hoping the slow one had
leased the message and entered its handler by then.

Neither is guaranteed. On a loaded runner the slow dispatcher can lose the
race to lease at all, in which case it returns the all-empty report; or it
can lease and then be shed by the lease-budget guard on the way to the
handler, in which case the message lands in `released`. Both report an
empty `fenced` and fail the assertion, which is what happened on main.

The handler now signals on entry and the test waits for that signal, which
establishes both facts the race needs: the lease is held, and the budget
guard has already been cleared, since it runs before the handler does. The
lapse itself no longer comes from waiting either — a lease is due again
once `leasedUntil <= now` and `now` is the caller's, so the rival simply
runs with its clock advanced past the lease. The lease is widened to 5s to
put the budget guard out of reach; nothing waits for it to expire.

Closes #7526

* test(process-manager): a delivery that never starts fails instead of hanging

Waiting on the entry signal alone had one bad outcome left: if the slow
dispatcher leased nothing, the await would never resolve and the run would
burn the full 60s test timeout before reporting a timeout rather than the
reason. Racing the run against the signal turns that into an assertion that
names what happened.

* fix(authz): answer a blank scope id as invalid input, not a wiring bug

A client that sent `projectId: ""` passed input validation — every router
schema declares `z.string()`, which accepts the empty string — and then
landed in the declared-permission middleware's wiring-bug backstop, which
logs at ERROR severity and returns an opaque 500.

The types guarantee the scope FIELD exists on the input; they never
guaranteed a caller fills it. So an ordinary bad request was being
reported as a platform fault, and it paged us: prod saw it as a new error
signature, from a first-render race at app boot where one query fires
before the project context resolves.

`resolveDeclaredScope` now says why it could not name a scope — `blank`
(the input named the field and left it empty) or `absent` (no usable
scope field at all). The middleware answers the first as a handled
`validation_error` at 400, and keeps the ERROR log and the 500 for the
second, which really is ours. A blank id still never shadows a wider tier
the caller did fill in, so an empty projectId alongside a real
organizationId checks at the organization exactly as before.

Decided at the one seam every declaration passes through, so all the
`.permission()` sites get it without touching ~197 input schemas.

Review asked for non-string and undefined values to be reclassified as

request, which is the failure this split exists to end. The distinction is
whose mistake it is, not the value's type — a field the caller was asked to
fill and filled badly is theirs to correct whatever they put in it. In the
real request path the point is moot, since the declaration's parser runs
ahead of the check and a wrong-typed id is already a 400 before it.

someone reading the same suggestion, and the doc now says "no usable id"
rather than "empty", which is what the code has always done.

`namesField` was written to survive a non-object input — its docblock calls
that "the very case this whole path exists to survive" — but the resolution
walk above it read `input[field]` first, so a `null` handed over by a
bypassed type layer threw instead of answering `absent`. The module promised
a guarantee it only half kept.

Which is this change's own lesson said twice. The bug it fixes is a value the
types said could not arrive, arriving; `input` is declared
`Partial<Record<ScopeTierField, unknown>>` and the declaration is not what
turns up at runtime. So the input is normalized once, before anything reads a
field off it, and both the walk and the blank/absent decision read the

* fix(identity): an unenrolled organization writes nothing extra on sign-up

The hook is deleted rather than gated, because gated it would be unreachable

* perf(identity): the gate costs one read per pod before anyone is enrolled

The read fork asks the gate on every authenticated request, so before any
operator has enrolled anybody it was one indexed lookup per active user per
TTL to learn something a single row settles: whether ANY user has finalized.

`hasFinalizedTenant` on the state port answers that, and the gate consults it
first through the same cache primitive with one constant subject - so it is
one read per pod per TTL, coalesced across concurrent requests, and it
disables itself the moment the first organization is enrolled. It fails in
the same direction as the per-user read (unreadable means closed) and lands
on the same counter, because to an operator it is the same failure with the
same consequence.

* feat(identity): ADR-116 - split Account along the truth line

The linkage half - who holds which sign-in method - is `Identifier`, built
by the fold. The credential half is a new `AccountCredential` table: row
truth, permanently, because tokens and passwords can never be events (the
payload rule) and OAuth refresh rewrites them on a cadence no event log
should carry. `AccountCredential.id` IS the old `Account.id`, which
`Identifier.accountId` already points at, so nothing is re-keyed.

`Identifier` gains `providerAccountId`, without which the projection cannot
answer the one question an IdP callback asks - "who is signing in?" - and
the legacy Account row stays the only answer, which is the duplication this
ADR removes. It was already part of the identifier's derived id; it just was
never stated on the fact. Free to add now and not later: the write gate
ships closed, so no identity event has ever been emitted anywhere.

Also lands `LIVE_IDENTIFIER_STATES` beside `isLiveIdentifierState`, so a
repository's SQL `IN` and the predicate cannot drift about whether a
tombstone may sign someone in.

Everything here is additive and dark. `Account` is untouched and stays
authoritative for every user until their backfill finalizes.

* feat(identity): better-auth reads accounts from the projection (ADR-116)

`IdentityAccountAdapter` fronts better-auth's `account` model and delegates
every other model to the stock prismaAdapter, method for method. Reads are
`Identifier` joined with `AccountCredential`; a token refresh writes secrets
and emits nothing, because a refresh is not a fact.

This is NOT the routing facade ADR-101 §2 removed. That one kept
better-auth's storage AND emitted events, which is exactly what made every
linkage fact exist twice. This one REPLACES storage for one model, so there
is one copy.

The query surface is enumerated (`account-queries.ts`) and an unrecognised
shape THROWS. That is load-bearing rather than bookkeeping: a `findOne`
answering null reads precisely like "no such account", which is how a person
gets told their sign-in method does not exist. A better-auth upgrade that
issues a new shape now fails a test instead of a sign-in.

The fallback to the legacy `Account` table is the migration, not a hedge: a
user whose backfill has not finalized holds no identifiers, the projection
answers nothing, and their legacy row answers - which is still their truth
and their only one. Per user, one source of truth, as ADR-110 has it. The
fallback goes when nobody is left on it, and that drop is the real exit gate.

* test(identity): stub the whole identity runtime in the router test

The router reaches the composition root for the ceremony; the module graph
behind it (auth -> better-auth) now reaches the same module for the account
adapter and the hooks, so a mock of one export leaves the graph unloadable.

* test(identity): drive better-auth end to end, and find the adapter's ceiling

Closes the two verification gaps ADR-116 shipped with, and in doing so
finds that the storage-replacing adapter cannot work in the shape it was
built.

Verification that was missing:

  - PrismaAccountCredentialsRepository had no integration tests while
    every other identity repository did. It has 14 now, over real
    Postgres: the ms/Date crossing, absent-vs-null patch semantics, the
    idempotent retry, and the one-credential-per-identifier index.
  - The three reads ADR-116 added to the heads repository had no
    integration coverage either - including the (provider, subject)
    lookup the whole read path depends on.
  - Two exact-shape assertions still described an IdentifierFact without
    `providerAccountId`, so they would have failed on the first
    datastore run. Fixed.
  - The account_credential_split migration had never touched a live
    Postgres. It applies, and its seed clauses were exercised against
    representative rows on a scratch database: providerAccountId is
    filled from the Account each identifier was adopted from, one
    credential row is written per adopted identifier with the Account's
    own timestamps, an unbackfilled user contributes nothing, and a
    re-run inserts nothing new.

What driving the real library found:

  1. better-auth runs sign-up inside `adapter.transaction`, and for that
     request `transaction` is the ONLY method it calls on the adapter.
     Passing the callback straight through handed better-auth the stock
     engine for the whole transaction, so `account` stopped being
     intercepted exactly where accounts are created. The transactional
     engine is now re-wrapped.

  2. The design has a ceiling that fix does not reach. `findUserByEmail`
     asks for the user with `join: { account: true }`. Joins are off by
     default, so `createAdapterFactory` satisfies the join itself with a
     second query through the adapter instance it was built around. This
     class wraps a FINISHED adapter, so it sits ABOVE that factory and
     never sees that query: a migrated user's sign-in reads the legacy
     table, finds nothing, and fails.

Wrapping a built adapter therefore cannot intercept a model completely -
the factory's own traffic is below the wrapper. The suite pins this
rather than hiding it: the direct queries are proven to answer from the
projection, and the sign-in that cannot work is marked as the defect it
is, to be inverted when the design is settled.

* refactor(identity): Account is a projection, not a peer (ADR-116 v2)

The storage-replacing adapter is deleted. Driving the real better-auth
library proved it cannot work, and the reason generalises rather than
being a slip:

  - `findUserByEmail(email, { includeAccounts: true })` asks for the user
    with `join: { account: true }`. Joins are off by default, and when
    they are off `createAdapterFactory` satisfies the join ITSELF, with a
    second query issued through the adapter instance it was built around.
    An adapter wrapping a finished `prismaAdapter` sits ABOVE that
    factory and never sees that query.
  - Sign-up runs inside `adapter.transaction`, and for that request
    `transaction` is the only method better-auth calls on the adapter.

One rule behind both: wrapping a built adapter cannot intercept a model,
because the factory's own traffic is below the wrapper. better-auth
documents no per-model storage routing at all.

So stop standing in front of it. `Account` is demoted from a source of
truth to a PROJECTION of the event log, alongside `Identifier`:

  - better-auth reads and writes `Account` with the completely stock
    adapter. Nothing intercepts it, so every join, transaction and query
    shape - present and future - is the library's own.
  - The fold owns its linkage columns and reconciles existence: a live
    identifier projects to a row, a tombstoned one projects to none.
  - The seam stays where better-auth documents it, `databaseHooks`, and
    does what it says: better-auth calls event sourcing.

Deleted: IdentityAccountAdapter, IdentityAccountStore, account-queries,
account-projection, AccountCredential and its repository - and with them
the enumerated query surface, the dual-read, the legacy-table fallback
and an error a better-auth upgrade could trip. `AccountCredential` was
not merely unnecessary once the adapter went, it was unreachable: the
stock adapter writes tokens to `Account.access_token` and can write them
nowhere else.

The fold's write set is `id`, `userId`, `provider`, `providerAccountId`
and nothing more. `type` is left to its default - a legacy NextAuth
column better-auth does not even map, so deriving it would be guessing.
An integration test writes real secrets, re-asserts the row from the
log, and fails if any of them moved: a replay that clobbered
`access_token` would undo a token refresh that legitimately happened
after the event.

The unshipped migration is corrected in place and renamed to what it
actually does - it adds `Identifier.providerAccountId` and its indexes,
without which the fold cannot reproduce `Account.providerAccountId`.

Verified: 65 tests in identity-server (including six driving real
better-auth end to end - sign-up, the joined sign-in read that defeated
the adapter, the account list, a password change, a link and a delete),
26 in identity, 23 identity integration tests against a freshly migrated
Postgres, 427 app unit tests, both packages typecheck, 39/39 scenarios
bound.

* docs(identity): ADR-116 - one storage adapter, and Account retires

better-auth keeps one database entry forever: an identity-owned adapter
built AT createAdapterFactory - the documented seam, and the only level
where the factory's own traffic (fallback joins, transactions) lands on
the implementation rather than below it. Inside it, the existing per-user
write gate routes between the stock Prisma behaviour (legacy users,
byte-for-byte) and event-sourced storage (latched users): linkage facts to
the event log folding into Identifier, secrets in a row-truth
AccountCredential. The end state serves the account model from
Identifier + AccountCredential and drops the Account table, restoring
"no table mixes truths" - every table single-truth, multi-email native.

Delivery is three phases, each deploy removing the previous phase's
mechanism: (1) the bridge - stock adapter, databaseHooks ceremonies, fold
dual-projection, no adapter at all; (2) the adapter goes live, latching
copies secrets across, and secrets mirror BOTH ways while the bridge
table exists so either branch authenticates at any moment; (3) last
tenant finalized - legacy branch, ceremonies, parity check and Account
are deleted.

The spec (specs/identity/identity-storage-adapter.feature, 31 scenarios,
@unimplemented until the adapter PR binds them) pins the routing rules,
the flagged sign-up as an idempotent sequence with retries rather than a
pretended cross-store transaction, cross-population email collisions at
verify time, the reverse secret heal, the OAuth callback resolution, the
account-id contract, deletion and erasure fan-out, and the loud-failure
codes (identity_engine_unavailable, identity_email_in_use,
identity_unsupported_storage_query) that reach the customer through the
presentation registry.

User-model reads are never routed - the User table stays complete for
both populations via the primary-identifier email polyfill, so admin
population queries never fork. Resolution reads join the migration-state
row directly instead of the gate's TTL cache, normalize the queried value
with the D01 normalizer, and fall through to the legacy branch on a miss
or a held user.

Cross-references updated to the phased shape: ADR-115's better-auth
subpath note, the identity-server README and module headers, the
better-auth composition comment, the D01 spec's truth-split header (the
Account row is a projection for as long as it exists), and D09's cutover
proof now reads Identifier, never Account.

(auto-link only on two-sided verification evidence, LinkProposed
otherwise), and the ADR-027 amendment - per-method policy owns the
decision, the before hook survives as the enforcement backstop, and every
locked semantic (startup-frozen license gate, constants table, route

for review: Q11 startup semantics kept, Q9 reset follows the identifier,
Q12 no-oracle scoped to sign-in. Named debt: the SAML engine choice, due
at D04 implementation. Under ADR-116 the router carries no per-user read
fork - resolution is the storage adapter's.

Four Wave 2 spec files, every scenario @unimplemented until its PR binds
it (LEGACY_INERT entries with removal notes, the identity-storage-adapter
pattern): signin-router (D03, 18 scenarios), signin-signup-screens (D13,
14), sso-connection-lifecycle (D04, 17), resilient-invitations (D11, 12).
Reviewed against the corpus: three scenarios that duplicated bound
anchors (reset no-oracle, half-created-account recovery, expired-invite

respects the no-email-installation invite-link rule.

The delivery plan gains the Wave 2 PR breakdown - docs/specs (this PR),

as the router's in-wave precondition.

* feat(invites): 14-day expiry, REVOKED state, and the acceptance claim

D11's state model (specs/identity/resilient-invitations.feature): the
expiry window grows from 48 hours to 14 days now that resend will be one
click, revocation becomes a visible REVOKED state instead of a row
delete, and EXPIRED is derived from the expiration column everywhere it
is asked - display, acceptance, resend - so there is no sweeper to run
and no row to forget.

Acceptance now CLAIMS the row: a conditional update on the expected
(status, inviteCode) pair inside the same transaction as the membership
write, recording who accepted and through which identifier. Two racers
on one PENDING invite cannot both win - the loser's claim matches
nothing, their membership write rolls back, and they see a stale-code
refusal; a caller racing its own accept re-runs the idempotent grant
tail instead, the same repair the ACCEPTED-retry path already made
reachable.

The accept endpoint stops conflating its refusals: a revoked invitation
reads exactly like a missing one on purpose (the journey ends quietly,
naming nothing), while expired gets its own handled code -
invite_expired, with registry copy pointing at the one-click resend -
because expiry is recoverable and a dead end here was the support pain.

The invitation list now returns expired and revoked rows with a derived
displayStatus, so an admin resends an EXPIRED invitation instead of
wondering where it went.

Schema: INVITE_STATUS gains REVOKED (WAITING_APPROVAL stays, deprecated,
pending its retirement commit), OrganizationInvite gains
acceptedByUserId + acceptedViaIdentifierId. Additive migration only.

* feat(invites): acceptance works through any verified identifier

The wrong-method dead end (D11): an invitation targets an address, and
any VERIFIED identifier holding that address vouches for the person -
password, Google, or the org's SSO. The user invited by email who signed
in with their Google account stops being a support ticket.

`matchableEmailsOf` (@langwatch/identity) answers every PRIMARY and
VERIFIED value whatever method proved it - wider than `primaryEmailOf`
on purpose, because acceptance asks "who vouches for this address",
not "which address is this person's". ATTACHED stays ineligible, same
rule for the same reason: an unproven address must never open someone
else's invitation. `IdentityEmailService.verifiedEmailsOf` serves it
behind the same gate-then-heads read fork as `resolveEmail`, null on
any failure so the acceptance path can never break on the fork.

The accept endpoint matches the invite's D01-normalized email against
that set for users on identifiers, recording which identifier vouched
(`acceptedViaIdentifierId`); a user not yet on identifiers keeps the
legacy case-insensitive session-email comparison byte-for-byte. For a
latched user the proven set is the authority - a session email nothing
verified does not accept.

* feat(invites): one-click resend

D11's recovery affordance: `resendInvite` mints a fresh invite code and a
fresh 14-day expiry on the same row and sends a new email - an expired
invitation stops being a dead end. Rotating the code IS the old link's
revocation: after the resend, a leaked stale link matches no row.

Resend claims the row the way acceptance does - a conditional update on
the (status, inviteCode) pair it read - so two admins racing a resend
mint exactly one live code and the loser reads as not found. Only
PENDING rows (including expired ones, which is the point) can be resent;
revoked and accepted invitations stay what they are. An email failure
never reverts the resend, matching approval's contract: the fresh link
exists and is returned as the fallback.

Exposed as organization.resendInvite behind organization:manage.

* refactor(invites): retire the member-approval workflow, show the states

The WAITING_APPROVAL flow is retired end to end (D11, epic Q13): the
member-wants-a-colleague-in motivation moves to D12's join requests, so
createInviteRequest, approveInvite, createMemberInviteRequest, the
WaitingApprovalActions component and the approval wiring on the members
page are deleted. Existing WAITING_APPROVAL rows close as REVOKED by
data migration - they were never actionable invitations (no email, no
shared code) - and the Postgres enum value stays, deprecated, because
dropping one means rebuilding the type. Duplicate checks, revocation,
listing and the license member count stop naming it.

The invites table now shows the D11 states: every invitation carries its
derived display status (Invited / Expired / Revoked) and expiry date, an
expired invitation offers one-click resend, revocation is a visible
state, and a revoked row keeps no actions. useInviteActions drops the
request/approve handlers and gains resend - which surfaces the fresh
link when the installation sends no email - and revoke with honest copy.

The invites integration suite is rewritten around the new lifecycle:
identifier-aware acceptance (the identity read fork mocked at the
boundary, values D01-normalized), the wrong-method dead end, both
support-pain replays, resend round-trips including the dead old link,
quiet revocation, exactly-once retry, and the visible states - 13
scenarios against real Postgres. Teardown covers the personal workspaces
acceptance provisions and deletes invitee users by accumulated id.

Also: handled 410s map to NOT_FOUND at the tRPC boundary instead of
falling through to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR - invite_expired is the first
410 a handled error raises.

* feat(invites): bind the D11 spec, slim the old one, match as a function

specs/identity/resilient-invitations.feature goes live: 11/11 scenarios
bound (unit and integration), off LEGACY_INERT; the one scenario still
@unimplemented - guided sign-up from an invite link - waits for D13's

(duplicate-skip on the attach, not a named idempotency key), and the

specs/members/update-pending-invitation.feature slims to what it still

The acceptance match moves into matchInviteToAcceptor, a pure exported

Delivery plan gains the D11 landed note: the identifier-aware match is
inert until users finalize (the read fork answers null pre-latch), the

* feat(identity): the sign-in router is a pure decision engine

Email in, decision out. The engine takes no user data at all, so
ADR-117's no-oracle rule holds by construction: an unknown address and a
known one on the same non-routing domain are the same call, and there is
no branch that could tell them apart.

Everything it needs arrives through two ports a composition layer fills
- an org-level domain lookup and an instance-level method policy - so
D04's swap from ssoDomain strings to the SsoConnection projection never
reaches the router.

The service around it records every decision with its reason code, and
with the domain of the address rather than the local part. Break-glass
reads nothing: the door exists for the days the connection store is what
is broken.

* feat(identity): one flag, and the router runs in shadow

IDENTITY_ROUTER_V2 is three-valued and ships off. Off, the legacy path
is byte-for-byte untouched: the shadow returns before it reads,
computes or logs anything. In shadow it decides on every live login and
compares its answer against what the legacy path actually gave, logging
the pair when they disagree. It throws nothing - the one thing a
comparison must never be is the reason someone cannot log in.

The comparison is a projection onto the one word the legacy front door
answers: email, or the provider it redirects to. That is what makes it a
comparison rather than two unrelated logs.

The router is composed here over the data that exists today - ssoDomain
strings for domains, NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER as the instance's one connection
- so D04's swap is a line in the runtime.

* refactor(auth): ADR-027 gates by method policy, the hook is the backstop

The before-hook used to ask the env and the license gate directly. It
now asks the router's method policy, which asks the same gate - the same
per-process memo, so a license still takes effect on restart and never
mid-flight. Every ADR-027 semantic survives: denied is email mode
exactly, the credential-mutation block holds in every state, the reset
pair stays open on deny.

The decision moved to where the data is. Enforcement did not, and could
not: absence from a picker enforces nothing for a pinned legacy callback
URL, and the hook is still the only interception point that sees the
callback rewrite.

That makes this a mechanism change to the guard a whole license gate
rests on, so the route-table canary is doubled rather than moved - one
over the path predicate, one driving the real hook end to end. Both read
one classification table, so a route better-auth adds fails both by
name.

* feat(identity): the callback links when the evidence is two-sided

A known subject signs straight in and states nothing new. An unambiguous
match auto-links. Everything short of that becomes a proposal a human
resolves, and no match at all is provisioned only where the connection
allows it.

Two-sided is the load-bearing word. Trusting the IdP's email_verified
alone would let any connection claim any row on its domain, so the
matched user has to hold the address themselves, verified, and hold
nothing the organization cannot vouch for. An ambiguous match proposes
against every candidate rather than picking one - picking one is the
guess the branch exists to avoid.

The service never writes an Account row and never attaches an identifier
itself. It asks the directory to create the provider account, which is
better-auth's write, which fires the ceremony that attaches through the
pipeline. LinkProposed joins the identity vocabulary as a real fact: the
refusal an operator is asked about later is evidenced rather than
reconstructed.

* test(identity): bind the sign-in router spec, drop its inert entry

17 of 18 scenarios bound, and the file leaves LEGACY_INERT with them. The
one left parked is the pendingSsoSetup reconciliation, which is bake-end
work: the column is still read, so declaring it done would be a lie the
check would then enforce.

* feat(identity): one endpoint for the questions a signed-out visitor asks

The screens hold no routing logic, so everything they need to know is a
question for the server: where does this address sign in, is this sign-up
address confirmed, and who is asking me to join. All three live in one
public router, rate-limited, with answers written to be safe in front of
whoever arrived rather than whoever they were meant for.

Routing is a mutation rather than a query on purpose. A query would be
cached per address, and a per-address cache entry is an account-existence
oracle built out of network timing - the engine cannot tell a registered
address from an unregistered one, and this keeps the transport from
learning it either.

The browser learns only the derived answer to the flag: whether the
identifier-first screens are live. The router also runs in shadow, and
screens never render then, so exposing the mode itself would be exposing
a state the browser must not act on.

* feat(identity): nothing exists until the address is confirmed

Sign-up asks for an address and stops there. What it leaves behind is a
single-use token with an hour on it and nothing else, so an abandoned
sign-up costs nothing and an expired one is recoverable by asking again.
The token rides the VerificationToken table, which is already a
single-use token store keyed by an opaque string, so this needs no schema
of its own.

A token may carry a pending credential: the password somebody typed into
the log-in form for an address nobody holds. That is the same journey
arriving from the other door, so it is answered the same way, and the
account is created when the link comes back. Only the hash is held, and
an address that gained an account in the meantime is left alone - the
link confirms an address, it does not entitle it to overwrite whatever
now answers for it.

Both doors write the account through one function. Two writers for a User
row and its credential Account row is how one of them ends up creating a
user nobody can sign in as.

* feat(auth): the front door is ours, and it has no dead ends

One funnel, entered from either side. The address goes first, the server
says where it signs in, and the screen renders that answer: a domain that
routes to an identity provider never shows a password field at all,
because the hand-off comes first.

Neither door refuses. Signing up with an address that already has an
account quietly becomes logging in - no banner, no notice, just the
log-in step with the address already in it. A password typed for an
address nobody holds becomes a sign-up, confirmed by email, with the same
"check your email" the other page would have shown. A wrong password for
an account that does exist still says so, in the words the failure-message
anchors hold.

The card is the same on every installation; a hosted signup wears its
pitch outside it, through slots the shell fills. The surface follows the
website - the brand orange, pill actions, the mesh band - through custom
properties declared for both colour modes, so the mode toggle moves these
screens with everything else. Motion is three small things and every one
of them stands down under prefers-reduced-motion.

Behind IDENTITY_ROUTER_V2. Not enforced, every legacy screen renders
exactly as before: the flag adds a branch in front of them and changes
nothing inside them.

* feat(auth): the hosted front door makes its case beside the card

A desktop signup gets two halves: the headline and its tagline over the
mesh band on the left, the card on the right behind a hairline. The card
does not change - it is the same component, in the same place, and
nothing inside it knows which half of the page it is on.

Everything the panel holds is a slot the shell fills. A company's own
installation renders none of it and gets the plain centred card, which is
the same code path with nothing passed to it. The trusted-by row stays an

Below the split it collapses to the headline alone. A tagline and a logo
row stacked above a log-in form on a phone are two screens of scrolling
in front of the thing the person came to do.

The gradient rides one word, split out of the copy string rather than
authored as markup, so the line stays something a writer can change
without opening a component.

* feat(auth): the mark the loading screen was showing walks into the card

Same mark, same size, same place it was already on screen - LoadingScreen
centres FullLogo at 155x38 scaled 1.2, and the flight starts from exactly
there - so the two screens read as one element moving rather than two
elements swapping. It lands on the card's own logo slot and cross-fades
into it, because the card's mark is the icon alone.

FLIP, transform only: the slot is measured, the difference is animated,
and no layout property moves, so the card underneath is composited rather
than reflowed. The rows rise in behind it, staggered from the stylesheet
rather than by threading an animation prop through every screen.

Three rules hold it in place. It plays once per page load, so a route
change, a step change and the sign-up morph are the same page continuing
rather than three arrivals. Nothing waits on it: the overlay is inert,
the card is mounted and typeable from the first frame, and the only thing
the motion gates is when focus is taken. Under prefers-reduced-motion
none of it runs at all - no overlay, no held-back mark, focus immediately.

The card gains two named hooks and no behavior: the entrance has to be
able to find the slot it is flying to.

* fix(auth): a red that reads on dark, and a wait that says how long

The light red fails contrast on the dark ground and comes out brown,
which is not a colour anybody reads as "wrong". It gets a dark step of
its own, alongside a detail step for focus rings and badges - the accent
that reads as an action on white disappears as a ring on a dark field.
Solid buttons keep the brand orange in both modes; only the details move.

The rate limiter's remaining window rides a response header the auth
client was discarding. Read on the way past, the screen can say how long
is actually left and count it down, and the submit stands down until it
runs out: the one thing that cannot help is now also the one thing that
cannot be done. A refusal that names no window changes nothing - the
general sentence, and a button that still works, because a submit
disabled for a duration nobody knows is a worse guess than no guess.

The failure-message anchor is untouched: the mapper still supplies the
sentence, and the real wait is added to it rather than replacing it.

One attempt at a password is now one function with three outcomes, which
is what it always was - signed in, signing up, or refused.

* feat(identity): a connection is an aggregate, not two strings

Enterprise SSO has been two hand-set columns on Organization: no history,
no guard, and no way to ask why an organization routes where it does. This
gives it the vocabulary of one - states, twelve verbs, the facts each states,
and the pure reducer that folds them - plus the guards that decide whether a
verb may state anything at all.

The guards read folded state and nothing else. verifyDomain refuses a domain
another ACTIVE connection already holds, and refuses it at the ceremony's
OPENING rather than at its end, so nobody publishes a TXT record we were
always going to reject. Activation needs a verified domain, a recorded test
login and a live break-glass binding - D05 owns the bindings, so the
requirement ships as a port every activation already calls. Teardown reads
the identity heads and refuses while anyone holds no other way in.

Grandfathering is the one verb that states HISTORY instead of commanding a
change, and it can only create. That is what makes "grandfathering never
weakens a guard" structural rather than careful: there is no grandfathered
branch in any guard, and a connection that already exists gets nothing, so
every later change is the ordinary guarded verb.

Secrets never appear. Events carry credential references and the DNS

hostname exactly the address it refuses. The overlay now vouches for the
simulator it just started.

And the domains a local walk claims are reserved names like `acme.test`
that no public resolver will ever answer for. The simulator is
authoritative for them; the machine's resolver has never heard of it. So
the overlay names the simulator's nameserver, and a domain proof asks
the one thing that can answer.

The nameserver port is haven's rather than the simulator's fixed
default. A second stack finds that default busy, falls back to an
ephemeral port and says so in a log nobody reads, leaving the app
pointed at the FIRST stack's nameserver -- which answers confidently for
somebody else's domains. Allocated here, both sides are told the same
number. A worktree that falls back to a baseline's simulator inherits
its nameserver too, which is why the baseline lookup now hands back the
whole service rather than one port.

Also: the users panel said only that login_hint skips the browser, to a
reader who had not yet been told the picker was the normal way in.

feat(agent-cache): a code agent logs in once for a whole run (#7545)

* docs(agents): a code agent can log in once and share the session across rows

The rows of an experiment or a dataset run are isolated on purpose, so each row
starts cold and logs in again. There is no per-batch cache and no shared-state
hook, and a customer asked what to do instead.

The project secret store answers it today. The platform reads every project
secret from the database when it prepares each row, so a row reads what an
earlier row wrote, and the REST secrets API accepts a project API key, so the
agent writes it back. The value is encrypted at rest and no API returns it,
which is what makes it correct for a session token. A dataset row is the
alternative and is kept in clear.

Adds the reference implementation, executed through the real runner.py against
a stub login service, a stub protected API and a stub secrets API. The tests
assert on what the stubs received, so an agent that logs in every row, or one
that carries a hardcoded token, cannot pass them.

The limit is stated rather than hidden: the secrets namespace a row reads is a
snapshot taken when the row starts, so the first parallel wave performs one
login per row in the wave. A lock cannot prevent this, and a scenario pins it.

* feat(secrets): a code agent reads a secret value back through the SDK

The shared-session example hand-rolled REST calls to the secrets API with
`requests`: a list, a create, a 409 branch and an update. It also could not
read a value at all, so it trusted the `secrets` snapshot taken when the row
was prepared.

Both are fixed at the source. `langwatch.secrets` gains `set(name, value)`,
which resolves create against update inside the SDK and falls through to an
update when another caller creates the name first, and `get_value(name)`,
which reads a value back. The example now imports `langwatch` and is short
enough to publish whole.

The value read is a new route, `GET /api/secrets/by-name/:name/value`, gated
on `secrets:manage` rather than `secrets:view`: a caller that can replace a
secret can already choose its next value, so reading the current one grants
nothing further, while a caller that can only list names stays away from the
values. Product-owned secrets read as not found, the same as the listing.

Two error codes ship with it, `secret_not_found` and
`secret_value_unreadable`, each with remediation tips and customer copy.

Because the agent reads the store when the row runs, a run over a dataset
logs in once and every row after it reuses the session. Only rows that start
at the same moment still log in once each.

The docs page carries the whole example, and a test compares the fenced block
to the committed file byte for byte so the two cannot drift. go-ci installs
the sandbox packages, the workspace SDK included, so the example tests run
rather than skip.

feat(identity): an identifier is an aggregate — the domain half (ADR-127) (#7595)

* feat(identity): an identifier is an aggregate — the domain half

The identity pipeline gives each PERSON one aggregate: `aggregateId = userId`,
one fold state holding every identifier they hold, one queue lane for every
ceremony they can run. ADR-127 makes an identifier its own aggregate — the
person stays the TENANT, and keeps a stream of their own for what is genuinely
about them (two-step verification, a link proposal, the erasure record).

This is the first slice: the domain decision, made concrete and provable,
wired nowhere. Nothing about the live pipeline changes.

  identityStreamsFor  the routing table — which aggregate a fact is stated on
  reduceIdentifier    one identifier's head, folded by one fact
  primaryChangeFacts  one promotion, plus a demotion per standing PRIMARY
  userErasureFacts    an erasure naming every head the person holds

The fold RULES do not move. `reduceIdentity` is now the same function plus a
delivery decision — hand every fact to every head — and a per-identifier fold
is the same function plus the routed delivery. A test folds one history both
ways and pins that they agree.

What the shared stream was quietly enforcing, and where it goes: a promotion
demoted every standing PRIMARY and an erasure wiped every head, both by
sweeping state no per-identifier fold can see. Both become routing, read from
the whole person at command time — ADR-110's principal-filter rule in
identity's terms — so the guards now state the facts rather than trusting the
fold to find the rest. Address uniqueness needed no move: `IdentifierReservation`
already externalised it (ADR-116 §6).

The tenant does not change, deliberately, so erasure stays a single tenant scan
and the D01 backfill, its migration state and the per-user write gate are
untouched. The ClickHouse user-tenant resolution problem is neither helped nor
worsened by this.

Spec: specs/identity/identifier-aggregate.feature (15 scenarios, all bound)
ADR: dev/docs/adr/127-an-identifier-is-an-aggregate.md, which lists the five
remaining slices — the envelope and the lanes, the fold and its cursor, the
ledger's wait, the erasure sweep, replay and ops.

* fix(identity): the review's findings — a race the lane was hiding, and three claims that were too strong

A read pass over the first commit found one design gap and several places
where the ADR said more than the code or the codebase supports.

**The gap: two guards were relying on the lane without saying so.**
`markPrimary` and `detachIdentifier` both read the WHOLE person and refuse on
what they read — every standing PRIMARY, and the ways in that would remain
(ADR-119's strands guard). Today the per-user lane is what makes those reads
decisive. Per identifier it would not be: two concurrent promotions each see no
standing PRIMARY and both state `previousIdentifierId: null`; two concurrent
detaches each see the other still VERIFIED and between them strand the account.
That is the class ADR-116 §6 already settled once — a read cannot decide a race.

So the ADR now separates the two things the aggregate was doing: a command's
aggregate id names its QUEUE LANE, the events it states carry their own, and
nothing in the framework ties them together. Attach and verify take per-identifier
lanes, because their cross-person race is decided by the address lock rather than
by a read. Promotion, detach, erasure and proposals keep the person's lane. The
concurrency this is for — attaches and verifies, at volume, and the backfill's
fan-out — is the concurrency it gains.

**Three claims corrected.**
- ADR-110's decision box draws two aggregate types; what shipped declares one and
  tells grants from roles by aggregate id. The ADR now cites the code, and says
  where the two differ.
- "No second copy of any fact" was true of history and false of new facts: a fact
  routed to N streams is appended as N events. That fan-out is now stated in the
  Decision, in the routing docblock, and in what `awaitFold` has to wait for.
- The legacy `primary_changed` gap is every legacy promotion, not only the ones
  naming no previous — one event keys to one stream, so the demotion half is
  unreplayable either way.

**"What one head cannot see"** is now a section, with the two histories where the
per-identifier fold and the per-person fold genuinely disagree, and tests that
pin both. Neither is reachable from a command; both need a partial replay window.
A fold that agreed everywhere would mean the split had changed nothing.

Also: `identityStreamsFor` returns a discriminated `IdentityStream` rather than a
bare id, so a person's stream cannot be handed to a per-identifier fold by
accident; ADR-101 gets its "Amended by" back-link; the routing forward-references
are tensed so a reader can tell which sentence describes today; and the tests
cover the branches that had none — a dead end, an ineligible promotion, a
proposal, and a foreign fact reaching a head the routing would never have sent
it to.

* fix(governance): wire the new source's credentials, and make the host check run on edit

which would have shipped.

threw them away. Secret-marked fields are dropped from parserConfig on
purpose — they belong in the credentials subtree, the only part the server
encrypts — and putting them back is the job of a per-source config builder
the new source did not have. Without one the composer falls through to a
bare adapter id: the source saves looking complete and every run fails for
want of a credential the form did ask for. The fields are renamed to the
credentials-prefixed convention the Databricks source already uses, and the
builder now assembles them.

The destination check did not run on edit. It dispatches on the adapter in
the config it is handed, and the edit form sends back only the fields it
renders — adapter is deliberately not one of them. So the host was pinned
when a source was created and free to change afterwards: an update could
repoint workspaceUrl or environmentUrl at any host and the check would
return without looking. It now takes the adapter from the stored row. This
was live for the Databricks source, not something this branch introduced.

The same edit also dropped adapter and schedule from the stored config,
because the carry-across list of client-invisible keys named credentials
and the underscore-prefixed internals but not those two. A rename would
leave a pull source the worker can no longer dispatch. Also pre-existing.

* fix(governance): pin a source's adapter once it holds a credential

The destination check reads the adapter off the stored row so a request
cannot dodge it by claiming to be something else. That decides which rule
to apply; on its own it does not stop the same request writing a different
adapter for the next run to use.

A caller with edit rights could satisfy the Databricks host rule with a
genuine workspace URL, ship adapter: "http_polling" and a URL of their own
in the same request, and have the worker hand the stored token to that URL
on the following tick. The caller never reads the secret; the server
delivers it. The stored credential survives the edit untouched, which is
correct behaviour and is exactly what makes the adapter dangerous to edit.

Pinning it is what lets the destination rule mean anything: a config can
only be judged against the rules of the adapter that will actually run it.
Absent still means unchanged, since the composer renders no adapter field.

Pre-existing rather than introduced here — on the base branch the same
request also persisted a hostile adapter, and the destination check
dispatched on the incoming value, so it did not even reach a host rule.
This branch narrowed it; this commit closes it.

* fix(governance): stop a bad activity taking down the whole run

Three ways a transcript could lose a conversation without saying so.

A null in the activities array passed Array.isArray and then threw on the
first property read. The caller has no try/catch, so one malformed activity
aborted routing for every conversation in the run, not just its own. The
row schema validates `content` as a string and never opens it, so this is
the only place anything checks inside it — each element is checked now, not
just the array.

A `from.role` outside {0, 1} fell off the end of the loop uncounted. The
docstring promises "skipped and counted, never invented", and that count is
the only downstream signal. A transcript where every message spelled its
role the other way produced no turns and no skips, reached the assembler as
an empty span list, and vanished with no log, no attribute and no error —
indistinguishable from a pull that found nothing. Both spellings are read
now, and anything else is counted.

Merged activities are ordered by batch and then by time. Batch order alone
is right whenever rows arrive as written; this is what makes it right when
they do not, because turns are paired by walking the list and one message
out of place attaches an answer to the wrong question. The batch comparator
returned 1 for both (a,b) and (b,a) when neither row had a number, which
left their order unspecified for the same reason.

* fix(governance): stop reporting a model the environment does not store

The mapper emitted copilot_studio.agent_model from a field nothing wrote.
The bot row carries name, schemaname, language, authenticationmode,
statecode, publishedon and modifiedon — checked against the captured row —
and no model, so neither the attribute nor the "possibly not the model that
answered" flag beside it could ever appear. Two tests hand-injected the
field and passed on data production cannot emit.

Worse than absent: a reader would have taken the missing attribute as "no
model configured" rather than "not knowable from here".

What the row does support is kept. modifiedon later than the conversation
means the agent was edited afterwards, which is the part that mattered —
anyone reading a trace as evidence of how an agent behaves needs to know it

* fix(governance): check the host on every request that carries the token

Three things the page walk got wrong, all on the same loop.

The next page is a URL taken from the response body, and the request that
follows it carries the access token. followRedirects: false stops the
server bouncing that credential elsewhere; this was the same hop by another
name, unchecked. The host allowlist has to hold for every request carrying
the secret, not only the first. Rows already read are kept — a bad link
ahead is no reason to discard them — and the run records an error.

The loop was bounded only by the deadline and the abort signal, both
optional on the run options. A server that keeps handing back a next-page
link could keep one run going indefinitely. Both sibling adapters carry a
page cap; this one now does too.

The row schema stripped every undeclared field, and the stripped object was
what got stored as raw_payload. That field is contracted to hold what the
source actually sent so a mapping written later can be replayed against old
rows instead of re-pulling them, and a field dropped at parse time is not
there to replay.

passed against a codebase with the known-broken source still in it. It now
asserts it can see what it is guarding before guarding it, and was checked

* fix(governance): stop one undated message scrambling the ones around it

The time sort added to `groupTranscriptRows` in the previous review pass
compared a null timestamp against a real one by position and every other
pair by time. Those two rules disagree, so the comparator is not a
consistent ordering: with A(pos 0, t=100), B(pos 1, undated) and
C(pos 2, t=50) it says A before B, B before C, and C before A. A sort
given a self-contradicting comparator may return anything, and V8
returns something specific and wrong:

    input   t100 undated t50 t70 t60 t90 t80 t40 t30 t20 t10
    result  t100 undated t10 t20 t30 t40 t50 t60 t70 t80 t90

The largest timestamp first, ahead of every smaller one — which is the
exact failure the sort was added to prevent. Turns are paired by walking
this list, so one undated activity anywhere in a merged conversation was
enough to attach an answer to the wrong question.

Sort the dated activities among themselves instead, and put them back
into the slots dated activities already held. An undateable activity
keeps its literal position rather than being ranked against messages it
cannot be compared to. The comment claiming stability protected them was
wrong on its own terms: stability only preserves pairs the comparator
calls equal, and this one never returned equal for them.

Undated activities are dropped further down regardless. The damage was
never to them — it was to the dated messages they sat between.

The existing ordering test uses two activities, both dated, and the
comparator is consistent when everything is dated, so it passed either
way. The new test puts an undateable activity between two dated ones in
the wrong order and fails on the old code.

Found by review of the previous review pass.

* fix(governance): pin a next-page link to the configured environment

The next-page URL arrives in the response body and the request that follows
it carries the access token. The check on that URL asked whether Microsoft
serves the host, which every tenant's environment answers yes to, so a link
naming another customer's environment passed and the token went with it.

Ask the narrower question instead: is this the environment the source is
configured against. `isSameDataverseEnvironment` keeps the existing suffix
and scheme checks as a first gate and then compares origins, so a link that
differs only in host case or a default port still counts as the same place.

The gap sat exactly between the two cases the tests already covered — a
foreign host that was rejected, and the configured host that was followed.
