* fix(governance): name the host in a refused next-page link

Pinning the next page to the configured environment traded one failure mode
for another: a link that is genuinely not the configured environment now
stops the walk, and the only record of it was a sentence with no host in it.

That matters because of what the stop costs downstream. The refusal raises
errorCount, and the worker treats a non-zero errorCount as a failed run, so
the events are dropped and the cursor stays put. An operator sees a source
that has quietly stopped moving. With no host in the log there is nothing to
tell an attack apart from an environment that legitimately pages on a second
address, and the two want opposite responses.

Log both hosts and say which question was asked. The host is the whole of the
useful part; the rest of the link is a skip token.

* fix(governance): read the agent from the bot table instead of asking for a join

The transcript query asked Dataverse to expand a navigation property named
`bot_conversationtranscriptid`. Nothing established that the property exists.
A wrong name there is not a missing field, it is a 400 on the very first page,
which would have meant every run of every source returning nothing at all.

The reads that were actually exercised against a real environment do not use
`$expand` anywhere on Dataverse. They take `_bot_conversationtranscriptid_value`
off the row, read the `bot` table separately, and join the two themselves. This
does the same: the lookup column joins the transcript's `$select`, and the run
reads the agents once and keeps them in a map.

Three things this had to get right, each now pinned by a test that was checked
by breaking the code under it and confirming that test and only that test
failed:

  * No `$expand` in the query. Without a test, it comes back.
  * The agent id is the lookup column, never the `BotId` inside the row's own
    metadata. Those two genuinely differ on a real row, and the metadata one
    joins to nothing, so reading it would attach a wrong name rather than no
    name. The fixture keeps them different for that reason.
  * A refused agent list is not an error. The worker discards a run's events
    and holds its cursor when the error count is not zero, so counting this
    would turn a missing name into a source that never moves again. It logs
    and delivers the conversations unnamed.

The join key is case-folded on both sides. Nothing promises Dataverse spells a
lookup id the same way in two tables, and a mismatch here fails silently.

scenarios join the feature file, so the parity check goes from 9511 to 9513.

Challenging the scenario written for a failed agent-list read turned up the

table say the realistic failure is the opposite shape: a credential holding a
role that reads that table at the wrong depth is answered with success and an
empty list, because the application user owns none of the rows, and that is
identical to the answer a tenant with no agents gives.

Nothing was logged on that path. Every conversation arrived unnamed and the
run reported a clean success, so the one signal an admin had was an absent
name they had no reason to attribute to a permission.

A run reading conversations that an agent wrote, told there are no agents,

table only proved half of it. The scenario promises both that the lookup

The logger is captured in this suite for the first time. One of this
adapter's promises is diagnostic, and a warning nothing asserts can be

* fix(governance): continue past the whole cursor, not just its id

The transcript read sorts by `createdon asc,conversationtranscriptid asc`
but resumed with "at or after the timestamp, except the saved id". That is
not a total order. On a timestamp holding several rows, a run whose cursor
is B gets A back first and saves A; the next run excludes A and gets B. The
pair alternates forever, the same transcripts are reprocessed every run, and
no later row is ever reached.

Resume lexicographically instead — everything strictly after the pair:

  (createdon gt T or (createdon eq T and conversationtranscriptid gt I))

The plain `createdon ge T` bound is kept alongside it. It says nothing the
disjunction does not, but it is the range the server can seek on where the
`or` alone invites a scan.

The sort moves to a shared constant, because the predicate is only a
continuation under exactly that sort and the two must not drift apart in
separate edits.

The tests drive the adapter against a table that answers the query it is
actually sent — filter applied, rows sorted, pages cut — rather than a
canned page. A canned page comes back whatever the filter says, so it cannot
tell a filter that walks in a circle from one that does not. Against the old
predicate the new tests report the alternation directly: three restarts
deliver row-a, row-b, row-a.

Also splits the agent-list read into the request, the rows it yields and the
two ways it can come back short, which is what carries fetchBots back under
the cognitive-complexity gate it was failing at 12. No behaviour change: the
same warnings on the same conditions, and a refusal still returns an empty
map without counting an error.

* fix(governance): keep a run that stepped past input it could not read

The worker threw whenever an adapter reported any error, before it wrote
the events or persisted the cursor. That is right for an adapter that could
not make progress, and wrong for one that made progress deliberately.

The S3 adapter advances past a malformed line and past an object it cannot
fetch at all, on purpose, and hands back the advanced cursor with a nonzero
error count. Throwing on it discarded both the events already collected and
the advance, so the next run read the same unreadable object and the source
never moved again.

The cursor is what tells the two cases apart, so the worker now reads it
alongside the error count: advanced means partial success — write, persist,
warn; unchanged means nothing was read, and the run still fails so the same
window is retried. A null cursor is never an advance; it is the drained
sentinel, and persisting it would rewind the source to the beginning.

The contract both halves depend on is now written down on `PullResult`,
where an adapter author will meet it.

* fix(parity): stop the binding check dropping a tag written the natural way

`ANNOTATION_RE` stops at the end of the tag's own line, so for the ordinary
JSDoc form the proximity scan starts inside the comment and has to walk out
of it before it can see the test call. It could step over whitespace, a
block comment and a line comment, but not over a `*` — so a continuation
line, or a `*/` sitting alone on its own line, fell through to the final

check saw nothing, and the disagreement surfaced only as an unbound

dropped without trace. The report is a warning, not a failure: `@scenario`
appears in prose that teaches the convention as well as in real tags, and a
check that fails on its own documentation is one people route around. A real
one already costs what it should — its scenario reports unbound.

`describe(` now counts as a test call alongside `it` and `test`. Tagging the
block that covers a scenario instead of every case inside it is a form
people already write, and the check refusing it was the second largest
source of dropped tags.

inside mapCopilotEventsToTraceRequest, which put it over both complexity limits
the repo enforces on new code — neither of which it tripped before. The span is
built the way turnSpan and toolSpan already are, beside them.

The tests for it were typed against span shapes that do not match ISpan: a
parentSpanId annotated as a string when OTLP allows bytes, an index signature
ISpan does not have, and three indexed reads that TypeScript cannot prove are
present. They now infer, and the two span names come from the exported
constants rather than repeating the literals.

No behaviour change — same spans, same attributes, same identifiers.

Moving the adapter guard chain into resolvePullAdapter left one of its three
exits untested: a pullConfig that names a registered adapter but does not
validate against it. Nothing proved the run stopped there rather than reaching
the network with a half-read config.

The case now drops the url from an otherwise-valid http_polling config and
asserts the run rejects naming that field, with no fetch, no OCSF write, and no
cursor update.

* fix(governance): keep an unusable value out of the transcript filter

The transcript id and timestamp are interpolated bare into the next run's $filter, because Dataverse compares an Edm.Guid and an Edm.DateTimeOffset against unquoted literals only. Neither was format-checked on the path that produces them, so a row carrying operator text would build a broken predicate — and since that value is persisted as the cursor, every later run would repeat the same HTTP 400 with nothing moving. Constrained at both ends: the row schema, and the cursor schema a later run reads back.

A page entry that is not an object was dropped by a bare continue while its sibling — a row failing the schema — was counted. Both are a row shaped unlike the rest, so both are counted now; a page of rubbish used to come back as a source with nothing in it.

Collapses botsPageSchema and pageSchema, which were identical, and derives Cursor from a schema instead of two casts behind hand-written typeof checks.

The secret-leak test asserted on JSON.stringify(result), which has never had anywhere to carry a message — it could not have failed. It now reads the text the logger was handed.

* refactor(governance): name the mapper's booleans as predicates

Renames incomplete, designMode, finished and completed to isIncomplete, isDesignMode, isFinished and isCompleted, so a call site can tell what true means. All four are internal to this module.

Writes down why the first trace for a tool call is safe to seed from: it is not arrival order that decides, it is that group.activities is time-ordered before any of this runs and toolCallTraceOf refuses a trace it cannot date, so an undated one never reaches the map. Pinned with a fixture that stores the completion above the start.

The multi-batch ordering assertion compared two findIndex results, and findIndex answers -1 for something absent — so batch 2 disappearing entirely would have satisfied it. Both entries are required to be present before they are compared.

Renames the scenario that reads "The agent's model is recorded when it can be trusted" in both the feature file and its binding: the step and the assertions require the opposite, that the trace claims nothing about a model.

The fixture helpers take named parameters, matching transcriptRow beside them.

* refactor(governance): give the two-argument destination checks named parameters

assertPullDestinationAllowed(parserConfig, adapterId) and isSameDataverseEnvironment(value, environmentUrl) both took positional arguments. The second is the one that matters: both are strings, so a transposed call compiles and compares the environment against itself — the check would pass on exactly the request that repoints the host.

Also drops an as const on a standalone string constant, where TypeScript already infers the literal type.

* refactor(governance): split the pull dispatcher into the steps it documents

runIngestionPull ran to 79 lines against a 60-line limit, which reviewdog has been reporting on this file since before this branch. Two seams were already there: running the adapter under the job deadline, and deciding whether a run that reported errors still counts as progress. Both move out with their reasoning intact, and the dispatcher reads as the sequence its docblock describes. No behaviour changes — same log fields, same messages, same thrown errors, same order.

Renames CONVERSATION_ROUTING_PROFILES to CONVERSATION_ROUTING_BY_SOURCE_TYPE: it holds ConversationRouting pairs and the reader takes .profile off the result, so the old name contradicted the call site.

Corrects the routing test's docblock, which implied it catches drift between the client declaration and the server map. It does not — it never reads the server map, and cannot from that bundle. Saying so beats implying a guard that is not there.

* test(governance): give three describe blocks the condition they were missing

The repo's BDD rule asks a nested describe to state a precondition or an action, so a failure message reads on its own. "credential handling on the wire" names a topic; the other two put their cases directly under the given block. Renamed and nested. No assertion changed.

* docs(governance): make ADR-088's contract match what shipped

Three sections still carried claims that later revisions overturned, and a reader taking the contract tables at face value would have built against them.

Decision 18 was re-locked on a host-suffix allowlist in v10, but the risk row still said BLOCKED, the pullConfig contract still said any host, and the consequences still said the secret goes wherever the admin typed. All three now describe the allowlist that is enforced, and name the four suffixes the code actually carries. The accepted cost changes with it: a custom-domain environment cannot self-serve.

The model field was withdrawn in v12 on the evidence that the bot table has no model column. The contract row named a path no query populates, and the mapping block still listed model attributes. Both now say the trace claims nothing about a model and record agent_changed_since instead.

The retired reference feature still required creating a new copilot_studio source, which the Dataverse feature requires to be impossible. That scenario is replaced by the one that still has to hold: a row configured before the retirement keeps being scheduled, and the picker never offers a new one.

* refactor(governance): type the assembled span from the schema that validates it

OtlpJsonSpan was any, with a comment explaining only why the transformer interface is wrong for the JSON path — it never said why the schema that validates these spans downstream could not describe them. It can. z.input rather than z.infer: several of spanSchema's fields carry .default(), so the parsed output has events, links, status and the dropped counts as required, while a mapper writes the input side where they are optional. Both mappers are now checked against the shape they have to emit, and the cast that papered over any is gone.

stringAttr and intAttr take named parameters. stringAttr is the one that matters: both halves are strings, so a transposed positional call compiled and emitted an attribute with its key and value the wrong way round, which nothing catches unless a test pins that exact attribute.

* fix(governance): make the conversation span cover the spans under it

The root span opened at the first turn and closed at the last, but a tool call attaches to the turn it falls inside by time and one that predates every turn attaches to the first rather than being dropped — so a tool span could begin before its parent opened or end after it closed, and a trace rendered with spans hanging outside the conversation that contains them.

The span's bounds are now taken across everything emitted under it. Kept separate from conversationEndMs, which answers a different question — when the conversation happened, which is what decides whether the agent was edited afterwards — and would have changed the agent_changed_since flag if the two were merged.

Splitting the per-conversation work out of mapCopilotEventsToTraceRequest keeps both functions inside the line limit; the extra bounds calculation had pushed the caller over it.

* test(governance): let the captured log line carry the field that could leak

The capture built each line with args.map(String), and every call in this adapter is logger.x({ context }, "message"). String({ error: "..." }) is "[object Object]", so the one argument that could carry a leaked secret never reached the string being asserted — the redaction check could only ever see the message.

This was the same defect as the JSON.stringify(result) assertion it replaced, moved one layer down. Non-string arguments are serialised now, so a secret in the error context fails the assertion.

* docs(governance): say why the log capture serialises instead of what it does

The helper's comment described the mechanism. What a reader needs is the reason it cannot be String(): that turns the structured context object into "[object Object]", which is the one argument a secret could travel in.

* fix(governance): correct two scenarios that asserted more than the code does

Both were written earlier this session and both were wrong in the direction that matters — a scenario is the yardstick, so an overstated one licenses deleting working code.

"The trace claims nothing about which model answered" is false. Every turn span carries gen_ai.request.model = "microsoft/copilot-studio", deliberately: cost enrichment runs on every llm span, and a routed conversation stays free only because that label resolves to no price row. A reader implementing to the old title could have deleted the attribute that keeps it free. The scenario now states both halves — the product label is emitted, and no attribute reports the model the agent was configured with — and the bound test asserts the first half rather than only the absences.

"A source configured before the retirement keeps running" had no When at all: it asserted a continuous state with no trigger and nothing observable at a point in time. Narrowed to the property that actually breaks if the retired adapter is unregistered — a scheduled run resolves an adapter instead of failing with "unknown ingestion pull adapter". The picker-absence line is dropped rather than restated; copilot-studio-dataverse.feature owns it and that copy has a test bound to it.

* fix(governance): step past a transcript row the walk cannot read

A row that fails the transcript schema was counted and skipped without
moving the cursor. With that row last on the page the source wedged: the
next run asked for everything after the last good row, got the bad one
back alone, and returned an unchanged cursor with an error against it,
which the worker fails as no progress. Every retry repeated it, until
some later row happened to arrive and drag the window past it.

Only the identifier and the timestamp go into the next run's filter, so
they are now read on their own. A row whose `name` came back as a number
is unreadable as an event and still perfectly readable as a position,
and the walk steps over it. Rows arrive sorted by that same pair, so a
row further down the page is always a cursor further forward.

A row whose own identifier is the unreadable part still holds the walk
where it is. That id is what the next filter would be built from, so
there is nowhere to move to, and failing loudly beats stepping over a
row nobody can name.

* test(governance): pin what stepping over rows costs when none of them read

Stepping past an unreadable row stops one bad row wedging a source, and the
other half of that is a page where every row is unreadable: the walk now runs
to the end of it and those events are gone rather than the run failing.

Guarding it — refusing to advance when a page yields no events — was tried and
rejected. It brings back the reported bug for the case where the malformed row
arrives on its own with nothing newer behind it, which is the shape the walk
sees most often.

So the count is the only signal that it happened, and this asserts the count is
the whole page rather than a sample of it.

* refactor(governance): keep the filter constraints in one place

The cursor fields were spelled out twice with the same types for the same
reason: both are interpolated bare into the next run's `$filter`, so both have
to reject anything carrying OData operator text. A copy is a thing that can be
loosened in one place, and this is the one spot where loosening it is what lets
that text reach the filter.

The row schema now extends the cursor schema instead of restating the two
fields, and the reason they are constrained lives with the schema that is only
those two.

* fix(cli): bound a daemon request so a wedged daemon cannot hang the caller

The daemon client bounded the connect (500ms) and the handshake (1s), but
nothing after `hello-ok`. Output is held back until the command finishes, so a
daemon that accepted the exec and then wedged left the client waiting with zero
bytes written. The daemon's own per-request timeout is ten minutes, far past
the 30 seconds an agent harness gives a command, so the harness killed the CLI
first and the caller read the empty result as the CLI answering nothing.

The whole request now has a 25 second deadline. On expiry the client prints
what happened and how to run without a daemon, exits 124, and asks the wedged
daemon to stop so the next command does not wedge in the same way. Nothing the
command produced is printed, because a partial result read as a whole one is
worse than none. The deadline is cleared once output commits: a command that is
streaming is visibly alive, and cutting it off would truncate a working stream.

25s leaves 5 seconds under a 30 second harness for the client to print and
exit, and clears the CLI's own longest in-command deadline, so a command with a
limit of its own always reports the failure itself.

* fix(langy): order the ui-action budgets under the agent harness

`langwatch ui call` runs inside an agent worker whose harness stops any command
at 30 seconds. The server ceiling on an action's execute budget was 30 seconds
too, so a max-budget action was a race the CLI always lost. The CLI's own

fix(clickhouse): a user is a tenant in its own right, so identity events can land (#7630)

* fix(clickhouse): a user is a tenant in its own right, so identity events can land

`user_identity` keeps one aggregate per person, so its tenantId is a user
id — and the client resolver knew only two kinds, project and organization.
Every append threw "is neither a project nor an organization", so no identity
event ever reached the log, the fold never ran, and the D01 backfill's parity
proof reported `identifier_missing` on every pass. Nothing was corrupted: the
guard refused rather than writing somewhere wrong. Nothing could finish
either. MFA enrolment failed the same way.

A user resolves to no organization on the way, deliberately. A tenant is a
project id, one person reaches many projects across many organizations, and
any mapping we invented would pick one of several equally true answers.
Identity history is platform-level, so it lands on the shared instance.

The exception is the case the guard exists for: a member of a
private-dataplane organization is refused rather than routed to shared, since
their identity events would sit in the shared platform log while their
organization's data stays on its private instance. `userMigrationPassCohort`
already excludes them from the backfill; re-proved here so the guarantee
holds for every caller rather than that one, and skipped entirely when no
private instance is configured. An id naming none of the three kinds still
throws.

The shared-user answer is cached with a TTL, because unlike a project's
owning organization it is not immutable — "belongs to no private-dataplane
organization" stops being true the moment they join one, and a write-only
cache would keep writing to the shared log for the life of the process.

Lifted from #7531 (identity wave 3), which carries this fix behind 778 other
files while the failure is live in production.

* fix(clickhouse): user data always lands on the shared instance

The first pass refused a user who belongs to a private-dataplane
organization, on the reading that their identity events would sit in the
shared platform log while their organization's data stays private. That
reading is wrong about what a user-tenanted event is. It records how somebody
signs in — true of them before, across and after every organization they
belong to — so it is platform data, not an organization's, and there is no
membership that could make it otherwise.

So membership does not enter into the routing at all: a user tenant resolves
to the shared instance, full stop. The tenant id stays the user's; it is the
instance that is global.

This deletes the `OrganizationUser` lookup, and with it the reason the cache
needed a TTL. The TTL existed only because "belongs to no private-dataplane
organization" could stop being true; "names a user" cannot, so the cache goes
back to being permanent like `tenantOrgCache` — a Set, not a timestamped Map.

`cohort.ts`: `userMigrationPassCohort` still excludes private-dataplane
members, but that is now pacing rather than correctness — such a person has a
perfectly good answer and would migrate like anybody else. Whether to backfill
them is a product call, recorded as one instead of as a routing limit.

* refactor(clickhouse): ask whether the tenant is a user, instead of deducing it

The user branch was reached by elimination: `organizationIdForTenant` returned
`null` to mean "not a project and not an organization, so it must be a
person", and the caller read that null as "route to shared". So the most
consequential routing decision in the file was the one nothing actually
stated, and any future tenant kind would silently join that same branch
rather than failing.

Now it is a question: `tenantIsUser` is asked first and directly, and
`organizationIdForTenant` answers only for the two kinds that genuinely
resolve per-organization — returning an org id or throwing, with no null to
interpret.

Both caches are still consulted before either query, so asking about the user
first costs a project tenant one extra lookup on its first resolution and
nothing after that.

No behaviour change: the same three kinds resolve to the same instances and
the same ids throw. Tests and spec are untouched.

* feat(migrations): a dedicated data plane no longer holds a person back

`userMigrationPassCohort` excepted anybody who belonged to a
private-dataplane organization, and the targeted run refused those
organizations outright. Both existed for one reason: a user tenant could not
be placed at all, so the only safe thing was to leave those people alone
rather than write their identity events somewhere wrong.

They can be placed now. A user tenant resolves to the shared instance
whoever they belong to, because what these events record is how a person
signs in rather than any organization's data. So the exception has nothing
left to protect, and keeping it would strand exactly those people on the
legacy path forever - the same reason this axis never held their
ORGANIZATIONS back.

Three things go: the per-user membership probe, the filter that dropped
private-dataplane organizations out of the enrolled set (so somebody who
reaches a migration only through one is now in the cohort), and the targeted
run's refusal, which turned an operator away at the door.

The organization SAMPLING defaults are untouched - drawing private-dataplane
organizations into a cohort is still an operator's deliberate choice, and
that is a pacing knob rather than a routing rule.

* fix(clickhouse): the refusal scenario stops describing a user as unplaceable

Address review comments.

- The unknown-tenant scenario still read "names neither a project nor an
  organization", which a user id satisfies and is no longer refused for. It
  now requires an id naming no project, no organization and no user, with the

- The private-dataplane routing case moves from a comment into a nested

* docs(clickhouse): say why a deleted user is not evicted from the cache

Raised in review. Recorded in the code rather than left to the next reader
or the next review to re-derive: the id keeps answering "shared" instead of
throwing, which softens only the guarantee that an unplaceable id throws -

fix(nlpgo): wire the dead engine timeout knobs — code-block timeout, SSE heartbeat, per-node timeout_ms (#7614)

* feat(nlpgo): let code nodes request a shorter timeout via timeout_ms

codeblock.Request.Timeout and the Execute code that honors it have both
existed since the block was written, but runCode never set the field, so
every code node ran on the executor default with no way to override it.
runHTTP already reads a timeout_ms parameter off the node; this wires the
code block into the same convention.

The clamp is the part that differs from its siblings. httpblock,
agentblock and evaluatorblock all let the node win outright and unbounded.
That is fine for an outbound call to the customer's own endpoint. It is not
fine here: the code-block timeout bounds how long untrusted customer Python
holds a worker, so an unbounded per-node override would let any workflow
author escape NLPGO_ENGINE_CODE_BLOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS by writing a bigger
number into their own node.

So the per-node value can only shorten the budget. The clamp lives in the
executor next to context.WithTimeout rather than in the engine, so no future
caller of codeblock.Request can route around it, and non-positive values are
normalized at both ends -- a negative duration reaching context.WithTimeout
would expire the run before the subprocess started.

* fix(nlpgo): stop a huge timeout_ms from overflowing into an instant failure

A node's `timeout_ms` was converted to a time.Duration before it was
compared with the operator's ceiling. Above ~9.2e12 ms that multiplication
overflows int64 and wraps negative, so the value read as "shorter than the
ceiling" and context.WithTimeout expired the call in ~80us — inverting the
documented rule that a node can only ask for LESS time, never more.

Fixed once in a new blocktimeout package rather than in four places: Clamp
compares in milliseconds before any conversion, FromMillis returns 0 for a
value that would overflow. Wired into httpblock, agentblock, evaluatorblock
and engine.nodeTimeout. codeblock takes an already-typed Duration and was
not affected.

Also: cap the code-agent adapter's fetch deadline at 15 minutes (just above
the engine's 12-minute ceiling, so the engine still reports its own timeout
first) instead of letting it reach Node's 24.9-day timer cap; give the
clamp tests a lower time bound and an errors.Is(context.DeadlineExceeded)
assertion so an instant failure can no longer pass them; split the
block-timeout spec so the negative-value case is actually exercised.

Addresses review comments 3872454374, 3872454390, 3872454400, 3872454416,
3872454425.

* fix(platform): make the scenario fetch ceiling an operator knob, not a hardcode

NLP_FETCH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS was hardcoded to 15 minutes while the engine
ceiling it sits above (NLPGO_ENGINE_CODE_BLOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) is
operator-configurable. Raising the engine ceiling past 900s made the
adapter abort first, losing the engine's own timeout diagnosis.

The cap now reads from NLP_FETCH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS, clamp-never-reject
(unset/empty/non-numeric/non-finite/zero/negative all fall back to the
unchanged 900000 default). Forwarded through buildChildProcessEnv's
allowlist, which is the only route into the scenario child process.

* Agent Testing v2: read a scope's previous configurations off its runs

The Run name dropdown lists the configurations a scope already ran with, and
configuration identity is wider than plan identity: one plan run twice with
different parameters, or a different repeat count, is two entries and both
must be listed and told apart. A plan row holds the configuration of its LAST
run, so the plan rows can only ever answer one entry per plan.

Every part of a configuration is already on the runs, so this is a GROUP BY
over the path the atom read already sweeps. No write path, no migration, no
new column.

Four folds, innermost out: the atoms in scope deduped to the latest version of
each run; one row per scenario and target of a batch, whose count IS the
repeat count the batch was started with; one row per batch, carrying its
targets, its models and the first scenario's parameters; and one row per
distinct configuration. The last fold is what makes the cap meaningful, since
a plan run nightly for a year with one setup costs one row and not three
hundred and sixty five.

The key is the contract. The dialog rebuilds the key of what it currently
holds to mark the matching entry, so a read that keys differently marks
nothing and offers the same configuration twice. Both sides call the one
recipe in server/suites/plan-config, and a unit test builds the same
configuration both ways, once through the client helper and once through this
read, and requires one string.

values takes the FIRST scenario's, which is what a person who set a parameter
in the dialog chose; a union would move the key whenever a scenario with a
different default joined the scope. And a run recorded before the models were
stamped reads as naming no model, which is correct: a configuration is what a
person chose, and the same choice has to key the same way after a project
default changes.

fix(gateway): a failure that never reached a provider stops calling itself a timeout (#7602)

* fix(gateway): a failure that never reached a provider stops calling itself a timeout

The dispatch engine reports a failure with no HTTP status when no HTTP call was
made, and the gateway read that absent status as a timeout. Every credential,
configuration and routing failure in the engine therefore reached clients as a
retryable 504 "Gateway Timeout", was attributed to the provider, was retried
across the whole credential chain, and counted a circuit-breaker failure against
a slot that was healthy.

Over one production week the mask covered 23 failures and not one was a timeout;
two thirds finished in under 100ms. They were "no keys found that support
model", "deployments not set", "chat_completion is not supported by elevenlabs
provider", and "failed to retrieve aws credentials" — four settings mistakes,
all terminal, none fixable by a retry. The reported Vertex case ("error creating
auth token source") is the same class.

Classification now reads what Bifrost actually states: IsBifrostError (did the
provider produce this, or the engine?), Error.Type, its own exported message
constants, and the cause it wrapped underneath its category message. Only the
request-timed-out signal produces provider_timeout.

Five codes replace the mask, each with its own status, fault, retry verdict and
customer copy: provider_credential_invalid, provider_credential_rejected,
provider_config_invalid, provider_connection_failed, request_abandoned. The
setup failures are terminal 4xx and the customer's to fix; only a genuine
transport failure stays retryable.

The wrapped cause survives as a herr reason and reaches the operator log line.
"error creating auth token source" is one sentence for five credential problems
with five different fixes, and the gateway was dropping the half that told them
apart. It stays out of meta, which is the client contract.

Bifrost's AllowFallbacks=false verdict is honored instead of ignored.

Remediation, so a terminal failure says what to change:

- A Go remediation registry (domain/remediation.go) attaches tips and a docs
  link at the single write choke point, keyed by code and sharpened by provider.
  "Check your credentials" means a service-account document for Vertex, an
  access key for Bedrock, a key plus an endpoint for Azure — so each names its
  own artefact, and each links that provider's own setup page. A test asserts
  every linked page exists in docs/.
- Tips are capped server-side at the client's MAX_TIPS with the specific advice
  first, so the cap drops what matters least rather than whatever was last.

Shown in the product:

- readHandledError could not read the canonical nested {error:{...}} envelope at
  all — its REST reading requires `error` to be a string — so every gateway
  failure, and every canonical-envelope route's, reached the UI as unhandled:
  generic "Something went wrong", no tips, no docs link, no trace id. Added
  fromCanonicalEnvelope, including the snake_case docs_url the flat reading was
  looking for under a camelCase name.
- presentation.ts gains copy for the five codes that names the provider and
  model from meta rather than saying "this provider".

* fix(gateway): US spelling in the remediation registry, which is what golangci-lint enforces

* fix(gateway): keep forwarding a provider answer bifrost could not parse

The first cut used IsBifrostError to decide whether an error was a provider
response worth forwarding verbatim. Bedrock breaks that: it sets the flag TRUE
on a real provider response whose error body it could not unmarshal, while
still carrying the provider's status and raw body. Reading the flag as "no
provider answered" would have collapsed every unparseable Bedrock 4xx into a
generic 502 — the guarantee error-transparency.feature exists to hold, broken
for the provider whose error bodies parse least reliably.

The discriminant is now the pair bifrost actually controls: a real status, from
something it did not synthesize itself. Bifrost synthesizes exactly two — 504
with request_timed_out, and 499 with request_cancelled — and only those two are
kept off the forwarding path.

Every field is load-bearing somewhere in that chain — tips and docs_url become
the remediation list and the docs link, fault picks the log level and the
headline, and meta.provider / meta.model are what let the copy say "Google
Vertex AI" and name the model instead of "this provider". Also pins that the
promoted fields do not ALSO sit in meta, and that the list stays inside the
client's MAX_TIPS so nothing is written only to be discarded.

Circuit breaker, the worst of them. classifyProviderError read Bifrost's
no-fallback marker before the code switch, and Bifrost's context-done
constructor is the only site in the engine that sets AllowFallbacks=false — so
in production every abandoned request carried the marker, matched there first,
and returned ReasonNonRetryable instead of ReasonContextDone. recordBreaker
credits anything that is neither a failure reason nor ContextDone as a SUCCESS,
and RecordSuccess force-closes the circuit and truncates the failure window.
Clients giving up during a provider outage were holding the breaker closed on
the dead slot — the exact inverse of the invariant this branch documents.

fix(agent-cache): a personal workspace run gets a key, and a project's runs share one (#7639)

* fix(agent-cache): a run in a personal workspace gets a key its owner holds

The sandbox key was minted as a service key, owned by no user. A personal
workspace admits no principal but its owner, so ApiKeyService.create
refused the mint there, the warning was swallowed, and every code agent
row in a personal workspace ran with no agent cache credential: every
row logged in, and the claim never arbitrated anything.

The mint now looks up whose workspace the project is. In a shared
project the key still belongs to no user. In a personal workspace it
belongs to the workspace owner, which is the owner acting
programmatically, the same way the Langy session key is minted, and
the owner's own ceiling caps it.

* feat(agent-cache): the runs of a project share one sandbox key

Every run minted its own sandbox key, and the reaper only revokes, so
each run left one revoked ApiKey row behind. Every run of a project
holds the same authority over the same cache, so one key serves them
all: the first run mints it, and the token is held encrypted for eight
of the key's twelve hours. Later runs pick it up, and the next mint
happens only once that window passes. A project that runs all day
mints three keys, not one per run; a project that runs nothing mints
none. The key stays short-lived, because the plaintext is held only in
the store and never written anywhere durable.

A held token the platform can no longer read (the encryption key
changed) is replaced by a fresh mint. Two runs that start together on
an empty store may both mint; both keys are valid.

fix(identity): accept better-auth 1.7's restated providerId on OAuth sign-in (#7642)

better-auth 1.7 rebuilt the sign-in token refresh in `oauth2/link-account`
to send `providerId` alongside the rotated tokens, echoing back the value it
had just read. 1.6 sent `scope` and no linkage column at all — the 1.7 guide
documents scopes accumulating across refresh, and this half of the change is
undocumented.

The storage adapter classifies every non-secret field on an `account` update
as a linkage rewrite and refuses it, so the echo failed EVERY OAuth sign-in
for a user on the identity branch. better-auth catches the throw and turns it
into a redirect, so the customer lands on `/auth/error` with
`identity_unsupported_storage_query` and no way back in.

The field alone cannot decide this; the field and its value together can. A
linkage column whose value already matches the row is a restatement that
writes nothing, and is accepted. One that differs is a real rewrite — it
would repoint the row at another IdP — and still refuses.

Linkage stays event-truth: the restated field is dropped from the payload
rather than written, so no command is skipped and a replay reproduces the
same projection. The legacy branch is untouched.

Also log the refusal. Both throw sites were silent, and the detail naming the
offending shape sat unread on the error's own `reasons`, so this failure ran
in production with zero log lines naming it — `handledErrorCode` was well
populated for every other code at the same time. It logs at error because it
is `fault: "platform"`.

The regression test drives better-auth's own `handleOAuthUserInfo` rather
than a hand-built payload, so it binds to what the library actually issues.
Verified as a negative control: with the fix disabled, both new tests fail
and the other 33 pass.

fix(scenarios): fix the seven defects found while dogfooding a customer onboarding demo (#7271)

* fix(scenarios): expand latest model aliases at simulation execution time

A scenario or run plan stores its simulator and judge model overrides
verbatim, so a virtual alias like openai/latest reached the prefetcher
unexpanded and providers received the literal model id "latest". The
prefetcher now passes every resolved override through expandLatestAlias
before it prepares litellm params. Storage keeps the alias verbatim so
the pick keeps tracking upstream releases.

Also validates the override shape at save time: the tRPC create and
update schemas for scenarios and run plans now reject a model id with
no provider prefix.

* fix(cli): make the agent dev tunnel session resilient to signals, crashes and dead tunnels

The session now restores the agent URL on SIGHUP, uncaughtException and
unhandledRejection (best-effort, exit nonzero), on a tunnel error event,
and on startup when a crashed session left a stale devTunnel stash. A
health monitor probes the local server through the public tunnel URL
every 30 seconds: the auth proxy's 401 counts as healthy, 530 or a
transport failure counts as unhealthy, three failures in a row provision
a replacement quick tunnel and re-point the agent, and a failed
replacement restores and ends the session. Healthy checks refresh a new
devTunnel.heartbeatAt field. Bring-your-own tunnels and --no-update-url
sessions only get a warning, since their URL is not ours to swap.
Shutdown is idempotent: a second signal shares the in-flight restore and
force-exits after a short grace instead of restoring twice.

* feat(scenario-api): expose model overrides and turn limits on the public scenarios and suites APIs

The UI edits simulatorModel, judgeModel, maxTurns and minTurns through
tRPC, but the public REST API dropped them: GET did not return them and
POST/PUT ignored them, so a scenario or run plan managed as code lost
its overrides. The routes now accept and return these fields, and null
clears an override back to the default.

`suite run` now speaks the output contract (rendersOwnResult +
printResult), so -o json|yaml|agents, --json <fields> and --jq work on

the schedule payload plus an outcome for plain runs, and for --wait the
hoisted tallies, the per-scenario results from the last poll, and the

other errno, or curl-style prose, fell through to the generic code. And
results a caller supplied went to storage unclassified, so the drawer
rendered the raw text as the judge's reasoning.

The adapter now wraps a transport failure in a typed error naming the
target host and the failure kind, keeping the underlying text so the
classifier still recognises it and the raw error as the cause. The
classifier learns the getaddrinfo and could-not-resolve-hostname
markers, which also lets an agent on a dead dev tunnel name itself when
its hostname stops resolving. Results whose reasoning is the raw failure
(or is missing) are classified before storage; results a judge wrote,
and any passing verdict, are stored untouched.

A `--tunnel-url` session starts neither a tunnel child process nor the
local auth proxy, and the health monitor's timer is unref'd, so nothing
held the event loop open. The command printed its banner and the process
ran out of work, which left the agent pointing at the caller's tunnel
with the real URL still stashed under devTunnel. The health check never
ran either, so the warning for a tunnel this session cannot replace was
unreachable.

runs, and clears it when the session ends.

A fork could hang the child. `os.register_at_fork` copies the lock in the
state it had, so a fork while the loop thread held it left the child with a

* fix(agents): a call is placed again only when it never reached an instance

The dispatcher retried on another instance whenever no ack was recorded.
The SDK sends `ack` and starts the function without waiting, and the gateway
writes the ack key after it reads the stored call, so a disconnect inside
that window left no key while the function was already running. The turn
then ran twice, against the at most once guarantee.

The retry now needs proof that the frame never reached an instance. Two
cases carry that proof: a publish that reached no subscriber, and a frame
the socket never took. The gateway writes to the socket before it counts the
call as in flight, and records `undelivered` on the result when the write
did not happen, so a socket that went away between the nudge and the write
does not cost the turn. A call routed at an instance that never registered
the agent is `undelivered` for the same reason.

Anything else fails as `agent_disconnected`. The copy says the turn may have
run and is not sent again.

fix(metrics): stop the rollup bucket read scanning retention with every column (#7691)

* fix(metrics): stop the rollup bucket read scanning retention with every column

The authoritative read behind `recomputeAffectedRollupsMany` fetched every
stored column through FINAL across the whole retention window, once per
affected bucket. FINAL materialises the selected columns for every row a
granule covers rather than the rows returned, so a statement returning ~100
rows was reading millions — and the server ran out of memory inside one of
the columns nothing reads (`while reading column PointAttributesJson`).

Two bounds, both on what the read looks at rather than on how large the
request is:

- ROLLUP_SELECT replaces AUTHORITATIVE_SELECT: the columns the fold reads and
  nothing else. The attribute and quantile JSON, resource and scope identity,
  description, flags and the accounting timestamps are not rollup inputs and
  were being decompressed and discarded. `MetricRollupSourcePoint` names the
  contract, so a builder cannot read a column the read does not fetch.

- The predecessor seek looks back an hour first, and widens to the rest of
  retention only for the buckets that found nothing there. The two windows
  abut, so their union is the single retention-wide window this replaced. The
  table partitions by ISO week, so the wide seek opened seven weekly parts to
  return one row; a live series now opens one.

RAW_SELECT and fromRaw go with them — nothing read whole rows any more.

* refactor(metrics): name the near-pass predecessor check

Biome's new-violation gate fails on a single added warning. Extracting
the unresolved-seek scan out of pointsForAffectedBuckets drops it back
under the complexity limit and gives the check a name.

* fix(metrics): say when the wide predecessor pass actually fires

Review feedback on #7691.

The comment claimed almost no bucket needs the wide pass. A series whose
first points are arriving has no predecessor at any distance, so every
one of its buckets falls through to it and the seek returns nothing.
Under series churn that is the common path. It costs one extra round
trip on top of what the single-pass read already cost, so it is not a
regression, but the comment was narrower than the behaviour.

The counted-reads integration test folds exactly such a series, which is
why it now expects three reads rather than two. The contract it exists
for is unchanged: the count stays flat as the chunk grows.

Also renames withBucketRows to shouldReadBucketRows for the boolean
naming rule.

original config forever — UpdateFunctionCodeCommand (the only update path)

demanded 100+ concurrent multi-query passes - exhausting the Prisma
connection pool inside resolveCallerProjectScope before the pull request
was even looked up. Measured: 4 queries per engine check, 160 queries

  reimplementing the deprecated walk (ADR-110).

feat(query): one door for raw LangWatchQL — REST at /api/v1/query, old routes removed (#7611)

* feat(query): promote LangWatchQL to its own JSON-RPC domain at /api/v1/query

LangWatchQL was reachable only as a sub-feature of charts, through
`/api/v1/projects/{projectId}/analytics/query/clickhouse` and its sibling
`.../analytics/schema`. Three things were wrong with that surface, and this
adds the door that fixes all three:

  1. The engine was in the URL. `/clickhouse` named the storage engine on a
     public path while Postgres-backed views already routed through the same
     service, so the name promised something the surface does not mean.
  2. The path parameter was decorative. `projectId` never selected anything —
     the tenant came from the credential, and a path naming any other project
     answered not found. A segment that cannot change the answer misleads.
  3. The domain had no family of its own. `analytics-sql` (directory),
     `analytics/query/clickhouse` (URL) and `lwql` (service) were three names
     for one thing; charts are a consumer of LangWatchQL, not its parent.

The surface is a verb, not a collection of addressable resources, so it is
JSON-RPC rather than REST: `query.run` and `query.schema` on one path, which
also gives the family somewhere to grow (`query.explain`, `query.cancel`)
without minting a path per verb. The version leads — `/api/v1/query` — putting
it where the rest of the platform already carries it.

Errors keep one vocabulary. The family's `onError` wraps this API's canonical
error envelope as the JSON-RPC `error.data` rather than replacing it, so a
client already parsing this app's errors needs no second parser, and failures
answer with their real HTTP status because CLIs and proxies branch on status
long before anything reads a body.

Two seams are documented rather than hidden, and pinned by tests so the docs
cannot quietly stop being true:

  - Auth failures (401/403) are raised beneath the family handler and arrive
    as the bare canonical envelope, NOT JSON-RPC-wrapped.
  - An unknown method is refused by the envelope as an invalid request (400),
    so no 404 is published for one; the handler's not-found branch stays as a
    guard for an enum/table disagreement.

Nothing is removed: the superseded routes stay registered and published, so
existing consumers are unaffected. Documentation pages land with the epic's
documentation phase, which is why the path is in the generator's skip list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(query): echo the JSON-RPC id on requests refused before dispatch

The id was recorded inside the route handler, which runs only after the
envelope validator has passed. That records it exactly when it is least
needed: a malformed envelope, an unknown method or a batch never reaches
the handler, so those refusals answered with no id at all.

That is the failure the mechanism exists to prevent. A client
multiplexing calls over one connection matches replies to requests by
id; an error it cannot match is an error it cannot route, and the call
it belongs to never settles. Unknown-method is the documented ordinary
path for a common client mistake, so this was not a marginal case.

Move the recording into a middleware that runs ahead of the validator
and reads the id off the raw body. Anything unparseable passes through
untouched — salvaging an id is this middleware's only job, and the
schema downstream still owns the diagnosis.

The existing unit test missed it by seeding the id into a stub context
by hand, proving only that the body builder echoes what it is handed.
The regression tests added here drive a real middleware chain, because
the bug was purely one of ordering and a stub cannot express ordering.

* fix(query): actually authenticate the query door

`handlerManagedAuth` applies no middleware. It is a declaration that the
HANDLER authenticates — the dataset family pairs it with an in-handler
call for signed upload sessions, the export families with a session
probe. The query handler declared it and then did none of the work: it
read the project straight off a context nothing had populated.

So the door stood open. Every anonymous call reached the dispatch table
and died on `project.id` of `undefined`, answering 500 rather than 401,
and `analytics:view` was enforced nowhere. The published document had
been promising `project_api_key` security the whole time, which is what
made this worse than a plain omission: the spec described a gate that
did not exist.

Use `apiKeyPermission("analytics:view")` — a real route-level chain, and
the sanctioned form for a public API-key surface, since it applies the
key ceiling rather than a strict role check.

The reasoning that led here was wrong twice over, and the comment it
left behind is replaced rather than trimmed: a route-level gate was
avoided on the theory that a future cross-project fan-out would resolve
the permission at the wrong scope. But this route is mounted on a
project app, where it resolves against the project the credential names,
and the fan-out will be a different app on a different mount that can
choose its own gate.

Pinned by tests driven through the real mounted app, because the hole
was that a declared policy installed nothing — only the assembled app
can show what was actually installed, and a stub would have reproduced
the mistake rather than caught it. They also pin that the refusal does
not double as a method directory.

* feat(sdk): make raw LangWatchQL reachable as LangWatch.query

Raw LWQL had no public SDK surface. `runQuery` lived on `ChartsApiService`
— the consumer owning the primitive — and that class is exported from
nowhere and is not a `LangWatch` field, so every caller reached it by deep
path. This adds the producer as its own first-class service.

`QueryApiService` speaks the JSON-RPC door at `POST /api/v1/query`:
`query()` sends `query.run`, `schema()` sends `query.schema`, and both
return the unwrapped payload rather than the envelope.

One path serves two methods, so the generated `200` types `result` as a
two-member union. The methods narrow it with `Extract` on a property unique
to each member rather than hand-written shapes, so a contract change breaks
compilation instead of drifting silently.

Wired eagerly, beside `analytics`. Lazy getters exist only because the
management families refuse an empty credential at construction; this one
takes the ordinary project config and has no such refusal — verified by
constructing `LangWatch` with an empty key without it throwing.

Also unwraps the JSON-RPC envelope before the shared error reader sees it.
That reader decides "did the platform name this failure?" by looking for
the canonical envelope at the top level of the body, which is where every
REST family puts it. This endpoint nests it one level deeper as
`error.data`, so handed the raw body the reader found only a numeric
`-32000`, judged the failure unnamed, and dropped the code, the trace id
and the platform's own sentence — every 400/422 degrading to a generic
error. Unwrapping happens here, in the one service that speaks JSON-RPC,
rather than by teaching the shared reader a transport the other twenty
families do not use.

Charts keeps its own `runQuery` for now; delegating it is separable.

* fix(feature-flags): resolve org memberships in one read instead of one per org

organizationIds and issuing one organizationUser.findUnique per id.
Prisma batches those into a single IN (...) statement, but the planner
still probes the composite primary key once per organization, and the
page issues three of these calls per load. For accounts in many
organizations this became the heaviest read on the database.

guard only inspects top-level model operations, so the nested read is
the same shape the MFA enrollment repository already uses for
cross-organization questions.

response cannot be used as a membership oracle.

surface calls and which previously had none.

`resolveMemberOrganizationIds` took three positional parameters, two of
which are strings, so a caller could swap them silently. The repo rule is

call sites, and the `buildMockPrisma` / `buildCaller` helpers in both unit
test files.

docs(agent-testing): connect from a function beside your service startup (#7698)

* docs(agent-testing): connect from a function beside your service startup

The connect step read as "decorate the function that runs your agent",
which is not what a customer writes. They add a small function beside
the code that starts their service, and that function calls the agent
they already have. It is the adapter: build the input the agent expects,
pass the run parameters into it, and read the reply out of what it
returns. Both examples now call an existing agent instead of standing in
for one, and the skill tells a coding agent to find two places, the
agent entry point and the file that starts the service.

Starting the process is no longer a step of its own. "Start the service
the way you always start it" next to a `node agent.ts` block read as two
different instructions. The connect function goes on the startup path,
the start command does not change, and `langwatch.agent.serve()` is a
note for an agent that has no service of its own.

`enabled` takes any boolean, so one expression can gate which
deployments connect. The option reference, the environments page and
both SDK doc comments show that now.

* fix(docs-ci): check every page the skills manifest generates, not two of them

The skills manifest drives five pages now. The pre-commit hook staged
two of them by name, and the CI staleness gate checked the same two, so
a change to a skill left `agent-testing/connect-your-agent.mdx` and the
two `coding-agents/` pages regenerated but unstaged, and CI reported
green with the published page behind its source.

`generate-skills-pages.mjs --list-pages` prints the pages it writes. The
hook stages that list and CI checks it, so a new manifest entry is
covered without a second copy of the list to remember.

Measured before and after: with the generated block in
connect-your-agent.mdx made stale, the old two-page diff exits 0 and the
new one exits non-zero.

* docs(agent-testing): cut the adapter paragraph to one sentence

* docs(agent-testing): correct the enabled examples and the TypeScript run command

`enabled` replaces the CI rule instead of adding to it. `resolveEnabled`
returns the explicit value before it reads `CI`, so
`enabled=APP_ENV != "production"` connects a CI job, which is what the
default exists to prevent. Both examples carry the `CI` half now, and
the text says why. The Python snippet also imports `os`.

`node agent.ts` needs Node 22.18 for native type stripping, and the SDK
declares `node >=20`. The sentence is about the connection holding the
event loop open, so it no longer names a command, and where a command
helps it points at the project's own runner.

Reported by CodeRabbit on #7698.

* docs(agent-testing): do not promise TypeScript keeps the script alive

The Note said the connection holds the event loop open. That is true of
an open WebSocket and not of the two waits around it: `wait()` in

both call `.unref()`, so a script with no server of its own can exit in

fix(authz): index the column an API-key permission check filters on (#7703)

* fix(authz): index the column an API-key permission check filters on

The holder lookup behind findCustomRolePermissions asks who else holds a
key's private role - (organizationId, roleKey), fenced on the row not
being revoked. Every index on Grant led with organizationId and then went
somewhere else, so for an organization holding more than a handful of
grants the leading column selected everything and there was nothing left
to descend. Postgres read every live grant the organization owned, on
every check, to return a few rows.

The regression test seeds a lopsided organization, drives the real public
method, captures the SQL Prisma emitted and asks the planner what it did
with it. It asserts rows EXAMINED rather than an index name or the
absence of a sequential scan, because those are shapes a future plan is
allowed to change; 20,001 rows read to return one is not.

Closes #7700

* docs(authz): name the invalid-index trap the concurrent path leaves behind

A CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY that fails leaves an invalid index under the
same name. IF NOT EXISTS would match it and skip, and the planner never
uses an invalid index - so the migration would report success while the
read stayed broken. The escape hatch now says how to check and recover.

* test(authz): type the principal instead of casting it away

`as never` on the principal would swallow a change to
AuthzPrincipalRef rather than fail the build, which is the one thing the
type is there to do.

* docs(authz): say what the grant index build costs and how to undo it

The migration described the lock but never sized it, so a reader could only
assume the worst: Grant is the live authorization projection, a revoke is a
write, and writes wait for the build. Measured on a 600,000-row reproduction
of the shape this index serves, the build is 575 ms for 4 MB of index - the
same order as every other migration here, and the same trade the two
comparable index migrations took for the same reason, that CONCURRENTLY
cannot run inside the transaction Prisma wraps a migration in.

Also adds the manual rollback step this directory expects on a reversible
migration.

* test(authz): nest the grant index check under a when block

CLAUDE.md asks for given/when nesting rather than a single given suite with
the condition folded into the test name.

* docs(authz): say where the grant index build was measured

The note gave a single figure with no context, so a reader could take it for a
production number and size a deploy window off it. It was measured on a local
container on developer hardware; a smaller or saturated instance should expect
single-digit seconds, which is the extrapolation the comparable migration in
this directory already makes from its own reproduction.

Also records that the figure was checked against two distributions - one
organization holding every row (524 ms) and a 7,000-organization spread
(399 ms) - because a btree deduplicates repeated keys and a lopsided seed
would have flattered it. It does not: the spread is the faster of the two.

Drops a wrong sentence that credited the partial predicate for the build cost.
The predicate excludes almost nothing here, since almost every row is live.

* docs(authz): name the lock the rollback takes

The build note is careful to say it blocks writes and not reads. The rollback
is the other way round - a plain DROP INDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and blocks
both - and saying nothing invited the reader to carry the build's reassurance
across. It is immaterial at this size (0.458 ms measured), and CONCURRENTLY is
available on the manual path, which is not inside Prisma's transaction.

fix(nlpgo): bound undici dispatcher timeouts so 630s deadline works (#7705)

* fix(nlpgo): bound undici dispatcher timeouts on scenario adapter fetch calls

nlpgo scenario adapters (code-agent, workflow-agent) called bare global
fetch() with only an AbortController deadline. undici's dispatcher-level
headersTimeout/bodyTimeout (default 300,000ms) sits below that and an
AbortController cannot override it, so requests were cut off with
"fetch failed (cause: HeadersTimeoutError)" at ~300,815ms in production
regardless of the caller's intended timeout.

Add createNlpFetchDispatcher() in nlpgo/timeouts.ts, building a per-call
undici Agent with headersTimeout/bodyTimeout set to the resolved fetch
timeout, and pass it via the dispatcher option at both adapter fetch
call sites. Fetch options are hoisted into an explicitly-typed
FetchInitWithDispatcher const before the call, since fetch()'s DOM-lib
RequestInit type has no dispatcher field and excess-property checking
rejects it inline.

Fetch call sites remain bare global fetch() (vi.stubGlobal("fetch", ...)
test mocking preserved). No new env vars. Does not route through
ssrfProtection.ts.

* fix(scenarios): extract postExecuteSync to satisfy Biome function-length gate

executeOnNlpService exceeded the 60-line Biome noExcessiveLinesPerFunction
limit after a prior commit hoisted timeoutMs/fetchInit into it. Pure
extraction of the fetch call and its error-wrapping catch into a new
postExecuteSync method; no behavior change, error message preserved
byte-for-byte.

* refactor(nlpgo): use named parameters for dispatcher factory and postExecuteSync

* fix(nlpgo): memoize undici dispatchers by timeoutMs to stop pool leak

createNlpFetchDispatcher built a fresh undici Agent on every call. An Agent
owns its own connection pool, so a per-request Agent meant connections were
never reused, keep-alive to nlpgo was defeated, and no pool was ever
destroyed — a socket/FD leak under load. Introduced by this PR's own
dispatcher change; caught in review before it shipped.

Memoizes by timeoutMs in a module-level Map. timeoutMs derives from
env-resolved config, so key cardinality is small and fixed for the
process's life and no eviction policy is needed.

Adds closeNlpFetchDispatchers() and registers it on the EXISTING
shutdownHandles teardown array in startWorkers.ts, right after
bootScenarioProcessor — no new shutdown subsystem, no process.on handler.

The two adapter unit tests reset the cache in beforeEach: with a
module-level cache, a dispatcher built by an earlier test for the same
timeoutMs is returned without touching the mocked Agent constructor, so
agentOptions stayed empty. Their headersTimeout/bodyTimeout assertions are
unchanged.

No new environment variables. No user-visible error strings changed.

fix(scenarios): pair the nlpgo dispatcher with undici's own fetch (#7714)

* fix(scenarios): pair the nlpgo dispatcher with undici's own fetch

langwatch#7705 gave the code and workflow scenario adapters an undici
dispatcher, to raise undici's 300s headersTimeout/bodyTimeout to the
630s deadline. But it passed that dispatcher to the GLOBAL fetch. Node's
global fetch is bound to the undici bundled with the Node runtime
(7.29.0 on Node 24), while the dispatcher comes from the npm undici
(8.10.0). The npm package rejects the older handler shape up front with
"InvalidArgumentError: invalid onRequestStart method", so every code and
workflow agent call failed in about a second, before a byte left the
process. The agent editor's test call and every simulation turn failed
the same way.

The fix is the one resend.ts already documents for this exact error:
import fetch from the undici package itself, so the fetch and the
dispatcher share one implementation. Verified at every level:

- A raw repro reproduces the production error byte for byte with the
  global fetch, and gets a 200 with undici's fetch.
- A new transport test drives both real adapters over real sockets
  against a loopback server, with no part of the transport mocked. With
  the bug present it fails with the exact production error.
- The adapter unit suites now intercept undici's fetch export, and the
  global fetch is stubbed to throw. A regression back to the global
  fetch fails 59 tests instead of passing silently, which is how the
  bug got through review the first time.
- FetchInitWithDispatcher is now undici's own RequestInit. It is not
  assignable to the DOM RequestInit the global fetch takes, so handing
  the dispatcher to the global fetch no longer compiles.
- The production scenario-child-process.cjs bundle was built and
  inspected: both call sites go through the single inlined undici copy,
  and an identically bundled adapter completes a real request.

A repo sweep found no other call site that mixes the two packages, and
no setGlobalDispatcher anywhere.

fix(ci): a manual usage refresh names the pull request's own commit (#7711)

Two defects in pr-token-usage, both found by review on the copies of this
workflow going to langwatch/scenario and langwatch/langwatch-saas.

A manual refresh passes a pull request number and nothing else. The workflow
fell back to `github.sha` for the commit line, which on a dispatch is the
branch the refresh ran from, not the pull request. Every manually refreshed
comment therefore ended "Updated for <default branch sha>", naming a commit
that has nothing to do with the work it reports. The same gap defeated the
fork guard: `github.event.pull_request` is absent on a dispatch, so the
job-level condition let every dispatched number through, fork or not.

The pull request answers both questions, so the script now asks it. The
workflow passes the head sha only when the event carries one, and an empty
value sends the script to the API for the head sha and the head repository.
A head branch in another repository, or a head repository that is gone with
a deleted fork, is refused.

Second, the comment search stopped after ten pages. A pull request with more
than a thousand comments would hide the marker past the cap, the search would
report "no existing comment", and the upsert would POST a second report
rather than update the first. GitHub's `Link` header is the listing's own
end signal, so the walk follows rel="next" and stops when there is no next.

Follows #7676, which is merged.

* fix(event-sourcing): a re-fold keeps the delivered event the history read missed

A connected-agent run records its served instance after the child exits,
with a timestamp later than the finished event the SDK sent. When the
fold processed the record first, the finished event was out of order and
the executor re-folded from the event log. That read came moments after
the append and, on a replicated log, did not return the finished event
yet. The state was written IN_PROGRESS and the event id was marked as
applied, so nothing folded it again and the run stayed running forever.

The out-of-order re-fold now merges the delivered events the history
read did not return, the same way the store-miss re-fold already did,
and logs how many it had to add.

feat(ci): refresh the usage comment once more when a pull request merges (#7721)

* feat(ci): refresh the usage comment once more when a pull request merges

pr-token-usage refreshes on every push, so the last comment a pull request
carries describes the world as it was at its last commit. Work continues
after that commit. Review agents read the diff, ask for changes and read it
again, and a pull request approved as it stands never gets another push to
trigger a refresh. Those tokens were spent on that pull request and belonged
in its report, and nothing was going to put them there.

Measured on #7676: its comment settled at 221 million tokens and $288.49
when its last commit landed. Reading the same pull request from its merge
commit gives 237 million and $317.32. Sixteen million tokens and twenty nine
dollars of review were spent after the last push and went unreported.

A merge is the moment the total stops moving, so pr-token-usage-final runs on
the push to the default branch, asks GitHub which pull requests that commit
merged, and refreshes each one's comment a last time. The stamp changes from
"Updated for <sha>" to "Final, at the merge of <sha>", so a reader can tell a
settled number from one still waiting for the next push.

It runs on a push rather than on `pull_request: closed` on purpose. A
`closed` trigger runs the workflow file from the pull request's own branch,
so no pull request opened before this change landed would ever get its last
refresh. A push trigger always runs the version on the default branch.

GitHub associates a commit with every pull request that contains it, not only
the one that merged it, so the association list is narrowed three ways: the
pull request must have merged, must have merged into the branch that was just
pushed, and must come from this repository. That last one keeps the promise
the per-pull-request workflow makes, which is that fork pull requests are
never commented on, and a merge is not the moment to start. A batch merge
refreshes each pull request it carried, once; a direct push refreshes nothing.

The two entry points share one `reportUsage`, so the numbers can never drift
into being reported differently. The job waits a minute before reading: usage
from a session that ended just before the merge is still landing, and the
per-pull-request run for the final commit may still be writing the comment
this job is about to rewrite. It blocks nothing while it waits, and like the
workflow it completes, a LangWatch outage is a warning and a green job.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Kw7WASVe7hE9vec3THQoo4

* fix(ci): resolve every commit in the push, not only its tip

Review finding. The final refresh asked GitHub which pull requests were
associated with `github.sha` alone. One push can land several merge commits:
a merge queue empties a batch at once, and a rebase merge lands each of a
pull request's commits. Only the last of them is `github.sha`, so every
earlier pull request in the push would have been left without its final
refresh, silently.

The workflow now passes the range, and the script compares it to list the
commits that arrived, resolves each one, and refreshes every pull request the
push merged. Each stamp names the commit that carried that pull request
rather than the batch's tip, so a reader lands on the right commit.

Measured on a five-commit range of this repository's own main: five pull
requests resolve and each takes its own merge commit, where the previous code
refreshed one. A push with no comparable range, a branch creation or a force
push whose `before` is unreachable, falls back to the tip and warns rather
than failing the job.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Kw7WASVe7hE9vec3THQoo4

* fix(ci): stamp a pull request with the last commit it landed on

Review finding. A rebase merge associates every one of a pull request's
commits with it, and the compare listing runs oldest first. Keeping the first
match named the commit the work started from rather than the one it is final
at, which is the opposite of what "final at the merge commit" promises.

The choice is now its own function, so it is tested rather than buried in the
loop that fetches: `landingCommits` takes the resolved commits in push order
and lets the last match win. A batch still gives each pull request the commit
that carried it, and a commit that carried no pull request names nothing.

fix(ci): stop check-feature-parity binding prose, and say when a run failed (#6672) (#6862)

* fix(ci): stop check-feature-parity binding prose, and say when a run failed (#6672)

Two reporting and parsing edges, both the same shape: the signal next to your
change says one thing and the exit code says another.

The annotation regex accepted an unquoted title anywhere the token appeared, so
an ordinary sentence bound a scenario. A comment reading "carries no @scenario
annotation: this guards a temporary exclusion" bound "annotation: this guards a
temporary", and the run then failed naming a scenario nobody wrote, at a line
whose comment says the opposite. The token now has to open its comment.

Which comment markers count is load-bearing in both directions. Requiring the
token to open a //, /* or * comment is enough to stop prose binding, and it also
silently drops every unquoted `# @scenario` in Python and Bats tests, because
their own hash pattern only accepts quoted titles. The whole-repo run does not
surface that: the nine bindings in sdks/python/tests/test_webhook_signature.py
disappear and the output stays byte-identical, since those scenarios are bound
from TypeScript too. So `#` is in the accepted set and a test pins it.

The per-file `✓ all bound` is scoped to one feature file, but unknown
annotations name scenarios in no feature file at all, so they sit in no section
and the tick next to your own work reads green on a failing run. The verdict now
prints above the per-file sections as well as below, built from the same reasons
the exit code is, and unknown annotations are grouped under the file they were
written in rather than listed flat at the end.

The three collectors shared this parsing loop by copy; they now share it for
real, which is what makes the rule testable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ci): make the annotation prefix a linear scan

CodeQL flagged the comment-marker prefix added in the previous commit as
js/redos, high severity: `/**` splits either as one `/*+` or as `/*`
followed by `*`, so a line of `/**/**/...` has exponentially many parses
and the engine walks all of them before failing. Measured at 7s for a
single 30-repetition line, and every source file in the repo is fed to
this on every run.

Spelling the same rule as one flat character class under one quantifier
removes the ambiguity: each character before the token is consumed

fix(event-sourcing): a re-fold never replaces state it cannot account for (#7725)

* fix(event-sourcing): a re-fold never replaces state it cannot account for

The out-of-order re-fold read the aggregate's history from a replicated
event log and replaced the loaded state with a replay of it. A read that
lagged could omit an event ALREADY folded into that state, and the
replay silently dropped it: loaded state A,B,C plus backdated D could
commit as B,C,D with no warning.

Two fences now guard the replay: every applied id the state was loaded
with must appear in the read or in the delivery, and the read plus the
delivery must reach the state's occurred-at checkpoint. A read that
fails a fence is re-read on a short backoff; if it still fails, the
loaded state is kept and the delivery applied on top, out of order but
with nothing thrown away, counted as es_fold_refold_total
outcome=incomplete and logged at error level.

Two test fixtures encoded exactly the overwrite the fence refuses (a
stored checkpoint from an event the mocked history never returned);
their histories are now complete.

An AggregatingMergeTree collapses every row that shares a sorting key when

ClickHouse 26.0 made that a create-time error, so a fresh install against
ClickHouse 26 or newer stopped on migration 00017 and created no schema at

columns so an install created on an older ClickHouse converges on the
identical schema. Storage is unchanged, so the ALTER is metadata-only.
