rollups. `migration-order` refuses that, correctly: those files have run
somewhere and cannot change.

deploy time rather than being quietly accepted.

fix(export): route every CSV writer through the formula guard (#7793)

* fix(export): route every CSV writer through the formula guard

Seven writers called papaparse directly and handed the result to a blob or a
response of their own, so the guard that was added for the annotations export
never ran for them. A cell opening with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, TAB or CR is
executed as a formula by Excel and Sheets, and RFC 4180 quoting does not stop
it — quoting protects the CSV grammar, not the spreadsheet reading the file.

The rule now lives in one place, `utils/csvFormulaGuard.ts`, with no DOM
dependency so the server serializers import it as readily as the browser ones.
The scenario-runs serializer, which had written the same rule independently,
delegates to it rather than keeping a second copy.

Four client writers move onto `downloadCsv`, which already applied the guard.
The two that cannot — a sectioned file with no single header row, and the
server-side trace serializer — apply it in place.

A structural test walks the tree and fails on any writer calling the raw
serializer outside a short allow-list, so this class cannot grow back
silently.

Closes #7783

* test(export): assert every allow-listed CSV writer still reaches for the guard

The allow-list carried a per-file claim that nothing checked. Deleting a
neutralizeRows call while leaving the file on the list would have passed both
existing assertions. Verified by removing the import from the one writer with
no behavioural test of its own and watching the run go red.

* test(export): fail loudly on unreadable scan roots and nest formula-injection suites

The structural guard swallowed a failed walk of a configured root: src alone
clears the scanned-file floor, so a broken ee scan passed silently without
checking enterprise CSV writers. A missing root now throws.

Also folds the formula-injection tests into nested when-blocks matching the
rest of the file and drops the banner comment that restated the suite title.

* test(export): catch aliased and destructured unparse references, not just direct calls

A destructured import or an alias assignment never writes `.unparse(`, so the
dot-anchored regex let those writers through. Every alias shape still has to
spell the word once, so a word-boundary match on the bare name covers them all
while the boundaries keep unparseable and urlunparse from matching.

The scenario executor reads `agent.role` with no guard, so an agent
decorated with `@langwatch.connect_agent` raised AttributeError when it

`ConnectedAgent` now answers `role` with `AgentRole.AGENT`. The executor

fix(sdk-ts): annotations methods return what their signatures promise (#7865)

* fix(sdk-ts): annotations methods return what their signatures promise

`annotations.getByTrace(traceId)` is typed `Promise<AnnotationResponse[]>`
but resolved to `{ data: [...] }`, so the obvious next call crashed:

    TypeError: (await client.annotations.getByTrace(id)).filter is not a function

The server was never the thing that changed. `/api/annotations*` has
wrapped every response in `{ data }` and rejected a missing `comment`
with a 400 since before the Hono migration — the same shapes are in the
Next.js handler it replaced. What was wrong is the hand-maintained
OpenAPI document the SDK types are generated from: it declared the GET
bodies as bare arrays and `comment`/`isThumbsUp` as optional. Omitting
`comment` type-checked and then failed at runtime, and the envelope was
invisible to the type system, so the service returned it untouched.

Corrects the document to describe the routes as they actually answer,
regenerates the client, and unwraps `data` in the service. `getAll`,
`get` and `create` carried the same defect and are fixed with it —
`annotation get` in the CLI had been printing `Annotation undefined`
with a dash for every field.

Also corrects the `Annotation` schema, which declared `required: ["name"]`
for a property it does not define. openapi-typescript dropped the
unresolvable entry and marked every field optional, which is why callers
read annotations through `?? "—"`. It now requires the columns the row
always carries and marks the nullable ones nullable.

If you were working around this by reading `.data` off the result
yourself, stop — that property is gone and the array is returned
directly.

The CLI's `annotation create` now refuses a missing `--comment` or
rating through the shared error port rather than spending a round trip
to be told the same thing, and `annotation list` loses the
`Array.isArray` shim it carried for the envelope.

The committed client was two commits stale before this change, so
regenerating it also picks up the `pull-request-usage` operation and a
connected-agent description field that have nothing to do with
annotations. Nothing in the repo uses either typed operation. That drift
is invisible to CI, because `prebuild` and `pretest` regenerate
`src/internal/generated` in place — worth a generate-and-diff step, in
its own change.

Fixes #7863

* fix(sdk-ts): the empty-state hint suggests a command that still runs

`annotation create` now requires a rating flag, so the hint printed by
`annotation list` on an empty result was a command that fails. Name
--thumbs-up in it, the way the other list commands name every required
flag in their hints.

* test(sdk-ts): assert the error document's registry key, not its reason label

`commandValidationError` sets both `code` and `kind` to
"validation_error", so the new guard tests passed either way, but every
other CLI test that pins this error asserts `code` — that is the key the
presentation layer is keyed by. Also names the type-contract block as a
`when` condition, like its siblings.

* fix(sdk-ts): refuse both rating flags instead of silently taking thumbs-up

`annotation create --thumbs-up --thumbs-down` resolved to thumbs-up and
said nothing, both before this branch and after its new guards. The
command already validates these two flags, so name the conflict there
rather than resolve it for the caller.

* test(sdk-ts): each refusal gets the describe its condition names

The conflicting-flags case landed inside `when a required flag is
missing`, where the condition is false for it: passing both flags is not
an omission. Split the three refusals into their own `when` blocks under
a shared `given --format json is active`, so the format setup stays in
one place.

The block comment claimed the server rejects every case with a 400. It
does that for the two omissions; the flag conflict never reaches the
wire, because `CreateAnnotationBody` carries a single `isThumbsUp`.

The both-flags case was also the only one not asserting `ok: false` —
the first field a machine reads.

* docs(sdk-ts): the conflict guard's comment carries the fact the code cannot

It restated the error string on the line below it and narrated the `if`.
The sibling guard's comment cites `routes/annotations.ts`, the rule you
cannot see from this file; this one now does the same job by naming why
it is the odd one out: the conflict is not a server rejection, it is a
state the wire type cannot represent, so no layer below the CLI can
catch it.

* docs(sdk-ts): --help says exactly one rating flag, now that both are refused

The flags advertised "one of --thumbs-up/--thumbs-down required", which
was the whole rule until this branch started refusing the pair. "Exactly
one" states both halves without a second clause.

* docs(specs): the annotation CLI spec covers the refusals the branch added

The feature file documented both `create` happy paths and nothing else,
so it now read as though a bare `--comment` still worked. Three
scenarios cover the refusals this branch introduced, in the style the
suite already uses for rejections — `Create an agent without required
type` in agent-cli, `Create a scenario without required situation` in
scenario-cli.

* feat(traces-v2): make thumbs_up_down events filterable without configuration (#7764)

Three defects kept feedback events out of reach in the trace explorer:

- The comfortable-density default section set omitted the Event name and
  Event attributes sections, so a fresh profile never saw them. Both are

  lookup, and the server routes event.attribute./span.attribute. facet
  keys to new bounded-sample lookups against stored_spans
  (Events.Attributes / SpanAttributes).
- Event rows had no drilldown. The events facet query now zips
  Events.Name with Events.Attributes and attaches per-event
  event.metrics.* value tallies (composite-key sumMap buckets, top-10
  capped, KEY_DISCOVERY_SETTINGS guarded) to the one discover query;
  a new EventDrilldown renders them evaluator-style and toggles a
  single top-level event.attribute.event.metrics.<k>:<v> clause.

The scenario claimed a thumbs_up_down event could carry
"event.metrics.latency_bucket" with the string value "p95". Ingest
rejects that with a 400 — `eventSchema.metrics` is a record of string to
number (src/server/tracer/types.ts:536), so a metric value is a decimal
on every path, and the projection mapper drops anything that fails its
decimal gate (event-attrs.mapper.ts:23).

The scenario passed anyway because its test fabricates a FacetItem in
memory, never touching ingest — a green test standing on a premise the
product refuses.

event with a numeric "stars" metric, which has no entry in the label map
and so renders as its stored value. Verified by ingesting both against a
live stack: stars=4 -> 200 and renders "stars 4", latency_bucket="p95"
-> 400 "Expected number, received string".

Moves the test out of the thumbs_up_down describe, since it no longer
renders a thumbs_up_down item.

* test(traces-v2): the drilldown Rule stops asserting things nothing checks

Two of the five scenarios under "Event rows drill down into their metric
values" were bound to no test at all. An unbound scenario is worse than a
wrong one: it reads as covered and guards nothing.

"An event type with no metrics shows no drilldown affordance" is now bound.
The behaviour was real — verified in a browser, one chevron across two event
rows — but the guard behind it had no automated cover. The test drives both
shapes: `eventMetrics` absent, which is what the server actually emits for an
event with no `event.metrics.*` attributes and what suppresses the chevron in
SectionRenderer:204, and the empty array, which no endpoint emits today.
Covering the second closes the hole raised in review and previously answered
with an argument about server behaviour rather than a test — an argument that
holds only until a payload changes.

Confirmed the test can fail: mutating the `metrics.length === 0` guard in
EventDrilldown.tsx turns it red, then green again on revert.

"The drilldown filter is trace-scoped, not same-event-scoped" asserts backend
query semantics and needs a repository-level test to mean anything. Tagged
@integration @unimplemented to declare the gap rather than leave it looking
enforced.

verbatim as "1" and "-1" — untrue since the vote labels landed.

typecheck 0, biome errors 0 across 8500 files, 12 files / 69 tests green,

* fix(traces-v2): a metric key carrying the separator no longer splits wrong

The doc on EVENT_METRIC_SEP claimed 0x1F "can't appear in either half". Half
true. Metric values are numbers everywhere (`eventSchema.metrics` is a record
of string to number), so the value half stringifies to a decimal and never
carries one. Metric keys are unconstrained strings — nothing stops a caller
sending one with an embedded 0x1F.

When that happens `indexOf` finds the caller's separator first, so the key is
truncated and the rest of it lands in the value: a drilldown row whose key and
value are both wrong, filtering on something that matches nothing. The mapper
now drops the bucket instead, and the doc says what is actually guaranteed.

Follows the file's convention and leaves `extractEventMetrics` private, so the
new guard is unit-tested no more than the `sep <= 0` guard directly above it.

blocks gained their `when` layer, and a comment restating its own assertion is
gone. The stored-value test now asserts the visible text as well as the
accessible name — the scenario says the drilldown *lists* the value, and only
the aria-label was checked.

and 91 files / 1783 server unit tests green.

Clicking a metric value on an inactive event drilldown row no longer

the user expanded.

separator (0x1F), since that character collides with the composite-key
encoding the drilldown decodes and previously made the value silently

* docs(traces-v2): record that clearing a metric leaves its event anchor behind

* docs(traces-v2): the orphan anchor matches how evaluator groups already behave

The @ prefix is an input sigil only: normalizeQueryString strips it at token
start (parse.ts:153-156) and serialize never re-adds it (parse.ts:98). A facet
click yields event:x, not @event:x, and cross-field clauses join with AND, not
a space. The bound tests already encoded this — filterStore.unit.test.ts:94-96

Every existing drilldown case handed toggleFacet a vi.fn() and asserted the

fix(sdks): one HTTP client per SDK, redirects followed only for an http to https upgrade (#7906)

* TypeScript SDK: one HTTP client, redirects followed only for an http to https upgrade

Every request to the LangWatch API goes through langwatchFetch. A 301, 302, 307 or 308 whose target is the same URL with http upgraded to https is replayed once with the same method, headers and body; every other redirect raises LangWatchRedirectError. A test fails on any raw fetch outside the shared module.

* Python SDK: one HTTP client, redirects followed only for an http to https upgrade

langwatch.http_client carries SchemeUpgradeTransport and
AsyncSchemeUpgradeTransport, the create_client and create_async_client
factories and RedirectRefusedError. A 301, 302, 307 or 308 to the same URL
with the scheme changed from http to https is followed once with the same
method, headers and body, with one warning per process; every other
redirect raises. Every hand written httpx call and the generated REST
client now go through the factories, and a test scans the source for raw
httpx constructions.

* TypeScript SDK: GET and HEAD follow redirects, other methods keep the scheme upgrade rule

A GET or HEAD follows a 301, 302, 303, 307 or 308 with the same method, up to five hops, drops Authorization, X-Auth-Token and X-Project-Id when the hop leaves the origin, and refuses a downgrade to http. Every other method still follows one http to https upgrade of the same URL only. The docs command goes through langwatchFetch.

* Python SDK: GET and HEAD follow redirects, other methods keep the scheme upgrade rule

SchemeUpgradeTransport and AsyncSchemeUpgradeTransport follow a GET or HEAD redirect with the same method, up to five hops, drop the credential headers when the hop leaves the origin, and refuse a downgrade to http. Every other method still follows one http to https upgrade of the same URL only.

* TypeScript SDK: the replay sends what init overrode, not the Request's own fields

fetch(input, init) lets init win over a Request field by field. The first send already honoured that, the replay read the Request instead, so an overridden method, headers or body were lost on the https upgrade. Both sends now derive from one effective Request.

* TypeScript SDK: the raw fetch guard counts calls per file instead of exempting whole files

The guard skipped the internal/http directory and exempted the two non-LangWatch files outright, so a new raw call in either scope passed. It now exempts only langwatchFetch.ts and holds each non-LangWatch file to the number of calls it has.

* TypeScript SDK: ui actions and ui call report a timeout that trips while reading the body

The deadline signal also aborts the response body read, which happened outside the try and crashed with a bare AbortError instead of printing the command's timeout message.

* SDKs: a cross origin hop also drops Cookie, Proxy-Authorization and X-Api-Key

Both clients stripped only the three names LangWatch keys on, so a caller supplied Cookie or X-Api-Key survived a GET or HEAD hop to another origin. The list now matches the Fetch standard's cross origin set plus the LangWatch names.

The TypeScript factory also moves its two redirect rules and the effective request builder out to module level, so createLangWatchFetch is the dispatch alone.

* Python SDK: a reconfiguration closes the httpx pools it replaces

setup() and the test reset replaced the REST client's httpx clients without closing them. The sync client now closes on replacement; the async one closes on a loop of its own when none is running, since awaiting it from a synchronous method is not possible and firing the coroutine at a running loop would leave it unobserved.

* docs: the SDK redirect paragraphs name HEAD alongside GET

Both clients apply the five hop rule to HEAD, which the docs described as an every other method request.

* Revert the httpx pool teardown on reconfiguration

PromptFacade captures the REST client at construction (prompts/prompt_facade.py), so a facade built before a re-setup keeps the previous LangWatchApiClient. Closing that client's httpx pool on replacement broke every live caller holding one, which the e2e suite caught with "Cannot send a request, as the client has been closed."

Releasing the pools needs the facades to resolve the client per call instead of capturing it, which is a wider ownership change than this transport work.

* Python SDK: the shared client keeps httpx's environment proxy discovery

httpx builds its proxy mounts from HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY only when it builds the transport itself (allow_env_proxies = trust_env and transport is None). Handing it a ready made transport dropped all of it, so every migrated call connected directly and ignored an operator's egress proxy.

The factories now build the client the stock way and wrap its transport and every proxy mount afterwards, so the redirect rule applies to direct and proxied requests alike. Five tests run against a loopback origin and a loopback proxy and assert which one answered, covering NO_PROXY and trust_env=False.

* TypeScript SDK: an aborted call settles while a streamed body is replayed

The stream refusal read init.body only, so a Request built with a stream and no init reached the replay. Reading that copy to the end never finishes, and the call stayed pending past the caller's abort.

The replay read now races the request's signal and cancels the copy it loses to, so an abort settles the call. A test drives a Request whose stream emits one chunk and stays open; without the fix it hangs.

* TypeScript SDK: the abort rejection in the replay body read is always an Error

eslint's prefer-promise-reject-errors flagged the raw abort reason. A non Error reason is wrapped in an AbortError.

* Python SDK: the redirect rule runs on the client so httpx picks the transport for every hop

SchemeUpgradeTransport and AsyncSchemeUpgradeTransport are replaced by LangWatchClient and LangWatchAsyncClient, which override send and issue one hop at a time through httpx.Client.send. httpx therefore selects the mount from each hop's own URL: the https replay leaves through the https mount and a GET hop to a NO_PROXY host leaves through that host's direct transport. create_client and create_async_client pass every argument to httpx unchanged. The evaluate tests patch the factories the module imports instead of httpx.Client.

* TypeScript SDK: the unread copy of a request body is released when no replay reads it

Request.clone tees the body stream, so the copy kept for a replay holds every
chunk the sent branch consumes until something cancels it. The copy is now
cancelled on every path that will not replay it. The cancellation is not
awaited: a tee settles that promise only once both branches are cancelled.

The abort test carries its own scenario name instead of repeating the one for
a refused stream replay.

* Python SDK: a hop that leaves the origin drops the auth the client was built with

Stripping the credential headers off the hop was not enough. httpx signs a
request from the auth the client holds, so a client built with httpx.BasicAuth
put Authorization back on a cross origin hop after the rule had removed it.

The hop now sends auth=None once it leaves the origin, and keeps it for a same
origin hop and for an https upgrade of the same host and port, matching the
header rule. Sync and async are both covered.

fix(traces): keep the chosen time range when opening a conversation (#7908)

* fix(traces): keep the chosen time range when opening a conversation

Opening a conversation from the Conversations tab reset the time range
back to the 30-day default, discarding whatever window the user had
picked.

The traces page keeps its bar state (active lens, query, time range) in
the URL fragment and writes it with a raw `history.replaceState`, which
React Router never observes. So from the first filter edit onwards, the
hash inside `router.asPath` is stale.

Every drawer URL is rebuilt from `asPath` and republished through
`router.push`. That turned the stale hash into a real navigation: the
fragment reverted to its pre-filter value, the page re-read it, found no
time-range statement, and applied the default window.

Read the fragment live from `window.location` instead. Path and query
still come from `asPath` — they only ever move through the router, so it
is authoritative for those; the fragment is the one axis something else
writes behind its back.

* fix(traces): keep bar state in the fragment instead of copying it to the query

Opening a drawer republishes the URL, and the fragment/query split lifted
any query it found after the `#` into the real query string. That rescue
exists for drawer params parked after the hash, but the traces bar keeps
its own state there (`#conversations?preset=24h`), so a preset ended up
duplicated on the URL as a stale `?preset=`.

Restrict the rescue to fragment queries that actually carry `drawer.`
params; everything else stays in the fragment, where its owner reads it.

* fix(traces): read the live fragment before splitting it, not after

Swapping the browser's fragment into the hash after splitAsPath had
already run meant the hash and the query it gives up came from two
different strings: a drawer param parked after the # was promoted into
the real query and a stale copy of it was left behind in the fragment,
where the next drawer navigation would promote it again.

Swap the fragment into asPath first, then split once, so both come out
of the same string.

* test(traces): nest the parked-fragment assertions under a when block

The last given block ran its action straight from the it bodies, with the
same setup copied into both, while every other block in the file states the
action in a nested when describe. Hoist the setup into a beforeEach and give
the two assertions the when block they belong under.

* fix(traces): rescue drawer params from the fragment when a query comes first

splitAsPath parsed the two URL orderings in separate branches, and only the
#fragment?query one lifted stray drawer. params back into the real query
string. So /acme/traces?filter=active#conversations?drawer.open=... left
drawer.open parked after the #, where router.query cannot see it — a filter
on the URL was enough to strand the drawer, purely because the real query
happened to be parsed first.

Pull the rescue into one rescueFragmentQuery helper both branches call, so
the ordering stops deciding whether it fires. The condition is unchanged:
only a fragment query actually carrying drawer. params is lifted, and bar
state like #conversations?preset=24h stays where its owner reads it.

* fix(traces): lift only the drawer params out of the fragment, not the bar state

A single drawer. key moved the whole fragment query into the real query
string. For #conversations?preset=24h&drawer.open=... that carried preset
out of the fragment the traces bar reads it from — losing the chosen time
range, which is the bug this branch exists to fix. The realistic shape, too:
the bar has already written preset by the time anything parks a drawer param
alongside it.

Split the fragment query instead. The drawer. pairs move to the query, every
other pair is written back into the fragment, and a fragment with nothing
left over keeps dropping its ?.

Also gives the two remaining flat given blocks the when describe the rest of
the file uses.

fix(security): move the connected-agent example onto the ai 6 line

Thirteen alerts sit on this example's lockfile, twelve of them undici and one
@ai-sdk/provider-utils. They all come from one chain:

  @ai-sdk/openai 2.0.122 -> @ai-sdk/provider-utils 3.0.35 -> undici 5.29.0

Neither end of that chain can be fixed in place. provider-utils 3.x tops out
at 3.0.36 and the advisory range is `<= 3.0.97`, so nothing on the 3.x line is
patched, and 3.0.35 pins `undici: ^5.29.0`, so overriding undici to 6.x would
break its own declared range. The escape is provider-utils 4.x, which declares
`undici: ^6.28.0`, and that arrives with @ai-sdk/openai 3.x and ai 6.

The example uses a small surface of that API: `openai()`, `generateText`,
`tool` and `ModelMessage`. All four are unchanged on ai 6, typechecked against
the installed packages.

The SDK peer-allows `@ai-sdk/openai` at `>=2.0.0 <5.0.0`, so 3.x needs no
change there. The example is private, is not a pnpm workspace member, and its
README tells readers to run `npm install`, so the committed lockfile is what a
reader gets and is worth keeping correct rather than deleting.

Closes alerts #2142 through #2154 (3 HIGH, 7 MODERATE, 3 LOW).

fix(gateway): self-map Azure deployments on the dispatch path (#7778)

* fix(gateway): self-map Azure deployments on the dispatch path (#7765)

Azure addresses a model by deployment name, so Bifrost refuses to build a
URL for a key whose AzureKeyConfig.Deployments is empty — the request never
leaves the gateway and the caller gets an opaque provider error.

The control plane only emits `deployment_map` when the provider row carries
an explicit deploymentMapping (config.materialiser.ts), which most Azure rows
do not: by default the model id IS the deployment name. Every other dispatch
path already closed that gap with domain.WithDeploymentSelfMap — nlpgo's
dispatcheradapter and gatewayproxy, added for #5760 — but the helper had zero
callers in services/aigateway. That is why the same Azure provider served the
playground and failed through a virtual key on every request.

BifrostRouter.Dispatch and DispatchStream now apply the self-map right after
the model is resolved, before any provider branch, so every lane (chat,
responses, embeddings, passthrough, Bedrock VPCE) sees the same credential.
An explicit mapping still wins: WithDeploymentSelfMap never overwrites an
existing entry.

The self-map is applied inside the adapter on a value copy, after credential
selection, so eligibility and routing are unaffected.

Tests drive the real router against a local upstream standing in for the
customer's Azure resource and assert the URL Bifrost actually builds. Without
the fix both self-map tests fail with provider_config_invalid, the taxonomy
entry for "deployments not set".

Binding the three new scenarios makes the feature file enforce scenarios for
the first time, so it comes off LEGACY_INERT.

* test(gateway): assert what the Azure self-map scenarios actually observe

Review of the scenarios turned up two places where the text described
something the test does not establish.

The Background spoke of "an Azure provider slot on a virtual key". The
test builds a domain.Credential and calls the provider router directly;
no virtual key, no auth, no pipeline take part. Reworded to the seam the
test really drives, so nobody reads these scenarios as coverage of
virtual-key resolution.

The chat scenario ended on "the dispatch does not fail with 'deployments
not set'". That string is a historical needle from the old Bifrost error
classifier; the failure this fix removes reports itself as a
provider-configuration error, which is what the positive control showed
and what the test asserts. Naming a message the system does not emit
makes the scenario unfalsifiable in the one direction that matters.

Also assert iter.Err() on the streaming lane. Without it a mid-stream
failure would leave the URL assertion passing on a request that never
produced a usable answer.

Scenario titles are unchanged, so the @scenario bindings still hold.

* test(gateway): name the stream flag and drop the field comment that restated itself

The upstream fixture's `paths` field carried a comment saying it held the
request paths, which the field declaration already said; the one property the
assertions rely on — arrival order — moves up into the type doc so it is stated
once. The chat-request helper's boolean parameter takes the `is` prefix the
repo's naming convention requires.

* fix(gateway): carry the Azure deployment into the raw-forwarded body

Bifrost v1.5 moved model->deployment resolution off AzureKeyConfig onto
Key.Aliases and stopped putting the deployment in the URL: the Azure chat
endpoint is now a flat /openai/v1/chat/completions, and the deployment is
named by the request body's `model` field.

Azure is raw-forwarded (isOpenAICompatibleProvider), so the client's own
bytes are what reach the wire and Bifrost's alias-resolved model never
lands in them. The deployment a provider names was therefore dropped on
the way out, and Azure was sent a deployment the customer's resource does
not have.

Resolve the deployment into the body on both dispatch lanes, mutating only
when it differs from the model id so the common case stays byte-identical
and OpenAI's prompt-prefix auto-cache keeps hitting -- the same rule
stripDropTuningParams follows.

The two WithDeploymentSelfMap calls stay: they fold a deployment named
alongside the credential into DeploymentMap, which is what both lanes read.

Tests drive the real dispatch path against a local upstream and observe the
deployment the request actually names. Verified each half is load-bearing:
without the body resolution both explicit-deployment tests fail, and without
the self-map the streaming one does.

* test(gateway): drop the helper comment that restated its own signature

* fix(gateway): resolve the Azure deployment without mutating the shared request

app.dispatch walks the credential chain with retry.Walk and hands the same
*domain.Request to Dispatch on every attempt. Writing the resolved deployment
back into that request left one credential's deployment in the body for the
next one: the resolver early-returns when the deployment equals the model id,
so nothing rewrote it back, and a fallback to a non-Azure credential returns
earlier still. The second resource was then asked for a deployment it does
not have, turning a single-key failure into a failure of the whole chain.

Resolve onto a shallow copy of the request instead, and only when the body
actually changes -- the unchanged case returns the original pointer, so the
common path shares the request exactly as before and stays byte-identical.

The test walks two Azure credentials with the same request, the first naming
a deployment and the second naming none, and asserts the second resource is
asked for the model id. It fails without the copy.

* spec(gateway): state that a resolved deployment belongs to one attempt

The retry-safety fix landed with a @scenario annotation pointing at a
scenario the feature file never gained, which fails the parity gate.

Write the two scenarios it needs. Both describe the same rule from the
outside — a deployment resolved for one credential must not decide what a
later attempt sends — for the two directions that actually reach the wire:
a second Azure resource, and a fallback to a provider that is not Azure.

Bind the non-Azure direction to the test that already covers it.

* feat(traces-v2): clicking a facet row opens its drilldown

The evaluator and event sections carry a second level — verdicts,
score range, per-event metric values — reachable only through a 12px
chevron at the row's trailing edge. Operators clicked the row itself,
got the filter, and never learned the sub-options existed.

Worse, the click looked inert: the section freezes its layout while the
pointer is inside, so the just-activated row stays in the list rather
than moving to the pinned block where the active drilldown renders. The
row lit up and nothing else happened until the pointer left the sidebar.

So the row's own click now opens the drilldown too, in place. State
mirrors the filter rather than latching, so undoing the click closes it
again and no row is left showing controls for a filter it no longer
contributes to. Sections whose rows have no sub-options are untouched.

The whole-tree `pnpm lint` step is blocking on errors, and the new test
file carried one: a ternary prop that Biome wraps across three lines. It

No behaviour change.

* test(traces-v2): bind the click-expand scenarios and nest them under when blocks

Two CodeRabbit findings on #7910, both house rules from CLAUDE.md:

1. The three new scenarios carried no binding tag. check-feature-parity
   only counts @unit/@integration/@e2e/@regression, so an untagged
   scenario reports itself as bound while binding nothing — the file read
   2/2 with the new rule enforcing none of it. Tagged @integration to
   match the .integration.test.tsx that covers them; the file now reports
   5/5 bound.

2. The suite grouped cases under "given" only. Each interaction now sits
   in its own describe("when ...") block, so the chevron path lives with
   the row-click path it contrasts with instead of as a sibling of the
   givens.

No production code touched.

* fix(traces-v2): tie a row's drilldown to its filter, and colour the verdict facet

Three follow-ups to the click-to-expand change, all in the same corner of
the filter sidebar.

Drilldown open-ness is now derived from the row's filter state instead of
latched in a Set on click. The Set could not tell the truth in two cases:
a row click cycles neutral -> include -> exclude -> neutral, so the second
click excluded the value while the Set treated it as an undo and collapsed
a drilldown whose filter was still standing; and a filter dropped from the
query bar, the pinned row, or a saved view left the sub-options open for a
filter the row no longer carried. Deriving also lines the inactive row up
with its pinned twin, which has always rendered extras unconditionally.
The trailing chevron keeps its override, recorded against the state it was
pressed on so it expires the moment that state changes.

The Evaluator Verdict facet had no colour or order rules, so it fell
through to the string hash: "pass" and "fail" drew arbitrary palette slots,
and the section listed Fail above Pass whenever failures outnumbered
passes. It now paints the same traffic light the evaluator drilldown does
-- green, red, yellow, in that fixed order -- at full strength rather than
dimmed.

The test harness modelled a two-state on/off toggle, which is why none of
this surfaced: the second-click assertion was passing against a transition
that does not exist. It now cycles all three states and carries an escape
hatch for clearing the filter from outside the sidebar. The feature file's
scenarios were rewritten to match.

* fix(traces-v2): order the verdict facet without seeding rows into it

Review of the previous commit turned up one real defect and one coverage
hole, both in the verdict-presentation half.

The defect: ordering was expressed by adding `evaluatorVerdict` to
FACET_DEFAULTS, but that map does two jobs. It also SEEDS — it feeds
`synthesizeDefaultDescriptors`, and its entries render as zero-count rows —
so ordering the facet through it also parked a permanent "Error 0" row in
the section, and conjured a whole synthetic Evaluator Verdict section into
the empty-project sidebar. Both in the one box the change was meant to make
easier to read. Ordering now lives in its own map, FACET_VALUE_ORDER, and
`orderValues` rank-sorts by it rather than prepending: it ranks what is
present and introduces nothing. Sort is stable, so unranked values keep the
count-sorted position they arrived with.

The coverage hole: nothing tested any of it. Stubbing the order out left
every suite green, and asserting FACET_COLORS directly would only have
proved the constant, not that a row ever receives its colour — the wiring
that matters is `dotColorFor` inside `buildFacetItems`. Both helpers are now
exported and covered there, against the rows themselves: verdict colours,
full-strength palette, pass/fail/error order however the counts fall, and no
row for a verdict the project never emitted. Four of the twelve fail when
the ordering or the colour lookup is stubbed.

The feature file gains the matching rule. Its three scenarios are bound to
the tests that assert rendered rows, not to the ones that poke the helper.

* refactor(traces-v2): buildFacetItems takes named parameters

This PR exported `buildFacetItems` so the colour and order wiring could be
covered directly, which turned a file-private helper into a shared surface —
and the surface it exposed was `buildFacetItems(cat, true)`, a bare positional
boolean that reads as nothing at the six call sites the tests added.

Object parameter, per the house rule. The one production caller passes
`synthetic: cat.synthetic ?? isSynthetic`, which now says at the call site
which of the two arguments it is.

No behaviour change: 12/12 unit and 79/79 component still pass.

* refactor(traces-v2): name the buildFacetItems boolean isSynthetic

The repo's own ast-grep rule `require-boolean-name-prefix-ts`
(dev/lint/ast-grep/rules/require-boolean-name-prefix.yml, scoped to
platform/app/{src,ee}/**/*.ts) fails a new boolean without an
is/has/should/can/will prefix. `buildFacetItems` is newly exported, so
its option is new surface and the rule applies.

The `FacetItem.synthetic` output field is unchanged — only the input
option is renamed.

fix(scenarios): structured error surfacing for SerializedCodeAgentAdapter (#3439) (#3698)

* fix(scenarios): structured error surfacing for SerializedCodeAgentAdapter (#3439)

The adapter previously collapsed every NLP-side failure into a single
"Code execution failed: HTTP 500 - <raw>" string with no distinction
between user code raising and the NLP service being down, and with AI SDK
warnings + OTEL flush chatter inlined alongside the actual cause.

This change:

- Introduces SerializedCodeAgentAdapterError with `source`
  (`user_code` | `nlp_service` | `network` | `timeout`), `endpoint`,
  `httpStatus`, and `rawDetail` so downstream code can branch on the
  failure mode without parsing message strings.
- Adds a dedicated formatter (format-execution-error.ts) that:
  - labels HTTP 500 with a `detail` payload as a user-code failure,
  - labels other non-2xx as an NLP service failure (with the endpoint),
  - strips ANSI escapes, AI SDK warnings, and OTEL flush noise from the
    rendered surface,
  - truncates >2k-char detail bodies with a marker referencing the
    original length, and preserves the unmodified blob on `rawDetail`.

The thrown message is now multi-line and starts with a clear "user code
raised an error" or "NLP service returned HTTP <status>" framing so the
worker log finally tells the customer what to do without stderr
archaeology.

Closes #3439

* fix(scenarios): classify against the Go engine's real error contract (review)

The classifier targeted FastAPI's `HTTPException(500, detail=…)`, but
/go/studio/execute_sync is served by nlpgo (Go). `grep '"detail"'
services/nlpgo` returns nothing and no Python execute_sync remains, so the
`user_code` branch could never fire in production.

Worse than the reviewer's P0: a failing user code block does not come back
non-2xx at all. The engine finalizes the run as HTTP 200 with
`{status:"error", error:{node_id,type,message,traceback}}` and omits
`result` (services/nlpgo/app/engine/engine.go `finalize`, shape at
app/app.go:121-137; asserted against the live engine in
services/nlpgo/tests/integration/code_block_spec_test.go, which requires
StatusOK and reads error.type = the Python exception class). The adapter
only inspected `!response.ok`, so a user's Python exception resolved to an
EMPTY agent reply — the silent-swallow #3439 reports.

Changes:
- classify the 200 status=error path off the engine's node-error type,
  denylisting the platform types from app/engine/faults.go so an unseen
  Python exception stays user_code instead of inverting to infra;
- classify non-2xx off the herr envelope's `type` (pkg/herr/http.go:30-74),
  mirroring handlerFault's customer set. Note herr does NOT put `fault` on
  the wire — ErrorBody is {type,message,meta,trace_id,span_id,reasons} — so
  the code allowlist is the mechanism, not a fallback. `unauthorized` and
  `not_found` deliberately stay infra: the adapter supplies the API key and
  the workflow id, so blaming user code for them is the same mislabelling;
- keep the legacy {detail} shape as a documented fallback;
- read the body ONCE as text, then parse. response.json() consumes the
  stream, so the text() fallback rejected with "Body is unusable" and
  .catch(()=>"") rendered every non-JSON body as "(empty)";
- parse inside the formatter, so a non-string `detail` (FastAPI validation
  arrays) no longer reaches .replace() and crashes the failure handler;
- hoist abort classification to cover the body read — the timer stays armed
  after headers arrive, and a bare "The operation was aborted." escaped
  unwrapped;
- redact host:port/URLs from the fetch-path cause. undici's cause carries
  `connect ECONNREFUSED 10.4.2.11:5561`, which this module's header promises
  to withhold from the persisted run record;
- drop `error.rawDetail` from customer copy; collapse 2+ blank lines.

Tests: every Response double is now a real `new Response(body,{status})`.
The plain `{ok,status,json,text}` literal is what let all of this ship green
— independently callable, infinitely re-readable bodies cannot reproduce
stream semantics. Falsifiability: with the tests kept and both source files
reverted to the previous HEAD, 33 tests fail; with the fix, 154 pass.

* fix(scenarios): address review — transport-agnostic blame, real redaction, reuse

Review of the previous commit found two blockers, both mine, plus several
correctness gaps. All are covered by tests that go RED without the fix.

Blocking:
- `invalid_workflow` was classified OPPOSITELY depending on transport: infra
  on the engine's 200 path, user_code on the herr non-2xx path. Same root
  cause, opposite blame, decided by which transport the engine happened to
  pick. Removed from the herr customer-fault set and the divergence comment
  now names it. New test asserts both paths agree.
- The module header promised the internal endpoint is withheld from EVERY
  rendered message, but only the fetch path redacted. An nginx/Envoy 502 page
  ("upstream connect error: connecting to 10.4.2.11:5561") or a herr
  `child_unavailable` message went to the persisted run record verbatim. The
  guarding test was VACUOUS — both its fixtures were address-free, so the
  absence assertion could never fail. Redaction now applies to the
  infra-detail branch, with fixtures that actually carry an address.
  Deliberately NOT applied to the user-code branch: that detail is the
  customer's own traceback and may contain a URL they wrote.

Correctness:
- A missing declared output threw a bare Error with no `kind`, no `source`
  and no span attribute — the untraced failure lw#3438 exists to remove. Now
  `kind: "output"`, `source: "user_code"`, span-tagged.
- A non-JSON 2xx was tagged `kind: "http"` with a hardcoded `httpStatus: 200`,
  re-conflating exactly what the new `execution` kind was introduced to
  separate. It gets `kind: "parse"` and the real status.
- The abort timer stayed armed after the body was in hand, so a later failure
  could be relabelled "the NLP service did not respond" — it demonstrably
  had. Disarmed at end-of-body, plus a latch for the narrow race where the
  timer fires mid-read and the body arrives anyway.
- The truncation marker reported `raw.length`, counting noise the formatter
  itself deleted — telling support there were thousands more characters of
  traceback to find. Reports the surviving length.

Reuse (hygiene):
- `parseErrorEnvelope` was a THIRD hand-rolled herr parser. It now uses the
  same exported Zod schema as `goHandledError.ts`, so a wire change lands in
  one place. Only the legacy `{detail}` fallback stays local — nlpgo never

- That schema's doc now records why `fault` must not be classified on: the
  shared `HerrEnvelope` type carries it, but Go's `toErrorBody` never writes
  it (it is a zap log field only), so it is always undefined on the wire.
  This is the exact misreading that produced the review's original P0 remedy.
- `parseExecutionResult` no longer hand-rolls a message the formatter already
  renders; it calls the shared `renderServiceFailure` via
  `formatMalformedBodyError`, so wording, truncation, noise-stripping and

- The previously-unused `NlpEngineResult` export is now the parse return type,

* fix(scenarios): real redaction, harness-frame stripping, de-vacuum the tests

Second review round. The security and test reviewers independently found that
the redaction I added was guarded by tests that could not fail.

De-vacuumed (must-fix):
- Both "does not leak the internal host and port" tests built their cause with
  `.code` set. `describeInnerCause` prefers `.code` and returns before
  redaction ever runs, so `redactInternalAddresses` could be DELETED and both
  still passed. The adapter-level test now uses a cause with no `.code` — the
  path that actually reaches the customer — and the unit-level one keeps the
  `.code` case but says plainly that it pins code-preference, not redaction.
  Neutering redaction now turns 9 tests RED; before, zero.

Security:
- The redaction regexes were both too narrow and too wide, verified by the
  reviewer against live Node errors. Too narrow: a bare address with no port
  (`getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND 10.4.2.11`) passed straight through — the actual
  shape a DNS failure produces. Too wide: `script.py:42` became `[redacted]`
  and `retry after 12:34:56` became `[redacted]:56`. Since redaction now runs
  over infra error bodies, that damage would be user-visible — and
  `script.py:42` is the most common substring in a Python traceback. Ports are
  now optional on addresses, hostnames must contain a `.` or `-`, and the
  ordinary-text cases are pinned by a table test.
- The engine's own execution-harness frames were rendered verbatim to the
  customer: `File "/tmp/nlpgo-codeblock-369240540/runner.py", line 143, in
  main`. Confirmed by the committed recording. The engine already anonymizes
  the customer's frame to `<code-block>`; its wrapper frames rode along in the
  same string that the "don't redact the customer's own traceback" rationale
  was written to protect — so that boundary was drawn at the wrong
  granularity. Harness frames are stripped; the customer's frame and exception
  line survive, asserted both ways.

Coverage (a dropped denylist entry could previously slip through):
- All four `PLATFORM_ENGINE_ERROR_TYPES` and all five remaining
  `CUSTOMER_FAULT_HERR_CODES` are now exercised; only two of nine were.
- `parseErrorEnvelope`'s non-object and no-recognised-key branches, and
  `classifyHttpFailure`'s legacy-detail-on-non-500 case, are covered.
- Dropped a `meta: { reason }` fixture field the code never reads — it implied
  a disambiguation rule that does not exist.

typecheck and feature-parity all pass.

* fix(scenarios): remove the ReDoS CodeQL found in the redaction pattern

CodeQL flagged `js/redos` (high) on the host:port pattern I added last round.
The "host is labels joined by separators" form —
`[A-Za-z0-9_-]*(?:[.-][A-Za-z0-9_-]+)+` — lets a `-` be consumed by either of
two adjacent quantifiers, so a dash-separated run that ultimately FAILS to
match backtracks exponentially. Measured on the old pattern:

  20 repeats of "-a"   37 ms
  24 repeats          570 ms
  26 repeats         2276 ms      <- a 60-character string

This runs over error bodies written by upstreams we do not control, so it was
reachable: a proxy error page echoing a long dashed token would hang the
worker. The new pattern does 200 repeats in under a millisecond.

The fix drops the nested quantifier entirely — one flat `token:port` match,
with "is this really a host?" decided in code. That also closes a hole the
previous guard only appeared to cover: `script.py:42` survived redaction ONLY
because the fixture happened to have a trailing colon; a bare
`File "script.py:42"` was still being rewritten to `[redacted]`. Source-file
locations are now excluded explicitly by suffix, asserted without the
trailing punctuation.

Also hardened `ENGINE_HARNESS_FRAME`: `\s` matches newlines in JS, so `\s{4,}`
under an outer `*` could cross lines and reintroduce the same ambiguity.
Restricted to horizontal whitespace.

* fix(lwql): self-provisioning owns the connection, so provision and query cannot split

`lwqlConnectionFromEnv` resolved the explicit `LWQL_*` connection whenever all
five were set, even under `LWQL_SELF_PROVISION=true`. `provisionLwql` builds the
access model on the connection *derived* from the admin `CLICKHOUSE_URL`, so a

`lwqlDerivedConnectionFromEnv` already refused this exact class for
`LWQL_DATABASE`; the URL had no equivalent guard. Now the self-provisioning
check runs before the per-field scan and always derives, and the derivation
refuses a `LWQL_CLICKHOUSE_URL` whose origin disagrees with the admin URL's,
naming the variable to drop rather than silently overriding it. Compared by
origin because the derived URL is normalised and an operator's value is not.

The chart sets `LWQL_SELF_PROVISION` and the two passwords but never
`LWQL_CLICKHOUSE_URL`, so the default install path is unchanged.

Alongside, from review:

- `charts/langwatch/values.yaml` + `README.md`: `lwql.enabled` provisions when
  the application starts, not on install/upgrade. The distinction is what an
  operator needs at `app.replicaCount: 0`, or when the app cannot boot.
- `selfProvisioning.unit.test.ts`: assert each catalog view's own `CREATE OR
  REPLACE VIEW` and `GRANT SELECT` per entry. The previous
  `toBeGreaterThan(0)` over the whole set stayed green when a single view or
  grant went missing, which is the one regression the test exists to catch.
- `charts/langwatch/tests/e2e.sh`: the unauthenticated 401 pins the auth gate,
  not `release_lwql_workbench`. Say so instead of labelling it the flag-off AC.

* fix(lwql): policies before grants, and never fall into the fatal path by accident

Two ways self-provisioning could fail in the direction it promises it cannot.

**A partial run could read across tenants.** `lwqlViewSetupStatements` emitted
every view, then every grant, then every row policy. In ClickHouse a table
carrying a SELECT grant and no row policy returns every row, and provisioning
is not atomic — a dropped connection or one refused statement between the grant
block and the policy block leaves the restricted identity able to read every
tenant, answering 200. `selfProvisionAll` deliberately swallows that error and
continues booting, so nothing downstream would ever close the window.

Row policies now come first. A partial run leaves the identity policed but not
yet granted, which refuses reads instead of widening them. Safe to hoist: every
table named is already present by that point — fact tables from migrations, the
PostgreSQL-engine tables from earlier in the same batch. Pinned as an ordering
test rather than a presence one.

**An incomplete Secret could brick the pod.** `execute()` chose its mode by
which inputs had arrived, not by what the operator asked for: with
`LWQL_SELF_PROVISION=true` and a hand-made Secret carrying only
`LWQL_CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD` (both keys are `optional: true` in the chart),
`lwqlSelfProvisionFromEnv()` returned null and the code fell through to the
explicit terraform path — whose `backfillKeyMap` is fatal, rethrown by the task
runner into `start.sh`'s `set -e`. A CrashLoopBackOff, for the feature whose
chart comment promises it "must degrade, not brick an upgrade". The mode is now
read from `LWQL_SELF_PROVISION`, and an incomplete self-provision configuration
declines loudly and lets the pod boot.

Also: eight doc comments across `provisioning.ts`, `views.ts` and
`postgresMapping.ts` still said "not called from any production path in this
repo". This PR makes each one a production caller on self-hosted while leaving
cloud infra-owned, so they now say both.

* style(lwql): satisfy the formatter, and lift the URL guard into its own helper

Two biome format errors from the previous two commits. Extracting
`disagreesWithDerivedServer` also brings `lwqlDerivedConnectionFromEnv` back
under the cognitive-complexity ceiling my guard had pushed it over.

* fix(lwql): the key map had the same grant-before-policy window

CI caught that the previous commit's fix was half a fix. Reordering
`lwqlViewSetupStatements` left `lwqlClickHouseSetupStatements` untouched, and
it grants `SELECT` on the key map (and on any `lwqlTables` passed) *before*
creating the row policies that constrain them — the identical window, on the
table that maps `KeyHash` to `TenantId`. A partial run there leaves the
restricted identity able to read every project's mapping. Policies now come
first in that block too.

The ordering test that caught it was itself wrong twice over, and both are
worth stating because the shape recurs:

- It asserted "every row policy precedes every grant" **globally**. That is
  false by construction — statements arrive in two blocks, so a grant from the
  first block legitimately precedes a policy from the second, and the
  assertion says nothing about whether any individual table is exposed. Now
  asserted per table, which is the property that actually protects a tenant.
- Its first per-table form then required every granted object to be policed.
  Also false by design: a view is granted but never policed, because the
  policies sit on the source tables it reads and that is what filters it.
  Narrowed to tables carrying both, with a non-vacuous guard.

Separately, `provisions the %s view with its own grant` matched the view name
as a substring, so `trace_metrics` also matched `trace_metrics_by_minute` and
two entries failed against a perfectly correct catalog. Anchored, with a
trailing non-identifier guard.

* test(lwql): match view statements by string prefix, not an escaped regex

CodeQL flagged js/incomplete-sanitization (high) on the view matcher this
branch added: `target.replace(/\./g, "\\.")` escapes dots but leaves
backslashes intact, so the interpolated identifier could still alter the
pattern it was being built into.

Nothing exploitable reaches it today — the identifier comes from
`qualified()` over catalog names that `assertIdentifier` has already
constrained to `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$` — but the fix is to stop
hand-rolling the escape rather than to complete it. The assertion only
ever needed a prefix match plus a non-identifier boundary, which plain
string comparison expresses directly and without escaping anything.

Behaviour is unchanged: still exactly one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW per
catalog entry, still guarding against `trace_metrics` matching
`trace_metrics_by_minute`.

* refactor(lwql): split the derived-connection reader and pin the protected table set

`lwqlDerivedConnectionFromEnv` had grown to 67 lines past the 60-line
ceiling. The six ways CLICKHOUSE_URL can fail to yield a server and a
database move into `derivedAdminTarget`, leaving the reader with one
"unconfigured" branch instead of six.

The row-policy-before-grant test derived its own subject from the
statements it was checking, so removing a policy would have dropped that
table out of the assertion and still passed. It now takes the expected
set from the catalog — the key map plus every distinct source table —
and requires both statements to exist before comparing their order, so a
deleted policy fails loudly. Views stay out: a view is granted but never
policed, its policies sitting on the source tables it reads.

* style(lwql): order the new views import after selfProvisioning

Biome's organize-imports assist is an error, not a warning, and the new
import landed out of order.

* feat(upgrade-access): KEEP_GOING so one run reports every AC verdict

The ladder exits at the first ac_fail. At REPLICAS=3 that meant AC8's total
access loss hid the eleven verdicts behind it — AC9, AC22, AC23, AC26, the
rollback pair, AC19 and the negative controls all went unmeasured.

continues. FAILED_ACS accumulates and main still exits 30 naming every AC
that failed. Nothing is softened: no assertion is relaxed, no failure is
downgraded to a warning, and a clean run still requires zero failures.

earlier failure (AC9 and AC22 cannot pass once the probe user is gone) are

* fix(upgrade-access): report AC19 as UNMEASURED when its precondition is gone

Run 3 at REPLICAS=3 passed AC19's "the below-quorum error carries a
ClickHouse error code" assertion, and then failed its recovery poll, for
the same wrong reason: AC8 had already lost every SQL-defined entity
across the upgrade, so up_probe did not exist. Every probe returned

  Code: 516. DB::Exception: up_probe: Authentication failed: password is
  incorrect, or there is no user with such name.. (AUTHENTICATION_FAILED)

at FULL quorum and below it alike. That string contains "Code:", so the
assertion went green while measuring nothing about Keeper quorum, and the
recovery poll could never go green however healthy Keeper was.

Establish the precondition explicitly (can up_probe authenticate at full
quorum?) and, when it does not hold, record the up_probe half of AC19 as
UNMEASURED rather than passing or failing it. A pass there would be
vacuous; a fail would blame AC19 for AC8's defect. The 'default' half is
unaffected and stays gated — default comes from users_xml, survives the
upgrade, and authenticating below quorum is a real measurement.

Adds a third reporting channel alongside pass and fail. UNMEASURED
assertions are listed separately in the run summary and never folded into
either column, because folding them is what turns a gap in the evidence
into a false claim.

No assertion is weakened: the bar AC19 sets is unchanged for any run where
the probe user survives.

* fix(upgrade-access): stop KEEP_GOING printing green over its own red

99d79abae5 made ac_fail return instead of exiting so one run could report
every AC verdict. That silently broke every assertion site that had been
relying on ac_fail never returning. Two failure modes, both observed in
ladder run 3:

1. FALSE GREEN. Every helper and phase that ended with an unconditional
   pass() now printed it directly underneath its own failure. Run 3's log
   contains pairs like

     [FAIL AC9] row policy limits up_probe to one row on ch-clickhouse-2:
       expected '1', got 'Code: 516...'
     [PASS] AC9 row policy limits up_probe to one row on ch-clickhouse-2

   The FAIL was real; the PASS was an artifact. Affected ac_assert_eq,
   ac_assert_contains, require_all_pods_ready, ac7b, ac12's envelope
   verdict, ac18, ac23's per-pod convergence, ac26's two verdicts, and
   P1.3's seeding gate.

2. NON-TERMINATING POLLS. Loops that called ac_fail on timeout expected it
   to exit. AC19's quorum-recovery poll ran past its own 300s budget to
   t+943s and 250 recorded failures before the run was killed; run 3 never
   reached P1.8 as a direct result. AC23's propagation poll had the same
   shape.

Each site now tracks its own verdict and emits the green line only when it
earned it, and each poll breaks itself. Guards return 0, not 1: under
`set -e` a non-zero return from a bare call would abort the run and defeat
KEEP_GOING entirely.

Also: a failed helm rollback/upgrade no longer proceeds to measure a
cluster that is not in the state the AC describes — it records the failure
and marks the remainder of that phase UNMEASURED. And a denial case with a
terminal verdict stops there instead of emitting duplicate reds for one
defect.

No assertion is weakened. Every bar is exactly where it was; these changes
only stop the harness reporting outcomes it did not measure.

* fix(upgrade-access): make AC24(a) a two-sided control that can actually fail

Ladder run 4 reported

  [FAIL AC24(a)] the AC8 check exits 30 (AC failure) with an entity
    destroyed: expected '30', got '0'
  [PASS] AC24(a) the harness detects a dropped entity

which is two separate defects in six lines, and neither of them is a
product finding.

The FAIL: the subshell inherited KEEP_GOING=true, so ac_fail returned
instead of exiting and ac8_five_classes exited 0 no matter what it found.
The control was measuring KEEP_GOING, not detection.

The PASS: an unconditional pass() after ac_assert_eq. The earlier sweep
missed it because the ac_fail lives inside ac_assert_eq, so it is not
lexically near the green line it printed over.

The deeper problem is attribution. AC24(a) exists to prove the detector
notices a destroyed entity. But in this experiment AC8 already fails for
all five classes, so the subshell exits 30 whether or not anything is
dropped — a red that would have happened anyway proves nothing. The
control was vacuous in exactly the run it most needed to be sound in.

Replaced with a two-sided control of the classifier itself: create the
entity, assert the detector says present-on-all; drop it, assert the same
detector says absent-on-all. Both halves run against the live cluster, and
this is sound here precisely because forward propagation works (AC23
measured 0s), which is independent of whether the upgrade preserved
anything. A detector that cannot separate those two states would
invalidate every AC8 verdict in this report.

The AC8-mediated form is kept but gated on every class being green
beforehand, so it runs only when its red would be attributable to the
drop; otherwise it is recorded UNMEASURED with the reason. KEEP_GOING is
disabled inside that subshell so ac_fail exits as the control expects.

The bar is raised, not lowered: the old form could pass without detecting
anything, the new one cannot.

* feat(clickhouse-serverless): refuse the unsupported replicas 1 -> 3 transition

Upgrading an existing single-node release to replicas=3 half-succeeds today.
Measured on kind (issue #1168, P1.7): existing tables stay plain MergeTree on
pod-0, so the new replicas come up with empty data directories. Per-pod
SELECT count() returned the full count on pod-0 and "Code: 81 ... Database up
does not exist (UNKNOWN_DATABASE)" on pods 1 and 2, and five identical
distributed SELECT count() calls returned the full count four times and
UNKNOWN_DATABASE once — the same query, twice, gives different answers with no
error saying the topology moved. The five SQL-defined access-entity classes are
not migrated either. The scale-up also crashlooped the new pods until Keeper
accepted connections (exit 231, KEEPER_EXCEPTION out of
NamedCollectionFactory::loadIfNot), failing helm --wait outright in 1 of 2
attempts.

There is no migration code on this path, so the chart now refuses it, following
the odd-replicas fail already in clickhouse-serverless.validate.

The current replica count is read from the live StatefulSet's spec.replicas
rather than the release's recorded values: Helm does not expose the previous
release's values to templates, and spec.replicas is the topology that actually
exists even if it was changed outside Helm. The guard is scoped to
.Release.IsUpgrade so fresh installs are never blocked, and 3 -> 3 upgrades pass
untouched.

Declared limitation, documented at the definition: lookup returns nil wherever
the renderer has no cluster access, so under ArgoCD and helm template the guard
is silently inert. Failing closed on nil would break every GitOps sync, so this
is a safety net for the interactive helm upgrade path, not a boundary.

* test(clickhouse-serverless): falsifiable check for the 1 -> 3 transition guard

AC11-D was chosen as a code branch rather than a docs branch precisely so it is
falsifiable by a command, so it gets a command. The script drives a real kind
cluster through all three cases the AC names and records each one's exact
command, exit code and full output:

  (a) install at replicas=1, then upgrade --set replicas=3 -> must exit
      non-zero AND stderr must contain "unsupported transition";
  (b) install at replicas=3, then upgrade at replicas=3 -> must exit 0;
  (c) fresh install at replicas=3 -> must exit 0.

(a) asserts on the message, not just the exit code: a timeout, an image pull
failure or a quota rejection are all non-zero too, and none of them would be
evidence the guard fired. It also asserts spec.replicas is still 1 afterwards,
so a guard that failed after mutating the StatefulSet would be caught.

(c) exists because the guard is lookup-based, and the failure mode of a
lookup-based guard is blocking first installs.

Verified on kind: all three cases behaved as required, and a negative control
(same cluster, same release at replicas=1, same upgrade command, guard include
removed) exits 0 where the guard exits 1 — so the refusal is attributable to
the guard and not to anything incidental in the transition.

* test(clickhouse-serverless): run the upgrade-access proof on EKS, not only kind

The harness could only prove the access-store relocation on a kind cluster it
built and threw away. Phase 2 of langwatch-saas#1168 needs the same proof on a
real arm64 EKS cluster, where the kubelet pulls from the actual registry and
EBS makes teardown slow and fallible.

Adds TARGET=kind|eks. Every eks branch is gated on that one variable, so
TARGET=kind is the behaviour that shipped, unchanged.

Under TARGET=eks:

- Refuses to run unless `kubectl config current-context` contains
  EXPECT_CLUSTER, and exits 40 before installing the EXIT trap, so a
  mis-aimed run mutates nothing. No cluster is created or deleted.
- Nothing is side-loaded. AC20 resolves the manifest-list form with
  `crane digest --platform linux/arm64` and compares it to what the running
  pods report in .status.containerStatuses[].imageID. A missing crane is a
  harness error (exit 10), never a skipped AC.
- R6 hygiene is explicit and verified, because there is no fresh cluster to
  give it for free: uninstall, delete the PVCs, delete the Secret carrying
  helm.sh/resource-policy: keep, delete the namespace, wait for it to really
  be gone, then assert namespace-absent and no-PVC-survives. A leftover PVC
  or Secret can manufacture a false "survived the upgrade" pass.
- NODE_SELECTOR_KEY/VALUE pin every replica to one node via
  scheduling.nodeSelector (run 2a); omitting them spreads (run 2b).
- TIMEOUT defaults to 1200 rather than 600, for real EBS attach/detach.
- Requirements are target-aware: helm, kubectl, crane, aws — not kind, not
  docker.
- image.pullPolicy is overridden to IfNotPresent; Never would ImagePullBackOff
  every pod and defeat the leg's whole point.
- KUBECONFIG survives the helper's sanitising unset, since it is the only
  route to the operator's cluster.

No AC is weakened or reinterpreted. The usage header documents every new
variable; usage() now prints the whole header instead of a hardcoded line
range that had already grown past its end.

fix(traces): keep a reading of zero on ingest (#7921)

* fix(traces): keep a reading of zero on ingest

The step that turns an OTLP attribute into a value asked whether the number
was truthy. Zero is not, so a tracked event whose metric was zero was
accepted with a 200 and then stored with that metric missing entirely, while
every other value on the same path stored fine.

A thumbs-up/down vote is allowed anywhere between -1 and 1, so 0 is a legal
neutral vote and the only one that could not survive ingest. The same went
for any custom metric that happened to be zero: a count of 0, a latency of 0,
a score of 0. Downstream - filters, the event drilldown, trigger matching -
the event read as carrying nothing rather than carrying a neutral reading.

Whole numbers and fractional ones now ask whether the value is there rather
than whether it is truthy, the question the boolean branch alongside them
already asked, so false and 0 are both kept and a genuinely empty attribute
is still dropped.

Three existing tests pinned the old behaviour and named it a bug in their
own comments; they now assert the value survives.

Closes #7869

* spec(traces): say what the zero-value scenarios actually observe

The Then steps claimed the reading reaches storage; what is asserted is the
normalization step every span event's attributes pass through on the way in.
No write is replayed and read back, and the scenario now says so rather than
promising more than it checks. The list scenario also drops its tracked-event
framing: the tracked-event endpoint sends one number per metric, so a list
only arrives on an ordinary span.

* test(traces): the non-zero control stands on its own, and drop a stray symlink

Review was right on both halves. `keeps a non-zero reading untouched`
asserted -1 while sitting under `when a numeric attribute is zero`, and
its annotation bound it to the neutral-vote scenario, which is about a
zero. It now has its own `when a numeric attribute is not zero` block
and no annotation: it is the control that widening the check to presence
moved nothing else, not a behaviour the spec claims. The comment above
it says so, so the missing annotation reads as deliberate.

Also removes `platform/app/src/generated/generated`, a symlink into
another local checkout that was picked up by an over-wide `git add` and
had no business in the tree. Nothing imports through it; both
typechecks are clean without it.

* fix(custom-chart-playground): concurrent LW.query support, fill-height charts, LW.useChartQuery hook

Root cause of the "Loading..." hang on multi-query widgets:
frameBridge.ts's handleQuery tracked a single global
activeRequestId/activeAbort ("one request at a time: a newer lw:query
aborts the one in flight"). A widget dispatching two LW.query calls via
Promise.all had its second dispatch abort the first, and the parent's
stale-reply guard (activeRequestId !== requestId) silently dropped the
aborted query's rejection instead of forwarding it back to the frame -
so that query's promise inside the iframe never settled, and Promise.all
never resolved. Fixed by tracking one AbortController per requestId (a
Map) instead of a single slot, matching what the shim's own `pending`
dict (keyed by requestId) already assumed on the frame side.

Chart fill: SandboxedChartFrame defaulted its iframe height to a fixed
240px and only grew via an author-called LW.setHeight - a resized card
never grew the chart with it. The iframe now defaults to (and tracks)
the card's own maxHeight, and buildSrcdoc gives #lw-root and html/body
height:100% so a widget's ResponsiveContainer height="100%" actually
has something to fill. LW.setHeight still works for a widget that wants
to size to its own content instead.

LW.useChartQuery(name, params) hook (shim addition): wraps LW.query's
promise in window.React.useState/useEffect so widget authors get
{data, loading, error} without hand-rolling it - never throws into the
component, ignores resolutions after unmount, refetches on page
param changes via the existing onParamsChange feed (now returns an
unsubscribe so a hook instance doesn't leak a listener per mount), and
compares params by value (JSON) so an inline object literal doesn't
cause a refetch loop. Starter widget template and Langy's page context
both updated to present this as the primary fetch API.

TanStack Query result contract — {data, isLoading, isFetching, isError,
