fix(gateway): re-read budget spend when its period ends (#7917)

* fix(gateway): re-read budget spend when its period ends

A cached bundle carries each budget's spend for the period it was read in,
and the config version token is built from the key's revision and its
provider set. Neither moves when a period ends, so the 60s staleness
refresh comes back 304 and the spend figures stay where they were.

For a budget that reached its limit that is a block with no way out. The
change event that would evict the entry is emitted by the debit of a
request that got through, and once the block is in force no request gets
through. The key stays rejected on the previous period's money until
someone edits it or the gateway restarts.

The wire already carries each budget's resets_at. Decode the earliest one
that belongs to a budget with a limit onto BundleConfig.Budget.ValidUntil,
treat an entry whose config was read before that instant as stale once it
passes, and drop the If-None-Match on that refresh so it cannot be
confirmed instead of answered.

The staleness check compares the boundary against configFetchedAt, so a
boundary that is permanently in the past (a MANUAL window, a skewed clock)
costs one re-read per entry rather than one per request.

No control-plane change: resets_at was already materialised and shipped,
just dropped at decode.

* docs(gateway): narrow the budget-rollover deadlock claim to what is true

Review found the rationale overstated. BUDGET_UPDATED evicts project-wide,
so a sibling key with traffic clears the block for the whole project within
a poll cycle. Only a project whose blocked key is its only traffic stays
stuck. That is still the case the change closes, but the spec is the
yardstick the change is measured by and it has to say what is actually
true.

* test(gateway): state the freshness precondition the running-period scenario relies on

The scenario asserted no refresh is triggered inside a live period, which
is only true while the config is also inside its staleness TTL. The test
happened to satisfy that by construction; now it asserts it, so the
scenario proves the boundary is what did nothing rather than a coincidence.

* style(gateway): use US spelling in the budget-rollover comments

The misspell linter rejects 'materialisation' and 'modelling' in the three
comment lines this change added. Comment text only; no behaviour change.

* fix(gateway): only an answered refresh closes out a rolled budget period

The roll was keyed on configFetchedAt, which endConfigRefresh stamps on every
outcome — a failed fetch included. So a control plane that could not be reached
counted as the re-read: the entry went back to offering its token, was answered
304, and kept enforcing spend from a period that had ended. With no staleness
clock configured it never retried at all.

The boundary now clears only on an answer from the control plane (a config or a
304), tracked separately from the fetch stamp. A failed attempt leaves the roll
standing, so the retry goes out unconditional too, paced by the ordinary clock
rather than fired on every request.

Entries built from a config read after the boundary start already answered, so a
boundary that never moves — a MANUAL window, a skewed clock — still costs one
re-read rather than one per refresh.

* fix(gateway): a 304 never closes out a rolled budget period

Acking the roll on any control-plane answer was wrong in both directions.

A 304 answering the unconditional refresh a roll forces carries no spend, so
treating it as the re-read left the entry holding the ended period's figures and
back on conditional revalidation — the deadlock again, reached through a control
plane that answers 304 to a request carrying no token.

Worse, the ack also fired on the ordinary in-period refresh. A daily budget on a
60s clock is confirmed hundreds of times before its boundary, and each of those
acked a boundary the entry had not reached yet, so the roll never fired at all.
The probe is in the test: with the ack in place the boundary produces no fetch
and the dead period's spend stays.

Only a config the gateway actually received clears a roll, and that arrives as a
new entry through storeL1, which already marks a boundary it read past. So there
is no ack on the refresh path at all.

test(langevals): pin the ragas litellm shim against the langchain-openai client contract (#7811)

The shim in model_to_langchain.py presents a litellm-backed object shaped
like the OpenAI client langchain expects, so it has to implement whatever
langchain reaches for. langchain-openai 0.3 started calling
`client.with_raw_response.create(...)` instead of `client.create(...)`,
the shim had no such member, and every ragas evaluator raised
AttributeError above the litellm layer on every provider, before a
credential was read or an LLM call was made. Nothing in CI said so: the
Azure/ragas tests need live credentials and skip without them, and the
deterministic credential-isolation suite covered every langevals
evaluator family but no ragas one.

The shim member itself now exists on main. What was missing is the test
that stops the next bump doing this again, so this adds it: the two
langchain entry points the shim has to survive (`invoke` on the sync
client, `ainvoke` on the async one), and one ragas evaluator end to end
with the provider stubbed at `litellm_patch.originals`, the same seam the
sibling credential-isolation tests use. The end-to-end case drives a real
Faithfulness evaluation through langchain, ragas and the shim, and
asserts both provider calls arrive carrying the request's credentials and
that the evaluation scores. A shim that only asserted the member exists
would pass against a future langchain that reaches for something else;
this one would not.

Deterministic, needs no key, runs on forks.

fix(system-migrations): answer the user cohort from the user's own memberships (#7710)

* fix(system-migrations): answer the user cohort from the user's own memberships

The user-pass cohort check shipped every enrolled organization id as an IN
list on every per-user membership probe. The rows read were cheap, but
Postgres re-plans that many-thousand-parameter statement on every call, a
cost that scales with total enrollment, repeats users x passes at every
worker boot, and never appears in execution-time stats
(pg_stat_statements.track_planning is off by default).

Fetch the user's own organization ids instead - one parameter, a handful
of rows - and intersect them in memory with the enrolled set the pass
already holds. Cohort semantics (automatic enrollment, empty enrollment,
self-hosted bypass, multi-org users) are unchanged and covered by the
existing tests plus a regression case pinning the probe to a single
parameter.

Fixes #7709

* fix(system-migrations): drop unbound @scenario tag that failed the parity gate

* fix(system-migrations): read cohort memberships as a relation of the user

The cohort probe read OrganizationUser top-level bounded only by userId —
a shape guardOrganizationId admits nowhere, so on cloud the real client
threw before the query ran and every non-automatic user migration failed
at its first candidate. The unit suite stubbed ~/server/db unguarded and
could not see it.

Read the memberships as a nested relation off the user's own row instead
(the guard checks top-level operations; User is not org-scoped), and
route the suite's stubbed delegates through the real guardOrganizationId
so a shape production refuses now fails the tests too — verified by
reinstating the old query, which fails 3 tests with the production error.

Addresses PR #7710 review (pullrequestreview-5068551265).

fix(traces): filter chips stop resizing on hover so the X stays put (#7980)

Chips paint a readable label (`evaluator:Ragas Response Relevancy`) over
the raw id in the document. On hover the CSS swapped that back to the id
at full size, and ids are far wider than names
(`evaluator:monitor_0005p7YMsdI0Oy56m6qklofZOl8zo`), so the pill grew in
place and pushed the remove button out from under the pointer. The
`:has(+ .filter-token-delete:hover)` half of the rule kept it expanded
once the pointer reached the X, so the button never settled and the

Drop both hover rules. The chip now paints the label in every pointer
state and its width never changes. The raw id moves to the chip's `title`
tooltip, which costs no layout — the live editor's decoration now sets
the same title string the placeholder renderer already used, so the two
renderers stay identical across the hand-off. Clicking a chip still opens
the value picker, and the query language is untouched: the document holds
the id and matching is still id-only.

specs/traces-v2/search.feature pinned the old behaviour, so its Rule is
rewritten: the two hover-to-id scenarios are replaced by ones asserting
the chip's text and width are unchanged on hover, that the remove button
does not move, and that the tooltip carries the id.

feat(datasets): search a dataset's rows from the editor (#7731) (#7734)

* feat(datasets): search a dataset's rows from the editor (#7731)

A 679-row dataset is 14 pages. Finding one row meant paging through
them, because the editor offered no way to search. This adds a search
box that narrows the whole dataset to the rows whose cell values
contain what was typed, and lets the pager page the matches.

The narrowing happens on the server, over the whole dataset, not over
the page already on screen. Datasets store their content as JSONL
chunks in object storage with no rows in Postgres at all, so matching
means reading chunks: the scan reads them one at a time, in the order
the stored offsets give, and stops at 50,000 rows. Past that the search
is refused with its own reason rather than returning the matches found
so far, because a user cannot tell an empty result from an abandoned
scan. Legacy Postgres-backed datasets take the same predicate through a
keyset walk, counting once for the whole scan.

Search is offered for saved datasets only. A dataset being drafted has
never been saved, so there is no server to ask, and every row is
already on screen.

Three things are withheld while a search is active, because each would
create a row that does not match and so vanishes the moment it is
made: the add-row button, the trailing empty row, and the CSV import
(including one already open when the search lands). Clearing the search
returns them, on the page the search started from -- searching from the
last page and being returned to the first would withdraw them for the
rest of the session.

Changing the search waits for a pending save and clears the row
selection. Rows are addressed by their position in the grid, so a
search that replaces which records occupy those positions would leave a
selection naming rows the user never picked.

Closes #7731

* fix(datasets): validate the whole chunk-offsets index before a search trusts it

A paged read rejects the entire `chunkOffsets` array when any one entry is
malformed and falls back to enumerating chunks by `chunkCount`. The search
accepted each entry on its own merits instead, keeping the ones that passed a
per-entry check and scanning only the chunks those entries named.

On a half-written offsets array — an interrupted migration that committed — the
two disagree about the same dataset: the pager displays rows the search reports
as absent, and the search answers "no records match" with the confidence of a
complete scan. Silence is the worst available failure here, because nothing on
screen distinguishes it from a genuine miss.

Both paths now read the index through one all-or-nothing helper,
`readValidChunkOffsets`, so a broken index takes both of them down the same
`chunkCount` fallback.

Regression test: an offsets array of one good entry, one entry missing its row
bounds, and a null. Before the change the search read 2 of 3 chunks and found
none of the matches; it now reads all 3 and finds both.

* fix(datasets): open each dataset in the editor unsearched

The editor is not torn down when the user moves between datasets client-side —
the route param changes under a grid that stays mounted — so every piece of
search state survived the move. The next dataset was fetched narrowed by a word
typed against the previous one, at a page that dataset may not have, with the
previous dataset's size still standing in as the total on the count chip. Rows
were missing and nothing on screen said why.

Three changes, one per surviving value:

- The search term is now debounced together with the dataset it was typed
  against. Debouncing the bare string left the old term live for 300ms after the
  switch, which is long enough to issue the narrowed request; pairing them lets
  the term be discarded the instant it stops belonging to what is on screen.
- Term, page, `pageBeforeSearch` and the remembered dataset total are reset
  during render rather than in an effect. An effect runs after the render that
  has already put the stale page into the query key, so the request goes out
  regardless; the page the query asks for is derived for the same reason.
- The dataset's own total is only remembered from a settled, non-placeholder
  read. `keepPreviousData` serves the previous dataset's result during the
  switch, and a total taken from it belongs to the wrong dataset.

The row selection needs no reset here — `setData` already clears it when the new
dataset's rows land.

Three regression tests, all red before the change: the new dataset was requested
with `search: "escalation"`, its count chip read "1 of 120" against a dataset of
3 rows, and page 2 was requested for a dataset that has one page.

* spec(datasets): state that a row edited out of its matches stays on screen

A matching row can be edited so that it no longer contains the searched text,
and the grid goes on showing it until the next search. That was unspecified,
which is the actual defect: it left the behaviour indistinguishable from an
oversight, and the obvious "fix" — re-running the search when the edit saves —
is worse than what it replaces.

Removing the row the moment its save settles takes it out from under the cursor
of the person still typing in it, and strands any further edit to the same row:
rows are addressed by grid position (`selectedRows` is a set of indices,
`rowData` reads `records[index]`), so the position that edit refers to now
belongs to a different record. The grid answers the search as it was run;
running it again re-answers it. This is what filtered grids elsewhere do, and it
is the behaviour worth keeping.

Adds the rule, the scenario, and a test that fails if someone later adds the
refetch. It is a characterization test — it passes on the code as it already
stood — so it pins the decision rather than a change.

* test(datasets): make the row-stays-on-screen test able to fail

The scenario asserted only that the edited value was still rendered. The
mocked refetch does nothing, so an editor that re-read on every save kept
the row on screen too and the assertion could not tell the two apart — the
test passed against the very change it was written to pin against.

Serve one shared refetch spy from the mocked query and assert the editor
did not re-read. Verified by applying a refetch-on-save to the component:
the test fails with it, passes without it.

* fix(datasets): stop retrying a search the server can never allow

A search over a dataset past the row cap is refused with
`dataset_too_large_to_search` (HTTP 413). That code was absent from the
permanent-failure set and 413 is not in the never-retry status list, so
`shouldRetryQuery` replayed it four times with exponential backoff. The
dataset does not shrink between attempts, so every replay read the same
row count and got the same refusal.

The cost is not just five wasted scans. React Query holds a retrying
query in `pending`, and the dataset editor serves `keepPreviousData`
while pending, so for the whole backoff the editor showed the last
unsearched page under a count chip reading "54,000 of 54,000 records" —
rows that were never matched against the search, presented as the
complete result of it.

Verified in a browser against a 54,000-row dataset on the local stack.
Before: five 413s at 0.4s, 1.4s, 3.4s, 7.5s and 15.5s, with the
unfiltered rows and the false count on screen for 15.5 seconds. After:
one 413 at 0.4s, and the refusal message in the grid from 0.4s onward.
The added unit test fails against the unfixed policy (expected false,
received true).

* fix(datasets): withdraw the ways of adding a row on the keystroke

The gates on the add-row button, the trailing empty row and the CSV
import all read `isSearching`, which is derived from the search term
after a 300ms debounce. Between the keystroke and the search running,
all three were still offered. A row added in that window is empty, so
the search arriving a moment later drops it from the grid: the user
adds a row and watches it disappear, with nothing on screen connecting
the two events. The gates now read a term the user has typed, settled
or not, while the presentation of search results stays on the debounced
value, which is the right gate for it.

Withdrawing the CSV import also left its disclosure believing it was
open: the render gate unmounted the dialog, and the only path that
cleared the flag was the dialog's own close handler. Clearing the
search reopened it on its own, seconds after the user last touched it
and empty of whatever they had chosen in it. The withdrawal now closes
the disclosure as well, so "withdrawn" and "closed" cannot disagree.

Both regression tests fail against the unfixed component: the add-row
button is still in the document immediately after the change event, and
one dialog is still on screen after the search is cleared. Also
confirmed in a browser against the local stack, where the import button
survived the keystroke by the length of the debounce and now does not.

* fix(datasets): stop reporting unsearched rows as the matches

The count chip switched to its two-number form the moment a search took
effect, and read the match count straight off the query result. While
the search's own read is in flight, that result is the last unsearched
page held over by `keepPreviousData`, and the count riding with it is
the dataset's own size. The chip rendered it as "54,000 of 54,000
records" — every row matched — above rows that had never been matched
against anything. On a large dataset the read takes seconds, and until
the retry fix in 89db11500b a refused search held that state for the
whole backoff.

Report a number of matches only once the search's own read has settled.
Otherwise fall back to the dataset's own size, which is what the chip
says with no search in effect and is true in either state. That
subsumes the refusal case, which was already handled separately for the
same reason, so the three-way branch collapses to the one rule.

The regression test serves what react-query serves during a key change
— the previous result flagged as a placeholder — and fails against the
unfixed chip with "expected element not to have text content 120 of
120; received 120 of 120 records".

* test(datasets): wait for the searched term, not the first empty message

The no-matches test typed "zzzznope" one character at a time and then
asserted on the first "no records match" message to appear. The search
waits 300ms after each keystroke, so an early prefix can settle
mid-typing and put up its own message for "z" or "zz" — which the
assertion then reads and fails on. This is the failure that turned
`test-component (3)` red on CI ("Expected: zzzznope, Received: No
records match “z”.").

Wait for the message that names the whole term instead. Reproduced
locally before the change (the run failed on “zz”) and passed three
consecutive runs after it.

* refactor(datasets): split the search scan per storage layout

`searchResolvedDataset` held the window arithmetic, the match collector
and both storage layouts' full scans in one method, at a cognitive
complexity of 28 against a limit of 10. That was a new violation of a
rule the repository already enforces on new code, and it failed the
lint gate on this pull request.

The two scans have nothing in common beyond the collector they feed, so
each becomes its own method taking that collector, and the chunk-index
enumeration — the part with the most branching and the longest
explanation — becomes a third. What remains in the caller is the window
arithmetic, the collector and the choice of layout.

No behaviour changes; the fourteen existing search unit tests pass
unaltered. The lint gate now reports the pull request as removing one
violation rather than adding one.

* refactor(datasets): give each search scan a name of its own

searchResolvedDataset held both scans inline, so the chunk walk and the
Postgres walk shared one function body and one comment block. Extracting
them into scanChunksForMatches and scanPostgresRecordsForMatches leaves
searchResolvedDataset stating which store it is reading and nothing else,
and gives each walk somewhere to document the limits it enforces.

No behaviour change.

* refactor(datasets): apply the house conventions to the search code

Four review findings on this pull request, all against conventions the
repository already states and all mechanical.

Named parameters: `matchesDatasetSearch` took `(entry, search)`
positionally, and the `searchPage` and `serveDatasetsById` test helpers
took theirs the same way. Each now takes one destructured object, and
every call site was updated.

Test structure: seven top-level `describe("given ...")` blocks held
their `it(...)` calls directly, with no `when` layer, while the ten
blocks in the first half of the same file have one. Each now names the
action its tests perform. One test asserting on the return-to-first-page
behaviour carried no `@scenario` annotation, so the scenario was bound
by only one of the two tests covering it; it now carries the same
annotation as its neighbour.

No behaviour changes. All 22 editor search tests and all 24 server
search tests pass, and feature parity reports the dataset editor at
37 of 37 scenarios bound.

* fix(datasets): bound a search by what it reads, not only by what it counts

A search scans, and what a scan costs is bytes fetched from storage and
parsed — not records counted. The only limit on it was a row count, and a
row is whatever columns it was given: an id and a status is a hundred
bytes, a stored model response is tens of kilobytes, and both count as
one. So the limit refused datasets by a number unrelated to their cost. A
54,000-row dataset of 5 MB was refused while a 9,800-row dataset of 18 MB
was allowed, though the second is more than three times the reading.

Adds a byte limit alongside the row limit, set to the ceiling the platform
already applies to reading a dataset in one request. Both are checked, and
neither covers the other: a dataset written before its size was recorded
has none to check, and a row count cannot see how wide a row is. A missing
size is not read as zero, which would make those datasets the smallest in
the platform and wave every one of them through.

The Postgres walk also gained the backstop its chunk counterpart already
had. Its only exits were a short batch and a missing cursor, and a dataset
being written to during the scan offers neither — so the walk ran as long
as the writer did, past a limit it had already been admitted under. Its
test could not report that: with nothing bounding the loop it exhausted
the heap and took the runner down, which reads as infrastructure trouble
rather than as a failed assertion. The fake now stops serving after twice
the cap, so the missing backstop shows up as that one test failing.

Same error and same code for both limits: to the user the dataset is past
what a search reads, and the way through is the same either way. Which
limit fired is in the log, not on screen.

* fix(datasets): bound a chunked search by the bytes it fetches, not only the ones it was promised

The byte limit was checked once, against `sizeBytes` on the dataset row,
before the scan started. That field is written when the dataset is
measured, not read when the search runs, so a dataset whose appends
landed without moving it passes the fence and is then fetched and parsed
with no byte bound at all. Rows already had both halves — an up-front
check and a running backstop; bytes had only the first.

The scan now accumulates each chunk's recorded `byteSize` as it walks
and refuses past the limit, mirroring the row backstop beside it. Bytes
are counted before the fetch rather than after: a chunk's size is known
in advance, so the chunk that would breach the limit is refused rather
than pulled down and objected to afterwards.

`readValidChunkOffsets` validates an offset's row bounds and not its
`byteSize`, so a valid array can carry an entry without one. Added to a
running total that value yields NaN, every later comparison against it
is false, and the backstop silently stops existing for the whole
dataset. Unrecorded sizes are therefore normalised to null at the point
the chunks are enumerated and skipped in the total — one chunk that
cannot be measured, not permission to stop measuring.

Verified by two tests that fail against the unfixed scan: a dataset
whose chunks outweigh its stale recorded size is refused after reading
the one chunk that fit, and a chunk with no recorded size no longer
stops the bytes after it from being counted. The row backstop still
stopped these scans eventually, which is why this was the smaller of the
two holes — but it stopped them on the wrong dimension.

Also binds three byte-limit scenarios that were added to the feature
file without annotations on the tests that prove them; the parity gate
was failing on this branch. And splits the two limit checks out of
`scanChunksForMatches` as named methods, which keeps the function under
the cognitive-complexity ceiling the lint gate enforces.

* fix(datasets): reject a chunk index that names the same chunk twice

`readValidChunkOffsets` checked each entry on its own and never checked
the array as a whole, so an index carrying two entries for chunk 0 —
one covering rows 0-1, one covering rows 2-3 — passed as valid. Its two
readers then key off different parts of it and disagree. The paged read
selects entries by row range and fetches whatever `index` each names, so
it reads chunk 0 twice and never reads the chunk no entry names; a
search deduplicates the indexes and reads it once. The user sees a row
in the grid and a search that reports no match for it, with nothing on
screen to explain the difference.

A negative index passed too. Chunk keys are built by zero-padding the
index, so it addresses no object: the read comes back empty and that
chunk's rows go missing from a dataset that still reports having them.

Both are now rejected, all-or-nothing like the existing per-entry
checks, which drops the dataset onto the repair path that reads every
chunk rather than onto a wrong answer.

Verified by two tests in dataset-chunking.unit.test.ts that fail against
the unfixed validator, both with "expected [ ...(2) ] to deeply equal
[]". With uniqueness now guaranteed at the source, the search's own
deduplication of the indexes is redundant and has been removed.

Declined from the same review finding: validating that the offsets cover
`chunkCount` and `rowCount`. Count drift between those fields and the
offsets is a state this codebase already treats as real and recoverable
— it is why the fallback paths exist — and rejecting an index on that
basis would send live datasets onto the unbounded read those paths guard
against. That trades a rare wrong answer for a routine memory risk.

* refactor(datasets): name the editor's new booleans for what they answer

The house rule is that a boolean carries an `is`/`has`/`should`/`can`/
`will` prefix, and the five booleans this branch added to the editor did
not, sitting alongside the `isSearching` and `isLastPage` that already
did. Renamed to `hasSearchTakenTheGrid`, `isSearchSettling`,
`isCsvModalOpen`, `hasSearchFailed` and `isMatchCountKnown`. No
behaviour changes; `searchFailedMessage` is a copy function, not a
boolean, and keeps its name.

Also repairs the self-check in the held-over-rows test. It asserted that
the CSV import button was gone, as proof that the editor had entered
search mode — which was true when it was written, and stopped being true
two commits later when the add-row affordances were moved to withdraw on
the keystroke rather than on the debounce. Their absence now proves only
that the term was typed, so the assertion could pass with the searched
read never sent and the chip merely still in its unsearched state. It
now waits for the searched request itself. Confirmed still able to fail:
against the un-fixed chip the test reports "Expected element not to have
text content".

And adds the missing test for the throw on an unreadable chunk index —
malformed offsets and a null `chunkCount` together, where reading the
count as zero would scan nothing and answer "no matches" for a dataset
that has them. Every other test in the file supplied a usable
`chunkCount`, so the fallback was covered and the throw was not.

* fix(datasets): stop a negative chunk size buying room for the chunks after it

The running byte total skipped a chunk whose size was missing or
unparseable but accepted one recorded as negative, and a negative is
worse than an absent value rather than merely equivalent to it. An
absent size leaves the total uninformed about one chunk; a negative one
sets the total back, so a single entry reading -100 MB pays for every
chunk that follows while the accumulated figure still looks comfortably
inside the limit. The bound is defeated across the whole dataset by one
bad field.

Negative sizes are now normalised the same way missing ones are — one
chunk that cannot be measured, contributing nothing — rather than
subtracted.

Verified by a test that fails against the unfixed accounting: a first
chunk recorded at minus half the limit followed by two chunks at half
the limit each completes the scan and returns matches, where it should
refuse on reaching the third. It now refuses after reading two.

Also groups this file's tests under `given`/`when` describes, which the
house convention asks for and which this file had never had. The
`@scenario` annotations stay: the review asked for them to be removed
along with the restructuring, but they are what binds each test to its
feature-file scenario, and `check-feature-parity.ts` is an enforced gate
that fails without them. Structure and annotations answer to different
rules and both are kept. Parity still reports 41/41 bound.

* fix(datasets): bound the search by the bytes it reads, not the bytes it was told about

The byte limit was judged entirely on numbers recorded against the dataset:
`sizeBytes` on the row, and `byteSize` on each chunk offset. Both are absent on
rows written before sizes were kept and on offsets a half-finished migration
left behind, and `chunksToScan` deliberately reports the absence as `null`,
which the running total added as zero. A ready s3_jsonl dataset under the
50,000-row cap could therefore fetch and parse unboundedly past the advertised
100 MB while both byte checks stayed green — and only ever on the damaged and
legacy metadata the defensive path exists to serve.

The scan now measures each chunk it reads and holds the larger of the measured
and the recorded totals against the limit. Recorded sizes keep their job of
refusing a doomed chunk before it is fetched, which measuring alone cannot do;
measuring covers the datasets that recorded nothing to judge, which the records
alone cannot. Where nothing was recorded the scan overshoots by the one chunk
that carried it over, because the size of a fetch is not knowable until it
lands — not by every chunk remaining.

Measuring also closes the understated-size case, where a recorded `byteSize`
smaller than the chunk bought passage for the chunks after it.

The existing test approving the missing-size path pinned the absence of a
refusal rather than the stated bound; it still passes, and now sits beside one
that reads four 30 MB chunks with nothing recorded and requires the refusal.
Verified it bites: reverted to the recorded-only total, the new test fails with
the search resolving a page after reading 120 MB.

* docs(datasets): say what measuring a chunk costs, where the cost is paid

`searchResolvedDataset` documents the heap it holds — one unit of input plus
the matched rows, whatever the dataset's size — as the reason the scan is safe
against a dataset of any size. Measuring a chunk re-serialises it, so while
that runs the heap holds a second copy of the chunk and the stated invariant
is false. Measured on a 16 MB chunk: 3.3 MB of parsed rows peaks at 18.7 MB.
The peak is twice one chunk rather than twice the scan, which is the part a
reader sizing a box needs, so it is stated rather than left to be rediscovered.

`measureRowsBytes` called its own cost proportional to the fetch and parse it
rides along with. True as an order of magnitude, but it reads as a fraction of
them and it is not one: on the same chunk, 9.3 ms of measuring against 6.1 ms
of parsing and 1.4 ms of matching. Still worth paying — 56 ms over a full
100 MB budget, against fetching 100 MB over the network — but the number
belongs next to the claim.

Recorded there too: the cheaper measure that was not taken. `readChunk` holds
the raw JSONL it parsed and throws it away, so returning its byte length would
be exact and free, and would measure the file rather than a re-encoding of it.
It changes the storage interface and all three implementations, which is not
this commit's scope.

Comments only; no behaviour changes.

fix(traces): stop the trace list deriving the version dedup twice per page (#7694)

* fix(traces): stop the trace list deriving the version dedup twice per page

`findAll` pages in two stages: an inner stage picks the page's traces, an
outer stage reads their heavy payload columns. Both stated the latest-version
dedup, which is a whole-window aggregate — it groups every row the tenant has
in the time range. The outer stage did not need it: the inner stage had
already resolved which exact row won each trace, so re-stating the dedup (and
the user filter) made ClickHouse rebuild that aggregate to arrive back at rows
it had just named.

The inner stage now hands over the winning rows' full identity
(TenantId, TraceId, UpdatedAt) rather than just their TraceIds, so the outer
stage selects exactly those rows. Dedup semantics are unchanged: it is still
decided on the base predicates alone, so a filter still chooses among current
traces rather than deciding which version is current.

Measured read-only against production, on a tenant with ~1.33M traces in a
30-day window (of which 2,206 — 0.17% — actually have more than one version):

  page read, wide columns   before: 4,449,207 rows  2.04 GiB  10,302 ms
                             after: 2,974,165 rows  1.90 GiB   5,722 ms

Rejected FINAL as the alternative: it wins on an unfiltered count
(489 -> 125 MiB) but loses badly once the list carries a filter
(467 -> 690 MiB, 3,876 -> 4,895 ms), because `trace_summaries` filters on an
unindexed `Attributes` Map that FINAL forces it to read for every row.

* fix(traces): keep the user filter on the outer page stage

The identity handover alone is not enough to pick a version. trace_summaries
is a ReplacingMergeTree, so a re-publish at the same UpdatedAt sits in its own
part until a merge collapses it, and both rows answer to the same
(TenantId, TraceId, UpdatedAt). Selecting on identity alone let the version
that does NOT match the filter into the page, and the page then disagreed with
its own total (2 rows returned, totalHits 1).

Re-applying whereClause on the outer stage restores the previous semantics
while keeping the win: the expensive part was the second whole-window dedup
aggregate, not the filter predicate, and on the unfiltered default view
whereClause IS baseWhereClause so it costs nothing.

Covered by a new integration test (two rows, one identity, separate parts) and
a unit assertion that the filter appears in both stages of the page read.

* test(traces): follow the directory's test conventions

Convention scan against the sibling repositories:
- captureFindAllQueries now wraps the real client in a Proxy rather than
  fabricating a one-method object and double-casting it, matching
  trace-summary.clickhouse.repository.integration.test.ts:95-106 and the four
  uses in span-storage.clickhouse.repository.integration.test.ts. The
  fabricated object had no exec/insert/close and worked only because findAll
  happens to call nothing else today.
- The unit file nests given/when describes, which CLAUDE.md requires and the
  directory majority follows.
- The filter test could pass vacuously (it only asserted absence); it is now
  paired with a count assertion that pins the positive side.

* style(traces): drop a stray trailing blank line

Left behind when the integration test's temporary probe block was removed.
biome check flagged it as a formatter diff.

* test(traces): stop the duplicate-row fixture depending on merge timing

The regression test for unmerged same-version rows is only meaningful while
the two rows are still in separate parts. A background merge landing between
the inserts and the read collapses them, and the assertion then passes or
fails on whichever version happened to survive rather than on the behaviour
under test.

Hold merges off `trace_summaries` for the fixture's lifetime, restart them in
cleanup, and assert both rows are still there before asserting what the read
returns.

Also make the query-log guard check what it claims to. It tested for the
table's existence, but `log_queries = 0` stops the recording and leaves the
table in place, so the guard passed and the read-cost assertions then failed
on an empty result. It now runs a probe query under a known id and looks for
its own row.

* test(traces): assert where the filter sits, not just how often it appears

Counting the filter's occurrences in the page read let the test pass with both
copies inside the inner stage, which is the arrangement it exists to rule out.
Split the SQL at the identity handover and assert one copy on each side.

Switch `occurrences` to a named-parameter object, per the repo's convention for
functions taking more than one argument.

* test(traces): use command() for the merge-control DDL, per the two existing callers

A timeout now reserves the caller slot for one further budget, so an early
retry is answered 429 instead of starting a second turn. That bounds a
misconfigured monitor to one turn per two budgets per caller. At the
documented 3-minute interval the reservation has always lapsed, and a 429
fails the check either way, so a correctly configured monitor is unaffected.
Every other outcome releases at once, since the turn is over.

Still per-process and per-caller by design: two monitors on two projects must
not block each other, and a cross-replica budget belongs to Langy turn
admission rather than to one health probe.

fix(navigation): scope the personal workspace lookup to the selected organization (#7985)

* fix(navigation): scope the personal workspace lookup to the selected organization

A personal workspace belongs to one organization — PersonalWorkspaceService
.ensure takes an organizationId and creates one per organization — so a user
in several organizations owns several personal projects.

findPersonalProject took no organization argument and returned the first
personal team it found across every organization, in a list the server sends
unordered. The Me sidebar's Traces entry therefore linked to another
organization's personal project, and since the header re-derives the
organization from the project slug in the URL, the organization in the chrome
flipped when the reader clicked it.

The parameter is now required, and both callers pass the organization the
chrome has resolved: PersonalSidebar (the Traces entry and the library entries
gated on the same project id) and FirstTraceRedirect, whose CLI approval was
granted against one specific organization. Where the selected organization
holds no personal workspace of the reader's, no Traces entry renders at all
rather than one addressing somewhere else.

Required rather than optional on purpose: scanning every organization is not a
choice any caller means to make, and an optional argument would let the defect
come back silently.

Regression cover: a unit suite for the resolution and a component suite
asserting the rendered href, both watched failing before the fix.

Closes #7984

* fix(cli): watch the approved organization's personal project, not the ambient one

The first-trace watcher resolved the personal project inside whichever
organization useOrganizationTeamProject happened to select — localStorage, or
the first organization in the payload. But the CLI approval is granted against
selectedOrgId: that is the id the page sends to /api/auth/cli/approve, and the
name it renders in the "LangWatch CLI is now authorized for <org>" card
directly above this widget.

A user who picks a different organization in the chooser than the one they
navigated in with was therefore watched against the wrong personal project,
and the widget silently contradicted the card beside it.

Pass the approved organization in as a prop instead of re-deriving it.

* docs(specs): state the real cause of the missing Me Traces entry

The scenario claimed the entry is absent when the selected organization
holds no personal workspace of mine. That state does not survive on a Me
page: visiting one calls api.user.personalContext, which ensures the
workspace in the selected organization. What actually keeps the entry
absent is the organization payload the sidebar reads, which is already
loaded and never refetched, so it stays absent for the rest of the session.

Say that instead. Also drop "rather than one for another organization"
from the Then: absence is observable, a counterfactual is not. The reason
absence is the wanted outcome moves into the comment above the scenario,
where it belongs. Renamed the matching test case to match.

* test(navigation): bind the two new sidebar scenarios and shape the suites the house way

The two @integration scenarios added to specs/navigation/product-sidebars.feature
carried no `@scenario` annotation, so the feature-parity check counted them as
unbound and failed: a scenario that binds nothing enforces nothing. Annotate the
two tests that already cover them.

While in the same files, two house rules the suites were breaking:

- Both `orgWithPersonalProject` helpers took positional arguments. They now take
  one options object, as every multi-argument function in this repo does.
- Four `it(...)` cases sat directly under their top-level suite with no `given`
  context. Each is now wrapped in the `describe("given ...")` that names the
  state it is asserting about, and its title says only what is observed.

* fix(cli): freeze the approved organization instead of reading the live selection

Passing selectedOrgId to FirstTraceRedirect stopped the watcher reading the
ambient organization, but it still read a value that can move. The organization
picker stays interactive while the approval request is in flight — only the
Approve and Deny buttons take the loading state — so a user who changes the
selection in that window has the approval go out for one organization and the
watcher poll another. The success card had the same hazard: it resolved the
organization name from selectedOrgId after the await, not from the id it sent.

Capture the id once at the top of the handler, send that, and carry it in the
success state. The card and the watcher now both name the organization the
approval was actually granted against, and neither can be moved afterwards.

useFirstTraceWatch takes its input as an object, matching every other function
in the file.

Regression cover: the page-level suite changes the organization while the
approval is held open and asserts the redirect lands on the approved
organization's personal project. Watched failing before the fix — it redirected
to the newly selected organization's personal project instead.

* test(cli): split the in-flight case into its given and its when

The new case carried its action in the given ("given the organization is
changed while the approval is in flight"), which leaves nothing for the when to
say. The state is an approval request that has not landed yet; the action is
changing the organization before it does. Say each in its own block, and lift
the deferred-response plumbing into a helper so the test body reads as the
three steps it performs.

fix(sdk-go): decode the annotations envelope and regenerate the REST client (#7989)

fix(sdk-go): decode the annotations envelope, and regenerate the REST client

The Annotations service could not read what the API returns. The annotation
endpoints wrap their payload in a `data` envelope, and the Go wrapper decoded
the bare value, so List, Get, ListByTrace, CreateForTrace and Update all failed
with:

  json: cannot unmarshal object into Go value of type []openapi.Annotation

Nothing was red. The test stubbed the bare shape, so the suite agreed with the
wrapper instead of with the schema.

All five now go through one `decodeAnnotationEnvelope` helper. Its `Data` field
is a pointer on purpose: JSON decoding ignores keys it was not asked for, so a
2xx body in some other shape — an older self-hosted server still sending the
bare value, or a future one that moves the payload again — decodes without
error. Against a value that silently yields a zero Annotation and a nil error,
which is a worse failure than the one being fixed here; against a pointer it is
a decode error naming the missing envelope. Three tests hold that behaviour
down, and they fail if the nil check is removed.

`AnnotationParams` claimed every field was optional. The API requires both
`comment` and `isThumbsUp` on create and on update, and rejects a body missing
either, so `Update`'s own documented example was a call the server always
refuses. Both are now documented as required, and the omitempty consequence —
an empty comment cannot be written — is stated rather than left to be
discovered.

The committed client was also eight spec commits behind. Regenerating picks up
15 added operations, drops 2 removed ones, and adds the `fields` and
`evaluations` properties that scenarios and simulation runs gained. Those are
additive.

This commit touches sdks/go and nothing else, so the break below reaches that
component alone. The spec that pins the envelope and the CI job that catches
the next drift land separately, for that reason.

BREAKING CHANGE: five Annotation fields are now values rather than pointers,
because the schema marks them required — Id, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, ProjectId
and TraceId. Callers that dereference them (`*a.Id`) no longer compile; read
the field directly. The remaining nullable fields — Comment, Email, IsThumbsUp,
UserId — are unchanged and stay pointers.

ci(sdk-go): pin the REST client response envelopes and fail when it goes stale (#7990)

ci(sdk-go): regenerate the Go client with the others, and fail when it is stale

The Go client drifted eight spec commits behind main and nothing said so.
There were two reasons, and this fixes both.

`make sync-all-openapi` regenerated the spec, the TypeScript client and the
Python client, and omitted Go. That is why the other two stayed current while
this one fell behind. It now regenerates Go too, so the command a developer
runs and the state CI demands cannot disagree.

Nothing verified the committed client either. The generated code is checked in,
no job regenerated it, and the OpenAPI document lives outside sdks/go, so a
spec-only change left sdk-go-ci's `relevant` filter false and skipped every Go
job. codegen-fresh regenerates and fails on a diff, watching the OpenAPI
document rather than sdks/go. Its filter also watches the two go.mod files and
the client's go.sum, because the toolchain formats the generated bytes: without
that, a Go bump lands unchecked and the next spec change fails here with a
whole-file gofmt diff it did not cause.

The check reads `git status --porcelain`, not `git diff --quiet`. The latter
exits 128 on a git failure, which `!` reads as "no difference", and it cannot
see untracked files. It also asserts the generated file exists first, because
`git status` on a path that is not there warns and exits 0 with empty output —
so a mistyped path or a generator that produced nothing would have read as
fresh. All three directions are exercised: current passes, stale fails,
missing fails.

The new filter key follows the pattern detect-changes documents: a key a caller
consumes must also be declared as an output and echoed into the force step, or
it silently lands as an empty string (#3461).

The spec states what a developer observes: annotations come back unwrapped, and
an answer holding no annotation is reported rather than returned blank. Ten
@unit scenarios, each bound to the test that proves it.

* feat(governance): rung 2 — puller health as a derived field

A cost number that silently stops updating reads as "we spent nothing",
which is worse than an error. Three signals were missing to tell a dead
puller from a quiet one, and this adds all three.

`LastSuccessAt` is a new stamp in the ingestionPullRunStatus fold, moved
on every completion including one that found nothing new. Neither field
that already existed could answer "when did the pull itself last work":
`LastRunAt` advances on failures too, and `lastEventAt` moves only when
data arrives, so a provider going dark looked exactly like a slow week.
The projection version moves with it, so replay backfills the column
from the existing event log rather than making every source fail three
more times before its health is knowable.

Health is derived, not stored — `deriveSourceHealth` reads the existing
consecutive-failure count and calls a source unhealthy at three in a
row. It is deliberately not a fourth `IngestionSource.status` value:
status is what an admin configured, and a provider outage must not be
able to rewrite that. The badge on the inventory list and the detail
header now shows health when the two disagree, because a green check on
a source whose last three runs all failed is how a broken integration
goes unnoticed for a week.

Coverage falls out of the same stamp. `sourceDataCoverage` marks every
day that begins after the last successful pull as uncovered, and the
shape carries no spend number for those days at all — the defect it
exists to prevent is an unpulled day being rendered as zero dollars, and
a field that can hold a number will eventually hold a zero.

Riding with the rung: the projection mirrors four columns back onto
`IngestionSource`, and that write was keyed on the source id alone. The
projection's tenant is the org's hidden governance project, so a
projection carrying another org's source id wrote that org's cursor,
error count and status. `IngestionSource` carries no projectId — it is
organization-scoped — so the predicate travels through the org that owns
the tenant project. Covered by a two-org test against real Postgres.

The table (migration 00087)
governance_cost_rollup_1d, a ReplacingMergeTree sorted on the fold's whole
group key — (TenantId, Day, CostSource, IngestionSourceId, Provider, Model,
AgentId, CurrencyCode, RawActorId). Every dimension the fold groups by is in
that key, which is the point: a dimension the fold groups by and the key omits
survives until the first background merge and is then deleted, taking one
spender's money with it. RawActorId is what keeps two spenders with identical
numbers two rows; CurrencyCode is what keeps two currencies two figures. Both
are asserted AFTER an OPTIMIZE ... FINAL, because before one they pass anyway.

ExactOrEstimate sits OUTSIDE the key on purpose: a provider moving a day from
estimate to exact is a restatement of that day, and the newer row must win on
version rather than survive beside the old one and double the day.
OrganizationId is payload for the same kind of reason — it says who the money
belongs to, not where the row lives.

Retention follows gateway_spend: a fixed 13-month TTL declared in the
migration, absent from both reconciler maps, so a tenant policy a customer can
shrink to weeks can never hard-delete a cost record. Pinned in
retentionTtl.unit.test.ts alongside the gateway_spend pins.

The fold, registered twice
governanceCostRollup runs on the gateway-spend pipeline AND the pulled-usage
pipeline, each as an optional dependency, so a deployment running no pullers
still summarizes gateway spend and one without ClickHouse degrades to a log
rather than a crash. The two lanes can never contend for a row because
CostSource is in the key. The trace lane is reserved and excluded: no pipeline
carrying trace cost registers this fold, so no row can carry trace cost under
any label.

refoldOnOutOfOrder is off EXPLICITLY. The executor's re-fold loads history by
context.aggregateId, which for these events is one gateway request or one
pulled item — never the day-wide cell the key names — so a replay would
rebuild the day out of one request and discard the rest of the money. It is
also unnecessary: the accumulators commute and the restatement rule keys on
observedAtMs carried by the event.

Money is integer nano units end to end. AmountNanoUsd is nullable and is NULL,
never 0, when no dollar figure is held — a zero charts as real free usage,
which is a different fact. Gateway failures that consumed tokens are counted,
because the shipped budget ledger charges for them and the two must state the
same money.

Reading it without lying
Reads are version-aware (argMax over EventTimestamp, ADR-015). The restatement
test asserts BEFORE compaction and carries the counterexample permanently: a
plain SUM over the same rows returns 21_340_000_000 where the read returns the
restated 9_000_000_000. Reverting the read to a plain SUM fails three tests.

The store implements getWithApplied so the executor's redelivery dedup
survives a cold cache; this fold accumulates, so without it a retry re-adds
the same money. Removing it makes one delivery-attempt-2 test report
10_000_000_000 where 5_000_000_000 is correct.

The watchdog
costRollupComparator re-derives a sampled day straight from event_log,
through the very projection that wrote the summary, and holds the two against
each other. A mismatch increments langwatch_governance_cost_rollup_mismatch_total
(labelled by cost source) and names both figures on the log line. It does NOT
self-heal — a comparator that rewrote the row it disagreed with would erase
the evidence of why they diverged. It also counts the harder direction: a
summary cell no event on the log explains. A lag gauge reports how far the
summary is behind in business time, so an idle lane sits flat rather than
climbing with the wall clock.

Runs on the ADR-044 calendar scheduler, worker-only, sampling yesterday — a
day still being written to is expected to disagree with its own summary.

Three lanes side by side — what the provider billed, what the gateway
metered, and seats — each labeled for what it measures and never summed

disagree on purpose; the gap between them is the thing worth looking at,

The reported defect is not real, so nothing is repaired here — but the property
it depends on was undocumented and untested, which is why it looked broken.

The claim was that compareDay selects events by envelope EventOccurredAt while
the fold buckets by payload occurred_at, so an event straddling midnight lands
in one query's day and the other's neighbour. The two timestamps are in fact
the same value on every path that produces these events:

  spendCommands.ts:81,129,177,224  occurredAt: data.occurred_at
  eventStoreUtils.ts:71            EventOccurredAt: event.occurredAt
  pullerWorker.ts:753              occurredAt: record.occurredAtMs

The append clock lands on EventTimestamp (eventStoreUtils.ts:70), a different
column that neither path reads for bucketing. Both event types make their
business timestamp a required field with no default, and each has a single
producer.

matching in-code filter would introduce the exact defect it was meant to

— a false mismatch on a day whose summary was correct.

day reports no drift while the second sees its own event. A producer that ever
set the envelope to wall-clock time would break it here rather than in a
comparator alert nobody can explain.

findSpendTotals ran a plain sumIf over governance_kpis, which is a
ReplacingMergeTree(LastEventOccurredAt) (00031_create_governance_kpis.sql:79)
whose own header at :22-25 mandates the dedup pattern. Until a background merge

This is worse than a replay hazard. The writer is LEVEL-TRIGGERED:

carrying $2, $5, $9 — several versions per key is ordinary operation, not a

The distortion is not symmetric across the ratio the evaluator computes. Long
traces bunch into the current window while the baseline averages six of them,
so the numerator inflates harder and the result reads as a spend spike that
never happened — a false-positive AnomalyAlert, every five minutes, from

The four existing evaluator tests pass unchanged, so the source-scoped and

* fix(clickhouse-client): clamp the fallback pool to the server's stated cap (#7670)

The fallback of 64 open connections was only safe against a server that
admits more than 64 concurrent queries. Every server we ship locally
admits fewer (haven 32, dev compose ~25, test endpoints 16), and the
sizing already parses CLICKHOUSE_SERVER_MAX_CONCURRENT_QUERIES - it just
discarded it unless CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT_REPLICAS was also set, which
nothing sets. So the derivation never ran, exceedsBudget was hardcoded
false, and the budget warning never fired once.

Now a stated cap bounds the fallback to what one process alone may claim
of it - floor(cap x nodes x 0.7 / clients) - and reports the budget as
exceeded so the operator learns to state the fleet size. A deployment
that states nothing keeps the historical 64; with the default cap of 300
the clamp is a no-op, so production does not move.

The same share also judges an explicit override when the fleet size is
unknown: the override still wins, but one set above the share is now
reported instead of sailing through silently - the review found that
CLICKHOUSE_MAX_OPEN_CONNECTIONS=64 against a stated cap of 32 raised no
warning at all.

Haven exports the cap from the same constant it renders into the
container's config, so the two sides cannot drift. It also exports
CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT_REPLICAS - one lane, or two when the workers run
standalone - which moves haven stacks off the clamped fallback onto the
real derivation, sized right and booting without the warning.

Closes #7666

Spec: specs/governance/pulled-usage-cost-reporting.feature
Decision: ADR-128 §3

* feat(governance): carry the currency a provider billed in, end to end

Azure bills our own subscription in euros. Every money field from the adapter
to the daily rollup assumed dollars, so a euro figure would have been filed as
dollars and summed with real ones.

The money on the durable event is now costNanoMinor — an integer of the
PROVIDER's own minor units — with currencyCode saying which, and costNanoUsd
holding the BILLER's own dollar conversion when it published one. Nothing
converts anywhere: no rate is invented at ingest, in the fold, or on read
(ADR-128 §3).

Both new fields default, and that is load-bearing: every event already on the
append-only log predates currencies and reported dollars, so a required field
would make the log unreadable. A test parses a pre-change event verbatim.

The rollup keys cells by the billed currency and states a dollar figure only
when it can: the amount itself when the cell is in dollars, the biller's own
figures when it is not and every item carries one, and null otherwise — a
partial dollar sum reads as the whole day's spend while omitting the rest.

The comparator now compares the billed amount. It was comparing the dollar
column, which on a non-dollar row is empty on both sides — it agreed with
itself while the real amounts could differ by anything.

The dollar ledger gets no row for money it cannot state in dollars, rather
than a native figure mislabelled as dollars or a zero that reads as free.

Also fixes a live trap in the existing fold test: its helper still wrote the
old field name, which the new schema reads as the biller-dollar field, so
amountNanoMinor went NaN and the amount assertions passed anyway. The helper
now names both fields and the restatement test asserts the billed amount too.

Spec: specs/governance/governance-cost-rollup.feature
Spec: specs/governance/pulled-usage-cost-reporting.feature
Decision: ADR-128 §3

* feat(governance): read Azure Cost Management's daily bill (pure mapper)

The pure half of the Azure cost read: no I/O, no clock, no fetch, so every
rule is decided against the REAL captured reply from a live subscription
(2026-08-30, 44 rows) in a unit test rather than against a shape invented to
match the code.

Three things that reply got wrong about the obvious design, each of which
produces a plausible-looking wrong number:

  - UsageDate is a Number column holding a PACKED integer, 20260823. Read as
    an epoch it lands in 1970. Parsed by position and round-tripped through
    Date, so an impossible day is refused rather than normalised into a
    neighbouring day and filed under the wrong bill.
  - A Currency column nobody asked for arrived in the MIDDLE of the row, so
    every value is read by column NAME. Keyed on position, the next column
    Azure adds turns the currency into a meter category.
  - Amounts are JSON floats, unlike Databricks whose numerics are strings.
    Converted to their exact decimal string exactly once, here; everything
    downstream is string and bigint.

The window always ends today and reaches back seven days, because today's
figure is partial by construction — the captured reply has today's load
balancer at 0.375 against 0.60 on every finished day. The start may only ever
widen, so a source that has fallen behind is not dragged forward and made to
skip the days in between.

totalCostUSD is requested beside totalCost from day one: we never invent a
rate, so Microsoft's own conversion is the only dollar figure we will state.

Spec: specs/ai-governance/puller-framework/copilot-studio-dataverse.feature
Decision: ADR-128 §3

* feat(governance): read the Azure bill inside the Copilot Studio source

Wires the pure Azure reader into the Dataverse puller, bundled into the
existing source rather than added as a new one: same customer, same app
registration, same environment, and a second source to configure would be a
second thing to get wrong for one number. Provider stays
copilot_studio_dataverse and the cost source stays "pulled", so the rollup
needs no change at all.

The sharpest rule here is not about money. The worker's assertRunMadeProgress
runs BEFORE the cursor write, and it discards a run that reports errors
without moving its cursor — the transcripts it already read included. So the
cost read never throws and never counts an error: every failure degrades to
"no cost this run", modelled on fetchBots which degrades the same way for the
same reason.

Being throttled is ordinary operation, not a fault — the first real request
against a live subscription was a 429 — so a refusal HOLDS the window instead
of pricing it at nothing. The next scheduled run is the retry; nothing sleeps
in-process, which would burn the run's deadline and risk it being killed
holding the transcripts. A window held past a week is given up, so a window
that can never be read cannot pin the source forever.

A day Azure returns no row for produces no event at all. It re-reads a
trailing week, so it constantly asks about days already recorded, and a zero
for a day whose bill has not landed is a correction downward that the
summarizing step would faithfully honour.

Also fixes a defect this wiring introduced and a test now pins: re-encoding an
unchanged position yields a DIFFERENT string, because the cost fields are now
spelled out — and the worker compares those strings to decide whether a run
progressed. It would have read that as an advance and persisted a run that
read nothing. The incoming string is now handed back verbatim when nothing
moved.

Cost signs in for Azure Resource Manager while transcripts sign in for the
environment: different audiences, and one token cannot stand in for the other.
The subscription id is a plain config field, NOT a credentials* one — that
prefix would bury it in the encrypted subtree the config schema never reads —
and the builder omits it when blank rather than saving an empty string the
uuid check would refuse.

Spec: specs/ai-governance/puller-framework/copilot-studio-dataverse.feature
Decision: ADR-128 §3

* fix(governance): close the money and progress defects a review found

Eight fixes, three of which would have shipped silently wrong money.

The ledger intent schema still had cost_nano_usd nonnegative, so every credit
Rung A exists to carry would have failed the intent's own schema and died in
the outbox after its retries — while the charge it reverses stayed on the
books. That is the exact failure the signed-money commit was written to
prevent, one layer further down than it reached.

Events already on the durable log name their money costNanoUsd and mean "the
amount". This build reuses that name for the biller's dollar conversion, so
read literally a historical event's amount is undefined — and nothing on the
read path parses these events, so the fold and the drift comparator took it
directly. A rebuild would have written NaN amounts under keys carrying a null
currency, and the watchdog would have reported every historical cell twice.
readPulledUsageMoney now translates at the two places that read it, with the
fold covered by a test that folds a verbatim legacy event.

A cost advance could stand in for transcript progress. The worker reads a
changed cursor as "advanced past input it could not read" and downgrades the
failure to a warning; the cost watermark moves on the first run of every UTC
day, so a stuck transcript walk would have been excused daily. Loudest case:
refusesNextLink, a next-page link pointing away from the customer's
environment, which is meant to fail the run rather than be absorbed by an
unrelated bill being read successfully. Only the transcript half may now
signal progress on a run that reported errors.

Also: a partial cost window is no longer reported as priced (the page cap, the
deadline and a refused next-page link all held it, and the refusal now logs
like the transcript walk's does); an HTTP 200 carrying an unrecognised body is
held rather than read as a genuinely free week; and the subscription id is out
of the restatement dimensions, where correcting a mistyped one would have
minted fresh keys for the trailing week and doubled every day in it.

Three tests were passing for the wrong reason and now cannot. The fold's
gateway helper kept the old field name, so its only commutativity test
compared NaN to NaN — Object.is says those are equal. The rollup and
comparator integration helpers had the same shape. The dedup claim that
currency and the biller figure both belong in the job id had no test at all.

* fix(governance): let the Azure cost page loop be read in one sitting

The page loop did four jobs at once — ask, judge the answer, judge the next
link, and decide whether the run had anything left — which Biome measured at a
cognitive complexity of 19 against a house limit of 10, and which the lint gate
reported on the added lines.

Split along the seams that were already there:

  * `readAzureCostPage` asks for one page and reads it, answering null for
    every refusal, because an HTTP refusal and a body of the wrong shape mean
    the same thing to the caller: hold the window.
  * `azureCostNextPageUrl` accepts a next-page link only from Azure Resource
    Manager, so the token cannot follow a link elsewhere.
  * The loop itself now reads the run's deadline and abort signal in its own
    condition, so leaving the loop always means one thing — a page is still
    owed and the window is held.

Behaviour is unchanged: same refusals, same log lines, same held windows. The
only difference visible anywhere is that `pageCount` in the ran-out-of-run
warning now counts pages actually asked for rather than one more than that.

Also formats the live-bill script, which was the one error failing the
blocking whole-tree lint.

* test(governance): cover the Azure bill that arrives in several pieces

The scenario "A cost reply spread over several pages is read whole" was bound
only to mapper tests that assert the next-page link is reported. Reporting the
link is not reading the pages: a caller that reported it and stopped would pass
every one of those tests and still hand back a bill missing most of its days.
The page walk itself had no test at all, which is why the split of it in the
previous commit could not be shown safe by anything but reading.

Five cases against the real walk, with only the outbound fetch mocked: it
follows an Azure Resource Manager next page and returns both pages; it holds
the window when the next page points elsewhere, without asking for it; it holds
the window at the page cap rather than record the pages it did read; it asks
for nothing when the run is already over; and a throttle mid-bill holds the
whole window, including the page already in hand.

* fix(governance): a partly failed run no longer resets source health

A run that advanced its cursor while some of its reads failed used to fold
exactly like a clean one: ConsecutiveErrors back to zero, LastSuccessAt
stamped. A source failing the same way every run could therefore launder
itself healthy forever by making any progress at all, and three-strikes
would never fire.

The run-completed event now carries the run's errorCount, threaded from
runIngestionPull (which already computed it) through IngestionPullRunPort
and recordRunCompleted into the event payload. The fold reads it: a partly
failed run keeps the previous ConsecutiveErrors and carries LastSuccessAt
forward instead of stamping now. Events written before the field existed
have no errorCount and fold as clean, which is what they claimed to be.

The field is optional, not defaulted, in the event schema: the fold reads
raw stored events without re-parsing, so a .default(0) would type the
field as always present while history lacks the key. The reader owns ?? 0.

Known residual, on purpose: a source that fails partially on every run
never trips three-strikes. Its LastSuccessAt now freezes, so the activity
monitor's staleness rule still catches it. A dedicated rule for eternal
partial failure is a follow-up, not this change.

* feat(governance): read a tenant's licence pool from Microsoft Graph (pure mapper)

New spec, specs/governance/pulled-seats.feature, and the pure half of the
read that binds most of it: subscribedSkus rows in, seat report events out,
no I/O. The puller integration is the next commit.

The shape mirrors the Azure cost mapper. readSubscribedSkuRows parses one
GET /v1.0/subscribedSkus response (that endpoint publishes no next link, so
there is deliberately no page loop), stepping over unreadable rows and
counting them, and distinguishing a malformed 200 body from a genuinely
empty tenant so an error page served with a 200 cannot read as "no
licences". microsoftSeatEvents emits one event per SKU per day with a
stable source_event_id (msgraph_seats:{skuId}:{day}) so a re-read replaces
rather than duplicates. Bought seats are enabled plus warning units:
Warning is the grace period, where the seats still work; suspended units
are excluded because nobody can sit in them.

nextSeatsCursor holds the day on any failure and gives up after
SEATS_MAX_HOLD_MS (7 days) by marking the day done while keeping the hold
start. That asymmetry is the cost cap for consent nobody granted: a tenant
that never grants Organization.Read.All costs one refused request per day,
not one per run, while an eventually granted consent exits through the
reported branch and clears the hold.

Seat events carry cost_usd "0" and no spend hint: a licence count is not
spend, and reporting it as zero dollars would sit a fake nothing beside
the real bill.

fix(me): pin personal virtual key list to the signed-in user (#8012)

* fix(me): pin personal virtual key list to the signed-in user

/me/configure omitted `targetUserId` on `personalVirtualKeys.list`. For a
caller holding `virtualKeys:viewOtherPersonal` at the organization tier the
absent target means an org-wide sweep, so that caller's own settings page
listed every member's personal keys as if they were their own — and revoking
one failed, because `revokePersonal` is scoped to the caller.

The procedure is correct: the sweep mode is deliberate and spec-bound to the
off-boarding audit. Only the call site was wrong. Pass the session user id and
gate the query on it, so the request cannot fire with an undefined principal.

Regression test in the component lane asserts both halves.

Fixes #8011

* test(vk-rbac): pin the self-target branch /me now depends on

The scope-RBAC suite covered every list path except the one the /me fix
routes through: a caller who HOLDS virtualKeys:viewOtherPersonal naming
their own id as targetUserId. That branch short-circuits before the
permission probe, which is the only reason pinning targetUserId gives an
admin a first-person view instead of the org-wide sweep.

Nothing pinned that ordering, so reordering the probe ahead of the
self-target check would have silently widened /me back to every member's
keys with the whole suite still green.

* fix(me): fail closed on the key scope while the session resolves

`undefined` is the literal value that means "sweep the whole org" at
personalVirtualKeys.list, so passing it through while the session is
unresolved left the entire guarantee resting on the `enabled` flag —
one refactor that flips a gate reopens the hole this PR closes.

Use the repo's sentinel idiom instead (`?? """ + enabled gate, ~208
call sites, including personalWorkspaceFeatures.get 30 lines away in
me/configure.tsx). An empty target takes the `!== undefined` branch:
FORBIDDEN for a member, zero rows for a permission holder. Never the
sweep. Found by convention scan during review.

* test(me): drop dangling @scenario tags, follow the file-naming convention

The two @scenario annotations named a title that exists in no .feature
file, which fails check:feature-parity — a required CI job whose path
filter covers platform/app/**. Reproduced locally:

  Annotations referencing unknown scenarios:
    x @scenario /me asks only for the signed-in user's own personal keys

Dropped rather than backfilled: this is a bug fix, and a bug fix earns a
regression test, not a spec scenario. Binding it to my-settings.feature
would also drag that file out of LEGACY_INERT and trip the partial-tag
rule.

Renamed to the dot-separated <Subject>.<concern>.<level> form that 136
sibling files use, and added the assertion pinning the fail-closed
sentinel from the previous commit.

* test(vk-rbac): assert the self-target read, drop the invisible @scenario

Two problems with the case added earlier in this PR, both found in review.

The assertion only excluded Leo's and Maya's keys, so an empty result passed
it: "scoped to me" and "returned nothing at all" were indistinguishable. The
auditor now owns a key of their own and the read is asserted as an exact set.

The `@scenario` above it named a title that exists in no feature file, and it
bound nothing: check-feature-parity's `isFollowedByTestCall` walks whitespace
and whole comments only, so the eight lines of prose between the tag and the
`it(` dropped it silently — the invisible-binding trap the checker's own
header warns about. Removed rather than backfilled: a bug fix earns a
regression test, not a spec, and inventing a scenario title to satisfy an

* fix(governance): environments go unmeasured when the source read does

The Inventory strip drew a dash for sources when that read had not answered, then counted environments off the same silence and printed 0. Environments are derived from the source list, not read separately, so an unanswered read made the derivation return an empty array and the count reported it as a measurement.

Proved by rendering the page with the sources query undefined: the strip read '0tools0 vendors0environments0 discovered from your sources-sources' in both the loading and the error case. One silence, reported two ways, in the same row.

environmentCount and discoveredEnvironmentCount now take number|null, mirroring the gate peopleSummary.ts already applies. The tab badge goes blank on the same condition, so Environments and Sources never disagree. Regression tests cover both loading and error.

* fix(governance): an unrecognised tool type degrades instead of crashing the pane

applicableRowsForTool spread TYPE_ROWS[tool.type] into a Set. That lookup is not total however much its Record type says so: AiToolEntry.type is a bare String column, the admin payload reaches the client through an as-unknown-as double cast that validates nothing, and AiToolTileType is a hand-written union that does not derive from the service's SUPPORTED_TILE_TYPES.

Measured rather than assumed. Adding a fourth member to SUPPORTED_TILE_TYPES and running typecheck exits 0, so the drift is silent; and [...undefined] throws TypeError: undefined is not iterable, so the first row carrying that type would take the whole Catalog pane down.

Guarded with ?? [] so such a row loses its two type-specific rows and keeps its card. Tests pin both the no-throw and the degraded shape. Deriving the union from SUPPORTED_TILE_TYPES is the real fix and belongs with the /me tile contract, not in a UI pass.

The overview hero carried four chips, three that add and one that

It is a menu item rendered as an anchor rather than the model picker's
bare footer control, because a non-item inside an Ark menu is out of

to a right-click the way the chip had it. The rule is a separator in a
negative-margin box rather than a sticky footer, because this menu is
four rows and never scrolls.

COST, STATED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED. The row now rides
`ingestionSources:manage`, since that grant is what draws the pill at

sources tab from this page. They still reach it: the tab itself is

Scenario titles unchanged. "The hero offers four ways in, three to add
and one to configure" stays literally true — three chips plus the menu

worker ever writes it, so a push source carrying failures rendered
