* Show departments on one table, and say each thing where it is read

The departments tab carried two stacked tables holding the same kind of
thing. A reader who saw "Engineering" twice was left to work out why. They
are one table now.

A created department and a directory name that fold to the same key are one
row, not two. The fold is case- and whitespace-insensitive, because the
collision it exists for is a human one: somebody creates "Engineering" and a
directory sends "engineering". The organization's own spelling wins the
display, since that is the name spend attributes under and the one the
assignment pickers show.

The distinction the second table was protecting is still enforced, it just
no longer costs a heading and a paragraph. Only a row with a record behind
it is offered Rename and Archive, because only a record can be renamed. A
row a directory named carries a badge naming that provider and nothing more.

This needed a data change rather than an invented vendor name. An observed
department previously carried only a name and a count, so the shape could
not say who named it. It now gathers the providers of the people filed under
that name, and the badge renders through the existing provider label, so a
directory slug resolves to the vendor's own catalog name and falls back to
the slug when the catalog has no entry.

A department nobody's directory named shows a dash for headcount rather than
zero. The figure counts the directory's people, not the members an
administrator assigned, so a zero would report a department empty when it
may hold half the company.

The paragraph under the people table is gone. It held two facts and each was
the page's only statement of its own, so both moved to where they are read
rather than being dropped. The twelve-month window is now on the spend and
requests headings, where a reader wondering what a figure covers is already
looking; both headings carry it, because one alone would leave the other
figure ambiguous. The sort's reach is now in the sort menu, said on the
control it is true of.

Four column hints tightened on one rule: a hint survives only where the
label cannot say the thing itself. One was deleted outright, because
"without a department" already states its whole condition. One changed
meaning on purpose rather than merely shortening, since the strip counts
only the departments the organization created and the tab below no longer
makes that obvious now the discovered ones share a table.

* Hold Cowork out of the sample Sources table without retiring the type

The sample table read as a claim about this deployment rather than as an
illustration, and a Cowork row was the case that made that visible. The type
itself is live: it is a real, creatable source type, it stays in the Add
source menu with its icon, its blurb and its configuration path, and nothing
a customer can configure changes here.

The flag sits on the catalog entry beside `deprecated`, not in a key list in
the sample module. A hand-written exclusion there would have reopened, in the
opposite direction, the drift that deriving the sample from the registry had
just closed: the sample could once again name something the registry did not,
or fail to name something it did.

Its comment leads with what it is not. A type held back from a mock-up is not
deprecated, and the next reader must not finish the job by retiring it. The
reason is that the two lists answer different questions. The menu answers
what can be connected and has to be complete. The sample answers what a
connected fleet looks like and is illustrative, so a row that reads as an
assertion about this deployment can be held back without being withdrawn from
the product.

The sample helper is derived from the offered helper rather than from the raw
list, which makes the subset relation structural instead of conventional: a
type cannot reach the sample without being on offer, whatever anyone does to
the flag later.

The spec keeps its existing scenario unchanged, since "every row is a source
type the Add source menu offers" was already the subset direction and is
still true. A new scenario names Cowork as the case that distinguishes the
two lists, asserting it has no sample row, is still offered by the menu, and
is not marked retired, so dropping the flag, deleting the entry and retiring
the type each break something different.

The sample's instance states are indexed positionally, so removing a row
shifts every state after it. Dropping Cowork happened to leave all four
badges on screen, but only by luck: the failure state landed on a pull source
where the count survives, and on a push source the push-mode rule would have
zeroed it and taken the badge away silently. A test now asserts the drawn set
is exactly those four badges, so the next type held back fails loudly rather
than quietly costing one.

* Let the hero address a page that has no tabs

The guard that stops the hero naming a tab its destination does not have
assumed every destination has tabs. It read each page's tab tuple and treated
a page without one as unreadable, so removing a page's tab bar looked like a
fault in the hero.

A page with no tuple is now a legal case held to a stricter rule rather than
an error: the hero must address it with no tab at all. The rule got tighter,
not looser. Ground that used to be unreachable is now checked, and it catches
a dead parameter that would otherwise sit in a link forever, read by nothing
and noticed by no one.

The throw for a page whose source cannot be found is untouched, because those
two failures need different reports. A page that moved must fail by name; a
page with no tab bar must not fail at all.

The agents link drops its tab accordingly, and carries a comment saying why
it alone has none, so the asymmetry with the links either side of it does not
read as an oversight later.

Both branches are exercised by the real tree: the agents page has no tuple
today while the people and inventory pages still do.

* Match departments on the name the writes match on, not a folded one

The merge folded case, on the reasoning that an administrator creating
"Engineering" while a directory sends "engineering" means one department. That
was a rule this screen invented, and the database does not agree with it.

Both paths that carry directory department text, the SCIM push and the daily
directory pull, trim it and resolve it through the same service, which looks
the name up with exact equality and creates a row when nothing matches. So
those two names are not one department. They are two records, and spend
attributes to them separately.

Folding them here would have printed that pair as one row and told the reader
their spend lands in one place when it lands in two. Worse, the merge is keyed,
so one of the two records would have been dropped from the table entirely,
leaving a real department that could never be renamed or archived from this
screen.

The match is now the trimmed name compared exactly, which is the predicate the
writes use. Trimming stays, because the writers trim before resolving, so
matching untrimmed text would miss rows they consider identical.

Two records still cannot collide on this key. A partial unique index on
organization and name, where the row is active, permits at most one live
department per name, so no record's row can be overwritten by another's. The
index is not visible in the schema file, having been carried over by rename
from the cost centre table it originally guarded.

* Make the agents page one surface, and let the list be the default

The page carried an Applications tab beside the agents, so a reader arriving
to see what was running had to notice a tab strip and choose a side before
seeing anything. The second tab is gone and the strip with it. What remains is
the thing the page is for.

The agents themselves now default to a list rather than a grid of cards. A
reader scanning for one agent among many reads a list faster than a wall of
tiles, and comparing two agents means comparing two rows rather than two
boxes. Cards stay available for anyone who prefers them, and the choice lives
in the address, so a chosen layout survives a reload and can be linked to.

Removing the strip removes the page's tab vocabulary entirely, which is why
the links pointing here no longer carry a tab parameter.

* Let a Cowork tile be created, since Cowork is a tool

The drawer's picker has been offering Cowork as a coding assistant while the
schema that gates the write rejected it, so an administrator could select it,
press save, and get an invalid value error. The picker builds its options from
the presets list and the write is gated by this enum, and nothing linked the
two, so the two lists drifted apart with nothing to catch it.

Cowork is a tool rather than a source, so the enum is what was wrong.

This makes a second thing work that has never worked. Cost attribution joins a
tile to incoming telemetry on the assistant kind, and no tile could hold this
kind, so for Cowork that join could never match. An administrator unticking
bundled subscription on Cowork was performing a gesture that did nothing, with
nothing on screen to say so. That untick now takes effect. Nothing changes for
anyone until an admin creates such a tile, since no stored row can carry a
value the schema always rejected, and the default is non-billable, so it takes
a deliberate choice.

Two comments elsewhere asserted things this makes false, and are corrected
rather than left to mislead. One justified passing Cowork telemetry through
under its own name on the grounds that no tile could ever hold it; the reason
is now the opposite and better, that a tile is keyed on exactly that name, and
folding it into Claude Code would make unticking the Claude Code tile silently
rebill Cowork as well. The other named the one assistant kind with no command
line wrapper, and there are now two.

The two lists are equal today and nothing yet keeps them equal. Guarding that
belongs with the wider work of linking the type lists, not here.

* Pin the Cowork billing join, now that it has a live left-hand side

Accepting `claude_cowork` as an assistant kind gave the bundled-plan join a
matching tile for the first time, so a decision about what a customer is
billed for became reachable with nothing asserting it.

Three cases on the join: unticking the Cowork tile bills Cowork, and neither
Cowork nor Claude Code moves when the other is unticked. Four on the mapper,
which had no test at all: the two renames, the agreements, and Cowork staying
its own source type. Verified the last one bites by folding Cowork into
Claude Code and watching that test alone fail.

* Register an agent in a drawer, like every other governance add

The modal was the last one on these pages: Add department, routing policy and
the rest already open as drawers from the registry, and the governance home
page's "Add agent" chip deep-linked into a Chakra dialog instead.

Content is unchanged, because it was never a form — an agent registers itself
from the process that runs it (ADR-128), so the drawer still shows the Python
and TypeScript connect snippets. `?add=1` keeps working for the chip and now
resolves to `drawer.open=addAgent`. Also corrects the routes comment that
still described this page as two tabs.

* Say what the department headcount counts

The figure counts the people a connected source filed under a department's
name, not the members an administrator assigned. Consolidating the two tables
deleted the panel heading that carried that fact, and an em dash means "no
source named anyone here" only to a reader who was told what was measured.
To anyone else, a dash beside a department they know has people in it reads
as a defect in the page.

The column now says it.

* Count an agent's age in one unit, so it never reads as zero years

`formatRegistered` counted months in thirty-day months and years in 365-day
years. The two units leave a gap: at 360 days the twelfth thirty-day month has
ended, so the months branch is done, but a 365-day year has not started, so the
years branch floors to zero. Days 360 through 364 rendered "0 years ago".

Years are now counted in the same months the months branch counts, which cannot
floor to zero on a value that reached the branch at all.

The formatters had no unit tests. They were exercised only through the list and
card integration tests, at whatever values the sample rows carry, and the
highest `registeredDaysAgo` in any sample is 320 — inside the months branch, so
the years branch was never reached. The new tests pin the branch boundaries and
then sweep every day inside four years asserting no phrase contains a zero
quantity, which is the rule the page already holds elsewhere: a value the
platform lacks reads as a dash, and one it has never reads as a zero.

* Close the department drawer once per dismissal, not twice

`Drawer.CloseTrigger` carried `onClick={closeDrawer}` while `Drawer.Root`
already called `closeDrawer` from `onOpenChange`. The trigger closes the
drawer, which fires `onOpenChange`, so one click on the X ran both.

`closeDrawer` ends in `router.push`, so the second call left a duplicate
history entry. A reader who closed the drawer and pressed Back saw nothing
happen, and on the second Back the drawer reopened.

Measured before the fix: one click on the close control called the navigation
twice; Cancel, which calls it directly and does not go through the trigger,
called it once.

The bound test asserted `toBeGreaterThan(0)` on the close count, which passes
at one and at two, so it went green for as long as the control was
double-wired. It now asserts exactly one, and a second test covers the X path
specifically — the Create path was never the broken one, so a guard on Create
alone would have missed this.

Seven of the 161 close triggers in `src/components` carry an `onClick`; the
other six are outside this change and untouched, but they have the same shape
and likely the same duplicate entry.

* Treat an unread answer as unread, not as a refusal

Four places decided something before the read behind it had answered,
and each landed on the wrong side of the decision.

The badge label moved under us. #8023 renamed the unhealthy source badge
from "Not pulling" to "Pulls failing"; this branch's new sample-row test
and three comments predate that rename and still named the old label, so
the sample rows failed the assertion that every badge the table can draw
reaches the screen.

The People strip read `!isLoading` as "answered". A tRPC query that was
never enabled is not loading and never will be: the spend read is off
for a reader without `activityMonitor:view` and off again for a
non-Enterprise organization, and the departments read is off until the
organization id arrives. Each printed a confident population counted
from the identity half alone, directly under a table showing that same
reader a permission notice. Success is what proves an answer.

The Add department drawer and the `?add=` deep link read an unresolved
grant as an absent one. `useOrganizationTeamProject` answers false for
every permission while its query is in flight, so a manager arriving on
the deep link read the refusal notice and watched the form replace it —
and the inventory effect went further, opening nothing and stripping the
flag off the address, so the link was spent on a refusal that was only
ever a timing artefact. The deep-link hook already carried this exact
reasoning for the plan gate; it now covers grants too.

Departments could not collide, said the comment. They can: the partial
unique index compares the name as stored and nothing on the write path
trims, so "Engineering" and "Engineering " are two active records that
folded to one key, and the first was dropped from the tab. Records now
key by id and the fold does only the job it had, which is letting a
directory name find its record.

Also splits the inventory page hook, whose composer half had pushed it
one line over the function-length limit CI enforces on new code.

* Settle the review findings on the governance pass

Catalog cards now read the billing override an admin actually set.
`billingForTool` chose payment rows and badges from `assistantKind`
alone, but the same registry entry carries `config.bundledPlan`, and the
cost-attribution policy reads `bundledPlan === false` as "these tokens
are billed". So a Claude Code tile with Bundled subscription unticked
was labelled Subscription, carried a subscriptions row, and hid the
token count that had just become the interesting figure on it — the
catalog contradicting the entry it is a summary of. The override now
ADDS the metered row and badge rather than replacing the contract's: the
plan is still bought, and unticking a box does not refund it.

Three assertions could not fail. `/^0 tools/` and `/\d+ sources · \d+
active/` were matched against single text nodes, and the strip draws
every figure and its label as separate nodes, so neither regex could
match anything and both passed whatever was on screen; a third asserted
an em dash somewhere in the strip, which a different pane's dash
satisfied. Each figure now carries a test id of its own and is read
where it is drawn. Reintroducing the zero-environments defect now fails
two tests; before, it failed none of them.

Departments could also be under-counted from the other direction: the
People strip counted a skipped read as a finished one, so the fix above
in `people.tsx` is now pinned by a case where the spend read was never
made at all, rather than only one where it is still running.

The button-weight scanner moves to `src/test-utils/buttonWeightScan.ts`,
beside the `markColourSites` and `parseSourceTexts` it is built on. It
had grown to 562 lines inside the suite that first needed it, and the
rule it implements is not specific to the governance tree. Its tag
vocabulary now covers pills and chips, since `HeroLeadPill` and
`AskChip` are pressable controls sitting in a scanned file, and what the
scan CANNOT see is stated in the module: a control that fills itself
from a prop of its own is invisible to it however loud it renders.

The rest are corrections to things that had drifted:

  - A drawer headed "Add tool" whose button said "Save tile", and a
    starter-pack import that reported "Imported 3 tiles". The rename was
    half-applied; the strings a reader sees now agree.
  - Four spec citations pointing at the wrong line, one of them at the
    wrong FILE — there are two `AgentCard.tsx` and the badge is in the
    other one. Citations name symbols now, so they cannot rot again.
  - A hero chip row drawing three icons from one library and the fourth
    from another; all four now come from the house one.
  - A doc comment claiming every applicable row on a sample card is
    filled, when six of eight carry a licence or token row on purpose.
  - A note recording a sibling spec as stale that this same change had
    already corrected.
  - A scenario asking for a menu row that its own Background could not
    produce, missing the grant that draws the menu.
  - An ownership comment crediting a panel with the mutations its child
    wires, and a component re-deriving two values off a query the hook
    beside it already exposes.
  - A reference badge left mounted in a second React root, so every
    query after it spanned two trees.
  - An abbreviation check that would have fired on the correct change:
    `" req"` is a prefix of `" requests"`, the word the rule wants.
  - A sparkline's only description for a reader who cannot see it,
    naming registrations in a window when the series is cumulative.

Not changed, and why. The seats row on a consumption-billed sample card
is not a contradiction of the rule that derived rows omit it — the two
describe different surfaces, and the scenario now says so. And the
all-zero-spend division is already guarded by `total <= 0`; the branch
was untested rather than broken, so it gets a test and not a fix.

* Split the department drawer's write out of its rendering

The three-state fix in the previous commit pushed this component past
the length the review rules hold new exported functions to, and it had
been doing four things anyway: resolving grants, holding the form,
owning the mutation, and drawing the drawer.

`useCreateDepartment` takes the form and the write. State and callbacks
only, no JSX, so the component is left deciding which of its three
states to draw — unresolved, refused, or the form — which is the thing
worth reading it for.

* Pin the corrected sparkline label in its own test

The label change two commits back left this assertion holding the old
string. It runs in the unit lane, which the component config does not
cover, so the governance component run stayed green over it.

* Update the starter-pack assertion the tool rename moved

The 'tile' to 'tool' rename covered the strings a reader sees; this
test pinned one of them from outside the governance tree, so the
governance suite stayed green over it.

* fix(annotations): walk the annotation queue one item at a time

The my-queue page resolved the reviewer's entire queue in order to render one
item of it: every queued trace id went to ClickHouse inside a single query
parameter, with every trace fully resolved. Past a certain queue length those
ids no longer fit in one parameter and the read fails outright — and long
before that, it quietly pays for thousands of traces to display one.

Replace `getOptimizedAnnotationQueues({ allQueueItems: true })` on that page
with `getQueueWalkStep`, which resolves the item the URL names (or the first
one still waiting), how many sort ahead of it, and the ids either side of it.
That is a fixed handful of rows and exactly one trace, whatever the queue's
length. The `allQueueItems` flag is gone; the list procedure keeps its
pagination untouched.

The bar used to release its buttons on a timer that knew nothing about the
read, so between the route settling and the next item arriving a click acted
on the item the reviewer had just left: it marked the wrong item done and
opened the wrong trace in the drawer. Every action now waits on the read for
the item it acts on, which no timer can stand in for, because the read
fetches a whole trace and routinely outlasts any beat short enough to feel
responsive.

Known and deliberately left: the two counts behind the position sort by a
column no index ends in, so this bounds the rows read rather than the work
done. A migration on that table is larger than this change.

Refs #8057

the `projectId` that clause already carried down one level.

`AnnotationQueueItem` is not in `SCOPED_MODELS`, so it falls to the default
multitenancy guard, and that guard reads tenancy at the top of the `where`
only — it never recurses into `AND`
(`src/utils/dbMultiTenancyProtection.ts:894`). With `projectId` hidden inside
the array the guard saw an unscoped read and refused it, so the procedure
failed before it could return anything:

    The findFirst action on the AnnotationQueueItem model requires a
    'projectId' or 'projectId.in' in the where clause

The page did not show an error. `useAnnotationQueueWalk` turns the failed step
into a null item, the drawer then resolves no thread id from it, and the
reviewer reads "No turns found in this conversation" — a working page with
nothing in it.

Narrow through one helper, `narrowQueueItemWhere`, which lifts `projectId`
back to the top and keeps the whole original clause inside the `AND`. What the
query matches is unchanged; only its shape is. That covers all four narrowing
sites: the named-item lookup in `findWalkItem`, and the count and two
neighbour seeks in `resolveWalkPlace`.

The existing tests could not catch this. Their Prisma stub answered directly,
so no guard ever ran against the `where` the router builds. The stub now routes
every `AnnotationQueueItem` read through the real `guardProjectId` middleware,
the same way `seedTopicModel.unit.test.ts` does for the equivalent bug in
ADR-051. A first test proves the guard can still refuse, so the suite cannot
pass on a guard that has been disarmed.

Reverting this change fails seven of the eight tests in that file with the
production error above.

Refs #8059

* style(annotations): join curried arrow in queue-walk test to satisfy formatter

Biome's formatter wants the curried `guardedQueueItemRead` arrow on a single
line. The split form failed `biome check` and turned the CI lint gate red on
PR #8065.

Whitespace only, no behaviour change. The unit test file still passes 8/8, and
`pnpm typecheck:all` exits 0 (plain `pnpm typecheck` never covered this file,
because `tsconfig.tsgo.json` excludes tests).

The two remaining warnings on annotation.ts (useMaxParams at :44,
noExcessiveLinesPerFunction at :1193) are pre-existing on main, are warnings
rather than errors, and are left alone.

feat(governance): discover and sync agents from connected providers (#8043)

* feat(governance): read and save the agent lists providers already hand us

Databricks Genie spaces and Copilot Studio bots were fetched on every pull,
used for a single display name, then dropped. DiscoveredAgent has existed
since the identity migration with no writer.

Three outcomes are kept apart because they mean different things to a reader:
listed, empty, and refused. The refused arm carries no agents field, so a
caller cannot silently treat a permission refusal as an absence of agents.

The credential seam keeps the organization in the WHERE predicate and strips
credentials from the config it hands over.

* feat(governance): trigger agent listing through the existing pull pipeline

The sync rides the ingestion_pull aggregate that already owns leasing, retry
and concurrency for this source. No cron, no timer, no queue beside it.

Outcomes are recorded as events in the shape of the existing run-completed and
run-failed pair. The refusal event carries a reason code and status, never
provider error text, matching the redaction contract in sourcePullStatus.

A sync must not disturb the source's pending scheduled wake. The process
manager owns that wake and every handler returns it explicitly, so a wrong
return here would silently stop a source from ever pulling again.

* feat(governance): show real agents on the agents page

The page issued no query at all: with sample mode off it was an honest empty
state, with it on the rows were invented. It now reads an organization-scoped
union of hand-registered agents and provider-found ones, each row saying which
it is.

An empty real result never falls back to sample rows. Advertising invented
figures beside a real read leaves the reader unable to act on either.

Loading and error branches did not exist on this page before.

* fix(governance): retype the command test helper against Event

The strict project config type-checks test files that the default config
skips, so this failed only under typecheck:all.

* test(governance): pin the connected-agent query and its scenarios

Covers the organization walk, archived and internal-governance exclusion,
the presence cutoff and the selected fields against a fake client.

* fix(governance): stop merging agents that only share a name

A shared name is not evidence that two agents are one. Agent.identityKey
has no counterpart in a provider's agent id, so an exact-name match has
nothing corroborating it.

The two failures are not symmetric. A duplicate row is visible and a
reader can act on it. A false merge silently removes an agent from an
inventory whose only job is to say what exists, and an absence cannot be
spotted. Over-counting is a nuisance; under-counting is a lie.

This also matches the people screen, where two providers naming the same
address stay two rows.

* fix(governance): say which agents the fleet trend cannot include

The fleet card headline counts every agent. The sparkline and the
"+N in the last 30 days" figure are folds over agents with a
registration date, which agents found at a provider do not have.

Unsaid, the card reads as twelve agents above a line reaching four,
and nothing tells a reader whether the count is inflated, the line is
broken, or four agents disappeared. Naming the excluded rows turns an
apparent error into a stated fact.

Wording only. The curve still leaves undated rows off rather than
pinning them to either end, and they still count in the headline. The
clause goes on the sparkline's label as well as the caption, so a
reader who hovers and a reader who cannot see it get the same story.

* feat(governance): pull the people list on the same pipeline as agents

A people listing is now an intent on the existing ingestionPull process
manager, with commands and events on the ingestion_pull aggregate. It
runs under the lease, attempt cap and concurrency the pull already has.
There is no timer, no queue and no path into the provider that does not
write an event first.

The join key is not the email. DiscoveredPerson is keyed on rawActorId,
so a listing keys on whatever that provider's activity rows already
write as actor: the member id for OpenAI and Anthropic, the directory
UUID for Microsoft, and userName then externalId then the SCIM id for
Databricks. The email travels as a fact about the person, never as the
key, because a tenant that re-issues an address would otherwise move
someone's whole history the day they change their name. Keying on the
email would have duplicated three providers out of four.

People and agents share the outcome shape, the refusal vocabulary and
one outbox handler body, because two copies of "a refusal is not a
retry" is how two lists drift into disagreeing about what a 403 means.
The events stay separate: a credential may enumerate agents and not
people, so one source can emit refused and listed in the same minute,
and a reader asking when we last learned who works here should not have
to filter a mixed stream.

Nothing writes DiscoveredPerson directly. The listing builds directory
sightings, runs them through the same erasure suppression the pull uses,
and hands the survivors to PersonDiscoveryService. Directory sightings
rather than activity ones, so refreshing a staff list does not report
every employee as active today. A tenant whose whole list is erased
reads as listed with nothing recorded, not as empty: they have staff, we
are right not to hold the names.

Databricks bulk SCIM has not been called against a live workspace. Both
shape assumptions degrade to a typed refusal rather than a crash, and a
legal empty page reads as empty rather than malformed.

142 files, 1612 tests pass. No provider was called.

* feat(governance): record what each listing actually answered

A source that refuses to enumerate its directory and a tenant that has
no agents both produced an empty table, and nothing on the run-status
row could tell them apart. An admin fixing a broken credential and an
admin with nothing to fix saw the same screen.

Adds eleven nullable columns in two sets, one per kind. They stay
separate rather than sharing a set with a kind discriminator because
one set would erase an agents refusal the moment somebody synced
people, making a broken source look healthy because a different sync
worked.

A listed outcome carries a count and clears the reason; a refusal
carries a reason and no count. Zero is a real answer from a working
provider. The two are never confusable, which is the point.

The listing handlers never write LastRunScheduledFor and never touch
the pull or mirror fields. The four listing events carry no
scheduledFor, so writing it would let a listing supersede a real pull
and freeze the cursor. A credential that cannot read a directory still
pulls cost perfectly, and a listing must never read as a failed pull.

The people counts are a pair: the directory count is everyone the
provider named, and the withheld count is how many of those erasure
kept us from storing. Withheld is a SUBSET, never an addition. Adding
them counts the same people twice; subtracting gives what we hold. The
withheld figure may be read as a current number only, never as a
series, because a drop from 500 to 499 at a known moment names the
person on a small tenant.

No projection version bump. A bump asserts replay produces different
rows. These events are new, so no history holds one to fold, and every
column is nullable with null meaning "no listing recorded", which is
the true reading for a source whose history predates them.

Also lifts the pipeline name into a constant in the leaf schemas
module, so a caller outside the directory can dispatch against it
without dragging the commands, projection and process manager into
every request-serving process.

* feat(governance): sync control and honest empty states on the agents page

The page could not ask a provider anything. The only way to see a newly
connected source's agents was to wait for the next scheduled pull, and
nothing on screen said so.

Adds a control that asks every connected source to list its agents. It
has four states and every unpressable one carries a sentence saying
why, so a disabled button is never a dead end.

The toast says we asked, not what came back, because at that moment we
do not know. A test asserts the copy does not match /found|listed \d/i
so a later edit cannot quietly turn a request into a claim.

The empty table names the connected providers rather than saying there
are no agents, because with no listing outcome recorded we cannot tell
an empty tenant from a source that never answered.

The fleet card no longer contradicts its own table: rows excluded from
the trend are excluded from the caption too.

Rows are not collapsed by name. A duplicate row is visible and somebody
can correct it; a false merge is invisible and nobody can.

* refactor(governance): split listing dispatch from failure handling

The provider dispatch carried a cognitive complexity of 11 against a
limit of 10, which the lint gate reads as a new violation because the
function arrived on this branch.

Splitting it is not just a way under the limit. Which credential each
provider needs and what a failure means to the caller are two different
questions, edited by different people for unrelated reasons. Adding a
provider now changes only the first.

Behaviour is unchanged: a failed sign-in and an unparseable config are
still refusals rather than throws, so one broken source in a list does
not fail the whole sync.

* fix(governance): stop exporting the erasure count on a telemetry span

The people-listed span carried the withheld count. Confirmed by
executing the real command's attribute function, which returned
"payload.withheld_person_count": 12 — live configuration, not dead.

Everywhere else this feature says that number may be read as a current
figure and never as a series. A span is emitted per run and retained
with a timestamp, so putting the number on one publishes exactly the
series the rule forbids. The count stepping from N to N+1 at a known
moment says an erasure happened then, and on a small tenant that
identifies the person as surely as a name would.

The comment beside it reasoned about spans and stopped at "counts,
never a name". That test is not sufficient for this field: the count IS
the sensitive fact, because it counts erasures.

The directory count stays. It is what the provider named, which our
erasure does not move, so it carries no such signal.

Nothing is lost to the operator. The run status row carries the
withheld figure as a current value, which is the one shape it is safe
in.

Not a regression this branch introduced: the base commit emitted a
survivor count on the same span, which leaks the same event equally.
Inherited, but inherited is only a statement about who caused it, not
about whether it is harmless.

* fix(governance): register the agent listing error and guard the withheld count

The agent listing refusal code was declared where it is raised but never
added to the shared registry, so a refusal reached the customer as a
generic unknown error with a trace id and no explanation. A registry test
already existed and had been failing since the code was introduced; it
named the code and both files to edit. That failure travelled into a
downstream branch by merge before anyone noticed.

Adds the code to the registry and gives it presentation copy.

Also lands the listing privacy guard, which walks the real output shape
and the span attributes of every listing command rather than a
hand-written list of fields, so a new command with a leaky attribute
fails rather than passing by omission.

The withheld people count and the HTTP status columns must not reach a
customer-facing surface. Until now that rule lived only in comments
written by the same head as the code, which inherits the author's belief
instead of testing it.

* fix(governance): correct the agents page copy and the stale comments

Three comments and a spec paragraph said the listing events exist but
nothing folds them. The same change that added the events also added the
fold, so the statement was false on arrival and it was load-bearing: it
was the stated reason the empty state refuses to tell a refusal from an
empty tenant, and the reason the asked state never clears. Restated to
say what is true and to name the gap that actually remains.

The unlisted empty state drew its button as an outlined primary while the
header control for the same action is a ghost. Two weights on one action
reads as two different actions.

The same copy told readers without the manage grant to press a button
they cannot see.

Makes the agent sync service take its dependencies as an object like its
six siblings, rather than three positional arguments.

* docs(governance): state where the withheld count may go, and where it is

The reason recorded for keeping this count off a span was wrong. It said
a per-run timestamped record publishes a series. That is equally true of
the event log, which keeps the same pair on every run with a timestamp by
design, so the stated reason would have forbidden our own store. Two
reviewers reached that independently.

The property that separates the two is reach. The event log and the run
status row sit inside our boundary, under our retention, readable only by
those granted this tenant's data. A telemetry export leaves over a plain
exporter to a backend with its own retention and a reader set of every
engineer holding a dashboard login.

Also corrects a claim in the same comment that the operator has not lost
the number. The column is written, but nothing reads it: no selector, no
endpoint, no page. A direct query is the only path. The comment now says
so, and says that the absence is intended rather than unfinished, because
the agnostic version invites the drive-by fix the rule exists to prevent.

* test(governance): make the listing privacy guard fail when it should

The first version of this guard passed against a real leak. It read a
property named `spanAttributes`, but the accessor is a static named
`getSpanAttributes`, so it read undefined, defaulted to an empty object,
and scanned nothing while reporting green. Only deliberately reintroducing
the leak exposed it.

It now discovers commands from the module and asserts the discovered set
is non-empty, so a rename fails loudly rather than silently scanning
nothing. Each of the three choke points was proven by mutation: a status
name added to a customer-facing row, a sensitive value routed through the
source mirror under an unrelated name, and the withheld count restored to
a span. The mirror case is the one a name scan cannot catch, because a
rename defeats a name scan and not a value scan.

A fourth assertion was removed rather than kept. It counted column
declarations and argued that a single overwritten column cannot express a
series. That encoded the reading we have since disproved, and would have
failed the day anyone added a legitimate internal per-run store. The event
log already is one.

* feat(governance): tell a refused agent listing apart from an empty one

The agents page could say only that it holds no agents. A provider that
refused to answer and a tenant that genuinely has none produced the same
sentence, so an operator had no way to tell a permission problem from a
true empty.

A pure selector narrows the two stored listing columns to listed, refused
with a cause of access or unreachable, or nothing recorded. Two causes,
not seven: either a credential or permission needs fixing, or the thing
is worth asking again later. A rate limit must not send someone to audit
a permission.

The batched read selects only those two columns, so the operator-only
HTTP status never enters the process that serves the page.

A refusal outranks a clean answer beside it, because agents behind the
refusing provider are missing from the list and any quieter sentence
overclaims. Saying the organization has no agents requires every
connected provider to have answered. Copy names only the providers that
refused, claims no count, and follows the manage grant.

* fix(governance): bind the listing privacy guard to its scenarios

My earlier commit added three scenario annotations to the privacy guard
and no matching scenarios, so the parity check failed on two of them.

The third was worse. Its annotation sat on the second line of the comment
block rather than the opening line, where the checker cannot see it at
all. It was not reported as unbound, it was invisible, so the guard
written because the span leak actually shipped was bound to nothing and
nothing said so.

Three scenarios added to the provider data boundaries feature, which is
already the home for what a provider value may and may not reach. The
span annotation now sits on its own self-closed line directly above the
test, matching the other two.

* fix(governance): report a network failure as unreachable, not unconfigured

A sign-in call sat inside a `try` whose catch was written for a broken
config, and inherited its verdict. Every DNS failure, TLS failure, timeout
and blocked egress during sign-in came out as `not_configured`, which the
agents page renders as "check that connection's credentials and
permissions" -- sending an administrator to audit access control over a
fault that was never theirs.

The scenario "A refusal that was only unreachable says to ask again" has
been in the spec and false since it shipped. Its test handed a refusal
straight to the fixture, so it never ran the code that decides the cause.

The comment on that catch described one case and the code covered all of
them. Each `try` is now scoped to its network calls alone, and config
parsing is hoisted out of reach via `safeParse`, so a broken config keeps
`not_configured` on its own path rather than inheriting it from a
fallback. An unclassified throw now defaults to `unreachable`: a wrong
credential misread as transient costs one retry, the reverse sends someone
to change permissions during an outage.

Tests drive the real classifier by rejecting the transport, and were
mutation-proven -- reverting the catch turns exactly the two network cases
red.

* test(governance): catch scenario annotations that bind to nothing

The parity checker drops an annotation it cannot bind with a bare
`continue` — no count, no file, no diagnostic. That is a fourth verdict
authors never see: unbound scenarios are reported, unknown annotations
are reported, and this one reads as coverage while being none.

The walk that looks for the test call starts at the end of the match and
cannot leave a comment it begins inside. So an annotation written as a
line WITHIN a block binds nothing, including one on the block's last
line, where the walk lands on the closing marker. Only an annotation
that CLOSES its own comment binds.

Eight real instances were found in the governance trees, all of them
credential-boundary requirements: the secret kept across a destination
change, the token restricted to a Databricks workspace, the environment
address Microsoft does not host, and the redirect that must not carry
credentials onward. Each named a scenario nothing was bound to.

The guard imports both halves of the acceptance rule rather than
restating either. An earlier attempt copied the extraction regex, passed
its own mutation, and sat in a file containing a real unbound annotation
the whole time.

Its fixture is the historical artefact, not a reconstruction: the privacy
guard whose third annotation shipped bound to nothing.

* test(governance): say what a green annotation guard does not cover

Review finding on the guard itself. The describe and the test name claimed
the property without naming the scope, so a green run read as "this
repository has no dangling annotations" when it means "these three trees
do not". That is the same failure the guard was built to catch: a check
that reads as broader coverage than it holds.

Names the scope in both, and records the residual in the file. The same
predicate over the whole app returns 98 across 3,582 test files, none of
them in these trees. A second session measured 113 with a looser
instrument and withdrew it as an upper bound after finding a prose
fragment among its titles.

Four of the 98 are not hygiene — cross-tenant read denial, an api key
ceiling, a lost queue marker, and a migration dropping a concurrent
write. Each has a passing test and nothing bound to it. Recorded rather
than fixed: widening this guard lands it red on 98, and a guard red on
arrival gets its scope cut instead of its findings fixed.

Both halves of the acceptance rule are mutation-proven. Forcing the
predicate to return true, and the extractor to return nothing, each turn
the fixture red.

* docs(governance): correct the cross-check count this guard records

The comment cited a figure the other session withdrew. Its first sweep
read 113 because it reached for the annotation's end offset through a
fallback instead of the `end` the extractor already returns, which starts
the proximity walk inside the annotation and over-reports. Rerun against
`end` it returns 103 over 3,880 files, against 98 over 3,582 here.

The gap is which files each walk collected, not the rule, and neither of
us is chasing 298 files to close five. What both corrected runs agree on
is the claim this guard's scope actually rests on: nothing under these
three trees dangles.

Recording the withdrawn number as if it stood would have left this file
citing a measurement its own author had already retracted.

* test(governance): widen the annotation-binding guard to the whole repo

A convention scan against the sibling guards found this one scoped to
three governance directories and justifying the narrowness in its own
comment as declining to report other people's debt.

That was wrong in the same shape as the bug the guard exists to catch.
A walk scoped to where the defect was found reports zero everywhere it
does not look, so a dangling annotation outside those three trees fails
nothing, ever. And the green check read as a statement about the
repository while checking a corner of it — a signal broader than what
fired it, one level up from the annotation that reads as coverage and
is not.

The house pattern answers the same concern without the blindness:
noRawErrorToasts.unit.test.ts:49 walks src and ee whole and carries its
exceptions as data, as does frontend-boundary.unit.test.ts:65. This now
walks src, ee and scripts and holds the pre-existing 98 dangling
annotations in KNOWN_DEBT.

Counts per file, not a file allowlist. The precedent warns in its own
comment that a file-level entry blinds the guard to every line that file
will ever grow, and eleven of these sit in one file, so allowing it
outright would silence the twelfth. An exact count keeps all 45 live and
ratchets: gain one and it fails, fix one and it fails asking you to
lower the number.

Verified by planting a dangling annotation in src/server/rbac, outside
the old scope. The guard names the file and line; the previous version
was structurally unable to see it.

Also from the scan, all cosmetic: dropped an SPDX header that was 1 of
54 in scripts/ and had been copied from the fixture's source file;
renamed to the directory's kebab convention with the .guard suffix the
one prior guard of this shape uses; nested describes per CLAUDE.md; and
removed the blank comment line each of the eight annotation moves left
behind before its close, which was residue from the deleted line rather
than a style — the only 8 such occurrences in the governance tree.

* test(governance): drive the agents inventory through the project-filter invariant

The invariant test enumerates every listing surface and proves each one
excludes the internal governance project. The agents inventory read was
missing from that list, so its filter was unguarded.

Registering it required recovering project ids from the agent rows the
read returns, since it hands back agents rather than projects. Driving it
any other way would assert about a query the screen does not run.

Removing the kind filter from the repository turns this red naming the
surface.

* fix(governance): report an unreachable people provider as unreachable

The people path carried the same defect already fixed for agents: one wide
try gave every throw the verdict not_configured, a comment written for a
config that no longer parses. A DNS failure or a timeout inside a sign-in
inherited it, so an unreachable provider told an administrator to go
re-enter a credential that was never at fault.

Each provider branch now parses its config first and scopes its own try to
the network calls, so a fifth provider inherits the safe default rather
than the config verdict. The branches were extracted behind one shared
parameter type, because four hand-written copies of that shape drift apart
where a single named one cannot.

The two reachability tests are driven through the Genie sign-in, not an
admin API: the admin pullers catch their own transport failures, so a
throw there never reaches the branch under test. Written against an admin
source they passed with the fix reverted.

* fix(governance): log why the last listing attempt failed

The terminal attempt returned before the only log statement in the path,
so the one failure that actually needs explaining was recorded nowhere.
The durable event carries a reason and no message on purpose, because a
provider's reply can quote a token or a person's name and that event
reaches a screen, which leaves the log as the only place the detail can
live.

The retry line and the terminal line now share one context object and
differ only in wording, so a search can tell a spent attempt from a
retried one.

Also deletes a one-line doc block that contradicted the block directly
below it. TypeScript attached only the second, so the stale one described
the opposite of the code to anyone reading the source.

* fix(governance): enumerate every page of Copilot agents, or refuse

The bot read returned one page and reported whether another existed; the
inventory discarded that flag and presented the first page as the whole
set. An environment with more than 500 agents produced a successful
inventory missing the rest, and every later Sync started at the same first
page, so pressing it again could never find them.

The walk is now opt-in. The transcript puller keeps reading one page,
because a missing agent name costs it a nicety, while the inventory
follows the continuation links to the end. A screen claiming to list the
organization's agents cannot treat a truncated list as a lesser answer.

Two bounds, both deliberate. The continuation URL is checked against the
environment's own origin before it is followed, because that URL arrives
in a response body and the next request carries the token. And the walk
stops after a fixed number of pages, since a provider echoing the same
link back would otherwise loop; reaching that bound is reported as a
refusal rather than as a finished list.

The fetch mock in this suite was never reset, which CodeRabbit also
flagged. It masked nothing before, but the paging cases count requests and
were reading the previous case's leftovers.

* fix(governance): refuse a Genie inventory the page bound cut short

The walk already reported whether it reached the end, and the listing
discarded that answer. A workspace whose spaces ran past the page bound
produced a successful inventory missing the rest, and the next Sync walked
the same pages and stopped in the same place, so repeating the action
could not uncover them.

Same rule as the Copilot inventory now: reaching the bound is reported as
a refusal, not as a list. A workspace holds tens of spaces, so hitting
twenty pages says something is wrong rather than that the workspace is
large.

* fix(governance): end the SCIM walk on the stated total, not a short page

SCIM treats count as a requested maximum rather than a promise, so a
workspace may serve fewer rows than asked while holding more. The walk
stopped on the first short page and reported the result as the workspace's
directory, which drops the rest without a trace.

totalResults was already parsed and thrown away. It now decides the end
where the workspace states one, and the short-page test survives as the
fallback for a workspace that omits it. A page that names nobody still
stops the walk whatever total it claims, since the next request would ask
from the same index and be answered the same way.

The comment above the old test claimed an index check below stopped a
workspace that ignores startIndex. There was no such check; the page bound
is what stops it.

* refactor(governance): give the new booleans the prefix the repo requires

Five new boolean properties and locals read as bare nouns, so a call site
seeing read.malformed or asked could not tell what true meant without
opening the declaration. The rule the repo enforces on new booleans is an
is/has/should/can/will prefix.

malformed becomes isMalformed in both provider reads, busy becomes isBusy
in the listing guard, and the sync control state takes isLoadingSources
and hasAsked, with the page's own state renamed to match rather than
mapped at the call site.

Also adds the SPDX header the sibling files in this cohort all carry and
this one test file was missing.

* fix(governance): tighten three reads the review found loose

The agents read handed its caller every DiscoveredAgent column, including
the provider's verbatim id and a provider-shaped metadata blob, neither of
which a screen row needs. It now selects the five fields it draws from and
returns a named row type, so what leaves this repository is a decision
recorded in one place rather than whatever the table happens to hold.

The annotation-binding guard swallowed every error from reading a
directory. A missing tree is genuinely not its problem, but a permission
or IO error is: the subtree goes unchecked while the file count stays
above its floor, so the guard reports the same verdict for looked and
found nothing as for could not look. Only ENOENT and ENOTDIR are ignored
now.

The listing-outcome migration carried no down step and no IRREVERSIBLE
block, which the repo's migration rule requires one of. The up step is
eleven nullable columns with no backfill, so the reversal is the drops and
nothing else, and the projection is folded from the event log, so a
re-apply restores every value.

* fix(governance): check the environment address before the token rides on it

The agent listing reaches the bot read without the adapter's validateConfig,
and the config schema behind it accepts any URL. So a plain http address
would have put the bearer token on the wire in clear, and a host outside
Power Platform would have sent it somewhere Microsoft does not serve. The
same-origin guard on continuation links did not help: it compares origins,
so http stays http.

The read now runs the adapter's own isDataverseEnvironmentOrigin rule
before it builds a URL, so no request is assembled around an address that
fails it. Removing the check turns both new cases red.

Also renames followPages to shouldFollowPages for the boolean prefix, and
adds errorType to the listing failure log so alerting can group on a
constructor-set name rather than on message text.

* feat(governance): per-currency money, a prior total that survives a reissue, and source rows that say how far they read

The cost screen stops implying a single dollar total it cannot honestly
compute, and starts saying what each currency actually holds.

Two production defects were found and fixed while binding this, both in the
rule for what a day previously held. Neither was a test artefact.

The first: a cell's creation instant was compared against the day's latest
revision to decide whether it existed beforehand. That column is stamped by
the fold's initialiser with the wall clock, so for any cell built from real
events it records when the ROW was written, which is always later than a past
business day's revision. Every folded cell therefore landed in the created
bucket and every restated day reported having previously held nothing. It
read correctly only against hand-written fixture rows that set the stamp
themselves, which is exactly why one area looked green while another did not.
The comparison now applies only when the creation stamp falls inside the
business day it belongs to; outside that window the stamp carries no business
ordering and the cell keeps the older, safe reading.

The second: the unpriced narrowing rescued a dollar-billed cell using its
minor-unit column. For a dollar cell that column holds the same number as the
dollar figure and goes on holding it after the provider withdraws the amount,
so reading it back resurrects precisely the figure that was taken back. Only
a non-dollar minor amount may rescue a cell now, and the rule lives in one
constant shared by all five reads that count unpriced cells.

Alongside: unpriced means no amount in any currency, so a euro cell holding
euros is priced; the single prior dollar figure is gone rather than guessed;
and ingestion source rows carry how far a run read and whether it finished,
so a page-capped run stops reading as a clean success.

One shipped assertion changed from 2 to 0. It claimed a euro cell and a yen

settled rule contradicts. It binds no scenario, so parity is unchanged, and

* fix(voice): audit recording access, and stop trusting the upstream

Four review findings on the whole-call audio route.

A call recording is personal data, so fetching one now writes an audit
entry naming the user, the project and the run, straight after the
permission check and before any bytes move. The entry is written
fire-and-forget so a failure to audit cannot turn a working download
into a 500, matching how the api-key routes already audit.

The provider base URL is customer-configured, so the upstream response
is not ours to trust. Every caller of the audio proxy now states the
content type it expects instead of echoing whatever came back, which
closes the door on an attacker-chosen type served from our own origin.

The Twilio recording lookup ran before the proxy's own timeout applied,
so a provider that withheld response headers could leave the request
pending until something else gave up. It now shares the same fifteen
second budget as every other voice HTTP call.

Finally, the new boolean on our dial interface reads `shouldRecord`, as
our naming rule asks. The SDK's published option is still `record`; the
translation happens at the one place we hand off to the vendor.

* feat(voice): let a voice worker discover its own public URL via a tunnel

A voice worker needs a publicly reachable wss:// endpoint because Twilio
dials in to deliver media (see dev/docs/adr/131-voice-media-transport.md).
Until now that endpoint had to be configured ahead of time, which meant a
load balancer, a certificate and a DNS record before a single call could be
placed.

The worker now opens a free cloudflared quick tunnel at boot and uses the
resulting hostname as its public base URL. It reuses the scenario SDK's own
exported openTwilioTunnel rather than reimplementing it. An explicitly set
VOICE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL still wins, so the stable-hostname deployment path is
unchanged; VOICE_TUNNEL=false restores the old hard failure when neither is
available.

The tunnel is opened before any scenario child is spawned, so the existing
child environment forwarding carries the URL down without new plumbing, and
its teardown is registered with the worker's other shutdown handles so a
restart cannot leak a cloudflared process.

Readiness is gated on the hostname actually resolving in public DNS. A fresh
trycloudflare hostname is not resolvable the moment cloudflared prints it,
and handing Twilio a name that does not resolve yet fails almost silently:
error 31920, a one second call, then a full connect timeout burned.

Also completes the per-call nonce handoff so the media listener can match an
incoming socket to the child that is waiting for it, and makes ordinary
workers refuse voice jobs rather than accepting work they cannot serve.

* fix(voice): make the worker's tunnel actually reachable

Three defects stood between the tunnel code and a working quick tunnel, none
of which any test could see.

The SDK helper was imported as a flat named export, but the package exports
its voice barrel as a namespace. The import type checked against the type
declarations and was undefined at runtime, so it failed only when the real
default was called, with nothing injected. That is worker boot in production
and nowhere else. A test now pins the binding.

Readiness asked the local system resolver. That is the wrong oracle twice
over. Twilio resolves the tunnel from its own network, so a public resolver
is what predicts success; and querying the local one before the name exists
caches the NXDOMAIN for the half hour this zone asks for, which makes the
gate deny a name that is live everywhere else. Readiness now asks two public
DNS-over-HTTPS resolvers and takes the first answer, with the timeout raised
to match the SDK's own equivalent gate.

The vendored SDK was three fixes behind: it predated the nonce-in-path media
URL, the conversation id capture, and the fix that keeps draining
cloudflared's output so its pipe buffer cannot fill and freeze the tunnel.
Rebuilt and re-pinned.

Building that SDK surfaced two type errors in its own upgrade path, both from
the shape Node actually hands an upgrade listener: method and url are
optional on IncomingMessage, and the socket is a Duplex rather than a
net.Socket. Widened both, which also keeps the external handoff path valid
since Socket extends Duplex.

Verified against the real thing, not a mock: a quick tunnel opened, became
globally resolvable in about ten seconds, accepted a real WebSocket upgrade
from the public internet on the nonce path, completed a frame round-trip, and
refused a wrong nonce.

* fix(voice): close the boot-order race and stop a voice typo killing the worker

Clears the seven review threads on #8071. Two were real defects.

**The media listener now binds before the scenario processor.** The processor
starts claiming queued jobs the instant it boots, and a voice job builds TwiML
naming this process's media socket. With the listener two stages behind it, a
job claimed in that gap handed Twilio a dial-back address nothing was bound to
yet, and the call failed on connect. The listener depends on nothing the
processor sets up, so it simply moves ahead of it. A boot-plan test now asserts
the ordering rather than only the membership.

**`readVoiceWorkerEnv` no longer throws.** Its contract said "never throws" and
it called `.parse()`. `startWorkers` reads it BEFORE the boot-stage `try` that
makes voice failures non-fatal, so a malformed `VOICE_WS_PORT` or a non-https
`VOICE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` took down a worker whose other eight subsystems were
healthy. Both now fall back to their documented defaults. The spec says a
non-https origin is "rejected", which it still is — it is just no longer
rejected by crashing, so the existing test moves from asserting a throw to
asserting the fallback.

The rest are smaller but real: the DNS-over-HTTPS probes had no timeout, so a
resolver that accepted the connection and then stalled would park worker boot
forever, since the 300-second deadline is only re-read between probes; and an
unguarded `tunnel.close()` in the readiness catch could escape in place of the
`VoiceTunnelNotReadyError` that actually names the URL and the timeout.

Two are style: a `describe` that named a topic instead of a precondition, and a
`settled` property that needed an `is` prefix.

Also corrects the env doc's no-endpoint description. It claimed the listener
boot was skipped when no public URL is configured. It is not — `voice-ws-listener`
is unconditional, so the socket still binds and a port conflict still surfaces;
only inbound reachability is lost.

fix(governance): keep the pages a refused OpenAI cost pull already read (#8088)

* fix(governance): keep the pages a refused OpenAI cost pull already read

A rate limit on page three of the admin cost report threw straight out of the
run, so the events from every page before it were dropped and the durable
cursor never moved. The next run asked for page one of the same window and was
refused at the same page again, so a source that met a rate limit mid-backfill
could never get past it, on any number of retries. The non-throwing failure
path had the same defect by another route: it returned the INCOMING cursor, so
even a run that ended normally made no forward progress.

A refusal that arrives with earlier pages already read now returns what a run
stopped short by the deadline returns — those events, and a cursor resuming at
the page that failed — with the refusal counted, which is what the worker reads
as a partial success: the events are written and the cursor is persisted. A
refusal on the FIRST page is unchanged: there is no progress to bank, so the
provider's Retry-After keeps travelling to the durable outbox, and the run
fails so the same window is retried.

Buckets read twice are restated, which the pipeline already handles. A window
that can never be read past is not recoverable at all.

* fix(governance): count a refused OpenAI page against the source that banked it

Keeping the pages a refused cost pull already read made the run a COMPLETION,
and the run-status fold held the failure count still on any completion that
reported errors. So a source refused after its first page banked its progress,
reported the refusal, and was counted as neither a success nor a failure. One
refused every run sat at zero consecutive failures forever: it never reached the
three that show a source as failing, it showed the amber partly-collected line
instead of the red one, and it collected a fraction of its spend every hour with
nothing anywhere saying so.

A completion now carries whether its errors include a page nobody could read, as
opposed to rows the run read and deliberately stepped over. The two are the same
error count and opposite news, and the fold could not tell them apart. Skipped
input still holds the count still, because a run working around one bad row is
not a failing source. A page that could not be read adds to the count and stamps
no success, so three such runs turn the source red. The banked events and cursor
are kept either way — the advance and the failure are separate answers, and the
fix is not to throw the progress away again.

The guard that decides whether to bank also promised something the code could
not do: it excluded non-retryable refusals, but only a 429 was ever built as
retryable, so every other status banked. A refused key (HTTP 401 or 403) now
leaves as a non-retryable error with a sentence an admin can act on and nothing
quoted back from a body that can echo a fragment of the key. It answers the same
way on every page, so there is no window to resume and no part of one worth
keeping, and the run fails. A 5xx stays a plain error and banks: a provider
having a bad minute carries no answer about this source and no wait to honour,
which is how the Anthropic puller reads the same status.

The feature file claimed a failed read always leaves the source where it was.
That is true of a first-page refusal only, and it now says so, alongside the
mid-window cases.

* refactor(governance): name the banked-progress flag for the question it answers

The flag saying a refusal arrived with earlier pages already read was called
`banked`, which reads as a past-tense verb rather than a question about state.
The repo asks a new boolean to carry an `is`/`has`/`should`/`can`/`will`
prefix, so it is `hasBankedProgress` now: the property on the page result, both
function parameters, and the local that decides whether a refusal travels.

Behaviour is untouched — the rename is type-aware, so every call site moved with
it and the doc comments that named the old flag name the new one.

* docs(governance): say which refusals bank that are not transient

The banking rule's comment listed what banks with pages in hand as "a rate
limit, a dropped socket, a provider having a bad minute (5xx)" and called each
one transient. A 4xx the adapter does not classify -- a 400 that is not the
key-breakdown cutoff, a 404, a 422 -- leaves the fetch on the same line a 5xx
does, so it banks too, and it is not transient.

Keeping those pages is still better than the old code throwing them away, but
the window never completes and the held cursor holds the consecutive count
instead of raising it, so a source wedged that way reads as partly collected
rather than failing. The comment now says so, rather than claiming everything
that banks is a bad minute. Turning those statuses into refusals would overturn
the two cases that already fix a differently-shaped 400 to a counted failure
rather than a throw, so it is a change of its own.

* fix(governance): stop banking a window the provider rejected the request for

A rejected request is not a bad minute. A 400 that is not the key-breakdown
cutoff, a 404 or a 422 earns the same answer on every page and every retry, so
resuming AT the rejected page parked the position on a page nothing will ever
read past. The banking rule could not tell one from a 503, because both left the
fetch as a plain error and the rule asked only whether the error was a dispatch
error.

A non-OK response now carries its status, and the rule refuses to bank when the
status says the provider answered about the request. 408 and 425 ask to be sent
again, so they stay bad minutes alongside the 5xx family.

What is thrown is unchanged, so a rejected request ends the run the way it always
did -- the pages read so far, the position where it was, the failure reported --
and the next run asks for the same window rather than for a page it cannot get
past. Making these non-retryable dispatch errors instead would dead-letter them
and overturn the two cases covering a differently-shaped 400 on the first page.

Also names the run-status fold's two new booleans for the questions they answer:
hasUnreadPage and hasPartialSuccess.

The new case fails without the rule change, on the advanced position.

* fix(voice): ship the cloudflared binary and fail fast when no public media URL exists

pnpm 10 only runs a dependency's postinstall when it is allowlisted in
onlyBuiltDependencies; cloudflared wasn't listed, so its postinstall (which
downloads the actual binary) was silently skipped everywhere, including in
CI. The voice worker's quick-tunnel mint then spawned a non-existent path
(ENOENT), no VOICE_PUBLIC_BASE_URL was ever set, and the phone transport
silently fell back to dialling BASE_HOST -- a URL with no voice media
listener -- producing Twilio error 31920 after a 120s timeout with nothing
on the run's trace.

phone transport fail fast instead of falling back: refuse to build the
outbound adapter when only BASE_HOST (or nothing) resolves, throwing
VoicePublicBaseUrlMissingError and recording it as an exception + ERROR span
on the run's own trace via tracer.withActiveSpan, so the failure is
immediately visible and actionable instead of a silent 120s timeout.

fix(data-privacy): stop redaction destroying opaque machine identifiers (#8092)

* fix(data-privacy): hold trace identifiers out of redaction on first-party traffic

The reserved-identifier catalog never fired on traffic from our own SDKs. The
REST collector rewrites caller metadata to a vendor-namespaced attribute key
before redaction runs, and the catalog only knew the canonical spellings, so a
trace id that happened to look like a phone number or a card number was
rewritten in place. Canonicalisation folds the namespace back afterwards, which
is why this was invisible downstream.

The namespace list now lives in one place, exported from the canonicalisation
extractor constants and consumed by the hold-out, so the two cannot drift. This
both widens the match to every namespace the collector actually emits and
narrows it to those namespaces only: a bare vendor-prefixed key that nothing
folds to a reserved name is no longer treated as reserved.

Also in this change, each independently reviewed and tested:

- Reserved names now gate on the value as well as the key, so a reserved name
  carrying prose is still analysed rather than waved through.
- Base58 bitcoin detection checks the version byte, so arbitrary base58 of the
  right length is no longer reported as an address.
- Uppercase bech32 addresses are recognised, matching the mixed-case rejection
  the validator already performed.
- The secret lane and the PII lane are separated where they were conflated on
  identifier-shaped attribute names.

Known residuals are disclosed in the source docstrings with measured rates
rather than left implicit: the shape rule submits a share of random tokens, and
identifier-named attributes skip two shape-only secret rules. Both are stated
with the numbers that were actually reproduced.

Tests cover the collector rewrite end to end, each namespace spelling, the
restriction to real namespaces, and the value-gating behaviour. Fixtures are
seeded and synthetic.

* test(data-privacy): exercise the attribute-name lookup on the submission path

The hold-out decides on the attribute's name, and a record can arrive keyed by
a flattened path with a side table carrying the real names. Both the in-place
rewrite and the analysis-submission path resolve the key through that table,
but only the rewrite had cover: deleting the lookup on the submission path left
every suite green.

The value matters here. A decimal identifier is withheld under every spelling
because a phone detector claims it, and a long hex value is withheld by the
value rule wherever it appears, so neither can show that the name was resolved.
Twelve hex characters sit under the opaque-run floor and carry no PII shape,
which leaves the reserved name as the only thing that can hold the value back.

Two flattened keys carry the same value, one mapped to a reserved trace address
and one not, and exactly one copy reaches analysis. Deleting the lookup sends
both copies out and fails the assertion.

* test(data-privacy): name the identifier-shape test for what it does

The ast-grep rule use-action-based-test-name-ts rejects a title that opens
with "should": the word adds length and removes certainty, and the title is
the only thing a future reader gets out of a failure. This was the only
offender across the branch's files.

feat(agent-plugin,cli): run the installed CLI from a committed launcher instead of a bundled hook (#8095)

* feat(agent-plugin,cli): run the installed CLI from a committed launcher instead of a bundled hook

The plugin's hooks run scripts/launch.mjs, which runs langwatch ingest hook
and langwatch ingest guidance from the installed CLI: the location the CLI
recorded about itself in its config first, langwatch on PATH second. The
bundle build, the tsup config and the two entry files are gone, and the
publish job mirrors the directory as committed.

The CLI records cli_location on login, claude and instrument, and the two
hook commands accept unknown arguments and exit zero so a plugin from any
version runs with a CLI from any version.

* fix(agent-plugin): the no-CLI test gets a PATH with only a git shim on it

The hook runs with `dirname(gitPath)` on PATH so the CLI can shell out to
git. On a machine where the global npm prefix and git share a directory,
that same entry also carries `langwatch`, and the case that must find no
CLI anywhere would resolve the host one instead. Put a single `git` shim
in a scratch directory and give the hook that.

Also correct the spec's header: a login is what the reported session
context needs, not the plugin as a whole. Guidance runs unsigned, and a
machine with no CLI gets its one installation message either way.

* fix(agent-plugin): the launcher waits for the install notice to reach the pipe

Claude Code reads a SessionStart hook's stdout as its answer to the
session, and that stdout is a pipe, so the write is asynchronous. The
forced exit could drop it, and the once-per-session marker is already on
disk by then, so the notice would never be said again. Pass the write a
callback and wait on it.

The exit stays forced. Reading stdin refs that handle, so a client that
never closes the pipe would otherwise keep the hook alive past its answer.

* fix(agent-plugin): a PATH langwatch has to be runnable to be the one we pick

The lookup took the first name that existed, so a directory called
langwatch, or a file with no execute bit, was chosen and then failed to
spawn while the real CLI sat further down PATH. The launcher swallows the
spawn error and exits zero, so the session recorded nothing and said
nothing. Require a regular file with the execute bit, which is what a PATH
lookup means.

Two unit tests cover it, one per shape, and both fail against the old
lookup.
