fix(cli): session context hooks report for a tool pinned with instrument --key (#8102)

* fix(cli): session context hooks report for a tool pinned with instrument --key

`resolveTarget` built its fallback target from `default_personal_ingest_keys`
alone, so a tool wired with `langwatch instrument <tool> --key` or `--project`
had no credential to read: while a pin stands the personal path is neither
consulted nor rewritten. The hook read that as "no telemetry configured" and
exited quietly, so those sessions' traces arrived and the repository, branch
and worktree never did, which is what left them unjoined to their pull
requests. It is the normal shape for a background agent, which traces to a
fixed project on a machine that may never have logged in.

The resolver now reads the two credentials in the order `langwatch instrument`
chooses between them: the tool's pin first, with the endpoint override the pin
carries, then the personal key under the control plane. `langwatch ingest
context` shares the resolver and is fixed with it.

A 401 on a pinned key is reported, never healed: minting a personal key in its
place would move the session's telemetry into another project without saying
so. The healer already declined a pinned tool for that reason, so the hook now
stops at the report rather than spending the round trip.

Also fixes the login-time wiring refresh, where the pinned-tool skip stood
ahead of the codex guidance install, so a pinned codex was never told to
declare the checkout it moved to. The guidance names no endpoint and no key,
so it now runs for a pinned tool as for a personal one, and only the mint and
the rewiring stay a pin's to refuse.

Fixes #8096

* fix(cli): warn once when the ingest key will travel to another host in the clear

The endpoint `langwatch instrument` settles on is the one every wire that
carries the ingest key uses: the tool's own OTel exporter posts that bearer to
it on every span batch, and the session context hook posts its record beside
them. So the scheme is decided once, where the endpoint is chosen, rather than
at each thing that later sends to it.

Plain http to a host that is not loopback now prints one line to stderr naming
the host and pointing at https, and the wiring continues. It is not a refusal
and there is no flag to allow it: a self-hosted deployment on a private network
over http is a real setup, and refusing it would take its telemetry while
protecting nothing. Loopback is exempt outright, `.localhost` included, since a
key that never leaves the machine is not exposed by the scheme and local
development is why plain http is reachable at all.

The `http://*.example.com` fixtures added with the pinned-key hooks move to
https, so the tests stop modelling plain http to a remote host as the ordinary
case, with one test keeping a loopback http pin to pin that local development
still reports.

* fix(gateway): publish image token quantities on the spend read surfaces

The spend read projection selected the five text token columns only, so

a gpt-image-2 generation rated at $0.004855 from 23 text input tokens and

perf(cli-login): the login wait is the round trip, not the poll interval (#7922)

* perf(cli-login): the login wait is the round trip, not the poll interval

`langwatch login --device` sat on "Waiting for you to approve in the
browser" long after the user had approved, because nothing told it that
anything had happened. Three things stretched the wait:

- `pollUntilDone` slept before its first poll, so the floor was a whole
  interval even when the approval landed while the browser was opening.
- The interval is 5 seconds.
- `/exchange` rate-limits a device code to one poll every 4 seconds, and
  a `slow_down` doubled the CLI's interval with no way back down, up to
  60 seconds.

The first poll now goes out immediately, and a new
`GET /api/auth/cli/device-approval` stream says the moment a code
settles: the browser's approve or deny publishes on a small Redis
channel, the stream emits one frame, and the CLI polls right then. That
poll skips the per-device window, since a settled code has nothing left
to rate limit and answering it with `slow_down` would put back the wait
the stream removes.

The stream carries no credential and grants nothing. The device code is
still the only thing it accepts, and the CLI still has to POST
`/exchange` to get its tokens, so this is a latency fix rather than a
second way to authenticate.

Polling stays the correctness floor. A server without the route, a proxy
that buffers the body, a Redis without pub/sub and an older CLI all fall
back to the interval they already used, and no failure in the signal path
can fail an approval.

* fix(cli-login): named parameters on the new helpers, a ceiling on open approval streams, and the denied frame under test

* fix(cli-login): the approval stream re-reads the code once its channel is live

Redis pub/sub keeps nothing for a late subscriber, so a code approved between the route's first read and its subscribe published to no one: the stream then held until the device code's deadline and the CLI fell back to its poll interval, which is the wait this route exists to remove.

waitForDeviceCodeSettled now hands back a subscribed promise alongside the settled one, and the route re-reads the record once the channel is live. From that point either the record already says the code settled or the publication reaches the stream.

* test(cli-login): pin the premise the approval re-read exists for, and name the status helper's parameters

The subscription-race test used Promise.all, which does not guarantee the
window it claims: an approval can land before the route's first read or
after its subscribe, so the test could pass without exercising the
re-read at all.

It is now two cases. One publishes before subscribing and asserts the
subscriber hears nothing, which pins the premise deterministically since
Redis keeps no history for a channel. The other drops the pod's
subscriber first, so the route's subscribe costs a connection handshake
while the approval runs on a connection already up, widening the window
by construction rather than by timing.

* fix(cli-login): one exchange redeems an approval, and an approval landing mid-poll is not lost

A settled device code skips the per-device poll window, and that window was
the only thing serialising concurrent /exchange calls. Two polls arriving
together could both hold the same approved record and both reach a 200: the
project-key branch returned the credential twice, the device-session branch
minted two token pairs, and the login-key mint inside the second could revoke
the key the first had just handed out. The approved branch now takes an
atomic SET NX EX claim on the device code before it reads anything, and
releases it on the returns that consume nothing. The loser gets the same
slow_down a too-fast poll gets, so the client contract does not change.

On the CLI side the approval wakeup was cleared the moment the frame arrived,
even if that was while an /exchange was in flight, so the next iteration slept
out a whole interval, the exact wait the stream exists to remove. The wakeup
is now tracked in two parts, arrival and spend, so a frame landing mid-poll
still sends the next poll out at once and is spent by it.

* test(cli-login): pin the other half of the subscribe boundary

The suite proved that a settlement published before the subscribe is lost.
It did not prove the complement, that one published after `subscribed`
resolves is always heard, which is what makes re-reading the code at that
point enough on its own: the gap the re-read has to cover is exactly
[the route's first read, `subscribed`], with nothing after it.

Deterministic, no race in it, and no change to the route.

fix(ingestion): codex helper threads no longer surface as sessions (#8103)

* fix(ingestion): codex helper threads no longer surface as sessions

Codex 0.154 generates the thread title (and the recap) on a hidden ephemeral
thread of its own, with its own thread id, through the same telemetry
exporter as the session it serves, so every title generation landed as a
second untitled session with one turn and a withheld prompt.

Nothing on the helper's turn span or events names the thread it serves, but
codex's temporary structured request helper mints the app-server request
ids for these threads with a fixed prefix, and the turn/start request span
carrying it is the root of the same trace as the helper's session_task.turn.
Ingestion now remembers such traces (Redis, since the request span and the
turn span arrive in different export batches) and stamps
langwatch.session.auxiliary on the kept spans of that trace. The
coding-agent session fold lifts the stamp into a sticky Auxiliary column,
and the Sessions list omits marked sessions while keeping their rows and
priced traces.

* test(ingestion): type the captured export batch as the OTLP request

* fix(coding-agent): drop helper sessions in the dedup group, not after the page

The sessions list read its `limit` from ClickHouse and only then removed the
sessions codex ran for itself, so a run of helper threads could spend the
whole page and leave the caller short. Through `getUsageTotals` that is an
omitted session's cost, not just a short list.

The exclusion moves into the dedup group as `HAVING max(Auxiliary) = 0`. It is
not the row predicate the query's docblock rules out: `HAVING` runs after the
grouping, so it changes no group's winner, and it drops a session whenever any
of its versions carried the mark, which is what the fold's sticky flag means.
`LIMIT` then counts only sessions the caller can see.

The auxiliary trace memo also outlived nothing useful at 24 hours: ingestion
accepts a span whose start time is up to 31 days old, and a memo that expired
first would store the helper's turn span unmarked. The TTL is now that same
bound, pinned to `SPAN_MAX_PAST_MS` by a unit test.

Also formats the captured codex span fixture, which was failing the lint gate.

* fix(ingestion): read the codex helper thread id off the request span's own batch

The helper request span and its queue child, which names the thread,
land in the same export batch, so the ingestion joins them there,
stores the request span stamped with the thread id and lets the
session fold derive the auxiliary fact from it. The Redis memo that
bridged the request span to the later turn span is gone, as is the
span-level auxiliary attribute.

* refactor(ingestion): split the codex helper thread join into its two halves

`codexHelperThreadMarkersOf` collected the request span ids and read the
thread id off the queue children in one function, at a cognitive complexity
of 15. The biome gate counts violations per file and rule against the merge
base, and the file is new here, so that one warning failed the lint job.

Collecting the request span ids and reading a queue child's thread id are now
their own functions, which is also where each of them is easiest to read.

* fix(ingestion): join the codex helper request to its queue child across every scope entry of the export

The helper-thread lookup is built once over all resource and scope entries
of the export request, with the marker scope-gated per entry, so a pair the
exporter splits over two scope entries still joins. Two decorative doc
comments are gone.

* fix(governance): give the pulled-usage withdrawal the envelope its command requires

A reissued charge's withdrawal never became an event. `defineCommand` derives
every command's payload schema by merging the envelope — `tenantId` and
`occurredAt`, both required — into the event data schema, and the withdrawal
dispatched neither. Validation rejected it at send time, so no `RETRACTED`
reached the fold.

That is the event this PR's new drift check subscribes to in order to put a
corrected day back on its list, so the handler it adds could not have fired:
currency, agent and raw-actor corrections left the superseded version standing
and the day was never re-compared.

- The dispatcher's parameter is now the event data AND the envelope, and the
  call site fills both from the payload it already holds: `tenant_id`, and
  `occurred_at_ms` as the date, which is the day the withdrawal CORRECTS and
  matches how the observation path dates its own command.
- `pipelineSet.ts` drops the `as never` at the late-bound holder. That cast is
  what let a payload missing two required fields type-check; with the holder
  typed, the compiler is what catches the next one.
- `RetractCommandEnvelope` is a type alias rather than an interface on purpose:
  the command payload is constrained to `Record<string, unknown>` and only an
  alias carries the implicit index signature that satisfies it.

The regression test drives the real `runRetractPulledUsage` and parses what it
dispatched with the REAL command schema, built the way `defineCommand` builds
it. It fails on the unfixed code — the parse reports `tenantId` and
`occurredAt` missing — which a shape assertion against a mocked dispatcher, the
way the existing suite checks withdrawals, could never have done.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(governance): wait for the cost rollup to catch up before judging drift

The rollup fold and the drift check are driven by two independent queues —
the projection queue keyed by rollup cell, the process manager's generated
subscriber keyed by organization — and nothing orders one against the other.
A charge landing shortly before the 04:23 slot could arm and fire the check
while its own projection job was still queued. The check then re-derived the
day from the event log INCLUDING that charge, read a summary written WITHOUT
it, and recorded the difference as drift on a rollup that was perfectly
correct and merely seconds behind. No retry followed, because the comparison
technically succeeded — and the wake had already cleared the day, so nothing
re-asked the question.

The removed nightly job had the same hole (it compared yesterday at 04:23
with no test that the summary covered it), but with hours of slack rather
than the seconds this design leaves: a charge at 04:22:59 arms 04:23:00.

The fix uses the watermark both sides already carry. `LastEventOccurredAt` is
the running maximum of the `occurredAt` of every event a fold applied to a
cell, and the comparator's re-fold runs the same projection, so it holds the
same quantity for the events it just read. Where a cell's derived watermark
is newer than the stored one — or the summary holds no row for that cell at
all — the comparison refuses rather than answers, throwing
`CostRollupSummaryBehindError` so the outbox's existing ladder
(5 attempts, ~30s to 8m) is the wait. A day that has caught up is compared
and reported exactly as before. A day still behind after every attempt dies
in the outbox and shows as lag on the gauge already written each attempt,
which is what a projection that stopped folding actually is — not drift.

No new tables, events, queues or schema: the watermark, the gauge and the
retry ladder all already existed.

Verified: the two new "waits" unit cases fail against the service without the
guard ("promise resolved instead of rejecting") and pass with it, while the
two control cases — a caught-up summary still reporting drift, and a charge
with no usable moment still being compared — pass either way. 469 governance
unit tests green, `pnpm typecheck:all` clean, biome 0 errors and no new
violations against origin/main, feature parity 42/42 bound. The integration
scenario needs a datastore and is proved by CI.

* fix(governance): stop the cost comparator judging a summary that has folded nothing

The freshness guard changed the contract for two existing comparator
integration cases, and both were expectations written against the old
behavior rather than defects in the guard:

- the midnight-bucketing pin wrote its summary stamped at 09:30 while its
  charges sat at 23:59:59.999, and gave the next day no summary at all. Both
  now read as still folding. It states its own preconditions instead: each

  row at a figure nothing explains, which pins the bucketing harder than the
  absent row did (a leak across midnight now reads 12_340_000_000).
- the lag case deliberately summarized nothing and read lagMs off the

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(governance): judge cost-rollup drift only when a mismatch survives the retry ladder

The freshness watermark added in b795807faf is not the settlement it was
written as. `LastEventOccurredAt` is a running MAXIMUM of provider
timestamps, so it cannot count: two charges on one cell stamped with the
same moment leave it unmoved, and the side that folded one reads as level
with the check that folded both. A charge arriving late but stamped OLDER
than the maximum cannot move it either — and the fold is explicitly
order-independent — so both are ordinary rather than contrived. Either way
the guard said "caught up", the comparison reported drift, and the day was
cleared.

Nothing else in the row does better. `LastObservedAt` is another maximum and
`RevisionCount` is an admitted under-count. An exact per-cell count of
applied events would settle it, but it is a new ClickHouse column that no
existing row carries: every row written before it would read as behind
forever, until a rebuild. Not worth it, and not in this PR.

So the judgment moves from one look to several. A fold that is behind
catches up between looks and drift does not, which is the only signal
available that separates them — and the check already has a retry ladder
(5 attempts, 30s/1m/2m/4m) built for comparisons that fail outright. A
disagreement now spends a rung of it instead of raising an alert, and only
one still standing on the last rung, some 7.5 minutes later, is counted and
logged. A comparison is a read, so the extra looks cost nothing.

That makes the comparator a reader and nothing else:

  - `compareDay` no longer logs, counts, or refuses. It returns the
    mismatches, the lag, and — as evidence rather than a gate — the cells
    whose watermark proves they are still folding. `CostRollupSummaryBehindError`
    is gone with it.
  - `reportCostRollupDrift` is the counter and the error line, exported so
    the one caller that knows how many looks are left can call it once.
  - The intent handler holds the whole decision, and completes on the last
    look rather than throwing: real drift filed as a dead outbox row is
    drift nobody reads.

Red before green: with the attempt guard disabled, three of the four new
handler tests fail on "promise resolved instead of rejecting" and the
fourth — the last-look case — still passes, which is the shape the change
predicts. The blind spot itself is pinned directly: equal watermarks, money
plainly different, nothing named as behind.

Also restores the two comparator expectations 36f3c214f9 had to restate.
They only needed restating because `compareDay` could refuse; it cannot any
more, so they go back to what their authors wrote.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(governance): restate two watch expectations against a comparator that returns

Both assumed `compareDay` could refuse, which it no longer does. CI caught
them; the integration lane needs real Postgres and ClickHouse and does not
run in this worktree.

The lag scenario asserted no comparison had happened on the first look. It
had — the comparator now returns what it saw and the handler decides — so it
asserts what the look actually found instead: one mismatch, one cell its own
watermark proves is still folding, and no drift line. That is the stronger
claim anyway: the difference is not hidden from anyone, it is just not called
drift yet.

"Comparing a day twice over" drained one look and then jumped the clock an
hour, which made the first comparison's retry fall due inside the second
check's drain — three comparisons where it expected two, and a count that
would read whatever the timing produced. Each check now runs to the end of
its own ladder before the next begins, and the last look is held against the
first.

Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(governance): look again when a summary is provably mid-fold, even if the figures agree

The retry ladder already judged mismatches correctly: a disagreement buys a
look, and the one that outlives every look is counted and logged while the
intent completes. A cell the summary holds no row for travels that same path
already, because `collectMismatches` states a missing row as a mismatch with
`summarizedNanoMinor: null` — so money on the log that never folded is
reported on the last look rather than dying as a dead outbox row. This commit
pins that with a test instead of leaving it to be re-derived.

What was genuinely missing is the other half of the same rule. A comparison
could come back with `behind` non-empty and `mismatches` empty — the watermark
PROVES the fold has not finished, and the two figures agree anyway. That
returned quietly and cleared the day. The agreement is a coincidence in that
state, not a verdict: the unfolded charge nets to nothing, or it lands on a
cell neither figure covers, and once the day is cleared nothing marks it
again. So `behind` now buys a look on the same ladder as a mismatch.

On the last look that case reports nothing — there is no disagreement to
count — but it writes one warn line naming the day, because that is the moment
the day is cleared on evidence that was never conclusive and the lag gauge
alone would not say which day went unjudged.

Red before green: with the guard back to `mismatches.length === 0`, "looks
again rather than clearing the day on a coincidence" fails with
`AssertionError: promise resolved "undefined" instead of rejecting`. The
missing-row test passes either way, by design — it is a regression pin on
behavior this commit does not change, not evidence for it.

refactor(governance): type the ingestion-pull outcome dispatches instead of casting them (#8118)

The six outcome commands an ingestion pull reports through are resolved late,
through a mutable holder filled once the pipeline exists, and every dispatch at
that seam carried an `as never`. #8111 is what such a cast costs: on the
sibling pulled-usage pipeline it let a withdrawal missing `tenantId` and
`occurredAt` past the compiler and into `queueManager`'s pre-send
`schema.validate`, which threw, and the retraction was lost.

No behaviour change here. Each of the six payloads was already complete:
`IngestionPullOutcomeCommands` names the envelope on every method, the
argument types match the event data schemas field for field, and
`IngestionPullRunReport` contributes nothing extra. Dropping the casts needed
no type plumbing at all — the code type-checks as written, which means the
casts were never load-bearing, only blinding.

Verified rather than assumed. With the casts gone, omitting `tenantId` at one
dispatch fails `pnpm typecheck` with "Property 'tenantId' is missing" — so the
compiler now catches exactly the class of defect #8111 was, and the green
typecheck is a result rather than a coincidence.

The new unit test covers what the compiler cannot: it drives the real effect
handlers and validates what each dispatched with `Command.schema.validate`,
the same object `queueManager` calls before enqueueing, taken off the real
command class. That catches value constraints (`.min(1)` ids and reasons,
`.int()` statuses) and drift in `commands.ts`. It was falsified against all six
commands — removing the envelope at the dispatch sites turns it red naming the
dropped field.

It closes a real gap between the two existing suites: `commands.unit.test.ts`
validates hand-written literals, so it proves the schemas behave but never that
a handler produces something they accept, while the effect suites mock the
commands and assert the cell each was handed, which says nothing about whether
the command takes it.

matcher — it is unreachable by construction. A reset link was therefore a

every organization that requires one, because that requirement is met by
enrolment rather than by anything the session proved.

The refusal goes in the minter rather than the caller so both doors
inherit it and a third cannot reintroduce it. Sign-up confirmation cannot
reach it today — a newborn account has enrolled nothing — and is guarded
anyway. It costs the person one screen: the reset succeeded, they sign in,

* fix(identity): retry the unlink that lost a serialization race, instead of throwing it at the person

Found writing the test for the "last way in" rule. The rule itself was
sound — the SERIALIZABLE transaction does stop two concurrent unlinks both
deciding from the same two-account snapshot — but only one of the two
repositories that use this shape retried, and it was not this one.

Serializable buys its guarantee by refusing to commit the loser of a race.
A caller that does not run it again therefore converts a race it correctly
detected into a raw driver write-conflict on its way to a person: a
double-clicked cross answered with a database exception rather than the
`would_strand_user` refusal the guard had already computed. Safe — nothing
was deleted twice — but indistinguishable from the database falling over.

The retry is lifted out of `passkey-removal.prisma.repository.ts` rather
than copied into a second place, since both repositories want exactly the
same four-attempt loop and the same two-shape conflict detection (Prisma's
`P2034` and the driver adapter's `TransactionWriteConflict`, which does not
arrive as a typed Prisma error). Retrying is safe precisely because the
loser committed nothing: the next attempt reads the state the winner left
and decides again, which is the answer a click a moment later would get.

The accompanying integration test races two unlinks against a real
Postgres, holding both transactions at the barrier after each has fixed
its snapshot so the race is deterministic rather than a matter of
scheduling luck. It pins BOTH halves: exactly one delete lands and an
account always survives, and the loser comes back as a refusal rather than
an exception — so the retry cannot be dropped again without a failure.

* refactor(identity): write the convergent ledger once, not four times

`StagedLedgerWriter` was extracted FROM these files and its own docblock
claims to be "the machinery the five identity ledger writers share" — but
only two of the five were ever moved onto it. The join-request, connection
and directory-sync writers stayed as the originals it was generalised from,
so the App-handle wait, the sender lookup, the append, the convergence loop
and the cursor comparison existed four times over, character for character,
and the three copies had no test of their own.

Their ports said as much. `JoinRequestLedger`, `SsoConnectionLedger` and
`MfaLedger` each describe their implementation as "exactly the shape the
identity, connection and grants ledgers already have" — three interfaces
asserting they are the same shape is the shape asking to be one
implementation.

So it is one. What actually differed between them was not behaviour but six
values: which pipeline stages them, which aggregate they append under, which
envelope turns a command into events, which field names the aggregate, what
they call themselves, and how long they wait. `ConvergentLedgerSpec` carries
those, `ConvergentLedgerWriter` carries the rest, and the three writers
become declarations of the first.

Two keep their own commit, deliberately. The identity ledger writes a
newborn's provisional heads before staging and exposes its two legs
separately so ADR-116 §3's born-finalized entrance can put row writes between
them. Directory sync swallows every failure on purpose, because a push must
never fail for want of its own bookkeeping — it takes the shared sender
machinery and keeps the policy. Those are different sequences, not different
configuration, and folding them in would be sharing that has to be undone.

Log field names are unchanged: the spec names the aggregate's own noun rather
than a uniform `aggregateId`, so nothing an operator filters on moves.

* feat(identity): run ADR-117 §3's evidence rule where a link is actually decided

`SignInCallbackLinkingService` was constructed by no composition root, so the
two-sided evidence rule it exists for never ran. The reason was not an
oversight: `complete()` is written to OWN a callback — resolve the person,
then link, propose or provision — and better-auth owns that resolution on
every deployment we run. The only moment it offers before a sign-in method
exists is `account.create.before`, which arrives with the link already chosen.
The service's entry point had nowhere to be called from.

So the RULE moves rather than the service. `refusalFor` becomes the exported
`linkRefusalFor`, and both callers share it: the service still applies it in
`complete`, and `SignInLinkEvidence` applies it at better-auth's seam. One
function, so a link refused in one place is refused in the other for the same
recorded reason — which for a security rule is the whole game.

A refusal now leaves something behind. It writes a link proposal, and
`linkProposals()` was already composed and already able to confirm or reject
one; until now nothing ever created one, so the resolution half of the feature
had no input. Failing to write the proposal does not un-refuse the link.

Scoped narrowly, on purpose:

  - only a method added to an account that ALREADY signs in some way.
    Somebody with no accounts is brand new or an orphan, and better-auth
    already refuses the unverified orphan — bound against a real callback in
    the commit before this one. Judging it twice would only add a way to lock
    a new signup out.
  - only when the identity provider actually asserted something. No ID token,
    no `email`, or no `email_verified` beside it means no evidence, and the
    link proceeds exactly as it did before.
  - not the domain half of the rule. A callback here carries no connection
    (D04 has not given the legacy env provider one), and "domains this
    connection cannot vouch for" has no answer without one.

`LINK_NEEDS_APPROVAL` joins the stable auth errors with copy that says an
administrator can review the request, rather than reusing
`OAuthAccountNotLinked`, whose copy would send them to retry the method that
was just refused.

Two scenarios in signin-router.feature bind the new seam. The four above them
describe the same rule through the service, and were bound to code no
deployment reaches — which parity cannot see and a reader should.

* fix(auth): say when the signed-out limits are counting the proxy, not the caller

The tRPC auth limiter is sound against spoofing — it resolves through
`getTrustedProxyClientIp`, which ignores every caller-controlled header and
takes the socket peer, and `buildReqShim` populates that peer from the real
connection. That part needed no change.

What it cannot see is a deployment sitting behind a load balancer that has not
set `TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES`. There the socket peer IS the balancer, so every
signed-out visitor shares one bucket — and these budgets are deliberately
small (sixty routing questions an hour, five reset requests). Shared, they
stop limiting an attacker and start capping the installation: one script
exhausts the hour for everyone, which reads as "sign-in is down".

Naming the address alongside the peer would not fix it, because the peer is
still shared and the shared budget still binds. Only the operator holds the
fact that recovers the real client. So this watches for the one combination
that proves the mistake — a forwarded-for header arriving while we vouch for
nobody — and says so once, naming the setting.

A warning rather than a refusal to boot: an installation genuinely not behind
a proxy is correct as it stands, and failing hard would strand deployments
that have been fine for years.

* docs(identity): ADR-135 — a write states its facts once

Every identity write currently decides twice: the guard runs on the calling
path, its facts go to a ledger writer, and the queued handler runs the same
guard again on state that may have moved. `identityEventsFor` dedupes the two
by `commandId:index`, which collapses them into one write only when the two
decisions are identical — the case the architecture cannot guarantee.

That leaves three truths where there should be one: the event log holds what
the queue decided, the projection briefly holds provisional rows derived from a
decision that was never written, and the caller is handed the decision that was
thrown away.

It already reaches a person. The join-request expiry gates a "your request
lapsed" email on the calling path's facts, so an administrator approving inside
that window can produce both a membership and the email. The comment above it
reasons about exactly this failure; the write path denies it the check.

The decision: a write states its facts once, on the queue. Services validate
and dispatch and answer with a receipt. The log becomes the only cause of a
projection row, so provisional heads go. A caller that needs an outcome awaits
application and then READS the projection, which makes its answer true by
construction rather than by coincidence.

The cost is named rather than hidden: this puts the queue on sign-up's critical
path, which is what provisional heads bought out of. We pay it in the UI — a
sign-up that outruns the window says it is still being set up — never in a row
asserting something the log does not say.

Numbered 135 because 132-134 are taken on the layout branch; 128 and 129 are
already duplicated in this tree and that is not worth repeating.

* spec(identity): the behavioural contract for one decision per write

Ten scenarios for ADR-135: that a command is decided once and on the queue,
that a caller is handed a receipt rather than a decision, that no projection
row exists which no event caused, that a caller needing an outcome reads what
landed, and — the one that reaches a person — that an expiry notice follows
what was recorded rather than what was proposed.

Three cover the new behaviour the change forces into the open: a sign-up whose
fold lands in time continues as before, one that outruns the window is told the
account is still being set up, and one that never lands is told so plainly with
a way to try again. None of them may render an address as though it were
already someone's.

Every scenario is @unimplemented, deliberately and temporarily. The write path
does not exist yet, so a binding tag would report a binding that is not there.
Each scenario names in a comment the tag it becomes, and the implementation
swaps it alongside the `@scenario` annotation.

The parity gate refuses a file that enforces nothing unless the reason is
written down, which is exactly the mechanism that was missing when
sso-orphan-user-linking sat untagged and read green. So the LEGACY_INERT entry
carries the reason and its own expiry: the implementation deletes it, and while
it is there the change is not done.

* refactor(identity): name the read-your-writes window for what it waits on

There were five copies of the wait's shape and they did not agree. Identity
said 2,000ms with a 25ms poll, written out four times — once each in
ledger.ts, mfa-ledger.ts, join-request-ledger.ts and sso-connection-ledger.ts,
each under a docblock claiming to be some other ledger's shape. Authz said
8,000ms with a 150ms poll. Same mechanism, same comparison against the same
kind of projection cursor, four times the window and six times the poll apart.

Neither number came from a latency distribution. Neither ledger exists on
main, so there was no production fold to measure when either was written, and
the spread is what that looks like: had either been derived, they would have
landed near each other.

Collapsing five constants to one was the easy half. The harder half is that one
number cannot be right, because the two waits are not answering the same
question. A person who submitted a form is spending every millisecond looking
at a button they already pressed, so the window is short and the honest
fallback beats holding the socket. A worker deciding what to do next has
nobody watching, and the only cost of waiting is a job slot — while the cost of
NOT waiting is acting on a fact the log may not hold, which is the class of
defect ADR-135 exists to remove. So the old numbers were not one argument with
a wrong answer; they were two questions nobody had distinguished, each answered
plausibly and then applied to both cases by whichever file was copied next.

Both timeouts are preserved exactly. What changes is that they are defined
once, named INTERACTIVE and BACKGROUND for the case each serves, and every use
site now says which it is and why. The polls widen — 25ms to 50ms, 150ms to
250ms — because at 25ms a two-second wait is eighty reads of one projection
row, and the fold either lands in the first few or is not landing on this
timescale at all.

The join-request ledger is the interesting one: its expiry wake is the single
caller here that would want the background window, and it does not get one,
because under ADR-135 it stops reading the return value at all and reads the
recorded state instead. A window that only mattered to a caller that no longer
depends on it is not worth splitting a ledger over.

The estimates are still estimates, and the new module is the one place that
says so rather than four files implying otherwise.
identity_commit_duration_seconds already times exactly what these bound; its
first production week is what should set them.

* fix(identity): tell people what was recorded, not what a thread decided

Three places read the facts a ledger RETURNED and acted on them. Those facts
are the guard's decision on the calling thread. The same guard runs again on
the queue, against state that may have moved in between, and only the queue's
run is stored — so each of these could state something the log does not hold.
All three reach a person.

The join request expiry is the one that had already been reasoned about and
still got it wrong. Its own comment says telling somebody their request lapsed
when it did not "would be worse than telling them nothing", and then it gated
the email on `facts.length === 0`. An administrator approving inside the expiry
window is exactly the divergence: the calling path reads PENDING and states an
expiry, the approval folds first, the queue's re-run reads APPROVED and states
nothing — and the person who just got in is emailed that their request lapsed.
It now reads the projection and announces only the PENDING -> EXPIRED
transition, which also keeps a replayed wake quiet about an expiry announced an
hour ago. An unconfirmed expiry says so in the log rather than returning in
silence, because a notice nobody receives is its own defect, just a quieter one.

Adding an address took `identifierId` off the attached fact and put it in a
confirmation link. A link naming a row the queue never wrote is a dead end the
person cannot diagnose or retry out of, so the identifier is read back from the
heads instead.

Completing a verification is the third, found while checking the other two. It
read the returned facts for a dead-end event, and both directions of that
divergence lie: decide "lost" here while the queue verifies and somebody is
told their own address belongs to a stranger; decide "won" here while the queue
dead-ends and they are told an address is theirs when it is not — the exact
harm the branch was written to prevent. It now answers from the identifier's
recorded state, which is conclusive because a uniqueness race is the only thing
that ever dead-ends one.

* docs(identity): the sign-up door does not wait, and three things the plan had wrong

The decision ADR-135 left open is made: sign-up returns once it has committed
its own rows and handed the command to the queue. It never blocks on the fold.
The wait moves to the surfaces that read projections, and those say "still being
set up" rather than rendering an empty state. Rejected: blocking briefly and
then showing that screen anyway (it puts the queue on the door to buy a state we
need regardless), and keeping the block with a wider window (it strands the tail,
and the window was never derived from data).

A review of the plan found three things worth more than the decision itself.

The session is NOT issued "from the event log", which is how the first draft of
this decision put it. `stage` is an enqueue, so at the moment a session is minted
the log has not been written and the fold has not run. What HAS landed is the
Postgres User row the entrance commits directly. The door is honest because it
claims only what it wrote with its own hands — and the wrong phrasing would have
sent somebody looking for a durability guarantee that isn't there.

`hasFolded` must survive, and the plan had it deleted. Today it only stops the
attach guard deduping against a provisional row. Once the rows are gone it
becomes the only signal separating "the fold has not run" from "this person
holds nothing" — two readings of an identical empty projection. Delete the
provisional WRITE; deleting the probe would leave every read surface guessing.
The surface that breaks first is /auth/join: verifiedEmailsOf answers [] rather
than null, the legacy fallback is keyed on null and so is skipped, and a new
account on a verified company domain gets told nothing matches it and is pushed
to start its own organization — the orphan workspace join-before-create exists
to prevent.

"Services validate and dispatch; the guard does not run" is too strong, and
shipping it literally would have been worse than the defect. The guards throw 37
domain errors synchronously: a wrong authenticator code, an address already
held, a request already answered. Move all of that to the queue and a wrong code
comes back as a receipt. Preconditions refuse and must stay on the calling path,
where running them twice is harmless because a refusal writes nothing;
decisions state facts and run once, on the queue. Only the second was ever the
problem.

Two counts were also wrong: 40 call sites and 4 readers, not 12 and 2 — the
first pass counted platform/app/src and missed 14 sites in identity-server,
two of them readers. And stage 1 cannot be built as written: awaitConvergence
compares the cursor against events it was handed, and a dispatch that no longer
decides has none to hand it, so applied/refused/not-yet collapse into one
answer. That blocks stages 3, 4 and 6 — not stage 2, which is why stage 2 is
already done.

The three sign-up scenarios encoded the rejected blocking screen and are
rewritten, with one added for the empty projection that is genuinely empty.

* feat(auth): come back to a screen that knows you, when it honestly can

The session gate sends every unauthenticated arrival to the same cold screen:
an empty address box greeting a stranger. For most arrivals that is the only
honest thing to show, because the browser has told us nothing. But the four
ways a request can arrive unauthenticated are not equally ignorant, and one of
them we know everything about.

  no cookie                 nothing known — new person, cleared cookies,
                            another browser, incognito, a shared link
  cookie, no session row     the session was ENDED ON PURPOSE
  cookie, row past expires   exactly who, and that this browser was signed in
  cookie, unknown token      a string somebody handed us; maybe a forgery

Only the third earns recovery. Sessions last thirty days, so it is rare and
unambiguous: the address is filled in and the person lands on the step that
asks them to prove it rather than the step that asks who they are. The card
stops saying "Log in to LangWatch" and says the one thing that is true — the
session ran out. Not an error: nothing went wrong, and an error tone sends
somebody looking for a fault that does not exist.

The second must NOT get recovery, and that is the security property here rather
than a nicety. Ending every session is what somebody does when they think a
machine is no longer theirs; printing the account's address on that machine
afterwards would undo exactly what they asked for. Revocation deletes the row,
so a revoked session reaches the read as a token with no row — the same shape a
forgery has — and both answer the same `unknown` a cookie-less stranger gets.
Nothing distinguishes them on screen and no reason code travels, because
confirming that a token parsed tells a forger how close they got. Never "your
signing key changed" either.

Three things this deliberately is not:

Not authentication. An expired session is a fact about the past, not a
credential. It shortens the walk by one step and never replaces a step of it —
the recovered address goes through the same `decide` call a typed one would, and
the method step still demands proof. There is a bound scenario for that alone.

Not an enumeration surface. The query takes NO input; it reads the cookie the
caller themselves presented, so the most it can ever describe is a session that
caller already holds. It cannot be turned into an oracle without adding a
parameter, which is also why it needs no rate limit: there is no budget to
exhaust on somebody else's behalf.

Not a cost to the common path. The question is asked alongside the routing
question rather than before it, so the cold screen — which is what nearly
everybody gets — is never held up waiting for an answer about a session that
does not exist. A failed query leaves the cold screen standing, which is the
right fallback rather than something to report.

The cookie's name, its `__Secure-` prefix and its dotted/dashed spellings stay
better-auth's business via `getSessionCookie`; a wrong guess there would fail
open into "unknown", which looks identical to working correctly.

Verified against the running stack: no cookie, a forged token, the secure
variant and the dashed spelling all return `{"kind":"unknown"}` — byte-identical
answers, which is the property. 7/7 scenarios bound, parity OK, typecheck:all
clean, 135 auth component tests and 233 identity unit tests pass.

Four feature files under specs/auth reported green while binding nothing:

The test that proves a sign-up states its identifier against the credential

* fix(auth): decide the caller once, from the connection, for both limiters

Signed-out authentication limits key on who is calling, so that answer is a
security control. This puts it in one place and gives both limiters the same
one.

The rule: the socket peer is the caller, and a forwarding header is read only
when that peer is one of the deployment's own hops -- an address named in
TRUSTED_PROXY_ADDRESSES, or, where none is named, a private, loopback or
link-local address, which is where an in-cluster ingress, mesh or sidecar
sits. A public peer is a caller whatever its headers say about itself.

That default is what makes an unconfigured deployment right in both
directions: one caller is never counted as many, and many callers are never
counted as one. Naming the hops is still stricter, and is the only way to
narrow trust inside a private network, so the setting stays and the log line
asks for it -- now only for the case it can help, a hop on a public address.

Better Auth runs its own limits over /api/auth/* and resolves the caller from
the request alone, because a fetch Request carries no connection. It is now
handed the resolved caller as the canonical header before the handler sees
the request, and its own trusted-proxy list is left empty, so its answer
reproduces this application's rather than competing with it.

* test(retention): ask the reconciler gate, not the customer set

This branch's TTL guard was written when the two were the same list. Main has
since given the governance cost tables a `_retention_days` column that defaults
to zero, so the reconciler installs the clause and nothing expires until a day
count is stamped on a row -- which is what `RETENTION_TTL_MANAGED_TABLES`
exists to name, and why the schema calls it deliberately wider than
`RETENTION_MANAGED_TABLES`.

Asked of the customer set, the guard read those two tables as unmanaged ones
carrying a stray column. Asked of the gate, it says what it meant to: a table
in the gate must carry a retention column, and a table outside it must not.

* fix(auth): rebuild the caller-stated request from its parts

`new Request(request, { headers })` is the obvious spelling and it is wrong

own and reaches for internals that object does not carry. Every `/api/auth/*`
request answered 500.

Passing only `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body` and `signal` asks for nothing an
adapter has to implement, so it holds for whatever the server hands us.

The unit test could not have caught this: it built its own `Request`, which is
exactly the case that works. The new one boots a real listener the way

Adding a test file changed the unit lane's shard split, and the streaming

its tests `await import("~/start")`, which pulls the whole server graph in, and
that import is ~17s cold. Whether it is paid at all depends on whether

* fix(identity): answer the callback key a provider's own issuer builds

better-auth keys Google, GitHub, GitLab and Azure AD accounts by the issuer
the provider itself asserts, and looks an account up on the OAuth callback by
`(issuer, accountId)` alone. No rule of ours derives a provider id from such
an issuer, so `parseAccountQuery` matched no shape and refused.

That key names no user, so it takes the fleet-wide gate rather than a per-user
one. The moment a single user anywhere reached `finalized`, every social
sign-in on the deployment failed — including for the people still held on the
legacy branch, because the refusal threw rather than returning null and so
left no legacy fallthrough.

The branch could always have answered it: `Identifier` stores the issuer
verbatim — the backfill copies the legacy column, the attach ceremony records
what better-auth was about to write — and `@@index([issuer, providerAccountId])`
was already there, unused. So this serves the pair rather than deriving the
provider id, and returns the provider id FROM resolution: a subject is unique
only within an issuer, and guessing the provider is how one IdP's subject
answers for another IdP's user.

A miss, or a user the backfill has not finalized, returns null and falls
through to the legacy row that is still their truth.

Also: the findMany sort/offset refusal now goes through `refused()` like every
sibling, instead of surfacing as a 500 with nothing in the log saying why.

The docblock claiming the branch stores no issuer was stale, and is the reason
this shape was never written. Corrected in place.

* fix(identity-lookup): bound how much of the trail a refused caller can write

The operator lookup records the attempt BEFORE it checks who is asking, which
is the right order — a refused attempt to reach across every organization is
exactly what the trail exists to hold. It also means every signed-in caller
reaches the write, carrying args they chose.

So the attempts the gate is about to refuse now spend a budget, through the
limiter the other unauthenticated write paths already use. Enough are kept
that somebody pointed at this surface who should not be stays legible in the
trail, and no more. An operator is never throttled: a support case is a burst
of real lookups, and a trail missing half of them is the thing this surface
exists to prevent. The refusal reads identically either way, so being
throttled tells a prober nothing the first refusal did not.

Two scenarios bound, one per half.

Worth recording separately: a refused lookup writes TWO rows, not one. The
second comes from `auditLogTRPCErrors`, mounted on every authenticated
procedure since Feb 2025, which writes a row for any non-500 error from a
signed-in caller. That is an app-wide unbounded write this change does not
address and does not make worse; the tests here count rows by action so they
measure only what this surface owns.

* chore(identity): stop naming a deployment mode in customer copy

`EMAIL_PASSWORD_DISABLED` is raised in two places with two messages. One said
"disabled in cloud/SSO mode", which names how we run rather than what the
customer can do about it — and this path is a better-auth APIError, whose
message ships verbatim on the auth error redirect. Both now use the wording
the other already had.

Also drops `clearSignUpConfirmationPending` from the identity runtime: the
exported wrapper had no caller anywhere, and the repository method it
delegates to is reached directly.

* fix(audit): bound how many refusals one caller can write to the trail

`auditLogTRPCErrors` sits on every authenticated procedure and records a row
for any non-500 refusal a signed-in caller provokes. Recording refused acts is
the right instinct; it is also a write anybody holding a session can repeat,
and a validation error is free to provoke on purpose. One account could grow
`AuditLog` at the speed it could issue requests.

Refusals now spend a per-caller hourly budget through the limiter the other
unauthenticated write paths already use. A person clicking around a broken
screen produces refusals in tens and stays fully recorded; a script produces
them in thousands and the trail keeps only enough to show that it happened.
The flood stays visible where an unbounded stream belongs — the logs — with
one line as the budget runs out rather than one per dropped row.

It fails OPEN: an unreadable budget writes the row. A refusal is never failed
over the bookkeeping that records it, and losing a record is worse than
keeping an extra one.

Predates this branch (Feb 2025) and is not identity-specific, but it is the
same unbounded-write shape as the operator lookup and is cheap to close here.

The audit-log spec leaves LEGACY_INERT for LEGACY_PARTIAL: it now enforces one
real scenario, and a file enforcing something is not inert. Its gateway half
is still unwritten and stays @unimplemented.

* feat(sso): refuse an issuer that resolves inside our own network

`public-egress.ts` was written for the two ceremonies that turn a customer's
string into a socket, and had no importer anywhere — the worst state for a
security control, because it reads as active to the next person who finds it.

It had no caller because neither ceremony dials from our code: the domain
proof makes no request, and the OpenID discovery fetch happens inside
better-auth, which takes `discoveryUrl` and no dispatcher from us. So the
guard now runs at the boundary this application does own — the moment an
operator types an issuer into `registerConnection` and we store a hostname we
will later ask better-auth to fetch.

Refused before the command goes out, so a rejected issuer registers nothing.
The copy names no address, interface or internal service: what was rejected is
the reader's own input, and describing our network back to them tells a prober
more than it tells an administrator.

This is a check at the door, NOT the pinned dial `fetchFollowingPublicHosts`
performs. A name that answers publicly now and privately a second later is not
stopped by it, and cannot be until this application owns discovery instead of
handing over a URL. That is a larger change than a guard; refusing what is
plainly private costs an operator nothing in the meantime, and the method says
so where somebody will read it.

The entrance is armed in exactly one place — a POST whose path ends

Two ways out are written down with a recommendation, and left for a decision
rather than taken in a pull request this size. Both code sites now point at
the amendment so the next reader does not assume the branch is live.

one in scenario-child-process.ts to keep the same judged-turn budget as

* feat(identity): mount every social provider whose credentials are present

The NextAuth-era rule mounted only the provider NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER names,
which made migrating off the Auth0 broker structurally impossible: the
native Google, GitHub and Microsoft providers must mount BESIDE it during
grace (D09). Credentials are the mounting decision now — an operator sets
a client id and secret for no reason other than to offer that provider —
and the policy layer already drew a multi-provider rail, deduped, with
NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER's method leading.

authProviderIsMounted answers for the NAMED provider specifically now:
'anything mounted' stopped implying 'the named provider mounted', and a
NEXTAUTH_PROVIDER typo must still land in email mode even while another
provider's credentials are present. The generic-OAuth builder still

fix(identity): a native social button never admits somebody to an SSO-enforced organization (#8149)

* fix(identity): a native social button never admits somebody to an SSO-enforced organization

The native Google, GitHub and Microsoft providers mount BESIDE the Auth0
broker now, so an employee at an organization pinned to an enterprise
connection can press "Continue with Google" and reach a door that was
written before those buttons existed.

What they got depended on a column: with the organization's `ssoDomain`
matching, an existing member was SOFT-blocked - signed in, flagged
`pendingSsoSetup`, and the Google account linked - and then that link was
deleted again by the reconciliation on their next broker sign-in. Somebody
with no account at all was refused. Neither answer is the organization's:
one hands an enterprise that enforces single sign-on a second door outside
the identity provider it deprovisions in, and the other dead-ends a real
employee.

So a native provider is refused outright at an SSO-enforced domain, whoever
is pressing it, with the code the error page already renders as "use your
organization's sign-in" - which tells them to enter their company email
address and sends them to their own provider. Nothing about the refusal is
new except the population it covers: `SSO_PROVIDER_NOT_ALLOWED` is already
a stable auth error, so it does not bounce them back to the identity
provider in a loop, and its recovery action is a federated logout that
clears the Auth0 session first.

The soft flag KEEPS its population, and the scoping is the point. Somebody
arriving through the broker on a connection the organization has since
stopped pinning is mid-migration; refusing them would send them to an
enterprise connection they may hold no account in, which is the lockout
`pendingSsoSetup` exists to avoid. No existing member's way in runs through
a native button, so nothing that works today stops working.

Linking the two identities, rather than refusing one, is the identity-sso
work's to answer - it owns the join request and the auto-link, with the
evidence to decide them. This is the interim door.

* fix(identity): the refusal sits on both callback paths, not only the one that creates a row

Review caught that the guard was half a guard. A provider is linked ONCE:
better-auth writes the `Account` row the first time and takes the
`updateAccount` branch on every sign-in after, which fires
`account.update.*` and never `account.create.before`. So the rule closed
the door to NEW native links while every link already made kept letting
its holder in - including the ones the old soft block wrote, which is
exactly the population this is for.

`refuseNativeProviderOnSignIn` now runs from `afterAccountUpdate` as well,
before its reconciliation and deliberately OUTSIDE that try/catch: a
refusal the catch swallowed would admit the sign-in it exists to stop. It
still weighs only native providers, so the brokered mid-migration member
is let through on this path too.

An organization that PINNED a native provider keeps its own front door,
and that is now pinned by a test rather than left to be inferred. The
suggestion to refuse native providers ahead of `isSsoProviderMatch` would
have locked those organizations out of their own setting - two bound
scenarios already say an organization with `ssoProvider` "google" signs in
with Google.

Also renames the verdict's boolean to `shouldRefuse` for the house rule on
boolean naming, and moves the existing "wrong provider does not clear the
flag" case onto a brokered provider, since the native one it used is
refused outright now.

fix(navigation): a workspace that has not answered is not one that answered with nothing (#8155)

* fix(navigation): a workspace that has not answered is not one that answered with nothing

Refreshing any /:project address drew the full-page 404 scene for as long as
the session fetch took, and "/" bounced a member who has organizations through
/onboarding/welcome before correcting itself. One cause under both.

The organization graph is read only once the session has resolved — the guard
that fixed the 401-that-never-retries. React Query derives `isLoading` as
`isPending && isFetching`, so while that guard holds the query off it reports
`isLoading: false` with no data: the exact shape of a read that came back
empty. `useOrganizationTeamProject` asked `isLoading` alone and so called the
workspace resolved for the width of the session fetch. Its callers believed
it. The project chrome finds no project for the slug in the address and draws
its not-found scene; the landing redirect finds no organizations and answers
with onboarding.

So the hook now reports on whether the read has ANSWERED, counting the wait for
the session as part of it. An address that asks for no graph at all — public,
signed out — still resolves immediately, which is what keeps the share page
from waiting forever on a read it never makes.

And the landing redirect's org-less test becomes affirmative: belonging to no
organization is something the graph SAID, never something inferred from its
silence. That also covers the case the loading fix cannot, where the graph
answered with a refusal rather than a list.

* fix(navigation): an address anybody can open does not wait for the session either

The session-wait added for the project chrome was unconditional, so it also
held the two addresses that never read an organization graph at all. On
/share/[id] and /auth/signin the session is still in flight on the first
render like everywhere else, and its answer cannot change what either page
draws — the graph query stays switched off for a signed-out visitor whatever
the session says. Waiting on it there bought nothing and cost the share page
and the sign-in screen a loading state for the width of a fetch they have no
use for.

So the wait is now counted only on an address that will need the graph
whichever way the session resolves. The feature file said this already
("An address anybody can open resolves without waiting for a graph") and its
scenario only covered a session that had already resolved to nobody, which is
the half the implementation got right; the new scenario covers the half it did
not, and fails without this change.

Raised by Copilot on the pull request.

* fix(navigation): a graph that refused the read is the third answer, and / says so

Reading an unanswered graph as an account with no organization was what sent a
member to /onboarding/welcome, and not reading it that way is the fix. But a
REFUSED read leaves the same absent list behind it as one still in flight, so
the new reading catches it too: nobody is sent to onboarding on a refusal,
which is right, and nothing else happens either, which is not.

On / that is terminal. The home resolver is asked for an organization, so a
refused graph leaves it switched off and answerless; the landing destination
stays null; and null is the signal to keep waiting. The page waits on a read
that has already failed and will not be repeated — a spinner with nothing
behind it, on the one address that has no project slug to fall back to. The
old behaviour was wrong in the other direction and at least drew a screen.

So the refusal now travels. useOrganizationTeamProject carries the error
itself rather than a flag, which is what lets the landing page resolve the
words a customer reads from the code-keyed registry instead of inventing them
(ADR-045), and / draws that failure with the retry that covers both a
transient fault and a session that has to be re-established. Every other
address keeps the behaviour it had: only / has nothing to fall back to.

The shell's own conflation is untouched and pre-existing — a project address
whose graph refused still draws the not-found scene rather than the failure.
That is wrong in the same way, but it is not a hang, and it is not this
change.
