fix(automations): resolve bare OTEL attributes in metadata.value trigger filters (#8167)

* fix(automations): resolve bare OTEL attributes in metadata.value filters

A trigger filter on `metadata.value` with a bare OpenTelemetry resource
attribute key — `service.name` is the one seen in production — never
matched, so the trigger silently never fired.

ClickHouse resolves such a key against three candidates (see
clickhouse/filter-conditions.ts:97-113): `metadata.{key}`,
`langwatch.metadata.{key}`, and the bare `{key}`. The in-memory matcher
resolved only the first two, because it reads `customMetadata`, and
`extractCustomMetadata` deliberately drops standard OTEL resource
prefixes (triggerFilter.matcher.ts:606,645 — pinned by the test at
triggerFilter.matcher.unit.test.ts:1090). The filter builder offers these
keys and the preview counts them, so the filter looked valid and saved
fine while never matching at trigger time.

Carry the raw attributes onto PreconditionTraceData and fall back to them
when customMetadata misses, giving the in-memory matcher the same three
candidates as ClickHouse. The exclusion list is unchanged, so
customMetadata keeps its current meaning.

Additive only: it can turn a previously-unresolvable lookup into a match,
never the reverse.

* fix(automations): OR the metadata.value candidates instead of taking the first

Review finding. ClickHouse ORs its three candidates for a metadata.value
key (clickhouse/filter-conditions.ts), while this matcher returned the
first by precedence. With `metadata.env = "a"` and a bare `env = "b"`, a
filter on ["b"] counted in the preview and never fired the trigger. The
same precedence made a present-but-blank canonical key block the bare
fallback entirely.

Return both candidates when they are both present and disagree, which is
the only case where OR differs from precedence. The engine already treats
an array as any-element-matches (triggerFilter.matcher.ts:332).

Deliberately NOT a plain array in every case: `matches_regex` runs
JSON.stringify over an array (evaluations/preconditions.ts), so always
returning a list makes `^prod` stop matching `production` — it would test
against `["production"]`. Verified by writing that exact fix and watching
the new regex test fail. Staying a plain string for a single candidate
keeps every existing consumer reading the value and not its encoding.

Adds the regex guard so the next person cannot make that trade silently.

* docs(evaluations): record why the other two builders have no attributes

Review finding. Three builders construct PreconditionTraceData and only
the automations one can supply the new `attributes` field. This file's
convention is that a builder unable to supply a field says so inline
(see the annotationIds notes), so the silent omission read as oversight.

Sets both explicitly to null with the reason. No behaviour change: the
field is optional and both already resolved to undefined.

Names the real gap while it stands: a metadata.value precondition on a
bare OTEL resource attribute still does not resolve on the monitor path,
because the command schema carries customMetadata and no raw attributes.
Fixing that crosses a persisted event-sourcing schema and is a different
feature, so it is not in this hotfix.

* fix(evaluations): matches_regex tests each array element, not the encoding

Review finding on the previous commit. Returning both metadata.value
candidates when they disagree hands `matches_regex` an array, and that rule
was the only one that tested JSON.stringify(value) instead of the values.
`^prod` against ["staging","production"] tested a string starting with `[`
and failed, losing a match ClickHouse counts.

The bug is wider than the case that surfaced it. `is`, `contains` and
`not_contains` already iterate array elements; `matches_regex` did not. Every
array-valued field reaching it — metadata.labels, metadata.prompt_ids,
spans.type, spans.model, topics.topics, topics.subtopics — could not be
matched by an anchored pattern.

Test each element and pass if any matches, which is the same any-element
semantics the other three rules use. The serialized array stays in the
candidate list, so a pattern written against the old JSON-encoded form keeps
working: this rule can only gain matches, never lose them.

A `g`-flagged regex carries lastIndex between .test() calls, so each
candidate gets a fresh instance rather than sharing one.

Two tests, both failing before this change: a conflicting canonical/bare pair
where only the bare value satisfies the pattern, and an anchored pattern over
a span-model list.

* fix(automations): read all three metadata.value key forms, not two

Review finding on the previous commits. ClickHouse reads three independent
attribute keys for one metadata key and ORs them: metadata.{key},
langwatch.metadata.{key} and the bare {key}. The matcher was reading two —
customMetadata plus the raw bare attribute — and customMetadata cannot stand
in for the other two.

extractCustomMetadata collapses every form of a key down to the
highest-priority one (triggerFilter.matcher.ts, priority 3/2/1). So a trace
carrying both metadata.env and langwatch.metadata.env exposes only the
canonical value there, while ClickHouse matches either. A filter on the
legacy value counted in the preview and never fired the trigger, which is the
same defect this branch set out to fix, one key form over.

Read the three attribute keys by the names the ClickHouse builder uses, keep
customMetadata in the list as the only source for callers that carry parsed
metadata and no raw attributes, then dedupe. A single distinct candidate
stays a plain string; several come back as a list the caller matches any of.

Tests cover the bare resource attribute customMetadata excludes, all three
forms present and distinct, and the collapse back to a plain string when they
agree.

* test(automations): stop two tests claiming more than they check

Both are review findings against tests added earlier on this branch.

The "anchors against the value itself, not a serialized container" test
carried a comment saying the resolver must stay a plain string for a single
candidate. It stopped pinning that the moment matches_regex began testing
array elements: the assertion passes whether the resolver returns "production"
or ["production"]. Verified by forcing the resolver to always return a list —
all 197 tests still passed. The comment now says what the test actually
covers and points at the shape guard, which asserts the return value
directly.

"falls back to the bare attribute when the canonical key is blank" named a
fallback the code does not take. A blank canonical value is a present
candidate, not a missing one, so it goes through the ordinary any-candidate
match. Renamed to match the path that runs.

* docs(automations): point the shape-guard comment at the right test file

The comment named triggerFilter.matcher.unit.test.ts, but the return-shape
guard lives in filters/__tests__/precondition-matchers.unit.test.ts. Left
over from moving that guard to its colocated home in 996fc168c8.

fix(model-providers): strip the whitespace around a stored credential (#8180)

* fix(model-providers): strip the whitespace around a stored credential

A credential pasted with padding is stored with the padding, and whether
that breaks the provider depends on where the credential is spent. In a
query string it is percent-encoded and the provider ignores it; in an
HTTP header it is refused before the request leaves the process. So the
settings page, which probes Gemini through `?key=`, reported "Connection
works" while every evaluation against the same row failed with
`litellm.APIConnectionError: GeminiException - Illegal header value
b' REDACTED'` -- the space before the mask is the padding itself.

The failure is quiet in the place anyone would look for it. Evaluators
that need a model credential fail; the ones that need none keep working,
so the evaluations chart thins out instead of stopping, and the settings
page stays green throughout.

Stripped on read rather than on write. Rows already hold padded values,
and healing them where they are read costs nobody a re-paste or a
backfill. Only strings are touched: the bag carries a provider's project
and location beside its key, and a value that is not a string has no
padding to lose.

* fix(model-providers): strip the whitespace around a stored header

Extra headers are the other credential bag on a provider row, and they were
not trimmed. Their values are spent as HTTP headers and nowhere else, and
http.client refuses a header name or value whose edges carry whitespace, so
a space a user never sees in the settings form would fail every request to
that provider.

This is worse than the same defect in an API key, which is what the previous
commit fixed: a key has a query-string variant that percent-encodes the
padding away, which is why the settings page could show a green "Connection
works" for a key that failed every real call. A header has no such variant.
It fails on every path, with nothing on the page to contradict it.

Both sides of the merge are trimmed, not just the incoming one. A masked
placeholder restores the value from the stored row, so trimming only the
submission would leave an already-padded row padded through every future
save.

The trim closes the hole on the header bag whether or not anything has
already fallen into it.

* fix(model-providers): restore each stored header at most once

Review of the previous commit found a case it introduced. Trimming can turn
two header names that differed only by surrounding whitespace into the same
name. The restore then looked the stored value up by first match, so both
placeholders took the first secret and the second one was dropped without a
word.

The merge now claims each stored header as it restores it, so a second
placeholder with the same name falls through to the next stored entry rather
than taking one already spent.

Before this change the added test stored "secret-one" under both names and
lost "secret-two" entirely.

* fix(model-providers): keep the webhook secret out of the read-time trim

Trimming a credential on the way out of the column is safe for one that is
spent as an HTTP header or a query parameter: both discard the padding
anyway, so stripping it early only spares the client refusing the value.

It is not safe for one spent as cryptographic key material.
ELEVENLABS_WEBHOOK_SECRET is the HMAC key in verifyElevenLabsSignature, so a
byte removed here changes every digest the route computes and a genuine
delivery answers 401, with a voice session left open behind it. The read
path reaches it through readCustomKeys like every other credential, so the
trim applied to it too.

Name it in a set the trim skips. The set is the exception list, not the rule:
a credential belongs in it only when its exact bytes are the contract.

The name is repeated rather than imported from elevenLabsCredential.service,
which imports this module.

Two tests cover it: the secret survives its padding exactly, and a credential
sitting beside it in the same bag is still trimmed.

* fix(model-providers): resolve a masked header by row before by name

Trimming can collapse two stored header names that differed only by
whitespace into one, and the settings form permits duplicate names outright.
Once two stored rows share a name, matching a masked placeholder by name
first can pick the wrong row.

Rename the first of two colliding rows and leave the second masked: the
renamed row finds no name to match, and its positional fallback is refused
because the name it used to carry is still somewhere in the submission, so it
is dropped. The second row then matches the first row's entry by name and
comes back carrying a secret that was never its own. The other secret is
lost.

Resolve in order of how strongly each match proves row identity: the same
name in the same row, then the same name somewhere else because the row
moved, then the same row under a new name because it was renamed. Each stored
row is spent once. A placeholder that resolves to nothing is still dropped
rather than stored literally, and a stored row whose name another placeholder
is still waiting on stays off limits, so a rename plus a reorder still cannot
copy one header's secret under another header's name.

The passes live in their own functions, one per kind of match, because the
rule is easier to check one claim at a time than as one nested loop.

A test covers the collision above. Without the fix it reports secret-one
where secret-two belongs.

* fix(model-providers): match a masked header on its raw name

The merge trimmed both sides before matching. Trimming is what collapses two
stored names that differ only by whitespace into one, so doing it first is
what made row identity ambiguous in the first place.

Delete the first of two such rows and the survivor submits the name it has
always had, now sitting at the index the deleted row used to hold. The
same-row pass matched it there and handed it the deleted row's secret; its
own was dropped.

The settings form round-trips a stored name unchanged, padding included, so
the raw name is the row's identity. Match on it, and on the raw row order.
Trimming moves to the end, on the way to the column: a header is still
stored with its edges stripped, and a placeholder that restores a padded
stored value still comes back trimmed, so a row stored padded before the
guard existed is still healed on its next save.

A test covers the deletion. Without the fix it reports secret-one where
secret-two belongs.

Also drops a doc comment that restated the function name, and rewrites the
mergeExtraHeaders comment that still described the old by-key-then-position
rule.

* fix(model-providers): exempt the AWS signing secret from the trim

The read-time trim exempts credentials whose exact bytes are the
contract, because the platform cannot check its copy against the
vendor's. `ELEVENLABS_WEBHOOK_SECRET` was listed. `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
meets the same rule and was not: SigV4 derives its signing key from the
secret by HMAC, so one changed byte changes every signature.

Also moves the exemption set above the doc comment it had orphaned, and
corrects that comment, which still claimed no credential means anything
different for the whitespace around it.

* refactor(model-providers): move the exact-bytes list to shared constants

The set of credentials exempt from the read-time trim lived as a private
const in customKeys.ts, with a comment claiming the names were repeated
there rather than imported because the modules holding them import
customKeys. That was wrong on both halves: registry.ts does not import
customKeys, and the AWS secret is not an exported constant anywhere, so
nothing was being worked around.

The codebase already has a home for a set of credential field names
classified by exact name, one module away: PUBLIC_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS in
utils/constants.ts, with a single reader and a test that walks the
provider registry to keep the list and the registry in step. The set now
sits beside it as EXACT_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS. There is no import cycle —
the sibling credentialMerge.ts already imports that module, and nothing
in its chain reaches back here.

The move brings the guard that was missing. Rename either field in the
registry and, before this, the set would quietly stop matching and the
signing key would go back to being trimmed on every read — invisible,
because a key that no longer matches the vendor's copy fails as an
authentication error rather than as a bad value. Two tests now hold it:
every listed name must exist in the registry, and every listed name must
already classify as a secret. Verified by renaming a field and watching
the first test fail.

Also converts the four restore helpers added earlier in this branch to
named parameters, which the repo's TypeScript guide requires for two or
more arguments and which their sibling mergeStoredCustomKeys already
does.

No behaviour change: same two credentials exempt, same trim everywhere
else. 870 tests pass across the model provider and gateway suites.

* docs(model-providers): cite where the AWS secret is signed with

The comment on EXACT_CREDENTIAL_FIELDS called AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY the
root of the SigV4 signing chain. True of the protocol, but no code here
signs anything, so a reader following the claim found nothing.

That is the same failure the commit before this one set out to remove: a
comment asserting something the citation does not support. Name the two
places the value leaves this process instead, and say the signing happens
downstream.

Comment only. No code change.

* test(evaluations): cover a padded credential reaching the worker

Drives setupModelEnv with only the database mocked, so the service, the
repository, readCustomKeys and prepareLitellmParams all run, and asserts
the api_key handed to the evaluator carries no padding.

The value is a sentinel and is asserted to be the stored one, because the
key resolves from the environment when the row does not supply it, which
would let the test pass on an ambient key and prove nothing.

Fails on the parent commit with the padding intact.

fix(event-sourcing): run the causality loop guard on the deferred-origin path (#8174)

* fix(event-sourcing): run the causality loop guard on the deferred-origin path

Evaluator-emitted traces can arrive with no root span. Their origin is
not resolved while spans stream in, so the originGate subscriber resolves
it afterwards and emits `origin_resolved`. That event carries no span
payload, and the evaluation-trigger loop guard only inspected the span
payload — so it returned "no loop" and dispatch proceeded unguarded. The
evaluator then evaluated its own output, which produced another rootless
evaluator trace, which dispatched again: a closed cycle.

Guard the deferred path off the fold state instead. Depth stays the sole
hard rule, matching the span path — origin remains a user-configurable
precondition, never a hardcoded subscriber rule.

Causality depth was not reaching the fold state, so accumulation now
folds `langwatch.reserved.causality_depth` in, accepting the int and
string encodings. Reserved keys are already exempt from analytics
trimming and already skipped by the filter builders, so nothing
user-facing changes.

Refs #8162

* test(event-sourcing): bind the deferred-origin guard to its spec and pin its limit

Review follow-ups on the causality guard change:

- Register "depth_fold" in the documented reason set for
  langwatch_evaluator_loop_blocked_total. The counter takes a bare
  string, so an unregistered reason reaches Prometheus silently.
- Add the deferred-origin scenarios to the loop-prevention feature file
  and bind the new tests to them with @scenario, matching how the
  sibling suite binds every depth scenario.
- Assert the counter and its reason label, which every depth scenario in
  the feature file states but no unit test checked.
- Pin the known limitation: a manual evaluation run inside the deferred
  window stamps depth on an application trace, fold accumulation is
  first-wins, and origin_resolved rewrites the folded origin — so that
  trace's evaluations are skipped. Documented as an accepted tradeoff
  against leaving the loop open, with the way out noted.

Refs #8162

* fix(event-sourcing): take the highest causality depth when folding a trace

A trace can carry both application spans (depth 0) and evaluator-emitted
spans (depth >= 1). Attribute accumulation merges as
`{ ...spanAttrs, ...state.attributes }`, so whichever span folded first
pinned the depth for the life of the trace: an application span landing
before the evaluator's held the trace at "0" and the deferred-origin loop
guard never fired on it. Depth answers "has this trace been through the
evaluator", so accumulate it as a max instead.

Also corrects the spec and the test that documented the manual-run
limitation. Both claimed the folded origin was rewritten to "application"
and that first-wins depth was the cause. Neither holds: the evaluator's
spans carry an evaluation origin onto the customer trace, so the trace
resolves as evaluator-produced on its own, and a monitor filtering on an
application origin already skips it. The guard only changes the outcome
for a monitor with no origin filter.

Scenarios rewritten as observable behaviour and dropped to @unit — the
tests backing them are unit tests, and the @integration tag claimed
coverage that does not exist. The comment block no longer asserts how
much traffic takes the deferred path, which was never measured.

Adds a test running the real accumulation service into the real
subscriber, so the depth being dropped between them is caught.

* docs(event-sourcing): correct the claim that folded causality depth is hidden

The behaviour is right and matches how langwatch.reserved.log_record_count
already reaches external consumers. Only the claim was wrong, so the claim is
what changes.

* fix(lwql): grant columns referenced by view where/join predicates (#8085)

A column a catalog view reads only in its `where` pre-filter or its join `ON`
predicate — never in a projected column's `sourceColumns` — was left out of the
restricted-identity grants, so `coding_tool_results` failed at query time with
`Missing permissions: SELECT(SpanName) ON ...stored_spans`.

Declare those columns explicitly (no SQL parsing): `whereSourceColumns` on the
view and `join.onSourceColumns` ({primary, joined}) on the join. They join the
base- and joined-table grants, and `lwqlViewStatement` now refuses a `where`
without `whereSourceColumns` or a join without `onSourceColumns`, so a missing
list is a loud provisioning error rather than a runtime ACCESS_DENIED.

Also move `LWQL_SOURCE_ALIAS` to a leaf module so a catalog entry can build its
`ON`/`where` SQL without importing the statement builder, breaking the import
cycle (catalogStatements -> lwqlViews -> overrides -> catalogStatements) that
left `coding_tool_results` undefined whenever its module initialised first.

* feat(query): one reference door for LWQL and trace filters, filter and facets on the traces API, langwatch query CLI, MCP run_query

LangWatch answers two query languages and described neither to an agent in
one place. LangWatchQL is SQL over the analytics datasets; the trace filter
is the Lucene-flavoured string the Trace Explorer speaks. A question belongs
to one or the other, and picking wrong is expensive.

Their pieces were published in four places to four readers, and one had
drifted: the MCP server's hand-copied list of 24 filter fields named renamed
fields and missed new ones, and QUERY_SYNTAX_DOC still documented
attribute.<key> while everything else had moved to trace.attribute.<key>.

GET /api/v1/query/reference now describes both languages in one payload:
datasets, columns and limits for the SQL half; fields, prefixes and syntax
for the filter half; worked examples in both; and a decision table saying
which language answers which question. It is built by describeQueryReference,
which is pure, so the endpoint answers from memory and the MCP fixture is
generated from it. Every published example is executed by a test against the
real validator, parser and ClickHouse compiler.

POST /api/traces/search gains filter, compiled at the boundary so a bad
filter is a 422 naming the field rather than a 500. GET /api/traces/facets
answers the value question, which the reference deliberately does not carry.

The CLI gains langwatch query (run, schema, reference, examples) with jsonl,
csv and keyset paging, plus trace facets and trace fields. The MCP server's
discover_schema is backed by the reference, search_traces takes the filter,
and run_query renders up to 50 rows as a markdown table.

See ADR-138.

* feat(lwql): eval functions judged by the classifier interface (Instant Evals)

A LangWatchQL projection can now ask a question about the text it extracts and
get a calibrated answer per row, in the same statement:

    SELECT ConversationId,
           eval(conversation_bounded(ConversationId, 8000, ''),
                'The customer sounds annoyed') AS annoyed
    FROM analytics.trace_metrics
    WHERE OccurredAt >= subtractDays(now(), 7) AND ConversationId != ''
    GROUP BY ConversationId LIMIT 100

Six functions on the PR 2 machinery unchanged: eval, eval_criteria,
eval_passed, eval_score, eval_category and eval_category_probs. A projection
UDF in ClickHouse, projection-only with an alias, options as literals, value
computed after the query.

An eval call may nest an extraction call one level deep, which is the only
nesting the validator allows anywhere: two identity UDFs compose to the
identity, so the column carries the inner function's key and hydration runs
the extraction first. Several eval calls over the same nested expression are
one classifier request carrying every question; rows are never packed together,
because the bench measured eleven accuracy points as the price of that saving.

eval(text, instructions, criteria) could not be a third arity of eval: a
ClickHouse SQL UDF is a lambda with a fixed parameter list and any other count
is BAD_ARGUMENTS (36), measured on 25.8. The criteria form is eval_criteria,
and a three-argument eval is refused by arity with a message naming it.

The classifier lives behind InstantEvalClassifier, which publishes its own
limits and pricing so nothing above it holds a provider constant. The shipped
implementation calls TypeSafe Jev with LangWatch's own key over an undici pool,
paced by a Redis token bucket shared by every pod; a deployment with no key
gets a null implementation that skips every question rather than failing every
query. Verified against the live API before anything depended on it.

Refusals: instant_eval_query_budget_exceeded (422) before anything is sent, and
instant_eval_classifier_unavailable (503, provider fault) when nothing at all
was judged. A query where some texts went unjudged answers normally with null
cells and an INSTANT_EVAL_SKIPPED diagnostic. One Cost row per query, carrying
our cost and the customer price at the markup.

Gated by release_instant_evals, dark by default, and by the presence of a
configured classifier.

* fix(lwql): key a score answer through its legend, cap the scale at ten, and cancel judging

Three findings from probing the live classifier, one of them a real bug.

A score answer's `probabilities` are keyed by level POSITION, and the answer's
`legend` is what says which level each position means: a range of 20 to 24 came
back as {"0":0, ..., "4":0.69} with legend {"0":"20", ..., "4":"24"}. The
reading now resolves each key through the legend first, then as a position, then
as a level written out, and accepts only levels the question actually offered.
That keeps the answer correct if the keys ever become the criteria themselves,
and a captured response pins it.

The API refuses more than ten score levels ("Too many score levels. Must have at
most 10 levels."), so eval_score(text, 'x', 0, 10) was accepted by the validator
and would have failed once per row at the provider. The ceiling is published
through the classifier's limits and refused where the caller wrote it.

`jev-latest` is a real model name and resolves to jev-1.13.0; a version written
out (`jev-1.13`) is refused as unknown. JEV_MODEL now pins one where a
deployment needs to.

Cancellation is threaded from the REST request to the classifier. A judged query
is the one LangWatchQL shape that keeps spending after its caller has gone, so
the runner checks the signal between classifications, hands it to each request,
and lets an abort propagate rather than counting it as a row that could not be
judged.

* fix(lwql): a failed judgement is a skip with a reason, not a key that named nothing

Review round one. The finding that mattered: when the classifier dropped one
text of several, `evaluateCalls` counted the failure and wrote no cell, so
`fillUnjudged` marked the key NOT_RESOLVED, which means "the key named no

broke the reporting contract the spec states: the key resolved, the text was
sent, and the classification failed. Those rows now record a
`classifier_failed` skip and a resolved null cell, so the result carries the
INSTANT_EVAL_SKIPPED diagnostic the spec asks for and no unresolved key.

- The per-query budget is estimated against the classifier's own published
  limits rather than the shipped constant, since the contract says limits are
  published by the implementation and never assumed.
- `createLangWatchQLInstantEvalSupport` takes the cost recorder as its port
  with the Prisma one as the default, so the concrete class is named in the
  factory that exists to wire it rather than reached for behind it.
- `InstantEvalClassifyRequest.text` documents the real contract: the caller
  passes the text it has, and the implementation cuts it to its own budget and
  reports that through `isTextTruncated`.
- The comment above the score rule still claimed a 255-level ceiling that the
  live API refuses at 11; the remediation tip called a query-wide token
  estimate "one request"; the eval arity scenario still described two arities.
  All three now say what the code does.

  `isLangWatchQLEvalFunction` predicate is gone and the extraction catalog is
  no longer exported, since nothing outside the module reads either.
- The limiter's capacity test counted the acquisition that waited and allowed
  eight grants of slack; it now asserts exactly the capacity.
- Both 422 ceilings are documented: the 1,000-text key cap as well as the
  per-query token budget.

* perf(lwql): only a statement that judges pays for the Instant Evals gate

Review round two. The finding that mattered most was a cost every query paid
for a feature almost none of them use: `execute` resolved the project's Instant
Evals gate, which is a Prisma project read plus a flag evaluation, and
`hydrateAndBill` built the classifier and its connection pool, whether or not
the statement called an eval function. Both are now conditional. The gate is
resolved only when the statement text names an eval function, and the
classifier only when the validated plan actually contains an eval call. The
text test is one-sided on purpose: a false positive costs one flag lookup, and
a statement that never names any of these functions cannot call one. The parse
stays single (ADR-083).

Also from the round:

- The limiter added permits it drew instead of assigning them. Two `acquire`
  calls can each be awaiting their own Redis draw, Redis has already deducted
  both chunks, and assigning threw away whichever landed first.
- The retry wait is abortable, so a cancelled query no longer sits out a
  `Retry-After` of up to thirty seconds for a caller that has gone.
- A too-large refusal on the final attempt reports
  `classifier_input_too_large` rather than `classifier_rate_limited`, which
  named the wrong cause.
- `JEV_BASE_URL` must be https: the classifier key travels in an Authorization
  header.
- `rateLimited`, `truncated` and `cutForSize` get their `is` prefixes.
- The two suites that asserted the gate no longer read the ambient
  `INSTANT_EVAL_CLASSIFIER` to decide what they were testing: the configured
  check is injectable, and the service suite states Instant Evals as off.
- The judged-hydration suite is split in two by what it claims — what a
  statement costs, and what a cell holds when the judge did not answer — with
  the fakes they share in one module.

Not applied: budgeting the text against `totalTokens - questions - reserve`.
Measured against the live API, the state cap covers the text and the questions
together. 33,000 estimated tokens of text alone is accepted (29,606 real input
tokens), while 31,000 of text beside a five-thousand-token question payload is
refused with `max_tokens_exceeded`. So the shipped formula is right and the
suggestion would over-fill every request carrying a large category question.
What was actually wrong is what led there: the comments called `stateTokens`
the text ceiling. They now say what it covers, and record the measurement.

New test: a statement that judges nothing resolves no gate and builds no
classifier.

* fix(e2e): wait for the nudge dismissal to be written before navigating

`passkeys.test.ts` has been failing all three attempts on this branch and on
main. The log names the cause precisely: the click on `create-passkey`
resolves the button as visible, enabled and stable, and then a dialog
positioner carrying "It is saved in your credential manager" swallows the
pointer event. That copy is the secure-account nudge, on a page the test
reached after dismissing it.

The nudge closes on local state and writes the dismissal behind it, so waiting
for the dialog to disappear says nothing about the write. The next line is a
`page.goto`, a document navigation that discards the page holding that local

deployment needs to.

verbatim. A page is two passes: keys (`SELECT TraceId, ThreadId, OccurredAt
FROM (<statement>) AS q`, hydration skipped, keyset predicate on `TraceId`
from the second page on) then judge (`WHERE q.TraceId IN
({instant_eval_page_ids:Array(String)})`). The cursor is one trace id, so no
event, process state or outbox payload carries a large id list.

that lifts the cap, and `instant_eval_row_cap_exceeded` past that with the cap
and plan in `meta`. One classifier request per row carrying every question, so
a four-column statement still sends one request per row. `POST /estimate`
prices a run from a key pass and a 50-row text sample. A finished run writes
one `Cost` row at the 1.3 markup through the PR 2b recorder.

the `judgments` LWQL dataset, a `InstantEvalRun` Prisma table, the

A score answer's `probabilities` are keyed by level POSITION, and the answer's

through the classifier's limits and refused where the caller wrote it.

deployment needs to.

is the one LangWatchQL shape that keeps spending after its caller has gone, so
the runner checks the signal between classifications, hands it to each request,

* feat(instant-evals): CLI, target shorthand and estimate for Instant Eval runs

An Instant Eval run still executes one LangWatchQL statement. This adds the
two things that make it usable without writing one first, and neither changes
what a run is.

The shorthand: a request may carry a target, a trace filter, a window and its
questions instead of `sql`. The server expands that into one statement from a
template per target, and the statement then goes through the same acceptance
gate a submitted one does. It is stored on the run and handed back, so the
shorthand teaches the primitive rather than hiding it. Sending both `sql` and
`target` is refused, and so is sending neither.

The filter is compiled into LangWatchQL rather than resolved into trace ids:
the existing trace compiler targets base tables a statement's identity cannot
see, and binding a hundred thousand ids would give back a statement nobody
could rerun. So there is a second dialect over the LangWatchQL trace view,
sharing the language's boolean walk with the trace compiler, and a field it
cannot answer is refused by name with the statement door named instead.

The CLI: `langwatch instant-eval run|estimate|status|list|results|sample|cancel`.
`run` prints the statement it ran under a Statement heading, `--wait` reports
`Judging... 3,200/10,000 (412 matched)`, and money is never spent by surprise:
`--estimate` prices and exits, and a run over a thousand rows prints the price
before it creates anything.

* fix(lwql): tell an eval function used outside the projection what to do instead

The APP_FUNCTION_POSITION refusal ended with "Project it there and filter,
group or sort on a plain column instead". That is right for an extraction

run it as an Instant Eval and read `instant-eval results --matched`.

evalCatalog.ts is what picks between them, so the two stay in step with the
catalog rather than with a second list.

plain-column sentence and the extraction one does not carry the Instant Eval

* feat(instant-evals): run waits for the answer by default, and the page respects the statement's key cap

`run` created a run and printed its id, which left the caller to poll for the
thing they asked for. It now follows the run: statement and price first, one
progress line while the judge works, then a headline and the rows that matched.
`--detach` is the previous behaviour, `--show N` sets how many rows to print,
the machine formats block too and emit one document, and Ctrl-C leaves the run
judging because it is already created and already being paid for. `--wait` is
kept as a hidden no-op.

Running it over ten thousand real conversations found three bugs:

- The hydration stage caps the keys one execution may read by the kind of key,
  200 for a thread against 1000 for a trace, but the page size was 500
  regardless, so every `--target threads` run past 200 conversations failed the
  whole run with `lwql_app_function_key_cap`. `instantEvalKeyCapFor` reads the
  caps of the functions the statement calls and lowers the page to the
  smallest.
- The finished headline read the row count the run set out to judge, so a run
  that died early announced rows it never read. It reads the progress unless the
  run finished.
- A label filter decoded escaped labels by trimming quote characters off the raw
  JSON element, and now uses `JSONExtractString`.

The three docs pages are rewritten around the new default, and the estimate's
sampling is stated where it is documented: the row count is exact, the price
comes from the first fifty rows, so it moves when rows vary in length.

* fix(instant-evals): price a run from a spread sample at the classifier's own byte ratio, and profile where a run's wall clock goes

The estimate was five times low on a ten thousand conversation run, from two
independent errors.

It measured the first fifty rows the statement returns. That is the head of the
ordering rather than a sample, and on real data row length correlates with the
order, so a statement ordered by conversation id priced itself on its fifty
lowest ids. The estimate now asks for fifty rows spread across the whole
selection with a `cityHash64(TraceId) % buckets = 0` predicate in the same
outer wrapper the page pass already uses, so the caller's statement is still
untouched inside the subquery. A stride over the key list would have needed the
whole key list read first, which is the read the count pass exists to avoid.
The run's page-size decision read the same head fifty rows and now reads the
same spread.

It also priced text at four bytes per token, which is calibrated on English
prose. A run judges conversation transcripts in markdown, and measured against
the live API those run 2.4 to 2.7 bytes per input token, so the prose rule
under-counted by about a third. The classifier now publishes
`bytesPerInputToken` alongside its caps and its pricing, and the estimate uses
it. The truncation cut keeps the prose rule on purpose, because the extraction
functions cut their own `max_tokens` argument with it.

On the ten thousand row seed the estimate went from 2.31M tokens and $0.13 to
11.87M and $0.65, against a run that really read 11.38M and cost $0.62.

`run` also logs one profile line per page at debug level: the gap before the
page, each read, the judging, the limiter wait and the write. It is what showed
the judge saturated at 166 classifications per second for 41% of the wall clock
while the hydration read took 34% and the per-page fixed costs 22%, and that
the limiter waits 26ms per request rather than owning the clock.

* perf(instant-evals): read the next page while the current one is judged, and never drop a page's traces to the thread read ceiling

A run's page was a read (statement, traces, texts) and then a judging, one
after the other, so every page's reads sat on the critical path of a job whose
judge is the bottleneck. The hydration stage now publishes its two halves,
prepareLangWatchQLHydration and judgeLangWatchQLHydration, the row source
exposes them as read and judgePrepared, and the run executor keeps one
prefetch per run keyed by the cursor the next intent will arrive with: page
n+1 is read while page n judges and handed over when the intent asks for it.
One page still judges at a time. The idempotency keys, the page events and the
cancel check are unchanged; a mismatched intent, a cancel, a failed page or a
finish drops what was read ahead and the intent reads for itself.

The thread read behind conversation extraction capped every call at a
thousand traces, so a page of two hundred conversations silently lost the
traces past that. The ceiling is now an option, sized by the LWQL trace
source at a thousand per thread asked for; every other caller keeps the old
default.

* fix(instant-evals): cut a page to the key cap of the statement's own functions

The hydration stage caps the keys one execution may read by the kind of key,
200 for a thread against 1000 for a trace, but a page was 500 rows regardless,
so a run over conversations failed on its first page with
lwql_app_function_key_cap instead of judging anything. The plan now reads the
caps of the functions the statement calls and lowers the page to the smallest.

* feat(instant-evals): the threads shorthand judges the whole conversation

`--target threads` expanded to `conversation_bounded(ConversationId, 8000, '')`.
A conversation is the thing people most want read end to end, and cutting it at
eight thousand tokens to save a fraction of a cent is the wrong trade, so the
template now writes `conversation(ConversationId)` and the only ceiling it meets
is the judge's own state, about thirty one thousand tokens once the questions
are in. `traces` and `llm_spans` keep their budget: a coding session renders to
many times it and those are the rows least worth reading in full.

A conversation past that ceiling is judged rather than lost. The classifier cuts
it to what the questions leave and the row comes back marked truncated, which
two tests now pin through the real request path.

That cut keeps the opening and drops the close, and writes no marker saying so,
which a third assertion pins because it is now on the default path.
`conversation_bounded` is the opposite, keeping both ends and naming how many
turns went missing, so it stays documented as the explicit-budget option and the
shorthand page points a question about how a conversation ended at it.

An unbounded conversation costs whatever it is long, up to roughly four times a
bounded one on the longest threads. The estimate prices the rows as they are, so
the number printed before a run already carries the difference.

* fix(instant-evals): cut an over-budget conversation through the bounded renderer, not by bytes

`--target threads` sends `conversation(ConversationId)`, which carries no budget
of its own, so a thread longer than the classifier's state reached the judge
whole and the classifier cut it. That cut works on bytes: it keeps the opening,
drops the close and writes nothing about what went missing. The close is the
part most questions are about.

The hydration stage now cuts first. A conversation text over the budget the
questions leave is re-rendered through the same bounded renderer
`conversation_bounded` uses, at that budget, so both ends are kept and a marker
names how many turns went from the middle. It is measured with the renderer's
own ruler rather than the classifier's denser one, so the text that comes back
satisfies the check the classifier is about to make and is not cut twice.

The row still reports itself truncated even though the classifier then has
nothing left to cut.

Three tests pin it through the real hydration path: the close survives, the
opening survives, the marker is there, the cell is marked truncated, and a
conversation inside the budget is passed through untouched. The classifier
suite keeps its own cut test for a text that arrives over budget by another
route, without the end-dropped assertion that this supersedes.

`conversation_bounded` stays documented as the explicit-budget option, for
naming the size yourself rather than taking the judge's.

The spec's two scenarios kept main's cost wording while this branch's tests

The two complexity findings are this branch's own code, and they surface now

cut from. judgeRunPageOrThrow gives up the page read, the read-ahead and the

* Give the judgments view its place in the manifest and the docs

The merge put the view in the application catalog but left the two things that
have to agree with it behind.

The Go manifest's lists are positional, so judgments belongs beside the
coding-agent views rather than at the end, and its source table at the same
index. The manifest also gained a sourceColumns map on main, which had no entry
for the view, so the grants are written from the catalog's own derivation. The
docs' view table lists it too.

* List the Instant Eval tables in the LWQL columns manifest

The two new migrations create instant_eval_judgments and instant_eval_runs, so
the manifest parity test failed on tables the migrations make but the manifest
does not list.

The generator can now also run against the ClickHouse named by
LANGWATCH_TEST_CLICKHOUSE_URL instead of always starting a container, which is

Every manifest table is either hand-written as a view, derived into one, or

session, the login holds no login key, or the platform answers its key with
a 401), the device login runs right away and the command continues. A
sign-in that still leaves no usable login ends with what to run:

--device`, then run `langwatch langy --share-control` again."

a failed sign-in comes back as an error it words instead of an exit.

its "local folder" pick in the browser, so after a reload it read "no
request" as "still waiting": with no expiry to count down to, the expired
branch could not render and the card kept spinning on "Waiting for you to
approve in the terminal" with nothing left for a terminal to approve.

`getLocalWorkspace` now returns `requestState`: open, approved, expired,
declined, ended or none. An open request answers from Redis. With none open
the state is read from the conversation's own record: the last
`local_control_requested` event carries the expiry, a
`local_workspace_connected` event with the same request id says it was
approved, and the approval mark covers the moment between the approval and
the folder coming online.

The card gains a closed state that names what happened ("This request
expired.", "This request was declined in the terminal.", "Sharing stopped.")
and offers "Try again". That calls the new `langy.renewLocalControlRequest`,
which opens a fresh request on the same conversation through
`openControlRequest`, the function the worker's route now shares. No
message is sent and no turn starts: the request shows up in a terminal that
is already waiting, and connecting the folder starts the next turn as it
does after the first ask. A card on screen when the countdown reaches zero
turns expired and re-reads the server once. Picking "Share local folder"
on a card whose request is already over opens a fresh one too.

* fix(langy): an empty reply with messages after it draws nothing

A reopened guided conversation showed an italic "No content" line between
the collapsed tour card and Langy's opener. The line is the empty reply row
of `MessageContent`: a settled assistant message with nothing visible.

The record keeps every reply. A turn that ends with nothing to show (a stop
before any text, or a reply with no text and no call that draws) is stored
as a message with one empty text part. Running the turn again replaces that
reply on screen, because a retry regenerates the last reply, but the record
keeps both, so a reload drew the empty one above the reply that answered.

The row now speaks only for the last message of the conversation, where it
says the turn ended with nothing. Above a later message it draws nothing.
The panel passes `isLatest`; the default keeps a lone message reading as it
did.

* fix(cli): a tool wrapper prints no note about a table

Inside a coding agent the CLI detects agent mode from the environment, and
every `langwatch codex ...` (and claude, copilot, code, cursor, gemini,
opencode) started with "note: `codex` does not emit structured output yet,
the table below is not machine-readable". A wrapper prints no table: it
hands the terminal to the tool it runs.

The seven wrappers are now registered with `rendersOwnResult`, the same way
`ingest hook` is, so the format gate lets them through with nothing printed.
They leave the holdout list of the command tree test, which keeps `open`.

The note itself, still printed for commands that do draw a table, reads as
two sentences.

* fix(cli): the sign-in inside langy --share-control prints only what it needs

With no usable login, `langwatch langy --share-control` runs the device
login, and it printed the whole `langwatch login` ceremony in the middle of
sharing a folder: the login header, the control plane, the mode line, the
list of AI tools, the model providers, the budgets and the dashboard line.

`runUnifiedLoginFlow` takes `quiet`. A quiet login prints the address to
open with its code, the "Logged in as" line, and any change it made to the
machine's tool wiring, then returns. It skips the budget overview request,
which only the ceremony reads. `langwatch login` is unchanged.

The terminal now reads: "No login on this machine yet. Signing in first.",
the address and code, "Logged in as ...", "Using your login as ...".

* test(langy): a scenario's own account is seeded in the local database

`seedGuidedOrganization` starts by giving the scenario a person of its own
through `signUpAccount`, which posted to `/api/auth/sign-up/email`. That
route answers 404 now: registration goes through `user.register`, which asks
for the proof an emailed link hands out, and a scenario has no mailbox to
read. Every guided onboarding scenario failed at its seed.

`signUpAccount` now seeds the account the way
`scripts/seed-dogfood-password.ts` does: a verified user plus the credential
account the email sign-in looks up (`issuer` `local:credential`, bcrypt
hash). The new `seed-account.ts` reads the database address from
`DATABASE_URL`, or from the app's own `.env`, and refuses to write unless
both the app under test and the database are on a loopback address. The
refusal names the address without its credentials.

* test(langy): the browser check signs in on the email first page

The sign-in page asks for the address first and shows the password box once
it knows the account signs in with one. `browser-qa.ts` filled the password
on the first screen, waited 30 seconds for a box that was not there, and
every scenario's browser check failed at its sign-in.

It now submits the address when no password box is on the page, waits for
the box, then fills it. A page that shows both boxes at once still works.

* fix(langy): a shared folder answers only to the owner of its conversation

A conversation shared with the project is readable by every member, and
`findByIdVisible` hands it to any of them. Both doors into local control
proved the conversation with that read alone, so a teammate reading a shared
conversation could ask for its folder again, answer one of its permission
cards, switch the permission checks off or close the folder from the panel,
and a Langy key of theirs could name the conversation on the worker's routes
and open a request or start a call in a folder on the owner's machine.

`own-conversation.ts` now holds the one rule: acting on a folder needs the
conversation to be the caller's own, and the refusal is the same not-found a
missing conversation gets. The panel's router uses it for every mutation and
keeps the visible read for the folder state, which a teammate may still see.
The worker's routes use it everywhere, since a turn only ever runs for the
owner.

* refactor(cli): two boolean options carry an is prefix

`asPerson` in the credential resolver becomes `isLoginKeyRequired`, which is
what it decides, and the login flow's `quiet` becomes `isQuiet`. The repo's
naming rule asks a new boolean for an is/has/should/can/will prefix.

* fix(cli): a login's key is only sent to the address that issued it

`langy --share-control` acts with the person's login key, and it paired that
key with whatever `LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT` resolved to. A folder's .env can set
that variable, so a cloned folder could point the command at an address of
its author's choosing and receive the key of whoever ran the command there.

The login records the address it was made against. When the command targets
another one, no key is resolved and the command ends naming both addresses,
with what to run to sign in to the other one. It does not sign in on its own:
the inline login runs against the login's own address, and replacing the
login on a machine because a folder said so is the person's call. Two
spellings of one address (a trailing slash, a capital letter) are the same
address.

* fix(cli): a host that only starts with localhost is not this machine

A login on this machine takes over a tool's wiring only when that wiring
already reports to this machine. For a tool wired through a shell function
the check searched the block for `://localhost`, which is also how
`https://localhost.acme.test` starts, so a local login could rewrite wiring
that reports to a deployment elsewhere.

The block's addresses are now read whole and judged by their parsed host,
the same `isLoopbackEndpoint` the claude and codex wiring already go through.

* fix(cli): what follows -- reaches a wrapped tool's help run as typed

A help or version run is recognised only before `--`, since everything from
there on is the tool's. The args handed to the tool were still stripped of
`--project`, `--personal` and `--tool-mode` on both sides of it, so
`langwatch codex --help -- --project acme` lost the tool's own `--project`.

The wrapper's flags are now stripped before `--` only, and the rest is passed
through unchanged.

* test(langy): a refused account seed names the host and nothing else

The refusal printed the app address as given and the database address with
its user and password cut out. An address can carry a secret in more places
than that: a token in the app address, an `sslpassword` or a token in the
database address's query. The refusal ends up in a CI log, so it now names
the parsed host alone, and says so plainly when the address does not parse.

* test(langy): a seeded account's two rows are written together

The verified user was committed before its password account was written. A
failure in between left a user with no way to sign in, and the next run
refused its address as taken, so the scenario could not recover.

The store now has one operation for both rows, run in one transaction: the
account's id is the user's id, so the user has to exist first, and either
both rows land or neither does.

* fix(guided-onboarding): a read that failed is not read as an empty space

`useSpaceInUse` answers unknown while a space's read is loading or failed,
and the offer stays hidden then. It looked at the data alone, and the query
cache keeps the last list through a failed refetch: an empty list from before
the space was used, plus a refetch that failed, read as "not in use" and the
offer showed.

A read that failed now answers unknown whatever the cache still holds, for
the gateway's keys, governance's sources and both personal reads.

* fix(cli): the device session's key goes only to the address that issued it

Every API-calling command resolves its credentials the same way: a key given
by flag, then `LANGWATCH_API_KEY`, then the device session's key. The endpoint
comes from `LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT` first, and a folder's .env can set it. With no
API key given, the session's key was paired with that endpoint, so a cloned
folder could point every command at an address of its author's choosing and
receive the key of whoever ran a command there.

The session's keys, the login key and the personal project's, are all read
in `resolveFromSession`, which now hands out nothing when the login was made
against another address than the one the command targets. `resolveCredentials`
ends such a command naming both addresses and what to run: `langwatch login
--device` against the other address, or unset `LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT`. Machine
callers get a `login_endpoint_mismatch` document. A key given by flag or in
`LANGWATCH_API_KEY` belongs to the address the command targets and is used as
given.

Addresses compare by origin: scheme, host in lower case and port, so a
trailing slash, a capital letter or `:443` do not make two addresses out of
one. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` stay two addresses. `langy --share-control`
words its refusal from the same message.

* fix(cli): a --tool-mode with no value does not swallow the option after it

`--tool-mode` took the next token as its value whatever it was. In
`langwatch codex --tool-mode --help` that token is `--help`: the run was
recognised as a help run, then `--help` was dropped as the mode's value and
codex started a session instead of printing its help.

A following option is now a missing value, the rule `--project` already
follows. A value that is no mode (`--tool-mode bogus`) is still dropped, so it
never reaches the tool as a stray positional.

* docs(guided-onboarding): the space reads' comments say why, not what

The comments above `SpaceRead`, `settled` and `hasAny` restated their
declarations. The one on the interface is gone; the other two now carry the
reason: the query cache keeps the last answer through a failed refetch, and
null is what keeps the offer hidden.

feat(instant-evals): meter judgements on the gateway spend spine, a Stripe meter and a 1 USD free budget (#8220)

* feat(instant-evals): meter judgements on the gateway spend spine with a one dollar free budget

Rebuilt on main after the run and CLI branches landed as squashes: replaying
this branch's own delta onto them is the same tree a merge would reach, without
44 add/add conflicts against commits main already holds.

Judgements are recorded as gateway spend of request type instant_eval at the
Jev cost plus 30 percent, reported to Stripe on the langwatch_instant_eval_usd
meter, and an organization without a paid plan may spend one dollar in total
across every project it owns. The budget is checked before anything is judged,
for both a run and a synchronous query, so it bounds what was spent rather than
arriving as a bill.

* Address the review: correct the budget in docs, isolate meter failures, stop publishing our cost

Docs still promised a three dollar free budget after the constant moved to one.

Each billing meter now fails on its own: the loop's comment already claimed a
meter that fails does not stop the next, but the catch was around the loop, so
a throw from one meter's checkpoint read, total query or intent write skipped
every meter after it, with no self-dispatch to come back for them.

costUsd is what the judging cost us and it sat next to priceUsd in the run and
estimate responses, which published the margin. It stays in the billing records
and leaves the public API.

Also from the review: the text pass refuses a truncated read like every other
length-sensitive pass, a judged probability map is shape-checked rather than
cast, the manifest generator re-encodes credentials it puts back into a URL,
the keyset advice names SpanId where the statement projects it, the migration
carries its IRREVERSIBLE note, and the ADR's judgment key matches the table.

* Stop a run under way from spending past the free budget, and wire the Instant Evals meter into Stripe

A run records its spend once, when it finishes, so the admission check reads a
ledger that knows nothing about a run already under way: one accepted run could
judge its whole selection however far past the budget that took it. The page
check now hands the budget what this run has judged so far, priced the way its
finish will price it, which bounds a single run to one page of overshoot.

Stripe gains GROWTH_INSTANT_EVAL_USD and the INSTANT_EVAL_USD meter. Both are
provisioned per mode by hand, so unlike every other name they are allowed to be
unmapped: resolution skips them instead of throwing, and a Growth checkout
carries the metered item only where it resolved. Without that, this code would
have failed the app at boot in any mode whose catalog had not been synced yet,
and a checkout that died over a meter for a separate feature would have blocked
every Growth signup.

* Give each meter's report its own function so its failure stays its own

The per-meter catch landed inline, which took the handler past the complexity
and line limits.

fix(coding-agent): charge a session's usage to the branch declared under it, not to its whole lifetime (#8169)

* fix(coding-agent): charge a session's usage to the branch declared under it, not to its whole lifetime

The pull-request usage split read only the per-call fact rows, which a span-only agent (codex) never writes, so a long-lived codex session declaring a branch per pull request was charged whole to one of them. Model-call spans are now stamped with the declared context like log records are, the session fold records what was spent under each context next to its counters (migration 00097), and the split reads that record first. Undeclared usage of a session that also declared work follows its first declared branch, and both read surfaces hand the tenure rule the same pull requests.

* fix(coding-agent): a saturated usage record charges its gap to no pull request, and split the two long reads

The lint gate caught four new Biome violations: shareOfPullRequest was one
over the cognitive-complexity limit, and three reads in the usage service
were one to six lines over the per-function limit. Each comes apart at a
join that already had a name: the undeclared-usage winner, the pull requests
a project's own work touched, one discovered pull request as a row, and the
mapped-pull-request lookup.

The review also found a real gap behind the bound. The fold stops opening
contexts at MAX_USAGE_CONTEXTS, so a session past that bound keeps charging
calls to its counters with nowhere to record where they went, and the read
was pricing that whole gap as pre-declaration usage and handing it to the
first declared branch. A session with more than two hundred contexts would
therefore charge a later branch's spend to its first pull request. The read
now recognises a record of exactly that size and gives the gap to nobody:
the weight stays in the denominator, so every pull request's share shrinks
by its own amount instead of one of them absorbing the lot.

MAX_USAGE_CONTEXTS moves to coding-agent-session.types.ts, beside the record
shape it bounds, because both the writer and the reader need it now.

* fix(coding-agent): the first declared branch only wins where it was declared

The undeclared-usage rule looked its first branch up among this repository's
pull requests using a bare name, and a name is not enough to say which
repository it belonged to. The row carries one repository field, overwritten
on every new declaration, beside a branch set that is never reset, so a
session that moved repositories keeps the old repository's branch names next
to the new one's. A session that began on `main` or `fix/...` in one
repository and later opened a pull request in another would hand the second
repository's pull request every token it spent in the first.

The ledger supplies what the name lacks, since its entries carry a whole
context. A first branch the ledger weighed only under another repository now
leaves this repository's unstamped bucket unowned. A first branch the ledger
never weighed at all is not evidence of another repository, so it still falls
through to the per-branch lookup, which answers undefined for a branch with
no pull request here; that is the case the existing default-branch scenario
covers and it reads the same as before.

* fix(coding-agent): a branch name worked in two repositories follows whichever declared it first

The repository guard asked whether ANY weighted context carried the first
branch's name on this repository. A session that worked `feat/linkage` under
another repository first and under this one later answered yes, so this
repository took the whole pre-declaration bucket even though the session had
begun elsewhere.

The record is ordered first seen first, so the first entry carrying that name
is the repository the branch was first declared under, and that is the one the
pre-declaration usage belongs behind. `find` rather than `filter` plus `some`.

The branch itself still comes from the row's branch set, which is what knows
the order and keeps branches the session spent nothing under; deriving it from
the record instead would skip a first branch that recorded no usage, which is
the default-branch scenario.

* feat(idpsim): a directory big enough to sync, and the changes between syncs

Two users is the right size for "does a sign-in work" and the wrong size for
every question about provisioning: whether a sync is incremental, whether the
receiving side pages its lists, whether a deactivation reaches the membership
table, what a thousand joiners does to the screen an administrator is reading.

THREE VERBS. `population` decides how many people there are — seeded, so the
same request twice produces the same directory, and growing keeps everybody
already there rather than regenerating the organization. `churn` decides what
happened to them since the last sync: join, leave, deactivate, reactivate,
rename, regroup, in counts rather than percentages. `scim-sync` carries the
difference across. Each is a control-API verb answering in JSON and a form on
the tenant page, because the question is usually asked while looking at a
screen.

A SYNC, NOT A REPLAY. `scim-push` sends every user as a create, which is right
exactly once and all conflicts afterwards — so the interesting question could
not be asked at all. The sync reads what the receiving side holds, matches it
the way a real provider does, and sends only creates, PUTs and a PATCH on
`active`. Run twice with nothing changed it sends nothing, which is what makes
every later run a measurement of the round rather than of the directory.

Two details, because they are the two that bite:

  PAGING. The read follows startIndex to the end of the collection. Reading
  only the first page would see 100 of 5,000 and call the other 4,900
  departures.

  IDENTITY. Matching is on externalId, falling back to userName. Somebody who
  changes their name and address keeps their external id, so they are an
  update and not a delete followed by a create — which is what matching on
  address alone produces, and what silently orphans whatever the receiving side
  had attached to them.

Every run reports elapsed and requests-per-second, so "how long does 5,000
take" has an answer. Failures are counted in full and reported up to 25.
Departures deactivate by default and delete on request; `dryRun` works out the
difference and sends nothing.

Verified against a live simulator, tenant 1 syncing into tenant 2's own SCIM
server: 5,000 created in 250ms; a 120/80/40 churn round carried as 117 creates,
38 updates and 77 deactivations; grown to 20,000 with 14,960 creates and no
spurious updates; two consecutive re-syncs sending nothing; delete mode
removing 579 records.

One bug found and fixed while verifying, with the regression tests that fail
without the fix: growing a directory that had already churned numbered the new
people from the COUNT rather than from the highest index in use. Those diverge
the moment somebody leaves, so the generator re-minted indices the joiners had
taken — two people under one id and one external id, and a receiving side
matching on external id then saw one person whose name changed back and forth
on every sync, for ever.
