fix(identity): a fleet that can boot, single sign-on that routes through the broker, and two stuck sign-in cohorts (#8244)

* fix(identity): the heal pass asks for the users whose secrets drifted, not for every user

The sign-in credential repair never finalizes a user — while both branches
can still write a secret there is no state in which one can no longer need
repairing — so the runner never treats a healed user as terminal and
re-proves everyone it is handed on every pass. Handed the whole User table,
that is a Redis claim, a state read, an Account read and a state write per
user per pass, and the boot preflight has to complete two passes before a
process may serve.

At a few thousand users that ran past the startup probe's budget, so no pod
bound its port, every replica sat in CrashLoopBackOff and the rollout timed
out waiting. Nothing was wrong with the preflight or with the migration: the
cohort simply became every user, and the cost is proportional to the cohort
rather than to the work outstanding.

So the enumeration carries the condition instead. A user can only need the
heal where one of their Account rows is ahead of the AccountCredential row
mirroring it — no credential row yet, or a legacy write after the copy — and
that is the comparison the carry service already makes per account, lifted
to the question of which users to visit at all. The heal then settles: the
carry writes the account's own updatedAt across, so a repaired user leaves
the set, and a later legacy write bumps Account.updatedAt and puts them back.
Level-triggered as before, without the sweep.

A migration declares that narrower set as `candidateTenants`, and a pass runs
one runner per distinct source. They cannot share one: a runner drives every
migration it holds over the one source it holds, so the narrowest declaration
would silently become everybody's cohort and the identifier backfill would
stop reaching the users it must finalize.

* fix(migrations): a peer's claims stop keeping a whole fleet from booting

Narrowing the heal's cohort was not enough. Every replica runs the boot
preflight, so a rolling deploy has a dozen of them sweeping the same tenants
at once and each reads the others' leases as `claimed`. Convergence required
`claimed === 0`, which none of them can reach while the others are still
booting, and none finishes booting until it does: each waits for peers who
are waiting for it. Measured on the deploy that widened the cohort:
`advanced: 0` every pass, `claimed` climbing 100 then 1243, twenty-five
passes, a preflight failure and a crash loop. No startup-probe budget fixes
that, because the loop never ends on its own.

So a pass that moved nothing and was shut out of only PART of the fleet now
counts toward settling, and three of those in a row start the process. The
tenants it could not claim are being driven by the peer holding them, their
migration gates stay closed and they are served on the legacy path — the same
bargain a held or parked tenant already gets — and the worker's re-drive
cadence covers a peer that dies mid-pass.

Total contention still never counts, however often it repeats. `lease.acquire`
fails safe to "held" on any Redis error, so being shut out of everything is
also exactly what an unreachable Redis looks like, and a process that learned
nothing about any tenant has no grounds to call anything settled.

Review findings, same change:

The heal's enumeration was missing its `@tenancy` opt-out. The raw-query guard
reads the SQL text and refuses a query with no tenancy predicate, and this one
scans two identity tables that carry no project or organization at all — so
the very first pass would have thrown out of `findTenantIdsAfter`, failed the
preflight and stopped the process from serving. It now carries the annotation
and a test drives the real query through the real guard, with a second case
proving the guard is running rather than waving the query through.

`groupByTenantSource` returned a map keyed by source, which merged a source
registered again later into its earlier bucket: [A(s1), B(s2), C(s1)] drove as
A, C, B, with C overtaking a migration it was registered after. It returns
contiguous runs now, so registration order survives grouping. A source that
appears twice is paged twice, which only a registration that actually
interleaves ever pays.

The enrollment suite's Prisma stub had no `$queryRaw`, so the pass threw
`TypeError` there as of the previous commit.

* fix(migrations): import PrismaClient from the generated client in the tenancy test

Prisma 7 does not re-export the type from `@prisma/client`, and the app
typecheck does not look at test files — so this only surfaced in
`typecheck:all`, which is what CI runs. Matches the repository under test.

* style(identity): sort the two import lists this branch added to

Biome's organizeImports assist runs at error severity in CI; both new import lines landed out of order. No behaviour change.

* test(system-migrations): drop a docblock that restated the helper it sat on

* fix(auth): the badge for the provider you last signed in with comes back

The sign-in screen stopped showing which social provider got you in last.
It still worked for a password or a passkey, because those record the badge
themselves the moment they succeed.

A federated dial cannot do that. The browser leaves for the provider and may
never come back signed in, so writing the badge at the click made "last used"
mean "last clicked" and a provider somebody tried once wore it forever. The
dial parks the method instead, and only a session may promote it.

Nothing promoted it. The promotion sat in an effect on the sign-in screen,
gated on a session — but a federated dial hands better-auth `callbackURL ??
"/"`, so the provider's callback returns the browser to the app root. That
screen is never mounted again, the effect never runs, and the parked method
never became the badge.

So the promotion moves to the session fetch, which is the one thing every
landing passes through and the only place a session is proof the hand-off
worked. It is a no-op when nothing is parked, so an ordinary landing pays
nothing for it. The sign-up screen, which parked a method and never promoted
one at all, is covered by the same move.

Reading the badge after that promotion also makes the sign-in screen's own
analytics name the method that just got the person in, rather than the one
before it.

The two scenarios that covered this were bound to tests that seeded the badge
into storage directly, so they proved the picker renders a badge it is handed
and never that anything hands it one. The new scenarios follow the round
trip: dial, land, badge — and they fail without the promotion.

* fix(auth): a dial you abandoned cannot take the badge from the method that let you in

Review caught the other end of the pending slot. Promoting on any session
made an abandoned dial outlive its own flow: back out of the consent screen,
sign in with a password instead, and the first session fetch after that
promotes the parked provider straight over the badge the password just
earned. "Last clicked" beating "last used" again, by a longer route.

So a method that actually gets somebody in retires whatever is parked, since
it has just settled the question the parked one was waiting to answer. A dial
still in flight in another tab is retired too, and a provider that does come
back signed in goes unbadged that once — the right way round, because a
missing badge costs a glance and a wrong one sends somebody to a button that
will not let them in.

* fix(identity): a real native account retires the derived identifier that predicted it

64 users on cloud are held at `migrated` and will never finalize. All of them
are Google or GitHub, which is exactly the set of Auth0 upstreams a broker
subject can be unfolded into.

The derivation states the native identity a broker subject implies, so a
native callback resolves before any native sign-in has happened. When one
does happen, better-auth writes the real Account row and the prediction has
been overtaken — but nothing retires it. The plan's `nativeSubjects` guard
keeps ONE pass from stating both facts at once and says nothing about a
derived identifier an earlier pass already wrote. That row stays live, its
source broker row is still live so the orphan compensation never reaches it,
and it holds the provider subject against the identifier the real row
implies, which carries that row's own business time and is therefore a
different identifier entirely.

So the attach loses the subject on every pass, the fold parks the loser, the
parity diff never clears and the user never finalizes — which also means
`carryForUser` never runs for them and their secrets stay on the legacy
branch. Sign-in still works, through the fallback ADR-116 exists to retire,
so this is a stuck cohort rather than an outage.

The compensation now detaches a derived identifier whose subject a real
native row asserts, before the adoptions rather than after, so the same pass
can then state the identifier that row implies. Toward the real row rather
than away from it, because that row is the stronger statement of the same
fact: the provider's own account as better-auth wrote it, able to hold
tokens, and outliving the broker's teardown. The derived identifier was only
ever an inference standing in until a native sign-in happened, and it has.

The service suite's double now models the projection's partial unique index
over the live states. Without it the harness folded two live rows onto one
subject, which is the precise failure this pass exists to avoid, so the
regression tests would have passed against a world where the bug cannot
happen. With it, both new tests fail if the compensation is removed.

* fix(sso): an organization pinned to a provider behind the broker is sent to the broker

People at brokered enterprise organizations typed their work address and
were told single sign-on was not finished being set up, then offered a
password form. Their single sign-on had been set up all along.

The router found their connection and judged it undialable, because
`configured` was strict equality between the provider the deployment mounts
and the organization's legacy pin. The pin is not a mounted provider id and
never was: `isSsoProviderMatch` defines it as a provider name or a
`providerAccountId` prefix, so on a deployment that brokers sign-in it names
the provider BEHIND the broker. Compared by equality against the broker's
own id it can never match, so every such organization read as one naming a
provider nobody here mounted. The same comparison existed twice, once over
the legacy columns and once for grandfathered rows in the projection.

It was undialable a second way as well. The pin was handed out as the method
id, and the sign-in surface can dial a connection, a bridge method or a
mounted provider, none of which a raw pin is.

`legacySsoDialOf` reads the pin as what it is and answers which mounted
method carries it: the pin itself when it names the mounted provider, the
broker when the deployment brokers, and nothing when the two genuinely
disagree, which still falls back to the local set with
`method_not_configured`. Both routing paths use it, and the projection
repository now takes the dial rather than a yes, so whether a connection is
dialable and what gets dialed cannot come apart again. The address already
rides along as the login hint, and the broker's own home-realm discovery
takes it from there, which is how these people signed in before.

This decides only whether there is a door. Who is let back through it is
unchanged: the callback still holds the pin against the arriving account.

The two tests that encoded the regressed rule paired a mounted broker with a
different pin and expected a refusal. They now pair two providers that
genuinely disagree, which is the case that must keep refusing. The new
regression test drives the real router over the real repository, and fails
with the broker branch removed.

* fix(auth): a provider my address was routed to earns the badge too

The button on the routed hand-off parks its method before dialling, so the landing can badge it. The automatic dial beside it did not: it called signIn directly. That is the dial nobody presses, and it is the ordinary way in for everybody whose organization owns their domain, so the people who sign in this way every day were the ones never badged, and the sign-in report named whichever method they had used before.

Parked inside RoutedToConnection rather than at its callers, because the sign-up screen reaches the same hand-off.

feat(traces-v2): enter to search, a routed search bar, instant evals in the filter bar, Langy in sync with the explorer (#8234)

* feat(traces-v2): Enter searches, and a sentence is routed before it runs

Typing in the Trace Explorer search bar no longer searches; Enter is the
one path out of the bar and blur keeps the text unsearched. A text with
bare words goes to the new tracesV2.routeSearch, where the classifier
(or, without it, the FAST model) decides whether it is a filter to build,
a judgement each trace needs, a literal phrase, or a question for Langy.
Every failure on the way is a phrase search, never an error state; with
no model at all a closable primer says what a model would add.

The translator's node ceiling gets its own code, filter_too_complex, with
copy that says to quote the sentence and a one-click fix on the table;
the client checks the same count before sending. Cmd+Enter is removed,
and Ask Langy now attaches the whole view chip before the filter chip.

The instant_eval route hands a typed payload to useInstantEvalRoute, which
applies the phrase search until the run itself lands (spec pending).

ADR-139 records the router, its fallbacks and why routing is counted, not
metered.

* feat(traces-v2): the sidebar counts read the same predicate as the table

The facet counts came from tracesV2.discover, which ignores the active
query, ignores the hidden Langy origin, and snaps the window to a
six-hour bucket from a shared cache, so the sidebar could show 33 next
to a value while the table showed 0 traces. The sidebar now reads
tracesV2.facets: every registry facet counted under the active query in
the exact window the list reads, with the list's hidden-origins rule.
Each facet is counted with its own field left out of the query, in the
compiler (createFacetFilterCompiler), so it keeps listing its other
values and each value's count is the list's total with that value
selected. Facets that share a predicate share one batched scan; facets
on stored_spans and evaluation_runs reach the query through a
membership test on the filtered traces (scopeTraceFilterToTable).

Nothing is cached server side for the filtered read; the client keys it
in React Query by query and window with the list's staleTime. discover
stays for the value lists, the attribute key lists and the warm start,
whose rows show no count until the filtered read lands.

One selector, useExplorerCounts, feeds the selection header, the
pagination line and the new sidebar total from the count the list read
already returns, so no two surfaces can disagree; it also carries the
page's trace ids for the explorer projection to come.

The legacy findFacetCounts and findRangeStats repository reads had no
caller left and are gone.

* feat(traces-v2): an eval chip runs an Instant Eval inside the Explorer

An instant_eval route now ends as one chip, eval:"<question>", with
eval.trace, eval.conversation and eval.llm forcing the unit judged. The
run behind a chip is registered under a key over the question, target,
the other chips and the window, kept in the filter store, written to the
URL fragment as run=<key>:<runId>, and sent as evalRuns with every list,
sessions, facets and new-count read. The server resolves each run
against the project and the compiler turns the chip into a TraceId IN
(SELECT ... FROM instant_eval_judgments ... HAVING argMax(Passed,
UpdatedAt) = 1) subquery; a forcing spelling with no run compiles to no
rows and the bare field keeps its evaluator-name lookup.

tracesV2.instantEval.{estimate,start,cancel,get} wraps the run service
with the shorthand. When the shorthand refuses a filter field by name
the service resolves the trace ids with the Explorer compiler and binds
them as instant_eval_selection_ids. Under 0.50 USD the run starts on the
estimate; at or over it a dialog shows the question, rows and cost. A
spent budget or a missing judge is a popover on the search bar, and
every refusal falls back to the phrase search. A determinate bar with
Stop polls the run every second and refetches the list and facets as
progress moves; the counts read the run's counters during the run.

* fix(traces-v2): type the test fixtures and split the router functions the gates flagged

The facet descriptor fixtures are typed as the discover output instead of cast from literals, the model role is the FAST enum member, and the router unit test's decision recorder is a typed mock. The search router is a set of module functions over its dependencies, the model route call and its interpretation are their own functions, and the search bar's submit and the Instant Eval route each hand one step to a hook of its own.

* refactor(traces-v2): the Explorer is one store with pure transforms

The filter, view and selection stores become slices of one explorerStore, joined by a rows slice that holds the open rows (out of component state) and the last read's count. A slice reaches another through get(), so a lens switch installs its filter and a sort change drops the keyset cursors inside one store. Every consumer imports explorerStore, and the types and lens helpers come from the slice that defines them.

The page state a change can touch is the ExplorerState pick. setFilter, toggleFacet, setTimeRange, setLens, setSort, setGrouping, setPage, setPageSize, select and expandRow are pure functions over it with a closed list of refusal codes, the sidebar's facet click runs the same function, commitExplorerState writes a transformed state back through the store's own actions, and readLiveExplorer answers the page with the count the header shows.

* feat(langy): Langy drives the Trace Explorer through explorer.* actions

The Explorer registers eight typed actions with Langy while it is open
(setFilter, setTimeRange, setLens, setSort, setPage, select, getState,
runInstantEval). Each change runs the pure transform and commits through
the store's own actions. getState waits for the list to answer the state
it reads, so the count it reports is the one on screen.

With no Explorer open, the three actions that can be a link answer an
href built by the page's own fragment encoder, labelled "View in Trace
Explorer", and the result card links there. getState answers the saved
defaults with no count. The rest are refused with langy_ui_no_browser.

The REST trace search leaves out Langy's own traces unless the request
names an origin, the same rule the Explorer applies, so a CLI count and
the Explorer count agree. The Explorer link on a trace search card now
carries --filter, --errors-only as status:error, and the lens the user
is on when that lens keeps the result set.

* feat(skills): find-traces skill, primary and secondary way of working

New recipe skills/recipes/find-traces. When finding traces is the ask,
Langy opens the Trace Explorer and drives explorer.setTimeRange and
explorer.setFilter, then reads the count with explorer.getState. When
traces are a step in another task, it stays on the page and answers with
trace search cards and their Explorer link.

The skill takes the window and the filter from the page context, names
no origin so its counts match the Explorer, and tries every form a
concept can take (events, annotations, evaluator results, attributes,
text, a wider window) before reporting that nothing matched.

Langy's routing table sends trace-finding asks to it, agent-performance
and tracing point at it, and drive-the-ui lists the explorer kinds. The
Trace origins rule no longer adds --origin application.

ADR-140 records the one-store decision. An e2e scenario with a fake
Explorer tab covers thumbs down stored only as events.

* chore(skills): regenerate the setup skill bodies for the tracing skill change

* fix(traces-v2): the sidebar total gets a row of its own

At the default sidebar width the total shared the header row with the
Configure chip and the two texts painted over each other. The total now
sits under the header and may wrap, which the Instant Eval summary needs
while a run judges.

* fix(traces-v2): the routed query replaces the sentence in a focused search bar

Enter keeps the editor focused, and the store-to-editor sync skipped a
focused editor, so after the router answered the bar still showed the
sentence with the Enter hint while the table ran the generated filter.
The sync now applies the answer to the user's own submit as long as the
editor still holds the submitted text.

* fix(instant-evals): a deployment with no query identity answers as not enabled

An estimate on a deployment that provisions no LangWatchQL identity died
inside the row source with a plain error, so the caller got a 500 with
"unknown error". The run service already treats a missing query
capability as the feature being off; the capability now also needs the
deployment identity, so the refusal is instant_eval_not_enabled.

* fix(cli): trace search reads epoch milliseconds for its window flags

The help says --start-date and --end-date take an ISO string or epoch ms,
but an integer string went through new Date() and reached the API as
null, which it refused with a validation error. The flags now use the
instant parser the other commands share.

* fix(traces-v2): the search bar names the estimate and the start of an Instant Eval

The Searching indicator covered the router only. A sentence routed to an
Instant Eval is followed by an estimate and a start before the progress
bar exists, each taking seconds, and the page stood still meanwhile.

* fix(traces-v2): an Explorer Instant Eval judges only the rows the table shows

The table hides Langy's own traces unless the query names an origin, but
a run over the bare chips judged them too: a window the table counted as
1,399 traces was planned as 1,450 rows. The Explorer's request now adds
the same origin exclusion to the run's filter.

* fix(traces-v2): pace the reads a running Instant Eval triggers

Every change of the run's counters, about one a second, invalidated the
list and the whole facet batch, and each invalidation replaced the read
in flight. The client cancelled the request but the server kept running
the query, so a run stacked a facet batch per second, each filtered by
the verdict subquery; locally that took ClickHouse down within a minute.
The list is now read at most every 2 seconds and the facets every 8
while the run judges, a read in flight is left to finish, and the read
after the run ends is never skipped.

* fix(sdk): an instant eval response with no body is reported as a failed request

A proxy answering 502 with an empty body left openapi-fetch's error empty, so status, list and cancel returned undefined and the CLI failed with a TypeError on a field read. The service now decides on the response status as well as the error.

* fix(ui): the pagination summary and the page numbers no longer overlap in a narrow table

With the Langy panel open beside the Trace Explorer the footer's 1fr auto 1fr grid squeezed the summary under the navigator. The summary track now keeps its max-content width and the empty third track gives way first, so the navigator stays centred while there is room and sits beside the summary when there is not.

* fix(langy): a reduced trace result keeps its row ids, and a card never reads unnamed rows as no matches

An oversized tool result is reduced before it is recorded, and wide objects kept their first keys in alphabetical order. A trace row kept error to metrics and lost trace_id, so the card read a total of 13 and no row it could name and said '13 traces, showing 0. No traces matched.' The reducer now keeps identity keys (id, *_id, *Id) ahead of the alphabetical fill, and both trace cards treat rows they cannot identify as unreadable output instead of an empty result.

* fix(traces-v2): the Enter hint follows the routed query instead of covering its chips

The bar keeps focus when the router's query replaces the submitted sentence, so the hint stays visible, but a programmatic content change skipped the refresh that measures where the text ends. The hint stayed where the sentence ended, drawn over the chips. The end anchor is now measured after the replace.

* fix(traces-v2): the Instant Eval dialog shows the criteria as written

The classifier returns whole sentences, and the dialog folded them into 'Yes when X. No when Y.', which read 'Yes when The user complains.. No when'. Each criterion is now shown verbatim under a Yes or a No label.

* fix(traces-v2): an empty table during an Instant Eval says matches are still coming

For the first seconds of every run the table is empty because no row is judged yet, and it read 'Nothing matches these filters. Your query is valid, there is just nothing matching it', with Clear filters as the main action. While a run behind one of the query's chips is active the empty state now says there are no matches yet and that the run is still judging, and it leaves Clear filters out.

* fix(traces): the origin filter check and the router test deps typecheck

* refactor(traces-v2): no new Biome violations, eval runs reach the filter translator by name

* chore(query): regenerate the MCP reference fixture and the LWQL columns manifest

* test(traces-v2): seed the facet and eval chip suites inside the retention window

* fix(sdk): nullish coalescing in the instant evals error path

* fix(langy): the agent prompt fits its size budget again

* fix(instant-evals): the classifier pool speaks HTTP/1.1, so a cancelled page cannot wedge the process

undici negotiates HTTP/2 by default. Stopping a run aborts every classification in flight at once, and that many stream resets on one session left Node's HTTP/2 writer spinning on the main thread: the process stopped answering every request until it was killed.

* fix(traces-v2): a stopped Instant Eval is read until its numbers hold still

The page stopped polling when the status turned terminal, while the page of rows the run held was still landing verdicts, so the chip, the header and the table could each freeze on a different number. The run is now read until a second read answers the same counters, the table and the sidebar read once more, and only then do the bar leave, the chip read partial and the counts read the list's total. The bar says it is stopping, a partial chip keeps its quotes, and a page in flight checks for a cancel every second.

* fix(traces-v2): the router knows a disabled provider and an unreleased flag, Back returns to the last search, and the ask shortcut has one owner

A FAST model whose provider is disabled threw model_provider_disabled, which the router logged as a generic failure, so the model primer stayed closed. With Instant Evals not released for the project the router no longer offers the judgement route to the classifier or the model. A submitted search pushes a history entry while run keys rewrite it in place. With Langy available the Explorer leaves the ask shortcut to the Langy panel, which already listens for it on every page.

* fix(langy): an action that reaches a page still mounting is held for that page

The first action after a navigation arrived before the Explorer had registered its handlers, went unclaimed, and the server answered from saved defaults that the agent then read as the screen. The panel now claims at once when the browser is already on the owning page, runs the handler when it registers, and reports langy_ui_page_not_ready if it never does. A saved read carries a note saying it is not the user's screen.

* fix(traces-v2): the Instant Eval refusal popover reads as plain sentences and stays under the search bar

The copy says what an Instant Eval does, what stopped it and what happens to the words meanwhile, one sentence each. The popover opens below the bar and does not flip over it, so the typed text stays readable.

* test(traces-v2): opening a View in Trace Explorer link selects no rows

* feat(langy): the dataset page offers its dataset to Langy by name

The route chip only knows the dataset id. The page registers a chip with the same id and the dataset name, and page-named chips go ahead of the route's in the merge, so the agent is handed the name with the same ref.

* fix(traces-v2): under any query, span and evaluation facets read the listed traces, the named facet included

A query naming only an evaluator or span facet left that facet counting the whole window, Langy's own traces and rows outside the window included, while every other facet read the listed traces. With no query it stays off: measured on the seeded project it reads about 2 KB of attributes per trace in the window on each read, which ADR-139 records.

* fix(traces-v2): an empty table under an unjudged eval chip offers to judge it

An eval chip whose run covered another window, lens or filter matches no
rows, and the table said "Nothing matches these filters", which is a wrong
answer: the rows were never judged. The empty state now says so and offers

* fix(langy): the e2e fake tab and the saved-read test follow the page-arrival contract

The fake tab still passed a fixed handlers map where executeUiAction now
reads getHandlers, and the saved-read test read a note its cast did not

* fix(traces-v2): a selection does not survive a search that changed while the page was away

The Explorer store outlives the page, and the hook that clears a stale
selection skipped its first run on every mount. So leaving the Explorer,

The find-traces skill knew a saved state is not the user's screen but not

The skill needs `trace fields`, `trace facets` and `trace search --filter`.

* fix(traces-v2): a second Instant Eval judges rows, not the first chip's verdicts

The estimate and the start sent the whole bar as the filter, eval chips
included, while the run key was computed without them. So a second
question on a query that already carried a chip asked the server to

* fix(traces-v2): the empty state and the selection slice keep their shape, and a submit option typechecks

Three gates in one pass. The view key held a NUL byte, which made a source
file binary to git. The hook returning the submit function still declared
one parameter, so naming a route from the empty state did not compile. And
the empty state and the selection slice each grew past the complexity the
repo enforces: the empty-state copy, its buttons and the members of a

* fix(traces-v2): a single result is named "1 trace", from the one string both counts read

A query matching exactly one row read "1 traces" on the pagination line and
on the sidebar total. The two surfaces also built their copy by different
routes: the sidebar rendered the summary the counts hook produces, while the
pagination line was handed the raw noun and assembled the line itself, so only
one of them could ever be fixed at a time.

The copy builders move into their own module and gain the singular, and the
pagination line now renders the same summary string the sidebar does. One
function owns the words, so the number and the noun cannot differ between the
places that show them.

Found while checking two Instant Eval chips in one query, where the result was
a single trace.

* fix(traces-v2): the filter language keeps OR grouping and negated operands

Three places where an AST rewrite changed what a query means:

- `filterAST` returned the original node for a `UnaryOperator`, so a caller
  removing terms from `NOT (status:error OR service:api)` kept the ones it
  had just removed. The facet sidebar counted Status under its own term.
- `combineQueries` read "already grouped" off the text, so `(a) OR (b)`
  looked like one group and joined as `(a) OR (b) AND c`. It now reads the
  parsed top level.
- `splitBareWords` lifted a word out from under an `OR`, and the router
  rejoins the halves with AND, so `status:error OR refund` came back as
  `status:error AND refund`. A word under an `OR` stays explicit.

* fix(traces-v2): boolean names, curated provider logs, bounded run windows

- The new boolean contracts take the prefix the house rule asks for:
  `isLangyAvailable`, `isInstantEvalAvailable`, `isModelUnavailable`. The
  predicate that reads a failure keeps a name of its own.
- The three `logger.error` calls in `ai-query.ts` were handing the raw
  provider exception to the log, and a rejected key makes the provider's
  response body the credential. They log what the customer-facing
  disclosure already logs: provider, model, status code.
- The Explorer's Instant Eval window is bounded to epoch milliseconds a
  date can represent, so a malformed request is a validation error rather
  than a `RangeError` while the instants are written.
- `ProviderPrimerPopover` keeps its popover content in a private component.
- The `filter_too_complex` tip names what `maxNodes` actually counts.

* fix(traces-v2): a live window does not cap the facet membership test

`TRACE_WINDOW_WHERE` always bound the subquery on both ends, while the reads
around it drop the upper bound for a rolling preset. A filtered facet on
`stored_spans` or `evaluation_runs` therefore stopped at the instant the
request was built and counted fewer traces than the table showed. The scope
takes the window's live state and leaves the predicate off with it.

* fix(traces-v2): a new search drops the Instant Eval estimate before it spends

The sequence guard only moved when another judgement reached the route, so an
estimate in flight survived a search that turned out to be a filter, a phrase
or a question for the assistant. It could then come back, start a run and put
its chip over results the reader had moved on from, and charge for it. Every
submit now abandons the pending run first, dialog and refusal popover with it.

The new-count baseline also resets when a run registers behind an eval chip:
the runs are part of the query identity, so a count from before the run is
not a baseline the 0 to N pulse can be read against.

* fix(traces-v2): a run's scope drops eval chips server side, and two scenarios say what they bind

An `eval` chip left in the filter a run judges has no run reference behind it,
so the selection compiler would fall back to the legacy evaluator-name meaning
of a bare `eval:` and judge a different set than the Explorer shows. The
client already stripped the chips; the boundary now strips them too, so the
invariant holds for any caller.

Two `@scenario` annotations claimed more than their tests checked: the counts
rule is split into the selector's answer and the two surfaces that print it,
and the facet cache test asks under a changed query and a changed window
rather than reading the freshness window alone.

* fix(traces-v2): a lens round trip keeps the run behind its eval chip

A fragment naming only a lens carries no `q`, so the apply set the runs to
none while the lens brought its own filter back. An `eval` chip in that filter
came back without its run: the table showed nothing, the empty state offered
"Judge these results", and taking it started a second run over rows the first
one had already judged and charged for it again.

The apply now keeps a held run whose key an eval chip of the restored query
computes to. The key is the scope, so this only carries a run whose question,
unit judged, other chips and window all still match; anything else stays
pending and is judged again.

The unjudged sentence also stopped naming a cause it cannot know. A chip
arrives with no run from a shared link or a saved lens as well as from an
edited scope, so it says the scope has not been judged.

* docs(langy): a trace search names no origin, an export may

The Langy secondary run put `origin:application` on the card's link, and the
counts only agreed because of it: the sidebar in the same frame showed
Application 10, Langy 8, Evaluation 1. The origin came from
`skills/agent-performance/SKILL.mdx`, whose Common Mistakes line read
"questions about production behavior are answered from `--origin application`
traffic" with no command named. `traceExplorerLink.ts` was faithful; it
carried what the search named.

The two commands are now told apart. An export is a local sample analysed
offline, so choosing its origins is part of the analysis and nothing links to
it. A `trace search` answers with cards and a "View in Trace Explorer" link
that carries whatever it named, so it names no origin unless the user does
and the Explorer opens on the same set the card counted.

Pinned by a test over every shipped skill: no `trace search` command prints
`--origin`, and the export keeps its narrowing with the reason next to it.

* refactor(traces-v2): the search router is four files, none over 300 lines

`route-search.ts` held the contracts, the classifier's question and context,
the four route builders and the orchestration in 666 lines, and its test 578.
Split along those lines, with no re-exports: callers import from the module
that declares what they use.

- `contracts.ts` what the router is asked and what it answers
- `classifier-context.ts` the category question and the context block
- `routes.ts` the four builders and their fallbacks
- `route-search.ts` which one runs

The test splits the same way, over a shared `__tests__/harness.ts`.

* refactor(traces-v2): the bare-word test is one named predicate

Adding the OR check to the `splitBareWords` filter took it past the cognitive
complexity limit, which the new-violations gate counts. The six conditions are
one `liftableWord` helper now, and the negated tags and the tags under an OR
arrive as a single set.

* fix(traces-v2): the provider-error log payload has one builder, and an annotation binds

Two things the unit shard caught that a targeted run could not.

The `@scenario` on the new eval-chip test sat on its `describe`, so the parity
checker read it and dropped it: a title that looks bound and is not. It sits
on the `it` now, and the dangling-annotation guard is back to its recorded
population.

The test that proved the log payload is curated mocked `ai`,
`@langwatch/observability`, `modelProviders/utils` and the field catalogue.
The unit lane runs `isolate: false`, so those replaced the modules for every
other file sharing the worker, and one of them failed on a module that had
been swapped underneath it. The three call sites build their payload through
`providerErrorLogPayload`, and the test calls that directly with no mocks at
all.

* fix(traces-v2): Clear empties the search bar while it has focus

Clear runs on mousedown and preventDefaults it, so the caret stays in the
bar. The sync effect leaves a focused editor alone so it cannot race with
typing, which meant Clear only emptied the store and the words stayed on
screen until the next blur. Text the user never submitted is not in the
store at all, so for that case the effect never even ran.

Clear now reaches the document directly, the way the chip X widget already
does: the button bumps a counter the editor watches, and the editor empties
itself whatever the store holds. `reset` was exported by the editor hook and
called by nobody; it is now the one path, and it guards the content change
with the programmatic flag like every other write in the hook.

* fix(identity): a click on the card does not start a second passkey ceremony

The passkey autofill offer armed itself from `document.activeElement` on
`pointerdown`. Focus moves after that event, so at that moment it still names
whatever the person is clicking away from, which on a screen that autofocuses
the address field is the address field. Any click on the card therefore
started a conditional-mediation ceremony, including the click on Continue,
which starts a ceremony of its own.

Two ceremonies share one server-side challenge: the second overwrites the
first, and both assertions are then refused. An end-to-end run caught it as
"We couldn't use that passkey" on a passkey the account really held, with two
`verify-authentication` calls returning 400.

A pointer now counts only where it is aimed. Typing still reads the focused
field, because a keystroke has no aim of its own and the entrance autofocuses
the field for you.

* fix(identity): the secure-account dismissal reaches the server before anything else

"Not now" sent the account write last, after an awaited cache cancel that
waits on a refetch still in flight. Answering is very often followed by a full
page load, and a document that goes away in that window takes the request with
it: an end-to-end run showed no dismissal POST at all, and the offer came back
as a modal over the settings page the person had just been sent to, where it
blocked the page.

The write now goes out before anything is awaited. The cache work follows and
still cancels the in-flight refetch first, so a client-side navigation reads
the answer too.

* fix(identity): the dismissal write outlives the page it was sent from

Sending it first was not enough. The browser cancels every request still in
flight when a document goes away, and an end-to-end run lost the answer in
exactly that window: the offer came back as a modal over the settings page and
blocked it, on two attempts out of three.

tRPC calls can now opt into `keepalive` with
`trpc: { context: { keepalive: true } }`, which routes them through an
unbatched link whose fetch carries the flag. That is the platform's own
guarantee that a request completes after its page is gone, the one sendBeacon
gives, with a real response. "Not now" takes it.

* fix(traces-v2): the out-of-budget popover says it in two lines

It ran to six lines, repeating the question, the spend and the free budget,
so the one thing a reader needs (upgrade, and the words are searched
meanwhile) was buried. The refusal now carries no numbers and no question:
the figures are in Settings, Subscription, and the question is right above

* feat(traces-v2): an eval chip is green, and sweeps while it judges

A pale blue chip on a pale bar read as disabled, which is the wrong word
for a chip that is about to spend money judging. Instant Eval chips now
wear green, and while the run is estimated, started or judging a band of
light sweeps across the chip from left to right, so the bar itself says
work is under way rather than leaving that to the progress bar alone.

The Enter hint learned to sit after a chip label: it measured the end of
the text, and a chip whose label is wider than its text (any facet name,
and every eval chip once it reads "(pending)") put the hint on top of it.

* fix(traces-v2): the eval chip glows while it judges, and its X is part of it

The sweeping band read as a grey-to-green gradient rather than as work in
progress, and it washed out the green it was meant to decorate. The chip is
now solid green and breathes a green halo while its run is estimated,
started or judging, the same affordance the ask button wears, quicker
because this one ends. The ask button drops its own halo meanwhile, so the
bar never pulses in two places at once.

The remove button stayed blue beside a green chip: it is a ProseMirror
widget in the live editor, which the sibling selector did not reach. Both
halves are now matched by the chip field they carry.

The refusal explains what an Instant Eval does again, without the example
and without the figures, and the title names the quota that upgrading
lifts.

* fix(traces-v2): a routed query leaves a caret, not a selection over the chips

setContent leaves a selection across everything it wrote. On a bar without
focus the browser paints that selection over the chips, which is what turned
a green eval chip into a washed grey in some recordings while a screenshot
of the same page showed it green. The caret now sits at the end instead.

fix(migrations): a pass visits only the tenants with a migration left to finish (#8247)

The boot preflight still could not finish inside the startup budget. Every
pass enumerated every tenant, and for each one took a lease, read its state
row per migration, found it terminal, released the lease and moved on. On a
settled fleet that is the whole of the work: the user leg visited 9,004
users of whom about 8,000 had finished everything, and took 4m43s a pass.
Two passes are mandatory, so a booting fleet crash-looped.

A tenant holding a terminal row for every migration a pass drives has
nothing left to do, so the two default tenant sources no longer name it.
`pendingFor` enumerates a tenant unless it is `finalized` or `rolled_back`
for every one of the pass's migrations. One still to finish, parked, held or
never touched is visited exactly as before, so the runner's own cohort check
and terminal short-circuit stay the authority and no outcome changes. The
terminal list is derived from `isTerminalTenantStatus` rather than written a
second time. At this fleet's size the query skips 8,884 finished users and
returns the rest in 13ms.

A migration that declares its own tenants keeps them. Targeted operator
passes are left alone on purpose: somebody asking for a re-run of a finished
tenant should still see the pass visit it.

Visiting so few tenants makes one thing newly possible. A pass can now find
every tenant it sees claimed by peers, which the convergence loop reads as
what an unreachable Redis looks like, and keeps trying until it fails the
preflight. It now settles on that once this process has been granted a claim
earlier in the same preflight: `acquire` fails safe to held on any Redis
error, so one granted claim is proof the lease store answers. A process
never granted a claim still keeps trying and still fails.

test(migrations): type the raw-query call tuple where it is read (#8248)

fix(migrations): a preflight that cannot drain its own work starts rather than refusing (#8249)

* fix(migrations): a preflight that cannot drain its own work starts rather than refusing

The boot preflight queues work, waits for it to drain, and refuses to start
when it has not drained in 60s. That refusal is the one a booting fleet cannot
answer. The barrier runs BEFORE the process consumes anything, so the work it
waits on drains only if some other process is already serving that queue, and
on a fleet booting together there is none. A claim whose worker an earlier
crash-loop killed outlives it and blocks its group's head; each boot queues
more behind that head and refuses over it, which is precisely what keeps the
consumer that would drain it from ever starting.

Seen on the identity backfill after #8247 removed the enumeration cost: one
group, `active: 1` with no owner alive, `pending` climbing 32 to 50 across
boots, every replica crash-looping on the same group id.

Work that has not drained leaves its tenant HELD, and a held tenant already
starts on the legacy path with its migration gate closed - the file says so
itself, and already boots past held, parked, and peer-claimed tenants on that
reasoning. The wait is how a pass finalizes such a tenant sooner, never how it
stays safe, so giving up on it costs a later pass rather than correctness.
`waitUntilPreflightIdle` now logs the groups it stopped waiting for, for
operator triage, and returns.

Work that FAILED is a different thing and still refuses: a later pass will not
clear a fault. That half of the barrier is the half worth keeping, so the
deadline path now runs the same success assertion the settled path does, and a
group that failed or blocked by the deadline prevents startup as before.

This narrows a contract the spec pinned deliberately, so the spec moves with
it: pending and delayed work no longer prevents startup, blocked and failed
work still does.

* test(migrations): bind the drain scenario to the tests rather than to their describe

The `@scenario` annotation sat above the `describe`, and the parity checker
only reads one directly above an `it(` or `test(`. It was the silent verdict
the binding guard exists to catch: the annotation extracts fine, the title is
good, and it never reaches the binding table, so the scenario reads as covered
while binding nothing.

It moves onto both tests, which is what the scenario's two halves are - one
that the barrier starts past undrained work, one that it still refuses over
failed work. `check:feature-parity` now reports 81/81 bound for the file.

`createQueueDefinition` already generates a unique queue name, so the tests
take `definition.name` instead of generating a second one.

* test(migrations): the drain barrier's tests reach the deadline without waiting for it

Both tests injected a 250ms deadline and then waited it out on the wall clock.
The deadline check runs after the settled check, so zero reaches the same
branch without the wait: a barrier with nothing draining it reads its targets
once, finds work outstanding, and takes the timeout path immediately.

* fix(migrations): the pending-tenant-source teardown names the tenants it deletes

`afterAll` bulk-deleted `SystemMigrationTenantState` by migration name alone,
and the multitenancy guard refuses a write that names no tenant, because one
would rewrite every tenant's migration state rather than this file's rows. The
suite therefore failed in teardown with all 2058 of its assertions passing -
the red that reached CI was the hook, not a test.

The rows it seeds belong to the four tenants in `EVERY_TENANT` that get state,
so naming that set deletes exactly what the file created and satisfies the
guard. Pre-existing on main, from #8247; it fails every run of the shared
integration shard, so it is fixed here rather than left to block this branch.

* fix(migrations): the pending-tenant-source teardown deletes one tenant at a time

The previous attempt named the tenants with an `in` list, which the guard
still refuses: it tests `typeof where.tenantId === "string"`, so only a scalar
counts and a list reads as migration-wide. Exercised against the real
predicate, `{ migrationName: { in: BOTH } }` and
`{ tenantId: { in: EVERY_TENANT } }` both throw, and `{ tenantId: "..." }`
passes.

So the teardown loops, one bulk delete per tenant. That is the shape the guard
is asking for - a bulk write names ONE tenant, because a migration-wide one
would drop every tenant's `finalized` latch and return switched-over
organizations to their legacy path.

fix(identity): separate serialization retries with a random wait (#8213)

`withSerializationRetry` ran a lost transaction again at once. Two
transactions that lose to each other therefore restarted at the same
instant, conflicted at the same instant, and did so until the four
attempts were spent — and the raw P2034 the helper exists to absorb
reached the caller after all. CI showed the shape: four conflicts three
milliseconds apart from one pair of overlapping passkey deletes (#8200).

Each retry now waits a draw from a window that doubles each round (10,
20, 40 ms), so a pair that restarted together is pulled apart and one
of them runs alone. Nothing about the decision changes: only conflicts
are retried, four attempts is still the limit, and what was thrown is
what the caller gets. The wait and the draw are injectable, so the new
unit test pins the exact waits — three, between attempts, none after
the last — without reproducing the race, and fails on the previous
code. Both last-way-in repositories go through this helper and are
covered by the change.

Closes #8200

fix(cli): --project everywhere, and six refusals that did not say what they meant (#8259)

* fix(cli): --project on every command that runs inside a project

The flag was added a family at a time, so the whole instant-eval family
shipped without it: an organization login could estimate and run nothing
against any project but the personal one, and the refusal named no way out.
Adding it to one more family by hand leaves the next family to repeat it, so
it is declared once over the finished command tree.

Two lists carry what is not a plain data-plane command, each entry with its
reason: the commands that touch only this machine or answer for the
organization, and the five that already spell --project meaning something else
(login writes a key to .env, spend-events filters a listing). A command in
neither list gets the flag, so a new one inherits it and leaving it out is a
deliberate edit. project-option.unit.test.ts walks the tree and names any leaf
that is neither marked nor listed, and refuses a listed command that no longer
exists.

The value does not travel through the commands. Threading it into every action
is the per-family work this exists to end, so the preAction hook reads it off
the command commander is about to run and publishes it into the request-scoped
credential holder, where resolveCredentials picks it up with nothing passed.

LANGWATCH_PROJECT_ID was read and then dropped. A legacy project key carries
its own project, so the server answered from the key and the variable changed
nothing: a project id that matched nothing returned another project's rows with
nothing on screen saying so. Naming a project that the key in hand cannot be
pointed at is now refused, and the same case from the environment warns and
says which project answered.

Also, a fault in our own code is no longer reported as a network failure.
`chart schema` read .views.length off a payload that had no views, and the
TypeError surfaced as network_error with "check your network connection": a fix
the reader cannot make, for a failure that was not theirs. The reader now
separates a program fault from a dead socket, the schema shape is checked
before it is read, and a TLS failure stops presenting its certificate code as
one the platform chose, which the classifier's own docstring already claimed it
did.

* fix(cli): say what a refusal was about, and accept the pipe people type

Four smaller things found while probing production, each one a case where the
CLI knew more than it said.

An authorization refusal now lists the permissions the login on this machine
carries. `api-keys create` answers 403 to an organization admin because a CLI
login key is minted without organization:manage on purpose, and the refusal
read as a missing role, so the way out looked like an escalation rather than a
re-login. An agent holding a device login could not tell the two apart at all.

Logging in as another organization says whose login it replaced. A login
overwrites the session in place, so signing in as a second account left every
command answering from the first account's organization with nothing on screen
saying the account had changed, which is how a CLI sat on a throwaway test
organization for a morning while the real organization's projects looked like
they did not exist. It is told rather than refused because the new identity is
only known after the browser approval, and refusing there would reject an
approval already given.

`--jq` accepts a pipe into a path. `.data[] | .slug` was refused while
`.data[].slug`, the same reading, worked, and the refusal pointed at real jq in
the shell. It is the plainest expression in the language the flag is named
after. The subset's own convention decides the two pipe readings: a path
distributes over an iteration so the result matches the inline spelling, and
`| length` sizes the collected array as it already did.

Bound the project-selector scenarios left unbound by the previous commit, and
narrowed one to what it actually pins.

* fix(traces-v2): the eval fields say Instant Evals, not Other

The four eval fields had no entry in the facet-group taxonomy the suggestion
dropdown buckets by, so they fell into the trailing Other with the unmapped
time and dynamic-prefix fields, under a question-mark icon. A reader browsing
the dropdown had nothing telling them what eval, eval.trace, eval.conversation
and eval.llm are.

Their own group rather than Quality: those are stored evaluator results with
facets to browse, and these are a question answered per row when the chip is
applied, which costs money to run.

SECTION_ORDER only sorts sections that already exist, and the facet manager
builds its groups from the facets a project has, so four keys with no facet
add an ordering entry and no empty section.

* fix(traces-v2): a typed eval chip starts its run, and its question takes spaces

Typing eval:"question" and pressing Enter applied the chip and nothing
else: a query with only field:value terms never reached the router, and
the chip is a filter over a run's verdicts, so with no run it sat at
(pending) over an empty table. Enter now starts the run for a chip no run
has answered, straight to the estimate and the cost rule. The question is
judged as written: the reader wrote it, so no model rewrites it on the
way, and a refusal leaves the chip in place instead of turning it into a
phrase search. "Judge these results" under the empty table goes through
the same path, so it no longer strips the eval: and searches the words.

A space could not be typed into the question: the filter language ends a
term at a space, so the words after the first one fell out of the chip.
A space typed into an unquoted eval value now quotes it and keeps the
caret inside; picking eval from the field list opens the quotes the same
way. While the caret is inside quotes the field list stays closed, so a
word of the question such as "user" no longer opens it, where Enter
would have accepted a field instead of searching.

* fix(cli): tell each credential apart, and warn every request that needs it

Review findings on the --project work.

The "LANGWATCH_PROJECT_ID was ignored" warning was latched on a module
variable, so under the daemon only the first command of the process saw
it and every later one ran against the key's own project in silence. The
latch moves into the request-scoped credential holder: once per request,
fresh for the next one.

The identity notice was suppressed whenever any project selector existed,
including an ambient LANGWATCH_PROJECT_ID that the session path does not
read. It is now suppressed only for a project named on the command line.

The permissions line on a 403 described the login stored on this machine
even when the request authenticated with --api-key or LANGWATCH_API_KEY.
It is emitted only when the resolved credential is the login key.

--api-key and LANGWATCH_API_KEY were one key source, so a project key
passed by flag was answered with "unset LANGWATCH_API_KEY". They are two
sources now, each with its own way out.

gateway-budgets list, reset, update and archive act on the organization's
budgets, so they join the commands that take no --project.

A transport failure is read off structured evidence on the cause (syscall,
errno, or a transport code such as ECONNREFUSED or CERT_HAS_EXPIRED)
rather than off the sentence "fetch failed", which a program fault can
raise too. SyntaxError leaves the program-fault list: with no HTTP status
it is a body that would not parse, which is infrastructure.

Also: replacedSessionNotice takes named parameters, withCliAdvice no
longer sits under the renderer's docstring, the projectOption docstring
names the suite that guards it, and four eslint errors are fixed.

* fix(traces-v2): the Instant Evals facet group has a place in every perspective

The group added for the suggestion dropdown was missing from the three
facet perspectives, so it fell to the end after Custom and the pinned
order test failed. It now sits after Quality in each of them.

A space typed in the middle of an eval question kept only the part before
the caret: the rest of the word fell outside the quotes. The whole token
is quoted now, with the space where the caret was.

The empty table's Judge these results button has a test: it hands the
query as typed to the search bar, which starts the chip's run the way
Enter does. The two functions that take eval chips out of a query share
one parse-filter-serialize helper. Two files reformatted.

* fix(cli): only the transport's own codes count as a transport failure

Reading transport evidence off the SHAPE of a code caught Node's own
program-fault codes with it: `new URL(path, endpoint)` against a
scheme-less endpoint throws `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_URL]`, which read as
a dead socket and sent the user to check their connection for a bug in
the call. The check now asks a named set of libuv and OpenSSL codes plus
undici's `UND_ERR_` prefix.

A program fault is also read before the platform envelope now. An Error
carrying a code of its own looked enough like the envelope to have that
code claimed as a domain discriminant, so the same bad URL came back as
a handled failure named ERR_INVALID_URL. With no HTTP status, a
TypeError, RangeError or ReferenceError is ours, whatever the runtime
hung on it, and it carries no meta.

* fix(traces-v2): the submit hook fits the house limits again

The router call and the filter branch move out of useSubmitSearch into
useRouteSubmit and applyFilter, so the hook and its submit callback sit
under the line and complexity limits the house rules gate on. The empty
state test mocks only the field it reads.

* fix(cli): find the transport under the wrapper, and name every organization

The SDK's HTTP layer wraps a throw as `originalError`, and the body reader
unwraps it, but the transport check looked only at the error and its
`cause`. An expired certificate arriving that way carries a code and no
errno, so it was read as a code the platform had chosen rather than as a
network failure. The check now scans `originalError` and its cause too.

The replacement notice named an organization by its name or slug, and a
session stored with neither read as an empty identity being signed out.
The id is the last fallback now, on both sides of the sentence.

* fix(traces-v2): a typed chip's run keeps the same question under another target

The chip taken out of the query for a run's filter was matched by its
question alone, so eval.llm:"annoyed" beside eval:"annoyed" lost both
when either started. The chip is now named by field and question together.

* fix(traces-v2): leaving a question, and the field list after the first clause

Arrow Right, End and a click already left the quotes an eval question
opens, and Enter searched from inside them, but typing the closing quote
added a second one. It now steps over the quote that is already there.

The editor writes U+00A0 between clauses, and the browser turns a typed
trailing space into one, but the search grammar ended a token only on a
plain space. Every clause after the first was read as more of the
previous value, so the field list stopped opening once the bar held a
chip. U+00A0 ends a token there now, as it already did everywhere else
that reads the bar.

feat(self-hosting): connected self-hosted, hosted services metered against the license (#8232)

* docs(self-hosting): ADR-139 and the behavioural contract for connected self-hosted

ADR-139 records the design for licensed self-hosted installs calling
LangWatch-hosted services: the license registry, the license token as a
gateway credential with one managed key per license, classify as a gateway
route that forwards to the one classifier, the signed sync lease as the seat
grace rule, invoice billing with a prepaid credit grant, and the langwatch
upstream provider. It includes the threat model for the credential and the
Stripe mechanics verified against the docs and in test mode.

The seven specs under specs/self-hosting/connected-services are committed as
.feature.draft. The parity gate fails closed on a .feature file that enforces
nothing, so each spec becomes a .feature in the milestone that binds its first
scenarios. No draft and no @unimplemented tag remains when the work is done.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjZFjZtrELL8f4ags4KBoj

* docs(self-hosting): align ADR-139 and the specs with the operations runbook

The registry stores sha256(token), a second hash, instead of a peppered HMAC:
the token has 256 bits of entropy, so the second hash cannot be reversed, the
issue script needs no extra secret, and read access to the registry is still
not credential access.

Billing follows the Stripe mechanics the runbook verified: the commit is a line
on the annual one-off invoice and the credit grant charges nothing, the grant
expires 14 days after the term, a renewal grant waits for the old term's last
usage invoice, the usage subscription is USD only while seats and the commit go
on one-off invoices, the seat true-up is its own invoice with proration from
the day after the quarter closes, roll-forward under 50 USD is an explicit
command, and an invoice paid by wire is marked paid out of band from the
backoffice. reportUsageForMonth skips organizations without SEAT_EVENT pricing,
confirmed in the code, so connected customers are admitted explicitly.

The sync lease carries warnAfter (14 days) and validUntil (30 days). The
default seat overage allowance is 20% of the seats, rounded up.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01QjZFjZtrELL8f4ags4KBoj

* feat(licensing): a registry of issued licenses, issued from the backoffice with a server-held signing key

Every license LangWatch issues is now recorded in IssuedLicense, linked to the
customer organization it belongs to: the backoffice, the payment link purchase
and scripts/generate-license.ts all write it, and a license signed before the
registry existed is registered by pasting it (signature verified, seats and
term read from the license). The row carries status, entitled hosted services,
the seat overage allowance, seat rate, prepaid commit, the overage switch and
maximum, and the instance binding. Status is derived, so a license past its
term reads as expired with no row edit.

The registry never stores the token an install presents. licenseTokenFromKey
derives lwl_<sha256> from the canonical re-serialized license, so line wrapping
or a trailing newline cannot split an install from its row, and the row keeps
sha256(token). A reissued license held for delivery is encrypted.

Issuing moves to Backoffice, Licenses (operator only, the shared 404 for
everyone else) and signs with LANGWATCH_LICENSE_PRIVATE_KEY. license.generate
and the form that took a pasted private key are removed: any organization admin
on any deployment could reach that mutation, and it bypassed the generation
service's validation.

A license key is credential material now, so the backoffice organizations list
no longer returns it (write-only, like the S3 fields), and the tRPC audit step
redacts licenseKey on every action. license.upload had been writing whole
license keys into audit rows.

Existing offline licenses are pinned by offlineLicenseCompat.unit.test.ts, on a
fixture minted with the licensing code of origin/main: same key, same schema,
same plan, same hard seat cap, no network call and no registry read. The
migration is additive: one enum, one empty table, one column with a default.

* feat(self-hosting): the license token as a gateway credential (M2)

A self-hosted license resolves on the gateway as `Bearer lwl_<sha256>` with
an `X-LangWatch-Instance` header, next to virtual keys (ADR-139).

Control plane:
- resolve-key branches on the `lwl_` prefix and asks the license registry.
  Refusals have stable codes and say nothing about the customer:
  connect_license_not_registered, connect_license_revoked,
  connect_license_expired, connect_instance_required, connect_wrong_instance.
- The first install to present a license is bound with one conditional update.
- Each license gets its own managed virtual key (purpose CONNECT), created on
  first use, scoped to the customer organization, with its spend on the hidden
  governance project. Its secret is discarded. It is hidden from customer reads,
  refuses customer mutations, and reaches none of the customer's own model
  providers.
- Revoking or re-linking a license ends its managed key, and resetting the
  binding invalidates it, so the existing change feed evicts gateway caches.
- Migration 20260919130000_connect_virtual_key: enum value CONNECT and
  IssuedLicense.virtualKeyId. Additive.

Gateway (Go):
- domain.PresentedKey{Token, InstanceID} replaces the bare token in the auth
  resolver. The instance is part of the cache key for a license token only.
- A malformed license token, or one without an instance id, is refused without
  asking the control plane. Final refusals are remembered for 30 seconds.
- The control plane's connect refusals keep their code instead of reading as a
  revoked key or a retryable 503. herrgen carries the codes into the app, each
  with customer copy.
- Virtual keys resolve, cache and are refused exactly as before.

CI fixes for M1: the backoffice Licenses view is split into small components
(biome new-violations gate), audit redaction moved into a helper, and
.gitleaks.toml allowlists the offline license fixture and a base64 test literal.

The offline compat test now also pins that no licensing or enforcement module
imports the registry.

* feat(self-hosting): hosted routes, classify, usage and budget, metered on the license's managed key

Three gateway routes in the /v1 auth group: POST /v1/instant-evals/classify,
GET /v1/usage, PUT /v1/budget. Classify runs the existing budget precheck and
402. Each forwards a signed envelope {virtual_key_id, organization_id,
project_id, payload} to POST /api/internal/gateway/connect/:operation and
relays status and body; a control plane 5xx is hosted_service_unavailable.

Control plane (ee/licensing/connect): the managed key is looked up in the
registry and that is the entitlement check. Classify runs the one classifier
under the hidden governance project and answers the list rate only. Spend is
summed per managed key and written every 5 s or 500 calls as one instant_eval
row with requests and virtual_key_id set; failed writes are kept; shutdown
flushes (connect-spend phase).

Contract budget: GatewayBudget ORGANIZATION, MANUAL, BLOCK,
externalId connect-contract, synced by the registry after issue, revoke, term
change and link. Default cap is the sum of counted commits; the customer may
set a cap up to commit plus the enabled overage maxima.

Also fixes the issuedLicense integration test that was missing the managedKeys
dependency.

judges through POST /v1/instant-evals/classify with the license token and the

ConnectGatewayClient maps the host's refusals to the same codes, adds
connect_budget_exhausted (402), connect_unreachable (host and port to allow)
and connect_disabled, and goes through EnvHttpProxyAgent when a proxy variable
is set. tRPC router connect: status, setService, setCap (audited mutations).

* feat(self-hosting): license sync with a signed lease, the seat allowance and license delivery over sync

Connect host on the app: POST /api/connect/v1/license/sync takes the license
token, the instance id, the version and the two seat counts, records the last
report on the registry row and the peak of the license term quarter in
LicenseSeatReport, and answers with a lease signed with the license key pair
(services, seat overage allowance, warnAfter +14 days, validUntil +30 days).
Refusals reuse the gateway codes; 48 syncs per license per day. POST
/api/connect/v1/stats shares the handler of /api/track_usage, which stays.

A reissued license rides in the sync answer until the install presents the new
token; the second sync marks the replaced license superseded, retires its
managed key and erases the encrypted copy held for delivery.

Install: licenseSyncWorker (Connect on only, daily) counts seats, syncs,
verifies the lease with the embedded public key and stores it on the
organization. getSelfHostedPlan adds the allowance while the lease is fresh or
in its warning window; the members page and the invite flow say which seats
will be invoiced at the next quarterly true-up. Settings, Connect shows the

Backoffice licenses show last sync, version, reported seats and the quarter
peak. The chart sets SERVICE_VERSION from the app image tag when Connect is on.

* fix(ci): fixtures carry the sync and lease fields

* feat(self-hosting): invoice billing, the langwatch upstream provider and the Connect docs

Billing (ee/billing/connected): the commit is agreed on the license and the
organization budget follows it. ConnectedBillingService onboards an invoice
customer (send_invoice, 30 days, bank transfer through the provider or
LangWatch's bank details in the footer), one quarterly USD usage subscription,
a paid credit grant for the commit (metered only, expires 14 days after the
term) and one annual invoice for seats and commit; every id is stored before
the next step, so a failed run resumes and a repeat creates nothing twice.
Renewal keeps the subscription, resets the budget, and creates the renewal
grant once the old term's last usage invoice is finalized. Usage invoices
under 50 USD roll forward once. Finance marks wired invoices paid out of band.
Credit grants go through a per-request API version adapter on the pinned SDK.
reportUsageForMonth admits self-hosted customers with a billing account; meter

billing contact for months with usage. Backoffice Billing panel and the
connectedBilling router (operator only). A daily Cloud worker runs it.

Managed models (M7): provider family langwatch, a direct HTTP lane on the
install's gateway that forwards OpenAI-compatible calls with the license token
and the instance id and relays answers unchanged, streamed or not. The
install's control plane synthesizes the slot when Connect and the service are
on. On LangWatch Cloud the bundle carries connect_services; dispatch refuses
connect_service_not_entitled before provider resolution and an entitled
managed key gets the platform's shared providers.

Docs: docs/self-hosting/connect.mdx and a pointer from the licensing page.

* fix(self-hosting): accept a loopback http Connect endpoint, and fold the scheme compare the linter asks for

* fix(gateway): reserve langwatch as a routing handle, it is a provider family now

* test(self-hosting): scope the Connect settings assertions to the Instant Evals entry
