* fix: type the Connect endpoint helpers for checkJs, format a test, and add UsageByContext to the LWQL columns manifest

The manifest entry is the one main's migration 00099 adds to
coding_agent_sessions. Main is red on columnsManifestParity for the same
reason. The generator needs a container runtime, so the entry was written
from the parity test's own diff; that test checks it against a live
ClickHouse.

* fix(connect): send is_contract on the usage route, which the install requires

The install parses every hosted answer against a published shape. Its budget
schema requires is_contract, and the host's budget wire never carried it, so
every usage read failed with hosted_service_unavailable and Settings > Connect
could neither show spend nor switch a service on. Found on an install stack.

Both sides had their own fixtures, so neither suite saw the gap. The usage
schema is now exported and the host's suite parses its own answer with it.

* chore(connect): order the import biome asked for

* fix(connect): the managed key is attached only while the license still admits the call

An operator revoking between the status check in resolve and the attach left a
freshly created ACTIVE key on a dead license, so the caller got a valid JWT
after revocation and the revocation had no key to end. attachVirtualKey now
carries the customer, the instance and the term into the write, so the database
decides; a lost write retires the key it created and answers with the refusal
for the state the license is in. An attach that throws retires it too.

* fix(connect): the registry writes its row last, and names a duplicate the table caught

Three findings from the review. Marking the customer as a self-hosted customer
now runs before the row is written, so a failure there no longer strands a
registry row whose license key the caller never saw, and a retry is not refused
as a duplicate. A unique violation on a plain write is mapped to
license_already_registered, which the read-then-write duplicate check misses
when two writes race; reissue keeps its own refusal for a replacesId clash. The
record, the ports and the derived rules move to issuedLicense.ts, writing a row
to issuedLicenseRows.ts and reading one back to issuedLicenseViews.ts, and the
service suite is split by concern over a shared harness.

* fix(connect): the mint script writes in one transaction, and the drawers reset what they show

The registry row and the organization's license now go through one
prisma.$transaction, so a failure on either leaves neither and a retry does not
mint a second license beside a stale row. The issue drawer resets its whole form
when it opens rather than only the key, and switching it to register puts the
customer field back on an existing customer, which is what that button submits.
Detail wraps its value in a div, so a value that is a Text of its own is no
longer a p inside a p. RevokeDialog is split into its reason and its actions.
The offline-license contract scan walks nested directories and names the two
subtrees that are allowed to read the registry. Every new migration carries an
IRREVERSIBLE block saying what a rollback would lose, the license-generator doc
says unlicensed baseline rather than FREE plan, the refusal-privacy scenario is
named for what it checks, and three comments that restated their code are gone.

* fix(connect): refused license commands are audited, and the organization drawer is split into its sections

A command the registry turns down now leaves an audit entry naming the attempt
and the refusal before the refusal travels on, which was the half of the trail
an operator most often needs back. The organization edit drawer is split into
its five field sections with the change diff as four pure functions beside them,
which is what Biome was reporting on the function this PR edited. The gating
test restores an unset ADMIN_EMAILS by deleting it rather than storing the
string undefined.

* refactor(connect): the license-token route harness moves to a support module, and the license forms take named parameters

The signed internal request, the registry on real Postgres and the per-run
cleanup are shared setup rather than part of the suite, so the test file keeps
only its cases. The three license form setters take a single { key, value },
which is what the repo asks of a function with more than one argument.

* fix(ci): put the two new scenario annotations on one comment line

check-feature-parity drops a @scenario the walker finds inside a multi-line
comment block, so both scenarios read as unbound.

* refactor(connect): the registry service keeps the commands, the rules move beside it

The commercial terms rule, the customer a license is issued to, and the two
writes that follow a change to a row (ending the managed key, syncing the
contract budget) are their own modules, so the service is the commands and
nothing else. Both remaining organization lookups go through the same customer
rule rather than repeating findById and its refusal.

* fix(connect): a duplicate is refused by the constraint the table names

A reissue used to read every unique violation as license_already_reissued, so a
tokenHash or licenseId clash told the operator to reissue the replacement
instead. The constraint name now decides: only a replacesId clash is a reissue
refusal, and everything else is the license already being registered. Prisma
reports the target as the column on some versions and the index on others, so
the column is looked for inside each name.

* fix(connect): find the clashing constraint wherever the client reports it

Prisma 7 on a driver adapter puts the constraint under
meta.driverAdapterError.cause, not meta.target, so a replacesId clash on real
Postgres was read as license_already_registered and the reissue integration test
caught it. The column is now looked for in the whole violation report, and the
suite covers all three shapes a client uses.

* fix(ci): the reissue scenario annotation sits on its test, not above a const

* feat(connect): the license decides what an install may call, not a switch

`LANGWATCH_CONNECT_ENABLED` made the connected path a side path: its absence
was doing the work the license should have been doing, and an operator who
wanted to know whether an install calls LangWatch had to read a deployment
file rather than the license they were sold.

The entitlement now travels inside the signed license, as
`LicenseData.connectServices`. A license that names a hosted service can reach
it; a license that names none reaches nothing, which an air-gapped operator
checks by decoding the blob. The field is optional and last in the schema, so a
license signed before this release parses and re-serializes byte for byte and
resolves to no entitlement at all.

`LANGWATCH_CONNECT_DISABLED` (Helm `app.connect.disabled`) replaces it as the
escape hatch an audit asks for. It only ever refuses: with it set the install
builds no client and opens no connection, whatever its license says.

A service the license names is on. `Organization.connectServicesDisabled`
records the refusals rather than the approvals, so a customer who bought hosted
judging has it working before anyone finds a settings page, and a service an
administrator switched off stays off when the license is reissued.

The compatibility guarantee holds and gained tests: the license main minted
names no hosted service, a sync pass over an install holding it reaches the
client for no organization, and the product statistics keep posting to
app.langwatch.ai until a license names a service.

* feat(connect): one identity per install, and a report that says whether it arrived

The usage report has always been identified by
`${organization.name}__${organization.id}`. That put the customer's name in
cleartext on every report, named one organization rather than one install, so
an install carrying three organizations sent three reports nothing could join
back together, and could not be matched to a license row without splitting a
string.

It is now a UUID in `InstanceIdentity`: one row, minted the first time anything
asks for it, never rewritten, overridable with `LANGWATCH_CONNECT_INSTANCE_ID`.
Two processes minting at once both insert and one re-reads the winner's id. A
reader asks `readInstanceId`, which returns null rather than minting, so
resolving a seat plan and opening a settings page never give an install an
identity it has not needed; the seat path decides from the license blob before
it reads anything at all.

The report is one per install rather than one per organization, so
`collectUsageStats` counts across the organizations it was given instead of
parsing an id to find one.

The sender used to treat any resolved `fetch` as a success, and the receiver
was `.strict()`. Together they meant a receiver one release behind its senders
refused every newer install's report while both sides looked healthy for as
long as they ran. The receiver drops unknown fields instead of refusing the
report, and counts them as `unknown_fields` so a receiver running behind says
so. The sender reads the status and writes a refusal to
`InstanceIdentity.lastReportError`.

Also fixes two suites the merge of main left pointing at `../../rbac`, which it
had moved to `app-layer/authz/permission-adapters`.

* feat(connect): the usage report is one dictionary, with windows and a ladder

Every field a self-hosted install reports is now declared once, in
`usage-report/dictionary.ts`, with its category, its window, why it is
collected and where its value is read from. Three lists used to be kept by
hand: what the sender put on the wire, what the receiver accepted, and what the
docs said. That is how the receiver ended up refusing reports from installs
newer than itself. A test compares the dictionary with the receiver, so a
declared field that the receiver would drop fails the build.

Categories are GitLab's, because they are what a security review asks about:
standard, operational, subscription, optional. The optional category is
switchable as a whole and hostname on its own, both on `InstanceIdentity`,
because hostname names the customer's own network. Switching the optional
category off leaves a report that still says which release runs and how big the
install is, and says nothing about what anyone does with it.

Every lifetime total that had one now has a seven day and a twenty-eight day
figure beside it. The lifetime total answers almost nothing on its own: an
install that ingested a million traces two years ago and none since reads
exactly like one ingesting a million a week.

New: the onboarding ladder, eleven rungs each carrying the day it was first
reached and null where it never was, which is the half that says where getting
started stalls. Aggregated user email domains with counts, never an address.
Active users and active projects over four weeks. Model providers by name.
Storage backend, whether email is configured, whether the gateway is.

Still to come in this dictionary: spans, gateway requests and spend, Langy
turns, coding agent sessions and instant eval runs. Each needs a ClickHouse
query that does not exist yet; adding one is now a dictionary entry and a
reader rather than an edit in three places.

* fix(docs): the connect page says what an unentitled license reaches, not 'nothing'

* fix(connect): one migration for the refusal column, not a pair that undoes itself

`20260919140000` added `Organization.connectServices` and `20260921120000`
dropped it again to add `connectServicesDisabled`. Neither has ever run on a
deployed database and both are unmerged, so the repo rule applies: a migration
not yet in production is fixed before merging rather than compensated.

`20260919140000` now creates `connectServicesDisabled` directly, carrying the
comment that explains why the column records refusals rather than approvals.
`20260921120000` is deleted. Nothing else is renumbered.

Verified by applying the whole folder to an empty database.

* perf(connect): aggregate email domains in Postgres, so no address reaches the app

`userEmailDomains` read every user row with `findMany({select: {email: true}})`
and split the addresses in JavaScript. On an install with tens of thousands of
users that materialised every raw address in the application process, once a
day, to produce a handful of counts.

It is now a grouped query: `split_part(lower(trim(email)), '@', 2)` with a
count, so the work happens where the index is and no address ever leaves

* feat(connect): activation codes, redeemable exactly once

A fresh install pastes a short code instead of a license blob. It posts the
code to the connect host, which mints the license the code describes and
answers with it signed. The license paste and the file upload stay, because an
air-gapped install has to activate with no network at all.

Redemption is the part that had to be exactly right, and it has a precedent on
this branch: the TOCTOU CodeRabbit found in attachVirtualKey, where a check
followed by a write let a revocation landing in between hand out a valid
credential. The same shape applies here. The state the caller read is part of
the write, so exactly one conditional UPDATE finds a row and every other
redemption is told the code has been used. Two tests prove it: a unit test that
holds two redemptions at a gate after both have read the row and releases them
together, which goes red if the write is not atomic, and an integration test
that fires five claims at one code against a real Postgres and asserts one
winner. Neither depends on timing.

The claim is made before the license is signed, so a code can only ever mint
one license. Signing then failing would burn the code, so a claim whose minting
failed is released again, conditionally on still being that install's claim.

The registry stores a hash of the code and never the code, and every lookup
hashes what the caller presented first. So the stored value is a step away from
anything presentable: posting it back is refused as malformed, which a test
pins against the real route. A revoked code reads exactly like one that was
never issued, because the caller may be holding a code it should not have.

The code is LW followed by sixteen characters of Crockford's base32 without I,
L, O and U, so nothing in it is misread as something else. Case, spaces and
dashes are decoration.

Also fixes a real type error from the metrics dictionary commit: model
providers are scoped to the organization, and the report was filtering them by
projectId, which does not exist on that model.

* fix(connect): a conditional write decides who won, which updateMany does not

CI caught it on the activation codes: five installs redeeming the same
single-use code, three of them told yes. The write was an `updateMany` with the
state in its WHERE clause, which reads like a claim that only one caller can
win, and is not one.

Prisma compiles `updateMany` to
`UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ... WHERE <conditions>)`. Two statements
meeting on one row serialize on the row lock as usual, but when the second wakes
up it re-checks only what its WHERE clause says, and that is the subquery, which
still runs on the statement's own older snapshot and still returns the row. So
the second write lands on a row the first already claimed.

Three writes on this branch had that shape, all of them deciding who holds a
credential: `claimSingleUse` on an activation code, and `bindInstance` and
`attachVirtualKey` on an issued license. The last one is the write the earlier
TOCTOU report was about, so that fix was never in force. All three now state
their conditions against the table, where the re-check sees the committed row
and the second write updates nothing.

Proving this needs an interleaving rather than a burst: five concurrent claims
pass on a fast machine whatever the write does, because the statements never
overlap. `src/test-utils/rowLockInterleaving.ts` holds the first write open in
its own transaction, waits until `pg_stat_activity` reports the second parked on
the row lock, and only then commits. Put `updateMany` back and all three tests
fail in under a second.

fix(identity): first-day follow-ups on the new sign-in, and a way for an organization to connect its own identity provider (#8251)

* fix(tenancy): two platform-scope reads stop being refused by their own guard

The operator's SCIM oversight list reads sync state across organizations by
design, and the periodic migration re-drive names every registered migration
in one list. The organization guard had no shape for the first and the
migration-state guard read a migration name as a bare string only, so both
threw on every call: the oversight page failed to load and the pass that heals
straggling tenants never ran.

ScimSyncState gains the read-only platform-scope grant for findMany and count,
the pair the list's pagination makes. The rows are sync bookkeeping, the route
is operator-gated and audited, and every organization-facing read still names
its organization. SystemMigrationTenantState reads accept a finite, non-empty
list of migration names; bulk writes still have to name a tenant.

Both are pinned by driving the real repository through the real middleware,
which is the room these two had never been put in together.

* fix(identity): a provider subject two users claim parks the loser instead of stopping their fold

Account is unique on (provider, providerAccountId) across every user, and the
fold upserts the bridge row by id. When another user's row already owns the
subject the insert is refused, nothing caught it, the group queue retried
until it blocked the group, and that user's identity stopped converging
altogether. The identifier write one table over already parks the same
collision on purpose; the bridge write now does too. The incumbent's row is
never touched, a P2002 with no incumbent behind it still propagates, and the
rest of the user's identifiers keep projecting.

Parking writes nothing, so every replay warned again about the same pair. A
pair is now reported once per process and at debug after that.

The parity proof gains a named reason. An absent identifier whose subject a
live row already holds is a subject_collision naming the holder, not an
identifier_missing: one heals on the next pass, the other only when a person
merges the two accounts, and the report used to tell operators to wait for
both.

ADR-116 said the losing user's bridge row is still written. Across users it
cannot be, and the section now says so.

* test(tenancy): the re-drive guard scenario exists in the feature file its test names

* fix(auth): the single sign-on banner stops asking members who already comply, and stops pointing at a dead end

The banner read one stored flag that only a later sign-in ever clears, so a
member whose correct sign-in never reached the clearing branch kept it for
good. Its button led to a settings page that offers an organization requiring
single sign-on no way to connect anything.

The status is now a live answer: pending only while the flag is set and none
of the member's sign-ins satisfies the organization's pin. The decision is the
one the sign-in hook already makes, extracted so the two cannot drift, and it
goes through the pin matcher rather than comparing provider ids. The read
never writes; the hook still clears the flag at the next sign-in.

The banner now says the one thing that works - sign out, then sign in with
your work email - and its action signs out.

Members admitted only through a newer connection are not re-checked here yet;
the comment on the read says so.

* fix(traces): a span whose time cannot be stored is refused at the door and skipped on replay, instead of blocking its project

Nothing bounded the future edge of a span's time. A value wrong by orders of
magnitude - nanoseconds sent where milliseconds belong - reached the id
generator, whose timestamp field is 48-bit seconds, and threw. The event was
already stored and the failure classed as retryable, so the queue retried,
blocked the group and re-staged the same job for good: one span stopped a
whole project's span storage and rollup lanes. Both fold projections
normalize the same event and threw the same way.

One predicate now says what a storable span time is: finite, positive and no
later than the DateTime64(3) ceiling the span columns can hold, which binds
long before the id does. The OTLP and REST doors refuse a span whose start or
end time fails it, counted into the rejected-span response the client already
reads. The four projections skip such an event with one warning rather than
throw, so stored events stop poisoning their lane, and span timing ignores
the value so it can never become a trace's min or max.

The id generator still throws on garbage: clamping there would mint colliding
ids. A far-future but storable time is still accepted.

The REST door used to let a zero start time through, because its digit check
skips falsy values; the OTLP door already refused it as older than the past
cutoff. Both now refuse it.

* feat(sso): an organization on the single sign-on we set up can connect its own identity provider from its settings

The command that registers a connection beside the one an organization
already signs in through was only reachable from the back office, so moving
to your own identity provider meant asking for it. The Single Sign-On page now
offers it to an administrator: the same registration form as the first-time
journey, given the connection it replaces. Before the fields it says what does
not change - everyone keeps signing in as they do today until an administrator
switches over, and switching back stays available. A reader without the
permission sees who can do this, not a disabled form.

The Authentication overview says the organization should update and links to
that step; once the update is under way it shows where it stands in every
phase. The progress panel speaks of an update, never a migration, gives each
phase one plain status line, and tells the administrator what to do about each
condition holding it up, with the full list on a tooltip a test pins to the
rules.

The plan refusal on these procedures is now the named enterprise_plan_required
error the registry already has copy for, rather than a bare FORBIDDEN that
rendered under the unknown-error title. Only the plan's own refusal is
translated. Nothing here skips a blocker, selects a route or finalizes.

* fix(auth): the dashboard never draws a refusal from a read that has not answered, and a declined arrival says why

Two screens could tell a member they had no access before anything had been
read. The join takeover treated an organization that was still loading the
same as no organization at all, so a pending request for a different
organization took the dashboard over while the organization read was out; and
the team-access refusal was computed from fields that do not exist until that
read lands. The takeover's organization prop now has three meanings kept
apart - not resolved yet, none, and an id - and decides nothing about the
first. The access gate holds the page body until the read has answered.

A single sign-on arrival that is not considered for admission used to leave no
trace, so a member found without access could not be told apart from one whose
arrival was never looked at. Each of the conditions the decision
distinguishes now logs one line with a stable reason. No decision changes.

fix(traces-v2): a sentence meant to be judged is judged, and Test Connection sends a real call (#8268)

* fix(traces-v2): a sentence meant to be judged is judged, with or without a model to sharpen it

The judge question is written by the project's FAST model. When that model
is missing or refuses, the router used to quote the sentence and search it
as a phrase, silently: the reader asked for a judgement and got a literal
string match with nothing on screen to say so.

Now the sentence is judged exactly as typed, the way a chip typed by hand
already is (no criteria, no model between Enter and the estimate), and a
strip under the bar names what the search was read as, with a dismissible
hint carrying the model provider settings. The once-per-page primer popover
goes with it: one affordance, and it is the one attached to the search that
just ran.

The router's own log line now names the cause inline (the handled code, the
model, the status) because the collector ships only the message field.

* feat(model-providers): Test Connection sends a real generation, so every chat provider can be tested

Listing models proves a key is shaped right and reaches the vendor, and
nothing else. An account with no credit left lists its models happily and
refuses the first completion; a plan-billed lane (Codex on a ChatGPT
account) has no listing endpoint at all and was reported as untestable
while working perfectly. Either way the row said something that was not
what the customer needed to know.

Test Connection now sends one generation of one token down the same road
the product uses at runtime: the nlpgo proxy for the OpenAI-compatible
lanes, the AI gateway for Codex. It runs the cheapest chat model the
provider lists, against the credential on the row that was asked about
rather than whatever the provider key collapses to. A credential the
listing already refused is not asked twice.

Two new refusals, because they are two different things to do about it:
the account is out of credit, or the plan is over its usage limit. Neither
sends the reader off to replace a key that is fine.

* fix(model-providers): a ping that never reached the provider is not reported as a refusal

Dogfooding the Codex row on a stack with no gateway running showed the
row saying "It answered, but wouldn't confirm the key", which is the
opposite of what happened: nothing was at the address. The classifier
was reading the words the SDK wrapped the failure in, and the AI SDK
says "Cannot connect to API" where undici says "fetch failed", so the
word list missed it and the failure fell through to a provider refusal.

What separates the two is whether anything came back. A refusal has an
HTTP status, a response body, or both; a failure carrying neither never
got that far, whatever it is called.

* fix(skills): a reproduced scenario invents its identifiers and seeds the lookup

A scenario is a simulation, so the names, emails and ids it needs are test data of its own rather than the customer's copied out of the trace, and a redacted value is invented too rather than asked for. The invented value is named in the situation, because an unnamed role lets the simulated user improvise a different address on every run. An identifier the agent looks up needs a record in the agent's fixtures or test data, added in the same change when it is missing: a lookup that always misses proves the miss rather than the behaviour under test.

* fix(skills): sync the Go embed copies with the rewritten grounding rule

* fix(agents): the owner-only refusal names the credential, not just the owner

The common case is one person holding two credentials, not two people: a project or service key names no person, so it cannot reach a personal development agent even when the same person registered it. The refusal now says that and names running with the registering key as the first way out, beside connecting your own copy and sharing the agent under a named environment.

* fix(review): the gate's comment says why it exists, and the AGENTS.md note returns to its block

* fix(skills): regenerate the setup skill bodies after the grounding rewrite

* chore(scenario): re-vendor the SDK at 1.7.0-dev.voice10 from scenario main

Built from langwatch/scenario 55de2020, which is main with scenario#1001 merged: criteria mapped by schema key, inconclusive criteria reported apart from unmet ones, a quiet period before a trace counts as settled, and a retry on an empty user-simulator answer. Retires the voice4 and voice9 tarballs, and the bundle test now asserts the inlined SDK knows traceQuietPeriodMs and inconclusiveCriteria, so a stale tarball cannot pass the gate the way the 1.2.0 re-vendor did.

* fix(identity): serialization retries wait a random moment before going again

Both sides of a lost race are told at the same instant, so an immediate retry put them back into the same microsecond and a race between two clicks could spend all four attempts without either getting through. That surfaced as a raw write conflict instead of the refusal the guard had computed, and it failed the passkey removal integration test in CI. Each retry now waits a random point inside a window that doubles per attempt, a few tens of milliseconds at worst.

Also fixes a clock race in the role read test: a read reports the fact's business time as createdAt, and the test timed two separate new Date() calls, so it only agreed while the clock held still between them.

* fix(identity): a serialization retry waits out the winner's transaction

The loser of a Serializable race is told it lost before the winner has committed, so a retry a few milliseconds later reads the same state, writes the same row and loses again. Four attempts inside a 35 ms budget could all be spent while the winning transaction was still open, and the raw write conflict reached the caller.

Five attempts now, each after a random draw from a window that starts at 50 ms and doubles, so the wait outlasts a whole transaction rather than a scheduler tick.

* test(migrations): the pending-tenant teardown names the tenant it deletes

The multitenancy guard refuses a bulk write on SystemMigrationTenantState that names no tenant, so the suite's afterAll threw and failed the file with every test in it passing. It now deletes one tenant at a time.

* fix(traces-v2): the redaction notice reads which identifiers the project redacts

The notice fired at every PII level but disabled, so a project on the custom level that left EMAIL_ADDRESS out of its entity list was told its addresses are redacted while they were stored in full, and sent looking for a setting that is already off. The custom level now has to name EMAIL_ADDRESS.

* fix(cli): pin the analytics metric list to the generated schema

KNOWN_METRICS hand-copied the metric enum, so a metric the platform renames would keep passing the CLI's own check and be refused by the API. It now satisfies the metric type the timeseries endpoint declares.

* fix(cli): the collapsed agent listing counts the rows it ships

The listing hid stale sibling rows but kept the untouched pagination block, so the machine document reported a total the data array did not match and read as a page cut short. The total now counts the rows shipped, and hiddenStaleRows says how many were collapsed.

fix(cli): say when a local instance takes over the machine's global wiring (#8165)

`langwatch login` and `langwatch instrument <tool>` write the machine's
global files: `~/.langwatch/config.json`, `~/.claude/settings.json`,
`~/.codex/config.toml`. Pointed at a local dev instance they repoint every
other session on the machine, so agent telemetry exports to a port that is
only up while the dev server runs and `langwatch ingest context` fails with
connection refused and spools.

Both commands now print one line when the endpoint they settle on is
loopback and `LANGWATCH_CLI_CONFIG` is unset, naming that env var plus
`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `CODEX_HOME` as the way to give a QA shell its own
home. A warning, never a refusal, and silent for a shell that already
relocated its config. Loopback detection reuses `isLoopbackHost` from
`ingest-endpoint-scheme.ts`.

Documents the isolation recipe in a CLAUDE.md row and
`dev/docs/best_practices/dogfooding-isolation.md`. The CLI state directory
`~/.langwatch/state` has no override, so the doc says so rather than naming
a variable that does not exist.

* fix(datasets): address review on attachment uploads and delivery

Review follow-ups on the dataset attachments PR.

Upload route: the caller is authorized and rate limited in a middleware
that runs before `bodyLimit`, so an anonymous request can no longer make
the server buffer a 21 MB envelope. The route now declares its
multipart request body, its `projectId` query parameter and its 200, 413,
415 and 429 responses, so the OpenAPI document describes the contract.

Delivery: the column type decides first for every value shape, so a text
cell that holds an `/api/files/...` reference stays the sentence it is.
An audio attachment gets its format from an allowlist (wav, mp3, ogg,
flac, webm, m4a, aac) and travels as a file part when the format is not
one a model names, instead of being labeled WAV. A connected agent turn
reads the stop signal once the attachments are read, so a stopped run
sends nothing.

Probe: `storedObjects.headById` now applies the object's own purpose
permission after the read, the same one the file route applies, so a
dataset-only viewer cannot probe trace or scenario media. The mapping
moved to `server/stored-objects/purpose-permission.ts` and both callers
read it from there.

Cells: a `data:` cell value opens as a blob, because a browser refuses a
top-level navigation to a data URL. The upload state moved into
`useAttachmentUpload`, and `AddOrEditDatasetDrawer` is split into a form
hook, a submit hook and three field components.

Engine: attachment-derived text is charged against a bounded free text
allowance before the shared trace budget, so many small inlined text
files cannot make the traced body unbounded.

Docs: hyphenate "30-second", drop `.svg` from the supported uploaded
formats and say why, document inline delivery for text and JSON, say
that `url` is the cell value, and add data URLs to the `file` column row.

docs(sso): customer guide for moving to your own identity provider, and the fixes that let the update finish (#8271)

* docs(sso): a customer guide for moving from the sign-in LangWatch set up to the organization's own identity provider

Adds docs/platform/sso-update.mdx to the Administration group, with light and dark screenshots of each state of the update taken against a local stack: the overview card, registering the replacement, setting it up, going live, switching over, and every check passed. The Complete state is not captured yet.

* docs(sso): the update guide's screenshots show ACME, every state through Complete, and no development badge

Retakes every capture with the organization named ACME and the development indicator hidden, and adds the Complete state now that finishing works locally.

* fix(sso): finishing an update no longer trips the tenancy guard, and a revoked legacy directory sync is not one to repoint

Finishing a self-serve update crashed with an unknown error at the first member: the shared-identity checks read OrganizationUser bounded only by organizationId: { not }, which the organization tenancy guard refuses. The other organizations a member belongs to are now read through the member's own memberships, where the relation carries the bound.

Once past that, finishing stopped on a directory-sync blocker it had just created: tearing the legacy connection down leaves a REVOKED sync-state row, and any legacy row counted as a sync to repoint. A revoked sync pushes nobody, so it no longer counts.

Both paths are bound to scenarios in specs/identity/sso-idp-termination.feature: a unit test that runs the real guard against the new lookup, and an integration case for the revoked sync.

* style(sso): biome orders the new helper import

* feat(sso): finishing an update moves the directory sync LangWatch set up across to the new connection

Customers on the sign-in LangWatch set up never held their directory sync's
token, so the update could not ask them to repoint it. Finishing now moves
the previous connection's tokens, and the people and external ids they
provisioned, to the replacement; whatever pushes today keeps pushing. The
scim-needs-repointing blocker goes, the Directory sync row reads Moves across
when you finish, and the guide says so.

* fix(sso): a person the previous connection's sync provisioned can sign in through the replacement before the update finishes

Verifying the hand-over end to end with a real legacy directory sync found
a deadlock for every organization whose people arrive through directory
sync: a provisioned member who had never signed in was refused by the
replacement, first because the provisioned-user resolver only looked for
the replacement's own directory rows, then because the update's link policy
refused any unverified address. The update cannot finish until every member
has signed in through the replacement, so it could never finish.

Both gates now honour a directory row held by either side of the migrating
pair, since the previous connection's sync moves to the replacement at
finish anyway. An unverified member no directory vouches for is still not
linked on address alone.

The guide's screenshots for the states that show the Directory sync row are
retaken with the sync in place, and the guide says provisioned people can
sign in during the update.

* feat(sso): an update waits only for the members the new connection cannot match, and two days after the switch-over rather than seven

Finishing used to wait until every member had signed in through the new
connection, although the new connection already matches most of them to
their account by address, before and after the update finishes. It now waits
only for members it cannot match (an address nobody confirmed and no
directory vouches for, an address another account also holds, or a domain
the new connection has not proved), for members whose only way in is the
previous provider, and for deactivated members in that position. Everyone
else is listed as moving across at their next sign-in.

The progress and the link policy share one matcher, so the page predicts
exactly what a real arrival will be told. Retirement accepts any verified way
in other than the previous provider, promotes it to primary when the
previous identity was, and refuses only when nothing but a passkey would be
left.

The quiet period now counts from the switch-over: finishing opens two days
after it, or seven days after the last sign-in through the previous provider
since then, whichever is later, and the page shows the time it opens.

* docs(sso): the update guide says what stays the same instead of what does not change, under the prose check

* fix(sso): two scenario annotations sit directly above the test that binds them, and llms-full.txt carries the update guide's current copy

The quiet-period annotation sat on a describe and the directory-sync one
inside a test body, so the parity checker dropped both without a
diagnostic. Each now closes its own comment directly above an it().

* feat(sso): finishing confirms the address the previous provider proved, so a member whose only way in it was no longer has to sign in first

A member the new connection could match still had to sign in through it
once when the previous provider was their only verified way in, because the
identity guards refuse to take a person's last way in away. Their account
already holds an address identity, unconfirmed, and the previous provider's
identity proved that same address when they signed in with it.

Finishing now confirms that address on the previous provider's word
(verified by oauth or saml, no verification record) before retiring the
identity, and makes it primary when the retired identity was. The progress
and retirement share addressFinishingConfirms, so the page lists these
members as moving across at their next sign-in only when retirement will
confirm them. Signing in once is left for the rare member whose previous
identity proved a different address, or whose address another account also
holds. Deactivated members are held on the same rule.

Sign-in routing is keyed on the address's domain, never on the address
identity, so a confirmed address opens no password or reset path on a
domain the new connection routes.

* fix(sso): members never hold the update, and the new connection recognises them by address on a domain it proved

An organization with two hundred people cannot be asked to have every one of
them sign in again before it finishes moving to its own identity provider.
Finishing no longer waits on anybody's sign-in or confirmed address.

- The replacement connection matches a member by address when that address is
  on a domain it proved and one account holds it, confirmed or not. A person
  who never signed in during the update moves across at their next sign-in.
- Retirement leaves the previous provider's identity in place for a person
  whose only verified way in it is, instead of stopping the finish. It stops
  working when the previous connection is torn down, and the replacement
  matches them at their next sign-in.
- The members-must-sign-in and deactivated-member blockers, the arrival
  module, the address-confirmation step and the way-in fallbacks are gone.
  The progress screen names why a member will not be recognised, and none of
  those reasons stops the finish.

* docs(sso): the guide says finishing never waits for members, and the screenshots show it

The update guide still promised nobody is locked out and said the directory
sync's word is what gets provisioned people recognised. It now says each
member moves across at their next sign-in, matched by address on a proved
domain whether or not they confirmed it, including someone who only ever
used the previous provider. The four screenshots that show member rows are
retaken on the current code.

* fix(sso): review follow-ups on the address count, the directory-sync move and the quiet-period copy

- A real arrival and the progress page count the accounts holding an
  address with one query. The link policy's case-insensitive Prisma
  `equals` compiles to ILIKE, so an address with an underscore counted a
  lookalike account as a second holder and was refused as shared while the
  page promised it would move across.
- Moving the directory sync starts the replacement's history before anything
  moves, moves only the tokens it was started for, and reads the
  replacement's own people and external ids inside the transaction that
  moves the rest. A crash at any point leaves a state the next attempt
  completes, and a push landing mid-move no longer collides with the key.
- The quiet-period line no longer says only a sign-in "before then" moves
  the finish time: any sign-in through the previous provider does.
- The shared lookups file is named for what it holds and carries the
  enterprise licence header.

* fix(sso): a directory-pushed member who never signed in is pinned as not holding the update, and the guide lists them like anyone else

The evidence test's members-not-signed-in case gains a member the previous
connection's directory sync pushed, and still asserts no blocker from either
the progress page or the finish check. The guide no longer says every
provisioned member is listed as moving across: one on a domain the new
connection has not proved is listed as not recognized, like any other member.

* refactor(scim): moving the directory sync keeps its row transfer in its own method

`moveToConnection` was over the 60-line limit for a new exported method. The
transactional move of tokens, people and external ids is now
`moveDirectoryRows`; `moveToConnection` announces, moves and revokes.

* fix(lwql): key a config-owned row policy by its ON target, not its short name alone (#8258)

ClickHouse identifies a row policy as `short_name ON database.table`, so two
tables can carry the same bare short name. The read-only access storage
(495) excuse compared only kind + short name, so an inventoried policy on one
table could excuse a failing CREATE ROW POLICY on another, leaving that table
granted to the restricted user with no tenant policy.

The inventory now reads database + table from system.row_policies, the
statement parser captures the ON target, and a 495 is excused only when short
name, table, and (when both sides qualify it) database all match. Regression
test: same short name on two tables must not be excused across them.

* fix(charts): make LWQL render RBAC and passwords pre-upgrade hooks so the first upgrade converges (#8258)

The render Job runs as a pre-upgrade hook on upgrade, which fires BEFORE
the main phase. On the first upgrade from a pre-LWQL release two inputs
it needs are new in this version and so absent from the main phase at
hook time, breaking every existing install's first upgrade:

- The render ServiceAccount/Role/RoleBinding were main-phase, so the
  pre-upgrade hook pod had no ServiceAccount and helm aborted the upgrade.
  They are now pre-install,pre-upgrade hooks at weight -10 (below the
  Job's 5), before-hook-creation and NOT hook-succeeded so they persist
  into the main phase for the main-phase install Job too.

- The two LWQL passwords lived in the app Secret, healed into it only in
  the main phase, so the pre-upgrade render failed with
  LwqlRenderConfigMissingInputError. They move to a dedicated chart-owned
  Secret (<release>-lwql-passwords, lookup-or-rand) that is a
  pre-install,pre-upgrade hook at weight -10; sharedEnv reads the
  passwords from it on the autogen path (existingSecret / hand-created
  app Secret pre-exist and are read as before). Install stays main-phase
  because DATABASE_URL still comes from the main-phase PostgreSQL Secret.

Also repoints two stale comments (values.yaml, render template) from
clickhouse.extraVolumes to clickhouse.lwqlAccess.secretName / the subchart
StatefulSet.

Proof: e2e.sh test_lwql_upgrade_from_main installs, strips the release to
a pre-LWQL state (deletes the RBAC and the password Secret), then
helm-upgrades with a bumped catalog annotation and asserts the pre-upgrade
hooks recreate RBAC + passwords, the render completes, and every ClickHouse
pod serves a tenant-filtered query with the freshly rendered identity.
lwql-connection-env.sh pins the hook topology at template level.

fix(selfhost): issues found dogfooding the 3.18 Helm install on EKS (#8313)

* fix(identity): sign-up on an installation with no email provider

With no email provider configured (the Helm chart default) the
verification-first sign-up mailed a link unconditionally, sendEmail
threw, and nobody could create an account.

Without a provider, requestSignUpVerification now returns a single-use,
address-bound unconfirmed proof instead of mailing, and user.register
accepts it only while no provider exists, creating the account with
emailVerified false so domain join requests and OAuth linking stay
closed. Passkey sign-up still requires a confirmed proof, and the
address confirmation resend refuses with auth_email_sending_unavailable.

* fix(clickhouse): serialize boot migrations across pods with an advisory lock

The app and the workers both run the ClickHouse migrations at boot, and
goose takes no lock on ClickHouse. On a fresh Helm install both applied
migration 00064 at once, one failed with TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS and the
pod crashlooped until the other finished. Several app replicas race the
same way. The migrate task now holds a Postgres advisory lock for the
whole run.

* fix(langevals): disable the gunicorn control socket

gunicorn 25.1+ opens a control socket under $HOME/.gunicorn by default.
The chart runs langevals on a read-only root filesystem with HOME=/, so
every boot logged 'Control server error: Read-only file system'.
Nothing uses gunicornc, so the socket is off.

* fix(checkup): stop showing the Redis password on the Checkup page

The Redis row printed REDIS_URL verbatim, so on the Helm chart (which
puts the generated password in the URL) Settings > Checkup showed the
Redis credential. The row now masks the user and password of any URL
it shows.

* fix(langy): dial the in-cluster gateway from the Langy worker on chart installs

The chart now sets LW_GATEWAY_INTERNAL_URL on the app and workers to the gateway Service, and the Langy worker prefers it over LW_GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL, which may not resolve inside the cluster. Codex models read the same variable.

* docs(self-hosting): gateway is on by default, and two installs in one cluster

* fix(identity): keep a misconfigured mailer on the mailed sign-up link

Only an installation with no email configuration at all issues an unconfirmed address proof; a named but unusable provider keeps the mailed link and fails loudly. The e2e suite runs as a mailerless install: UI sign-up follows the no-email path, and account fixtures confirm the address in Postgres the way the link would.

* fix(pii): keep model and tool names out of strict name detection

Strict redaction sent every attribute to the name detector, which reads
a bare model id like claude-sonnet-4-6 as a first name and stored it as
[PERSON]. Single-token values under known model and tool attributes are
now held back from that pass. Prose, emails and phone numbers under the
same keys are still redacted.

Closes #8331

* fix(pii): send URLs under model names to detection, name the length cap

A URL written under a model or tool attribute can carry a person in its
path, so it is no longer held back. The 128-character cap is now a named
constant, and the rule has its own unit cases: the cap edge, the values
it sends on, and the single-token names it knowingly holds back.

* test(pii): add the phone number scenario for model name attributes

* fix(pii): hold model and tool names back only after the native pass

With no tenant, the kill switch set, or a failed policy lookup, the
analysis batch is the only redaction. Holding a model name back there
stored a phone or card number under it in the clear. The hold-out now
applies only on the path where the native pass has already run.

Also lists the model and tool name rule in the module header and states
that only scheme-qualified URLs are sent on.

* fix(pii): send scheme-less URLs under model names to detection

A dotted host before the first slash (www.acme.example/u/...) marks a
URL; vendor namespaces in model ids never carry one. Also renames the
native-pass flag to hasNativePassRun per the boolean naming rule.

A custom level that selects only analysis-service identifiers, with

The flag now reports whether it ran instead of assuming it did.

* fix(pii): spare model and tool names name detection only, not all analysis

Holding model and tool names back from the analysis batch left them
scanned by nothing wherever the native pass does not reach: no policy,
a custom level it has nothing to do for, and national ids it never
covers. They now go in a second call with PERSON and LOCATION removed
from the entity list, so every other identifier is still looked for on
every path. The two calls run in parallel.

When the call does not look for names or places (the essential level,
or a custom level without them) model names now go in the single call.

fix(selfhost): issues found on a fresh 3.18.0 Helm install on EKS (#8326)

* fix(clickhouse): boot migrations wait for a ClickHouse that is still starting

On a fresh Helm install the chart-managed ClickHouse takes about a minute to
accept connections. The migration preflight pinged it once, and ping() reports
failure in its result instead of throwing, so the check passed and bootstrap
then died on ECONNREFUSED. The app and workers pods restarted once on every
new install.

The preflight now pings with a SELECT (which also checks the credentials) and
retries connection failures (ECONNREFUSED, ENOTFOUND, timeouts and similar)
every 2s for up to CLICKHOUSE_MIGRATE_WAIT_SECONDS (default 180, 0 turns the
wait off), logging a waiting line at most every 10s. A server that answers
with an error, such as refused credentials, still fails on the first attempt.
Logged URLs carry no credentials.

The clickhouseMigrate task waits before it queues on the Postgres migration
lock, so a pod waiting for ClickHouse never holds up the others.

* fix(mcp): check for an MCP config without logging an error on every boot

createMcpHandler probed for an existing config by calling getConfig() and
catching the throw, and getConfig() logs a "[MCP config] getConfig() failed"
line with a stack before it throws, so every app boot printed it. The config
module now exports hasConfig(), which neither logs nor throws, and the handler
uses it. The app builds mcp-server's dist in start:prepare:files, so no extra
build step is needed.

* fix(ci): stamp the release version into the published Go images

The Go Dockerfiles already take a VERSION (langyagent: SERVICE_VERSION) build
arg for -X main.Version, but the Docker Hub and ECR publish workflows never
passed one, so langwatch/ai-gateway, langwatch/langwatch_nlp and
langwatch/langyagent reported "version":"dev" on every log line and in the
OTel resource. The release version is now passed (git-<sha> for a dispatch
or main build).

The "env":"local" field is the ENVIRONMENT variable's default. It stays as
is: the gateway treats any other value as a hosted deployment and then
requires BLOCK_LOCAL_HTTP_CALLS and REQUIRE_HTTPS_CUSTOM_ENDPOINTS, so the
chart setting it would change egress behaviour on self-hosted installs.

* fix(lwql): write the key-map row on every project creation path

The tRPC project router (used by onboarding and the projects screen), the
REST API and personal workspace provisioning created projects without a
LangWatchQL key-map row, so a new project read zero rows from LangWatchQL,
custom chart widgets and Instant Evals until the next deploy's boot-time
backfill. Every path now calls ProjectService.syncLwqlKeyMapRow, best effort.

* fix(lwql): name the column in an unknown identifier refusal inside a function call

ClickHouse 25.x words a name passed to a function as "Unknown expression or
function identifier", which the extractor did not match, so
lwql_unknown_identifier arrived without meta.identifier.

* docs(self-hosting): fix first-install gaps found on a fresh 3.18.0 Helm install

Pin the chart version in the quick starts and take the size-dev overlay from
the pulled chart instead of main. Correct the overlay request table. Langy is
on by default and runs unsandboxed unless a RuntimeClass is set. Document
ADMIN_EMAILS and the two feature flags custom LangWatchQL charts need.

* fix(checkup): stop false alarms on a default Helm install

The gateway control plane check accepts any address this app is reached
at (BASE_HOST, the in-cluster callback URL, GATEWAY_CONTROL_PLANE_URL),
so a gateway pointed at http://<release>-app:5560 passes while one
pointed at another install still fails.

The Langy canary asks hasLangyAccess, the gate the Langy panel uses, and
sends its turn in process as the administrator who ran the checkup,
instead of calling /api/health/langy with the project key, which sits
behind the separate API key surface flag and refuses ownerless keys.

The model provider test decrypts customKeys before probing, so an OpenAI
row with a real key is tested, and an untested provider names why.

* fix(langy): show the chats-improve-Langy note on LangWatch Cloud only

A self-hosted install sends none of its Langy chats to LangWatch, so the
composer no longer says it does there. The layout provides IS_SAAS
through a context the composer reads, defaulting to hidden.

* fix(checkup): link only docs pages that exist

Add the self-hosting Checkup page the checkup rows already named, point the
AI Gateway rows at the gateway Helm page instead of a missing overview, and
pin every checkup docs path to a real page in the docs navigation.

* docs(self-hosting): install commands track the latest release instead of pinning one

Quick starts and upgrade commands no longer pass --version; the pin section,
the ArgoCD example and the mirroring example use a <version> placeholder or
the latest release. docscheck now reports any concrete LangWatch release in
the docs instead of requiring it to match the chart, so release PRs no longer
have to edit docs, and docs-ci stops running on chart version bumps.

* docs(self-hosting): release-please bumps the copyable version examples

The quick starts and upgrade commands still install the latest release. The
examples that need a concrete version (ArgoCD targetRevision, the image
mirroring script and values, the pin-a-version upgrade) keep one, marked
x-release-please-version and listed as release-please extra-files, so every
release PR bumps them and docscheck's drift rule stays green. The drift rule
is restored, and its remedy now says how to mark a new pin.

* fix(selfhost): address review on the 3.18 fresh-install fixes

- checkup: a provider whose stored keys will not decrypt fails both provider rows naming the decryption failure
- REST project routes use the App's ProjectService; lwqlKeyMap is private again
- personal workspace writes its key-map row before the owner grant
- redactUrl drops user and password query params
- Langy data-use flag resolves below the layout's memo boundary
- test and TSDoc fixes

* style(checkup): format the docs-link test

* fix(checkup): Langy canary passes the admin's email to the access gate; docs say Langy ships enabled and unsandboxed by default

* style: clear the two new biome warnings (split the ClickHouse wait loop, assert inside the key-map tests)

fix(langy): write the project credentials without asking, and retry a transient model failure (#8325)

* feat(langy): a transient model or tool failure retries inside the turn

A model call that fails for a transient reason (an overloaded provider, a
dropped stream, a network error, a timeout, a 5xx or a 429) is made again up
to five times, waiting 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds with jitter, or the wait the
provider names. pi's own retry loop runs it, with the policy in model-retry.ts
deciding which failures retry and how long to wait, so the failed answer is
dropped and every tool call that already ran keeps its result.

The worker reports each retry as a retrying event that the manager draws as the
panel's status line (Retrying (2 of 5)), cleared once the call answers. The
relay no longer cuts an in-stream error that names no plan limit, since the
worker's budget now ends those. A local call's start is sent again only on 429
or 503, and its polls retry transient failures on the same schedule.

* fix(langy): the credentials call gets the project key through the device session

The CLI's langy session fetched the project key with GET
/api/projects/:id/api-key, which refuses every API key with 403, so on
production the credentials write always failed and Langy told the person to
paste LANGWATCH_API_KEY and LANGWATCH_ENDPOINT by hand. The session now looks
the project's slug up by id and trades the developer's device session for the

* fix(analytics): apply per-series filters and percentage mode in the ClickHouse builder

The ClickHouse timeseries builder dropped a series' own `filters` entirely:
the per-series loop passed only metric/aggregation/key/subkey on, and the
only filter translation was the graph-wide one. Two series differing only by
`filters: {"traces.error": ["true"|"false"]}` therefore compiled to
byte-identical SQL, drew the same line, and every alert built on a filtered
series watched the wrong number. This is an Elasticsearch-to-ClickHouse
regression — the deleted ES builder implemented it as a `__filters` wrapper
aggregation — and nothing covered it.

Each series' filters now compile to a predicate that is folded into that
series' own aggregate via the `-If` combinator, so the graph-wide WHERE stays
shared: `sum(x)` becomes `sumIf(x, pred)`, `count()` becomes `countIf(pred)`,
and an aggregate that is already conditional (evaluation metrics) has the
predicate ANDed into the condition it carries. Every filter class resolves to
a predicate on `trace_summaries` — span, event and evaluation facets as
`ts.TraceId IN (SELECT ...)` subqueries — so none needs a JOIN to be scoped to
one series; a future one that does now fails loudly instead of narrowing the
whole graph. The two paths that aggregate over a CTE hoist the predicate as a
per-trace boolean column first, since the raw predicate reads an alias those
outer SELECTs do not have. Per-entity (pipeline) series take their filter in
their own subquery's WHERE, because the filter decides which entities exist.

`asPercent` ("show in percentages") was read by nothing. It now reproduces the
ES `bucket_script` it replaces — `all > 0 ? filtered / all * 100 : 0` — so an
empty bucket reads as 0% rather than no value, and percentage mode on an
unfiltered series stays the no-op it was in ES. A percentage on a filtered
per-entity series is refused with a handled `analytics_series_percentage_
unsupported` rather than answered with a plausible wrong number.

Grouping by `error.has_error` read the span-level `StatusCode` through a
stored_spans JOIN, so a trace with one failing span and several healthy ones
landed in BOTH buckets and the buckets could not add up to the total. It now
groups on the trace-level `ContainsErrorStatus` the filter and the field
mapping already agree on, and drops the JOIN.

Also invalidates every `graphs.getAll` key when a graph is deleted from a
dashboard: the page refetched only its own `{projectId, dashboardId}` query,
so the alert composer — which reads the list keyed by `{projectId}` alone —
kept offering the deleted graph until a full reload.

Closes #6718

* fix(analytics): keep the percentage refusal out of the alert lane and stop filtered extrema fabricating zeros

Review follow-ups on the per-series filter work.

The `analytics_series_percentage_unsupported` refusal was a poison pill in the
graph-trigger evaluator: that worker rethrows anything it does not recognise,
a rethrow is a redelivery, and the composer still lets an author save a
per-entity series with a percentage — so one such trigger would re-fail on
every delivery until it quarantined its tenant's whole alert lane, taking
every OTHER trigger in the project down with it. It is now classified
alongside the row-ceiling refusal the same file already documents: skipped and
logged with the trigger id and the offending series, never rethrown.

Filtered non-additive aggregates fabricated zeros. ClickHouse's `-If`
combinators do NOT return NULL for an empty match set when the source column is
non-nullable — `minIf` returns 0 — so a filtered latency floor drew a real
0ms line for every bucket the filter excluded, where the row parser and
Elasticsearch both leave a non-additive series absent. Non-additive series
(per `isZeroWhenAbsentSeries`) now carry an emptiness guard:
`if(countIf(<cond>) > 0, minIf(x, <cond>), NULL)`. Additive series are left
alone, because no matching rows genuinely IS zero there.

The error dropped its `meta.metric`: nothing read it. The presentation copy
cannot name an internal metric key at a customer, and the one caller that
needs to know which series is at fault — the evaluator — has the series in its
own scope and logs it there.

Coverage: integration tests now execute a per-series filter on both paths that
carry the hoisted per-trace boolean (the grouped/arrayJoin CTE and the mixed
evaluation CTE), plus the non-additive gap and its matching control.

The aggregate-call scanner was also split into named steps so the three new
helpers stay under the cognitive-complexity limit rather than adding lint
warnings.

* fix(api): redact delivery credentials at the /api/triggers boundary

Every `/api/triggers` response — list, read, create, update — now carries
`actionParams` with each delivery credential replaced by the `[redacted]`
placeholder. The delivery shape survives: which channel is configured, which
destination is set and which header names are in play all stay readable, so an
integrator or an agent can still reason about an automation.

The redaction is structured. `server/app-layer/automations/trigger-redaction.ts`
declares, per delivery channel, which `actionParams` fields hold a credential
and substitutes the placeholder there; nothing scans prose for something
secret-shaped. The module also holds `redactTriggerForRead`, moved out of
`routers/automations.ts` so the dashboard read and the public API read state
their rules side by side — the dashboard keeps the fields its composer
round-trips, the public API keeps none of them.

Read-modify-write stays safe: the write path treats the placeholder as "keep
what is stored", so an integrator who reads an automation, renames it and
writes the whole object back keeps the live credential. On a create there is
nothing behind the placeholder, so the field is dropped rather than stored.

The command line consumes the response as it arrives and its client-side
redaction module is gone. The MCP trigger tools read the same REST payload and
needed no change.

* fix(api): resolve public API credential placeholders through the provider

A save on `/api/triggers` now hands `actionParams` to the delivery channel's
own persist hook, which is what owns the at-rest form: the encrypted Slack bot
token (ADR-041), the encrypted webhook header values and signing secret
(ADR-040 §3). The wire name and the at-rest name differ for each of those, and
the hook is the only thing that knows both, so the advertised contract — send
back what you were given and the stored credential stays — holds on every
channel rather than only where the two names happen to match.

`trigger-redaction.ts` now declares, per credential field, how "keep the stored
value" reaches the provider that owns it: the channel's own kept sentinel where
the hook resolves it against the ciphertext, the stored value substituted here
where the hook stores the field exactly as it is given.

A row whose saved credentials cannot be read back — one written while a
different credentials secret was in force — lists with an empty delivery
configuration and a warning in the log, rather than ending the listing for
every other automation in the project.

Tests: read-modify-write round trips over the real route for an encrypted
customer endpoint (header value and signing secret both still decrypt to what
was stored) and for a Slack bot connection (token still decrypts); a typed
destination is saved as typed; the webhook fixtures use the encrypted at-rest
shape the product writes, with one legacy plaintext row kept to prove those
still read; the delete response body is asserted.

Refs #6716

* fix(api): keep a public API save to the delivery configuration it owns

`actionParams` carries two things: how the automation delivers, and the rule
it fires by — a graph alert's series, threshold and time window, a report's
source and schedule. A provider states its own delivery fields exhaustively,
dropping anything it does not recognise so a channel can never keep another
channel's stale credential, so handing it the whole object made that stripping
apply to the rule as well.

A save now separates the two by the channel's own schema: the provider decides
the delivery half and the rule half is carried across untouched, which is the
same split the dashboard save makes. A graph alert or a report delivered over
Slack survives a read-modify-write with the rule it fires by intact, and the
channel still states its delivery fields on its own terms.

A row naming a channel this server does not offer has no provider to prepare
an at-rest form, so its payload is stored as it was sent rather than ending the
request; the read still declines to return it.

The update schema now documents what it has always done — the delivery
configuration is replaced as a whole, so a field left out is removed, and a
credential sent back as the placeholder (or a bot connection sent back with the
flag the read echoes) keeps the one already stored.

Tests: read-modify-write round trips over the real route for a Slack-delivered
graph alert and a Slack-delivered report, each asserting the saved rule still
parses as the evaluator and the report dispatcher read it; an update that
states no headers removes them; an unclaimed channel is stored as sent.

Refs #6716

* test(automations): hold every delivery channel to a named field set

A public API save reads the fields a channel owns off the schema that channel
publishes, and a schema resolving to something other than an object shape names
none — every field the caller sent would then go to the provider persist hook,
which states its own fields exhaustively, and the rule the automation fires by
would be dropped on the way to storage with a 200 and no log. That shape is now
held by a test rather than by whichever change first reaches for a union, an
intersection, or a schema library whose objects are a different class.

The module also records why slicing by the current channel alone is sound: an
update cannot change a trigger's action, so the channel that owns the stored
delivery fields is the one that owns the incoming ones. Making the channel
switchable widens the split to the union of every provider's field names.

* feat(api): let the public API write every automation the dashboard writes

An automation over `/api/triggers` could only ever be a trace automation
with an untyped delivery blob. It can now be any of the three kinds the
composer writes — matching traces, a metric crossing a threshold, a

and a report owns a calendar entry. And a webhook automation pointed at a

`platform_create_trigger` sent no delivery configuration at all, so every
call it made was refused: a channel with nothing configured cannot deliver.

so a Slack automation can be created in one call and the schema says what it

* fix(ci): drop the import the cadence move left behind, and name the key type zod wants

* fix(api): cap what a test fire can send, and refuse a field instead of dropping it

Four things the API answered with a 200 that it should have refused, or
should not have let happen at all.

A test fire is the one verb here that makes LangWatch send on the caller's
say-so, to an address the same caller chose — an email through the shared
provider, a request from our workers at any destination. The dashboard caps
that per user; over the API it was uncapped, so setting an automation's
recipients and firing it in a loop was an outbound mailer. It is now capped
per project, on the same window, with Slack exempt as it is there because
its destination is pinned to Slack's own hosts. The comment claiming the
saved destination was itself the safeguard now says what actually bounds it.

A field the channel does not have is refused rather than dropped, so
`slackChannelID` is answered instead of saving an automation that delivers
nowhere. The payload is read against the channel on the stored row rather
than against whichever shape it resembles, which is also what stops another
channel's field being parked on a row where a later conversion could adopt
it as live configuration. The credential split now reads every channel's
field names, so such a field cannot reach the rule half by any route.

The rule an automation fires by is stated in `graphAlert` or `report`. Sent
inside the delivery configuration it was overwritten by the stored rule on
the way to storage — a save that changed nothing and said it had. It is
refused with the field it belongs in, and the read now hands the rule back
in that same field, so writing the response back means what it says.

* docs(api): say it where the reader is, and answer a report with report copy

Three things a reader outside this repo could not see or could not act on.

`actionParams` explained itself in a TSDoc comment: the redaction rule, what
sending the placeholder back means, and that the automation's rule is not in
this field. None of that reached the published document, the generated
client or the API reference — and the reader holding those is exactly the
one who would otherwise put the rule in `actionParams` and take a 422. It is
said in `.describe()` now, on both the read and the write.

An MCP client could read a scheduled report but not write one, while REST
could do both. Both write tools take `report`, structured like `graphAlert`
rather than as a loose record: an agent that cannot see the field names has
to guess them, and a guess here is a refusal. The tolerance this file keeps
for reads is about deployments answering with less, which is not a reason to
describe a write badly.

A report whose stored configuration can no longer be read was answered with
"pick one of those channels", when the channel is fine and what is missing is
the report. It now says to state what it sends and when.

The test-fire cap's copy reads `meta.resetAt` and says how long to wait,
which is the only thing the caller wanted from it.

* feat(automations): the View drawer becomes the in-depth view (#6716)

The View drawer answered "what is this automation?" and almost nothing
else: a thin "Recent fires" list, no sense of what happens next, and — for
an alert that has never fired — total silence. The evaluator computes an
observed value on every check and records none of it, so "why is this not
firing?" had no answer anywhere in the product (#6716 G3).

The drawer now answers two questions about one automation: what has it
done, and what will it do next.

- History: the whole firing history, paged (keyset on createdAt + id, so a
  burst inside one millisecond cannot skip or repeat rows), with the last
  check of an alert on the same timeline — "Checked · The alert did not
  fire / observed 42, fires when greater than 100 over 1 hour".
- What happens next: a schedule's instant from the scheduler that owns the
  calendar entry, a digest's from the same boundary computeScheduledFor
  would snap a match to, and an alert's cadence rather than an invented
  instant.
- Run the conditions now: the composer's matched-traces read, asked from a
  saved automation's own view, with input and output excerpts. On demand,
  never on open.

Alerts persist their latest evaluation in a new TriggerLatestEvaluation
table — one upserted row per trigger, kept out of the TriggerSent ledger
that every "last fired" / "currently firing" read counts. Skips carry a
stable code (result_too_large, incomplete_configuration, subject_missing,
inactive) that the drawer turns into copy naming what to change. Recording
is best-effort at two levels: an observation of an alert can never become
a way to break the alert.

scenarios).

fix(chart): stop committing charts/langwatch/Chart.lock so releases cannot publish with a stale lock (#8386)

The committed lock pinned the file:// subcharts at their previous versions, so every release that bumped them broke helm dependency build until a separate job rewrote the lock on the release PR. The 3.19.1 release PR merged before that job ran and the chart release failed. Without a committed lock, helm dependency build resolves the subcharts from the checkout and prometheus from its exact pin in Chart.yaml. The lock-sync workflow is removed, and a chart test asserts dependencies build after a subchart version bump.

fix(sso): link an unconfirmed password account when the connection verified its domain (#8387)

On a self-hosted install with no mailer, a password account never confirms its address, so single sign-on refused to link it ("account not linked"), including the admin's setup test sign-in. The link is now allowed on self-hosted when the connection has verified the address's domain and the identity provider asserts the address is verified. LangWatch Cloud keeps the previous rule. Other refusals get the named code sso_existing_account_unconfirmed with copy on the sign-in and SSO settings screens.

fix(sso): let the link evidence hook see the resolver's confirmation (#8389)

The account-create hook re-checked a single sign-on link's evidence by reading the user outside the callback transaction, so it missed the confirmation the resolver had just written and refused every link with LINK_NEEDS_APPROVAL on self-hosted installs without a mailer. The facts repository now reads through the identity callback transaction when one is open. The regression test builds better-auth with the production database hooks. The sso_existing_account_unconfirmed copy names both causes.
